summary: 1. Result Let Q_d be the real d-dimensional manifold on which a particle sector lives. For every positive particle mode n, set N=n-1. There is a canonical rank-S(n,d) mode bundle over Q_d: \mathcal E_{N,d} = \operatornam
text:
Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Result Let Q_d be the real d-dimensional manifold on which a particle sector lives. For every positive particle mode n, set N=n-1. There is a canonical rank-S(n,d) mode bundle over Q_d: \mathcal E_{N,d} = \operatorname{Sym}^{N} \left( \mathbf 1_{\mathbb C}\oplus T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C ight). Its rank is \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}\mathcal E_{N,d} =  inom{N+d}{d} =  inom{n+d-1}{d} =S(n,d). The additional trivial line \mathbf1_{\mathbb C} homogenizes the cumulative occupation condition: \operatorname{Sym}^{N}(\mathbb C\oplus V) \cong  igoplus_{k=0}^{N}\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(V). For V=T_q^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C, the right-hand side contains every d-direction oscillator shell from 0 through N. The extra occupation number records the unused portion of the total excitation. The Hermitian fibre W_{d,q}=\mathbb C\oplus T_q^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C has ray space \mathbb P(W_{d,q})\cong\mathbb{CP}^{d}. On \mathcal E_{N,d,q}=\operatorname{Sym}^{N}(W_{d,q}), rank-one support on the occupied coherent ray, covariance, and unit normalization uniquely determine a positive localization density \Lambda_{N,d}([z]) =D_{N,d}\, |z;Nangle\langle z;N|, \qquad D_{N,d}=S(N+1,d), where |z;Nangle=z^{\odot N} is the normalized symmetric coherent state. This operator obeys \int_{\mathbb{CP}^{d}} \Lambda_{N,d}([z])\,d
u_{m FS}([z]) =I_{\mathcal E_{N,d}}, and \Lambda_{N,d}([z])^2 =D_{N,d}\Lambda_{N,d}([z]). It therefore has one nonzero eigenvalue, exactly D_{N,d}. A scalar self-contact contribution \mathcal M_{N,d}([z]) =\mu_d\Lambda_{N,d}([z]) has the coherent localized mode as an eigenvector with rest mass  oxed{ m(n,d)=\mu_dD_{N,d} =\mu_d inom{n+d-1}{d}. } This derives the combinatorial multiplier as the eigenvalue of the localized contact density on the cumulative tangent-mode bundle. The proposed physical identification assumes the following additional occupied-ray prescription for the scalar self-interaction: The master Dirac interaction is algebraic in the local scalar current and its sector coordinates, with no derivatives of that current. The current is evaluated at the occupied projective mode ray determined by the field's local amplitude and covariant derivatives. The rank-one formula requires contact at a specified occupied coherent ray in the auxiliary projective fibre, with the stated measure and evaluation map. Locality in the physical base coordinate alone does not imply this. A local identity operator has a delta kernel too, yet band compression gives the identity on the band, not the rank-one operator \Lambda_{N,d}([z]). The combinatorial multiplier is therefore derived for the explicitly assumed coherent-ray contact operator. Deriving that operator, its band-independent coefficient \mu_d, and the occupied modes from the master action remains open; normalization is not the only remaining problem. There is also a distinct conformal scalar construction: the critical conformal differential operator on a round even-dimensional spatial sphere has the exact normalized eigenvalues S(n,d). Its conformal recurrence and spatial factorization derive that scalar spectrum without a mode-ray point insertion. The construction uses different geometric and operator assumptions; its realization in the master spinor action, the occupied scalar harmonic degrees and the common sector normalization remain unproved. The Killing-spinor transfer constructs an exact local spinor version on that specified round geometry. Its opposite Dirac signs carry adjacent simplex values. Direct insertion as a scalar mass fails Hermiticity; the real action gives their average. The scalar-to-spinor transfer is therefore explicit, while the physical master mass term remains unresolved. A local projective spinor construction has a different outcome on the specified physical CP3 geometry. On the full bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(2), the polynomial X(X+4)(X+6)/720, with X=R^2\mathscr D_2^2/4, gives exactly S(n,6) on its first paired form family. It is local and permits a Hermitian scalar insertion on both Dirac signs. All additional families remain explicit. A geometric covariant derivative now obtains its zero-form polynomial from the symmetric third holomorphic derivative on that line bundle and its physical adjoint. The relative coefficients follow from the derivative norm. The connection and the derivative energy still need a master-action origin, with their normalization and full physical frequencies. Working backward, the inverse polynomial dynamics classify explicit local Hermitian actions with exact simplex frequencies on the complete paired family. They modify both kinetic and scalar terms and retain the complementary spinor equation. The inverse action has a consistent canonical norm. Its full curved commutator now excludes finite propagation when the polynomial acts on every spatial mode. A causal nonlinear origin for selected particle masses remains open. The inverse scalar-law test retains the original Dirac kinetics and reconstructs an interaction from complete spatial fields. It requires both a scalar full residual and one common function of the actual current. Pure unchanged Jacobi pairs fail the assigned two-frequency target, while dressed nonlinear controls recover the same local law and its coupling derivative. A dressed excited-branch response now derives a near-resonance from that common scalar action and checks its instability with full spatial derivatives and increasing cutoffs. The interaction that supports a proposed mass state must also give its required spatial stability and reciprocal coupling response. The natural projective jet lift has a nonconstant induced kinetic norm. When that lifted field is canonical, the derivative coefficient becomes P(X)/Z(X). Its canonically compressed algebraic scalar response remains bounded on a fixed smooth background; this particular lift does not derive the unbounded simplex polynomial as a mass term. A fixed-line cumulative spatial band also has the exact simplex rank up to one sector constant, with a matching polarized physical point eigenvalue. Its smooth local scalar self-current instead has a different coefficient and drives additional spatial components. This derives a possible spatial carrier count while leaving the required point interaction and occupied full spinor unresolved. The scalar-current insertion has also been tested on an exact round-sphere Killing background. Its full spatial response puts the simplex coefficient inside a frequency polynomial and has unstable high harmonics for every nonzero derivative-current coefficient. This is a result for that specified action and background. An exact local scalar-gap solution is available on the ordinary spinor bundle of a specified round six-space. It has nonzero constant scalar current and complete spatial spectral stability. Its coefficient is fixed by the local self-consistency equation and depends on norm, volume and radius. This closes a conditional spatial field construction, while leaving the simplex enhancement, master geometry and observed mass identification unresolved. An explicit normal Dirac extension supplies the absolute spatial Dirac operator from a specified half-cylinder of the same field. Its induced kinetic norm cancels the corresponding factor in a constant bulk scalar mass. Local scalar contact retains an inverse-width coefficient but excites complementary normal profiles. This identifies a concrete spatial reduction without yet deriving the complete simplex operator or a physical normal binding law. In the fixed spatial Killing channel, a full-line theorem also excludes a finite-norm stationary normal profile for that local product-space model. 2. The cumulative oscillator bundle At a point q\in Q_d, the complexified cotangent space V_{d,q}=T_q^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C has complex rank d. Its degree-k symmetric power has rank \operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(V_{d,q}) = inom{k+d-1}{d-1}. This is the shell multiplicity of d commuting creation directions. The cumulative band through degree N is \mathcal B_{N,d} = igoplus_{k=0}^{N}\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(V_{d,q}). Consequently, \operatorname{rank}\mathcal B_{N,d} =\sum_{k=0}^{N} inom{k+d-1}{d-1} = inom{N+d}{d}. The count is independent of coordinates. Changes of orthonormal cotangent frame act through U(d) on V_{d,q} and through its symmetric powers on the band. The band can be written as one homogeneous representation. For arbitrary vector spaces A and B, \operatorname{Sym}^{N}(A\oplus B) \cong  igoplus_{k=0}^{N} \operatorname{Sym}^{N-k}(A)\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(B). Taking A=\mathbb C gives \operatorname{Sym}^{N}(\mathbb C\oplus V_{d,q}) \cong  igoplus_{k=0}^{N}\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(V_{d,q}), because every symmetric power of a one-dimensional vector space is one-dimensional. In occupation numbers, a monomial in the cumulative band is labelled by (a_1,\ldots,a_d), \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{d}a_j\leq N. Introduce a_0=N-\sum_{j=1}^{d}a_j. Then a_0+\cdots+a_d=N, \qquad a_j\geq0, and stars-and-bars gives \#\{(a_0,\ldots,a_d):a_0+\cdots+a_d=N\} = inom{N+d}{d}. Thus a d-direction cumulative spectrum has d+1 homogeneous slots while its base remains d-dimensional. 3. Particle manifold and mode-ray fibre Two projective spaces can occur in the electron construction and must be kept distinct. The electron lives on Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^{3}, \qquad \dim_{\mathbb R}Q_6=6. Its cumulative six-direction mode fibre has rays \mathbb P \left( \mathbb C\oplus T_q^*Q_6\otimes\mathbb C ight) \cong\mathbb{CP}^{6}. Thus \dim H^0(\mathbb{CP}^{3},\mathcal O(L)) = inom{L+3}{3} and \operatorname{rank}\mathcal E_{n-1,6} = inom{n+5}{6} are both correct. They count different structures:  inom{L+3}{3} counts degree-L holomorphic flux states on the electron's configuration manifold;  inom{n+5}{6} counts the cumulative symmetric tangent-mode band through degree n-1. The first governs the projective orbital representation. The second supplies the mass multiplier. The labels L and n belong to these two distinct counts. For a general sector, \mathbb{CP}^{d} is the ray space of the rank-(d+1) homogenized mode fibre over the particle manifold Q_d. 4. Covariant localization forces the dimension factor Fix q\in Q_d and write W=W_{d,q}, \qquad \mathcal H_N=\operatorname{Sym}^{N}(W), \qquad D=\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H_N. Give W its metric-induced Hermitian structure. For a unit vector z\in W, define |z;Nangle=z^{\odot N}, \qquad \langle z;N|z;Nangle=1. Its projector depends only on the ray [z]: P_N([z])=|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Let d
u_{m FS} be the U(d+1)-invariant probability measure on \mathbb P(W). Consider A_N=\int_{\mathbb P(W)}P_N([z])\,d
u_{m FS}([z]). The representation \operatorname{Sym}^{N}(W) of U(d+1) is irreducible. Invariance of the measure gives U A_N U^\dagger=A_N for every U\in U(d+1). Schur's lemma therefore gives A_N=c_NI. Taking the trace fixes the coefficient: 1 =\int\operatorname{tr}P_N([z])\,d
u_{m FS} =\operatorname{tr}A_N =c_ND. Hence A_N= rac{I}{D}. The covariant localization density resolving the identity is consequently \Lambda_N([z])=DP_N([z]). Once the localization operator has rank-one support on the coherent line, covariance, positivity, and resolution of the identity force the factor D. This is the finite-dimensional coherent-state resolution of the identity used in geometric quantization. General coherent-state and reproducing-kernel constructions on compact integral symplectic manifolds are reviewed by Kirwin; explicit SU(N) coherent-state resolutions are constructed by Mathur and Mani. 5. From localization density to rest mass Let the sector spinor bundle be \Sigma_d. For a spin sector this is the ordinary spin bundle. For a \mathrm{Spin}^c sector it includes the required line connection. The mode-N field is a section of \Sigma_d\otimes\mathcal E_{N,d}. A spatial operator can commute with every Clifford matrix without being boost invariant. The rest-current carrier and dynamical rest-frame construction supply conditional completions with responsive frames and induced connections. Their additional dynamics and stability limitations must be retained; they do not derive the mode bundle from the master field. Subject to a complete such specification, the effective projected Dirac equation may take the form \left( i\gamma^a
abla_a -\mu_d\widehat\Lambda_{N,d}([z]) ight)\psi_{N,d}=0. For a localized coherent mode \psi_{N,d}=\chi\otimes|z;Nangle, the contact operator gives \widehat\Lambda_{N,d}([z])\psi_{N,d} =D_{N,d}\psi_{N,d}. The rest equation is therefore \left(i\gamma^a
abla_a-m(n,d)ight)\psi_{N,d}=0, with m(n,d)=\mu_dD_{N,d} =\mu_dS(n,d). The symmetric power acts on the bosonic orbital or derivative directions of one spinor field. 6. Projection from the master field Let P_{d,N} project the master spinor onto the particle manifold Q_d and the cumulative mode bundle \mathcal E_{N,d}. Separate the master Dirac operator into its kinetic and self-interaction parts: \mathcal D_\infty =i\Gamma^A

The mass theorem applies if the scalar contact component satisfies P_{d,N}\mathcal K_\infty P_{d,N}  ig|_{m scalar,contact} =\mu_d\widehat\Lambda_{N,d}([z]). The following subsections specify the additional occupied-ray insertion and derive its exact finite-band projection. The minimal local scalar interaction alone does not supply that insertion. 6.1 The projective ray is local mode-phase data The fibre W_{d,q} =\mathbb C\oplus T_q^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C is the homogenized oscillator-symbol fibre. The cotangent factor contains the d complex oscillator amplitudes. In an orthonormal frame centred on the mode, they combine displacement x_a and conjugate momentum p_a as a_a = rac{1}{\sqrt2} \left(  rac{x_a}{\ell_d} +i rac{\ell_dp_a}{\hbar} ight), \qquad a=1,\ldots,d. Here \ell_d is the spatial sector length. The connection identifies p_a with the covariant derivative symbol of the field. Both quadratures are dimensionless. Real orthonormal sector-frame changes act through O(d), a subgroup of U(d). The larger unitary oscillator symmetry also mixes canonical quadratures; it is not supplied by spatial frame changes alone. The additional component a_0 records the unused part of the cumulative excitation bound. The completed vector z=(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in W_{d,q} defines the projective mode-phase ray [z]\in\mathbb P(W_{d,q}). Common complex rescaling leaves the ray invariant. The value of \ell_d changes the physical phase-space embedding while preserving the rank of \mathcal E_{N,d} and the diagonal trace identity. This is the classical projective completion of the cumulative oscillator band. Quantization at homogeneous degree N gives \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^{d+1}). The same construction therefore produces both the ray space and its simplex dimension. Higher oscillator degree fills the degree-N representation of the same spatial coordinates: \operatorname{Sym}^N(W_{d,q}), and the definite ray becomes the coherent line |z;Nangle=z^{\odot N}. Equivalently, the filtered symbols through derivative order N have associated graded bundle  igoplus_{k=0}^{N} \operatorname{Sym}^k(T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C). The sector connection splits this filtration into the homogenized bundle \mathcal E_{N,d}. The ray is the local oscillator phase of the field on Q_d. A definite orbit supplies a definite [z] at each instant. The direct calculation on physical field derivatives keeps the distinction between this carrier identification and an interaction derivation. The written local scalar term acts on Taylor derivatives by a triangular product rule: the count repeats its local source blocks, while their eigenvalues retain the original coefficient. Changing the derivative normalization preserves that result. A physical oscillator projection also needs its induced kinetic metric and control of the next derivatives entering the spatial Dirac equation. 6.2 Conditional occupied-ray insertion Lift the scalar current to the graph of its occupied projective symbol: \mathcal J_d(q,[u]) =J_d(q)\, \delta_{m FS} \left([u],[z_{\Psi_d}(q)]ight), \qquad J_d= ar\Psi_d\Psi_d. The invariant delta is normalized by \int_{\mathbb P(W_{d,q})} f([u])\delta_{m FS}([u],[z])\,d
u_{m FS}([u]) =f([z]). This graph lift assigns a specified ray to the source. Its identification with the field's physical amplitude-gradient data is an additional premise, not a consequence of scalar locality on Q_d. Consider the leading scalar self-interaction of a nonlinear Dirac field: \mathcal L_{m sc} =- rac{\kappa_d}{2}J_d^2. Its Euler--Lagrange contribution is  rac{\partial\mathcal L_{m sc}}{\partial ar\Psi_d} =-\kappa_dJ_d\Psi_d. In integral-kernel language, multiplication by the current has distribution kernel \kappa_dJ_d(q)\, \delta_{Q_d}(q,q')\, \delta_{m FS}([u],[u']). The diagonal delta is the kernel representation of multiplication. In the ray variable it represents the identity, not a point insertion at a selected ray. Its band compression is P_N I P_N=I_{\mathcal H_N}, which has full rank. General order-zero multiplication can also have a nonconstant coefficient in [u]; locality does not determine that coefficient. To obtain the point insertion \kappa_d\delta_{[z]}, separately assume that the interaction evaluates against the graph-supported source at the occupied ray. Its finite-band projection is computed in the next section. A physical derivation must specify the lifted action, its measure, and its pairing; formally squaring the distributional graph current in a quartic action is not a defined replacement for those data. A defined graph-measure pairing with one finite-band kernel retains the simplex coefficient. Its complete self-variation is a scalar-current variation: the moving ray contributes no self-orientation stiffness. This candidate action still needs its physical origin and normalized spatial solutions. 6.3 Exact projection of a point contact Let \mathcal H_N =\operatorname{Sym}^{N}(W_{d,q}) and let P_N be the orthogonal projector onto its holomorphic realization over \mathbb P(W_{d,q}). Denote its reproducing kernel by K_N. For every s\in\mathcal H_N, s([z])=\langle K_{N,z},sangle, \qquad K_{N,z}(\,\cdot\,)=K_N(\,\cdot\,,[z]). Define the Toeplitz projection of the point contact by its quadratic form: \langle s,T_{N,[z]}tangle = \int \overline{s([u])}\, \delta_{m FS}([u],[z])\, t([u])\,d
u_{m FS}([u]). Evaluation gives \langle s,T_{N,[z]}tangle =\overline{s([z])}t([z]) =\langle s,K_{N,z}angle \langle K_{N,z},tangle. Therefore T_{N,[z]} =P_N\delta_{[z]}P_N =|K_{N,z}angle\langle K_{N,z}|. Its nonzero eigenvalue is \|K_{N,z}\|^2=K_N([z],[z]). The diagonal is constant because U(d+1) acts transitively on \mathbb{CP}^{d} and preserves both P_N and d
u_{m FS}. Its value is fixed by the trace: \int_{\mathbb{CP}^{d}} K_N([u],[u])\,d
u_{m FS}([u]) =\operatorname{tr}P_N =\dim\mathcal H_N. The measure has total volume one, hence K_N([z],[z]) =\dim\mathcal H_N = inom{N+d}{d} =S(N+1,d). Writing |z;Nangle = rac{K_{N,z}}{\sqrt{K_N([z],[z])}} gives the exact identity  oxed{ P_N\delta_{[z]}P_N =S(N+1,d)|z;Nangle\langle z;N| =\Lambda_{N,d}([z]). } Here U(d+1) is the covariance of the homogenized cumulative mode fibre. The original U(d) rotates the d derivative directions. Projective completion adds the homogeneous slack component and extends the finite band to the irreducible U(d+1) representation \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^{d+1}). Treating that completion isotropically is a necessary mode-space premise of the exact simplex law. This is the required projection theorem. Toeplitz operators with singular measure and distribution symbols are part of the general reproducing-kernel framework described by Rozenblum and Vasilevski. Here the finite-dimensional projective case is an exact consequence of the reproducing property. 6.4 Conditional projected nonlinear Dirac equation Assume the occupied-ray interaction of Section 6.2 supplies the following term, with the ray held fixed during this operator evaluation, and project it onto the mode band: P_{d,N} \left(\kappa_dJ_d\delta_{[z]}ight) P_{d,N} = \mu_dP_N\delta_{[z]}P_N, where \mu_d is the sector-normalized scalar contact strength after the Q_d profile and spinor normalization have been taken. The projection theorem gives P_{d,N}\mathcal K_\infty P_{d,N}  ig|_{m scalar,contact} = \mu_dS(N+1,d) |z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Acting on the occupied coherent line, P_{d,N}\mathcal K_\infty P_{d,N}|z;Nangle =\mu_dS(N+1,d)|z;Nangle. With n=N+1, the projected Dirac equation therefore contains the rest mass  oxed{ m(n,d)=\mu_dS(n,d). } All explicit N-dependence comes from the diagonal of the finite-band reproducing kernel. The resulting \mu_d is shared by all ordinary particle modes in sector d provided the normalized one-particle scalar-current contraction is the same in every band. This is automatic for a universal unit-normalized point current, but must be checked for the normalized spinor convention used by the projected master action. The action-level derivation has four necessary ingredients: Locality in the mode ray. The self-interaction evaluates the wave against its own phase-space ray [z]. Covariance. Rotating the mode frame sends \Lambda([z]) to \Lambda([Uz]) by conjugation. Resolution normalization. Integrating the mutually overlapping localized rays over invariant measure gives the identity. Band-blind contact strength. The coefficient \mu_d depends on the sector and is independent of N. The graph-supported contact is the first premise; it is not forced by the local scalar current. The Bergman projection proves the second and third within the chosen isotropic mode space and produces the factor S(n,d). Absence of a band label in a bare coupling does not by itself establish the fourth: normalized projected profiles and scalar-current matrix elements can depend on the band. Their independence must also be demonstrated. If the occupied ray is itself a function of the varied field or its derivatives, variation of the lifted action must include that dependence. The fixed-ray operator calculation does not already derive those additional Euler--Lagrange terms or prove a self-consistent occupied-ray solution. At one fixed ray, \Lambda_{N,d}([z]) has a (D_{N,d}-1)-dimensional nullspace. The coherent rays form an overcomplete family and \int\Lambda_{N,d}([z])\,d
u_{m FS}=I, so every nonzero state is detected by some contact density. At a given [z], the occupied localized particle is the one nonzero eigenline. 7. Kinetic and contact operators A spatial Dirac or Laplace operator on Q_d supplies kinetic eigenvalues and their multiplicities through \slashed D_{Q_d} and \Delta_{Q_d} respectively. The localized contact operator supplies the rest-energy endomorphism whose eigenvalue grows as S(n,d)\sim n^d. The kinetic operator constructs the mode eigenspace. The contact density then maps its rank D to the eigenvalue of a normalized localized operator. This is the two-stage origin of the mass multiplier. 8. Boundaries of the theorem 8.1 The photon The construction begins at n=1, where N=0 and S(1,d)=1. The proposed photon assignment has n=0. Extending the count by S(0,2)=0 records a vanishing contribution from this mode family. The formal empty bundle \mathcal E_{-1,d}=0 has no nonzero state and therefore supplies neither a zero eigenvalue nor a propagating photon. A physical photon requires a nonempty transverse state space and a contact operator satisfying \mathcal M\psi_\gamma=0,\qquad \psi_\gamma
e0. Its kinetic propagation, complete energy–momentum response and stability must follow from the same field action. The zero-count boundary alone does not prove these conditions or the protection of a massless branch. 8.2 The bottom beat The ordinary theorem gives the single-band masses m(n,3)=\mu_3S(n,3). The bottom formula m_b=\mu_3\sqrt{S(16,3)S(17,3)} requires a two-band coupling. Its closure condition is that the off-diagonal contact operator between \mathcal E_{15,3} and \mathcal E_{16,3} have a singular value equal to the geometric mean of their diagonal contact eigenvalues. 8.3 Sector scales For a band-blind master contact coefficient, one \mu_d multiplies every ordinary occupied band in a sector. Numerical projection must determine \mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_4,\mu_5,\mu_6,\mu_{10} and their cross-sector relations from the normalized master kernel and its overlap between the corresponding Q_d sectors. Observed masses provide the empirical test of those projected values. 8.4 Mode selection The operator supplies a collective mass eigenbranch for every positive integer n. A separate stability or resonance condition must select which branches occur as particles. The accuracy of the mass-depth scan is conditional on those occupied indices. 8.5 Occupied-ray and ray-averaged quartic densities The distinction between contact at the occupied ray and averaging over all rays is mathematically observable. For a normalized coherent state |w;Nangle, define its normalized phase-ray density ho_w([z]) =D_N|\langle z;N|w;Nangle|^2. It obeys \intho_w\,d
u_{m FS}=1. Because |\langle z;N|w;Nangle|^2 =|\langle z|wangle|^{2N}, the invariant moment formula gives \int_{\mathbb{CP}^{d}} |\langle z|wangle|^{4N}\,d
u_{m FS} = rac{1}{D_{2N}}, \qquad D_{2N}= inom{2N+d}{d}. A quartic energy averaged over the whole ray space is \intho_w([z])^2\,d
u_{m FS} = rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}, while occupied-ray self-contact has eigenvalue D_N. The two interactions are 	ext{occupied-ray self-contact} \quad\longrightarrow\quad D_N, 	ext{ray-averaged quartic density} \quad\longrightarrow\quad rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}. Of these two specified prescriptions, only the point contact has the simplex multiplier with a band-independent coefficient. This comparison does not establish uniqueness among nonlinear actions. The full smooth quartic variation establishes coherent stationary solutions, a complete mode Hessian and finite-mode orbital stability for the second action. Its nonlinear frequency retains D_N^2/D_{2N}. Deriving a coherent branch and deriving the point-contact multiplier are therefore separate requirements. The specified spatial CP3 scalar branch tests another necessary step: restoring the physical spatial Dirac complement. On that proposed geometry, the normalized local-contact branch has a nonzero cubic frequency correction and an oscillatory radial instability at every positive section degree for sufficiently small coupling. A smooth spatial moment kernel changes that response and avoids the radial instability in the same regime. The physical CP3 section count uses  inom{L+3}{3}; it must not be identified with the auxiliary cumulative count D_N= inom{N+6}{6}. These conditional field calculations do not yet select a stable physical particle, its occupied index, or its mass. 8.6 Coordinate harmonic kernel and phase-ray contact A scalar coordinate kernel whose isotropic mean field is V_d(q)=\lambda_d|q|^2 derives a harmonic well and hence the shell spaces \operatorname{Sym}^k(T_q^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C). That is enough to derive the rank D_N of the cumulative band. The corresponding band projection is P_{N,d}|q|^2P_{N,d} and the phase-ray contact density is D_N|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Their relation requires either a master interaction written locally on the homogenized phase-ray bundle; or a derivation showing that the coordinate-space nonlinear kernel transforms into the occupied-ray contact density after the oscillator and sector projections. This step completes the map from coordinate confinement to phase-ray self-contact. The actual spatial oscillator point form provides a separate explicit comparison: its eigenvalue is the spatial reproducing kernel on the diagonal, with a weighted Hockey-Stick central value and fixed-width growth of degree d/2. The simplex dimension is its integrated trace, so spatial point evaluation alone does not supply the projective coefficient at every point. Consistency across cumulative bands adds a test for one underlying kernel, distinguishing fixed bare compression from a dynamical Schur reduction. The specified band embeddings and any eliminated modes are part of that bridge. 9. Sector normalization The universal combinatorial part of the scalar contact projection is now fixed: P_N\delta_{[z]}P_N =S(N+1,d)|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Write the scalar coefficient left after sector projection as \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d. Here \kappa_d is the projected master-contact coefficient, R_d is the normalized spatial-profile overlap on Q_d, and B_d is the scalar spinor contraction. Suppose the order-zero vertex is a scalar identity on the normalized non-mode factors, its coefficient is constant on the occupied contact graph, and its coefficient is independent of the band projector. Under these band-blind hypotheses, all three factors are independent of N. The contact theorem then gives m(n,d)=\kappa_dR_dB_d\,S(n,d). For the stated band-blind scalar vertex, \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d is independent of N. Derivative vertices, nonconstant order-zero coefficients, finite contact width, spectral functions, mode-dependent spinor polarization, and band-dependent state normalization generate testable modifications of the mass sequence. For two sectors with equal self-couplings, the ratio of mass units is  rac{\mu_a}{\mu_b}= rac{R_aB_a}{R_bB_b}. Thus the proposed \mu_6=\mu_{10} symmetry requires both g_{66}=g_{10,10} and equality of the normalized projected overlaps. The local scalar profile calculation shows explicitly how normalization can change the frequency produced by a contact coefficient. Its virial and exact massive benchmark concern a flat local comparison; they do not replace the physical geometry and bundle terms needed for the occupied particle solutions. The nonlinear spatial reduction now derives the effective stationary action and induced norm after complementary Dirac modes respond. For a normalized chiral zero-mode branch, the frequency is gA-4g^3C+O(g^5) while the total energy is gA/2-g^3C+O(g^5). Under the stated positive-potential hypotheses, C vanishes exactly when the scalar source preserves the selected zero-mode line. A common graph coefficient g_N=\kappa D_N must therefore also control these spatial corrections before it supplies a common physical mass scale. The graph coefficient itself remains to be derived from the master action. The physical tangent-band point projection computes the complete holomorphic zero-form contact spectrum with the natural curved connection. Its eigenvalues depend on fibre polarization. At fixed line twist their maximum grows cubically with the cumulative degree on CP3, while the auxiliary simplex rank grows as its sixth power. This is a derived distinction between specified operators; it does not change the particle assignments or identify a physical rest mass. The constant-density local branch solves the written local scalar equation on that specified curved kinetic bundle. Five holomorphic polarization fields occupy five orthogonal tangent copies already in the carrier. Their total density is constant, so the scalar coefficient is exact; at common norm and volume it is independent of the carrier rank. The action also retains copy symmetries that leave the occupied pattern unselected. The coherent curved mode-bundle construction retains the natural tangent-mode connection and gives pointwise coherent spatial fields with balanced first moments. The specified scalar moment action has exact linear branches on these fields, but local scalar contact and a spatially transported graph pairing retain different normalization factors. Their master origin and full stability remain open. The balanced spatial branch supplies an exact unit-norm field with frequency g and energy g/2 for the specified smooth moment kernel. Its noncoherent holomorphic shape has an isotropic first spatial moment, and its complete spatial linearization has no exponential modes. This is a constructive solution of a conditional spatial normalization problem; the master origin of the kernel and coherent-ray coefficient, nonlinear stability and physical rest-mass identification remain to be established. On the specified physical CP3 geometry, exact source preservation forces a smooth real scalar potential on a holomorphic section to be constant. A covariant kernel preserving the coherent branch then makes every holomorphic shape in that degree degenerate. The genuine mean kernel gives an exact, nonlinearly stable phase orbit, while a finite same-field static response retains a bounded nonzero spatial correction. Exact linearity therefore does not by itself select the occupied shape. The scalar self-consistency comparison constructs a nonzero scalar coefficient and an exact collective response frequency from one specified global kernel. Its leading coefficient is M\simeq\kappa Q, where Q is the full canonical norm. A cumulative count enhances it only when that norm grows with the number of modes; at unit total norm, |M|\le\kappa for every band. This locates a normalization requirement that a physical mass derivation must supply. 9.1 The conditional common-anchor relation There is a compact way to state the scale relations that have direct mass tests. Let n_d^\star be a specified reference band in sector d and define its contact mass M_d^\star=\mu_dS(n_d^\star,d). Under the projected fixed-point condition  rac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} =  rac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}. the sector scale is  oxed{ \mu_d =  rac{m_e}{S(n_d^\star,d)} \sqrt{ rac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} }. The square root is the direct algebraic consequence of this quadratic fixed-point equation. The master equation of motion must supply that equation. For the proposed reference choices, the formula reads  egin{aligned} \mu_6&= rac{m_e}{S(13,6)},\ \mu_3&=m_e\sqrt{ rac{g_{33}}{g_{66}}},\ \mu_4&= rac{m_e}{S(3,4)} \sqrt{ rac{g_{44}}{g_{66}}}. \end{aligned} The electron fixes the unit. The d=3 and d=4 expressions then make conditional predictions to compare with inferred quark-mass parameters. A quantitative comparison must specify the mass definition, renormalization scheme, scale and matching to measured hadronic or scattering observables. These parameters are not directly measured free-particle masses; see the PDG quark-mass review. No common-scheme refit is performed here. The proposed d=2 formula \mu_2=m_e\sqrt{ rac{g_{22}}{g_{66}}} uses a unit-count back-reaction reference. It is testable because it predicts the absolute W, Z, and Higgs masses after their mode indices are specified. Likewise, \mu_{10}=\mu_6 is testable against the tau mass, but still requires the normalized 6\leftrightarrow10 overlap equality just identified. These are the direct empirical checks of the conditional fixed-point equation and coupling counts. 9.2 The neutrino scale is unresolved The proposed relation \mu_5 =  rac34 rac{\mu_6^3}{\mu_4^2} is a phenomenological normalization calibrated to the observed neutrino order of magnitude. V2 treats \mu_5 as an undetermined projected normalization. An operator equation must select the factor 3/4 and powers (3,-2) before this expression becomes a derived scale law. Neutrino oscillations measure mass-squared differences. Given the proposed mode indices, they constrain a common \mu_5. An absolute neutrino-mass measurement will provide the direct scale test. The current status is  oxed{\mu_5	ext{ remains an undetermined projected normalization.}} A derivation requires evaluating \kappa_5R_5B_5 from the master action. 9.3 Remaining numerical calculation The outstanding work is to evaluate (\kappa_d,R_d,B_d), \qquad d\in\{2,3,4,5,6,10\}, from one normalized projected action and recover the cross-sector relations. The simplex multiplier is derived, the non-neutrino scale relations are conditional and empirically testable, and the neutrino expression is a phenomenological ansatz. The construction also makes sharp deformation predictions: a finite ray-contact width replaces the constant diagonal evaluation with a convolution of the Bergman kernel and changes the mass sequence; derivatives of the contact delta insert powers of the representation generators and generate additional N-dependence; a band-dependent scalar coefficient spoils the scale-free family ratios; a mixed state on several projective rays splits or averages the rank-one mass eigenvalue. Order-zero self-contact at a definite projective mode ray is one operator realization of the simplex spectrum. The homogeneous coherent actions provide other exact occupied eigenvalues with different complete mode responses. Their nonconstant spatial solutions have canonical energy and full linear stability for the specified independent kinetic bundle. The functional normalization and master-field carrier remain assumptions; the direct derivative identification fails finite propagation in its stated flat control. The spectrum therefore constrains a master interaction without determining it uniquely.

title: Dimensional constriction and hadronic mass
summary: Current scope: This is an exploratory calculation ledger, not a derived hadron-mass formula. Numerical residuals and trial normalizations below are conditional comparisons. Neither 154.808228 MeV nor twice that value is
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Current scope: This is an exploratory calculation ledger, not a derived hadron-mass formula. Numerical residuals and trial normalizations below are conditional comparisons. Neither 154.808228 MeV nor twice that value is an established constriction eigenfrequency. Section 2 distinguishes action from frequency; Sections 64--76 give the normalization and spectral limitations. 1. Question The quark sectors in V2 are assigned different spatial depths: Q_4 \quad \text{for up-type quarks}, and Q_3 \quad \text{for down-type quarks}. The cross-depth geometry is asymmetric. A four-dimensional mode projected into a three-dimensional hadronic sector loses one independent spatial oscillator direction. The three-dimensional state does not gain one. This raises a specific dynamical question: Can the large difference between light current-quark masses and observed hadron masses be interpreted as the energy cost of constraining a four-dimensional oscillator into three dimensions? The calculation below separates what follows mathematically from dimensional constriction from what remains an empirical or dynamical input. 2. Oscillator action and the separate frequency-rescaling hypothesis For an isotropic oscillator with d directions, E_d=\omega_d I_{\rm total}^{(d)} =d\,\omega_d I_{\rm per}^{(d)}. Conservation of total action under a hypothetical 4\to3 transfer gives 4I_{\rm per}^{(4)}=3I_{\rm per}^{(3)}. This fixes the action per surviving direction, not the frequency. If both total action and total oscillator energy are conserved, the displayed Hamiltonian instead gives \omega_3=\omega_4. The equation 4\omega_4 I_1=3\omega_3 I_1 assumes equal energy and the same per-direction action on both sides. It yields \omega_3=4\omega_4/3, but changes total action from 4I_1 to 3I_1. It is not a consequence of total-action conservation. The numerical explorations below use \boxed{\omega_3=\frac43\omega_4} as a separate frequency-rescaling hypothesis. No current V2 dynamics derives it. Transferring eliminated action into surviving directions, by itself, does not establish this hypothesis. 3. Mass-like energy from the constriction For a relativistic bound mode, oscillator or confinement energy contributes to the rest energy observed in the lower-dimensional sector. Define the effective confinement contribution per valence quark by \epsilon_h = \frac{M_h-\sum_i m_{q_i}}{N_q}, where M_h is the observed hadron mass; m_{q_i} are the current-quark masses used by V2; N_q is the number of valence quarks in the minimal quark assignment. If the observed three-dimensional confinement quantum is the constricted oscillator quantum, \epsilon_h=\hbar\omega_3, then the corresponding pre-constriction four-dimensional quantum is \boxed{ E_{4,h} =\hbar\omega_4 =\frac34\epsilon_h. } If the four-dimensional oscillator has characteristic spatial scale R_h, dimensional analysis gives E_{4,h}\sim\frac{\hbar c}{R_h}, so the effective constriction radius inferred from a hadron mass is \boxed{ R_h =\frac{4\hbar c}{3\epsilon_h}. } Equivalently, \boxed{ M_h =\sum_i m_{q_i} +N_q\frac43\frac{\hbar c}{R_h}. } This is the simplest quantitative hadronic-mass law produced by the 4\to3 constricted-oscillator hypothesis. 4. Nucleon test Using the V2 light-quark masses m_u=2.16\ {\rm MeV}, \qquad m_d=4.70\ {\rm MeV}, the proton current-quark sum is 2m_u+m_d=9.02\ {\rm MeV}. With m_p=938.272088\ {\rm MeV}, the excess mass is \Delta M_p =929.252088\ {\rm MeV}. Per valence quark, \boxed{ \epsilon_p =309.750696\ {\rm MeV}. } The inferred pre-constriction oscillator quantum is E_{4,p} =\frac34\epsilon_p =232.313022\ {\rm MeV}, and therefore \boxed{ R_p^{\rm constr} =\frac{\hbar c}{E_{4,p}} =0.8494\ {\rm fm}. } The neutron gives almost the same result. With m_n=939.565421\ {\rm MeV}, and m_u+2m_d=11.56\ {\rm MeV}, one finds \boxed{ \epsilon_n =309.335140\ {\rm MeV}, } E_{4,n}=232.001355\ {\rm MeV}, and \boxed{ R_n^{\rm constr} =0.8505\ {\rm fm}. } Thus proton and neutron independently select essentially the same constriction scale: \boxed{ R_N^{\rm constr}\simeq0.850\ {\rm fm}, } with a three-dimensional confinement quantum \boxed{ \hbar\omega_3\simeq309.5\ {\rm MeV}. } The near equality of the proton and neutron values is nontrivial because their current-quark sums differ. 5. Relation to the measured nucleon size The proton charge radius is approximately r_p\simeq0.84\ {\rm fm}. The mass-derived constriction radius R_p^{\rm constr}\simeq0.849\ {\rm fm} is therefore within roughly one percent of the observed proton charge-radius scale. Conversely, inserting a radius near 0.84 fm into \epsilon=\frac43\frac{\hbar c}{R} gives a confinement quantum near 313\ {\rm MeV}, close to the 309--310 MeV required by the proton and neutron masses. This is the strongest numerical result of the dimensional-constriction test. It does not by itself prove the mechanism because the relation E_4=\hbar c/R is a characteristic confinement estimate rather than a derived eigenvalue of the present V2 master operator. Any dependence they create in a proposed generator must be derived, eliminated exactly, or proved to cancel before making a frequency prediction. 69.1 What changing units and projecting a state do not prove Writing an unknown coefficient as the electron reference times an unknown dimensionless ratio changes its units, not whether that ratio has been determined. Likewise, projecting a state and then renormalizing it does not automatically justify replacing its generator by a compressed matrix. Section 74 gives an exact example in which a projection factor changes spectral weight but not the surviving frequency. The normalized-marginal example showed no universal 7/6 multiplier for that example. Its failure is neither erased merely by using frequency notation nor promoted into a universal theorem about a different operator. The required endpoint is a derived frequency ratio, with no fitted amplitude. In a nonlinear theory, any background dependence of the linearized frequency operator also has to be specified or eliminated; eigenvalue notation alone does not establish independence from it. 70. Electron anchoring: historical V1 provenance and the correct V2 target The historical dimensional architecture does not by itself establish the projected dynamics. V1 states explicitly that the electron mass is the sole unit reference for the particle spectrum. In frequency language, the construction is \boxed{ \omega_{n,d} = \omega_e\,R_{n,d}, } where every R_{n,d} is dimensionless. For example, the V1 scale hierarchy was written as \frac{\varpi_3}{\omega_e} = \sqrt{\frac{g_{33}}{g_{66}}}, and \frac{\varpi_4}{\omega_e} = \frac{1}{S(3,4)} \sqrt{\frac{g_{44}}{g_{66}}}. The electron does not explain a human unit such as MeV. It supplies the single measured reference frequency. MeV enters only when that measured reference is expressed numerically in human units. This is also the natural interpretation of the V2 common-anchor relation \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} = \frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}. Dividing through by m_e^2 shows that its physical content is entirely dimensionless: \boxed{ \left(\frac{M_d^\star}{m_e}\right)^2 = \frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}. } In frequency notation, \boxed{ \left(\frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}\right)^2 = \frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}. } Thus the foundational V2 problem is not to derive an absolute energy unit. It is to derive this dimensionless spectral relation from the projected master dynamics. 71. Cross-depth coupling audit in frequency language The original cross-depth coupling module defines an allowed invariant vertex space \mathcal V_{abc} = \operatorname{Inv}_{Spin(a)\times Spin(q)} \left(F_a\otimes R_b^*\otimes R_c\right). A nonzero invariant space permits a coupling, while the source explicitly leaves its dynamical effect to the projected equations. The adopted couplings satisfy g_{34}^2=g_{33}g_{44}, and in the adopted convention g_{66}=1/4 is dimensionless. The fixed-point relation gives [g_{dd}]=[g_{66}], and the rank-one relation gives [g_{34}]^2=[g_{33}][g_{44}]. Thus these couplings are dimensionless in that convention; the ratio equation alone would not establish their absolute engineering dimension. This is exactly what should happen in an electron-anchored frequency theory: g_{34} can determine a ratio or dimensionless spectral deformation, while \omega_e supplies the sole measured unit reference. Therefore the correct cross-depth spectral ansatz is not \text{new dimensionful coefficient}\times g_{33}, but \boxed{ \omega_{34}^{\rm con} = \omega_e\,R_{34}^{\rm con}, } with \boxed{ R_{34}^{\rm con} = F_{34}(g_{33},g_{34},g_{44},S,\text{projected spectral data}). } If the depth-three sector is first established relative to the electron, this can equivalently be written \boxed{ \omega_{34}^{\rm con} = r_{34}\varpi_3, \qquad r_{34}:=\frac{\omega_{34}^{\rm con}}{\varpi_3}. } The strongest simple hypothesis is r_{34}=g_{33}, but that remains to be derived from the spectrum of the projected cross-depth operator. 71.1 Status of 7/6 and 4/3 The two previously proposed projection factors are also dimensionless and therefore belong naturally in a frequency-ratio calculation. The reciprocal candidate is \frac76, and the action-transfer candidate is \frac43. The audits already established: 7/6 is a natural symmetric dimension-counting normalization but is not yet forced by the written V2 cross-depth operator; 4/3 is not the generic result of ordinary symplectic 4\to3 reduction and requires explicit transfer dynamics. Thus a candidate chain such as \frac{\omega_{\rm con}}{\varpi_3} = \frac76\frac43\,g_{33} must be regarded as a product of separate hypotheses until each factor is obtained from the spectral dynamics. No amplitude is involved in this statement. 72. Fixed-point audit restated as a pure frequency-ratio problem The V2 source writes the conditional common-anchor relation \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} = \frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}. Its observable content is the dimensionless frequency ratio \boxed{ \frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e} = \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. } For a sector whose first occupied particle lies at simplex factor S(n_d^\star,d), \omega_d^\star = \varpi_d S(n_d^\star,d), so \boxed{ \frac{\varpi_d}{\omega_e} = \frac{1}{S(n_d^\star,d)} \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. } For d=3, because S(1,3)=1, \boxed{ \frac{\varpi_3}{\omega_e} = \sqrt{\frac{g_{33}}{g_{66}}}. } This mathematics is dimensionally and conceptually clean: it solves only for a measurable frequency ratio. The unresolved point is dynamical rather than dimensional. The V2 source itself states that the master equation of motion must supply the common-anchor fixed-point equation. A corpus audit found no independent derivation of it elsewhere in V2. Therefore the current status is: the simplex contact eigenvalue S(n,d) follows under the stated finite-band, occupied-ray, measure and band-blind-vertex hypotheses; the identity g_{34}^2/g_{44}=g_{33} gives the removed static relaxation contribution; the actual static Schur complement is zero; the electron-relative fixed-point law (\omega_d^\star/\omega_e)^2=g_{dd}/g_{66} is still conditional on the projected master dynamics; the cross-depth ratio r_{34}=\omega_{34}^{\rm con}/\varpi_3 is not yet derived; the candidate factors 7/6 and 4/3 remain separately unproved for the reasons already established. 72.1 Math audit: no amplitude is being solved for The surviving hadronic equations after this revision involve only integer spectral counts S(n,d); dimensionless couplings g_{dd'}; observable frequencies \omega; ratios of observable frequencies. The central unknowns are \boxed{ \frac{\varpi_3}{\omega_e} } and \boxed{ \frac{\omega_{34}^{\rm con}}{\varpi_3}. } No field amplitude, probability amplitude, profile normalization, current magnitude, or overlap normalization is being solved for. This is the correct formulation for the next stage of the V2 proof/disproof program. 73. Coupling audit corrected: static relaxation is not a frequency-spectrum theorem This section replaces the earlier, overly broad coupling-only no-go claim. The tested couplings are the values adopted in the preceding investigation; this calculation does not derive them from the V2 master action. Write G=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a=8\sqrt7,\quad b=4\sqrt6,\quad c=\frac{12}{\sqrt7}. Then b^2=ac and G is positive semidefinite of rank one. 73.1 Three different static quantities The actual static Schur complement of the depth-four block is \boxed{a-bc^{-1}b=0.} The removed relaxation contribution is \boxed{bc^{-1}b=a,} while clamping the second channel leaves the principal block a. Section 32 distinguished the relaxed and clamped quadratic forms. Later summaries incorrectly called the removed contribution itself the Schur complement. Neither that contribution nor a static stiffness is automatically an observable frequency. 73.2 The spectral Schur equation retains its frequency dependence For the matrix eigenvalue parameter z, exact elimination gives f(z)=a-z-\frac{b^2}{c-z}, \qquad z\ne c, and (c-z)f(z)=\det(G-zI)=z(z-a-c). The full matrix eigenvalues are therefore 0 and a+c=68/\sqrt7. Setting z=0 inside the eliminated block before solving is a static approximation, not an exact frequency calculation. The excluded denominator value must be checked in the original matrix problem. 73.3 The common-anchor relation does not define a full coupled generator The source relation \left(\frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}\right)^2 =\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}} concerns specified sector reference frequencies. It does not by itself identify G/g_{66} with the frequency-squared operator of an interacting baryon. Conditional test only: if one additionally defines the coupled frequency generator as \sqrt{G/g_{66}}, its positive frequency satisfies \frac{\omega_+}{\varpi_3}=\sqrt{\frac{a+c}{a}} =\sqrt{\frac{17}{14}}, where \varpi_3/\omega_e=\sqrt{a/g_{66}} is the conditional depth-three fundamental. Taking the square root after clamping instead gives the ratio one. These results test those particular operator prescriptions. They do not prohibit a term linear in a dimensionless coupling in a different frequency generator. Such a term would require its own derivation; it is neither established nor contradicted by the diagonal anchor relation alone. 73.4 Projection and the operator square root do not commute For this rank-one matrix, \sqrt G=\frac{G}{\sqrt{a+c}}. On the first channel, \frac{\langle3|\sqrt G|3\rangle}{\sqrt a} =\sqrt{\frac{14}{17}}, \qquad \frac{\sqrt{\langle3|G|3\rangle}}{\sqrt a}=1. Thus projecting a first-order generator and taking the square root of a projected second-order operator are different operations. The master dynamics must specify the appropriate operation. 73.5 The old numerical factor remains an identity, not a prediction The algebraic identity \frac{28}{9}=\frac23\frac{g_{33}}{g_{44}} is exact for the adopted couplings. Section 76 derives a signed -2/3 coefficient in a specified color-pair operator. Equality of numerical magnitudes does not identify that operator with the old constriction chain. Its sign, pair counting, remaining kernel, and frequency dependence must all be retained. 73.6 Corrected conclusion The two-by-two matrix calculations have been solved exactly, but their identification with a hadronic frequency operator has not been derived. The previous universal exclusion of linear coupling dependence is withdrawn. The unresolved task is the interacting spectral problem, not an amplitude fit or the invention of a new human energy unit. 74. Color projection: spectral weights, compressed generators, and observed frequencies The earlier 64/6 computation was algebraically correct for one compressed rank-one operator. Its interpretation as a universal color-induced reduction of frequency was not correct. 74.1 Carrier content does not determine the generator The proposed carrier W=\mathbb C\Omega\oplus U, with U\cong\mathbf3, has \dim W^{\otimes3}=64. Its two SU(3) singlets are the vacuum-like line \Omega^{\otimes3} and the determinant line \Lambda^3U. This is a representation statement. It does not establish that W^{\otimes3} is the baryon carrier or that its dimension is a baryon frequency multiplier. 74.2 What the identical-vector zero actually excludes The determinant projection obeys P_{\Lambda^3U}(z\otimes z\otimes z)=0. This excludes the identical-vector product as a determinant-color state. It does not exclude three particles in the same orbital mode with a separate antisymmetric color factor. Color and orbital tensor factors must not be conflated. 74.3 Compression changes the operator unless the subspace reduces it Let v=|123\rangle be an ordered orthonormal color tensor and let P_\epsilon project onto the normalized determinant singlet. For A=64|v\rangle\langle v| one obtains P_\epsilon A P_\epsilon=\frac{32}{3}P_\epsilon. However, [A,P_\epsilon]\ne0. This is not restriction to a reducing subspace: using the compressed operator as a closed generator discards the coupling to its complement. No master-action argument previously justified that discard. 74.4 Exact observation preserves a surviving frequency, not necessarily its weight For a time-independent linear projection P, a stationary mode satisfies P\!\left(u\,e^{-i\omega t}\right)=(Pu)e^{-i\omega t}. If Pu\ne0 and the same clock is used, its frequency is unchanged. A vanishing projection removes the line; it does not divide its frequency. The distinction is explicit in the rank-one test above. In dimensionless spectral units, the exact projected resolvent is P_\epsilon(z-A)^{-1}P_\epsilon =\left[\frac{1}{6(z-64)}+\frac{5}{6z}\right]P_\epsilon. It has poles at 64 and 0, not at 32/3. The factor 1/6 is the residue of the frequency-64 pole. It is fixed geometrically in this diagnostic, not fitted from an amplitude measurement. The exact reduced generator on this line is A_{\rm eff}(z)=\frac{32z}{3z-160}, \qquad z-A_{\rm eff}(z)=\frac{3z(z-64)}{3z-160}. Retaining the eliminated-channel term recovers the original poles. The apparent singularity at z=160/3 is not an eigenvalue of the original matrix. This example distinguishes observation and exact elimination from physically imposing a new clamped generator. It does not claim that a non-invariant ordered-color contact is the physical baryon Hamiltonian. 74.5 A singlet constraint need not attenuate orbital eigenfrequencies If the generator factorizes as \mathsf H=I_{\rm color}\otimes A_{\rm mode}, then color-singlet restriction gives (P_\epsilon\otimes I)\mathsf H(P_\epsilon\otimes I) =P_\epsilon\otimes A_{\rm mode}. Every allowed mode eigenfrequency of A_{\rm mode} survives unchanged. More generally, in a closed three-quark model with color-neutral remaining factors, an SU(3)-invariant generator preserves its color-singlet subspace. Additional colored dynamical fields require a total-color constraint, not an unjustified valence-only truncation. Corrected result: color projection neither derives the candidate 64 nor universally suppresses it by 1/6. The claimed suppression-based exclusion is withdrawn. Whether 64 occurs must be decided from the actual invariant interacting generator, without treating proximity to a previously selected numerical target as a derivation. 75. Three-body relative coordinates: an effective domain, not a new particle depth 75.1 The observed-coordinate kinematics For three positions in a common observed \mathbb R^3, an orthogonal Jacobi transformation separates the center coordinate and two vectors \rho,\lambda\in\mathbb R^3. Their relative configuration space is \mathbb R^6. With the Euclidean metric and R^2=|\rho|^2+|\lambda|^2, a fixed-R surface is S^5. Mass-weighted Jacobi coordinates can be used when the kinetic metric requires them. These statements concern three-body configuration coordinates, not six spatial directions available to a single particle. 75.2 Native depth is not configuration-space dimension V2 assigns the constituent fields to their native manifolds Q_d. Observing three positions in a common three-space does not prove that the native higher-depth coordinates disappear from the dynamics. Consequently neither the six Jacobi coordinates nor their S^5 angular surface can be identified with the electron's depth-six manifold or the neutrino's depth-five sector merely by matching dimensions or manifold names. Such an identification needs an explicit map of operators, metrics, bundles, measures, and constraints. 75.3 Degeneracy is not automatically a frequency For scalar harmonics on the unit round S^5, -\Delta_{S^5}Y_{\ell}=\ell(\ell+4)Y_{\ell}, \qquad h_\ell=\binom{\ell+5}{5}-\binom{\ell+3}{5}. The Laplacian eigenvalue and its degeneracy are different quantities. Neither is automatically the spectrum of the composite Dirac/contact frequency generator. The previous degeneracy scan therefore did not test a specified V2 baryon operator. 75.4 A conditional valence-space representation After deriving an appropriate observed-coordinate reduction, a three-quark valence model could use a physical subspace of L^2(\mathbb R^6_{\rho,\lambda}) \otimes\Lambda^3U_{\rm color} \otimes\mathcal H_{\rm spin/flavor}, with the total fermionic permutation constraint enforced. This is a possible effective representation, not a derivation of the complete baryon Hilbert space. Native coordinates and other dynamical channels must either be retained or eliminated with their induced spectral terms. 75.5 Predict the whole baryon pole The primary target is the complete rest-frequency ratio \boxed{z_B=\omega_B/\omega_e.} The earlier approximately 309--310 MeV quantity was a per-constituent allocation of a residual after subtracting chosen quark contributions. It is not, without an additional decomposition theorem, a separate measured eigenfrequency that the operator must contain. 75.6 Corrected status The Jacobi construction provides useful observed three-body kinematics. It does not establish a new particle sector, a baryon-to-neutrino identification, or the elimination of native coordinates. Passive projection alone does not generate a larger frequency. A physical frequency shift requires the interacting generator or a specified change of dynamics; exact elimination represents that interaction rather than replacing it with dimension counting. 76. Exact frequency-domain reduction and the color-singlet pair coefficient This section records the constructive result of the revised audit. The block identities are exact for the finite matrices checked here. Applying them to the full master operator additionally requires specified domains, a stationary background where needed, and a controlled treatment of its infinite-dimensional channels. 76.1 A frequency equation with no fitted field amplitude Let \mathsf H be a dimensionless stationary time-evolution generator, defined using the electron reference and the common phase variable \tau=\omega_e t: i\partial_\tau\Psi=\mathsf H\Psi. An eigenvalue z is then a frequency ratio \omega/\omega_e. A covariant spacetime Dirac operator is not automatically this generator; its time direction and stationary reduction must first be specified. For an orthogonal model-space projector P_B and Q_B=I-P_B, define \mathsf H_{\rm eff}(z) =P_B\mathsf H P_B +P_B\mathsf H Q_B (z-Q_B\mathsf H Q_B)^{-1} Q_B\mathsf H P_B. The inverse acts on \operatorname{Ran}Q_B. Where it exists, the projected resolvent is P_B(z-\mathsf H)^{-1}P_B =\left[zI_{P_B}-\mathsf H_{\rm eff}(z)\right]^{-1}. Thus the bound-state calculation seeks \boxed{\ker\!\left[z_BI_{P_B}-\mathsf H_{\rm eff}(z_B)\right]\ne\{0\}.} A determinant equation is available in a finite representation. At excluded complementary eigenvalues, the original system must be checked or the model space enlarged; denominator clearing alone is insufficient. This is standard Feshbach-Schur reduction, not a newly derived V2 interaction. See Dusson, Sigal, and Stamm, The Feshbach-Schur map and perturbation theory, Theorem 1.2 and equations (1.15)--(1.16). The independently checked two-channel example in Section 74 fixes the sign convention used here. 76.2 Derive the color factor from the specified generators The V2 gauge-block proposal uses fundamental generators T^a=\lambda^a/2. With \operatorname{tr}(T^aT^b)=\delta^{ab}/2, define C_{ij}=\sum_{a=1}^8T_i^aT_j^a =\frac12\left(\mathsf X_{ij}-\frac13I\right), where \mathsf X_{ij} exchanges the two color slots. The generator normalization and completeness identity are standard; see Haber, Useful relations among the generators in the defining and adjoint representations of SU(N). On the determinant singlet, \mathsf X_{ij}=-I. Therefore \boxed{P_\epsilon C_{ij}P_\epsilon=-\frac23P_\epsilon,} \qquad \boxed{P_\epsilon\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}P_\epsilon=-2P_\epsilon.} The sum contains three unordered pairs. These are operator eigenvalues from representation theory, not field amplitudes and not an inserted hadron-mass fit. 76.3 What this fixes in an actual pair interaction If the derived dimensionless interaction has the form \mathsf V_{\rm pair}(z)=\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}\otimes K_{ij}(z), with K_{ij}(z) acting on the remaining factors, its singlet restriction is \boxed{\mathsf V_{{\rm pair},B}(z)=-\frac23\sum_{i<j}K_{ij}(z).} It reduces to -2K(z) only when the three remaining pair operators actually coincide. It does not supply a universal frequency ratio of two or 2/3. The sign is retained; whether this is an attractive contribution depends on the remaining operator convention. This form is a conditional template for matching to the V2 master interaction. The audit has derived its color coefficient, not the existence, radial dependence, spin dependence, or normalization of K_{ij}. 76.4 What has and has not been solved The static/spectral Schur distinction, the projection-versus-frequency error, and the singlet pair coefficient have been resolved exactly. A normalized eigenvector may be used to represent a mode, but no measured field amplitude is used as an input. Electron anchoring fixes the unit. It does not, by itself, determine every dimensionless interaction coefficient. The next calculation must derive the remaining blocks and their spectral dependence from the V2 dynamics, retaining induced terms rather than guessing an integer near the desired mass. No numerical baryon-frequency prediction is claimed by this revision.

title: Neutrino mass splittings and the simplex spectrum
text:
Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. 1. Result In the V2 neutrino sector, the three occupied modes are (n_{
u_1},n_{
u_2},n_{
u_3})=(10,15,22), at depth d_
u=5. The bare mass law is m_i=\mu_5 S(n_i,5), \qquad S(n,d)= inom{n+d-1}{d}. For the three neutrino modes, S(10,5)=2002, S(15,5)=11628, S(22,5)=65780. Therefore (m_1,m_2,m_3) =\mu_5(2002,11628,65780). The common normalization \mu_5 cancels exactly from the ratio of the two independent mass-squared splittings. The V2 neutrino assignments therefore make a parameter-free prediction:  oxed{  rac{\Delta m_{21}^2}{\Delta m_{31}^2} =  rac{11628^2-2002^2}{65780^2-2002^2} =0.030349842234897634. } The depth-scan companion uses a different PDG-2024 benchmark and reports 1.98\% for that comparison. The 2.68\% below belongs specifically to the two inputs displayed here; these benchmarks must not be interchanged when quoting accuracy. Using the benchmark oscillation values \Delta m_{21}^2=7.49	imes10^{-5}\ {m eV}^2, \Delta m_{31}^2=2.534	imes10^{-3}\ {m eV}^2, the observed ratio is  rac{\Delta m_{21}^2}{\Delta m_{31}^2} =0.029558011049723762. The V2 simplex prediction is therefore high by approximately  oxed{2.68\%}. This comparison contains no fitted neutrino mass scale. 2. Independent reconstruction of the neutrino scale The same mass law permits \mu_5 to be inferred independently from either measured splitting. From the solar splitting, \Delta m_{21}^2 =\mu_5^2\left[S(15,5)^2-S(10,5)^2ight], so \mu_5^{(21)} = \sqrt{  rac{\Delta m_{21}^2} {11628^2-2002^2} } =7.5556190385	imes10^{-7}\ {m eV}. From the atmospheric splitting, \Delta m_{31}^2 =\mu_5^2\left[S(22,5)^2-S(10,5)^2ight], so \mu_5^{(31)} = \sqrt{  rac{\Delta m_{31}^2} {65780^2-2002^2} } =7.6561541256	imes10^{-7}\ {m eV}. Their ratio is  rac{\mu_5^{(21)}}{\mu_5^{(31)}} =0.9868687221. Thus the two experimentally independent splittings infer the same sector normalization to approximately  oxed{1.31\%}. This is a direct internal consistency test of the one-scale neutrino-sector hypothesis. 3. Absolute neutrino masses Once either splitting fixes \mu_5, the simplex law determines the absolute neutrino masses. Using \Delta m_{21}^2 gives m_1=0.00151263\ {m eV}, m_2=0.00878567\ {m eV}, m_3=0.04970086\ {m eV}, and hence  oxed{ \sum_i m_i=0.05999917\ {m eV}. } Using \Delta m_{31}^2 instead gives m_1=0.00153276\ {m eV}, m_2=0.00890258\ {m eV}, m_3=0.05036218\ {m eV}, with  oxed{ \sum_i m_i=0.06079752\ {m eV}. } The two independent absolute-spectrum reconstructions therefore lie in the narrow interval \sum_i m_i\simeq0.0600	ext{--}0.0608\ {m eV}. The absolute spectrum is not an additional fit once one measured splitting fixes the common normalization. The second splitting then tests the mode pattern. 4. Joint one-scale reconstruction A single common scale may also be chosen to reproduce both measured splittings simultaneously. If a=S(15,5)^2-S(10,5)^2, b=S(22,5)^2-S(10,5)^2, and x=\mu_5^2, the unweighted least-squares value minimizing (xa-\Delta m_{21}^2)^2 +(xb-\Delta m_{31}^2)^2 is x=  rac{a\Delta m_{21}^2+b\Delta m_{31}^2} {a^2+b^2}. This gives \mu_5=7.6560622136	imes10^{-7}\ {m eV}, and (m_1,m_2,m_3) = (0.00153274,0.00890247,0.05036158)\ {m eV}. The corresponding mass sum is  oxed{ \sum_i m_i=0.06079679\ {m eV}. } The reconstructed splittings are \Delta m_{21}^2=7.69047	imes10^{-5}\ {m eV}^2, \Delta m_{31}^2=2.53394	imes10^{-3}\ {m eV}^2. Because the atmospheric splitting is numerically much larger, an unweighted fit in absolute squared residuals is dominated by it. The scale-free ratio in Section 1 is the cleaner test of the simplex pattern itself. 5. Why the result is nontrivial For three masses obeying m_i=\mu_5 S(n_i,5), the two measured splittings are \Delta m_{21}^2 =\mu_5^2 \left[S(n_2,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2ight], \Delta m_{31}^2 =\mu_5^2 \left[S(n_3,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2ight]. Their ratio removes the only continuous parameter: R_
u =  rac{S(n_2,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2} {S(n_3,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2}. Once the discrete mode triple (10,15,22) and depth d=5 are specified, R_
u is fixed. The comparison with oscillation data is therefore not a three-mass fit and not a one-parameter fit. It is a test of the discrete spectrum shape. The second form of the same test is to infer \mu_5 separately from each measured splitting. If the simplex mode assignments were badly wrong, the two inferred scales would generally disagree. Instead they differ by only about 1.31\%. 6. Relation to depth selection The same scale-free ratio can be evaluated while keeping the mode indices fixed and varying the candidate depth: R_
u(d)=  rac{S(15,d)^2-S(10,d)^2} {S(22,d)^2-S(10,d)^2}. For the neighboring depths, R_
u(4)\approx0.05550, R_
u(5)\approx0.03035, R_
u(6)\approx0.01686. Thus the observed oscillation hierarchy selects d=5 sharply relative to the adjacent integer depths. This result is also summarized in the mass-spectrum depth test. 7. What is established and what remains conditional Established mathematics Given the V2 mass law and the stated neutrino mode assignments: the simplex counts are exactly (2002,11628,65780); the predicted splitting ratio is exactly 0.030349842234897634; the ratio is independent of \mu_5; the two measured splittings independently infer nearly the same \mu_5; fixing \mu_5 from either splitting determines the complete absolute spectrum; the resulting mass sum is approximately 0.060--0.061\ {m eV}. Conditional inputs The physical interpretation remains conditional on the mode assignments (10,15,22) being selected independently of the measured neutrino splittings; the neutrino sector obeying the same one-scale simplex mass law as the other V2 sectors; normal mass ordering; the benchmark oscillation measurements used in the numerical comparison. The result does not by itself derive the mode-selection rule or the projected normalization \mu_5 from the master geometry. 8. Discrete null tests The immediate null test is discrete rather than continuous. For all ordered integer triples 1\leq n_1<n_2<n_3\leq N, at fixed depth d=5, define R(n_1,n_2,n_3) =  rac{S(n_2,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2} {S(n_3,5)^2-S(n_1,5)^2}. 8.1 Unrestricted integer triples The unrestricted search is deliberately permissive: every increasing integer triple is allowed, without imposing the V2 mode-selection construction. Using the benchmark ratio R_{m obs}=0.02955801105, the committed V2 triple (10,15,22) has relative error 2.6789\%. It is good but not unique in the unrestricted search. Its rank remains near the best 0.6\% of triples as the cutoff grows: Maximum index N Number of triples Rank of (10,15,22) Percentile 22 1,540 10 0.649% 30 4,060 24 0.591% 50 19,600 111 0.566% 75 67,525 390 0.578% 100 161,700 909 0.562% 150 551,300 3,153 0.572% 200 1,313,400 7,269 0.553% Many arbitrary triples fit the oscillation ratio more closely. For example, (5,10,15) gives a relative error of about 0.099\%, and by N=200 some accidental triples match at the 10^{-3}\% level. Therefore the oscillation ratio by itself is not strong evidence for the particular integers (10,15,22). The unrestricted null does exactly what it should: it shows that one real-valued ratio can be approximated well by many freely chosen discrete triples. 8.2 Null constrained by the V2 mode-generation rule The physically relevant comparison is narrower because the V2 indices are not arbitrary integers. The mode-selection construction generates the first two neutrino indices from a common seed k through adjacent simplex firings, n_1(k)=S(k,3), n_2(k)=S(k,4), and generates the third through the inclusion--exclusion pushout n_3(k)=n_1(k)+n_2(k)-k. For the committed seed k=3 this gives S(3,3)=10, \qquad S(3,4)=15, \qquad 10+15-3=22. The resulting index triple is then passed through the independent depth-five mass law, m_i(k)=\mu_5 S(n_i(k),5). Scanning the seed family 1\leq k\leq100 gives the following leading results: Seed k Generated triple Predicted R_
u Relative error 3 (10,15,22) 0.03034984 2.679% 5 (35,70,100) 0.03064535 3.679% 4 (20,35,51) 0.02724713 7.818% 6 (56,126,176) 0.03695042 25.010% 7 (84,210,287) 0.04511132 52.620% 8 (120,330,442) 0.05464059 84.859% 2 (4,5,7) 0.06057782 104.946% Within this constrained family,  oxed{k=3\ 	ext{ranks first among all tested seeds }1\leq k\leq100.} This distinction is essential. The unrestricted null shows that arbitrary integer triples can fit the measured ratio easily. The constrained null shows that the specific triple generated by the V2 contact-resonance construction is the best member of the tested seed-generated family. The evidential content therefore lies not in the ratio alone but in the composition of two independent structures: 	ext{mode selection} \longrightarrow (10,15,22) \longrightarrow 	ext{depth-five simplex masses} \longrightarrow R_
u. The remaining question is whether the seed rule and pushout are themselves uniquely forced by the projected master interaction rather than chosen after the spectrum is known. 9. summary: This reading sequence brings the current calculations into twenty manageable documents. Each document includes selected equations and results from the maintained research. Source links lead to the full record; the conden
text: This reading sequence brings the current calculations into twenty manageable documents. Each document includes selected equations and results from the maintained research. Source links lead to the full record; the condensed set does not reproduce abandoned research routes. Research map and current status — The physical mass operator remains the central open problem. This reading set follows the active spatial, current, support, coupling and inertia calculations. Mathematical existence within a stipulated action is kept distinct from a derived same-field law or an observed particle. Physical premises and nested spatial sectors — Depth counts ordinary physical spatial dimensions in one nested manifold. A particle pattern may rotate independently of its sector. Lower-dimensional sectors are nested, but particle solutions at different depths need not be restrictions of one another. Spatial operator and contact toolkit — The simplex factor must arise from an actual physical spatial operator or a justified effective reduction. Mode counting, one eigenfrequency, a contact trace, and a pair vertex are different objects. Same-field actions and canonical normalization — A candidate mass and coupling mechanism must follow from one varied action with its canonical norm, retained modes and complete energy. The calculations here are conditional action constructions; they do not establish a unique master-field reduction. Simplex spectrum and sector assignments — Observed frequencies provide the targets. The assigned spatial depth and harmonic index determine a proposed cumulative mode count, while the physical frequency unit and occupation rule require dynamics. Spatial carriers and compatible geometry — A carrier must live in the physical sector and support the proposed spectrum, polarization and spatial variation. Candidate geometries at different depths must coexist in one nested chain before their field equations are compared. Localization and same-field support — The same-field interaction may sustain a finite spatial pattern and set its oscillation frequency. A radial minimum is only one necessary part of a stationary spatial field; angular stress and the response of the sustaining structure matter. Current mass-operator candidates — The finite component carrier, inverse current law and density-current simplification are candidate routes to the assigned frequencies. Their exact finite-chain and current calculations should be read with their stated geometric and normalization assumptions. Common scales across particle sectors — One operator must account for frequencies at all maintained depths without fitting each particle independently. Radius, gap, spatial conversion and canonical norm must be compared under the same assumptions. The competing outer depth-ten branch — The extra depth-ten branch is a candidate state of the same harmonic, not an established particle identification. Its local frequency, retained same-field response and shifted-radius checks are useful even though one fitted law does not reproduce every known sector. Spatial and dynamical stability — Stability claims depend on which field, polarization and geometric perturbations were varied. The current-action component and angular results and the conformal background calculation belong to specified, distinct actions. Complete energy, inertia and causal motion — Mass is the selected oscillation frequency in equivalent units, while positive inertia requires the momentum response of the complete particle and its sustaining field. Partial wave momentum and an assigned frequency do not settle that response. Photon geometry and physical polarization — Depth-two light supplies the explicit transverse polarization control. A massive higher-depth sector may have a different polarization rule; the proposed photon zero and its radiative protection remain separate questions. Same-field coupling across sectors — Coupling is compatibility and reciprocal response of actual spatial patterns in the one field. A response coefficient, pair vertex, encounter probability and rest frequency require separate normalizations before they can be related. Pair geometry and reciprocal encounters — Both particles carry orientation, phase and a responding spatial field. Fixed overlap is a snapshot; a complete encounter calculation must include the reciprocal motion of both patterns and preserve the common field law. Neutrino frequency and interaction controls — Neutrino patterns may have different physical support sizes and nonzero but rare encounters. Oscillation measurements constrain mass differences; a particular positive absolute mass is not imposed by this synthesis. Composite and hadronic mass — A composite frequency and complete energy can contain a substantial interaction contribution. The normal response, quark-pattern coupling and canonical normalization must be calculated from one action before identifying a nucleon mass mechanism. Orbits, binding and observed spatial patterns — A projected picture, a circulating coefficient ray and an actual spatial orbit are distinct. The available orbit calculations make the observer map explicit and test a conditional Coulomb-driven spatial pattern. Flavor, charge and gauge geometry — Mass assignments alone do not produce a mixing matrix or a physical gauge field. Candidate projected operators and bundle data give finite tests whose physical source and normalization remain to be derived. Observational comparisons and remaining proofs — A candidate law must pass simultaneous frequency, normalization, spatial-state, stability and response tests. This document keeps the maintained depth controls and explicit proof obligations together without promoting an inverse fit into a physical derivation.
