The fixed-line spatial spectral band is a distinct construction: it adds nonholomorphic spatial harmonics on one line bundle. That band has a different evaluation spectrum and an exact simplex dimension up to a constant. Matching a dimension does not identify it with the tangent-mode bundle considered here. Use the specified physical geometry Q=\mathrm{CP}^m, with m=3 for six ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. The radius R remains undetermined, and no dimensions are compactified. Formulas at other m\ge2 are conditional geometric comparisons, not particle identifications. Let T=T^{1,0}Q, and retain W=\mathbf1\oplus T\oplus T^*,\qquad E_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N W,\qquad F_{N,L}=\mathcal O(L)\otimes E_N,\qquad L\ge0. 	ag{1} The connection and Hermitian metric are induced by the spatial geometry. The fixed line degree L and cumulative mode degree N are different data. The carrier rank remains D_{N,2m}= inom{N+2m}{2m}. 	ag{2} For the canonical Spin^c operator twisted by F_{N,L}, define \mathcal H_{N,L}=H^0(Q,F_{N,L}). 	ag{3} This is its complete holomorphic zero-form channel. The full Dirac kernel also contains the higher Dolbeault cohomologies H^j(Q,F_{N,L}), which need not vanish. A scalar multiplication source acting on a zero-form remains a zero-form, so (3) is its full projection onto the Dirac kernel. The operator calculation below does not bound all the other form channels or replace a continued nonlinear spatial solution. Use unit spatial measure d
u first. At q\in Q, let \operatorname{ev}_q:\mathcal H_{N,L}\longrightarrow F_{N,L,q}, \qquad s\longmapsto s(q),\qquad C_{N,L}(q)=\operatorname{ev}_q\operatorname{ev}_q^\dagger. 	ag{4} The physical point form on the global section space is T_q=\operatorname{ev}_q^\dagger\operatorname{ev}_q. Its nonzero eigenvalues are precisely those of C_{N,L}(q). For a specified unit fibre polarization \xi, the polarized point form is rank one, with nonzero eigenvalue \langle\xi,C_{N,L}(q)\xiangle when that number is nonzero. The physical position q is not an auxiliary mode-phase ray. Decompose every tangent-mode component The slack component in (1) gives the orthogonal parallel decomposition E_N= igoplus_{k+j\le N}\operatorname{Sym}^k T \otimes\operatorname{Sym}^j T^*. 	ag{5} Contracting one tangent and one cotangent index decomposes each summand into trace-free pieces. Write p=k-\ell, q=j-\ell, where 0\le\ell\le\min(k,j). Use q as an integer label in the formulas below, rather than as the spatial point in (4). The trace-free piece has fibre rank r_{p,q}^{(m)} = inom{p+m-1}{m-1} inom{q+m-1}{m-1} - inom{p+m-2}{m-1} inom{q+m-2}{m-1}, 	ag{6} where the second term is zero if p=0 or q=0. Its multiplicity in E_N is 
u_{N,p,q}=\left\lfloor rac{N-p-q}{2}ightfloor+1, \qquad p,q\ge0,\quad p+q\le N. 	ag{7} The contraction and trace insertion are parallel maps, so these are holomorphic orthogonal subbundles with the induced metric. Their ranks satisfy \sum_{p+q\le N}
u_{N,p,q}r_{p,q}^{(m)}=D_{N,2m}. 	ag{8} An independent character identity checks the complete decomposition, not only its rank. If h_p(x) is the complete symmetric polynomial in m variables, the trace-free character is h_p(x)h_q(x^{-1})-h_{p-1}(x)h_{q-1}(x^{-1}). Multiplying by the line character to power p-q and summing with (7) reproduces the degree-N symmetric character of all 2m+1 entries of W. Holomorphic sections fix the evaluation eigenvalues Let \mathcal Q be the rank-m tautological quotient bundle on projective space. The Euler sequence gives T=\mathcal O(1)\otimes\mathcal Q. The trace-free piece labelled by (p,q) consequently has the quotient-bundle highest weight (p,0,\ldots,0,-q) and line twist t=L+p-q. For the Borel–Weil–Bott calculation, its complete weight and shift are \lambda=(p,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{m-2},-q,-t), \qquad \varrho=(m,m-1,\ldots,0). 	ag{9} If \lambda+\varrho has a repeated entry, all cohomology vanishes. Otherwise sorting those entries gives the unique cohomology degree; subtracting \varrho gives the corresponding highest weight. This is the homogeneous-bundle cohomology rule, with the dual and quotient conventions described in Marian, Oprea and Sam, Section 2.3.2. The explicit application (9) is also checked against the independent Euler index below. There are holomorphic sections precisely when (9) is already dominant:  oxed{L+p\ge2q.} 	ag{10} When (10) holds, the Weyl dimension formula divides into the fibre dimension (6) and the factors involving the last weight in (9):  oxed{ b_{p,q,L}^{(m)} = rac{(L+p-2q+1)(L+2p-q+m)}{m!} \prod_{j=2}^{m-1}(L+p-q+j). } 	ag{11} The product is empty for m=2. More explicitly, \dim H^0(F_{p,q,L})=r_{p,q}^{(m)}b_{p,q,L}^{(m)}. This follows directly by separating the factors with last index m+1 in \prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j+j-i)/(j-i). Spatial homogeneity makes the diagonal evaluation operator on each irreducible fibre block a scalar. Its trace integral is the dimension of the global section space. Since the measure has total volume one, that scalar is the dimension divided by the fibre rank, namely (11). Thus the complete nonzero spectrum of C_{N,L} is  oxed{b_{p,q,L}^{(m)} \quad	ext{with multiplicity }
u_{N,p,q}r_{p,q}^{(m)}, \quad p+q\le N,\quad L+p\ge2q.} 	ag{12} The other fibre blocks have zero evaluation. On the global section space, T_q has these same nonzero eigenvalues and its remaining kernel. Equivalent copies in (7) remain orthogonal copies with the same scalar; their number does not multiply the eigenvalue on one copy. The sharp physical contact strength All positive factors in (11) are maximized at p=N, q=0. Therefore  oxed{ \|T_q\|=\|C_{N,L}(q)\|=B_{N,L}^{(m)} = rac{L+2N+m}{m} inom{L+N+m-1}{m-1}. } 	ag{13} For fixed L, this grows as 2N^m/m!. It differs from the auxiliary mode-fibre point-contact eigenvalue D_{N,2m}, which grows as N^{2m}/(2m)!. They are evaluations on different spaces with different metrics and sections. There is also a particularly simple coherent polarization: the pure slack vector e_0^{\odot N}. Its physical evaluation strength is  oxed{ \langle e_0^{\odot N},C_{N,L}e_0^{\odot N}angle = inom{L+m}{m}, } 	ag{14} independent of N. The auxiliary isotropic ray contact instead assigns D_{N,2m} to that coherent ray as well. The natural spatial connection does not supply the larger isotropy of the homogenized mode fibre. For the six-dimensional candidate with L=0: Cumulative degree N Carrier rank D_{N,6} Largest physical point eigenvalue B_{N,0}^{(3)} Physical slack eigenvalue 12 18\,564 819 1 34 3\,838\,380 14\,910 1 These are normalized operator eigenvalues, not particle masses. A different fibre polarization can have a smaller point expectation. The table does not establish that no independently selected pair of physical states could fit a particular finite ratio, nor does it compare alternative particle dimensionalities. It shows that this specified physical projection does not itself produce the isotropic simplex operator. With physical volume \mathcal V, every value in (12)–(14) gains the same factor 1/\mathcal V. A common sector scale cannot remove their different dependence on N. An explicit spatial field attains the bound The largest value in (13) has an independent spatial realization. Let X be the holomorphic projective vector field induced by the matrix E_{10}. For unit homogeneous coordinates, put p_j=|Z_j|^2. The tangent metric gives \|X\|^2=p_0(1-p_1),\qquad s_{N,L}=Z_0^L X^{\odot N},\qquad \|s_{N,L}\|^2=p_0^{L+N}(1-p_1)^N. 	ag{15} This is a global section in the \operatorname{Sym}^N T component, including its zeros. It is pointwise coherent where it is nonzero. At the coordinate pole Z=e_0, its squared norm is one. Under unit FS measure, p_1 has beta distribution (1,m), while p_0/(1-p_1) conditionally has beta distribution (1,m-1). Hence  egin{aligned} \int\|s_{N,L}\|^2d
u &= rac{m}{L+2N+m}  rac{(m-1)!(L+N)!}{(L+N+m-1)!}\ &= rac1{B_{N,L}^{(m)}}. \end{aligned} 	ag{16} Thus \sqrt{B_{N,L}^{(m)}}s_{N,L} has unit norm and squared value B_{N,L}^{(m)} at the pole, attaining (13). No representation dimension formula is used in this integral. The same field's normalized local quartic is  oxed{ \intho_{N,L}^2d
u = rac{(B_{N,L}^{(m)})^2}{B_{2N,2L}^{(m)}}. } 	ag{17} More generally, every unit section in (3) obeys ho(q)\le B_{N,L}^{(m)} and therefore \intho^2d
u\le B_{N,L}^{(m)}. This is a bound on the stated holomorphic channel. A finite nonlinear branch with complementary Dirac components has to be solved separately. The source-preservation criterion continues to distinguish an occupied expectation from an exact linear stationary frequency. Check the higher forms through an independent index The Euler sequence gives the K-theory class [W]=(m+1)[\mathcal O(1)]+(m+1)[\mathcal O(-1)]-[\mathbf1]. If H is the hyperplane class and z is a formal counting variable, the symmetric-power character is \sum_{N\ge0}\operatorname{ch}(E_N)z^N = rac{1-z}{(1-ze^H)^{m+1}(1-ze^{-H})^{m+1}}. 	ag{18} Taking its coefficient and using \chi(\mathcal O(k))=\prod_{j=1}^m(k+j)/m! gives an independent Euler characteristic, including negative line degrees. It agrees with the alternating sum of all cohomology groups from (9). Serre duality also gives h^j(E_N(L))=h^{m-j}(E_N(-L-m-1)), because E_N is self-dual. For CP3 the result simplifies exactly:  oxed{ \chi(E_N(L)) = inom{N+6}{6}\chi(\mathcal O(L)) +4(L+2) inom{N+7}{8}. } 	ag{19} To see the second term, expand the cubic polynomial \chi(\mathcal O(L+k)). Symmetry between the positive and negative line summands makes its odd k moments cancel. The coefficient of k^2 is (L+2)/2, and (18) gives second moment 8 inom{N+7}{8}. This separates the carrier rank from the contribution of its curvature. For example, at N=2, L=0, the Dolbeault cohomology dimensions in form degrees zero through three are (101,1,0,0), with index 100. At N=12 they are (840\,636,35\,106,11\,873,194\,183), with index 623\,220. The holomorphic section count alone is therefore not the entire Dirac zero-mode count or its chiral index. Verification and consequence for the master projection tangent_band_contact_checks.py checks complete characters and ranks, the full cohomology algorithm, the independent Euler index, Serre duality, every point eigenvalue and the explicit extremizer integrals. A separate spatial calculation constructs all 15 holomorphic tangent vector fields on CP3 from traceless matrices. Direct integration normalizes their Gram matrix and gives three point eigenvalues equal to 5. Their 120 symmetric products have an integrated Gram matrix of rank 84. Using its inverse on that support gives six physical point eigenvalues equal to 14, in agreement with (13) at N=2. The calculation retains the product relations and uses two independent spatial cubature orders. Counting all 120 generators as orthonormal sections would give the wrong operator. The natural cumulative inclusions preserve the existing degree blocks and their connections, as required by consistent band contacts. This spatial projection is also distinct from the flat oscillator point form, whose spatial profiles and metric are different. The calculation derives the evaluation operator once the specified spatial point form and kinetic bundle are adopted. A smooth local scalar current still does not itself impose a point insertion. Deriving the master field's actual interaction, projection and canonical normalization remains necessary before the auxiliary simplex eigenvalue can be identified with a physical mass.

title: When a two-frequency spatial symmetry exists
summary: A constant antilinear reduction requires a specific involution of the complete spatial Dirac matrices, and its existence, scalar interference and compatibility with nested field projections can be checked directly.
text: Summary: A constant antilinear reduction requires a specific involution of the complete spatial Dirac matrices, and its existence, scalar interference and compatibility with nested field projections can be checked directly. A special solution family need not be a symmetry of arbitrary fields The radial two-frequency map constructs full solutions from arbitrary complex radial profiles. Extending that map to arbitrary spatial perturbations requires an additional matrix identity. The number of field components alone does not supply it. Here r counts the ordinary macroscopic spatial derivatives actually retained in the equation. A bound depth d has r=d when normal motion is suppressed, and r=d+1 when one existing normal direction is included. These coordinates belong to the one nested manifold. Matrix ranks and conjugation operations describe its field components; they do not introduce new physical dimensions. Consider H=-i\sum_{j=1}^r\alpha_j\partial_j+\beta\mathfrak m, \qquad \mathfrak m\in\mathbb R. \tag{1} Use constant Clifford matrices in the stated flat spatial model, on a common domain preserved by the proposed conjugation and boundary conditions. A matrix identity alone does not establish a symmetry of a different operator domain or of a curved spatial bundle. A coordinate-preserving antilinear partner C=B\mathsf K, where \mathsf K conjugates the field components, must obey \boxed{B\alpha_j^*=\alpha_jB,\qquad B\beta^*=-\beta B,\qquad B^\dagger B=I.} \tag{2} These identities give CH=-HC, including every retained derivative. They also give (C\psi)^\dagger\beta(C\psi)=-\psi^\dagger\beta\psi. To mix \psi and C\psi while preserving the scalar source for arbitrary complex fields, their cross bilinear must vanish. This requires \boxed{(\beta B)^T=-\beta B, \qquad C^2=BB^*=I.} \tag{3} Under (2), the two conditions in (3) are equivalent. For example, BB^*=I makes the unitary B symmetric, and then (\beta B)^T=B\beta^*=-\beta B. The related nonlinear Dirac symmetry and its matrix requirements are discussed by Boussaïd and Comech. The calculations below check the actual spatial matrices and the centered moment source used here, rather than assuming a symmetry from a smaller field representation. Check the complete Clifford representation The standard complex Clifford representation can be constructed from Pauli matrices: \gamma_{2j-1}=Z^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes X\otimes I^{\otimes(k-j)}, \qquad \gamma_{2j}=Z^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Y\otimes I^{\otimes(k-j)}. \tag{4} For an odd number 2k+1 of generators, append \gamma_{2k+1}=Z^{\otimes k}. Use the first r generators as \alpha_j and the last as \beta. This is an irreducible complex representation of the full indicated Clifford algebra. Each generator has \gamma_j^*=\epsilon_j\gamma_j, with \epsilon_j=\pm1. For a product B=\prod_{j\in S}\gamma_j of m=|S| distinct generators, B\gamma_jB^{-1}=(-1)^{m-\mathbf1_{j\in S}}\gamma_j, \qquad BB^*=(-1)^{N_{\rm imag}+m(m-1)/2}I. \tag{5} Here N_{\rm imag} counts imaginary generators in the product. The required signs are \epsilon_j on spatial generators and -\epsilon_\beta on the scalar generator. Equations (4)–(5) provide explicit intertwiners and their squares. For r=4 and r=8, the product of all r+1 generators is a nonzero real scalar times I. Equations (2) would make antilinear conjugation change its sign, but a real scalar cannot change under such conjugation. No B satisfying (2) exists in those stated representations. When a solution exists, any two invertible solutions of (2) differ by a matrix commuting with every generator. Irreducibility makes that matrix a scalar. A phase change of B cannot change BB^*, so a computed negative square cannot be replaced by a positive square in the same irreducible representation. retained spatial derivatives r complex field components result for C^2 1 2 +I 2 2 +I 3 4 +I 4 4 no intertwiner satisfying (2) 5 8 -I 6 8 -I 7 16 -I 8 16 no intertwiner satisfying (2) 9 32 +I 10 32 +I 11 64 +I Thus the minimal five- and six-dimensional bound equations do not have the involution (3). Including one normal derivative gives r=6 or r=7 and still has a negative square. The corresponding ten-dimensional examples have a positive square. These are matrix statements about the specified operators, not assignments of particle charge, stability or interaction strength. A positive square gives a controlled nonlinear map When (2)–(3) hold, define \mathcal T\psi=a\psi+bC\psi, \qquad s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0. \tag{6} Pointwise scalar interference vanishes, giving \sigma[\mathcal T\psi]=s\sigma[\psi]. In the centered moment source, the scalar center is unchanged and its second moment is multiplied by s, provided its scalar normalization is nonzero. Consequently, if \psi solves the complete spatial source equation at coefficient g_0s, then \mathcal T\psi solves it at g_0 with the same bare scalar term. This follows directly by applying (2) to each derivative and using the transformed scalar moment. The real-linear map has \boxed{\mathcal T^{-1}=\frac{\bar a-bC}{s},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\langle\mathcal T u,\mathcal T v\rangle =s\operatorname{Im}\langle u,v\rangle.} \tag{7} At fixed nonzero s it is invertible and transfers the growth exponents of the corresponding full real field linearizations. The map becomes poorly conditioned when its two weights approach equality: \operatorname{cond}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal T =\frac{|a|+|b|}{|a|-|b|}. \tag{8} The number norm is generally different from the radial isometry: \boxed{\|\mathcal T\psi\|^2 =(|a|^2+|b|^2)\|\psi\|^2 +2\operatorname{Re}\big[\bar a b\langle\psi,C\psi\rangle\big].} \tag{9} The cross term need not vanish on arbitrary fields. A stationary nonzero-frequency eigenfunction is orthogonal to its opposite-frequency partner, but that fact must not be applied to every perturbation. For C^2=-I, equation (2) instead makes \beta B symmetric. Generic complex fields then have nonzero \psi^\dagger\beta C\psi, so the single scalar scaling used in (6) fails. Exact radial and real anisotropic two-frequency families can still exist through their own spatial identities. They do not require a global transformation of every field perturbation. Include the existing normal direction before using the symmetry A symmetry of the bound equation must also satisfy BY^*=YB to include its normal derivative. In the tested three-dimensional bound representation, the involution instead has BY^*=-YB. At normal momentum q, it therefore obeys B H_{-q}^*+H_qB=2qYB, \qquad H_q=H_b+qY. \tag{10} Its bound-space reduction fails as soon as that normal propagation is retained. In the tested five-dimensional case, the negative-square partner respects the normal derivative but still fails the arbitrary-field scalar-interference condition. These are distinct requirements, checked separately in the full spatial source. The occupied polarizations also matter. A background generated by (6) must have Y\phi_2=C\phi_1, or \phi_2=YC\phi_1. That is a specific correlation between the two occupied profiles. It cannot be presumed for independent polarizations. For the deformed three-dimensional profile in a 2\subset3 pair, this correlated preparation cancels all scalar rest sidebands. The full normal response still opens them. The analogous orthogonal preparation in the deformed five-dimensional profile of a 3\subset5 pair has nonzero scalar sidebands even at rest. Orthogonality alone therefore does not substitute for the full spatial symmetry calculation. The reciprocal periodic response retains these channels directly. A containing-space involution need not preserve a projected sector Suppose a higher representation has C^2=I, and P selects a lower field copy while retaining its lower spatial Clifford operators and \beta. If CP=PC, restricting C to that copy would give a positive-square solution of (2) there. That is impossible when the selected minimal lower representation requires C^2=-I. The containing involution must then leave that selected copy. This can be checked explicitly in the 64-component representation with ten bound derivatives and one common normal derivative. Commuting rotation projectors on the other containing directions select a lower minimal copy of rank 8 for bound depth five or rank 16 for bound depth six. For the checked projectors, \boxed{PBP^*=0,\qquad \|(I-P)BP^*\|_F^2=\operatorname{rank}P.} \tag{11} The transformation's full norm goes into complementary field components. Those components still describe the same nested physical manifold. This is a compatibility condition on a symmetry and a chosen field projection, not an obstruction to the nesting of the spatial sectors. The spatial reflection analysis provides related constraints on their polarization multiplicities. Verification and scope antilinear_dirac_checks.py constructs (4)–(5), checks every spatial matrix relation, and independently solves the complete complex linear intertwiner equations at the smaller ranks. It checks scalar interference, the real kinetic form, the inverse and number norm on arbitrary complex field vectors. Complete centered nonlinear source evaluations test the map beyond a stationary ansatz. Independent prepared spatial resolvents test the correlated-polarization sidebands. Explicit containing-space projectors verify (11). Reports are timestamped and checks remain active with Python optimization. The obstruction concerns constant coordinate-preserving antilinear maps in the specified representations. Additional field multiplicities, spatial reflections, nonlocal transformations and special solution families require their own analysis. The full periodic source equation remains available without assuming this reduction.

title: Axial spatial Dirac packets
summary: An exact angular family retains complete complex polarization vectors and transverse localization in odd-dimensional scalar Dirac dynamics, with a variational radial and axial regulator for reciprocal packet encounters.
text:
Summary: An exact angular family retains complete complex polarization vectors and transverse localization in odd-dimensional scalar Dirac dynamics, with a variational radial and axial regulator for reciprocal packet encounters. An ordinary spatial family with explicit angular dependence Consider the same local scalar equation used by the positive-frequency vertices, now in odd ordinary spatial dimension D\ge3: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot
abla\Psi+g\sigma eta\Psi, \qquad \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi. 	ag{1} This is a specified flat-space scalar term. The following packets are unbound fields, not identified photons, neutrinos or leptons. Choosing a spatial symmetry of their preparation does not introduce compactified or internal dimensions. Write x=(x_\perp,z)\in\mathbb R^{D-1}	imes\mathbb R, r=|x_\perp|, and s=D-1. Let \Gamma_j be a minimal complex Clifford representation for the D spatial directions. Choose \alpha_j= egin{pmatrix}\Gamma_j&0\0&-\Gamma_j\end{pmatrix}, \qquad  eta= egin{pmatrix}0&I\I&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Gamma_r=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma_j rac{x_j}{r}. 	ag{2} The two blocks are the opposite complete kinetic chiralities. Let W contain an entire orthonormal basis of the +1 eigenspace of \Gamma_z. Its dimension is P=2^{(D-3)/2}. Since \{\Gamma_z,\Gamma_r\}=0, W^\dagger W=I_P, \qquad W^\dagger\Gamma_r W=0, \qquad (\Gamma_r W)^\dagger\Gamma_r W=I_P. 	ag{3} At each nonzero transverse position, (W,\Gamma_r W) spans the complete chiral spinor space. Take the full spatial field  oxed{ \Psi_u=W F_u(t,r,z)+\Gamma_r W G_u(t,r,z),\qquad \Psi_v=W F_v(t,r,z)+\Gamma_r W G_v(t,r,z), } 	ag{4} where every F_b,G_b is a complex P-component vector. Their polarization can vary with radius and axial position. The retained angular dependence is the actual matrix \Gamma_r. This is a restricted angular family, not a representation of arbitrary angular textures. Its pointwise completeness does not remove that restriction on how different positions are related. For D=3, choose W=(1,0)^T. Equation (4) reads \Psi=(F_u,e^{i\varphi}G_u,F_v,e^{i\varphi}G_v)^T. 	ag{5} The axial angular structure is familiar from the three-dimensional Dirac separation described by Fillion-Gourdeau, Lorin and Bandrauk, section 2, after a constant change of spinor basis. The nonlinear closure and higher-dimensional formulas below follow directly from (1)–(4). For smooth Cartesian fields at the axis, F_b is smooth in r^2, and G_b=r times a function smooth in r^2. The full local equation closes exactly The scalar is independent of transverse angle, but retains the complete complex interference:  oxed{\sigma=2\operatorname{Re}(F_u^\dagger F_v+G_u^\dagger G_v).} 	ag{6} This expression follows from the complete field before any spatial integration. It is not a density average replacing its polarization. The Clifford derivative gives \Gamma_\perp\cdot
abla_\perp(WF)=\Gamma_r W\partial_rF, \qquad \Gamma_\perp\cdot
abla_\perp(\Gamma_r WG) =W\left(\partial_r+ rac{s-1}{r}ight)G. 	ag{7} Indeed, \sum_j\Gamma_j\partial_j\Gamma_r=(s-1)I/r. Together with \Gamma_zW=W and \Gamma_z\Gamma_rW=-\Gamma_rW, this yields  oxed{  egin{aligned} i\partial_tF_u&=-i\partial_zF_u -i\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-2}{r}ight)G_u+g\sigma F_v,\ i\partial_tG_u&=+i\partial_zG_u-i\partial_rF_u+g\sigma G_v,\ i\partial_tF_v&=+i\partial_zF_v +i\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-2}{r}ight)G_v+g\sigma F_u,\ i\partial_tG_v&=-i\partial_zG_v+i\partial_rF_v+g\sigma G_u. \end{aligned}} 	ag{8} Every source and derivative stays in (4). Thus any sufficiently regular solution of (8) reconstructs a solution of (1), with its full angular spinor factor. Both incoming patterns evolve. A common rotation of the physical coordinates, axis and spinor frame transports the same solution. Physical norm, source and conserved polarization Let S_{s-1}=2\pi^{s/2}/\Gamma(s/2) be the area of the unit transverse sphere. The physical volume element and positive norm are dV=S_{s-1}r^{s-1}dr\,dz, \qquad Q=\int dV\sum_{b=u,v}(F_b^\dagger F_b+G_b^\dagger G_b). 	ag{9} The energy is the full Dirac kinetic energy plus g\int\sigma^2dV/2. In particular, the radial derivative's adjoint in this norm is (\partial_r)^\dagger=-\partial_r- rac{s-1}{r}, 	ag{10} with the stated regularity and sufficient decay. Dropping the divergence term would change both the dynamics and norm. The reduced action is invariant under the same constant unitary transformation of all four polarization vectors. Consequently the entire Hermitian matrix  oxed{\mathcal P=\int dV\sum_{b=u,v} (F_bF_b^\dagger+G_bG_b^\dagger)} 	ag{11} is conserved. Its trace is Q. This is a symmetry of the specified angular family. It does not state that a local spatial overlap or either object's individual polarization matrix is fixed. Writing c=F_u^\dagger F_v+G_u^\dagger G_v gives the reciprocal law \dot Q_u=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2dV, \qquad \dot Q_v=-\dot Q_u. 	ag{12} A complete single-chirality field has \sigma=0 and evolves freely. Another exact control occurs when all F_u,G_u lie in a fixed polarization subspace orthogonal to the subspace containing F_v,G_v. Then c=0 pointwise and the free evolution preserves the mismatch. At P\ge2 this admits nonzero localized fields on both sides. It neither forces the occupied patterns into those subspaces nor makes five dimensions uniquely noninteracting. Spatially varying textures can span the whole polarization space. A finite regulator derived from the same local energy For numerical work, choose a radial scale w and retain N functions in each of the two radial families. Put x=r^2/w^2 and \alpha=s/2-1. Define  egin{aligned} \phi_n^0(r)&=A_n e^{-x/2}L_n^\alpha(x),& A_n^2&= rac{2n!}{S_{s-1}w^s\Gamma(n+s/2)},\ \phi_n^1(r)&=B_n\sqrt{x}e^{-x/2}L_n^{\alpha+1}(x),& B_n^2&= rac{2n!}{S_{s-1}w^s\Gamma(n+s/2+1)}. \end{aligned} 	ag{13} Each family is orthonormal in S_{s-1}r^{s-1}dr. This extends the independently normalized radial spatial Dirac basis. The exact derivative identity is \partial_r\phi_n^0=- rac1w \left[\sqrt{n+s/2}\,\phi_n^1+\sqrt n\,\phi_{n-1}^1ight]. 	ag{14} Let D_{mn} be that derivative matrix, with G rows and F columns. For axial Fourier momentum k, the upper chiral Galerkin operator is H_u(k)= egin{pmatrix}kI&iD^\dagger\-iD&-kI\end{pmatrix}, \qquad H_v(k)=-H_u(k). 	ag{15} It is self-adjoint in the canonical coefficient norm. The reverse derivative has a complementary radial component at the finite cutoff; convergence in N is required. The finite regulator is not an assertion that the continuum field occupies only these modes. If D=U\Lambda V^\dagger, transform F by V^\dagger and G by U^\dagger. Each free block has frequencies \pm\sqrt{k^2+\lambda_j^2}, supplying its exact propagator and positive-frequency projector. Applying that projector prepares an incoming field. The nonlinear evolution retains both free-frequency signs thereafter; neither is assigned an antiparticle interpretation. The local quartic has exact finite-basis radial quadrature. Write the polynomial parts of F,G as f,g, including \sqrt x in the G basis, so \sigma=e^{-x}\sigma_{m pol}. Changing variable to u=2x gives  oxed{ E_{m int}= rac g2 rac{S_{s-1}w^s}{2^{s/2+1}} \int dz\int_0^\infty du\,u^{s/2-1}e^{-u} \sigma_{m pol}(u/2,z)^2. } 	ag{16} Every quartic product contains an even number of G factors. The remaining integrand is polynomial in u, of degree at most 4N-2. A generalized Gauss–Laguerre rule of order 2N or higher therefore integrates (16) exactly in this retained radial space. The nonlinear coefficient source is its full complex derivative. The axis uses a finite Fourier interval as numerical storage for localized fields. For an even number N_z of retained complex modes, zero-padding to 2N_z before evaluating (16), followed by orthogonal projection of the source, integrates the quartic without Fourier aliasing. This preserves the finite action's axial translation symmetry and corresponding momentum. The interval and radial scale are numerical choices requiring convergence checks; they do not specify a physical compactification or the geometry of the observed three-dimensional space. Verification and limits axial_scalar_checks.py reconstructs the complete Cartesian spinor and differentiates it in every ordinary direction at D=3,5,7,9. It checks (6)–(8), physical rotation covariance, the normalized radial basis and its independent derivatives, full complex source variation, exact quartic quadrature, conserved norm, axial momentum and the matrix (11). Independent full matrix exponentials verify the free propagator and complete positive-frequency projection implemented by axial_scalar_packets.py. The diagnostic runs 192 checks, including full nonlinear evolution of complex spatial textures and a five-dimensional localized comparison with both zero and nonzero scalar sources. Spatial, radial and temporal refinement remain necessary for any particular collision result. The family provides transverse localization and several spatial polarizations with a tractable full-source equation. It supplies no bound-particle depth assignment or electric and weak channel embedding. With dimensionless Q and \hbar=c=1, [g]=\mathrm{length}^{D-1}. Choosing equal numerical g values at different D does not by itself define one physically normalized interaction across nested sectors. Changing compatibility of localized spatial packets uses this full angular family to compare both outgoing complex patterns after removing their known free evolution. A precisely specified future encounter has either increased or decreased scalar contact for different five-dimensional preparations under the same local dynamics. A separate spherical vector family works in both odd and even dimensions, including six and ten. Its full radial polarization vectors retain tangential current while scalar density is radial. It has one radial center and does not extend the present axial encounter ansatz to a general even-dimensional collision.

title: Geometric response of balanced normal populations
summary: Paired normal Dirac populations leave a stationary scalar source unchanged while supplying a common geometric response across target grades, including a finite kinetic gap and the complete probe self-interaction.
text: Summary: Paired normal Dirac populations leave a stationary scalar source unchanged while supplying a common geometric response across target grades, including a finite kinetic gap and the complete probe self-interaction. A stationary source need not measure a moving polarization The complementary Dirac reduction derives a stationary source from occupied normal modes of the same field. Its full positive-space occupation has an even frequency response. There is a different preparation in the same scalar interaction: add equal populations in the positive and negative normal branches, with a nonuniform distribution over coefficient directions. The added populations cancel in the stationary scalar current and energy. Their polarization nevertheless changes when the retained geometry moves. The resulting leading geometric response is independent of the retained mode degree for a specified common probe. The calculation below includes both Dirac signs, their positive canonical norms, a finite normal kinetic gap and the complete probe scalar self-interaction. The normal signs are not assigned an antiparticle interpretation. Their occupied columns must represent actual orthogonal modes of the same field; their geometry and populations have not been dynamically selected. Matrix directions describe coefficients over ordinary spatial sectors, rather than extra physical dimensions or compactification. Balanced populations at zero kinetic gap First take a positive Hermitian normal insertion R and Hamiltonian H=g\tau_z\otimes R, with g>0. Let U\ge0 commute with R. Choose the two normal densities \mathcal D_+=U+qI_r,\qquad \mathcal D_-=U, \qquad q>0. \tag{1} Each density can be realized by an explicit square-root matrix of occupied spectator columns. Their scalar current, energy and canonical norm are \begin{aligned} C_f&=\mathcal D_+-\mathcal D_-=qI_r,\\ E_f&=g\operatorname{Tr}(RC_f)=qg\operatorname{Tr}R,\\ Q_f&=\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal D_++\mathcal D_-) =qr+2\operatorname{Tr}U. \end{aligned} \tag{2} Thus U changes the positive canonical norm even though its stationary scalar energy cancels between the two normal signs. That norm is retained; it is not identified with electric charge or particle number. The mixed normal preparation is not a passive energy minimum. The complete density equations are i\dot{\mathcal D}_\pm=\pm g[R,\mathcal D_\pm]. \tag{3} For a perturbation \delta R\,e^{-i\Omega t}, work in a common eigenbasis of R and U, with eigenvalues r_i,u_i. Applying the density linearization to both signs gives \boxed{\delta(gC_f)_{ij} =\frac{2g^2\Omega(u_j-u_i)} {\Omega^2-g^2(r_i-r_j)^2}\,\delta R_{ij}.} \tag{4} The uniform excess q cancels from (4). The balanced response is odd in frequency and vanishes statically when the relevant spectral gaps are nonzero. For small frequency, \delta(gC_f)_{ij} =-\frac{2\Omega(u_j-u_i)}{(r_i-r_j)^2}\delta R_{ij} +O(\Omega^3). \tag{5} This is a geometric, phase-shifted response to motion. A single complex frequency amplitude need not itself be Hermitian; the physical real drive combines its positive and negative frequency components. Degenerate eigenspaces with unequal occupations need their own transport analysis. The actual common probe of the scalar master kernel Let the retained coherent current have degree N, norm J and ray z, and let the normal probe have fixed degree one. Set r=d+1. The exact scalar projection gives \begin{aligned} V_{N\to1}(C_N)&=a_N\left[J I+N\rho_{N,1}\right], &a_N&=\frac{d+1}{N+d+1},\\ C_N=JP_{z,N}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_N=a_NJI+B_NP_z, &B_N&=a_NJN. \end{aligned} \tag{6} Here \rho_{N,1} is the one-index contraction with trace J. The parallel ray and its orthogonal complement are independent of N. Their eigenvalue gap B_N depends on N. At depth six and J=1, B_{12}=84/19 and B_{34}=238/41. Choose the same probe preparation at the two target grades: U=u_\perp I+\Delta u P_z, \qquad \Delta u=u_\parallel-u_\perp, \qquad u_\parallel,u_\perp\ge0. \tag{7} Near z=e_0, use the normalized local ray z=(1,x+iy,0,\ldots)/\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2}. On its active two-direction plane, the actual external current vertices are \partial_xR_N=B_N\sigma_x,\qquad \partial_yR_N=B_N\sigma_y. \tag{8} Insert both vertices in (4). The response of the x energy gradient to a moving y is \boxed{ \lim_{\Omega\to0} \frac{\operatorname{Tr} [(\partial_xR_N)\,\delta(gC_f)[\partial_yR_N]]} {-i\Omega}=4\Delta u.} \tag{9} The two vertex factors B_N^2 cancel the spectral denominator. No division by the target mass and no inverse reconstruction of the raw current has been introduced. This is a common leading geometric response for the specified common population. Its finite-frequency corrections still depend on the normal gaps. Equivalently, the balanced population contributes the Berry one-form 2\Delta u\,i z^\dagger dz. Its curvature on this local plane is -4\Delta u\,dx\wedge dy. The induced energy gradient is minus the curvature acting on the ray velocity, giving the sign in (9). The uniform population contributes the trace connection of a complete coefficient frame, which has zero curvature in this local calculation. The same algebra works on a chosen two-direction plane at other physical depths. Consequently it does not by itself explain weak depth-five coupling. A physical rule for which normal patterns occur and how their sectors engage remains necessary. Ordinary spatial rotation is a more specific test An arbitrary unitary change of the d+1 coefficient entries is broader than a rotation of physical space. In W=\mathbf1\oplus(T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C), an ordinary spatial rotation acts on the tangent entries and leaves the homogenizing scalar entry fixed. Let A,B be two real antisymmetric tangent rotation generators, extended by zero on that scalar entry. Then \partial_AR_N=B_N[A,P_z],\qquad \boxed{\mathcal G(A,B)=4\Delta u\, \operatorname{Im}\langle Az,Bz\rangle.} \tag{9a} Equation (9a) is the actual spatial-rotation instance of (9). It also survives the finite-gap self-consistency below. The result concerns the coefficient-current component of the full response; spinor and spatial kinetic contributions must accompany it in a physical moving field. For a concrete check, take z=(1,\sqrt2,i,0,\ldots)/2, where the first entry is the scalar slot. Let A rotate tangent directions one and three, and B rotate tangent directions two and three. Then \mathcal G=\sqrt2\Delta u. Replacing i by 1 leaves the norm and occupied degrees unchanged but makes this geometric component zero. Independent complete normal-response calculations verify both controls at the assigned degrees and each stated finite kinetic gap. This zero follows from the actual complex polarization, rather than an inserted neutral projector. It does not make an entire particle noninteracting: other response directions and the scalar density channel remain present. Nor does the calculation assign the real preparation to one physical depth. A specified uniform complex-ray distribution supplies a useful depth comparison. With r=d+1, its normalized squared amplitudes obey \langle |z_1|^2|z_2|^2\rangle=1/[r(r+1)], and uniform relative phase gives \langle\sin^2\varphi\rangle=1/2. For the two rotations above, \langle\mathcal G\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\mathcal G^2\rangle= \frac{8(\Delta u)^2}{(d+1)(d+2)}. \tag{9b} Direct amplitude and phase quadrature verifies these moments. The depth-five variance is 4/3 of the depth-six variance at common \Delta u, so this uniform preparation provides no neutrino suppression. That conditional comparison identifies the missing selection of physical polarization; it does not exclude other depth-dependent spatial patterns. The probe's own scalar term The complete degree-one self-projection is V_{1\to1}(C)=b\left[\operatorname{Tr}C\,I+C\right], \qquad b=\frac{d+1}{d+2}. \tag{10} At the zero-gap stationary preparation C=qI, this adds an identity insertion. A variation adds b\delta C in each off-diagonal direction. The resulting self-consistent response is \delta(gC)_{ij}= \frac{2g^2\Omega(u_j-u_i)} {\Omega^2-g^2(r_i-r_j)^2-2gb\Omega(u_j-u_i)} \delta(R_N)_{ij}. \tag{11} Its finite-frequency form differs from (4), but the leading term (5) and common external coefficient (9) survive. Thus the cancellation does not depend on omitting the probe self-interaction. A finite normal kinetic gap preserves the balanced cancellation For H(R)=\epsilon\tau_x\otimes I+g\tau_z\otimes R, let P_+(R) be the complete positive projector. The stationary density is now \boxed{\mathcal D=I_2\otimes U+qP_+(R)}, \qquad [R,U]=0, \qquad E_i=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r_i^2}. \tag{12} In each coefficient eigendirection its positive and negative occupations are u_i+q and u_i. The contribution I_2\otimes U commutes with the full Hamiltonian and has zero scalar current and zero energy, including the normal kinetic term. Its norm remains 2\operatorname{Tr}U. The stationary scalar eigenvalues therefore are c_i=q\frac{gr_i}{E_i}, \tag{13} independent of the balanced occupation. The unbalanced q population has the even susceptibility \chi^q_{ij} derived in the linked mass-source note. The balanced contribution is \begin{aligned} \chi^U_{ij}(\Omega)&=2g^2\Omega(u_j-u_i) \left[\frac{1-T_{ij}}{\Omega^2-(E_i-E_j)^2} +\frac{T_{ij}}{\Omega^2-(E_i+E_j)^2}\right],\\ T_{ij}&=\frac{E_iE_j+\epsilon^2-g^2r_ir_j}{2E_iE_j}. \end{aligned} \tag{14} The first fraction comes from transitions within the same Dirac sign, and the second from transitions between the signs. Both are required. For distinct positive r_i,r_j, elementary substitution gives \boxed{g^2\left[ \frac{1-T_{ij}}{(E_i-E_j)^2} +\frac{T_{ij}}{(E_i+E_j)^2}\right] =\frac1{(r_i-r_j)^2}.} \tag{15} Thus the leading balanced geometric response is exactly (5), even at finite \epsilon. The formula presumes an adiabatic spectral separation; it must not be extended through unresolved degeneracies by assigning values to zero divided by zero. Finite-gap scalar self-consistency For the coherent target (6), the complete stationary insertion and normal scalar current share the same two eigenspaces. Their eigenvalues satisfy r_i=r_i^{\rm ext}+b\left[\sum_jc_j+c_i\right], \qquad c_i=q\frac{gr_i}{\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r_i^2}}, \tag{16} where r_\parallel^{\rm ext}=a_NJ+B_N and r_\perp^{\rm ext}=a_NJ. The perpendicular value occurs d times. All scalar self-terms are retained, including the trace. For positive external values, monotone iteration from r^{\rm ext} is bounded above by r^{\rm ext}+bq(r+1) in each entry, so a positive solution exists. It is unique in the positive cone: the map is monotone, and strict sublinearity under a common factor greater than one follows from the positive external term and concavity of r/\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r^2} for r>0. If two positive fixed points differed, compare them at the largest component ratio; strict sublinearity would contradict the component attaining that ratio. Let \Delta r=r_\parallel-r_\perp and \Delta c=c_\parallel-c_\perp. The gap equation and static off-diagonal susceptibility obey \Delta r=B_N+b\Delta c, \qquad \chi^q_{\parallel\perp}(0)=g\frac{\Delta c}{\Delta r}, \qquad 1-\frac bg\chi^q_{\parallel\perp}(0)=\frac{B_N}{\Delta r}. \tag{17} For an off-diagonal external drive, put \chi=\chi^q+\chi^U. Full self-consistency replaces it by \chi_{\rm full}=\frac{\chi}{1-b\chi/g}. \tag{18} Its leading odd part is \chi^U/(1-b\chi^q(0)/g)^2. Equation (15) supplies 1/(\Delta r)^2; equation (17) supplies the factor (\Delta r/B_N)^2. The two external vertices again supply B_N^2. Hence (9) survives the finite-gap complete scalar square. Diagonal responses additionally couple through the trace term in (16); the executable full Liouvillian retains that coupling as well. At the assigned depth-five, depth-six and depth-ten degrees, independent finite matrix calculations with \epsilon=0.1,1,5 reproduce the same coefficient 4\Delta u=2.4 for the declared \Delta u=0.6. No physical coupling value or normal kinetic gap is fitted here. Reciprocal motion under the same complete interaction A coherent target and a degree-one normal probe form an invariant zero-spatial-kinetic control. Keep the entire probe rank r=d+1, its complex occupied matrices Y_+,Y_- and the target's unit ray z. Define \mathcal D_\pm=Y_\pm Y_\pm^\dagger, C=\mathcal D_+-\mathcal D_- and W=\mathcal D_++\mathcal D_-. The varying scalar energy is E=g a_NJ\left[\operatorname{Tr}C+N z^\dagger Cz\right] +\frac{gb}{2}\left[(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2+\operatorname{Tr}C^2\right]. \tag{19} The coherent target's own term gJ^2\lambda_N/2 is constant on this fixed-norm ray manifold, but its full scalar phase is retained when reconstructing the target field. Its induced ray kinetic coefficient is JN, obtained from the canonical field \sqrt J\,z^{\otimes N}. The resulting equations are \begin{aligned} i\dot z&=g a_N C z,\\ i\dot Y_\pm&=\pm g L Y_\pm,\\ L&=\left[a_NJ+b\operatorname{Tr}C\right]I+B_NP_z+bC. \end{aligned} \tag{20} The target's additional scalar phase rate is g a_N\operatorname{Tr}C+gJ\lambda_N. The scalar identity terms in L remain in the full complex-field evolution; they are not removed merely because they commute with densities. Direct variation of the complete symmetric tensor verifies that the degree-one insertion maps this coherent ray manifold into its tangent. The source contains all N index insertions, plus that scalar phase. Both objects respond. In particular, \boxed{JN P_z+W\ \text{is conserved}},\qquad Y_\pm^\dagger Y_\pm\ \text{are conserved},\qquad \|z\|=1. \tag{21} The first is the common coefficient-rotation moment. It follows directly by adding the projector equation to i\dot W=g[L,C]. The full energy is conserved as well. If initially C=qI but the balanced population U is misaligned with P_z, the target initially has only a scalar phase. Its subsequent interaction is not zero: \dot C(0)=-2igB_N[P_z,U]. \tag{22} The scalar current becomes anisotropic and then moves the target ray. This is an explicit reciprocal mechanism for changing compatibility, derived from the same interaction instead of an imposed alignment rule. For an aligned stationary preparation, the active orientation block at fixed total rotation moment has signed frequencies \boxed{\Omega_\pm=-gb\Delta u \pm g\sqrt{b^2(\Delta u)^2+a_N^2JN(JN+2\Delta u)}.} \tag{23} One obtains them by linearizing the full density equations for (P_z,C,W) and using JN\delta P_z+\delta W=0. They are real for the stated \Delta u>0. This checks the local orientation block; it is not a theorem of complete spatial stability. A nonlinear control at depth six uses the same J=1, g=0.7, q=0.4, u_\perp=0.2, \Delta u=0.6 and initial complex misalignment at N=12,34. Initially both normal polarizations have target overlap 0.671823. During 0\le t\le60, the positive population's overlap decreases to 0.642635 and 0.640150, respectively; the negative population's overlap increases to 0.743467 and 0.718852. Their subsequent motion oscillates. There is no automatic common alignment or imposed dissipation. Independent time refinement changes the full complex fields by less than 4.1\times10^{-7}. In the refined runs, energy drift is below 3.5\times10^{-10}, each occupied Gram drift below 9.4\times10^{-11}, and total rotation-moment drift below 1.4\times10^{-10}. These trajectories retain both polarizations and their phases. They remain finite mode controls with zero spatial kinetic operator, rather than localized encounters between identified particles. What this establishes and what still needs selection This supplies a common geometric response across distinct retained grades under the actual scalar projection, with canonical normalization and self-consistent normal dynamics. A stationary scalar excess can still carry the complementary mode count described in the linked mass-source note. The geometric cancellation therefore permits different stationary sources and a shared moving-polarization response within one interaction. It is only one response component. Scalar density vertices and the full interaction energy retain their occupation and band dependence. No electric current, measured charge, encounter rate or neutrino suppression has been identified by equation (9). The chosen populations are additional physical preparation data; common \Delta u is not derived by the scalar kernel. At zero gap their occupied density spectra are conserved by (3), so this closed mode model cannot dynamically choose those spectra from arbitrary initial data. Physical spatial geometry must supply the normal modes, their preparation and their overlap with other nested sectors. The sectors are nested; one particle is not a constituent inside another. The full spatial Dirac residual and finite-norm binding must be checked when passing from this mode control to particle fields. The positive-current localization condition states one relevant flat-space restriction. Neither a physical mass operator nor a complete coupling law is claimed here. Verification The reciprocal stability calculation now retains the complete finite-gap normal density and target ray. Its exact angular quartic and full nonlinear fields distinguish a bounded and a growing preparation at equal total canonical norm and stationary scalar source. The geometric response alone does not select the population's dynamical viability. balanced_dirac_response_checks.py checks independent two-sign Liouvillians, the exact master projection, coherent tensor tangents, frame covariance, full action gradients, geometric vertices and the complete orientation spectrum. An additional exact rotating-ray control checks both normal density equations directly. The finite laws are in balanced_dirac_response.py. gapped_balanced_response_checks.py checks both transition families, finite-gap cancellation, the positive scalar fixed point and complete matrix self-feedback; its implementation is gapped_balanced_response.py. balanced_dirac_reciprocal_flow.py stores the entire complex reciprocal trajectories, and dirac_response_trajectory_checks.py independently verifies refinement, energy and the common rotation moment.

title: Stability of reciprocal normal polarization
summary: The complete finite-gap normal density and reciprocal coherent target have an exact quartic orientation dispersion, with bounded and growing nonlinear controls at equal canonical norm and stationary scalar source.
text: Summary: The complete finite-gap normal density and reciprocal coherent target have an exact quartic orientation dispersion, with bounded and growing nonlinear controls at equal canonical norm and stationary scalar source. Test whether the response preparation persists The balanced normal response has a common leading geometric coefficient across retained grades under specified canonical populations. A stationary preparation with that response need not persist when disturbed. This calculation retains the entire normal density, both normal Dirac signs and the reciprocal target ray to test the finite mode dynamics. The normal kinetic gap and occupied spectator modes remain conditional reductions of the same field. The target has zero spatial kinetic operator in this control. Its coherent tensor ray is an invariant mode manifold of the degree-one interaction, not an established localized particle. No new physical dimensions, compactification or interaction particle is introduced. Use the definitions of the linked response note: physical depth d, coefficient rank r=d+1, target degree N, target canonical norm J, and common coefficients a=\frac{d+1}{N+d+1},\qquad b=\frac{d+1}{d+2},\qquad B=aJN. \tag{1} Let P=zz^\dagger be the target ray projector and let Y be the complete 2r-row normal field, including both signs and its explicit occupied spectator columns. Its density and scalar current are \mathcal D=YY^\dagger,\qquad C=\mathcal D_{++}-\mathcal D_{--},\qquad L=(aJ+b\operatorname{Tr}C)I+BP+bC. \tag{2} The exact canonical field equations are i\dot z=gaCz,\qquad i\dot Y=H(L)Y,\qquad H(L)=\epsilon\tau_x\otimes I+g\tau_z\otimes L. \tag{3} The induced target ray kinetic coefficient is JN. The full normal Gram matrix Y^\dagger Y and all positive canonical norms are retained. The target's additional scalar phase includes its own self-insertion; it does not change the projector dynamics at fixed J. The complete reciprocal linearization At a stationary coherent target, L, C and the population matrix U have parallel and perpendicular eigenspaces. The positive scalar fixed point of the response note gives the insertion eigenvalues r_0,r_1, scalar eigenvalues c_0,c_1, and normal density \mathcal D_0=I_2\otimes U+qP_+(L),\qquad U=u_\perp I+\Delta u P, \qquad u_\perp\ge0,\quad u_\perp+\Delta u\ge0. \tag{4} Here r_1,c_1 each have multiplicity d. Both populations are nonnegative even when \Delta u<0. The balanced part has zero scalar current and zero normal energy but a positive canonical norm. Write \delta C=\delta\mathcal D_{++}-\delta\mathcal D_{--}. Linearizing (3) gives the complete finite density system \begin{aligned} i\delta\dot P&=ga\left([C,\delta P]+[\delta C,P]\right),\\ i\delta\dot{\mathcal D}&=[H,\delta\mathcal D] +[\delta H,\mathcal D_0],\\ \delta H&=g\tau_z\otimes \left[B\delta P+b(\operatorname{Tr}\delta C\,I+\delta C)\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{5} The common coefficient-rotation moment is conserved: JN P+\operatorname{Tr}_{\rm normal}\mathcal D \quad\text{is constant}. \tag{6} Indeed, the \epsilon\tau_x term commutes with coefficient rotations. The cross commutators cancel between the target and normal parts of (6), and the scalar self-commutators cancel among themselves. Equation (5) obeys the linearized version for arbitrary complete matrix variations. At depth six the diagnostic retains all 49 complexified target matrix entries and all 196 normal entries. Hermitian variations give the physical density perturbations; the coherent target tangent and fixed normal-population orbit are invariant subspaces. A growing mode below is explicitly realized by canonical fields on those physical subspaces. No instability is inferred solely from an inadmissible density direction. An independent five-variable orientation block Choose one perpendicular coefficient direction. Let p=\delta P_{01} and let D be the full two-by-two normal-spin block \delta\mathcal D_{s0,t1}. Define \begin{aligned} H_i&=\epsilon\tau_x+gr_i\tau_z,& E_i&=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r_i^2},\\ D_i&=u_iI_2+\frac q2\left(I_2+\frac{H_i}{E_i}\right),& \delta c&=\operatorname{Tr}(\tau_zD),\quad \ell=Bp+b\delta c. \end{aligned} \tag{7} With the convention e^{-i\Omega t}, the exact block is \boxed{\begin{aligned} \Omega p&=ga\left[(c_0-c_1)p-\delta c\right],\\ \Omega D&=H_0D-DH_1+g\ell(\tau_zD_1-D_0\tau_z). \end{aligned}} \tag{8} This has five complex variables and retains every normal-spin transition. Independent matrix embedding checks that it is exactly a block of (5). The common rotation moment supplies its zero-frequency mode. The remaining four frequencies are roots of an explicit real quartic. Put \begin{aligned} \Delta r&=r_0-r_1,& R&=r_0+r_1,& \Delta c&=c_0-c_1,& S&=E_0^{-1}+E_1^{-1},\\ Z(\Omega)&=\frac12\left(\Delta c-\frac\Omega{ga}\right),& \Lambda(\Omega)&=\Delta r-\frac{b\Omega}{ga},& F(\Omega)&=\Omega^2-g^2R^2. \end{aligned} \tag{9} Then the dispersion equation is \boxed{\begin{aligned} 0={}&\Omega\left[F(\Omega)-4\epsilon^2\right]Z(\Omega)\\ &+g\left[\Delta u F(\Omega)+q\epsilon^2S\Omega\right] \Lambda(\Omega) +\frac{g\Delta r JN}{2}F(\Omega). \end{aligned}} \tag{10} For a derivation, expand D=A I+X\tau_x+Y\tau_y+Z\tau_z. The conserved moment at nonzero frequency gives A=-JNp/2; the target equation gives Z=Z(\Omega)p. The fixed-point gap relation \Delta r=B+b\Delta c gives \ell=\Lambda(\Omega)p. Eliminating X and Y from the remaining normal equations yields (10). The diagnostic compares its coefficients with the characteristic polynomial of the independent block (8). At exceptional degeneracies the matrix equation, rather than a cancelled fraction, defines the complete spectrum. The zero-gap restriction and the finite-gap difference At zero kinetic gap, \Delta c=0 and \Delta r=B. Equation (10) factors into the two normal frequencies \pm gR and the two reciprocal orientation frequencies \Omega_\pm=-gb\Delta u \pm g\sqrt{b^2(\Delta u)^2+a^2JN(JN+2\Delta u)}. \tag{11} The radical is nonnegative for every real \Delta u when N\ge1: \begin{aligned} &b^2(\Delta u)^2+a^2JN(JN+2\Delta u)\\ &\quad=b^2\left(\Delta u+\frac{a^2JN}{b^2}\right)^2 +a^2(JN)^2\left(1-\frac{a^2}{b^2}\right)\ge0, \end{aligned} \tag{12} because a\le b. The full scalar self-term is essential to this completed-square statement. Real frequencies still allow polynomial growth at a defective degenerate root; this is an exclusion of exponential orientation growth in the stated zero-gap block. Finite \epsilon couples the orientation motion to the other normal transitions. The full quartic can then have nonreal roots. At d=6, N=12, J=1, g=0.7, q=0.4, \epsilon=20 and \Delta u=-20, the growing frequency is \boxed{\Omega=0.1129776272+0.4392350957\,i.} \tag{13} It occurs in the complete density system (5), not just the reduced polynomial. Taking u_\perp=20.2 gives u_\parallel=0.2, so all occupied canonical eigenvalues are strictly positive. The specified positive-imbalance controls \Delta u=0.6 at N=12,34 and gaps 0.1,1,5,20 have no exponentially growing eigenfrequency in the complete finite linearization. This is a tested set, not a proof for all positive imbalances or all spatial fields. Nonlinear comparison at equal norm and scalar source Two controls use the same d=6, N=12, J=1, g=0.7, q=0.4 and \epsilon=20. Fix \operatorname{Tr}U=121.4 and compare \Delta u=0.6 with \Delta u=-20, setting u_\perp=(121.4-\Delta u)/7 in each case. Both have normal canonical norm Q_f=245.6, the same stationary scalar current and the same stationary normal energy. Only the balanced population distribution differs. These are declared mode controls; none of these quantities is fitted to a particle measurement. An eigenmode of (8) is embedded into the complete density matrices. To make a valid nonlinear initial field, the perturbation is implemented by unitary rotations of the target ray and the occupied normal columns. Their exact norms and the entire normal Gram matrix are therefore unchanged at initialization. All complex fields then evolve by (3), including their fast phases and the reciprocal change of the target. For initial density amplitude 10^{-5} and 0\le t\le15, the reversed population amplifies by approximately 726.709, matching \exp(15\times0.4392350957). The full nonlinear density remains close to the growing linear mode over that interval. A corresponding oscillatory mode of the positive-imbalance control stays bounded. Independent time refinement checks the complete complex fields, energy, occupied Gram matrix and common rotation moment. The exact source programs and raw trajectories accompany the reports. Conservation of those quantities does not by itself imply stability; the growing solution conserves them while its polarization changes. The two complete field refinements differ by less than 8.8\times10^{-9}. The refined growing rate is 0.439235095730, compared with the linear value 0.439235095738. Energy drift is below 7.7\times10^{-11}, occupied Gram drift below 8.8\times10^{-11} and rotation-moment drift below 1.3\times10^{-10} in these controls. Consequence for physical selection The stationary scalar source and a canonical norm do not uniquely select the polarization preparation, even within this one action. Reciprocal finite-gap dynamics distinguishes some preparations that those stationary quantities cannot distinguish. It supplies a concrete stability constraint on the proposed common geometric response. It does not yet select a unique population, identify the observed coupling currents or produce a spatial particle. The mass-source calculation retains the separate occupation, band matching and total-energy questions. Physical spatial geometry and full Dirac residuals must be supplied before these finite controls can establish particle stability or dimensionality. Verification gapped_reciprocal_normal_checks.py compares the complete reciprocal density generator, independent angular block, eliminated quartic, canonical action variations, conserved moments and zero-gap completed square. With the two trajectory reports supplied, it also checks complete-field refinement and nonlinear amplification. The exact finite equations are implemented in gapped_reciprocal_normal.py. gapped_reciprocal_normal_flow.py stores the complete canonical fields for the equal-norm comparison.

title: Nonlinear response of the bending modes
summary: The same surface curvature energy that gives simplex frequencies has nonzero canonical mode couplings, an exact quadratic resonance and a scale response that must enter any nonlinear particle fixed point.
text: Summary: The same surface curvature energy that gives simplex frequencies has nonzero canonical mode couplings, an exact quadratic resonance and a scale response that must enter any nonlinear particle fixed point. A frequency calculation also needs its interaction The bending construction gives the exact frequency sequence under a declared geometric action. Its nonlinear curvature energy supplies a way to test interactions without inserting a separate coupling matrix for each pair of modes. This note uses the four-dimensional round surface in ordinary six-dimensional space. It is a conditional feature of a field, not a replacement of that physical space. The calculation retains both normal directions. Individual zonal harmonics are specified spatial polarizations within the complete harmonic multiplets; they do not exhaust possible particle patterns. The mass-frequency targets are unchanged. The small displacements below differentiate the geometry and test its nonlinear response. They are not variables used to fit particle masses. Physical magnitude may be needed in a full nonlinear fixed-point solution, after specifying its frequency. Canonical coordinates on the actual graph Let \theta\in S^m be a unit radial vector and describe the surface by \begin{aligned} F(\theta)&=(r(\theta)\theta,z(\theta)),\\ F(\theta)&\in\mathbb R^{m+1}\times\mathbb R. \end{aligned} \tag{1} The last coordinate specifies the chosen axis of this round comparison. Rotating the complete geometry changes that axis; it is not a distinguished spatial dimension of a physical sector. The geometric symplectic form on this chart is exactly \Omega=\Gamma\int_{S^m}r^m\,\delta r\wedge\delta z\,d\Omega_m. \tag{2} To obtain (2), contract the containing volume form with the two variations and the m graph tangents. Terms involving tangential derivatives of r or z repeat one of the variation directions and drop out of the determinant. Each remaining spherical tangent contributes one factor r. Consequently a canonical radial graph coordinate is q=\frac{r^{m+1}-R^{m+1}}{(m+1)R^m},\qquad v=z, \qquad \Omega=\Gamma R^m\int\delta q\wedge\delta v\,d\Omega_m. \tag{3} Linear radial displacement equals q at r=R, but their higher variations differ. That difference matters for nonlinear coupling. This is canonical normalization, obtained from the kinetic form of the same action. For m=4 and R=1, r=(1+5q)^{1/5}=1+q-2q^2+6q^3+O(q^4). \tag{4} The following numerical coefficients use R=\Gamma=\kappa=1 and real harmonics Y_\ell normalized by \int_{S^4}Y_\ell^2dA=1. The associated mode coordinates are q_\ell,v_\ell. Their quadratic Hamiltonian is H_2=\frac12\sum_\ell\omega_\ell(q_\ell^2+v_\ell^2),\qquad \omega_\ell=\frac14(\ell-1)\ell\cdots(\ell+4). \tag{5} Differentiate the curvature of the spatial surface There is an analytic expression for the full cubic interaction. Let A,B be geodesic normal coordinates about the equator in S^{m+2}, with B pointing toward the stereographic pole. Reversing both normal coordinates is an ambient isometry fixing the equator. Consequently the conformal bending energy has no odd terms in (A,B) at that equator. Stereographic projection to the Euclidean graph gives, to second order, r=1+B+\frac12(B^2-A^2)+O(3),\qquad z=A+AB+O(3). \tag{5a} Combining this with the exact canonical coordinate (3) gives B=q-\frac{m+1}{2}q^2+\frac12v^2+O(3),\qquad A=v-qv+O(3). \tag{5b} Let K=\mathcal J/m be the frequency operator in the common unit normalization. The spherical quadratic energy is \tfrac12\int(AKA+BKB)dA. Its cubic contribution after (5b) is exactly \boxed{ H_3=-\frac{m+1}{2}\int q^2Kq\,dA -\int qvKv\,dA+\frac12\int v^2Kq\,dA. } \tag{5c} There is no omitted spherical cubic term, by the normal-reflection symmetry. If G_{abc}=\int Y_aY_bY_c\,dA, (5c) therefore gives \begin{aligned} \partial_{q_a}\partial_{q_b}\partial_{q_c}H &=-(m+1)(\omega_a+\omega_b+\omega_c)G_{abc},\\ \partial_{q_a}\partial_{v_b}\partial_{v_c}H &=(\omega_a-\omega_b-\omega_c)G_{abc}. \end{aligned} \tag{5d} These identities apply to the full real harmonic multiplets, including mixed spatial polarizations. The following direct curvature calculation provides an independent check at the specified zonal modes. For zonal modes, use a surface of revolution F(\vartheta,\eta) =(a(\vartheta)\eta,b(\vartheta),z(\vartheta)),\qquad \eta\in S^3,\quad a=r\sin\vartheta,\quad b=r\cos\vartheta. \tag{6} Write C=(a,b,z), s=|C'|, T=C'/s and e_a=(1,0,0). The two principal curvature vectors, with the spherical one repeated three times, are K_\vartheta=\frac{T'}s,\qquad K_\eta=\frac{-e_a+(e_a\cdot T)T}{a},\qquad H=K_\vartheta+3K_\eta. \tag{7} The required contractions are \begin{aligned} |\nabla^\perp H|^2&= \frac{|H'|^2-(H'\cdot T)^2}{s^2},\\ |A_H|^2&=(H\cdot K_\vartheta)^2+3(H\cdot K_\eta)^2,\\ dA&=s a^3\,d\vartheta\,dA_{S^3}. \end{aligned} \tag{8} The angular derivatives of H are tangent to the surface and have no normal component. Equations (7)–(8), inserted into the explicit curvature energy, differentiate the actual spatial geometry. No spectral polynomial is substituted for the nonlinear energy. The implementation uses two independent methods: symmetric variations of the nonlinear integral, and third-order Taylor arithmetic applied to its curvature expressions. Angular quadrature is independently refined. An exact resonance has a nonzero interaction The simplex recurrence implies \frac{S(n+1,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac{n+d}{n}. \tag{9} At n=d, the ratio is exactly two. For the six-dimensional comparison, the corresponding surface degrees are \ell_a=7 and \ell_c=8: \omega_a=83\,160,\qquad\omega_c=166\,320=2\omega_a. \tag{10} These are available modes of the trial operator, not new particle assignments. Their real zonal harmonics have nonzero spatial overlap G=\int_{S^4}Y_7^2Y_8dA=0.368980006548\ldots. \tag{11} The diagnostic evaluates this integral exactly using Gegenbauer polynomials and the measure 2\pi^2(1-t^2)dt, then compares the value with the curvature quadrature. Define three canonical third derivatives of the same energy: C_q=\partial_{q_a}^2\partial_{q_c}H,\qquad C_v=\partial_{v_a}^2\partial_{q_c}H,\qquad C_\times=\partial_{q_a}\partial_{v_a}\partial_{v_c}H. \tag{12} At the round surface their analytic and directly computed values agree: Third derivative Value in the stated normalization C_q -613687.546891 C_v 0 exactly by (5d) and the resonance condition C_\times -61368.7546891 The positive-frequency equation for w_c=q_c-iv_c contains a doubled frequency source from the rotating a mode. Its coefficient is F_{caa}=\frac{C_q-C_v+2C_\times}{8} =-92053.1320336\ldots. \tag{13} In fact, (5d) and \omega_c=2\omega_a give the general exact expression F_{caa}=-(m+2)\omega_aG_{aac}/2=-d\omega_aG_{aac}/2. Thus the temporal resonance in (10) is enabled by a nonzero spatial interaction. An eigenvalue coincidence alone would not establish that. Retain the reciprocal response In the canonical complex coordinates a=(q_a-iv_a)/\sqrt2 and c=(q_c-iv_c)/\sqrt2, the resonant cubic Hamiltonian is H_{\mathrm{res}}=\omega_a|a|^2+\omega_c|c|^2 +g(c^*a^2+c(a^*)^2),\qquad g=\sqrt2 F_{caa}. \tag{14} Both interaction directions come from (14). After removing the two linear phases, its complete complex equations are i\dot A=2gA^*C,\qquad i\dot C=gA^2. \tag{15} They conserve |A|^2+2|C|^2 and the interaction energy. With a small test displacement A(0)=a_0 real and C(0)=0, the exact solution is A(t)=a_0\operatorname{sech}(\sqrt2ga_0t),\qquad C(t)=-\frac{ia_0}{\sqrt2}\tanh(\sqrt2ga_0t). \tag{16} Numerical integration checks both complex modes and their conserved quantities against (16). The initial displacement tests energy transfer; it does not set either mass-frequency in (10). This is the cubic resonant truncation. It has not been established as a controlled approximation to the complete nonlinear spatial equation over arbitrary times. Complementary harmonics, the slow background response and higher-order frequency shifts still require their own equations. The assigned modes also force the background At each of the unchanged assignments (d,n)=(6,13),(6,35),(10,23), there is no available degree with exactly twice its frequency inside the angular product range 2\le\ell_c\le2(n+1). This checks one specified quadratic self-resonance. It neither proves nonlinear stability nor selects these particle indices uniquely. There is a separate zero-frequency response. Let Y_0=1/\sqrt{A_m} be the normalized constant harmonic. Scale invariance fixes its third derivatives without fitting a coefficient: \begin{aligned} \partial_{q_0}\partial_{q_\ell}^2H &=-\frac{(2m+2)\omega_\ell}{\sqrt{A_m}},\\ \partial_{q_0}\partial_{v_\ell}^2H &=-\frac{2\omega_\ell}{\sqrt{A_m}},\\ \partial_{v_0}\partial_{q_\ell}\partial_{v_\ell}H&=0. \end{aligned} \tag{17} Here the common units are again R=\Gamma=\kappa=1. For the derivation, move the constant-radius background to r. At fixed physical normal displacement, its quadratic bending energy scales as r^{-2}. The canonical radial displacement in (3) additionally satisfies \delta r=r^{-m}\delta q. Thus the radial quadratic coefficient scales as r^{-2m-2} and the axial coefficient as r^{-2}. Differentiating with respect to q_0, for which \delta r=\delta q_0/\sqrt{A_m} at unit radius, gives the first two identities. Independence of the energy under uniform axial translation gives the third. Direct third variations verify (17) at surface degrees 7,14,36. For a circular test motion q_\ell=b\cos\omega_\ell t, v_\ell=b\sin\omega_\ell t, the constant part of its force is \left\langle\partial_{q_0}H_3\right\rangle =-\frac{(m+2)\omega_\ell b^2}{2\sqrt{A_m}}. \tag{18} Since q_0 and v_0 are conjugate, this term produces axial motion of the background. A circular linear mode on an unchanged stationary round surface therefore omits a nonlinear equation. It must be included when finding a complete oscillating fixed point or its moving-frame version. Equation (18) is a response to an oscillation of specified frequency; it is not a second prescription for that mode's mass. Consequences for a shared coupling response The same action fixes both the simplex spectrum and the geometric coupling. At a common radius and common canonical normalization, the scale vertices in (17) are proportional to \omega_\ell. Their muon-to-electron ratio is therefore the simplex ratio, approximately 206.7647, in this particular channel. The fractional frequency response to a radius change is common, \delta\omega/\omega=-d\,\delta R/R, but the absolute canonical vertex is not. This reproduces the distinction emphasized in the common-cavity coupling calculation. A universal fractional shift is insufficient to establish the required grouping of physical particle couplings by depth. These computations identify a concrete nonlinear response of a natural geometric frequency operator. Its realization in the master field, the particle fixed points, their complete inertial response and the physical pair-interaction channel remain open. The time law also retains the finite-propagation limitation stated in the bending construction. Verification bending_surface_checks.py checks the canonical curvature derivatives, their independent finite variations and quadrature refinements, the exact Gaunt integral, the unchanged particle-index resonance test and the scale identities. bending_curvature_jets.py provides the direct Taylor differentiation of the actual spatial energy. The full reciprocal complex trajectories and their exact controls are preserved with the numerical report.

title: Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents
summary: Opposite-frequency components of the same spatial Dirac field give exact current oscillations at twice the bound frequency, with a common scalar source and explicit normalization, size and response constraints.
text: Summary: Opposite-frequency components of the same spatial Dirac field give exact current oscillations at twice the bound frequency, with a common scalar source and explicit normalization, size and response constraints. Construct a spatial clock from the bound field itself A stationary field's common phase cancels from its bilinear observables. Nevertheless, the scalar Dirac model admits exact fields whose spatial currents oscillate at a frequency fixed by their bound profile. This provides a concrete construction to examine when asking whether slow particle oscillations can weaken coupling. Use ordinary bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and one existing normal coordinate y in a containing sector of the same nested physical manifold. The two components below belong to one field. No interaction particle or extra internal spatial direction is introduced. The specific source model used here is local in time and y, with a centered spatial moment over the bound coordinates: \begin{gathered} \sigma=\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi,\qquad Q_\sigma=\int\sigma\,dx\ne0,\qquad X_\sigma=Q_\sigma^{-1}\int x\sigma\,dx,\\ M_\sigma=\int(x-X_\sigma)(x-X_\sigma)^T\sigma\,dx,\\ i\partial_t\Psi=\left[-i\alpha_i\partial_i-i\alpha_y\partial_y +\beta\left(m_0+g_0(x-X_\sigma)^TM_\sigma(x-X_\sigma)\right)\right]\Psi. \end{gathered} The Hermitian matrices obey the ordinary spatial Clifford relations; \beta anticommutes with each \alpha. With X_\sigma=0 and a radial source, the bound operator is H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta(m_0+a_{\rm source}r^2). Only boosts in the (t,y) plane are used below; full spacetime Lorentz covariance of this bound-coordinate kernel is not assumed. For a real radial bound profile, the normal-partner construction supplies H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b(\alpha_y\phi)=-M\alpha_y\phi, \qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} The two fields are orthogonal. The stronger pointwise scalar identity is \phi^\dagger\beta\alpha_y\phi=0, \qquad (\alpha_y\phi)^\dagger\beta(\alpha_y\phi) =-\phi^\dagger\beta\phi. \tag{2} It follows from the full upper and lower radial components, as established for all selected rest polarizations in Spatial Dirac polarization waves. An exact nonlinear two-frequency family Choose complex constants a,b and define \boxed{\Psi(t,x)=a\phi(x)e^{-iMt} +b\alpha_y\phi(x)e^{iMt}.} \tag{3} Set n=|a|^2+|b|^2 and s=|a|^2-|b|^2. Equation (2) gives \boxed{\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi=s\,\phi^\dagger\beta\phi, \qquad \int\Psi^\dagger\Psi\,dx=n.} \tag{4} Solve the bound profile with this same scalar weight s. Its scalar center and every scalar binding moment are then constant. Each frequency component solves the same frozen bound equation, and their sum preserves exactly the source which defined that equation. Thus (3) solves the full nonlinear scalar moment equation, uniformly in y. Two-frequency solitary waves also occur in nonlinear Dirac models with local scalar interaction; see Boussaïd and Comech. Equations (1)–(4) prove the present construction directly for the specified spatial moment source. Stability results for a different source model are not being assumed here. The current and number-density pattern really move Write the reference bilinears as \rho_0=\phi^\dagger\phi, j_{i0}=\phi^\dagger\alpha_i\phi and j_{y0}=\phi^\dagger\alpha_y\phi. Define z(t)=\bar a b e^{2iMt},\qquad v_i(x)=\phi^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_y)\phi\in\mathbb R. Direct multiplication of the complete spatial field gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \rho(t,x)&=n\rho_0(x)+2\operatorname{Re}z(t)\,j_{y0}(x),\\ j_y(t,x)&=n j_{y0}(x)+2\operatorname{Re}z(t)\,\rho_0(x),\\ j_i(t,x)&=s j_{i0}(x)-2\operatorname{Im}z(t)\,v_i(x). \end{aligned}} \tag{5} These are currents over literal spatial coordinates. Their identification with a particular electromagnetic source still requires the physical current map. The scalar binding density in (4) does not move with them. For n=1, the integrated normal current has oscillation amplitude 2|ab|=\sqrt{1-s^2}. It can remain large when the bound frequency is small. The bound number-density centroid provides another check. For a radial rest polarization w, put J_{iy}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_y)w,\qquad F_0=\frac{1-2G/d}{2M}, \quad G=\int g(r)^2r^{d-1}dr. \tag{6} Then \boxed{X_{\rho,i}(t)=2\operatorname{Re}z(t)F_0J_{iy}, \qquad \dot X_{\rho,i}=-4M\operatorname{Im}z(t)F_0J_{iy}.} \tag{7} Independent integration of j_i yields precisely the second expression, checking spatial continuity. The scalar center stays fixed. For the tested pure odd-dimensional preparations, \sum_iJ_{iy}^2=1; the selected six-dimensional rest chirality instead has J_{iy}=0. A slower clock increases the excursion scale F_0\propto1/M at fixed radial shape. The corresponding speed amplitude is \sqrt{1-s^2}(1-2G/d) for the unit odd-dimensional circulation. It stays finite: low frequency alone does not imply a small moving current. The five-dimensional field still occupies all five bound spatial directions. Keep the canonical norm and the common coefficient fixed Set n=1, 0<s\le1, and choose |a|^2=\frac{1+s}{2},\qquad |b|^2=\frac{1-s}{2}. \tag{8} For the zero-bare-mass scalar moment branch, let M_* and \phi_* denote the profile at s=1 with a fixed coefficient g_0. The exact self-consistent scaling is \boxed{\lambda=s^{1/5},\qquad \phi_s(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi_*(\lambda x),\qquad M(s)=\lambda M_*,\qquad a_{\rm source}(s)=\lambda^3a_{\rm source}(1).} \tag{9} Both frequency components use this readjusted profile. The full field's source satisfies a_{\rm source}=g_0sT/d, where T=\int r^2\phi_s^\dagger\beta\phi_s\,dx. Under dilation, T\mapsto\lambda^{-2}T, so self-consistency gives \lambda^3=s\lambda^{-2} and hence \lambda=s^{1/5}. The full field's canonical norm remains one; s measures their signed scalar balance. The total scalar second moment scales as s\lambda^{-2}=s^{3/5}, while the squared number-density radius scales as s^{-2/5}. Reducing the scalar balance therefore makes the current clock slower and the bound field broader using the same g_0. For d=5, g_0=6.5 and zero bare mass, independent spatial solves give: scalar balance s bound frequency M current frequency 2M bound centroid excursion amplitude centroid speed amplitude 1 2.472753 4.945506 0 0 0.5 2.152656 4.305313 0.185593 0.799034 0.05 1.358234 2.716469 0.339224 0.921491 0.001 0.621127 1.242255 0.742718 0.922645 These are model units and a continuous family, not a neutrino mass table. The same construction works at the tested depths three and six. The action has not selected a particular s or a uniquely five-dimensional preparation. As s\to0, the bound profile spreads without limit, so the endpoint is not a finite localized zero-frequency particle. The conserved full field energy per chosen normal normalization interval is the bound kinetic expectation plus \mathcal E_{\rm int}=g_0\operatorname{tr}(M_\sigma^2)/2. For the zero-bare-mass family it is \boxed{\mathcal E(s) =sM(s)-\mathcal E_{\rm int}(s) =\frac56sM(s)=\frac56M_*s^{6/5}.} \tag{10} The first equality retains the opposite signs of the two frequencies; the last uses the spatial dilation law. A periodic field containing both signs is not a single stationary energy eigenmode. Neither M nor (10) can be assigned a measured neutrino mass without deriving that particle identification and its propagation normalization.
