A small mean scalar source does not fix its response The shrinking scalar moment in (9) reduces its diagonal scalar cross energy against a fixed partner in the specified moment kernel. The other partner must readjust at finite coupling, and the full variation still includes changes of s, shape and polarization. For example, parametrize (8) by a=\cos\theta, |b|=\sin\theta, with 0\le\theta<\pi/4, so s=\cos2\theta. Differentiating the readjusted energy gives \frac{d\mathcal E}{d\theta} =-2M(s)\sqrt{1-s^2},\qquad \boxed{\frac{d^2\mathcal E}{d\theta^2} =\frac{4M(s)}{5s}(1-6s^2).} \tag{11} For small positive s, the second derivative grows as s^{-4/5}. Thus a small mean binding source can coexist with a large response to changing the relative components. This curvature is not a stability proof for the periodic field. Its linearized source also has explicit time dependence. If the spatial moment columns are C(t)=aC_+e^{-iMt}+bC_-e^{iMt}, the ordinary and conjugate feedback blocks contain respectively C(t)\kappa C(t)^\dagger, \qquad C(t)\kappa C(t)^T. \tag{12} Here \kappa is the constant moment curvature at the unchanged scalar source, including the scalar-center response where required. The blocks in (12) contain frequencies 0,\pm2M. A perturbation can therefore drive sidebands separated by 2M. Its response requires a calculation with periodic coefficients, or an equivalent Floquet expansion; substituting 2M into a stationary single-frequency susceptibility does not supply it. Periodic spatial source response derives that complete equation. Some scalar readouts satisfy an exact finite spectral cancellation at rest, while normal propagation reopens their sidebands. The full shape response provides the relevant spatial source columns, with the time dependence retained here. Motion changes the source phase seen by the partner The normal boost symmetry gives another exact solution: \Psi_\eta(t,x,y) =e^{\eta\alpha_y/2}\Psi_0(\tau,x),\qquad \tau=\cosh\eta\,t-\sinh\eta\,y. \tag{13} Its scalar source remains the same pointwise. The current's oscillating phase is 2M\tau, with frequency 2M\cosh\eta and normal wavenumber 2M\sinh\eta in these coordinates. Along a comoving trajectory it accumulates at 2M per proper time. At a fixed position the uniform boosted pattern instead oscillates at 2M\cosh\eta. A finite encounter also includes the spatial envelope and overlap of both objects. Their motion cannot be represented by inserting the rest clock alone into a target response. The general source-frequency accounting is in Source frequencies in spatial coupling. Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields extends this stationary construction to arbitrary complex radial motion. It proves the distinct number and kinetic weights and transfers an existing radial instability into the full two-frequency field. Verification source_frequency_checks.py recomputes the scalar profile at fixed common coefficient and unit total norm for several scalar balances and depths. Full spatial quadrature checks the density, moments, currents, centroid and conserved energy. Independent finite derivatives in every bound coordinate, time and the normal direction verify both unboosted and boosted nonlinear solutions. Independent temporal Fourier transforms recover the twice-frequency current and the periodic source-feedback blocks. Energy differences verify (11). The construction supplies an exact spatial clock and its limitations; full stability, the occupied neutrino geometry and physical photon coupling remain to be established. Related Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — supplies the partner, boost and current-moment identities. Spatial Dirac polarization waves — supplies the complete spatial polarization frame. Source frequencies in spatial coupling — explains the clock sampled by a physical output map.

title: Bilateral polarization coupling
summary: Keeping both objects polarized gives covariant tensor pairings, distinct source and response zeros, and a reciprocal orientation model with exactly conserved relative overlap.
text: Summary: Keeping both objects polarized gives covariant tensor pairings, distinct source and response zeros, and a reciprocal orientation model with exactly conserved relative overlap. Both objects carry spatial polarization Let the two particle patterns carry spatial tensors J_a(x;\alpha) and J_b(y;\beta), where \alpha,\beta label their respective preparations. These parameters describe fields on actual nested macroscopic spatial submanifolds of one infinite manifold. They are not additional physical dimensions. Each object has its own polarization and can change in response to the other; a fixed-target calculation is a conditional snapshot. The working physical hypothesis is that this reciprocal motion can improve or worsen the match between the spatial patterns. An encounter may therefore strengthen its subsequent coupling or move the patterns toward incompatibility. Changing compatibility is a proposed part of the mechanism, to be tested from the same field equations. The calculation must follow both patterns during the encounter and determine which responses initiate and sustain that change. Initial overlap alone does not determine the outcome. Neither automatic alignment nor conserved relative overlap is a general requirement; the exactly conserved overlap in the benchmark below is a property of its specified restricted dynamics. A specified reciprocal two-form term can be written U[\alpha,\beta] =-g\operatorname{Re}\int\!\int \left\langle J_a(x;\alpha), \mathcal K_{ab}(x,y)J_b(y;\beta)\right\rangle d\mu_a(x)d\mu_b(y). \tag{1} The kernel includes the actual spatial maps, frame transport, and any derivatives prescribed by the action. All tensors must be paired in compatible frames. Reciprocity uses the adjoint kernel for the reverse variation. Equation (1) is a conditional term of the one field's energy; the kernel and tensor observables must come from its action. Under a common rotation of all physical geometric data, J\mapsto RJR^T and \mathcal K transforms correspondingly, leaving (1) unchanged. Rotating only the particles while keeping an anisotropic environment fixed is a different physical preparation and need not preserve the energy. For a local isotropic benchmark, with two real tensors at one common point, the expression reduces to U=-g\langle A,B\rangle, \qquad\langle A,B\rangle=-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(AB). \tag{2} If A=R_aA_0R_a^T and B=R_bB_0R_b^T, this depends on the relative rotation R_a^TR_b. Either tensor can be the lower or higher pattern. The formula does not privilege one as the only polarized object. Plane alignment includes both principal directions For oriented orthonormal pairs u_1,u_2 and v_1,v_2, put A=u_1\wedge u_2 and B=v_1\wedge v_2, with u\wedge v=uv^T-vu^T. Direct expansion gives \boxed{ \langle A,B\rangle =(u_1\cdot v_1)(u_2\cdot v_2) -(u_1\cdot v_2)(u_2\cdot v_1) =\det(U^TV),} \tag{3} where U=(u_1,u_2) and V=(v_1,v_2). The singular values of U^TV are \cos\theta_1,\cos\theta_2, the two principal-angle cosines. Hence the squared pairing is |\langle A,B\rangle|^2 =\cos^2\theta_1\cos^2\theta_2. \tag{4} The sign of (3) also retains relative orientation. For several rotational planes, expand A=\sum_i a_i A_i and B=\sum_j b_j B_j: \langle A,B\rangle =\sum_{i,j}a_i b_j\det(U_i^TV_j). \tag{5} Contributions to this same scalar pairing add before it is squared. Opposite orientations can cancel despite nonzero overlap of individual planes. Complex oscillating tensors additionally retain their relative phases through the Hermitian pairing. A temporal or ensemble average must be justified by the specified preparation. A zero static source need not be a zero response Let a photon amplitude a couple to a target preparation \beta through U(a,\beta)=-g\,a\,s(\beta), \qquad s(\beta)=\langle B_\gamma,J_b(\beta)\rangle \tag{6} for one real wave quadrature. The background can satisfy s(\beta_0)=0 while the mixed derivative is nonzero: \boxed{\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial a\,\partial\beta} =-g\left\langle B_\gamma, \frac{\partial J_b}{\partial\beta}\right\rangle.} \tag{7} For an exact example in three ordinary spatial directions, choose B_\gamma=e_1\wedge e_2 and J_b(\theta) =\cos\theta\,(e_2\wedge e_3) +\sin\theta\,(e_1\wedge e_2). This is a unit simple two-form for every \theta. Its static pairing at zero is zero, but s'(0)=1. An incoming wave can therefore drive the target's angular variation even when the target's unperturbed projection supplies no source in that wave direction. For two varying target patterns and a fixed kernel, the mixed variation of (1) contains \delta_a\delta_b U =-g\operatorname{Re}\int\!\int \langle\delta J_a,\mathcal K_{ab}\delta J_b\rangle d\mu_a d\mu_b. \tag{8} When the kernel, embeddings, or measures also change, include those derivatives. A claim of no linear coupling must test all allowed response tangents and the other action terms. The value of (1) at one preparation, by itself, is insufficient. A complete mode-fibre pair action provides a conditional deformation benchmark: two initially coherent patterns leave the coherent subset, and their changing density contact is constrained by energy and rotation moments. This positive-density component model retains shape responses beyond two ray angles; its auxiliary mode-space dynamics still require a physical spatial and Dirac-current reduction. A solvable reciprocal orientation benchmark For the finite isotropic energy (2), give A and B fixed coadjoint orbits of SO(D) and positive symplectic weights \ell_a,\ell_b. Specify the Lie–Poisson convention \ell_a\dot A=[A,\nabla_AU], \qquad \ell_b\dot B=[B,\nabla_BU]. The equations are \ell_a\dot A=-g[A,B], \qquad \ell_b\dot B=g[A,B]. \tag{9} Both polarizations respond. Their weighted sum S=\ell_aA+\ell_bB is constant, as are their individual spectra, the overlap \langle A,B\rangle, and the energy. Since \dot A=\frac{g}{\ell_a\ell_b}[S,A], \qquad \dot B=\frac{g}{\ell_a\ell_b}[S,B], the exact solution is \boxed{ R(t)=\exp\left(\frac{gt}{\ell_a\ell_b}S\right), \qquad A(t)=R(t)A(0)R(t)^T, \qquad B(t)=R(t)B(0)R(t)^T.} \tag{10} The weights are coefficients of a specified first-order orientation action, not values inferred from spatial depth. These orbit dynamics preserve tensor spectra and rotate both objects together. They produce precession, with no attraction toward a better matched relative angle. Testing the proposed improvement or loss of compatibility during an encounter therefore requires derived spatial motion, anisotropy, or response structure beyond this benchmark. The direction of that change must follow from the equations, rather than a rule that always favors alignment. Equation (9) assumes the displayed orbit variations are admissible. Fixed sector embeddings or geometric constraints can restrict the allowed generators and require reaction terms. The benchmark does not establish that arbitrary rotations preserve every global nested embedding. Following the full field beyond its mean rotation tensor The coadjoint benchmark follows the two-form observables. They need not specify the complete polarized field at a higher spatial depth. Equal-current spatial polarizations derives a reciprocal six-inside-ten example from a rotation-moment energy and both full spatial kinetic terms. Its mean tensors remain fixed while the higher field can rotate into an orthogonal polarization. Thus even a two-form interaction can require more field information to describe its response than the mean two-forms alone retain. Relation to the photon and higher-sector calculations The tensor J_d in photon plane coupling already specifies one target polarization, while E,k,c specify the photon's polarization and propagation. Its projector calculation freezes the target at that preparation. Equations (7)–(8) supply the additional test when both can respond. The descending source starts from the higher pattern; its derivative gives the reverse response. The Dirac source derivative computes that derivative explicitly for one written nonlinear term. These descriptions can coexist: the higher geometry may determine the source while the two objects' relative polarizations determine which response is engaged. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Descending photon source — separates the source value from its reciprocal derivative. Photon plane coupling — fixes both spatial preparations for one instantaneous overlap. Dirac source linearization — retains the changes of the higher field and its nonlinear source. Canonical free-pair operator — gives an earlier two-electron example whose invariants depend on both complex structures. Polarized response spectrum weights the spatially allowed responses by their frequencies and finite exposure time. Coherent spatial overlap evaluates both objects' shapes and phases in exact Gaussian and opposing-lobe examples.

title: Canonical coupling normalization
summary: Kinetic Gram matrices fix normalized transition vertices and conserved generators, separating charge universality from profile-dependent interaction strength.
text: Summary: Kinetic Gram matrices fix normalized transition vertices and conserved generators, separating charge universality from profile-dependent interaction strength. Modes and the kinetic metric Use finite sets of linearly independent, admissible mode sections in arbitrary nested physical sectors. Their coefficient labels are not additional spatial dimensions. Let S_d map coefficients c_d to the spatial field, and let the positive time-kinetic form induce Z_d=S_d^\dagger S_d>0,\qquad L_{\rm kin}=\sum_d i c_d^\dagger Z_d\dot c_d. The dagger includes the specified spatial measure and bundle inner product. The block form assumes kinetic orthogonality between the retained families. Spatial nesting alone does not imply it. If cross terms occur, use the full positive Gram matrix for the independent combined basis and normalize that matrix. Redundant sections must first be removed; a singular Gram matrix cannot be normalized with an inverse. With \hbar=1, define z_d=Z_d^{1/2}c_d. The kinetic term becomes i z_d^\dagger\dot z_d. For a coherent cross-sector vertex with a single real perturbation amplitude A of the same field, U_{\rm tr}=A\,c_a^\dagger K_{ab}c_b+\text{complex conjugate}, Here A is a retained variation of \Psi_\infty, and the trilinear term is conditional on its expansion from that field's action. It does not introduce a separate interaction field or a mediator particle. The matter-normalized vertex is \widehat K_{ab}=Z_a^{-1/2}K_{ab}Z_b^{-1/2}. \tag{1} If A has time-kinetic coefficient Z_A>0, its canonical amplitude is A_c=\sqrt{Z_A}A, and the fully normalized vertex is \widehat K_{ab}/\sqrt{Z_A}. Matrix-valued response metrics require the corresponding transformation on their own index. For a density source j_d=c_d^\dagger T_dc_d, the transformation instead is j_d=z_d^\dagger\widehat T_dz_d,\qquad \widehat T_d=Z_d^{-1/2}T_dZ_d^{-1/2}. \tag{2} Each current has two matter legs. A current-current interaction therefore cannot be normalized by applying (1) just once to its matrix of scalar coefficients. Measures and spatial maps must be transformed consistently. Independence of coefficient conventions Under any invertible basis change c_d=T_d'\widetilde c_d, \widetilde Z_d=T_d'^\dagger Z_dT_d',\qquad \widetilde K_{ab}=T_a'^\dagger K_{ab}T_b'. The matrix U_d=Z_d^{1/2}T_d'\widetilde Z_d^{-1/2} is unitary, because U_d^\dagger U_d=I. Substitution proves \widetilde{\widehat K}_{ab}=U_a^\dagger\widehat K_{ab}U_b. \tag{3} Thus rank and singular values of the normalized vertex are independent of the arbitrary normalization of its basis sections. Its entries still depend on which physical states are used; mass eigenbases and their relative phases have to be determined to predict particular transitions. The existing CKM calculation is a concrete application. For a single mode per family, |K_{ab}|/\sqrt{Z_aZ_bZ_A} is invariant. The pair energy g_{ab}j_aj_b, a transition vertex, and a mass-operator coefficient remain different objects even if all are called couplings. Generators, charge, and selection Let a self-adjoint generator \mathsf Q preserve each retained mode subspace, so \mathsf Q S_d=S_d q_d,\qquad q_d^\dagger Z_d=Z_dq_d. The normalized generator is Hermitian: \widehat q_d=Z_d^{1/2}q_dZ_d^{-1/2}. If the underlying generator is the same scalar q on two families, \mathsf Q S_a=qS_a and \mathsf Q S_b=qS_b, then their unnormalized charge matrices are qZ_a,qZ_b. After normalization both become qI, regardless of spatial depth, profile width, or the number of retained modes. This proves preservation of a common charge under projection and normalization. It does not derive which master generator is electric charge, its eigenvalues, or why both physical sectors carry the same one. A neutral field perturbation preserves this charge when \widehat q_a\widehat K_{ab}=\widehat K_{ab}\widehat q_b. \tag{4} For charge eigenvectors with eigenvalues q_i,q_j, (4) reads (q_i-q_j)\widehat K_{ij}=0. A charged complex field amplitude transforming as A\mapsto e^{i q_A\theta}A, with matter transforming as z_d\mapsto e^{i\widehat q_d\theta}z_d, changes the criterion to \widehat q_a\widehat K_{ab}-\widehat K_{ab}\widehat q_b =q_A\widehat K_{ab}. \tag{5} This is the infinitesimal invariance of A z_a^\dagger\widehat K_{ab}z_b. It is a selection rule, not a numerical prediction of an allowed entry. For non-Abelian generators the perturbation index transforms too, giving an invariant tensor rather than a single charge-difference equation. Universal charge and resolved spatial structure For a normalized positive density \rho_d carrying the same charge q, the projected spatial form factor is F_d(k)=q\int_{Q_d}e^{ik\cdot r(x)}\rho_d(x)\,d\mu_d(x), \qquad F_d(0)=q. Here r is the specified readout onto shared spatial coordinates. The zero-momentum identity uses the complete conserved marginal. It does not require all the F_d(k) to agree at nonzero momentum. For a centered Gaussian shared marginal with covariance C_d, F_d(k)=q\,e^{-k^{\mathsf T}C_dk/2}. Thus equal charge is consistent with unequal spatial response and contact integrals. A mode count or spatial width need not multiply a normalized particle's charge. This statement concerns an assumed conserved charge; neutral composite distributions or other electromagnetic operators need their own form factors. The quantum-field benchmark is charge universality in the Thomson limit, described in PDG, Electroweak Model, §10.3.1. The calculation above is an action-level projection identity, not an all-orders proof of that benchmark for V2. A common gauge-field kinetic normalization and a gauge-consistent elimination of omitted modes remain necessary. The projected current note gives the exact local conservation defect when a truncation drops such modes. Related and verification Generalized sector coupling — the theory-wide calculation and its physical inputs. Nested sector reciprocity — fixes the spatial pairing used in the raw vertex. Common field response — applies response factorization only after the source convention is specified. Neutrino channel control — applies charge selection without suppressing every interaction. generalized_coupling_checks.py tests nonorthogonal bases, nonunitary basis changes, conserved generators, charged transition selection, and independently integrated form factors.

title: Canonical spatial spin response
summary: The full moving spatial frame fixes the canonical particle center and relates its electric spin-orbit response to the magnetic moment without an independent coefficient.
text: Summary: The full moving spatial frame fixes the canonical particle center and relates its electric spin-orbit response to the magnetic moment without an independent coefficient. Retain the entire occupied polarization The conditional spatial current calculation supplies a normalized radial Dirac profile on d ordinary spatial coordinates. Its centered scalar binding determines the translation inertia \mathcal I and current moment F_0. With a normalized complex vector z in the complete occupied multiplet, write J_{ij}=z^\dagger B_{ij}z,\qquad B_{ij}=W_{\rm rest}^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)W_{\rm rest}, \qquad g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0. \tag{1} Here W_{\rm rest} embeds the upper radial polarization at rest. The full spatial field includes its lower radial component. These matrices describe spatial rotations and add no physical dimensions. The complete polarization description keeps the whole vector z even when its bivector J does not determine every higher-dimensional polarization observable. The soft current derivation gives the velocity tangent \zeta_i=iMx_i\phi+\alpha_i\phi/2 and the number centroid R_\rho=X+F_0Jv. The charge q and minimal connection of that same field remain conditional inputs. Work to first order in a weak electric field and to the leading nontrivial order in the particle velocity. Normalize the moving spatial frame Let W(x) contain every normalized rest profile as columns, and let Z_i(x)=iMx_iW+\alpha_iW/2. Full spatial integration gives matrix identities \int W^\dagger W=I,\qquad \int W^\dagger Z_i=0,\qquad K_{ij}-K_{ji}=-\frac i2B_{ij},\qquad K_{ij}=\int Z_i^\dagger Z_j. \tag{2} The first mixed integral vanishes by parity. The last identity is the matrix version of the velocity symplectic curvature; it holds before choosing the occupied ray. Normalize W_v=W+v_iZ_i by its integrated Gram matrix: \widetilde W_v=W_v(\int W_v^\dagger W_v)^{-1/2}. For the field \widetilde W_vz, the term containing dz remains the canonical \tfrac i2(z^\dagger dz-dz^\dagger z). Equation (2) fixes the leading velocity connection as i\int\widetilde W_v^\dagger d\widetilde W_v =\tfrac14v_iB_{ij}dv_j+\cdots. A local frame gauge can absorb the symmetric connection terms of a higher-order profile completion; the curvature at rest is fixed by its actual first tangents. Together with the translation momentum, the retained action one-form is \theta=\frac i2(z^\dagger dz-dz^\dagger z) +\mathcal I v\cdot dX+\frac14v_iJ_{ij}dv_j. \tag{3} This states the orders needed below, not an all-velocity canonical description of the scalar-bound particle. Find the canonical spatial center Define \boxed{ P=\mathcal I v,\qquad r=X+\frac{Jv}{4\mathcal I}.} \tag{4} Then P\cdot dr=\mathcal I v\cdot dX+\tfrac14v\cdot J\,dv. This remains true when z changes: the extra term is \tfrac14v_i(dJ_{ij})v_j=0 because dJ is antisymmetric. Thus (3) becomes the usual P\cdot dr plus the full polarization one-form. No frozen-spin assumption is needed for this coordinate identity. The physical number centroid is consequently \boxed{ R_\rho=r+\frac{g_{\rm mag}-1}{4\mathcal I^2}JP.} \tag{5} The scalar center, canonical center and number centroid describe different moments of the same moving spatial field. They are not separate physical spaces or a division of the six-dimensional electron. Obtain the electric spin-orbit coefficient For a uniform electric field, the actual charge energy is -qE\cdot R_\rho. Its velocity-dependent part in canonical coordinates is \boxed{ H_{\rm SO} =-\frac{q(g_{\rm mag}-1)}{4\mathcal I^2} \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}(E_iP_j-E_jP_i).} \tag{6} For a chosen three-dimensional measurement plane, J_{ij}=2\epsilon_{ijk}S_k, so H_{\rm SO} =-\frac{q(g_{\rm mag}-1)}{2\mathcal I^2} \,S\cdot(E\times P). \tag{7} The same current gives the rest magnetic term H_B=-qg_{\rm mag}S\cdot B/(2\mathcal I) in that plane. With the conventional coefficient names c_F=g_{\rm mag}/2 and c_S=g_{\rm mag}-1, \boxed{c_S=2c_F-1.} \tag{8} This agrees with the low-velocity spin-half electromagnetic coefficient relation derived from Lorentz invariance; see the explicit Lagrangian and matching discussion in Paz, An Introduction to NRQED, equation (3). The comparison concerns the response coefficients of an individual particle. It imports no mediator-particle interpretation and does not model an atom. There is a direct consistency check. Put c=(g_{\rm mag}-1)/(4\mathcal I^2) and keep J fixed at linear order in the applied field. Equations (5)–(6) give \dot P=qE, \dot r=P/\mathcal I+qcJE and therefore \dot R_\rho=v+2qcJE. This is exactly the full spatial current derived independently from the complete source resolvent. The result fixes the leading uniform-field spin-orbit response. Spatial field gradients, the Darwin term, finite-frequency deformation and an all-velocity spin-precession law require further calculation. The scalar six-dimensional ground profile still gives g_{\rm mag}\simeq2.07691916, so this coefficient relation does not repair its mismatch with the electron magnetic moment. The same parameters also control the soft forward scattering term; these related tests must be satisfied together. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py integrates (2) as full spatial matrices at depths three and six, normalizes the moving frame, and independently differentiates its overlap to recover the Berry connection. Halving the velocity tests the omitted order. Arbitrary complex polarization variations check (4), while the canonical equations are compared with the independently derived spatial current. All checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Spatial and moving-cavity response
summary: Exact oscillator matrix elements connect cumulative state counts to polarized spatial response and energy-transfer distributions, while moving scalar and Dirac modes show why a frozen cavity overlap is only one part of coupling.
text: Summary: Exact oscillator matrix elements connect cumulative state counts to polarized spatial response and energy-transfer distributions, while moving scalar and Dirac modes show why a frozen cavity overlap is only one part of coupling. A spatial operator with a specified meaning Let P_{N,d} project onto the normalized isotropic oscillator modes of total degree at most N in d ordinary spatial coordinates. Their common oscillator length is L and their count is D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}. The operator A(k)=e^{ik\cdot x},\qquad \eta=\frac{|k|^2L^2}{2}, \tag{1} is a Fourier component of a declared scalar density probe. It is unitary on the complete spatial Hilbert space. Its compressed matrix can lose weight to modes outside a selected band. These are conditional spatial controls. Positive density is not automatically electric charge or a Dirac scalar. A band trace represents specified equal weights; a coherent field instead requires its actual complex coefficients. The calculation neither changes the particle depth assignments nor adds compactified coordinates. Hockey-Stick gives an exact form factor For one normalized oscillator mode, \langle a|e^{ikx}|a\rangle =e^{-\eta/2}L_a(\eta), \tag{2} where L_a is a Laguerre polynomial. Align the first coordinate with k. The other d-1 coordinates contribute their oscillator multiplicities. The generating function for the shell traces is e^{-\eta/2}(1-t)^{-d} \exp\left(-\frac{\eta t}{1-t}\right). \tag{3} Multiplication by (1-t)^{-1} performs the cumulative Hockey-Stick sum. Comparison with the generalized Laguerre generating function gives \begin{aligned} F_{N,d}(k)&=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(P_{N,d}A(k))}{D_N}\\ &=e^{-\eta/2}\frac{L_N^{(d)}(\eta)}{D_N}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} In particular F_{N,d}(0)=1. Its small-k expansion gives \langle |x|^2\rangle_N =dL^2\left(\frac{N}{d+1}+\frac12\right). \tag{5} This explicitly separates a common well length from the spatial extent of different modes. Equation (4) is a normalized trace amplitude. Squaring it is not generally the probability of remaining in a band: amplitudes may cancel in a trace, while transitions to different final modes are distinct. Complete transition weights For \ell=\min(a,b) and h=\max(a,b), the one-coordinate displacement matrix A_{ba}=\langle b|A(k)|a\rangle, with k chosen positive along that coordinate, is \begin{aligned} A_{ba}&=e^{-\eta/2}\sqrt{\frac{\ell!}{h!}}\\ &\quad\times(i\sqrt\eta)^{h-\ell}L_\ell^{(h-\ell)}(\eta). \end{aligned} \tag{6} Let r be the total degree in the spectator coordinates. Their shell multiplicity is g_{d-1}(r)=\binom{r+d-2}{d-2} for d\ge2. For d=1, only r=0 contributes, with weight one. The probability weight captured in a final cumulative band M is \begin{aligned} I_{N\to M}(\eta) ={}&\frac1{D_N}\sum_{r=0}^{\min(N,M)}g_{d-1}(r)\\ &\times\sum_{a=0}^{N-r}\sum_{b=0}^{M-r} |A_{ba}|^2. \end{aligned} \tag{7} This retains every allowed final mode. It obeys \begin{aligned} D_NI_{N\to M}&=D_MI_{M\to N},\\ \lim_{M\to\infty}I_{N\to M}&=1. \end{aligned} \tag{8} The first identity follows from the symmetric squared entries in (6); the second follows from completeness and unitarity. It is a reciprocity identity for this operator, not a complete two-particle scattering law. Occupation blocking, an energy budget or a specified time-dependent probe would impose additional physical conditions. Resolve the response by energy as well as by band Take oscillator energies \hbar\omega(k+d/2). A transition from degree a to b in the active coordinate changes the energy by \hbar\omega j, where j=b-a can be positive, zero or negative. Resolve the sum (7) by this signed difference and let w_N(j) denote the resulting complete weight, with the final cutoff removed. Put u(t)=4\eta\sinh^2(t/2). The exact one-coordinate generating function is \begin{aligned} G_a(t)&=\sum_b|A_{ba}|^2e^{t(b-a)}\\ &=e^{\eta(e^t-1)}L_a(-u(t)). \end{aligned} \tag{9} The same spectator and cumulative sums give the full moment-generating function \begin{aligned} \mathcal G_N(t)&=\sum_jw_N(j)e^{tj}\\ &=e^{\eta(e^t-1)} \frac{L_N^{(d)}(-u(t))}{D_N}. \end{aligned} \tag{10} At t=0, this is one. Its first two cumulants are \begin{aligned} \langle j\rangle&=\eta,\\ \operatorname{Var}(j)&=\eta\left(1+\frac{2N}{d+1}\right). \end{aligned} \tag{11} There is an independent spatial check. Conjugating the oscillator Hamiltonian by A(k) adds \hbar k\cdot p/m_{\rm kin} and \hbar^2|k|^2/(2m_{\rm kin}). The band has zero mean momentum, and its directional momentum variance gives the second line of (11). Thus the generating function and the actual kinetic operator give the same two sum rules. The inclusive weight remains one, but it need not lie in the frequencies available to a particular encounter. For example, every t<0 gives the rigorous bound \Pr(j\le J)\le e^{-tJ}\mathcal G_N(t). \tag{12} This follows by applying the elementary exponential Markov inequality to e^{tj}. The program evaluates the logarithm before optimizing t, so an exponentially small bound is not confused with floating-point zero. Neither (11) nor (12) determines an IDWT encounter's available energy; that requires its actual field dynamics and conservation equations. Complex polarization and a nested spatial probe An isotropic trace removes orientation information. A normalized complex polarization v\in\mathbb C^d instead defines the degree-N mode |N,v\rangle=\frac{(v\cdot a^\dagger)^N}{\sqrt{N!}}|0\rangle. \tag{13} Its actual spatial density form factor is F_{N,v}(k)=e^{-\eta/2} L_N\!\left(\frac{L^2|v^\dagger k|^2}{2}\right). \tag{14} Relative complex phases enter |v^\dagger k|^2. Circular and linear polarizations give different directional responses. The diagnostic compares (14) with complete complex mode vectors and separately integrates a general complex superposition in physical coordinates. Let E be the real isometric inclusion of a lower spatial sector into a containing sector. For a declared product of two density profiles, a shared wavevector k samples the higher profile at Ek. Its Fourier pairing contains both factors F_{N_a,v_a}(k)\,F_{N_b,v_b}(-Ek). \tag{15} A common physical rotation of v_b and E leaves the result unchanged. Both polarizations are retained. A rotation of only one object is a different preparation. The normal marginal must be formed from the bilinear current before constructing this pairing. Equation (15) remains a specified profile overlap until both fields and their reciprocal motion are derived from an interaction action. A moving final cavity has a different spectral projector The moving-cavity calculation gives an exact identity for quadratic kinetics: \begin{aligned} H_v&=H_0-v\cdot p,\\ U_v&=e^{im_{\rm kin}v\cdot x/\hbar},\\ P_v&=U_vP_0U_v^\dagger. \end{aligned} \tag{16} For k=m_{\rm kin}(v_f-v_i)/\hbar, the spatial phase A(k) maps the initial moving band isometrically onto the corresponding final moving band. In consistently related bases, \langle U_{v_f}u_b|A(k)|U_{v_i}u_a\rangle =\delta_{ab}. \tag{17} Projection back into an unchanged cavity is a different operation. In the fifteen-state quasiperiodically perturbed oscillator used for the inertia control, a boost of 1.4 in its nonrelativistic units leaves fixed-band weights 0.65253335 and 0.65394785 for the two well phases. The corresponding moving-band weights are one to within 3\times10^{-14}. The prescribed well and its velocity are part of this calculation. The identity does not derive a physical collision that accelerates the well, or remove the need to include its source and energy. It shows why a frozen profile overlap alone cannot decide whether a moving particle pattern can persist after receiving momentum. Full first-order Dirac current overlaps For the exact Dirac control H=\sigma_xp+b\sigma_yx+m_0\sigma_z, \tag{18} use the complete normalized moving spinors derived in the inertia note. With \hbar=c=1, the current matrix element is \begin{aligned} J_\Gamma(k,v)={}&\int dx\,\phi_{n,v}^\dagger(x)\\ &\qquad\times\Gamma\phi_{n,0}(x)e^{ikx}. \end{aligned} \tag{19} The vertices I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z give the density, spatial, pseudoscalar and scalar channels of this two-component comparison. Both spinor components, the boost phase and the changed width remain inside the integral. At b=0.8, m_0=0, n=1, v=0.8, choose the phase-matched wavevector k=E'\gamma v=1.30639453. This matches the spinor phase; it is not automatically the total conserved momentum transfer of a collision. The calculated density amplitudes give Density comparison Squared amplitude Both spatial profiles held at zero velocity 0.07494905 Final profile is the complete moving mode 0.75019526 For the moving mode, the spatial-current amplitude is 0.43306907, the scalar amplitude is 0.01397361, and the pseudoscalar amplitude is 0.00698680i. They are distinct channels. Independent coordinate quadrature at orders 80 and 160 verifies the complete complex integrals. This comparison contains an external well; it is not a closed reciprocal IDWT encounter or a prediction of a physical interaction rate. The large inverse-scale ratio is a conditional suppression test The existing mass-scale benchmarks suggest L_5/L_6\simeq3.6\times10^7 if the geometric conversion factors in the common-size relation are equal. For the illustrative probe |k|L_6=10^{-3}, (4) gives F_e=0.9999988929 and F_\mu=0.9999973214 at the unchanged degree assignments. The same probe has \eta=6.48\times10^8 in the depth-five oscillator comparison. At depth-five degrees 9,14,21, the logarithms of the absolute fixed-band trace amplitudes are approximately -3.24\times10^8. The finite-band capture weights are also exponentially small. Equation (12) gives a similarly small bound if the allowed increase in oscillator energy is only ten quanta. All these statements retain the prescribed stationary well and specified energy window. This establishes strong suppression for those operator channels. It does not yet explain rare neutrino interactions: the oscillator frequency in the energy window, the physical current, allowed final states, moving confinement and both objects' response must be supplied by the same-field action. In particular, neither a trace amplitude nor a positive density marginal establishes electric neutrality. The broader spatial contact calculation also keeps the physical measure and its units explicit. Reproduction cavity_form_factors.py implements the exact matrix elements and generating functions. cavity_form_factor_checks.py checks direct finite matrices, independent complex coordinate integration, reciprocal band weights, energy moment sum rules, the complete transfer generating function, rotated polarized profiles, moving bands and Dirac currents. The numerical controls retain the fixed particle indices; their success establishes the stated mathematics under the stated operators.

title: Coherent spatial overlap
summary: Exact complex Gaussian overlaps retain both objects' shapes, polarizations, and spatial phases, while normalized opposing lobes give a concrete low-momentum source cancellation.
text: Summary: Exact complex Gaussian overlaps retain both objects' shapes, polarizations, and spatial phases, while normalized opposing lobes give a concrete low-momentum source cancellation. Spatial source patterns, before averaging After deriving a source or response operator, a local overlap may take the form \mathcal A(k)=\int \langle F_a(x),F_b(x)\rangle e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d^Dx. \tag{1} Both F_a and F_b are polarized spatial patterns. Their components must be expressed in compatible frames and normalized according to the action. Equation (1) adopts a local identity pairing; a derivative or nonlocal kernel must be retained when the action supplies one. The coordinates belong to one common physical chart of the nested manifold. This benchmark uses finite test functions or wavepackets after the spatial mode maps have been specified. It does not replace a lower field's cylindrical continuation by a thin sheet, or identify wavepacket localization in a free direction with a new bound dimension. For an actual nonlinear source, first calculate F_b from the higher field as in descending photon source. Substituting a bare wavefunction or a positive density for a different source would change (1). Exact overlap of two Gaussian amplitude profiles Let A,B be real positive-definite D\times D matrices. Choose \psi_a(x)=\left(\frac{\det A}{\pi^D}\right)^{1/4} \exp\left[-\frac12(x-X_a)^TA(x-X_a)+ip_a\cdot x+i\phi_a\right], and the analogous \psi_b using B,X_b,p_b,\phi_b. Both have unit L^2 norm. If F_a=\psi_a T_a and F_b=\psi_b T_b with constant normalized tensors, the result is \mathcal A(k)=\langle T_a,T_b\rangle\,I_{ab}(k). \tag{2} Put S=A+B,\qquad m=S^{-1}(AX_a+BX_b), \qquad q=p_b-p_a-k,\qquad \Delta X=X_a-X_b. Completing the real square gives (x-X_a)^TA(x-X_a)+(x-X_b)^TB(x-X_b) =(x-m)^TS(x-m)+D_0, where D_0=X_a^TAX_a+X_b^TBX_b-m^TSm =\Delta X^T(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\Delta X. The last identity holds without assuming that A and B commute. Diagonalizing S and taking the characteristic function of the centered Gaussian now yields \boxed{ I_{ab}(k)= \frac{2^{D/2}(\det A\det B)^{1/4}}{\sqrt{\det S}} \exp\left[-\frac12D_0-\frac12q^TS^{-1}q +iq\cdot m+i(\phi_b-\phi_a)\right].} \tag{3} Thus spatial separation, shape covariance, phase-gradient mismatch, and tensor polarization all remain visible. At equal profiles and k=0, I_{aa}=1. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |I_{ab}(k)|\leq1 for every k, since the Fourier phase has unit magnitude. The positive density overlap in Gaussian contact profiles is a different quantity: it has different normalization and no relative wave phase. It cannot stand in for (3) when interference is relevant. Two structured objects For finite patterns F_a=\sum_i a_i\psi_{ai}T_{ai}, \qquad F_b=\sum_j b_j\psi_{bj}T_{bj}, linearity gives the exact amplitude \boxed{\mathcal A(k)= \sum_{i,j}\overline a_i b_j \langle T_{ai},T_{bj}\rangle I_{ai,bj}(k).} \tag{4} Both objects' orientations and phases occur in every term. Individual nonzero overlaps can cancel in the sum. The full Gram matrix of the component profiles determines the normalization of a and b; the lobes are not assumed orthogonal merely because their centers differ. If physical dynamics makes some outputs distinguishable, sum their intensities only after separating those outputs. A normalized shape with a vanishing long-wavelength source For an explicit finite source use the real normalized amplitude \psi_\sigma(x)=(\pi\sigma^2)^{-D/4} e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad \sigma>0. For a fixed nonzero displacement L, define opposing lobes f_-(x)= \frac{\psi_\sigma(x-L/2)-\psi_\sigma(x+L/2)} {\sqrt{2\left(1-e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}\right)}}. \tag{5} Their overlap is e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}, so \|f_-\|_2=1. With Fourier convention \widetilde f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}d^Dx, \boxed{ \widetilde f_-(k)= \frac{-2i\sin(k\cdot L/2)} {\sqrt{2\left(1-e^{-|L|^2/(4\sigma^2)}\right)}} \widetilde\psi_\sigma(k),} \tag{6} where \widetilde\psi_\sigma(k) =2^{D/2}\pi^{D/4}\sigma^{D/2} e^{-\sigma^2|k|^2/2}. The zero at k=0 comes from spatial cancellation while the source has unit norm. For fixed L,\sigma and |k\cdot L|\ll1, its squared Fourier amplitude begins at order (k\cdot L)^2. Directions with k\cdot L=0 remain exactly dark for this source. This is a shape-induced selection within the declared linear source map, not a small coefficient inserted into that map. For a tensor source f_-(x)T_b, additionally contract its tensor with the other object's polarized test pattern. The node in (6) and the tensor pairing are separate factors only for this separated preparation. General moment cancellation Suppose an integrable scalar or tensor source s(x) has finite absolute moment of order m and \int x^\alpha s(x)d^Dx=0 \quad\text{for every multi-index }|\alpha|<m. Subtract the degree-m-1 Taylor polynomial of e^{-ik\cdot x} under the integral. Its real-variable integral remainder is bounded by |k\cdot x|^m/m!, which proves \boxed{ \|\widetilde s(k)\| \leq\frac{|k|^m}{m!} \int |x|^m\|s(x)\|d^Dx.} \tag{7} This gives a calculable low-momentum suppression from vanishing source moments. The moments must vanish for the source produced by the actual field equation. Squaring an odd field can remove its odd parity, so an odd bare shape alone does not establish the moment conditions. The same construction is available at many depths. A distinctive particle prediction requires the field dynamics to select the relevant shape, scale, and source symmetry, and requires the coupling to allowed response tangents to be checked as well. A zero source does not by itself exclude a nonzero susceptibility. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Bilateral polarization coupling — retains both tensor states and distinguishes source values from mixed response derivatives. Descending photon source — defines which higher-field source is projected. Polarized response spectrum — combines spatial matrix elements with frequency and exposure. Gaussian contact profiles — contrasts density contact with the complex amplitude overlap derived here.

title: Collective translation waves
summary: Full source feedback gives the normal propagation of spatial translation modes, with exact inertia and stiffness identities and a subluminal two-polarization branch at bound depth two.
text: Summary: Full source feedback gives the normal propagation of spatial translation modes, with exact inertia and stiffness identities and a subluminal two-polarization branch at bound depth two. Translate a complete bound field A field bound in two spatial directions has two independent displacement directions. If those displacements vary along a perpendicular propagation coordinate, they provide a concrete candidate for a two-polarization wave. The propagation speed must follow from the complete field equation. Use the scalar Dirac moment branch, with actual bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and an existing perpendicular coordinate y in a containing sector. All coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions in the one nested physical manifold. Set the underlying Dirac wave speed to one. The normalized resting profile satisfies H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta(m+a|x|^2),\qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} Here M is the profile's stationary frequency and m its bare scalar coefficient. The full centered moment energy determines a: Q_\sigma=\int\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx,\qquad T_\sigma=\int |x|^2\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx,\qquad a=\frac{g_0T_\sigma}{d}. \tag{2} Q_\sigma denotes scalar normalization, not electric charge. The source is local in (t,y) and uses the centered scalar moments in the bound coordinates, as specified in Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes. A small displacement has spatial tangent \eta_i=-\partial_i\phi,\qquad \Psi=e^{-iMt}\big[\phi+X_i(t,y)\eta_i+\cdots\big]. \tag{3} The omitted terms include the velocity and normal-gradient response of the full spatial profile. Retaining only the displaced density would miss them, just as a general polarization texture can omit a nonzero Dirac complement. Identify when the dipole source closes Let Y=\alpha_y anticommute with every bound \alpha_i and with \beta. For even d, define the Hermitian involutions \Gamma_b=i^{d/2}\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_d,\qquad \Xi=\beta\Gamma_b. \tag{4} They obey [\Xi,H_b]=0,\qquad [\Xi,\beta f(x)]=0,\qquad \{\Xi,Y\}=0. \tag{5} Choose one complete spatial chirality, \Xi\phi=\phi. Every scalar source column \beta f(x)\phi then has that same chirality, while its normal partner has the opposite chirality. This is a decomposition of spatial field components, with no additional physical dimensions. Consequently the term linear in qY between scalar source columns vanishes in the exact normal resolvent. The remaining terms are even in the normal wavenumber q. The parity \beta\mathcal R, where \mathcal R\phi(x)=\phi(-x), further separates odd dipole sources from even second-moment sources. Thus all scalar shape sources can be retained while the dipole block closes. This proof uses the selected even-dimensional chirality. At odd bound depth, normal propagation can mix dipole and shape sources through the field's mixed circulation. An isolated odd-dimensional dipole formula must not be substituted for that full coupled problem. Keep the complete normal and conjugate response The dipole source columns and their curvature are b_i=\beta x_i\phi,\qquad \kappa=-\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}. \tag{6} The curvature comes from varying the scalar center, as derived in Translational Dirac response. For a circular eigenpolarization \lambda of the radial circulation, let w_{\lambda n}\ge0 be the squared source projections on the complete bound eigenfields with energies E_n. Both angular Dirac families belong in this spectral sum. The full bare dipole response is \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \chi_\lambda(\omega,q) ={}&\sum_n w_{\lambda n} \frac{\omega+M+E_n}{(\omega+M)^2-E_n^2-q^2}\\ &+\sum_n w_{-\lambda n} \frac{-\omega+M+E_n}{(-\omega+M)^2-E_n^2-q^2}. \end{aligned}} \tag{7} The second line retains the conjugate fluctuation. At q=0 this reduces to the usual two signed frequency resolvents. Equation (7) follows from the exact Clifford inverse, not a fixed-profile envelope dispersion. The source-carrying modes solve 1-\kappa\chi_\lambda(\omega,q)=0. \tag{8} Source-free modes and any canceled frozen poles remain part of the full field spectrum. For example, the normal partner of a degenerate stationary polarization can have zero dipole residue; it must not be counted as a dipole pole merely because it appears in the frozen denominator. Translation invariance and commuting momentum generators give \kappa\chi_\lambda(0,0)=1,\qquad \partial_\omega\chi_\lambda(0,0)=0. \tag{9} Expand the dipole response at the origin as \chi_\lambda=\frac1\kappa+ \frac12\chi_{\omega\omega}\omega^2+ \chi_{q^2}q^2+ O(\omega^3,\omega q^2,q^4). \tag{10} The inverse force response then has leading coefficients \boxed{ \mathcal I=-2a^2\chi_{\omega\omega},\qquad \mathcal K=4a^2\chi_{q^2},\qquad c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{\mathcal K}{\mathcal I}.} \tag{11} Indeed, a scalar force coefficient f_i adds energy f_i\delta P_i=Q_\sigma f_iX_i. The full dipole response becomes \delta P_i=Q_\sigma^2f_i/(\mathcal I\omega^2-\mathcal Kq^2) to this order. This fixes the normalization of both coefficients. Derive the coefficients directly in physical space Put L=H_b-M. The spatial Dirac identities [H_b,x_i]=-i\alpha_i,\qquad \{H_b,\alpha_i\}=-2i\partial_i \tag{12} give explicit inhomogeneous solutions: \boxed{ L^{-1}\eta_i=Mx_i\phi-\frac i2\alpha_i\phi,\qquad (H_b+M)^{-1}\eta_i=-\frac i2\alpha_i\phi.} \tag{13} These inverses are taken on the relevant complementary subspaces. Equivalently, apply the displayed operators to the right sides to verify the equations directly. Kernel components have zero dipole residue and do not contribute to the coefficients. The velocity correction is iL^{-1}\eta_i. Its first scalar-density variation is zero pointwise: the iMx_i\phi term is a phase variation, and \beta\alpha_i is anti-Hermitian. The full source therefore permits this generalized translation partner. The normal correction lies in the opposite \Xi sector and has no first-order scalar-source feedback by (5). The complete ordinary/conjugate response gives \mathcal I=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta_i,L^{-1}\eta_i\rangle, \qquad \mathcal K=2\operatorname{Re} \langle\eta_i,(H_b+M)^{-1}\eta_i\rangle. \tag{14} Define the actual bound kinetic contribution in direction i: T_i=\langle\phi,\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)\phi\rangle. \tag{15} Localization and unit normalization imply 2\operatorname{Re}\langle-\partial_i\phi,x_i\phi\rangle=1. Integration by parts in the other term gives -i\langle-\partial_i\phi,\alpha_i\phi\rangle=T_i. Substitution into (13)–(14) proves \boxed{\mathcal I=M+T_i,\qquad \mathcal K=T_i,\qquad c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{T_i}{M+T_i}.} \tag{16} For a radial field, T_i=T/d with T=\langle\phi,-i\alpha_i\partial_i\phi\rangle. The quadratic scalar virial identity is T=2aT_\sigma, while M=T+mQ_\sigma+aT_\sigma. Thus \boxed{ T_i=\frac{2(M-mQ_\sigma)}{3d},\qquad m=0\ \Longrightarrow\ c_{\rm tr}^2=\frac{2}{3d+2}.} \tag{17} This also explains the previously computed translation inertias without fitting their numerical values. Two transverse polarizations do not fix the speed For the zero-bare-mass branch, the small-wavenumber speeds are: bound spatial depth number of displacement directions speed in Dirac units 2 2 \frac12 6 6 \frac1{\sqrt{10}} 10 10 \frac14 The depth-two modes are genuine source-carrying, gapless spatial displacements with two transverse polarizations. Within this specified scalar moment model they propagate at half the underlying wave speed. Changing the common scalar coupling only rescales the zero-bare-mass profile; it does not change (17). This is distinct from the lightlike propagation required by the photon construction. The action's covariance in (t,y) does not make every collective excitation lightlike about a finite-frequency, finite-density background. Likewise, covariance under rotations within the bound space does not complete the kernel's dynamics under rotations mixing bound and free directions. At higher orders the circular branches can differ. Positivity of \mathcal I and \mathcal K describes this low-frequency displacement sector; it does not remove separate radial instabilities or establish a stable physical particle. The same full velocity partner determines the low-frequency current and magnetic moment in Soft spatial current response. Null spatial pulses supplies a constructive stationary-background comparison with equal time and propagation norms, while keeping its component action distinct from this scalar Dirac branch. Verification collective_translation_wave_checks.py evaluates both full angular radial families and their normal partners. It compares the exact coefficients with independent spatial derivatives and radial/angular quadrature, and verifies the source equation against the full normal and conjugate matrices. A separate Cartesian Hermite construction retains every scalar second moment and both scalar-center sources at bound depth two. Independent nonlinear source variations verify its curvature. Increasing its total degree from 24 through 30 to 36 brings the displacement frequency toward the independently calculated radial result. Reports are timestamped and all checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Coupling response of combined coherent bands
summary: Joint coherent currents expose substantial band dependence hidden by isolated susceptibilities, and exact tensor-current reconstruction identifies the finite-band corrections needed for a different geometric contact.
text:
Summary: Joint coherent currents expose substantial band dependence hidden by isolated susceptibilities, and exact tensor-current reconstruction identifies the finite-band corrections needed for a different geometric contact. At A=B=1, the occupied source coefficients relative to their isolated values are approximately 0.51870 and 0.999991. Their unequal response follows from the common action; it is not removed by the exact isolated mass relationship. This tests the extension (2). It is not a no-go theorem for every action with the same isolated masses. The smooth action has a different joint peak width For the smooth coherent action, a single positive coherent current has the expansion F_N(A)=\mu D_N- rac{\mu d\sigma}{A}+O(\sigma^2),\qquad F_N'(A)= rac{\mu d\sigma}{A^2}+O(\sigma^2), 	ag{5} at fixed N,d,A>0 as \sigma	o0. Its isolated leading curvature depends on depth but not on the mass-band count. This is a useful lead, but it does not give the mixed derivative of a combined action. Put both currents into the same local functional: U_\sigma=\mu\sigma\log\int \exp\left[ rac{j_{N,z}+j_{M,z}}{\sigma}ight]d

Its partition integral is Z=d\int_0^1(1-u)^{d-1}e^{au^N+bu^M}du. 	ag{7} Near its unique endpoint peak the width is controlled by H=Na+Mb= rac{ND_NA+MD_MB}{\sigma}, 	ag{8} not by either isolated peak width. With y=H(1-u), the leading integral has the Gamma weight y^{d-1}e^{-y}. Thus  egin{aligned} U_\sigma ={}&\mu(D_NA+D_MB)-\mu\sigma d\log H +\mu\sigma\log(d!)+O(\sigma^2),\  oxed{\partial_A\partial_B U_\sigma} ={}& oxed{\mu\sigma d\,  rac{(ND_N)(MD_M)}{(ND_NA+MD_MB)^2}+O(\sigma^2).} \end{aligned} 	ag{9} Here the expansion holds with both degrees and positive currents fixed. The complete finite-\sigma Hessian is the covariance matrix of D_Nu^N and D_Mu^M, multiplied by \mu/\sigma. This supplies an independent numerical calculation of (9) and retains both reciprocal responses. At depth six, ND_N for degrees 12 and 34 has ratio 3515/6=585.8333333. With A=B=\mu=1 and \sigma=0.01, resolved quadrature gives Degree pair Mixed density curvature (12,12) 0.01500002592 (12,34) 0.0001020694543 (34,34) 0.01500000013 The mixed-band value is about 0.00680463 times the equal-band leading value. Therefore the isolated curvature (5) did not establish a universal coupling group for the common action (6). These are local current controls. They are not measured lepton vertices, particle encounter rates or alternative assignments of physical depth. Exact linear mass and amplitude curvature There is also a simple general constraint. If a differentiable stationary branch has E_N(Q)=m_NQ on an open interval of canonical norms, then \omega_N= rac{dE_N}{dQ}=m_N, \qquad  rac{d\omega_N}{dQ}=0. 	ag{10} A nonzero density curvature cannot coexist with that exact linear branch on the same interval. The constraint does not exclude polarization couplings, a physically selected isolated norm or a different stationary branch. It does explain why smoothing the peak generates both a response and a mass correction. The exact entropy energy-frequency defect of (6) must also be retained. The old nonconstant spatial profiles need a solvability test The limiting peak action has an exact family of nonconstant holomorphic fields on the conditional physical CP3 bundle. At unknown physical radius, let X_A be its specified holomorphic tangent field and put w_t=(1,\sqrt t\,X_A,0),\qquad h_t=1+t|X_A|^2,\qquad \phi_{N,t}= rac{w_t^{\otimes N}} {\sqrt{\mathcal V\int h_t^N d
u_Q}},\quad t>0. 	ag{11} The parameter t here scales the spatial section; it is not time. These fields have unit canonical norm. The nonconstant field and its full connection solve the limiting equation, so differentiation in t is an actual zero direction of its stationary Hessian. The first soft energy correction depending on that profile is -\mu d\sigma\int\log|\phi_{N,t}|^2dV. A differentiable small-\sigma stationary continuation approaching a specified member must make its derivative vanish along this zero direction. Set v=|X_A|^2 and Z_t=\int h_t^Nd
u_Q. Direct differentiation, including the physical normalization, gives  rac{d}{dt}\int\log|\phi_{N,t}|^2d
u_Q =N\left[ \int rac{v}{h_t}d
u_Q -\int rac{h_t^N}{Z_t} rac{v}{h_t}d
u_Q ight]<0. 	ag{12} Both h_t^N and v/h_t increase strictly with nonconstant v. Their positive covariance proves the strict sign. Consequently these finite-t nonconstant members fail the first-order stationary solvability condition. Their exact validity for the peak action does not establish their validity for its smooth replacement. The parallel slack field remains an exact smooth-action control. The argument excludes a differentiable continuation to the specified nonconstant member; it does not exclude other spatial profiles, drift to a different limiting member, or singular limits where the field vanishes. The physical CP3 geometry itself remains conditional, with no dimensions compactified. Reconstructing a fixed-order current from a coherent symbol The adjacent-current contact uses exact one- and two-index contractions of the field. A raw coherent symbol does not already equal either contraction. Write r=d+1 and, for one grade, define the raw moments M_k=\int|z^{\otimes k}angle\langle z^{\otimes k}|\, j_{N,z}\,d
u(z),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}M_k=J. 	ag{13} Let ho_1,ho_2 be its actual reduced tensor currents, and let \mathcal S(A) be A\otimes I compressed to the symmetric square. Direct integration of normalized monomials gives  egin{aligned} M_1&= rac{Nho_1+JI}{N+r},\ M_2&= rac{N(N-1)ho_2+4N\mathcal S(ho_1)+2JI_2} {(N+r)(N+r+1)}. \end{aligned} 	ag{14} For example, at ho_1=JP_{e_0} and ho_2=J|e_0^2angle\langle e_0^2|, the three degree sectors of M_2/J have numerators (N+1)(N+2), 2(N+1) and 2 over the common denominator in (14). These are the independent Dirichlet monomial integrals. Covariance and polarization extend the identity to every matrix current, including the full signed scalar current. The trace factors can be checked without a large band: \operatorname{Tr}\mathcal S(A)= rac{r+1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}A, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal S(A)\mathcal S(B)] = rac{(r+2)\operatorname{Tr}(AB)+\operatorname{Tr}A\operatorname{Tr}B}{4}. 	ag{15} Equations (14) are the first two cases of the symmetric-tensor coherent moment identities discussed by Lewin, Nam and Rougerie, Theorem 2.2. Only the tensor identities are used here; that paper's many-particle interpretation is not a premise about constituent particles in IDWT. For N\ge2, the exact inverse is  oxed{  egin{aligned} ho_1&= rac{(N+r)M_1-JI}{N},\ ho_2&= rac{(N+r)(N+r+1)M_2 -4(N+r)\mathcal S(M_1)+2JI_2}{N(N-1)}. \end{aligned} } 	ag{16} These coefficients are fixed by the projection and its normalization. They are not a freedom to fit a separate coupling to each mass band. They nevertheless have to be produced by the proposed master reduction; knowing their inverse formula does not establish that the master action implements it. In particular, applying a fixed raw ray kernel |z^\dagger w|^2-|z^\dagger w|^4 to j_{N,z}j_{M,w} gives \operatorname{Tr}(M_{N,1}M_{M,1})- \operatorname{Tr}(M_{N,2}M_{M,2}). It does not give the adjacent reduced-current action. A finite-band coherent symbol is spread over rays, and this raw action has a nonzero isolated coherent self contact. The corrected contractions (16) cancel it exactly. This identifies a concrete remaining operator problem: derive the normalized low-order current from the same physical master field, with its actual kinetic metric.
