title: Common field response
summary: Eliminating stable response modes of the same field gives a Gram correction to the direct coupling, with exact reciprocity and a proportional-profile criterion for rank one.
text: Summary: Eliminating stable response modes of the same field gives a Gram correction to the direct coupling, with exact reciprocity and a proportional-profile criterion for rank one. Direct coupling and reduction of one field IDWT has one field \Psi_\infty and no mediator particles. Its cross-sector interactions belong to that field's own action. Start with a specified background and independent real coordinates for its admissible variations in a finite region: \delta\Psi_\infty=S_{\rm r}j+S_{\rm s}X. Here j describes retained variations and X describes other variations of the same field. The maps must respect the actual spatial embeddings, constraints, and normalization. Real coordinates may describe a complex classical field or a specified mean-field energy; they add no physical dimensions. Independent variations do not imply separate physical fields. At a stationary background, the energy's second variation has blocks E^{(2)}=\frac12\langle j,H_{\rm rr}j\rangle +\langle X,H_{\rm sr}j\rangle+\frac12\langle X,LX\rangle, \qquad H_{\rm rs}=H_{\rm sr}^{*}. Set B=-H_{\rm sr}. Thus both the direct block H_{\rm rr} and the response source Bj are derived from the same Hessian. A physical application must calculate these blocks; specifying them as a benchmark does not derive them from IDWT. Constraints and any zero modes must be handled before an inverse is taken. For retained source currents j_d on a finite collection of nested sectors, a source term \sum_dB_dj_d is a further specified reduction of this one-field energy. Each map includes spatial identifications, measures, and polarization contractions. Its range is a real space \mathcal H of response profiles of the same field. Nonlinear bilinear currents require the corresponding expansion and variations; they are not automatically identical to the linear coordinates above. Assume a fixed positive self-adjoint stiffness L\ge\ell_0 I>0 on \mathcal H and sources for which L^{-1/2}B_dj_d exist. Work in a finite region with stated boundary conditions, or on a domain where these operator assumptions hold. An operator with zero modes requires a separate constraint, boundary, or limiting treatment. For this conditional response reduction, write E[X,j]=E_{\rm direct}[j]+\frac12\langle X,LX\rangle -\left\langle X,\sum_dB_dj_d\right\rangle. \tag{1} The currents and all maps use a specified common unit convention. Field normalization acts on every leg of a current as explained in Canonical coupling normalization. Exact elimination and reciprocity Set S=\sum_dB_dj_d. Completing the square gives E=E_{\rm direct} +\frac12\|L^{1/2}(X-L^{-1}S)\|^2 -\frac12\langle S,L^{-1}S\rangle. At fixed sources the unique minimizing response is X_*=L^{-1}S. The eliminated energy and its blocks are therefore E_{\rm eff}=E_{\rm direct}-\frac12\sum_{a,b} \langle j_a,G_{ab}j_b\rangle,\qquad G_{ab}=B_a^*L^{-1}B_b,\qquad G_{ba}=G_{ab}^*. \tag{2} The induced source potential is -\sum_bG_{ab}j_b, including the sign from (1). In the quadratic case the complete retained Hessian is H_{\rm eff}=H_{\rm rr}-B^*L^{-1}B. The Gram expression is a response correction, not the entire direct interaction. The full energy must still control stability as sources vary; positivity of the response stiffness alone does not do that. Different physical interaction channels can have different signs, constraints, derivative vertices, and tensor contractions. Equations (1)–(2) give every pair in this correction from the same field-response operator and source maps. There is no independently adjustable coefficient for each pair in the correction once B_d and L have been specified. There can still be sector parameters inside B_d: a reduction in pairwise freedom is not their derivation. Rank measures independent response profiles Collect B=(B_1,\ldots,B_N) and define C=L^{-1/2}B. Then G=C^*C,\qquad \langle j,Gj\rangle=\|Cj\|^2\ge0,\qquad \ker G=\ker C. \tag{3} On a finite retained source space, \operatorname{rank}G=\operatorname{rank}C. It is bounded by the number of independent response modes of the field to which the retained sources couple. One field has many spatial modes, so one field does not force this rank to be one. For one fixed, normalized source profile f_d in each sector, let b_d=B_df_d and v_d=L^{-1/2}b_d. The pair numbers are g_{ab}=\langle v_a,v_b\rangle,\qquad |g_{ab}|^2\le g_{aa}g_{bb}. \tag{4} This is Cauchy–Schwarz in the response metric. If g_{aa}=0, then v_a=0 and g_{ab}=0 for every b in this channel. Vanishing coupling to one particular other source only establishes orthogonality to that source's response, not absence from the whole channel. When g_{aa},g_{bb}>0, equality in (4) holds precisely when v_a,v_b are proportional. The complete nonzero matrix has rank one precisely when all nonzero response profiles lie on one common line: v_d=\alpha_d v,\qquad g_{ab}=\alpha_a\alpha_b\|v\|^2. \tag{5} For complex channel amplitudes, transpose becomes Hermitian adjoint, and the last product is \overline{\alpha_a}\alpha_b\|v\|^2. The rank and inequality statements are unchanged. Thus a factorization B_d=\alpha_d\widetilde B_d of bare coefficients is insufficient for (5); the \widetilde B_df_d must generate the same spatial response up to scale. This is the exact additional condition needed by a common-anchor response. That note's subsequent conversion of source potentials to occupied mass poles still needs its kinetic and reference-count factors. Its displayed positive current-current energy also differs in sign from the negative term induced by (1). The shared rank criterion does not identify the two actions: an application must derive the interaction sign and the physical mass branch as well as the profile factorization. These positivity and rank statements concern the static scalar response in (1). They are not universal inequalities for the sum of all gauge, gravitational, and matter interaction coefficients. A direct matter term can change the total quadratic form. Spatial example across all depths Choose a shared spatial chart \mathbb R^s, s\le d, and normalized sector densities \rho_d(x,y)=p_{\sigma_d}(x)f_d(y),\quad \int f_d\,dy=1,\quad p_\sigma(x)=\frac{e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{s/2}}. Take source image b_d=h_d p_{\sigma_d} and the local stiffness L=\kappa I, \kappa>0. This is a declared static contact benchmark, not a derived electromagnetic or weak response law. The exact overlap is g_{ab}=\frac{h_ah_b}{\kappa} \frac{1}{[2\pi(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2)]^{s/2}}, \qquad g_{aa}=\frac{h_a^2}{\kappa(4\pi\sigma_a^2)^{s/2}}. \tag{6} For nonzero h_a,h_b, the magnitude of the normalized correlation is \frac{|g_{ab}|}{\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}} =\left(\frac{2\sigma_a\sigma_b}{\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2}\right)^{s/2}. \tag{7} The Gaussian integral can be evaluated one coordinate at a time. The inequality 2\sigma_a\sigma_b\le\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2 proves (4) explicitly, with equality exactly at equal widths. Displaced centers multiply (7) by \exp[-|x_a-x_b|^2/(2(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_b^2))]. Shared preparation Coupling consequence Equal marginal, any normalized containing fibre No multiplicative dependence on the containing depth Same center and width \lvert g_{ab}\rvert/\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}=1 \sigma_b=2\sigma_a, s=3 \lvert g_{ab}\rvert/\sqrt{g_{aa}g_{bb}}=(4/5)^{3/2} h_a=0 in this channel g_{ab}=0 for every b in this channel For finitely many distinct positive widths, these centered Gaussians are linearly independent: along a radial line their exponentials have distinct decay rates, and the slowest-decaying term in any putative vanishing linear combination must have zero coefficient; repeat. Their Gram matrix is therefore strictly positive definite. A single scalar response component of the field can produce full rank among these preparations. Equal widths with differing containing depths instead give (5), including for the assigned depths 3,4,5,6,10 whenever the same shared marginal and vertex are chosen. Depth five is not singled out by this geometric contact model. A neutral sector's suppression has to enter through its derived channel map, not an arbitrary factor of five. Retarded response and a controlled static limit For linearized equations of the same field, let D(\omega) be their operator in retained and remaining coordinates. Wherever the retarded inverse of D_{\rm ss} exists, eliminating the remaining coordinates gives the exact block expression D_{\rm eff}(\omega)=D_{\rm rr}(\omega) -D_{\rm rs}(\omega)D_{\rm ss}^{-1}(\omega)D_{\rm sr}(\omega). The inverse is a response kernel for field evolution. This step assumes no exchanged particles. Both the blocks and their causal boundary conditions come from the original equations. If that reduction yields harmonic response coordinates with positive inertia M, their equation is M\ddot X+LX=S(t). With Fourier convention e^{-i\omega t} and retarded boundary conditions, G_{ab}^{R}(\omega) =B_a^*\left[L-(\omega+i0)^2M\right]^{-1}B_b. \tag{8} For real reciprocal coefficients its transpose reverses source indices at the same frequency. Above accessible resonances it need not be a positive static Gram matrix. An instantaneous interaction is the low-frequency approximation to this specified response, not proof of instantaneous physical signalling. In a finite-mode model put A=L^{-1/2}ML^{-1/2} and C=L^{-1/2}B. For \epsilon=\omega^2\|A\|<1, the Neumann series gives G(\omega)=C^*(I-\omega^2A)^{-1}C,\qquad \|G(\omega)-G(0)\| \le \|C\|^2\frac{\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}. \tag{9} This states when one static coupling matrix approximates the dynamic response. The field stiffness, inertia, and source maps must be derived before treating the resulting frequency dependence as a particle prediction. Related and verification Generalized sector coupling — combines spatial reciprocity, normalization, and channel tests. Neutrino channel control — distinguishes a vanishing interaction term from suppressed field response. Cross-sector moment kernel — an existing example in which coordinate tensors obstruct automatic factorization. Gaussian contact profiles — derives the more general covariance and displacement overlap. generalized_coupling_checks.py independently minimizes response energies, checks source gradients and response ranks, integrates the Gaussian profiles, and tests (9) against the full frequency-dependent inverse.

title: One spatial kernel on a projective chain
summary: A single bounded spatial moment kernel gives reciprocal full-spinor Dirac equations on specified nested projective sectors, with conserved norms, global evolution and no independent interaction coefficient for each pair.
text: Summary: A single bounded spatial moment kernel gives reciprocal full-spinor Dirac equations on specified nested projective sectors, with conserved norms, global evolution and no independent interaction coefficient for each pair. A declared common spatial action Consider any finite nested family of linear projective spatial submanifolds inside one specified containing projective space. Their metric, embeddings and spin or Spin^c connections are fixed. These are ordinary physical spatial directions within the same manifold; no dimension is compactified. The projective geometry and its physical scale remain conditional inputs. This finite family is a partial chain of even-dimensional submanifolds. The intermediate-depth calculation shows why it cannot automatically be filled in at every ordinary spatial depth: for example, the standard CP3-to-CP5 inclusion admits no seven- or nine-dimensional intermediate submanifold. The pair action below remains conditional on its specified partial family; it does not complete the geometry of the full hierarchy. For each family d, let \psi_d be its complete spatial spinor and D_d its self-adjoint Dirac operator, with chirality involution \beta_d. Use canonical positive kinetic norms. This specifies an orthogonal decomposition of retained mode families of the one field and the additive scalar source below. If another decomposition has cross kinetic or cross-current terms, those terms must be retained rather than inferred away from spatial nesting; see canonical normalization. Let i_d embed the spatial sector in the common projective space and put P_X=XX^\dagger/(X^\dagger X). Specify the same kernel everywhere: \boxed{K(X,Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_XP_Y) =\frac{|X^\dagger Y|^2}{|X|^2|Y|^2}.} \tag{1} There is no dimension-dependent multiplier in (1). Its unit-FS integral on CPm is 1/(m+1), which follows from the geometry. Normalizing it separately to one at every depth would change the common kernel. Using each sector's physical spatial measure, define \sigma_d=\psi_d^\dagger\beta_d\psi_d,\qquad M_d=\int P_{i_d(x)}\sigma_d(x)\,d\mathrm{vol}_d(x),\qquad M=\sum_dM_d. \tag{2} The matrices M_d are moments of the same field's scalar currents. They are not extra spatial dimensions, independent dynamical fields or mediator particles. The complete energy is \boxed{E=\sum_d\langle\psi_d,D_d\psi_d\rangle +\frac\kappa2\operatorname{Tr}M^2.} \tag{3} Writing Q_d=\|\psi_d\|^2, the single coefficient has units [\kappa]=[E]/[Q_d]^2. A common radius can be used to express time and \kappa dimensionlessly. No separate self or pair coefficient is fitted. This is a specified reduction to test, not a derivation of (1)–(3) from the master action. Scalar bilinears make the interaction globally defined without a spinor-to-spinor bundle identification between different sectors. It describes scalar-current interaction, not a particle-changing vertex. The normal spinor factors remain relevant when such a vertex or a nonscalar current is proposed. The interaction in (3) is spatially nonlocal and instantaneous: every potential uses the other sources at the same time. Its mathematical well-posedness below does not establish relativistic causal propagation. A physical use as an effective interaction requires a controlled reduction of local master-field dynamics, with the omitted propagation times and response frequencies specified. The local-current causality test now gives smooth, norm-preserving separated initial data for which this instantaneous equation changes the target's current derivative immediately. The spatial harmonic comparison identifies the kernel as a specific low-harmonic truncation, and shows why the direct term and signed induced response of local Dirac dynamics do not yet derive it. Both complete spatial responses Varying (3), including the dependence of every moment on its field, gives \boxed{i\partial_t\psi_d =\left[D_d+\kappa\operatorname{Tr}(P_{i_d(x)}M)\beta_d\right]\psi_d.} \tag{4} For two families, the cross energy is \kappa\operatorname{Tr}(M_aM_b). The response of either family uses the other one's same moment matrix. In particular, the lower response and the higher response contain the weighted marginal and its adjoint; the higher-dimensional potential is a smooth function on its full space. Every spinor component and relative phase within each field remains in (4). This particular additive scalar-current action has an independent overall phase symmetry for each family. Consequently Q_d=\|\psi_d\|^2 is separately conserved, while energy can move between the families. These phase norms have not been assigned physical electric charges. For static geometry, (3) is conserved on sufficiently regular solutions. The entire construction is covariant under a common projective isometry of the fields and all embeddings: P\mapsto UPU^\dagger and M\mapsto UMU^\dagger. Rotating one source while holding its physical embedding fixed is a different configuration, not this covariance test. Global evolution follows from the conserved norms The signed scalar current satisfies |\sigma_d|\le|\psi_d|^2. Hence, with Q_{\rm tot}=\sum_dQ_d, \boxed{\|M\|_{\rm op}\le Q_{\rm tot},\qquad |\kappa\operatorname{Tr}(P_XM)|\le|\kappa|Q_{\rm tot}.} \tag{5} On the direct sum of the sector L^2 spaces, write the nonlinear part of (4) as F(\psi). For two fields in the ball of squared norm at most Q_*, the moment difference obeys \|M(\psi)-M(\phi)\|_{\rm op} \le(\|\psi\|+\|\phi\|)\|\psi-\phi\|. Adding and subtracting the potential of \psi acting on \phi gives \boxed{\|F(\psi)-F(\phi)\| \le3|\kappa|Q_*\|\psi-\phi\|.} \tag{6} The free Dirac group is unitary. Its Duhamel equation with the locally Lipschitz nonlinearity (6) therefore has a unique local mild L^2 solution. Conservation of the positive norms keeps it in the same ball, so it extends for all finite times. The norm identity can first be proved for smooth approximations and then passed to their L^2 limit. Smooth initial fields remain smooth. All spatial derivatives of the potential are bounded by a geometry-dependent constant times |\kappa|Q_{\rm tot}, because it is a finite linear combination of smooth projective moment functions. Standard differentiated energy estimates bound every fixed Sobolev norm on finite time intervals. This argument concerns the complete spinor equations, independently of a finite-mode approximation or a profile symmetry. Global existence is not stability of a particular particle. The spatial Dirac energy has both signs; (5) does not supply an orbital stability theorem or a preferred occupied mode. Spatial phase information changes subsequent interaction For a fixed scalar test function f, the scalar moment is m_f=\langle\psi,f\beta\psi\rangle. On a regular solution, \boxed{\dot m_f=i\langle\psi,[D,f\beta]\psi\rangle.} \tag{7} The nonlinear term cancels from this first derivative because two scalar multiplication operators times \beta commute. It changes the field and therefore changes later values of (7). A holomorphic or other finite projection can alter this commutator, so its moment flow must not be substituted for the uncompressed spatial equation. The spatially varying relative phase between even and odd form components is consequential. Multiplying all odd components by e^{i\theta} leaves the instantaneous scalar density unchanged, but generally changes (7). Opposite phase preparations can therefore have identical initial scalar interaction overlap and different subsequent responses. The full spatial pair calculation supplies an explicit example and checks its coordinate residuals. Relation to the single-sector kernel and mass question On a single CP3 sector, (1) is one quarter of the normalized kernel in the smooth moment-contact calculation. That conversion must be included when using its stationary solver. For general complex dimension m, its normalized-kernel strength is \kappa Q/(m+1) in common radius units. A normalized coherent holomorphic section of degree L on a projective subspace with projector P_A has M=Q\frac{P_A+LP_z}{L+m+1},\qquad \boxed{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}M^2}{Q^2} =\frac{(L+1)^2+m}{(L+m+1)^2}\le1.} \tag{8} Thus this fixed bounded kernel does not itself produce an unbounded simplex mass multiplier. Its constructive role is a common, reciprocal, well-defined spatial interaction whose field response can be tested. Its derivation, physical scale, occupied patterns and observed electric and weak channels remain separate requirements. Verification projective_spatial_pair.py implements the same action and both full complex source derivatives in an exact spatial symmetry class. projective_spatial_pair_checks.py checks the ordinary and conjugate response, canonical kinetic forms, independent coordinate equations, conserved norms and energy, and refined spatial pair trajectories. The global existence argument above is analytic and does not follow merely from successful finite evolution.

title: Complete scalar response and null directions
summary: The complete local scalar-source derivative is invertible at nonzero scalar density, while a scalar-null field retains one real response direction whose kinetic protection and projected channel meaning must be tested separately.
text: Summary: The complete local scalar-source derivative is invertible at nonzero scalar density, while a scalar-null field retains one real response direction whose kinetic protection and projected channel meaning must be tested separately. Source response is distinct from a projected vertex At a physical spatial point, consider the written scalar contribution \mathcal N(\phi)=g s\beta\phi,\qquad s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi,\qquad \rho=\phi^\dagger\phi, \tag{1} with real g, Hermitian \beta^2=I, and the full spinor fiber retained. The invariants obey |s|\le\rho. They are scalar and positive densities over ordinary physical space; spinor components do not introduce more spatial dimensions. The complete derivative is \boxed{J_\phi\eta=D\mathcal N(\phi)\eta =g\left[s\beta\eta+2\beta\phi\, \operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\beta\eta)\right].} \tag{2} This note determines its entire pointwise response spectrum. It does not assert that every projected particle vertex is nonzero. A vertex includes spatial wavefunctions, an output projection, kinetic normalization and the appropriate current channel. Also, J_\phi is only the nonlinear source derivative: the complete rotating-frame operator includes D-\mu. Its symmetry zero modes or cancellations are not excluded by an invertible J_\phi alone. Exact real response spectrum Let \beta have p\ge1 positive and q\ge1 negative complex directions, with n=p+q. Regard the complex fiber as a real 2n-dimensional Hilbert space with inner product \operatorname{Re}(\eta^\dagger\xi). Writing v=\beta\phi, equation (2) is the real symmetric operator \boxed{J_\phi=g\left(s\beta+2v\otimes_{\mathbb R}v\right).} \tag{3} The real Hessian of the energy density g s^2/2 is 2J_\phi; the factor two follows from \delta E=2\operatorname{Re} (\mathcal N^\dagger\delta\phi). The rank-one term in (3) is real-linear, not a complex-linear rank-one operator acting alone. Diagonalize \beta and use unitary changes within its two eigenspaces to put \phi=(a,b) in one real direction of each, where a^2=\frac{\rho+s}{2},\qquad b^2=\frac{\rho-s}{2}. The remaining real directions give g s with multiplicity 2p-1 and -g s with multiplicity 2q-1. On the two displayed real directions, J_\phi/g is \begin{pmatrix} 3a^2-b^2&-2ab\\-2ab&-a^2+3b^2 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} Its trace is 2\rho and determinant is -3s^2. Thus the full spectrum is \boxed{g s\ (2p-1),\quad -g s\ (2q-1),\quad g\left(\rho+\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}\right),\quad g\left(\rho-\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}\right).} \tag{5} The multiplicities in parentheses count real directions. Formula (5) also has the correct pure-chirality limits |s|=\rho. No spatial-depth counting identity changes this pointwise spectrum. Nonzero scalar density leaves no full source kernel If g\ne0 and s\ne0, every eigenvalue in (5) is nonzero. In particular, \boxed{\det_{\mathbb R}J_\phi=3g^{2n}s^{2n},} \tag{6} and the exact real-linear inverse is \boxed{J_\phi^{-1}\xi=\frac1{g s} \left[\beta\xi-\frac{2\phi}{3s} \operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\xi)\right].} \tag{7} Substitution in (2) verifies (7). Equivalently, apply the rank-one inverse identity to sI+2\phi\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\beta\,\cdot), whose rank-one functional takes value 2s on \phi. For example, suppose \phi^\dagger\beta\eta=0. The scalar itself has zero first variation in that direction, but the full source still changes by g s\beta\eta. Freezing the final field factor would erase this term and create an artificial nullspace. The nonlinear map has a related exact invariant: \omega=\mathcal N(\phi)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega^\dagger\beta\omega=g^2s^3. \tag{8} For nonzero output scalar t=\omega^\dagger\beta\omega, take the real cube root s=(t/g^2)^{1/3} and recover \phi=\beta\omega/(g s). The scalar-null input cone maps to zero. A nonzero scalar-null output does not occur in the image of this local cubic map. A small scalar does not suppress every response The exact smallest singular value in the canonical real metric is \boxed{s_{\min}(J_\phi)=|g| \left(\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}-\rho\right) =\frac{3|g|s^2}{\sqrt{\rho^2+3s^2}+\rho}.} \tag{9} The second expression avoids subtractive numerical cancellation. It is no greater than |g s|, because |s|\le\rho. For 0<|s|\ll\rho, the weakest response is approximately 3|g|s^2/(2\rho), but the largest is approximately 2|g|\rho. |s|/\rho, with g=\rho=1 Smallest singular value Largest singular value 1 1 3 0.1 0.0148892 2.0148892 0.01 0.000149989 2.000149989 0 0 2 Near cancellation of the background scalar can therefore leave a very weak direction and a strong direction simultaneously. It is insufficient to explain universal rare interaction without specifying the actual incident and observed spatial channels. If a spatial perturbation is supported where |s(x)|\ge s_*>0 and \rho(x)\le\rho_{\max}, integrating (9) gives \|J_\phi\eta\|_{L^2}\ge |g|\left(\sqrt{\rho_{\max}^2+3s_*^2}-\rho_{\max}\right) \|\eta\|_{L^2}. \tag{10} This is a full-source estimate on the stated support. A localized field generally has s\to0 in its tails, so (10) must not be promoted to a uniform gap over all space. For a complete orthonormal output family f_a, Parseval gives \sum_a|\langle f_a,J_\phi\eta\rangle|^2=\|J_\phi\eta\|^2. A selected channel can still vanish, and a finite output band can miss the response altogether. Counting that band is not a substitute for evaluating its spatial projection. What the rank-one null response actually means At s=0 and \rho>0, \boxed{\mathcal N(\phi)=0,\qquad J_\phi=2g(\beta\phi)\otimes_{\mathbb R}(\beta\phi).} \tag{11} The complete source derivative has one real responsive direction and 2n-1 real null directions. In particular, J_\phi(\beta\phi)=2g\rho\beta\phi. A zero background self-source therefore does not mean an absence of interaction with a probe. This rank-one operator also does not provide an occupied-ray self-contact. Let P_\phi=\phi\phi^\dagger/\rho. At scalar nullity, \phi^\dagger\beta\phi=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_\phi J_\phi=0. \tag{12} Its responsive direction is orthogonal to the occupied complex ray. Projecting onto that ray removes the response. The rank-one source derivative cannot be identified with a nonzero mass operator on the occupied ray. The graph-contact variation likewise distinguishes an occupied coefficient from the complete field-dependent response; its graph kernel and normalization are separate specified ingredients. Spatial kinetics can activate an initially null scalar The exact zero crossings of local polarized pulses use their actual traveling solutions and full spatial compatibility. Nullity of the scalar at one time alone does not impose that dynamics. A simple control uses two ordinary spatial directions x,y, with anticommuting \alpha_x,\alpha_y,\beta. Choose a unit initial spinor \phi_0 satisfying \alpha_x\phi_0=\phi_0,\qquad \alpha_y\phi_0=-i\beta\phi_0. \tag{13} The full plane field \Psi(t,y)=e^{iky}\phi(t) obeys i\dot\phi=(k\alpha_y+g s\beta)\phi,\qquad s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi, \tag{14} and begins with s(0)=0, \rho=1. Direct differentiation gives \dot s(0)=-2k, independently of g. The actual transverse kinetic term immediately produces a scalar source. This is an unbound plane control per unit volume. The preparation in (13) mixes both signs of the free energy associated with its actual momentum along y; it is not proposed as a positive-energy particle state. An eigenplane with \alpha_y\phi_0=\phi_0 instead has an invariant scalar zero and solves the full equation as a free positive-frequency wave. The difference is the occupied kinetic mode, not scalar nullity alone. For completeness, the nonlinear scalar evolution in (14) closes exactly. On the invariant two-component plane use \alpha_x=\sigma_z, \alpha_y=-\sigma_y, \beta=\sigma_x. Writing v=\langle\sigma_y\rangle, w=\langle\sigma_z\rangle, the conserved energy is -kv+g s^2/2=0 and \dot s=-2kw. The Bloch equations therefore imply \boxed{\ddot s+4k^2s+2g^2s^3=0,\qquad s(0)=0,\quad\dot s(0)=-2k,} \tag{15} \dot s^2+4k^2s^2+g^2s^4=4k^2. \tag{16} For k>0, its amplitude is \boxed{|s|_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{2k}{\sqrt{k^2+g^2}+k}}.} \tag{17} At g=0, s(t)=-\sin(2kt). This exact source activation occurs with conserved positive norm and conserved total energy; the scalar term has not introduced an external driving field or a mediator particle. Consequence for physical coupling tests The classification of scalar-null fields identifies constant linear preparations whose zero source survives every spatial derivative. The full null-plane response separately determines whether perturbations outside an exact zero-source background stay bounded. Its stability threshold shows why invariance alone is insufficient. The local scalar term admits real source nullspaces at particular fields and exact mismatched traveling solutions. Its nonzero-scalar response is nevertheless full rank before projection, and its null cone is not invariant under arbitrary spatial motion. A protected physical suppression therefore requires the actual occupied solution, its full kinetic evolution and the derived channel map. These statements do not establish electric neutrality or eliminate weak vertices. The neutrino channel control keeps those physical requirements separate. No special depth-five zero, band-independent mass coefficient or observed rate follows from (5) or (11). Verification local_scalar_response_rank_checks.py runs 2,116 checks. title: Complete spatial polarization data
summary: Complete spatial Clifford tensors retain the amplitudes and phases of a polarized field, exposing information that a circulation tensor captures at six dimensions but can omit at ten.
text: Summary: Complete spatial Clifford tensors retain the amplitudes and phases of a polarized field, exposing information that a circulation tensor captures at six dimensions but can omit at ten. Begin with the full oscillating field For a monochromatic vector with complex amplitude a+ib, where a,b are real spatial vectors, E(t)=\operatorname{Re}[(a+ib)e^{-i\omega t}] =a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t. \tag{1} Its trajectory lies in \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{a,b\}, even when the containing physical space has many dimensions. The squared ellipse axes are the eigenvalues of \begin{pmatrix}|a|^2&a\cdot b\\a\cdot b&|b|^2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} Parallel a,b give linear polarization; orthogonal equal-length a,b give circular polarization. More spatial dimensions permit more plane orientations. A field with several modes, spatially varying amplitudes or different frequencies has further structure which (1) does not describe. The Dirac polarization waves give an exact multimode example with a shared scalar source and changing spatial currents. For a particle field, the allowed components must come from its actual spatial equation. In a fixed degenerate spatial multiplet, write \Psi_z(x,t)=e^{-iMt}W(x)z,\qquad \int W^\dagger W\,dx=I_N,\qquad z^\dagger z=1. \tag{3} The spatial Dirac construction supplies examples where W(x) includes both radial components and all bound coordinates. The coefficients z describe the polarization of this field. Their number is not the number of physical spatial dimensions. All x coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions in the one nested manifold. Equation (3) is a fixed-multiplet description. It does not assert that every physical particle has that profile, or that its other spatial modes can be discarded. Retain amplitudes and relative phases without selecting one tensor The matrix \varrho=zz^\dagger,\qquad \varrho^\dagger=\varrho,\quad \varrho^2=\varrho,\quad \operatorname{tr}\varrho=1 \tag{4} retains every relative amplitude and phase in z. It removes only the common constant phase. For any operator O on the multiplet, \langle O\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho O). \tag{5} A common phase relative to another coherent field must still be retained in the combined field and its transition terms. Likewise, replacing z by a position-dependent phase cannot be justified by (4); its derivatives enter the spatial equation, as shown in Spatial polarization textures. To express (4) as spatial tensors, choose Hermitian Euclidean Clifford matrices \gamma_i, satisfying \{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I. They describe how the field transforms under rotations of its actual spatial coordinates. For even depth use one specified chiral representation; for odd depth use the stated irreducible spin representation. Define the Hermitian spatial operators B_{ij}=-i\gamma_i\gamma_j,\qquad C_{ijkl}=\gamma_i\gamma_j\gamma_k\gamma_l, \qquad i<j<k<l. \tag{6} Restriction to the selected chiral space is understood. Their expectation values are the two-form J_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho B_{ij}) and four-form K_{ijkl}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho C_{ijkl}). Count and verify a complete operator basis At the depths below, the listed operators \Gamma_A form a complete Hermitian basis on the indicated polarization multiplet: physical spatial depth complex components N complete operator grades number of operators 3 2 scalar and two-form 1+3=4 5 4 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+10+5=16 6, one chirality 4 scalar and two-form 1+15=16 10, one chirality 16 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+45+210=256 In five dimensions a four-form is dual to a vector in those same five spatial directions. The table counts descriptions of fields, not additional spatial coordinates or independent particles. The Clifford trace identities give \operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_A\Gamma_B)=N\delta_{AB}. \tag{7} To see why the stated grades suffice, products of distinct Clifford generators are trace-orthogonal unless their index sets agree or are related by the top-dimensional duality. In an irreducible odd-dimensional module, the top product is scalar; on an even-dimensional chiral module it is fixed by chirality. The table selects one representative of each dual pair. Its N^2 orthogonal operators span the entire N\times N matrix algebra. Consequently \boxed{\varrho=\frac1N\sum_A \operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)\Gamma_A.} \tag{8} The scalar coefficient is one. For a single normalized coherent polarization, purity also gives \sum_{A\ne0}\operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)^2=N-1. \tag{9} The coefficients are constrained by the full equation \varrho^2=\varrho; (9) alone is insufficient. Mixtures obey (8) too, but must satisfy positivity and have \operatorname{tr}\varrho^2\le1. At six dimensions, J therefore determines the entire polarization matrix within the selected four-component multiplet: \boxed{\varrho_6=\frac14\left(I+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}B_{ij}\right).} \tag{10} For a pure ray, its J satisfies J^2=-I_6. One way to establish this for every ray is to note that the fifteen traceless B_{ij} span the Hermitian generators of SU(4). Their spin representation acts transitively on the rays, and rotates J as a physical two-form. A reference ray has three unit orthogonal planes; rotating it preserves J^2=-I_6. Arbitrary complex coefficients in this fixed chiral multiplet already include all its constant polarizations. Additional six-dimensional complexity must also consider other spatial modes and textures. At ten dimensions the complete expression is instead \boxed{\varrho_{10}=\frac1{16} \left(I+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}B_{ij} +\sum_{i<j<k<l}K_{ijkl}C_{ijkl}\right).} \tag{11} The circulation tensor alone can lose relative-phase information. An explicit ten-dimensional coherent family Construct five fermionic matrix pairs a_j=(\gamma_{2j-1}+i\gamma_{2j})/2. Let |0\rangle be their common vacuum and |1234\rangle=a_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_4^\dagger|0\rangle, with its phase fixed so that \langle0|C_{1357}|1234\rangle=1. These are basis labels for components of one spatial field, not constituent particles or extra coordinates. The normalized same-chirality family \boxed{z_{\eta,\theta} =\cos\eta\,|0\rangle+e^{i\theta}\sin\eta\,|1234\rangle} \tag{12} has \boxed{J=\operatorname{diag} (\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,J_2), \quad \lambda=\cos2\eta,\quad J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.} \tag{13} Every off-diagonal occupation transition in a two-form changes at most two matrix occupations, so it cannot connect the two components in (12). The diagonal two-forms are 1-2a_j^\dagger a_j, giving (13). The four-form does connect them: \boxed{K_{1357}=\sin2\eta\cos\theta.} \tag{14} Thus \theta can change the field polarization without changing any component of J. At \eta=\pi/4, the fields with \theta=0,\pi are orthogonal, yet have exactly the same J. Every vector in (12) is a pure coherent state in the sense of (4). The term Cartan-pure spinor imposes a separate algebraic condition: the complex spatial vectors v satisfying \gamma(v)z=0 span a maximal five-dimensional complex annihilator. The vacuum has that property; for 0<\eta\le\pi/4, (12) has only a one-dimensional complex annihilator. Indeed, write a general complex Clifford vector as \sum_j(u_j a_j+v_j a_j^\dagger). Acting on (12), its one-occupation terms force every v_j=0, while its three-occupation terms force u_1=\cdots=u_4=0. Both coefficients in (12) are nonzero in this range, and the distinct occupation grades cannot cancel each other. Only a_5 remains. On the vacuum, all five a_j annihilate the field coefficient. This complex algebraic test concerns combinations of the existing spatial directions. It does not remove real physical directions from the particle. The Clifford construction and distinction between pure and general spinors provide a mathematical comparison; (7)–(14) are checked directly here. Even a two-form interaction can read the additional information Let a specified complex spatial rotation pattern act through O_f=\sum_A f_A B_A, where A labels coordinate planes. For a pure polarization, its component orthogonal to the initial mode has squared norm \boxed{\|(I-\varrho)O_fz\|^2=f^\dagger\mathcal V f,\qquad \mathcal V_{AB}=z^\dagger B_AB_Bz-J_AJ_B.} \tag{15} This is a positive response matrix. It retains relative phases in the incoming pattern f as well as the occupied field z. For disjoint ordered planes, B_{ij}B_{kl}=-C_{ijkl}. Shared indices instead reduce to a two-form, and identical planes give the identity. Consequently the response to a two-form probe can depend on four-form polarization data even though its mean source depends only on J. No additional four-form interaction term is required for this distinction. Equal-current spatial polarizations constructs the full bound fields and a reciprocal six-inside-ten example. The periodic polarization test supplies the corresponding approach when complete field resolvents and sidebands are needed. Neither an instantaneous response norm nor this operator classification is a physical scattering rate. Verification spatial_polarization_structure_checks.py constructs all the actual matrices and verifies their full trace Gram matrices, reconstruction of arbitrary complex rays and mixtures, the ten-dimensional phase family and its Clifford annihilators. Independent operator products check the response in (15). Reports are timestamped and checks remain active under Python optimization.

summary: The complete normal source has a derived common endpoint response but drives a zero-cost geometric deformation, so the linked radial profile is not yet a stationary occupied particle.
text: The bounded connected carrier gives a concrete spatial frequency operator. Its occupied wave also supplies a reciprocal source for the supporting texture and connection. Computing both sources reveals a useful common response and a remaining dynamical constraint: the wave drives a genuine deformation along which the proposed geometric functional is constant. Thus solving the geometry without its occupied wave does not yet give a stationary particle. The calculation concerns the linked normal operator on an ordinary unbounded plane. All spinor and canonical-pair components are retained. The coefficients have not been assigned an independent physical interaction field or a physical energy separate from the one IDWT field. The forces below are model derivatives in the stated units, not measured couplings or encounter rates. Complete normal response Write the full field as psi=Phi+eta/Lambda+O(Lambda^(-2)), where Phi contains the complete n-mode kernel and both canonical components. The first complementary equation is D\eta=(\omega-V)\Phi,\qquad \eta\perp\ker D. \tag{1} For the connected profile, the positive-chiral radial inverses are \begin{aligned} K_{j,+}&=-\partial_r^2-r^{-1}\partial_r +(j-n+a/2)^2/r^2+1,\\ K_{j,-}&=-\partial_r^2-r^{-1}\partial_r +(j+1-a/2)^2/r^2+1. \end{aligned} \tag{2} These are the complete radial operators for each forced angular label. They replace both the earlier monomial scalar inverse and the bounded unconnected two-component inverse. Regular origin conditions and decaying outer conditions select their inverses. The weighted polarization source also has the exact inverse given in the carrier note. At leading nonzero order, the sources of the normal coefficients are \begin{aligned} \mathcal J_W&=\sum_\chi\left[ \Phi_\chi^\dagger(\Gamma_1+i\Gamma_2)\eta_\chi+ \eta_\chi^\dagger(\Gamma_1+i\Gamma_2)\Phi_\chi\right],\\ \mathcal J_{A_i}&=\operatorname{Re}\sum_\chi \Phi_\chi^\dagger\alpha_i\tau_3\eta_\chi. \end{aligned} \tag{3} The factor Lambda multiplying the normal operator cancels the factor 1/Lambda in the field correction. One must additionally vary the explicit bounded polarization term whenever a changes. Its leading contribution is one half of Phi^dagger S chi_1 Phi times delta a. An independent radial check replaces w(r),a(r) by w(s r),a(s r), leaving h(r) fixed. Recomputing every normal mode and projected frequency gives the same derivative as integrating (3), including the explicit polarization variation. At depth six the relative frequency derivative is about 1.1915 for both assigned branches. Keeping only W would miss most of this response; the connection supplies a substantial contribution. Deform the linked geometry itself The full planar geometric rule can be written with a holomorphic polynomial P and a real function u: W=e^{-u}P(z),\qquad \boldsymbol A=\nabla^\perp u, \qquad \Delta u=2(1-e^{-2u}|P|^2). \tag{4} The radial reference has P=z^n and a=r u'. Move along this same rule with P=z^n+epsilon z^(n-k), where 1<=k<=n. For real epsilon, write delta u=f_k(r) cos(k theta). Linearizing (4) gives \boxed{ \left[-\partial_r^2-r^{-1}\partial_r+k^2/r^2+4w^2\right]f_k =4w^2 r^{-k}.} \tag{5} The solution is regular as r^k at zero and approaches r^(-k) at infinity. Its associated linked variations are \begin{aligned} \delta W&=w\left[(r^{-k}-f_k/2)e^{i(n-k)\theta} -(f_k/2)e^{i(n+k)\theta}\right],\\ \delta A_r&=k f_k\sin(k\theta)/r,\qquad \delta A_\theta=f_k'\cos(k\theta). \end{aligned} \tag{6} For a purely imaginary epsilon replace the cosine by a sine and retain the corresponding complex coefficients. This preserves the full phase information. For k>=2 the center is unchanged, and the explicit polarization weight varies through delta a=r delta A_theta. The k=1 case is an independent control. Equation (5) has the exact solution f_1=a/(n r). If the center and h move too, (6) is a common translation. The complete frequency derivative then vanishes. Numerical refinement verifies that cancellation. Fourier contraction is used directly for the smallest responses; subtracting large angular samples would otherwise obscure the translation check through roundoff. For arbitrary zeros of P the same first-order geometric rule has cost G=2 pi n. Moving those zeros therefore supplies genuine constant-cost directions. It preserves the complete normal gap and kernel count, but need not preserve the projected particle frequency. One spatial endpoint coefficient gives the response grouping For k=n the polynomial changes by a constant. Angular selection now makes the projected variation especially simple. The polarization variation has angular difference n, larger than the largest difference n-1 between retained labels, and gives no projected entry. The variation of the degree-one multiplier h can reach only the opposite endpoints: \boxed{\delta T=\gamma\,\kappa_n\epsilon\, |0\rangle\langle n-1|.} \tag{7} Here kappa_n is a real spatial integral, independent of beta or any particle frequency. It is not the binding coefficient in the separate polarization-core action. There is an explicit independent formula for this integral. Let f=f_n, U=U_0, V=V_0 and define \begin{aligned} b_0&=w(r^{-n}-f/2)U+\tfrac14(nf/r+f')V,\\ b_1&=\tfrac14(nf/r-f')U+\tfrac12wfV. \end{aligned} \tag{8} Let (Y_0,Y_1) be the two positive-chiral radial components of D^(-1)(I-P) h Phi_(n-1), with their known angular factors removed. They are computed from (2). Reflection between the endpoint modes gives \boxed{\kappa_n=-4\pi\int_0^\infty r(b_0Y_0+b_1Y_1)\,dr.} \tag{9} For a jointly normalized pair (u,v), the complete projected response is \boxed{\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial\epsilon} =2\gamma\kappa_n\operatorname{Re}(v_0^*u_{n-1}).} \tag{10} Both vectors have norm approaching 1/sqrt(2) on the small-frequency branch. Their endpoint product tends to (-1)^(n-1)/2, independently of beta. Thus different masses within one depth approach a common absolute shape response by the same spatial rule. No division by mass or separately chosen particle coefficient produces this grouping. The computed geometric derivatives are approximately -0.0802981 at n=5, -0.0339063 at n=6 and -0.000529886 at n=10. These are defined in the same chosen dimensionless coefficient convention; they do not derive physical relative sector scales or neutrino suppression. At n=6 and gamma=10000, the independently refined shape derivatives are about 339.061284 for beta=15.5 and 339.053384 for beta=37.5. The frequencies differ by approximately the assigned simplex ratio, while this response differs by about 2.33e-5 in relative terms. The sign follows the retained phase and endpoint convention. It is not a sign assigned to inertia. The force in (10) is nonzero along the constant-cost geometric direction. Therefore an additive geometric functional alone does not hold the occupied radial configuration stationary. The wave and sustaining motion must be solved together, or a different explicit common geometric rule must be tested. The near-equal response is useful evidence about this candidate operator, not a completed physical particle-pair coupling. A precise finite-hopping limitation on the mass law Put d_l=beta+l-(n-1)/2>0 and let \omega_{\rm lead}=\frac{\prod_l d_l}{\gamma^{n-1}\prod_l h_l}, \qquad M(\beta)=\omega_{\rm lead}T^{-1}. \tag{11} The exact smallest positive frequency is omega=omega_lead/||M||_2. After fixed alternating signs are removed, every entry of M is a positive product of the diagonal factors outside one interval, divided by fixed positive hopping factors. Its lower-left entry is one. All other nonzero entries increase with beta. The positive matrix M^T M has a strictly increasing largest eigenvalue. Hence, for n>=2 and finite positive gamma, 0<\frac{\omega}{\omega_{\rm lead}}<1, \qquad \frac{\omega}{\omega_{\rm lead}} \text{ strictly decreases as }\beta\text{ increases}. \tag{12} The exact ratio of two projected frequencies is therefore strictly smaller than their simplex-product ratio when the second beta is larger. The finite canonical matrix does not give an exactly proportional simplex spectrum at finite hopping. The first correction is explicit: \frac{\omega}{\omega_{\rm lead}} =1-\frac{1}{2\gamma^2} \left(\frac{d_0^2}{h_0^2} +\frac{d_{n-1}^2}{h_{n-2}^2}\right)+O(\gamma^{-4}). \tag{13} The full normal complementary correction remains separately controlled by the spatial gap. Equation (12) describes this projected operator; it is not an exclusion of other IDWT dynamics or mode assignments. Reproducible checks connected-source-20260914T130824_340126Z.json passes 50 checks of the full source equation, independent radial frequency derivatives, linked nonradial variations, common translations, complex rotation and refinement. title: Conserved spatial charge
summary: A local charge generator must preserve the complete spatial Dirac kinetics, distinguishing a conserved electric-charge candidate from a rotation-neutral polarization of one probe.
text: Summary: A local charge generator must preserve the complete spatial Dirac kinetics, distinguishing a conserved electric-charge candidate from a rotation-neutral polarization of one probe. A neutral pattern must remain neutral under its field equation A spatial polarization can be annihilated by a particular rotation operator. That supplies an exact compatibility condition for that probe. An electric-charge assignment requires more: its density and current must obey continuity under the complete spatial dynamics. This matters for the conditional current used in Soft spatial current response. Its leading charged-particle response cannot be suppressed by simply freezing an unfavorable orientation. A proposed geometric origin of neutrality must specify the physical generator and preserve its kernel. All derivatives below act on ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinates in the one nested manifold. A matrix acting on field components does not introduce further spatial dimensions. Compute the full local continuity equation Take i\partial_t\Psi =-i\alpha_i\partial_i\Psi+V[\Psi]\Psi, \qquad V^\dagger=V, \tag{1} with constant Hermitian spatial Dirac matrices \alpha_i. For a Hermitian, possibly position-dependent matrix Q(x,t), define n_Q=\Psi^\dagger Q\Psi,\qquad j_{Q,i}=\frac12\Psi^\dagger\{Q,\alpha_i\}\Psi. \tag{2} These are candidate charge density and current, not an electric identification by definition. Differentiating (2) using (1) gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \partial_t n_Q+\partial_i j_{Q,i} ={}&\Psi^\dagger \left[\partial_tQ+\frac12\{\alpha_i,\partial_iQ\} +i[V,Q]\right]\Psi\\ &+\frac12\left[ (\partial_i\Psi^\dagger)[Q,\alpha_i]\Psi -\Psi^\dagger[Q,\alpha_i]\partial_i\Psi \right]. \end{aligned}} \tag{3} For example, the two derivative terms in \partial_t n_Q are -(\partial_i\Psi^\dagger)\alpha_iQ\Psi -\Psi^\dagger Q\alpha_i\partial_i\Psi. Combining them with \partial_i j_{Q,i} gives exactly the second line. The potential contributes i\Psi^\dagger[V,Q]\Psi. This proof includes arbitrary complex field values and derivatives. For a constant Q and a scalar Dirac potential V=\beta\mathfrak m[\Psi], conservation for arbitrary local field data requires \boxed{[Q,\alpha_i]=0\quad\hbox{for every retained direction}, \qquad [Q,\beta]=0.} \tag{4} The second condition applies where the scalar potential is nonzero. The first follows because the first spatial derivatives at a point can be varied independently. It cannot be replaced by vanishing expectation of the second line for one stationary field. Apply the complete kinetic representation If \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d,\beta act irreducibly on the full complex field module, their common commutant consists of scalar matrices. One proof uses the associative matrix algebra they generate: irreducibility makes this the full matrix algebra, whose commuting matrices are qI. Consequently (4) gives Q=qI. \tag{5} This does not derive q. It says that a constant local phase-type charge on one such complete module is the same for all its spatial polarizations. The canonical normalization preserves that supplied charge. Several equivalent copies instead permit Q=I_{\rm Dirac}\otimes q_{\rm copies}, provided the remaining dynamics preserves it. Inequivalent invariant blocks may also have different scalar charges. Assigning and occupying those blocks requires a physical derivation. Their labels are field components, not additional spatial dimensions. Every retained propagation direction matters. For example, a containing representation of six bound coordinates and one existing normal coordinate has \Xi=\beta i^3\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_6,\qquad [\Xi,\alpha_i]=[\Xi,\beta]=0,\qquad \{\Xi,\alpha_y\}=0. \tag{6} The bound operator alone permits separate constants on the two \Xi blocks. Its normal kinetic term connects them and removes that freedom as a conserved local charge of the complete equation. Normal Dirac propagation explicitly retains this normal partner. The example concerns the stated representation; it does not forbid distinct invariant particle families in a larger derived master field. Test the balanced five-dimensional rotation The rotation-neutral construction uses Q_{\rm rot}=\frac12(B_{12}+B_{34}),\qquad B_{ij}=-i\alpha_i\alpha_j,\qquad P_0=I-Q_{\rm rot}^2. \tag{7} On the positive-\beta rest polarization module, P_0 has rank two. Every w in that doublet satisfies Q_{\rm rot}w=0. However, [Q_{\rm rot},\alpha_1]=i\alpha_2,\qquad [Q_{\rm rot},\alpha_5]=0. \tag{8} Thus this spin-only rotation generator does not satisfy (4). The same issue appears as a missing transverse kinetic complement in Neutral doublet transport. An exact spatial plane-wave evolution makes the distinction explicit. Choose normalized \beta w=w, Q_{\rm rot}w=0, and initial field e^{ipx_1}w. Under the full free Dirac operator, \Psi(t,x)=e^{ipx_1} \left[\cos(Et)-i\frac{p\alpha_1+m\beta}{E}\sin(Et)\right]w, \qquad E=\sqrt{p^2+m^2}. \tag{9} Applying (8) gives \boxed{ \|Q_{\rm rot}\Psi\|^2 =\frac{p^2}{p^2+m^2}\sin^2(Et).} \tag{10} The mean is \Psi^\dagger Q_{\rm rot}\Psi=-\|Q_{\rm rot}\Psi\|^2 w^\dagger B_{12}w. It remains zero for an equal-weight preparation of the two opposite B_{12} eigenpolarizations, despite the nonzero response norm. General complex preparations can change both the mean and the norm. Propagation along x_5 instead preserves the kernel because the second commutator in (8) vanishes. A favorable propagation direction is therefore a conditional geometric property, not a conserved electric-neutral particle assignment. Equation (9) is a full spatial Dirac initial-value example, not an identified neutrino mode. It tests the proposed matrix generator on allowed spatial data. Full spatial rotations have an orbital term The actual rotation generator is \mathcal L_{ij} =-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) -\frac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j. \tag{11} For a radial scalar source, [\mathcal L_{ij},H_b]=0. The orbital commutator cancels the spin commutator with the spatial kinetic operator. This is why the full rotation-neutral Dirac field can remain neutral under a chosen total rotation while its spin components alone do not satisfy (4). That conserved quantity is an angular momentum of the actual spatial field. It is a first-order differential generator, so it lies outside the constant zero-order phase-charge hypothesis of (4)–(5). Promoting such a spatial rotation to a local coupling requires its coordinate and derivative terms too. Formally replacing a derivative by \partial_\mu+iA_\mu\mathcal L changes the principal spatial operator through the orbital part of \mathcal L. The action must then derive the corresponding frame dynamics, connection source, conservation law and photon modes. Retaining only its spin matrix would discard the very term which conserved the rotation charge. The useful distinction is therefore between a specified probe's geometric nullspace and a conserved physical source. Both can be geometrical. Their identification must follow from the complete same-field action and its occupied spatial solutions. Particle and antiparticle identification remains open V2 has not yet supplied a physical account of antiparticles or specified what changes in a particle's spatial pattern to produce its antiparticle. The conserved-generator conditions above constrain a candidate charge assignment; they do not identify that physical transformation. Assigning opposite charge labels or using opposite-frequency solutions still requires a derivation connecting those mathematical descriptions to the occupied particle and antiparticle fields. Verification spatial_charge_generator_checks.py checks (3) against direct field time derivatives for arbitrary complex spatial data. Independent commutant calculations include all Dirac matrices through depth ten and verify the effect of the normal derivative. Exact matrix evolution checks (9)–(10) for arbitrary complex doublet polarizations, momenta and masses. Direct spatial polynomial derivatives verify the orbital-plus-spin kinetic cancellation in (11). All checks remain active under Python optimization and reports use timestamped filenames.

title: Reciprocal scalar envelopes

Summary: Readjusting both nested spatial Dirac profiles derives a reciprocal scalar coupling matrix and distinct common and relative amplitude responses from one interaction coefficient. Couple both envelopes through their actual spatial profiles The nested Dirac pair determines both spatial profiles from one scalar moment interaction. The scalar envelope reduction determines how one profile responds when its amplitude changes. Combining these constructions gives the mutual amplitude response without introducing a new coefficient for each pair. Use nested spatial sectors Q_p\subset Q_{p+q} and one ordinary free coordinate in a sector containing both. All these directions belong to the same infinite physical manifold. The two envelope amplitudes describe orthogonal projected channels of \Psi_\infty with the kinetic measures specified in the nested-pair construction; they are not independent interaction particles or further physical dimensions. Keep the two centers and rest polarizations fixed in this scalar envelope reduction. The scalar stationary profiles retain that polarization degeneracy; changing spatial shapes and orientations has the additional responses in Dynamical shape opening. Hence the reduced normal frequencies are real. The tested pairs satisfy the stronger bound 0\prec\mathcal A\preceq D/5. title: Equal-current spatial polarizations
summary: Complete ten-dimensional fields can share density and circulation yet respond differently to the same six-dimensional partner, because reciprocal rotation dynamics retains polarization information beyond the current tensor.
text:
Summary: Complete ten-dimensional fields can share density and circulation yet respond differently to the same six-dimensional partner, because reciprocal rotation dynamics retains polarization information beyond the current tensor. Put the additional polarization into an actual spatial field The complete polarization tensors identify information absent from a ten-dimensional circulation tensor. That information can be carried by full spatial solutions, rather than only by vectors with no specified spatial profile. Use the declared flat scalar Dirac moment model on ordinary macroscopic bound coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d. All sectors belong to the one nested physical manifold. With spatial Clifford matrices \gamma_i, define \alpha_i=\sigma_1\otimes\gamma_i,\qquad  eta=\sigma_3\otimes I,\qquad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+ eta A r^2. 	ag{1} For w=(z,0)^T and a real normalized radial solution F,G,  oxed{\Phi_z(x)=  rac{F(r)w+iG(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w}{\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}}, \qquad H_b\Phi_z=M\Phi_z.} 	ag{2} The radial source obeys A=g_0T_\sigma/d, with T_\sigma=\int r^2\Phi_z^\dagger eta\Phi_z\,dx. The scalar moment branch supplies the equations, normalization and separate stability qualifications. Its pointwise bilinears are  oxed{ho= rac{F^2+G^2}{\Omega_{d-1}},\qquad \sigma= rac{F^2-G^2}{\Omega_{d-1}},\qquad j_i=- rac{2FG}{\Omega_{d-1}}J_{ij}\widehat x_j.} 	ag{3} These identities follow by multiplying the complete upper and lower components, using  eta w=w and J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w. The scalar density and every self-binding moment are independent of normalized z. Two fields have the same complete Dirac current At d=10, take the two same-chirality polarizations  oxed{z_+= rac{|0angle+|1234angle}{\sqrt2},\qquad z_-= rac{|0angle-|1234angle}{\sqrt2}.} 	ag{4} The component basis and its phase convention are defined in Complete spatial polarization data. Both have only J_{9,10}=1 nonzero. Equations (2)–(3) therefore give the same number density, scalar binding density and every bound component of the Dirac number current, at every spatial point. Nevertheless, \langle\Phi_+,\Phi_-angle=0,\qquad \Phi_+^\dagger(x)\Phi_-(x)=0. 	ag{5} The local identity follows from W^\dagger W=ho I for the frame in (2). A four-form distinguishes them. On the ordinary spatial axis x=r e_9,  oxed{\Phi_\pm^\dagger \alpha_1\alpha_3\alpha_5\alpha_7\Phi_\pm=\pmho(r).} 	ag{6} The operator in (6) commutes with \alpha_9, so both radial components carry the same sign there. The field still occupies all ten bound coordinates through (2). One nonzero current plane does not reduce its physical spatial dimensionality. Complete spatial rotations distinguish the fields The total generator of a rotation in the ij coordinate plane is \mathscr J_{ij}=-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) - rac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j. 	ag{7} It contains the orbital derivative and the field's spin action, as derived for complete spatial rotations. For a common physical rotation R and its spin lift S(R), S(R)\Phi_z(R^Tx)=\Phi_{S_{m rest}(R)z}(x),\qquad \mathscr J_{ij}\Phi_z=\Phi_{B_{ij}z/2}. 	ag{8} This is a rotation of the spatial field. Its integrated kinetic norm is the same as the norm of its rest coefficient because (2) is an isometry. Consider the particular spatial generator G= rac12(B_{13}+B_{57}). 	ag{9} Direct Clifford multiplication gives  oxed{Gz_+=0,\qquad G^2z_-=z_-,\qquad z_-^\dagger Gz_-=0.} 	ag{10} Thus the two fields respond differently to the same rotation, despite having identical mean rotation tensors. Their overlaps with their initial spatial modes after rotation by \vartheta are  oxed{|\langle\Phi_+,\Phi_{e^{-i\vartheta G}z_+}angle|^2=1, \qquad |\langle\Phi_-,\Phi_{e^{-i\vartheta G}z_-}angle|^2 =\cos^2\vartheta.} 	ag{11} The difference is the rotation variance z^\dagger G^2z-(z^\dagger Gz)^2, which contains four-form information. A vanishing change in the mean current tensor is insufficient to conclude that the full spatial polarization is unchanged. Obtain the rotation from a polarized lower partner A reciprocal example uses the existing bilateral rotation-moment energy. Specify normalized field channels on Q_6\subset Q_{10}, with a fixed local spatial inclusion I:\mathbb R^6	o\mathbb R^{10}, and energy  oxed{U_{m rot}= rac{\kappa}{2} \langle I J_a I^T,J_bangle,\qquad \langle A,Bangle=\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}B_{ij}.} 	ag{12} The coefficient \kappa is one specified interaction parameter for this benchmark. It is not an electromagnetic coupling derived from particle data. The channel projection and rotational moment term are assumptions of the declared reduced action for modes of the same field. Give both full spatial channels their ordinary first-order kinetic terms. To define (12) away from the radial family, take J_{ij}=2\langle\Phi,\mathscr J_{ij}\Phiangle as its integrated rotation-moment observable. Equation (8) makes this equal to the rest two-form on that family. Variation of this specified full-field energy gives the source operators  oxed{ \delta H_a=\kappa\sum_{\mu<
u}(I^TJ_bI)_{\mu
u}\mathscr J^a_{\mu
u}, \quad \delta H_b=\kappa\sum_{i<j}(I J_a I^T)_{ij}\mathscr J^b_{ij}.} 	ag{13} In the invariant radial family these become  oxed{ i\dot z_a= rac{\kappa}{2} \sum_{\mu<
u}(I^TJ_bI)_{\mu
u}B^a_{\mu
u}z_a, \quad i\dot z_b= rac{\kappa}{2} \sum_{i<j}(I J_a I^T)_{ij}B^b_{ij}z_b.} 	ag{14} Both sources follow from the same energy, and both polarizations remain dynamical. Each channel may have its own radial carrier; it is factored out in (14). Choose the six shared directions as (e_1,e_3,e_5,e_7,e_9,e_{10}) and a lower polarization whose embedded tensor has unit planes 13, 57 and 9\,10. This is a particular relative orientation in the nested space. It makes no direction intrinsically different to either particle. With either z_b=z_+ or z_b=z_-, the higher tensor has only its 9\,10 plane. The lower source is therefore its local 56 rotation. Choose the lower unit state z_{a0} with all three local plane weights +1. The exact pair solution is  oxed{ z_a(t)=e^{-i\kappa t/2}z_{a0},\qquad z_b(t)=e^{-i\kappa t/2}e^{-i\kappa tG}z_b(0).} 	ag{15} The lower tensor remains fixed. The higher J_b also remains fixed: the rotation generated by G acts in directions where that tensor is zero and commutes with its 9\,10 plane. Substitution into (14) therefore reproduces the same generators at every time, proving reciprocal closure. Both norms and U_{m rot}=\kappa/2 are conserved. higher initial polarization mean current tensor during the interaction overlap with its initial full spatial mode z_+ unchanged 1 z_- the same unchanged tensor \cos^2(\kappa t) The second field has nontrivial spatial polarization motion that a model following only J_a,J_b misses. Even an energy expressed entirely in their two-forms requires the larger polarization dynamics to recover that motion. Scope of the spatial solution Multiplying (15) by the complete profiles and radial carrier phases gives solutions of the declared nonlinear spatial channel equations including (13). Rotations preserve the radial scalar density, so their original self-binding sources remain valid. The derivative part of (13) also adds the corresponding rotational advection to the local conserved number current. That drift is the same in the two compared preparations; (3) names the Dirac current rather than silently including this extra term. The example uses two individual spatial field channels. It does not introduce an atom, a mediator particle, or a new physical dimension. It also does not identify the lower field as an actual electron or the higher field as an actual tau merely from their depths. Their occupied mode, physical interaction operator and stability remain separate tasks. The scalar branch's known radial instabilities are not removed by (15). The normal polarization waves provide a different exact motion with a preserved scalar source. Allowing polarization to vary across the bound coordinates instead requires the full kinetic remainder derived in Spatial polarization textures. Verification spatial_polarization_structure_checks.py solves normalized radial fields at one common scalar coefficient g_0=6.5 and two radial resolutions. Spatial quadrature reconstructs their binding sources; independent derivatives check the original Dirac equations. It compares all pointwise number currents, the four-form in (6), and actual orbital-plus-spin rotations. Independent complex energy variations and nonlinear integration verify both equations in (14), their conserved quantities and (15). Independent spatial and temporal derivatives then verify the full driven field equations, including the orbital source terms.
