title: The kinetic current and the chosen endpoint interaction
summary: The conserved kinetic flux and the chosen endpoint interaction have different spatial matrix elements, so their coupling interpretations must remain distinct.
text: The first-order parent fixes a conserved norm and its spatial flux. That flux is different from the endpoint bilinear used in the quartic control. The distinction can be calculated exactly. The nearly equal endpoint coefficients therefore do not, on their own, derive physical coupling strengths from the kinetic equation. This comparison preserves the preceding endpoint-current calculation as a declared interaction model. An interaction need not be built from a conserved current, but choosing another bilinear requires its own origin in the master action. Neither current is identified here with electric charge or an observed force. The current fixed by canonical evolution Let S exchange the x and y halves of the chain: S=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\I_d&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1} All derivative links in the Hodge parent have the same principal symbol c gamma_a. Consequently its complete spatial norm flux is \boxed{j_a=c\Psi^\dagger(S\otimes\gamma_a)\Psi =2c\operatorname{Re}\sum_{r=1}^d y_r^\dagger\gamma_a x_{r-1}.} \tag{2} The canonical density includes every chain field. The local continuity equation is partial_t rho+div j=0. Algebraic curvature shifts and gap terms cancel in this identity because they are Hermitian. By comparison, the declared endpoint current is j_a^{\rm end}=x_0^\dagger\gamma_a x_0+ y_d^\dagger\gamma_a y_d. \tag{3} Its coefficient near one is a legitimate matrix element of (3), but (3) is not the flux of the canonical norm. A single stationary harmonic can have zero divergence for either vector; interference between two different frequencies makes the distinction explicit. An exact divided-difference identity Write b=beta/R for an eigenvalue of the actual spatial Hodge operator B. On its normalized form eigenfield, the chain matrix is H(b)=c b S+H_0, where H_0 contains the shifts and the common gap. Let u_a,u_b be two unit positive-frequency chain eigenvectors. Subtracting their two eigenvalue equations gives \boxed{c\,u_a^\dagger S u_b =\frac{\omega_b-\omega_a}{b_b-b_a} u_a^\dagger u_b.} \tag{4} For equal b the diagonal limit is the Hellmann–Feynman identity c u^dagger S u=d omega/db. If dimensionless beta is used instead, the right side of (4) carries an additional R. The complete pointwise cross-current is the coefficient on the left of (4), multiplying chi_a^dagger gamma chi_b. The Hodge equation implies div(chi_a^dagger gamma chi_b)=i(b_b-b_a)chi_a^dagger chi_b. Equation (4) therefore verifies the full interference continuity law \operatorname{div}j_{ab} =i(\omega_b-\omega_a)\rho_{ab}. \tag{5} This is a constraint from the actual evolution, independent of how an interaction is subsequently chosen. In units R=c=1, at G=10,000, the diagonal kinetic-current coefficients for depth-six degrees 14 and 36 are respectively 5.2381149445e-14 and 4.4309346846e-12. Their endpoint coefficients are 0.9999975350 and 0.9999858750. The mixed kinetic coefficient is 1.2501008459e-12, while the mixed endpoint coefficient is 0.9999917050. These are values in the specified inverse parent, not empirical interaction strengths. At large gap, the kinetic coefficient behaves as \frac{d\omega}{db} \simeq R\omega\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \frac{1}{\beta+j-(d-1)/2}. \tag{6} It therefore retains strong mode dependence. The norm density still has its own canonical unit integral; neither that conserved norm nor its current is automatically ordinary electric charge. Exact parity of the endpoint overlap The signed Hodge branches have equal positive low frequencies. For the positive beta branch choose real endpoint coefficients e_\ell^+=(A_\ell,(-1)^{d-1}B_\ell),\qquad A_\ell,B_\ell>0. \tag{7} Reversal of the full bidiagonal chain gives, on negative beta at the same positive parent frequency, e_\ell^-=(B_\ell,-A_\ell). \tag{8} This follows by reversing the x and y equations and their alternating signs; it is also checked with the complete chain eigenvectors. Hence (e_\ell^+)^\dagger e_\ell^-= \begin{cases}0,&d\text{ odd},\\2A_\ell B_\ell,&d\text{ even}. \end{cases} \tag{9} For an operator acting equally on both endpoints, the odd-depth off-diagonal matrix element vanishes throughout that fixed-degree polarization pair. This is an operator selection within the specified subspace, rather than merely a vanishing expectation for one vector. It does not remove the diagonal channels. At unequal degrees, the odd-depth overlap instead obeys (e_a^+)^\dagger e_b^-= \frac{(d-1)(a-b)}{2\eta^2}+O(\eta^{-4}), \qquad \eta=GR/c. \tag{10} The expansion uses A_ell=2^(-1/2)[1-(ell-1)^2/(2 eta^2)+...] and B_ell=2^(-1/2)[1-(ell+m)^2/(2 eta^2)+...]. The effect holds at other odd depths as well as five. An endpoint operator with opposite weights would have a different rule. Equal endpoint weighting remains part of this trial action, not a derived universal force law. The kinetic current provides a useful control: equation (4) makes its matrix element between opposite b at the same omega vanish at every depth. Thus the even/odd rule in (9) belongs to the selected endpoint interaction and cannot be attributed to every current of the geometry. Resolve the small components before computing flux The earlier scaled-inverse singular value calculation accurately resolves the low frequency, canonical norm and endpoint weights. A standard floating-point singular vector can nevertheless lose relative accuracy in intermediate entries many orders smaller than its norm. The kinetic flux in (2) depends on those small entries. The scaled inverse has separable row and column signs. Taking its entrywise absolute value gives a positive matrix P. Alternating the normalized products u=P^T v and v=P u restores relative precision in the small components without cancellation; the signs are then restored. Eight iterations suffice in the tested large-gap cases. This is a numerical method for those cases, not a uniform iteration bound for arbitrary gap. Independent 100-digit singular decomposition checks every component. The old unrefined vectors would give kinetic-flux errors of about 17% and 11% in the depth-ten degree-two and degree-24 controls. Those were not previously adopted flux results. The newly resolved vectors agree with the high-precision calculation and the derivative identity. The earlier frequencies, endpoint interaction and norm results are unchanged at their stated accuracy. curvature-noether-current-20260914T003117_040924Z.json passes 75 checks, including complete small components, high-precision flux, exact divided differences, endpoint reversal and parity, and direct pointwise continuity in the actual surface coordinates. This comparison narrows what the endpoint calculation establishes; it does not derive a master interaction or complete particle inertia. Related research Spatial mass operator: results and remaining dynamics — connects this calculation to its premises, later corrections and the complete source question.

title: Descending photon source
summary: A higher-sector field sources a photon mode by projection over its bound coordinates while retaining normal propagation, with reciprocal feedback fixed by the same action.
text: Summary: A higher-sector field sources a photon mode by projection over its bound coordinates while retaining normal propagation, with reciprocal feedback fixed by the same action. Start with the higher-dimensional field pattern There is one infinite physical manifold and one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. A higher-sector particle may determine an interaction through its complete spatial field pattern. A photon response is then a particular projection of that interaction. This construction does not assume that the lower particle's bound depth sets the strength of the source. All retained amplitudes below belong to the single field \Psi_\infty. There are no mediator particles. A separation into target and photon amplitudes is a mode decomposition to be derived and normalized, not a postulate of independent physical fields. The photon geometry separates two bound spatial coordinates from the perpendicular phase directions. In a fixed product chart of a containing depth b\geq3, write x=(u,y),\qquad u\in E\simeq\mathbb R^2, \qquad y\in N\simeq\mathbb R^{b-2}. \tag{1} This is a relation to the photon plane. It does not divide the higher particle's dimensions into different physical kinds. A product chart, fixed frame, and product measure are assumptions for the formulas below; curved or moving frames require their Jacobians and connection terms. Project the bound mode and retain the propagation coordinates Let \chi_0(u) be a normalized bound profile, \int_E|\chi_0|^2du=1. Let S_\gamma:\mathbb C^2\to\mathcal F_x be an isometric map from the two photon amplitudes to the relevant field components in this chart. The bundle \mathcal F is the field's amplitude bundle over physical space. Deriving S_\gamma from the master field is part of the sector construction; its two columns are not extra spatial coordinates. For a vector-wave diagnostic they can be the two spatial polarization vectors in E. Define an isometric inclusion and its Hilbert-space adjoint by (I_\gamma a)(u,y)=\chi_0(u)S_\gamma a(y), \qquad (P_\gamma\Psi)(y)=\int_E\overline{\chi_0(u)} S_\gamma^\dagger\Psi(u,y)\,du. \tag{2} For square-integrable packets, P_\gamma I_\gamma=I and \|I_\gamma a\|_{L^2(E\times N)}=\|a\|_{L^2(N)}. Set Q=I-I_\gamma P_\gamma. Every field in the domain decomposes as \Psi=I_\gamma a+h,\qquad P_\gamma h=0. \tag{3} The complement h is not automatically one particle sector. A proposed higher-particle family must be embedded into it, or a nonorthogonal family must use the full kinetic Gram normalization. The photon amplitude a(y,t) retains its propagation phase, for example e^{i(k\cdot y-\omega t)}. Integrating over y would erase this dependence or select a particular Fourier component. It is not the projection in (2). The source marginal in nested sector reciprocity serves a different purpose and must not be substituted for a propagating-mode projection. Exact projected field equation Write the specified field equation as L\Psi+\mathcal N[\Psi]=0, where L contains the selected linear spatial and temporal operators and \mathcal N contains the remaining terms. All operator products below require a common valid domain. With fixed I_\gamma, define D_\gamma=P_\gamma L I_\gamma. Substitution of (3) gives the exact row \boxed{D_\gamma a =-P_\gamma Lh-P_\gamma\mathcal N[I_\gamma a+h].} \tag{4} If the linear operator preserves the photon mode and its orthogonal complement, P_\gamma Lh=0. That is an intertwining property to check; bound-depth assignment alone does not establish it. Even then, the nonlinear projected term need not close on a. The initial photon-sector forcing of a prescribed higher field h is s_\gamma[h]=-P_\gamma\big(Lh+\mathcal N[h]\big). \tag{5} Thus the source is first computed from the higher-dimensional pattern and its field equations. Photon polarization and the bound profile then select which parts enter the output. Its strength need not be a function of the number two. A configuration with s_\gamma[h]\ne0 is not a complete stationary solution with a=0. Its lower-sector background response must be solved before a stability or small-scattering calculation is made. A nonzero static source also does not by itself imply radiation: outgoing waves depend on the source frequency and the propagating spectrum of D_\gamma. One action determines the reverse response Let \mathcal E[\Psi] be a twice differentiable real energy on a real Hilbert space of field variations. Complex fields may be treated as their real and imaginary components. Around a valid background \Psi_0, let H=D^2\mathcal E[\Psi_0] be the self-adjoint Hessian. For fixed isometric target and photon inclusions I_b,I_\gamma, the quadratic cross term is \mathcal E_{\rm cross}(a,q)=\langle a,Bq\rangle, \qquad B=I_\gamma^*H I_b. \tag{6} Variation gives the photon force Bq and target force B^*a: \boxed{B_{\gamma b}=I_\gamma^*H I_b, \qquad B_{b\gamma}=I_b^*H I_\gamma=B_{\gamma b}^*.} \tag{7} This reciprocal pairing permits a source-led, downward calculation. It does not require equal responses to unequal preparations, occupations, or incident fluxes. A genuinely time-dependent background can exchange energy with perturbations and requires its time-dependent variational equations. Reciprocity of the real Hessian is not automatically a time-reversal symmetry of a scattering experiment. When coordinates depend on the field, vary the inclusions, frame, and kinetic terms too. Holding an action-dependent projector fixed can omit part of the source. When a selected higher solution already contains photon components, expand around that complete solution rather than counting those components twice. A direct finite projection check For a normalized bound vector \chi and discrete normal-coordinate vector f, I_\gamma f=\chi\otimes f and P_\gamma(\chi\otimes f)=f. A nonconstant phase sequence in f therefore survives exactly. A bound profile \eta\perp\chi obeys P_\gamma(\eta\otimes f)=0, independently of that phase. For a separated linear operator L=L_E\otimes I+I\otimes L_N with L_E\chi=\lambda_0\chi, the projected operator is D_\gamma=\lambda_0I+L_N. An off-diagonal term connecting \eta to \chi supplies a nonzero P_\gamma Lh, as retained explicitly in (4). These finite identities check the projection; they do not prescribe the physical photon dispersion. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Nested sector reciprocity — distinguishes full source marginalization from propagation-preserving mode selection. Photon plane coupling — gives the conditional two-form selection at a specified output wavevector. Canonical coupling normalization — handles nonorthogonal mode families and physical vertex normalization. Generalized sector coupling — organizes the source and response calculation across all sectors. Dirac source linearization computes the source and its reciprocal response explicitly for the written scalar self-interaction. Spatial source complementarity gives exact bounds on which vector and rotation descriptors survive a lower projection. Bilateral polarization coupling retains both objects' polarization and response. A zero static source overlap does not by itself make the mixed response derivative vanish.

title: Spatial Dirac polarization waves
summary: The full spatial Dirac field supports exact linear polarization waves and nonlinear polarized plane superpositions whose scalar binding source stays fixed while their spatial currents change.
text: Summary: The full spatial Dirac field supports exact linear polarization waves and nonlinear polarized plane superpositions whose scalar binding source stays fixed while their spatial currents change. Restore the polarizations omitted by a single-amplitude envelope The scalar envelope fixes a rest polarization while following changes of the bound profile. The scalar spatial source itself leaves a family of rest polarizations degenerate. Their normal propagation can be derived from the full spatial Dirac equation, without assuming that those motions are frozen or gapped. All fields below occupy the same ordinary bound spatial coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d and an existing normal coordinate y in a containing sector. The polarization amplitudes specify spatial field patterns on that manifold. Their component labels do not add physical dimensions. Choose an orthonormal set of allowed rest spinors collected in a matrix V, with V^\dagger V=I_N and \beta V=V. Every column belongs to the containing spatial Clifford representation. A further selected chirality can be imposed when it defines the intended radial family, but scalar binding alone does not select that chirality or the occupied polarization. A full spatial frame for the polarization amplitudes For a normalized real radial profile f,g, define F(x)=\frac{[f(r)I+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)]V} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad W(x)=\big(F(x),\alpha_yF(x)\big). \tag{1} The bound equation and its normal partner satisfy H_bF=MF,\qquad H_b\alpha_yF=-M\alpha_yF, \quad H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta\mathfrak m(x), \tag{2} with M>0. Thus, after integration over the actual bound coordinates, W^\dagger W=I_{2N},\qquad \alpha_yW=W(\sigma_1\otimes I_N),\qquad H_bW=W(M\sigma_3\otimes I_N). \tag{3} The normalized spinor amplitudes therefore retain the normal kinetic operator. They have not been obtained by dropping its negative-frequency partner. The scalar identity is stronger: it holds pointwise, \boxed{W(x)^\dagger\beta W(x) =\sigma_0(x)(\sigma_3\otimes I_N),\qquad \sigma_0(x)=\frac{f(r)^2-g(r)^2}{\Omega_{d-1}}.} \tag{4} To check it, the diagonal blocks follow from \beta V=V and anticommutation with \alpha(\widehat x). The mixed block vanishes: F^\dagger\beta\alpha_yF=0. Its radial cross terms cancel because \beta\alpha_y commutes with \alpha(\widehat x), and the remaining terms connect opposite \beta eigenspaces. For any complex amplitude \chi\in\mathbb C^{2N}, the reconstructed field has \Psi=W\chi,\qquad \overline\Psi\Psi=\sigma_0(x)s, \qquad s=\chi^\dagger(\sigma_3\otimes I_N)\chi. \tag{5} Its scalar source depends on the total proper scalar density, while its full spatial current can distinguish the polarizations and their phases. Linear polarization waves are full-field modes Let the rest background be \chi_0=\sqrt{s_0}(z,0)^Te^{-iMt}, with z^\dagger z=1. Readjust the radial profile to its scalar density s_0 as usual. Take a perturbation in any rest polarization z_\perp orthogonal to z. Equation (4) gives \delta(\overline\Psi\Psi)=0 \tag{6} at every bound spatial point, for either component of its normal partner. The scalar center and all scalar moments consequently have zero first variation too. The linearized full field equation in this direction has no additional source-feedback term. In the frame rotating at the background phase frequency, the two normal amplitudes \eta obey \boxed{i\partial_t\eta =\big[-i\sigma_1\partial_y+M\sigma_3-MI_2\big]\eta.} \tag{7} These are exact linearized modes of the specified full spatial source model. Their physical normal wavenumber k gives \boxed{\omega_\pm(k)=-M\pm\sqrt{M^2+k^2}.} \tag{8} In particular, \omega_+(k)=\frac{k^2}{2M}+O(k^4/M^3). \tag{9} There is no positive gap isolating one chosen rest polarization from its orthogonal neighbors. At k=0, this branch is the tangent to the stationary polarization family. Its long-wave frequency is quadratic, which must be retained if these modes are included in a coupling reduction. It is not a derived photon dispersion relation. The radial source can have separate unstable modes; (8) does not establish stability of the entire background. It identifies a specific set of polarization motions that a fixed-polarization envelope omits. Exact finite polarized waves can share one unchanged source The same pointwise identity also gives nonlinear solutions beyond first order. Choose mutually orthonormal rest polarizations z_j and positive proper densities s_j with \sum_j s_j=s_0. Solve the radial source once at s_0, obtaining M. For arbitrary normal momenta k_j, put E_j=\sqrt{M^2+k_j^2},\qquad u_j=\begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{(E_j+M)/(2E_j)}\\ k_j/\sqrt{2E_j(E_j+M)} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{10} The amplitude field \boxed{\chi(t,y)= \sum_j\sqrt{\frac{s_jE_j}{M}}\, (u_j\otimes z_j)e^{i(k_jy-E_jt)}} \tag{11} has constant scalar density s_0. Indeed, u_j^\dagger\sigma_3u_j=M/E_j, and every cross term in (5) vanishes by z_i^\dagger z_j=0 for i\ne j. Each term solves the same frozen normal Dirac equation, and their sum preserves precisely the scalar source which made that operator self-consistent. Therefore \Psi=W\chi solves the full nonlinear scalar source equation exactly. The laboratory number density and normal current, integrated over the bound coordinates, are \boxed{n=\sum_j\frac{s_jE_j}{M},\qquad j_y=\sum_j\frac{s_jk_j}{M}.} \tag{12} The relativistic normalization factors in (11) are needed for both the source and the current. Replacing them by unit laboratory amplitudes would generally change the scalar source and require another profile. These uniform waves are modes of the same field sharing one bound profile. This construction does not replace the distinct-depth, mutually deformed pair problem with two independently assigned particles. Scalar density does not describe the complete spatial motion Orthogonal polarizations remove the scalar cross terms in (5). They need not remove cross terms in \Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi. Distinct E_j,k_j can therefore produce a changing bound spatial current even while every scalar binding moment remains constant. The diagnostic uses s_1=0.7, s_2=0.3, k_1=0.4M and k_2=-0.7M with two complex orthogonal spatial polarizations. At depths three, five and six, it verifies the unchanged scalar source and an explicitly changing local bound current. Both full spatial polarizations are needed to describe that solution; the scalar density alone loses the motion. For a varying total s(t,y), the bound profile also varies. Replacing W by W_s restores the profile-derivative residual calculated in the scalar-envelope note, now with \sigma_1\otimes I_N. Constant s makes that residual vanish, including (11). General wavepackets require the actual radial, shape and center response as well. This gives a precise coupling limit: scalar self-binding permits and transports different polarizations, but does not choose the occupied one. A physical neutrality mechanism must supply that selection and the current sampled by an incoming field; it cannot infer them from the unchanged scalar source alone. Reflection symmetry of scalar Dirac sources shows why this degeneracy can persist with unequal scalar confinement axes. It also checks the nonlinear moment source before treating a frozen eigenspace as a degenerate family of self-consistent fields. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents uses opposite-frequency components of this same frame to construct an exact current oscillating at twice the bound frequency. Its unit-norm family separates a slow clock from a small current or a small source response. Complete spatial polarization data identifies which tensors retain all constant amplitudes and phases in the chosen multiplet. Spatial polarization textures derives the additional kinetic terms when those amplitudes vary across the bound coordinates, including the component outside the retained frame. The source-preserving normal waves above and bound-coordinate textures therefore require their respective complete spatial equations. Verification dirac_polarization_wave_checks.py constructs the full containing Clifford fields, checks (4) at spatial points for arbitrary complex amplitudes, and integrates the canonical norm over the bound coordinates. Independent source integrals and finite spatial derivatives verify the linear polarization modes. For the finite two-wave solutions it recomputes the scalar moment and checks the complete nonlinear equation using independent finite derivatives in time, the normal coordinate and every bound coordinate. It also checks both normalization factors, the normal current and the changing bound current. Conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes — supplies the full normal partner and boost convention. Scalar envelope of a bound Dirac field — supplies the profile response when total scalar density changes. Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the complete polarized bound field and its currents. Polarized Dirac shape response — supplies additional spatial shape motions beyond this radial polarization family. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the source equation and separate radial stability limits.

title: Reflection symmetry of scalar Dirac sources
summary: Spatial reflection symmetries force degenerate Dirac polarization multiplets even for unequal scalar confinement axes, and identify when those families also preserve the nonlinear moment source.
text: Summary: Spatial reflection symmetries force degenerate Dirac polarization multiplets even for unequal scalar confinement axes, and identify when those families also preserve the nonlinear moment source. Anisotropic scalar confinement can retain polarization degeneracy The spatial polarization waves use the rest-polarization family of a radial Dirac profile. A stronger statement applies to scalar potentials which are even in each principal spatial coordinate: unequal confinement strengths do not by themselves remove the entire degeneracy. Work in the stated flat-coordinate spatial model, with a self-adjoint operator and a domain preserved by the reflections below. The bound coordinates are ordinary macroscopic directions of the physical sector. A curved global sector or different boundary conditions require their own symmetry check; a coordinate expression alone does not establish these global symmetries there. Let H_0=-i\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta M(x), \qquad M(x_1,\ldots,-x_i,\ldots,x_d)=M(x). \tag{1} The matrices are Hermitian and satisfy \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I, \{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0, and \beta^2=I. A scalar quadratic source with a real symmetric coefficient matrix can be written in this form after choosing its principal axes. Combine each actual coordinate reflection with its Clifford matrix Define \mathcal P_i\Psi(x)=\Psi(R_ix), where R_i reverses the ith coordinate, and put \boxed{C_i=\alpha_i\mathcal P_i.} \tag{2} These are unitary Hermitian operators on the spatial field. The coordinate reflections commute with the constant Clifford matrices, so C_i^2=I,\qquad C_iC_j=-C_jC_i\quad(i\ne j). \tag{3} Conjugating the kinetic operator by C_i reverses every term: the coordinate reflection reverses the ith derivative, while \alpha_i reverses the other Clifford matrices. The even scalar mass changes sign because \alpha_i\beta\alpha_i=-\beta. Hence \boxed{C_iH_0C_i=-H_0,\qquad [H_0,C_iC_j]=0.} \tag{4} Every even product preserves the same energy eigenspace. These operators act on actual spatial coordinates and field components; their labels do not describe another physical space. An identity potential V_0(x)I which is also even in every coordinate commutes with each C_i. It therefore preserves the second identity in (4) for H=H_0+V_0I, although the first identity then need not hold. The multiplicity argument only needs the even products to commute with H. Derive the minimum multiplicity without an assumed particle label For m=\lfloor d/2\rfloor, define commuting Hermitian involutions W_j=-iC_{2j-1}C_{2j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m. \tag{5} Each commutes with H. In a finite isolated energy eigenspace, choose a joint eigenvector with signs w_j=\pm1. For odd d=2m+1, the energy-preserving operator C_{2j}C_d flips w_j and leaves every other sign unchanged. Its unitarity keeps the result nonzero. Applying these operators produces all 2^m sign patterns at the same energy. Different sign patterns are orthogonal. For even d=2m, use C_{2j}C_{2m} for j<m. It flips w_j and w_m together, producing 2^{m-1} orthogonal patterns with fixed total sign product. Therefore every such eigenspace contains a multiplet of size at least \boxed{N_d=2^{\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor}.} \tag{6} Repeated multiplets can make the degeneracy larger. The minimum sizes at the working depths are: spatial depth minimum scalar-source multiplet 3 2 5 4 6 4 10 16 The proof permits unequal strengths along every axis. It requires the reflection symmetries and operator domain, rather than spherical symmetry. These numbers count degenerate field modes, not additional spatial coordinates or a physical particle census. For the central five-dimensional family, the balanced total spatial rotation has two neutral members within its four-mode family, as derived in Rotation-neutral Dirac fields. Scalar confinement with the symmetries above cannot create an isolated two-mode energy band by splitting a four-mode multiplet. Occupation may depend on formation and other source terms, which require their own derivation. Check the nonlinear source before declaring a degenerate solution family A degeneracy of a frozen operator alone is insufficient for a nonlinear field equation. Different eigenvectors could change the source which was used to construct that operator. For the centered quadratic moment kernel, the relevant source data can be checked explicitly. Suppose a finite eigenspace consists of exactly one minimal multiplet. For any operator commuting with all the even reflection transformations, its compression onto that multiplet is scalar. This follows directly from the sign proof: commuting with the W_j makes it diagonal in the distinct sign states, and commuting with their flips makes all diagonal entries equal. Every diagonal scalar moment operator \beta x_i^2 commutes with the even transformations. Its expectation is therefore independent of the chosen normalized polarization in that eigenspace. For a pure scalar quadratic source M(x)=m+\sum_i a_ix_i^2, \tag{7} assume the a_i are distinct. The full ordinary spatial rotation generator J_{ij}=-i(x_i\partial_j-x_j\partial_i) -\frac i2\alpha_i\alpha_j \tag{8} obeys \boxed{[J_{ij},H_0] =2i(a_i-a_j)\beta x_ix_j.} \tag{9} The orbital and spin commutators cancel in the kinetic term. Between any two vectors at the same energy, the left side has zero matrix element. Thus the mixed scalar moment operator has zero compression onto that whole eigenspace. The parity operator \Pi=\beta\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_d also commutes with H_0 and the even transformations. A minimal multiplet has one parity sign. Its scalar density is even under x\mapsto-x, so its scalar first moment vanishes. Provided the total scalar integral is nonzero, its scalar center is the origin. Consequently every normalized member has the same centered scalar moment matrix. If one solves the nonlinear quadratic moment source equation, all members of that minimal multiplet solve the same source equation. This statement concerns a kernel determined by those moments; another nonlinearity depending on further local density data needs another check. When some axis coefficients coincide, (9) alone does not determine the corresponding mixed moments. The explicit central and two-block fields in Scalar Dirac modes and Nested Dirac pair separately verify their polarization-independent scalar sources. Implication for coupling calculations The scalar model can bind spatial profiles, deform a nested pair and produce polarization-dependent dynamical shape response. Its persistent polarization families explain why those results do not yet select an occupied neutral mode. Increasing axis anisotropy while preserving the same scalar reflection symmetries does not supply that missing energy splitting. The full shape response can still distinguish prepared polarizations through its angular spectrum and source matrix. The required physical calculation must retain that response and determine which polarization is occupied and which current the incoming field samples. A source symmetry and a transition selection rule are separate parts of that calculation. Verification dirac_reflection_symmetry_checks.py checks (4) by differentiating complete spatial fields at coordinate points, including an even nonquadratic scalar potential. An independent Cartesian Hermite regulator with unequal axis coefficients preserves the reflections and reproduces the predicted multiplet sizes at depths three, five, six and ten. These spectra verify multiplicity, not converged physical masses. The diagnostic checks each sign-flipping operation, the complete orbital-plus-spin commutator, scalar moment compression and parity within one minimal eigenspace. It also verifies that the multiplicity requirement is conditional on the source symmetry. All conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Spatial Dirac polarization waves — derives normal propagation of the degenerate polarization family. Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the total spatial generator and the central neutral subspace. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the nonlinear moment source and its stability limits. Self-consistent nested Dirac pair — verifies the source for the two-block spatial profile. Polarized Dirac shape response — retains polarization-dependent response despite stationary degeneracy.

title: Polarized Dirac shape response
summary: Full spatial Dirac quadrupole sources split into two calculable angular families whose polarization weights, radial spectra and reciprocal source feedback determine the allowed shape response.
text: Summary: Full spatial Dirac quadrupole sources split into two calculable angular families whose polarization weights, radial spectra and reciprocal source feedback determine the allowed shape response. Calculate the shapes the field can actually change into The transition-density interaction compares both objects' changing spatial patterns. A complete calculation also needs the motions those patterns can undergo. Here those motions are calculated from the full first-order Dirac operator and the same scalar moment source which determines the stationary profile. This is a conditional model on ordinary spatial coordinates x\in\mathbb R^d within the one nested physical manifold. Field components, angular basis functions and shape coefficients are descriptions of this field, not further physical dimensions. The radial profile is the stated scalar model's solution; it does not replace the actual electron orbit. Use Hermitian Clifford matrices \alpha_i,\beta and a unit rest polarization w with \beta w=w. Write the normalized stationary field as \Phi(x)=\frac{f(r)w+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \int_0^\infty(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr=1. \tag{1} Its self-consistent central operator is H_0=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla+\beta(m+ar^2),\qquad H_0\Phi=E\Phi. \tag{2} Scalar Dirac moment modes derives a=g_0T/d, where T=\int r^2(f^2-g^2)r^{d-1}dr. The common coefficient g_0 also fixes the feedback below. A quadrupole has two different Dirac angular responses Let A be a real symmetric traceless spatial matrix. Its source vertex is V_A(x)=\beta(x^TAx),\qquad v_A=V_A\Phi. \tag{3} Both signs in \beta matter. In particular the source acts on the lower radial component as well as the upper one. For any x, define spinor-valued homogeneous polynomials \begin{aligned} p_A(x)&=(x^TAx)w,\\ N_A(x)&=\frac{2}{d+2}\alpha(Ax)w,\\ M_A(x)&=p_A(x)-\alpha(x)N_A(x). \end{aligned} \tag{4} They obey \boxed{\alpha\cdot\partial\,M_A=0,\qquad \alpha\cdot\partial\,N_A=0,\qquad p_A=M_A+\alpha(x)N_A.} \tag{5} A polynomial annihilated by \alpha\cdot\partial is called monogenic. Here (5) follows directly: \alpha\cdot\partial p_A=2\alpha(Ax)w, \alpha\cdot\partial N_A=2\operatorname{tr}A\,w/(d+2)=0, and \alpha\cdot\partial(\alpha(x)N_A)=(d+2)N_A. Thus the two functions are derived from the actual source. On the unit sphere, equation (3) becomes \sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}\,v_A =r^2\left[fM_A-i g\alpha(\widehat x)M_A\right] +r^2\left[f\alpha(\widehat x)N_A-i gN_A\right]. \tag{6} The first family has upper angular degree two and lower degree three. The second has upper degree two and lower degree one. Both retain the original d spatial coordinates. Their different radial Dirac operators give different spectra even though they arise from the same quadrupole. The target's polarization fixes the angular weights Choose a real orthonormal basis A_r of traceless symmetric matrices, \operatorname{tr}(A_rA_s)=\delta_{rs}, and define J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w\quad(i<j), \qquad J_{ji}=-J_{ij}. \tag{7} J is the ordinary spatial circulation tensor of the prepared field. Its action on the shape basis is the real skew matrix \mathcal K_{rs} =\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}[A_r,A_s]_{ij} =\frac12\operatorname{tr}\left(A_r[J,A_s]\right). \tag{8} Use the normalized spherical average \langle1\rangle_S=1 and set c_0=2/[d(d+2)], c_1=4/[d(d+2)^2]. Direct second and fourth spherical moments give \boxed{G_N=\big[\langle N_r^\dagger N_s\rangle_S\big] =c_1(I+i\mathcal K),\qquad G_M=\big[\langle M_r^\dagger M_s\rangle_S\big] =c_0I-G_N.} \tag{9} The cross average \langle M_r^\dagger\alpha(\widehat x)N_s\rangle_S vanishes. For example, the first identity follows by averaging \alpha(A_r\widehat x)\alpha(A_s\widehat x) and retaining both its scalar part \operatorname{tr}(A_rA_s) and its bivector part in (8). Both Gram matrices are positive semidefinite because they are actual spatial inner products. For a complex incident shape c_rA_r, the two source strengths are c^\dagger G_Mc and c^\dagger G_Nc, with their radial factors restored below. Thus the target polarization J and the incident shape and phase c enter together. A common physical rotation of J and every A_r leaves the prediction unchanged. For pure rest polarizations at depths five and six, diagonalizing i\mathcal K gives: spatial depth shape helicity \lambda and multiplicity \operatorname{rank}G_M \operatorname{rank}G_N 5 -1:3,\;-\frac12:2,\;0:4,\;\frac12:2,\;1:3 14 11 6 -1:6,\;0:8,\;1:6 20 14 Here helicity labels a complex rotating spatial quadrupole relative to J. It is not an independently assigned particle charge. The five-dimensional null direction supplies the half-helicity channels. At \lambda=-1, the N family has zero source weight, but the M family remains available. A zero in one family is therefore not a zero of the whole interaction. Derive the radial operators without removing angular components For a monogenic polynomial of degree \ell, the ordinary angular Dirac pair has radial equations \begin{aligned} (E-M)F&=G'+\frac{d+\ell-1}{r}G,\\ (E+M)G&=-F'+\frac\ell rF. \end{aligned} \tag{10} Writing F=r^\ell f_\ell, G=r^\ell g_\ell converts the radial integration weight to r^{d+2\ell-1}dr. Its matrix is the previously derived radial matrix evaluated at the numerical parameter d+2\ell. This parameter accounts for powers of the same radius; it introduces no additional spatial directions. Let H_D denote that radial matrix with the unchanged scalar coefficients m,a. For the two families in (6), H_M=H_{d+4},\qquad H_N=-XH_{d+2}X,\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{11} The second formula follows by exchanging the upper and lower radial angular roles. Its signs can also be checked directly with \alpha\cdot\partial(F\alpha(\widehat x)N) =(F'+(d+\ell-1)F/r)N. Project the two radial source pairs (r^2f,-r^2g) onto their respective orthonormal physical radial bases, obtaining real vectors u_M,u_N. Their complete-basis norms satisfy \|u_M\|^2=\|u_N\|^2 =\int_0^\infty r^4(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{12} In particular the total source norm has the isotropic value c_0\int r^4(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr for every unit complex shape. The polarization dependence enters how that strength is divided between families with different dynamics, not a depth-specific zero inserted in the total norm. Keep both ordinary and conjugate feedback Put L=\operatorname{diag}(H_M-E,H_N-E) and define u_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{c_0-c_1(1+\lambda)}\,u_M\\ \sqrt{c_1(1+\lambda)}\,u_N \end{pmatrix}. \tag{13} A real spatial source pairs helicities \lambda and -\lambda. The full ordinary/conjugate fluctuation block is \boxed{\mathcal B_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} L+g_0u_\lambda u_\lambda^T&g_0u_\lambda u_{-\lambda}^T\\ -g_0u_{-\lambda}u_\lambda^T&-L-g_0u_{-\lambda}u_{-\lambda}^T \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{14} Its coefficient is the same g_0 as in the stationary source. Multiplication by \operatorname{diag}(I,-I) gives a Hermitian energy Hessian. The matrix itself need not be Hermitian or have a positive energy, because the full Dirac fluctuation problem retains both signs of the spectrum. For z away from the indicated poles define the bare shape response \chi_\lambda(z)= u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{15} Eliminating the responding field from (14) gives \boxed{\chi^{\rm full}_\lambda(z) =\frac{\chi_\lambda(z)}{1-g_0\chi_\lambda(z)}.} \tag{16} This is the response to an additional specified scalar shape source. It is also a building block for a reciprocal pair calculation: each object's induced shape becomes part of the other's source. A scattering probability still requires the physical incoming/outgoing mode map, appropriate boundary conditions and flux normalization. A spectral example from the self-consistent profiles At a=1, m=0.5, the first positive frequencies of the finite quadrupole block converge as follows: depth \lambda first positive frequency second positive frequency 5 0 1.311394217 1.758838889 5 \frac12 1.283179965 1.844170152 5 1 1.261523857 1.924425431 6 0 1.263961888 1.674646832 6 1 1.216595363 1.821722236 These are model fluctuation frequencies, not fitted particle masses or weak-interaction rates. The table fixes a, so the self-consistent g_0 differs between depths. Both geometries retain nonzero shape responses. Their differing helicity spectra provide a calculable distinction without establishing anomalously weak five-dimensional coupling. No growing quadrupole modes were found in these finite calculations or in the corresponding m=0 examples. The latter backgrounds nevertheless have the radial instability documented in the profile note. Stability of one angular response does not remove an instability elsewhere. Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels uses this complete response to calculate how a higher shape with zero static restriction can drive a lower polarized field at nonzero frequency. Incoming spatial shape modes compares these active modes at depths five and six using one common interaction coefficient, checks their moment restrictions and distinguishes their incident amplitudes from forces which first create a higher-sector response. Verification angular_dirac_response_checks.py constructs full Clifford fields, differentiates their spatial polynomials, and independently integrates their angular Gram matrices with a positive spherical rule. It tests both radial operators against differentiated physical radial functions, source completeness, low-frequency convergence, and the full matrix resolvent against (16). The centered full-field energy is separately varied by finite differences. Conditions remain active with Python optimization enabled. Related Rotation-neutral Dirac fields — supplies the full spatial field and its circulation tensor. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the stationary profiles and their radial stability test. Translational Dirac response — applies the same method to center motion and its exact zero mode.

title: Dirac source linearization
summary: The written scalar Dirac self-interaction gives an explicit real-linear response with ordinary and conjugate mode couplings determined by the higher spatial field.
text: Summary: The written scalar Dirac self-interaction gives an explicit real-linear response with ordinary and conjugate mode couplings determined by the higher spatial field. The existing nonlinear term Use the scalar self-interaction present in the projected Dirac action. In units \hbar=1, its Hamiltonian form is i\partial_t\Psi=H_0\Psi+\mathcal N[\Psi], \qquad \mathcal N[\Psi]=\kappa(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi. \tag{1} Here \beta=\beta^\dagger, \beta^2=I, \kappa is real, and H_0 is the specified self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator including whichever fixed background terms have actually been adopted. Its domain and the spatial measure must make the following pairings valid. The energy is \mathcal E[\Psi] =\langle\Psi,H_0\Psi\rangle +\frac\kappa2\int(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)^2d\mu. \tag{2} This is one field on the nested macroscopic spatial manifold. Spinor components describe amplitudes over that space, not independent spatial dimensions. Equation (1) is a specified contribution to V2 dynamics, not the completed master action or a derivation of occupied particle geometries. No mediator particle is introduced. Nonlinear Dirac equations with this scalar structure and linearization about solitary waves are treated in Boussaïd and Comech. The sign convention here is fixed directly by (2). Differentiate the complete source At a spatial field \phi, set s=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\in\mathbb R, \qquad v=\beta\phi. For a variation \eta, the scalar changes by \delta s=v^\dagger\eta+\eta^\dagger v. Therefore D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta =\kappa\left[s\beta\eta +v(v^\dagger\eta+\eta^\dagger v)\right]. \tag{3} Equivalently, \boxed{ D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta=A_N\eta+B_N\overline\eta, \qquad A_N=\kappa(s\beta+vv^\dagger), \qquad B_N=\kappa vv^T.} \tag{4} The s\beta term is the variation of the final field factor. The two rank-one terms come from changing the source scalar itself. Retaining only s\beta\eta would freeze the higher particle's source while it is being perturbed. The complete derivative is real-linear; generally D\mathcal N[i\eta]\ne iD\mathcal N[\eta]. The matrices obey A_N=A_N^\dagger and B_N=B_N^T. Spatial variation of s(x) and v(x) retains the target's local shape and polarization. Replacing them by spatial averages is an additional approximation. Linearized dynamics about a stationary profile Suppose \Psi_0=e^{-i\mu t}\phi is an actual solution of (1), so (H_0+\kappa s\beta)\phi=\mu\phi. \tag{5} In the same rotating frame put \Psi=e^{-i\mu t}(\phi+\eta). The linearized equation is i\partial_t\eta=A\eta+B\overline\eta, \qquad A=H_0-\mu+A_N, \qquad B=B_N. \tag{6} Its doubled representation is i\partial_t \begin{pmatrix}\eta\\\overline\eta\end{pmatrix} =\mathcal L \begin{pmatrix}\eta\\\overline\eta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal L= \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\-\overline B&-\overline A\end{pmatrix}. \tag{7} The second row is the conjugate of the first; it does not add another physical field or another set of spatial dimensions. With \Sigma_3=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I), \mathcal H=\Sigma_3\mathcal L =\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\\overline B&\overline A\end{pmatrix} =\mathcal H^\dagger. \tag{8} This is the quadratic-energy structure. \mathcal L itself need not be Hermitian or have a real spectrum. Stability cannot be inferred merely from the Hermiticity of H_0. The global phase tangent supplies the consistency identity \mathcal L \begin{pmatrix}i\phi\\-i\overline\phi\end{pmatrix}=0, \tag{9} which follows immediately from (5). A moving orbit or a background with several temporal frequencies instead requires time-dependent coefficients; a stationary spectral analysis cannot silently replace that motion. Spatial coupling between mode families Let f_a(x) be photon-sector test modes and u_\lambda(x) target variation modes, normalized by the action's kinetic metric. The ordinary and conjugate matrix elements of the interaction derivative are K_{a\lambda}=\int f_a^\dagger A_Nu_\lambda\,d\mu, \qquad C_{a\lambda}=\int f_a^\dagger B_N\overline{u_\lambda}\,d\mu. \tag{10} Thus a target amplitude vector q produces the linearized source Kq+C\overline q. The spatial integrals include polarization, relative phase, and all of the higher-dimensional profile present in (4). Any cross-family kinetic matrix element of H_0 must also be retained. Interchanging target and photon mode labels gives Hermitian reciprocity for K and transpose symmetry for C: K_{\lambda a}=\overline{K_{a\lambda}}, \qquad C_{\lambda a}=C_{a\lambda}. \tag{11} For the second equality, use B_N^T=B_N and transpose the scalar pairing. In the doubled mode space these are precisely the symmetries of the real quadratic energy. They do not require treating the conjugate variation as an independent particle. A zero of one matrix element excludes that particular linear response. It is not a zero of the complete interaction unless all relevant ordinary, conjugate, and kinetic blocks vanish. The criterion must be applied to the actual nonlinear source, not to the parity of a bare field alone; angular kernel parity gives an explicit example of this distinction. Which temporal frequencies the source contains For a finite prescribed field h(x,t)=\sum_j c_j\phi_j(x)e^{-i\Omega_jt}, equation (1) gives \mathcal N[h] =\kappa\sum_{j,\ell,m} \overline c_jc_\ell c_m (\phi_j^\dagger\beta\phi_\ell)\beta\phi_m e^{-i(\Omega_\ell+\Omega_m-\Omega_j)t}. \tag{12} Projection onto an output mode f_a uses the full cubic spatial overlap T_{a;j\ell m} =\kappa\int f_a^\dagger\beta\phi_m (\phi_j^\dagger\beta\phi_\ell)\,d\mu. \tag{13} The frequency combination and spatial compatibility follow from the same written term. Frequency matching alone does not make (13) nonzero. Several triples reaching the same output frequency interfere coherently. Equations (10)–(13) assume a linear output-mode inclusion in the master field. If a photon is instead realized as a nonlinear collective observable of that field, derive its tangent map and induced equations. For example a bilinear observable contains frequency differences, whereas the cubic field source in (12) contains the displayed three-term combinations. Their different frequency rules cannot be interchanged without deriving that output map. Scope of the concrete calculation Complete scalar response determines the full pointwise rank, singular values and inverse of (3). At nonzero scalar density the complete source derivative is invertible; at scalar nullity it retains one real response direction. Those facts concern the full source before a spatial channel projection and before adding H_0-\mu. Transition-density coupling derives the corresponding nonlocal source derivative and full quartic mode tensor for the projected bilocal density interaction, with both patterns retained. The operator D\mathcal N[\phi] is now explicit for this term. The remaining physical inputs are the actual higher-sector solution, the photon embedding or collective map, all additional action terms, and the boundary conditions selecting incoming and outgoing modes. The matrix formulas apply at any depth supporting the specified Dirac structure and do not themselves single out depth five. Local scalar contact normalization adds the spatial virial and an exact normalized massive profile for the same local source convention. It makes explicit why a scalar vertex coefficient does not by itself determine a stationary particle frequency. Verification Local polarized pulse coupling retains the exact cross-current of two traveling components of this same field. Its complete local equations give source zeros and both reciprocal weak-scattering maps without first postulating a bilocal spatial kernel. Causal scalar response solves this complete derivative about a specified uniform spatial background, including every scalar angular mode, both signed propagation channels and the conserved zero mode. The background is a control, not an identified particle. polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Source frequencies in spatial coupling tracks the distinct temporal frequencies in the bilinear density, complete cubic field source and perturbations relative to the stationary carrier. Related Descending photon source — retains normal propagation when projecting the higher-field source. Projected Dirac current — supplies the written scalar interaction and its action conventions. Canonical coupling normalization — fixes the mode metrics used in (10). Angular kernel parity — distinguishes source selection from parity of the underlying field.

title: Dressed spatial source vertices
summary: Eliminating spatial modes dresses both the interaction vertex and its kinetic normalization, with exact finite-frequency conservation identities and nonzero responses that a bare projection can miss.
text: Summary: Eliminating spatial modes dresses both the interaction vertex and its kinetic normalization, with exact finite-frequency conservation identities and nonzero responses that a bare projection can miss. Carry the source through the same reduction as the dynamics The projected Dirac current shows why a current can lose required terms under direct mode compression. This note calculates those terms by eliminating the omitted modes of the same field. It supplies the physical normalization and the complete source matrix for a specified linear Hermitian problem. All modes describe \Psi_\infty on the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. Retained and omitted components are a mathematical decomposition of that field. They are not extra dimensions, independent interaction fields or mediator particles. Let a fixed orthogonal mode projector define a block decomposition H=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^\dagger&C\end{pmatrix}, \qquad H=H^\dagger. \tag{1} The formulas apply to a finite regulator or to operators with compatible domains and the stated inverses. Work at a real spectral parameter E outside the spectrum of C. A continuum or a resonance requires the appropriate boundary-value resolvent and flux normalization; the positive norm identities below concern this Hermitian, real-energy setting. The full real-linear Dirac fluctuation problem may also require its ordinary and conjugate blocks before this reduction is applicable. Exact reconstruction and the norm of a reduced amplitude The omitted row of (H-E)\Psi=0 gives R(E)=(E-C)^{-1},\qquad \Psi=\Omega(E)u,\qquad \Omega(E)=\begin{pmatrix}I\\R(E)B^\dagger\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} The retained equation and its inverse operator are H_{\rm eff}(E)=A+BR(E)B^\dagger, \qquad K(E)=EI-H_{\rm eff}(E),\qquad K(E)u=0. \tag{3} This is the effective-operator construction explained in Compression and effective dynamics. It obeys the useful exact identity (E-H)\Omega(E)=\begin{pmatrix}K(E)\\0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} The full field norm is not generally u^\dagger u. Since \partial_E R=-R^2, \boxed{Z(E)=\Omega^\dagger\Omega =I+BR(E)^2B^\dagger =I-\partial_EH_{\rm eff}(E),\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=u^\dagger Z(E)u.} \tag{5} Z is positive and at least I in this setting. For a selected energy, b=Z^{1/2}u gives a normalized physical amplitude and \widehat\Omega=\Omega Z^{-1/2} is an isometry. Energy dependence makes this a mode normalization; replacing Z(E) by one constant over an entire broad spectrum is an extra approximation. Differentiate the entire effective operator Let H(a)=H+aV+O(a^2), where a is a specified source perturbation amplitude and V=V^\dagger is its full spatial vertex. The same-field interpretation requires that amplitude and vertex to be obtained from the adopted action. This calculation does not identify a with a physical photon in advance. At fixed E and fixed mode projector, direct differentiation gives \begin{aligned} \partial_aH_{\rm eff}={}&V_{PP} +V_{PQ}RB^\dagger+BRV_{QP} +BRV_{QQ}RB^\dagger\\ ={}&\Omega^\dagger V\Omega. \end{aligned} \tag{6} The final term follows from differentiating the inverse: \partial_aR=RV_{QQ}R. The middle terms retain the probe's effect on the coupling to the omitted modes. Their signs and coefficients are fixed by the same full operator. Consequently the normalized static source vertex is \boxed{\widehat V(E)=Z(E)^{-1/2}\Omega(E)^\dagger V\Omega(E)Z(E)^{-1/2}.} \tag{7} For an isolated eigenvalue E(a) and reduced eigenvector u, differentiating K(E(a),a)u=0 yields \frac{dE}{da} =\frac{u^\dagger(\partial_aH_{\rm eff})u}{u^\dagger Zu}. \tag{8} This equals the full-field expectation of V in the normalized eigenstate. Both the source and its normalization are therefore required to predict an energy shift. A probe-dependent projector adds its own variation terms; (6) is explicitly the fixed-projector formula. For a transition between two retained spatial modes, the corresponding vertex is \Gamma_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger V_{fi}\Omega_i, \qquad \widehat\Gamma_{fi}=Z_f^{-1/2}\Gamma_{fi}Z_i^{-1/2}. \tag{9} The two lifts include both mode preparations. If the full vertex satisfies V_{if}=V_{fi}^\dagger, then \widehat\Gamma_{if}=\widehat\Gamma_{fi}^\dagger. Polarization and shape enter through both full spatial states and the source operator; this relation does not replace either preparation by an isotropic average. Charge normalization and a finite-frequency identity If the adopted action already supplies one conserved generator qI on the full mode family, its normalized equal-energy density vertex is exactly Z^{-1/2}\Omega^\dagger(qI)\Omega Z^{-1/2}=qI. \tag{10} A small retained fraction cannot turn this supplied charge into a neutral particle. This preserves a given charge; it does not assign q to any sector or identify the physical electromagnetic symmetry. For two different energies at the same spatial momentum, the resolvent identity gives R(E_f)-R(E_i)=-(E_f-E_i)R(E_f)R(E_i). Hence the complete density vertex obeys \boxed{\Omega_f^\dagger\Omega_i =I-\frac{H_{\rm eff}(E_f)-H_{\rm eff}(E_i)}{E_f-E_i}.} \tag{11} Its coincident limit is (5). Equation (11) ties the energy dependence of the dynamics to the finite-frequency density response, so they cannot be chosen independently. The full spatial current retains continuity For an affine spatial symbol H(p)=M+\sum_a\alpha_a p_a, \qquad M=M^\dagger,\quad\alpha_a=\alpha_a^\dagger, \tag{12} use the same fixed retained projector at incoming and outgoing momenta. The minimally varied density and spatial-current matrices, without their common supplied charge factor, are \Gamma^0_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger\Omega_i, \qquad \Gamma^a_{fi}=\Omega_f^\dagger\alpha_a\Omega_i. \tag{13} Apply (4) on the left and right of the exact full-operator difference. Writing \omega=E_f-E_i and k=p_f-p_i gives \boxed{\omega\Gamma^0_{fi}-k_a\Gamma^a_{fi} =K(E_f,p_f)-K(E_i,p_i).} \tag{14} Between actual incoming and outgoing solutions, the right side has zero matrix element. This is the reduced continuity identity. It remains valid when M and the velocities mix the retained and omitted modes strongly, as long as the stated reconstruction exists. For a nonlinear spatial symbol, the finite-momentum current must instead be obtained by varying its actual coupling to the probe. Replacing that vertex by a derivative at one momentum need not satisfy the finite-difference identity. A transverse photon would contract the correctly derived spatial vertex with its physical polarization; continuity fixes the longitudinal relation but does not supply the transverse interaction by itself. A bare zero can miss a real source Consider the completely specified two-mode model H=\begin{pmatrix}0&t\\t&\Delta\end{pmatrix}, \qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta>0. \tag{15} Retain the first component. Its bare vertex is V_{PP}=0, but H_{\rm eff}=t^2/(E-\Delta) and \partial_aH_{\rm eff}=2t/(E-\Delta) when the probe changes t to t+a. The full lower eigenvalue gives \frac{dE_-}{da}\bigg|_{a=0} =-\frac{2t}{\sqrt{\Delta^2+4t^2}}. \tag{16} At t=0.4, \Delta=2, the physical vertex is about -0.37139. Equation (7) reproduces it exactly. This is a source through the components of the same field which the bare projection omitted. Even a truly invariant retained space at zero probe can retain a nonlinear response. Set t=0 in (15). The first derivative vanishes, but E_-(a)=\frac{\Delta-\sqrt{\Delta^2+4a^2}}2 =-\frac{a^2}{\Delta}+O(a^4),\qquad E_-''(0)=-\frac2\Delta. \tag{17} The induced source is linear in a small applied amplitude even though the unperturbed source expectation is zero. Thus a neutral charge, a vanishing linear transition vertex, and absence of polarizability are separate tests. The geometric response examples require this same distinction. Application to the neutral spatial modes Spatial transport of a neutral doublet shows that a fixed spinor projection can remove the first-order Dirac action of perpendicular spatial momenta. Equations (2)–(14) provide a way to retain that contribution in both the dynamics and the source before identifying a physical coupling. They also prevent a missing projected current from being mistaken for derived electromagnetic neutrality. The required next inputs are the full spatial particle solution, the actual photon inclusion or collective map, and the action which defines V. The descending photon source specifies the propagation-preserving output projection; its complete current must be carried through the same reduction. Verification dressed_coupling_checks.py compares the source derivative with independent finite differences of the full effective operator, reconstructs full eigenstates, and checks their energy shifts against direct diagonalization. Independent incoming and outgoing momenta test (14), including on-shell matrix elements. The two-mode examples verify both the nonzero dressed source and quadratic response. All conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Canonical coupling normalization — establishes the kinetic-metric normalization extended here to eliminated modes. Projected Dirac current — supplies the current and projection-defect problem addressed by the full vertex.

title: Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels
summary: The full Dirac response can rotate a statically inaccessible higher-dimensional shape into a lower-sector source, producing a derived low-frequency barrier with both objects' polarizations retained.
text: Summary: The full Dirac response can rotate a statically inaccessible higher-dimensional shape into a lower-sector source, producing a derived low-frequency barrier with both objects' polarizations retained. A shape can fail to match statically and still respond dynamically For the spatial moment interaction, a source in a higher sector acts on a lower one through its restricted shape tensor. A mixed shape with one direction perpendicular to the lower sector has zero restriction. The full field can nevertheless move that pattern into another spatial shape which does have a nonzero restriction. This note calculates that process using the self-consistent Dirac profiles and complete quadrupole response in Dirac shape response. All coordinates belong to the same nested manifold of literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. The tensors label actual spatial patterns; their component counts do not introduce other physical dimensions. The result is a conditional spatial coupling mechanism. It does not assign the chosen quadrupole to a photon, or identify its suppression with a measured neutrino rate. Two radial functions determine the entire polarized shape response Let L_M,L_N be the two radial Dirac fluctuation operators, with normalized radial source vectors u_M,u_N. Define R_M(z)=u_M^T(z-L_M)^{-1}u_M,\qquad R_N(z)=u_N^T(z-L_N)^{-1}u_N. \tag{1} The spectral parameter z has the same time convention as the Dirac equation; a retarded boundary value requires the appropriate prescription at the real spectrum. The derivation uses values away from poles. For a real orthonormal traceless shape basis A_r, the target's spatial circulation tensor J acts by \mathcal K_{rs}=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(A_r[J,A_s]). \tag{2} Put c_0=2/[d(d+2)] and c_1=4/[d(d+2)^2]. The angular Gram matrices derived from the full Clifford field give the exact bare matrix response \boxed{\chi_0(z,J)=A(z)I+B(z)i\mathcal K,} \tag{3} where \begin{aligned} A(z)&=(c_0-c_1)[R_M(z)+R_M(-z)] +c_1[R_N(z)+R_N(-z)],\\ B(z)&=c_1[R_N(z)-R_M(z)-R_N(-z)+R_M(-z)]. \end{aligned} \tag{4} A is even in frequency and B is odd. Thus the static response is isotropic in the shape basis, while the rotating part of the response retains the prepared spatial polarization J. The source's own feedback supplies the complete response \boxed{\chi(z,J)=\big[I-g_0\chi_0(z,J)\big]^{-1}\chi_0(z,J),} \tag{5} with the same scalar coefficient g_0 as in the stationary profile. Equations (3)–(5) contain all the shape helicities and both ordinary and conjugate Dirac fluctuations. They do not replace the latter by a positive scalar oscillator. Both target preparation and source shape are essential. If the source has complex shape coefficients c, its response is \chi(z,J)c. Reversing the prepared circulation gives the transpose identity \chi(z,J)^T=\chi(z,-J),\qquad \chi(-\bar z,J)=\overline{\chi(z,J)}. \tag{6} A fixed polarized preparation need not have a symmetric response matrix. These relations retain the underlying real energy and its reciprocal variation without assuming that reversing a process leaves its preparations unchanged. Restriction can change the type of spatial shape For an isometric inclusion I:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^d, the moment source restricts as \mathcal R(C)=I^TCI. \tag{7} A traceless shape in d dimensions need not remain traceless after restriction. Its lower trace is a breathing source and must be retained when calculating the complete interaction. With Hilbert–Schmidt-normalized tensor bases, the map from higher traceless shapes to all lower symmetric shapes has singular values \underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{p(p+1)/2-1}, \qquad \sqrt{\frac{d-p}{d}}. \tag{8} To derive the last value, apply the adjoint map to the normalized lower breathing shape I_p/\sqrt p and remove its higher trace. The squared norm is 1-p/d. Lower traceless shapes already embed as higher traceless shapes with the same norm, giving the unit values. For five dimensions inside six, fourteen lower quadrupoles have unit restriction singular value and the lower breathing channel has value 1/\sqrt6. Five independent higher mixed shapes have zero static restriction. This is a statement about this spatial tensor kernel, not about the entire physical coupling of a particle species. The higher field's rotation opens the mixed shapes Take a six-dimensional orthogonal circulation tensor J, with J^2=-I, and let the lower five-plane be n^\perp. Put u=Jn, so u lies in that plane and has unit norm. Relative to this particular inclusion, J=\begin{pmatrix}J_5&u\\-u^T&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{9} The block notation describes the relation between the two objects. It does not make any of the six spatial directions inherently different. Every traceless symmetric C with zero full restriction has the form C=\begin{pmatrix}0&v\\v^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad v\in\mathbb R^5. \tag{10} Its spatial rotation satisfies \boxed{\mathcal R\left(\frac12[J,C]\right) =\frac12(uv^T+vu^T).} \tag{11} For unit u, the right side is zero only when v=0. For example, multiplying by u gives v+(u\cdot v)u=0, whose component along u then gives u\cdot v=0 and hence v=0. Thus none of the five nonzero statically hidden mixed quadrupoles remains hidden after this first spatial rotation. In matrix form, \ker\mathcal R\cap\ker(\mathcal R\mathcal K)=\{0\}. This retains the mixed part of the higher geometry instead of discarding it during restriction. There are still input combinations with zero output at an individual frequency, because the output has fewer components. The result concerns a fixed spatial pattern being invisible throughout the response, which is a stronger condition than a zero at one selected frequency. A derived low-frequency matching barrier Away from a static collective pole, equations (3)–(5) give \chi(z,J)=\frac{A(0)}{1-g_0A(0)}I +\frac{B'(0)}{[1-g_0A(0)]^2}z\,i\mathcal K+O(z^2). \tag{12} The coefficient is fixed by the actual radial modes: B'(0)=2c_1\left( \|L_M^{-1}u_M\|^2-\|L_N^{-1}u_N\|^2\right). \tag{13} For a source c with \mathcal Rc=0, \boxed{\mathcal R\chi(z,J)c =\frac{iB'(0)}{[1-g_0A(0)]^2}z\, \mathcal R\mathcal Kc+O(z^2).} \tag{14} The original static mismatch is exact, but a nonzero-frequency field motion opens the channel. The resulting mode amplitude is linear in small frequency when the coefficient in (13) is nonzero. Its squared amplitude is then quadratic; a physical transition rate also requires the relevant mode map, state density and incident flux. This is an explicit version of a spatial matching barrier produced by the field's own dynamics. It does not require assigning a special small coupling coefficient to the five-dimensional particle. Include the lower object's response as well Let \chi_a,\chi_b be the two objects' own complete shape responses. For a weak cross term with coefficient \epsilon multiplying their moment pairing, the leading response of the lower shape to a higher applied source h_b is \boxed{\delta M_a(z) =\epsilon\,\chi_a(z,J_a)\mathcal R\chi_b(z,J_b)h_b(z) +O(\epsilon^2).} \tag{15} Both polarizations and both spatial spectra enter. The reverse response uses \mathcal R^T, obtained from the same real pair energy. Common physical rotations transform both circulation tensors, both shape bases and the inclusion together, leaving the physical prediction unchanged. The coefficient \epsilon here controls a perturbative contact expansion; it is not an independently fitted constant for each particle pair. At leading order one may use the isolated self-consistent profiles. Their static deformation changes (15) at the next order. A finite interaction requires the corresponding complete pair background, as illustrated by Self-consistent nested Dirac pair. For a specified quadratic fluctuation energy, both responses can be solved exactly from \begin{aligned} \delta M_a&=\chi_a(h_a+\epsilon\mathcal R\delta M_b),\\ \delta M_b&=\chi_b(h_b+\epsilon\mathcal R^T\delta M_a). \end{aligned} \tag{16} This gives reciprocal feedback and collective poles. Applying that finite quadratic model to a nonlinear physical pair requires its Hessian at the correct background; it is not supplied just by combining two isolated profiles at an arbitrary large contact coefficient. A normalized example Choose J_6 with unit rotations in planes 12,34,56, and the lower five-plane spanned by axes 1 through 5. Apply the unit complex shape C=\frac12(e_3e_6^T+e_6e_3^T) +\frac i2(e_4e_6^T+e_6e_4^T). \tag{17} Its static restriction vanishes. Its entire response lies in a spatial subspace whose lower projection is traceless, so the lower breathing channel is not needed for this particular example. Take m=0.5 and one common interaction coefficient g_0=6.5. Self-consistency determines the isolated source strengths a_5=1.031769686 and a_6=0.998746098; they are not separately fitted interaction coefficients. Retain both profiles' complete source feedback. For the lower circulation with unit rotations in 12 and 34, the norm of the transfer coefficient \chi_5\mathcal R\chi_6C is: frequency lower response norm per unit weak-contact coefficient 0 0 0.1 9.40182\times10^{-6} 0.05 4.70316\times10^{-6} 0.025 2.35182\times10^{-6} 0.0125 1.17593\times10^{-6} The amplitude divided by frequency tends to approximately 9.40742\times10^{-5} in these model units, as calculated directly from the zero-frequency radial derivative. Reversing the lower target's 34 circulation while keeping the higher preparation fixed changes the finite-frequency response. The static zero is therefore compatible with both genuine dynamical access and a dependence on both polarizations. The incoming quadrupole in (17) is a specified spatial source, not a derived photon inclusion. This example supplies a mechanism to test against that physical inclusion; it does not establish universal five-dimensional suppression. Persistent spatial shape barriers extends this calculation across the hierarchy. It classifies shapes with a permanent zero and those whose first opening is quadratic in frequency, retaining the lower breathing response when needed. Verification spatial_shape_transfer_checks.py compares (3)–(5) with the full complex ordinary/conjugate source matrix, including every shape direction. It checks restriction singular values, the rank statement following (11), low-frequency scaling, both target preparations, covariance of the whole nested geometry, and reverse transfer. It also checks the controlled weak-contact expansion against exact finite quadratic feedback. As a separate completeness test, the equal norms of u_M,u_N cancel the would-be 1/z rotating response at large frequency. The response begins with A=O(z^{-2}), B=O(z^{-3}). title: Generalized sector coupling
summary: A common interaction on arbitrary nested sectors yields reciprocal responses, normalized vertices, and testable coupling relations, with neutrinos as a channel-specific control.
text: Summary: A common interaction on arbitrary nested sectors yields reciprocal responses, normalized vertices, and testable coupling relations, with neutrinos as a channel-specific control. Physical scope There is one infinite physical manifold with one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. Particles at different depths are structures of \Psi_\infty on that chain. All directions belonging to a given particle are of the same spatial kind. A decomposition relative to another particle's submanifold describes their relation; it does not give either particle an inherent division into different kinds of space. The following construction applies to arbitrary finite collections of sectors, including the working depths 2,3,4,5,6,10. It assumes specified spatial maps, measures, mode subspaces, and an interaction channel. It does not require accepting a particular list of global sphere or projective topologies. Actual embeddings and their domain conditions must be supplied wherever a proposed topology is used. IDWT has no mediator particles. The source profiles, response modes, and representation indices below describe the one field on this physical space. Coupling starts with its direct interaction terms. Eliminating some of its modes is a conditional reduction of those equations, not a particle-exchange mechanism. The working coupling hypothesis includes a changing geometric match: each particle can drive the other's spatial pattern toward greater compatibility or toward incompatibility during an encounter. Bilateral polarization coupling separates that physical target from a restricted orientation benchmark whose relative overlap remains constant. Both the change in compatibility and its effect on subsequent interaction must follow from the same dynamics. The concrete shape calculation is developed in Transition-density coupling, followed by Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes. The complementary route through rotation-neutral modes and their spatial transport tests how one geometric operation can be blocked while another remains active. The constructions below provide their common spatial maps and normalization. Localized spatial fields and reciprocal feedback Positive-frequency scalar vertices retain complete incoming bands and the off-diagonal spatial interference that builds the local source. A fixed normalized incoming polarization has massless inclusive squared strength \sin^2(\theta/2); a count of output components supplies no further multiplier. Available channels and the actual coherent contraction are separate parts of the calculation. A full Cartesian calculation independently checks its three-dimensional head-on response. At the stated three-dimensional benchmark, opposite relative phases reverse an approximately 1.77\% classical chiral-norm transfer, with conserved total norm and a continuum reflection law. Changing spatial compatibility compares the incoming and outgoing full patterns through the same prescribed free encounter, after removing their known free evolution. At fixed five-dimensional preparation rules and one coefficient, different complex phases give either increased or decreased contact. The effects are small and survive positive unit normalization of each outgoing pattern. Time ordering of the source derives the first nonzero contact coefficient from the complete local equation. Its independent coupling variations retain both partners' spatial response; no steering toward alignment is added. Scalar Born frequency accounting supplies a further constraint. Complete scalar vertices remove the negative-output resonant Born channel for positive incoming scattering data, while a finite-time positive preparation can still have a nonresonant signed response. Selecting stable occupied particle patterns, projecting one physically normalized interaction across distinct depths, and identifying observed electric and weak channels remain necessary. The full nonlinear collision changes normalized spatial compatibility in either direction under the same local equation. These are transversely unbound flat pulse controls, not identified particles or a completed distinct-depth coupling law. Causal local Dirac response derives two retarded scalar channels from the written local term at a specified uniform background. The instantaneous moment causality test exhibits an immediate remote influence in the candidate nonlocal equation. Its spatial harmonic comparison shows that matching one screened denominator does not derive that candidate: the higher spatial modes, response sign and direct contact all matter. Collective translation waves derives \mathcal I=M+T/d from the complete scalar Dirac field. The two displacement polarizations at depth two propagate at half the underlying Dirac speed on the zero-bare-mass branch. Their count alone does not identify photons. With an explicitly supplied minimal connection of the same field, Soft spatial current response derives the Thomson current, magnetic moment and uniform polarization correction. The matrix across (2,3,4,5,6,10) has rank six when every u_d is nonzero. Its normalized pair correlations are \sqrt{\min(d,e)/\max(d,e)}, independent of those scales. Selecting only the trace of the spatial moment tensor would instead give the rank-one geometric factor de/D in a containing depth D. The complete kernel also includes a nonzero traceless response. This identifies a definite physical projection to derive if a scalar common response is to follow from this kernel. Physical inputs still needed for numerical predictions The common construction fixes relations after its operators are specified. To predict particle couplings, V2 must supply the actual spatial and polarization maps B_d, the field's linearized evolution operator, the mode kinetic metrics, and the occupied preparations from its field equations. Depth-dependent parameters hidden inside those maps remain parameters. The electric, weak, and colour identifications also require the correct generators and representations on every sector. For the photon this includes its protected zero mode and transverse propagating field. The positive scalar confinement model developed below has no localized zero bound frequency; its massive normal branch cannot by itself supply that photon mode. This statement concerns the frozen bound eigenproblem. Collective fluctuations also vary the source and can have zero modes; their propagation requires the full fluctuation operator.
