title: Common probes of different self-mass branches
summary: Reduced currents give exact common-probe responses across different coherent mass grades, with reciprocal shape evolution, same-grade interference and vacuum regularity kept explicit.
text: Summary: Reduced currents give exact common-probe responses across different coherent mass grades, with reciprocal shape evolution, same-grade interference and vacuum regularity kept explicit. Use the self-mass action for the second pattern too The self-mass construction defines the canonical fields, exact contraction maps T_{Nk}, reduced scalar currents \rho_{N,k} and their adjoints B_{Nk}. Its common law is U=\sum_k h_{k,d}\Phi(\|R_k\|_{\rm HS}),\qquad R_k=\sum_{N\ge k}\rho_{N,k},\qquad h_{k,d}=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}. \tag{1} All currents are evaluated at the same physical spatial point before integration. Spatial profiles, both polarizations and their phases remain part of the fields. The independent canonical grade decomposition and weights in (1) are inverse-action premises, not a derived master reduction. The quartic pair kernel For \Phi(r)=\kappa r^2/2, take two coherent fields in distinct grades: \Psi_N=\chi_a\otimes z^N and \Psi_M=\chi_b\otimes w^M. Write A=\chi_a^\dagger\beta\chi_a, B=\chi_b^\dagger\beta\chi_b and \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2. The cross energy is exactly \boxed{V_{NM}=\kappa ABG_K(\tau),\qquad G_K(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^K\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}\tau^k, \qquad K=\min(N,M).} \tag{2} The same action has isolated self-source \kappa D_NA on the first coherent field. At perfect compatibility, G_K(1)=D_K by Hockey-Stick. At a fixed \tau<1, however, G_K(\tau)\longrightarrow(1-\tau)^{-d},\qquad (1-\tau)^dG_K(\tau)=I_{1-\tau}(d,K+1), \tag{3} where I is the regularized incomplete beta function. Equation (3) quantifies a region where the response becomes insensitive to the occupied degrees while the isolated self-source continues to grow as D_N. At depth six, Compatibility \tau G_{12}(\tau) G_{34}(\tau) 0.2 3.814687653888 3.814697265625 0.7 638.7104282927 1359.920365828 1 18564 3838380 This is not uniform agreement over orientations. Order zero also gives G_K(0)=1, so orthogonal coherent rays do not eliminate the quartic interaction. No electric or weak channel has been identified by this scalar compatibility polynomial. A fixed probe gives a stronger exact statement Let a probe have fixed degree M, arbitrary complex mode coefficients and every spinor component. Its currents only reach order M. Any coherent target of degree N\ge M has \rho_{N,k}=A P_{z,k},\qquad 0\le k\le M. \tag{4} Therefore its full cross energy with that probe, and its diagonal source on the target's occupied ray, are independent of N at the same local A and z. This does not require the probe itself to be coherent. The complete target gradient still contains B_{Nk} and depends on N: equal diagonal responses do not imply equal changes of shape. For the root or smooth law \Phi_\sigma(r)=\mu(\sqrt{r^2+\sigma^2}-\sigma), linearize about a nonzero coherent target and a zero probe field. Since the probe current is quadratic in its amplitude, its complete linear source operator is \boxed{\mathcal V_M(x)= \mu\,s_\sigma(A(x))\,\beta \sum_{k=0}^Mh_{k,d}B_{Mk}(P_{z(x),k}),\qquad s_\sigma(A)=\frac{A}{\sqrt{A^2+\sigma^2}}.} \tag{5} At the positive root endpoint, s_0(A)=1 for every A>0. Equation (5) is then independent of both target degree and target density. Different nonconstant target profiles sharing the same local ray texture give the same full probe Dirac operator, including every probe coefficient and spinor component. This is stronger than equality of one expectation value. For a parallel slack target ray, its transverse probe occupation j has source coefficient \mu\,s_\sigma(A)\frac{D_M}{D_j}\,\beta, \qquad D_j=\binom{j+d}{d}. \tag{6} The contraction identity used in (6) is the first sum in equation (14) of the self-mass note. Both the spatial kinetic operator and these coefficient sectors must be retained when computing a physical response. The target responds at second order in the small probe amplitude. That backreaction comes from the same energy; fixing the target in the linear probe equation is the stated perturbative limit. It does not remove the reciprocal variation of the full action. Nor does a weak field perturbation automatically represent a separately normalized massive particle. Root interaction and the vacuum limit For positive coherent currents in two different grades, the contribution of a shared order is \mu h_{k,d}\left[\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\tau^k+\sigma^2}-\sigma\right]. \tag{7} Unshared orders contain only their own grade's current. At \sigma=0, subtracting the two isolated energies gives a nonpositive cross term. At alignment it vanishes; at other orientations it generally remains. In particular, the order-zero root is additive for positive currents. It must not be confused with the quartic action's uniform order-zero cross term in (2). The endpoint also has a physical limitation. Equation (5) remains nonzero as a positive target density tends to zero, if the probe amplitude is taken to zero first. Reversing those limits gives the isolated probe problem. A globally weak tail cannot simply be assigned the same physical meaning as a finite normalized particle while ignoring this noncommuting vacuum limit. Positive \sigma restores decay of (5) when the target disappears. It also restores dependence on the actual target density and changes the spatial self-source. Near-equal weighted matrix elements do not establish equality of every spatially localized probe response. The separate spatial calculation retains this distinction. Ordinary rotations and orientation averages An average over real spatial directions is different from a Haar average over complex mode rays. For real unit tangent directions in d ordinary dimensions, \tau=(z\cdot w)^2 has beta distribution \operatorname{Beta}(1/2,(d-1)/2). Hence \langle\tau^k\rangle_{SO(d)} =\frac{(1/2)_k}{(d/2)_k}. \tag{8} At depth six the means of G_{12} and G_{34} are approximately 59.40644 and 1023.83613. Their second moments are approximately 190632.19 and 649947765.65. The high-compatibility region matters strongly even though (3) converges away from it. More generally, any polynomial F_N(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^Nc_{N,k}\tau^k with nonnegative coefficients summing to D_N satisfies \langle F_N\rangle_{SO(d)} \ge D_N\frac{(1/2)_N}{(d/2)_N}. \tag{9} The moments in (8) decrease with k, proving the bound term by term. At fixed d, its right side grows as N^{(d+1)/2}. Thus fixed-overlap agreement does not imply a degree-independent average over all these ordinary rotations. Equation (9) has the stated positive- polynomial scope; it is not a bound on every geometric interaction. Same-grade contributions retain interference If two contributions occupy the same canonical grade, their sum is one field. It is incorrect to replace it by two independently phased carriers. For \Psi=\chi_a z^N+\chi_b w^N, define t=\chi_b^\dagger\beta\chi_a,\qquad s=w^\dagger z,\qquad\tau=|s|^2. The exact current is \rho_k=AP_{z,k}+BP_{w,k} +t s^{N-k}|z^k\rangle\langle w^k|+\text{Hermitian conjugate}. \tag{10} Direct multiplication gives \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Tr}\rho_k^2={}&A^2+B^2+2AB\tau^k +2|t|^2\tau^{N-k}\\ &+2\operatorname{Re}(t^2s^{2N}) +4(A+B)\operatorname{Re}(ts^N). \end{aligned} \tag{11} Summing (11) includes both G_N(\tau) and H_N(\tau)=\sum_kh_{k,d}\tau^{N-k}, with H_N(0)=h_{N,d}. Averaging relative phase removes the explicitly oscillating terms but leaves the |t|^2 term. The canonical norm also contains the corresponding spinor Gram interference. These features concern field superposition, not particles nested inside other particles. Reciprocal evolution and a small scalar self-source A complete coefficient evolution at d=6, N=12,34, unit norms, \kappa=1/D_{12} and initial \tau=0.7 tests the quartic action. Two active coefficient directions and one positive-\beta spin line form an invariant subspace; every occupation within those directions evolves. It is a coefficient control, not a spatial particle encounter. Over time 20, the cross energy changes from 0.0344058623299 to 0.0405001677154. The first-current compatibility changes from 0.7 to 0.7018348509519, and the second-current compatibility from 0.49 to 0.4989699515065. The first-current purities finish at approximately 0.9896030421225 and 0.9999999338726: one pattern deforms substantially more than the other. Total energy, both norms and the total rotation moment are conserved to numerical accuracy. Tighter integration tolerances change the complete complex trajectory by at most 4.49\times10^{-8}. The root law at the same grades, norms, initial compatibility and duration, with \mu=1/D_{12}, gives a different but equally reciprocal evolution. Its first-current purities finish at 0.91769258 and 0.9999999919; the first- and second-current compatibilities reach 0.71452485 and 0.51880053. The cross energy changes from -0.56192935 to -0.51481218, with total energy and both norms conserved. Tighter time integration changes the complete complex pair trajectory by at most 4.46\times10^{-8}. The light pattern again deforms more strongly. The evolution is not restricted to a prescribed changing overlap. Small self-source requires a separate interpretation. At a scalar-null coherent spinor with positive canonical density \rho, the quartic source vanishes, but its occupied real derivative has a nonzero singular value 2\kappa D_N\rho. Cancellation between spinor components therefore does not suppress every response. A small field norm, a small scalar balance and a small microscopic coefficient are different mechanisms. The existing odd-depth scalar-null classes also annihilate every current in (1) when all coefficient spinors belong to the same class. They provide no self-binding or selected small nonzero mass, and a general external scalar source can drive complementary components. These checks do not yet identify the neutrino's electric or weak channels, or derive a suppression scale for the assigned depth-five states. Verification The later localized response calculation extends the comparison to solved spatial target profiles under one binding and self-mass action. A finite normalized lower-grade probe has identical cross energy, complete probe source and reciprocal translation force for targets with the same profile and different larger grades. Their full shape responses and frequency-proportional inertias still differ. The test does not identify the probe as an observed particle or settle a full encounter. A different forward calculation uses the actual scalar master projection and balanced normal populations. Their stationary scalar contribution cancels while their moving polarization produces a common geometric response. It retains finite normal kinetic gaps, complete probe self-interaction and ordinary tangent rotations, without replacing the raw projection weights by shell weights. graded_current_tower_checks.py checks complete reciprocal sources, same-grade interference, ordinary rotations, common probes and the scalar-null derivative. graded_current_actions_checks.py checks the full root and smooth probe operators and pair energies. graded_current_tower_flow.py evolves the stated coefficient control with all active occupations. graded_current_root_flow.py uses the same complete coefficient space for the root or smooth action. graded_current_flow_comparison.py checks both refined trajectories and all stated conserved quantities. The self-source, response and evolution all use the same canonical action.

title: Higher angular response of the localized current field
summary: Homogeneous closed and coclosed polynomial forms give complete angular blocks for the even-depth matrix field; independent Cartesian checks and expanded electron and muon scans retain the distinction between angular classification and full spatial stability.
text: Summary: Homogeneous closed and coclosed polynomial forms give complete angular blocks for the even-depth matrix field; independent Cartesian checks and expanded electron and muon scans retain the distinction between angular classification and full spatial stability. Three different indices The earlier localized response calculation used constant Clifford forms. Those angular families include translations but only a bounded range of ordinary spherical harmonics. Here d is an even ordinary spatial depth, k is a Clifford form degree, and \ell is a polynomial angular degree. Neither k nor \ell is the occupied mass grade N. The electron and muon retain N=12 and N=34 at d=6. At even depth, the full complex r\times r matrix space, r=2^{d/2}, is represented by all Clifford forms. No spinor or partner directions are discarded by using that matrix basis. Let P_{\ell,k}(x) be a Hermitian Clifford k-form whose coefficients are homogeneous polynomials of degree \ell, satisfying \sum_a\alpha_a\partial_aP_{\ell,k}=0,\qquad \sum_a(\partial_aP_{\ell,k})\alpha_a=0. \tag{1} These are simultaneously closed and coclosed polynomial differential forms. A concrete nonzero example for 1\leq k\leq d-1 uses z=x_1+ix_2: P_{\ell,k}(x)=i^{k(k-1)/2} \left[\operatorname{Re}(z^\ell)\alpha_1 -\operatorname{Im}(z^\ell)\alpha_2\right] \alpha_3\cdots\alpha_{k+1}. \tag{2} The final product is empty for k=1. Direct differentiation proves both equations (1). Real linear combinations and rotations provide the other polarization patterns in the same polynomial space. A closed radial block at every angular degree Write x=r_xn and T(n)=P_{\ell,k}(n), normalized by its mean squared trace on the unit sphere. Introduce B_0=T,\quad B_1=i\alpha_nT,\quad B_2=iT\alpha_n, \quad B_3=\alpha_nT\alpha_n, \qquad s_k=(-1)^k(d-2k). \tag{3} These B_i are angular basis matrices, not the scalar insertions of the action. Homogeneity and (1) give \alpha\cdot\nabla T(n)=-\ell\alpha_nT/r_x. The complete spatial Dirac operator D=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla acts as \begin{aligned} D(aB_0)&=-(a'-\ell a/r_x)B_1,\\ D(bB_1)&=[b'+(d+\ell-1)b/r_x]B_0,\\ D(cB_2)&=s_kcB_0/r_x+[c'-(\ell+1)c/r_x]B_3,\\ D(eB_3)&=s_keB_1/r_x-[e'+(d+\ell)e/r_x]B_2. \end{aligned} \tag{4} These identities follow by the Cartesian product rule. They do not replace d by an effective physical depth. All derivatives still act in the original d ordinary directions. The four diagonal angular Gram entries are one. The only nonzero off-diagonal entries are G_{03}=G_{30}=G_{12}=G_{21}=t_{\ell,k},\qquad t_{\ell,k}=\frac{s_k}{d+2\ell}. \tag{5} For example, \Delta(\alpha_xP_{\ell,k}\alpha_x)=2s_kP_{\ell,k}, while \Delta(r_x^2P_{\ell,k})=2(d+2\ell)P_{\ell,k}. Their harmonic difference is orthogonal to degree \ell, proving (5). This argument applies to every solution of (1), not only (2). An orthonormal angular basis is E_0=B_0,\quad E_+=\frac{B_1+B_2}{\sqrt{2(1+t_{\ell,k})}},\quad E_-=\frac{B_1-B_2}{\sqrt{2(1-t_{\ell,k})}},\quad E_3=\frac{B_3-t_{\ell,k}B_0}{\sqrt{1-t_{\ell,k}^2}}. \tag{6} Their ordinary harmonic degrees are \ell,\ell+1,\ell+1,\ell+2. At \ell=0, (4)–(6) recover the earlier constant-form blocks. The exceptional constant scalar and pseudoscalar forms have two angular components rather than four. The complete local binding Hessian closes on this span. Clifford grade fixes \beta T\beta=(-1)^kT, and Hermitian conjugation exchanges the required basis expressions without discarding complex coefficients. For k=1, the trace term also closes because \alpha_nT+T\alpha_n is a scalar matrix. Other interior form degrees have the corresponding zero traces. Thus the ordinary and conjugate coefficients of every upper and lower matrix variation remain present. The current-metric comparison changes the upper partner curvature by its stated factor q and preserves this closure. Why the angular blocks cover the matrix field The Fischer decomposition for closed and coclosed polynomial forms states that arbitrary Clifford-valued polynomials are generated from solutions of (1) by radial powers, exterior multiplication by x, and contraction with x. On the sphere these operations are exactly the span (3), with the two exceptional constant families. This gives the angular classification; the radial functions remain unrestricted. See Theorem 1 of Delanghe, Lávička and Souček. The multiplicities provide an independent count. For 1\leq k\leq d-1, the dimension of the polynomial space in (1) is h_{\ell,k}=\binom{d-2}{k-1}\binom{\ell+d-2}{d-2} \frac{(2\ell+d)(\ell+d-1)}{(\ell+k)(\ell+d-k)}. \tag{7} Set h_{0,0}=h_{0,d}=1, h_{\ell,0}=h_{\ell,d}=0 for \ell>0, and every negative-degree multiplicity to zero. Formula (7) follows by solving the dimension recurrence for the harmonic pieces: \binom dk\left[\binom{j+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{j+d-3}{d-1}\right] =h_{j,k}+h_{j-1,k-1}+h_{j-1,k+1}+h_{j-2,k}, \tag{8} for interior k; the final term is absent at the two endpoint form degrees. Unavailable binomials are zero. Counting (6) at a fixed ordinary harmonic degree j, including the exceptional constant families, yields exactly 2^d\left[\binom{j+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{j+d-3}{d-1}\right]. \tag{9} This is the full scalar-harmonic dimension times the r^2=2^d matrix components. Polynomial restrictions are dense on the sphere, so the classification extends to the angular Hilbert space. It does not turn any finite radial calculation into a stability theorem. Including radial Gaussian polynomial degrees recovers the usual shell count 2^d\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}. This is a count for that chosen polynomial basis. It is not a derivation that the nonlinear particle cavity has an oscillator spectrum, nor does it select the weights of its mass operator. Expanded tests of the actual smooth core The calculation uses the solved smooth core with central-shape parameter 10^{-4}, common gap one, sustaining coefficient g=7.875370789623267 and unit norm. Its root mean squared radius is 1.276658598123441 in gap units. Both current norms use that same fixed point. Independent Cartesian differentiation checks (4) at depths six and ten, all interior form degrees, and \ell=0,1,2,5. The largest normalized error is 5.67\times10^{-12}. Full arbitrary-complex matrix Hessian checks have maximum relative residual 1.04\times10^{-15}. Angular quadrature independently checks the Gram matrix. The entire finite \ell=0 projected matrices also agree with the earlier implementation. The spatial scan uses every combination of \ell=1,2,4,8,16 and k=1,\ldots,5 at physical depth six; the assigned electron and muon frequencies 18564 and 3838380; the original norm q=1 and equal-contraction norm q=1/9; 26 radial functions with scale 0.5 and 180 quadrature points, and 40 radial functions with scale 0.55 and 260 quadrature points. The 200 finite spectra retain both frequency signs, ordinary and conjugate variations, and every component of each stated angular block. The largest computed real growth parts are Current curvature Electron Muon q=1 3.96\times10^{-11} 8.15\times10^{-9} q=1/9 2.95\times10^{-11} 1.01\times10^{-8} These real parts are unresolved at the numerical scale of the large frequency blocks. The scan establishes no resolved exponentially growing mode within its stated finite ranges. It does not cover every \ell, arbitrarily short radial wavelengths, or finite nonlinear disturbances. Real eigenvalues also do not exclude transient amplification; the current-metric note gives a separate exact limiting-operator analysis. Reproduction and limits localized_harmonic_response.py constructs the angular matrices and multiplicities. localized_harmonic_response_checks.py performs the independent Cartesian and full-Hessian checks, exact dimension counts, and all 200 spectra using localized_clifford_response.py. The report preserves the full finite eigenvalue arrays and each discretization, rather than only favorable selected frequencies. This supplies the angular blocks needed for a complete future spatial analysis. It does not prove nonlinear stability, determine the physical mass carrier, derive the shell weights, or identify observed interaction vertices. The matrix decomposition and the absence of resolved growth in these finite calculations have precisely those separate scopes.

title: Complete normal currents and the two-wave coupling
summary: The complete two-wave current retains mixed terms, both polarizations, surface overlaps and reciprocal separation forces, with comparable conditional responses across depth-six frequencies.
text: The gapped normal carrier admits a concrete polarized two-wave current calculation. Its large-gap limit has two distinct angular contributions: the overlap of separate self currents and a mixed current between the waves. Keeping both removes a false inference of zero interaction from a zero of the separate-current overlap. Under common parameters, the normal response is nearly independent of the occupied surface degree within a winding. Actual surface overlaps retain additional degree and orientation dependence. This is a conditional geometric interaction on the inverse spatial carrier, not a derived physical IDWT force or a rate of particle encounters. The operator, source and complete normal corrections are defined in the carrier, the inertia calculation, and the endpoint source response. The local quartic used here is a declared probe of those fields. Its failure to generate the prescribed normal texture remains unresolved. Keep the complete same-field phase average For two distinct carrier frequencies, write the field at a given position as A exp(-i omega_a t)+B exp(-i omega_b t). With the same two Hermitian normal matrices Gamma_i, define J_i^A=A^\dagger\Gamma_iA,\qquad J_i^B=B^\dagger\Gamma_iB,\qquad K_i=A^\dagger\Gamma_iB. \tag{1} The quartic U=g sum_i J_i^2/2 is an interaction of this one field. Expansion and averaging over the relative oscillation phase gives the cross term \boxed{\overline U_{AB} =g\left(\boldsymbol J^A\cdot\boldsymbol J^B +\sum_i|K_i|^2\right).} \tag{2} The second term is interference of the two waves in the same local current. It is not an exchanged particle. Equation (2) is an algebraic phase average for distinct frequencies. At equal or resonant frequencies the relevant phases must instead remain in the dynamics. The unaveraged quartic retains them in either case. For the normal kernel both currents in (1) vanish at leading chiral order. Inserting the complete correction eta/Lambda gives their first nonzero terms. The calculation retains all normal Fourier powers and all four normal spinor components in both members of the canonical pair. The normal angular factors Write vartheta for a normal polarization orientation and theta for the ordinary polar coordinate in the normal plane. Let q=n-1, A_0=U_0, B_0=V_0, and define the positive scalar responses \begin{aligned} Y&=K_0^{-1}\left[ \frac{2(1+r^2/2)}{(1+r^2)^{3/2}}U_0\right],\\ Z&=K_{n+1}^{-1}\left[ \frac{r^2}{(1+r^2)^{3/2}}V_0\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{3} The inverse K_m is the complete half-line inverse, not a normal-mode cutoff. In the large-gamma endpoint limit, the complex self current scaled by Lambda is j_1+i j_2= -2(-1)^q\gamma A_0Y e^{in\vartheta} +2(-1)^q\gamma B_0Z e^{-in\vartheta}e^{i2n\theta}. \tag{4} Both terms survive at leading order. Define the positive common spatial coefficient C_n=4\int_{\mathbb R^2} \left(A_0^2Y^2+B_0^2Z^2\right)d^2x. \tag{5} Angular integration of (4), and a separate contraction of the mixed spinors, then give \begin{aligned} D_{ab}&:=\int\boldsymbol j_a\cdot\boldsymbol j_b\,d^2x \longrightarrow C_n\gamma^2\cos(n\Delta\vartheta),\\ X_{ab}&:=\int\sum_i|k_{i,ab}|^2\,d^2x \longrightarrow C_n\gamma^2\cos^2(\Delta\vartheta/2). \end{aligned} \tag{6} Here Delta vartheta=vartheta_b-vartheta_a. The coefficients k_i are the first mixed-current terms scaled by Lambda, matching the scaling of j_i. The endpoint result follows from the actual wavefunctions, with their canonical norm. It contains no division by particle frequency. Numerically C_5=0.0935501816, C_6=0.0920762937 and C_10=0.0868345076. Thus the winding-five normal channel has no large suppression under the same dimensionless normal action parameters. This is not a derivation of neutrino interactions. The full depth-five geometry, physical units and cross-sector interaction still have to be supplied. At gamma=10000, the aligned electron and muon normal source profiles differ by about 0.00328 in relative L2 norm. Their direct and mixed normal overlap coefficients are respectively about 9.20738332e6 and 9.20740815e6, close to the common endpoint value 9.20762937e6. At Delta vartheta=pi/12 the depth-six separate-current overlap is nearly zero, but the mixed contribution is about 0.98294 of its aligned endpoint scale. That preparation is not a zero of (2). The cross term can also be negative at other orientations; the complete quartic, including the separate self terms, remains nonnegative for positive g. Neither the sign of this cross energy nor an energy gradient alone establishes the dynamics of an encounter. Restore the actual depth-six surface patterns For the monogenic surface family with one common spinor vacuum z_0, \chi_{L,u}=Y_{L,u}z_0,\qquad Y_{L,u}=\frac{(u_1z_1+u_2z_2)^L}{\sqrt{V B(L)}}, \quad B(L)=\frac{\Gamma(L+1)\Gamma(5/2)}{\Gamma(L+5/2)}, \quad V=\frac{8\pi^2}{3}. \tag{7} These are actual spinor fields on the conditional four-sphere surface feature in six ordinary dimensions. The two ordinary normal coordinates remain spatial coordinates. This surface/normal description does not impose a special three-plus-three split of electron space. The two terms in (2) generally multiply different surface overlaps: integral rho_a rho_b and integral |chi_a^dagger chi_b|^2. For the common-vacuum family (7) those overlaps coincide pointwise. Their exact integral is I_{ab}(x)=\frac{B(a+b)}{V B(a)B(b)} \frac{\sum_{j=0}^{\min(a,b)}\binom aj\binom bj x^j} {\binom{a+b}{a}},\qquad x=|u^\dagger v|^2. \tag{8} The earlier surface spinor overlap contains an additional tangent-current factor. It is absent from (8) because the present matrices act in the normal spinor factor. Reusing that tangent-current integral unchanged would give the wrong coefficient. The complete reference cross coefficient for (7) is I_ab(D_ab+X_ab). For a common degree-two mathematical probe and the electron and muon surface assignments, the ratio of responses is: Relative surface angle Muon response / electron response 0 1.11231580 0.3 1.09720285 0.7 1.01237516 pi/2 0.18986898 The normal orientations are aligned and all action parameters and norms are common. The particle-frequency ratio is 206.75894 at the tested finite gamma. The degree-two probe is a depth-six mathematical mode, not a photon. These results illustrate comparable responses for some preparations and substantial geometric variation for others; they do not establish an orientation-independent universal coupling. The physical normalization removes an apparent width suppression Let the surface radius be R and the normal profile width be a. Both are ordinary spatial lengths. The normal width is a field-profile scale on an unbounded plane, not a compactified dimension. Equal physical wave speeds give Lambda=R/a. Canonical normalization of a d-dimensional product profile requires \Psi_{\rm phys} =a^{-1}R^{-(d-2)/2}\psi_{\rm dimensionless}. \tag{9} Its first nonzero normal current therefore scales as J_{\rm phys} =a^{-2}R^{-(d-2)}\Lambda^{-1}j =a^{-1}R^{-(d-1)}j. \tag{10} The complete volume element contributes a^2 R^(d-2). Hence \boxed{\int J_{\rm phys}^2\,d^dx =R^{-d}\int j^2\,d^2r\,dA} \tag{11} at this leading order. The apparent Lambda^(-2) suppression is exactly offset by the increasingly concentrated physical profile. If g_d is the physical quartic coefficient in frequency-times-volume units, the pair coefficient is \overline U_{ab} =\frac{g_d}{R^d}I_{ab}(D_{ab}+X_{ab}). \tag{12} Thus narrowing this normal profile alone does not weaken the physical interaction at fixed g_d and R. Taking Lambda large at fixed dimensionless quartic g instead changes the corresponding physical coupling. That distinction is necessary when comparing the normal gap with the source and response. Across different d, the physical normalization and sector measure still require a common master-field derivation; the numerical C_n values alone do not settle that relation. Separate the two ordinary spatial profiles The complete normal fields can also be placed at different centers. Let s be their separation along the axial normal direction, in units of the common normal width a. This axial displacement is an ordinary Cartesian translation. It is distinct from displacing the radial coordinate of the round surface, which would change the profile of the feature rather than translate the whole feature. The separate and mixed terms are evaluated on the actual complex fields at x+s/2 and x-s/2, with all their spinor components and normal angles. For aligned normal polarization, the depth-six electron/muon comparison gives the following normal cross coefficient, divided by the common endpoint value 2 C_6 gamma^2: Axial separation / normal width Relative normal cross coefficient 0 0.99997463 1 0.52100688 2 0.03799068 3 3.64177e-7 4 approximately 1.90225e-35 The dimensionless normal width cancels from the leading coincident strength in (11), but the physical separation is a s. It therefore still sets the range of this overlap. This distinction does not supply a physical value for a or an interaction rate. Polarized coefficients are more varied than this aligned example. At relative angle pi/6 the complete cross term is negative at coincident centers, positive at separations one and two, and negative again at separation three. The separate and mixed contributions have different spatial envelopes. A sign-changing cross energy alone does not prove a bound particle pair or a stable dynamical trajectory. Direct differentiation of the full complex spatial fields gives the gradient of this cross energy. Independent displaced-profile differences agree with it. Interchanging the two profiles leaves their cross energy unchanged and reverses its separation derivative. A common rotation of both polarized fields and the separation vector also leaves it unchanged. These checks establish reciprocity of this interaction contribution; the inertial and supporting-field terms needed for motion remain absent. Scope and verification The normal report holomorphic-normal-pair-20260914T062613_882235Z.json passes 256 checks. It includes all mixed currents, spatial refinement, the full first normal equation, reciprocity, common physical rotations, and an independent phase average of the complete complex local spinors. It also checks the winding-five control with no inserted suppression. holomorphic-surface-pair-20260914T062853_406360Z.json passes 75 checks of actual ordinary surface integration, arbitrary complex coherent lines, canonical norms, and the physical volume factors. holomorphic-normal-separation-20260914T064513_632049Z.json passes 138 checks of complete Cartesian overlap, polarization, physical rotations, reciprocity and the spatial energy derivative. The very small separation-four tail uses a denser radial profile and independent Cartesian quadratures. The preceding report and its source remain preserved: its last radial tail comparison missed the required three-parts-per-million tolerance. The calculations concern prescribed overlapping or separated reference profiles and an initial weak-interaction coefficient. They do not yet supply self-supported particles, a physical background, a dynamical encounter trajectory, or reciprocal evolution of the normal texture. Those require the same-field source and its kinetic and stress terms. The negative wave-only inertia found in the companion calculation is not repaired by the present pair overlap. Related research Spatial mass operator: results and remaining dynamics — connects this calculation to its premises, later corrections and the complete source question.

title: The spatial source and the endpoint response of the simplex carrier
summary: The full normal current tests the assumed texture and opens an endpoint link with nearly equal electron and muon responses despite their different simplex frequencies.
text: The full normal wave supplies a concrete source test for the prescribed texture W=z^n. Its simplest local matrix-current closure does not reproduce that texture: the dominant current has winding zero. That same component has a precise spectral effect. A constant deformation W=z^n+a opens a coupling between the two ends of the projected chain. The electron and muon assignments have almost the same absolute response to this deformation under one common normal operator, while their frequencies follow different simplex counts. This is a conditional example of the combination of different mass-frequencies and similar response within a depth. The sustaining field, its stiffness, and the physical coupling law are not derived by this example. The starting spatial operator and all its normal modes are defined in the gapped carrier. Its complete first normal response and wave stress are calculated in the normal inertia note. No independently interacting scalar field or particle-exchange mechanism is introduced. The actual local source of the normal coefficient Let Gamma_1 and Gamma_2 denote the two Hermitian normal potential matrices called beta_1 and beta_2 in the carrier note. At a fixed surface mode, define the local currents J_a(x)=\psi(x)^\dagger\Gamma_a\psi(x),\qquad a=1,2. \tag{1} The pair components are summed in this contraction. Both Gamma matrices reverse normal chirality. Therefore the complete kernel state psi_0 has J_a=0 pointwise. With the full complementary correction eta, \psi=\psi_0+\Lambda^{-1}\eta+O(\Lambda^{-2}),\qquad J_a=\Lambda^{-1}j_a^{(1)}+O(\Lambda^{-2}), \tag{2} j_a^{(1)}=2\operatorname{Re} (\psi_0^\dagger\Gamma_a\eta). \tag{3} Thus the finite-kernel state alone would miss the source entirely. For the normal component ordering used in that note, the complex current is particularly simple: j_1^{(1)}+i j_2^{(1)} =2\sum_\chi \left(\eta_{\chi,0}^*\psi_{0,\chi,1} -\psi_{0,\chi,2}^*\eta_{\chi,3}\right). \tag{4} Every forced angular Fourier coefficient of (4) is retained. The complete first-order Dirac residual, radial refinement and independent contractions of the four-component spinors verify the result. A specific local quartic closure A minimal same-field source comparison is the declared quartic U=\frac g2(J_1^2+J_2^2). \tag{5} Its variation gives the local term g(J_1 Gamma_1+J_2 Gamma_2)psi. Consequently, reproducing the assumed normal potential Lambda(Gamma_1 Re W+Gamma_2 Im W) would require \Lambda W=g(J_1+iJ_2), \quad\text{or at leading order}\quad \Lambda^2 W=g(j_1^{(1)}+i j_2^{(1)}). \tag{6} This is a test of (5), not a claim that (5) is the established master interaction. It keeps a real common coefficient g and does not fit individual particle amplitudes. Write the complete complex source as sum_m j_m(r) exp(i m theta). For W=r^n exp(i n theta), equation (6) requires only harmonic m=n. The calculated source instead has a dominant m=0 term. At gamma=10000: Winding n Beta Fraction of source squared norm at m=0 Fraction at m=n 6 15.5 0.9999874017 5.04721e-34 6 37.5 0.9999614143 2.15766e-29 10 27.5 0.9999806896 2.18066e-50 The fraction uses the actual full-plane L2 norm of the source, summing all its Fourier powers. Orthogonality makes the unwanted angular components impossible to remove by changing a single real coefficient. An independent fit weighted by the actual wave density also has a relative residual essentially equal to one. This avoids giving the unbounded target coefficient an artificial finite global norm. There is also a separate asymptotic issue: a polynomial current of a single localized wave decays at infinity, whereas W=z^n grows. A fuller same-field background or a different spatial completion would have to address both the local angular source and the outer spatial behavior. These observations constrain this source comparison; they do not rule out an ambient IDWT field or every possible self-interaction. The dominant source has an analytic endpoint formula Put q=n-1 and use the normalized radial functions U_l,V_l of the complete normal kernel. The reflection symmetry gives V_q=U_0 and U_q=V_0. Define the positive scalar response Y=K_0^{-1}\left[ \frac{2(1+r^2/2)}{(1+r^2)^{3/2}}U_0\right], \tag{7} where K_0 is the full radial operator in the normal inertia note. For large gamma at fixed beta, the two canonical vectors approach the opposite endpoints, with their normalization fixed jointly. Then j_0(r)=-2(-1)^q\gamma U_0(r)Y(r) \,[1+O(\gamma^{-2})] \tag{8} in the integrated comparison. The leading expression is independent of beta. Positivity of the scalar Green function makes its coefficient nonzero. A smaller harmonic at m=2n also survives the endpoint limit; it is retained in the source norm and cannot be dropped in an exact polarization calculation. title: Incoming spatial shape modes
summary: A specified incoming spatial moment and an applied force have different response maps; individual shape helicities obey exact hyperplane restriction bounds which clarify the frequency-dependent cancellation mechanism.
text: Summary: A specified incoming spatial moment and an applied force have different response maps; individual shape helicities obey exact hyperplane restriction bounds which clarify the frequency-dependent cancellation mechanism. Distinguish an incoming pattern from a force that creates it Dynamical shape opening follows a fixed force applied to a higher spatial field. The higher response converts that force into a changing moment, which then drives the lower partner. A freely propagating particle must also satisfy its own field equation, so its actual moment cannot automatically be identified with that forcing vector. The two objects occupy nested submanifolds of the same ordinary macroscopic spatial manifold. Both polarizations, the actual spatial inclusion and the response of each object remain in the following equations. Moment and helicity labels describe spatial patterns; they are not additional spatial dimensions or physical particle assignments. Retain both responses without processing the incident mode twice Let \mathcal R(C)=I^TCI restrict a higher spatial moment into the lower sector. Its adjoint uses the full Frobenius moment norm, including lower breathing. Let \chi_a,\chi_b be the corresponding complete response operators at a specified frequency and normal momentum, and let \epsilon denote the common contact coefficient. For a prescribed unperturbed incoming moment b_{\rm in}, the coupled linear response equations are a=\epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R b,\qquad b=b_{\rm in}+\epsilon\chi_b\mathcal R^\dagger a. \tag{1} They give, wherever the indicated inverse exists, \boxed{a= [I-\epsilon^2\chi_a\mathcal R\chi_b\mathcal R^\dagger]^{-1} \epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R b_{\rm in}.} \tag{2} Both objects readjust, and the denominator retains repeated feedback. If the incident moment is instead produced by an applied force f_b, then b_{\rm in}=\chi_bf_b. Substituting it into (2) recovers the previous leading response \epsilon\chi_a\mathcal R\chi_b f_b. An actual incoming moment is already the result of its own spatial dynamics; applying \chi_b to it again would change the physical input. Consequently \mathcal R b_{\rm in}=0 gives zero lower response in this specified channel, while \mathcal R f_b=0 need not. The latter force can produce \mathcal R\chi_bf_b\ne0. For a scattering problem the incoming field and outgoing response use their specified propagation boundary conditions. At a discrete pole or resonance, use the full coupled operator or its appropriate limiting resolvent. A finite pair of free bound oscillators has hybridized mode frequencies; an inverse evaluated directly at an uncoupled pole does not replace that eigenproblem. At finite nonlinear contact, the background must also be the readjusted nested pair. Individual rotating shapes preserve their geometric restriction Take an even-dimensional higher sector with orthogonal circulation J^T=-J, J^2=-I. On complex symmetric traceless spatial tensors define \mathcal K(C)=\frac12[J,C],\qquad T=i\mathcal K. \tag{3} The eigenvalues of T are 0,\pm1. A shape helicity is an eigenvector Tc=\lambda c; it labels rotation of the actual spatial pattern relative to J. For the full radial Dirac response, \chi(z)c=\chi_\lambda(z)c, \qquad \chi_\lambda(z)= \frac{A(z)+\lambda B(z)}{1-g_0[A(z)+\lambda B(z)]}. \tag{4} Therefore \boxed{\mathcal R\chi(z)c=\chi_\lambda(z)\mathcal Rc.} \tag{5} Changing frequency changes the amplitude of an individual helicity, while its relative spatial restriction stays the same. Degenerate modes can be combined within a helicity; (5) holds for that whole subspace. Combinations of different helicities can instead acquire different relative responses. A hyperplane retains a fixed fraction of every pure helicity Let the containing sector have d=2m, with m\ge2, and let the lower sector be any hyperplane of dimension d-1. Choose coordinates in which J rotates the planes 12,34,\ldots and the omitted normal is axis d. This is a common change of coordinates for the geometry and inclusion, not a preferred division of the higher particle's spatial dimensions. The singular values of the restriction map on each normalized helicity subspace are: helicity singular value multiplicity +1 or -1 1 m(m-1)/2 +1 or -1 1/\sqrt2 m-1 +1 or -1 1/2 1 0 1 (m-1)^2-1 0 \sqrt{(m+1)/(2m)} 1 0 1/\sqrt2 2(m-1) To derive the nonzero-helicity rows, take the orthonormal complex spatial vectors v_j=(e_{2j-1}+ie_{2j})/\sqrt2. Their symmetric squares and products span one helicity, with the conjugates spanning the other. Restriction preserves v_j for j<m and gives I^Tv_m=e_{d-1}/\sqrt2 at the vector level. A square of v_m therefore loses a factor 1/2 in tensor norm; a normalized mixed product loses 1/\sqrt2; the remaining products retain norm one. For helicity zero, represent the commuting real tensors by Hermitian m\times m matrices. Write their final row and column as a vector v and scalar a, with upper block H_0 and \operatorname{tr}H_0=-a. The full and restricted squared spatial norms are respectively 2\|H_0\|^2+4\|v\|^2+2|a|^2, \qquad 2\|H_0\|^2+2\|v\|^2+|a|^2. \tag{6} Split H_0 into its traceless part and -aI/(m-1). These orthogonal parts give the final three rows. Complexification preserves the same singular values for complex forcing amplitudes. In particular, for six dimensions restricted to five, \boxed{\|\mathcal Rc\|\ge\frac12\|c\| \quad\text{on each nonzero helicity subspace},} \tag{7} and the zero-helicity lower bound is 1/\sqrt2. Every individual helicity therefore retains a nonzero full five-dimensional moment. This is a geometric norm bound, not a lower bound on a physical neutrino interaction probability. The mode's radial source magnitude, the target's allowed preparations, its output map and flux normalization remain essential. In particular, the output here is all symmetric five-dimensional moments, not the physical photon channel. The full Dirac modes realize these helicities The spatial Dirac shape calculation gives radial source vectors u_\lambda,u_{-\lambda} and the complete ordinary/conjugate fluctuation matrix \mathcal B_\lambda= \begin{pmatrix} L+g_0u_\lambda u_\lambda^T&g_0u_\lambda u_{-\lambda}^T\\ -g_0u_{-\lambda}u_\lambda^T&-L-g_0u_{-\lambda}u_{-\lambda}^T \end{pmatrix}. \tag{8} An eigenvector (p,q) has moment amplitude h=u_\lambda^Tp+u_{-\lambda}^Tq. When h\ne0, its moment pattern has helicity \lambda. Independently, its frequency obeys 1-g_0\chi_{0,\lambda}(\omega)=0, \quad \chi_{0,\lambda}(z) =u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{9} The diagnostic solves (8) and checks (9), retaining both signs of the radial Dirac spectrum. With one common g_0=6.5 and bare scalar coefficient m_0=0.5, the first active six-dimensional shape frequencies are approximately: helicity first active frequency second active frequency -1 1.414313 2.402246 0 1.263426 1.673915 +1 1.216080 1.820918 The bound background frequency is 3.091416 in these model units. Radial refinement and the independent resolvent condition agree. These are shape excitations of the declared scalar model, not observed particle masses or a complete stability calculation. The analogous five-dimensional calculation uses the same g_0 and retains its additional half-helicities. The slow applied frequencies used in the earlier opening example are below these active shape frequencies. They should not be assigned to a free particle merely because the applied response is well defined there. Frequency opening describes cancellation between visible components Decompose a specified force as f=\sum_\lambda f_\lambda. Then \mathcal R\chi(z)f =\sum_\lambda\chi_\lambda(z)\mathcal Rf_\lambda. \tag{10} At z=0, the odd function B vanishes, so all \chi_\lambda(0) are equal. A force with \sum_\lambda\mathcal Rf_\lambda=0 is therefore statically hidden even though its individual components remain visible. As frequency changes, their different responses can spoil that cancellation. This is the mechanism behind linear or quadratic opening in Persistent spatial shape barriers. An actual occupied particle could realize a coherent combination or a frequency-dependent spatial mode, but its field equation must establish that preparation. A low bound frequency alone does not choose the cancelling combination. Source frequencies also explains why the frequency driving that combination must be derived from its actual spatial source. Verification incoming_shape_mode_checks.py compares singular values with independent coordinate tensors, including explicit tensors attaining the lower bounds at depths four, six and ten. Common rotations transform the circulation and inclusion together. Full ordinary/conjugate Dirac eigenvectors and independent radial resolvents verify the active modes at two radial resolutions and a common interaction coefficient. Independent coupled block equations check (2) with both objects responding, and explicitly distinguish an incident moment from an applied force. All checks remain active under Python optimization. Related Dynamical opening of spatial shape channels — supplies the forced response which (2) specializes. Persistent spatial shape barriers — supplies the complete fixed-force frequency classification. Polarized Dirac shape response — supplies the actual spatial fluctuation operators and their polarization weights. Source frequencies in spatial coupling — supplies the temporal interpretation needed for a particle application.

title: Causal limit of an instantaneous scalar moment interaction
summary: Smooth spatially separated initial data show that the instantaneous scalar moment equation changes a local current before causal contact, so its physical use requires a controlled retarded reduction.

A local observable tests the domain of dependence The common projective moment action gives i\partial_t\Psi=(D+V[\Psi] eta)\Psi, \qquad V_\Psi(X)=\kappa\int K(X,Y)\sigma(Y)\,d
u(Y), \quad \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi, 	ag{1} where K(X,Y)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_XP_Y) and d

Consider two smooth initial fields that agree on an open neighborhood of X, including all spinor components, and differ only in separated regions. Their local Dirac derivatives at X agree. Equation (1) gives  oxed{\Delta\dot j_e(X) =i\Delta V(X)\Psi(X)^\dagger[ eta,\alpha(e)]\Psi(X).} 	ag{2} This follows by differentiating both field factors in j_e and using \Delta\dot\Psi=-i\Delta V eta\Psi. The commutator is generally nonzero because  eta anticommutes with the spatial velocity matrices. A state with both chirality components can therefore have a different local current derivative immediately, even though all its initial data near the target are identical. For a local relativistic initial-value equation, changes outside a target's past domain of dependence cannot do this. Equation (2) identifies a specific failure of that property in the standalone instantaneous scalar model. No instantaneous potential plus compensating local constraint has been derived for (1); such a structure cannot be presumed. u= rac{d^2u}{\pi(1+|u|^2)^2}. 	ag{3} This is a conditional projective geometry of radius one, not a compactified direction. The target is u=0. Let b_c(u) be a normalized nonnegative smooth bump supported on the disk |u-c|<0.07, and define M_c=\int P(u)b_c(u)d
u(u),\qquad\operatorname{Tr}M_c=1. 	ag{4} Move a scalar density a=0.1 from the disk centered at c_2=1.2i to the disk centered at c_1=0.6. Both disks are disjoint from the target. This can be realized by smooth even-chirality field densities on top of a common positive background, with the same spinor in a neighborhood of the target. At \kappa=1 the target potential difference is \Delta V(0)=0.1\operatorname{Tr}[P(0)(M_{c_1}-M_{c_2})] \simeq0.03253166758. 	ag{5} Choose a local Clifford frame with  eta=\sigma_z, \alpha(e)=\sigma_x, and the common target spinor \Psi(0)=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2. Then  oxed{\Delta\dot j_e(0)=-2\Delta V(0) \simeq-0.06506333516.} 	ag{6} The minimum distances of the two source disks from the target are \arctan(0.53)\simeq0.48736 and \arctan(1.13)\simeq0.84636. Equation (6) holds at the initial time, before either distance can be traversed at speed one. Restoring R multiplies these distances by R; it does not remove the immediate response. Consequence for the candidate interaction The reciprocal spatial pair remains a valid calculation of its specified mathematical action. Its overlap changes and full-spinor deformations cannot yet be interpreted as a causal fundamental particle interaction. An effective instantaneous approximation could still be useful in a regime derived from local same-field dynamics. It must specify the retained spatial modes, response frequencies, initial conditions and error from neglecting propagation. The local Dirac retarded response supplies one explicit calculation in which both propagation channels follow from the written scalar term and signals have the required delayed support. Its static approximation has a frequency bound. That calculation does not derive the projective moment action or identify a physical background.
