All checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Two localized cores and regular binding
summary: Two independently solved cores have an exact reciprocal initial interaction and a binding-current cancellation; a smooth inverse binding removes that specific singularity while retaining localized simplex-frequency branches.
text: Summary: Two independently solved cores have an exact reciprocal initial interaction and a binding-current cancellation; a smooth inverse binding removes that specific singularity while retaining localized simplex-frequency branches. Start with two solved spatial fields The localized current action supports a common spatial core at different simplex frequencies. Its finite probe identity applies to arbitrary probe fields. A sharper test prepares both objects as independently solved localized cores, retaining the complete field equation after they overlap. Use natural units \hbar=c=1 and one ordinary spatial depth d. Prepare distinct grades N>M with unit canonical norm: \begin{aligned} \Psi_N(x)&=\begin{pmatrix}\phi(x-X)\\0\end{pmatrix} \otimes\overline z^{\,N},\\ \Psi_M(x)&=\begin{pmatrix}\phi(x-Y)\\0\end{pmatrix} \otimes\overline w^{\,M},\qquad \|z\|=\|w\|=1. \end{aligned} \tag{1} Each isolated field oscillates at its assigned \omega_R=\omega_{0,d}\binom{R+d}{d}. These are initial data for a pair, not a claim that their overlapping sum is a stationary solution. The grades label distinct components of the same field. At the same grade, one must instead retain coherent interference in one summed field. Write \phi^\dagger\phi=\rho I_{r_d} for the core at X, use \sigma for the corresponding density at Y, and let s=|z^\dagger w|^2,\qquad 0\le s\le1. \tag{2} The scalar s summarizes the two coherent coefficient rays in this particular preparation. Their actual radial spinor textures remain in \phi(x-X) and \phi(x-Y) and enter the complete binding source. It is not a replacement for spatial polarization in a general encounter. The exact initial cross energy At every shared current order k\le M, the complete mass current is R_k=I_{r_d}\otimes(\rho P_{z,k}+\sigma P_{w,k}),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}(P_{z,k}P_{w,k})=s^k. \tag{3} Subtract the two isolated potentials from the combined potential. Unshared orders cancel. Both upper-only fields have J=0, so the binding potential has zero value on this initial set. The full initial cross energy density is therefore \boxed{\mathcal V(x)=\omega_{0,d}r_d \sum_{k=1}^{M}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1} \left[\sqrt{\rho^2+\sigma^2+2\rho\sigma s^k} -\rho-\sigma\right].} \tag{4} The order-zero term vanishes because s^0=1. The factor r_d includes the common root normalization and every partner in the canonical density. Equation (4) does not depend on the larger target grade N. Differentiating it with respect to either center gives the reciprocal initial translation forces, in agreement with the complete field gradients. For coincident cores, \rho=\sigma and r_d\int\rho=1. Their integrated cross energy has the profile-independent value \boxed{V(X=Y)=\omega_{0,d} \sum_{k=1}^{M}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1} \left[\sqrt{2+2s^k}-2\right].} \tag{5} This is an interaction energy of the prepared pair, not a new isolated mass formula. A common phase of either grade does not change it. General relative phases within the two polarized rays affect s and the full shape response. The root contribution gives an initial attractive force Every bracket in (4) is nonpositive. For t=s^k, define its positive magnitude F_t(\rho,\sigma)=\rho+\sigma -\sqrt{\rho^2+\sigma^2+2t\rho\sigma}. \tag{6} Direct differentiation gives \frac{\partial^2F_t}{\partial\rho\partial\sigma} =\frac{\rho\sigma(1-t^2)} {(\rho^2+\sigma^2+2t\rho\sigma)^{3/2}}\ge0. \tag{7} Also F_t(0,\sigma)=F_t(\rho,0)=0. Thus F_t is the double integral of the nonnegative weight (7), over density thresholds below \rho and \sigma. The spatial integral is a positive weighted sum of volumes where the two density superlevel sets overlap. For the nodeless radial cores, (12) of the core calculation gives \rho'=-4fh-2(d-1)h^2/r<0 away from the origin. The superlevel sets are balls. Their intersection volume decreases as their centers separate. Consequently the magnitude of the negative cross energy decreases with separation: the root contribution is initially attractive for nonaligned rays. It vanishes identically for s=1. Translation invariance of the integrated energy gives equal and opposite center forces. Their accelerations differ because the isolated inertial coefficients are \omega_N and \omega_M at Q=1. This is a conditional initial force law of the inverse model, not a derivation of observed electric charges or a solution of the ensuing encounter. Zero initial energy does not mean zero coupling Take coincident cores with the same coherent ray. The root cross energy and both initial translation forces vanish. However, their binding currents add before the interaction is varied: J_{\mathrm{total}}=0,\qquad K_{\mathrm{total}}=2K_\phi, \qquad K_\phi=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi. \tag{8} For the original fractional binding function f(K)=\operatorname{sgn}(K)|K|^a, the complete source on each field differs from its isolated source by \boxed{\Delta\mathcal N_R =\begin{pmatrix}0\\-g(2^a-1)\rho^a\phi\end{pmatrix} \otimes\overline z^{\,R},\qquad R=N,M.} \tag{9} The shared gap term is linear and cancels in this difference. The root source stays equal to its isolated value. Equation (9) is nonzero: both objects immediately develop lower-component motion. Restricting the variation to the upper-only initial family would miss it. This supplies a response from the same binding law that sustains each core. Its normalized spatial coefficient is common across the grades, although subsequent dynamics can depend on their different frequencies. It does not establish automatic alignment, repulsion or identical trajectories. The full evolving spatial shapes must be retained to decide those questions. Two regular isolated currents can cancel For the radial matrix core \phi=fI+ih\alpha_{\hat x}, Clifford multiplication gives K_\phi=(f^2-h^2)\beta+2ifh\beta\alpha_{\hat x}. \tag{10} Its eigenvalues are \pm\rho, so it is invertible at every finite point of a nonzero isolated core. Now put two identical cores on opposite sides of a midpoint. Their radial directions at the midpoint are opposite. At equal distance r from their centers, K_{\mathrm{total}}=2(f(r)^2-h(r)^2)\beta. \tag{11} The solved profiles have a radius r_* at which f=h. Therefore their combined current vanishes at the midpoint when the center separation is 2r_*. The fractional core values in m_c=1 units are: Ordinary depth Radius r_* Separation 2r_*/L_{\mathrm{rms}} 5 2.12123849 2.93887781 6 2.20364754 2.84485508 10 2.50670916 2.64022650 This is a specific allowed pair preparation. It is not a claim that every trajectory reaches that separation or polarization. It does show that invertibility of each isolated current does not ensure invertibility of their sum in a coupling calculation. An explicit failure of the fractional variation At the midpoint write the two upper matrices as \phi_\pm=A(I\pm i\alpha_1) and put \rho=2A^2. Introduce small, allowed upper and lower variations of these two grade fields: \Psi_\pm(\epsilon,t)= \begin{pmatrix} \phi_\pm+\epsilon\beta\phi_\pm\\ t\beta\phi_\pm \end{pmatrix}. \tag{12} The symbol t in (12) is a dimensionless variation parameter, not time. The coefficient rays have unit norm and drop out of the traced binding currents. Exact matrix multiplication gives \begin{aligned} K_{\mathrm{total}}&=4\epsilon\rho I,\\ J_{\mathrm{total}}&=4t\rho I,\\ C_{\mathrm{total}}&=2\rho(1+\epsilon^2-t^2)I. \end{aligned} \tag{13} For small |t|, the mass current stays strictly positive. The problem here is specifically the fractional binding law. Its potential along this path is U_{\mathrm{bind}}=-g r_d t(4\rho)^{1+a} \operatorname{sgn}(\epsilon)|\epsilon|^a. \tag{14} The gap trace vanishes because \operatorname{Tr}\beta_p=0. At every nonzero t and 0<a<1, the derivative with respect to \epsilon diverges as |\epsilon|^{a-1}. Such configurations occur arbitrarily close to the upper-only cancelling pair. At the exact point t=\epsilon=0, the binding potential has zero first derivative, since its leading joint variation has degree 1+a>1. That special value does not provide a differentiable neighborhood: the nearby configurations with t\ne0, \epsilon=0 have no finite derivative. The ordinary quadratic kinetic and gap terms cannot cancel (14). This is a concrete regularity obstruction in the written fractional action. It is stronger than checking isolated tails or assigning a value to f(0) alone. No particle lifetime or actual collision outcome is inferred from it. A smooth inverse binding retains the frequency branch A positive current scale \kappa supplies an explicit smooth comparison: \boxed{f_\kappa(K)=K(K^2+\kappa^2I)^{(a-1)/2},\qquad \kappa>0.} \tag{15} Replace f by f_\kappa in the same binding potential and vary it completely. The source is still \mathcal N_{\mathrm{bind}}= m_cB_1\Psi\beta_p-g\left[B_1\Psi f_\kappa(K) +B_2\Psi Df_{\kappa,K}(J)\right]. \tag{16} For a scalar eigenvalue x, f_\kappa'(x)=(\kappa^2+a x^2) (x^2+\kappa^2)^{(a-3)/2},\qquad 0<f_\kappa'(x)\le\kappa^{a-1}. \tag{17} The off-diagonal matrix divided differences obey the same bound by the scalar mean-value theorem. Hence the full derivative has Hilbert–Schmidt operator norm at most \kappa^{a-1}, including repeated, opposite-sign and zero eigenspaces. In particular, Df_{\kappa,0}(J)=\kappa^{a-1}J. \tag{18} The cancelling-current pair now has a finite complete source and variation. This removes the specific defect (14). A small chosen \kappa can still give a large response coefficient; finite does not mean weak or stable. The separate zero mass-current root and the polarized kinetic limitation of the proposed rest-frame carrier have not been repaired by (15). The matrix function is odd and respects unitary conjugation. Thus the radial isotropic core reduction and the original boost argument still apply. Its radial binding coefficient is now F(\rho)=g\rho(\rho^2+\kappa^2)^{(a-1)/2}, \qquad f'=-(1+F)h,\quad h'=(F-1)f-\frac{d-1}{r}h \tag{19} in m_c=1 units. A spatial solution of this equation gives the same exact current-hierarchy frequency \omega_N=\omega_{0,d}D_N and the same canonical inertia \hbar\omega_NQ/c^2. The binding profile can change without changing the isolated mass ratios. Two verified smooth depth-six cores Use central-normalized profiles with f(0)=1 and set a=1/6. Let \delta be the current scale in those temporary shape units, and solve (19) for its unknown coefficient p. If q is that shape's full canonical norm, the common unit-norm physical profile has g=pq^{1/6},\qquad \kappa=\delta/q. \tag{20} The two independently refined numerical examples are: Shape parameter \delta Common coefficient g Current scale \kappa L_{\mathrm{rms}} in unit-gap coordinates 10^{-6} 7.96477241 3.23577831\times10^{-8} 1.53585064 10^{-4} 7.87537079 8.66605017\times10^{-6} 1.27665860 Each row specifies one action used for both the electron and muon grades. Its field magnitude solves the fixed point at Q=1; it is never identified as either particle's mass. The two rows are alternative inverse bindings, not independent tuning of the electron and muon. The new current scale has units of field density. A proposed common-gap scale law can write \kappa=\widehat\kappa(m_c/c)^d with dimensionless \widehat\kappa, but selecting that coefficient is additional physical input. The original fractional size factors remain results of their original law. Smoothing changes them, as this table demonstrates. The smooth spatial functional uses the vacuum-subtracted primitive H(\rho)=g[(\rho^2+\kappa^2)^{(1+a)/2}-\kappa^{1+a}]/(1+a). Writing R=\int r_d\rho F(\rho) and V=\int r_d H(\rho), its independent virials are T+S=R and T=d(R-V) at unit gap. These are fixed-point identities. This auxiliary functional is not added to the full particle energy. Full component response of the smooth core The complete occupied-ray Hessian uses the same matrix reduction as the original localized action, with its actual smooth potential and stiffness: F(\rho)=g\rho(\rho^2+\kappa^2)^{(a-1)/2},\qquad 2\rho F'(\rho)=2g\rho(\kappa^2+a\rho^2) (\rho^2+\kappa^2)^{(a-3)/2}. \tag{21} Independent arbitrary complex variations of the full source verify this ordinary/conjugate Hessian, retaining both spinor blocks and every partner. The \delta=10^{-4} core was then tested in all constant-Clifford angular multiplets k=0,\ldots,6, with 26 and 40 radial basis functions, at \omega=18564 and 3838380. The complete unsymmetrized matrices and their canonical structure are retained. The largest displayed electron real growth part is approximately 2.32\times10^{-11} in core units. Direct muon diagonalization produces an apparent growth 1.48873194\times10^{-4} in the 40-function k=6 block. It fails the exact slow-block matching equation: the smallest matching singular value there is 2.68574013\times10^{-8}, rather than zero. The true slow squared growth of that block is -4.69417325\times10^{-9}. At 26, 40 and 55 radial functions, the independently matched muon slow oscillation frequencies are 1.87198029\times10^{-3}, 6.85140369\times10^{-5} and 9.38787993\times10^{-6}, approaching the phase-symmetry zero mode. Thus the apparent growing result is a numerical cancellation artifact for this finite block. Other tested real parts remain at numerical precision. These checks find no resolved instability in their stated scope; they do not cover higher angular representations, all radial wavelengths, finite encounters or nonlinear stability. Verification and remaining scope localized_core_pair_checks.py verifies 122 conditions for the initial pair: full tensor-current energies, both reciprocal source variations, the nonzero aligned shape response, ordinary spatial energy integrals, the three current cancellations, and the exact fractional derivative exponents. Its arrays retain the actual currents, gradients and spatial interaction values. The scalar integral implementation is localized_core_pair.py. smooth_current_core_checks.py checks 110 conditions for independent smooth matrix and field variations, including the cancelling pair, both refined localized profiles and their virials, the unchanged assigned frequencies, full boosted equations and every stress component, full ordinary/conjugate Hessians, bounded spatial spectra and the exact muon slow-block comparison. Its data retain the misleading direct eigenvalue as well as the independently matched result. The action and solver are in smooth_current_core.py. The pair is still an initial preparation. A complete nonlinear encounter, observed interaction channels, cross-depth maps and neutrino suppression remain to be derived. The smooth binding establishes a local repair and new spatial witnesses; its master origin, parameter selection and complete spatial stability remain open. The physical oscillator-mode carrier is also still required before this inverse construction can be identified with particles. The later trace-current comparison keeps this smooth core and its binding law, while adding a positive trace contraction to the mass norm. The resulting initial pair energy remains independent of the larger target grade, with an explicitly changed angular coefficient. Its improved constant far-field response and additional spatial tests apply to that declared comparison.

title: Response of localized simplex-frequency fields
summary: Solved localized branches have identical finite lower-grade probe energies and forces at common profile, while complete current Hessians and bounded spatial spectra distinguish that coupling identity from stability.
text: Summary: Solved localized branches have identical finite lower-grade probe energies and forces at common profile, while complete current Hessians and bounded spatial spectra distinguish that coupling identity from stability. A common probe of actual localized targets The localized current action has spatial solutions with \omega_N=\omega_{0,d}D_N and common canonical norm and profile at a fixed depth. Its binding and mass terms belong to one action. This allows a finite probe comparison that retains both the probe source and the target's reciprocal force. Write a target as \Psi_N=e^{-i\omega_Nt}(\phi,0)^T\otimes\overline z^{\,N}, where \phi^\dagger\phi=\rho I_r. A fixed test pattern occupies a distinct lower grade M<N and may have arbitrary complex spinor, partner and oscillator coefficients. Its physical spatial profile is part of that field, rather than a prescribed overlap number. The exact target mass current at every order accessible to the probe is R_{N,k}(x)=\rho(x)I_r\otimes P_{z,k},\qquad 0\le k\le M. \tag{1} It is independent of N. Define the local cross interaction by subtracting the two isolated energies from the combined action: V_{N,M}(x)=U(\Psi_N,\Psi_M)-U(\Psi_N,0)-U(0,\Psi_M). \tag{2} Every unshared mass-current order cancels. Every shared order contains the same target current (1). The binding currents trace all oscillator coefficients; the target's J=0 and K=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi are also independent of N. Thus the entire cross interaction is the same for different targets with the same \phi and z. Where the complete source is differentiable, this proves \boxed{ V_{N,M}=V_{N',M},\quad \frac{\delta V_{N,M}}{\delta\overline\Psi_M} =\frac{\delta V_{N',M}}{\delta\overline\Psi_M},\quad -\partial_XV_{N,M}=-\partial_XV_{N',M},\quad N,N'>M. } \tag{3} Here X translates the actual target profile. Integrating these identities gives the same cross energy and translation force whenever the integrals and their variations exist. No limit of vanishing probe amplitude is required. The independently normalized probe and target can both have Q=1. The complete shape derivative on the target still contains the lifting maps T_{Nk}^\dagger(\cdot\otimes I)T_{Nk} and depends on N. Equal force does not mean equal acceleration: its inertial coefficient is \hbar\omega_N/c^2. Subsequent shape changes can likewise differ. The statement therefore concerns an exact initial response and an energy functional, not identical encounter trajectories. Independent tensor calculations use all seven coefficient slots at depth six, target grades two and three, and a grade-one Gaussian test pattern with unit norm and arbitrary full complex polarization. At three spatial points, the cross energies, full probe sources and reciprocal translation forces agree to numerical precision. The analytic identity (3) covers the assigned electron and muon grades for M<12 without materializing their enormous full coefficient arrays. The test probe has not been identified as an observed particle solution. Oscillator grade is not physical spatial depth. Consequently (3) does not yet derive cross-depth coupling, photon vertices or neutrino suppression. The existing common-probe analysis also retains same-grade interference: two contributions to the same grade are one coherent sum, so treating them as two independent carriers is invalid. The root law's noncommuting weak-field and vanishing-target limits still exist. Equation (3) avoids using that limit to infer a finite coupling, but it does not cure nonsmooth zero currents or fractional eigenvalue crossings during a general encounter. The later two-core calculation prepares both objects as independently solved localized fields. It derives their full initial cross energy and reciprocal forces, and shows why aligned cores can have zero initial cross energy but nonzero shape response. It also finds a concrete cancellation of their fractional binding current and constructs smooth inverse bindings that retain the isolated frequency law. Those smooth actions require their own response checks; the spectra below continue to describe the original binding law. Full oscillator directions of the occupied grade The current hierarchy supplies two contraction identities. If j counts oscillator occupations outside the occupied coherent ray, they are \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^Nh_{k,d}\frac{\binom{N-j}{k}}{\binom Nk} &=\frac{D_N}{D_j},\\ \sum_{k=0}^Nh_{k,d}\frac{\binom kj}{\binom Nj} &=D_N\frac d{d+j},\qquad D_j=\binom{j+d}{d}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} Unavailable binomials are zero. Retaining the new matrix partners gives the complete root-source derivative for j\ge1: \delta\mathcal N_{\mathrm{mass},j} =\omega_N\left(\frac{B_0}{D_j}+\frac d{d+j}\Pi_u\right)\eta_j. \tag{5} The binding currents have zero first variation in these orthogonal oscillator directions. Their derivative is complex-linear, \delta\mathcal N_{\mathrm{bind},j} =m_cB_1\eta_j\beta_p-gB_1\eta_jf(K). \tag{6} Each matrix insertion in (5) and (6) is Hermitian on the complete spinor and partner space. With the full self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator, these blocks conserve their linear perturbation norm. This is an exact statement for the stated transverse oscillator blocks, not for the occupied ray's spatial and partner response. Independent full tensor variations at d=6,N=3 and d=10,N=1 verify (5), including every oscillator slot. They also verify the complete occupied block against the actual nonlinear gradient, with ordinary and conjugate variations both present. An absent higher grade has additional previously zero root currents. Their leading directional source is generally nonlinear in the perturbation, so a single global linear Hessian cannot be assigned there without more regularity assumptions. The action does have an independent phase symmetry in every grade. Along a sufficiently regular solution with the required boundary decay, it conserves each grade's canonical norm. In the declared finite grade domain, a small absent-grade norm therefore stays small for as long as that solution exists. This conditional conservation statement does not establish existence or uniqueness at a zero current. This does not derive transitions between grades or mode selection. Spatial and partner Hessian on the occupied ray Use natural units and write \phi=\sqrt\rho U, with U unitary. Define the full spatial binding operator \mathcal B(\phi)=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla\phi +m_c\beta\phi\beta_p-g\beta\phi f(\phi^\dagger\beta\phi). \tag{7} In the rotating frame, the complete ordinary/conjugate Hessian has block form \mathcal H'\begin{pmatrix}\eta_u\\\eta_l\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} \mathcal A\eta_u+\mathcal B'_\phi\eta_l\\ \mathcal B'_\phi\eta_u-2\omega_N\eta_l \end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathcal A(UX)=2\omega_N U\left(\operatorname{Herm}X -\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Herm}X)}rI\right). \tag{8} The real-linear derivative \mathcal B'_\phi includes all spectral divided differences of the matrix function. A phase-only or positive-spinor truncation is not this Hessian. For a radial matrix core \phi=fI+ih\alpha_{\hat x}, the complex radial subspace retains both upper and lower pairs. Conjugate away the radial measure, put v=(f,h)^T, P=2vv^T/\rho-I and define \begin{aligned} D_r&=\begin{pmatrix} 0&\partial_{r_x}+\dfrac{d-1}{2r_x}\\ -\partial_{r_x}+\dfrac{d-1}{2r_x}&0 \end{pmatrix},\\ L_+&=D_r+m_c\sigma_z-F(\rho)I-2F'(\rho)vv^T,\\ L_-&=D_r+m_c\sigma_z-F(\rho)P,\\ A&=2\omega_N(I-vv^T/\rho). \end{aligned} \tag{9} Here F(\rho)=g\rho^a for the power law. If upper perturbations are x+iy and lower perturbations are u+iw, the full radial equations are \begin{aligned} \dot x&=Ay+L_-w,&\dot y&=-L_+u,\\ \dot u&=L_-y-2\omega_Nw,&\dot w&=-L_+x+2\omega_Nu. \end{aligned} \tag{10} A regular Laguerre basis and independent differential-equation matching test this same system. The latter propagates four regular origin solutions and four decaying solutions from infinity and compares their subspaces. Fixing the final subspace basis gauge is necessary before root finding; arbitrary eigenvector phases do not define a continuous matching determinant. For the analytic critical core at d=6,R=1,\omega=1, both methods find a genuine growing mode e^{\lambda t}: \lambda=0.983987427901+2.46986730435i. \tag{11} Changing the origin cutoff, outer endpoint and integration tolerance leaves this value unchanged at the displayed accuracy. A smooth polynomial binding control, F(\rho)=6\rho(1-\rho^2) with zero core gap, also has a localized core. At \omega=1 its independently matched growing mode is \lambda=3.01769256948+3.72920233603i. Thus neither exact localization nor smoothing the binding law alone proves stable particles. Ordinary nonradial polarization multiplets For a Hermitian Clifford k-form T, T^2=I, the radial background preserves the angular span B_0=T,\quad B_1=i\alpha_{\hat x}T,\quad B_2=iT\alpha_{\hat x},\quad B_3=\alpha_{\hat x}T\alpha_{\hat x}. \tag{12} These basis names are local to this section and do not denote the scalar insertions of the action. For 0<k<d let s_k=(-1)^k(d-2k) and t_k=s_k/d. Angular integration gives diagonal Gram entries one and off-diagonal entries G_{03}=G_{12}=t_k and their transposes. A normalized angular basis is E_0=B_0,\quad E_+=\frac{B_1+B_2}{\sqrt{2(1+t_k)}},\quad E_-=\frac{B_1-B_2}{\sqrt{2(1-t_k)}},\quad E_3=\frac{B_3-t_kB_0}{\sqrt{1-t_k^2}}. \tag{13} Its ordinary spherical-harmonic degrees are 0,1,1,2. At k=0,d, only B_0,B_1 are independent. The spatial Dirac action on radial coefficients is exactly \begin{aligned} D(aB_0)&=-a'B_1,\\ D(bB_1)&=[b'+(d-1)b/r_x]B_0,\\ D(cB_2)&=s_kcB_0/r_x+[c'-c/r_x]B_3,\\ D(eB_3)&=s_keB_1/r_x-[e'+de/r_x]B_2. \end{aligned} \tag{14} Clifford multiplication and the complete matrix Hessian preserve this span. Independent arbitrary-normal matrix variations and Cartesian derivatives verify closure and (14) in six and ten ordinary dimensions. The k=1 sector includes translations. These are the constant-Clifford angular multiplets; higher angular representations remain untested. Large frequency, canonical conditioning and a slow symmetry mode The common-gap core uses m_c=1 and a=1/6. Its assigned electron and muon coefficients are \omega=18564 and 3838380 if the stated inverse identification m_c=\omega_{0,6} is made. Direct diagonalization then mixes very large and very small frequencies. Write perturbations as UX, where U=(fI+ih\alpha_{\hat x})/\sqrt\rho. This is pointwise unitary and preserves the canonical norm. Its radial phase angle satisfies \theta'=F(\rho)-m_c\frac{f^2-h^2}{\rho} -\frac{(d-1)fh}{r_x\rho}. \tag{15} Transform the kinetic operator and the full Hessian together. In this frame the mass blocks are exact constant integer matrices times \omega. Forming the small binding Hessian before adding those blocks avoids subtracting nearly equal large numbers. A canonical squeeze q\mapsto q/\sqrt\omega, p\mapsto\sqrt\omega p in stiff directions then improves conditioning without changing the symplectic form. The calculation retains raw unsymmetrized matrices and checks their Hermiticity independently. The common-gap core has growing controls at \omega=1. Across every k=0,\ldots,6 in the tested bases, the \omega=30 and electron scans show no resolved growth. The electron's largest real parts are about 10^{-11} in core units, while the fast frequencies are about 37128. Refinement changes radial basis size, length and quadrature together. These are bounded numerical observations, not a statement about the entire spatial spectrum. One muon computation produces an apparent real growth rate near 5.398\times10^{-4} in the k=6 symmetry sector. An exact Schur elimination diagnoses it. In this sector the real and imaginary Hessians have the finite projected blocks H_R=\begin{pmatrix}2\omega I&L_R\\L_R&-2\omega I\end{pmatrix},\qquad H_I=\begin{pmatrix}0&L_I\\L_I&-2\omega I\end{pmatrix}. \tag{16} Put z=\lambda^2, A(z)=(zI+L_IL_R)/(4\omega^2). Eliminating the fast block gives the exact slow matching matrix \boxed{\mathcal F(z)=zI+L_I^2 -L_I[I+A(z)]^{-1}A(z)(L_I-L_R).} \tag{17} This form avoids cancellation of terms of order \omega^2. Evaluating it in the raw L_I eigenbasis further resolves its smallest mode without forcing either Hessian to be symmetric numerically. The apparent growing value fails (17): its smallest matching singular value is approximately 2.927\times10^{-7}, instead of zero. The elimination does not assume that L_I and L_R commute. Where I+A(z) is invertible, it also gives the exact determinant identity \det(zI+H_IH_R)=(4\omega^2)^p\det[I+A(z)]\det\mathcal F(z), \tag{18} where p is the size of L_I. Independent noncommuting matrix tests check both the direct Schur complement and this characteristic determinant. The actual slow squared growth is negative. With 26, 40 and 55 radial basis functions, its oscillation frequencies are respectively 8.99508\times10^{-4}, 3.59022\times10^{-5} and 1.16970\times10^{-6}. They approach the exact phase-symmetry zero mode, rather than a growing disturbance. Thus a small residual relative to the enormous original generator is insufficient to identify this mode; the well-conditioned reduced equation is the decisive control. The other tested muon multiplets have real parts at floating-point accuracy. Neither this scan nor (17) proves stability for all angular momenta, radial wavelengths or finite perturbations. The action's nonsmooth currents also remain a separate evolution question. The full classical Hamiltonian also has no lower bound at fixed unit norm, even for positive mass current and strictly timelike field current; the localized-action calculation gives an explicit smooth family. This precludes a global energy-minimum argument. It does not turn the unresolved spectral questions into a proved instability. What the combined result establishes The same reconstructed action now supports a localized spatial fixed point, the selected simplex carrier frequencies, their exact canonical inertia, and a finite common-probe identity. The pair comparison retains both polarizations and reciprocal translation variation. Its continuing limitations concern the actual physical carrier, observed interaction channels, full encounter evolution and complete spatial stability. In particular, the oscillator labels still need to arise as modes of the same physical field. Their tensor interpretation and complete spacetime transformation law cannot be inferred from the dimension count alone. The inverse action is a concrete target for that derivation, not evidence that its premises are already realized by particles. The later rest-frame carrier calculation provides an explicit covariant tensor connection from the field's own current. Its additional kinetic term preserves these linear calculations on zero-rotation-moment rays and preserves the finite common-probe identity for such targets. For complex polarized rays it changes the kinetic form and produces a defective principal response. Those new terms cannot be omitted when assessing that completed action's general stability. The later higher angular response gives the complete polynomial angular block classification at even depth and tests additional electron and muon blocks. Its finite spectra retain their stated radial and angular limits. The trace-current comparison also identifies a secular high-momentum response that real frequencies alone do not exclude. Adding a positive trace contraction removes that specific degeneracy and yields a positive conserved norm for the complete constant far-field operator. Its localized frequency and common-probe identities survive, while its changed Hessian requires its own tests. Verification localized_current_response_checks.py checks the full angular source and spatial derivatives, independent direct radial matching, complete asymptotic spinor/partner symbols, raw canonical structure, finite angular spectra and the exact slow Schur equation. It preserves the complete finite eigenvalue arrays, representative eigenvectors and projected generators, including the misleading unconditioned slow result rather than silently deleting it. The response implementations are localized_clifford_response.py, localized_radial_galerkin.py, localized_radial_evans.py and localized_full_asymptotic.py. The smooth binding control is implemented in polynomial_localized_core.py. The finite probe and inertia calculation uses localized_current_inertia_checks.py. localized_action_audit_checks.py independently checks (17) and (18) by block Gaussian elimination and a full characteristic determinant, and compares arbitrary complex mixed second variations of the actual potential with the complete Hessian.

title: Localized scalar wave encounters
summary: Complete three-dimensional packet evolution retains phase-sensitive reciprocal transfer beyond a plane-wave truncation, with a continuum reflection law and independent spatial, temporal and boundary refinements.
text: Summary: Complete three-dimensional packet evolution retains phase-sensitive reciprocal transfer beyond a plane-wave truncation, with a continuum reflection law and independent spatial, temporal and boundary refinements. From a resonant contraction to the full spatial equation The resonant quartet calculation identifies a coherent channel through which two complex spatial patterns can exchange positive canonical norm. The full local scalar equation also generates momenta outside that quartet. A localized preparation further contains a continuum of directions and frequencies. Here evolve all four complex components on all three ordinary coordinates: i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla\Psi +g(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi)\beta\Psi, \quad \alpha_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,-\sigma_j), \quad \beta=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1} The \sigma_j in the matrix definition are Pauli matrices. Write \Psi=(u,v)^T and c=u^\dagger v. The scalar current is \sigma=2\operatorname{Re}c. The full positive-frequency vertex gives Q_u=\int u^\dagger u\,d^3x,\qquad Q_v=\int v^\dagger v\,d^3x,\qquad \dot Q_u=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2d^3x=-\dot Q_v. \tag{2} The two blocks are components of the same classical field. Their norms are not electric charges or identified particle counts. These are unbound spatial wave controls; no bound elementary pair has been selected. A precise four-packet preparation For a center x_0, carrier p, width w and constant four-component seed \xi, define a canonically normalized packet by \widehat R(k;p,x_0,w,\xi)=\mathcal N P_+(k)\xi\, e^{-w^2|k-p|^2/2-ik\cdot x_0}, \qquad P_+(k)=\frac12\left(I+\frac{\alpha\cdot k}{|k|}\right). \tag{3} Choose \mathcal N>0 so its full spatial norm is one. The continuum zero-momentum point has measure zero; the numerical preparation sets that grid coefficient to zero. Positive-frequency projection is applied once at preparation. Evolution under (1) retains every subsequently generated component. Frequency sign is not assigned an antiparticle interpretation. Put e_p=e_z, e_q=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta), and s=\sin(\theta/2), c_\theta=\cos(\theta/2). The incident seeds are u_+=(1,0,0,0)^T,\quad u_-=(0,1,0,0)^T, \quad v_+=(0,0,-s,c_\theta)^T, \quad v_-=(0,0,c_\theta,s)^T. \tag{4} With w=2 and carrier magnitude 2, define \begin{aligned} u_0&=\frac{R(2e_p,-4e_p,2,u_+)+R(-2e_p,4e_p,2,u_-)}{\sqrt2},\\ v_0&=\frac{e^{i\varphi}}{\sqrt2} \left[R(2e_q,-4e_q,2,v_+)+R(-2e_q,4e_q,2,v_-)\right],\\ \Psi(0)&=u_0/\|u_0\|+v_0/\|v_0\|. \end{aligned} \tag{5} There are four localized incoming packets organized into two complete complex chiral patterns, each of norm one. Both patterns propagate, diffract and respond. Here \varphi is a global phase of the entire second pattern. This differs from the main-mode phase in the textured five-dimensional compatibility preparation. Why opposite phases reverse the transfer There is an exact continuum symmetry of (1) and (5). Let n=\frac{e_p-e_q}{|e_p-e_q|}=(-c_\theta,0,s),\qquad O=I_3-2nn^T,\qquad U=-i\,\sigma\cdot n,\qquad S=\beta\operatorname{diag}(U,U). \tag{6} The ordinary spatial reflection O exchanges e_p and e_q. Its spinor lift satisfies S\alpha_jS^\dagger=\sum_kO_{kj}\alpha_k, \qquad S\beta S^\dagger=\beta. \tag{7} Thus \Psi(x,t)\mapsto S\Psi(O^{-1}x,t) preserves the entire kinetic operator and the nonlinear scalar source, while exchanging the two chiral blocks. The isotropic Gaussian and complete projector in (3) transform covariantly. Directly, Su_\pm=i v_\pm,\qquad Sv_\pm=i u_\pm, \qquad S\Psi_\varphi(O^{-1}x,0)=i e^{i\varphi}\Psi_{-\varphi}(x,0). \tag{8} Uniqueness on any interval of regular evolution and the constant phase symmetry of (1) therefore imply \boxed{Q_u(-\varphi,t)=Q_v(\varphi,t),\qquad \Delta Q_u(-\varphi,t)=-\Delta Q_u(\varphi,t).} \tag{9} The second identity uses initial norms one and total norm two. It holds for the full continuum evolution, including generated modes. It is not limited to the four-mode resonant approximation. An oblique reflection does not preserve a finite periodic cube; exact finite-grid oddness is consequently not the numerical requirement. Refinement must recover the continuum comparison. Localized transfer and its numerical scale At fixed g=2, T=10 and \cos\theta=0.6, full evolution gives \Delta Q_u\simeq+0.01770 for \varphi=+\pi/4 and the opposite sign for -\pi/4. Thus about 1.77\% of the initial first-block norm is transferred, with equal and opposite change of the second. These are specified model units, not a measured conversion probability. The two nonzero traces use the same N=80, \delta t=0.04 grid. The right-angle trace uses N=64 at the same step. Recorded numerical data, the vector figure and plotting code retain the preparations and numerical quantities used in the display. The numerical operator uses an exact free Fourier propagator and an exact local reaction, \Psi\longmapsto \cos(g\sigma\,\delta t)\Psi -i\sin(g\sigma\,\delta t)\beta\Psi, \tag{10} in symmetric Strang splitting. The reaction keeps its own pointwise scalar and positive density fixed; the spatial step changes the pattern. The box [-L,L]^3 is storage for a localized-field approximation, not physical compactification. Positive-frequency packets have tails, so exact compact support or a strictly zero boundary signal is not assumed. Points per axis N L Step \delta t \Delta Q_u, phase +\pi/4 Maximum energy drift 64 16 0.04 0.01769528052 7.95\times10^{-7} 80 16 0.04 0.01770118605 8.04\times10^{-7} 96 16 0.04 0.01770118604 8.04\times10^{-7} 80 16 0.02 0.01770168036 2.01\times10^{-7} 100 20 0.04 0.01770118606 8.04\times10^{-7} Time-step halving reduces the energy error by approximately four, as expected for this splitting. Spatial refinement from 80 to 96 changes the transfer by about 10^{-11}; the remaining time error is larger. Reporting many numerical digits here exposes convergence, not physical precision. The full complex fields also converge. Fourier interpolation from 80 to 96 points changes the final field by 1.83\times10^{-7} in positive L^2 norm. Halving the time step changes it by 2.28\times10^{-6}. At the same spacing, increasing L from 16 to 20 changes the nonlinear response in the common central cube by 2.84\times10^{-6}; the larger total-field difference, about 3.84\times10^{-5}, includes the changed initial and free tails. At N=80, changing only the phase gives \Delta Q_u=-0.01770118590, within 1.6\times10^{-10} of the opposite-phase magnitude. At N=64 and right angles, the transfer stays below 3.2\times10^{-10} over the encounter, while the full field still differs from its free control by about 0.0369 in positive L^2 norm. This is a numerical control for the one-polarization transfer node. It does not establish an exact right-angle theorem for all localized continuum data, and it is not zero interaction. Independent spatial control A simpler head-on preparation contains one packet in each chiral pattern, with carriers \pm2e_z, centers \mp4e_z, width two and unit norms. At the same g=2, T=10, its full field differs from free evolution by approximately 0.05013, with only about 7\times10^{-10} chiral norm transfer in the stated refinement. There is phase and spatial deformation without a large norm exchange. The independently derived axial spatial equation reconstructs this same three-dimensional field using radial Laguerre modes and axial Fourier modes. Its refined nonlinear response agrees with the Cartesian N=96, \delta t=0.04 response to about 3.2\times10^{-6} in full positive L^2 norm. Comparing the response means comparing \Psi_g(T)-U(T)\Psi(0); the total fields have larger differences from their initial and freely propagated tails. This cross-check uses two different spatial discretizations of the same complete equation. Reproduction and scope scalar_packet_collision_checks.py constructs (5), evolves all spatial components through scalar_wave_packets.py, and records both chiral norms, full field changes, energy and momentum. For the positive-phase preparation: OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \ python experiments/scalar_packet_collision_checks.py \ --packet-size 80 --quartet-cosine .6 --phase .7853981633974483 \ --step .04 --output-dir experiments/results --save-fields Change the phase sign for the reciprocal comparison, or set --quartet-cosine 0 for the right-angle control. Without --packet-size, the diagnostic runs 101 checks, including independent full spatial ODE integration, energy variation, time convergence and the complete reflection identities (7)–(8). Reports and optional field archives have timestamped filenames. The calculation confirms a permitted spatial mechanism of the specified scalar term beyond plane-wave truncation. Bound particle shapes, their common physical normalization, their nested-sector channel maps and their measured interaction rates remain to be derived.

title: Geometric currents across mass families
summary: Fixed-order tensor currents give a common geometric contact with band-independent coherent elastic vertices, a depth-dependent source count and reciprocal spatial dynamics, while the simplex mass term and master-field realization remain inputs.
text: Summary: Fixed-order tensor currents give a common geometric contact with band-independent coherent elastic vertices, a depth-dependent source count and reciprocal spatial dynamics, while the simplex mass term and master-field realization remain inputs. Separate the mass count from the current being compared A mass band can contain many coefficients while an interaction reads a fixed number of spatial tensor indices. That distinction gives a concrete inverse construction with different masses and a common coherent elastic vertex. Its initial coupling source has a count fixed by physical depth, even when the mass-band count changes greatly. The construction below specifies the simplex mass operator. It does not derive that operator from the original master action. What is derived is the complete response of a common interaction added to it: both source variations, the canonical vertex, its geometric zeros, its full coherent Hessian and its effect on spatial fields. There is one interaction coefficient within a physical sector, rather than one coefficient per pair. Use the coherent spatial carrier at physical spatial depth d: W=\mathbf1\oplus(T^*Q_d\otimes\mathbb C),\qquad E_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N W,\qquad D_N=\binom{N+d}{d},\qquad N=n-1. \tag{1} The components of W and its tensor powers are coefficient data over an actual physical point. They add no physical spatial dimensions. The directions of Q_d remain ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. For this inverse action, the retained grades are independent, canonically normalized components of one effective field. Their interpretation as a reduction of \Psi_\infty is an assumption. In particular, they are not silently identified with constrained derivatives of one smaller spinor. Only spatial sectors are nested; individual particles are not nested objects. A trace-preserving geometric current For a fixed integer 1\le k\le N, split off k tensor indices using the isometry T_{Nk}:E_N\longrightarrow E_k\otimes E_{N-k}. \tag{2} In normalized occupation states, with |\alpha|=k and |\beta|=N-k, its nonzero coefficient is \langle\alpha,\beta|T_{Nk}|\alpha+\beta\rangle =\sqrt{\frac{\binom{k}{\alpha}\binom{N-k}{\beta}} {\binom{N}{\alpha+\beta}}}. \tag{3} Here \binom{N}{\gamma}=N!/\prod_i\gamma_i!. The multinomial Vandermonde identity gives T_{Nk}^\dagger T_{Nk}=I. The two tensor factors in (2) are groups of field indices, not constituent particles. Let \Psi_N retain all its ordinary spatial spinor components. Contract the spectator indices in T_{Nk}\Psi_N using the scalar spinor bilinear \beta: \rho_{N,k} =\operatorname{Tr}_{\Sigma,E_{N-k}} \left[|T_{Nk}\Psi_N\rangle\langle T_{Nk}\Psi_N| (\beta\otimes I)\right],\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\rho_{N,k}=J_N=\Psi_N^\dagger\beta\Psi_N. \tag{4} The current is Hermitian. It need not be positive for a general Dirac field; none of the full variation below replaces it by a positive density. At a coherent field \Psi_N=\chi\otimes z^{\otimes N}, with \|z\|=1, \boxed{\rho_{N,k}=J_N|z^{\otimes k}\rangle\langle z^{\otimes k}|.} \tag{5} Thus the same geometric pattern has the same retained current at different N. This follows from a trace-preserving contraction; no division by the particle mass has been made. The dual operator for a Hermitian current H on E_k is \mathcal B_{Nk}(H)=T_{Nk}^\dagger(H\otimes I)T_{Nk},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}(H\rho_{N,k}) =\Psi_N^\dagger[\beta\otimes\mathcal B_{Nk}(H)]\Psi_N. \tag{6} It is unital, \mathcal B_{Nk}(I)=I, and \|\mathcal B_{Nk}(H)\|\le\|H\|. With the declared canonical kinetic metric, (6) is the normalized two-matter-leg vertex for this current. The general normalization rule still applies if a different master reduction supplies a nontrivial metric. For k=1, \mathcal B_{N1}(H) is the average of H acting on each of the N indices. A geometric rotation generator instead sums those actions. The averaged intensity current is therefore not automatically a Noether charge or the electric current. The diagonal coherent vertex is independent of N, but a transition between different rays retains the spectators: \langle w^{\otimes N}|\mathcal B_{Nk}(H)|z^{\otimes N}\rangle =(w^\dagger z)^{N-k} \langle w^{\otimes k}|H|z^{\otimes k}\rangle. \tag{7} Equal elastic vertices do not imply equal transition form factors, polarizabilities or response times. The minimal adjacent-current contact For a finite set of grades with N\ge2, set R_k=\sum_N\rho_{N,k},\qquad k=1,2. Consider the real potential density \boxed{ U=\sum_N m_NJ_N+ \frac\kappa2\left[\operatorname{Tr}(R_1^2) -\operatorname{Tr}(R_2^2)\right],\qquad m_N=\mu D_N. } \tag{8} At one physical depth, \mu has units of energy and \kappa has units of energy times spatial volume when the canonical norm is dimensionless. Comparing absolute coefficients at different depths additionally requires the physical normal integrals and their kinetic normalization. A dimensionless fibre comparison does not supply those factors. There is a limited minimality argument for (8). Restrict the ansatz to the three isotropic contractions J_{\rm total}^2, \operatorname{Tr}R_1^2 and \operatorname{Tr}R_2^2. For two coherent patterns their common quartic cross term is a polynomial AB(c_0+c_1\tau+c_2\tau^2), where \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2. Preserving an isolated coherent mass at every amplitude requires its value at \tau=1 to vanish. Requiring the complete interaction to vanish for orthogonal coherent patterns requires c_0=0. The smallest nonzero polynomial satisfying both conditions is proportional to \tau(1-\tau), which gives (8). This is uniqueness within that specified contraction ansatz. Physical rotation covariance alone permits additional tensor and spinor invariants. Neither the ansatz nor the mass polynomial in (8) has been obtained from the original master interaction. With the full self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D_N, use the canonical action S=\int dt\,dV\left[ \sum_N\frac i2(\Psi_N^\dagger\dot\Psi_N- \dot\Psi_N^\dagger\Psi_N) -\sum_N\Psi_N^\dagger\mathscr D_N\Psi_N-U\right]. \tag{9} Varying every current in (8) gives \boxed{ i\partial_t\Psi_N =\mathscr D_N\Psi_N+m_N\beta\Psi_N+ \kappa\beta\left[\mathcal B_{N1}(R_1) -\mathcal B_{N2}(R_2)\right]\Psi_N. } \tag{10} No target current is frozen. Each partner's source is the derivative of the same real potential, so its full real Hessian is reciprocal. All complex spinor components and relative phases remain in (4) and (10). The action is invariant under an independent phase of every retained grade and conserves each grade's canonical norm. It therefore has no vertex converting one mass grade into another. Such conversion processes would require additional terms from the common master reduction. The action is a smooth local polynomial on the independent carrier, including scalar-null fields and the vacuum. It preserves the principal Dirac symbol. The usual local difference-energy estimate consequently gives finite propagation for smooth solutions on their interval of existence. It does not prove global nonlinear existence or a complete spacetime-covariant embedding of the proposed mode bundle. Exact masses and the complete coherent response For an isolated coherent field, both terms in the square brackets of (10) act as J_NI on its occupied vector. The entire interaction source vanishes. Its mass remains m_N, including its complementary equations. This also gives exact nonconstant spatial fields on the specified physical CP3 bundle. That geometry has unknown physical radius and volume; its mathematically compact topology is not a compactification of extra dimensions. For the holomorphic section w=(1,X_A,0) described there, take \phi_N=\sqrt{\frac{Q_N}{\mathcal V\mathcal Z_N}}w^{\otimes N},\qquad \mathcal Z_N=\int\|w\|^{2N}d\nu_Q. \tag{11} The full connection gives \mathscr D_N\phi_N=0 and \beta\phi_N=\phi_N. Therefore \Psi_N(t)=e^{-im_Nt}\phi_N,\qquad \omega_N=m_N,\qquad E_N=m_NQ_N. \tag{12} Several grades with the same local ray w/\|w\| also have zero complete interaction source, even when their densities differ. Equation (12) then holds for that joint configuration. At common Q, the unchanged degrees 12,34 give E_{34}/E_{12}=D_{34}/D_{12}=3515/17. This preserves the input simplex relationship; it is not a new derivation of the observed lepton masses or of the selected canonical norm. The response must include the current variation. At a coherent field in the frame z=e_0, let P_j project onto transverse occupation j and define a_{kj}=\frac{\binom{N-j}{k}}{\binom Nk},\qquad b_{kj}=\frac{\binom kj}{\binom Nj}, \tag{13} with an unavailable binomial set to zero. For j\ge1, the complete interaction Hessian has the spin block \boxed{ A_j^{\rm int}=\kappa\left[ J_N(a_{1j}-a_{2j})\beta+ (b_{1j}-b_{2j})\beta\chi\chi^\dagger\beta \right],\qquad B_j^{\rm int}=0. } \tag{14} The j=0 interaction block is zero. The formula is polynomial in \chi; it does not divide by J_N. To derive (14), split a degree-j transverse occupation using (3). Its probability of leaving all retained indices in e_0 is a_{kj}. Its off-diagonal contraction with the coherent vector is nonzero only when all j transverse indices are retained; that coefficient is \sqrt{b_{kj}}. These two terms give the ordinary derivative. A conjugate term would need opposite transverse occupations; only the radial term can contribute, and the two adjacent currents cancel it. This proves (14) for the entire spinor multiplet. For a positive-chirality occupied spin line, the j=1 interaction coefficient vanishes, as required for a moving coherent ray. At j=2 it is 2\kappa J_N(N-3)/[N(N-1)]. The other spinor polarizations are retained in (14), rather than inferred from that one coefficient. Every block is Hermitian. On the exact spatial field (11), the rotating linearization is the actual spatial Dirac operator plus a smooth bounded Hermitian endomorphism. It is self-adjoint and conserves the complete positive L^2 perturbation norm. This is full spatial linear stability, not nonlinear orbital stability, confinement or a physical identification of the independent carrier. No unproved global ordering of the two current purities is needed for that conclusion. The pair vertex and its Hockey-Stick source count Take two independent coherent grades with scalar intensities A,B and mode rays z,w. Equations (5) and (8) give exactly \boxed{U_{\rm int}=\kappa AB\,\tau(1-\tau),\qquad \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2.} \tag{15} There is no factor D_N, D_M, N or M in this elastic current vertex. Its geometric factor also has the projector identity \tau(1-\tau)=\tfrac12\|[P_z,P_w]\|_{\rm HS}^2, \qquad P_z=zz^\dagger. \tag{16} Aligned and orthogonal projectors commute. In both cases the complete cross-source vanishes, not only its expectation value. For positive coherent mixtures the interaction can likewise be written as a weighted sum of these squared commutators. A general field need not have such a positive coherent-mixture representation, so that observation is not a global positivity proof for arbitrary Dirac fields. For the full initial source, set z=e_0, w=ce_0+se_1 with c,s\ge0 and c^2+s^2=1. After factoring out \kappa B\beta\chi, the coefficients in the first grade are \begin{aligned} g_0&=\tau(1-\tau),\\ g_1&=\frac{cs(1-2\tau)}{\sqrt N},\\ g_2&=-\frac{c^2s^2}{\sqrt{\binom N2}},\\ g_j&=0\quad(j>2). \end{aligned} \tag{17} The reciprocal source exchanges the two fields. In particular, the j=2 term drives a genuine deformation outside the coherent-ray tangent space. At \tau=1/2, the first-order ray motion vanishes while this deformation remains nonzero. Allowing every partner orientation spans the complete degree-j transverse spaces through j=2. Their ranks are \binom{j+d-1}{d-1}. Thus the initial source count is the Hockey-Stick identity \boxed{ \sum_{j=0}^{2}\binom{j+d-1}{d-1} =\binom{d+2}{d}. } \tag{18} At depths 2,3,4,5,6,10 these counts are 6,10,15,21,28,66. They are source-channel counts for the specified current, not counts of observed gauge vertices. In contrast to D_N, they do not grow when the occupied mass band changes at fixed depth. Later evolution can populate higher occupations through repeated action of the full equation; (18) does not justify truncating the evolving field to these initial terms. Canonical shape response still knows N. The coherent-ray kinetic metric is NQ times its projective metric. For an aligned pair, a canonically normalized tangent direction has the interaction block \kappa\begin{pmatrix} B/N&-\sqrt{AB/(NM)}\\ -\sqrt{AB/(NM)}&A/M \end{pmatrix}. \tag{19} It has one common-rotation zero mode and one frequency \kappa(B/N+A/M). Equation (19) is why a common elastic vertex should not be reported as equality of all dynamical susceptibilities. Interference within one grade Two contributions to the same field grade are not orthogonal carrier blocks. Write \Psi=\chi_a\otimes z^{\otimes N}+\chi_b\otimes w^{\otimes N}, A=\chi_a^\dagger\beta\chi_a, B=\chi_b^\dagger\beta\chi_b and t=\chi_b^\dagger\beta\chi_a. Retaining the off-diagonal contractions gives \boxed{ U_{\rm int}=\kappa(1-\tau) \left[AB\tau-|t|^2\tau^{N-2}\right]. } \tag{20} For N\ge3, this is (15) times 1-|t|^2\tau^{N-3}/(AB) when AB\ne0. The explicit form (20) also covers zero scalar products without division. To verify it, the cross term in \rho_{N,k} is t(w^\dagger z)^{N-k}|z^{\otimes k}\rangle\langle w^{\otimes k}| plus its adjoint. Squaring the two complete currents cancels the terms linear in this cross term and leaves (20). The initial potential is independent of a relative phase assigned to one contribution. Their combined canonical norm includes interference, and the general field equation still retains complex phase. A two-mode description must include its Gram matrix before treating the amplitudes as canonical independent coordinates. Equation (20) is not a derivation of particle statistics or an antiparticle mechanism. Reciprocal deformation The complete coefficient dynamics can be tested without a two-ray restriction. A positive-spin preparation on two geometric directions stays in \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^2)\oplus \operatorname{Sym}^M(\mathbb C^2) because its full conserved rotation moment has support there. All N+1 and M+1 complex coefficients evolve. This is an invariant-subspace argument for this preparation, rather than a declaration that the physical sector has only two dimensions. With N=12, M=34, unit norms and \kappa=1, an initial ray overlap \tau=0.7 gives first-index compatibility from 0.7 to approximately 0.76919, and second-index compatibility from 0.49 to approximately 0.63550, over the tested interval of 150 time units. Starting at \tau=0.2 gives the corresponding ranges 0.2 to 0.23859 and 0.04 to 0.10867. Both patterns deform. For these coherent initial preparations, conservation of N\rho_{N,1}+M\rho_{M,1} gives the exact balance \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{N,1}(t)\rho_{M,1}(t))-AB\tau ={}&\frac{N^2[A^2-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{N,1}(t)^2]}{2NM}\\ &+\frac{M^2[B^2-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{M,1}(t)^2]}{2NM}\ge0. \end{aligned} \tag{21} The inequality uses positivity in this coefficient preparation. It is relative to the initial coherent state and does not imply monotonic alignment for arbitrary fields. Reversed complex preparations give the reversed motion. General spatial Dirac currents need not be positive, and their actual transport must be retained. An actual spatial Dirac encounter Equation (10) also permits a direct spatial control, with both fields evolving. Use a flat six-dimensional spatial patch and let one ordinary coordinate vary, keeping translation invariance in the other five. These are cylindrical pulse controls with norms per unit transverse volume, not localized six-dimensional bound particles. The calculation retains all eight spinor components and all 13+35 complex coefficients in the invariant two-direction preparation. The rest masses are prescribed as 1 and 3515/17, with \kappa=5, unit norms, Gaussian widths 3, initial centers -12,0, and central momenta 0.75,0. Both spinors have complex polarization. The two coherent mode rays initially obey |z^\dagger w|^2=0.7. The central-momentum spin preparation is an initial Dirac pulse; it is not a solved bound state or an exact positive-energy spectral packet. Through time 50, the full equations give \begin{aligned} P_{12}:&\quad 0.75\longrightarrow 0.61477473,\\ P_{34}:&\quad 0\longrightarrow 0.13522527. \end{aligned} Both spatial patterns deform. Their density-weighted two-index mode purities change from one to approximately 0.9711931 and 0.9981039. Here purity uses the positive spin contraction, rather than the signed scalar current: if \rho^+_{N,2} is that contraction and q_N=\Psi_N^\dagger\Psi_N, the reported quantity is \int\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho^+_{N,2})^2]dx/\int q_N^2dx. Exact Fourier Dirac steps alternate with the local nonlinear update. In a spatial interval of length 192, a 512-point grid with time step 0.02 gives energy drift below 3.7\times10^{-7}, norm drift below 9.0\times10^{-13} and total momentum drift below 5.1\times10^{-13}. Doubling the time step changes the final individual momenta by less than 2.1\times10^{-8} and the complete complex fields by less than 1.7\times10^{-5} in canonical L^2 norm. The comparison uses the same phases and masses, without fitting either endpoint. An independent 384-point grid at the same time step changes the two complete endpoint fields by less than 5.4\times10^{-9} in L^2. The largest boundary-region density across the three controls is below 9.2\times10^{-24}. These comparisons resolve the reported transfer and deformation against the tested numerical discretizations. The spatial verification record retains the complete field comparisons and hashes of the source and raw states. The figure uses the finer time step and spatial grid. The residual interaction energy is about 0.011 at the endpoint. This is a resolved finite-time encounter, not an asymptotic scattering amplitude or a measured interaction rate. It demonstrates reciprocal momentum and shape response under the proposed action; it does not identify these pulses with the physical electron and muon. Physical depth, orientation and the neutrino test The current maps compare actual tensor directions in nested tangent spaces. They must transform together with both fields and the physical inclusion. For example, a coherent higher ray has zero restricted k-index current when it is orthogonal to the entire specified lower space. This is a geometric condition on the occupied pattern, not a depth-specific coefficient. Physical rotation averages are different from averages over all complex mode rays. For real unit vectors in d ordinary spatial directions, \langle\tau\rangle_{SO(d)}=\frac1d,\qquad \langle\tau^2\rangle_{SO(d)}=\frac3{d(d+2)},\qquad \langle\tau(1-\tau)\rangle_{SO(d)}=\frac{d-1}{d(d+2)}. \tag{22} Complex polarization retains more information. For d\ge3, define e_u=|u^Tu|^2 and e_v=|v^Tv|^2 for two complex unit directions. The complete physical rotation average is \left\langle|u^\dagger Rv|^4\right\rangle_{SO(d)} =\frac{e_ue_v}{d^2} +\frac{(1-e_u/d)(1-e_v/d)}{d(d+1)/2-1}. \tag{23} To derive (23), decompose each symmetric square into its trace and traceless symmetric tensor. Their squared norms are e_u/d and 1-e_u/d. The traceless representation has dimension d(d+1)/2-1; averaging over physical rotations pairs equal irreducible components and removes unequal ones. Both polarization invariants remain. At d=2, the two oriented helicities must be treated separately; replacing them by this single traceless representation would lose their distinction. These formulas do not make a generic five-dimensional pattern unusually weak. The real-polarization value is 4/35 at depth five and 5/48 at depth six. The assigned neutrino degrees 9,14,21 have the same coherent vertex formula as the charged-lepton degrees; no small neutrino coefficient has appeared. Moreover, a pattern invisible to one fixed photon plane can be visible to another allowed orientation. If all planes in the shared three-space are admissible, a coherent vector invisible to every one must lie normal to that entire space. This same simple restricted current would then also be invisible to a probe confined to those three directions. The calculation therefore has not derived zero ordinary electric charge together with the observed nonzero weak response. The neutrino channel requirement still needs the selected physical state and the actual electromagnetic and weak current maps. Equations (22) and (23) are dimensionless geometric comparisons. They are not interaction rates or a substitute for physical spatial normalization. Canonical spatial overlap still matters The local identity (15) does not remove the physical envelopes from an integrated particle vertex. This can be tested on the exact fields (11), without assuming a constant spatial density for the massive state. Keep A=\operatorname{diag}(1,i,-1,-i) and compare the two holomorphic patterns w=(1,X_A,0) and w_\theta=(1,e^{i\theta}X_A,0). The angle changes their complex tangent polarization relative to the slack component; it is not a global phase of the entire field. Both have the same h=1+\|X_A\|^2. Their pointwise overlap is \tau_\theta= \frac{|1+e^{i\theta}(h-1)|^2}{h^2} =1-\frac{2a(h-1)}{h^2},\qquad a=1-\cos\theta. With s=N+M, the dimensionless spatial pair coefficient is exactly \begin{aligned} I_{NM}(\theta) &=\frac{\int h^{N+M}\tau_\theta(1-\tau_\theta)d\nu_Q} {\mathcal Z_N\mathcal Z_M}\\ &=\frac{2a(\mathcal Z_{s-1}-\mathcal Z_{s-2}) -4a^2(\mathcal Z_{s-2}-2\mathcal Z_{s-3}+\mathcal Z_{s-4})} {\mathcal Z_N\mathcal Z_M}. \end{aligned} The physical initial interaction energy for independent grades is \kappa Q_NQ_M I_{NM}/\mathcal V. This is an initial matrix element between exact isolated fields, not a solved interacting stationary pair. The exact factorial expression for \mathcal Z_N and independent positive spatial cubature give the following values. Degrees (N,M) I_{NM}(\pi/2) I_{NM}(\pi) (12,12) 0.3773967521 0.0032325400 (12,34) 0.4720130793 0.0013384312 (34,34) 0.7087981270 0.0009850869 The diagonal entries are bilinear current reference values. Two fields in one grade also have the interference and canonical Gram terms in (20); those diagonal references must not be called complete same-grade particle interactions. The off-diagonal entry needs no such identification. A complementary comparison holds the probe's physical density constant at 1/\mathcal V, with the same normalized local ray w_\theta/\sqrt h for both massive branches. The probe can be an admissible initial field in one common retained grade; no stationary particle has been selected for it. Its dimensionless occupied vertex is F_N(\theta)= \frac{2a(\mathcal Z_{N-1}-\mathcal Z_{N-2}) -4a^2(\mathcal Z_{N-2}-2\mathcal Z_{N-3}+\mathcal Z_{N-4})} {\mathcal Z_N}. At \theta=\pi/2, F_{12}=0.2499455223 and F_{34}=0.2499974696: the same probe gives very similar response despite the prescribed mass ratio 3515/17. At \theta=\pi, the values are 0.0056018126 and 0.0012047321. Near a geometric zero, differences in the occupied spatial profiles matter greatly. Thus this action demonstrates a possible grouping of elastic responses, but not equality for every polarization or resolved encounter. The calculations use one physical volume, one coupling coefficient and the same normalization law. No mass division or separate fitted coefficient produces the comparison. Deriving the actual particle profiles and their observed current remains essential. A constraint on deriving this contact from the master quartic The interaction in (8) cannot be obtained by a bare complex-linear projection of a positive sum of squared Hermitian scalar currents onto the full independent carrier. This restriction can be proved using only positive-chirality fields; it does not require a negative-energy example. Fix one spin polarization and one spatial envelope. A linear lift of its mode coefficient c into such a master interaction would give a quartic functional of the form V(c)=\frac12\int g(y)[c^\dagger A_yc]^2d\mu(y), \qquad A_y=A_y^\dagger,\quad g(y)\ge0. \tag{24} The candidate contact vanishes for every coherent c=z^{\otimes N}. If (24) equalled that contact, positivity would force \langle z^{\otimes N}|A_y|z^{\otimes N}\rangle=0 for every ray, almost everywhere on the support of g. A countable dense set of rays and continuity suffice to choose the same full-measure set of y. These coherent diagonal values determine the entire Hermitian matrix: expand the homogeneous polynomial in z and \bar z. Its independent monomial coefficients are precisely the matrix entries of A_y, with nonzero normalization factors. Consequently A_y=0 there, and (24) would vanish for every c. But the adjacent-current action is nonzero away from the coherent set. For a normalized perturbation from e_0^{\otimes N} toward the occupation |N-2,2\rangle, its positive-spin interaction begins as V(c_\epsilon) =\frac{2\kappa(N-3)}{N(N-1)}|\epsilon|^2 +O(|\epsilon|^4),\qquad N>3. \tag{25} This includes the assigned degrees 12 and 34 and contradicts the consequence of (24). Thus the simple positive scalar-square projection cannot supply this new contact. A genuine effective reduction involving the complementary dynamics of the same field, or a different master invariant, would have to be derived and tested. This is a specific constraint on the proposed action's origin, not an exclusion of the particle dimensionalities or of all master reductions. Scope and executable verification The useful inverse result is a common local action that preserves the specified coherent simplex masses while giving an elastic geometric vertex independent of the mass band and a coupling-source count depending on depth. It includes reciprocal shape deformation and a full spatial linear stability calculation on its exact coherent fields. Its mass operator, canonical carrier, current selection and master-field origin remain inputs. Its aligned transparent configurations have not been identified with observed charged particles. A local scalar contact also does not establish the long-range electromagnetic current. The physical geometry, selected particle norm, neutrino channels and nonlinear particle stability remain to be derived. marginal_contact_checks.py constructs the complete normalized contractions and their derivatives. adjacent_marginal_checks.py tests the action (8), arbitrary complex eight-component fields, both reciprocal responses, physical rotation covariance, all coherent source occupations, same-grade interference and full coefficient evolution. nested_marginal_geometry_checks.py checks physical rotation averages and complete nested occupation counts. marginal_spatial_overlap_checks.py computes the normalized physical matrix elements using exact factorial sums and independent spatial cubature, retaining both complex patterns. marginal_spatial_pulses.py evolves the spatial Dirac encounter, and marginal_spatial_verification.py compares its complete complex fields under independent time and grid refinement. Both final momenta and both deformed fields are retained. The combined-band comparison explains why isolated mass agreement and isolated susceptibility were insufficient tests of the earlier root and smooth current actions.

title: Moving nonlinear scalar planes and their response
summary: The local scalar Dirac equation has continuous nonnull traveling-plane branches whose complete self-consistent response has a covariant closed form, with proper density, conjugate modes and the conserved norm treated explicitly.
