No radiation weight is fitted. In a normalized spatial eigenmode with eigenvalue \ell, the amplitude h_\ell(t,q) obeys \ddot h_\ell+\left(q^2+\frac{\ell}{\lambda^2}\right)h_\ell =\frac{f_\ell}{\lambda^2}S(t,q). \tag{7} Its full-field kinetic energy has coefficient \mathcal T\lambda^2/4 for each real quadrupole component. Solving (7) with zero incoming data and evaluating its outgoing energy therefore gives \boxed{ E_{\rm out} =\frac{\mathcal T}{2\lambda^2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq}{2\pi} \int_0^\infty d\mu(\ell)\, \left\| \widetilde S\!\left( \sqrt{q^2+\ell/\lambda^2},q \right) \right\|^2.} \tag{8} This is the leading emitted energy, fourth order in the incoming weak slopes. The integral is positive and symmetric under exchanging the two pulses, which sends q to -q. It includes the full radial continuum and both quadrupole polarizations. For a real forced oscillator, the same normalization follows directly: after the source has ceased, |\dot h|^2+\omega^2|h|^2=|\widetilde f(\omega)|^2. Combining the q and -q components gives (8) for real spatial fields. This also fixes the factors of two from Fourier and kinetic conventions. Retain the energy lost by each incoming pulse Write dE_{\rm out}(\ell,q) for the positive measure in (8), including both quadrupole components, and put \Omega=\sqrt{q^2+\ell/\lambda^2}. The outgoing normal momentum is P_{\rm out}=\int(q/\Omega)\,dE_{\rm out}. The same source coupling fixes the two leading pulse energy losses: \boxed{ \Delta E_A=\int\frac{\Omega+q}{2\Omega}\,dE_{\rm out}, \qquad \Delta E_B=\int\frac{\Omega-q}{2\Omega}\,dE_{\rm out}.} \tag{8a} Both are nonnegative. Their sum is E_{\rm out}, while their difference is P_{\rm out}, as required by the opposite incoming propagation directions. Equivalently, their weights are \alpha/(\alpha+\beta) and \beta/(\alpha+\beta). This partition can be checked directly from the full coupling. In dimensionless radial coordinates its term is \tfrac{\mathcal T}{2}\sum_{c=1}^2\langle h_c,fS_c\rangle_w. Varying the first incoming waveform by its time translation gives \partial_uS_c; varying the second gives \partial_vS_c. Thus the integrated work removed from the first pulse is -\tfrac{\mathcal T}{2}\sum_{c=1}^2\int dt\,dy\, \langle h_c,f\partial_uS_c\rangle_w, and similarly for the second. Their sum integrates by parts to the work on the complementary field. Using its retarded solution supplies exactly (8a). There is no independently assigned absorption coefficient for either pulse. The losses refer to the outgoing complement at leading fourth order in weak slopes, with the retained right- and left-moving wave energies computed from their reciprocal response. The local conservative delays are part of the same expansion, but the local action alone omits these finite-width losses. Obtain the long-pulse law The outgoing low-frequency response derived from the complete spatial Hessian is \operatorname{Im}F(\omega+i0)=\pi\omega^2/4+o(\omega^2). Thus the continuum density near threshold is d\mu/d\ell=\ell/4+o(\ell). For pulses concentrated at frequencies small compared with 1/\lambda, substitute this into (8) and change variables to \alpha=(\Omega+q)/2, \beta=(\Omega-q)/2: \boxed{ \frac{E_{\rm out}}{\mathcal T} =\frac{\lambda^2}{\pi} \int_0^\infty d\alpha\int_0^\infty d\beta\, \alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta) \|C(\widetilde a(\alpha),\widetilde b(\beta))\|^2 +\hbox{higher-frequency corrections}.} \tag{9} The Jacobian is d(\Omega^2-q^2)\,dq=4(\alpha+\beta)\,d\alpha\,d\beta. The powers in (9) follow from the spatial spectral density and source derivatives, rather than a presumed frequency filter. For equal Gaussian displacement pulses in real unit directions, A(u)=\epsilon L e^{-u^2/(2L^2)}e_a,\qquad B(v)=\epsilon L e^{-v^2/(2L^2)}e_b,\qquad L\gg\lambda, \tag{10} the derivative spectrum satisfies |\widetilde a(\alpha)|^2= 2\pi\epsilon^2L^4\alpha^2e^{-L^2\alpha^2}. The elementary Gaussian moments in (9) give \boxed{ \frac{E_{\rm out}}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}2\, \frac{\epsilon^4\lambda^2}{L} +o\!\left(\frac{\epsilon^4\lambda^2}{L}\right),\qquad \frac{E_{\rm out}}{E_A+E_B} =\frac{3\pi}{2}\epsilon^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{L}\right)^2 +o\!\left(\epsilon^2\frac{\lambda^2}{L^2}\right).} \tag{11} The small-frequency limit here is L/\lambda\to\infty at fixed weak slope, within the leading weak-field radiation calculation. Higher orders in the slope are separate corrections. The incoming pair energy is E_A+E_B=\mathcal T\epsilon^2L\sqrt\pi. For unequal widths L_A,L_B and weak slopes \epsilon_A,\epsilon_B in real unit directions, the corresponding leading individual losses are \boxed{ \frac{\Delta E_A}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}4 \frac{\lambda^2\epsilon_A^2\epsilon_B^2}{L_A}, \qquad \frac{\Delta E_B}{\mathcal T} =\frac{3\pi^{3/2}}4 \frac{\lambda^2\epsilon_A^2\epsilon_B^2}{L_B}.} \tag{12} The shorter pulse contributes more emitted energy at fixed slopes. Swapping the complete incoming profiles swaps the two results. For \lambda=1, the complete radial spectral calculation gives E_{\rm out}/E_{\rm soft} approximately 0.99717, 0.99986 and 0.999992 at L=5,10,20, with agreement under radial refinement. No coefficient is changed between these comparisons. This establishes a concrete frequency-dependent suppression and a two-polarization cancellation for one specified outgoing channel. Its frequency is the actual incoming spatial waveform frequency, as distinguished in Source frequencies in spatial coupling. The calculation does not assign a neutrino mode, an electric charge, or a measured electromagnetic or weak rate. Verification polarized_pulse_collision_checks.py checks the complex source identity, exchange symmetry, common spatial rotation and both circular senses. Independent Fourier transforms of real multi-frequency waveforms retain all conjugate components and check the timelike cancellation alongside its nonzero spacelike source. Direct forced-mode time integration checks the emitted-energy normalization against an independent temporal Fourier integral. Unequal-width pulses additionally test both direct source-work integrals against (8a) and the actual outgoing mode energy. A separate full radial eigensystem and source measure evaluate (8), with radial resolution and outer-domain refinement, and recover (11). The companion nonlinear evolution tests the conservative pulse delays. Reports have timestamps and checks survive Python optimization.

title: Positive-frequency scalar vertices
summary: The full positive-frequency scalar Dirac vertex has an exact canonical singular strength, with a massless half-angle law, chirality-dependent zeros and reciprocal spatial interference that must be retained before channel counting.
text: Summary: The full positive-frequency scalar Dirac vertex has an exact canonical singular strength, with a massless half-angle law, chirality-dependent zeros and reciprocal spatial interference that must be retained before channel counting. Normalize the complete incoming bands Use the scalar matrix \beta appearing in the written Dirac source, on one flat containing spatial chart with d\ge2 ordinary directions and \hbar=c=1. Let H(p)=\alpha\cdot p+m\beta,\qquad E_p=\sqrt{|p|^2+m^2},\qquad P_p=\frac{I+H(p)/E_p}{2}, \tag{1} where m\ge0 is a specified mass coefficient of this free-band comparison. At m=0, exclude the single zero-momentum point when defining the positive band. The minimal full complex module has dimension n=2^{\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor}. Choose any isometric positive-frequency frame U_p, U_p^\dagger U_p=I_{n/2} and U_pU_p^\dagger=P_p. The complete scalar vertex between momenta q and p is \boxed{C(p,q)=U_p^\dagger\beta U_q.} \tag{2} This is the canonical positive-norm convention used by the massive current projection. Changing to a different external-wave normalization would change its factors and the associated kinetic metric together. The input and output spaces retain every positive-frequency polarization, not a single selected spin direction. Exact singular strength The Clifford relations give \beta P_p\beta= \frac12\left[I+\frac{-\alpha\cdot p+m\beta}{E_p}\right]. \tag{3} For A=-\alpha\cdot p+m\beta, its anticommutator with H(q) is \{A,H(q)\}=2(m^2-p\cdot q)I. Compressing this identity to the +E_q eigenspace yields P_q A P_q=\frac{m^2-p\cdot q}{E_q}P_q. \tag{4} Consequently \boxed{C(p,q)^\dagger C(p,q)=\tau(p,q)I_{n/2},\qquad \tau(p,q)=\frac12\left[1+\frac{m^2-p\cdot q}{E_pE_q}\right].} \tag{5} The reciprocal identity is CC^\dagger=\tau I_{n/2}, and C(q,p)=C(p,q)^\dagger. Every singular value is exactly \sqrt{\tau}. For \tau>0 the full vertex is a scaled unitary map between the two canonical bands. Its unitary part still contains polarization and phase information. For m>0 and finite momenta, \tau>0. At p=q, (2) reduces to (m/E_p)I, recovering \tau=m^2/E_p^2. The forward scalar-density factor is a particular momentum configuration, not a general nonforward interaction strength. The massless angular law For m=0, let \theta be the angle between the two nonzero spatial momenta. Then \boxed{\tau(p,q)=\frac{1-\widehat p\cdot\widehat q}{2} =\sin^2\frac\theta2.} \tag{6} Exactly co-propagating bands have C=0, even for different momentum magnitudes. Opposite directions have unit singular strength. At every nonzero angle, a nonzero input polarization has a nonzero response somewhere in the complete output band. This does not make every individual vertex nonzero. For unit polarizations a,b, |a^\dagger C(p,q)b|^2\le\tau(p,q), \tag{7} and the chosen two patterns can be orthogonal under that map. A particular observed channel also involves its actual spatial inclusion and readout. Equation (6) alone neither identifies an electromagnetic channel nor predicts a scattering rate. Under a common physical rotation, transform both momenta and spinor frames by the covering spin rotation. The scalar vertex is unchanged in the transported frames because the spin rotation commutes with \beta. Independent changes of polarization bases instead give C\mapsto V_p^\dagger C V_q and preserve (5). Chirality gives a channel zero, not a depth-five exception At odd total spatial dimension, the kinetic involution commutes with every massless P_p and anticommutes with \beta. Its positive-frequency eigenspaces each have dimension n/4. Writing the restricted involutions as C_p^{\rm kin} and C_q^{\rm kin} gives C_p^{\rm kin}C(p,q)=-C(p,q)C_q^{\rm kin}. \tag{8} Thus the scalar vertex vanishes between two equal kinetic chiralities for every pair of momenta. Between opposite chiralities, its singular strength is still \sqrt\tau. The complete vertex remains consistent with (5): its nonzero response is in the opposite output block. This occurs at every odd total spatial dimension, including three, five, seven and nine. It supplies no unique depth-five selection and no electric-charge assignment. The neutrino control continues to require a derived neutral electromagnetic channel and surviving weak vertices. Both kinetic signs refer to components of the same field; their particle-antiparticle meaning remains open. If a field also propagates through containing spatial directions, use the complete containing kinetic operator. A lower odd-dimensional involution anticommutes with every additional normal \alpha_j. The lower class can therefore mix under normal motion. The corresponding protection question is treated explicitly in spatially invariant scalar-null fields. Assemble the actual spatial current before projecting A positive-frequency free packet has the form \Psi(x,t)=\int\frac{d^dp}{(2\pi)^{d/2}}\, U_p a(p)e^{ip\cdot x-iE_pt},\qquad \|\Psi\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|a(p)\|^2d^dp. \tag{9} Its scalar current is the full coherent contraction \boxed{\sigma(x,t)= \iint\frac{d^dp\,d^dq}{(2\pi)^d}\, a(p)^\dagger C(p,q)a(q) e^{i(q-p)\cdot x-i(E_q-E_p)t}.} \tag{10} At m=0 every monochromatic forward scalar is zero, but the off-diagonal momentum pairs in (10) can remain nonzero. A spatial packet cannot generally be replaced by an incoherent sum of those forward scalars. A packet confined to one complete odd-dimensional kinetic chirality does have zero scalar, because every matrix element in (10) then vanishes. For two such packets of opposite kinetic chirality, denote them by \psi_+ and \psi_- and put c(x,t)=\psi_+^\dagger\beta\psi_-. Their individual scalar self-currents vanish, while the total scalar is \sigma=2\operatorname{Re}c. \tag{11} For the local equation i\partial_t\Psi=D\Psi+g\sigma\beta\Psi, the exact two rows are \boxed{ i\partial_t\psi_+=D\psi_++g\sigma\beta\psi_-, \qquad i\partial_t\psi_-=D\psi_-+g\sigma\beta\psi_+. } \tag{12} Both patterns respond to the same local scalar. For sufficiently decaying fields, their positive norms satisfy \boxed{\frac{dQ_+}{dt}=2g\operatorname{Im}\int c^2dx,\qquad \frac{dQ_-}{dt}=-\frac{dQ_+}{dt}.} \tag{13} The derivative follows from 2\operatorname{Re}\langle\psi_+,-ig\sigma\beta\psi_-\rangle. Its sign depends on the full complex cross pattern. Individual norms need not be conserved even though their sum is. Equation (12) retains all generated frequency components; positive frequency is an initial preparation, not a projection imposed at every nonlinear time step. These full spatial equations generalize the local cross-source structure of polarized traveling pulses. They do not assume automatic alignment, a fixed target or a mediator particle. What counting can and cannot multiply For a fixed unit incoming polarization b, summing over a complete orthonormal output band gives \sum_{j=1}^{n/2}|e_j^\dagger Cb|^2=\tau. \tag{14} Summing additionally over all orthonormal inputs gives \operatorname{Tr}(C^\dagger C)=(n/2)\tau, while averaging over those inputs gives \tau again. The number of available components is not an extra enhancement of one normalized incident field. Similarly, a cumulative spatial-mode count can organize the available channels, but their actual current contraction, kinetic metric and spectral weights remain necessary. The oscillator source marginals show how Hockey-Stick sums enter a specified projection after those ingredients are supplied. They do not replace (10) by a depth-only coupling coefficient. Verification positive_scalar_vertex_checks.py checks full positive-frequency eigenspaces, all singular values, reciprocity, projector identities and physical rotations in every spatial dimension from two through ten. Independent spatial superpositions verify the complete current, including diagonal massive terms and complex interference. General angular superpositions check the exact chiral source zeros and both reciprocal nonlinear source rows. Containing-direction tests retain every additional Clifford matrix and distinguish lower-class leakage from a scalar zero protected by a complete containing symmetry. These results verify the specified scalar operator and incoming preparations; a physical particle-channel embedding, flux normalization and observed rate remain separate calculations. scalar_wave_packets.py implements (12) on a full three-dimensional Cartesian grid with all four complex components. Its incoming Fourier Gaussian is projected onto the complete positive-frequency band once, then evolved with the exact local reaction and exact free Fourier propagator in a symmetric time splitting. The numerical periodic box is a regulator for localized ordinary spatial fields, not a physical compactification. scalar_packet_collision_checks.py checks that solver against an independently assembled four-component nonlinear differential equation. The default 101 checks include energy variation, reciprocal norm transfer, positive-frequency preparation and second-order time convergence. Its optional larger packet runs record spatial and temporal refinement data; a finite-grid collision is a conditional unbound-field benchmark, not an identified particle pair. Axial spatial Dirac packets retain transverse localization and complete complex polarization vectors in an exact angular family at odd total spatial dimension. Their radial and axial equation comes from the same local scalar, with both patterns evolving and the full angular spinor dependence reconstructed explicitly. Resonant scalar wave quartets provide a multi-directional positive-frequency preparation with reciprocal chiral norm transfer. The exact coherent contraction has a sharp normalized bound. A right-angle cancellation for one polarization per selected chiral band is removed by allowed complete higher-dimensional vectors; counting the components cannot determine that contraction. Frequency accounting for scalar Born response uses both complete vertices to control the negative-output source. A resonant cancellation for positive incoming scattering data coexists with nonzero finite-time forcing from a positive initial preparation.

title: Reciprocal spatial Dirac pair
summary: The same spatial moment interaction drives reciprocal deformation of complete complex Dirac profiles in an exact CP3–CP5 symmetry class, including a generated two-form component and phase-dependent changes in interaction overlap.
text: Summary: The same spatial moment interaction drives reciprocal deformation of complete complex Dirac profiles in an exact CP3–CP5 symmetry class, including a generated two-form component and phase-dependent changes in interaction overlap. The physical comparison and its scope Use the single spatial moment kernel on the specified linear inclusion \mathbb{CP}^a\subset\mathbb{CP}^{a+q}. The six-to-ten comparison has a=3,q=2. All spatial directions remain ordinary macroscopic dimensions of the same manifold. The projective topology, common metric scale, spin twists and current-family decomposition are explicit assumptions; no compactification is introduced. Take the lower spinor bundle to be \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(L) and the higher one \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(K), with their FS/Chern Dirac operators. The integer section degrees are independent of the auxiliary mass-band labels. Their normal bundle relation does not supply an occupied-state assignment. This calculation tests an aligned-center spatial symmetry class while retaining its complete complex field profiles. It is not a generic relative-orientation calculation or a replacement for the evolving electron–nucleus orbit. Its purpose is to determine whether the stated common kernel can actually change both spatial patterns under one action. A larger exact higher-dimensional spatial class Choose homogeneous coordinate blocks \mathbb C^{a+q+1}=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C^a\oplus\mathbb C^q. The first coordinate fixes the common profile center, the next a belong to the rest of the lower projective subspace, and the final q are normal to that chosen subspace. These are coordinate descriptions relative to the pair. A common physical isometry rotates all three blocks, both fields and the embedding together. Define the global intensity functions x=\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad z=\frac{\|Z_{\rm normal}\|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad y=1-x-z, \tag{1} and the normalized holomorphic section \chi=\sqrt{\binom{K+a+q}{a+q}}Z_0^K. The higher field class is \boxed{\varphi_b=\chi\left[F+A\bar\partial x+C\bar\partial z +B\bar\partial x\wedge\bar\partial z\right],} \tag{2} with all four profiles arbitrary complex functions of (x,z). The exterior degrees are zero, one, one and two; their chirality signs are +,-,-,+. These are spinor components, not additional spatial dimensions. Smooth profiles define global sections, including where \chi or a displayed differential vanishes. The lower field retains the complete complex radial zero-form/one-form class in the spatial scalar branch. The higher field needs both variables: the lower source distinguishes shared directions from normal directions in the higher field equation. Measure, scalar current and the full Dirac derivative After angular integration, the norm of (2) uses the Dirichlet probability measure with parameters (K+1,a,q): w(x,z)\,dx\,dz =\frac{\Gamma(K+a+q+1)}{\Gamma(K+1)\Gamma(a)\Gamma(q)} x^K y^{a-1}z^{q-1}\,dx\,dz. \tag{3} The one-form metric and two-form squared norm are \boxed{G=2\begin{pmatrix}x(1-x)&-xz\\-xz&z(1-z)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta=\det G=4xyz.} \tag{4} Thus the positive norm density relative to w is |F|^2+(A,C)^\dagger G(A,C)+\Delta|B|^2, while the scalar current has the one-form term with a minus sign. No polarization component is discarded from this specified class. Write \mathscr S=K+a+q+1 and let d denote the restriction of \bar\partial to the displayed forms. Then dF=(F_x,F_z),\qquad d(A,C)=C_x-A_z,\qquad dB=0. \tag{5} Its weighted adjoints, computed with (3)–(4), are \boxed{d^\dagger(A,C)=-\frac1w\operatorname{div}\!\left[wG \begin{pmatrix}A\\C\end{pmatrix}\right],} \tag{6} \boxed{d^\dagger B=2\begin{pmatrix} z(1-z)B_z-xzB_x+(q-\mathscr S z)B\\ xzB_z-x(1-x)B_x+(\mathscr S x-K-1)B \end{pmatrix}.} \tag{7} The complete spatial Dirac operator in this class is D=\sqrt2(d+d^\dagger). These formulas can also be derived directly in all a+q complex chart coordinates using the FS inverse metric and the line connection. The three-form derivative vanishes identically; the other omitted form components are not generated. A scalar potential depending on x,z preserves the class. Equations (2) and (5)–(7) therefore define an exact invariant class of the spatial PDE. Local phase current Let \eta=(A,C)^{\mathsf T}. The positive norm obeys a local continuity equation after angular integration: \partial_t\left[w(|F|^2+\eta^\dagger G\eta+\Delta|B|^2)\right] +\partial_x(wj^x)+\partial_z(wj^z)=0, \tag{8} where \boxed{\begin{pmatrix}j^x\\j^z\end{pmatrix} =2\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\left[ \bar F G\eta-\bar B\Delta\begin{pmatrix}C\\-A\end{pmatrix} \right].} \tag{9} The real scalar potential adds no source to (8). It changes the relative phases and thereby changes these spatial currents. Equation (9) retains the two-form contribution as well as the zero-form/one-form one. The positive phase norm is not an assigned electric charge. One interaction and both evolving moment matrices Let the lower scalar block moments be (u_a,v_a) and the higher ones be (u_b,v_b,w_b), obtained by integrating the signed scalar current against the three coordinate intensities. The lower field has no normal block. Their ambient matrices are M_a=\operatorname{diag}\left(u_a,\frac{v_a}{a}I_a,0_q\right), \qquad M_b=\operatorname{diag}\left(u_b,\frac{v_b}{a}I_a, \frac{w_b}{q}I_q\right). \tag{10} Put U=u_a+u_b, V=v_a+v_b, W=w_b. The same interaction energy is \boxed{E_{\rm int}=\frac\kappa2 \left[U^2+\frac{V^2}{a}+\frac{W^2}{q}\right], \qquad I_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(M_aM_b) =u_au_b+\frac{v_av_b}{a}.} \tag{11} Its full higher potential is \kappa[Ux+Vy/a+Wz/q]. The lower potential is its restriction to the lower space, \kappa[Ut+V(1-t)/a]. Every moment varies with its own complete complex field. The coefficients 1/a,1/q are the normalized block multiplicities of the same ambient trace, not separate pair couplings. A canonical approximation with a spatial residual Use polynomial degrees at most N for F, N-1 for each of A,C, and N-2 for B. This entire polynomial form complex is invariant under the linear operator (5)–(7). It has \boxed{2N^2+2N+1} \tag{12} complex modes, with both Dirac signs and one zero mode. No nonlinear invariance is claimed for a finite cutoff; the moment potential can generate higher polynomial degree. The zero-form basis uses the normalized polynomials (1-x)^jP_i^{(a+q+2j-1,K)}(2x-1) P_j^{(a-1,q-1)}\!\left(\frac{2z}{1-x}-1\right), \qquad i+j\le N. Their norms follow from the two beta measures in the coordinates x and z/(1-x). The one-form and two-form Gram matrices include G and \Delta; positive Cholesky transformations make all coefficient kinetic norms canonical. The nonlinear energy remains (11), so its ordinary and conjugate Hessians follow from the same three moment matrices. Refinement checks the time derivative against the uncompressed differential expressions (5)–(7) on a separate spatial grid. Agreement of a few moment values alone is not the convergence criterion. Reciprocal changing overlap in a specified preparation For a=3,q=2,L=K=1, set both phase norms to one and use \kappa=2 in common radius units. Prepare each field in its own stationary branch of the same smooth kernel, then evolve their autonomous complete pair action. No target is held fixed and no time-dependent alignment force is imposed. Over the sampled interval 0\le t\le20: Scalar interaction overlap Value Initial I_{ab} 0.199482310985 Sampled minimum, at t=6.1 0.194893252070 Sampled maximum, at t=6.7 0.200660187556 The overlap becomes both smaller and larger than its initial value. It is not monotone. The initially absent higher two-form component acquires a squared norm of about 1.049\times10^{-7} by the sampled time t=18.8. This component belongs to the actual spatial spinor equation; freezing the original one-variable profile removes it. Cutoffs N=5 and N=7 agree on these overlap values to better than 10^{-10}. At the listed times and two additional checks, the maximum uncompressed spatial residual drops from about 1.2\times10^{-9} to 2.4\times10^{-13}. These are deterministic numerical checks of the stated model, not measured particle interaction strengths. The phase dependence is separately observable in the equations. Starting from the same two self profiles, multiply all lower odd components by e^{0.6i} and all higher odd components by e^{-0.4i}. The entire initial positive and scalar densities remain unchanged, as does I_{ab}. Its initial derivative becomes approximately -0.000820812710. Conjugating both preparations gives the same instantaneous densities and +0.000820812710 instead. This is a mathematical phase/reversal comparison, with no antiparticle assignment. What has been established The common kernel can drive reciprocal changes in complete spatial profiles within this exact symmetry class, with conserved norms and energy. Both signs of changing scalar overlap occur without an imposed steering rule. This is a spatial Dirac counterpart to the finite coherent-mode deformation example, with its own action and different constraints. The aligned embedding and profile symmetry remain restrictions. Stable occupied particles, arbitrary relative orientations, phase-sensitive cross-current terms from the master field, the actual electron orbit, and observed electromagnetic and weak vertices have not been derived. The calculation supplies a reproducible full-equation test for a common kernel, rather than a depth-only interaction coefficient. Verification projective_spatial_pair_checks.py checks the actual coordinate Dirac operator through two-form degree, three-form closure, local continuity, complete canonical mode metrics, both nonlinear Hessian blocks, same-kernel self-branch normalization, reciprocal trajectories, phase preparations and refined spatial residuals. The maintained solver is projective_spatial_pair.py.

title: Spatial harmonics of the moment kernel and local response
summary: The projective moment kernel is exactly a screened inverse truncated to two scalar harmonic levels, while the derived local Dirac response retains higher harmonics, its induced sign and the direct contact term.
text:
Summary: The projective moment kernel is exactly a screened inverse truncated to two scalar harmonic levels, while the derived local Dirac response retains higher harmonics, its induced sign and the direct contact term. Scalar harmonics on the specified physical geometry Use CPm with physical Fubini–Study radius R, unit measure d
u, and r=m+1. This is a conditional ordinary spatial geometry with an undetermined physical scale; there is no compactification. Let \Pi_\ell denote the scalar Laplace eigenspace projector. Then A\Pi_\ell=\lambda_\ell^2\Pi_\ell,\qquad \lambda_\ell^2= rac{4\ell(\ell+m)}{R^2}, 	ag{1} \dim\Pi_\ell=  inom{\ell+m}{m}^2- inom{\ell+m-1}{m}^2, \qquad \dim\Pi_0=1. 	ag{2} One construction uses bihomogeneous polynomials of degree (\ell,\ell) on \mathbb C^{m+1} restricted to the unit sphere and invariant under its common phase. Removing the trace, or |Z|^2 times the preceding polynomial space, gives (2). These are spatial scalar functions, not the holomorphic wave-band dimension alone. For t=|X^\dagger Y|^2 with unit representatives and fixed X, the measure is m(1-t)^{m-1}dt. The normalized zonal eigenfunction is Z_\ell(t)= rac{P_\ell^{(m-1,0)}(2t-1)}{ inom{\ell+m-1}{\ell}}, \qquad Z_\ell(1)=1. 	ag{3} The radial operator is -4R^{-2}[t(1-t)\partial_t^2+(1-(m+1)t)\partial_t]. The Jacobi differential equation gives (1), and projective isometries generate the complete eigenspace from its zonal functions. Exactly which harmonics the spatial moment retains The common kernel is K_0(X,Y)=t. Unit-FS moment identities give \int P_Yd
u(Y)= rac{I}{r},\qquad \int\operatorname{Tr}(P_YB)P_Yd
u(Y) = rac{B+\operatorname{Tr}(B)I}{r(r+1)}. 	ag{4} They follow by unitary invariance: the second moment on two copies of \mathbb C^r is (I+\mathrm{Swap})/[r(r+1)], with its coefficient fixed by taking the trace. Constants form \Pi_0, and the traceless moment functions \operatorname{Tr}(P_XB) form \Pi_1. Thus, as an integral operator,  oxed{K_0= rac{\Pi_0}{r}+ rac{\Pi_1}{r(r+1)},\qquad K_1=rK_0=\Pi_0+ rac{\Pi_1}{r+1}.} 	ag{5} Here K_1 is a convenient normalized single-sector comparison. The common action itself does not multiply its kernel separately by r at each depth. For a real scalar source \sigma, let S=\int\sigma d
u and M=\int P_X\sigma(X)d
u(X). Then  oxed{\Pi_{\le1}\sigma(X)=r(r+1)\operatorname{Tr}(P_XM)-rS,} 	ag{6} \|\Pi_{\le1}\sigma\|_2^2=r(r+1)\operatorname{Tr}M^2-rS^2. 	ag{7} All higher scalar spatial harmonics are discarded, even if they came from a complete complex spinor current. The extension K_p(X,Y)= inom{p+m}{m}t^p, p\ge0, has multipliers  oxed{r_{\ell,p}= rac{p!(p+m)!}{(p-\ell)!(p+m+\ell)!} \quad(0\le\ell\le p),\qquad r_{\ell,p}=0\quad(\ell>p).} 	ag{8} To derive them, evaluate the convolution on the zonal eigenfunction at its pole: r_{\ell,p}= inom{p+m}{m}m\int_0^1 t^p(1-t)^{m-1}Z_\ell(t)dt. The Jacobi Rodrigues formula followed by \ell integrations by parts leaves the beta integral of t^p(1-t)^{m+\ell-1} times p!/(p-\ell)! and the normalization in (3). Its factorials give (8). For \ell>p the differentiated polynomial is zero. This is a scalar convolution on actual spatial points. It is distinct from applying a finite ray-resolution operator to a holomorphic coefficient band. The spatial source-preservation calculation uses these harmonic multipliers to determine which kernels preserve a holomorphic field exactly. It also bounds the cubic branch correction when the full direct-plus-induced response in (13) approaches a constant potential on a fixed coherent source band. A screened inverse with an explicit truncation Since \lambda_1^2=4r/R^2, equation (5) implies  oxed{K_1= rac4{R^2}\Pi_{\le1} \left(A+ rac4{R^2}ight)^{-1}\Pi_{\le1}.} 	ag{9} This is an exact identity. The full screened inverse on the right without the projectors has nonzero multipliers 4/[4\ell(\ell+m)+4] at every \ell. The equality fixes a screening scale 2/R but does not establish a physical origin for that scale or justify the truncation. For p>1, matching the \ell=1 multiplier in (8) to a normalized single screened inverse requires screening parameter \mu^2R^2=4p. At \ell=2 the two respective multipliers are  rac{p(p-1)}{(p+m+1)(p+m+2)},\qquad  rac{p}{p+2(m+2)}, 	ag{10} which differ for finite p\ge2. A higher-power coherent kernel is not obtained merely by changing one screening length. The local Dirac response retains the direct term At the specified uniform background of the local Dirac calculation, \varepsilon=gho_0, the exact static response for \ell>0 is \delta\sigma_\ell=- rac{4\varepsilonho_0} {\lambda_\ell^2+4\varepsilon^2}J_\ell. 	ag{11} At |\varepsilon|R=1, the denominator has the scale used in (9). That alone does not derive the moment action: the response has its derived sign, includes all \ell>0, and has a separate conserved zero mode. Suppose, additionally, that a specified decomposition into retained and responding modes makes their scalar sources additive, and a retained source j perturbs the background through J=g j. This source assumption must be derived for the intended particle families; arbitrary spinor sums can have cross-current terms. Within that declared source model, \delta\sigma_\ell=- rac{4\varepsilon^2} {\lambda_\ell^2+4\varepsilon^2}j_\ell, \qquad \ell>0. 	ag{12} The total potential includes the original g j as well as the induced g\delta\sigma. Consequently  oxed{\delta V_\ell=g rac{\lambda_\ell^2} {\lambda_\ell^2+4\varepsilon^2}j_\ell\quad(\ell>0), \qquad\delta V_0=g j_0.} 	ag{13} Equivalently, its operator is g\Pi_0+gA(A+4\varepsilon^2)^{-1}(I-\Pi_0). It approaches the direct contact coefficient g at high spatial frequency; it is not the positive finite-rank kernel (5). The common field-response framework similarly distinguishes the induced contribution from a direct interaction term. Here the actual Dirac response has both canonical energy signs, so the stable positive-mode elimination assumptions of a different model cannot be imported silently. How much structure a deformed pair source loses The reciprocal spatial pair evolves full complex 0-, 1- and 2-form profiles on the higher CP5, in its stated exact symmetry class. Its scalar source is \sigma(x,z)=D_Kx^K\left(|F|^2-|H_1|^2-|H_2|^2+|H_3|^2ight). 	ag{14} The H_j are the pointwise orthonormal form components; their squared metric factors matter. At wave cutoff N, the complete source is a polynomial of degree at most 2N+K. Projecting (14), rather than the bare wavefunction, onto scalar polynomials through that degree reconstructs the source independently. Equation (6) checks the first two levels from its moment matrix. For a=3,q=2,L=K=1,\kappa=2, with both same-kernel stationary preparations and unit positive norms, define e_\sigma= rac{\|(I-\Pi_{\le1})\sigma\|_2}{\|\sigma\|_2},\qquad e_R= rac{\|(I-\Pi_{\le1})(A+4)^{-1}(I-\Pi_0)\sigma\|_2} {\|(A+4)^{-1}(I-\Pi_0)\sigma\|_2}. 	ag{15} The second quantity is a specified radius-one screened comparison, not a claim that this nonlocal pair follows the local uniform response. Time Omitted source norm e_\sigma Omitted screened response norm e_R 0 0.001941 0.001405 6.1 0.040542 0.030505 6.7 0.016059 0.011424 10 0.024804 0.018396 20 0.008056 0.005809 Wave cutoffs N=5 and N=7 agree to better than 10^{-10} in these fractions. They are relative L^2 amplitudes, not probabilities or rates. A small initial omission does not remain constant during the encounter. Even an undeformed coherent density \sigma=D_Lt^L contains scalar levels through \ell=L. Only L=1 is exactly retained by (5). On CP3, the omitted fractions for L=2,6,12 are respectively 0.25820, 0.76636, and 0.93095. Choosing a temporal static limit does not remove this spatial information. Verification and physical scope local_dirac_response_checks.py checks the Laplace equation, every kernel multiplier in (8) through p=8 against direct spatial quadrature, the complete moment convolution, the direct-plus-induced coefficient, and scalar reconstruction of the evolving full-spinor pair at two wave cutoffs. These identities constrain a master-kernel derivation. The simple moment action requires an independently justified spatial restriction and a causal origin; the local calculation requires an actual physical background and source decomposition. Neither calculation yet selects observed electric or weak vertices, determines their rates, or fixes a physical radius.

title: Normal spinors in projective nesting
summary: The standard physical CP3 inclusion in CP5 has an explicit global normal-spinor decomposition and Abelian normal holonomy, with twist-dependent parallel factors that sharpen the six-to-ten coupling test.
text:
Summary: The standard physical CP3 inclusion in CP5 has an explicit global normal-spinor decomposition and Abelian normal holonomy, with twist-dependent parallel factors that sharpen the six-to-ten coupling test. The specified spatial embedding Consider the candidate physical inclusion \mathbb{CP}^a\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^{a+q},\qquad [Z]\longmapsto[Z,0], 	ag{1} with the same FS metric scale and its induced connections. Here a,q are complex dimensions: the lower spatial depth is 2a, the higher depth is 2(a+q) and the normal spatial depth is 2q. The electron–tau comparison is a=3,q=2. These are ordinary spatial submanifolds of the same physical manifold. The split is relative to the chosen lower submanifold, not a division into different kinds of dimensions in the higher particle. No dimension is compactified. The global projective geometries, embedding and metric are explicit hypotheses, rather than consequences of depth alone. The pointwise branching S_{10}^+=(S_6^+\otimes S_4^+)\oplus(S_6^-\otimes S_4^-) does not yet specify the bundles or their connection. Equation (1) allows those data to be computed. Normal bundle and actual holonomy Write A=\mathbb C^{a+1}, W=\mathbb C^q and let \ell\subset A denote the tautological line at a spatial point. The tangent space of the ambient projective manifold restricts as \operatorname{Hom}(\ell,(A\oplus W)/\ell) =\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,A/\ell) \oplus\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,W). Thus the complex normal bundle is  oxed{N=\mathcal O(1)\otimes W.} 	ag{2} The linear projective subspace is totally geodesic. Its normal connection is the Chern connection on \mathcal O(1) tensored with the constant identity on W. This can be verified directly from the ambient spatial metric. In the chart [1,z,w], put t=(1+|z|^2)^{-1} on w=0. The normal Hermitian metric is tI_q, so its connection in a holomorphic frame is  oxed{
abla^N=d+\alpha I_q,\qquad \alpha=\partial\log t=-t\sum_i ar z_i\,dz_i.} 	ag{3} The ambient Christoffel symbols satisfy \Gamma^\mu_{i
u}=-t ar z_i\delta^\mu_
u and \Gamma^\mu_{ij}=0 for normal indices \mu,
u and tangent indices i,j. The latter equality is the vanishing second fundamental form. In the curvature-four convention, F^N=-2i\omega_{m FS}I_q. 	ag{4} For radius R, write the same formula as F^N=-2i\omega_R I_q/R^2. All curvature endomorphisms lie on one central line. Since they are nonzero and the base is simply connected, the normal vector holonomy is exactly the central U(1). The available normal-frame group SO(2q) is much larger than this particular connection's holonomy. The complete normal spinor factors For even q, c_1(N)=qH is even and the normal bundle is spin. Using the complex structure and its unique spin structure gives \Sigma N=\Lambda^*N\otimes(\det N)^{-1/2} = igoplus_{k=0}^{q} \mathcal O(k-q/2)\otimes\Lambda^kW. 	ag{5} Here the Hermitian metric identifies the usual antiholomorphic cotangent description of spinors with \Lambda^*N. Exterior parity specifies chirality. Formula (5) is a unitary, connection-preserving decomposition; the normal-bundle identification and parallel splitting also appear in Ginoux and Habib, Lemma 4.2 and Corollary 4.4. The normal holonomy weight is k-q/2 and its multiplicity is  inom qk. The curvature on that summand is (k-q/2)F_{\mathcal O(1)}. Therefore its covariantly constant sections vanish unless k=q/2. Precisely  oxed{\dim\ker
abla^{\Sigma N}= inom q{q/2}.} 	ag{6} This is a count of parallel normal polarizations on the specified lower space, not the number of particles or the kernel of the full ambient Dirac operator. If q is odd, the normal bundle in (2) is not spin; a Spin^c construction and its determinant line must be retained. For a=3,q=2, the two chiral normal bundles are  oxed{\Sigma^+N=\mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1), \qquad \Sigma^-N=\mathbf1\otimes\mathbb C^2.} 	ag{7} The second doublet is globally parallel; the first consists of two curved line bundles. In these chirality conventions the global version of the sixteen-dimensional branching is  oxed{ \left.\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^5ight|_{\mathbb{CP}^3} =\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes [\mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1)] \ \oplus\ \Sigma^-\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes\mathbb C^2.} 	ag{8} It is a splitting along the lower spatial submanifold. It does not split T\mathbb{CP}^5 into rank three and rank two over all of CP5, which the global tangent obstruction excludes. Retain the physical line twists The selected electron construction uses \Sigma\mathbb{CP}^3\otimes\mathcal O(L+2), rather than the untwisted spinor bundle. More generally, on odd complex dimension a, write \mathcal S_a(L)=\Sigma\mathbb{CP}^a \otimes\mathcal O igl(L+(a+1)/2 igr) =\Lambda^{0,*}T^*\mathbb{CP}^a\otimes\mathcal O(L). Restrict the corresponding higher bundle \mathcal S_{a+q}(K). Combining its relative line twist with (5) yields  oxed{ \left.\mathcal S_{a+q}(K)ight|_{\mathbb{CP}^a} = igoplus_{k=0}^{q} \mathcal S_a(L)\,\widehat\otimes\,  igl[\mathcal O(K-L+k)\otimes\Lambda^kW igr].} 	ag{9} The hat retains normal exterior parity. This formula also has the canonical Spin^c interpretation when an ordinary spin splitting is unavailable. Its relative factor is parallel exactly when k=L-K. Consequently the number of parallel normal factors is  oxed{  egin{cases}  inom q{L-K},&0\le L-K\le q,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}} 	ag{10} For the six-to-ten comparison this becomes: Relative section degree Parallel normal factor Normal exterior parity L=K 1 even, k=0 L=K+1 2 odd, k=1 L=K+2 1 even, k=2 Other L-K 0 none In particular, matching two holomorphic degree-zero spinor components with the same section degree uses k=0. It does not automatically occupy the two-state normal factor. A full projected field can contain other form components, but their dynamics and occupation must be computed. The section degrees here are not the auxiliary cumulative mass-band labels. These line weights are geometric connection weights, with no electric charge or particle–antiparticle assignment made here. The projective mass inheritance test applies this connection formula to the new simplex polynomial. Canonical CP5 contains its required lower line degree at top normal degree. Full normal Clifford derivatives mix that component, and complete form-degree matching constrains a shared construction at both depths. Global intermediate spatial depths The normal characteristic obstruction adds a constraint to (2): its real normal Euler class is H^q. When q\le a, the specified inclusion cannot factor through a smooth odd-dimensional intermediate space. For CP3 inside CP5, this excludes intermediate depths seven and nine. A parallel normal spinor doublet is compatible with that obstruction: it is not a frame of ordinary normal vectors. The direct six-to-ten inclusion and its branching remain valid; the missing intermediate embeddings cannot be inferred from them. What the geometry permits and what it selects Parallel normal endomorphisms may mix equal holonomy weights. Their complex dimension in (5) is \dim\operatorname{End}_{m Hol}(\Sigma N) =\sum_{k=0}^{q} inom qk^2= inom{2q}q. 	ag{11} For q=2, this is six: two scalar blocks on \Sigma^+N and the four-dimensional matrix algebra on the parallel doublet \Sigma^-N. Thus parallel transport alone permits a full two-by-two matrix there; it does not determine that matrix or its eigenvalues. There is a second symmetry constraint. Normal rotations of W are ambient isometries fixing the entire embedded lower subspace. Their SU(2) action on the parallel doublet is irreducible. An interaction invariant under all those rotations acts as a scalar on the doublet. It cannot choose a unique line or split its two eigenvalues. Selecting a normal pattern can break that symmetry, but then the pattern and its response are additional dynamical data of the same field. The standard FS normal connection itself remains Abelian. A non-Abelian normal response needs a changed geometry or a derived field-dependent connection; the existence of an SU(2) frame action does not supply it. The separate gauge-carrier construction makes the same structure-group/holonomy distinction on a different bundle. Equations (8)–(10) sharpen the charged-lepton test: the proposed pair's twists, form components and normal current must match a global factor. The resulting vertex still needs its spatial matrix element and canonical kinetic normalization. Neither the parallel multiplicity nor the invariant-endomorphism count fixes a mass ratio, an observed weak coupling or neutrino neutrality. Verification projective_normal_bundle_checks.py checks the ambient coordinate connection and vanishing mixed second fundamental form, normal curvature and loop transport, full Clifford holonomy weights and chiral restrictions, twist-dependent parallel multiplicities, Chern-character compatibility and invariant matrix spaces.

title: Spatial projective source marginals
summary: A specified projective nesting has an exact almost-everywhere spatial disintegration, weighted reciprocal source maps and complete holomorphic current contractions, with distinct restriction and marginal normalization.
text:
Summary: A specified projective nesting has an exact almost-everywhere spatial disintegration, weighted reciprocal source maps and complete holomorphic current contractions, with distinct restriction and marginal normalization. Geometry and the domain of the spatial projection Use the specified linear physical inclusion \mathbb{CP}^a\subset\mathbb{CP}^b, a\ge1, q\ge1, b=a+q, with homogeneous coordinates [Z,W] in \mathbb C^{a+1}\oplus\mathbb C^q. The normal geometry is described by the global normal-spinor calculation. All these directions are ordinary spatial dimensions. No compactification is assumed; results using the global FS geometry remain conditional on it. The coordinate projection \pi[Z,W]=[Z] 	ag{1} is defined off the projective subspace Z=0. It cannot extend to a continuous retraction of the whole higher space onto the lower one. Indeed, if r were such a retraction, its action on the integral hyperplane class would satisfy r^*H_a=H_b. But then 0=r^*(H_a^{a+1})=H_b^{a+1}
e0 for b>a. The canonical inclusion and this almost-everywhere map are distinct geometric objects. The exceptional set has FS measure zero. Therefore (1) still provides an exact disintegration for integrable scalar sources. It does not justify discarding the exceptional set when differentiating a pulled-back field or asserting global smoothness. The full spatial measure Let d
u_a,d
u_b be the unit-volume FS measures. At fixed base representative z\in\mathbb C^{a+1}, |z|=1, write the higher point as [\sqrt T\,z,\sqrt{1-T}\,w],\qquad 0<T<1,\quad w\in S^{2q-1}. The sphere variable includes the relative phase of the normal coordinates. The invariant unit measure disintegrates as  oxed{d
u_b=d
u_a(z)\,  rac{T^a(1-T)^{q-1}}{\mathrm B(a+1,q)}\,dT\,d\omega(w),} 	ag{2} where d\omega is unit sphere measure. One direct derivation uses a normalized complex Gaussian vector: the squared norms of its two orthogonal blocks are independent gamma variables before normalization. Their ratio has the displayed beta distribution, independently of the two directions. Changing the phase of z is absorbed by the sphere integration, so (2) is globally well-defined as a scalar measure identity. For an integrable scalar current j, define (R_pj)(z)=\int_0^1\int_{S^{2q-1}} T^p j([\sqrt Tz,\sqrt{1-T}w]) \,d\omega(w) rac{T^a(1-T)^{q-1}}{\mathrm B(a+1,q)}dT, \qquad p\ge0. 	ag{3} R_0 is the ordinary marginal. Its weighted relatives have the exact adjoints  oxed{(R_p^*f)(X)=T(X)^pf(\pi X),\qquad \langle f,R_pjangle_a=\langle R_p^*f,jangle_b.} 	ag{4} Since T is independent of z in (2),  oxed{R_pR_p^*=  rac{(a+1)_{2p}}{(b+1)_{2p}}I, \qquad \|R_p\|^2= rac{(a+1)_{2p}}{(b+1)_{2p}}.} 	ag{5} Here (u)_v=\Gamma(u+v)/\Gamma(u); integer p suffices for the polynomial kernels below. In particular R_0 is a coisometry between the stated scalar L^2 spaces, rather than multiplication by a mode count. Physical volumes must be restored consistently. For a common radius R, \mathcal V_d=\pi^dR^{2d}/d! on complex dimension d. The marginal in physical volume measures is R_p^{m phys}=(\mathcal V_b/\mathcal V_a)R_p. A normalized physical wave uses \Phi/\sqrt{\mathcal V_b}; its density marginal then has the lower normalization R_0|\Phi|^2/\mathcal V_a. No arbitrary volume factor is discarded. A weighted map follows from one smooth kernel Consider the same dimension-independent kernel on every nested projective subspace: K_p(X,Y)= rac{|X^\dagger Y|^{2p}}{|X|^{2p}|Y|^{2p}}, \qquad p\in\mathbb N. 	ag{6} The kernel is a specified interaction candidate. It is not normalized independently at each depth. For a lower point z and higher point X, K_p(i z,X)=T(X)^pK_p(z,\pi X). 	ag{7} Thus the cross energy of two complete scalar sources is  oxed{U_{ab}=\kappa\langle j_a,K_pR_pj_bangle_a,\qquad V_a=\kappa K_pR_pj_b,\quad V_b=\kappa R_p^*K_pj_a.} 	ag{8} The weight T^p is fixed by the common kernel and spatial embedding. It is not an independently adjusted suppression coefficient. Both variations in (8) follow from the same energy, as required by nested reciprocity. A bare pullback of a smooth nonconstant f generally fails to extend smoothly across Z=0. The actual response in (8) avoids this problem: T^p(K_pj_a)(\pi X) is the globally smooth ambient polynomial potential \int K_p(i z,X)j_a(z)d
u_a(z). The same kernel fixes both the weight and the regular extension. Along a compatible chain, the geometric weights multiply: T_{c	o a}=T_{c	o b}T_{b	o a}. Conditional integration therefore gives R_{p,c	o a}=R_{p,b	o a}R_{p,c	o b}, with the reverse order for adjoints. This is source reduction, not propagation through another particle. Section branching and restriction For a specified holomorphic line family of degree K, normalized monomial sections on CPb are s_{\alpha eta}(Z,W)= \sqrt{ rac{(K+b)!}{b!\,\alpha!\, eta!}}\, Z^\alpha W^ eta,\qquad |\alpha|+| eta|=K, 	ag{9} evaluated on unit homogeneous representatives. Normal occupation r=| eta| gives the complete branching H^0(\mathbb{CP}^b,\mathcal O(K)) = igoplus_{r=0}^{K} \operatorname{Sym}^{K-r}(\mathbb C^{a+1})^* \otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{r}(\mathbb C^q)^*. 	ag{10} Counting these terms gives the exact convolution  oxed{ inom{K+b}{b} =\sum_{r=0}^{K} inom{K-r+a}{a} inom{r+q-1}{q-1}.} 	ag{11} For q=1, this reduces to the ordinary Hockey-Stick identity. The corresponding flat spatial oscillator source calculation has different integration weights. Restriction to W=0 retains only r=0. In unit-volume kinetic norms, every nonzero singular value of this restriction has square  oxed{ rac{D_b(K)}{D_a(K)},\qquad D_d(K)= inom{K+d}{d},} 	ag{12} with multiplicity D_a(K). For CP3 inside CP5 the ratio is (K+5)(K+4)/20. In physical-volume norms (12) also carries \mathcal V_a/\mathcal V_b, as appropriate for a restriction to a lower-dimensional spatial submanifold. The complete current marginal is different Let \Phi=\sum_{\alpha, eta}c_{\alpha eta}s_{\alpha eta}, with arbitrary complex coefficients, and put k=K-| eta|. Construct the current |\Phi|^2 before integrating it. The sphere phase integrals remove cross terms with unequal normal occupations, while preserving every cross term with the same  eta. The remaining beta integral gives  oxed{R_p|\Phi|^2(z)= \sum_{ eta}  rac{(k+a+1)_p}{(K+b+1)_p} \left|\sum_{|\alpha|=k}c_{\alpha eta} s^{(a)}_{\alpha}(z)ight|^2.} 	ag{13} To check the coefficient directly, use \int|w^ eta|^2d\omega=(q-1)! eta!/(r+q-1)! and \mathbb E[T^{k+p}(1-T)^r] =\mathrm B(a+1+k+p,q+r)/\mathrm B(a+1,q). Multiplying by the normalizations in (9) leaves precisely the normalized lower section and the factor in (13). At p=0 there is no external count factor. Even a higher mode that vanishes under restriction can have a nonzero density marginal. At p=1 each block instead carries (k+a+1)/(K+b+1), fixed by the same smooth kernel as (8). For a chain, these factors telescope to the direct coefficient. Equation (13) is a scalar-current example in the specified holomorphic spinor line. It does not replace the full spatial spinor bundle, its Dirac complement or its velocity current. Other complete scalar currents can be inserted directly into (3). A vector or tensor current additionally needs its bundle transport and contraction; integrating unrelated components does not define a covariant source map. Verification projective_source_projection_checks.py checks full complex monomial fields by independent spatial fibre quadrature, weighted current contractions, normalized restriction matrices, direct and staged projection, common-kernel covariance and both reciprocal variations.

title: Radial dynamics of two-frequency fields
summary: An exact map from complex radial motion to the full two-frequency spatial field separates number norm from kinetic weight and transfers radial dynamics, source response and instability without a dimension-specific symmetry assumption.
text: Summary: An exact map from complex radial motion to the full two-frequency spatial field separates number norm from kinetic weight and transfers radial dynamics, source response and instability without a dimension-specific symmetry assumption. Extend the stationary construction to radial motion The two-frequency current construction uses two stationary components of one spatial field. Its radial dynamics can also be derived exactly when the profile changes with time. The map below is defined on actual radial functions over d ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, with one existing containing normal direction used for the partner matrix \alpha_y. All sectors remain submanifolds of the one nested physical manifold. Choose fixed unit rest polarizations w_1,w_2 satisfying \beta w_j=w_j. They need not coincide. For arbitrary complex radial functions u=(F,G), define \Phi_w[u]\,(x)=\frac{F(r)w+iG(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \|u\|_r^2=\int_0^\infty(|F|^2+|G|^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{1} Here \Omega_{d-1} is the area of the unit sphere. The functions obey regularity at the origin and the decay needed for the stated integrals and integrations by parts. For constants a,b, put \boxed{\Psi[u]=a\Phi_{w_1}[u]+b\alpha_y\Phi_{w_2}[u^*], \quad n=|a|^2+|b|^2,\quad s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0.} \tag{2} Conjugation in u^* acts on the radial functions F,G. It does not conjugate the fixed spatial Clifford matrices or the chosen rest polarization. Equation (2) defines a real-linear map into the full field. It does not assume a global antilinear symmetry on arbitrary spatial fields. When a two-frequency spatial symmetry exists derives the separate matrix and scalar-interference requirements for such a global map, including its compatibility with normal propagation. The scalar source remains radial pointwise The Clifford relations give \Phi_{w_1}[u]^\dagger\beta\alpha_y\Phi_{w_2}[u^*]=0. \tag{3} The diagonal terms connect opposite \beta eigenspaces and vanish. The two radial cross terms cancel because their coefficient is F^*G^*-G^*F^*=0 and \beta\alpha_y commutes with \alpha(\widehat x). This holds for complex F,G and both independent rest polarizations. Consequently \boxed{\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi =\frac{s}{\Omega_{d-1}}(|F|^2-|G|^2).} \tag{4} The scalar center stays at the origin whenever its defining scalar normalization is nonzero. Its second-moment tensor is M_\sigma=(sT/d)I_d, where T[u]=\int_0^\infty r^2(|F|^2-|G|^2)r^{d-1}dr. \tag{5} Thus the common scalar moment interaction g_0 gives \mathfrak m(r)=m_0+(g_0s/d)T[u]r^2. A nonlinear radial equation generates the full spatial solution The real radial Dirac differential operator is H_r[u]= \begin{pmatrix} \mathfrak m(r)&\partial_r+(d-1)/r\\ -\partial_r&-\mathfrak m(r) \end{pmatrix}. \tag{6} It is self-adjoint on the appropriate radial domain with measure r^{d-1}dr. Suppose \boxed{i\partial_tu=H_r[u]u.} \tag{7} The field \Phi_w[u] then satisfies the complete bound-coordinate Dirac equation. Since (6) has real coefficients, the conjugate radial functions satisfy i\partial_tu^*=-H_r[u]u^*. Anticommutation of the full bound operator with \alpha_y supplies that same negative sign for the second term of (2). Both terms therefore solve the full spatial equation with precisely the scalar source in (4). This proves an exact invariant radial family, uniform in the normal coordinate y. A varying y-dependent amplitude or an angular shape perturbation requires the additional spatial dynamics. The complete periodic response retains those possibilities rather than assuming this radial family exhausts the field. For a stationary real profile u_0, u(t)=u_0e^{-iMt} makes (2) the original two-frequency solution. Time-dependent complex profiles in (7) also give full nonlinear spatial solutions; the construction is not confined to harmonic motion. Number norm and kinetic normalization have different weights The positive and normal-partner radial frames are orthogonal after integration over the actual bound spatial directions. For variations \delta u,\delta v, equation (2) gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \|\Psi[u]\|^2&=n\|u\|_r^2,\\ \operatorname{Re}\langle\delta\Psi[u],\delta\Psi[v]\rangle &=n\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta u,\delta v\rangle_r,\\ \operatorname{Im}\langle\delta\Psi[u],\delta\Psi[v]\rangle &=s\operatorname{Im}\langle\delta u,\delta v\rangle_r. \end{aligned}} \tag{8} The second component is conjugated, so it reverses the imaginary part of the radial inner product. At n=1, the map preserves the real perturbation norm exactly. Its symplectic form, and hence the first-order kinetic term, instead has weight s. Let H_{r,0} be (6) with the bare scalar coefficient m_0 and no self-interaction. The full energy restricted to (2) is \boxed{\mathcal E_{\rm full} =s\langle u,H_{r,0}u\rangle_r+ \frac{g_0s^2}{2d}T[u]^2 =s\,\mathcal E_{r,g_0s}[u].} \tag{9} The kinetic term has the same overall factor s. Therefore the complete restricted action is s times the radial action with coefficient g_0s, and variation gives (7) for fixed a,b. The amplitudes and their relative polarizations remain additional possible variations outside this restricted calculation. For a radial scalar moment, a tangent source variation has the form \delta(sT)=2s\operatorname{Re}\langle u,Q\delta u\rangle_r, where Q is the signed radial second-moment operator. In the canonical coordinate \xi=\sqrt{s}\,\delta u, this becomes \boxed{\delta(sT)=2\sqrt{s}\operatorname{Re}\langle u,Q\xi\rangle_r.} \tag{10} Both the changing profile and its kinetic weight must enter the normalized coupling vertex. Unit total number norm alone does not determine the normalization of every collective coordinate. Radial instability is inherited Let u_0e^{-iMt} be a radial stationary solution at coefficient g_0s. A growing perturbation of its radial equation maps through (2) into a perturbation of the full two-frequency field. At n=1, equation (8) preserves its norm at every time. A radial exponential growth rate is therefore preserved by the map, including an oscillating growing mode. The negative-frequency component cannot remove that instability. This statement is conditional on the radial instability being present. It does not assert that every scalar Dirac source is unstable. The zero-bare-mass moment branches already have such modes. Direct nonlinear evolution of the five- and six-dimensional radial equations confirms their transfer through (2), while both the full number norm and energy remain conserved. A phase rotation of the stationary background should be removed when comparing a nonlinear perturbation with a tangent mode. If its real linearization has eigenvalue \lambda with nonzero imaginary part, the physical radial tangent evolves as \operatorname{Re}(e^{\lambda t}v) in real coordinates. Retaining only e^{\operatorname{Re}\lambda t}\operatorname{Re}v would miss its oscillation and give an incorrect verification. The current retains both polarizations and the radial phase Integrating the normal number current gives \boxed{\int j_y\,dx =2\operatorname{Re}\left[ \bar a b\,\langle w_1,w_2\rangle \int_0^\infty(F^{*2}+G^{*2})r^{d-1}dr\right].} \tag{11} For a real unit stationary profile this reduces to a 2M oscillation, with an additional factor from the overlap of the two rest polarizations. Orthogonal rest polarizations can remove this integrated normal-current oscillation. That is a statement about one integrated current; local bound-direction currents and other response channels still need to be calculated. The current in (11) is the spatial number current of the single Dirac field. Identifying its projection with a physical photon source remains a separate dynamical step. A readjusted stationary current clock The frequency of a nearby stationary branch changes when its scalar source changes. Add an isotropic coefficient f_{\rm ext} multiplying r^2/\sqrt d. On the zero-bare-mass branch, write the total quadratic coefficient as A to distinguish it from the amplitude a in (2). Self-consistency and spatial scaling give A=\frac{f_{\rm ext}}{\sqrt d}+\frac{g_0s}{d}T(A),\qquad T(A)=\frac{M(A)}{3A},\qquad M(A)\propto A^{1/3}. \tag{12} At zero external coefficient, \boxed{\frac{dA}{df_{\rm ext}}=\frac{3}{5\sqrt d},\qquad \frac{dM}{df_{\rm ext}}=\frac{M}{5A\sqrt d}.} \tag{13} The frozen-profile scalar matrix element is T/\sqrt d=M/(3A\sqrt d). Profile readjustment reduces that derivative by a factor 3/5 in this specific homogeneous source model. Independent stationary solves verify (13). Following the derivative as an actual slow dynamical evolution would also require stability; a stationary branch derivative does not supply it. Verification radial_bifrequency_checks.py uses arbitrary complex radial profiles and independent rest polarizations. Full spatial quadrature checks the scalar density, center, moments, number current, tangent metric and kinetic form. Independent finite derivatives in every bound coordinate verify (7) as an actual spatial field equation. A nonlinear radial trajectory and its reconstructed two-component field check the source equation, conserved norm and energy, and the complete oscillating growth mode. Separate stationary profile solves check the current-clock derivative. Reports preserve previous runs with timestamped filenames and all checks remain active under Python optimization. Related Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents — supplies the stationary family extended here. Periodic spatial source response — retains normal propagation and angular motions outside the radial family. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the radial equation, scaling and stability calculation. Canonical coupling normalization — explains why a source coefficient must be combined with its kinetic normalization. Complete radial polarization fields allows independent complex vector profiles in both radial components. That separate family closes under the local scalar equation in even and odd dimensions and retains the full tangential current. It does not assume the two components share one scalar radial profile or require a partner normal matrix.

title: Complete radial polarization fields
summary: A spherical scalar Dirac family retains independent complex radial polarization vectors, tangential spatial currents and reciprocal source variations in both odd and even dimensions, including six and ten.
text:
Summary: A spherical scalar Dirac family retains independent complex radial polarization vectors, tangential spatial currents and reciprocal source variations in both odd and even dimensions, including six and ten. A spatial family available in even dimensions The localized axial family uses odd-dimensional kinetic chiral blocks. A separate spherical family works for every D\ge2, including the proposed depths six and ten. It extends the fixed-polarization radial construction by allowing every radial polarization component to have its own complex profile. The spatial domain here is a specified flat chart, not a selected global particle geometry. Let the Hermitian matrices \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_D, eta obey the complete Dirac Clifford relations. Their minimal complex size is n=2^{\lfloor(D+1)/2floor}. Choose an orthonormal matrix W whose P=n/2 columns span the entire  eta=+1 eigenspace. For r=|x|>0, put \alpha_r=\alpha\cdot\widehat x and set  oxed{\Psi(x,t)=W F(r,t)+\alpha_r W G(r,t), \qquad F,G\in\mathbb C^P.} 	ag{1} The vectors F and G are independent functions of radius and time. They need not be scalar functions multiplying one fixed polarization. Their components describe a field on D ordinary spatial coordinates; they introduce no additional physical dimensions. At the origin, sufficient smoothness conditions are that F is a smooth function of r^2 and G=r\widetilde G(r^2) with smooth \widetilde G. Then \alpha_rG=\alpha\cdot x\,\widetilde G is regular in the original Cartesian coordinates. Decay or appropriate boundary conditions must also support the stated integrations by parts. Spatial dimension D Complete Dirac size n Components of each radial vector P 3 4 2 5 8 4 6 8 4 10 32 16 These counts belong to (1); they are not extra interaction multipliers. The scalar and positive density are radial Because  eta\alpha_r=-\alpha_r eta, the columns of \alpha_rW span the opposite  eta eigenspace. Thus W^\dagger\alpha_rW=0 and \alpha_r^2=I give pointwise  oxed{ho=\Psi^\dagger\Psi=F^\dagger F+G^\dagger G, \qquad \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi=F^\dagger F-G^\dagger G.} 	ag{2} No angular averaging is used to obtain either identity. If two radial patterns are superposed, their complete vector sums enter (2). In particular their scalar includes 2\operatorname{Re}(F_1^\dagger F_2-G_1^\dagger G_2). Their phases and polarization contractions remain present. Exact closure under the local scalar equation Consider the same specified local interaction, i\partial_t\Psi=-i\alpha\cdot
abla\Psi +[m+g\sigma] eta\Psi,\qquad m\ge0, 	ag{3} and define M(r,t)=m+g\sigma(r,t). The two Cartesian identities \alpha\cdot
abla(WF)=\alpha_rWF',\qquad \alpha\cdot
abla(\alpha_rWG) =W\left(G'+ rac{D-1}{r}Gight) 	ag{4} follow from \partial_i\widehat x_j=(\delta_{ij}-\widehat x_i\widehat x_j)/r and the Clifford anticommutators. Substitution gives the exact vector equations  egin{aligned} i\partial_tF&=-i\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-1}{r}ight)G+MF,\ i\partial_tG&=-i\partial_rF-MG. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} Every regular solution of (5) reconstructs a solution of the full D-dimensional equation through (1). The nonlinearity preserves this angular family because its scalar (2) is radial. It still couples all occupied vector components through the common M. This is an invariant spatial family, not a claim that arbitrary angular patterns solve (5). The full scalar-source variation is also retained. For independent variations \delta F,\delta G, \delta\sigma=2\operatorname{Re} (F^\dagger\delta F-G^\dagger\delta G),\quad \delta inom{\sigma F}{-\sigma G} = inom{\delta\sigma F+\sigma\delta F} {-\delta\sigma G-\sigma\delta G}. 	ag{6} Both ordinary and conjugate-dependent responses remain in this real-linear derivative. No fixed partner or additional pair coefficient is inserted. A radial density can carry a tangential current The full spatial number current is not determined by ho alone. For a unit direction \widehat x, define K_i(\widehat x)=W^\dagger\alpha_i\alpha_rW-\widehat x_iI_P. 	ag{7} These matrices are anti-Hermitian and obey \sum_i\widehat x_iK_i=0. Direct reconstruction of j_i=\Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi yields  oxed{j_i=2\widehat x_i\operatorname{Re}(F^\dagger G) +2\operatorname{Re}(F^\dagger K_iG).} 	ag{8} The second term is tangential. Its coefficients retain the complete spatial rotation matrices and complex polarization texture. For fixed radius it is a linear combination of tangential rotation fields on the sphere; its divergence is zero. The radial component j_r=2\operatorname{Re}(F^\dagger G) therefore gives \partial_tho+ rac1{r^{D-1}}\partial_r(r^{D-1}j_r)=0. 	ag{9} Thus a radial scalar and density do not imply absence of angular current. Nor is this number current already an identified electromagnetic current. Canonical norm and the full polarization matrix Let \Omega_{D-1}=2\pi^{D/2}/\Gamma(D/2). The physical norm and its matrix refinement are \mathcal Q=\Omega_{D-1}\int_0^\infty (FF^\dagger+GG^\dagger)r^{D-1}dr, \qquad Q=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal Q. 	ag{10} The convention in (1) includes no factor 1/\sqrt{\Omega_{D-1}}; that physical area consequently remains in (10). Using (5), the matrix integrand obeys \partial_t(FF^\dagger+GG^\dagger) =-\left(\partial_r+ rac{D-1}{r}ight) (GF^\dagger+FG^\dagger). 	ag{11} The real scalar terms cancel, including the nonlinear part of M. Vanishing endpoint flux proves conservation of every entry of \mathcal Q, not just its trace. This is a property of the stated radial family; it does not assert a new unrestricted internal symmetry of every spatial Dirac field. Local polarization profiles and tangential currents can still change while their integrated matrix is conserved. For a common physical rotation O with spin lift S, S commutes with  eta and induces the unitary matrix U=W^\dagger SW. Transforming F,G to UF,UG reconstructs S\Psi(O^{-1}x), so (2)–(11) are covariant under rotation of all physical data. Verification and scope radial_polarization_fields.py implements reconstruction, the vector time derivatives and the complete spatial current. radial_polarization_checks.py runs 234 checks of complete Clifford modules in every dimension from two through ten. Independent Cartesian derivatives verify (5) on complex profiles whose polarizations vary with radius. The checks also reconstruct every current component, rotate the full field, retain the complete scalar Hessian and integrate the derivative of the full conserved matrix (10). This supplies a controlled spatial family at the even particle depths as well as at odd depths. Its patterns share one radial center. General separated-center encounters, arbitrary angular textures, stable occupied particle states and physically normalized cross-depth coupling require additional calculations. The family does not select the global geometry of our three-dimensional space or of a higher sector.

title: Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes
summary: A solved conservative wave model turns a two-sided spatial overlap into reflection and transmission, separating protected polarization mismatch from narrow resonances and coherent transparency.
text: Summary: A solved conservative wave model turns a two-sided spatial overlap into reflection and transmission, separating protected polarization mismatch from narrow resonances and coherent transparency. From an allowed overlap to an actual encounter A nonzero geometric vertex does not specify how much of an incident wave scatters. The target responds, and that response changes the wave which drives it. This note solves that reciprocal problem in a conservative mode benchmark, including both incident polarizations and all retained target shape modes. The variables are modes of the one field on the nested macroscopic spatial manifold. The propagating modes represent a chosen physical propagation direction, with their bound transverse profiles already included in their normalization. The target variables represent localized spatial changes of the same field. They are not additional mediator particles or additional physical spatial dimensions. The model is conditional on a self-adjoint first-order mode reduction. A general Dirac linearization retains the ordinary and conjugate blocks in Dirac source linearization; reducing it to the form below requires justification. The lattice dispersion below is an exact solvable benchmark, not a proposed photon dispersion law. One reciprocal quadratic energy Let a_n\in\mathbb C^p, n\in\mathbb Z, describe p propagating polarization amplitudes on a line, and let b\in\mathbb C^m describe the target response modes. Take E=-J\sum_n\left(a_n^\dagger a_{n+1}+a_{n+1}^\dagger a_n\right) +b^\dagger H_b b+b^\dagger Va_0+a_0^\dagger V^\dagger b, \tag{1} with J>0, H_b=H_b^\dagger and an m\times p spatial vertex V. The two preparations enter through the target profiles which determine V and through the incident polarization. Their canonical normalization must come from the field action. A shared frequency offset can be added to all modes if positive absolute frequencies are required; the calculation uses frequencies relative to that offset and sets \hbar=1. Variation yields i\dot a_n=-J(a_{n-1}+a_{n+1})+\delta_{n0}V^\dagger b, \qquad i\dot b=H_bb+Va_0. \tag{2} The conserved mode norm is \sum_n\|a_n\|^2+\|b\|^2. Both appearances of V in (2) are fixed by the same energy. No independently chosen one-way response coefficient is allowed. The scalar version belongs to the exactly solvable family of discrete wave resonance models studied by Miroshnichenko and Kivshar. The following matrix formulas are derived directly from (2). Solve the incoming and outgoing wave equations Choose 0<k<\pi. A free wave has relative frequency and positive group velocity \varepsilon=-2J\cos k,\qquad v=2J\sin k. \tag{3} For an incident polarization c, use the stationary amplitudes a_n=e^{ikn}c+e^{-ikn}r\quad(n\leq0), \qquad a_n=e^{ikn}t\quad(n\geq0). \tag{4} The value at the shared site gives t=c+r. Substitution into its original difference equation gives iv r=V^\dagger b. Combining that equation with the target equation gives D(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon I-H_b+\frac{i}{v}VV^\dagger, \qquad \boxed{b=D^{-1}Vc,\quad r=\mathsf r c=-\frac{i}{v}V^\dagger D^{-1}Vc,\quad t=\mathsf t c=(I+\mathsf r)c.} \tag{5} The inverse is evaluated with outgoing boundary conditions. If an exact decoupled target eigenmode makes it singular, use the limiting resolvent on the coupled subspace; an unexcited dark bound mode does not spoil the scattering solution. The term iVV^\dagger/v is the response into the propagating modes of the same field. Its size and sign have been derived from the spatial junction equation, not inserted as a phenomenological loss rate. Exact flux conservation Because D-D^\dagger=2iVV^\dagger/v, the inverse identity gives D^{-1}-D^{-\dagger} =-\frac{2i}{v}D^{-\dagger}VV^\dagger D^{-1}. Consequently \mathsf r+\mathsf r^\dagger=-2\mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf r, \qquad \boxed{\mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf r+\mathsf t^\dagger\mathsf t=I.} \tag{6} The two-port scattering matrix and its second unitarity identity are S=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf r&\mathsf t\\\mathsf t&\mathsf r\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathsf r^\dagger\mathsf t+\mathsf t^\dagger\mathsf r=0, \qquad S^\dagger S=I. \tag{7} All propagating polarizations here have the same group velocity. If their dispersions differ, the flux metric must be included. Complex polarized targets need not give S=S^T while that preparation is held fixed: time reversal transforms the target and probe preparations as well. Adjoint terms in one energy establish conservative mutual coupling; they do not erase those polarization conditions. One shape channel: exact mismatch and a narrow resonance Let there be one target mode of frequency \Omega, and write V=gq^\dagger, where q^\dagger q=1 is the normalized spatial coupling direction in the two incident polarizations. Then P=q q^\dagger,\qquad \delta=\varepsilon-\Omega, \qquad \Gamma(\varepsilon)=\frac{g^2}{v(\varepsilon)}, \qquad \mathsf r=-\frac{i\Gamma}{\delta+i\Gamma}P. \tag{8} For c^\dagger c=1, the reflected fraction is \boxed{\mathcal R(\varepsilon,c) =\frac{\Gamma^2}{\delta^2+\Gamma^2}|q^\dagger c|^2.} \tag{9} This separates two effects with different physical meanings: If q^\dagger c=0, the target is never driven: b=0, r=0, t=c. This is a geometric polarization mismatch for the specified channel. For the matched polarization c=q, any nonzero g gives complete reflection at \delta=0. A small coupling makes the resonance narrow; it does not make its peak small. Away from a band edge and at weak coupling, v varies little across the resonance. Its full width at half maximum is approximately 2\Gamma, and its integrated reflected spectral weight is approximately \pi\Gamma. The exact expression remains (9) with its energy-dependent velocity. A broad incident spectrum can therefore scatter weakly even when a finely tuned monochromatic wave scatters strongly. For a quadrupole channel with g=g_0\cos(2\theta) from transition-density coupling, the width scales as \cos^2(2\theta). At exactly zero overlap the channel closes. For arbitrarily small nonzero overlap its ideal resonant peak can remain large. The limits of zero coupling and exact resonant frequency do not commute. Real finite-time preparations must be evaluated with their actual bandwidth. Coherent transparency can retain target motion Take one incident polarization and two target modes, H_b=\begin{pmatrix}-\Omega&0\\0&\Omega\end{pmatrix}, \qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}g\\g\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Omega\ne0. At the central relative frequency \varepsilon=0, (5) has b=\frac g\Omega\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}c, \qquad V^\dagger b=0,\qquad r=0,\qquad t=c. \tag{10} The two target responses cancel in the outgoing source while both are nonzero. This is a frequency-specific transparency, unlike the invariant input nullspace \ker V. It illustrates why observing transmission alone does not establish that the incoming pattern never engaged the target. Independent spatial wavepacket check The diagnostic evolves (2) directly on 501 sites with two polarizations and one target mode. Before evaluating it, the benchmark fixes J=1, g=0.6, \Omega=0, carrier k=\pi/2, an incident Gaussian intensity width 12 centred at site -80, and final time 100. The boundaries are at \pm250, outside the relevant encounter and outgoing packets. The target direction is q=(\cos0.43,e^{0.71i}\sin0.43)^T; its complex polarization is retained. Integration of (9) over the incoming packet spectrum predicts matched reflection 0.8590726693. Direct evolution gives: incident polarization reflected norm transmitted norm q 0.859071525 0.140926211 c_\perp, q^\dagger c_\perp=0 below 10^{-27} 1.000000000 (q+c_\perp)/\sqrt2 0.429535762 0.570463105 Reflected and transmitted packets are counted outside 25 sites from the target. Their values agree with the integrated stationary prediction to within 1.2\times10^{-6}; a small remainder is still near the target at the finite stopping time. The full evolving norm and energy are conserved. The dark input leaves the target unexcited throughout the sampled evolution. These are model units and mode norms. They are not measured particle cross sections or an assignment of a lattice to physical space. Consequence for the coupling mechanism Shape and polarization enter the spatial vertex. Reciprocal field dynamics then determine its resonant enhancement, interference and outgoing flux. An exact rotation-neutral source can close a specified vertex entirely. A small but nonzero overlap instead requires a bandwidth and spectrum calculation before it can explain rare scattering. To apply this result across the particle hierarchy, derive V, H_b, the continuum dispersion and the background preparation from the same field action. The higher spatial geometry may determine the full vertex; the two photon polarizations specify the incident channel on which it acts. Verification and related spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py checks the unreduced spatial equations, multichannel unitarity, a protected dark input, resonant reflection, coherent transparency and full wavepacket evolution. The propagating lattice is solved directly for the final check; the scattering formula is not used to evolve it. Transition-density coupling — supplies spatial vertices with both shape preparations retained. Polarized response spectrum — gives finite-exposure response before completing the reciprocal scattering problem. Coherent spatial overlap — includes spatial phase and interference in the input source profiles.

title: Resonant scalar wave quartets
