u)},\qquad \chi_{m null}(0,0)= rac{ho}{p-
u}\quad(
u<p). 	ag{13} In contrast, a nonzero purely transverse static momentum has \chi_{m null}(0,q)=0. General static poles satisfy |q|^2=2a|q_\parallel|: two elastic-scattering spheres centered at \pm ae, each of radius a. These directional limits and resonances exclude treating this background's response as one universal positive elliptic overlap coefficient. Nonlinear comparison and scope The nonnull moving branches emerge at the same threshold and have a continuously connecting scalar response. Neither family is a localized particle or a discrete mass selection. scalar_plane_response_checks.py compares (4) with the complete spinor symbol in spatial dimensions two through six and ten, with complex polarizations and general momenta. Independent Fourier differences of the nonlinear source check both ordinary and conjugate blocks. The diagnostic verifies the full spectrum, positive metric, evolution bound, critical Jordan mode and scalar resolvent. It also evolves the original eight-component nonlinear plane at p=ho=1 and 
u=0.3,1,1.4. Halving the initial perturbation from 10^{-5} to 5	imes10^{-6} approximately halves the error divided by that perturbation amplitude, as required for a first variation. Over 0\le t\le4, the selected linear perturbations amplify by approximately 1.016, 8.062 and 157.53, respectively. Positive norm and the complete kinetic-plus-scalar energy remain conserved. These are dynamical checks of the stated controls; they do not measure a physical particle coupling.

title: Slow shape poles and their signed response
summary: The two-frequency scalar shape response has poles whose frequency and residue decrease together, but their canonical sign and finite total response prevent identifying them from softness alone as stable weakly coupled particles.
text:
Summary: The two-frequency scalar shape response has poles whose frequency and residue decrease together, but their canonical sign and finite total response prevent identifying them from softness alone as stable weakly coupled particles. Solve for the collective frequency instead of supplying it The complete periodic response distinguishes the bound field's carrier from its collective source poles. In the radial rest examples, scalar quadrupole sidebands cancel and the remaining frequency equation can be solved directly. This gives a concrete test of whether a slow source also has a weak response. Use the zero-bare-mass scalar model with one fixed g_0, unit number norm and scalar balance s=|a|^2-|b|^2>0. The bound profile dilates by \ell=s^{1/5}. Let A(z) and B(z) be the even and odd scalar functions of the full single-frequency spatial shape response, calculated at s=1. For a tensor eigenvector of the circulation action T with eigenvalue h, the two-frequency bare response is  oxed{\Pi_h(\omega;s)=A(z)+ rac{h}{s}B(z),\qquad z= rac{\omega}{\ell},\qquad \chi_h= rac{\Pi_h}{1-g_0\Pi_h}.} 	ag{1} The tensor labels describe spatial shape patterns over the existing macroscopic dimensions. They are not new physical directions. The 1/s factor comes from retaining both frequency components and their different scalar and canonical weights; it is not a chosen weak-coupling coefficient. Derive the slow pole and its residue Suppose the frozen source resolvents are analytic near z=0, and put A(z)=A_0+O(z^2),\qquad B(z)=B_1z+O(z^3), \qquad D_0=1-g_0A_0. 	ag{2} For hB_1
e0 and D_0
e0, set z=s\zeta in the denominator of (1). The implicit-function theorem gives the simple root  oxed{\omega_h(s) =s^{6/5} rac{D_0}{g_0hB_1} \left[1+O(s^2)ight].} 	ag{3} The source residue R_h is defined by \chi_h(\omega)=R_h/(\omega-\omega_h)+O(1). At the pole \Pi_h=1/g_0, so  oxed{R_h=- rac{1}{g_0^2\partial_\omega\Pi_h(\omega_h)} =- rac{s^{6/5}}{g_0^2hB_1}\left[1+O(s^2)ight].} 	ag{4} Thus both the pole frequency and its source weight become small. Their signs also matter. The checked profiles have A_0<0, B_1<0 and D_0>0. The h=+1 member has negative frequency and positive residue; its conjugate h=-1 member has positive frequency and negative residue. At one common g_0=6.5 and s=0.001, full radial response calculations give: spatial depth positive slow frequency, h=-1 its signed residue static full response 3 0.004989695 -0.000487181 -0.056209060 5 0.005806261 -0.000575196 -0.054789326 6 0.006199339 -0.000616903 -0.054348207 The same calculation supplies the slow poles at all three depths. It does not select a uniquely five-dimensional particle or an occupied mode. Check the sign with the full canonical field realization The scalar functions in (1) arise from both angular radial families and both signs of the Dirac spectrum. Let L be their complete reference radial operator with its bound carrier subtracted, and let v_h,v_{-h} be the respective spatial source vectors. The four-block realization is  egin{gathered} L_4=\operatorname{diag}(\ell L,-\ell L,-\ell L,\ell L),\qquad \Sigma_4=\operatorname{diag}(I,I,-I,-I),\ t=\ell^{-2}(a v_h,-b v_h,a v_{-h},-b v_{-h})^T,\  oxed{\mathcal B_4=L_4+g_0\Sigma_4tt^\dagger,\qquad \chi_h=t^\dagger(\omega-\mathcal B_4)^{-1}\Sigma_4t.} \end{gathered} 	ag{5} The amplitudes may be taken real in this single-helicity realization, with a^2=(1+s)/2 and b^2=(1-s)/2. The \ell^{-2} factors are the dilated quadratic source moments. Expanding the four frozen blocks recovers (1), including its 1/s term. The matrix obeys \Sigma_4\mathcal B_4= (\Sigma_4\mathcal B_4)^\dagger. For a simple real mode \mathcal B_4v=\omega_hv with v^\dagger\Sigma_4v
e0, its resolvent residue is  oxed{R_h= rac{|t^\dagger v|^2}{v^\dagger\Sigma_4v}.} 	ag{6} This independent normalization reproduces (4). Replacing the denominator by the positive Euclidean norm would erase the sign of the physical canonical form. A small source residue must be assessed with that form. Interpret the work sign with the stability qualification For a real source term H_{m ext}=f(t)O, let f(t)=\operatorname{Re}(f_0e^{-i\omega t}) and let a bounded particular output have amplitude \chi f_0. The mean supplied power is  oxed{\langle\dot f\,\delta Oangle =- rac{\omega|f_0|^2}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi.} 	ag{7} A simple real pole continued as R/(\omega-\omega_0+i0) has positive absorptive weight at positive \omega_0 when R>0 and the opposite work sign when R<0. Equation (6) identifies this signed contribution without assigning an absolute physical energy to a Floquet frequency, which can be shifted by the background frequency. An unstable full background has no generic settled periodic response. For it, (1) is a meromorphic source resolvent, and its individual real-pole weight does not establish stable absorption. The radial dynamics already transfer existing radial instabilities to these two-frequency fields. Stability and selection of the occupied field must therefore precede any particle interpretation. A real canonical two-mode example checks the effect of opposite signs: H= rac12(p_a^2+\omega_a^2q_a^2) - rac12(p_b^2+\omega_b^2q_b^2)+\varepsilon q_aq_b. 	ag{8} Both reciprocal equations follow from this same energy. Their frequencies satisfy  oxed{(\omega^2-\omega_a^2)(\omega^2-\omega_b^2) +\varepsilon^2=0.} 	ag{9} At equal uncoupled frequencies a nonzero coupling gives growth, while the indefinite total energy remains conserved. This illustrates the normalization issue; it is not an added interaction field or a derived physical two-particle model. A small pole weight does not make the full response small At zero forcing frequency, B(0)=0, so  oxed{\chi_h(0;s)= rac{A_0}{1-g_0A_0},} 	ag{10} independent of s. At fixed nonzero z=\omega/\ell with hB(z)
e0, the 1/s term instead becomes large. Source feedback then gives  oxed{\chi_h(\ell z;s)\longrightarrow- rac1{g_0}.} 	ag{11} Neither limit is a weak total scalar response. The frequency of an incoming field, its selected spatial pattern, the pole residue and the full output map are separate parts of a coupling calculation, as explained in source frequencies. Verification slow_shape_pole_checks.py compares full four-block field resolvents with (1), locates the slow poles independently, and checks their residues using both source derivatives and the complete canonical eigenvectors. Increasing radial resolution verifies the quoted frequencies and signed residues. Both source components, both angular radial families and both signs of the Dirac spectrum are retained. Direct real-time work verifies the convention in (7), and the complete canonical pair checks (9) and energy conservation during growth. Reports use timestamped filenames and verification remains active under Python optimization. The results establish the stated source spectrum and its limits, without a stable weak-particle identification.

title: Soft polarized scattering
summary: Retaining the photon spatial phase and the target's complete polarization multiplet gives the low-frequency forward spin response in the conditionally gauged scalar Dirac model.
text: Summary: Retaining the photon spatial phase and the target's complete polarization multiplet gives the low-frequency forward spin response in the conditionally gauged scalar Dirac model. Keep the incoming wave's spatial structure Use the normalized full spatial profile and conditional current coupling derived in Soft spatial current response. The particle occupies its stated d ordinary spatial directions in the one nested manifold. Choose propagation along x_3 and transverse polarizations along x_1,x_2. This selects three measurement directions; it does not split the particle's space into different kinds of dimension. The incident photon amplitude is a complex transverse vector \varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2), with \varepsilon^\dagger\varepsilon=1. Its source operator includes \alpha_i e^{ikx_3} =V_i^{(0)}+ikV_i^{(1)} -\frac{k^2}{2}V_i^{(2)}+O(k^3), \qquad V_i^{(n)}=x_3^n\alpha_i,\quad i=1,2. \tag{1} The current readout includes the opposite spatial phase. Thus a uniform electric-field calculation cannot simply be called the real-photon amplitude. Set k=\omega for the conditional case where photon speed equals the underlying Dirac speed, both set to one. The target also retains its complete complex polarization z in \phi_z(x)=W(x)z,\qquad \int W^\dagger W\,dx=I_N,\qquad z^\dagger z=1. \tag{2} These coefficients describe the field's spatial pattern. The complete tensor description explains which relative amplitudes and phases a single circulation tensor can omit. The complete zero-frequency multiplet contributes Let P project on the full resting multiplet (2), and let B_{ij} denote -i\alpha_i\alpha_j restricted to its constant upper polarization frame. Spatial parity and direct radial integration give PV_i^{(0)}P=0,\qquad PV_i^{(1)}P=-F_0B_{i3}. \tag{3} The coefficient F_0=(1-2G/d)/(2M) is the full field's current moment, including its lower radial component. A polarization variation within W orthogonal to the occupied ray changes neither scalar density nor scalar source at first order. These are exact degenerate stationary directions, as in Dirac polarization waves. The ordinary and conjugate zero-frequency resolvents therefore give \begin{aligned} \Pi^{(11)}_{ij}(\omega) &=\frac1\omega z^\dagger[PV_i^{(1)}P,PV_j^{(1)}P]z+O(1)\\ &=\frac{2iF_0^2}{\omega}J_{ij}+O(1). \end{aligned} \tag{4} Here J_{ij}=z^\dagger B_{ij}z. The commutator identity [B_{i3},B_{j3}]=2iB_{ij} gives the second line. Projection only onto the occupied ray would miss this term. The global phase direction cancels between the two signed responses; the full multiplet commutator retains the physical polarization changes. The phase coefficients in the incoming and outgoing vertices make (4) contribute +k^2\Pi^{(11)}. At k=\omega, this is an order-\omega spin response, despite being second order in spatial phase. Include the other spatial-phase terms and shape feedback For Hermitian source labels A,B, use \Pi_{AB}= \langle A\phi,(\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}B\phi\rangle +\langle B\phi,(-\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}A\phi\rangle. \tag{5} Let C contain all scalar first moments and all scalar second moments, including breathing. With their curvature matrix \mathcal K, the complete source response is \chi_{VV} =\Pi_{VV} +\Pi_{VC}\mathcal K (I-\Pi_{CC}\mathcal K)^{-1}\Pi_{CV}. \tag{6} This is the actual scalar source variation, not a fixed-target prescription. The connection is sourced reciprocally by that same current in the conditional action. A physical scattering rate additionally needs its derived radiation operator and incident/outgoing flux normalization. Parity separates V^{(0)},V^{(2)} from V^{(1)}. It removes the single phase cross term even with all shape feedback retained. The V^{(0)}–V^{(2)} response must also be checked: multiplied by k^2, a spurious inverse-frequency pole could contaminate the soft limit. The complete angular calculation below retains that cross response. In the tested radial branches and transverse preparations it remains bounded, so it cannot change the order-\omega term. The only singular even-source contribution needed at that order is (4). Higher phase terms are suppressed by additional powers of k, with odd cross terms removed by parity. This expansion assumes an isolated stationary multiplet and translation sector, with no additional zero-frequency shape instability. The angular construction uses the complete monogenic families of degrees zero, one and two and their opposite radial partners. For example, a harmonic spinor polynomial p_\ell(x)w decomposes as p_\ell(x)w=M_\ell(x)+\alpha(x)N_{\ell-1}(x),\qquad N_{\ell-1}=\frac{\alpha_i\partial_i(p_\ell w)} {d+2\ell-2}. \tag{7} Both M_\ell and N_{\ell-1} are monogenic. Their radial Dirac operators retain the full upper and lower profile functions. Formal radial dimension shifts account for the radial weight; they add no physical spatial directions. The unused cubic angular family is orthogonal to every V^{(0)} and scalar dipole source, so it does not enter the V^{(0)}–V^{(2)} cross term. Combine the two spin contributions The spatially uniform current kernel has the independently derived term \chi^{(00)}_{ij} =\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\mathcal I} +i\omega\left(\frac1{2\mathcal I^2} -\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}\right)J_{ij} +O(\omega^2). \tag{8} Adding (4) on shell gives \boxed{ \chi^{\rm forward}_{ij} =\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\mathcal I} +i\omega\,\frac{(g_{\rm mag}-2)^2}{8\mathcal I^2}J_{ij} +O(\omega^2),\qquad g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0.} \tag{9} The cancellation is \frac1{2\mathcal I^2}-\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}+2F_0^2 =2\left(F_0-\frac1{2\mathcal I}\right)^2. \tag{10} For an outgoing polarization \varepsilon', the coherent response is \varepsilon'^\dagger\chi^{\rm forward}\varepsilon. Both photon phases and both complex polarization components remain present, together with the target's spatial circulation. Compare the form with the low-energy scattering theorem For the conventional normalized electromagnetic radiation equation, a forward amplitude has factor -q^2/(4\pi) times the current kernel used here. Put \kappa_{\rm mag}=(g_{\rm mag}-2)/2. Equations (9)–(10) then give the spin-amplitude coefficient -\frac{q^2\kappa_{\rm mag}^2}{8\pi\mathcal I^2}\,\omega. \tag{11} This is the anomalous-moment-squared structure of the electromagnetic low-energy theorem. Equation (4) of Gorchtein and Zhang states the corresponding forward expansion with their explicit electromagnetic normalization. Here it is a comparison of response formulas; their separate weak-current analysis is not a V2 interaction mechanism. For arbitrary outgoing direction \widehat n', the same leading uniform current would give, with that radiation normalization, \frac{d\sigma_{\varepsilon'\varepsilon}}{d\Omega} =r_q^2|\varepsilon'^\dagger\varepsilon|^2,\qquad r_q=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\mathcal I}, \tag{12} at sufficiently low energy and negligible recoil. Summing the two outgoing transverse polarizations gives r_q^2(1-|\widehat n'\cdot\varepsilon|^2). For a normalized incident polarization the angular integral is 8\pi r_q^2/3. Consequently a chosen polarization can eliminate a particular output channel without making a freely moving charged target transparent to every output. This complements the complete target-transition test. Equations (11)–(12) require a correctly normalized physical photon action. The present calculation derives the target current kernel under the declared coupling hypothesis; it does not derive that radiation action. The six-dimensional scalar profile's magnetic moment also disagrees with the single-electron benchmark, as quantified in the companion note. Matching the structural identity (11) is therefore a useful consistency test, not a completed observational interaction law. The photon speed matters as well. If its speed in the same units is c_\gamma, then k=\omega/c_\gamma and the two terms combine as \frac1{2\mathcal I^2}-\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I} +\frac{2F_0^2}{c_\gamma^2}. \tag{13} The cancellation in (10) requires c_\gamma=1 in the stated model. The depth-two scalar translation wave has c_{\rm tr}=1/2 in these Dirac units. Identifying it as the photon would therefore require a different, fully consistent completion of its propagation and coupling. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py constructs the angular source functions directly on the actual spatial sphere, orthonormalizes their complete monogenic spans, and integrates their radial profiles independently of the soft formula. It retains every scalar first and second moment in (6), both frequency signs, and all three displayed phase vertices. Checks compare the low-frequency coefficients for aligned and arbitrary complex target polarizations and tilted incident planes at depths 3, 5 and 6, with two radial resolutions. Direct full-spatial integrals and separate radial circular-channel resolvents check the ingredients of (8) up to depth 10. The executable reports the conditional electron magnetic-moment discrepancy rather than treating the benchmark as fitted.

title: Soft spatial current response
summary: The full spatial translation and velocity tangents determine the low-frequency electric current, its polarization correction, and the magnetic moment of a conditionally gauged scalar Dirac profile.
text: Summary: The full spatial translation and velocity tangents determine the low-frequency electric current, its polarization correction, and the magnetic moment of a conditionally gauged scalar Dirac profile. Specify the physical current being tested Let a normalized localized field on d ordinary spatial coordinates obey H_b\phi=M\phi,\qquad H_b=\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)+\beta(m+a|x|^2),\qquad \int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx=1. \tag{1} Its quadratic scalar source is varied with its own centered moment functional. The coordinates belong to the one nested macroscopic spatial manifold. The field components describe its spatial polarization. For this calculation, make an explicit additional hypothesis: a retained connection amplitude of the same field enters the equation as H[A,\Phi]=\alpha_i(-i\partial_i-qA_i) +\beta\mathfrak m[\Psi]+q\Phi. \tag{2} The connection, charge generator qI, and its eventual radiation normalization must be derived from the master action to identify this with a physical interaction. Equation (2) is a conditional test of the resulting particle response. It introduces no mediator particle. Varying this same action gives the reciprocal connection source \rho_{\rm em}=q\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\qquad j_{{\rm em},i}=q\Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi. \tag{3} The scalar binding functional is invariant under local common phase changes, so it preserves the corresponding number continuity equation. Keeping the full spatial field also keeps the kinetic normalization required by Dressed source vertices. Keep the field's displacement and velocity Write the normalized radial field as \phi(x)=\frac{f(r)w+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)w} {\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}},\qquad \beta w=w,\quad w^\dagger w=1. \tag{4} The constant vector w may have arbitrary complex polarization in the selected complete spatial multiplet. Define J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w,\qquad G=\int_0^\infty g(r)^2r^{d-1}dr, \qquad F_0=\frac2d\int_0^\infty r^d f(r)g(r)\,dr. \tag{5} The radial Dirac equations imply F_0=\frac{1-2G/d}{2M}. \tag{6} This current-moment identity is derived in Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes. The total spatial angular momentum includes the orbital contribution and satisfies \langle\mathcal L_{ij}\rangle=J_{ij}/2 on (4). The complete translation calculation supplies the two tangent fields \eta_i=-\partial_i\phi,\qquad \zeta_i=iMx_i\phi+\frac12\alpha_i\phi, \qquad \Psi=e^{-iMt}[\phi+X_i\eta_i+v_i\zeta_i+\cdots]. \tag{7} Here X is the scalar center and v its generalized velocity coordinate. The first variation of every scalar binding source under v_i\zeta_i vanishes pointwise. The profile's inertial coefficient is \mathcal I=M+\frac{T}{d},\qquad T=\langle\phi,\alpha_i(-i\partial_i)\phi\rangle. \tag{8} The stationary frequency M and translation inertia \mathcal I must not be interchanged. For the zero-bare-mass quadratic scalar branch, \mathcal I=M(1+2/(3d)). Derive the spatial symplectic coefficients The original field action has kinetic term \tfrac i2\int(\Psi^\dagger\dot\Psi-\dot\Psi^\dagger\Psi)\,dx. Direct spatial integration gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\eta_i,\eta_j\rangle&=0,\\ 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\eta_i,\zeta_j\rangle &=\mathcal I\delta_{ij},\\ 2\operatorname{Im}\langle\zeta_i,\zeta_j\rangle &=-\frac12J_{ij}. \end{aligned}} \tag{9} The first identity follows from commuting translation generators. The second includes the full Dirac velocity partner in (7). For the third, put \chi_i=Mx_i\phi-i\alpha_i\phi/2, so \zeta_i=i\chi_i. Its cross terms give -MF_0J_{ij} to the imaginary overlap, while the Dirac spin term gives \frac14\langle\phi,-i\alpha_i\alpha_j\phi\rangle =\frac14\left(1-\frac{4G}{d}\right)J_{ij}. \tag{10} Equation (6) makes their sum -J_{ij}/4, proving the last line of (9). The orbital and lower radial components are essential to these identities. The number-density centroid differs from the scalar center. Since 2\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger\zeta_j)=\phi^\dagger\alpha_j\phi, \boxed{R_{\rho,i}=X_i+F_0J_{ij}v_j.} \tag{11} Indeed, \int x_i\phi^\dagger\alpha_j\phi\,dx=F_0J_{ij}. Number continuity then identifies the integrated number current with \dot R_\rho. All quantities in (9)–(11) are integrals of fields and derivatives on the actual spatial coordinates. Apply a slowly varying uniform electric field To the required order, use energy \mathcal I|v|^2/2-qE\cdot R_\rho. The symplectic matrix from the stated field-action convention is \begin{pmatrix} 0&-\mathcal I I_d\\ \mathcal I I_d&J/2 \end{pmatrix} \tag{12} in coordinates (X,v). Its equations give \mathcal I\dot v=qE,\qquad \mathcal I\dot X+\frac12J\dot v =\mathcal I v+qF_0JE. \tag{13} Keeping J at its unperturbed value suffices at linear order in this uniform electric perturbation. Therefore \dot R_\rho =v+q\left(\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I} -\frac1{2\mathcal I^2}\right)JE. \tag{14} For time dependence e^{-i\omega t} and E=i\omega A, the induced current is \boxed{ \delta j_{\rm em} =-q^2\left[ \frac1{\mathcal I}I_d +i\omega\left(\frac1{2\mathcal I^2} -\frac{2F_0}{\mathcal I}\right)J +O(\omega^2)\right]A.} \tag{15} The leading coefficient is independent of target polarization. It gives the usual Thomson current structure if \mathcal I is the physical inertial mass and (2) is the physical normalized connection coupling. Those identifications are additional to the derivation. Check against the complete source response There is an independent route which keeps the entire radial spectrum. Let c_i=\beta x_i\phi and u_i=\alpha_i\phi be the scalar-center and current source columns. For any Hermitian source labels A,B, define \Pi_{AB}(\omega)= \langle A\phi,(\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}B\phi\rangle +\langle B\phi,(-\omega-H_b+M)^{-1}A\phi\rangle. \tag{16} Both signed frequency terms are required. The center curvature is \kappa=-2a/Q_\sigma, where Q_\sigma=\int\phi^\dagger\beta\phi\,dx. Its feedback gives \boxed{\chi_{uu}=\Pi_{uu} +\Pi_{uc}\kappa(I-\Pi_{cc}\kappa)^{-1}\Pi_{cu}.} \tag{17} All coordinate indices are retained. Parity separates these odd source columns from the even scalar shape sources at zero spatial wavenumber. The current columns can also be generated without a current ansatz: u_i=i(H_b-M)(x_i\phi). \tag{18} Complete angular radial families in (16)–(18) reproduce every coefficient of (15). The frozen-profile response \Pi_{uu} tends to zero; the moving center supplies the finite leading term. This distinguishes a vanishing frozen overlap from a vanishing physical response. Relate the current moment to a measured particle property The actual antisymmetric magnetic moment tensor from (3) is \mu_{ij}=\frac12\int(x_i j_{{\rm em},j} -x_j j_{{\rm em},i})\,dx=qF_0J_{ij}. \tag{19} Using S_{ij}=J_{ij}/2 and defining the gyromagnetic factor by \mu_{ij}=g_{\rm mag}qS_{ij}/(2\mathcal I) gives \boxed{g_{\rm mag}=4\mathcal I F_0,\qquad \chi_{uu}(\omega,0) =\frac1{\mathcal I}I_d +i\omega\frac{1-g_{\rm mag}}{2\mathcal I^2}J+O(\omega^2).} \tag{20} For a selected three-dimensional observation plane this is the ordinary magnetic-moment convention. Selecting that plane distinguishes a measurement geometry; it introduces no inherent split in an electron's six spatial directions. The zero-bare-mass scalar ground profiles give: bound spatial depth conditional g_{\rm mag} 3 2.14608436 5 2.09132914 6 2.07691916 A single-electron measurement in 2023 found g/2=1.00115965218059(13), hence g=2.00231930436118(26). This is the benchmark reported by Fan, Myers, Sukra and Gabrielse, not an atomic-system calculation. Thus the stated six-dimensional scalar profile, with the current (3), does not reproduce the electron magnetic moment. Changing the common coupling rescales the zero-bare-mass profile and leaves this dimensionless factor unchanged. A different occupied field or a derived modification of the physical current would have to supply its own prediction. The spatially uniform kernel (20) is not yet the on-shell photon amplitude. The photon phase and the complete degenerate target polarizations supply another term, calculated in Soft polarized scattering. Conserved spatial charge gives the full kinetic conditions a proposed geometric charge generator must satisfy. Canonical spatial spin response uses the full moving polarization frame to derive the canonical center and the electric spin-orbit coefficient from this same current moment. Verification soft_photon_response_checks.py checks (9)–(11) by direct radial and angular integration of the full spatial fields, including arbitrary complex polarizations. A separate angular radial resolvent calculation verifies (15) and (20) at depths 3, 5, 6 and 10, with zero and positive bare scalar mass. The companion scattering check retains the photon phase and all scalar shape feedback. Reports have timestamped names and checks remain active under Python optimization. These checks establish the stated conditional mathematics; the connection, charge assignment, stable occupied particles and empirical interaction law remain to be derived.

title: Source frequencies in spatial coupling
summary: The full field source, spatial observables and changing mode patterns carry different temporal frequencies, whose relation to normalized response determines whether a slow bound oscillation weakens coupling.
text: Summary: The full field source, spatial observables and changing mode patterns carry different temporal frequencies, whose relation to normalized response determines whether a slow bound oscillation weakens coupling. Identify the clock carried by the interacting spatial pattern A low bound oscillation frequency can affect coupling only through the source actually sampled by the other object. In particular, the frequency in a spatial susceptibility need not equal the phase frequency of the unperturbed bound field. The distinction can be established directly from the written source, without assigning a weak coefficient to depth five. All fields below live on the one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. Mode indices and amplitude components describe fields over that space. They introduce neither further spatial directions nor interaction particles. A finite expansion illustrates the source algebra; it is an exact solution of the nonlinear field equation only when its profiles and amplitudes also satisfy that equation. Bilinear sources carry transition frequencies For normalized spatial modes, write \Psi(t,x,y)=\sum_j c_j\Phi_j(x) e^{i(k_jy-E_jt)}. \tag{1} The normal coordinate y is an existing containing spatial direction. For any time-independent Hermitian source matrix A(x), \boxed{\rho_A=\Psi^\dagger A\Psi =\sum_{i,j}\bar c_i c_j\Phi_i^\dagger A\Phi_j e^{i[(k_j-k_i)y-(E_j-E_i)t]}.} \tag{2} The transition density includes both spatial polarizations, their relative phase and the overlap required by the adopted nested inclusion. Integrating it against a spatial kernel preserves its temporal frequency. Its contribution can vanish geometrically even when that frequency is allowed. The complete spatial vertex is derived in Transition-density coupling. For a single stationary field e^{-iMt}\phi(x), every such bilinear is stationary. This applies to its scalar density and ordinary Dirac current. For a superposition, off-diagonal terms can describe actual moving spatial patterns. Their frequencies are differences, rather than a common phase. A pure occupied mode can still have nonzero transition matrix elements to other modes. The absence of a pre-existing off-diagonal mean density is not the absence of a response to an applied source. The complete nonlinear field source retains a carrier A bilinear density is only one factor in the scalar Dirac source. For \mathcal N[\Psi]=(K\rho_\beta)\beta\Psi, the complete term has \boxed{\Omega_{i;j\ell}=E_j+E_\ell-E_i, \qquad q_{i;j\ell}=k_j+k_\ell-k_i.} \tag{3} Here K is a time-local spatial kernel; a specified kernel with temporal memory would add its own response. The source coefficient includes the full cubic spatial overlap, as derived in Dirac source linearization. For a single frequency, \mathcal N[e^{-iMt}\phi]=e^{-iMt}\mathcal N[\phi]. \tag{4} Thus cancellation of the phase from \Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi does not make the full nonlinear field source time independent. A linear output-mode projection of \Psi samples (3); a photon realized as a bilinear collective observable samples (2) and its tangent response. The physical output map must decide which construction applies. They cannot be identified solely because each contains a small frequency. The principal clocks can be recorded without conflating them: object being followed temporal frequency stationary field component M bilinear spatial transition E_j-E_i cubic field source E_j+E_\ell-E_i perturbation about e^{-iMt}\phi frequency relative to the background carrier opposite-frequency spatial-current beat 2M in its rest description The last row is an exact nonlinear construction in Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents. It supplies a real spatial clock tied to the bound frequency; its amplitude and coupling still need to be calculated. Slow inter-mode clocks can survive large normal momentum For the normal Dirac branch, let E_i(k)=\sqrt{M_i^2+k^2} in units \hbar=c=1. At the same normal momentum, \boxed{E_j(k)-E_i(k) =\frac{M_j^2-M_i^2}{E_j(k)+E_i(k)}.} \tag{5} It equals M_j-M_i at rest and approaches (M_j^2-M_i^2)/(2|k|) at large |k|. Therefore a hierarchy of small bound frequencies can provide slow transition clocks even for energetic propagation. The frequency relation alone does not supply the required spatial transition matrix element or a physical neutrino assignment. Other transitions have different clocks. Within one branch, E(k+q)-E(k) =\frac{2kq+q^2}{E(k+q)+E(k)}. \tag{6} At fixed nonzero forward momentum transfer, this need not vanish as M tends to zero. The complete interaction must retain such channels when its source permits them. The already derived polarization wave has \omega(k)=\sqrt{M^2+k^2}-M. Consequently \frac{\partial\omega}{\partial M}\bigg|_k =\frac{M}{\sqrt{M^2+k^2}}-1<0\quad(k\ne0). \tag{7} Reducing the bound frequency at fixed normal wavelength increases this particular fluctuation frequency. Scaling the wavelength together with M is a different comparison. The scalar moment source of these orthogonal polarization waves has zero first variation at every depth where the stated construction applies. A source phase \Omega t-qy sampled by a target moving with speed v in that direction has proper-time frequency \gamma_v(\Omega-vq). Both the temporal and spatial phase are needed when comparing clocks in different preparations. Include the response scale and normalization The frequency barriers are expansions about zero forcing frequency with fixed profiles and regular response functions. An amplitude proportional to \omega or \omega^2 is small relative to the corresponding spectral and source scales. Those coefficients can change when the particle's bound scale changes. The zero-bare-mass scalar moment branch gives an exact control. Let D_\lambda\phi(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi(\lambda x). For unit spatial norm, dilating a complete bound solution gives \phi_\lambda=D_\lambda\phi, \quad M_\lambda=\lambda M, \quad a_\lambda=\lambda^3a, \quad g_\lambda=\lambda^5g. \tag{8} The scalar second moment scales as \lambda^{-2}. A quadrupole source column b_A=\beta(x^TAx)\phi therefore scales as \lambda^{-2}D_\lambda b_A, while the full fluctuation operator scales as \lambda D_\lambda L D_\lambda^\dagger. Both ordinary and conjugate resolvents yield \boxed{\chi_\lambda(\omega) =\lambda^{-5}\chi_1(\omega/\lambda), \qquad g_\lambda\chi_\lambda(\lambda z)=g\chi_1(z).} \tag{9} This holds for the complete self-consistent shape response, not just a bare overlap. A common change of bound scale does not suppress this dimensionless response at a fixed frequency ratio. There is a corresponding fixed-g statement for the single-frequency family of proper density s=\lambda^5. Its field has the additional factor \sqrt{s}. Each source column gains \sqrt{s}, cancelling the \lambda^{-5} factor in the susceptibility. At fixed g, \chi_s(\omega)=\chi_1(\omega/\lambda). \tag{10} This is a density-family identity, not permission to vary an isolated particle's norm to fit its mass. A two-frequency background has additional periodic response coefficients and must be treated separately. Different physical particle scales could still provide a small frequency ratio; their selected profiles and normalization must establish it. Conditions for the proposed neutrino mechanism The proposed five-dimensional application requires a selected spatial mode whose actual source has no unsuppressed static contribution, followed by a derived slow source clock in the frame of its interaction partner. The full response must include both polarizations and all accessible ordinary, conjugate and spatial channels. An incoming mode also has to satisfy its own field equation; Incoming spatial shape modes checks that distinction explicitly. A physical photon additionally has a massless propagating branch. Its outgoing Green function can have poles where a regular static susceptibility does not. The low-frequency power of a gapped shape response cannot by itself determine the normalized photon amplitude or its emitted or scattered flux. V2's neutrino spectrum provides proposed mass indices and a conditional scale reconstruction. The projected mass-operator construction still leaves the depth-five normalization to be derived. Neither the frequency rules nor a chosen small normalization complete that task. Verification source_frequency_checks.py compares full complex spatial bilinears and a nonlocal cubic source with independent temporal Fourier transforms. It checks normal transition clocks, observer phases and complete scalar matrix elements. Independent spatial radial solves and both signs of the fluctuation resolvent verify (8)–(10). Reports preserve previous runs with timestamped filenames; all conditions remain active under Python optimization. Related Dirac source linearization — fixes the complete field-source and rotating-background conventions. Transition-density coupling — supplies the two-sided spatial vertices accompanying the clocks. Two-frequency spatial Dirac currents — gives an exact changing current with a bound-frequency clock. Incoming spatial shape modes — distinguishes a free pattern from a forcing coefficient.

title: Time ordering of spatial compatibility
summary: The leading change of the prescribed spatial contact is a Poisson bracket with the second time-ordered source generator, identifying a reciprocal feedback contribution that a single integrated overlap omits.
text:
Summary: The leading change of the prescribed spatial contact is a Poisson bracket with the second time-ordered source generator, identifying a reciprocal feedback contribution that a single integrated overlap omits. Keep the full spatial Hamiltonian at each stage The localized compatibility functional compares the same free encounter for the incoming field and the fully evolved outgoing field after removing known free propagation. Its leading scattering variation preserves that functional. The next term can be derived from the same scalar source without adding an alignment rule. Use the local scalar Dirac equation, i\partial_t\Psi=D\Psi+g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) eta\Psi, \qquad U(t)=e^{-iDt},\qquad \psi_I(t)=U(-t)\Psi(t). 	ag{1} For a canonical field argument \psi, define \chi_t=U(t)\psi,\quad \sigma_t=\chi_t^\dagger eta\chi_t, \qquad h_t[\psi]= rac12\int\sigma_t^2\,d^Dx. 	ag{2} These are full spatial functionals; both complex patterns enter the same local scalar. The interaction-picture equation is Hamiltonian with g h_t. Its explicit time dependence comes from the free spatial operator, even though (1) is autonomous. Use the positive spatial inner product and gradient convention \delta F=2\operatorname{Re}\langle
abla_*F,\delta\psiangle. The canonical Poisson bracket is  oxed{\{F,G\}=2\operatorname{Im} \langle
abla_*F,
abla_*Gangle,\qquad \dot F=\{F,G\}\quad\hbox{when }\dot\psi=-i
abla_*G.} 	ag{3} All formulas below are finite-order, fixed-duration expansions where regular solutions depend smoothly on g. They hold directly in a finite canonical spatial regulator. A continuum use additionally needs sufficient regularity and control of the displayed derivatives and integrals; no convergence of an infinite Magnus series is asserted. The first two source generators Let T>0 be fixed. Define  oxed{ K_1=\int_0^T h_t\,dt= rac12\mathcal C_T, \qquad K_2= rac12\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\,\{h_t,h_s\}. } 	ag{4} For any sufficiently differentiable real functional F, the complete interaction-picture map gives  egin{aligned} F[\psi_I(T)]={}&F[\psi_I(0)]+g\{F,K_1\}\ &+g^2\left(\{F,K_2\} + rac12\{\{F,K_1\},K_1\}ight)+O(g^3), \end{aligned} 	ag{5} with the brackets on the right evaluated at the incoming field. For the sign convention, write L_G F=\{F,G\}. Two stages, h_s first and h_t second, pull back observables in the order e^{gL_{h_s}}e^{gL_{h_t}}. The Jacobi identity gives [L_{h_s},L_{h_t}]=L_{\{h_t,h_s\}}. Expanding that ordered product through second order yields (4)–(5). Integrating over all ordered pairs gives the displayed time triangle. This is the Hamiltonian form of the standard chronological expansion; see Blanes, Casas, Oteo and Ros, section 3.4.1. Taking F=\mathcal C_T=2K_1 eliminates both the first-order term and the repeated first-generator bracket:  oxed{\Delta\mathcal C_T =g^2\{\mathcal C_T,K_2\}[\psi_{m in}]+O(g^3).} 	ag{6} Thus the first contact change is controlled by how the full spatial Hamiltonians at different encounter stages fail to commute. The integral of their separate contact strengths is insufficient to determine it. The sign of (6) is not fixed by the nonnegativity of \mathcal C_T. If \{h_t,h_s\}=0 as functionals for every pair of stages on the relevant domain, then \{\mathcal C_T,h_t\}=0 and the full interaction-picture evolution conserves \mathcal C_T exactly. By contrast, a zero numerical value of K_2 at one incoming field does not ensure a zero gradient or a zero bracket in (6). The coefficient retains both complete complex variations The full source gradient and its real-linear derivative are  egin{aligned} f_t=
abla_*h_t &=U(-t)[\sigma_t eta\chi_t],\ H_t\eta=(\mathrm d f_t)_\psi[\eta] &=U(-t)\left[ 2\operatorname{Re}(\chi_t^\dagger eta U(t)\eta)\, eta\chi_t +\sigma_t eta U(t)\etaight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{7} The inner product inside the real part in (7) is pointwise; the outer source remains a complete spatial field. In a Galerkin implementation, the local product is followed by the same orthogonal spatial projection as the original energy variation. Since H_t is symmetric for the real canonical inner product,  egin{aligned} K_2&=\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\, \operatorname{Im}\langle f_t,f_sangle,\ 
abla_*K_2 &= rac12\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\, \left[H_t(-if_s)+H_s(if_t)ight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} For example, varying the integrand of \{h_t,h_s\} gives 2\operatorname{Im}(\langle H_t\eta,f_sangle+ \langle f_t,H_s\etaangle); moving the two real-symmetric Hessians to the other slot gives (8). With F_1=\int_0^T f_tdt, the coefficient in (6) is  oxed{\{\mathcal C_T,K_2\} =4\operatorname{Im}\langle F_1,
abla_*K_2angle.} 	ag{9} Dropping the conjugate-dependent part of (7), holding one pattern fixed, or replacing its local scalar by an average would change (8)–(9). No independent coefficient has been introduced: g is still the single scalar coefficient of (1). An independent full-field expansion Iterating the interaction-picture differential equation directly gives \psi_I(T)=\psi_{m in}-igF_1+g^2 B_2+O(g^3), \quad B_2=-i\int_0^Tdt\int_0^t ds\,H_t(-if_s). 	ag{10} The generator formula instead gives B_2=-i
abla_*K_2- rac{i}{2} \int_0^T H_t(-iF_1)dt. 	ag{11} Splitting the square time integral in (11) into its two triangles and using (8) reproduces (10). This provides a check on the source ordering and the factors of two, without interpreting the generator as a new physical field. Reversing the prescribed sequence h_t\mapsto h_{T-t} leaves K_1 unchanged and sends K_2\mapsto-K_2. It therefore reverses the coefficient (6). This is a control on a sequence of Hamiltonians, not a claim that freely departing spatial packets reverse themselves or naturally repeat an encounter. Compute the coefficient by direct coupling variations The same coefficient can be calculated without the double time integral. Expand the physical field at fixed preparation as \Psi_g=\chi+g a+g^2 b+O(g^3), with \chi=U(t)\psi_{m in}. Writing N(\chi)=(\chi^\dagger eta\chi) eta\chi, direct variation of the complete spatial equation gives  egin{aligned} i\partial_t a&=Da+N(\chi),&a(0)&=0,\ i\partial_t b&=Db+(\mathrm dN)_\chi[a],&b(0)&=0. \end{aligned} 	ag{12} The source derivative is the full real-linear expression in (7), before conjugation by the free propagators. It includes the response of both spatial patterns. In the interaction picture, a_I(T)=-iF_1 and b_I(T)=B_2. Let \mathcal H_C=2\int_0^T H_tdt be the real Hessian of the prescribed contact. Taylor expansion of that same functional gives  oxed{c_2=2\operatorname{Re}\langle
abla_*\mathcal C_T,b_I(T)angle +\operatorname{Re}\langle a_I(T),\mathcal H_C a_I(T)angle, \qquad \Delta\mathcal C_T=g^2 c_2+O(g^3).} 	ag{13} Equations (6) and (13) give the same coefficient using different calculations. The direct method integrates two inhomogeneous spatial variations and one single time quadrature. It does not fit a coefficient to completed nonlinear collisions. spatial_packet_variations.py implements (12)–(13), with timestamped results and optional variation fields. Its local Hessian differentiates every quadrature component of the original scalar energy. spatial_packet_variation_checks.py runs 28 checks, including independent cubic polarization, scalar energy variation, both norm coefficients, comparison with the ordered generator and full nonlinear evolution. The same checks include positive renormalization of both complete outgoing patterns. Verification and physical scope packet_time_order.py evaluates the two generators and both full-field expressions using the normalized axial spatial equation. For its homogeneous cubic source, the Hessian also has the exact polarization identity H_t\eta= rac{f_t(\psi+\eta)-f_t(\psi-\eta)}2-f_t(\eta). 	ag{14} packet_time_order_checks.py runs 50 checks. It checks (14) by independent directional differentiation, verifies real Hessian symmetry and the scalar variation of K_2, refines the time quadrature and checks source-order reversal. Complete nonlinear spatial evolution at dimensions three and five approaches (10) with cubic field error and approaches the contact coefficient (9) under small-coupling refinement. A frozen-transport control conserves the same contact under its full spatial nonlinear source. The result explains a conditional feedback contribution in the stated comparison protocol. It does not select occupied bound-particle patterns, fix their physical sizes, assign observed interaction channels, or imply a universal tendency toward improved compatibility.

title: Rotation-neutral Dirac fields in physical space
summary: A full radial Dirac field can preserve an exactly neutral total spatial rotation through compensating orbital and spin motion, even though a projector on neutral spin components discards part of the field.
text: Summary: A full radial Dirac field can preserve an exactly neutral total spatial rotation through compensating orbital and spin motion, even though a projector on neutral spin components discards part of the field. Keep the position dependence of the polarization The neutral-doublet calculation shows that projecting the first-order spatial Dirac operator onto neutral spin components removes some momentum responses. Full spatial modes provide a constructive way to retain those components. The conserved rotation acts on position and spin together. Work on a flat d-dimensional spatial model of a sector in the one nested macroscopic manifold. All d directions are ordinary spatial dimensions. The finite spinor components below describe the same field on those coordinates. Choosing rotation planes specifies a probe or a physical preparation; it does not divide a particle's dimensions into different kinds. This note derives neutrality under that specified spatial rotation. Its identification with an electromagnetic interaction remains a separate current calculation. No mediator particle or additional physical dimension is introduced. The full Dirac representation Let Hermitian matrices satisfy \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I, \qquad \{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0, \qquad\beta^2=I. \tag{1} Let V be an isometric basis of the positive rest eigenspace, \beta V=V, V^\dagger V=I. The map \alpha(v)V lies in the opposite \beta eigenspace for every spatial vector v. The two eigenspaces are field components, not parts of physical space. The full central spatial Hamiltonian is H=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta M(r)+V_0(r)I, \qquad r=|x|. \tag{2} Its radial coefficients may be specified backgrounds or come from a self-consistent source. A derivation must say which applies and keep their response when they are dynamical. For z^\dagger z=1, consider the spatial field \boxed{\Psi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Omega_{d-1}}} \left[f(r)Vz+i g(r)\alpha(\widehat x)Vz\right],} \qquad \widehat x=x/r, \tag{3} where \Omega_{d-1} is the area of the unit (d-1)-sphere and f,g are real radial functions. Regularity requires g(r)=O(r) at the origin. The norm and scalar source are \|\Psi\|^2=\int_0^\infty(f^2+g^2)r^{d-1}dr, \qquad \overline\Psi\Psi=\frac{f^2-g^2}{\Omega_{d-1}}. \tag{4} The lower component has a direction-dependent polarization. Removing it would change both the field equation and the scalar source. Substitution into H\Psi=E\Psi gives the full radial equations \boxed{(E-M-V_0)f=g'+\frac{d-1}{r}g, \qquad (E+M-V_0)g=-f'.} \tag{5} They follow from \alpha(\widehat x)^2=I and \alpha_i\partial_i\alpha(\widehat x)=(d-1)I/r. No nonrelativistic approximation has been made. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes solves these radial equations with the potential generated by the existing nonlocal scalar source, and checks its complete radial response. Orbital motion preserves the same total rotation weight Choose m=\lfloor d/2\rfloor ordinary orthogonal rotation planes and set S=-\frac i2\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{2j-1}\alpha_{2j}, \qquad L=-i\sum_{j=1}^{m} \left(x_{2j-1}\partial_{2j}-x_{2j}\partial_{2j-1}\right), \qquad\mathscr Q=L+S. \tag{6} The Dirac matrices rotate with their spatial arguments. Explicitly, [S,\alpha(x)]=-L\alpha(x),\qquad [\mathscr Q,\alpha(\widehat x)]=0. \tag{7} Every radial function is annihilated by L. If the rest polarization has S Vz=qVz, equation (3) therefore obeys \boxed{\mathscr Q\Psi=q\Psi.} \tag{8} This is an operator identity for the entire position-dependent field. For a physical rotation R(\theta) in the chosen planes, its finite version is e^{-i\theta S}\Psi\big(R(\theta)^{-1}x\big) =e^{-iq\theta}\Psi(x). \tag{9} The kinetic operator and both central terms in (2) commute with \mathscr Q. A rotation-equivariant nonlinear scalar source also preserves an initially fixed rotation sector, subject to the adopted domains and uniqueness of evolution. Retaining the lower component is fully consistent with that conservation. The five-dimensional neutral modes remain available The rest weights are the spin lifts of the chosen spatial rotations. At depth five the four-component rest module has weights (-1,0,0,1), so two independent choices in (3) give \mathscr Q\Psi=0. Those fields can have nonzero density throughout all five spatial coordinates. At depth six the rest module is a selected four-component half-spin representation. Three equal rotation planes give half-integer weights with no zero. The five-plane depth-ten construction likewise has no zero weight. With ordinary single-valued spatial wavefunctions, the full 2\pi rotation acts as -I when the number of planes is odd; orbital integer weights cannot turn it into a zero eigenvalue. The rotation-weight note gives the representation assumptions and the other depths, including the even-plane cases which also admit zero weights. The comparison concerns the same type of geometric operation. It is not a proof that this operation is the photon current or that all five-dimensional particles occupy its neutral modes. Neutral and nonneutral radial polarizations in (3) have the same scalar density and radial equations. Their occupation still requires a dynamical explanation. What a spin-only projection would discard Let F=\int f^2r^{d-1}dr,\qquad G=\int g^2r^{d-1}dr, \qquad F+G=1. Spherical averaging and the Clifford identity \sum_i\alpha_iS\alpha_i=(d-4)S give \langle S\rangle=q\left(1-\frac{4G}{d}\right), \qquad \langle L\rangle=\frac{4Gq}{d}, \qquad\langle\mathscr Q\rangle=q. \tag{10} For a five-dimensional zero-weight state, the lower component also obeys \boxed{\langle S^2\rangle=\langle L^2\rangle=\frac45G, \qquad\mathscr Q\Psi=0.} \tag{11} The spin and orbital actions cancel on the full field, although each can have a nonzero norm. One way to obtain (11) is to use S^2=I/2+ a Clifford grade-four term and \sum_i\alpha_iT_4\alpha_i=(d-8)T_4. On a rest state with S^2Vz=0, the lower angular average gives 4/5. A projector onto \ker S alone discards a fraction 4G/5 of the complete field norm: the lower component in four of the five spatial directions has nonzero spin weight, compensated by its orbital dependence. That discarded norm is not a violation of the conserved total neutrality in (8). Equations (7)–(11) specify the distinction exactly. A neutral total rotation does not imply zero local current Define the rest polarization bivector by J_{ij}=z^\dagger V^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)Vz, \quad i<j, \qquad J_{ji}=-J_{ij}. \tag{12} Direct substitution of (3) into the Dirac velocity current yields \boxed{j_i(x)=\Psi^\dagger\alpha_i\Psi =-\frac{2f(r)g(r)}{\Omega_{d-1}}J_{ij}\widehat x_j.} \tag{13} The current is tangent to the radial spheres. Its divergence vanishes: J is skew, x^TJx=0, and \operatorname{tr}J=0. These are literal spatial circulation planes of the field. The unpaired direction of a five-dimensional rotation can be a null direction of its current tensor while remaining a direction in which the field has spatial extent. For a specified charged minimal action, the electric current would include its supplied charge factor. Equation (13) itself is the velocity current; zero weight under \mathscr Q does not make this current vanish. The physical source must be obtained from the same action and the appropriate photon projection. Dressed source vertices shows how to retain the required current if modes are subsequently eliminated. Compatibility with the entire nested geometry The rotation used here can move lower members of a nested chain. Rotations of nested sectors distinguishes preserving each fixed member from transporting the whole chain while preserving its nesting. A physical application must include those embedding motions and both interacting objects' polarizations. Equations (8)–(13) retain full spatial motion but do not select a universal embedding or assign a charge generator to every particle. Normal propagation of spatial Dirac modes retains the containing-space Dirac partner and derives exact free-direction boosts of this full spatial field, including its scalar source and current. Verification spatial_dirac_mode_checks.py builds full Clifford matrices independently at depths three, five, six and ten. It tests finite rotations of position-dependent fields, spatial finite differences of L, the complete current, and positive spherical cubature for the spin variance and discarded fraction. Its independent radial checks also retain both equations in (5). Related Rotation-neutral spatial modes — establishes the equal-plane weights and source-compression conditions. Spatial transport of a neutral doublet — identifies the first-order components whose orbital completion is retained here. Dressed spatial source vertices — carries the complete field response through a subsequent mode reduction.

title: Spatial displacement action
summary: Full spatial deformation gives the exact constant-gradient action and a common leading interaction between two polarized displacement waves, with the complementary field retained explicitly.
text:
Summary: Full spatial deformation gives the exact constant-gradient action and a common leading interaction between two polarized displacement waves, with the complementary field retained explicitly. Retain both incoming spatial polarizations Use the declared unit-vector field action of Null spatial pulses: S= rac Z2\int dt\,dy\,d^2x\, \partial_\mu n\cdot\partial^\mu n,\qquad n^2=1. 	ag{1} Its static profile is n_0(x)= rac{(2\lambda x_1,2\lambda x_2,|x|^2-\lambda^2)} {|x|^2+\lambda^2},\qquad \mathcal T=4\pi Z. 	ag{2} The coordinates are ordinary spatial directions in one containing manifold; n has three constrained field components. Equation (1) remains a conditional component action to be derived from the master field before any physical photon identification. Each one-way pulse n_0(x-X(t\mp y)) solves the complete field equation. To examine an interaction, retain both real vector profiles: X(t,y)=A(t-y)+B(t+y),\qquad a=A'(t-y),\quad b=B'(t+y). 	ag{3} Both a and b have their own two-dimensional spatial polarization. A relative angle is physical data; replacing either vector by its norm before varying the field would discard it. Compute the omitted spatial deformation Let n_i=\partial_i n_0 and define the tangent second derivative \mathcal H_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_jn_0 +(n_i\cdot n_j)n_0. 	ag{4} The static field equation gives \mathcal H_{11}+\mathcal H_{22}=0. Substituting the rigidly shifted profile into the complete field equation leaves \mathcal R= (\dot X_i\dot X_j-X_{y,i}X_{y,j})\mathcal H_{ij} =S_{ij}\mathcal H_{ij}, 	ag{5} because \Box_{t,y}X=0, with  oxed{ S=2\left(ab^T+ba^T-(a\cdot b)I_2ight).} 	ag{6} The trace has dropped out using (4). The residual is tangent to the field-value constraint and represents an actual change of the spatial profile. In two bound directions,  oxed{S^2=4|a|^2|b|^2I_2,\qquad \operatorname{tr}S^2=8|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{7} Thus a nonzero pair of opposite pulses always has a nonzero quadrupole source. Perpendicular polarizations have a\cdot b=0 but still S
e0. For example, a=e_1,b=e_2 gives S=2 egin{pmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{pmatrix}; a=b=e_1 gives S=2\operatorname{diag}(1,-1). The source orientation changes while its norm stays the same. This is a full-field example of the distinction between a vanishing overlap and a vanishing reciprocal response in Bilateral polarization coupling. For (2), direct differentiation sharpens (5): \mathcal R =- rac4{|x|^2+\lambda^2}(Sx)_i n_i, \qquad  oxed{\int|\mathcal R|^2d^2x = rac{128\pi}{3\lambda^2}|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{8} Its projection onto each translation tangent vanishes by spatial parity: \int n_i\cdot\mathcal R\,d^2x=0. A calculation retaining only X would therefore miss this entire complementary source, just as a projected polarization texture can miss its full field residual. Complete a uniformly moving and tilted plane exactly For constant velocity v and slope w, put C=I_2+ww^T-vv^T,\qquad C>0,\qquad L=C^{-1/2}. 	ag{9} The full profile  oxed{n(t,x,y)=n_0\!\left(L(x-vt-wy)ight)} 	ag{10} solves the nonlinear field equation. In fact, LCL^T=I_2, so the derivatives of its two spatial arguments have exactly the static orthonormal contraction. The positive-definiteness condition states that their normal plane is spacelike. This construction includes the required rotation and contraction of the spatial profile. It does not hold that profile rigid while changing its motion. Integrating the original action over the actual x plane gives  oxed{\mathscr L(v,w) =-\mathcal T\sqrt{\det(I_2+ww^T-vv^T)}.} 	ag{11} The factor is the Jacobian 1/\det L. Equivalently, \det C=(1-|v|^2)(1+|w|^2)+(v\cdot w)^2. 	ag{12} Equation (11) is the induced-area action, often called the Nambu–Goto form, here obtained by integrating the explicit full spatial solution. No independent interaction coefficient is assigned to each polarization. Derive the common quartic term in two ways Expanding (11) about a straight resting background gives  egin{aligned} \mathscr L ={}&-\mathcal T+ rac{\mathcal T}{2}(|v|^2-|w|^2)\ &+ rac{\mathcal T}{8}(|v|^2-|w|^2)^2 + rac{\mathcal T}{2} \left[|v|^2|w|^2-(v\cdot w)^2ight] +O((v,w)^6). \end{aligned} 	ag{13} Using v=a+b,w=-a+b, its quartic part is  oxed{\mathscr L_4=2\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2 = rac2{\mathcal T} |\partial_{u_-}\varphi|^2|\partial_{u_+}\varphi|^2,\qquad \varphi=\sqrt{\mathcal T}\,X,} 	ag{14} where u_-=t-y and u_+=t+y. Here \varphi is the canonically normalized displacement field. The same \mathcal T fixes propagation normalization and the interaction coefficient. There is an independent spatial-response derivation of (14). Let \mathcal J be the constrained static energy Hessian divided by Z, on tangents perpendicular to n_0. Its quadratic form is \langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle =\int\left[|
abla\eta|^2-|
abla n_0|^2|\eta|^2ight]d^2x. 	ag{15} The trace-free part of the completed profile's second-order change is \eta= rac12(Sx)_i n_i,\qquad \mathcal J\eta=-\mathcal R. 	ag{16} The trace part is a static size variation and has zero Hessian at this order. Direct integration gives  oxed{ Z\langle\eta,\mathcal Rangle=-4\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2,\qquad Z\langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle=4\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2.} 	ag{17} Substituting this response into -Z\langle\eta,\mathcal Rangle -	frac Z2\langle\eta,\mathcal J\etaangle gives 2\mathcal T|a|^2|b|^2, precisely (14). The complementary spatial field supplies the interaction that the rigid translation projection misses. Domain of the interaction result Equation (11) is exact for constant gradients. Equation (14) is its leading local term with four first derivatives, with its coefficient also fixed by the static response calculation. It is not the complete scattering law of arbitrary finite pulses. The correction (16) has a 1/r tail. Its static quadratic-form energy is finite, but its L^2 norm grows logarithmically with transverse cutoff. The original sigma model also has a gapless transverse continuum. title: Reciprocal evolution within degenerate frequency families
summary: Averaging the same quartic action gives reciprocal evolution within complete degenerate form families, retaining changing spatial compatibility.
text: The complete source calculation identifies resonant forcing of spatial patterns outside the initial two modes. The appropriate leading weak interaction equation therefore retains each entire degenerate family in the stated spatial symmetry class. It follows by averaging the declared quartic action over the relative particle oscillation phase. This is an interaction calculation on overlapping spherical features. The feature, common gap and endpoint interaction are inverse assumptions. It does not describe separated trajectories or derive their sustaining geometry. The endpoint bilinear is also distinct from the kinetic norm flux, as derived in The kinetic current and the chosen endpoint interaction. Average the full action, including both objects' currents Write the field at leading order as \Psi(t,x)=e^{-i\omega_a t}A(s,x)+e^{-i\omega_b t}B(s,x), \qquad s=g t. \tag{1} Here A and B are arbitrary complex vectors in their respective positive parent-frequency eigenspaces. The unit-radius notation absorbs the spatial units of g. Each eigenspace includes both signed B polarizations; neither is a particle-antiparticle assignment. The amplitudes describe the evolving spatial pattern and canonical norm. Mass is still the selected particle frequency, not any one of these amplitudes. Using the equal-endpoint bilinear, define j_A=\sum_eA_e^\dagger\gamma A_e,\quad j_B=\sum_eB_e^\dagger\gamma B_e,\quad z=\sum_eA_e^\dagger\gamma B_e. \tag{2} The full current is j_A+j_B+exp[-i(omega_b-omega_a)t]z plus its complex conjugate interference term. Integrating its square over one relative phase gives the exact averaged energy \boxed{\mathcal U_{\rm av} =\frac12\int|j_A+j_B|^2dA+\int|z|^2dA.} \tag{3} The currents of A and B need not vanish during the evolution. Let P_a and P_b be the full orthogonal spectral projections onto the retained frequency families. Varying (3) gives both equations: \begin{aligned} i\partial_s A&=P_a\big[(j_A+j_B)\cdot\gamma A +z^*\cdot\gamma B\big],\\ i\partial_s B&=P_b\big[(j_A+j_B)\cdot\gamma B +z\cdot\gamma A\big]. \end{aligned} \tag{4} This is a Hamiltonian evolution. Independent phase symmetry in each family conserves Q_A and Q_B separately, while (3) and the common rotation momentum are conserved. It need not decrease an overlap monotonically. Energy can move between the individual currents and their mutual interference, so coupling can weaken and subsequently strengthen without an imposed alignment rule. For the O(m-1)-invariant basic spatial class, a degree L family contains q=-L,-L+2,...,L and both Hodge signs. This gives 2(L+1) complex canonical coefficients. The depth-six degree-14/36 pair therefore has 104 coefficients, with every allowed relative phase and both signed form polarizations. They are evaluated as actual spatial forms using the normalized Jacobi basis, not as an isotropic density trace. What makes this an approximation Equation (3) is an exact phase average of the declared interaction. Using (4) as dynamics is a weak-interaction reduction. Off-resonant frequencies remain in the complete parent and have the explicit first response in Complete form response to the current interaction. Their forcing divided by their detuning must be small for the average to be adequate. A large intermediate gap alone is insufficient, because additional low form families exist. No nonzero cross-frequency resonance was found in the initial cubic source at the assigned controls, beyond the two complete original frequency families. title: Complete form response to the current interaction
summary: The full spatial form source predominantly forces low branches and resonant patterns, so a large intermediate gap cannot justify a two-mode closure.
text: The local source in Spatial currents and orientation-dependent coupling drives modes outside the two initially occupied patterns. Resolving its full spatial form content shows that almost all of this forcing lies on low branches of the parent. The large intermediate gap therefore does not justify discarding it. Some of the additional patterns are exactly degenerate with the original frequency and require resonant evolution within the full mode family. This calculation uses coincident spherical field features and a declared quartic interaction. It does not yet describe separated particle motion, derive the sustaining geometry, or identify observed interaction channels. Mass remains the selected particle frequency in equivalent units. An invariant spatial class with all generated form components On the unit S^m write ds^2=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2+ \cos^2\theta\,ds_{S^{m-2}}^2,\quad 0\le\theta\le\pi/2,\quad t=\sin^2\theta. \tag{1} The two-plane patterns are invariant under O(m-1) acting on the remaining ambient directions. The corresponding basic forms have four components: scalar, one-form along theta, one-form along phi, and their exterior two-form. The Hodge operator and the specified local current source preserve this class. The pointwise source was also checked against every exterior component outside it. This is not a claim of stability against all nonsymmetric spatial perturbations. Use the orthonormal components (f,a,b,c) multiplying (1,dtheta,sin(theta)dphi,dtheta wedge sin(theta)dphi), with azimuthal dependence exp(iq phi). Direct exterior differentiation and its weighted adjoint give (d_S+\delta_S) \begin{pmatrix}f\\a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} -a'+[-\cot\theta+(m-2)\tan\theta]a-iq b/\sin\theta\\ f'+iq c/\sin\theta\\ iq f/\sin\theta-c'+(m-2)\tan\theta\,c\\ -iq a/\sin\theta+b'+\cot\theta\,b \end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} Primes denote theta derivatives. The weight is sin(theta) cos(theta)^(m-2). In t, normalized angular integration uses k(1-t)^(k-1)dt with k=(m-1)/2. Both complete harmonic families Let q be any integer and j a nonnegative integer. A scalar seed is f_{qj}=C_{qj}t^{|q|/2} P_j^{(k-1,|q|)}(2t-1)e^{iq\phi},\qquad L=|q|+2j,\quad \lambda_0=L(L+m-1). \tag{3} The constant C normalizes its actual surface L2 norm. Together with d_S f/sqrt(lambda_0), it gives the scalar/exact-one-form pair. The constant scalar has no exact-one-form partner. The second seed is a two-form with coefficient c_{qj}=\widetilde C_{qj}t^{|q|/2}(1-t)^{1/2} P_j^{(k,|q|)}(2t-1)e^{iq\phi},\qquad L=|q|+1+2j,\quad \lambda_1=(L+1)(L+m-2). \tag{4} Its partner is delta_S c/sqrt(lambda_1), a coexact one-form. The identities obtained by substituting the Jacobi differential equation in (2) establish both eigenvalue formulas. Jacobi orthogonality, and orthogonality of exact and coexact forms, give a complete orthonormal resolution in this basic spatial class. These formulas agree with the spherical form spectra of Ikeda and Taniguchi. For B=d_S+delta_S+k Gamma, the two respective signed eigenvalues are \beta_0=\pm(L+k),\qquad \beta_1=\pm\sqrt{(L+k)^2+m-2}. \tag{5} The second family has a different sequence. Insert every signed beta into the same full first-order chain with links beta+j-(d-1)/2, j=0,...,d-1. Both low signs and all high chain modes remain present. The low eigenvalues are calculated with the stable scaled inverse; large eigenvalues use the ordinary Hermitian decomposition. Exact signed reversal is retained when evaluating degenerate frequencies. Resolve the actual time-dependent source At zeroth order take real spatial patterns A and B at their two positive parent frequencies, with coefficients sqrt(0.6) and sqrt(0.4). Factoring out exp(-i omega_a t), their relative phase advances at -(omega_b-omega_a)t. The complete cubic source has four Fourier orders r=-1,0,1,2,\qquad \Omega_r=\omega_a+r(\omega_b-\omega_a). \tag{6} With kappa from the preceding current note and real initial coefficients a,b, its spatial coefficients are F_{-1}=-ig a^2b\,\kappa\cdot\gamma A,\quad F_1=ig a^2b\,\kappa\cdot\gamma A,\quad F_0=-ig ab^2\,\kappa\cdot\gamma B,\quad F_2=ig ab^2\,\kappa\cdot\gamma B. \tag{7} The direct nonlinear source agrees with their sum at arbitrary relative phase. Each F is then projected onto (3)-(5) and every canonical chain eigenvector. Reconstruction in physical space and the complete 4-by-4 source Gram matrix check that this resolution has retained the forcing. The cubic source has finite angular degree; additional degrees and independent quadrature refinement verify the cutoff. If f_mu,r is one of these coefficients, the first response in an empty mode with frequency nu_mu is exactly \delta c_\mu(t)=\sum_r f_{\mu,r} \frac{e^{-i\Omega_rt}-e^{-i\nu_\mu t}}{\Omega_r-\nu_\mu}. \tag{8} At equality of the frequencies the quotient is -it exp(-i nu_mu t). The implementation uses a sinc expression for that limit. Independent matrix-exponential evolution of the driven full chain verifies (8), including resonance. This is first order in g, with its usual limitation that the perturbation must remain small. Low response and exact degeneracy At eta=10,000, the fraction of summed source-channel norm carried by low chain modes is 0.9999974073 for depth-five degrees 11/16 and 0.9999846774 for depth-six degrees 14/36. The remainder is retained and its high-frequency response is bounded using its actual denominators. The small high response cannot account for the substantial low forcing outside the original pair. For a reproducible weak-coupling comparison set g=epsilon omega_a and tau=omega_a t. The following are response norm squares divided by epsilon squared at tau=1. They include all low frequencies and both signed form polarizations. The degree-two rows are mathematical controls, not a photon assignment. The r=0 and r=1 channels contain exact resonances in the original frequency families. For example, the degree-36 family also receives q=+8 and q=-8, j=14 patterns when it interacts with the degree-14 pattern. They have the same scalar degree and parent frequency, but a different spatial distribution. The opposite signed B polarization must also be kept. Such a response changes a spatial pattern without requiring a change of its leading particle frequency. It motivates the complete resonant-family calculation rather than a closed two-mode ansatz. Exact scalar beta values and signed reversal also prevent floating-point splitting of a known degeneracy. The original reports and source versions are retained. The calculation does not establish nonlinear stability, an encounter cross section, ordinary electric neutrality, or a complete particle mass operator. It supplies the missing full spatial source and its first reciprocal response for the stated inverse action.
