title: Spatial polarization textures
summary: Allowing polarization to vary across a bound particle can preserve its scalar density while creating a full spatial kinetic residual, whose omitted components must be solved before the texture is a physical mode.
text: Summary: Allowing polarization to vary across a bound particle can preserve its scalar density while creating a full spatial kinetic residual, whose omitted components must be solved before the texture is a physical mode. Allow the polarization to vary over the actual bound coordinates A constant vector of complex amplitudes describes one part of a particle's polarization; Complete spatial polarization data identifies its full tensor description. Its phase and orientation can also vary across its spatial profile. That possibility must be tested in the field equation rather than accepted because it preserves a selected density. Use the complete stationary radial frame of Equal-current spatial polarizations: H_bW=MW,\qquad W^\dagger W=\rho(x)I,\qquad W^\dagger\beta W=\sigma(x)I. \tag{1} The bound coordinates x are ordinary macroscopic directions in the particle's submanifold. There is only the one infinite nested physical manifold. The frame's column labels describe field components over it. Consider \boxed{\Psi(x,t)=e^{-iMt}W(x)z(x,t),\qquad z^\dagger z=1.} \tag{2} At every point, the number and scalar densities remain \rho and \sigma. For a scalar self-binding source depending only on the latter density's centered moments, its coefficient is unchanged. This statement holds regardless of how rapidly z varies. It establishes the source value, not the full spatial equation. The spatial derivative supplies an additional response With H_b=-i\alpha_i\partial_i+\beta m_{\rm eff}(x), direct application of the product rule gives \boxed{ H_b(Wz)=MWz-i\sum_i\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{3} Consequently the remaining field equation after removing the carrier is \boxed{iW\partial_tz=-i\sum_i\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{4} The right side need not lie in the image of W(x). Where \rho(x)>0, define the actual local projector and compressed current matrices \boxed{ P_W=\frac{WW^\dagger}{\rho},\qquad A_i=\frac{W^\dagger\alpha_iW}{\rho}.} \tag{5} Equation (4) is equivalent to the projected equation together with its complementary condition: \boxed{ i\partial_tz=-i\sum_i A_i\partial_i z,\qquad 0=-i\sum_i(I-P_W)\alpha_iW\,\partial_i z.} \tag{6} The second equality is essential. Solving only the first can manufacture an apparent polarization mode while omitting a nonzero spatial response. For a real evolving field, additional profile components can be excited, and its source must then be recomputed. The radial frame gives the full matrix identity \boxed{W^\dagger\alpha_iW =-\frac{2FG}{\Omega_{d-1}} \sum_j B_{ij}\widehat x_j,} \tag{7} where B_{ji}=-B_{ij} and B_{ii}=0. The diagonal bilinear of (7) recovers the ordinary Dirac current. Its entire matrix is needed for the varying amplitudes in (6). The first equation also carries the number continuity condition. Because \partial_i(\rho A_i)=0 for this fixed radial frame, \partial_t(\rho\,z^\dagger z) +\partial_i(\rho\,z^\dagger A_i z)=0 \tag{8} follows from it. Maintaining the pointwise constraint z^\dagger z=1 requires the resulting current to have zero divergence. An arbitrary initial texture need not preserve that constraint under its dynamics. A concrete texture lies outside the retained equation Take a normalized constant z_0 and a Hermitian spatial rotation matrix B with B^2=I, and set z(x)=e^{ikx_1B}z_0. \tag{9} Only \partial_1z=ikBz is nonzero, so its stationary kinetic remainder is \boxed{\mathcal R=k\alpha_1WBz,\qquad \|\mathcal R(x)\|^2=k^2\rho(x).} \tag{10} On the physical axis x=r e_1, equation (7) gives A_1=0. Thus \boxed{P_W\mathcal R=0,\qquad \|(I-P_W)\mathcal R\|^2=k^2\rho.} \tag{11} At that point the entire nonzero response is missed by the projected polarization equation. The example identifies precisely which part of the full spatial equation must be retained; it does not claim that the imposed texture is a stationary particle. Even a common spatial phase can conceal the missing motion Let \Phi be a unit-normalized stationary field of the same model. For a smooth real function \theta(x), put \widetilde\Phi(x)=e^{i\theta(x)}\Phi(x). \tag{12} Every local nondifferential bilinear is unchanged: \widetilde\Phi^\dagger O\widetilde\Phi=\Phi^\dagger O\Phi \tag{13} for a local component operator O. This includes the number density, the scalar source and every local Dirac current component. The spatial equation nevertheless gives \boxed{ (H_b-M)\widetilde\Phi =e^{i\theta}\alpha(\nabla\theta)\Phi,\qquad \|(H_b-M)\widetilde\Phi\|_{L^2}^2 =\int\rho\,|\nabla\theta|^2\,dx.} \tag{14} The last equality uses the full Clifford identity \alpha(v)^\dagger\alpha(v)=|v|^2I for real v. For \theta=kx_1, the residual norm is exactly |k| for a normalized field. This is a physical spatial phase gradient, despite all the unchanged bilinears in (13). The original scalar Dirac equation has a global phase symmetry. A local phase with its connection held fixed changes the field dynamics. If a gauge connection is part of a different specified action, transform that connection too before declaring two configurations gauge-equivalent. What a complete polarization calculation must add The constant polarization waves supply exact solutions with their own normal partner and unchanged scalar source. The scalar envelope derives a separate remainder when the bound profile changes with its amplitude. Equations (3)–(14) add the bound-coordinate texture response. A proposed richer particle pattern must therefore supply its spatial amplitudes and phases, satisfy the complete kinetic equation, and retain the profile components and source changes generated by that equation. The neutral-doublet transport provides another example where a projected derivative omits a necessary Dirac complement. Neither a density plot nor the number of polarization parameters is sufficient to establish a physical mode. Verification spatial_polarization_structure_checks.py uses complete self-consistent spatial fields at depths three, five, six and ten. It tests their local metrics and projectors, then differentiates the textured fields in every actual bound coordinate. Independent full Dirac evaluations verify (3), the projected and complementary terms in (6), the wholly omitted response in (11), and the spatial-phase norm in (14). The scalar source and every Dirac current are recomputed rather than inferred from a plotted profile. Reports are timestamped and all checks remain active under Python optimization.

title: Spatial source complementarity
summary: Projecting a normalized odd-dimensional rotation tensor and its null-axis vector onto a lower spatial subspace gives an exact complementarity identity and conditional source-strength bound.
text: Summary: Projecting a normalized odd-dimensional rotation tensor and its null-axis vector onto a lower spatial subspace gives an exact complementarity identity and conditional source-strength bound. A source determined by the higher geometry This calculation starts with a higher-dimensional spatial source and asks which of its components survive on a chosen lower subspace. All spaces are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in one nested manifold. The split is relative to that lower subspace; it is not an inherent division of the higher particle. Use the normalized skew tensor and unit null vector from the dimensional magnetic kernel: J^T=-J,\qquad J^2=-I+nn^T,\qquad |n|=1 \tag{1} in dimension d=2m+1. These imply Jn=0 and unit rotational singular values on n^\perp. At depth five, the specified pure spatial spinor model supplies both J and n. For other odd dimensions, (1) defines a conditional tensor family rather than a claim about all spinors or physical particles. Let W be an r-dimensional lower spatial subspace and let Z=W^\perp, of dimension s=d-r. In adapted orthonormal frames, J=\begin{pmatrix}A&Q\\-Q^T&C\end{pmatrix}, \qquad n=\begin{pmatrix}n_W\\n_Z\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} A is the restriction of the rotational two-form to W, while n_W is the projected vector. Use \|A\|^2=-\operatorname{tr}(A^2)/2 for skew matrices and the ordinary Euclidean norm for vectors. Exact projection identity The diagonal blocks of (1) are A^2-QQ^T=-I_r+n_Wn_W^T, \qquad C^2-Q^TQ=-I_s+n_Zn_Z^T. Writing t=|n_W|^2 and using |n_Z|^2=1-t, their traces give 2\|A\|^2+\|Q\|_F^2=r-t, \qquad 2\|C\|^2+\|Q\|_F^2=s-1+t. Subtracting eliminates every mixed component and yields \boxed{\|A\|^2+|n_W|^2-\|C\|^2=r-m.} \tag{3} Consequently \|A\|^2+|n_W|^2\geq r-m. \tag{4} The lower bound is useful when r>m. It is a statement about projected source descriptors, before identifying an interaction channel or rate. Five-dimensional source viewed in three dimensions For d=5 and r=3, equation (3) reads \boxed{\|A\|^2+|n_W|^2=1+\|C\|^2\geq1.} \tag{5} Every real three-dimensional skew matrix has one rotational singular value a\geq0, with \|A\|^2=a^2. Since A is a compression of a norm-one operator, a\leq1. These bounds sharpen two endpoint cases: If n_W=0, then \|A\|^2=1 and C=0. If A=0, then |n_W|=1 and C=0. Both cases are attainable. In an orthonormal basis of \mathbb R^5, take J=e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4 and n=e_5. The first case is W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3); the second is W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_3,e_5). Thus orientation alone cannot make both projected descriptors small in this normalized family. If a response reads these as orthogonal, distinguishable channels with positive weights g_B,g_V, then g_B\|A\|^2+g_V|n_W|^2\geq\min(g_B,g_V). \tag{6} This bound requires both channels to be present with the stated positive metric. A physical map might omit one channel, assign different derived normalizations, or coherently combine contributions. In those cases the actual map must be evaluated; (6) does not replace it. In particular, the five-dimensional vector supplied by the scalar-exchange benchmark has not been identified as an electromagnetic source by this identity. Relation to photon observations in a shared three-plane Let k\in W be a unit propagation direction and take the observer's photon plane E=W\cap k^\perp. Because k^TJk=0, P_EJk=Ak. \tag{7} Write Av=b\times v in an oriented frame on W; this three-dimensional axial-vector notation is only a way of describing the restricted two-form. Then |b|^2=\|A\|^2 and C(E,k;J)=|b|^2-(b\cdot k)^2. \tag{8} For a uniform propagation direction within this fixed W, \mathbb E_{k\in S(W)}C=\frac23\|A\|^2. \tag{9} This is the sum over two photon polarizations. An unpolarized average has the additional factor 1/2. If A=0, every such photon direction has zero magnetic overlap, even though the higher tensor J is nonzero. For the five-dimensional model, (5) then requires a fully projected vector n_W. Its physical coupling must be evaluated separately. The preparation in (9) fixes the observer subspace and target tensor. It differs from the full isotropic relative-preparation ensemble in isotropic polarization comparison. Even-dimensional comparison For a normalized even-dimensional tensor J^2=-I in d=2m, the same trace calculation gives \boxed{\|A\|^2-\|C\|^2=r-m.} \tag{10} At d=6,r=3, the two restricted norms are equal and both may vanish. For example J=e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4+e_5\wedge e_6 and W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_3,e_5) give A=C=0, while the mixed block carries the complete rotation. This is a relation to a chosen observer three-plane; the electron's six spatial dimensions remain equivalent and have no inherent split. The odd/even identities provide exact tests of a proposed descending source map. They do not determine a particle's global spatial topology, prepare the required orientations, or assign empirical coupling strengths. Verification polarization_coupling_checks.py checks the displayed identities with independent spatial quadrature, energy variations, or full finite-system evolution as appropriate. These checks verify the declared mathematics and benchmarks, not empirical couplings. Related Dimensional magnetic kernel — derives the particular five-dimensional vector and rotational tensor and distinguishes candidate interaction terms. Descending photon source — derives the higher-field source before selecting its lower response. Photon plane coupling — supplies the overlap used in (7)–(9). Isotropic polarization comparison — evaluates a different, explicitly averaged ensemble.

title: A binomial compatibility law for actual spatial spinors
summary: Integrating actual polarized surface spinors gives an exact binomial compatibility factor and a reciprocal orientation response within the declared interaction.
text: A family of circulating spinor patterns gives an exact orientation dependence for the declared local current interaction. The individual linear frequencies stay fixed under spatial rotation, while the interaction integral can become very small. Its binomial factor comes from integrating the actual spatial modes, rather than assigning a small coefficient to a particle sector. The construction uses the conditional round four-sphere feature in ordinary six-dimensional space and the spinor parent already defined in A spatial spinor parent for the curvature frequency. It is one spatial family at depth six. It is not a photon model, a depth-five neutrality mechanism or a calculation of interaction rates in matter. The common surface, normal carrier and endpoint-current action remain assumptions. Complete local spinor identity In the Killing frame use five Hermitian ambient Clifford matrices Gamma_A on C^4. At a unit surface point x, the tangent matrices are gamma_a=-i Gamma_x Gamma_(P_x e_a), and C=Gamma_x is surface chirality. For every full complex spinor psi, direct Clifford algebra gives \sum_{A=1}^5(\psi^\dagger\Gamma_A\psi)^2 =(\psi^\dagger\psi)^2. \tag{1} The analogous local set of four tangent matrices and C also satisfies (1). Thus rho=psi^dagger psi, sigma=psi^dagger C psi and the actual tangent current obey |j|^2=rho^2-sigma^2. No spinor component or complex phase has been discarded in this identity. Polarize (1) with two arbitrary complex spinors A and B, average their relative phase, and remove their separate self terms. The complete unit-endpoint mixed current factor becomes \boxed{ j_A\cdot j_B+\sum_a|A^\dagger\gamma_aB|^2 =\rho_A\rho_B+|A^\dagger B|^2 -\sigma_A\sigma_B-|A^\dagger C B|^2.} \tag{2} The chirality terms are physical polarization bilinears of this specified surface spinor. They are not electric charges or assigned neutral projectors. Equation (2) concerns rank-four surface spinors; its unrestricted extension to other spinor ranks has not been assumed. An actual rotating spatial family Write z_1=x_1+i x_2 and z_2=x_3+i x_4 on the unit four-sphere, and choose the unit spinor z_0=(1,0,0,0). It is annihilated by both Gamma_1+i Gamma_2 and Gamma_3+i Gamma_4. Every normalized field \chi_{L,u}(x)=\frac{(u_1z_1+u_2z_2)^L}{\sqrt{V B(L)}}z_0, \quad |u_1|^2+|u_2|^2=1, \quad V=\frac{8\pi^2}{3}, \tag{3} with B(L)=Gamma(L+1)Gamma(5/2)/Gamma(L+5/2), is a monogenic positive B_K eigenfield with eigenvalue L+3/2. Therefore its chain frequency depends on L and the common radius and gap, and does not depend on u. The parameter u labels a complex line in the actual four ambient coordinates. These lines are a restricted family of oriented real planes; they do not exhaust all relative planes or polarizations in the full spinor multiplet. Parameter spaces and spinor components add no physical dimensions. The full tangent current of z_0 is explicitly j_0(x)=(-x_2,x_1,-x_4,x_3,0),\qquad |j_0|^2=1-x_5^2. \tag{4} For (3), multiply (4) by the scalar density. Cross bilinears between two such spinors contain the same vector with the complete complex scalar product. Thus every tangent component of the interaction is retained, including its interference term. Let e_L be the two real endpoint coefficients of the complete normalized positive chain state. Define k_L=e_L^Te_L,\qquad k_{ab}=e_a^Te_b,\qquad A_{ab}=k_a k_b+k_{ab}^2. \tag{5} The phase-averaged cross term from the same action is g times \mathcal C_{ab}(u,v) =A_{ab}\int |Y_{a,u}|^2|Y_{b,v}|^2(1-x_5^2)\,dA. \tag{6} The phase average applies to the two distinct rapid carrier frequencies. It does not assert that arbitrary coherent phases are irrelevant to the unaveraged field equation. Derive the binomial factor Common spatial SU(2) rotations allow u=(1,0) and v=(cos(theta),sin(theta)). Put x=|u^dagger v|^2=cos^2(theta). The squared radii (|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2,x_5^2) have surface integration weights corresponding to parameters (1,1,1/2). Expanding the two ordinary azimuths therefore gives, exactly, \boxed{ \frac{\mathcal C_{ab}(u,v)}{\mathcal C_{ab}(u,u)} =F_{ab}(x)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\min(a,b)} \binom aj\binom bj x^j}{\binom{a+b}{a}}.} \tag{7} One explicit derivation first expands the degree-b field, producing sum_k binom(b,k) binom(a+k,k) x^k(1-x)^(b-k), divided by binom(a+b,a). Use binom(a+k,k)=sum_j binom(a,j)binom(k,j). The binomial average of binom(k,j) is binom(b,j)x^j, giving (7). Vandermonde's identity then supplies F_{ab}(1)=1,\quad F_{ab}(0)=\binom{a+b}{a}^{-1},\quad F'_{ab}(1)=\frac{ab}{a+b}. \tag{8} The complete aligned integral, including the spatial current and canonical endpoint weights, is \boxed{\mathcal C_{ab}(u,u) =A_{ab}\frac{B(a+b)}{V B(a)B(b)} \left(1-\frac1{2(a+b)+5}\right).} \tag{9} At radius R the integral gains the common factor R^(-4). It has not been divided by either particle's frequency to make responses appear similar. For the assigned degree-14/36 patterns at R=1 and gap G=10000, the aligned integral is approximately 2.088613623. At theta=0.7 radians it is 0.012767877. For perpendicular planes it is 2.227033423e-12, with the exact relative factor 1/binom(50,14)=1.066273532e-12. This suppression is conditional on that spatial preparation; it is not a depth-five prediction. A low-degree mathematical probe also provides a useful comparison. The aligned degree-2/14 and degree-2/36 integrals are 0.268861396 and 0.303574875 under the same normalization. Their difference is modest compared with the electron-to-muon frequency ratio. These degree-two fields belong to this depth-six surface family and must not be identified with photons. Both rigid orientations follow the canonical kinetic term Pull the complete normalized field kinetic term back to (3). The spinor z_0 is invariant under the spatial SU(2) subgroup in question, so the orbital Berry curvature is that of spin L/2. Direct surface integration gives -L sin(vartheta)/2 in polar-angle coordinates, with the sign fixed by the canonical time convention. For unit Bloch vectors n_a,n_b representing the two complex lines, x=(1+n_a dot n_b)/2. Hamiltonian H=g C_ab(1) F_ab(x) gives \dot n_a=\frac{H'(x)}a(n_b\times n_a),\qquad \dot n_b=-\frac{H'(x)}b(n_b\times n_a). \tag{10} Both responses come from the same action. Their total angular momentum a n_a/2+b n_b/2 and their relative x are conserved. They precess around that constant total vector. A potential gradient alone therefore does not justify imposing an alignment rule on the rigid family. Changing compatibility requires a spatial deformation, another retained mode or a separately derived physical process. spinor-geometric-overlap-20260914T021339_299491Z.json passes 88 checks: the exact full-complex quartic identity, phase averaging, actual spatial integration at two resolutions, all binomial factors, the canonical field curvature and both reciprocal orientations. An independent exact precession verifies the latter. Its earlier 021023_940799 report is preserved; its looser trajectory tolerance failed three small conservation checks. The current run tightens that tolerance and adds the exact trajectory comparison. The complete compatible polynomial shape space, used to go beyond these rigid orientations, is developed in the companion resonant spinor calculation. The physical carrier and full self-supported particle construction remain open. title: Reciprocal shape response in the spinor family
summary: Both complex spinor patterns evolve under one resonant action and can strengthen or weaken their subsequent spatial overlap.
text: The same endpoint-current action has a complete resonant evolution within a specified polynomial spinor family. Both shapes change, and their interaction integral can change even though rigid canonical rotation would preserve its orientation overlap. The exchange is fixed by the same self-interaction and cross-interaction energy. This is a weak-interaction average on an overlapping round field feature. It is not a separated-particle encounter, a solution for the normal carrier or the complete spatial field equation at arbitrary coupling. All complex coefficients in the stated resonant family are retained; its symmetry and spectral restriction are described below. The complete compatible resonant space Use the actual depth-six surface spinors in A binomial compatibility law for actual spatial spinors. Replace the single coherent polynomial (u_1 z_1+u_2 z_2)^L by every homogeneous holomorphic polynomial of degree L, multiplying the same vacuum spinor z_0. The full normalized basis is \Phi_{L,k}(x)= \sqrt{\frac{\Gamma(L+5/2)}{V\Gamma(5/2)(L-k)!k!}} \,z_1^{L-k}z_2^k z_0,\qquad k=0,\ldots,L. \tag{1} Its coefficient vector has L+1 arbitrary complex entries. Both the canonical norm and all three spatial SU(2) angular generators are retained. The spinor and orbital basis labels add no spatial dimensions. This family is complete within its stated resonant symmetry class. Under the common rotation of the two complex planes, the base vacuum spinor's character fixes the other spinor components' required orbital charges to L+1, L+1 and L+2. At scalar degree L these are impossible: an orbital charge cannot exceed its harmonic degree. The surviving component has charge L and is precisely a holomorphic degree-L polynomial. Every such polynomial is monogenic and has B_K eigenvalue L+3/2. Thus no other spinor or signed-B component at the same degree has been arbitrarily removed from this rotation class. The opposite parent frequency and higher scalar degrees are not resonant at the original positive frequency. They do receive forcing in the full equation. Their response must be controlled before using the average at a finite physical coupling. The nonlinear fixed-point calculation already demonstrates this complementary forcing for the single circulating branches. Multiply the actual spatial polynomials For coefficient vectors A in degree a and B in degree b, define [M_{ab}(A,B)]_s =\sum_{i+j=s} \sqrt{\frac{\binom ai\binom bj}{\binom{a+b}s}}\,A_iB_j. \tag{2} This is the maximal total angular-momentum projection. Vandermonde's identity gives unit norm to each row of its matrix. Therefore the linear map on the product space is a coisometry and \|M_{ab}(A,B)\|^2\le\|A\|^2\|B\|^2. \tag{3} It has rank a+b+1 on a product space of dimension (a+1)(b+1). It is not a globally rank-one interaction operator. Its rank-one blocks at fixed total angular weight follow from the actual spatial integral, rather than from an assumed sector coupling matrix. Let I_{ab}=\frac{B(a+b)}{V B(a)B(b)} \left(1-\frac1{2(a+b)+5}\right), \tag{4} with the moment B(q) defined in the geometric coupling note. The full ordinary spatial integral is exactly integral |Phi_A|^2 |Phi_B|^2(1-x_5^2)dA =I_ab ||M_ab(A,B)||^2. Thus (2) is a compact evaluation of actual surface spinors, not a substitute for their spatial overlap. One Hamiltonian supplies both responses Use the complete canonical endpoint coefficients k_a, k_b and k_ab. Set \kappa_a=k_a^2 I_{aa},\qquad \kappa_b=k_b^2 I_{bb},\qquad \kappa_{ab}=(k_a k_b+k_{ab}^2)I_{ab}. \tag{5} They are matrix elements of the same action, not separately fitted pair constants. At R=1 remove the two rapid linear carrier phases and use slow time s=gt. The averaged Hamiltonian is \boxed{ H=\frac{\kappa_a}{2}\|M_{aa}(A,A)\|^2 +\frac{\kappa_b}{2}\|M_{bb}(B,B)\|^2 +\kappa_{ab}\|M_{ab}(A,B)\|^2.} \tag{6} Variation with respect to both complex conjugate vectors gives i dA/ds=partial H/partial A^* and i dB/ds=partial H/partial B^*. For example, the cross source in the first equation is kappa_ab M_ab(B)^dagger M_ab(A,B), with the corresponding adjoint map in the second equation. The complete self terms remain in both. The real-linear response also retains conjugate perturbations. The two canonical norms, total H and all three components of the common spatial angular momentum are conserved. No imposed alignment, loss or damping is present. Deformation changes the compatibility At unit norm in each band define P_a=\|M_{aa}(A,A)\|^2,\quad P_b=\|M_{bb}(B,B)\|^2,\quad C=\|M_{ab}(A,B)\|^2. \tag{7} Each quantity is a spatial projection norm, and each is at most one. The absolute interaction integral is kappa_ab C. It is not divided by a particle mass. A coherent single-plane pattern has P_a=1 or P_b=1. For two initially coherent patterns, conservation of (6) gives \boxed{\kappa_{ab}[C(s)-C(0)] =\frac{\kappa_a}{2}[1-P_a(s)] +\frac{\kappa_b}{2}[1-P_b(s)].} \tag{8} Thus this positive-current action cannot lower C below its initial value for that particular preparation. It can increase C as the initially concentrated shapes redistribute their self energy. This is a consequence of the action and the starting shapes, not an imposed alignment rule. More general initial shapes do not have P_a=P_b=1. Equation (8) then contains their actual initial P values, and compatibility can increase or decrease. The real coefficient Hamiltonian also permits the exact reversed trajectory A(T-s)^, B(T-s)^. Forward integration from that deformed state reverses the energy exchange under the same action. This mathematical operation has no antiparticle interpretation. Rigid coherent orientations alone miss this response. Projecting the initial full velocity onto each coherent shape's phase, norm and rotation tangents leaves a nonzero complement at intermediate relative angles. For the assigned degrees at angle 0.7 radians its norm is approximately 0.0665421 in slow-time units. The largest difference between the two complete complex trajectories in the reported controls is below 2e-10. Canonical norms, energy, all three angular momenta and (8) pass independent checks. title: Controlling the full source of the reciprocal spinor pair
summary: All four source frequencies, angular components and opposite parent branches support a controlled finite-slow-time approximation of the reciprocal spinor evolution.
text: The reciprocal polynomial evolution has a controlled weak-coupling interpretation in the complete surface equation. Its cubic source contains four temporal frequencies. Each source has finite angular support, including the non-vacuum spinor components and the opposite parent frequencies. Explicit nonzero detunings permit a first spatial correction and a finite-slow-time averaging argument. This concerns the conditional depth-six surface action in Nonlinear spinor frequencies under one common surface action and Reciprocal shape response in the spinor family. It retains all 48 complex field components on the specified four-sphere. It does not construct the supporting field in the two ordinary normal directions, establish particle stability, or determine the physical coupling coefficient. The surface is a proposed field feature in ordinary space, not compactification. The complete cubic source Set the common radius and wave speed to one. Let H be the complete Hermitian chain Hamiltonian, with common gap G. At its two endpoints, the interaction is U=\frac12\int J_aJ_a\,dA,\qquad J_a=\sum_e\Psi_e^\dagger\gamma_a\Psi_e,\qquad N_e=J_a\gamma_a\Psi_e. \tag{1} All other components of N vanish, but the free Hamiltonian propagates this forcing through every chain component. The endpoint current in (1) remains an inverse interaction premise, distinct from the canonical kinetic flux. This is a local same-field action without mediators. For two complete holomorphic polynomial shapes A(x) and B(x), of degrees a and b, respectively, write the leading field as \Psi^{(0)}=u_a A(x)z_0e^{-i\omega_a t} +u_b B(x)z_0e^{-i\omega_b t}. \tag{2} The vectors u_a and u_b are the complete unit canonical chain states. Both polynomial coefficient vectors have norm one. Define their two endpoint vectors e_a,e_b and k_a=e_a^Te_a,\quad k_b=e_b^Te_b,\quad k_{ab}=e_a^Te_b. \tag{3} In actual Cartesian coordinates on the unit four-sphere, use z_1=x_1+ix_2, z_2=x_3+ix_4 and the vacuum spinor z_0. Its tangent current is j_0=(-x_2,x_1,-x_4,x_3,0). Full Clifford multiplication gives v(x)=\gamma(j_0)z_0=z_0-x_5\Gamma_xz_0 =(F,-x_5z_2,-x_5z_1,0)^T,\qquad F=1-x_5^2,\quad\|v\|^2=F. \tag{4} In particular, the non-vacuum components have squared norm x_5^2 F. They cannot be replaced by the vacuum projection F z_0. The complete source at each endpoint is a sum of S_e(x)v(x) with the following temporal factors: \begin{array}{c|l} \text{frequency}&S_e\\\hline \omega_a&[e_{a,e}k_a|A|^2+(e_{a,e}k_b+e_{b,e}k_{ab})|B|^2]A\\ \omega_b&[e_{b,e}k_b|B|^2+(e_{b,e}k_a+e_{a,e}k_{ab})|A|^2]B\\ 2\omega_a-\omega_b&e_{a,e}k_{ab}A^2\overline B\\ 2\omega_b-\omega_a&e_{b,e}k_{ab}B^2\overline A. \end{array} \tag{5} Direct Fourier decomposition of the actual Clifford current verifies all four terms for arbitrary complex polynomials. No restriction to real amplitudes or one fixed relative phase is used. The complete spectral support is finite Under a common rotation of the two complex planes, the four source classes have vacuum orbital charges q=(a,b,2a-b,2b-a). \tag{6} The other spinor components carry the compensating orbital charges q+1,q+1,q+2. Their total spinor rotation character is the same within each class. Since a and b differ, the four classes are mutually orthogonal. The free Hamiltonian preserves them. The polynomial degrees in (5), including the degree-two vector (4), give the following upper bounds on scalar harmonic degree K: K_{\max}=(a+2\max(a,b)+2,\ b+2\max(a,b)+2, 2a+b+2,\ 2b+a+2). \tag{7} In each class K has the parity of q. For the two positive central charges, K is at least q. For either combination class a conservative lower bound is max(0,|q|-2), adjusted to that parity. This bound can include harmonics with zero source; including them only weakens a resolvent estimate. For each such K, retain both B eigenvalues and both signs of every parent frequency. The smallest positive parent frequency is obtained from the full six-link singular problem. The two signs of B give the same singular frequencies by reflection and diagonal sign changes. The other singular frequencies are at least G-(K_max+4), by the singular-value perturbation bound relative to the gap shift. Consequently, their detuning from a source frequency Omega is at least G-(K_max+4)-|Omega|. This is positive for the cases below. At each central frequency, remove only its complete resonant polynomial family. Its projection is precisely the force derived from the Hamiltonian in Reciprocal shape response in the spinor family. The opposite parent frequency at that same degree remains forced. For the combination frequencies, the enumerated signed low branches have nonzero detuning in all reported cases. Thus no additional resonant source has been silently omitted. The positive combination frequency for degrees 14 and 36 illustrates the geometric restriction. Its charge is 58, so K is conservatively at least 56. A frequency comparison that ignores this charge would include lower-degree modes to which the actual source cannot couple. Bound the first complementary response Let F_j be the complete nonresonant source at frequency Omega_j, with its central resonant projection removed when necessary. Let R_j=(Omega_j-H)^{-1} on that source's finite invariant complementary space. The inverse is needed only there, not on unrelated angular sectors. If delta_j bounds every retained detuning, then \|R_jF_j\|_2\le\frac{\|F_j\|_2}{\delta_j}. \tag{8} The first response with zero initial correction is \xi^{(1)}(t)=-ig\int_0^t e^{-iH(t-r)} \sum_j e^{-i\Omega_jr}F_j\,dr. \tag{9} For fixed shapes, orthogonality of the four rotation classes gives \boxed{\|\xi^{(1)}(t)\|_2 \le2|g|\left[\sum_j\frac{\|F_j\|_2^2}{\delta_j^2}\right]^{1/2}.} \tag{10} The bound is uniform in t. At a central frequency one can also resolve the same-degree opposite-parent projection separately. Its detuning is 2 omega_a or 2 omega_b; its orthogonal remainder uses the larger applicable gap. Their squared bounds add. This retains the small opposite-parent component without letting its small detuning inflate every other component. All source differences are formed directly in ordinary coordinates. For example, subtracting a resonant polynomial R at a central frequency gives endpoint squared residual \sum_{e=0,1}|S_eF-u_{e}R|^2 +\sum_e|S_e|^2x_5^2F, \tag{11} plus the complete intermediate-chain contribution sum |u_i R|^2. This avoids subtracting two nearly equal squared norms. The opposite-parent subtraction changes the upper and lower chain polynomials to R+R_minus and R-R_minus, respectively. Verified magnitudes under one common action Use G=10000 and the common linear electron frequency omega_e^0=1.3366047052613313e-13. Define epsilon=g/omega_e^0 for every pair; it is not reset using each pair's smaller frequency. The following are coefficients C in the frozen bound ||xi^(1)|| <= C |epsilon|: Degrees Plane angle C 14, 36 0.3 3.34710227 14, 36 0.7 0.84919762 14, 36 1.2 0.82836086 2, 14 0.7 1253.62972 2, 36 0.7 1476.86195 These bounds include self-source deformation as well as cross-source response. A small cross-overlap alone therefore does not make the entire complementary source small. Degree two is a mathematical control within this depth-six construction, not a photon. Its much smaller spectral gap makes the same averaging approximation require a weaker common interaction. For the degree-14/36 angle-0.7 pair, the source norms at the four frequencies are approximately 0.79405147, 2.89797426, 0.02166322 and 0.08574321. The resonant norms at the first two frequencies are 0.64642895 and 2.35324052. The remaining central norms are 0.46113702 and 1.69130538. These are actual full-field L2 norms. spinor-pair-source-20260914T045034_198193Z.json passes 459 checks. Independent coherent moment formulas, complete Clifford currents, arbitrary complex shapes, conjugate derivatives, two ordinary-coordinate quadratures and 80-digit signed detunings verify the calculation. Check counts are numerical evidence for the stated implementation, not a replacement for the support argument above. Follow the changing shapes The reciprocal shapes vary with slow time s=gt. Integrating (9) by parts with the complete varying F_j gives the bound \|\xi^{(1)}(t)\|_2\le |g| \left[\mathcal R(s)+\mathcal R(0) +\int_0^s\mathcal R_1(\sigma)\,d\sigma\right], \tag{12} where R(s) is an upper bound for the Hilbert norm of the orthogonal sum of R_jF_j(s), and R_1 uses dF_j/ds. The latter derivative follows from both complete complex shape equations, including their conjugate variations. This remains a first forced response, not the full nonlinear error at a specified finite epsilon. For the independently refined degree-14/36, angle-0.7 trajectory, the frozen coefficient grows from 0.84919762 to 1.25663633 through slow time 20. The integral of the corresponding derivative coefficient is 16.00941368. Equation (12) therefore gives an endpoint first-response estimate of 9.05762382 |epsilon|. Two slow-time quadratures differ by 2.60e-6 in that integral. The estimate is numerically refined, not interval certified. Report spinor-source-trajectory-20260914T045545_833184Z.json passes 31 checks, including full spatial and conjugate-derivative refinements at deformed points along the trajectory. There is also a direct inverse calculation for aligned coherent pairs. It expands all four sources in their complete signed-rotation spinor harmonics through (7), with four further degrees used as a zero-source check. Both signed B projections and every canonical parent eigenvector are retained. The full chain inverse is computed at 80-digit precision. For the aligned degree-14/36 pair, the four norms of omega_e^0 R_j F_j are approximately 2.19168906, 0.02932807, 0.00542109 and 0.00059714. They give the stronger frozen bound 4.38378412 |epsilon|, compared with the conservative gap bound 6.04185324 |epsilon| for that alignment. This aligned example is different from the angle-0.7 trajectory above. spinor-source-resolvent-20260914T051854_908897Z.json passes 569 checks. Source reconstruction retains every generated spinor component and has L2 residual below 1.7e-12 in the assigned-degree examples. Independent quadrature, additional angular degrees, complete Dirac-square identities and a directly applied ordinary angular equation at a smaller, well-conditioned gap verify the inverse calculation. A finite-slow-time theorem for the complete surface equation Normalize H and all rapid frequencies by omega_e^0, and time by its inverse. The full equation is i\partial_t\Psi=\widehat H\Psi+\epsilon N(\Psi). \tag{13} Fix any finite slow interval 0 <= s <= S and an initial pair in the specified resonant polynomial spaces. Suppose its four complete source classes have the nonzero complementary detunings just verified. Then the exact solution of (13), with that initial pair, converges to the reciprocal resonant evolution as epsilon approaches zero, uniformly for 0 <= t <= S/epsilon in H^3 on the four-sphere. Here is the argument, including the full field space. The chain Hamiltonian is self-adjoint and commutes with the componentwise spherical Laplacian, because B^2=-Delta+9/4. Its group is therefore unitary in every spectral Sobolev norm. H^3 on the four-dimensional surface is an algebra, and the smooth tangent Clifford coefficients make N locally Lipschitz in H^3. The usual product bound follows from Leibniz' rule, H^3 embedding into L-infinity and the applicable H^1-to-L^4 derivative estimates. It applies to all 48 complex components. The finite polynomial averaged system preserves the two norms, so its solution and every derivative remain bounded on a fixed S. Its source has the finite support (7). In normalized units define \begin{aligned} W(t,s)&=\sum_j e^{-i\widehat\Omega_jt} (\widehat\Omega_j-\widehat H)^{-1}F_j(s),\\ \widetilde W(t,s)&=W(t,s)-e^{-it\widehat H}W(0,0),\\ \Psi_{\rm app}(t)&=\Psi^{(0)}(t,\epsilon t) +\epsilon\widetilde W(t,\epsilon t). \end{aligned} \tag{14} The second line enforces the original initial field exactly. The leading residual is minus epsilon times the complementary source; the fast derivative of the correction cancels it. The remaining residual is \epsilon^2 i\partial_s W -\epsilon\{N(\Psi^{(0)}+\epsilon\widetilde W) -N(\Psi^{(0)})\}, \tag{15} and hence is bounded by A epsilon^2 in H^3, uniformly on the interval. A is finite because the source support, its inverse detunings and the shape derivatives are all bounded there. Choose a fixed H^3 ball containing the approximate trajectory, and let L be the local Lipschitz constant of N on a slightly larger ball. Duhamel's formula and Gronwall give \|\Psi(t)-\Psi_{\rm app}(t)\|_{H^3} \le\frac{A\epsilon}{L}(e^{LS}-1). \tag{16} Taking epsilon sufficiently small closes the ball bootstrap and continues the exact local solution through S/epsilon. The correction in (14) is also O(epsilon), proving the claimed convergence. No harmonic cutoff is imposed on the exact solution. Newly generated modes and subsequent nonlinear responses are covered by the full Sobolev estimate. This theorem supplies a conditional asymptotic justification for the shape calculation. A coarse Sobolev bound can make its explicit smallness threshold extremely restrictive. It does not certify that an example such as epsilon=0.01 accurately follows the average for slow time 20. The informative L2 first-response coefficients in the table do not replace that nonlinear estimate. Neither result derives the surface, the master-field interaction, a depth-five neutral branch, or the particle's full inertia. Mass remains the selected frequency; the slower shape evolution is its interaction response. title: Transition-density coupling
summary: The complete derivative of a bilocal density interaction pairs both objects' transition densities, giving reciprocal mode vertices and an exact signed quadrupole matching law from the existing spatial kernel.
text: Summary: The complete derivative of a bilocal density interaction pairs both objects' transition densities, giving reciprocal mode vertices and an exact signed quadrupole matching law from the existing spatial kernel. The spatial patterns which must match A coupling calculation compares the changes that two spatial patterns can undergo. For a density interaction the relevant objects are their transition densities, which can have signs and complex phases even when each original density is positive. Their pairing provides a precise version of shape matching with both objects polarized. Use one field \Psi(t,x) on a specified finite containing spatial region of the nested macroscopic manifold. The labels x,y below are two points in that same physical space. Let A_\alpha(x) be fixed Hermitian matrices on its field components, and define real scalar bilinears \rho_\alpha(x)=\Psi(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\Psi(x). \tag{1} For a compatible Dirac scalar channel one may take A_\alpha=\beta P_\alpha when \beta P_\alpha is Hermitian. Positivity of the bilinear is not assumed. The channel labels do not supply spatial embeddings; the appropriate nested maps, transport and measures must be included in the kernel used for a physical application. The same energy fixes both responses Take a real exchange-symmetric spatial kernel K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)=K_{\beta\alpha}(y,x) and the energy term E_{\rm int}[\Psi]=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta} \iint\rho_\alpha(x)K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)\rho_\beta(y) d\mu_xd\mu_y. \tag{2} Define U=K\rho with the indicated integrals. Its field source is \big(\mathcal N[\Psi]\big)(x)=\sum_\alpha U_\alpha(x)A_\alpha(x)\Psi(x). \tag{3} This is the Hamiltonian convention \delta E=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta\Psi,\mathcal N\rangle. The bilocal variation derives (3) directly from the two density factors in (2). At a specified background \phi, let (D\eta)_\alpha(x)=2\operatorname{Re} \big[\phi(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\eta(x)\big], \qquad V_\phi=\sum_\alpha(K\rho[\phi])_\alpha A_\alpha. \tag{4} D\eta is the change in the source density. Differentiating the whole source, including that change, gives \boxed{D\mathcal N[\phi]\eta =V_\phi\eta+\sum_\alpha A_\alpha\phi\,(KD\eta)_\alpha.} \tag{5} The first term is multiplication by the existing potential. The second term is the response of the potential to the changing pattern. It is generally real-linear and depends on \eta and its conjugate. For two independent field variations, the complete mixed second derivative is \boxed{\big(E_{\rm int}''[\phi]\big)(\eta,\zeta) =2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,V_\phi\zeta\rangle +\langle D\eta,KD\zeta\rangle_{\rm real}.} \tag{6} Exchange symmetry of K makes (6) symmetric in the two variations. This is reciprocity before any mode truncation or amplitude convention. With the real field pairing \operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,\zeta\rangle, the density-map adjoint satisfies D^*f=2\sum_\alpha A_\alpha\phi f_\alpha; thus (5) is also V_\phi+\tfrac12D^*KD. A response with D\eta=0 has no density-feedback term, but it can still respond through V_\phi, kinetic cross terms or other action terms. In particular D(i\phi)=0 while D\mathcal N[\phi]\,(i\phi)=i\mathcal N[\phi]. The full phase zero mode requires an actual stationary solution and the kinetic part of its equation. The complete coherent mode vertex Let \Phi_i(x) be modes normalized in the derived kinetic metric. If they are not orthonormal, apply the canonical normalization before interpreting amplitude magnitudes. Define transition densities r_{ij}^{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_i(x)^\dagger A_\alpha(x)\Phi_j(x). \tag{7} For \Psi=\sum_i c_i\Phi_i the exact quartic term is E_{\rm int}=\frac12\sum_{i,j,k,l} \bar c_i c_j\bar c_kc_l\,T_{ij;kl}, \qquad T_{ij;kl}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\iint r_{ij}^{\alpha}(x)K_{\alpha\beta}(x,y)r_{kl}^{\beta}(y) d\mu_xd\mu_y. \tag{8} Both pairs of modes enter. Reversing a transition changes its density to its complex conjugate, giving T_{ij;kl}=T_{kl;ij},\qquad \overline{T_{ij;kl}}=T_{ji;lk}. \tag{9} This retains the spatial shapes and relative phases required by the one field. The diagonal densities alone do not determine (8). Likewise, frequency matching does not guarantee a nonzero spatial vertex. A rotating wave approximation can select resonant terms only after this full tensor and the temporal frequencies have been calculated. Exact factorization for the spatial dot-square kernel For two prescribed spatial charts and their rectangular identification B:\mathbb R^e\to\mathbb R^d, adopt the scalar term K(x,y)=g(x^TBy)^2. Define complex transition moments M_{ij}^{(a)}=\int xx^T\bar\Phi_i^{(a)}\Phi_j^{(a)}\,dx, \qquad M_{kl}^{(b)}=\int yy^T\bar\Phi_k^{(b)}\Phi_l^{(b)}\,dy. Expansion of the two dot products gives \boxed{T_{ij;kl}=g\operatorname{tr} \left(M_{ij}^{(a)}B M_{kl}^{(b)}B^T\right).} \tag{10} There is no extra complex conjugate in this bilinear expression; the reversal identities are already in (9). The geometric action supplies the identification B, and common physical rotations transform all three tensor factors consistently. Centre motion or a position-dependent contact factor must also be varied when they belong to the adopted energy. The source channel has at most d(d+1)/2 independent symmetric moment components at fixed depth. These are descriptions of spatial shape, not additional spatial axes. Higher spatial structure can enter other terms of the action even when it is absent from this particular kernel. A normalized shape-matching example Use ordinary flat Gaussian modes with width parameter \omega>0, \phi_0(x)=\left(\frac\omega\pi\right)^{d/4} e^{-\omega|x|^2/2}. For a real symmetric matrix A with \operatorname{tr}A^2=1, define the polarized quadratic shape mode \phi_A(x)=\sqrt2\,\omega \left(x^TAx-\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{2\omega}\right)\phi_0(x). \tag{11} Gaussian second and fourth moments give \langle\phi_0,\phi_A\rangle=0,\qquad \|\phi_A\|=1,\qquad \int xx^T\phi_0\phi_A\,dx=\frac{A}{\sqrt2\,\omega}. \tag{12} For example the covariance of x^TAx under |\phi_0|^2 is \operatorname{tr}A^2/(2\omega^2), establishing the normalization. The covariance of xx^T with x^TAx is A/(2\omega^2), establishing the transition moment. Two such patterns, with shape tensors A,C and widths \omega_a,\omega_b, therefore have the exact vertex T_{0A;0C}=\frac{g}{2\omega_a\omega_b} \operatorname{tr}(A B C B^T). \tag{13} For two real fluctuation amplitudes q_a,q_b about the respective backgrounds, the mixed second derivative of the cross energy is four times (13): each density variation contributes a factor two. Equation (13) itself is the normalized quartic mode vertex, not that Hessian. In a shared two-plane take B=I and A=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad C=R(\theta)A R(\theta)^T. Then \boxed{T_{0A;0C}=\frac{g}{2\omega_a\omega_b}\cos(2\theta).} \tag{14} The patterns have the same nonzero spatial support and norm, yet this transition is exactly blocked at \theta=\pi/4. At \theta=\pi/2 the amplitude reverses sign. Rotating both objects by the same angle changes neither result. Squaring the amplitude gives a \cos^2(2\theta) angular factor for an otherwise specified transition probability. There is also an orientation-independent mismatch: a traceless shape A has zero pairing with the breathing shape C=I/\sqrt d for every relative rotation in this isotropic kernel. Other compatible shape transitions can remain nonzero. These are explicit geometric selection rules obtained from the existing interaction, without assigning a separate zero to a selected particle species. Scope of the selection rule For harmonic-oscillator basis functions, multiplication by x_ix_j changes total oscillator number by 0 or \pm2. Thus (10) connects only the corresponding mode pairs on each side. This is a rule for the transition density and its moment; it is not a claim that an odd spatial field has zero self-energy. The distinction is derived in angular kernel parity. Equations (11)–(14) are a conditional flat-profile example. They do not replace the actual Coulomb-plus-precession electron orbit or specify a neutrino profile. Their role is to demonstrate, using an explicit kernel, how polarization becomes a higher-order spatial shape selection rule. The occupied particle solutions, photon map, accessible target motions, kinetic scales and scattering boundary conditions remain to be derived. Verification spatial_coupling_mechanism_checks.py compares (5)–(6) with finite differences of the full nonlocal complex-field energy using unequal spatial weights, indefinite bilinears and both positive and indefinite kernels. It reconstructs the complete quartic energy from (8), checks reciprocity, and independently evaluates (12)–(14) by Gaussian double quadrature with both shape orientations varied. Related Projected bilocal variation — supplies the action and first variation extended here. Dirac source linearization — gives the local scalar analogue, including conjugate response blocks. Cross-sector moment kernel — derives the tensor identification and its covariance. Bilateral polarization coupling — motivates varying both spatial patterns.

title: Translational Dirac response
summary: Varying the scalar center restores the exact translation zero mode and yields a calculable inertial response of the full self-bound spatial Dirac field.
text: Summary: Varying the scalar center restores the exact translation zero mode and yields a calculable inertial response of the full self-bound spatial Dirac field. A self-bound field must be able to move The centered scalar interaction determines its own spatial profile and center. Holding that center fixed while varying the field would replace part of its dynamics by an external constraint. This note retains the center and derives its response from the same energy as the scalar Dirac moment modes. All coordinates are ordinary spatial coordinates in a sector of the one nested physical manifold. Translation moves the field within those coordinates. Response coefficients and angular functions add no physical dimensions or interaction particles. Use \sigma=\Phi^\dagger\beta\Phi, Q_\sigma=\int\sigma\ne0, P_\sigma=\int x\sigma, X=P_\sigma/Q_\sigma, and M_\sigma=\int(x-X)(x-X)^T\sigma\,dx, \qquad \mathcal E_{\rm int}=\frac{g_0}{2}\operatorname{tr}M_\sigma^2. \tag{1} Q_\sigma is a scalar bilinear integral, not an electric charge. It need not equal the separately normalized field norm. The center contributes a required dipole feedback At a centered radial background, M_\sigma=(T/d)I and a=g_0T/d. For an arbitrary field variation let \delta\sigma=2\operatorname{Re}(\Phi^\dagger\beta\eta),\qquad \delta P=\int x\,\delta\sigma\,dx,\qquad \delta C=\int xx^T\delta\sigma\,dx. The first variation of the central moment is \delta M=\delta C, but the source also depends on x-X. Differentiating the entire scalar potential gives \boxed{\delta U(x)=g_0x^T\delta Cx -\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}x\cdot\delta P.} \tag{2} The second term supplies the center's dipole response. Its coefficient \kappa=-2a/Q_\sigma follows from the same centered energy, including its sign; it is not an independently chosen interaction strength. For two variations the full interaction Hessian is \begin{aligned} \mathcal E_{\rm int}''(\eta,\zeta) ={}&2\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,\beta ar^2\zeta\rangle +g_0\operatorname{tr}(\delta C_\eta\delta C_\zeta)\\ &-\frac{2a}{Q_\sigma}\delta P_\eta\cdot\delta P_\zeta. \end{aligned} \tag{3} This is symmetric in both variations, as required for reciprocal dynamics. The negative center term is consistent with translation invariance: a shift of the entire field does not cost binding energy. The dipole source has a full spatial Dirac decomposition With the rest polarization w and Clifford matrices of the profile note, a dipole source in direction b is v_b=\beta(b\cdot x)\Phi. Its angular polynomial splits as \begin{aligned} p_b(x)&=(b\cdot x)w=M_b(x)+\alpha(x)N_b,\\ N_b&=\frac1d\alpha(b)w,\qquad M_b(x)=(b\cdot x)w-\frac1d\alpha(x)\alpha(b)w. \end{aligned} \tag{4} Both M_b and N_b are annihilated by \alpha\cdot\partial. The radial operators and source norms follow by the same direct method as Polarized Dirac shape response, now with degrees one and zero. For the circulation tensor J_{ij}=w^\dagger(-i\alpha_i\alpha_j)w their angular Gram matrices are G_N=\frac{I+iJ}{d^2},\qquad G_M=\frac Id-G_N. \tag{5} The two radial operators are H_{d+2} and -XH_dX, with the same physical scalar coefficients m,a. The larger numerical radial parameter again accounts only for powers of the existing radius. Let L contain these two operators minus the stationary frequency. For helicity \lambda of iJ, let u_\lambda,u_{-\lambda} be the normalized radial source vectors with squared angular weights 1/d-(1+\lambda)/d^2 and (1+\lambda)/d^2. Their bare response is \chi_\lambda(z)=u_\lambda^T(z-L)^{-1}u_\lambda +u_{-\lambda}^T(-z-L)^{-1}u_{-\lambda}. \tag{6} The complete dipole response is \chi_\lambda/(1-\kappa\chi_\lambda), with the center coefficient from (2). The ordinary and conjugate blocks are both retained. Translation gives an exact response identity For a translated stationary field \Phi(x-\epsilon b), the tangent is \eta_b=-b\cdot\nabla\Phi. Translation leaves the central moment unchanged and gives \delta P=Q_\sigma b. Differentiating the stationary equation therefore gives \boxed{\kappa\chi_\lambda(0)=1.} \tag{7} This places a zero-frequency collective mode in the complete response, even though the frozen confining Dirac operator has finite excitation gaps. The identity holds in all physical translation directions. Commuting translations also have zero mutual symplectic pairing. In the radial representation this is \|L^{-1}u_\lambda\|^2=\|L^{-1}u_{-\lambda}\|^2, \qquad \chi_\lambda'(0)=0. \tag{8} The first identity follows equivalently from the spatial integral of the commutator of momentum generators. It is a useful independent check of the angular decomposition and both Dirac radial branches. At finite numerical resolution the translation zero and its conjugate momentum direction can produce small spurious growth rates. Fixing total momentum and quotienting the translation direction removes that pair. This operation preserves the remaining fluctuation frequencies; it does not remove a nonzero physical instability. The inertial coefficient follows from the low-frequency response Apply a specified slowly varying scalar source h(t)\cdot x\,\beta. Its contribution to the energy is h\cdot P_\sigma and the force on the translated field is -Q_\sigma h to first order. Expanding (6) at zero frequency and using (7)–(8) gives \chi^{\rm full}_\lambda(z) =-\frac{2}{\kappa^2\chi_\lambda''(0)z^2}+O(z^{-1}). \tag{9} Comparing \delta X=\delta P/Q_\sigma with the force response defines the inertial coefficient \boxed{\mathcal M_{\mathrm{tr}} =-\frac{\kappa^2Q_\sigma^2}{2}\chi_\lambda''(0) =-2a^2\chi_\lambda''(0).} \tag{10} The second derivative involves the sum of opposite helicities, so this leading inertia is isotropic for the radial background. Higher-frequency response can still depend on J. In the present examples it is positive. At a=1, m=0, the numerical values are approximately 2.080669220 at depth three, 2.770370932 at five, 3.084232390 at six, and 4.210308101 at ten. These are coefficients in the specified model's translation dynamics. The instantaneous nonlocal energy does not supply a Lorentz-covariant completion, so equality to the stationary frequency or total binding energy is not presumed. At depths with a separate radial instability, this translation response does not make the whole background stable. Relation to a force between two patterns This calculation supplies a field's response when a reciprocal pair interaction exerts a force. The force itself must come from differentiating that pair energy with respect to its two positions. A moment pairing which depends only on separately centered shapes and a fixed identification matrix has no dependence on their relative translation. Its orientation and shape responses remain meaningful, while a separation-dependent force requires the corresponding spatial contact or propagation kernel. Verification angular_dirac_response_checks.py checks the dipole source by full Clifford angular integration and the physical radial equations. It verifies the translation identity and the vanishing first frequency derivative, then compares the remaining spectra at increased radial resolution. Independent finite differences of the centered full-field energy and source check (2)–(3), including the sign of the center contribution. Related Centroid-relative self-binding — derives the center variation in the scalar spatial model. Self-consistent scalar Dirac moment modes — supplies the full first-order stationary profile. Polarized Dirac shape response — derives the angular and ordinary/conjugate response method used here.

title: Circulating isotropic orbitals
summary: Auxiliary model only: Pure excited orbitals can have isotropic position moments while carrying a full-rank circulation that supplies a conditional singlet spin source.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Auxiliary model only: Pure excited orbitals can have isotropic position moments while carrying a full-rank circulation that supplies a conditional singlet spin source. Interpretation correction This calculation concerns an auxiliary field or local spin model, not the actual electron orbit constructed in the 6D demo. Its stationary states, angular expectations, and stability results have not been mapped to that trajectory or its observer readout. They must not be used as a replacement for the existing orbit-shape derivation. See Actual orbit research correction. 1. Position moments do not exhaust orbital data The positive scalar ground-state result remains intact. The following is an excited-state construction, not another ground-state minimum. It shows why isotropic second moments do not imply vanishing orbital current. Use a flat six-dimensional oscillator H_omega=p^2+omega^2 r^2, with unit norm, and split its real basis into O=(e1,e2,e3) and H=(e4,e5,e6). Define orthonormal circular modes z_a=(e_a-i e_(a+3))/sqrt(2), a=1,2,3. In the oscillator shell of total degree N>=2 take \phi_N=\frac1{\sqrt3}\sum_{a=1}^3|N\hbox{ quanta in }z_a\rangle. This is a pure superposition, not a mixture. The coordinate polynomials (x_a-i x_(a+3))^N are harmonic, so the state lies in ell=N as well as shell N. Its one-body cross matrix elements vanish because a one-body operator cannot transfer all N>=2 quanta between two orthogonal modes. With rho the trace-N one-body density matrix, \rho=\frac N3 P_-,\qquad P_-=\frac12(I+iJ_0),\qquad J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_3\\-I_3&0\end{pmatrix}. Thus Re rho=N I/6, while Im rho=N J_0/6 is nonzero. For a fixed shell, the anomalous expectations of two creation or two annihilation operators vanish, giving M=\langle xx^T\rangle=\frac{N+3}{6\omega}I_6, \qquad \langle L\rangle=-2\operatorname{Im}\rho=-\frac N3J_0. The position covariance is isotropic and the circulation has full rank six. The density itself need not be isotropic: the quadratic scalar kernel sees only its second moments, not its higher angular moments. 2. These are scalar self-consistent stationary solutions For the single-sector functional E=T+(g/2)tr M^2 with g>0, variation gives the mean-field potential g x^T M x. It equals omega^2 r^2 precisely when \omega_N^3=\frac{g(N+3)}6. At that width, phi_N is an exact stationary scalar Hartree solution, with phase eigenvalue mu=(2N+6)omega_N. Its energy is E=(3/2)(N+3)omega_N, not mu. For N=2, choosing omega=1 gives g=6/5, M=5I/6, and mu=10. The scalar problem supplies an entire symmetry-related family, not a chosen absolute J_0 or a particle-index selector. The state is above the unconstrained scalar ground state. Its linear stability is a separate calculation. 3. Conditional spin source and the circulation sign If this orbital is used in the local vector-potential Dirac reduction of the spin-orbit audit, its angular expectation produces \mathcal S=-\frac N3\sum_{a=1}^3\Sigma_{a,a+3}. In the stated chiral convention this has eigenvalues {-N,N/3,N/3,N/3}. For a positive spin-orbit coefficient the unique lowest ray lies in the locked orbit, with complex structure J_0. Reversing the orbital circulation negates the matrix and gives a triply degenerate lowest eigenvalue instead. Thus the current sign relative to chirality and the interaction coefficient must be retained; a magnitude-only source calculation misses the distinction. The scalar Hartree functional does not prove that its potential is the time-component vector potential of the Dirac model. Nor does a projected spin matrix identify the spatial Dirac-section fibre with the homogeneous CP3 base coordinate. These bridges remain open. 4. A shared-well normalization constraint With fixed g and unit norm, these isolated self-bound solutions have N-dependent omega_N. They cannot all be treated as excitations of one fixed harmonic well while each is simultaneously taken to source that well alone. For charge Q the relation becomes omega_N^3=g Q(N+3)/6. Keeping omega fixed would require Q proportional to 1/(N+3), or a separate dominant background that fixes the well. Neither is supplied by the one-quantum normalization. This does not disprove a fixed-background cumulative-band construction. It specifies what must distinguish that construction from isolated self-binding. N here is a flat oscillator degree, not an independently derived assignment to an electron, a chemistry orbital, or a V2 projective band. Verification circulating_hartree_checks.py verifies the N=2 state's norm, moment matrix, self-consistent width, one-body current, and both signed chiral spectra. Its further linearized checks are documented separately. The general N>=2 statements follow from the one-body selection rule and the displayed moment identities. Related Self-consistent moment lock test — the ground-state theorem is not an exclusion of these excited current-carrying states. Orbital projection source test — the earlier two-plane construction is extended to three planes and isotropic position moments. Spin-orbit source audit — supplies the conditional derivative vertex and its approximation limits. Research status — current proof boundaries and correction routes.

title: Controlled orbital gap

Choose an integer N ≥ 2 with N > 3r/2, and set \alpha^2=\frac12-\frac{3r}{4N},\qquad \beta^2=\frac12+\frac{3r}{4N},\qquad \omega^3=v_6^2\left(\frac{N+3}{6}+\frac r4\right). Use three orthonormal complex oscillator modes z_a = αe_a − iβe_(a+3), and the pure shell state φ = 3^(-1/2) Σ_a |N quanta in z_a⟩. For α ≠ β its coordinate polynomial is not simply a harmonic power: it is defined by applying the oscillator creation operator N times. It remains in the oscillator shell N, but need not have a single angular degree ℓ. N is not identified with a CP3 band. Take the nuclear field to be the oscillator ground state with frequency ω₃ = rω. The moments are M_3=aI_3,\quad a=\frac1{2r\omega},\qquad M_6=\operatorname{diag}(m_OI_3,m_HI_3), m_O=\frac{1/2+N\alpha^2/3}{\omega},\qquad m_H=\frac{1/2+N\beta^2/3}{\omega}. The mixed position covariance vanishes, but the angular expectation is \langle L\rangle=-\frac{2N\alpha\beta}{3}J_0. It has full rank for the strict threshold N > 3r/2. Its signs at u = 0,16,24,32 are respectively negative, positive, negative, positive for every N > 3/2. Thus it has three distinct positive roots, one in each intervening interval. It does not turn its scalar potential into a Dirac vector potential, derive a nonfactorizing transition, identify a spatial spinor fiber with a CP3 base coordinate, or select an observed particle index. It is invariant under SO(6), and its Hamiltonian evolution conserves the angular-momentum tensor. In particular fix \mathcal J=\sum_{a=1}^3L_{a,a+3},\qquad \langle\mathcal J\rangle=-j,\quad j\ge0. j is an expectation constraint and need not be an integer. This is not a new quantization rule. The states φ_N constructed earlier have j = N. The oscillator identity is p^2+\omega^2r^2+2\omega\mathcal J =4\omega N_++6\omega. Choose ω³ = g(j+3)/6 and m = ω²/g. Completing the matrix square gives the exact expectation identity E-\frac32\omega(j+3) =4\omega\langle N_+\rangle +\frac g2\|M-mI_6\|_F^2\ge0. It is therefore a global constrained energy minimum, despite being excited relative to the unconstrained scalar ground state. What this controls dynamically At fixed initial j, the chosen ω is fixed. Both E and j are conserved by the isolated scalar evolution, so the entire right-hand side is conserved. An initially small energy excess controls the opposite-circulation occupation and the Frobenius deviation of M from mI at all times for which the evolution exists. Since N₊ has integer spectrum with gap one above its kernel, the squared Hilbert-space norm outside that kernel is also bounded by ⟨N₊⟩. This is a nonlinear invariant bound for these observables. It is not stability of a particular wavefunction modulo phase. Many states have the same constraints and second moments; their spatial evolution and higher moments need not stay near one representative φ_N. No unique orientation, selected degree, or radiative lifetime follows. The result complements rather than replaces the linear spectral analysis. For a general quadratic mean-field potential xᵀ W x, the covariance equations give \frac{d}{dt}\langle L\rangle=2[W,M]. Self-interaction W = gM makes this vanish. An added nuclear matrix need not commute with M, and the scalar constrained-minimum proof then cannot be carried across unchanged. Even initially isotropic M does not ensure that anisotropic W preserves the circulating stationary solution. Radiation and other channels can likewise exchange angular momentum. Exact moment dynamics Consider the single scalar equation i partial_t psi=(p^2+g x^T M x)psi, M=<xx^T>, g>0, with unit conserved norm and the flat, fixed-centroid assumptions of the circulating-orbital note. Define real matrices K_{ab}=\langle p_ap_b\rangle,\qquad C_{ab}=\tfrac12\langle x_ap_b+p_bx_a\rangle. Quadratic operator commutators close exactly, even for a non-Gaussian state: \dot M=2(C+C^T),\qquad \dot C=2K-2gM^2,\qquad \dot K=-2g(MC+C^TM). There is no moment-factorization approximation here. In particular C-C^T, the angular-momentum tensor, is conserved because dot C is symmetric. These equations use the scalar Schrödinger-type functional, not the full Dirac master dynamics or a dissipative radiative model. 2. Linearize about an isotropic circulating stationary point Let M=mI, K=g m^2 I and C=A, with A real antisymmetric. Write omega^2=g m. Let X,Y,Z be the symmetric perturbations of M,K,C. The antisymmetric perturbation of C is separately constant. Then \dot X=4Z,\qquad \dot Z=2Y-4gmX,\qquad \dot Y=-4gmZ-2g[X,A]. Eliminating Y and Z gives X^{(3)}+24\omega^2\dot X+16g[X,A]=0. The commutator map X-> [X,A] on symmetric matrices is skew-adjoint for the Frobenius inner product. Its complex eigenvalues are i a with real a, and |a| is at most twice the largest rotation rate of A. Positivity of the phase-space covariance gives ||A||_op<=m omega, hence |g a|<=2 omega^3. For example this follows from the Schur complement of the positive matrix [[mI,A],[-A,gm^2 I]]. The stronger quantum uncertainty inequality is not needed for this bound. For a moment proportional to exp(-i Omega t), the frequency equation is \Omega^3-24\omega^2\Omega+16ga=0. Its discriminant is bounded below by 4(24\omega^2)^3-27(16ga)^2 \ge27648\omega^6>0. Thus each commutator channel has three real frequencies. The a=0 channels include a zero frequency and plus/minus sqrt(24) omega. This proves absence of exponential growth in the linearized moment system, not nonlinear orbital stability or damping toward a unique state. 3. Relation to the complete scalar linearization Write psi=exp(-i mu t)(phi+eta) around a harmonic-shell stationary state. The linearized field equation is i\dot\eta=(H_\omega-\mu)\eta +g\sum_{a,b}\delta M_{ab}\,x_ax_b\phi. The homogeneous operator is self-adjoint; the forcing depends only on the closed moment perturbations. A perturbation invisible to all delta M evolves under this homogeneous operator. A nonzero exponential instability could therefore neither hide in a zero-moment perturbation nor be generated by the bounded-frequency moment channels. Resonant forcing and neutral directions can still produce polynomial behavior; bounded norm for every linearized perturbation and nonlinear stability are not claimed. For phi in shell N=2, every x_a x_b phi lies in shells 0,2,4. The entire nonlinear part of the Bogoliubov operator is therefore captured in their 148-dimensional scalar sum, doubled to 296 dimensions. All omitted shell directions have free real frequencies. With q_ab=x_a x_b phi, the blocks are \mathcal A=H_\omega-\mu+g\sum_{a,b}|q_{ab}\rangle\langle q_{ab}|, \qquad \mathcal B=g\sum_{a,b}q_{ab}q_{ab}^T, \qquad \mathcal L=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal A&\mathcal B\\-\bar{\mathcal B}&-\bar{\mathcal A}\end{pmatrix}. The transpose in B is not an adjoint; the background is complex. Summing over a<=b instead requires a factor sqrt(2) in off-diagonal q_ab columns. 4. Explicit circulating N=2 result For omega=1, g=6/5, m=5/6 and A=-J_0/3, the nonzero commutator rates are a=plus/minus 2/3. The additional cubic is Omega^3-24 Omega+64/5=0. The distinct positive field frequencies in the active block are approximately 0.5398903, 4, 4.6066714, 4.8989795 and 5.1465617, along with their negatives and neutral modes. The non-cubic sqrt(24) and free-shell frequency 4 are included in this list. circulating_hartree_checks.py compares the analytic roots with all 296 numerical eigenvalues. Raw near-zero eigenvalues have imaginary roundoff around 4e-8; nonzero modes agree with real values to numerical precision. The proof uses the analytic closure, not a claim that floating-point zero eigenvalues are exactly diagonalizable. 5. Implication for the V2 search There is a genuine current-carrying stationary branch with no exponential linear instability in this scalar model. It is not excluded by the earlier ground-state covariance theorem. But the argument applies broadly to isotropic harmonic-shell stationary states, so passing this test cannot select the observed particle indices. The missing cross-sector, radiative, spinor, and background-selection dynamics remain essential. Correction to the rank-three requirement: a generic rank-two orbital bivector uniquely selects an SO(3) frame by orientation-preserving Procrustes completion Section 55 correctly proved that the mixed block of one simple orbital bivector has rank at most two, E_L=x_Op_H^T-p_Ox_H^T, \qquad \operatorname{rank}E_L\le2. It then drew the stronger conclusion that rank two is insufficient to determine a complete three-frame relation. That conclusion is false once the desired frame map is restricted to Q\in SO(3). Two independent oriented vector correspondences determine the third axis by orientation. Equivalently, a generic rank-two 3\times3 tensor has a unique orientation-preserving orthogonal Procrustes factor. This materially strengthens the scattering route. 99.1 Exact factorization of the orbital mixed block Write A_O=[x_O\;p_O], \qquad A_H=[x_H\;p_H], and J_2= \begin{pmatrix} 0&1\\ -1&0 \end{pmatrix}. Then \boxed{ E_L=A_OJ_2A_H^T. } If x_O\not\parallel p_O and x_H\not\parallel p_H, both A_O and A_H have column rank two and J_2 is invertible. Therefore \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}E_L=2. } Its left and right null directions are exactly the two orbital-plane normals: \boxed{ E_L^T(x_O\times p_O)=0, } \boxed{ E_L(x_H\times p_H)=0. } Thus the missing third axis is not absent geometrically. It is already fixed, up to sign, by the oriented normals of the two rank-two planes. 99.2 Rank-two 3\times3 tensors have a unique SO(3) Procrustes maximizer Let a real rank-two tensor have singular-value decomposition E=U \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1&0&0\\ 0&\sigma_2&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix} V^T, \qquad \sigma_1,\sigma_2>0. Because the third singular vectors correspond to zero singular value, their signs may be chosen so that U,V\in SO(3). Consider the orientation-preserving Procrustes problem \max_{Q\in SO(3)}\operatorname{tr}(Q^TE). Write Q=URV^T, \qquad R\in SO(3). Then \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) = \sigma_1R_{11}+\sigma_2R_{22}. Since every diagonal entry of an orthogonal matrix is at most one, \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) \le \sigma_1+\sigma_2. Equality requires R_{11}=R_{22}=1. Orthogonality then forces the first two rows and columns to be the first two coordinate basis vectors, and the condition \det R=1 forces R_{33}=1. Hence R=I_3 is the unique maximizer. Therefore \boxed{ Q_E=UV^T } is a uniquely selected element of SO(3) even though \det E=0. So full matrix rank is not required for full orientation selection in three dimensions. 99.3 Canonical exact example For E= \begin{pmatrix} 0&a&0\\ -b&0&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a,b>0, one has E=Q_0 \operatorname{diag}(b,a,0), with \boxed{ Q_0= \begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\\ -1&0&0\\ 0&0&1 \end{pmatrix} \in SO(3). } For any Q=Q_0R, \qquad R\in SO(3), the trace objective is \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) =bR_{11}+aR_{22} \le a+b, with equality only for R=I. This provides a completely elementary exact verification of the rank-two theorem. 99.4 Consequence for the scattering hierarchy The ranking in Section 55 must therefore be revised. A rank-one mixed source leaves a continuous axial ambiguity and is insufficient. But a generic rank-two source already fixes two independent directions, and the orientation condition fixes the third. Thus \boxed{ \operatorname{rank}E=2 \quad\text{is generically sufficient to select a unique }Q\in SO(3). } The scattering-triad tensor E_{\rm tri} remains a valid full-rank construction, but it is no longer the minimal one. A much smaller transition can produce P_Q and hence T_Q at second order. Section 99 now removes an analogous unnecessary requirement on the classical orientation source. The source tensor need not be full rank either. It only has to determine a unique orientation-preserving frame map. Therefore the required chain can be weakened from \text{full-rank }E_{\rm tri} \longrightarrow Q_{\rm scat} to \boxed{ \text{generic rank-two }E_L \longrightarrow Q_L \longrightarrow P_{Q_L} \longrightarrow T_{Q_L}. } This is a genuine reduction in the amount of dynamical structure V2 must derive. 99.6 Degenerate cases are now sharply classified For the orbital tensor E_L=A_OJ_2A_H^T, rank falls below two exactly when at least one orbital plane degenerates: x_O\parallel p_O or x_H\parallel p_H. Then only one or zero independent directions are correlated and a continuous frame ambiguity returns. Thus the physical distinction is not \text{rank three versus rank two}, but \boxed{ \text{two independent oriented directions versus fewer than two}. } This matches ordinary three-dimensional frame geometry: two noncollinear axes determine the third by the right-hand rule. 99.7 Revised bottleneck The source audit of Section 98 remains valid: the current non-note V2 corpus does not yet insert an orbital/scattering bifundamental into the electron--nucleus kernel. But the missing source is now simpler than Section 98 assumed. One no longer needs to derive a full-rank tensor such as E_{\rm tri}. It is enough to derive a nondegenerate mixed orbital block \boxed{ E_L=P_O(x\wedge p)P_H } or any equivalent rank-two bifundamental whose SO(3) Procrustes completion is unique. The next source-level test is therefore: \boxed{ \text{does the actual }3\leftrightarrow6\text{ projected interaction retain the mixed orbital bivector }P_O(x\wedge p)P_H\text{ or an equivalent two-direction correlation?} } If yes, the orientation problem is much closer to closure than the earlier full-rank criterion suggested. If every source-level cross-depth term removes or averages away this rank-two orbital information, the orientation route still fails. The integer block charges (-2,3) are the primitive solution of 3a+2b=0, up to simultaneous sign reversal. Dividing by six gives the existing hypercharge generator Y=diag(-1/3,-1/3,-1/3,1/2,1/2). The choice of degree-one L and of this auxiliary carrier is an additional construction, not a background selection derived from the master action. For a unitary connection a on L and traceless unitary connections A_c,A_w on the displayed trivial multiplicity bundles, a compatible connection is \nabla^g=\operatorname{diag}(d-2aI_3+A_c,\ d+3aI_2+A_w). The expression is interpreted in local line frames with their transition functions; the global tensor-product connection is what is defined. Its trace is zero and its mixed blocks vanish. With A_c=A_w=0, its actual holonomy is only a U(1) subgroup; the allowed structure group is not a proof that every non-Abelian gauge interaction is dynamically generated. 2. The entire charge table is a global exterior bundle Use F_g=Lambda^even E_g, of rank 16. Its decomposition is Exterior component SU(3) x SU(2) Line factor Y Conventional field label Lambda^0 (1,1) L^0 0 nu^c Lambda^2 colour (bar3,1) L^-4 -2/3 u^c colour tensor weak (3,2) L^1 1/6 Q Lambda^2 weak (1,1) L^6 1 e^c Lambda^3 colour tensor weak (1,2) L^-3 -1/2 leptons Lambda^2 colour tensor Lambda^2 weak (bar3,1) L^2 1/3 d^c The line exponents are just sums of the five primitive weights. Their multiplicities are 1,3,6,1,2,3. This is the same fibre branching as the existing gauge module, now on a specified global bundle. If read as one family of left-handed 4D fields, the usual hypercharge, mixed, and weak-doublet anomaly checks pass; that is a representation check, not a derivation of 4D field content. 3. It is not a disguised tangent or tangent-spinor bundle The carrier has c(E_g)=(1-2H)^3(1+3H)^2 =1-15H^2+10H^3+60H^4-72H^5, which differs from c(T CP5). Even the rank-16 fibre resemblance does not identify F_g with the geometric half-spin bundle. Their second Chern-character components are \operatorname{ch}_2(F_g)=60H^2,\qquad \operatorname{ch}_2(\Sigma^+\mathbb{CP}^5)=12H^2. For the first value sum one-half the squares of all 16 line exponents. For the second, the half-spin weights give 2 sum(x_i^2), with x_i the tangent Chern roots; sum(x_i^2)=c1^2-2c2=6H^2. Both rank-16 bundles have c1=0, so a nontrivial line twist cannot equate them while preserving c1. The global matter carrier is genuinely additional data. 4. Fibre multiplicities are not zero-mode multiplicities If one were additionally to use the ordinary spin Dirac operator on CP5 twisted by a line L^q, its index would be \operatorname{ind}(D\otimes L^q)=\chi(\mathcal O(q-3)) =\binom{q+2}{5}, where the binomial is the polynomial extension for negative arguments and K^(1/2)=O(-3).
