The remaining symmetrized quadratic generator term and the scalar contraction in (10) come from the two possible contractions of the added coordinate factors. Together with (6), this yields  oxed{G= rac{(L+r)G_0+I/r}{L+r+1},\qquad G_1= rac{I/r-G_0}{L+r+1}.} 	ag{11} The complement has strictly positive norm for every nonzero traceless T. Otherwise f_T\chi would be holomorphic, and the real source-preservation theorem would force f_T to be constant. That is impossible for nonzero traceless T. Since G_0\ge0, each eigenvalue \gamma of G_1 consequently obeys  oxed{0<r\gamma\le rac1{L+r+1}<1.} 	ag{12} This bound controls the complete source spectrum without choosing one polarization or one angular harmonic. For the explicit section (4) and L\ge3, G_0 has eigenvalues  rac{L^2}{r(L+r)^2}\quad(r-1	ext{ copies}),\qquad  rac{L}{r(L+r)^2}\quad(r(r-1)	ext{ copies}). 	ag{13} Diagonal generators and off-diagonal generators give these two values. For L=2, the nonzero value is 4/[r(L+r)^2] with multiplicity (r-1)(r+2)/2; zero has multiplicity r(r-1)/2. The zero directions are the real orthogonal symmetries of the quadratic polynomial. Equation (11) gives the complementary eigenvalues in all cases. The complete spatial linearization has no exponential modes Linearize the field in the rotating frame of (3). Let U have columns u_a in orthonormal spatial source coordinates, with \chi embedded in the full retained zero space. The ordinary and conjugate variations are  egin{aligned} i\dot\eta&=A\eta+B ar\eta,\ A&=\mathscr D_L+g eta-gI+g\chi\chi^\dagger+grUU^\dagger,\ B&=g\chi\chi^T+grUU^T. \end{aligned} 	ag{14} The \chi terms retain the response of the scalar trace, including changes of the total norm. The U terms retain every traceless spatial moment and both quadratures. Freezing the moment matrix would remove these terms and give an incomplete stability test. Because the source Gram matrices are real, choose orthonormal coordinates in which their source vectors are real. On a first excited zero-form and its Dirac one-form partner, the free rotating operator is A_0= egin{pmatrix}0&\lambda\\lambda&-2g\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{15} The real quadrature in the retained zero space is constant under the linearized evolution. For a nonzero-frequency mode it must therefore vanish. Its conjugate quadrature can still respond; it is retained in (14). After diagonalizing G_1, the remaining pair at eigenvalue \gamma has squared-frequency matrix A_0\left[A_0+2gr\gamma  egin{pmatrix}1&0\0&0\end{pmatrix}ight]. Its two eigenvalues are  oxed{\Omega_\pm^2=\lambda^2+2g^2 \pm2|g|\sqrt{g^2+(1-r\gamma)\lambda^2}.} 	ag{16} By (12), the square root is real. The sum of the two eigenvalues is positive and their product is \lambda^4+4g^2r\gamma\lambda^2>0, so both are positive. Thus all nonzero source modes oscillate rather than grow exponentially, at every real coupling g. Norm, phase, polarization and possible Jordan directions remain at zero frequency; this is not a claim that every linear perturbation stays bounded for all time. Finally, the orthogonal complement of the exact source space in (8) has zero linear scalar-moment source. Self-adjointness of \mathscr D_L and invariance under  eta make it a reducing subspace. Its evolution is generated by the self-adjoint operator \mathscr D_L+g eta-gI. It therefore cannot add an exponential mode. This includes the other spatial harmonics and form polarizations omitted by a radial ansatz. The conclusion concerns the complete spatial linearization of (1). What is now available for the mass calculation These balanced fields have a common normalized frequency \omega=g without a profile-dependent cubic or higher-order correction. They therefore satisfy the spatial source-preservation requirement identified by the nonlinear reduction, and their complete linear spectrum passes the stability test above. Restoring the physical volume \mathcal V and a fixed canonical norm Q, the normalized moment convention gives \omega_{\mathrm{physical}}= rac{g_{\mathrm{physical}}Q}{\mathcal V}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{physical}}= rac{g_{\mathrm{physical}}Q^2}{2\mathcal V}. 	ag{17} If an independent master derivation supplied g_{\mathrm{physical},N}=\kappa D_N, this spatial family would preserve its linear count dependence at common Q and \mathcal V. That premise has not been supplied by this calculation. Compatibility with the occupied auxiliary coherent-ray prescription must also be established; coherence of that mode-bundle ray is distinct from coherence of a holomorphic spatial section on CP3. The frequency-energy distinction remains visible in (17). The observed rest mass, physical metric scale, occupied section degree, causal master kernel and nonlinear orbital stability are not determined here. Balance supplies a family of spatial shapes, not selection of a unique particle. Its isotropic first moment leaves higher spatial harmonics intact; their role in a reciprocal interaction must be calculated with the appropriate same-field source. The coherent spatial mode-bundle construction retains the curved tangent-mode carrier and gives a separate family with pointwise mode coherence and balanced spatial moments. Its exact norm makes the distinction between scalar and transported graph contractions explicit. That larger field bundle has a different spatial response, so the linear stability theorem above is not automatically its theorem. Verification balanced_spatial_mass_checks.py uses independent projective monomial integrals for the norm, balance, Toeplitz projection and full fourth-moment Gram matrix. A separate physical-chart derivative checks (7). The diagnostic assembles (14) with the entire holomorphic zero multiplet and both excited form components, then compares every nonzero eigenfrequency with (16), retaining the zero-frequency directions. The CP3 controls use L=2,3,4,6, including a complex spatial rotation of the quadratic field. Lower-complex-dimension controls test the general identities without reassigning any particle depth. The calculation is finite because the linear source closes exactly; the free orthogonal spatial complement is handled by the self-adjoint argument above.

title: Finite biased support and the mode-selection boundary
summary: One positive response bias can satisfy the field-orthogonality equations for a finite selected set at each depth, but the same bias fails the next unselected mode and therefore requires a derived mode-selection law.
text: The positive particle-sourced response fails spectral transparency when it has no independent bias. A natural extension is to add one common bias per depth. This note determines exactly what that buys and where it stops. Orthogonality with a common bias Let A>0 be the response stiffness, S_i the quadratic source of the selected mode i, and b a depth-wide bias. Eliminating the response gives the source energy U_{\mathrm{eff},i} =-\frac12\langle S_i+b,A^{-1}(S_i+b)\rangle. \tag{1} Under a field-amplitude variation, S_i scales as |a|^2. Vanishing of the resulting frequency shift requires \boxed{\langle S_i,A^{-1}b\rangle =-\langle S_i,A^{-1}S_i\rangle.} \tag{2} Writing u_i=A^{-1/2}S_i and q=A^{-1/2}b, these are linear conditions \langle u_i,q\rangle=-\|u_i\|^2. \tag{3} For a finite linearly independent set of u_i, a solution exists. The minimum-norm solution is obtained from the exact Gram system Gc=-r,\qquad G_{ij}=\langle u_i,u_j\rangle, \qquad r_i=\|u_i\|^2, \qquad q=\sum_jc_ju_j. \tag{4} This is a common bias for the depth, not an independently fitted bias for each selected mode. It can therefore be a legitimate inverse construction if a single action derives both the source vectors and the bias. The finite-set boundary The construction does not automatically support the next mode. Applying the same q to an additional source u_* requires \langle u_*,q\rangle+\|u_*\|^2=0. \tag{5} Using the maintained source controls (u_i)_\ell=\frac{i+\ell+d}{i+2\ell+d+1}, \qquad \langle u_i,u_j\rangle =\sum_{\ell\in H}\frac{(u_i)_\ell(u_j)_\ell} {\mathcal L_d(\ell)}, \tag{6} the first calculation used the finite harmonic control H=H_{d,I}=\{2,4,\ldots,2\max I\}. \tag{7} Its Gram matrices are nonsingular for every maintained depth. The exact finite-dimensional solution of (4) satisfies (3) for all selected indices at depths 2,3,4,5,6,10, but (5) is nonzero for the next index at every depth. This establishes a finite-control obstruction. It does not by itself establish the same statement for the infinite even-harmonic space. The minimum bias norm \|q\|^2 from (4) quantifies the cost of this finite construction. For the algebraic source controls in (6) and cutoff (7), it is: Depth Selected indices Minimum \|q\|^2 2 76, 81, 95 5.25 3 1, 4, 16, 17 2.21\times10^3 4 3, 20, 72 56.7 5 10, 15, 22 65.1 6 13, 35 13.5 10 23 1.19 These values are controls of the stated source model, not physical support energies. They show why the bias cannot be treated as an innocuous constant: its norm is a derived part of the action and must be included in the total energy and stress. Infinite even-harmonic completion The projected Jacobi inverse has the exact factorization \frac{1}{\mathcal L_d(2k)} =\frac{d}{(2k-1)(2k+d)}. \tag{8} Consequently the infinite inner product in (6), now with H=\{2,4,6,\ldots\}, converges because its summand is O(k^{-2}). Direct high-precision summation at 50 and 80 decimal digits gives the following cutoff-independent controls: Depth Minimum \|q\|^2 Gram condition estimate Next-mode residual 2 4.97618 1.19\times10^9 1.11\times10^{-6} 3 79.7667 4.21\times10^8 2.43\times10^{-5} 4 43.4310 1.87\times10^4 4.46\times10^{-4} 5 35.0233 2.97\times10^6 1.21\times10^{-4} 6 13.3677 7.50\times10^3 -7.02\times10^{-4} 10 1.22498 1 3.61\times10^{-3} The next-mode residual is the left side of (5). It remains nonzero at every maintained depth, so the finite-set boundary survives completion of the stated harmonic space. The large depth-two and depth-three condition numbers are a separate limitation: their solved biases are highly sensitive to small changes in the assumed source law. The calculation therefore establishes compatibility for these specified algebraic controls, not a robust physical selection mechanism. Stationarity is not amplitude stability The orthogonality condition cancels the first amplitude derivative, but the eliminated positive response has a fixed second derivative. Write s=|a|^2, so the selected source is s u_i, and subtract the constant energy of the bias alone. The response contribution is \Delta U_i(s) =-s\langle q,u_i\rangle-\frac12s^2\|u_i\|^2. \tag{9} Using (3) gives \left.\frac{d\Delta U_i}{ds}\right|_{s=1}=0, \qquad \left.\frac{d^2\Delta U_i}{ds^2}\right|_{s=1} =-\|u_i\|^2<0. \tag{10} For a real amplitude varied about a=1, the corresponding curvature is \left.\frac{d^2\Delta U_i(|a|^2)}{da^2}\right|_{a=1} =-4\|u_i\|^2. \tag{11} Thus the bias makes the normalized amplitude stationary but does not stabilize it. Within the response sector alone, the stationary point is a strict local maximum in the amplitude direction. A viable joint action needs a bare-field or constrained contribution whose positive curvature exceeds 4\|u_i\|^2 for every selected mode in the common normalization. This is the amplitude block of the full Schur-complement condition, not a complete instability proof for a model that includes such an additional term. This is a boundary of the common-bias transparency calculation. A physical action could select occupations through a nonlinear law, a finite band, a conserved charge sector, or a boundary condition. The failed cancellation does not establish that the next mode is absent: it could have a shifted frequency, remain unoccupied, be unstable, or describe an exotic branch. Continue that branch under the same action and test its stability and observable response. The bias and any occupation rule require a same-field derivation; choosing the bias after listing observed modes fits the spectrum. There is also a simple incompatibility when two sources are proportional. If u_j=\alpha u_i, equations (3) demand both \langle u_i,q\rangle=-\|u_i\|^2 and \alpha\langle u_i,q\rangle=-\alpha^2\|u_i\|^2. For a nonzero source, these agree only when \alpha=1. A common bias cannot transparently support arbitrary rescalings of one source direction. What this adds to the support problem The result leaves three conditional routes: an independently present background with a derived bias and a finite mode-selection law; a constrained or indefinite response for which the positive overlap argument no longer applies; or a nonlinear same-field support whose stationary equations generate the orthogonality conditions without mode-by-mode tuning. The first route is algebraically consistent for a finite selected set, but it introduces a new physical obligation: derive the bias and the selection mechanism together. It does not establish the mass operator, a complete particle, or a neutrino interaction rate. Verification biased_source_compatibility_checks.py solves the exact finite Gram systems and tests the next unselected mode at every maintained depth. The normal and optimized runs each pass 40 conditions. The selected exact report contains the source vectors, solved bias coefficients, and unselected-mode residuals. biased_source_infinite_checks.py performs the infinite even-harmonic sums independently at 50 and 80 decimal digits. Its normal and optimized runs each pass 48 convergence, compatibility and amplitude-curvature conditions. The selected infinite-space report contains the converged norms, coefficients, condition estimates and next-mode residuals. The source components are algebraic controls; they are not measured particle densities.

title: A constraint on smooth homogeneous spinor interactions
summary: Boost invariance and degree-two homogeneity force a potential that is differentiable on all nonzero spinor fields to be quadratic, precisely delimiting the role of the retained frame and null-current domain.
text: The retained frame in the regular current model is not merely an awkward way to write a spinor-only invariant. Within a precise class of local potentials, removing it while preserving both global regularity and the existing homogeneity removes the nonlinear interaction itself. This is a mathematical constraint on that class of actions. It does not forbid nonlinear spinor theories, a retained degree of the same field, or an effective action restricted to a regular current domain. It also does not identify the sign of a potential with the inertia of a particle. Assumptions and statement Let V be a finite complex spinor multiplet, including any finite number of partner columns and retained coefficient components that act as spectators under the chosen spinor boost. Let A be its Hermitian boost involution, A^2=I,\qquad B(t)=e^{tA/2},\qquad V=V_+\oplus V_-,\quad A|_{V_\pm}=\pm I. \tag{1} The parameter t is rapidity, not elapsed time. Consider a real local potential U:V\to\mathbb R, without field derivatives or an independently transforming frame, satisfying U(\lambda\Psi)=\lambda^2U(\Psi)\quad(\lambda>0), \qquad U(B(t)\Psi)=U(\Psi). \tag{2} Assume that U is differentiable at every nonzero field, including the pure boost eigenspaces. No second derivative at the total-field origin is assumed. Then U is a real bilinear pairing between V_+ and V_-. If it also has the canonical common phase symmetry U(e^{i\theta}\Psi)=U(\Psi), it is a Hermitian quadratic form \boxed{U(\Psi)=\Psi^\dagger H\Psi,\qquad H^\dagger=H,\quad \{H,A\}=0.} \tag{3} The flattened vector notation includes every spinor, partner and finite coefficient entry. This is not a restriction to a coherent ray. Proof from independent scaling of the boost eigenspaces Write \Psi=x+y, with x\in V_+ and y\in V_-. Combining a uniform scaling \lambda=\sqrt{ab} with rapidity t=\log(a/b) gives \boxed{U(ax+by)=ab\,U(x+y),\qquad a,b>0.} \tag{4} For a pure eigenspace vector, the boost is itself a uniform scaling. The two equations in (2) therefore force U(x)=U(y)=0. Fix a nonzero x. Differentiability there and (4) imply \begin{aligned} U(x+\epsilon y)&=\epsilon U(x+y),\quad\epsilon>0,\\ U(x+y)&=D U(x)[y]. \end{aligned} \tag{5} The derivative is a real-linear functional of y, so the potential is linear in its second argument. Applying the same argument at each nonzero y makes it linear in the first argument as well. Continuity extends the result when either argument is zero. Thus U(x+y)=b(x,y), where b is a real bilinear pairing. For complex fields, common phase invariance eliminates the pairings with two unconjugated or two conjugated factors. The remaining expression is 2\operatorname{Re}(x^\dagger K y). Its Hermitian matrix is H=\begin{pmatrix}0&K\\K^\dagger&0\end{pmatrix} \quad\text{in }V_+\oplus V_-. \tag{6} Equation (3) follows. Invariance under every physical boost further gives \{H,A_a\}=0 for each physical spatial direction a. This completes the classification under the stated hypotheses. A nonnegative potential makes the restriction stronger If H anticommutes with A, its eigenvalues occur in pairs: H v=\lambda v implies H(Av)=-\lambda Av. Consequently U(\Psi)\ge0\text{ for every }\Psi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H=0. \tag{7} No nonzero nonnegative potential satisfies all the hypotheses. A signed quadratic scalar potential is allowed, and can support positive-frequency particle branches. Equation (7) is not a statement that particle inertia can be negative. The complete branch energy and momentum determine that separate physical response. For the doubled spinor representations used in the current calculations, the full Hermitian spinor-matrix space anticommuting with all physical A_a has real dimension four at even depth and eight at the tested odd depths. Partner matrices supply additional constant quadratic coefficients. These counts are representation algebra, not spatial dimensions or a particle selection rule. If independent grade phases are also symmetries, the quadratic matrix cannot mix different grades. The current-root cusp is the explicit boundary Every scalar insertion B_j in the current model anticommutes with the boost involution. Let \Phi be a conformal-unitary upper core and put x=P_+^A\Phi, y=P_-^A\Phi, where P_\pm^A=(I\pm A)/2. The pure eigenspace currents vanish: x^\dagger B_jx=y^\dagger B_jy=0. For the root mass current F_q(C)=\sqrt{qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2}, the complete path \Phi_\epsilon=x+\epsilon y satisfies \boxed{F_q(C[\Phi_\epsilon]) =|\epsilon|F_q(C[\Phi]).} \tag{8} The one-sided derivatives at \epsilon=0 are opposite. The field x itself is nonzero. Thus the original root law retains its nonlinearity by failing differentiability on the null-current set, exactly where the classification requires it. The positive density normalization instead uses \rho_u=u\cdot j in a retained future timelike frame. The simultaneous transformation is (\Psi,u)\longmapsto(B\Psi,\Lambda u). Holding u fixed while boosting only \Psi is a different transformation and is not a symmetry of that regularized potential. It therefore lies outside (2). The frame dependence is explicit and mathematically consequential; assigning the frame its own response is still required by that candidate action. What the constraint leaves for the mass derivation The homogeneous local action gives the useful stationary identity E=\omega Q. The classification shows why extending a nonlinear version smoothly across every spinor current while retaining ordinary boost covariance requires additional structure or a changed hypothesis. An effective current law on a regular domain remains possible. So do higher-degree microscopic interactions, derivative interactions, and retained modes with their own transformation law. Their energy, kinetic normalization and source must be included when deriving the particle frequency and inertia. This is a restriction on proposed reconstructions, not a proof selecting one of those extensions. In particular, the simplex shell weights and their physical spatial carrier are still to be derived. A model with a frame must account for that frame within the same field; the theorem does not introduce another particle or an exchanged interaction. Verification boost_homogeneity_checks.py checks the complete Pauli representation of the physical boosts, the dimension and sign pairing of the allowed quadratic matrices, the exact null-current path (8), and simultaneous retained-frame transformations. The 228-check report passes at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. It supports the representation and examples; the classification itself is proved in (4)–(6).

title: The bottom geometric mean and cumulative-count response
summary: Positive canonical quadratures can produce the retained bottom geometric mean, but the actual surface-partner signs give a stringent phase-resolved coupling test and leave the spatial pairing to be derived.
text: The retained bottom count \sqrt{816\cdot969} can arise as the frequency of a positive canonical oscillator. This is different from the ordinary two-positive-frequency Hermitian mixing excluded by the cross-sector controls. It gives a concrete inverse target for the field's kinetic projection. It does not yet establish that the two spatial components are canonical quadratures of one physical particle. The coupling calculation is an equally important part of this target. Keeping the actual surface-partner signs gives a different answer from assuming that both quadratures have the same response. Frequency from two positive quadrature coefficients For real canonical coordinates q,p, let H=\frac12(ap^2+bq^2),\qquad a>0,\quad b>0. \tag{1} Hamilton's equations give \dot q=ap, \dot p=-bq, and hence \boxed{\omega=\sqrt{ab}.} \tag{2} The Hamiltonian is positive. The canonical rescaling Q=(b/a)^{1/4}q, P=(a/b)^{1/4}p gives H=\omega(P^2+Q^2)/2. Thus the action variable I=(P^2+Q^2)/2 obeys E=\omega I. The frequency is independent of oscillator magnitude; imposing I=1 would fix the normalization, not turn an amplitude into mass. For the circle surface operator B=-i\partial_\theta, put D_L=\frac{L(L-1)(L+1)}6. The bottom components have L=17,18, so choosing a=\omega_{0,3}D_{17}, b=\omega_{0,3}D_{18} gives \omega=\omega_{0,3}\sqrt{816\cdot969} =889.21538448\ldots\,\omega_{0,3}. This is a conditional frequency construction using the maintained counts. Its positive oscillator energy does not independently derive the full particle's relativistic inertia or the physical canonical pairing. An actual circle relation between the two components In the specified bounding spin structure, a spinor can be written \psi=e^{i\theta/2}F, with periodic F, and \mathscr D=B+1/2. Complex conjugation on the spinor induces \Theta F=e^{-i\theta}\overline F, \qquad \Theta B\Theta^{-1}=-B-1. \tag{3} Consequently B=17 and B=-18 are the two signs of one absolute Dirac level, |\mathscr D|=17.5. Their positive normal frequencies correspond to the counts 816 and 969, using the previously established reflection symmetry of the full normal singular spectrum. For j=L+1/2, the adjacent-count geometric mean has the exact form \sqrt{D_LD_{L+1}}= \frac{j^2-1/4}{6}\sqrt{j^2-9/4}. \tag{4} Equation (3) is a surface identity. It has not been extended here to a symmetry of the complete occupied normal texture or given a particle-charge interpretation. Nor does it by itself change the canonical inner product: ordinary distinct circle harmonics remain orthogonal. A symplectic pairing between the proposed quadratures must come from the full spatial kinetic term, including any real-structure or orientation constraint that is used. The complete phase-dependent geometric response Let \xi be one physical geometric deformation, with a'=\partial_\xi a and b'=\partial_\xi b. At fixed action I, write the solution as q=\sqrt{2I}(a/b)^{1/4}\cos\vartheta,\qquad p=-\sqrt{2I}(b/a)^{1/4}\sin\vartheta, \qquad \vartheta=\omega t+\vartheta_0. The instantaneous source is the partial derivative at fixed physical canonical coordinates q,p, evaluated on this orbit. Expressing it in action and phase after taking that derivative gives \begin{aligned} \partial_\xi H ={}&I\left[a'\sqrt{b/a}\sin^2\vartheta +b'\sqrt{a/b}\cos^2\vartheta\right]\\ ={}&\frac I2\left(a'\sqrt{b/a}+b'\sqrt{a/b}\right) +\frac I2\left(b'\sqrt{a/b}-a'\sqrt{b/a}\right) \cos(2\vartheta). \end{aligned} \tag{5} Its average is I\partial_\xi\omega, as follows independently by differentiating (2). Equation (5) keeps the actual temporal phase; it is not an interpretation of a static force sign as negative inertia. The bottom ratio is exactly b/a=969/816=19/16. If both coefficients had the same additive derivative a'=b'=F, their mean response would be \frac{\langle\partial_\xi H\rangle}{IF} =\frac{35}{8\sqrt{19}}=1.00369383568\ldots \tag{6} with twice-frequency coefficient -3/(8\sqrt{19}). This hypothetical equal-sign pairing would nearly preserve a common geometric response despite the geometric-mean frequency. The actual surface-conjugation candidate requires a separate sign test. The existing complete normal source satisfies F_{N,d}(-\beta)=(-1)^dF_{N,d}(+\beta). At depth three, the B=17 and B=-18 partners therefore have opposite signed responses to the same surface-independent normal deformation. In the common-leading-response limit, a'=F, b'=-F, so (5) instead gives \frac{\langle\partial_\xi H\rangle}{IF} =\frac{3}{8\sqrt{19}}=0.08603090020\ldots, \tag{7} and twice-frequency coefficient -35/(8\sqrt{19}). The average is suppressed while the oscillating source remains large. Finite-hopping differences between the two original derivatives can be inserted directly into (5); no equality of their exact values is assumed. Thus a positive geometric-mean oscillator is compatible with very different responses depending on its actual spatial pairing. The equal-sign result (6) must not be attributed automatically to the conjugation relation (3). An independent rotation or change of deformation coordinate must also be derived and compared using the same physical probe, rather than used to flip one sign by hand. The Hockey-Stick identity gives the general response factors The same calculation applies to adjacent cumulative bands at any depth. Write D_{N,d}=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}=\binom{N+d}{d}. Then \frac{D_{N+1,d}}{D_{N,d}}=\frac{N+d+1}{N+1},\qquad D_{N+1,d}-D_{N,d}=\binom{N+d}{d-1}. For a positive quadrature pair with coefficients proportional to these adjacent counts, and common-magnitude additive geometric derivatives, the two possible mean response factors are exactly R_+=\frac{2N+d+2}{2\sqrt{(N+1)(N+d+1)}},\qquad R_-=\frac{d}{2\sqrt{(N+1)(N+d+1)}}. \tag{8} They obey R_+^2-R_-^2=1. Equivalently, the opposite-sign factor is one shell count divided by twice the geometric mean of the neighboring integrated counts. Thus the IDOS interpretation gives an explicit combinatorial statement about the proposed coupling response, rather than only about the mass ratio. At large fixed-depth index, R_+ approaches one while R_- decreases as d/(2N). This is conditional on the positive quadrature pairing and the stated additive derivatives. It is not a scattering rate, a unique neutrino suppression mechanism, or permission to change the maintained single-band particle assignments. The 240-check count identity report verifies the exact sums, shell differences, ratios and response factors at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. What the common field model still has to supply Three conditions are required before (2) is a bottom mass mechanism. The physical kinetic projection must give the proposed canonical pair; the same spatial action must supply its two positive coefficients with consistent rotation and frame behavior; and its occupied branch must have the required mass and geometric response. Selection is not automatic. Applying the adjacent-count rule to down and strange as well would give counts 2 and \sqrt{700}, replacing their maintained counts 1 and 20. A common action would therefore need an actual branch distinction between paired and unpaired oscillation patterns. The surface identity alone does not provide that distinction. The quadrature diagnostic checks exact count identities, direct Hamiltonian trajectories, positive energy, unit canonical action, the circle conjugation map, and both complete phase-dependent response signs. It establishes these mathematical targets; it does not establish a spatial bottom solution or an observed coupling rate. The 30-check report preserves the exact identities and full phase-resolved trajectories.

title: Preserving the simplex factors in the full radial operator
summary: A bounded Hermitian completion preserves the rising-factorial leading mass coefficient with the full radial dressing retained; angular endpoint selection also supplies a common leading shape response within each depth.
text:
The simplex numerator can survive the complete radial normal field, rather than only its finite kernel projection. An explicit bounded completion of the spatial operator achieves this at the leading order in the normal-to-tangential scale ratio. Its radial coefficient is common to all particle indices at one depth. The completion is an inverse construction from the target angular structure. It is not a forward derivation from the master action. It retains the original highest-derivative part, but changes specified lower terms. Finite-scale corrections, the occupied supporting geometry and the physical shared scales remain to be derived. Mass is the resulting frequency in equivalent units throughout. The later spatial dimension and frame audit establishes the positive-dimensional reference surface formula, while identifying a missing surface harmonic tower at depth two. Its depth-two radial calculation therefore still uses a prescribed surface parameter. The same audit specifies how the angular operator must be transported under a local component-frame change. The full radial field has two protected endpoints Use the linked geometric operator D=D_{m geo}, normal chirality C, and the two existing canonical blocks described by \chi_i. These are field components, not additional spatial dimensions. In the \Gamma=-1 block their angular weights are l-(d-2)/2; in the \Gamma=+1 block they are l-d/2, with l=0,\ldots,d-1. Thus the perturbation norm is at most v=g\sqrt d, compared with the rigorous unperturbed gap \delta_d=2/\sqrt{d+1}. When v<\delta_d/2, each isolated one-dimensional endpoint cluster must stay at zero: chiral symmetry would require a nonzero eigenvalue to have an opposite partner in the same cluster. Interior sectors instead have leading splitting gh_l>0. Chirality removes the quadratic static Schur term, leaving the conservative remainder bound  rac{v^3}{\delta_d(\delta_d-v)}. 	ag{4} If this is smaller than g\min_l h_l, there are no interior zero modes. Both conditions hold for all six depths at the tested g=0.02 and 0.05, with the hopping integrals checked by independent radial refinement. The endpoint modes are therefore isolated and independent of the particle index. Their fields include positive normal-chiral components induced by g; those components are retained. This protection concerns the radial leading operator A_g. It is not yet protection of a photon under the complete occupied dynamics or an arbitrary nonradial deformation. Derive a bounded link from the angular factors The angular link B_-=-C\chi_-( eta+J) 	ag{5} lowers \mathscr K by one. Its scalar factor between weights k and k-1 is  eta+k-1/2. Connecting the two endpoints requires d lowering steps, which produces precisely \prod_{l=0}^{d-1}\left( eta+l- rac{d-1}{2}ight). 	ag{6} Using (5) directly as an added physical term would introduce an unbounded angular derivative. Instead, the geometric anticommutator gives a bounded completion. Put \mathcal R=-iS\alpha\cdot x,\qquad K_{m nat}=\{D,\mathcal R\}-2J =S+(a-d)	au_3-aI, \qquad S_-= rac12C\mathcal R\chi_-. 	ag{7} Here \mathcal R^2=r^2I, and S_-^2=0. The full differential commutator is [A_g,S_-]=- rac12C\{D,\mathcal R\}\chi_- - rac g2\mathcal R ar h. 	ag{8} Consequently the new neighboring link is the multiplication operator  oxed{\widetilde B_-=B_--[A_g,S_-] =-C eta\chi_-+ rac12CK_{m nat}\chi_- + rac g2\mathcal R ar h.} 	ag{9} There is one required two-step link:  oxed{C_{--}=-S_-A_gS_-= rac g4Cr^2 ar h\chi_-.} 	ag{10} Both (9) and (10) are bounded for the decaying linked curvature. Their coefficients follow from the same identity; they are not independently chosen for a particle or fitted to its mass. With \epsilon=1/\Lambda, the exact directed identity on the smooth decaying mode domain is (I+\epsilon S_-)(A_g+\epsilon B_-)(I-\epsilon S_-) =A_g+\epsilon\widetilde B_-+\epsilon^2C_{--}. 	ag{11} The coordinate multiplier S_- itself is unbounded on the whole plane. Equation (11) is used for its finite-order identity on the exponentially decaying modes, not as an assertion of bounded global similarity of two self-adjoint operators. The completed Hermitian parent Add each raising adjoint and restore the normal scale:  oxed{ H_{m c}=\Lambda A_g+ (\widetilde B_-+\widetilde B_-^\dagger) +\Lambda^{-1}(C_{--}+C_{--}^\dagger).} 	ag{12} Equivalently,  egin{aligned} H_{m c}={}&\Lambda D-\gamma CH_h-C eta\chi_1 + rac12CK_{m nat}\chi_1+g\mathcal R\operatorname{Re}h\ &+ rac g{4\Lambda}Cr^2(\chi_- ar h+\chi_+h), \qquad \gamma=g\Lambda. \end{aligned} 	ag{13} It is Hermitian and anticommutes with \Gamma. Every new spatial coefficient is bounded; the original normal and tangential principal symbols remain unchanged. On the negative normal kernel the new polarization agrees with the maintained -K\chi_1/2. Its extension off that kernel, and its additional curvature terms, are specified changes to the full parent. The coordinate multipliers refer to the chosen geometric normal origin. A rigid translation must move that origin and all profile coefficients together. Translating only W,A while holding the coordinate factors fixed tests a different, externally anchored operator. The moving-frame contributions must be retained in a later occupied-state calculation. A local phase change also transports the angular lift: J\mapsto UJU^\dagger, with U=\exp[-i(	au_3-I)\lambda/2]. Transforming only the profile and connection while keeping the literal J fixed changes the completed operator. The explicit covariance identity retains the reference spectrum and identifies the required frame data. At order \epsilon^d, any path joining the angular endpoints must lower at every step. A raising step would require at least two additional powers of \epsilon. The leading coefficient of the Hermitian operator (12) therefore equals that of the directed identity (11), and hence contains the product (6). This includes all interior radial resolvents and both dressed endpoint fields. For the maintained positive branch  eta=n+(d-1)/2, the result is  oxed{ \omega_{n,d}= rac cR\,  rac{|F_d(g)|}{\gamma^{d-1}}\, d! inom{n+d-1}{d} \left[1+O_{d,g,n}(\Lambda^{-2})ight].} 	ag{14} The radial coefficient F_d(g) is independent of n, with F_d(g)	o(-1)^{d-1}/\prod_lh_l as g	o0. The negative surface branch reverses the signs of the factors and has the same leading positive frequency. Neither surface sign is retuned. The complete spatial error bound makes this remainder explicit using the complementary gap and angular selection. The remainder notation holds at fixed nonzero g and fixed assigned index as \Lambda grows. It is not a bound uniform in arbitrarily large n, nor a claim of an exact finite-scale simplex law. At a formal zero of (6), the leading coefficient vanishes, but higher orders have not been shown to vanish. Such a root cannot yet be identified with an exactly massless photon. title: A canonical mode-field realization of the collective source
summary: A current-dependent oscillator square realizes the collective source inside one canonical mode field and preserves its frequencies exactly; replacing its moment interaction by an operator product creates an omitted source and shifts those frequencies.
text: The collective geometric source has an exact realization in a single canonical coefficient field. The realization specifies the interaction through mode averages. This assumption makes its coherent family invariant and keeps all the additional oscillator modes under control at linear order. The oscillator indices describe candidate modes of the same field. They are not extra physical dimensions or additional particles. Identifying these modes with the actual spatial carrier remains a separate derivation. In particular, a moment of a whole mode is not automatically a local interaction on the physical manifold. The complete action Let the finite carrier Hilbert space be V, with Hermitian frequency operator H_0 and two bounded Hermitian source matrices O_j. Retain one field \Xi\in V\otimes\mathcal F_1\otimes\mathcal F_2, \qquad Q=\langle\Xi,\Xi\rangle>0, \qquad g_j=\frac{\langle\Xi,O_j\Xi\rangle}{Q}. \tag{1} Here \mathcal F_j is the usual oscillator mode space and b_j its lowering operator. No occupation statistics or particle exchange is being assigned to this notation. The matrices O_j act on V and the b_j on the oscillator factors. For common positive K,\Omega, define u=\frac1{\sqrt{2K\Omega}},\qquad A_j=b_j+u g_j, \qquad \boxed{E[\Xi]=\langle\Xi,H_0\Xi\rangle +\Omega\sum_j\|A_j\Xi\|^2.} \tag{2} Use the canonical kinetic term \tfrac i2\langle\Xi,\overleftrightarrow{\partial_t}\Xi\rangle. The current-dependent displacement in (2) is a stated inverse kernel. It is homogeneous of degree two in \Xi; it is not a primitive quartic interaction with a discarded source norm. Write h_j=\operatorname{Re}\langle\Xi,A_j\Xi\rangle/Q. The full field equation is \boxed{i\dot\Xi=H_0\Xi+\Omega\sum_j \left[A_j^\dagger A_j\Xi+2u h_j(O_j-g_j)\Xi\right].} \tag{3} The second term inside the brackets is required by variation of the current in A_j. Both Q and the complete energy are conserved. Homogeneity gives \operatorname{Re}\langle\Xi,i\dot\Xi\rangle=E. Exact frequency preservation For a normalized carrier eigenvector H_0\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n, take the oscillator coherent states with amplitudes \alpha_j=-u g_{j,n}, where g_{j,n}=\langle\psi_n,O_j\psi_n\rangle. Then \Xi_n=\psi_n\otimes|\alpha_1,\alpha_2\rangle, \qquad A_j\Xi_n=0. \tag{4} Every added term in the energy and its first variation vanishes. Consequently \Xi_n(t)=e^{-i\lambda_nt}\Xi_n(0),\qquad E_n=\lambda_n Q. \tag{5} Mass is this selected frequency in equivalent units. Its value does not come from adjusting Q. The construction preserves whichever spectrum the stated H_0 actually has. Applied to the linked carrier it therefore preserves its finite-hopping corrections as well; it does not turn them into an exact simplex law or derive the carrier's mode assignments. The collective kinetic term follows from the same field On a product coherent state write \alpha_j=\sqrt{I\Omega/2}\,a_j +\frac{i p_j}{\sqrt{2I\Omega}},\qquad I=K/\Omega^2. \tag{6} Choose the coherent-state phase convention whose Berry one-form is p\cdot da. The product field's canonical one-form is then \frac i2\psi^\dagger\overleftrightarrow{d}\psi +Qp\cdot da. Thus P=Qp is the geometric canonical momentum, including when the field normalization is varied. Equation (2) restricts exactly to E=\psi^\dagger H_0\psi+ \frac{Q}{2K}|Ka+g|^2+\frac{|P|^2}{2IQ}. \tag{7} This supplies the earlier collective norm factors from an explicit canonical field ansatz. The coherent family is also dynamically invariant: the complete generator obtained by expanding (3) is a sum of a state-dependent operator on V, a forced harmonic oscillator operator, and a scalar. Such evolution preserves product states, and a forced harmonic oscillator preserves coherent states. More generally, even an entangled initial coefficient field evolves by a product of time-dependent unitary operators on its factors. The eigenvalues of its reduced density matrices, or Schmidt weights, are conserved. This strong restriction follows from the chosen moment interaction. It is a physical modeling assumption to assess, not a generic property of local field interactions. All additional modes have a known linear response Displace the oscillator basis so that (4) is \psi_n\otimes|0,0\rangle. Let v_j=(O_j-g_{j,n})\psi_n. The variation of each completed square is \delta(A_j\Xi)=b_j\eta+ 2u\,\Xi_n\operatorname{Re}\langle v_j\otimes0,\eta\rangle \quad(Q=1). \tag{8} Its active subspace consists of every other carrier vector tensored with the oscillator vacuum, together with the occupied carrier vector and one quantum in either oscillator. Its complete real Hessian is exactly the collective Hessian already derived from (7). Every remaining mode is a spectator at linear order. Its rotating frequency is \boxed{\nu_{l,k}=\lambda_l-\lambda_n+\Omega(k_1+k_2).} \tag{9} It evolves by multiplication by a phase. Coincident frequencies, including zero, do not create a coupling between these spectators. Thus the proven finite collective stability result extends to the entire oscillator complement of this particular moment model. This statement includes both signs of every retained carrier frequency. It does not establish stability in the physical normal complement that has not been identified with these oscillator modes. Equal restricted energies do not determine the full source A superficially similar action replaces the product of moments by an operator product. Put c=\sqrt{\Omega/(2K)}, X_j=b_j+b_j^\dagger and N_j=b_j^\dagger b_j. That comparison is E_{\rm op}=\left\langle H_0+\Omega\sum_jN_j +c\sum_jO_jX_j\right\rangle Q +\frac Q{2K}\sum_jg_j^2. \tag{10} Angle brackets in (10) are normalized field expectations. Its difference from (2) is precisely the covariance E_{\rm op}-E=cQ\sum_j \left(\langle O_jX_j\rangle-\langle O_j\rangle\langle X_j\rangle\right). \tag{11} It vanishes on product fields, but its first variation need not vanish there. At the proposed stationary product (4), the omitted full-field source is R=c\sum_j (O_j-g_j)\psi_n\otimes|1_j;\alpha\rangle, \qquad \boxed{\|R\|^2=c^2\sum_j\operatorname{Var}_{\psi_n}(O_j).} \tag{12} For the two-endpoint limit H_0=D\sigma_z, with source operators \sigma_z,\sigma_x, the variance sum is one. The product is therefore not an exact stationary state of (10). Solving that action's full nonlinear stationary equation at K=16,\Omega=1/4 gives a frequency increase 0.00442969434406 at D=1, and 0.000262336796110 at D=15. Refining the oscillator cutoff preserves these shifts. An independent small-transverse-coupling expansion includes the complete longitudinal oscillator displacement. Its second-order coefficient is \delta\omega^{(2)}=c^2\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^m/m!}{2D+2/K-\Omega(m+1)}, \qquad \mu=\frac2{K\Omega}, \tag{13} away from a denominator resonance. The checked small-coupling solutions approach (13). The comparison demonstrates why restricting an energy to a coherent ansatz is insufficient: the source normal to that ansatz must also vanish. A local spatial current requires its own calculation, as developed in the locality tests. Verification moment_square_checks.py checks arbitrary complex variations, normalization, Schmidt invariance, the exact collective block, every retained spectator through two quanta per oscillator, and maintained simplex endpoint counts across depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. Its 141-check report passes. The infinite spectator statement follows from (8)–(9), rather than from extrapolating that finite cutoff. oscillator_parent_checks.py independently verifies (10), its full real-linear Hessian, stationary energy accounting and the expansion (13). Its 21-check report also records the complete signed response at three oscillator cutoffs for D=1. Those finite spectra do not supply an infinite-cutoff theorem for (10).

title: Inertia of a moving cavity
summary: A moving-well sum rule gives count-additive inertia for quadratic kinetics, while an exact Dirac cavity derives inertia from confined field motion and exposes the confinement stress needed for a closed particle.
text:
Summary: A moving-well sum rule gives count-additive inertia for quadratic kinetics, while an exact Dirac cavity derives inertia from confined field motion and exposes the confinement stress needed for a closed particle. The inertial quantity to calculate The mass-frequency relationship is already available: \omega_m=mc^2/\hbar. The proposed spectrum is  egin{aligned} m(n,d)&=\mu_dD_N,\ D_N&= inom{N+d}{d},\qquad N=n-1. \end{aligned} 	ag{1} A route to its dynamics is to calculate the momentum response of an oscillating spatial pattern when its overall velocity changes. Continuous internal oscillation is compatible with zero total momentum. In a translation-invariant setting, the target coefficient is \left. rac{\partial P_i}{\partial v_j}ight|_{v=0} =\mu_dD_N\delta_{ij}. 	ag{2} The following two controls isolate the required calculation. They are declared spatial wave equations, rather than derived IDWT particles. The quadratic comparison contains a kinetic mass parameter. The Dirac comparison admits zero bare mass and has explicit spatial confinement. Its confining background is prescribed, so its momentum must not be silently identified with that of a closed particle plus its well. All coordinates used below are ordinary spatial coordinates. The controls do not change the particle depth assignments, impose compactification, or make one particle a constituent of another. An exact translation sum rule Consider a fixed Hermitian multiplication potential V(x) and H_X= rac{p^2}{2m_{m kin}}+V(x-X),\qquad p=-i\hbar
abla. 	ag{3} Assume its selected discrete states are separated from the complementary spectrum. Moving to coordinates y=x-X(t) gives, at constant velocity, the generator H_v=H_0-v\cdot p. 	ag{4} Complete the momentum square, keeping its phase transformation:  egin{aligned} U_v&=\exp(i m_{m kin}v\cdot y/\hbar),\ H_v&=U_vH_0U_v^\dagger- rac12m_{m kin}|v|^2. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} Every selected eigenvalue therefore changes by the same amount, \epsilon_a(v)=\epsilon_a(0)-m_{m kin}|v|^2/2, and its full moving field is U_vu_a. This statement holds for an anharmonic or quasiperiodically perturbed well as well as for a harmonic one. Suppose there are D equally occupied orthogonal modes, each with canonical norm q. The occupied generator trace and the resulting translation term in the effective action are \mathcal E(v)=q\sum_{a=1}^{D}\epsilon_a(0) - rac12qDm_{m kin}|v|^2, \qquad L_{m trans}= rac12qDm_{m kin}|v|^2. 	ag{6} Hence  oxed{M_{ij}=qDm_{m kin}\delta_{ij}.} 	ag{7} The equal contribution follows from the kinetic translation symmetry; it does not require equal individual eigenfrequencies. For a cumulative oscillator band, D=D_N gives the simplex multiplier exactly. The two physical inputs in this comparison remain explicit. The single-mode inertia m_{m kin} is present in (3), and equal occupation q is a stated preparation. At fixed total norm Q=qD, (7) is M=m_{m kin}Q and has no count enhancement. The calculation does not select q, identify canonical norm with electric charge, or derive a physical kinetic mass from the IDWT master field. The spectral response includes every complementary mode Differentiating (4) by ordinary eigenvalue perturbation theory gives another expression for the same inertia. Let P denote the occupied spectral subspace and put \Delta_{ba}=\epsilon_b-\epsilon_a. Summing over the occupied modes cancels transitions internal to P: M_{ij}(0)=2q\operatorname{Re} \sum_{a\in P,\ b
otin P}  rac{\langle a|p_i|bangle\langle b|p_j|aangle} {\Delta_{ba}}. 	ag{8} For a time-reversal-invariant real well, the symmetric response at angular frequency \Omega is M_{ij}(\Omega)=2q\operatorname{Re} \sum_{a\in P,\ b
otin P}  rac{\Delta_{ba}\langle a|p_i|bangle\langle b|p_j|aangle} {\Delta_{ba}^2-(\hbar\Omega)^2}. 	ag{9} The retarded continuation specifies how a pole is approached. Equation (7) constrains (9) at zero frequency; it does not make the entire response independent of the well. Eigenfunction overlaps and transition gaps remain in the finite-frequency result. No division of a response by a fitted particle mass has been used to obtain (7). For an isolated excited level, rather than an occupied trace, the sum is over every other level and retains the signed denominators. Dropping lower or negative-energy levels changes that response. A first-order Dirac cavity with no bare mass Set \hbar=c=1 for this section. On one ordinary spatial coordinate, consider the local two-component operator H=\sigma_xp+b\sigma_yx+m_0\sigma_z, \qquad b>0. 	ag{10} The linear pseudoscalar profile confines the wave. The parameter m_0 is a stated constant mass offset, and can be set to zero. The complete operator retains both Dirac signs; these signs receive no particle–antiparticle interpretation here. With oscillator length b^{-1/2}, (10) couples the upper Hermite mode h_{n-1} to the lower mode h_n. The two eigenvalues for n\ge1 are E_{n,\pm}=\pm\sqrt{m_0^2+2bn}. 	ag{11} There is also an unpaired lowest state. The finite-basis calculations below explicitly check the spatial residual of each selected paired state so that an artificial cutoff state cannot replace it. For the prescribed translated well b(x-vt), let r=\sqrt{1-v^2} and use the generator H-vp. Its exact paired spectrum is  oxed{\mathcal E_{n,\pm}(v) =\pm r\sqrt{m_0^2+2bnr}.} 	ag{12} This formula follows from the full Dirac transformation, including the well. In coordinates x'=\gamma(x-vt), its slope is b'=b/\gamma. The stationary frequency there is E'=\pm\sqrt{m_0^2+2b'n}. Writing t'=t/\gamma-\gamma v(x-vt) gives (12). In terms of a normalized stationary spinor u_{n,b'}, the actual moving profile is \phi_{n,v}(y) =e^{iE'\gamma vy} e^{ rac12\operatorname{artanh}(v)\sigma_x} u_{n,b'}(\gamma y),\qquad y=x-vt. 	ag{13} The boost phase, the two spinor components and the changed spatial width all matter. Replacing (13) by an unchanged real envelope loses part of the momentum response. For the positive branch, differentiating the moving eigenvalue gives the momentum of this field: P_n(v)=- rac{d\mathcal E_n(v)}{dv} =v\left[  rac{\sqrt{m_0^2+2bnr}}{r} + rac{bn}{\sqrt{m_0^2+2bnr}} ight]. 	ag{14} Consequently its adiabatic translation coefficient is  oxed{M_n=E_n+ rac{bn}{E_n}.} 	ag{15} The second term is precisely the integrated kinetic stress: \langle\sigma_xpangle=bn/E_n. It follows either from the two Hermite components or from the spatial virial identity. In particular,  oxed{m_0=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M_n= rac32E_n>0.} 	ag{16} This derives nonzero translational inertia from a confined, continuously oscillating Dirac field with no bare mass offset. It does not derive the inertia of a closed physical particle: the source maintaining the linear well has been held external to (10). The confinement stress belongs in the particle calculation For a stationary localized stress-energy distribution, a small boost gives a translational momentum coefficient  rac{\partial P_i}{\partial v_j} = rac1{c^2}\left(E\delta_{ij} +\int T^{ij}\,d^dxight). 	ag{17} For a complete conserved tensor in a flat translation-invariant domain, the integrated stationary stresses vanish under the required decay conditions. To see the condition, integrate \partial_k(x^iT^{kj})=T^{ij}+x^i\partial_kT^{kj}. Conservation and a vanishing boundary term give \int T^{ij}=0 for a stationary tensor. A periodic localized tensor gives the corresponding cycle-averaged identity. The covariant total momentum of a closed system then gives M=E/c^2. The geometric hypotheses and background-field qualifications are developed by Giulini. The positive stress in (15) is therefore a specific term that a self-contained confinement calculation must balance. Within IDWT, the balancing contribution must come from the same master field and its spatial geometry. An uncounted external wall is not that derivation. On a curved sector, the available translation or Killing symmetries and the appropriate momentum definition must be stated separately. Numerical and full-field checks The scalar control uses a two-dimensional oscillator with a bounded quasiperiodic perturbation of operator norm at most 0.3. Its cumulative degree-four band has fifteen states and remains separated by a gap. Two choices of the three phases change the spatial eigenfunctions and occupied energy sums, but give M(0)=15I 	ag{18} to below 5	imes10^{-13} in the final spatial basis. At \Omega=0.6, their xx responses are approximately 23.86076 and 23.69556, respectively. Thus count-additive inertia coexists with different finite-frequency response in this specified action. The driven calculation evolves all fifteen complex occupied columns under H-v(t)p_x, with v(t)=10^{-3}\sin(0.4t) through one period. Halving the drive amplitude reduces the leading response error by approximately four, as expected for the first nonlinear correction. The linear prediction differs from the refined full momentum by 7.24	imes10^{-8}. Time refinement changes the complete fields by about 1.00	imes10^{-9}. Increasing the spatial cutoff from 24 to 32 changes the complete fields, after a fixed initial spectator-basis alignment, by 5.47	imes10^{-7} in the reported norm. The actual complex trajectories and bases are retained with the report. The Dirac checks use slopes b=0.8, offsets m_0=0,0.7, levels n=1,4,12, and velocities through |v|=0.5. Complete signed spectral sums reproduce (15). Independent coordinate quadrature verifies the norm, momentum, uncompressed spatial Dirac equation and the analytic complex spinor (13). The final residuals and profile errors are of order 10^{-14} to 10^{-13}, with spatial cutoffs 64 and 96 agreeing. For example, at m_0=0.7,n=1, the energy is 1.44568323 and the inertia is 1.99905480. Negative-energy intermediate modes contribute -0.09890517 to that inertia. Omitting them would give a different answer even though the occupied branch is positive. The implementations are cavity_inertia.py and cavity_inertia_checks.py. Consequence for the inverse mass problem The count in (1) can enter a collective inertial trace without being the eigenvalue of a rank-one point-contact operator. Equation (7) establishes that possibility for a concrete kinetic law. Equations (10)–(17) identify the extra calculation required when inertia comes from the actual Dirac field motion: its full spatial spectrum and confinement stress must be included. The route remains conditional on deriving the common per-mode inertia, the occupied mode content, the physical cavity and its same-field confinement. A count of available states alone supplies none of these dynamical inputs. The complementary Dirac calculation provides a related normal-mode energy and response construction; the homogeneous inverse action instead supplies prescribed simplex frequencies with a different mass mechanism. The exact oscillator level moments are relevant when computing the energy of an occupied cavity. Summing oscillator energies and counting equally weighted modes are distinct operations. Finally, the spatial localization conditions remain necessary when promoting a finite mode or external-well control to an actual localized same-field particle.

title: A smooth two-current polynomial with conditional mass and reciprocal pair response
summary: A positive polynomial of two same-field scalar currents gives a conditional energy-frequency identity and polarized pair response, but its coherent core has an exact fixed-norm lower-field energy saddle; a simple third-current repair creates frozen growth.
text: The two-current quartic produces a simplex self frequency and a polarized pair term on a stipulated coherent constant-density spatial zero mode. At canonical norm one, its quartic energy is half its standing frequency. A nonhomogeneous current function can remove that algebraic discrepancy at a density stationary under support-volume variation. The following construction is an inverse action candidate, not a derivation of the physical particle state or master interaction. One local function and its complete source At retained order k, write C_k=\Psi^\dagger B_0\Psi and K_k=\Psi^\dagger B_2\Psi with the retained current maps understood. Both matrices are Hermitian Lorentz scalars in the specified doubled-field representation. Define L_{\pm,k}=C_k\pm K_k and, in units of one common current scale, f_\epsilon(y)=y^2[(y-1)^2+\epsilon] =y^4-2y^3+(1+\epsilon)y^2, \qquad 0<\epsilon<\frac13. \tag{1} For h_{k,d}=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}, the candidate action is \boxed{U=g_d\sum_{k\ge0}h_{k,d}\operatorname{Tr} \left[f_\epsilon(L_{+,k})+f_\epsilon(L_{-,k})\right].} \tag{2} One f_\epsilon governs self and pair terms. It is a polynomial in the current, hence smooth through zero field and current cancellation. Equation (1) is nonnegative for every real eigenvalue, so (2) is nonnegative even for indefinite currents. The complete local field source, before lifting through the retained maps, is \frac{\partial U}{\partial\Psi^\dagger} =g_d\sum_k h_{k,d}\left[ (B_0+B_2)\Psi f_\epsilon'(L_{+,k}) +(B_0-B_2)\Psi f_\epsilon'(L_{-,k})\right]. \tag{3} The executable batch checks the full complex field derivative and actual grade-zero retained source maps at all six maintained depths. For odd d, it uses the doubled Clifford representation of rank 2^{(d+1)/2}: an irreducible odd-dimensional spinor has no matrix that anticommutes with every spatial Dirac matrix, so the spatial involution requires both inequivalent Clifford blocks. The earlier rank-2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor} odd-depth matrix control did not represent this spatial algebra. The physical reason for this doubling and its canonical norm must still be established. The polynomial and equal channel coefficients remain choices in this inverse construction. The current unit, strength, shell weights and sector scales have no forward master derivation. A selected density and exact energy-frequency identity Assume a spatial zero mode whose upper-only partner field is pointwise \phi=\sqrt\rho U, with U a square unitary frame and constant \rho. Then L_+=2\rho P_+ and L_-=2\rho P_- on the occupied oscillator ray, where P_++P_-=I_r. Put y=2\rho and D_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}h_{k,d}=\binom{N+d}{d}. Equations (2)–(3) give \omega_N=2g_d f_\epsilon'(y)D_N,\qquad U_N=g_d r f_\epsilon(y)D_N,\qquad Q=r\rho\mathcal V_d. \tag{4} The displayed energy takes unit spatial volume; restoring \mathcal V_d multiplies it by that volume. At fixed canonical norm, the local interaction energy per norm is proportional to f_\epsilon(y)/y. Its nonzero stationary densities solve f_\epsilon(y)=y f_\epsilon'(y): y_\pm=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{1-3\epsilon}}{3}. \tag{5} y_+ is the local minimum and y_- the intervening local maximum. At y_+, if the spatial kinetic eigenvalue is zero, (4) gives the exact conditional identity E_N=\omega_N Q. A physical field normalization, spatial volume and relation among depths must determine it; setting it algebraically does not derive those quantities. For Q=1, unit volume would require r\rho=1, which is false at ranks other than the matching value. Thus the unit-volume calculation alone is not a one-particle normalization across depths. On an unbounded flat carrier, a smooth field of fixed norm can spread over volume V, making its density y\propto V^{-1}. Equation (1) gives U\sim\mathrm{const}/V\to0, while a massless first-order spatial kinetic expectation can also tend to zero with increasing size. The finite-density y_+ branch is only a local interaction-energy minimum; this action without a derived spatial support cannot make it the global isolated particle minimum. The constant-density CP3 field is a concrete noncoherent spatial zero mode, but it has neither the required square-unitary current pattern nor the simplex enhancement of (4). Reciprocal prepared-pair energy For equal-density coherent upper fields with matching spatial involutions, let s=|z^\dagger w|^{2k} be their ray overlap at order k. Their two nonzero current eigenvalues are y(1\pm\sqrt s) in each occupied spatial channel. Subtracting the isolated energies and using (5) yields \boxed{V_{AB,k}^{\rm match} =2g_d r y^3s[(3+s)y-2]h_{k,d}\ge0.} \tag{7} The inequality holds for y=y_+>2/3 and 0\le s\le1. The expression is symmetric and its complete source varies both fields. For opposite spatial involutions, L_+ and L_- place the two fields in orthogonal current channels and the prepared cross term vanishes exactly, even when their oscillator rays overlap. At (6), equation (7) per partner rank is 77/60 for s=1 and 693/4000 for s=3/10. The actual retained grade-zero calculation uses s=1, independently of the full coherent-ray angle, and checks both reciprocal derivatives. This is a polarization-sensitive pair energy, not a measured vertex or interaction rate. Matching gives a positive cross cost under this preparation. The spatial orientations, phase-bearing photon states, encounter trajectories and nested cross-depth maps remain unselected. Frozen stability boundary At the selected density, the normalized density curvature simplifies to q_\epsilon=\frac{y_+f_\epsilon''(y_+)}{f_\epsilon'(y_+)} =\frac{3y_+-2}{1-y_+}. \tag{8} Thus q_\epsilon\le1 exactly when \epsilon\ge5/16. This numerical result is consistent with (8); it is not an all-momentum stability theorem. The odd-depth checks in the batch establish Clifford algebra and retained maps in the doubled representation, not odd-dimensional spatial spectra. Neither complete spatial stability, positive collective inertia nor the physical photon response follows from a uniform frozen test. Fixed-norm energy saddle and a third-current control There is a decisive missing direction in the apparent stable window. Let the full-rank upper field be \sqrt\rho I_r and choose a unit vector v in the \beta=+1 spinor subspace. Add a lower field t vv^\dagger, while multiplying the upper field by a_t=\sqrt{1-t^2/(r\rho)}. This keeps the total canonical norm Q=r\rho exactly fixed. With P_v=vv^\dagger, the two currents have spectra equivalent to L_+=y a_t^2P_+, \qquad L_-=y a_t^2P_- -2t^2P_v. \tag{9} Thus one shell has the exact energy U(t)=g_d\{r f_\epsilon(y-2t^2/r)+f_\epsilon(-2t^2)\} =U(0)-2g_df_\epsilon'(y)t^2+O(t^4). \tag{10} At the unit-frequency normalization in (6), the coefficient is -1. The batch checks the fixed norm and approaches that coefficient at all six depths; at t=0.001 the computed coefficients lie between -0.999991 and -0.999990. If the upper spatial field is a zero mode of an off-diagonal Dirac kinetic operator, its kinetic cross term with an arbitrary lower perturbation vanishes by self-adjointness. The lower-only quadratic kinetic term also vanishes for that off-diagonal operator. Consequently the same negative direction persists for that spatial zero-mode realization. Real frozen frequencies do not remove this constrained energy saddle. The existing third scalar current J=\Psi^\dagger B_1\Psi suggests one simple repair. Add g_da\operatorname{Tr}J^2 to (2). It vanishes with zero first source on the isolated upper field, and does not change the prepared upper-field pair formula (7). In the direction (9), its energy curvature changes the coefficient to -1+4g_d\rho a. Energetic repair requires \boxed{a>\frac{f_\epsilon'(y)}{y}.} \tag{11} The complete frozen tests expose the countervailing response. At \epsilon=8/25 the threshold is a=0.391111\ldots; the frozen uniform field already has high-momentum growth about 0.5 at that value. At \epsilon=0.33 the threshold is a=0.42: a=0.41 retains a negative energy direction, while a=0.43 has positive curvature in that direction but sampled growth 0.153653 at intermediate momentum and 0.077152 at momentum 1000. Depths two, four and six give the same values within numerical precision. The tested simple J^2 completion therefore has no interval with both positive curvature in this direction and no resolved frozen growth. This is a bounded result for that completion, not a theorem excluding all same-field actions. As a diagnostic, equal squares of J_x=\Psi^\dagger (\sigma_x\otimes\beta)\Psi and J_y=\Psi^\dagger(\sigma_y\otimes\beta)\Psi have a tuned coefficient a=2f_\epsilon'(y)/y. At \epsilon=0.33 this is a=0.84. The complete local rotating Hessian is nonnegative in the tested rank-two, four and eight blocks, and sampled frozen frequencies are real; moving the coefficient by 0.01 restores a negative Hessian direction or growth. This apparent completion is not Lorentz scalar in the action's boost representation. For boost generator G=\sigma_x\otimes\alpha_1, \{G,\sigma_y\otimes\beta\}\ne0, whereas the corresponding anticommutators vanish for B_0,B_1,B_2. A direct boost changes J_y at every tested depth. The symmetric result therefore identifies a response that would be needed, not an admissible physical term in this same-field action. There is a different fourth bilinear, J_0=\Psi^\dagger (\sigma_y\otimes I)\Psi, which is scalar under these boosts. Testing its square alongside J_x^2 leaves the minimum rotating Hessian at -2 in particle-frequency units for every tested coefficient. The remaining negative direction has a direct algebraic explanation that applies to a much larger class than (2). Restricted no-go for algebraic scalar currents Let F(C,K,J_x,J_0) be any differentiable local function of these four Hermitian Lorentz-scalar currents. Suppose its coherent upper-only square-unitary branch \Psi_0=(\sqrt\rho I_r,0)^\mathsf T has a positive standing self frequency \omega and the canonical norm Q=r\rho. At even depth in the irreducible complex spatial Clifford representation, these four exhaust the Hermitian bilinear scalar insertions for the stipulated boosts. Indeed, decompose an insertion as I\otimes A_0+\sigma_x\otimes A_x+ \sigma_y\otimes A_y+\sigma_z\otimes A_z. Anticommutation with every boost generator \sigma_x\otimes\alpha_i requires A_0,A_x to anticommute with every \alpha_i, hence each is proportional to \beta; A_y,A_z commute with every \alpha_i, hence each is proportional to I. The odd-depth doubled representation can have additional commutant structure, so the theorem below is stated for these four currents there. Choose one Hermitian spatial Clifford matrix \alpha_1 that anticommutes with \beta. The fixed-norm variation \Psi_t=\begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{1-t^2/(r\rho)}\sqrt\rho I_r\\ t\alpha_1/\sqrt r \end{pmatrix} \tag{12} has, exactly, C_t=\left(\rho-\frac{2t^2}{r}\right)I_r, \quad K_t=\left(\rho-\frac{2t^2}{r}\right)\beta, \quad J_{x,t}=J_{0,t}=0. \tag{13} Thus every action in this restricted class follows its original coherent current ray toward smaller density. On that ray the standing source implies dU/d\rho=r\omega. Consequently \boxed{U(\Psi_t)-U(\Psi_0)=-2\omega t^2+O(t^4)<0.} \tag{14} The batch checks (12)–(14) at depths two, three, four, five, six and ten, both with the original polynomial and after adding tested J_x^2, J_0^2 and \operatorname{Tr}(C^2-K^2) coefficients. The computed quadratic coefficients approach -2 throughout. If the upper field is an exact spatial zero mode of an off-diagonal Dirac operator, that quadratic kinetic energy also vanishes by self-adjointness. The result obstructs a constrained energy minimum for that upper-only zero-mode class. It does not prove exponential growth, exclude occupied lower components or rule out derivative or Lorentz-tensor interactions with a different complete response. The same direction has a broader Lorentz explanation. Let G=\sigma_x\otimes\alpha_1 be a Hermitian boost generator, G^2=I, and set S_\theta=e^{\theta G/2}. For an upper-only field, \langle\Psi_0,G\Psi_0\rangle=0, so Q(S_\theta\Psi_0)=Q_0\cosh\theta. The normalized field \widehat\Psi_\theta=(\cosh\theta)^{-1/2}S_\theta\Psi_0 \tag{15} has exactly the original canonical norm. Let U be any differentiable algebraic Lorentz-scalar potential made only from the field, with no derivatives or fixed Lorentz-breaking background. Pointwise boost invariance gives U(\widehat\Psi_\theta)= U((\cosh\theta)^{-1/2}\Psi_0). If its occupied stationary source is \omega\Psi_0 with \omega>0, amplitude variation gives dU(\lambda\Psi_0)/d\lambda|_{\lambda=1}=2\omega Q_0. Since (\cosh\theta)^{-1/2}=1-\theta^2/4+O(\theta^4), \boxed{U(\widehat\Psi_\theta)-U(\Psi_0) =-\frac12\omega Q_0\theta^2+O(\theta^4)<0.} \tag{16} This is the same coefficient as (14) after expressing the lower-field norm in terms of \theta. For an upper zero mode of a self-adjoint off-diagonal spatial Dirac operator, the kinetic cross term with the induced lower field vanishes, and a lower-only field has no quadratic kinetic expectation. A smooth local boost in a spatial patch suffices when a global tangent frame is unavailable. Equation (16) therefore extends the fixed-geometry constrained-energy obstruction to every algebraic Lorentz-scalar field potential in this upper-only zero-mode class. It does not apply to a state with occupied lower components, a derivative-dependent interaction or a nonzero spatial kinetic balance, and it is not a dynamical growth theorem. The polynomial repairs the quartic branch's algebraic E/\omega Q factor on a selected constant-density zero mode, and it supplies a reciprocal polarized pair response. Equations (12)–(16) show why this does not establish a stable one-law mass operator. A successful action must change the occupied upper/lower structure or supply a response outside this upper-only algebraic class whose complete spatial dynamics remains sound. Canonical norm, spatial size, master selection, photon structure and cross-sector coupling remain unresolved. The calculation report records the tested values.

title: Derivative constraints and coherent mass propagation
summary: Restricting the homogeneous coherent action to normalized derivatives of one spinor preserves its massive plane waves but gives an exactly nonlocal linear response, so this specified lift does not preserve finite propagation.
text: Summary: Restricting the homogeneous coherent action to normalized derivatives of one spinor preserves its massive plane waves but gives an exactly nonlocal linear response, so this specified lift does not preserve finite propagation. The carrier must have a physical realization The homogeneous coherent action has exact simplex mass branches and finite propagation when its components are independent canonical fields in the specified spatial mode bundle. A different proposal identifies those components with derivatives of one smaller spinor. That proposal must retain both their compatibility conditions and their induced kinetic norm. Here this identification is tested in a flat constant-coefficient control on ordinary physical spatial coordinates. The calculation does not choose a new geometry for the electron or compactify any directions. It excludes this particular derivative realization, not all reductions of the master field on the curved physical sector. A complete, normalized derivative lift For |\alpha|\le N, define the coherent-normalized derivatives (T_N\psi)_\alpha =\sqrt{\frac{N!}{(N-|\alpha|)!\,\alpha!}} \ell^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\psi, \tag{1} where \ell is a fixed physical normalization length. The coefficients are the same normalized cumulative occupations used in the local-current derivative calculation. They are not independent functions: differentiating a lower component fixes the appropriate higher one. On a Fourier component of wavevector k, the complete coefficient vector is the unnormalized coherent tensor generated by (1,i\ell k). Summing every occupation gives \boxed{Z_N(k)=T_N(k)^\dagger T_N(k) =(1+\ell^2|k|^2)^N.} \tag{2} Indeed, the degree-j contribution is \binom Nj(\ell^2|k|^2)^j, by the multinomial theorem. When the lifted field has the canonical time derivative, the parent field's time metric is Z_N, not the identity. The free constant-coefficient Dirac operator commutes with this lift. Restricting the complete action, rather than just substituting the source in one component, gives iZ_N\partial_t\psi =Z_N\mathscr D\psi+T_N^\dagger G_p[T_N\psi]. \tag{3} This is a specified new action for the parent field. It is distinct from prolonging the original master equation by its product rule. Exact massive plane waves survive For a plane wave \psi=\chi e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}, the lifted field is pointwise coherent. If \chi^\dagger\beta\chi>0, the complete source is G_p[T_N\psi]=m_N\beta T_N\psi, with m_N=\mu D_N. Therefore (3) reduces exactly to (\alpha\cdot k+m_N\beta)\chi=\omega\chi, \qquad \omega=\sqrt{|k|^2+m_N^2} \tag{4} on its positive-energy branch. The induced norm cancels consistently in both the equation and E/Q=\omega. These are plane-wave controls, not localized particle solutions. The complete perturbation response, however, contains information that the dispersion relation (4) does not test. Compress the full Hessian with the same kinetic norm Take the constant coherent background in the slack occupation, with unit positive-chirality spinor \chi_0. Put P_\chi=\chi_0\chi_0^\dagger, s=\ell^2|k|^2 and \begin{aligned} r_j&=\frac{(N)_{\underline j}}{(pN)_{\underline j}},\\ a_{N,p}(s)&=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^N\binom Nj r_js^j} {(1+s)^N},\\ b_{N,p}(s)&=(p-1)\left[a_{N,p}(s)-(1+s)^{-N}\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{5} The full coherent Hessian of the independent action is complex-linear. Its degree-zero spin matrix is m_N\beta; its degree-j>0 matrix is m_Nr_j[\beta+(p-1)P_\chi]. Multiplying each by its contribution to (2) proves the complete canonical compression \boxed{ Z_N^{-1}T_N^\dagger A_pT_N =m_N[a_{N,p}(s)\beta+b_{N,p}(s)P_\chi]. } \tag{6} The rotating-frame generator adds \alpha\cdot k-m_NI to (6). It is Hermitian at each real k. Thus the calculation does not uncover an exponentially unstable Fourier mode. Its obstruction concerns spatial locality and finite propagation. For N=1, the response along the occupied spin line happens to have a+b=1. This cancellation does not hold in all the other spinor polarizations. Retaining them is essential to the test. The denominator cannot cancel Let P_{N,p}(s) be the numerator of a_{N,p}. The finite Vandermonde identity gives \boxed{ \begin{aligned} P_{N,p}(-1) &=\sum_{j=0}^N(-1)^j\binom Nj \frac{(N)_{\underline j}}{(pN)_{\underline j}}\\ &=\frac{[(p-1)N]!^2}{[(p-2)N]!\,(pN)!}>0. \end{aligned} } \tag{7} One elementary proof draws N objects without replacement from pN objects, of which N are marked. The sum is inclusion-exclusion for drawing no marked objects. The direct probability is \binom{(p-1)N}{N}/\binom{pN}{N}, equal to the last expression. This supplies an independent combinatorial derivation of the nonzero remainder. Along a single physical Fourier direction, a_{N,p}(\ell^2k^2) therefore has poles of order N at k=\pm i/\ell. It is a nonpolynomial rational multiplier. A translation-invariant local generator has a convolution kernel supported at the origin, hence a polynomial Fourier symbol. Equation (7) proves that this compressed response is not local. For a concrete spin channel in six dimensions, use the exterior-form Clifford representation and choose a positive two-form polarization orthogonal to the zero-form \chi_0. Its partner under the first Clifford matrix is a negative one-form, also orthogonal to \chi_0. This two-state channel is preserved by that one-direction Dirac symbol; P_\chi vanishes on it. The nonlocal coefficient a_{N,p} cannot be removed by the occupied-spin term in (6). An explicit instantaneous tail Already at N=1, a_{1,p}(\ell^2k^2) =\frac1p+\frac{1-1/p}{1+\ell^2k^2}. \tag{8} In one physical direction the second term has convolution kernel K(x)=\frac{1-1/p}{2\ell}e^{-|x|/\ell}. \tag{9} For any nonnegative nonzero smooth perturbation supported in [-1,1], the convolution K*f is strictly positive for x>1. The local Dirac derivative and local mass terms vanish there initially, while (9) gives a nonzero initial time derivative. The same rational symbol in d physical coordinates is a nonlocal Helmholtz resolvent and has the same support obstruction. Finite-speed differentiable evolution would require its generator to preserve initial support: outside that support, the solution is zero for a nonzero interval of time. Its derivative at time zero must then also vanish there. Equations (7)–(9) violate this necessary condition. The pole proof applies to every finite even p\ge2 and every N\ge1, including the unchanged degrees 12 and 34. The nonlocality arises because the independent nonlinear source does not preserve the derivative constraints. Restricting its action projects the response back to the allowed derivatives through Z_N^{-1}T_N^\dagger. That spatial projection is not an instantaneous local operation. Why canonical independent jets impose a strong restriction There is a general local explanation. Consider a first-derivative field (f,g) with g=\ell\partial_xf, in a fixed flat canonical metric. Suppose an algebraic source (F_0,F_1) both comes from a real local potential and preserves this constraint for every smooth f. Then F_1=\ell\partial_xF_0 =(D_fF_0)g+\ell(D_gF_0)\partial_xg. \tag{10} The second derivative \partial_xg is arbitrary at a point. Since the source is algebraic in (f,g), (10) forces D_gF_0=0 and F_1=DF_0(f)g. Work in real and imaginary components. A real potential has a symmetric real Hessian. Its upper off-diagonal block is zero, so the lower one must also vanish: D_fF_1=(D^2F_0)(f)[\,\cdot\,,g]=0 \quad\hbox{for every }g. \tag{11} Thus F_0 is affine. With phase covariance its constant term and conjugate-linear part vanish; it is one fixed Hermitian complex-linear map, repeated on the derivative components. A nonlinear local gradient on independent canonical jets generally fails this compatibility test. This argument has stated limits: it assumes an algebraic source, a fixed flat canonical fibre metric and exact first-derivative compatibility. A dynamical complementary field, a different induced kinetic structure, or a frequency-dependent elimination is not covered by it. Such ingredients must be derived from modes of the same master field; they are not mediator particles or unspecified extra physical dimensions. Consequence for the mass investigation The homogeneous action remains a valid conditional construction on its independent kinetic bundle. Its interpretation as the particular normalized derivative lift (1) is excluded as an exact finite-speed law by the full response, despite the plane-wave success (4). A viable master reduction must therefore specify how the carrier is realized, retain its actual norm and complementary response, and pass a propagation test on perturbations. Equality of carrier dimensions or an exact rest-frequency sequence does not supply those missing steps. Verification coherent_jet_causality_checks.py constructs every small-band derivative component, compresses the complete spinor Hessian with its induced norm, and measures the omitted response. It also verifies massive plane waves, exact rational pole coefficients through degree 34, and the nonzero convolution outside compact initial support. The analytic support argument, rather than a finite numerical cutoff, establishes the failure of finite propagation for this lift.
