The pairing accounts for every zero-form and the image of its Dirac derivative. Its orthogonal complement is Dirac-invariant, has no zero-form component and receives no conjugate source. All transverse mode sectors are also retained: the slack line is parallel, so their degree projectors are parallel, and their coherent response has B=0 with a Hermitian spin matrix. Each therefore gives a self-adjoint spatial operator. This establishes the scope of (13) beyond a restricted radial ansatz. The criterion is directly calculable from (9):  rac bM=a rac{\operatorname{Var}_p(u^N)}{\langle u^Nangle_p}. 	ag{14} At d=6,N=34,a=30 it is about 22.94, well inside the unstable regime. At a=10^4 it is about 0.000601. Smoothing does not guarantee spectral stability at every current density. A common-scale comparison Let \eta=\sigma\mathcal V/Q. Their finite-\sigma corrections are physical consequences of the specified action, not numerical errors to remove. The combined peak has width controlled by ND_NA+MD_MB, so the leading mixed susceptibility does not inherit the isolated band's apparent universality. It also gives the first-order solvability condition for continuing the nonconstant physical CP3 fields into the smooth action. title: Coherent spatial mode-bundle fields
summary: Pointwise coherent fields on the curved tangent-mode bundle can have balanced spatial moments, but local contact and a transported graph pairing retain different band-dependent normalizations.
text:

It gives a direct test of leakage from the whole zero space, without restricting the spatial perturbations to a chosen radial basis. The assigned cumulative indices give the following diagnostic values. A_N is an interaction expectation on the specified field, not a mass or the frequency of a solved local-contact branch. On the positive-chirality coefficient fields under consideration, the transported graph extension is the well-defined quartic \mathcal E_{\mathrm{pair}}(\psi)=  rac{\kappa D_N}{2}\int\!\int K_1(q,q') |\langle\psi(q),U_{q\leftarrow q'}\psi(q')angle|^2d

u(q'). 	ag{18} This operator contraction differs from multiplying \psi(q) by the convolution of its scalar density. That distinction remains even when the scalar spatial moment is balanced. This is a necessary occupied equation, not a proof that the other equations admit that profile. The strictly increasing \mathcal Z_N prevents a common frequency-to-count coefficient on these fields for this particular action. The constructive result (14) and the constraint (19) can coexist because their actions contract the source differently. Deriving which contraction the master field supplies is essential to a physical mass operator. title: Coherent phase and polarization tests of the supporting multiplet
summary: The balanced averaged multiplet still has coherent beat-frequency sources; an exact endpoint determinant and a combinatorial bound retain every two-state polarization, while explicit pure-state choices quantify source suppression without changing any frequency.
text: The curvature-moment carrier has a positive complete averaged shape Hessian. A coherent field occupying those bands is a stricter test than its averaged density. Its different frequencies produce oscillating sources, and changing their phases cannot generally remove them. Within one fixed surface harmonic, a determinant identity tests every polarization of the positive squared-carrier doublet. For resolved distinct beat frequencies and nonzero occupation of all bands, no such polarization choice makes even the two endpoint sources vanish at every time when at least three bands are occupied. The result does not exclude responsive geometry or additional surface-harmonic content. Continuous supporting motion remains a possible part of the model. A normalized coherent supporting field Take T u_j=s_jv_j, T^\dagger v_j=s_ju_j, with real, unit-normalized singular vectors and s_j>0. In the positive retained oscillator action L_2=\|\partial_t[B(\alpha)c]\|^2-c^\dagger H_P^2c, the squared coefficient operator has the degenerate eigenvectors \phi_j=(\eta_j u_j,\zeta_j v_j),\qquad |\eta_j|^2+|\zeta_j|^2=1. \tag{1} Retain arbitrary complex \eta_j,\zeta_j, including their phases. The coherent coefficients and their spatial field are c(t)=A\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-is_jt}\phi_j,\qquad\Psi=Bc, \qquad A^2=\frac1{2\sum_js_j}. \tag{2} Its total positive canonical phase charge is one. Each band has charge q_j=2s_jA^2, exactly the frequency-weighted population that cancels the averaged source. The amplitudes in (2) fix that common normalization; they do not assign the masses. Every frequency is still s_j. For a shape coordinate a, its instantaneous source is \mathcal F_a(t)=c^\dagger K_a c, \qquad K_a=\partial_a(H_P^2)=\{H_P,H_a\}. \tag{3} The diagonal terms sum to zero by the complete trace identity. The remaining terms oscillate at the positive frequency differences |s_j-s_r|. Averaging (3) removes them; it does not prove they are absent from the actual field equation. An endpoint determinant keeps both polarizations The endpoint derivatives have T_x=g_*|0\rangle\langle d-1|, T_y=i g_*|0\rangle\langle d-1|, where g_*=\gamma\kappa_d\ne0. For a distinct pair of bands define a=g_*(v_j)_0(u_r)_{d-1},\qquad b=g_*(v_r)_0(u_j)_{d-1}. In the two pure chiral blocks, the real/imaginary endpoint source vectors are respectively \mathbf U_{jr}=\begin{pmatrix}s_j a+s_r b\\i(s_j a-s_r b)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf V_{jr}=\begin{pmatrix}s_r a+s_j b\\i(s_r a-s_j b)\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} Their determinant is \boxed{\det[\mathbf U_{jr},\mathbf V_{jr}] =2i(s_r^2-s_j^2)ab\ne0.} \tag{5} The nonvanishing endpoint components do not require an assumption about an arbitrary eigenvector. The symmetric tridiagonal matrices T^\dagger T and TT^\dagger have nonzero adjacent entries. If an eigenvector's endpoint vanished, their row recurrence would force every component to vanish. The same recurrence makes each eigenspace one-dimensional; their eigenvalues are simple. Thus every factor in (5) is nonzero for the stated finite carrier and nonzero endpoint coefficient. For the general polarization (1), the pair's source coefficient is \eta_j^*\eta_r\,\mathbf U_{jr} +\zeta_j^*\zeta_r\,\mathbf V_{jr}. \tag{6} If the beat gaps are distinct, each Fourier coefficient must vanish separately for a time-independent source. Equation (5) would then require both \eta_j^*\eta_r=0 and \zeta_j^*\zeta_r=0. Every pair would have to occupy opposite pure chiral blocks. At most two nonzero bands can satisfy that condition pairwise. For d\ge3, this cancellation is impossible. At depth two, the two bands can occupy opposite blocks, and the centered source vanishes exactly, including its diagonal sum. See the depth-two calculation. The distinct-gap condition is explicit. At \gamma=10000, the computed gaps are distinct for all maintained controls and both surface signs, with separations well resolved under the stated spatial and normal integration refinements. This is not a claim of nondegeneracy at every possible parameter value. The two blocks in (1) are not assigned a particle–antiparticle interpretation. A phase-independent combinatorial lower bound Let \ell_{jr}>0 be the smallest squared singular value of the two columns in (5), and put p_j=|\eta_j|^2. Equation (6) implies \|\text{pair source}\|^2\ge \ell_{jr}\left[p_jp_r+(1-p_j)(1-p_r)\right]. \tag{7} The sum on the right is linear in each p_j when all other entries are fixed, so its minimum over [0,1]^d occurs at a binary assignment. Consequently the endpoint force obeys \boxed{ \overline{\mathcal F_x^2+\mathcal F_y^2} \ge\frac1{2(\sum_js_j)^2} \min_{\epsilon_j\in\{0,1\}} \sum_{j<r:\,\epsilon_j=\epsilon_r}\ell_{jr}\ge0.} \tag{8} Any two-color assignment of d bands leaves at least \lfloor(d-1)^2/4\rfloor same-color pairs. This gives a simpler positive bound by replacing every \ell_{jr} with their minimum. The combinatorics concerns compatibility of the source polarizations; it is not an additional factor inserted into the mass formula. The bound is strictly positive for three or more occupied bands. It is zero at depth two, where an opposite-block assignment attains zero source. For higher depths the bound can be very small. It excludes exact static cancellation in this restricted coherent state, but does not by itself exclude weak forcing or small sustained geometric motion. A displacement or stability claim needs the actual kinetic response to (3). Constructive polarization choices can suppress the source The same calculation can find useful coherent comparison states. Assign each occupied band to either pure chiral block, keeping its frequency and canonical population unchanged. Cross-block pair sources vanish exactly. Within-block pair sources remain. Exhaustively testing the 2^d assignments gives the smallest force variance in this discrete family. Here the variance includes every centered real and imaginary deformation, with each covector component normalized by its actual positive geometric metric. Relative to equal chiral mixing, representative source RMS ratios are approximately: Control Best pure-block assignment / equal mixing Depth-two W, Z and Higgs 0 Depth-three down 0.000882 Depth-four up 0.001847 Depth-five first neutrino 0.2141 Depth-six electron 0.3127 Depth-ten tau 0.3386 These are constructive polarization controls of the same operator, not mass fits. The search covers all pure assignments, but not the full continuous polarization space; its minimum is an upper bound on that larger optimization problem. The field's dynamics has not been shown to select minimum variance. Nor are these internal supporting-source ratios particle encounter rates or a derivation of neutrino interaction suppression. The comparison does show why retaining polarization matters: a positive averaged shape Hessian and the same frequency spectrum can coexist with very different oscillating sources. The next dynamical calculation must retain that source and its reciprocal geometry, rather than replacing it by the zero time average. Verification coherent_support_checks.py verifies (5), the complete finite binary bound in (8), arbitrary complex polarization controls and resolved beat gaps across all maintained sectors. Its 704-check report records the exact source hashes and refinement settings. The bound is computed with stable positive Gram eigenvalues, retaining small endpoint components at high precision. polarized_support_checks.py uses every centered source matrix, compares them with direct differentiation of the full squared operator, and checks the selected assignments by an independent full polarization projection. Low- and high-depth spatial refinements test the force suppression. These are conditional field-source calculations; no complete particle inertia is inferred. The 82-check report preserves the full discrete searches and their independent controls. The generalization to more polarization channels shows why the channel count must be established physically before this threshold can be interpreted as a law about spatial depth or inertia.

title: Common-anchor action audit
summary: Action and kinetic-normalization tests locate the unresolved fixed-reference bridge.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Summary: Action and kinetic-normalization tests locate the unresolved fixed-reference bridge. NOT A PHYSICS MODULE. This note records the action-level attempt to derive or falsify the V2 common-anchor law as it proceeds. 1. Target The relation under test is \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}}=\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}, or, in frequency language, \frac{\omega_d^\star}{\omega_e}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. The task is to determine whether this follows from the written V2 projected dynamics rather than being an additional scale ansatz. 2. First source-level result The self-contact module explicitly starts from a sector-diagonal scalar interaction \mathcal L_{\rm sc}=-\frac{\kappa_d}{2}J_d^2 and derives the projected scalar coefficient \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d. The finite-band contact theorem then gives M_{n,d}=\mu_dS(n,d). Therefore the written operator ordering is \boxed{\mu_d\;\longrightarrow\;\mu_dS(n,d)}. The sector coefficient is formed first; the simplex/contact eigenvalue multiplies it afterward. Section 9.1 of the self-contact module introduces the common-anchor equation separately as a projected fixed-point condition and explicitly states that the master equation of motion must supply that equation. No equation in the inspected self-contact passage identifies \kappa_dR_dB_d with g_{dd} or \sqrt{g_{dd}}. 3. Cross-depth source audit The bound/free module writes reciprocal cross-depth interactions schematically as S_{ab}=g_{ab}\int dt\,I_{ab}, whose variations give g_{ab} times the other sector's marginal/contact density. The higher-dimensional-polarization module writes a schematic current/gauge interaction S_{\rm int}=g_{ab}\int_{Q_a}\langle A_a,(\pi_{ba})_*J_b\rangle. These establish incidence, reciprocity, representation filtering, and the existence of coupling coefficients. In the inspected passages they do not identify the scalar self-contact coefficient \kappa_d, the projected scalar coefficient \mu_d, or an occupied reference frequency with g_{dd} or \sqrt{g_{dd}}. The polarization source in fact says that a nonzero invariant vertex leaves its coupling coefficient to the projected dynamics. 4. Exact placement test for the rank-one proposal Let v_d=\sqrt{g_{dd}},\qquad G=vv^T, and for the proposed depth-3, depth-4, and electron reference bands define D_\star=\operatorname{diag}(1,15,18564). If the rank-one response acts on primitive pre-contact coefficients, \sigma=GJ=v(v^TJ), then the written contact projection gives M^\star=D_\star\sigma=(D_\star v)(v^TJ). Hence \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} =\frac{D_d^\star\sqrt{g_{dd}}}{D_6^\star\sqrt{g_{66}}} }. This is Case B, not the desired common-anchor law. If instead a deeper master equation acts directly on the already-projected occupied reference coefficients, M^\star=vC, then \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} }. This is Case A. The algebraic way to begin before contact multiplication and still end in Case A is to use \widetilde G=D_\star^{-1}vv^TD_\star^{-1}, so that D_\star\widetilde GJ lies along v. But this changes the primitive diagonal couplings to \widetilde g_{dd}=\frac{g_{dd}}{(D_d^\star)^2}. That is not a harmless relabeling of the quoted V2 couplings unless an independent projection or kinetic-normalization theorem derives exactly this weighting. 5. Interim verdict The naive rank-one source-to-self-energy mechanism does not derive the common-anchor law when attached directly to the scalar coefficient already written in V2. With the explicit self-contact ordering it produces Case B. Case A remains possible only if the deeper projected master dynamics supplies additional structure, for example: a rank-one equation acting directly on occupied reference frequencies; an independently derived two-sided reference-count weighting before contact projection; sector-dependent projected overlap or kinetic factors that cancel the reference counts exactly; or a nonlinear fixed-point equation in which the reference-band factors enter before the final ratio is formed. None of those mechanisms has yet been found in the inspected source passages. The identity g_{34}^2=g_{33}g_{44} is therefore insufficient by itself. It establishes rank one for a coupling-coefficient matrix, but does not determine the operator layer on which that matrix acts. Since D_\star v is not proportional to v, the simplex projection and the proposed rank-one image do not commute in the way required by the anchor law. The remaining problem is an operator-ordering and normalization problem, not an unknown-amplitude problem. 6. Next proof obligation Trace the actual derivation and mathematical role of g_{33}=8\sqrt7,\qquad g_{44}=12/\sqrt7,\qquad g_{34}=4\sqrt6,\qquad g_{66}=1/4. For each value, determine whether it is defined as a scalar self-interaction coefficient, a polarization/gauge normalization, a stiffness, a kernel eigenvalue, or another object. Only then can the use of these same numbers in the scalar reference-frequency fixed-point equation be classified as derived, merely compatible, or category-invalid. No V1 material is used as evidence here. 7. Historical V2 action supplies a real candidate mechanism - but not yet a current-V2 derivation The git history contains an earlier V2, not V1, formulation from August 28, 2026. It is useful provenance because it shows what the common-anchor statement was intended to mean before the present projective-contact modules were written. That historical V2 wrote one quartic master interaction S_{\rm int} =\frac12\sum_{d,e}g_{de} \int K_{de}(\xi_d,\xi_e)\,\rho_d\rho_e, with g_{de}=v_dv_e, \qquad g_{dd}=v_d^2. For the displayed kernel, K_{de}=(\xi_d\cdot\xi_e)^2. The same historical text then states the lightest-mode fixed point \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} =\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}, which is exactly the present common-anchor condition. This matters because the rank-one-response idea was not invented during the present audit: an earlier V2 master action already contained a rank-one coupling matrix and explicitly described one collective interaction channel. 7.1 Exact variation of the historical rank-one action Let \rho_d=\bar\Psi P_d\Psi. For a symmetric kernel and symmetric coupling matrix, variation of the quadratic density functional with respect to \rho_d gives \Sigma_d =\sum_e g_{de}K_{de}\rho_e. Using g_{de}=v_dv_e, \boxed{ \Sigma_d =v_d\sum_e v_eK_{de}\rho_e. } This is an important refinement of the simpler toy calculation \Sigma=v(v^TJ). Rank one of the coefficient matrix alone does not yet imply \Sigma_d=v_dC with one sector-independent scalar C, because the geometric kernel still carries the external sector label d through K_{de}. The required additional condition is \boxed{ \sum_e v_eK_{de}\rho_e=C \quad\text{independent of }d } on the relevant fixed-point branch, or an equivalent projector/normalization theorem that reduces the full kernel to a common scalar functional. The historical prose asserts precisely such a common condensate, but the displayed action by itself does not prove that the K_{de} dependence collapses this way. 7.2 Why this still does not automatically solve the present projective-contact problem The historical V2 and current V2 place the spectral count at different conceptual stages. The current self-contact theorem derives M_d^\star=D_d^\star\mu_d, where \mu_d is the sector-normalized scalar contact coefficient before multiplication by the occupied-band dimension. Therefore, if the historical rank-one response \Sigma_d is identified with the current primitive coefficient \mu_d, then M_d^\star =D_d^\star v_dC, which is Case B: \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} =\frac{D_d^\star v_d}{D_6^\star v_6}. To recover Case A in the current architecture, one must establish one of two precise identifications: post-projection response: the historical \Sigma_d corresponds directly to the occupied reference eigenvalue M_d^\star, not to \mu_d; or count-compensated primitive response: projection of the historical kernel produces \mu_d\propto\frac{v_d}{D_d^\star}, so that the subsequent contact multiplier restores M_d^\star\propto v_d. The historical source does not perform the present finite-band projective-contact calculation, so it cannot decide between these two identifications. 7.3 A second incompatibility that must be resolved The historical V2 derives a self-consistent harmonic stiffness \lambda_d=\left(\frac{g_{dd}}2\right)^{2/3} from the quartic kernel, and then separately states that the physical mass spectrum is m(n,d)=m_{{\rm scale},d}S(n,d). But the ordinary isotropic harmonic-oscillator eigenvalues scale linearly with excitation number and with \sqrt{\lambda_d}; their degeneracy count is S(n,d) only after cumulative counting. The historical source does not derive why the eigenfrequency itself equals the cumulative degeneracy rather than the usual oscillator eigenvalue. The current projective-contact theorem was written precisely to supply a genuine operator whose occupied eigenvalue is S(n,d). Consequently, importing the historical harmonic-well fixed point wholesale would mix two distinct spectral mechanisms. 7.4 Result of the historical-source test Survives as provenance and a candidate mechanism: V2 originally intended g_{de} to be one rank-one quartic self-interaction matrix; V2 originally intended the electron-relative scale law to be a kernel-vacuum fixed point; the square-root coupling ratios therefore have a coherent action-level motivation, not merely a numerical coincidence. Does not yet survive as a derivation in the current V2 operator architecture: rank one of g_{de} does not by itself remove the sector dependence of the geometric kernel K_{de}; the historical action does not derive the inverse reference-count factor required if its response is pre-contact; the historical harmonic-well spectrum and the current projective-contact spectrum are not the same operator construction. The common anchor is therefore better motivated than the current files alone made visible, but still unproved in present V2. 8. Sharpened next calculation The next decisive calculation is now concrete. Project the historical-style rank-one master kernel through the current finite-band projectors and ask whether its occupied-line matrix element has the form \langle z_d;N_d|P_d\mathcal K_\infty P_d|z_d;N_d\rangle =C\sqrt{g_{dd}} or =C\sqrt{g_{dd}}\,D_d^\star, or instead acquires a compensating factor 1/D_d^\star before the contact eigenvalue is applied. Equivalently, define the projected source functional F_d[\rho] =\sum_e v_e\,\langle z_d;N_d|P_dK_{de}[\rho_e]P_d|z_d;N_d\rangle. Case A requires D_d^\star F_d[\rho] \propto \text{constant in }d, when the primitive scalar coefficient is used, whereas a direct post-projection formulation requires simply F_d[\rho]\propto\text{constant in }d. This is now the exact normalization theorem to prove or falsify. 9. Fixed reference normalization is compatible with band blindness The current self-contact theorem states that, for the ordinary family law, M_{n,d}=\mu_dS(n,d), with all explicit band dependence carried by the reproducing-kernel diagonal S(n,d). Its action-level domain explicitly requires the scalar contact strength \mu_d to be band-blind. This sharpens the Case A/Case B fork. Suppose the historical rank-one master response is attached to the current primitive scalar coefficient: \mu_d=v_dC, \qquad v_d=\sqrt{g_{dd}}. Then the present contact theorem gives M_d^\star=D_d^\star v_dC, and therefore Case B. The only primitive-level algebraic rescue previously identified was \mu_d\propto\frac{v_d}{D_d^\star}. Here D_d^\star is fixed once per sector. Dependence on that fixed reference does not imply dependence on the varying occupied band n or N=n-1. Thus \mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star is band-blind and gives M_{n,d}=Cv_dD_{n,d}/D_d^\star, with M_d^\star=Cv_d. The earlier claim that band blindness alone excludes this normalization is withdrawn. Replacing D_d^\star by the running D_{n,d} would violate band blindness, but that is a different prescription. Therefore: \boxed{ \mu_d=Cv_d\text{ forces Case B; fixed }\mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star\text{ gives Case A.} } A fixed inverse-reference normalization changes the primitive-response identification, not the band-blind contact theorem. Its physical origin remains unproved; it cannot be silently inserted as a result of the historical kernel. This rules out only the simultaneous unweighted primitive response \mu_d=Cv_d and the desired reference ratios with unequal reference counts. Case A can follow from a post-contact / occupied-reference fixed point, or from a derived fixed sector normalization at the primitive layer. Neither route has been derived from the current master action. 10. Current V2 explicitly records the missing coordinate-kernel to phase-ray bridge Section 8.6 of the present self-contact module distinguishes two operators: P_{N,d}|q|^2P_{N,d} from the coordinate harmonic kernel, and D_N|z;N\rangle\langle z;N| from phase-ray point contact. It then states that their relation still requires either: a master interaction written locally on the homogenized phase-ray bundle; or a derivation showing that the coordinate-space nonlinear kernel transforms into occupied-ray contact after oscillator and sector projection. This is exactly the missing bridge between the historical V2 master kernel (\xi_d\cdot\xi_e)^2 and the present projective-contact mass operator. So the source audit now yields a stronger documentary conclusion: \boxed{ \text{the current V2 source itself identifies the historical-to-current operator bridge as unfinished.} } Consequently, the historical statement that the kernel vacuum supplies the common anchor cannot presently be imported as a completed derivation. It points to the right location in the dynamics, but the required projection theorem has not yet been written. 11. Revised status after the bridge audit Established in current V2: occupied phase-ray point contact gives the exact simplex eigenvalue D_N=S(n,d); the ordinary family law has a band-blind primitive coefficient \mu_d; therefore a primitive response proportional to \sqrt{g_{dd}} produces Case B. Established as historical V2 provenance: an earlier V2 master action used a rank-one coupling matrix g_{de}=v_dv_e; it intended one collective self-interaction channel; it stated the electron-relative common-anchor law as a kernel-vacuum fixed point. Still missing: the projection of that coordinate-space rank-one kernel into the current occupied phase-ray scalar-contact operator; a proof that the resulting complete occupied reference eigenvalue, rather than the primitive coefficient, lies along v_d; or any other current-V2 equation that yields M_d^\star\propto\sqrt{g_{dd}} with a derived fixed sector normalization or occupied-reference fixed point. The common-anchor law is not disproved. The unweighted primitive identification is excluded; a fixed inverse-reference normalization remains algebraically allowed but physically underived. 12. Kinetic-normalization audit: no present rescue of the primitive rank-one anchor The remaining obvious place for a compensating factor was canonical or kinetic normalization. The current V2 mass module does not provide one. Its operator ordering is explicit: the spatial Dirac/Laplace operator constructs the mode eigenspace; the localized contact operator maps the rank of that eigenspace to the rest-energy eigenvalue; the sector coefficient is \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d, and is independent of the band label under the ordinary mass theorem. No reference-band wavefunction renormalization or kinetic factor proportional to \frac1{D_d^\star} appears in that derivation. A separate gauge/polarization module does say that propagation laws and kinetic normalizations of the projected gauge connection remain to be obtained from the master action. But that statement concerns projected connection components and cross-sector propagation; no current source identifies such a normalization with the scalar rest-energy contact coefficient, and no formula supplies the reference-band dependence required here. The cross-depth contact theorem also preserves complete normalized marginal weight: \int \bar\rho_{b\to a}=1. Thus full marginalization does not furnish an inverse simplex factor either. Combining these facts gives the following present-V2 no-go statement. 12.1 Primitive-rank-one incompatibility theorem Assume simultaneously: the ordinary current V2 contact law M_{n,d}=\mu_dD_{n,d}, \qquad D_{n,d}=S(n,d); band blindness of the primitive scalar contact coefficient \mu_d; normalized cross-depth marginalization with no band-dependent loss of weight; identification of the historical rank-one response with that primitive coefficient, \mu_d=C\sqrt{g_{dd}} for one sector-independent C. Then for any chosen reference bands, \boxed{ \frac{M_d^\star}{M_6^\star} = \frac{D_d^\star}{D_6^\star} \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} } and not \sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} unless accidentally D_d^\star=D_6^\star. For the adopted references, D_3^\star=S(1,3)=1, \qquad D_4^\star=S(3,4)=15, \qquad D_6^\star=S(13,6)=18564, so the accidental-equality condition fails drastically. Therefore the four assumptions above are mutually incompatible with the common-anchor law. At least one must change. Since assumptions 1--3 are explicit parts of the current V2 contact construction, the natural conclusion is: \boxed{ \text{the desired anchor is incompatible with the unweighted identification }\mu_d=Cv_d. } It can instead act on the complete occupied reference eigenvalues, or arise from a derived fixed sector weighting such as \mu_d=Cv_d/D_d^\star. The latter preserves assumptions 1--3 but replaces assumption 4; it is not excluded merely because it acts at the primitive layer. 12.2 Numerical size of the contradiction The difference is not perturbative. The desired Case A factors relative to the electron reference are \sqrt{g_{33}/g_{66}}\approx 9.2013065, \qquad \sqrt{g_{44}/g_{66}}\approx 4.2593773. A primitive rank-one response followed by the present contact theorem instead gives \frac{1}{18564}\sqrt{g_{33}/g_{66}} \approx 4.9565\times10^{-4}, and \frac{15}{18564}\sqrt{g_{44}/g_{66}} \approx 3.4416\times10^{-3}. These differ from the required reference-frequency ratios by factors exactly equal to the missing count ratios. This cannot be repaired by unit conventions. 13. Status of the common-anchor attack The first attempted action-level derivation has therefore failed in a precise way. It did not fail because rank-one coupling is useless. Historical V2 shows why rank one is a serious clue. It failed because the current exact simplex theorem fixes where the count enters, and a primitive rank-one response then places that count on the wrong side of the proposed fixed point. The surviving proof target is now narrower: Derive a fixed-point equation for the complete occupied reference eigenvalue M_d^\star, or derive the fixed sector normalization of the primitive coefficient (for example 1/D_d^\star) from the master projection. Any future derivation that merely writes \mu_d\propto\sqrt{g_{dd}} has already been ruled out for the present V2 mass operator. Related Research status — current proof boundaries and correction guidance.

title: A common background action and its radial stability threshold
summary: One inverse background action cancels the finite carrier's radius force and field-radius mixing for every assigned mode, while its actual radial Hessian sets a shared background-curvature threshold and leaves angular curvature unselected.
text: The positive-background construction previously canceled the angular force at first order but left the geometric Hessian unspecified. This calculation gives one complete radial inverse action for the maintained finite carrier. It derives the radius force, field--radius mixing and radial curvature from that action, and identifies exactly what remains undetermined for nonuniform geometry. The separate whole-depth conformal-current candidate does specify its metric dependence and has its own calculated two-direction Hessian; the two carriers are not one action and their curvatures cannot be combined. One action for every harmonic in a sector Let H_d(R)=D_d/R+gK_d be the Hermitian finite carrier at fixed normal width and fixed hopping strength g. The component chain has diagonal entries (n+j)/R and adjacent entries g h_j, where the h_j come from the same linked spatial normal-mode calculation for all harmonics at depth d. The assigned index n labels the occupied spatial eigenstate; the operators and coefficients are shared. Choose a reference radius R_0, a nonzero retained background value v, and a positive background curvature a. Write x=v+\xi and define the single sector action through its energy E[\Psi,R,\xi]=\langle\Psi,H_d(R)\Psi\rangle +\frac a2\xi^2 -\frac{R-R_0}{v}(v+\xi) \langle\Psi,C_d\Psi\rangle, \qquad C_d=\left.\partial_RH_d\right|_{R_0} =-\frac{D_d}{R_0^2}. \tag{1} The retained action is S=\int dt\,[\tfrac i2\Psi^\dagger \overleftrightarrow{\partial_t}\Psi +\tfrac{I_R}{2}\dot R^2+\tfrac Z2\dot\xi^2-E], with positive I_R,Z. The wave has its canonical first-order time term. The collective kinetic coefficients are inputs whose physical values are not determined here. Equation (1) is an explicit inverse choice. In particular, the background coupling is made from the carrier's reference derivative; its origin in \Psi_\infty, the value of a, and the selection of R_0 have not been derived. At R=R_0, \xi=0, the extra term and its wave derivative vanish. Every normalized positive carrier eigenstate therefore retains its standing frequency \omega_{n,d}>0 and energy Q\omega_{n,d}, where Q=\langle\Psi,\Psi\rangle. Neither amplitude nor a supporting energy is substituted for mass. Full reference variations and radial Hessian Because C_d is an operator shared by the sector, rather than a number fitted to each particle, the radius and field--radius variations cancel for every wave field at the reference: \partial_RE\big|_*=\langle\Psi,C_d\Psi\rangle -\langle\Psi,C_d\Psi\rangle=0, \qquad D_\Psi\partial_RE\big|_*=0. \tag{2} The background variation also vanishes there. Put p_{n,d}=-R_0\omega_R/\omega, with the physical hopping strength held fixed. The finite-carrier inverse identity gives 1<p_{n,d}<d and the Hellmann--Feynman relation \langle\Psi,D_d\Psi\rangle=Qp_{n,d}\omega_{n,d}R_0. \tag{3} The three nontrivial second derivatives of (1) are therefore \boxed{G_R=\partial_R^2E\big|_*= \frac{2Qp\omega}{R_0^2},\qquad F_R=\partial_\xi\partial_RE\big|_*= \frac{Qp\omega}{vR_0},\qquad A_\xi=a.} \tag{4} The field--radius mixed block vanishes by (2), including the derivative of the carrier itself. Eliminating the relaxing background yields the actual radial curvature of this action, \boxed{G_{R,\mathrm{eff}}= \frac{2Qp\omega}{R_0^2} -\frac{Q^2p^2\omega^2}{a v^2R_0^2},\qquad a v^2>\frac{Qp\omega}{2}\quad\text{for positive curvature}.} \tag{5} All occupied harmonics at one depth can use one common a,v,R_0 only if the inequality holds at the largest Qp\omega/2 among them. This is a derived threshold, not a determination of a. It is specifically a radial result; it does not test the angular Hessian. With positive radius and background kinetic coefficients I_R,Z, the two retained squared normal frequencies are \Omega_\pm^2=\frac12\left[\frac{G_R}{I_R}+\frac aZ \pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{G_R}{I_R}-\frac aZ\right)^2 +\frac{4F_R^2}{I_RZ}}\right]. \tag{6} Both are positive precisely when (5) holds. The wave perturbations decouple at quadratic order because the mixed block is zero. This gives a conditional finite-carrier linear result, not stability of the full spatial field. The constrained first-order wave Hessian still has a negative direction toward the negative-frequency partner, so the positive-field-block assumption of the earlier Schur inequality is not met for the entire pair. That negative energy direction alone does not imply exponential growth when it is decoupled. Common-threshold calculation The extended unified script uses the archived linked-mode hopping integrals and the unchanged particle assignments. It checks the pressure identity independently through the smallest singular vector of the finite carrier, verifies the first radius derivative by a centered difference, and verifies (5) by differentiating the eliminated action. The input hopping values are finite-precision numerical data; extra working digits in the matrix calculation do not certify their last digits. The table reports \max_n p\omega/2 at Q=v=R_0=1. The two common gaps are dimensionless diagnostics, not fitted physical sector scales; values from different depths cannot be compared as physical stiffnesses without the common kinetic and length units. Depth Gap 1000: a> Gap 10000: a> 2 17.7 1.91 3 1.92\times10^{-2} 1.92\times10^{-4} 4 9.54\times10^{-2} 9.65\times10^{-5} 5 1.98\times10^{-5} 1.98\times10^{-9} 6 4.35\times10^{-6} 4.36\times10^{-11} 10 1.75\times10^{-14} 1.75\times10^{-23} These are maxima over the maintained modes within each depth, so no particle gets its own background curvature. A sufficiently stiff background can make the radial block positive for this finite set, while an arbitrarily soft one cannot. The dependence on the chosen gap shows that the present calculation does not select a physical stiffness or a measured length. Why angular stability remains unselected The force-canceling rule fixes only the first geometric derivative. For an angular coordinate q, write a carrier with the same reference operator and first derivative as H(q)=H_0+qC+\frac{q^2}{2}D+O(q^3),\qquad B(q)=-\frac qv\langle\Psi,C\Psi\rangle. \tag{7} The force and field--geometry mixed block cancel at q=0 for every choice of D, while the bare angular curvature is \langle\Psi,D\Psi\rangle. Changing D changes its sign without changing the frequency or first variation at the reference. This proves that the previously established first-order angular force and transparent background do not determine the angular stability calculation. The full conformally transported spatial carrier, background geometry and their second derivatives must be specified. Choosing D solely to pass the stability test would be a fit. The same caution applies to (1): adding a term quadratic in R-R_0 can change (4) while preserving (2). Equation (1) is the minimal linear-in-radius background completion that was actually tested. Its successful radial cancellation does not establish the master-field origin, photon behavior, a common compatible geometry across depths, nonlinear stability or reciprocal particle coupling. The unified calculation passed 356 conditions at this radial stage. Its radial-stage report contains every maintained mode, two common gap controls and the exact source fingerprints. The later conformal-current calculation in the same script supplies a separate candidate's two-direction metric Hessian. A derived background stiffness and the complete spatial Hessian remain open.

title: Common cavity size and collective coupling
summary: A common cavity radius and count-additive energy constrain the balancing terms of an inverse action, while its canonical probe response requires a separate count scaling that can be tested against actual spatial contacts.
text: Summary: A common cavity radius and count-additive energy constrain the balancing terms of an inverse action, while its canonical probe response requires a separate count scaling that can be tested against actual spatial contacts. Frequency scale and spatial scale The proposed mass law supplies a frequency unit directly from the fixed particle assignments: \begin{aligned} D_N&=\binom{N+d}{d},\\ N&=n-1,\\ \mu_d&=\frac{m(n,d)}{D_N},\\ \omega_{0,d}&=\frac{\mu_dc^2}{\hbar}. \end{aligned} \tag{1} Different particles in one depth test whether this is a common unit. The mass-frequency conversion is already available. Identifying the unit with a cavity's spatial scale additionally requires its spatial operator. For example, if that operator gives \omega_{0,d}=\gamma_d\frac{c}{L_d}, \qquad \frac{L_d}{L_e}=\frac{\gamma_d}{\gamma_6} \frac{\mu_6}{\mu_d}, \tag{2} then the inverse mass-scale ratio is the length ratio when the geometric factors agree. Here L_e denotes the electron-sector reference length and \gamma_d is a dimensionless factor to derive from the geometry and wave operator. It cannot be independently retuned for each particle. A common characteristic well size does not imply equal spatial extent of every occupied mode. Nor does the cavity terminology require an external wall, compactification, or particles occupying one shared location. The following inverse actions test the common-size premise; their origin in the same master field remains to be established. Relative units at the fixed particle assignments The existing mass-spectrum benchmarks give the following energy units \mu_dc^2 and inverse ratios. For the multi-entry quark and boson families, the table uses the geometric mean of their individual m_ic^2/D_i values. The electron itself fixes the depth-six anchor. These are the current repository's stated benchmark inputs, not a new fit of particle indices or a new mass measurement. Depth Energy unit in eV Inverse ratio \mu_6/\mu_d 2 2.7460464\times10^7 1.0023989\times10^{-6} 3 4.6930314\times10^6 5.8653643\times10^{-6} 4 1.4324413\times10^5 1.9216381\times10^{-4} 5, solar splitting 7.5757674\times10^{-7} 3.6334720\times10^7 5, atmospheric splitting 7.6505625\times10^{-7} 3.5979496\times10^7 6, electron anchor 27.5263386 1 10, direct tau value 27.5440754 0.9993561 The neutrino rows use the unchanged counts (2002,11628,65780). Their separate units are obtained from \begin{aligned} \mu_{5,\mathrm{solar}}c^2 &=\sqrt{\frac{\Delta m_{21}^2c^4}{D_2^2-D_1^2}},\\ \mu_{5,\mathrm{atm}}c^2 &=\sqrt{\frac{\Delta m_{31}^2c^4}{D_3^2-D_1^2}}. \end{aligned} Their difference is the same finite bare-ratio discrepancy recorded in the mass-spectrum test. The tau row is the scale extracted directly from its benchmark; the proposed shared charged-lepton scale instead sets \mu_{10}=\mu_6 and retains the documented tau residual. The last column becomes a physical length ratio only after multiplication by \gamma_d/\gamma_6 in (2). Conversely, one common length across all depths would require those geometric factors to carry the direct mass-unit ratios. This is a quantitative condition for the spatial operator, rather than an already measured hierarchy of particle sizes. spectral_count_checks.py records the individual units and their family residuals using the exact current benchmark source. An exact condition on two balancing energies Write D for the cumulative count and suppose a declared positive energy has two terms, with A,B,a,b>0: E(D,L)=A D^rL^{-a}+B D^sL^b. \tag{3} The first term grows as the cavity contracts and the second as it expands. The exponents describe this specified model; they do not prescribe the geometry of an IDWT sector. Its unique positive stationary size follows from \partial_LE=0. With L_1=(aA/bB)^{1/(a+b)}, \begin{aligned} L_*(D)&=L_1D^{(r-s)/(a+b)},\\ E_*(D)&\propto D^{(br+as)/(a+b)}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} The energy diverges at both ends of the positive length axis, so this stationary point is its minimum. A common size requires r=s. With this condition, linear energy requires r=s=1. Thus, within (3), \boxed{r=s=1.} \tag{5} Both contributions must then carry the same count factor. A fixed confinement energy added to an increasing number of oscillations generally changes the minimizing size. Equation (5) is not a theorem about all possible actions. An additional term D^2(L-L_0)^2 has zero value and first derivative at L_0, but changes the restoring stiffness there. Such a term can preserve common size and linear stationary energy while changing the dynamics. Testing the response therefore adds information beyond fitting stationary masses. Count and oscillator energy give different balances At the unchanged electron and muon assignments, \begin{aligned} (N_e,N_\mu)&=(12,34),\qquad d=6,\\ (D_e,D_\mu)&=(18564,3838380),\\ \frac{D_\mu}{D_e}&=206.76470588\ldots. \end{aligned} \tag{6} Consider the comparison E=A D/L+B L^6, with a count-independent positive volume energy. Minimizing it gives a muon-to-electron radius ratio of 2.14181691 and energy ratio of 96.53705902. This action does not give the proposed common size or count-additive energy. If the cavity contains equally occupied ordinary harmonic levels, the energy sum in oscillator-frequency units is instead the exact level moment \begin{aligned} W_N&=\sum_{k=0}^N(k+d/2) \binom{k+d-1}{d-1}\\ &=d\left(\frac{N}{d+1}+\frac12\right)D_N. \end{aligned} \tag{7} The two six-dimensional values are 246636 and 123376500, whose ratio is 500.23719165. Replacing D by W_N in the contraction term gives radius ratio 2.42994570 and energy ratio 205.86352708. The latter is near the target ratio, but this is a different balance with a different radius. It does not establish the exact mass law. The moving-cavity inertia calculation gives an exact count-additive translation coefficient for a specified quadratic kinetic law. Equation (7) explains why that result cannot simply be relabelled as the total energy of the harmonic cavity. A closed relativistic particle must include its confinement contribution and stress. The per-mode kinetic law and the occupied field content need their own derivation. What a common kinetic gap would have to do A large common gap is one possible source of nearly equal per-mode energies. Consider the declared positive spectrum \begin{aligned} E_k&=\Delta\sqrt{1+\lambda(k+d/2)},\\ \lambda&=\frac{\Lambda}{\Delta^2},\qquad \Delta>0,\quad\Lambda\ge0. \end{aligned} \tag{7a} Here \Lambda has units of energy squared and the shell multiplicity is \binom{k+d-1}{d-1}. This is a spectral comparison. It is not asserted to be the full spinor spectrum of the proposed physical geometry. Let \overline E_N be the mean of these energies through degree N. Equal occupation gives total energy qD_N\overline E_N. For any \Lambda>0, adding higher shells strictly raises the mean. Thus the normalized energy is not exactly common at the electron and muon bands. At d=6 and small relative spread, the exact finite sums give \frac{\overline E_{34}}{\overline E_{12}}-1 =\frac{66}{7}\lambda+O(\lambda^2). \tag{7b} As a stated accuracy budget, requiring this departure to be at most 2\times10^{-5} gives the numerical finite-band condition \begin{aligned} \lambda&\le2.12129418\times10^{-6},\\ \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt\Lambda}&\ge686.59328. \end{aligned} \tag{7c} This is an illustrative tolerance, not an uncertainty-weighted experimental bound. No particle indices or wave amplitudes have been changed. The diagnostic evaluates the complete finite sums and checks independent concavity and Taylor bounds on their means. The gap route can approximate a count-additive energy, but it requires a substantial separation between the common gap and the oscillator energy scale in this model. Its origin must be supplied by the same field. If the spatial scale were \hbar c/\sqrt\Lambda, it would also differ from the inverse gap scale \hbar c/\Delta. This is another reason to derive the spatial conversion in (2), rather than silently identifying every mass unit with the fundamental of an ordinary harmonic well. Pressure of a gapped band The gap approximation also needs a pressure test. Let s=k+d/2 and let \langle\cdot\rangle_N denote the normalized cumulative oscillator average. Consider positive common coefficients in the energy \begin{aligned} \mathcal E_N(L)&=D_N\left(\overline E_N(L)+B L^d\right),\\ \overline E_N(L)&=\left\langle\sqrt{\Delta^2+As/L^2}\right\rangle_N. \end{aligned} \tag{7d} The support term is extensive in the count. Its equilibrium condition is \begin{aligned} BdL^{d-1}&=\frac{A}{L^3}f_N(L),\\ f_N(L)&=\left\langle\frac{s}{\sqrt{\Delta^2+As/L^2}}\right\rangle_N. \end{aligned} \tag{7e} At fixed L, the function of s on the right increases strictly. Adding higher shells therefore raises that side, while the left side is common. Two different cumulative bands cannot have exactly the same equilibrium length under this specified supporting law. For example, set \Delta=1, A=10^{-6} and choose one common B so that the electron band has L_e=1. Independent minimization gives L_\mu=1.11676579. The optimized energy ratio differs from the count ratio by only 8.32\times10^{-6}, while the radii differ by 11.7 percent. Thus an accurate count-like energy does not ensure the common size. A supporting field with a different derived response may satisfy both conditions; this volume-energy comparison does not. An extensive collective action with a common radius A useful inverse family has a collective radius coordinate R and action \mathcal L_D=\frac D2\dot R^2-D f(R). \tag{8} The displayed units absorb common kinetic and energy scales. If f'(R_0)=0 and f''(R_0)>0, every count has the same equilibrium radius, stationary energy D f(R_0) and complete nonlinear equation \ddot R+f'(R)=0. \tag{9} For f(R)=R^{-1}+R^6/6, the equilibrium is R_0=1 and the small oscillation frequency squared is seven. Direct integrations starting at R=1.03, \dot R=0 for counts 1 and D_\mu/D_e agree in the actual, unscaled radius trajectory to 3.01\times10^{-14}. The complete conserved energies differ by the count factor. This supplies a consistent collective pattern to seek in the master-field reduction. It does not supply the reduction itself. In particular, D in both terms of (8) is a declared hypothesis about the field content, not a fit of an eigenfunction amplitude. The physical coupling must be normalized independently Let a probe coordinate z couple near equilibrium through C_Dz\,\delta R, where \delta R=R-R_0. Write the quadratic reciprocal action as \begin{aligned} \mathcal L^{(2)}={}&\frac D2\dot{\delta R}^{\,2}+\frac12\dot z^2\\ &-\frac D2\omega_R^2\delta R^2-\frac12\omega_z^2z^2\\ &-C_Dz\,\delta R. \end{aligned} \tag{10} Both responses follow from the same energy. In the canonical coordinate x=\sqrt D\,\delta R, the physical off-diagonal vertex is g_D=\frac{C_D}{\sqrt D}. \tag{11} This is kinetic normalization, not an arbitrary division of a measured response by mass. Eliminating the radius at frequency \Omega produces a probe stiffness correction with magnitude \left|\frac{C_D^2}{D(\omega_R^2-\Omega^2)}\right|. \tag{12} For C_D\propto D^p, the three distinct scalings are: Quantity Count dependence Radius displacement per probe drive D^{p-1} Canonical vertex D^{p-1/2} Probe self-response away from a pole D^{2p-1} Consequently C_D\propto\sqrt D gives a common canonical coupling and probe response. The choice C_D\propto D gives the same radius motion under a fixed drive, but a probe response proportional to D. Equal motion alone is not equal coupling. The diagnostic verifies this distinction using both eigenvalues of the full reciprocal two-coordinate problem, independently computed with the original kinetic metric and in canonical coordinates. A spatial contact supplies an instructive scaling test There is a direct comparison with the previously derived spatial oscillator contact. For normalized Hermite modes of common length L, its central trace K_{N,d}(0)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le N}|h_\alpha^L(0)|^2 is \begin{aligned} K_{N,d}(0)&=\pi^{-d/2}L^{-d}C_{N,d},\\ C_{N,d}&=\binom{\lfloor N/2\rfloor+d/2}{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}. \end{aligned} \tag{13} As N grows at fixed d, this behaves as N^{d/2}, whereas D_N behaves as N^d. Hence K_{N,d}/\sqrt{D_N} tends to a constant. This scaling has an explicit conditional use. Take the positive occupied density \rho_N=q\sum|h_\alpha^L|^2 with common occupation q, a central density probe, and the collective kinetic term of (8). Its interaction gz\rho_N(0) gives a radius vertex \begin{aligned} C_N&=gq\,\partial_LK_{N,d}(0)\\ &=-\frac{d gq}{L}K_{N,d}(0). \end{aligned} \tag{14} At common L, the normalized vertex therefore has the leading count behavior required by (11). The actual electron and muon central coefficients, after removing \pi^{-3}L^{-6}, are 84 and 1140: \begin{aligned} \frac{g_\mu}{g_e}&=\frac{1140/84}{\sqrt{D_\mu/D_e}}\\ &=0.94381606\ldots. \end{aligned} \tag{15} This is a 5.6 percent difference in this specified density-and-radius model, rather than an exact universal vertex. It does not identify a Dirac scalar or electromagnetic current with positive density. Nested-sector marginalization changes the result A probe occupying only a shared ordinary coordinates of a containing b-dimensional sector samples a different density. Integrate the normal coordinates of the complete occupied density before applying the local probe. The bilinear marginal rule gives at the shared origin the value k_N=K^{\rm marg}_{N,b\to a}(0): \begin{aligned} k_N&=\pi^{-a/2}L^{-a}c_N,\\ c_N&=\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}w_r \binom{N-2r+b-a}{b-a},\\ w_r&=\frac{(a/2)_r}{r!}. \end{aligned} \tag{16} The generating function for the dimensionless coefficients is (1-t^2)^{-a/2}(1-t)^{-(b-a+1)}. \tag{17} The first factor counts the even shared-coordinate values at the origin. The second counts every normalized normal mode and performs the cumulative sum. This is a density trace; integrating a linear wave and then squaring would be a different operation. Equation (17) has leading growth N^{b-a/2}. After normalization by \sqrt{D_b(N)}, the vertex scales as N^{(b-a)/2}. Only a=b has the preceding constant leading behavior. At the actual six-dimensional degrees, the conditional muon-to-electron canonical vertex ratios are: Shared dimension a Vertex ratio 2 5.91750718 3 3.79171524 4 2.42695557 6 0.94381606 These compare branches at the same containing depth, common width and common probe rule. The dimensional units of the probe coefficient change with a; the rows are not absolute couplings between different sectors. The complete band trace is isotropic. It is a useful exact control, but does not test the polarized spatial patterns of an actual particle pair. Their spinor vertices, both complex polarizations, relative orientation and reciprocal spatial evolution remain necessary. What the inverse test supplies The localized current fixed point supplies a further concrete same-field inverse example. Its depth-six nodeless profile has root mean squared radius 1.549216\ldots c/m_c, with the same profile at every occupied mass grade. If its common core coefficient is identified with \omega_{0,6}, this gives an explicit geometric factor in (2). That coefficient identification and a common unit canonical norm remain stated inverse premises; neither is derived by extracting a frequency unit from the observed masses. The full matrix action also gives the corresponding canonical inertia, while physical mode-carrier selection and complete stability remain open. The dimensionless binding calculation extends this spatial fixed point to depths five and ten and supplies the factors \gamma_5=1.44357039, \gamma_6=1.54921602 and \gamma_{10}=1.89885917. With the explicit shared-gap and shared-frequency identifications, the depth-ten to depth-six size ratio is 1.22569038. These are radii of the reconstructed field profiles; their measured interaction form factors and cross-depth vertices remain to be derived. The common-size premise constrains confinement as well as oscillation. Equations (3)–(9) supply explicit balances with measurable collective consequences. Equations (10)–(17) show how the requested grouping of coupling responses imposes a further condition on the same reduction. The point-contact comparison is close to that condition within one full spatial sector, but its ordinary nested marginal does not retain it. The spatial and moving-cavity response resolves these probes by momentum and energy transfer, retaining complex polarizations and consistently moving final modes. The open derivation is a same-field action that supplies the count-additive kinetic and supporting energies, selects the occupied modes, and produces the physical normalized vertex. These calculations constrain that action; they do not establish a completed mass operator. The surface-bending frequency calculation tests a concrete geometric restoring energy with the exact simplex eigenvalues. Its conformal scale remains undetermined, and ordinary tension changes the frequency ratios. The associated nonlinear mode response derives a scale vertex from that same energy and distinguishes its absolute canonical strength from a common fractional frequency shift. cavity_balance_checks.py verifies the independent positive-energy minima, exact energy moments, full nonlinear breathing trajectories, reciprocal canonical spectra and the spatial marginal formula against direct normalized Hermite quadrature.

title: Size variation of a common positive response
summary: A scale-covariant positive Laplacian response shifts the standing frequency but cannot by itself stabilize a common cavity size; its fixed-profile size extremum is absent or unstable at every maintained depth.
text: A shared length among the harmonics of one depth must follow from the same spatial action as their standing frequencies. The fixed-norm response result gives a frequency shift, but it does not yet determine a length. This note varies that length for a minimal local response whose source, stiffness and kinetic normalization all scale together. The calculation supplies a necessary test for that class of candidate actions, not a general theorem about every same-field support mechanism. One scale-covariant sector model Work at one physical depth d\geq2. Let a common reference region or profile family have length L. It need not be a hard-walled cavity or a compactified dimension. For a normalized spatial pattern write \psi_{i,L}(x)=\sqrt{Q_i}\,L^{-d/2}u_i(x/L),\qquad \int |u_i(y)|^2\,d^dy=1. \tag{1} The canonical norm Q_i can differ between solutions. At this stage u_i is held fixed during the dilation; allowing it to relax can change the result. Assume that the positive-frequency bare branch has E_{0,i}(Q_i,L)=Q_i\frac{c\mu_i}{L},\qquad \mu_i>0, \tag{2} as for a scale-covariant first-order spatial operator. The dimensionless \mu_i is an output of that operator, not automatically a simplex count. For the proposed mass law, one would need \mu_i=\gamma_d\mathcal S(i,d) with a single factor \gamma_d at that depth. Let z be a retained, relaxing component of the same field. Consider its quadratic energy and a local quadratic source, E_z=\frac12\langle z,A_Lz\rangle -g\langle z,S[\psi]\rangle, \quad A_L=L^{-2}U_L\widehat A U_L^{-1}>0, \quad S[\psi_{i,L}]\bigl(x\bigr)=Q_iL^{-d}\sigma_i(x/L). \tag{3} Here U_L f(x)=L^{-d/2}f(x/L) is unitary between the reference and physical L^2 spaces. The reference operator \widehat A may be a positive dimensionless Laplacian plus a positive gap. The gap in (3) scales with L^{-2}; a fixed external gap introduces another length and is outside this one-scale test. The source shape \sigma_i includes the actual spatial polarization contractions if the action supplies them. Its arbitrary normalization cannot be absorbed separately for each mode. Eliminating z gives the exact fixed-profile coefficient K_i=\langle\sigma_i,\widehat A^{-1}\sigma_i\rangle>0, \qquad E_i(Q_i,L)=\frac{Q_ic\mu_i}{L} -\frac{g^2Q_i^2K_i}{2L^{d-2}}. \tag{4} The power L^{2-d} follows from the physical d-volume, the two factors L^{-d} in the source and the inverse stiffness L^2. It does not depend on a chosen radial ansatz. At fixed norm the standing frequency is the canonical multiplier \boxed{\omega_i=\left.\frac{\partial E_i}{\partial Q_i}\right|_L =\frac{c\mu_i}{L}-\frac{g^2Q_iK_i}{L^{d-2}}.} \tag{5} Mass is read from this frequency in equivalent units. The second term can depend on amplitude and profile without making amplitude itself mass. The size extremum Put A_i=Q_ic\mu_i>0, B_i=g^2Q_i^2K_i/2>0, and p=d-2. Along the specified norm-preserving dilation, E_i(L)=\frac{A_i}{L}-\frac{B_i}{L^p},\qquad E_i'(L)=-\frac{A_i}{L^2}+\frac{pB_i}{L^{p+1}}. \tag{6} This one-dimensional variation is a necessary direction for spatial stability. It gives the following exhaustive cases for the maintained depths: Depth Response power p Fixed-profile size result 2 0 The response is independent of L; E_i'(L)<0 for finite L. 3 1 E_i=(A_i-B_i)/L; only A_i=B_i is stationary, and then the dilation is flat. Its standing frequency is negative. 4, 5, 6, 10 d-2>1 A finite extremum exists, but E_i''(L_*)=(3-d)A_i/L_*^3<0. At depth four its standing frequency is zero. For d>3, its position obeys L_*^{d-3}=\frac{(d-2)B_i}{A_i} =\frac{(d-2)g^2Q_iK_i}{2c\mu_i}. \tag{7} The energy tends to -\infty under contraction in this restricted model. Thus the extremum is a maximum even before other field and geometric perturbations are considered. A stationary common length across harmonics would also require the right side of (7) to be mode-independent. Equal Q_i makes that a condition on K_i/\mu_i. The existing equal-norm source controls fail its simplex version at every multi-mode maintained depth. Adjusting Q_i after seeing the masses or lengths would not derive a selection law. Substituting the stationary-size condition into the multiplier (5) gives \omega_i(L_*)=\left(1-\frac{2}{d-2}\right)\frac{c\mu_i}{L_*} =\frac{d-4}{d-2}\frac{c\mu_i}{L_*}. \tag{8} At depth three the flat condition gives \omega_i=-c\mu_i/L<0. The depth-four extremum has \omega_i=0, so it cannot represent a positive mass-frequency branch. The depth-five, six and ten extrema have positive multipliers, respectively one-third, one-half and three-quarters of the bare frequency, but remain size maxima. Energy per norm and the canonical frequency differ because the eliminated response is quadratic in Q_i; the positive energy at those maxima does not repair their negative size curvature. For the positive response alone, unconstrained amplitude does not repair the problem. At fixed L, \partial_{Q_i}^2E_i=-g^2K_i/L^{d-2}<0. A specified conserved norm removes that radial direction from the constrained tangent space; it does not select its value or supply a positive size curvature. What an additional stabilizer must accomplish If the complete same-field energy contains a further term G_i(Q_i,L), a stable common length L_d must satisfy, for every occupied harmonic at that depth, \left.\partial_LG_i\right|_{L_d} =\frac{A_i}{L_d^2}-\frac{pB_i}{L_d^{p+1}}, \qquad \left.\partial_L^2(E_i+G_i)\right|_{L_d}>0. \tag{9} The same G must also enter the canonical multiplier and the complete energy-momentum response. A mode-independent geometric cost is not automatically sufficient: its one size derivative must equal the mode-dependent right side of (8) for all occupied harmonics. A coupling or stiffness coefficient independently chosen for each harmonic would hide the missing mechanism. A different spatial order, a fixed physical gap, nonlinear profile relaxation or a constrained off-diagonal field equation can change the scaling argument; each must be calculated from its own full action. The localized current construction, for example, uses an auxiliary spatial fixed-point functional whose value is not additional particle energy, so (4) is not its size law. The next constructive task is to derive a common stabilizing term and solve its profile and norm equations together with (5) and (9), then check the full Hessian and reciprocal pair response. The present result shows exactly why a positive quadratic response and a common length symbol alone cannot complete that task.

title: Counting, Frequency Selection and Internal-Motion Inertia
summary: Pascal incidence supplies exact phase weights; localized profiles, canonical action and full boosts expose the additional conditions needed for a physical mass spectrum.
text:
A count becomes a particle mass only when the same dynamics supplies a localized state, its normalization and its complete energy. The construction below makes each step explicit. It is an inverse candidate action on ordinary physical space, not a derivation of the maintained particle spectrum. Counts From a Common Incidence Rule Consider complex components of one proposed field on \mathbb R^d, with canonical kinetic density \sum_a(|\partial_t\phi_a|^2-|
abla\phi_a|^2) in units c=1. Components are labeled by a Pascal graph. All boundary entries refer to one common component b. A cubic incidence couples each child to its two parents. Phase invariance requires q_c=q_p+q_z,\qquad q_{k,0}=q_{0,r}=1, \qquad q_{k,r}= inom{k+r}{r}. This is a derived graph charge assignment. The graph labels are not spatial coordinates and do not establish physical depth. A separate matched vacuum gap \mu q_c is assumed in the potential V=\mu^2|b|^2+\sum_c\left[(\mu^2q_c^2-\mu^2)|\phi_c|^2+ \left|\mu\phi_c- rac g\mu\phi_p\phi_zight|^2ight]. Reflected adjacent parents with opposite amplitudes, together with their common child, form an exact invariant three-component configuration. Their counts are q,q,2q, where q= inom{2k+1}{k}=3,10,35,126,\ldots,\qquad k\ge1. Destructive interference makes every exterior classical source vanish. This closure holds at every encompassing graph cutoff. It establishes a useful count family, which differs from the maintained electron, muon and other particle assignments. Actual Spatial Profiles and Complete Energy In \mu=g=1 units let the parents be P=\sqrt2F(r)e^{-i\omega t} and Z=-P, and the child C=-2H(r)e^{-2i\omega t}. The profiles obey \Delta F=\delta F-2HF+2F^3,\qquad \Delta H=4\delta H-F^2,\qquad \omega=\sqrt{q^2-\delta},\quad 0<\delta< rac14. For regular decaying real profiles define I=\int(F^2+4H^2),\quad T=\int(|
abla F|^2+|
abla H|^2), \quad P_0=\int HF^2,\quad K=\int F^4. All integrals use the full d-dimensional spatial measure. Multiplication of the profile equations and spatial dilation give \delta I= rac{6-d}{d}T+K,\qquad P_0-K= rac{2T}{d}. The primitive phase action J, graph charge Q and complete rest energy are J=8\omega I,\qquad Q=qJ,\qquad E=\omega J+ rac{8T}{d}. The supporting gradients are part of the particle candidate. Its complete mass-frequency is E/\hbar and rest mass is E/c^2. The carrier phase rate \omega=dE/dJ is a collective coordinate rate; assigning it the complete particle energy without checking normalization would omit the supporting contribution. Internal Motion Enters the Translational Momentum A boost of speed u changes both envelope and phase. To first order each harmonic becomes f_l(x-ut)e^{-il\omega(t-ux_1)}. Direct substitution in the canonical momentum, followed by the virial identity, gives P_1=u\left(8\omega^2 I+ rac{8T}{d}ight)+O(u^2)=uE+O(u^2). Thus the internal oscillation contributes to the same kinetic momentum as translation even when the unboosted center is at rest. For a computed depth-three q=3 profile with \delta=0.109762540262, the two displayed contributions are approximately 29816.50124 and 60.92649, totaling 29877.42773. Translating only its envelope omits nearly all the inertia. This is a result within the declared Lorentz-covariant action and its stationary stress balance. Conditional Action Selection The parent mean and relative phases (\varphi, eta) have the identification (\varphi, eta)\sim(\varphi+\pi, eta+\pi). An untwisted collective wavefunction has integer labels m,n with m+n even. Relative-neutral states therefore require even m. Conditional quantization at fixed depth gives 8\sqrt{q^2-\delta}\,I_d(\delta)=m\eta, \qquad \eta= rac{\hbar g^2}{\mu^{5-d}}. One common m=10000, n=0, \eta=1 gives the following depth-three boundary-value solutions: Count q Selected \delta Complete E/(\hbar\mu) RMS radius in 1/\mu 3 0.1097625403 29877.43 4.46686 10 0.0616521486 99983.90 5.39049 35 0.01746988883 349999.04 9.53428 The charge condition was solved with the profile equations. These are conditional large-action examples, not elementary-particle predictions. Quantization, the physical action unit and the desired spatial assignments remain to be justified. A regular weak cubic endpoint has I_d\sim C_d\delta^{2-d/2} only for d<6. Its action tends to zero at depths two and three, a nonzero limit at four, and infinity at five. The Pohozaev identity excludes this particular endpoint at six and ten. Depth five also has \eta=\hbar g^2, independent of \mu: changing the sector frequency scale cannot evade an action threshold there. This is a specific dimensional consequence of this candidate, not a neutrino prediction. Stability and Interaction Belong to the Same Action Exact closure does not guarantee stability. Higher q=10,35 examples have growing incoming-component modes in refined finite-domain calculations. At exactly opposing parent phases the lowest q=3 pattern instead has a positive conserved exterior quadratic energy. Small departures in its internal relative phase couple a disturbance to an opposite-sign continuum; outgoing calculations at depths three and five support growth. There is no established finite stable phase-acceptance interval. For well separated copies of the same grade, the canonical stress and phase current produce leading interaction terms proportional to \cos\Delta\varphi and \sin\Delta\varphi, respectively. A quarter-cycle mean-phase difference can suppress the leading force while retaining phase-action transfer. Those initial tail calculations do not establish a full collision. Mean phase between two patterns and relative phase inside one pattern are different variables. The scale-covariant contact action changes the interaction law to obtain exact complete-energy scaling and a different exterior stability result. Its results must not be assigned to the original action above. The subsequent field evolution tests reciprocal contact under that amended action. Classical profiles still form a continuous family; no physical frequency-selection law has been completed.

title: Searching compatible nested geometries with one field law
summary: A joint geometry parameterization enforces sector compatibility before testing the standing field and necessary supporting variations across all maintained depths.
text: A geometry search must retain the nesting of physical sectors. A good independent fit at depth two and another at depth three do not constitute a joint solution unless their metrics can occur in the same containing geometry. This calculation imposes that compatibility before solving for any particle frequency. The first implemented family consists of nested, conformally deformed spheres. It is a finite-dimensional search within the existing spherical spatial candidate, not an enumeration of all geometries in ten or fewer dimensions. Its global spherical topology is an assumption of this candidate. It does not introduce compactified physical dimensions. One metric and its compatible restrictions Start with an intrinsic ten-sphere of radius R_{10}. Mathematical Euclidean embedding coordinates X describe nested latitude spheres; they do not introduce an additional physical dimension. Choose 0<R_2\le R_3\le R_4\le R_5\le R_6\le R_{10}. Each lower sphere is a latitude sphere of the next containing sphere. For a jump of several dimensions, fix the necessary additional embedding coordinates. The squared coordinate offsets sum to the difference of the squared radii. Equal radii give equatorial inclusions. On the containing sphere define Q=\frac{X_1^2+X_2^2}{R_{10}^2},\qquad \sigma(Q)=a_1(Q-\tfrac12)+a_2(1-6Q+6Q^2) +a_3(-1+12Q-30Q^2+20Q^3). The containing metric is g_{10}=e^{2\sigma(Q)}g_{10,0}. On a depth-d member, let q=(X_1^2+X_2^2)/R_d^2. Its metric is \boxed{g_d=e^{2\sigma((R_d/R_{10})^2q)}g_{d,0}.} Every lower metric is therefore the actual pullback of the higher one. Direct restriction and restriction through intermediate depths agree. The radii are parameterized by one outer radius and five ratios in [0.65,1]; the three shape coefficients are shared. Different particles at the same depth always see the same candidate radius and metric. This restriction is particular to the latitude-sphere family. It is not a theorem that all nested physical sectors must have ordered curvature radii or spherical topology. Particle fields are not required to be restrictions of one another. Curvature and the stated supporting law For the unit round metric at depth d, |\nabla q|^2=4q(1-q),\qquad \Delta_+f=-4q(1-q)f''+[2(d+1)q-4]f', where \Delta_+ is the positive Laplacian. The curvature scale of the conformal metric is \kappa_d=\frac{e^{-\sigma}}{R_d} \sqrt{1+\frac2d\Delta_+\sigma -\frac{d-2}{d}|\nabla\sigma|^2}. The square-root argument is a polynomial. Its minimum is evaluated at both endpoints and every real stationary point in [0,1], rather than only at integration nodes. This is a floating-point domain check, not an interval certificate. The screen retains the stated inverse supporting law g(\kappa)=\frac{100\kappa^4}{1+\kappa^4} in units with the reference length and wave speed equal to one. Its coefficient and functional form are common inputs. They have not been derived from the master field. A negative scalar curvature is a failure of this particular real-curvature law's domain, not a failure of metric compatibility or a proof that such a geometry is physically impossible. The field and profile tests The finite calculation uses the same timelike current source F[\psi]=H_0\psi-\frac{g}{s} \left[jK+\eta_d^2(\rho I-z\Sigma)\right]\psi, \qquad s^2=j^2+\eta_d^2(\rho^2-z^2). Here \rho=\psi^\dagger\psi, j=\psi^\dagger K\psi, and z=\psi^\dagger\Sigma\psi, with \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(I_d,-I_d). The fixed matrix K links adjacent components of the existing finite chain. For spinors, H_0=\chi D_g+\kappa A, where \chi exchanges the two component blocks and A=\chi\operatorname{diag}(a-d/2), a=0,\ldots,d-1. The depth-two form version uses its actual Hodge operator and parity-dependent curvature offsets. The positive action is \|\partial_t\psi\|^2-\|F[\psi]\|^2. The six values of \eta_d are taken from the preceding pair calculation, with one fixed value per depth. They are not refitted for a particle or geometry. A separate saturated calculation uses \eta=0 on the strictly negative-current branch. All maintained spectral controls enter each joint candidate: W, Z and Higgs; down, strange and the two bottom constituent indices; up, charm and top; the three neutrino indices; electron and muon; and tau. The bottom constituent indices are not two separate particles. The bosonic depth-two calculation retains scalar and differential-form components. Each reference spinor field has canonical conformal transport \widetilde D_\sigma=e^{-\sigma/2}D e^{-\sigma/2}. Two spatial profiles are tested: the canonically transported reference field and its normalized multiple e^{\sigma/2}. The latter cancels the explicit conformal derivative term in this restricted field family. For depth-two forms, the corresponding transport is E_\sigma D_{\mathrm f}E_\sigma, where E_\sigma=e^{-\sigma}P_{\rm even}+P_{\rm odd}. Its alternative profile multiplies the even component by e^\sigma. It is not assigned the spinor weight. The real component vector adjusts through the complete finite chain and, for finite \eta_d, its nonlinear current fixed point. Its selected positive frequency remains the mass in frequency units. Profile normalization is not used as mass. The principal field diagnostic is r_F=\frac{\|F[\phi]-\omega\phi\|}{\omega\|\phi\|}. This tests the inherited first-order standing branch, which supplies a solution of the positive wave action when it holds. It does not exhaust all possible solutions of the second-order equation involving DF^*F. The full spatial field is not freely optimized: only the stated profiles and real component vectors are retained. Necessary supporting tests differentiate the generating energy along a common scale change and the three shared shape changes. For the adapted profiles these paths change both geometry and profile. Vanishing path derivatives would be necessary for a full joint stationary solution; it would not establish stationarity against independent, arbitrary field and tensor-metric variations. A nonzero derivative rules out stationarity of that tested configuration. A joint score is the worst particle's combined field defect and largest normalized path derivative. Opposing errors from different particles are never summed to cancel one another. Passing thresholds are numerical screening tolerances, not observational error bars or a stability theorem. Independent orientations inside the same compatible geometry For spinors at depths three and above, rotate the complex spatial pattern plane through the same angle \theta in two coordinate planes. The geometry stays fixed. For a degree-n field, the normalized marginal law of its geometric coordinate q is \sum_{\ell=0}^{n} \binom n\ell p^\ell(1-p)^{n-\ell} \operatorname{Beta}\!\left(\ell+1,n-\ell+\frac{d-1}{2}\right), \qquad p=\cos^2\theta. This follows by expanding the rotated complex harmonic, averaging its relative phases, and using the sphere's coordinate-square distribution. Its moments independently verify the numerical integration. On a round metric, the frequency is independent of \theta. The orientation refinement retains seven angles and both profiles on selected complete metric chains. It includes the frequency derivative with respect to orientation at interior angles. This is one continuous rotation family, not the entire orientation space. The depth-two form calculation does not use this four-coordinate spinor construction. An axisymmetric marginal must not be mistaken for an axisymmetric full field or an isotropic tensor stress. Search bounds and interpretation The initial design contains 1,208 compatible chains: 1,024 reproducible Sobol samples, round boundary families, and explicit small deformations. The outer radius ranges from 0.4 to 2.5; shape coefficients range over [-0.3,0.3], [-0.06,0.06], and [-0.02,0.02]. Three starting configurations are refined jointly within the same bounds. Higher-order integration checks the best retained results. The completed results and verification receipts are recorded below. Even a successful screen would still need unrestricted field adjustment, independent metric-stress tests, stability, mass-ratio checks and physical scale selection. Failure of this screen excludes only the tested configurations and profiles under the stated law. Why a spatially varying component pattern is necessary in this family There is a structural limitation in the first profile screen. For a spinor reference eigenfield Du=\beta u, put \psi=f(q)\phi\otimes u, with one real component vector \phi throughout space. If f=e^{\alpha\sigma}, canonical transport gives \widetilde D_\sigma(fu)= f e^{-\sigma}\left[\beta u+ (\alpha-\tfrac12)\operatorname{cl}(d\sigma)u\right]. The Clifford term has no real cross term with the retained real component ray. Its squared norm supplies a nonnegative contribution to the field residual. Thus the unchanged profile cannot give an exact standing field on a nonconstant conformal metric. The covariant choice \alpha=1/2 removes this particular obstruction. There is still a second restriction. Define \chi\phi=(v,u) for \phi=(u,v), and let A=\chi\operatorname{diag}(j-d/2). The finite-current contribution on this separated ray is a fixed matrix J multiplied by the local strength g(q). The remaining equation is \left[a(q)\chi+\kappa(q)A+g(q)J\right]\phi=\omega\phi, \qquad a(q)=\frac{\beta e^{-\sigma(q)}}{R_d}. For the retained positive arithmetic-diagonal component chain at d\ge3, the vectors \phi,\chi\phi,A\phi are linearly independent. All components of the lowest singular vectors are nonzero. A proposed relation would require (s+t(j-d/2))^2=r^2 at three or more distinct values of j. This forces t=0, leaving a possible \chi-eigenvector. That would make the left and right singular vectors equal up to sign. The first row of the lower-triangular chain and the last row of its transpose would then require its distinct endpoint diagonal entries to coincide. They do not. The averaged eigen-equation consequently makes \chi\phi,A\phi,J\phi independent as well. Subtracting the averaged equation from the pointwise one forces all three scalar coefficients to be constant. In particular, a(q) constant forces \sigma constant. This is a restriction of the separated component-ray ansatz, not an exclusion of deformed geometries in IDWT.
