A meaningful extension must allow the component pattern itself to vary with position. The follow-up calculation therefore retains an axial spatial basis in every component, including both spatial spectral signs. Its local nonlinear source is integrated before projection; the norm of the residual outside the retained basis is included. Every such field is tested on the same compatible metric chain. This is a larger conditional search, not yet a complete spatial or geometric variational solution. A second compatible family: complete flat sectors The flat chain \mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^3\subset\cdots \subset\mathbb R^{10} is compatible without selecting radii or shape coefficients. Under the particular curvature-dependent candidate tested here, \kappa=0 gives g(0)=0, and the curvature offsets vanish. The remaining spatial operator is the free Dirac operator, or the actual free Hodge operator for the depth-two forms. Its square is c^2(-\Delta) on the appropriate components. A square-integrable standing field on a complete flat sector would obey (-c^2\Delta-\omega^2)\psi=0. Fourier transformation requires its square-integrable transform to be supported on |k|^2=\omega^2/c^2. This set has Lebesgue measure zero, including the zero-frequency case. The only such square-integrable field is zero. Thus this supporting-law candidate cannot provide a localized standing particle anywhere in the complete flat chain. This is an analytic exclusion under the stated law, with no artificial boundary, external potential or altered asymptotic conditions. It does not exclude locally flat regions of a curved geometry, confinement from a different same-field law, or flat directions outside the bound sector. It also does not assert that ordinary physical space has measured nonzero curvature. No empirical geometric conclusion follows from this conditional calculation. Spatial-pattern refinement on one compatible chain All sixteen controls were relaxed on the same chain with every radius 0.8 and shared coefficients (0.003, -0.0002, 0.0001). The calculation retained a spatial basis through cutoff two, then expanded it to cutoff three for the first maintained control at each depth. The normalized pointwise first-order field residuals were: Depth Control Initial residual Expanded-basis residual Largest metric path derivative / frequency 2 W 0.00156088 6.81884e-06 5.17755 3 down 2.99778 0.0111373 1.85365 4 up 6.79341 0.024939 4.53209 5 neutrino 1 2.05422 0.000257419 20.2712 6 electron 2.9595 0.000329197 27.6463 10 tau 4.1822 0.000590969 54.1317 Residuals are fractions, not percentages. These are computed field defects, not discrepancies from measured particle masses. The cutoff-three fits except the depth-two W control reached their iteration limits. Their remaining residuals must not be reported as converged minima or exact solutions. The cutoff-two fields agree under 100- and 200-point integration; that does not prove convergence with respect to the spatial basis. The results demonstrate that spatially varying component patterns can substantially reduce the first screen's defects without changing the nested metric independently for each particle. They do not eliminate the supporting forces. None of these configurations supplies a fully self-supported particle geometry. The raw minimum-current diagnostic for the high-index depth-two Higgs control includes extremely small polar tails, where normalized-current diagnostics are set to zero below the numerical density cutoff. This is not evidence of a physical null-current boundary. The weighted residuals are checked by integration refinement; a pointwise domain certificate for every tail is not supplied. Common-strength controls A separate control changes the common coefficient in the curvature law for the whole chain, using 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 at each of four common radii (0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 2.5). No particle-specific strength is fitted. None of these sixteen complete round chains has zero radial force for every maintained control. At the larger strengths, the previously fixed finite regularizers also prevent the algorithm from retaining a positive branch for some modes. That is a domain limitation of this candidate and branch procedure, not a proof against every nonlinear branch or supporting law. Completed joint scan Both current-law versions completed the same 1,208 compatible metric configurations. Each retained 1,010 configurations in its tested curvature and component-branch domain; 198 were outside that domain. These are not 198 failures of nesting compatibility: every generated chain was compatible by construction. Three joint refinements were completed for each law. Current law Best tradeoff score Largest relative field defect at that point Largest normalized path force Saturated 7.2151719 3.5089233 7.2110505 Finite timelike 7.215221 3.5087623 7.2111023 No sampled or optimized candidate passed the simultaneous field tolerance of 1e-6 and path-force tolerance of 1e-5. The score only ranks unsuccessful tradeoffs; its minimum is not an approximate physical solution. The best points also approach the lower radius bound, so the finite search does not establish a global minimum over the metric family. The orientation refinement improves some necessary force diagnostics, but none of its five metric chains passes either. The strongest statement is therefore a completed conditional screen, together with a concrete reason to enlarge the spatial field ansatz. The scan does not establish which geometry nature realizes or finish the mass operator. Reproducible verification The six identity and implementation reports pass 1,489 checks in total. They cover nested metric restriction, curvature, derivative identities, normalization, finite-current fixed points, orientation moments, actual bosonic form transport, the spatial residual gradient and agreement between the screening formulas and an independently assembled pointwise spatial operator. Completed numerical screens are recorded separately from passing identity checks. Their failures, iteration limits, coefficient arrays and integration refinements are preserved with the source hashes. The main entry points are joint_geometry_fast_scan.py and joint_geometry_finite_scan.py for the joint metric search, joint_orientation_screen.py for independent pattern headings, joint_spatial_screen.py for component textures, and joint_strength_audit.py for common-strength controls. The checkpoint manifest identifies their exact archived versions and the raw numerical arrays.

title: Self-source from complementary Dirac modes
summary: An explicit canonical normal-mode reduction produces a spectral square-root source and its full response; the projected count, total norm and complete scalar square determine what remains missing from a physical mass law.
text: Summary: An explicit canonical normal-mode reduction produces a spectral square-root source and its full response; the projected count, total norm and complete scalar square determine what remains missing from a physical mass law. Derive a source before interpreting it as mass The current hierarchy reconstructs an action with a simplex self-source. A complementary calculation starts from an explicit canonical Dirac pair and derives the interaction obtained by following its occupied modes. The reduction explains a square-root law, but also fixes its matrix meaning, its occupation dependence and its frequency response. Those details cannot be chosen independently afterward. All retained and complementary variables below are conditional modes of the same field. Their normal kinetic matrix must ultimately follow from the physical spatial Dirac operator and its geometry. No extra interaction particle is introduced. The matrix rank counts coefficient modes; it adds no physical spatial dimensions and imposes no compactification. Let a Hermitian retained current be R on an r-dimensional coefficient space. Consider the complementary Hamiltonian H(R)=\epsilon\tau_x\otimes I+g\tau_z\otimes R, \qquad \epsilon>0, \qquad E_i=\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r_i^2}. \tag{1} Here r_i are the eigenvalues of R, \tau_x,\tau_z are Pauli matrices, and \epsilon is a specified normal kinetic frequency. It is not an inserted physical particle mass. The two signs of the Dirac spectrum are retained without assigning them a particle–antiparticle interpretation. Canonical occupation and the spectral root Represent the occupied complementary field by a matrix Y whose columns are explicitly orthogonal spectator modes of the same field. With one common canonical norm q per positive eigenmode, its density is Y^\dagger Y=qI_r,\qquad YY^\dagger=qP_+(R),\qquad Q_f=\operatorname{Tr}Y^\dagger Y=qr. \tag{2} A single pure coefficient vector does not automatically give the complete projector in (2). The physical spectator modes and their occupation need an origin in the master field. A quantum filled sea is not assumed. The positive spectral space maximizes \operatorname{Tr}(Y^\dagger H Y) at this fixed Gram matrix: diagonalizing H bounds the occupied trace by the sum of its r largest eigenvalues. This is an energy maximum, rather than a passive ground state. Its dynamical viability must be checked in the coupled system and in its actual spatial domain. Subtracting the specified R=0 reference energy gives the adiabatic law \begin{aligned} U_{\rm ad}(R)&=q\operatorname{Tr} \left[\sqrt{\epsilon^2I+g^2R^2}-\epsilon I\right],\\ K(R)&=\frac{\partial U_{\rm ad}}{\partial R} =qg^2R(\epsilon^2I+g^2R^2)^{-1/2}. \end{aligned} \tag{3} For a scalar current this is exactly the smooth saturating law, with \mu=q|g| and \sigma=\epsilon/|g|. For a matrix current it is a trace of spectral roots. It is not \mu\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}R^2+\sigma^2}. Those two functions agree on an isolated rank-one current but give different finite interactions. For example, let R=AP_z+BP_w, A,B>0, and \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2. Its two nonzero eigenvalues are \lambda_\pm=\frac{A+B\pm \sqrt{(A-B)^2+4AB\tau}}2. \tag{4} At positive \epsilon, (3) gives a nonnegative cross energy which increases with \tau and vanishes for orthogonal rays. At zero gap, \operatorname{Tr}|R|=\operatorname{Tr}R=A+B: the positive-current cross energy vanishes at every orientation. The Hilbert–Schmidt root instead gives \sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\tau}-A-B, which is generally negative. The zero-gap and zero-probe limits also fail to commute at a current with a null eigenspace. At every positive gap an infinitesimal probe orthogonal to a rank-one target has zero first derivative, whereas a finite positive probe has a nonzero slope after taking the root limit. An isolated source coefficient therefore does not determine the pair law. The complete frequency response Use the convention e^{-i\Omega t}, with a positive imaginary part of \Omega for the retarded continuation. In an eigenbasis of R, the linear response acts entry by entry on \delta R: \begin{aligned} \delta K_{ij}&=\chi_{ij}(\Omega)\delta R_{ij},\\ \chi_{ij}(\Omega)&= \frac{2qg^2T_{ij}(E_i+E_j)}{(E_i+E_j)^2-\Omega^2},\\ T_{ij}&=\frac{E_iE_j+\epsilon^2-g^2r_ir_j}{2E_iE_j}. \end{aligned} \tag{5} To derive (5), linearize the complete density equation i\dot D=[H,D] about D=qP_+. In the full Dirac eigenbasis, (\delta D)_{ab}= \frac{(D_b-D_a)(\delta H)_{ab}} {\Omega-(H_a-H_b)}. \tag{6} Only transitions between the equally occupied positive space and the unoccupied negative space contribute. Their squared scalar transition matrix element is T_{ij}; combining both directions gives (5). Taking the scalar current of \delta D supplies the second factor of g. At zero frequency this is the divided difference of qg^2r/\sqrt{\epsilon^2+g^2r^2}. The diagonal is \chi_{ii}(\Omega)= \frac{4qg^2\epsilon^2}{E_i(4E_i^2-\Omega^2)}. \tag{7} The full response is even in frequency. In a smooth positive frame, the trace Berry connection vanishes, although the matrix connection can be nonzero. The leading susceptibility correction is proportional to \Omega^2 and is positive along a Hermitian probe below the poles. Its eliminated real-time derivative term has the sign associated with expansion about the constrained energy maximum. This is a low-frequency expansion of the explicit canonical system, not a fundamental higher-time- derivative theory or a proof of spatial causality. Retain the actual master projection The smooth coherent scalar projection defines D_N=\binom{N+d}{d} and the normalized current symbol j_N(z)=D_N\langle z^N|C_N|z^N\rangle. A complementary degree-M space sees the actual insertion V_{N\to M}(C_N)=D_M\int j_N(z)P_{z,M}\,d\nu(z). \tag{8} The ray measure describes coefficient directions over physical space. It is not a new spatial sector. The exact contractions of the linked projection note evaluate (8) without replacing its weights by shell weights. For an isolated coherent current C_N=JP_{u,N}, the eigenvalue at transverse occupation j and its multiplicity are v_j=J\frac{D_ND_M}{D_{N+M}} \frac{(M)_{\underline j}}{(N+M)_{\underline j}}, \qquad h_{j,d}=\binom{j+d-1}{d-1},\quad 0\le j\le M. \tag{9} One derivation sets t=|z^\dagger u|^2. The sum of coherent probabilities in the jth transverse shell is \binom Mj t^{M-j}(1-t)^j, and its measure is d(1-t)^{d-1}dt. The beta integral, divided by h_{j,d}, gives (9). The trace identity is particularly restrictive: \boxed{\sum_{j=0}^M h_{j,d}v_j=D_MJ.} \tag{10} Thus the zero-gap, completely occupied positive complementary space gives cross source q|g|D_M. It counts the populated complementary band, independently of the retained degree N. Obtaining D_N requires the additional rule M=N. At fixed total complementary norm Q_f, q=Q_f/D_M removes that enhancement. At common norm per mode, Q_f=qD_M grows with the count. The scalar gap normalization explains the corresponding distinction in a global self-consistent model. A single coherent normal source has a different preparation from the complete population in (2). Its full target insertion approaches qD_NP_{z,N} at fixed canonical norm as the normal degree tends to infinity. That construction derives an explicit contact approximation and its divergent scalar self-energy cost; it does not require matching the populated band to the target. For a positive kinetic gap, insert (9) into (3). At J=q=g=1, matched depth-six bands N=12,34 give the following cross-only ratios. The width is \sigma=\epsilon/|g| in the same declared current units. Width Excess-energy ratio Source ratio 10^{-6} 206.7648723 206.7647007 10^{-3} 206.8935178 206.7827363 0.1 211.6067621 208.2020296 1 229.9706123 215.9223027 These are controlled model values, with no fitted physical gap. The smallest insertion at N=34 is approximately 2.80\times10^{-15} in these units. Adiabatic following must compare the actual frequencies of current variation with the relevant transition gaps. A stationary field's overall phase cancels from its current; its phase frequency alone is not a time scale for that test. Restore the complete scalar square The cross interaction alone is not the entire scalar master kernel. At zero normal kinetic gap, take a coherent retained current JP_{u,N} and a uniformly populated complementary current qI_M. The complete projected square gives \begin{aligned} \lambda_N&=\frac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}},\\ E_{\rm total}&=\frac g2 \left[J^2\lambda_N+2JqD_M+q^2D_M^2\right],\\ \boxed{\omega_N}&=\boxed{g\left[J\lambda_N+qD_M\right]}. \end{aligned} \tag{11} Here g>0 is the common scalar-square coefficient in the same normalized mode units, and \omega_N is the retained positive-spinor phase frequency. The complementary self-insertion is qD_MI_M. It commutes with the complete complementary density, so that density stays invariant while its complex occupied modes acquire their actual phases. The total canonical norm is J+qD_M. Above the specified complementary- only reference, the excess energy is E_{\rm excess}=gJqD_M+\frac g2J^2\lambda_N, \qquad \frac{\partial E_{\rm excess}}{\partial J}=\omega_N. \tag{12} For M=N and J=q=1, the depth-six source-frequency ratio is 204.6505814, and the excess-energy ratio is 205.6913738. The simplex ratio is D_{34}/D_{12}=3515/17=206.7647059. The retained self-term in (11) therefore matters. Dropping it would change the action under investigation. The full energy also contains the complementary self-energy, proportional to q^2D_M^2. Identifying only the retained phase or a subtracted energy with a particle's physical rest mass requires an explicit physical preparation and energy prescription. A coefficient that contains a count does not settle that identification. The complete normal band at finite kinetic gap The full self-consistent normal band can be calculated without constructing a D_M-dimensional dense matrix. In the coherent target frame, let c_j be the scalar eigenvalue of the normal current on transverse shell j, with multiplicity h_{j,d}. Its coherent symbol is D_M\sum_jc_j\binom Mj t^{M-j}(1-t)^j. Integrating the product of two such symbols gives the exact self-insertion matrix \boxed{\mathcal K_{kj}= \frac{D_M^2d}{h_{k,d}}\binom Mk\binom Mj \mathrm B(2M-k-j+1,d+k+j),} \tag{12a} where \mathrm B is the Euler beta function. Every entry is positive, \sum_j\mathcal K_{kj}=D_M, and h_{k,d}\mathcal K_{kj}=h_{j,d}\mathcal K_{jk}. The latter is reciprocity with the actual shell multiplicities. The weighted matrix is a positive Gram matrix of the coherent shell symbols. Write w_k=v_k/J from (9) and \sigma=\epsilon/g. Equal positive occupation q in each normal eigenspinor now requires r_k=Jw_k+\sum_j\mathcal K_{kj}c_j, \qquad c_k=\frac{qr_k}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+r_k^2}}. \tag{12b} For positive J,q,\sigma, monotone iteration from r_k=Jw_k is bounded above by Jw_k+qD_M. Positivity and strict sublinearity of the scalar response give a unique positive solution by the component-ratio argument also used in the linked balanced-response calculation. The target's complete source is \boxed{\frac{\omega_N}{g} =J\lambda_N+\sum_kh_{k,d}w_kc_k.} \tag{12c} This calculation includes the normal kinetic energy as well as both self-terms and the cross-term: \begin{aligned} \frac{E}{g}={}&\sum_k \frac{h_{k,d}q\sigma^2}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+r_k^2}} +\frac12J^2\lambda_N +J\sum_kh_{k,d}w_kc_k\\ &+\frac12\sum_{k,j}h_{k,d}c_k\mathcal K_{kj}c_j. \end{aligned} \tag{12d} At the stationary normal solution, differentiation at fixed canonical normal occupations gives \partial E/\partial J=\omega_N. Independent fifty-digit energy differences verify that statement, even when the normal energy is much larger than the retained derivative. The total canonical norm remains J+qD_M; finite gap does not erase the occupation. For matched depth-six bands and J=q=1, the complete source ratios at common widths \sigma=1,10^3,10^6 are respectively 204.6505816, 204.9364800 and 6505.0628511. These common-width controls are not physical fits. They show that the kinetic scale changes the ratio continuously and cannot be ignored or chosen independently for each target. The normal self-field also changes the smallest insertion. At width one it is approximately 18564.0002 for N=12 and 3838380.0000 for N=34, rather than the very small values of the cross-only operator (9). Normal response must use the complete self-consistent Hamiltonian when that is the declared action. At vanishing retained current, a uniform positive normal branch obeys r=D_Mc and exists for qD_M>\sigma, with c=\sqrt{q^2-(\sigma/D_M)^2}. This is the uniform instance of the canonical scalar gap mechanism. It still requires the stated occupation and a physical normal spectrum; it does not select a particle norm. Reciprocal time evolution checks the elimination A finite control retains an eight-component spatial Dirac spinor with two coefficient directions, one specified momentum, and both complementary normal signs with two occupied spectator columns. Its exact energy is E=p\langle X,\alpha_1X\rangle+ \operatorname{Tr}\left[Y^\dagger \left(\epsilon\tau_x\otimes I+g\tau_z\otimes C_X\right)Y\right], \qquad (C_X)_{ab}=\sum_{s,t}X_{sa}\beta_{ts}\overline{X_{tb}}. \tag{13} Both fields evolve by the complete complex gradient of this declared cross-action. It is a check of (3), not a claim that the retained and normal self-terms of (11) have been included in this control. Scaling (\epsilon,g,q) to (\Lambda\epsilon,\Lambda g,q/\Lambda) keeps (3) fixed while increasing the normal transition frequencies. For p=0.35, baseline (\epsilon,g)=(0.8,0.6) and time interval 0\le t\le20, the maximum complete retained-field error relative to the adiabatic evolution is \Lambda Full complex field error 4 2.41478\times10^{-2} 8 6.05970\times10^{-3} 16 1.47299\times10^{-3} 32 3.80655\times10^{-4} 64 9.35992\times10^{-5} The observed convergence is approximately second order in 1/\Lambda. Independent time refinement changes the full fields by less than 7.1\times10^{-9} for the last two cases. The full norms, occupied Gram matrix, energy and total coefficient-rotation moment are conserved to the reported numerical accuracy. This is a one-momentum mode control, not a localized particle or a spatial scattering calculation. The joint mass and coupling question Equation (3) is a derived effective source for the specified canonical normal-mode preparation. Equations (10)–(12) identify the missing band matching, occupation and physical mass interpretation. The spatial normal spectrum itself must also come from the same physical manifold. The localization conditions remain relevant when searching for actual finite-norm spatial particles. A further balanced-population calculation retains paired positive and negative normal occupations. Their stationary scalar contributions cancel while their moving polarization gives a nonzero geometric response. That result supplies a way for a shared response to coexist with count-dependent stationary sources under the same scalar interaction. It does not select those populations or derive the physical mass operator. Verification dirac_current_reduction_checks.py checks the full spectral variation, independent Dirac Liouvillian, canonical occupations, actual coherent master insertion and all terms of (11). Its finite equations are implemented in dirac_current_reduction.py. dirac_current_reciprocal_flow.py stores the complete complex trajectories, and dirac_response_trajectory_checks.py independently checks their refinement and conserved total rotation moment. projected_normal_self_consistency_checks.py checks the finite-gap complete square with independent beta quadrature, signed full tensor insertions, canonical shell reciprocity and fifty-digit energy derivatives. The exact shell reduction and positive normal solver are in projected_normal_self_consistency.py.

title: Testing slow geometric motion with every centered deformation
summary: The complete wave curvature does not justify a Berry-only slow supporting law; its formal velocities violate the small signed partner's adiabatic condition across all maintained sectors.
text: The radial geometry has a nonzero wave source. Allowing it to move is a possible alternative to static force balance, but the proposed motion must respect the approximation used to calculate it. Including the actual moving spatial basis gives a precise test: the simplest first-order slow action predicts motion far outside its own range of validity. This result applies to the stated Berry-only action and the tested symmetric profile. It does not rule out faster same-field dynamics, other shapes or a complete sustaining kinetic action. No formal velocity reported here is asserted to be a physical trajectory. The candidate law and its required condition Use the complete curvature from the moving normal basis, the fixed bounded hopping h=z/\sqrt{1+r^2}, and every centered coordinate \alpha_k=x_k+i y_k, k=2,\ldots,d. The proposed slow action for a unit canonical wave is L_{\rm slow}=A_a(\alpha)\dot\alpha_a-\lambda(\alpha). \tag{1} At a real radial reference state, the imaginary forces vanish and F_{xx}=F_{yy}=0. Put M_{kh}=F^{\rm wave}_{x_k y_h}, f_k=\partial_{x_k}\lambda. The complete first-order equations give \boxed{M\dot y=f,\qquad \dot x=0.} \tag{2} For the occupied wave to follow one instantaneous eigenbranch, every other signed eigenmode must satisfy the necessary condition \boxed{ \eta_r= \frac{\left|\sum_h\dot y_h\langle r,H_{y_h}n\rangle\right|} {|\lambda_r-\lambda_n|^2}\ll1.} \tag{3} It is enough to find one violation of (3); changing the normal gap cannot remove a violation within the retained carrier itself. A common canonical wave norm multiplies both terms in (1), so it cancels from (2). A common change of time unit also leaves (3) invariant. Neither convention can repair this test. The small signed partner supplies the strongest constraint The carrier has chiral form H_P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&T^\dagger\\T&0\end{smallmatrix}\right). At the real reference state, a real source has zero matrix element between the two opposite small signed partners. An imaginary source generally has a nonzero matrix element there. Thus that partner's contribution to the real–imaginary curvature is zero, even though it imposes the strongest condition (3). Its two roles cannot be inferred from curvature alone. The calculation retains all centered coordinates, both surface signs and all maintained particle controls. At \gamma=10000, examples for the geometric carrier on the positive surface sign are: Control Maximum \eta_r Depth-three down 1.53\times10^{21} Depth-four up 2.54\times10^{25} Depth-five first neutrino 3.93\times10^{27} Depth-six electron 9.49\times10^{31} Depth-ten tau 1.44\times10^{49} Even the smallest value among the positive-sign geometric controls is about 1.63\times10^{15}. The original carrier also violates (3). Independent radial-grid and outer-domain refinements change the selected ratios by less than 5\times10^{-7} relatively. The violation is not a consequence of resolving the finite curvature matrix inaccurately. The asymptotic mismatch For the geometric carrier define B_d=\frac12\left[ (F^{\rm normal}_{x_d y_d})_{00} +(F^{\rm normal}_{x_d y_d})_{d-1,d-1}\right]. \tag{4} At every tested depth B_d>0. The large-hopping normal density has equal endpoint weights. Its full centered limiting curvature is diagonal and nonsingular; cross-order entries vanish in that limit. Let \kappa_d be the endpoint hopping derivative and let \lambda_{\rm lead}\propto\gamma^{-(d-1)} be the leading small frequency. The dominant source and opposite-partner vertex both scale as \gamma\kappa_d. Equations (2) and (3) therefore give \boxed{\eta_{\rm pair}\sim \frac{\gamma^2\kappa_d^2}{4\lambda_{\rm lead}^2|B_d|} \propto\gamma^{2d}.} \tag{5} The full-coordinate calculations at hopping strengths 1000 and 10000 verify this leading expression. Improving the simplex approximation by increasing hopping worsens this particular slow-motion condition. The result identifies what the candidate action lacks: a self-consistent sustaining response capable of keeping the occupied motion in the regime being modeled. The complete particle's positive inertia is still a joint energy-and-momentum question. The signed modes in (3) have no assigned particle–antiparticle interpretation. Verification normal_motion_checks.py uses the complete spatial curvature and a high-precision signed singular system. Its 293-check report checks all centered equations, the zero real partner vertex, the strongest adiabatic condition, asymptotic scaling and domain refinements. This is a necessary consistency test of (1), not a numerical integration outside the approximation's validity.

title: The complete shape source and surface-branch balance
summary: Keeping every polynomial deformation leaves a nonzero even-order source at each maintained depth; mixing positive-frequency surface signs cannot hold this symmetric trial geometry stationary.
text: The two surface-sign branches can cancel some geometric forces, but they cannot cancel the complete source of the symmetric linked carrier. At all maintained depths there is an even-order deformation driven with the same sign by both positive-frequency branches. The proposed geometric cost has zero first derivative in that direction. This is a necessary source-balance test of a specific trial configuration. It does not exclude other shapes, other sustaining motion or the broader IDWT proposal. A source coefficient is not a signed particle inertia. The surface signs are not assigned a particle–antiparticle interpretation. A full matrix derivative replaces separate source terms Use the connected normal carrier with winding d, normal modes \Phi_l, and the complete projected pair H_P=\begin{pmatrix}0&T^\dagger\\T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad T_{ll}=\beta+l-\frac{d-1}{2},\qquad T_{l+1,l}=\gamma h_l. \tag{1} All h_l>0 are spatial integrals, with \gamma>0. For a polynomial deformation P(z)=z^d+\alpha_kz^{d-k}, let \delta D_k include both the texture and connection variations. Choose the orthogonal mode derivative \delta\Phi_l=-D^{-1}(I-P)\delta D_k\Phi_l. Then the full derivative is \delta T_k=\mathcal P_k+\gamma\mathcal H_k, \qquad (\mathcal H_k)_{ij}= -\langle\delta D_k\Phi_i,D^{-1}(I-P)h\Phi_j\rangle -\langle D^{-1}(I-P)\bar h\Phi_i,\delta D_k\Phi_j\rangle. \tag{2} The first term \mathcal P_k originally contains the explicit polarization variation and both changes of its mode basis. The local anticommutator identity proves \boxed{\mathcal P_k=0\quad\text{at the radial configuration}.} \tag{3} These terms cancel only after their complete variations are included. They must not be individually omitted from an unreduced field equation. The result is not shape independence to higher order. For a jointly unit-normalized positive-frequency state (u,v), the complete first frequency derivative is therefore \boxed{F_k(\beta)=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}(v^\dagger\mathcal H_k u).} \tag{4} An independent calculation integrates the original full spatial texture, connection and explicit polarization sources. It agrees with (4) for every maintained control, every k=2,\ldots,d, both surface signs, and complex deformation orientations. Reflection explains which sources cancel Let R reverse the normal labels and S_0=\operatorname{diag}((-1)^l). The original carrier has h_l=h_{d-2-l}, and its real deformation matrices satisfy R\mathcal H_k^T R=\mathcal H_k,\qquad S_0\mathcal H_kS_0=(-1)^{k-1}\mathcal H_k, \qquad T(-\beta)=-S_0R T(\beta)^T RS_0. \tag{5} Transforming both singular vectors in (4) gives \boxed{F_k(-\beta)=(-1)^kF_k(\beta).} \tag{6} Equal positive-frequency populations of the two signs cancel odd-order sources and leave even-order sources unchanged. The previously known endpoint relation is the special case k=d. Retaining the other orders is essential at odd depth. For mutually orthogonal surface harmonics, the surface integral of the source is their population-weighted sum: the interference terms integrate to zero. This is only an integrated necessary condition. Vanishing of an integral would not establish pointwise balance of a coherent field. A nonzero surviving source at every depth The endpoint order k=d has the single entry \mathcal H_d=\kappa_d|0\rangle\langle d-1|,\qquad \kappa_d<0. \tag{7} The positive Green contraction fixes its sign. At the next order, \boxed{\mathcal H_{d-1} =a_d\left(|0\rangle\langle d-2|+|1\rangle\langle d-1|\right), \qquad a_d<0.} \tag{8} The sign also follows from a spatial integral. Let (U,V) be the positive horizontal geometric mode for k=d-1, in its \tau=c_0\alpha coordinate. Write Y^+_{d-2,0} for the first positive-chiral component of D^{-1}(I-P)h\Phi_{d-2}, and Y^-_{0,1} for the second radial component of D^{-1}(I-P)\bar h\Phi_0, in the phase conventions of (2). Then a_d=-2\pi c_0\int_0^\infty r\left[ (UU_0+VV_0)Y^+_{d-2,0} -(UV_{d-2}+VU_{d-2})Y^-_{0,1}\right]dr. \tag{9} The first Green source is strictly positive and the second strictly negative. Their regular decaying scalar inverses preserve those signs. Since the radial modes are positive, the bracket is positive on a set of nonzero measure. The horizontal basis-phase correction has angular order d-1; its only possible retained endpoint entry vanishes by the endpoint reflection identity. Thus (9) gives the same coefficient as (2). For \beta>(d-1)/2, every diagonal of T is positive. The matrix S_0T^{-1}S_0 is triangular with positive entries on and below its diagonal. Its two singular Perron vectors are strictly positive. Consequently the smallest-frequency vectors u,v have matching alternating signs, with every component nonzero. Equation (7) then has F_d>0 when d is even. Equation (8) has F_{d-1}>0 when d is odd. Reflection gives the same sign at -\beta. Equivalently, choose the largest even integer k_*\le d. title: Spatial response of a conformal scalar-current interaction
summary: An exact zero-current Killing field has a closed full-variation response to a conformal scalar-current interaction, whose simplex coefficient enters collective frequencies and makes this branch unstable at high harmonic degree.
text: Summary: An exact zero-current Killing field has a closed full-variation response to a conformal scalar-current interaction, whose simplex coefficient enters collective frequencies and makes this branch unstable at high harmonic degree. Test the scalar-current route in the field equation The conformal scalar operator has a simplex spectrum, but an interaction in which it acts on the scalar current must be varied and solved as a nonlinear field equation. There is an exact spatial background on which this response can be calculated. The simplex value enters the collective response; it is not directly the background frequency or an observed particle mass. Specify the actual physical geometry as a round six-dimensional sphere with undetermined radius R. Its six directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, with no compactification. This is a conditional geometry, not a determination of the electron's physical topology. Use the ordinary complex rank-eight spinor bundle, the self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D and Hermitian chirality \beta. Initially set R=1 and normalize spatial measure to total volume one. The proposed energy is E(\psi)=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psi\rangle +\frac12\langle J,(g_0I+g_1\widehat P_6)J\rangle, \qquad J=\psi^\dagger\beta\psi. \tag{1} Here \widehat P_6=\Delta(\Delta+4)(\Delta+6)/6! and \widehat P_6Y_{\ell,a}=p_\ell Y_{\ell,a},\qquad p_\ell=S(\ell,6),\qquad p_0=0. \tag{2} The g_0 term is the local scalar interaction. The derivative-current term proportional to g_1 is an additional candidate, not a reduction already supplied by the master action. Its full variation gives i\partial_t\psi=\mathscr D\psi+ \bigl[(g_0I+g_1\widehat P_6)J\bigr]\beta\psi. \tag{3} Both ordinary and conjugate variations of the source are retained, as required by the complete scalar response. A full spatial field with zero scalar current Six-dimensional Clifford multiplication can be represented by real skew-symmetric 8 by 8 matrices c_i. A concrete construction uses X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{4} The six tensor words IIJ_2,\ IJ_2X,\ XJ_2Z,\ J_2IZ,\ J_2XX,\ J_2ZX give the c_i. They obey c_ic_j+c_jc_i=-2\delta_{ij}I. Take \beta=i c_1c_2\cdots c_6. It is Hermitian, purely imaginary and antisymmetric, and anticommutes with each c_i. In the complete Killing frame, choose a constant real unit vector v and put \varepsilon=Uv. The explicit stereographic frame U=(I-x_ic_i)/\sqrt{1+|x|^2} is real. Thus, globally, \begin{aligned} \mathscr D\varepsilon&=3\varepsilon,& \varepsilon^\dagger\varepsilon&=1,& \varepsilon^\dagger\beta\varepsilon&=0,\\ \varepsilon^\dagger c(X)\varepsilon&=0,& \varepsilon^\dagger c(X)\beta\varepsilon&=0. \end{aligned} \tag{5} The bilinear identities follow from antisymmetry; the mixed matrix c(X)\beta is also antisymmetric. They are properties of this particular spatial field, not imposed zeros for an observed particle coupling. Choosing this real family does not remove complex perturbations. Let \xi=\beta\varepsilon, so \mathscr D\xi=-3\xi. Equation (3) has the exact solution \boxed{\psi_0(t,q)=e^{-3it}\varepsilon(q)} \tag{6} for every g_0,g_1. Its scalar current is zero and its ordinary norm is nonzero. Neither its Dirac sign nor its zero scalar current identifies an antiparticle, electric neutrality or an observed particle. The complete response on an invariant spatial subspace Put \psi=e^{-3it}(\varepsilon+\eta). Since the background current vanishes, the complete linearization is i\partial_t\eta=(\mathscr D-3)\eta +2\xi(g_0I+g_1\widehat P_6) \operatorname{Re}(\xi^\dagger\eta). \tag{7} Take any real degree-\ell scalar harmonic u, normalized by \int u^2=1, with \ell\ge1 and \Lambda=\ell(\ell+5). Define \chi_0=u\xi,\qquad \chi_1=c(du)\xi. \tag{8} All physical derivatives of the spinor are included. The Killing equation and the scalar harmonic equation give \begin{aligned} (\mathscr D-3)\chi_0&=-6\chi_0+\chi_1,\\ (\mathscr D-3)\chi_1&=\Lambda\chi_0-\chi_1. \end{aligned} \tag{9} The bilinear identities (5) also give \xi^\dagger\chi_1=0 pointwise. For arbitrary complex z_0,z_1, \operatorname{Re}\bigl[\xi^\dagger(z_0\chi_0+z_1\chi_1)\bigr] =u\,\operatorname{Re}z_0. \tag{10} Thus the complex span of (8) is invariant under the full real-linear equation (7). It includes the spatial derivative partner and both phase quadratures. It is an invariant subspace of the full field problem, not a claim that all perturbations have this form. Its physical Gram matrix is \operatorname{diag}(1,\Lambda). In the orthonormal basis (\chi_0,\chi_1/\sqrt{\Lambda}), define L_\ell=\begin{pmatrix}-6&\sqrt{\Lambda}\\ \sqrt{\Lambda}&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad a_\ell=g_0+g_1p_\ell,\qquad E_{00}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{11} Writing the coefficient vector as z=x+iy, the equations are \dot x=L_\ell y,\qquad \dot y=-(L_\ell+2a_\ell E_{00})x. \tag{12} The quadratic canonical energy is z^\dagger L_\ell z+2a_\ell x_0^2. The response frequencies therefore satisfy \boxed{ \Omega^4-T_\ell\Omega^2+D_\ell=0, } \tag{13} where \begin{aligned} T_\ell&=37+2\Lambda-12a_\ell,\\ D_\ell&=(\Lambda-6)(\Lambda-6+2a_\ell). \end{aligned} \tag{14} These are eigenvalues of L_\ell(L_\ell+2a_\ell E_{00}). They are not \Omega=p_\ell. At \ell=1, one squared frequency is zero and the other is 49-12a_1. At \ell=0, the derivative partner vanishes; that separate block has squared frequency 36-12g_0 and a phase-space description of one complex amplitude. High harmonics give an exact instability result for this branch For \ell\ge2, exponential growth occurs if D_\ell<0, or if T_\ell<0, or if T_\ell^2-4D_\ell<0. A negative squared frequency gives real growth; nonreal squared frequencies give a complex quartet. At large degree, with fixed finite g_0, p_\ell\sim\frac{\ell^6}{720},\qquad T_\ell\sim-\frac{g_1}{60}\ell^6,\qquad D_\ell\sim\frac{g_1}{360}\ell^8. \tag{15} If g_1>0, the trace eventually becomes negative. If g_1<0, the determinant eventually becomes negative. Therefore every nonzero g_1 gives an unstable harmonic of this exact background in the unrestricted continuum problem. The invariant subspace (8) is enough to establish instability of the full linearized field. For g_0=0, exact rational arithmetic gives these first unstable degrees within the family: Dimensionless g_1 First unstable degree Initial instability condition \frac1{1000} 10 T_\ell^2-4D_\ell<0 -\frac1{1000} 22 D_\ell<0 \frac1{10^6} 35 T_\ell^2-4D_\ell<0 -\frac1{10^6} 136 D_\ell<0 These are dimensionless model benchmarks, not fitted particle indices. A finite cutoff can omit the unstable degrees, but then its physical origin and the discarded response must be justified. Other backgrounds, different kinetic operators or a derived nonlocal response require their own analysis; (15) is not a no-go theorem for all IDWT dynamics. An exact nonzero local scalar branch has complete spatial spectral stability before the derivative-current term is added. Its full response has also been tested: the added term leaves that constant-current background unchanged but again destabilizes its high harmonics. Thus the source response matters even when a local self-consistent scalar coefficient is already present. Restore the physical scale Let the actual sphere have volume \mathcal V and fix canonical norm Q. The background becomes \sqrt{Q/\mathcal V}\,e^{-3it/R}\varepsilon. If the dimensional interaction coefficients multiplying J^2/2 and J\widehat P_6J/2 are \kappa and \eta, respectively, then g_0=\frac{R\kappa Q}{\mathcal V},\qquad g_1=\frac{R\eta Q}{\mathcal V}. \tag{16} Equations (11)–(15) use time t/R; physical response frequencies are \Omega/R. No radius, canonical norm, master coefficient or occupied particle mode is selected by this calculation. Verification conformal_current_response_checks.py checks the full real Clifford representation, Killing fields and all bilinear cancellations. Independent stereographic differentiation verifies (9) for zonal and angular harmonics, with arbitrary complex perturbation coefficients. The nonlinear current on this perturbation plane and its complete first variation are checked directly. Exact matrix algebra derives (13)–(15). Independent variations of the canonical quadratic energy and the full four-real-component generator verify the frequencies and growth conditions. Exact rational scans give the table. The normalized scalar spectrum enters a specified nonlinear response; it has not been derived as the master mass operator.

title: Exact local scalar fields with constant spatial density
summary: Five holomorphic polarization fields give an exact constant-density branch of the local scalar Dirac action on the curved mode bundle, while its common coefficient and copy symmetries leave the mass count unselected.
text:
Summary: Five holomorphic polarization fields give an exact constant-density branch of the local scalar Dirac action on the curved mode bundle, while its common coefficient and copy symmetries leave the mass count unselected. Solve the written local interaction The coherent curved-bundle construction gave exact spatial fields for a specified smooth moment interaction. The written local scalar interaction can also be solved exactly on the same kinetic bundle, using a different polarization pattern. Retain the candidate physical CP3 geometry and its undetermined metric radius R. Its six directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. No dimensions are compactified. Set T=T^{1,0}\mathrm{CP}^3,\qquad W=\mathbf1\oplus T\oplus T^*,\qquad E_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N W, 	ag{1} with the natural Hermitian metric and connection. Use the specified canonical Spin^c operator \mathscr D_N=\sqrt2( ar\partial_{E_N}+ ar\partial_{E_N}^{\dagger}), \qquad  eta=(-1)^{	ext{form degree}}, 	ag{2} on all exterior-form components, with degree-zero line twist. The interaction is the local scalar action itself: \mathcal E(\psi)=\langle\psi,\mathscr D_N\psiangle + rac{\kappa}{2}\int(\psi^\dagger eta\psi)^2d
u. 	ag{3} Initially d
u has total spatial volume one. There is no additional spatial response kernel in (3). The bundle and kinetic operator remain specified candidate data; their master-field projection and holonomic interpretation have not been derived. The construction below supplies a nontrivial holomorphic zero-form \chi_N with \|\chi_N(q)\|^2=1 everywhere. Then \mathscr D_N\chi_N=0, its scalar current is constant, and the complete local equation has an exact stationary solution. Five fields whose tangent norms add to a constant Let \sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z be the Pauli matrices, and define five Hermitian 4 by 4 matrices  egin{aligned} \Gamma_1&=\sigma_x\otimes I_2,& \Gamma_2&=\sigma_y\otimes I_2,\ \Gamma_3&=\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_x,& \Gamma_4&=\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_y,& \Gamma_5&=\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z. \end{aligned} 	ag{4} They obey \Gamma_a\Gamma_b+\Gamma_b\Gamma_a=2\delta_{ab}I_4. They generate five particular holomorphic projective vector fields on the same physical CP3. Their number does not count spatial dimensions. For a unit homogeneous vector Z=(a,b,c,d), put r_j=Z^\dagger\Gamma_jZ. Direct multiplication gives  egin{aligned} r_1+ir_2&=2( ar a c+ ar b d),\ r_3+ir_4&=2( ar a b- ar c d),\ r_5&=|a|^2+|d|^2-|b|^2-|c|^2. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} Let A=|a|^2+|d|^2 and B=|b|^2+|c|^2. The cross terms cancel in | ar a c+ ar b d|^2+| ar a b- ar c d|^2=AB. Hence  oxed{\sum_{j=1}^5r_j^2=4AB+(A-B)^2=(A+B)^2=1.} 	ag{6} This is the quadratic identity associated with the quaternionic Hopf construction; Baez, Section 3.1 describes its projective setting. Here it is used only as the explicit polynomial identity (5)–(6). It introduces no additional physical space. For any complex matrix A, write X_A for its holomorphic projective vector field. With the common unit-radius tangent normalization, \|X_A(Z)\|^2=Z^\dagger A^\dagger AZ-|Z^\dagger AZ|^2. 	ag{7} In the chart Z_0
e0, it has the holomorphic components X_A^j(z)=(A(1,z))_j-z_j(A(1,z))_0,\qquad j=1,2,3. 	ag{8} Equations (4), (6) and (7) now prove  oxed{\sum_{j=1}^5\|X_{\Gamma_j}(q)\|^2=5-\sum_{j=1}^5r_j(q)^2=4} 	ag{9} at every physical point. The five separate densities vary with position. Their sum is constant. Put the five fields into orthogonal copies already in the carrier The complete tangent-band decomposition shows that E_N contains \lfloor(N-1)/2floor+1 orthogonal parallel copies of T. In particular, it has at least five when N\ge9. An explicit normalized inclusion removes any ambiguity about the metric of these copies. Temporarily let m=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}T; here m=3. In an orthonormal tangent frame, use normalized symmetric occupation notation |s;\alpha;\gammaangle for slack, tangent and cotangent degrees. These are polynomial coefficient labels, not extra particles or spatial coordinates. For \ell\ge0 and 2\ell+1\le N, define  oxed{ \mathcal I_{\ell,N}(v)= \sum_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_m=\ell\i=1,\ldots,m}} \sqrt{ rac{n_i+1}{ inom{\ell+m}{m}}}\, v_i\,|N-2\ell-1;\,n+e_i;\,nangle. } 	ag{10} Every term has homogeneous degree N. The identity \sum_{|n|=\ell}(n_i+1)= inom{\ell+m}{m} 	ag{11} gives \langle\mathcal I_{\ell,N}(v),\mathcal I_{\ell,N}(w)angle =v^\dagger w. One proof of (11) takes the coefficient of t^\ell in (1-t)^{-2}(1-t)^{-(m-1)}. Thus the trace insertion has a definite Hockey-Stick normalization, which makes it an isometry. There is also a basis-independent description. Contract one tangent and one cotangent factor with the parallel identity tensor, insert \ell such pairs, and add the remaining slack factors. In formal normalized creation notation, this is \mathcal I_{\ell,N}(v)=  rac{(a_0^\dagger)^{N-2\ell-1} (\sum_i a_i^\dagger b_i^\dagger)^\ell a_v^\dagger|0angle} {\sqrt{(N-2\ell-1)!\,\ell!\,(m+1)_\ell}}, 	ag{12} where (m+1)_\ell=(m+1)\cdots(m+\ell) and the empty product is one. Expanding (12) gives (10). The maps are parallel and holomorphic because the contraction and slack line are parallel. Their images for different \ell are orthogonal: they have different total tangent and cotangent degrees. An exact noncoherent branch of the full local equation For every N\ge9, set  oxed{ \chi_N(q)= rac12\sum_{\ell=0}^4 \mathcal I_{\ell,N} igl(X_{\Gamma_{\ell+1}}(q) igr). } 	ag{13} The five terms are orthogonal at every point. Therefore (9)–(10) give \|\chi_N(q)\|^2=1,\qquad  ar\partial_{E_N}\chi_N=0,\qquad \mathscr D_N\chi_N=0,\qquad  eta\chi_N=\chi_N. 	ag{14} All components of the spatial polarization pattern have been included. The field is not parallel: its separate copy densities vary, even though their sum is constant. For N>9, the field is also noncoherent in the homogeneous carrier. Every occupied term has a positive slack degree, but the pure-slack coefficient is zero. A coherent vector (s,u,v)^{\odot N} with s
e0 has nonzero pure-slack coefficient s^N; with s=0 it has no slack occupations. Neither case equals the nonzero field (13). This proves the distinction at both assigned indices N=12 and 34. The full equation from (3) is i\partial_t\psi =\mathscr D_N\psi+\kappa(\psi^\dagger eta\psi) eta\psi. 	ag{15} Substitution of (14) proves  oxed{\psi(t,q)=e^{-i\kappa t}\chi_N(q),\qquad \omega=\kappa,\qquad \mathcal E(\chi_N)=\kappa/2.} 	ag{16} Restoring physical volume \mathcal V and canonical field norm Q gives  oxed{ \psi(t,q)=\sqrt{ rac Q{\mathcal V}}\, e^{-i\omega t}\chi_N(q),\qquad \omega= rac{\kappa Q}{\mathcal V},\qquad \mathcal E= rac{\kappa Q^2}{2\mathcal V}. } 	ag{17} The common physical tangent normalization is restored with the same metric scale for every N. Holomorphicity and constant density survive that common rescaling. The nonlinear scalar endomorphism on this background is \kappa Q\, eta/\mathcal V. It is a self-consistent constant scalar coefficient of the specified field equation. Its identification with an observed rest mass, rather than merely this equation's carrier frequency, requires further physical justification. Cumulative degree N Carrier rank  inom{N+6}{6} Frequency of (17) 12 18\,564 \kappa Q/\mathcal V 34 3\,838\,380 \kappa Q/\mathcal V The same normalized spatial field is carried from E_{12} to E_{34} by the natural cumulative inclusion, which adds slack occupation while preserving each existing degree block. This exact solution therefore does not turn the larger carrier rank into a larger scalar coefficient. The sufficient construction threshold N\ge9 is not a particle mode-selection rule or a claim that it is the smallest possible threshold. Why a nontrivial coherent field cannot use this constant source There is a precise result for the same degree-zero line twist. Suppose s is a nonzero holomorphic section of E_N, with N\ge1, which is pointwise coherent and has a constant positive norm. Locally, s has a holomorphic root w satisfying s=w^{\odot N}. This follows by choosing a nonzero component of the coherent generating line, taking a local Nth root of its pure coefficient, and recovering the other components from the mixed coefficients. On overlapping charts, two such roots differ by a constant Nth root of unity. CP3 is simply connected: the homotopy sequence of S^1	o S^7	o\mathrm{CP}^3 gives \pi_1(\mathrm{CP}^3)=0. The finite root covering therefore has a global branch. Thus w is a global holomorphic section of W, with constant norm. The holomorphic sections of W have the form w=(c,X_A,0). 	ag{18} Here c is constant, H^0(T^*)=0, and all holomorphic tangent fields are projective matrix fields. These facts follow from the Euler sequence or the degree-one cases of the tangent-band calculation. Every complex matrix A has an eigenvector. At its projective eigenline, X_A vanishes. Since \|w\|^2=|c|^2+\|X_A\|^2 is constant, that zero forces X_A to vanish everywhere. Consequently,  oxed{ 	ext{A constant-norm coherent holomorphic section of }E_N 	ext{ is a pure-slack section.} } 	ag{19} The statement is restricted to this bundle and its degree-zero line twist. It does not classify nonlinear fields with complementary Dirac components or nonzero twists. The real-source preservation criterion shows why (19) matters: an exact local scalar branch that remains on a holomorphic zero line requires constant density. The nontrivial solution (13) meets that condition through its full multiplet. The local action leaves copy norms and pattern choices free Each parallel projector onto an isomorphic T copy commutes with \mathscr D_N and  eta. Writing \psi_a for the full spinor in copy a, the local equation gives  rac d{dt}\langle\psi_a,\psi_bangle=0. 	ag{20} Indeed, both copies evolve with the same instantaneous self-adjoint operator \mathscr D_T+\kappa J(q,t) eta. Its contributions to the derivative of the inner product cancel. This includes a spatially varying self-consistent current and both form parities. The action has a common unitary symmetry mixing the five equivalent copies. Such mixing preserves the total pointwise density, holomorphicity and the frequency in (16). For the particular field (13), every copy has norm 1/5: unit projective measure gives \int r_j^2d
u=\operatorname{Tr}(\Gamma_j^2)/(4\cdot5)=1/5, so \int\|X_{\Gamma_j}\|^2d
u=4/5. These equal copy weights describe the constructed solution; the action does not dynamically enforce them on arbitrary initial fields. This is a symmetry of the specified kinetic and local scalar action. It is not an identification with an observed gauge symmetry. A master projection could impose additional constraints or terms that change it. The physical derivative calculation is one reason to distinguish independent coefficient sections from derivatives of the master field. Full spatial stability remains a separate calculation Constant background density does not freeze the density of a perturbation. At unit norm and volume, put \psi=e^{-i\kappa t}(\chi_N+\eta). Retaining the complete variation of (15) gives i\partial_t\eta =\mathscr D_N\eta+\kappa( eta-I)\eta +2\kappa\chi_N\operatorname{Re}(\chi_N^\dagger\eta). 	ag{21} The last term responds to every local density perturbation, and \chi_N has a nonconstant spatial polarization. Replacing (21) by a frozen linear massive Dirac operator would omit that response. No complete spectral or nonlinear stability theorem is established here. The earlier line-bundle stability result uses a different spatial source closure and does not transfer automatically. The graph contact action would multiply the scalar coefficient by D_N if adopted separately. The construction above solves the written local scalar action before that extra premise. It establishes a possible exact spatial source, while leaving the master interaction, the count enhancement, state selection and observed mass identification unresolved. Verification constant_density_bundle_checks.py proves (6) by symbolic expansion in all eight real homogeneous coefficients. Direct occupation sums and independent repeated pair creation verify (10)–(12), including their complete complex connection intertwining. Spatial chart changes, physical tangent norms and full Dolbeault derivatives check (13)–(14) at N=9,12,34. The diagnostic also checks the scalar stationary equation with different common norms and volumes, both signs of the scalar coefficient, and the distinction between energy and frequency. The copy-charge cancellation is independently checked with full complex fields and both spin parities; that finite identity test is not a spatial stability calculation. Matrix eigenlines verify the elementary zero used in (19). The global root-covering argument itself is a mathematical proof, not a numerical test.

title: Fixed-norm response as an eigenvalue contribution
summary: A canonical-norm constraint converts the positive response force into a standing-frequency shift; equal-norm frozen source controls do not follow the simplex spectrum, while dynamically determined amplitudes and profiles remain open.
text: A fixed canonical norm is a natural way to prevent the support calculation from turning particle masses into adjustable amplitudes. It changes the question, however. The response no longer has to be transparent in the radial field direction, because that direction is excluded from the constrained tangent space. Its radial derivative instead enters the Lagrange multiplier, which is the standing frequency. This note determines what that means for the current positive response model. The constrained multiplier Let a reference mode satisfy Q[\phi_i]=1, and write a radial extension as \Psi=\sqrt{s}\,\phi_i, so Q[\Psi]=s. The physical stationary value s=Q_i need not be the same for every solution. Even at fixed global Q_i, the local amplitude can vary with the spatial profile. Suppose the bare energy on this ray is E_{0,i}(s)=s\omega_{0,i}. \tag{1} This equation does not identify amplitude with mass. It states the usual linear dependence of the energy on canonical norm for a mode whose eigenvalue is \omega_{0,i}. Let a positive response z have energy E_z=\frac12\langle z,Az\rangle -\gamma\langle z,S(\Psi)\rangle, \qquad A>0, \qquad S(\sqrt{s}\phi_i)=sS_i. \tag{2} Eliminating z gives E_{\mathrm{eff},i}(s) =s\omega_{0,i}-\frac{\gamma^2}{2}s^2K_i, \qquad K_i=\langle S_i,A^{-1}S_i\rangle>0. \tag{3} Stationarity of E-\omega(Q-Q_i) at s=Q_i therefore fixes the standing frequency to \boxed{\omega_i=\omega_{0,i}-\gamma^2Q_iK_i.} \tag{4} The fixed-norm constraint removes the radial amplitude direction from the constrained Hessian. It does not remove the response effect. It converts that effect into a stationary phase-frequency shift. That shift affects the nonlinear eigenproblem, but its identification with physical mass needs an additional complete-energy calculation. In the units of this reduction, E_{\mathrm{eff},i}(Q_i)-Q_i\omega_i =\frac{\gamma^2}{2}Q_i^2K_i>0. Thus even at unit canonical norm the energy differs from this phase multiplier. The mass-equivalent frequency remains \omega_m=E_{\rm rest}/\hbar=mc^2/\hbar. Establishing that a particular phase rate equals it requires the complete same-field supporting action, its conserved normalization and its energy–momentum response. See mass and energy response. Amplitude remains in the dynamics: it can affect the phase frequency through Q_i, and changes of the normalized spatial profile can change K_i. The same amplitude and profile can enter coupling overlaps. Neither the amplitude alone nor this unconsolidated phase multiplier establishes mass. Equal-norm control against the simplex spectrum For the current algebraic controls, (S_i)_\ell=\frac{i+\ell+d}{i+2\ell+d+1}, \qquad K_i=\sum_{\ell=2,4,\ldots} \frac{(S_i)_\ell^2}{\mathcal L_d(\ell)}. \tag{5} The converged values of K_i lie between approximately 0.400 and 1.225 over all maintained controls. They vary far more slowly than the simplex count \mathcal S(i,d)=\binom{i+d-1}{d}. \tag{6} For the diagnostic choice Q_i=1, if a bare simplex spectrum \omega_{0,i}=\Omega_{0,d}\mathcal S(i,d) is to remain a simplex spectrum after the response, with one possibly renormalized scale \Omega_d, equation (4) requires \frac{K_i}{\mathcal S(i,d)} =\frac{\Omega_{0,d}-\Omega_d}{\gamma^2} \tag{7} to be independent of i at fixed depth. The tested ratios fail that condition at every depth containing more than one maintained mode. Their largest-to-smallest spreads are: Depth Ratio spread 2 1.53 3 561 4 4.62\times10^4 5 28.4 6 176 10 single-mode control The one-mode depth-ten sector cannot test proportionality. At the other depths, a nonzero common coupling changes the simplex ratios rather than renormalizing their common frequency unit. The response alone also cannot generate the count law, because K_i is not proportional to \mathcal S(i,d) under these equal-norm frozen-source assumptions. If the dynamics selects unequal Q_i, the corresponding condition is that Q_iK_i/\mathcal S(i,d) obey one common sector rule. Choosing Q_i\propto\mathcal S/K_i after the fact would merely move the spectral fit into amplitude. Deriving such amplitudes from the same stationary equations would instead be a legitimate nonlinear result. The present calculation does not decide between those possibilities because it holds the normalized source vectors fixed. What the constraint does and does not solve The canonical constraint is still useful. It removes the radial direction from perturbations at a specified conserved Q_i and turns the support problem into an honest nonlinear eigenvalue problem whose output is a frequency. It does not require equal peak amplitudes, equal profiles or even equal conserved norms unless the common action supplies that rule. The present equal-norm source controls are not sufficient as that eigenvalue problem. Preserving the established simplex law requires the complete amplitude-dependent Rayleigh contribution to follow one common spectral rule. A compensating mode-dependent bare term would merely move the fit into the bare operator. The useful next target is therefore a constrained same-field action in which the spatial operator, source, response and amplitude are derived together. At each depth, the particle harmonics must follow one common field law and shared fundamental parameters. That law may generate different sizes, effective stiffnesses, conserved norms, amplitudes and profiles. Equal size is a testable subclass; independent per-particle retuning does not derive a spectrum. The resulting phase eigenvalue remains a spectral diagnostic until its relation to complete rest energy and inertia is established. Verification constrained_response_spectrum_checks.py evaluates the infinite even-harmonic norms at 50 and 80 decimal digits, checks the fixed-norm multiplier identity and compares each response norm with its simplex count. The normal and optimized runs each pass 69 checks. The selected report records the converged shifts and ratio spreads. The source components remain algebraic controls, not measured densities or a derived master-field source.

title: Canonical contact normalization and finite combinatorial bounds
summary: Fixed-charge normalization changes a local quartic's frequency weight; exact harmonic and Hockey-Stick band counts bound which proposed contact scalings can realize the simplex hierarchy.
text: Counting can constrain a proposed operator without being a derivation of its frequency. This calculation combines canonical normalization with the exact dimension of a space of angular functions. It rules out specific scalar-contact reductions under a shared normal profile, while leaving derivative interactions and dynamically changing normal profiles open. 1. A local quartic has a frequency denominator at fixed charge Let a normalized spatial eigenmode have frequency \Omega_n(R) and \int|u_{n,R}|^4=W_nR^{-d}. For an ordinary quadratic time norm, the unperturbed fixed-charge amplitude satisfies a^2=Q/(2\kappa\Omega_n). A local positive potential g\int|X|^4 therefore contributes, at first order in g, \Delta E_4=\frac{gQ^2W_nR^{-d}}{4\kappa^2\Omega_n^2}. Replacing this by a constant times Q^2W_nR^{-d} omits canonical normalization. The latter can be studied as a stipulated effective energy, but requires a different derived interaction. For the particular hypothetical gap law G=g_0R^{-2}, the high-gap chain gives \Omega_n=A P_n R^m, where P_n=d!S(n,d), m=d-2, and d>2. With a positive current support cost \sigma R^{-d}, the corrected reduced energy is E=A P_n Q R^m+\sigma R^{-d} +B\frac{W_n}{P_n^2}Q^2R^{-q},\qquad q=3d-4. It is an exact algebraic model if stipulated; for a plain local quartic it is only the first-order reduction. At simultaneous radius balance and the additional identification target E=\omega Q, B\frac{W_n}{P_n^2}Q^2R^{-q}=\sigma R^{-d},\qquad m A P_n Q R^m=(d+q)\sigma R^{-d}. Thus R^q=\frac{d+q}{mA}\frac{\sqrt{\sigma BW_n}}{P_n^2},\qquad \omega\propto P_n^{d/q}W_n^{m/(2q)}. For mode-independent \sigma,B, a linear frequency in P_n requires W_n\propto P_n^4. If the charge is also common while the solved support cost may change with branch, linear frequency implies constant radius and requires \sigma_n\propto P_n, W_n\propto P_n^3. These are consequences of this reduction, not functions that may be fitted into a claimed derivation. There is a further control on the approximation. At that formal joint balance the quartic energy divided by the linear wave energy is fixed: \frac{\Delta E_4}{Q\Omega_n}=\frac{d-2}{4d-4}. It is 3/16 at depth five, 1/5 at six, and 2/9 at ten. These do not tend to zero by sending g to zero while imposing both balances. Accordingly the formal equality branch is not justified as a controlled weak-quartic solution by this truncation alone. A full nonlinear calculation could change it. Positive contact also changes the spatial profile. At depth five, \langle U_l^3,U_j\rangle=j+1 for j\le l of the same parity, and zero for opposite parity. The nearest same-parity mode therefore has a cubic source of size l-1. The prior adjacent-mode stabilization estimates had first-order profile changes around 0.27–0.28 in this channel. They are useful diagnostics, not full-profile stability results. 2. A finite harmonic bound tests every scalar shape in a degree On S^m, the degree-l scalar harmonic dimension is D_{l,m}=\binom{l+m}{m}-\binom{l+m-2}{m}, where the second term vanishes below degree two. These count homogeneous polynomials modulo their traces. The diagonal of the orthogonal projector is constant by rotations and equals D_{l,m}/\mathcal A_m, with \mathcal A_m the sphere area. Consequently every real or complex normalized harmonic obeys \frac1{\mathcal A_m}\le\int|Y_l|^4 \le\frac{D_{l,m}}{\mathcal A_m}. The lower bound is Cauchy–Schwarz; the upper follows from the projector's pointwise norm. It includes arbitrary mixtures within that degree. At depth five, m=3, the maintained indices n=10,15,22 give l=11,16,23, products 240240,1395360,7893600, and dimensions 144,289,576. The extreme product ratio is exactly 230/7. A common scalar contact scaling W_n=cP_n^k would require (230/7)^k\le576. Already (230/7)^2=52900/49>576. Thus every integer power k\ge2 is excluded in this same-degree scalar class with a common normal factor. No numerical shape search is needed. 3. The Hockey-Stick extension includes all lower degrees For every scalar harmonic through degree L, summing the dimension formula gives N_{L,m}=\binom{L+m+1}{m+1}-\binom{L+m-1}{m+1}. This is the Hockey-Stick Identity applied to the two polynomial counts. It counts available coefficients, not occupied particles or a selected frequency. The band projector gives the same fourth-norm bound with D_{l,m} replaced by N_{L,m}. At depth five and L=23, N_{23,3}=\sum_{j=1}^{24}j^2=4900, \qquad (230/7)^3=12167000/343>4900. Therefore permitting all lower scalar degrees still cannot supply the P_n^3 or P_n^4 contact scaling in this model, with one common normal factor. The square ratio is below 4900, so this band bound does not exclude the distinct stipulated-effective P_n^2 requirement. Full Hodge form components, derivative contacts, or a normal profile whose response is derived from the wave change the quantity being bounded. They must be calculated under the same action. Depth two's old scalar S^0 feature has no such ladder. These exact finite-mode exclusions do not establish a general prohibition on the physical mass operator. Verification Independent verification checks the normalized powers, exact product and dimension ratios, and the complete band sum. An effective quartic model that omits the canonical frequency denominator is a separate stipulated interaction; its results do not verify the plain local-potential normalization.

title: Coupling as the source of localization and mass-frequency
summary: A same-field interaction may generate mass by sustaining a localized oscillating pattern. A scale calculation shows why simple contact alone does not bind and how competing terms can select a radius, while the complete frequency, inertia and pair response remain to be derived.
text:
The physical proposal is that interactions within one field hold a particle pattern together. The resulting confined motion selects its oscillation frequency and inertial response; mass is that frequency in equivalent units. A self-interaction is one possible sustaining contribution. Coupling to other modes of the same field, or to a supporting field pattern, may also be necessary. The same action must then govern how two particles respond to each other. This proposal does not require a bare interaction coefficient, an observed encounter rate, and a mass-frequency to have the same numerical value. The canonical scalar-response identities already show the precise relation for a first-order candidate action: on a smooth stationary branch at fixed spatial geometry, dE/dQ=\omega, where Q is canonical norm, while the response to another field pattern comes from higher variations of the same energy. Thus frequency and pair coupling are related derivatives of one action, but neither derivative can be inferred from the other without the stationary spatial field and its normalization. The identity is conditional on that first-order action; it is not a universal mass law. That can be tested, but low coupling cannot simply be taken to zero in (3): below the finite threshold (4), this particular scale model has no localized stationary radius. title: Local contact instability on proposed CP3
summary: Every positive-degree coherent branch of the specified massless local scalar Dirac action on physical CP3 has a small-coupling oscillatory instability in its complete radial Dirac complement.
text: Summary: Every positive-degree coherent branch of the specified massless local scalar Dirac action on physical CP3 has a small-coupling oscillatory instability in its complete radial Dirac complement. Precise statement Use the metric, twist, normalization and full spatial equation of the specified CP3 scalar branch. The physical space is CP3, the bare mass is zero, and the interaction is local \varepsilon(\varphi^\dagger\beta\varphi)\beta\varphi. For each fixed integer L\ge1, its branch through the coherent holomorphic section is spectrally unstable for every sufficiently small nonzero \varepsilon. The proof retains both Dirac signs and conjugate variations. The unstable mode belongs to an exact invariant class of spatial spinors, so it is also an instability of the full specified field equation. The statement does not extend automatically to other kernels, additional field terms, other branches or arbitrary coupling strengths. It does not make a particle–antiparticle identification from Dirac signs. Full complex linearization Expand both chirality components in the complete Jacobi modes and write their complex coefficients as c. At a real stationary profile, the linearized gradient in its rotating frame has the form i\dot\eta=(A-\Omega I)\eta+B\bar\eta, \qquad A=A^\dagger,\quad B=B^{\mathsf T}. \tag{1} The bar denotes conjugation of the mode coefficients in this linearization. Setting \eta=x+iy gives \dot x=L_-y,\qquad \dot y=-L_+x, \qquad L_\pm=A\pm B-\Omega I. \tag{2} For a real spatial background with components F and H=\sqrt aG, the nonlinear part of L_+ has pointwise blocks \varepsilon\rho_0 \begin{pmatrix}3F^2-H^2&-2FH\\-2FH&3H^2-F^2\end{pmatrix}, \tag{3} integrated with the respective zero-form and one-form basis functions. The nonlinear part of L_- is \varepsilon\rho_0(F^2-H^2)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1). Both include the full Dirac off-diagonal operator and subtract \Omega. In particular L_-c=0 is the exact phase-symmetry zero mode. Opposite-energy modes form a resonant pair At zero coupling, let u_n=\chi p_n and v_n=\mathscr D_Lu_n/\lambda_n. The complete Dirac modes are (u_n\pm v_n)/\sqrt2 with energies \pm\lambda_n. In (1), a positive-energy coefficient and the conjugate of a negative-energy coefficient have the same unperturbed frequency +\lambda_n. Dropping either removes this resonance. Let A_0=\int\rho_0^2d\nu,\qquad U_n=\int_0^1w\rho_0p_n^2dt,\qquad V_n=\int_0^1w\rho_0Q_n^2dt. The first-order matrix on this two-dimensional frequency subspace is \boxed{\lambda_n I+\varepsilon \begin{pmatrix}a_n&b_n\\-b_n&-a_n\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a_n=U_n-\frac{V_n}{2}-A_0, \quad b_n=\frac{U_n}{2}.} \tag{4} Thus its frequencies are \nu_{n,\pm}=\lambda_n\pm\varepsilon \sqrt{a_n^2-b_n^2}+O(\varepsilon^2). \tag{5} The actual stationary profile differs from \chi at order \varepsilon. Since it enters the nonlinear Hessian multiplied by \varepsilon, that correction changes (4) only at the next order. The first level is unstable at every positive degree For n=1, put s=L+m+1. The normalized Jacobi mode is p_1(t)=\sqrt{\frac{s+1}{(L+1)m}}[st-(L+1)], \qquad Q_1(t)=\sqrt{\frac{s(s+1)}{(L+1)m}}\sqrt{t(1-t)}. \tag{6} The measure w\rho_0/A_0 is the beta distribution with parameters (2L+1,m). Its first two moments evaluate (4). At m=3 this gives \frac{U_1}{A_0}=\frac{2(L+1)(L+5)}{(L+2)(2L+5)},\qquad \frac{V_1}{A_0}= \frac{(L+4)(L+5)(2L+1)}{2(L+1)(L+2)(2L+5)}. \tag{7} Substitution and factorization produce the exact sign: \boxed{\frac{a_1^2-b_1^2}{A_0^2} =-\frac{L(2L^2+21L+7)(6L^3+35L^2+81L+40)} {16(L+1)^2(L+2)^2(2L+5)^2}<0\quad(L\ge1).} \tag{8} Every factor other than the displayed minus sign is positive. The physical exponential growth rate is consequently \Gamma=\frac{|\varepsilon|}{R}\sqrt{b_1^2-a_1^2} +O(\varepsilon^2/R), \tag{9} while the mode oscillates at frequency close to \lambda_1/R. This is an oscillatory instability, not the phase zero mode. For L=1, the coefficients reduce to A_0=\frac85,\quad U_1=\frac{64}{35},\quad V_1=\frac{12}{7}, \quad a_1=-\frac{22}{35},\quad b_1=\frac{32}{35}, \quad \boxed{\Gamma R=\sqrt{\frac{108}{245}}|\varepsilon| +O(\varepsilon^2).} \tag{10} At \varepsilon=10^{-3}, the leading growth is 0.0006639400022/R. Independent finite approximations to the corrected branch give the first growth pair near 0.0006639375673/R, with oscillation frequency near 4.4721371142/R. Why this is not an artifact of a finite cutoff In the complete radial class, the unperturbed frequencies \lambda_n=2\sqrt{n(n+L+3)} are discrete and separated. The cluster at +\lambda_1 has dimension two in the doubled equation (1). The smooth background on the specified global CP3 geometry makes the perturbation a bounded analytic operator on the same Dirac domain. Its Riesz projection is therefore an analytic finite-dimensional cluster, with first-order matrix exactly (4). The two nonreal eigenvalues supplied by (8) are distinct at first order. They persist for sufficiently small nonzero coupling; higher orders cannot cancel their leading imaginary parts. This proves the spectral statement for the complete symmetry class. The class is invariant under the full spatial equation, so these eigenmodes are valid spatial perturbations even when all other angular and spinor components are admitted. No convergence of the largest growth rate over all modes is needed for this proof. One unstable isolated pair is sufficient. Numerical near-zero roots associated with the phase Jordan block are also not the modes used in (8)–(10). Relation to the projected coherent calculation Restricting the action to holomorphic zero forms gives the smooth quartic with coefficient D_L^2/D_{2L}. Its finite holomorphic coherent set is orbitally stable within that finite action, taking its projective complex dimension to be three here. The missing radial one-form partners create the instability just proved. The comparison therefore distinguishes a stable projected pattern from a stable solution of the spatial Dirac equation. The smooth moment-kernel calculation changes the actual scalar interaction and tests which part of this resonance survives; it does not reinterpret the local-contact result. Verification cp3_scalar_dirac_checks.py checks the real and conjugate Hessian by independent differences, the exact beta moments and factorization, the first resonant pair at successively refined mode cutoffs, and the uncompressed spatial equation for each background. Its nonlinear evolutions retain both complex chirality profiles and the conserved norm and energy.
