title: The remaining lengths and coupling in the frequency unit
summary: Restoring the existing spatial lengths identifies the shared frequency unit; an inverse-matrix bound tests equal six/ten scales, while conditional radius ratios retain their finite-hopping limitations.
text: The curvature-moment rule removes an independent spatial function. It does not fix the remaining dimensional scales. Restoring their units makes the missing physical input explicit and gives a useful constraint on the charged-lepton comparison. Mass is frequency in equivalent units throughout. This calculation asks which physical geometry and coupling produce that frequency; it does not rederive the conversion mc^2=\hbar\omega. Restore the lengths already present in the carrier Let R_d be the tangential length parameter and L_d the normal profile's length unit. These are ordinary spatial lengths, common to the particle modes at one depth. Write the dimensionless normal coordinate as y=x/L_d. The physical coefficient in the curvature-moment rule has inverse-length units: h_{\rm phys}=\frac{z_{\rm phys}B_{\rm phys}}2 =\frac1{L_d}h(y). \tag{1} With a common wave speed c and a dimensionless physical coefficient g_d, the frequency matrix therefore has diagonal entries c(\beta+j_z)/R_d and adjacent entries cg_dh_l/L_d. Equivalently, \boxed{\gamma_d=g_dR_d/L_d,\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\frac c{R_d}\lambda_{n,d}(\gamma_d).} \tag{2} The normal separation parameter is R_d/L_d. This is a restoration of the existing parameters, not an additional adjustable length for each particle. In the large-hopping limit the common unit is \boxed{\omega_{0,d}= \frac{c\,d!}{g_d^{d-1}\prod_lh_l} \frac{L_d^{d-1}}{R_d^d},\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\omega_{0,d}\binom{n+d-1}{d} [1+O(\gamma_d^{-2})].} \tag{3} Thus a measured common frequency unit constrains a combination of the lengths, coupling and computed spatial integrals. It does not determine all of them separately. The geometric factor is fixed by the operator, and cannot be dropped when comparing inferred sizes across depths. A common radius, width and coefficient fail the six/ten comparison As an optional stronger trial, set R_{10}=R_6, L_{10}=L_6 and g_{10}=g_6. Then both matrices have the same \gamma and the physical frequency ratio equals their dimensionless singular-value ratio. There is an upper bound valid at every \gamma\ge0, not only in the asymptotic approximation. The maintained anchor indices are n_e=13, n_\tau=23. Take the central six-by-six block of the depth-ten triangular matrix, using normal labels 2 through 7. Its diagonal magnitudes, ordered increasingly, are 25,26,\ldots,30, whereas the depth-six magnitudes are 13,14,\ldots,18. The computed five adjacent integrals of this central block each exceed every depth-six adjacent integral. Reversing and transposing a negative surface-sign matrix orders its diagonal magnitudes without changing its singular values. The same comparison therefore covers all four choices of the two surface signs. The absolute entries of a triangular inverse are products of its adjacent coefficients divided by products of its diagonal coefficients. Consequently the central inverse block dominates the depth-six inverse entrywise up to the factor C=\prod_{l=0}^5\frac{25+l}{13+l}. \tag{4} The norm of a nonnegative matrix is monotone under entrywise increase. The norm of the full inverse is at least that of its central submatrix. Therefore \boxed{\frac{\lambda_{\tau,10}}{\lambda_{e,6}}\le C,} \tag{5} which is far below the assigned simplex ratio \frac{S(23,10)}{S(13,6)} =\frac{64512240}{18564}\simeq3475.12605. \tag{6} The positive-sign pair has the sharper bound \prod_{l=0}^5(23+l)/(13+l)=20.29411765. These are comparisons between separate particle matrices. They do not identify one particle solution with a part of the other. This excludes the simultaneous equal-radius, equal-width, equal-coupling trial within the current carrier. Equal radius alone is not excluded; the normal length or coupling may depend on depth. The IDWT premise of one common size for all modes at a given depth is also unaffected. Conditional radius requirements are computable For illustration, retain a common L and g across the two depths but allow their radii to differ. Put r=R_{10}/R_6. Then \gamma_{10}=r\gamma_6, and the positive-sign anchor equation is \boxed{ \frac{\lambda_{23,10}(r\gamma_6)} {r\lambda_{13,6}(\gamma_6)} =\frac{S(23,10)}{S(13,6)}.} \tag{7} The small singular value strictly decreases as positive hopping grows: the nonnegative absolute triangular inverse increases entrywise. Thus the left side of (7) decreases from infinity to zero with r, giving a unique conditional radius ratio at each stated \gamma_6. The leading expression is r_{\rm lead}= \left[\frac{10!}{6!} \frac{\prod_lh_l^{(6)}}{\prod_lh_l^{(10)}} \frac1{\gamma_6^4}\right]^{1/10}. \tag{8} Full finite-matrix solutions give: \gamma_6 Required R_{10}/R_6 Resulting \gamma_{10} 100 0.23713045 23.7130 1000 0.10320217 103.2022 10000 0.04125312 412.5312 100000 0.01642733 1642.7334 These values impose the assigned anchor ratio under the extra common L,g assumption. They are not a forward derivation of actual particle sizes. They also do not remove the finite within-depth correction: at \gamma_6=10000, the computed muon/electron ratio is about 1.10\times10^{-5} below its ideal simplex ratio. Matching one cross-depth anchor cannot silently eliminate that remaining correction. The physical kernel must still determine the shared lengths and coupling and satisfy the normal-complement control needed for the projected spectrum. This dimensional accounting also leaves the supporting state's energy and coherent motion unresolved. Neither issue is a mass–frequency separation. Verification curvature_scale_checks.py checks the entrywise spatial comparison, the analytic inverse bounds at multiple hopping strengths and all surface-sign choices, the exact conditional radius roots, and the dimensional reparametrization. It uses the maintained indices and verified spatial integrals. It does not scan alternative particle assignments or fit a separate coefficient for each mass. The 50-check report records these comparisons and the hashes of the input spatial report.

title: A bounded curvature-moment carrier with positive averaged shape stiffness
summary: The rule h=zB/2 removes an independent spatial function, preserves the simplex numerator and grouped response, and gives a positive complete centered Hessian for the balanced averaged multiplet across all maintained depths.
text: A simple coefficient obtained from the existing linked geometry survives both the spectral and complete averaged-stiffness tests: \boxed{h=z(1-|W|^2)=\frac{zB}{2}.} \tag{1} It removes the independently prescribed radial multiplier. Unlike the density-gradient choice, it retains positive shape stiffness when the actual nonlinear geometry is included. The same rule is used at depths 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10, with every maintained particle index and both surface signs. The result is a stronger candidate spatial carrier. It is not yet a complete physical mass operator: the averaged supporting state has a large energy cost, and its coherent field still has time-dependent sources. Its physical normalization and sustaining motion remain to be derived from the one field. One scalar profile determines the spatial coefficients In the same ordinary dimensionless normal coordinates, use \boxed{ \Delta u=2(1-e^{-2u}|P(z)|^2),\qquad W=e^{-u}P(z),\quad A=\nabla^\perp u,\quad B=\Delta u.} \tag{2} The radial reference has P=z^d, W=w(r)e^{id\theta}, A=a(r)e_\theta/r, with w'=\frac{d-a}{r}w,\qquad a'=2r(1-w^2). \tag{3} These same fields determine the geometric normal operator, its bounded polarization and the new multiplier: \begin{aligned} D_{\rm geo}&=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla+ \frac12\alpha\cdot A(\tau_3-I)+2\Gamma\cdot W,\\ K&=(d+1-a)S-aI,\qquad h=\frac{zB}{2}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} Equation (1) is an explicit candidate choice using an existing geometric quantity. The physical master action has not uniquely selected it or fixed its overall coupling. There is no new fitted spatial profile in (4), and none of these normal coordinates is compactified. At the radial reference, h=r(1-w^2)e^{i\theta}. Monotonicity of w gives a(r)=2\int_0^r s(1-w(s)^2)ds\ge r^2(1-w(r)^2), so \boxed{|h|\le\min(r,d/r)\le\sqrt d.} \tag{5} The coefficient is regular at zero and decays at infinity. Bound (5) applies to this radial reference; arbitrary separated nonradial shapes require their own bound. A common translation carries the center and its relative coordinate z together. Spectrum and grouped response survive For normalized normal modes \Phi_l, the adjacent integrals are h_l=2\pi\int_0^\infty r^2(1-w^2) (U_{l+1}U_l+V_{l+1}V_l)dr>0. \tag{6} The projected pair still has H_P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&T^\dagger\\T&0\end{smallmatrix}\right), with T_{ll}=\beta+l-\frac{d-1}{2},\qquad T_{l+1,l}=\gamma h_l. \tag{7} For \beta=n+(d-1)/2, the product of its diagonal entries is d!\binom{n+d-1}{d}. Therefore its small frequency remains \boxed{\lambda_{n,d}= \frac{d!}{\gamma^{d-1}\prod_l h_l} \binom{n+d-1}{d}\,[1+O(\gamma^{-2})].} \tag{8} The finite-hopping correction remains nonzero. The equality of the charged-lepton frequency units between depths six and ten is not proved by the numerator in (8). For a real polynomial deformation, the density derivative is \delta\rho=2wU_k\cos k\theta. The coefficient now has \delta h=-z\delta\rho, \qquad \delta_{x_k}h=-rwU_k \left(e^{i(1-k)\theta}+e^{i(1+k)\theta}\right). \tag{9} For the imaginary coordinate, multiply the first angular coefficient by i and the second by -i. The complete derivative also includes both moving normal modes. The polarization's full first derivative still cancels by its independent angular-generator identity. The endpoint coefficient \kappa_d, normalized by the actual positive geometric metric M_d, is: Depth \kappa_d/\sqrt{M_d} 2 -0.55216758 3 -0.70703135 4 -0.84344101 5 -0.96798865 6 -1.08333628 10 -1.47836995 Its frequency response is 2\gamma\kappa_d\operatorname{Re}(v_0^*u_{d-1}). For a fixed surface sign, the endpoint product approaches a common value across the assigned indices within each depth. This retains different frequencies with similar within-depth response. These dimensionless integrals do not themselves derive neutrino suppression, physical gauge couplings or encounter rates. Retain the full nonlinear shape Hessian Use the positive averaged populations q_j=s_j(T_0), where s_j are all positive singular values. Their complete centered source is zero by the weighted trace identity. Keep these canonical populations fixed during an energy variation. The canonical interpretation here uses the explicitly defined retained positive action. Projecting the full parent's square would add a complementary-mode term unless its invariant low subspace has first been derived. For real coordinates x_k, define \mathcal A_{kh}=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr} (T_k^\dagger T_h+T_0^\dagger T_{kh}),\qquad F_{jk}=\partial_{x_k}s_j. \tag{10} The complete static energy Hessian is \boxed{\mathcal H_{xx}=\mathcal A-F^TF,\qquad \mathcal H_{yy}=\mathcal A,\qquad \mathcal H_{xy}=0.} \tag{11} The zero mixed real–imaginary block follows from complex conjugation at the real reference. It does not set the dynamical Berry curvature to zero. The imaginary first frequency gradients vanish there, and the first matrix norms and relevant second spatial traces agree on the two quadratures. Thus \mathcal H_{yy}-\mathcal H_{xx}=F^TF\ge0. Angular selection makes \mathcal A tridiagonal in the centered orders k=2,\ldots,d. The full real Hessian is nevertheless generally dense because of the frequency-gradient Gram matrix. Discarding its mixed entries would not test (11). The diagonal nonlinear terms use the complete second geometry, with h''_0=-z\rho''_0. For adjacent orders h=k+1, the required mixed geometric harmonic solves \boxed{(-\Delta_1+4w^2)g_{k,k+1}=4U_kU_{k+1}.} \tag{12} It follows by taking the mixed derivative of (2) and retaining the angular difference harmonic. Its density coefficient is 2U_kU_{k+1}-2w^2g_{k,k+1}. The second moving mode also includes D_k\Phi_h+D_h\Phi_k, the explicit D_{kh}, and its symmetric in-kernel normalization. All these terms are retained. They supply \mathcal A_{k,k+1}= \gamma\sum_l\left(\beta+l-\frac{d-1}{2}\right)(h_{kh})_{ll} -\frac\gamma2\sum_lh_l(K_{kh})_{l+1,l}. \tag{13} Orders separated by more than one cannot contribute to this nonlinear trace. Equation (12) is checked independently with a scalar boundary value solver, and (13) with direct finite spatial integrals. The complete centered Hessian is positive in the tested controls Normalize to unit canonical charge \mathcal Q=\sum_js_j(T_0) and use the diagonal positive geometric metric M_k. At \gamma=10000, the smallest eigenvalues of \mathcal H_{xx,kh}/(\mathcal Q\sqrt{M_kM_h}) include: Control Smallest real-shape eigenvalue Depth-two W 2489.69 Depth-three down 1711.22 Depth-four up 1275.03 Depth-five first neutrino 1033.74 Depth-six electron 739.18 Depth-ten tau 81.63 The complete matrices are positive for every maintained control and both surface signs. Equation (11) then also gives positivity of the entire imaginary block. This establishes a local minimum of the stated averaged energy over all centered complex polynomial deformations at fixed populations, within the declared spatial reduction. It is stronger than the earlier separate-coordinate test. It does not establish a pointwise coherent equilibrium or dynamical stability of the full master field. The positive-band energy bound still places the supporting state's energy per canonical charge well above the small frequency. A coherent occupation also has beat-frequency sources that averaging removes, as quantified in the coherent polarization test. Those two issues remain physical work for the same-field action; they are not repaired by calling a static Hessian an inertia. Dimensional normalization remains explicit Let R_d be the tangential length and L_d the normal profile's length unit. Both are ordinary spatial lengths shared by the particles at one depth. With a common wave speed c, the physical coefficient z_{\rm phys}B_{\rm phys}/2 has units of inverse length. If its dimensionless physical multiplier is g_d, then \gamma_d=g_d\frac{R_d}{L_d},\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\frac c{R_d}\lambda_{n,d}, and (8) gives \boxed{\omega_{0,d}=\frac{c\,d!}{g_d^{d-1}\prod_lh_l} \frac{L_d^{d-1}}{R_d^d}.} \tag{14} Equation (14) identifies the combinations that must be supplied by the physical geometry and coupling law. It does not assign independent lengths to different particle modes, derive a common size across all depths, or introduce compactified dimensions. Mass is already frequency in equivalent units; the unresolved step is the dynamics that fixes these shared physical coefficients. The dimensional comparison tests those remaining parameters explicitly, including all surface-sign choices in the six/ten equal-parameter trial. The depth-two extension reruns the common calculation at all six depths, with 102 positive real coordinate controls and the complete complex Hessians. It also identifies an exact two-band coherent source cancellation. The polarization-dimension test examines its generalization and distinguishes it from cancellation of inertia. Verification flux_moment_hopping.py implements the coefficient and its explicit first and second responses. flux_moment_checks.py verifies the bounded profile, independent first spatial contractions, finite second spatial differences on both quadratures, the common spectral numerator, grouped response and positive-support energy bound. Its 140-check report includes all 96 real coordinate-curvature controls. curvature_moment_mixed.py and curvature_moment_mixed_checks.py retain the full mixed nonlinear geometry and every centered coordinate. The 132-check report checks the complete matrices, the independent mixed scalar profile, finite spatial derivatives and low/high-depth refinements. Raw geometry, matrices and exact executed source versions are stored separately.

title: Curvature forces on the linked mass-carrier geometry
summary: The actual tube weight gives an exact leading restoring-to-metric ratio, but also a centered shape force; the symmetric planar profile is not a complete curved stationary source.
text: The actual spatial curvature supplies a positive restoring coefficient for the carrier's constant-polynomial deformation at depths 4, 5, 6 and 10. That contribution vanishes at depth 3. The ratio of its leading coefficient to the deformation metric is an exact polynomial in depth, with no independent numerical integral. The same calculation also finds a force on a different centered shape coordinate. Consequently this restoring coefficient does not make the round reference a stationary occupied particle. A common-radius pressure balance must be accompanied by a balance of the internal shape forces. These statements concern the declared geometric coefficient functional. Its physical energy and time normalization, its identification with sustaining modes of the one field, and the complete curved wave source remain open. Mass is the particle's selected frequency in equivalent units. The ordinary spatial tube Let a round field feature S_R^m lie in ordinary \mathbb R^{m+2}, with m=d-2. Use the outward radial normal y_1 and the fixed binormal y_2. This normal frame is flat; no normal Chern class is inserted. In the nonsingular tube r<R, r^2=y_1^2+y_2^2,\qquad J(y)=\left(1+\frac{y_1}{R}\right)^m. \tag{1} The following expressions are per unit area of the reference feature. They retain normal derivatives of the linked coefficients and their exact tube volume factor. They restrict those coefficients to the planar first-order family; they are not the full Euler–Lagrange equations of a curved stationary solution. The linked planar rule is W=e^{-u}P(z),\quad A=\nabla^\perp u,\quad B=\Delta u=2(1-|W|^2),\qquad (D_1+iD_2)W=0, where D_i=\partial_i-iA_i. Its positive geometric density and cost are e=|DW|^2+\frac{B^2}{4}+(1-|W|^2)^2,\qquad G_J=\int Je\,d^2y. \tag{2} At J=1, every degree-d polynomial in this family has G_1=2\pi d, independently of its zero locations. The local identity \boxed{e=B+\frac12\Delta |W|^2} \tag{3} follows by applying the covariant Laplacian to |W|^2 and using the first-order rule. Changes of the localized density decay exponentially, which controls the boundary terms in the integrations below. The finite tube is used where J is a physical Jacobian; replacing its localized integrals by full-plane integrals has an exponentially small tail error when the core is well inside the tube. The constant-polynomial restoring coefficient At P=z^d, write w=|W|, a=ru_0'. For P=z^d+\alpha, the expansion is u=u_0+\alpha f_d\cos d\theta+ \alpha^2(g_0+g_2\cos2d\theta)+O(\alpha^3). The metric calculation gives \begin{aligned} (-\Delta+d^2/r^2+4w^2)f_d&=4w^2r^{-d},\\ (-\Delta+4w^2)g_0&=2w^2(r^{-d}-f_d)^2,\\ \int g_0\,d^2y&=\frac d2M_d. \end{aligned} \tag{4} The angular mean of the second coefficient of |W|^2 is -\Delta g_0/2. The degree of J is m=d-2<d, so its product with every nonzero angular harmonic of this deformation integrates to zero. Using (3) twice by parts yields G_J(\alpha)-G_J(0)=G_2\alpha^2+O(\alpha^4),\qquad \boxed{G_2=\int\left(\Delta J-\frac14\Delta^2J\right)g_0\,d^2y.} \tag{5} Rotation of the normal plane changes the phase of \alpha. Since J cannot see the nonzero multiples of d, the restricted cost depends on |\alpha|; the real expansion is even. In particular, G_2=\frac{m(m-1)}{R^2}\int g_0\,d^2y+O(R^{-4}), \qquad \boxed{\frac{G_2}{M_d} =\frac{d(d-2)(d-3)}{2R^2}+O(R^{-4}).} \tag{6} At depths 4 and 5 the displayed leading term is exact for this restricted tube polynomial. At depth 3 it is identically zero. Higher inverse-radius terms remain at depths 6 and 10. If a kinetic comparison has M_d|\dot\alpha|^2, its real kinetic and restoring Hessians both acquire a factor two, so the ratio in (6) is unchanged. It is nevertheless not yet a physical shape frequency: the complete reference is not stationary, and the curved kinetic metric also changes at higher orders. A physical geometric action would supply its energy and time units before this ratio could become a frequency. For the well-conditioned coordinate \tau=c_0\alpha, with w\sim c_0r^d, numerical coefficients at R=40 are: Depth Coefficient of \tau^2 in G_J 3 0 4 0.007760334864 5 0.029320061767 6 0.070598093673 10 0.556519629104 The coordinate factor changes both G_2 and M_d equally. These entries are geometric comparisons, not measured couplings. The other polynomial directions carry forces For P=z^d+\alpha_kz^{d-k}, let U_k=w(r^{-k}-f_k). The first density variation is \delta|W|^2=2wU_k\cos k\theta. Equation (3) gives the finite formula F_k=\partial_{\alpha_k}G_J =-2\int\left(2J-\frac12\Delta J\right)wU_k\cos k\theta\,d^2y. \tag{7} The holomorphic moment identity \int_0^\infty r^{k+1}wU_k\,dr=k/2 fixes its leading term: \boxed{F_k=-\frac{2^{2-k}\pi k}{R^k}\binom{m}{k} +O(R^{-k-2}),\qquad k\le m.} \tag{8} For k>m, the first derivative vanishes by angular selection. When m-k<2, no higher tube-polynomial term contributes to (8). In particular, F_1=-\frac{2\pi m}{R}+O(R^{-3}),\qquad F_2=-\frac{\pi m(m-1)}{R^2}+O(R^{-4}). \tag{9} The first coordinate shifts the center by -\alpha_1/d, giving the usual mean-curvature tension force of a cost 2\pi d. The second coordinate keeps the center fixed. Positive \alpha_2 splits a pair of zeros along the binormal and lowers the weighted cost at leading order. Therefore fixing the center does not hold the coincident polynomial stationary for d\ge4. For d=3, J is linear. Every centered planar first-order configuration has the same restricted cost. This follows from (3) and the first holomorphic moment; it is not merely a numerical zero in one quadratic coefficient. The full first variation and complementary fields It is useful to check the full energy rather than just its restriction. At any planar first-order solution, varying arbitrary W,A gives \begin{aligned} \frac{\delta G_J}{\delta W^*}&=-(\partial_iJ)D_iW,\\ \frac{\delta G_J}{\delta A}&=-\frac12B\nabla^\perp J. \end{aligned} \tag{10} The constant-weight Euler–Lagrange terms cancel, leaving derivatives of J. For a linear weight J=1+\varkappa y_1, define the horizontal translation vector Z_1=(-D_1W,-B e_2),\qquad \|\delta\|_M^2=\int(|\delta W|^2+|\delta A|^2/4)d^2y. Then \boxed{dG_J[\delta]=2\varkappa\langle Z_1,\delta\rangle_M, \qquad \|Z_1\|_M^2=\pi d.} \tag{11} Thus the order-R^{-1} source is purely a translation in this specified metric. If translation is removed by the corresponding orthogonal projection, there is no order-R^{-1} force on complementary fields. The usual second-order energy lowering from relaxing such a forced complement therefore vanishes in this particular projected problem. That projection does not derive physical pressure. A different imposed center constraint, or the occupied wave's actual support stress, can act on the complementary fields differently. The full physical source still needs its own equation. At order R^{-2}, the nonzero quadrupole force already lies within the geometric zero-mode space and remains explicit. title: A simpler current action with the same mass-core response
summary: Total-density normalization removes the cutoff functions and their thresholds while preserving the coherent mass branches, canonical inertia and complete core Hessian, including finite graded currents and their common-target interaction.
text: The regular polarization model admits a genuine simplification. Its two cutoff applications can be replaced by ordinary rational functions of the same field's total density. No cutoff thresholds remain. The maintained coherent mass-frequency branches, common spatial profiles and complete linearized equations on those branches are unchanged. The replacement is a different nonlinear interaction away from the core. The statement proved here is equality of the potential, its first variation and its full second variation on the core, together with global regularity of the fixed-frame source. It is not an assertion that all nonlinear encounters are identical. The spatial carrier of the simplex weights and the physical selection of occupied branches remain open. All physical coordinates are ordinary and uncompactified. Mass remains the selected frequency, with mc^2=\hbar\omega. The single-grade formula Use the complete 2s-by-s matrix field \Psi=(\phi,\chi)^T, where s is the partner representation rank. The matrices and currents are those of the localized polarization core: A_a=\sigma_x\otimes\alpha_a,\quad B_0=\sigma_z\otimes I_s,\quad B_1=\sigma_x\otimes\beta,\quad B_2=I_2\otimes\beta, \qquad C=\Psi^\dagger B_0\Psi,\quad J=\Psi^\dagger B_1\Psi,\quad K=\Psi^\dagger B_2\Psi. Here the Hermitian \alpha_a,\beta anticommute and square to one. Let \rho=\operatorname{Tr}\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\qquad \Delta_C=s\operatorname{Tr}C^2-(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2. For \rho>0, the simplified potential is \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \widetilde U={}&\frac{\omega}{2\rho}\left[\rho^2+ qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2\right] +m_c\operatorname{Tr}(J\beta)\\ &-\frac{s\kappa}{\rho^2} \operatorname{Tr}(\beta K)\operatorname{Tr}(JK) +\mu\|P_\perp\phi\|_F^2. \end{aligned}} \tag{1} The physical spatial principal operator remains -iA_a\partial_a. The projector P_\perp removes the scalar and physical-vector matrix components, as defined in the shape-response calculation. The common contraction choice remains q=1/(s+1). No parameter is adjusted for an individual particle. At \Psi=0, set both the potential and its source to zero. A zero scalar or polarization current in a nonzero field no longer causes any division by zero. The density denominators do not introduce a new field, a density scale, or a mass obtained by fitting the field magnitude. Compared with the cutoff construction, (1) removes the cutoff function, both uses of it, its two threshold constants, and all derivatives of the cutoff. It also removes the square root from the occupied-grade mass potential. The binding, shape and responding-frame structures still have distinct mathematical roles. Equality of the complete core derivatives At every point of the radial core, \phi_0=fI_s+i h\alpha_{\hat x},\quad \chi_0=0,\qquad c=f^2+h^2,\quad C_0=cI_s,\quad K_0^2=c^2I_s, \quad J_0=0,\quad\rho_0=sc. \tag{2} The original mass expression was F_q(C)=\sqrt{qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2} =\sqrt{t^2+q\Delta_C},\qquad t=\operatorname{Tr}C. The normalized mass expression satisfies the exact identity \boxed{\widetilde F=\frac{\rho^2+F_q^2}{2\rho},\qquad \widetilde F-F_q=\frac{(\rho-F_q)^2}{2\rho}\ge0.} \tag{3} It is positive at every nonzero field and even under reversal of the scalar current. There is no square root in its implemented formula. On the core, F_q=\rho and \delta F_q=\delta\rho for every complete field variation. Consequently \rho-F_q=O(\epsilon^2), so the potential difference starts at fourth order. The complete Hessian and third potential variation agree. The same argument applies to a conformal-unitary lower-only core, where C=-cI_s. Equivalently, the upper-core expansion is \widetilde F=t+q\Delta_C/(2\rho)+(\rho-t)^2/(2\rho). The last term preserves the reversed-current symmetry while having zero variation through third order at the upper core. No new coefficient is introduced. For the binding term, put D=\operatorname{Tr}K^2. At the core, D=\frac{\rho^2}{s},\qquad \delta D=2c\,\delta\rho =\delta\left(\frac{\rho^2}{s}\right). \tag{4} The numerator \operatorname{Tr}(\beta K)\operatorname{Tr}(JK) vanishes there because J_0=0, and starts at first order. Replacing D by \rho^2/s changes the potential only at third order. The binding potential, full source and complete Hessian therefore agree. These are identities for arbitrary complex spinor and partner variations, including variations outside the scalar/vector shape of the core. The transverse-mode reduction further separates the complete finite hierarchy into one occupied coefficient block and complex-linear spatial blocks. The complete spatial linearized differential operator is consequently the same as before, with the same canonical kinetic term. Its existing local Clifford decomposition, spatial angular equations and outgoing matching controls transfer directly. This does not turn those limited stability results into a complete stability theorem. The source includes the density derivatives The normalized expression must be varied as an action. For example, let L=qsC+(1-q)tI_s,\qquad B=qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)t^2,\qquad b=\operatorname{Tr}(\beta K),\quad v=\operatorname{Tr}(JK). The complete mass source is \widetilde S_{\rm mass} =\omega\left[\frac{B_0\Psi L}{\rho} +\frac12\left(1-\frac{B}{\rho^2}\right)\Psi\right], and the binding source is \widetilde S_{\rm bind} =m_c B_1\Psi\beta -s\kappa\left[ \frac{B_1\Psi(bK)+B_2\Psi(v\beta+bJ)}{\rho^2} -\frac{2bv}{\rho^3}\Psi\right]. \tag{5} The last term in each expression is required by reciprocity. Omitting it would change both the action and the branch comparison. Retaining the whole finite current hierarchy The simplification is not confined to an occupied coefficient ray. For a finite set of grades, retain the canonical fields and exact symmetric-tensor splitting maps of the graded current construction. At retained order k, let R_k be the sum of the scalar-insertion currents from grades N\ge k, and define \rho_k=\sum_{N\ge k}\|\Psi_N\|_F^2,\qquad h_{k,d}=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}. The mass action becomes \boxed{ \widetilde U_{\rm mass} =\frac{\omega_{0,d}}2\sum_k h_{k,d} \left[\rho_k+ \frac{qs\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2} {\rho_k}\right].} \tag{6} An empty active channel contributes zero. The numerator uses the partner rank s, not the generally larger size of the retained current matrix. The binding currents instead trace the oscillator indices and sum all grades; their denominator uses the total canonical density. At an isolated coherent upper core, R_k=cI_s\otimes P_{z,k} and \rho_k=sc. The auxiliary defect s\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2-(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2 and its first field variation vanish. To see the latter, write \Pi=I_s\otimes P_{z,k}. The first current variation has no (I-\Pi)-to-(I-\Pi) block: one of its two field factors is still the occupied coherent field. Hence \delta\{s\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2-(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2\} =2sc\operatorname{Tr}[(\Pi-I)\delta R_k]=0. Therefore \delta F_q=\delta\operatorname{Tr}R_k=\delta\rho_k, and the exact remainder (3) includes every retained oscillator component, not just partner variations inside the occupied ray. It also includes an initially empty lower grade used as a weak probe. The same Hockey-Stick sum gives \omega_{N,d}=\omega_{0,d}\sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d} =\omega_{0,d}\binom{N+d}{d}. \tag{7} The weights in (6) remain an inverse prescription. Rewriting the action does not derive their physical carrier. An initially empty channel above the highest occupied grade has a Lipschitz source but need not have a linear derivative at its zero field. No infinite-grade differentiability or uniform infinite-grade evolution estimate is asserted here. The polarization-sensitive interaction survives For two coherent upper cores of grades N\ge M, let \rho,\sigma be their total local canonical densities and let \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2 be the overlap of their coefficient rays. Subtracting the isolated mass energies in (6) gives exactly \boxed{ V_{\rm mass} =-\omega_{0,d}q\frac{\rho\sigma}{\rho+\sigma} \sum_{k=1}^M h_{k,d}(1-\tau^k).} \tag{8} This is a nonzero polarization-sensitive interaction under the same stated conditions as the earlier current comparison. It remains independent of the larger grade. The complete initial source seen by the lower-grade probe has the same common-target identity, because every channel accessible to that probe contains the same target current and density. Its finite-overlap numerical value differs from the original square-root interaction. In the weak-probe limit the original and new laws agree at leading order, as also follows from the complete Hessian equality. Neither expression is an observed gauge vertex or an encounter rate, and subsequent particle deformations need not be identical. Setting q=0 would remove (8) entirely. On upper-only fields, (6) would then collapse to a sum of prescribed quadratic grade masses. A mass-only comparison would miss this loss of the polarization-sensitive self-interaction. Retaining the positive contraction term is therefore part of preserving the joint mass-and-coupling construction. Regularity, the frame and positive inertia For any fixed finite tower, the new potential is smooth on each nonzero active field sphere and homogeneous of degree two. Every denominator is bounded away from zero on that sphere. Its source is homogeneous of degree one with bounded angular derivative, and extends by zero as a globally Lipschitz map. A finite sum of these active-channel sources has the same property. The fixed-frame nonlinear Dirac system therefore retains global canonical L^2 mild evolution and finite propagation. This is not a nonlinear orbital-stability theorem. Evaluate the normalized quantities in the retained future timelike frame, transforming the partner representation with its induced spatial rotation. Composition with this frame map preserves the core derivative identities. Thus the replacements add no new mixed frame-wave or frame-frame quadratic term. The existing responding-frame kinetic term and its vacuum-domain question remain. The complete boosted branch and its canonical translation–boost pairing are unchanged: M_{ab}=\frac{\hbar\omega Q}{c^2}\delta_{ab}>0. The common Q=1 premise still fixes canonical normalization. No amplitude has been identified as mass. Reproducible calculations density_polarization_binding.py contains the complete source and real directional derivative. The 2,325-check report checks arbitrary full matrix variations, reciprocity, conservation, zero-current domains, actual Cartesian fields, boosts and complete core Hessians at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. density_partner_tower.py retains the full canonical grade splitting and pooled binding. The 161-check report checks complete low-grade oscillator spaces at all five depths, all maintained indices in an explicitly stated two-direction coefficient subspace, and the exact finite polarized interaction and common-target source. The bottom entries remain its two component controls; they do not supply the missing spatial quadrature pairing. The 85-check identity report checks the exact positive remainder, reversed-current symmetry, and both upper and lower coherent-core mass Hessians. Its executable is density_mass_identity_checks.py.

summary: The depth-two normal carrier passes the spectral and centered stiffness tests at its prescribed surface parameter; the round-feature construction has no depth-two harmonic tower, while two occupied bands can cancel coherent beat sources.
text: The common curvature-moment calculation now includes all six active depths, d=2,3,4,5,6,10. Thus the centered source vanishes at every time, although the field continues oscillating at both frequencies. Reversing the block assignment works as well. The general combinatorial bound agrees: two bands can have opposite colors with no same-color pair, whereas three or more occupied bands cannot. Dependent scripts take the curvature report filename with --input-report; original executed source versions and raw spatial arrays are preserved with their reports. Its derivative controls the ordinary and conjugate feedback in (5), with g replaced by the appropriate local F'(J) in the source derivative. A law that gives a desired frequency can still produce an unacceptable spatial response. This gives a concrete additional inverse condition: the same interaction must pass the full spatial source test, the common-law test and the required stability test. Changing the scalar response to repair an unstable branch also changes coupling; those adjustments cannot be treated as unrelated parameters. The local quartic law supplies a reproducible example of this constraint, while the physical particle fields remain unidentified. Verification excited_scalar_resonance_checks.py derives (6) from the full action Hessian and independently from curved spatial current integrals. It continues the normalized nonlinear fields, retains both complex response blocks, checks phase and norm identities, and enlarges every spatial cutoff. The stationary and response residuals are evaluated through actual spatial derivatives on separate refined quadrature grids. The near-resonant response is checked directly, including the apparently stable controls, instead of selecting an arbitrary high-frequency numerical eigenvector from tiny roundoff growth. These calculations provide numerical convergence evidence; the finite matrix alone is not a continuum stability proof.

title: Finite-chain mass ratios and an inverse current correction
summary: A finite positive component chain has a strict simplex-ratio drift at every depth; an exact depth-two inverse current law and a common dimension-aware correction identify what a same-field mass source would need to supply.
text: The current whole-depth carrier and the linked normal carrier have the same finite matrix structure on each occupied spatial harmonic. That structure allows an exact test of their proposed simplex mass ratios, independently of the still unknown supporting geometry. A local normalized-current action can also change the finite-chain frequency without assigning a coefficient to each particle. The calculations below distinguish this inverse design from a mass operator derived from the one master field. A strict finite-chain ratio theorem For spatial depth d\ge2, let B_n be the real lower bidiagonal component matrix (B_n)_{jj}=n+j\quad(0\le j<d),\qquad (B_n)_{j,j-1}=b_j>0\quad(1\le j<d), \tag{1} where the b_j are independent of the harmonic label n. The current carrier has b_j=g for all j, while the linked carrier has b_j=g h_j, with one positive geometric hopping list per depth. At a fixed physical radius, the smallest singular value \epsilon_n is the positive oscillation frequency of this component carrier. Write P_{n,d}=\det B_n=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j)=d!S(n,d). \tag{2} The adjugate identity gives an exact normalization formula: \boxed{\frac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} =\frac1{\|\operatorname{adj}B_n\|_2}.} \tag{3} Conjugating the adjugate by alternating diagonal signs makes it a nonnegative lower triangular matrix A_n. Its entries are (A_n)_{ij}= \left(\prod_{a=j+1}^{i}b_a\right) \left(\prod_{a<j\,\text{or}\,a>i}(n+a)\right), \qquad i\ge j, \tag{4} with zero entries above the diagonal. Every entry is nondecreasing in n>0, and some entries increase strictly. The bottom row is positive, so the leading left and right singular vectors can be chosen strictly positive. Their bilinear characterization then makes \|A_n\|_2 strictly increasing. Equation (3) proves \boxed{\frac{\epsilon_{n_2}}{S(n_2,d)} <\frac{\epsilon_{n_1}}{S(n_1,d)} \quad\text{whenever }n_2>n_1>0.} \tag{5} This holds at every finite positive hopping strength, including different positive h_j that are common to all modes at one depth. It covers the maintained depths two, three, four, five, six and ten. Depth ten has only one maintained mode, so it has no within-depth ratio test. The theorem does not cover nonlinear self-consistent hopping that changes with n, different physical radii for particles in one sector, or an added direct mass interaction. When all b_j grow at fixed positive ratios, expanding the largest singular value of the adjugate gives \frac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} =\frac1{\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}b_j} \left[1- \frac12\left(\frac{n^2}{b_1^2} +\frac{(n+d-1)^2}{b_{d-1}^2}\right) +O(g^{-4})\right]. \tag{6} Here the remainder is at fixed n,d as the common edge scale g increases. This correction is the positive norm of internal component content in the causal parent, rather than an error from computing a tiny singular value. The unified calculation verifies (3) independently of direct singular-value decomposition on every maintained mode. For the benchmark masses already used in the mass-spectrum comparison, the observed electron-to-muon ratio is 206.76828299, while the bare simplex ratio at depth six is 3515/17=206.76470588. The latter is low by about 0.00173\%. Equation (5) means an uncorrected finite chain at one common radius and hopping strength lowers its prediction further. At dimensionless current edge g=5000, the whole-depth current ratio is 206.75506228; the linked carrier at its specified strength 10000 gives 206.76242640. These are conditional model predictions against the stated benchmark, not uncertainty-weighted experimental exclusions. An exact depth-two inverse current law on a finite branch For d=2, put P=n(n+1) and use a common positive edge G. The two singular values \epsilon<\Omega satisfy \epsilon(P,G)=\frac12 \left[\sqrt{G^2+4P+1}-\sqrt{G^2+1}\right], \qquad \partial_P\epsilon=\frac1{\sqrt{G^2+4P+1}}. \tag{7} Consider the local homogeneous generating density \rho f(k), where \rho=\Psi^\dagger\Psi, k=\Psi^\dagger K\Psi/\rho, and the same component current matrix K acts on the full form carrier. Complete variation gives the edge G=f'(k), scalar offset C=f(k)-Gk, and standing frequency \lambda=\epsilon(P,G)+C. The envelope identity is d\lambda/dP=\partial_P\epsilon along a self-consistent branch. Choose a reference edge g>0 and set \mu=(1+g^2)^{-1/2}. Requiring \lambda(P)=\mu P through a continuous finite band makes (7) imply G(P)^2=g^2-4P, \qquad k(G)=\frac G2\left(\mu-\frac1{\sqrt{1+G^2}}\right)<0. \tag{8} The following one function of the local current supplies exactly that edge and scalar offset: \boxed{ f(k(G))= \frac{\mu(g^2+G^2)}4- \frac1{2\mu}+ \frac1{2\sqrt{1+G^2}}. } \tag{9} It has f(0)=0 at G=g and direct differentiation gives f'(k)=G. Substitution into the full frequency, including C, then gives the exact identity \boxed{\lambda_n=\mu n(n+1)=2\mu S(n,2).} \tag{10} There is no particle-index coefficient in (9). At the two tested reference strengths g=500 and g=5000, all three maintained depth-two indices 76,81,95 lie in its regular branch. In that branch, G>\sqrt{(1+g^2)^{1/3}-1}, the map G\mapsto k is one-to-one and f''(k)=\frac{2}{\mu-(1+G^2)^{-3/2}}>0. \tag{11} The branch has a finite upper mode bound because G^2=g^2-4P>0, and its one-to-one condition is slightly stronger. An extension of f outside this current interval has not been specified. The exact law therefore applies to the stated finite band, not to every harmonic and not to a derived photon zero mode. Since the interaction is local and algebraic in the normalized current, it preserves the spatial eigenspace and does not change the Dirac or form principal symbol on this branch at fixed geometry. With the already specified positive squared-wave action, its homogeneous gradient supplies exact oscillating solutions at (10) and canonical phase charge \mathcal Q=2\lambda\|\Psi\|^2. Its geometric force, full field Hessian, nonlinear continuation and origin in the master action remain to be established. On the fixed round depth-two form geometry, the complete component derivative has an additional finite control. Its real and imaginary blocks are L_x=A+2f''vv^T and L_y=A, with v=(K-kI)\phi, A=H_0+GK+C, and the entire signed component space retained. At both reference strengths and all three maintained indices, every eigenvalue outside the occupied \lambda ray has absolute value greater than \lambda. Hence the rotating component quadratic stiffness is nonnegative. The separate form spatial scan retains all four form types, electric and quadrature polarizations, azimuth shifts one and three, and angular cutoffs two, four and six. Its 72-case report has positive complete projected Hessians and no resolved growing frequency; the largest growth-to-particle-frequency value is 4.40\times10^{-11}, at numerical resolution. Doubling the quadrature order changes the complete matrix by at most 3.08\times10^{-15} after scaling by the squared strength. This is finite spatial evidence, not a theorem of full field stability. The exact proportionality also makes an on-branch radial comparison possible without moving each mode to a different size. Restore the physical radius and speed through h(R)=g(R)R/c. If the same inverse current function is scaled consistently at each radius, (10) gives \lambda_n(R)=\frac{cP_{n,2}}{R\sqrt{1+h(R)^2}}. \tag{12} As one explicit curvature trial, take the previously tested bounded law g(R)=g_0/[1+(R/R_0)^4], set x=R/R_0 and \gamma=g_0R_0/c. Every n then has the same stationary radius equation 2\gamma^2x^2(x^4-1)=(1+x^4)^3. \tag{13} At \gamma=1000 and 10000, its inner roots are respectively 1.0000010000025R_0 and 1.00000001000000025R_0. The logarithmic on-branch frequency curvatures there are approximately 3.999976 and 3.99999976, both positive. A second, outer stationary root is a maximum, and the frequency tends to zero as R\to\infty. Thus the inner branch has a common local minimum, not global binding. The curvature law and its radius scale are inputs; the full field-radius mixed Hessian and supporting energy remain open. The earlier depth-two angular-stress calculation still constrains this route. If its geometry dependence enters only through a scalar curvature function and any additional first metric variation is isotropic, the electric form's degree-two, degree-four and degree-six density components cannot all be stationary. Changing the current function changes one curvature-response coefficient but does not remove that three-component incompatibility. A patterned same-field supporting response or a different spatial state is still required. The sign in (11) matters. Eliminating a linearly coupled stable same-field response coordinate from a positive quadratic potential V(x)+xk gives f_{\mathrm{eff}}''=-1/V''<0. That elementary Schur result cannot produce the positive curvature required by (9). A direct positive current contribution or a more involved retained dynamics would be needed; the exact inverse function alone does not supply it. The sign obstruction extends to any stable set of response coordinates that enters affinely in the current: the minimized energy \inf_x[V(x)+kB(x)] is an infimum of affine functions of k, so it is concave wherever finite. At a smooth positive Hessian its curvature is -B_x^T(V_{xx}+kB_{xx})^{-1}B_x\le0. This does not exclude the direct convex current term used below, a response that remains dynamical, or nonlinear coupling to k. One dimension-aware correction across all tested depths The strong-gap calculation also suggests a simpler common formula for a candidate current source. On the negative-current branch, let p_d=1+\frac2d,\qquad a_d=(d-1)^{-p_d}, \qquad f_d(k)=gk+a_dg|k|^{p_d}. \tag{14} These are functions of the spatial depth, not fitted mode coefficients. Because k\simeq-(d-1)P_{n,d}/g^d, the second term adds P_{n,d}n^2/g^{d+1} at large n, canceling the leading -P_{n,d}n^2/g^{d+1} part of (6). The finite-index terms and the next powers of 1/g remain. Full variation gives G=g\big[1-a_dp_d|k|^{p_d-1}\big],\qquad C=-a_dg(p_d-1)|k|^{p_d},\qquad \lambda_n=\epsilon_n(G)+C. \tag{15} The unified script solves (15) rather than substituting a prescribed G. The table gives largest-to-smallest spreads of \lambda_n/S(n,d) within each maintained depth. Here the reference edge is g=\text{strength}/2; both strengths are diagnostics, not measured coupling values. Depth Fixed current, strength 1000 Corrected current, 1000 Fixed current, 10000 Corrected current, 10000 2 1.012077525 1.000000097 1.000130611 1.000000000008 3 1.001281644 1.000002078 1.000012800 1.000000001074 4 1.022002484 1.000492062 1.000215327 1.000000046360 5 1.001731997 1.000004387 1.000017280 1.000000000253 6 1.004690472 1.000024970 1.000046643 1.000000002041 Depth ten has one assigned mode, so neither formula has a within-depth spread there. All 32 tested corrected fixed points have positive frequency and positive derivative of their scalar fixed-point equation. The correction improves agreement with the bare simplex rule, not with the electron-to-muon benchmark: at strength 10000 its ratio is 206.76470546, still below the benchmark 206.76828299 and slightly below the bare simplex value 206.76470588. The complete finite-component derivative has real and imaginary blocks L_x=A+2f_d''(k)vv^T,\qquad L_y=A, \quad A=H_0+GK+C,\quad v=(K-kI)\phi. \tag{16} The component-Hessian batch uses the prior report's branch locations but recomputes the fixed points at high precision before diagonalizing all signed components. In all 32 cases every eigenvalue outside the occupied ray has absolute value greater than \lambda. The smallest ratio is 1.0000001761, at depth three and strength 10000. This supplies nonnegative rotating component quadratic stiffness at fixed geometry. The separate fractional depth-two spatial scan then evaluates 72 finite form channels with the same modes, strengths, polarizations, shifts and cutoffs as the exact-law scan. Every complete projected Hessian is positive and the largest growth-to-particle-frequency value is 5.65\times10^{-11}, at numerical resolution. Neither scan establishes stability of the full spatial field or its geometry. For d>2, the fractional term is only C^1 at k=0; the second variation there needs a smooth completion. Its dimension-dependent exponent and coefficient were chosen to cancel the known finite-gap correction. Neither their master-field origin nor the required common six/ten physical frequency unit follows from this calculation. The exponent is forced within this restricted single-current correction class. At a fixed index and large reference gap, the current scales as |k|\sim(d-1)P_{n,d}g^{-d}, while the unwanted leading frequency correction scales as g^{-(d+1)}. A first nonlinear term ag|k|^p scales as g^{1-dp}; matching these powers requires p=1+2/d. Its dependence on the harmonic index also matches the leading n^{d+2} drift. Thus one universal nonzero leading power of this scalar current cannot cancel the leading drift at two different depths. In particular, an analytic current function with a quadratic first correction can do so at depth two, but its correction decays too quickly with the gap at every higher depth. This is a restriction on a current-only cancellation mechanism, not on a master action containing other field or geometric invariants. Continuous inverse branches and the six-to-ten scale The exact depth-two function suggests a general inverse problem. For a reference dimensionless edge g, set \mu_d(g)=\|\operatorname{adj}B_0(g)\|_2^{-1},\qquad P_d(n)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j). \tag{17} The value of \mu_d is the exact zero-mode slope of the smallest singular value divided by P_d'(0). At n=0 the adjugate has only its first column nonzero, with row-i entry (d-1)!g^i/i!. Consequently the reference unit is available without a matrix decomposition: \boxed{\mu_d(g)=\frac1{(d-1)!} \left[\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\frac{g^{2i}}{(i!)^2}\right]^{-1/2}.} \tag{17a} If a differentiable branch is to have \lambda_n=\mu_d(g)P_d(n) continuously, the envelope theorem requires \partial_n\epsilon_n(G_d(n))=\mu_d(g)P_d'(n). \tag{18} Let k_d(n)=\partial_G\epsilon_n(G_d(n)). On any interval where this current is one-to-one, the one local inverse density specified by f_d(k_d(n))=\mu_d(g)P_d(n)-\epsilon_n(G_d(n))+G_d(n)k_d(n) \tag{19} obeys f_d'(k_d(n))=G_d(n). Indeed, differentiating (19) and using (18) cancels the explicit n-derivatives, leaving df_d/dn=G_d\,dk_d/dn. Its full varied standing frequency is therefore the target \mu_dP_d. This is a constructive identity conditional on an invertible branch, not a physical origin for f_d. The exact inverse function is locally smoother at zero current than the fractional approximation in (14). Let Z_d(g)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}g^{2i}/(i!)^2, w_i=g^{2i}/[(i!)^2Z_d(g)], and a_d(g)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}w_i \sum_{j=i+1}^{d-1}\frac1j>0. \tag{19a} This is the derivative of \log\|\operatorname{adj}B_n\|_2 at n=0: only the first adjugate column contributes at first order. Writing P_d'(0)=(d-1)!, implicit differentiation of (18) at (n,G)=(0,g) gives G_d'(0)=\frac{2\mu_d(g)a_d(g)P_d'(0)} {\mu_d'(g)P_d'(0)},\qquad k_d'(0)=\mu_d'(g)P_d'(0), \quad \boxed{f_d''(0^-)= \frac{2\mu_d(g)a_d(g)} {[\mu_d'(g)]^2P_d'(0)}>0.} \tag{19b} Thus each finite-gap inverse branch has a one-sided finite positive second derivative at k=0, and the implicit-function theorem gives a smooth local continuation there. This does not supply one universal function across different depths or settle regularity at zero field density, where k=j/\rho is a separate issue. The inverse-depth batch and its selected report samples each maintained depth at both reference gaps, including points between the maintained indices. All 12 sampled depth-gap branches have decreasing positive G_d(n), decreasing negative k_d(n), and positive secant estimates of f_d''. The calculation does not prove these properties between all sampled points or beyond the assigned band. For example, at g=5000, the effective edge falls from 0.9999974952g at electron index 13 to 0.9999850569g at muon index 35. The required finite-band correction divided by g|k|^{1+2/d} approaches the dimension-aware leading coefficient in (14), while retaining finite-index variation. The exact inverse function remains depth dependent. Restoring a physical radius gives the simplex frequency unit \omega_{0,d}=\frac c{R_d}\,d!\mu_d(h_d),\qquad h_d=\frac{G_dR_d}{c}, \tag{20} where G_d here denotes the reference physical edge, rather than the self-consistent edge on a particular mode. With equal dimensionless reference gaps h_6=h_{10}=500, an equal six-to-ten frequency unit requires R_{10}/R_6=8.06309677\times10^{-8}; at h=5000, it requires 8.06399097\times10^{-12}. These are exact finite-chain reference-unit ratios, close to the leading 5040/h^4. If instead the physical reference gap is shared, so h_{10}=h_6R_{10}/R_6, solving (20) gives R_{10}/R_6=0.19519654 at h_6=500 and 0.07773980 at h_6=5000. The resulting depth-ten gaps are about 97.60 and 388.70; the index-23 inverse branch exists at both sampled values. These radius ratios are conditional requirements, not predictions of a supporting geometry. The inverse-depth batch also varies the same bounded curvature trial of (13) at every maintained depth, using one g_0 and one R_0. From (17a), define the exact dimensionless elasticity q_d(h)=-\frac{d\log\mu_d}{d\log h} =\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} i h^{2i}/(i!)^2} {\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} h^{2i}/(i!)^2}. \tag{21} With x=R/R_0, h=\gamma x/(1+x^4), and q_g=4x^4/(1+x^4), the shared radial unit in (20) is stationary precisely when (q_g-1)q_d(h)=1. The inner local minima have R_{10}/R_6=0.97330930 at \gamma=1000 and 0.97330927 at \gamma=10000. Yet their ten-to-six frequency-unit ratios are only 4.84522\times10^{-8} and 4.84564\times10^{-12}. Thus this one specified common curvature trial does not supply the charged-lepton scale relation, even after the inverse current law makes the within-depth ratios exact. These are necessary local radial minima; no full field or metric stationarity has been shown. The same-field metric stress and a compatible nested geometry still have to determine the cross-depth scales. There is also an exact boundary on the tempting equal-radius, equal-dimensionless-gap option. At one radius the reference-unit ratio is (10/6)\sqrt{Z_6(h)/Z_{10}(h)}, where Z_d(h)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}h^{2i}/(i!)^2. It decreases from 10/6 to zero as h grows: the extra terms in Z_{10}/Z_6 have powers higher than every term of Z_6, so their ratio to Z_6 increases strictly. The unit ratio equals one only at h=6.5440289929. But B_n'(n)=I, so the smallest singular value is 1-Lipschitz in n and |\partial_n\epsilon_n|\le1. Equation (18) would require slopes 320.71 for the electron index, 27129.62 for the muon index, and 1.04565\times10^6 for the tau index at that gap. Hence the exact inverse current law with its zero-mode normalization has no occupied branch at the unique equal-radius shared-gap crossing. This excludes that restricted normalization choice, not distinct sector radii or a different same-field operator. More generally, the same slope bound imposes a minimum reference gap for every occupied inverse branch. The largest necessary bound within each maintained depth is: Depth Controlling index Necessary h above 2 95 190.9974 3 17 31.1288 4 72 116.6521 5 22 35.7856 6 35 53.5700 10 23 35.2139 Each bound solves \mu_d(h)P_d'(n)=1 using (17a). It is necessary, not sufficient for existence, invertibility or stability of the branch. The exact depth-two law (9) and the approximate common rule (14) are separate inverse actions. They must not borrow the conformal Hessian or background threshold computed for the saturated current law. The joint candidate calculation keeps all of them on the same modes and records its source fingerprints and fixed-point outputs in its report. The next physical test is to derive a current term of the required sign and depth dependence from the master field, then vary the complete metric, field and supporting background together. The common-scale response bound shows that no positive common gap law with nondecreasing logarithmic falloff can make the occupied inverse-current depth-six and depth-ten frequency units agree. It states the separate depth-two condition and the nonmonotone response required to evade that bound.

The complete zero-mode space The horizontal polynomial variations have the form \Xi_l=(0,e^{il	heta}U_l, i e^{i(l-d+1)	heta}V_l,0)^T, \qquad l=d-k, where U_l'= rac{l-a}{r}U_l-2wV_l,\qquad V_l'= rac{d-1-l}{r}V_l-2wU_l. 	ag{10} The d polynomial coordinates k=1,\ldots,d give regular, decaying solutions. Verification and physical scope linked_geometric_jacobi.py and geometric_jacobi_checks.py verify (6) with independent Cartesian differentiation, (7) on arbitrary positive-chiral fields, the complete uncompleted energy's second variation, and every geometric zero mode at all five maintained depths. Equation (5) is now a candidate common differential expression for the geometry and the normal mass carrier. Its carrier comparison distinguishes the geometric rotation representation from an ordinary spinor representation. A common expression is useful structure, but does not by itself derive the same-field kinetic action, the occupied curved equilibrium, or the complete particle's positive inertia.

title: A common geometric and mass-carrier differential operator
summary: The geometric Jacobi operator also has the required projected polarization and simplex numerator; an exact anticommutator removes the complete first polarization source, while the physical rotation module and occupied geometry remain unresolved.
text:

It has exactly the required number of localized modes, equally spaced projected polarization, positive adjacent hopping integrals, and a controlled normal complement. This comparison is made at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 with the maintained particle indices. There is also a simplification that applies to both the old and new carriers: a local anticommutator proves that their entire first projected polarization variation vanishes at the radial configuration. The full first shape source comes from one hopping matrix. The geometric carrier changes the spatial integrals. It is a candidate consolidation of two differential expressions, rather than an assertion that all previous numerical predictions are unchanged. Its geometric fluctuation module and an ordinary spinor module have different full-turn rotation laws. Their physical identification, the occupied same-field geometry and its total inertia remain to be constructed. Mass remains frequency, in equivalent units. Later calculations replace the independent hopping profile by the curvature moment, include depth two, and derive the leading complementary kinetic correction. The bounded angular completion specifies a full extension that preserves the leading simplex factors after radial dressing. Its finite-scale bound controls the remaining spectral error. title: Null motion and positive inertia of the linked geometry
summary: A positive Lorentz completion of the existing geometric cost supplies exact null disturbances and complete positive supporting inertia; its stress bound distinguishes the disturbance from the extended background.
text:
The linked spatial geometry admits a positive dynamical completion in which a disturbance can keep oscillating and carry null energy–momentum. The same action gives positive inertia to its supporting structure. No negative kinetic contribution is needed for either result. This closes the time-to-space normalization within a specified effective geometric action. It does not derive that action from the master field, identify its disturbance with the photon, or solve the occupied massive particle. The coefficients below describe proposed modes of the same field. They are not additional particles or a particle-exchange mechanism. All spatial coordinates are ordinary and uncompactified. Complete the existing geometric cost Use coordinates (t,x_1,x_2,y), where (x_1,x_2) is the normal plane and y is an available perpendicular direction in the containing space. In that case (5) supplies the temporal connection, and all coordinates of the path must share the same null variable. The construction is conditional on the smooth static family and its regular horizontal lift. The radial linear modes below and finite translated profiles are explicit controls of that statement. This null-coordinate mechanism has a mathematical precedent in Dziarmaga's traveling multivortex calculation. The normalization, field equations and stress used here are those of (1). For a pulse returning to the same center at both ends, with square-integrable X', integration gives  oxed{E_{m pulse}=\mathcal T\int|X'|^2du, \quad P_y=E_{m pulse},\quad P_i=\mathcal T[X_i(+\infty)-X_i(-\infty)]=0.} 	ag{12} These are finite excess quantities over the same static background.
