title: The linked carrier's induced geometric response
summary: Complete signed resolvents determine the actual carrier's static, Berry and time-derivative response; the dominant transverse coefficient scales as minus the inverse cube of its frequency and does not supply the assumed positive collective kinetic term.

title: Reconstructing a scalar interaction from spatial particle fields
summary: Complete spatial fields determine a scalar interaction only when their full residual is scalar and equal-current points require the same law; unchanged Jacobi pairs cannot share the assigned simplex frequencies through such a law, while nonlinear dressed controls reconstruct both the common action and its coupling derivative.
text:
Summary: Complete spatial fields determine a scalar interaction only when their full residual is scalar and equal-current points require the same law; unchanged Jacobi pairs cannot share the assigned simplex frequencies through such a law, while nonlinear dressed controls reconstruct both the common action and its coupling derivative. Keep the causal kinetic equation and invert the interaction The quadratic inverse construction matches the complete simplex frequencies, but its unrestricted polynomial dynamics fail the curved finite-propagation test. A different inverse problem keeps the original first-order spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D and asks for one real local scalar law:  oxed{ i\partial_	au\psi=\mathscr D\psi+F(J) eta\psi,\qquad J=\psi^\dagger eta\psi. } 	ag{1} Here  eta^\dagger= eta,  eta^2=I and \{\mathscr D, eta\}=0. The physical geometry, connection, measure and canonical field normalization are fixed inputs. The scalar current is not identified with electric charge. All complex spinor components remain in (1). For a smooth real F, this is a semilinear first-order equation. As long as its smooth solutions exist and remain locally bounded, the difference of two solutions has the original Dirac principal part and a locally Lipschitz source. The usual exterior-cone energy estimate and Gronwall inequality preserve the Dirac domain of dependence. This does not prove global existence or stable particle solutions, but it avoids replacing the kinetic equation by an unrestricted sixth-order spatial dispersion. Equation (1) is a candidate class of same-field laws. Its inverse conditions apply to arbitrary spatial polarizations. The explicit Jacobi comparison below is a narrower fixed-profile test on physical CP3 with \mathcal O(2) and one common radius R. No dimensions are compactified, and the radius is not selected. Sector nesting does not require one particle field to be a restriction or constituent of another. A complete pointwise test for a real scalar source Suppose a proposed stationary field and frequency are given: \psi(	au,x)=e^{-i\omega	au}\phi(x). Define the source that its full differential equation requires: r(x)=(\omega-\mathscr D)\phi(x),\qquad ho(x)=\phi^\dagger\phi,\qquad v(x)= eta\phi(x). 	ag{2} At every point where ho>0, the best real scalar coefficient is uniquely determined:  oxed{ M_\phi(x)=  rac{\operatorname{Re}[v(x)^\dagger r(x)]}{ho(x)},\qquad r_\perp(x)=r(x)-M_\phi(x)v(x). } 	ag{3} Indeed, for any real trial coefficient M, \|r-Mv\|^2 =\|r_\perp\|^2+ho(M-M_\phi)^2. 	ag{4} The cross term vanishes by the definition in (3). Thus the full stationary equation admits a real scalar multiplication coefficient precisely when r_\perp=0. An imaginary coefficient or an orthogonal spinor source remains in that residual; a scalar expectation alone cannot remove it. At a zero of the complete field, stationarity requires r=0, and that point does not determine a scalar coefficient. These are pointwise statements on actual spatial fields, with all their covariant derivatives included in \mathscr D\phi. They are invariant under a common change of spinor basis when the field, operator and  eta are transformed consistently. A spatially varying change of frame also transforms the connection. One action requires one function of the actual current Passing (3) is only the first condition. For a collection of proposed particle fields \phi_a, one law (1) additionally needs  oxed{M_{\phi_a}(x)=F(J_{\phi_a}(x))} 	ag{5} with the same smooth real function F for every field and point. In particular, J_{\phi_a}(x)=J_{\phi_b}(y) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad M_{\phi_a}(x)=M_{\phi_b}(y). 	ag{6} This compares independently occupied field structures; it does not impose inheritance between their spatial profiles. Equal-current compatibility is necessary. A smooth extension through critical current values and the boundaries of the sampled current ranges is required as well. Where 
abla J
e0, a differentiable law must satisfy 
abla M_\phi=F'(J_\phi)
abla J_\phi,\qquad F'(J_\phi)=  rac{
abla M_\phi\cdot
abla J_\phi}{|
abla J_\phi|^2}. 	ag{7} The derivative inferred at equal-current points must also agree. Physical norms and density units must be fixed before applying this test; rescaling each candidate afterward changes the argument of F. Different depths additionally need their common master-field reduction and normalization. If (3)–(5) hold with a smooth law on the required current range, put U(J)=\int_0^J F(s)\,ds. The real action is  egin{aligned} \mathcal S[\psi]&=\int d	au\left[  rac i2 igl(\langle\psi,\dot\psiangle- \langle\dot\psi,\psiangle igr)-E[\psi]ight],\ E[\psi]&=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psiangle+\int U(J)\,dV. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} Its full complex variation gives exactly (1). The same scalar law fixes the complete local response:  oxed{ \delta\!\left(F(J) eta\psiight) =F(J) eta h+ 2F'(J)\operatorname{Re}(\psi^\dagger eta h)\, eta\psi. } 	ag{9} This includes both ordinary and conjugate variations, as in the complete scalar source linearization. Coupling is therefore a constraint on the inverse law itself. The inverse spectral response comparison likewise distinguishes shared frequencies from a complete interaction. There is no independent coefficient for each particle pair. The total current of an encounter includes its spatial interference before U(J) is evaluated. The inferred law need not be unique outside the sampled current ranges. A background with constant current determines F at one value but generally leaves F' undetermined there. Thus mass frequencies alone do not determine every coupling response or the complete master dynamics. The excited spatial response calculation tests this constraint on nonlinearly deformed assigned modes. The same local interaction produces a calculable resonance in their full complex response, showing why stationary source compatibility and spatial stability must be assessed together. Apply the test to unchanged spatial Dirac pairs Let \phi_n be a normalized zero-form eigenfield and let \eta_n=\mathscr D\phi_n/\lambda_n be its normalized exact one-form partner: \mathscr D\phi_n=\lambda_n\eta_n,\qquad \mathscr D\eta_n=\lambda_n\phi_n,\qquad \lambda_n= rac{2\sqrt{n(n+5)}}R. 	ag{10} Consider the unchanged paired spatial profile \chi_n=c_n\phi_n+s_n\eta_n, with real constant weights, c_n^2+s_n^2=1, and both nonzero. The common overall phase is arbitrary. The two form equations require  egin{aligned} \lambda_ns_n+M(x)c_n&=\omega_nc_n,\ \lambda_nc_n-M(x)s_n&=\omega_ns_n. \end{aligned} 	ag{11} Where the respective spatial components are nonzero, these give M=\omega_n-\lambda_n rac{s_n}{c_n} =\lambda_n rac{c_n}{s_n}-\omega_n. 	ag{12} Continuity extends this one constant coefficient over the remaining points of the explicit Jacobi profile. In particular,  oxed{\omega_n^2=\lambda_n^2+M_n^2.} 	ag{13} Changing F does not alter this fixed-profile requirement. It follows from the full spatial equation, before taking any expectation or dropping a complementary source. For the pole-centered physical CP3 field at line degree two, write p_n(t)=P_n^{(2,2)}(2t-1). Up to its positive common normalization, the two local densities are |\phi_n|^2\propto t^2p_n^2,\qquad |\eta_n|^2\propto  rac{t^3(1-t)(p_n')^2}{n(n+5)}. 	ag{14} For every n\ge1, the polynomial has simple interior zeros. At such a zero the scalar current of \chi_n is negative, because the odd component is nonzero. At t=1 the odd component vanishes and the scalar current is positive. Between the last polynomial zero and that pole, the current therefore crosses zero while the complete spinor is nonzero. Every such unchanged pure pair consequently requires  oxed{F(0)=M_n.} 	ag{15} Its complete current image is an interval containing zero. The same field forces F to be constant on that interval, so F'=0 in its interior. Multiplying the physical norm by a positive factor preserves the zero-current argument. The written massless scalar law F(J)=gJ has F(0)=0 and therefore cannot support these unchanged profiles with M_n
e0. A nonzero bare value F(0) would instead give the same constant coefficient to every such pair. Neither option supplies distinct simplex coefficients on the unchanged spatial profiles. The assigned two-frequency target fails this pure-profile test Keep the common six-dimensional geometry and its one fixed radius. The assigned target is \omega_n=\mu S(n,6) at n=13,35. Equations (13) and (15) would require one real constant M. For x_n=n(n+5), this gives  rac{\omega_{35}}{\omega_{13}} =\sqrt{ rac{x_{35}+(MR/2)^2}{x_{13}+(MR/2)^2}} \le\sqrt{ rac{x_{35}}{x_{13}}}. 	ag{16} The actual numbers are: Quantity Value Largest ratio from a shared real gap on this fixed geometry \sqrt{ rac{1400}{234}}\approx2.445998 Assigned simplex frequency ratio  rac{ inom{40}{6}}{ inom{18}{6}}= rac{3515}{17}\approx206.764706 No smooth scalar function of J can resolve this discrepancy while retaining those unchanged pure spatial pairs and the same fixed geometry. This extends the earlier holomorphic source-preservation condition to an explicit nonzero-kinetic paired family. The result does not cover nonlinear spatial dressing, other polarization textures or a self-consistently changing geometry. The round-space scalar branch, for example, has constant nonzero current and does not satisfy the current-crossing hypothesis used in (15). These distinctions are part of the theorem's scope, rather than reasons to reassign the particle depths or mass indices. A dressed field can pass the same inverse test The local curved scalar construction already supplies nonlinear branches whose even and odd spatial profiles change together. They provide a positive control for the reconstruction, independently of the desired particle masses. Use the radius-one, unit-volume convention and fix one local law F(J)=\kappa J with \kappa=0.15. Take physical norms Q=1 and Q=3. The normalized branch solver then uses g=\kappa Q: Physical norm Q Normalized solver coefficient g Stationary frequency 1 0.15 0.417382662446 3 0.45 1.106712764874 At successively larger paired cutoffs 8,14,22, independent uncompressed spatial derivatives reduce the full residual below 6	imes10^{-15} in this numerical control. Both profiles retain nonzero odd spatial dressing. At equal physical currents J=0.25,1,3, the inverse formula recovers the same M=\kappa J from both fields. Their spatial derivatives also recover the same F'(J)=0.15. This validates both parts of the inverse procedure on solutions of a common local action. It is not a mass prediction, a quantization of Q or a stability proof for those branches. It demonstrates why solving the changed spatial field can succeed where the unchanged-profile test fails. Frequency and rest energy still need separate identification For a stationary solution of (1), (8) gives  oxed{\omega Q-E =\int\left[J F(J)-U(J)ight]\,dV.} 	ag{17} Along a smooth family of constrained stationary solutions, dE/dQ=\omega. Neither identity makes E/Q equal to \omega for a general nonlinear interaction. This agrees with the local scalar normalization calculation. Thus the inverse frequency target, the total energy of a localized particle and an observed rest mass must be connected by the same physical normalization and dynamics. The current calculation reconstructs and tests a candidate scalar law; it does not establish that final physical identification. The energy constraints from scalar response make the next comparison explicit. A common energy-frequency conversion can preserve the ratios, but its agreement across spatial branches must be checked. The same F' fixes the energy defect and full norm response; the latter also determines how a common change of action moves the energy and frequency targets. Verification inverse_scalar_law_checks.py checks the real scalar minimization and its complete complex residual at spinor ranks two, eight and thirty-two. General complex basis changes, imaginary-source controls and full action variations retain the ordinary and conjugate responses. Actual curved derivatives verify the constant coefficient of the paired Jacobi fields and locate their nonvanishing-spinor current zeros. Exact integer comparisons check (16) at the unchanged assigned indices. Independent spatial derivatives, quadrature and increasing paired cutoffs reconstruct the common law and its coupling derivative on the dressed controls.

title: Testing spatial patterns, compatible geometry and the mass law together
summary: Joint field and metric variations expose finite-chain mass drift and a rigorous radial obstruction in the round depth-two reference branches.
text: A spatial field can nearly solve its standing equation while having the wrong mass ratios or an unbalanced supporting variation. All three must be kept visible. This continuation retains the same finite-current candidate, the same compatible nested conformal-sphere geometry and all six maintained depths. Mass is the selected positive frequency. The geometry remains one containing metric and its restrictions. Particle patterns vary independently inside their sectors; they are not restrictions of other particles. Global spherical topology is a conditional geometric choice, not compactification. What the joint test asks For a canonically normalized field, write E_1[\psi;g]=\langle\psi,F_g[\psi]\rangle, \qquad \omega=E_1[\psi;g],\qquad R=F_g[\psi]-\omega\psi. The inherited standing branch requires R=0. It is a sufficient branch of the positive wave action, not every possible solution of its second-order equation. The expectation E_1 is the trial eigenvalue in this first-order search; it is not the physical frequency of every other standing branch. An exact extension below makes that distinction explicit while always identifying mass with the actual oscillation frequency. Four necessary support tests vary the common logarithmic radius and the three shared conformal coefficients: f_a=\partial_a E_1\big|_\psi, \qquad a=0,1,2,3. These are derivatives with the canonical field fixed. They test the specific hypothesis that this occupied field and its curvature-dependent interaction supply the support, without an additional geometric action or background stress. An externally supported geometry need not make these derivatives vanish. Neither alternative has been derived from the master field here. Passing these four paths would also not prove stationarity against every tensor-metric variation. The mass check uses u_{n,d}=\frac{\omega_{n,d}}{S(n,d)},\qquad S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d}. The units must agree within a depth, with the maintained shared unit also checked between depths six and ten. There are no fitted particle-specific mass coefficients. The two bottom constituent indices remain separate spectral controls; deriving their physical combined branch is still open. The joint numerical objective sums the squared relative field defects, the squared f_a/\omega, and the squared deviations of \log u from the mean within each required group. Equal weights are an explicit numerical search choice. They do not change the physical action or make a nonzero tradeoff minimum a solution. Efficient full spatial evaluation For a fixed spatial pattern, the pointwise field has the form F=aU_0+bU_1+\kappa U_2+g(\kappa)U_3, \quad a=\frac{e^{-\sigma}}{R_d},\quad b=-a\sigma'. Here U_0 is the reference spatial Dirac or Hodge term, U_1 is its conformal-gradient term, U_2 is the stated component curvature offset, and U_3 is the full local finite-current source per unit coupling. Each contains the actual spatially varying component field. Their values can be retained while the compatible geometry is varied. The residual is evaluated pointwise, including components outside the finite spectral basis. It is not replaced by its projection alone. The complete real derivative of the current enters the field-residual gradient. Homogeneity and the variational symmetry of F give \delta E_1=2\operatorname{Re}\langle\delta\psi,F\rangle, \qquad \delta f_a=2\operatorname{Re} \langle\delta\psi,\partial_aF\rangle. Canonical normalization projects these derivatives onto the tangent space of the unit sphere of fields. These identities permit support and mass defects to vary along with the field defect, rather than optimizing each condition in isolation. Independent directional differences check the implemented derivatives. Exact finite-chain drift away from the simplex law There is a useful exact result for the round reference carrier with saturated negative current. In units with wave speed one, let T_{jj}=\frac{n+j}{R},\qquad T_{j,j-1}=G, \qquad \gamma=GR, where j=0,\ldots,d-1. Its smallest singular frequency is \epsilon=1/\|T^{-1}\|_2. Signs in the inverse can be removed by diagonal orthogonal transformations. The inverse magnitudes are |(T^{-1})_{ji}|= R\frac{\gamma^{j-i}}{\prod_{k=i}^{j}(n+k)},\qquad j\ge i. Divide this matrix by its lower-left entry C=R\gamma^{d-1}/(n)_d, where (n)_d=n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-1)=d!S(n,d). The resulting matrix has M_{ji}= \frac{\prod_{k\notin\{i,\ldots,j\}}(n+k)} {\gamma^{d-1-j+i}},\qquad \boxed{\frac{\epsilon}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d!}{R\gamma^{d-1}}\frac1{\|M(n,\gamma)\|_2}.} The lower-left entry of M is one. Every other nonzero entry strictly increases with n. Its positive left and right leading singular vectors therefore make \|M\|_2 strictly increase with n. Consequently, at a fixed finite \gamma, the mass unit \epsilon/S(n,d) strictly decreases with mode index. Thus the exact round saturated reference branch does not give the exact simplex mass law at any finite gap. It approaches that law as the corner entry dominates at large \gamma. This theorem concerns that reference branch. A finite-current correction, another spatial branch, or a deformed geometry requires its own calculation. The norm of the first column supplies the quantitative bound \frac{\epsilon}{d!S(n,d)/(R\gamma^{d-1})} \le\frac1{\sqrt{1+[(n+d-1)/\gamma]^2}}. For the current round trial law, G=g(R)=\frac{100}{1+R^4},\qquad \gamma\le\frac{100\,3^{3/4}}4\simeq56.9877. For example, one-percent accuracy to the leading simplex expression for the depth-four index-72 control requires at least \gamma\ge75/\sqrt{0.99^{-2}-1}, approximately 526.3. The present strength cannot reach that regime at any round radius. This comparison is to the leading expression, not by itself a fitted within-sector observational error bound. A rigorous round depth-two radial obstruction The finite-current round reference state has an effective gap G\le g. Let \epsilon be its positive singular frequency, k<0 its normalized component current, and C=\frac{g\eta_2^2}{\sqrt{k^2+\eta_2^2}},\qquad \omega=\epsilon-C,\qquad 0\le C\le g\eta_2. Define A=-G\epsilon_G/\epsilon and q_g=-d\log g/d\log R. The fixed-point envelope derivative is \frac{d\omega}{d\log R} =-\epsilon[1-(q_g-1)A]+q_g C. For depth two the singular-value formula gives, with \Gamma=GR, A=\frac{\Gamma^2} {\sqrt{\Gamma^2+1}\sqrt{\Gamma^2+(2n+1)^2}} <\frac{\Gamma}{2n+1}. For the stated curvature law, 0\le q_g<4. A direct maximization with x=R^4 gives \max_R (q_g-1)_+\,gR=100B,\qquad B=\frac{x_*^{1/4}(3x_*-1)}{(1+x_*)^2} \simeq0.667555,\quad x_*=\frac{11+4\sqrt7}{9}. Let \gamma_{\max}=100\,3^{3/4}/4 and b_n=100B/(2n+1). The smallest singular-value perturbation bound gives \epsilon\ge R^{-1}(n-\gamma_{\max}). For the three maintained indices, n>\gamma_{\max} and b_n<1, hence \boxed{R\frac{d\omega}{d\log R} \le -(1-b_n)(n-\gamma_{\max}) +4\gamma_{\max}\eta_2.} With the unchanged \eta_2=0.02264240274802975, the right-hand side is approximately -5.556, -9.017 and -19.565 for indices 76, 81 and 95. It is strictly negative. No radius can balance these round reference branches under this particular supporting law, wherever their retained finite-current branch exists. The statement includes the actual depth-two form carrier. It does not exclude other textured states or another supporting law. Compatibility also constrains the large-gap radial limit For the saturated large-gap limit, radial balance under the same law gives R_*(d)=\left(\frac{d}{3d-4}\right)^{1/4}. This decreases strictly with depth. Nested round latitude spheres instead require R_2\le R_3\le\cdots\le R_{10}. Thus the leading radial equilibria cannot be assembled into that compatible round family, even though each radius separately solves its leading radial equation. Finite-chain corrections and deformed geometries are distinct tests. There is no conclusion here about arbitrary nested metrics or the measured geometry of ordinary space. Changing the curvature normalization does not suffice The previous supporting law uses the normalized curvature scale \kappa^2=\mathrm{Scal}/[d(d-1)]. An alternative common law can use scalar curvature itself: g=G_0\frac{\mathrm{Scal}^2}{1+\mathrm{Scal}^2},\qquad \mathrm{Scal}=\frac{d(d-1)}{R_d^2}. Lengths and curvature are expressed in the same fixed reference units at every depth. This is a different trial law, not a correction of an incorrect formula. It introduces no particle-specific coefficient. Its leading stationary radii are R_d=\sqrt{d(d-1)}\left(\frac{d}{3d-4}\right)^{1/4}. They increase with depth, so this entire round chain is compatible before any field test. Nine controls use this chain, three common radius multipliers and three common strengths. Improving the radius ordering does not restore the required shared electron–tau unit. There is an exact bound for that shared unit on the chain at its leading stationary radii, using the saturated finite matrices without a large-gap approximation. Let I_d(h)=|T_d(h)^{-1}|, where h>0 is the common strength. Then \frac{\epsilon_{23,10}/S(23,10)} {\epsilon_{13,6}/S(13,6)} =\frac{S(13,6)}{S(23,10)} \frac{\|I_6(h)\|_2}{\|I_{10}(h)\|_2}. Each inverse entry is a positive monomial in h, of degree at most d-1. On an interval [h_-,h_+], bound the numerator norm by the sum of its entries at h_+, and the denominator norm by its largest entry at h_-. Rational upper and lower enclosures of the two radii make this an exact rational inequality. At small strength, the denominator's diagonal entries give a nonzero bound. At large strength, the numerator grows at most as h^5, while the denominator's corner grows as h^9. Fifty-nine intervals, including both unbounded end ranges, give \boxed{\frac{\epsilon_{23,10}/S(23,10)} {\epsilon_{13,6}/S(13,6)}<0.008 \quad\text{for every }h>0.} The largest recorded upper bound is approximately 0.00765128. The certificate uses rational arithmetic, not floating-point sampling of strengths. Thus this compatible round chain cannot supply the shared unit simply by choosing another common saturated coupling strength. It is not a theorem about other metrics or finite-current corrections. An exact family of full positive-wave states The positive wave action also has standing states outside the first-order eigenfield ansatz. This extension follows from the structure of the candidate itself. Write the two component blocks as \psi=(u,v). The spatial linear operator and K are off diagonal between these blocks. For positive real numbers a,b, the finite-current norm scales as s[au,bv]=ab\,s[u,v], including for spatially varying fields. Consequently, \boxed{F[au,bv]=(bF_u[u,v],\ aF_v[u,v]).} Suppose F[u,v]=\Omega(u,v), with \Omega>0, and \|u\|^2+\|v\|^2=1. The generating energy is homogeneous of degree one in each block separately. Its variational identity gives \|u\|^2=\|v\|^2=1/2. Choose a=\cos\theta+\sin\theta,\quad b=\cos\theta-\sin\theta,\quad |\theta|<\frac\pi4. Then \psi_\theta=(au,bv) stays normalized, and F[\psi_\theta]=\Omega(bu,av),\qquad DF[\psi_\theta]^*F[\psi_\theta]=\Omega^2\psi_\theta. To obtain the second identity, differentiate the boxed block-scaling identity in the direction (bu,av), and use the real variational self-adjointness of DF. Thus e^{-i\Omega t}\psi_\theta solves the complete positive wave equation whenever the starting field does. The differentiated identities apply on the smooth timelike-current domain. Spatial nodal sets retain the same weak or limiting interpretation required by the starting field; this construction adds no new regularity claim there. Every member has the same oscillation frequency and the same mass. Its first-order expectation instead equals \langle\psi_\theta,F[\psi_\theta]\rangle =\Omega\cos(2\theta). That expectation is not its oscillation frequency unless the state belongs to the first-order eigenbranch. The difference does not separate mass from frequency; it identifies which spectral equation supplies the frequency. Overall field magnitude is not being used as mass. The positive block factors redistribute the component pattern. They do not derive physical polarization counts, rotations of spatial directions, antiparticles or photon behavior. The endpoint where one block disappears is excluded because the current norm reaches its singular boundary. This freedom does not remove the supporting stress. For a parameter variation preserving the stated block structure, the real matrix elements \langle u,\partial F_u\rangle and \langle v,\partial F_v\rangle are equal by the same separate homogeneity. Since a^2+b^2=2, \partial\|F[\psi_\theta]\|^2 =\partial\|F[\psi_0]\|^2. The normalized wave family therefore has the same metric source as its starting eigenfield. It extends the solution space of the candidate, but cannot repair an unbalanced radius by choosing different block weights. The resulting neutral direction is not a proof of stability against all other perturbations. Free-direction factorization at the action level There is a stronger propagation statement than constructing a particular first-order moving eigenfield. Retain the previously stated product extension, a parallel Hermitian normal symbol \Sigma, \Sigma^2=I, and the anticommutators \{H_0,\Sigma\}=\{K,\Sigma\}=0. For a constant normal momentum p in frequency units, write F_p[\psi]=F_0[\psi]+p\Sigma\psi. Self-adjointness and anticommutation give \operatorname{Re}\langle H_0\psi,\Sigma\psi\rangle=0. For the current term, the corresponding real inner product vanishes pointwise: the jK term has zero real part, and the other two terms cancel as \rho z-z\rho=0. Expanding the norm therefore gives the exact functional identity \boxed{\|F_p[\psi]\|^2 =\|F_0[\psi]\|^2+p^2\|\psi\|^2.} Variation of this identity yields DF_p[\psi]^*F_p[\psi] =DF_0[\psi]^*F_0[\psi]+p^2\psi. Every valid bound standing field of the full positive wave equation, not just a first-order eigenfield, consequently has a constant-momentum product extension with \boxed{\Omega(p)^2=\omega^2+p^2.} Its bound profile can remain unchanged. At zero net normal momentum, \partial_p^2\Omega=1/\omega>0. The bound field still oscillates. This preserves mass as its selected frequency and extends the previous free-direction inertial calculation to all valid standing branches of this candidate. This is an action identity under explicit product and domain assumptions. It does not establish nonlinear superposition of different normal momenta, a localized particle packet, arbitrary bound-direction motion, or a globally free normal geometry. In particular, the nested latitude metrics tested in the joint search have not been shown to realize this product extension. The propagation lemma and that global geometry must not be combined into a claimed physical solution without establishing their compatibility. Numerical results The alternating search completed three cycles of shared metric adjustment and spatial field relaxation. Its final largest relative field defect was 0.4613 and its largest normalized metric-path force was 30.063. Doubling the quadrature changed its field defects by at most 2.14e-8. Neither condition is close to a solution, and the required mass units also remain inconsistent. The simultaneous search varied all sixteen spatial patterns and the nine compatible metric parameters in one objective. It stopped after 49 iterations at its specified computation limit. Its endpoint is not converged, and six controls failed the subsequent integration-refinement check. The original reports retain those failures. The problem is especially clear where the optimized local current reverses sign. Its numerator is a polynomial of degree at most twice the retained axial cutoff after removing the common harmonic density factor. Locating all its interior roots allows adaptive integration to split around the finite-current transition widths. For the depth-five index-22 control, the relative field defect rises from the optimizer-grid value 8.5414 to 9.8044. For depth-ten index 23 it rises from 19.0004 to 21.7907. These are large failed field equations, not small corrections to particle masses. The apparent objective reduction must not be interpreted as a physical improvement. The full positive-wave derivative also fails at these endpoints; its projected residual already suffices to exclude them. This search retains a finite axial basis with a fixed spatial heading, including both spectral signs and complex component coefficients. It is not unrestricted angular or orientation variation. Further basis refinement cannot be replaced by quadrature refinement. No global minimum or exhaustive exclusion of the conformal family is claimed. Eight identity and implementation reports pass 1,505 checks. A separate 32-check endpoint integration audit contains six failures, which motivated the adaptive investigation rather than being discarded. Four completed numerical screens record the alternating search, simultaneous search, scalar-curvature controls and adaptive audit. These categories are kept distinct from a successful physical solution. The clearest positive result is the larger full-wave family and the action-level propagation identity. The clearest restriction is that the tested scalar-curvature support constructions do not simultaneously produce supported compatible geometry and the maintained mass units. Developing the supporting term from the same field remains the central open step; none of these calculations completes the mass operator.

title: The competing depth-ten branch and the self-coupling mass hypothesis
summary: The fitted common radius law has an occupied but unselected outer depth-ten branch near 86 eV mass-energy; its electron-calibrated spectrum does not reproduce all known assignments, which does not exclude an additional exotic state.
text: The shared rational reference law has two depth-ten local minima on the exact inverse-current reference frequency curve. Its inner minimum was fitted to the observed tau frequency unit relative to the maintained depth-six unit. The outer minimum is a separate candidate state of the same sector and index, not a new mode assignment. This note tests its occupied branch and asks whether a low selected frequency must imply weak self-coupling. The frequency and its origin At fixed depth ten, the common simplex factor cancels between the two radii. With h=g(R)R/c, the exact ratio is \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{out}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{in}}} =\frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R_{\mathrm{out}}} \sqrt{\frac{Z_{10}(h_{\mathrm{in}})}{Z_{10}(h_{\mathrm{out}})}}, \qquad Z_{10}(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{9}\frac{h^{2j}}{(j!)^2}. \tag{1} For the fitted positive rational law with b=1.34, C=18.00753138, and h_2=500, the inner branch is at R_{\mathrm{in}}/R_0=1.06721483, h_{\mathrm{in}}=116.63970; the outer branch is at R_{\mathrm{out}}/R_0=14.18017176, h_{\mathrm{out}}=568.77005. Equation (1) gives \omega_{\mathrm{out}}/\omega_{\mathrm{in}} =4.84170206\times10^{-8}. Calibrating the fitted inner branch to the 1776.93 MeV tau benchmark gives an outer equivalent mass-energy of 86.03366 eV and a cyclic frequency of 2.08028\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{Hz}. These are conditional values inherited from the fit, not an independent experimental mass measurement. The large suppression has an exact spectral origin. Writing Z_{10}(h)=h^{18}T_{10}(h)/(9!)^2, where T_{10}(h)\to1 at large h, equation (1) becomes \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{out}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{in}}} =\frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R_{\mathrm{out}}} \left(\frac{h_{\mathrm{in}}}{h_{\mathrm{out}}}\right)^9 \sqrt{\frac{T_{10}(h_{\mathrm{in}})} {T_{10}(h_{\mathrm{out}})}}. \tag{2} Thus a reference-gap increase of a factor about 4.88 is amplified by the ninth power. The outer radius is about 13.29 times the inner radius. The calculation does not establish that either radius is realized by a physical tau structure. An independent shape grid also varies b and C separately by \pm0.5\% around the reference values, retaining only the depth-two gap anchor and not refitting C to the inner tau/electron unit. All nine trials retain two depth-ten reference-frequency minima; the outer one has positive radial frequency curvature and passes the necessary occupied-slope condition. Its energy after calibrating each inner branch to the tau benchmark spans 72.16–103.00 eV. The inner tau/electron unit ratio simultaneously ranges from 0.8353 to 1.1922 times its benchmark. The grid report therefore supports local branch existence, while the narrow 86.03348–86.03414 eV range under correlated refits is not an unfitted mass prediction. This finite grid does not establish full spatial stability or the physical probability of the state. A two-channel route to the radius law The fitted rational shape is exactly a sum of two positive response terms. Put x=(R/R_0)^4, a=b^{-4}, and c=C^{-4}. Then \frac{1+ax}{(1+x)(1+cx)} =\frac{w_s}{1+x}+\frac{w_l}{1+cx}, \qquad w_s=\frac{1-a}{1-c},\quad w_l=\frac{a-c}{1-c}. \tag{2a} Both weights are positive for the fitted 1<b<C. At b=1.34, w_s=0.68985012 and w_l=0.31014988. The two terms contribute almost equally to the gap at the inner radius, whereas the long-scale term supplies 99.99238% at the outer radius. The two-channel audit checks the identity and the branch fractions for all four fitted shapes in its selected report. This makes a long-scale same-field response a concrete candidate source of the extra branch; it does not derive that response. For example, let two retained same-field amplitudes q_i have positive stiffnesses D_s=1+x, D_l=1+cx, and local energy D_iq_i^2/2-J_iq_i+\beta_iq_i k, where k is the normalized current. Choosing J_i=\beta_i=\sqrt{\gamma w_i} and eliminating these amplitudes gives F_{\rm eff}(k,R)=F_0(k) -\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)} +\gamma\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}k -\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}k^2. \tag{2b} The coefficient of the linear current is exactly the fitted gap g(R)=\gamma[w_s/D_s+w_l/D_l], with \gamma=179.0387654 for the reference fit. However, the eliminated response subtracts g(R) from current curvature, so the direct same-field contribution must satisfy F_0''>g(R) on a convex occupied branch. The conditional lower bounds are 109.294 and 40.110 in the source units at the inner and outer radii. This is a necessary sign test, not a derivation of F_0. The eliminated response also contributes to the radial energy. At a fixed current k, its derivative is \left.\partial_R E_{\rm response}\right|_k =2\gamma(1-k)^2R^3\left[ \frac{w_s}{(1+R^4)^2} +\frac{cw_l}{(1+cR^4)^2}\right]>0, \tag{2c} in units where R_0=1. At k=0, the audit obtains 56.898 at the inner and 1.571 at the outer radius; the occupied currents change these values only slightly. The frequency minima therefore do not establish stationarity of the complete energy. Other same-field terms and shape response must balance this radial stress while preserving the occupied spectrum. The fourth power, channel scales, source amplitudes, canonical kinetic term and such a balancing term still require derivation from the master field. The preceding expression is an uncompleted response per canonical norm. Its zero-current offset would shift the particle frequency by -54.647 at the inner radius and -20.055 at the outer radius in c/R_0 units for the equal-source choice. The corresponding occupied frequencies are only 5.4732\times10^{-5} and 2.6500\times10^{-12}. This offset cannot be left out of the mass-operator calculation. A completed-square same-field action One homogeneous retained-mode alternative includes the zero-current normalization in a positive square. Per canonical norm, consider \mathcal E=\langle H_0(R)\rangle+F_0(k) +\sum_{i=s,l}\left[ \frac{D_i(R)}2\left(q_i-\frac{J_i}{D_i(R)}\right)^2 +\beta_iq_i k\right], \quad J_i=\sqrt{r\gamma w_i},\quad \beta_i=\sqrt{\gamma w_i/r},\quad r>0. \tag{2d} Here q_i are retained modes of the same field, rather than independent particles. Their kinetic terms and actual spatial profiles have not been specified. Eliminating their static values q_i=(J_i-\beta_i k)/D_i gives F_{\rm eff}(k,R)=F_0(k)+g(R)k -\frac{g(R)}{2r}k^2, \qquad g(R)=\gamma\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}. \tag{2e} The square cancels the uncompleted response's zero-current frequency offset and its associated zero-current radial stress. Its Schur contribution to current curvature is -g/r, so the direct term must supply F_0''=f_{\rm target}''+g/r on an occupied inverse branch. Without square completion, reducing r lowers the offset but increases the negative curvature: channel by channel, 2|E_{0,i}||F_{i,kk}|=g_i^2. For general two-channel coefficients, Cauchy's inequality gives 2|E_0||F_{kk}|\ge g^2. The same-action batch tests whether one radius-independent F_0(k) could at least match both sampled inverse-current bands. It maps target values and derivatives to F_0 at harmonics 5, 20, 22.5, 23, 23.5, 26 and 30 on each radius, plus F_0(0)=F_0'(0)=0. All adjacent secant slopes lie between their endpoint derivatives for tested r=0.001,0.01,1,100 and the zero-current matching ratio below. The selected report records the samples. These are necessary convex-interpolation checks, not a constructed smooth F_0, a full spatial state, or a test at the other depths. The same proposed action has a radial force test. At fixed canonical norm and on the stationary component field, its derivative is \partial_R\mathcal E =-\frac{\epsilon/R-Gk}{R} +g'(R)k-\frac{g'(R)}{2r}k^2, \qquad G=g(R)-\frac{g(R)}r k+F_0'(k), \tag{2f} where \epsilon is the dimensionless finite-chain singular frequency and G is the physical current edge. At the inherited inner and outer radii, this derivative is positive for all five tested positive r. At r=1 it is 3.248\times10^{-6} and 4.749\times10^{-16} in the corresponding c/R_0 energy-per-norm units. This completed-square action therefore does not make either inherited radius an exact stationary state. At r=1 the outer residual is small relative to its frequency, leaving a nearby shifted equilibrium possible; the complete field, radius and metric Hessian has not been solved. There is a sharper condition if the exact inverse current law must continue smoothly from each branch to k=0. One radius-independent direct term must then have the same F_0''(0) at both radii: f_{{\rm inv},\mathrm{in}}''(0)+\frac{g_{\rm in}}r =f_{{\rm inv},\mathrm{out}}''(0)+\frac{g_{\rm out}}r. \tag{2g} The exact zero-current inverse formula gives physical curvatures 2.31215\times10^{12} and 2.69108\times10^{17} in c/R_0 units. Equation (2g) fixes r=2.570865\times10^{-16}, rather than leaving the source/current amplitude ratio free. Its sampled convexity inequalities still pass. But its fixed-norm radial forces at the inherited radii become 4.548\times10^6 and 2.162\times10^{-9}, respectively. Thus the simple completed-square action cannot simultaneously keep the inherited radii stationary and realize one smooth zero-current direct law under that full inverse continuation. A shifted solution, additional same-field stress, or a law that applies only on occupied finite bands remains possible. The magnitude is a diagnostic in this action's chosen normalization, not a measured force. The action is a candidate construction with specific force and spatial tests remaining, not a derived physical mass operator. A local continuation of this action finds nearby stationary radii with positive restricted radial curvature on both depth-ten branches. Its scalar-current angular controls pass under an assumed nonnegative retained-mode gradient stiffness; the complete polarized field and geometric spatial variations remain open. Absolute spectrum across the maintained sectors The rational law was fitted to the depth-six electron and inner depth-ten tau frequency units; the other depths were only checked for local roots and necessary inverse slopes. To test the candidate as one common mass operator, fix the remaining physical scale c/R_0 with the observed electron mass-energy. With no further depth-dependent conversion, every assigned mode then has the definite prediction m_{n,d}^{\rm trial}c^2 =m_ec^2\frac{u_d}{u_6} \frac{S(n,d)}{S(13,6)},\qquad S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d}. \tag{3} The selected whole-spectrum calculation records all 16 maintained mode values under this one calibration. Representative results are: Assigned mode Trial mass-energy Observed comparison Depth two, W index 76 21.10 TeV 80.369 GeV PDG Depth five, neutrino index 10 5.194 MeV Sub-eV laboratory scale; effective electron-neutrino mass <0.45 eV at 90% confidence KATRIN Depth six, muon index 35 105.65655 MeV About 105.658 MeV Depth ten, tau index 23, inner radius 1776.93 MeV Fitted input Depth ten, tau index 23, outer radius 86.03366 eV Competing conditional branch The W discrepancy is over two orders of magnitude at the selected h_2=500 fit, and the neutrino discrepancy is much larger, so the common rational law with this reference normalization fails the full assigned mass spectrum. The neutrino bound cited is a measurement of an effective electron-neutrino mass, whereas the maintained depth-five assignments are model labels. The KATRIN result is an upper bound on an effective electron-neutrino mass, not a measured nonzero value or a lower bound on any neutrino mass. The MeV trial values are incompatible with treating these assigned modes as the observed light neutrinos without an additional, derived mixing or suppression mechanism. A dimension-dependent spatial conversion could change (3), but it would need to follow from the common field and geometric operator. Assigning a new fitted conversion to each depth would not repair this candidate as a predictive law for all known assignments. These comparisons do not exclude a separate, possibly unseen exotic state. They only limit the claim that this one fitted law also explains the named W and neutrino states. The outer depth-ten branch remains a mathematical solution with no derived selection or detection channel. The same script refits C at depth-two reference gaps 220, 300, 500, and 1000 with b=1.34. Across those four trials, the lightest assigned depth-five neutrino ranges from 2.286 to 10.389 MeV, and the assigned W from 0.791 to 337.6 TeV. This finite scan shows the failure is not confined to h_2=500. It is not a proof that no other common spatial law or normalization can work. The h_2=220 trial also has the independently observed depth-two n=95 finite spatial growth, so lowering that gap is not a verified stability remedy. Occupied branch and local controls The reproducible batch checks four neighboring shared-law shapes b=1.332,1.34,1.35,1.36. For each shape the one outer scale C is refitted to the same inner tau/electron unit ratio, so this variation is a local fit sensitivity test, not an independent prediction. In the selected report, the conditional outer mass-energy ranges from 86.03348 to 86.03414 eV. All four outer points are strict local minima of the reference frequency curve and pass the assigned necessary occupied-slope inequality. At b=1.34, exact finite-chain inverse roots exist at sampled harmonics 1, 5, 20, 23, 26, and 30 on the outer branch. Their edge and negative normalized current decrease in order, as required by the sampled convex inverse-current construction. At the assigned index 23, the outer normalized current is -5.9474\times10^{-13}. The inner branch current is -4.5331\times10^{-6}. The sampled controls do not prove invertibility across every intermediate point. The inner depth-ten frequency minimum and its following maximum occur at 1.0672R_0 and 1.2557R_0. That maximum is only 1.02684 times the inner minimum. The second minimum is at 14.1802R_0, with a much lower frequency. This maximum is not a calculated particle decay barrier. The complete radius energy, supporting field and collective radius inertia have not been supplied. Changing b over the four cases changes the frequency maximum over the inner minimum from 1.00222 to 1.14515, even though the outer frequency remains close under refitting. The necessary occupied-slope limit for the assigned depth-ten index is h>35.21386344. Along the outward side of the b=1.34 outer branch, the shared law reaches this limit at R/R_0=54.72550. Thus the inverse occupied branch is not established out to arbitrarily large radius. The reference-frequency curve beyond this limit cannot be interpreted as the same physical particle branch without a different current continuation. Neither the local outer minimum nor this finite domain proves global binding. The complete signed finite-component matrix at fixed geometry gives the nearest other component magnitude divided by the occupied frequency as 1.02401 for the inner branch and 1.000928 for the outer branch. Both exceed one. The local inverse-current curvature is positive on the sampled branch, so its rank-one real-component correction also has the favorable sign. This is a finite component control only: the outer branch has not passed a depth-ten spatial or full field–metric stability calculation. Does low mass imply weak self-coupling? In the proposed normalized-current density \rho f_d(k), the same function controls both the frequency shift and a local current response. On the exact inverse branch, f_d'(k)=G and f_d''(k)=dG/dk. A symmetric secant between harmonics 22.5 and 23.5 at depth ten gives f_{10}''\approx4.1340\times10^4 on the inner branch and 5.8948\times10^{10} on the outer branch, in the stated dimensionless c/R normalization. The latter local curvature is about 1.426\times10^6 times larger, although its oscillation frequency is about 4.842\times10^{-8} as large. The outer current magnitude is only 1.312\times10^{-7} of the inner one. Hence neither current magnitude nor current curvature alone is a universal mass proxy in this candidate. These derivatives are not a physical two-particle vertex or encounter rate. There is nevertheless an exact conditional relation between the current action and a pair interaction. Suppose two patterns overlap at one position, their field components are pointwise orthogonal, and their cross current vanishes, so that their densities and currents add: \rho=\rho_i+\rho_j and j=\rho_i k_i+\rho_j k_j. If both see the same local function f, their contact contribution relative to isolated patterns is \Delta U_{ij}=(\rho_i+\rho_j) f\!\left(\frac{\rho_i k_i+\rho_j k_j}{\rho_i+\rho_j}\right) -\rho_i f(k_i)-\rho_j f(k_j). \tag{4} For convex f, Jensen's inequality gives \Delta U_{ij}\le0, with equality when the currents agree or the law is affine between them. This is a negative mixed contribution to the stated generating density under the orthogonality assumptions. Its relation to complete pair energy and force requires the canonical action and both particles' spatial response. Actual patterns need not be orthogonal at each point, and their relative phase, geometry and reciprocal deformation can change the result. The inner and outer tau radii also use different local reference gaps, so (4) cannot be applied across those branches without deriving one spatial action that defines f through the intervening field configuration. A testable version of the self-coupling hypothesis asks whether one canonically normalized same-field interaction supplies both the selected self-frequency and the response between two occupied spatial patterns. For example, a scalar contact U[\Psi]=(\lambda/2)\int(\Psi^\dagger\Psi)^2 has a self term (\lambda/2)\int\rho_i^2. For mutually orthogonal field components at overlapping positions it also has a pair term \lambda\int\rho_i\rho_j. The common \lambda does not make the self frequency equal to that pair coefficient: they involve different density integrals, canonical norms, and the stationary field equation. Relative polarization and phase can change the pair term for nonorthogonal patterns. This is an algebraic illustration, not a derivation of IDWT's particle profiles. The neutrino and nucleon examples motivate different checks. Rare neutrino encounters in ordinary matter do not, by themselves, measure the neutrino pattern's self-coupling. Electron and muon weak vertices are closely constrained despite very different lepton masses, so a universal rule equating mass to an external vertex strength is not supported by those observations; the one-field theory would need to derive both quantities from state-dependent spatial patterns. See the Particle Data Group electroweak review. For a nucleon, energy stored in interacting quark and gluon dynamics accounts for most of its rest energy in a lattice QCD mass decomposition. That supports testing a composite field's complete energy against its constituents, but it does not identify an IDWT self-coupling coefficient or imply that every bound composite is heavier than the sum of the isolated constituents' total energies. The exact inverse current interaction is quadratic-homogeneous in field amplitude, while a pure scalar quartic contact is fourth-order. The fixed linear projection obstruction in the preceding note still applies. A nonzero same-field background, nonlinear reduction, fixed norm, or additional master invariant must supply the needed effective interaction, its positive current curvature, and its spatial support. The rational gap shape can be written as a positive source divided by a positive stiffness, but choosing those radius functions to reproduce the fit is an inverse construction, not their derivation from the master field. Observable channels The 86.03 eV value is the equivalent rest energy of the outer candidate. It does not by itself predict a light-emission line at 86.03 eV. A transition from the fitted inner branch to the outer one would release approximately 1776.929914 MeV before recoil and any other products. Production or emission predictions require the same-field coupling vertex, conservation laws, line width, and a channel connecting the states. The current model gives none of those quantities. A spectral feature near 86 eV cannot be assigned to this branch by its energy alone.

title: Exact metric identities for the linked spatial deformations
summary: The actual linked zero modes have a positive horizontal metric and exact moment identities that remove an independent integral from their curvature response.
text:
The bounded normal carrier's geometric deformations have a simple metric once changes of component basis are removed. Its radial equations imply an exact identity between that metric and the second change of the geometric profile. This supplies the normalization needed to compare shape responses without confusing a small coordinate coefficient with a small physical vertex. The metric is a stated positive kinetic comparison for the spatial coefficients. Its physical coefficient and origin in the one master field remain to be derived. It is not a calculation of the complete particle's inertia. The normal coordinates are ordinary unbounded spatial coordinates. Linked geometric zero modes Use the bounded linked profile with winding equal to the tested depth d: W=w(r)e^{id	heta},\quad A= rac{a(r)}r e_	heta,\qquad w'= rac{d-a}{r}w,\quad a'=2r(1-w^2). 	ag{1} More generally, the common rule is W=e^{-u}P(z), A=
abla^\perp u, \Delta u=2(1-|W|^2). Consider the real polynomial deformation P(z)=z^d+\alpha_kz^{d-k},\qquad \partial_{\alpha_k}u=f_k(r)\cos k	heta,\quad 1\le k\le d. Its linear equation is \left(-\partial_r^2-r^{-1}\partial_r+k^2/r^2+4w^2ight)f_k =4w^2r^{-k}. 	ag{2} The regular solution behaves as r^k at zero and as r^{-k} at infinity. Its unprojected field variations are those obtained by varying both W and A in the common rule. Retaining both is essential for the metric and the wave source. Removing a change of component basis Define the real positive metric by minimizing over an infinitesimal basis phase a_0(x,y): M_k=\inf_{a_0}\int_{\mathbb R^2} \left(|\delta W-i a_0W|^2+  rac14|\delta A-
abla a_0|^2ight)d^2y. 	ag{3} This specifies what is meant by the geometric kinetic comparison; it has not been inferred from the wave-induced response coefficient. Variation with respect to a_0 gives (-\Delta+4w^2)a_0 =4\operatorname{Im}(W^*\delta W)-
abla\cdot\delta A. Equation (2) then gives a_0=-f_k\sin k	heta. The horizontal variations simplify to  egin{aligned} \delta W_h&=U_ke^{i(d-k)	heta},\ (\delta A_{h,r},\delta A_{h,	heta}) &=2V_k(\sin k	heta,\cos k	heta),\ U_k&=w(r^{-k}-f_k),\qquad V_k= rac12(f_k'+kf_k/r),\ M_k&= oxed{2\pi\int_0^\infty r(U_k^2+V_k^2)dr.} \end{aligned} 	ag{4} The imaginary polynomial variation has the same metric. Their real cross term vanishes at the radial configuration by rotational symmetry. Differentiating (4), using (1) and (2), gives another first-order pair: U_k'= rac{d-k-a}{r}U_k-2wV_k,\qquad V_k'= rac{k-1}{r}V_k-2wU_k. 	ag{5} Consequently the integral of [r^2(U_k^2-V_k^2)]' vanishes, giving \int (d-k+1-a)U_k^2\,d^2y =k\int V_k^2\,d^2y. 	ag{6} For k=1, f_1=a/(dr) is exact. The polynomial coordinate moves the center by -\alpha_1/d, and (4) gives M_1=\pi/d. The actual translation coordinate therefore has metric \pi d, half the flat geometric cost 2\pi d. The second profile and the same bounded weight Expand the exact planar solution through second order: u=u_0+\alpha_k f_k\cos k	heta +\alpha_k^2(g_{0,k}+g_{2,k}\cos2k	heta)+O(\alpha_k^3). The angular mean obeys (-\Delta+4w^2)g_{0,k}=2U_k^2. 	ag{7} The bounded polarization weight used in the mass carrier also obeys an exact identity: (-\Delta+4w^2)(d+1-a)=4. 	ag{8} To verify it, differentiate a'=2r(1-w^2), giving \Delta a=4-4(d+1-a)w^2. Pairing (7) and (8), with their regular and decaying boundary conditions, yields \int g_{0,k}\,d^2y = rac12\int(d+1-a)U_k^2\,d^2y = oxed{ rac{k}{2}M_k}. 	ag{9} The last equality uses (6). Thus the same linked weight that gives the carrier's equally spaced projected polarization also fixes this geometric metric identity. No separately fitted stiffness-to-metric ratio enters it. Holomorphic moments fix the leading forces The asymptotic expansion of u agrees with \log|P| up to decaying corrections. Green's identity against a holomorphic monomial therefore gives \int z^k B\,d^2y=2\pi\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^k, \qquad B=\Delta u, 	ag{10} where z_i are the zeros of P, counted with multiplicity. For the first variation in \alpha_k, Newton's polynomial identity gives \partial_{\alpha_k}\sum_i z_i^k=-k. Equivalently,  oxed{\int_0^\infty r^{k+1}wU_k\,dr= rac{k}{2}.} 	ag{11} The boundary calculation in (10) matters: f_k itself has a harmonic r^{-k} tail. Integrating it against a growing tube polynomial and discarding its boundary term would give a wrong force. The decaying combination U_k avoids that problem. Numerical normalization and verification Near the center, w=c_0r^d+\cdots. The computation uses 	au_k=c_0\alpha_k to avoid poorly scaled polynomial coefficients. Metrics and second profile integrals acquire the same factor c_0^{-2}; physical conclusions cannot depend on this coordinate conversion.
