title: The exact carrier pressure and a common cavity size
summary: A positive-inverse identity bounds the finite carrier's radial pressure; bare geometric area tension gives stable branch-dependent radii but fails the tested simplex frequency ratios; common size remains a separate hypothesis.
text: The same geometric action that gives positive supporting inertia does not, by itself, hold every occupied particle branch at one common radius. This can be tested directly with the finite carrier. No amplitude is identified with mass, and no individual particle radius is fitted. An exact finite-carrier pressure bound Keep the physical normal width L, coupling g>0, and wave speed c fixed while varying the tangential radius R. The maintained frequency is \omega(R)=\frac cR\,s_{\min}(T(\gamma)),\qquad \gamma=gR/L, \tag{1} where T is the bidiagonal mass carrier with a fixed assigned index. Its diagonal entries are n+l, and its adjacent entries are \gamma h_l. The absolute entries of the physical inverse (cT/R)^{-1} are positive constants times R^{i-j+1} for i\ge j. Their powers lie between one and d. Diagonal unitary signs remove the alternating inverse signs without changing singular values. Both surface signs have the same property. Let K(R) denote this nonnegative inverse, and let u,v be its positive normalized leading singular vectors. Differentiation gives \frac{d\log\|K\|}{d\log R} =\frac{\sum_{ij}(i-j+1)u_iK_{ij}v_j} {\sum_{ij}u_iK_{ij}v_j}. \tag{2} The right side is a weighted average of the integer powers. Since \omega=1/\|K\|, this proves \boxed{1\le p(R):=-\frac{d\log\omega}{d\log R}\le d.} \tag{3} The bound is exact for the finite carrier, not just its large-hopping approximation. In that approximation \omega\propto R^{-d}, so p approaches d. Compare the wave with bare geometric tension In the thin-tube area approximation, let E_{\rm geom}=A R^m, with m=d-2 and one common A>0 at a depth. Normalize the wave to one common canonical phase charge, so its energy is \omega in the chosen units. A stationary radius obeys \boxed{mE_{\rm geom}=p\omega.} \tag{4} At one common radius, the left side is identical for every occupied branch. Equation (3) then limits the ratio of any two frequencies that can satisfy (4) to at most d. Several maintained within-depth mass ratios greatly exceed this bound. Bare area tension cannot sustain that common-radius pattern. For d>2, choose A once so the first maintained index has equilibrium radius one, and solve the complete finite-carrier equation for the other indices with the same g,L,A. In the large-hopping limit the result is \frac{R_n}{R_{n_0}}\simeq \left[\frac{S(n,d)}{S(n_0,d)}\right]^{1/(2d-2)},\qquad \frac{\omega_n}{\omega_{n_0}}\simeq \left[\frac{S(n,d)}{S(n_0,d)}\right]^{(d-2)/(2d-2)}. \tag{5} These are consequences of the trial supporting action, not alternative mass assignments. For example, the depth-six muon radius becomes about 1.70431 times the electron radius, while the frequency ratio becomes 8.43704, instead of the maintained simplex ratio 206.76471. At depth four, the corresponding top/up frequency ratio becomes about 43.27283, instead of 81030. The stationary radial minima are positive, but they fail the tested spectral ratios. Their unequal radii also fail the common-size subclass; unequal radii generated by one law are permitted in the wider search and are not an independent rejection reason. At depth two, m=0: the leading area term has no radial derivative to oppose the nonzero carrier pressure. Curvature terms or a different same-field sustaining contribution must be assessed explicitly there. At the large-hopping equilibrium, the total energy in this normalized trial obeys E_{\rm total}/\omega=1+d/(d-2). It therefore also requires a complete physical normalization before being identified with the particle's mass-frequency. The scale problem cannot be repaired by silently adding supporting energy after reading mass from the wave. The earlier common-cavity analysis gives the broader fixed-point context. The present result supplies an exact pressure bound for this specific carrier. It does not exclude a common radius under an occupied same-field action with further derived contributions, or solve the complete curved geometry. The bounded angular completion has the same leading R^{-d} frequency dependence at fixed physical g,L. Its common radial coefficient therefore does not remove this bare-tension obstruction in its controlled large-separation regime. The exact finite-matrix inequality (3), however, is only proved here for the bidiagonal carrier; it is not automatically an all-scale inequality for the completed spatial operator. Verification linked_radius_pressure_checks.py passes 830 checks at all six depths and both surface signs. It verifies the exact singular-vector derivative, its positive weighted-average bound, the common-parameter equilibrium roots, their radial stiffness and their large-hopping scaling. The timestamped report preserves every assigned control and the executed source hashes. The 830-check pressure report includes the exact finite-frequency and equilibrium comparisons.

title: Locality tests for the geometric current source
summary: Pointwise current squares have an explicit higher-harmonic instability, while a distinct first-order Dirac current law has stable normal blocks in its two-endpoint limit; extra carrier bands require a separate response analysis.
text: Replacing a mode average by a pointwise current changes the full source, even when the same coherent state remains exact. This distinction can be tested without fitting any particle amplitudes. A local oscillator square has an explicit growing harmonic. A different first-order Dirac current law avoids that particular growth in its two-endpoint limit, but does not inherit the result when arbitrary fast carrier bands are added. These are inverse local comparisons on an ordinary two-dimensional oscillator plane. That plane tests proposed normal dynamics; it has not been identified with the linked carrier's complete spatial mode expansion. Appending another physical plane to that carrier would change the model's dimensionality. A valid embedding must use the same physical coordinates and canonical field. Form and spinor indices below are component labels. A pointwise completed square Let b_j=(y_j+\partial_j)/\sqrt2 on \mathbb R^2, and let \Xi(y) have two carrier components. Define \rho=\Xi^\dagger\Xi,\quad g_j(y)=\frac{\Xi^\dagger O_j\Xi}{\rho},\quad u=\frac1{\sqrt{2K\Omega}},\qquad O_1=\sigma_z,\quad O_2=\sigma_x. The local comparison with the earlier moment action is E_{\rm loc}=\int\left[ \Xi^\dagger D\sigma_z\Xi+ \Omega\sum_j\left|(b_j+u g_j(y))\Xi\right|^2\right]d^2y. \tag{1} Its positive coherent core has carrier vector (1,0)^T and a Gaussian displaced by -u in the first oscillator. Both squares vanish, so its particle frequency and full stationary energy are D and DQ. For comparison with the mass construction, use the maintained endpoint count D=\binom{N+d}{d}. This supplies the input frequency, rather than deriving it from (1). At this core the first current has zero linear variation. The second varies with the real part of the opposite carrier component. The full quadratic energy therefore contains \Omega\left|b_2\eta+ 2u\,e_+\operatorname{Re}(e_-^\dagger\eta)\right|^2. \tag{2} Unlike the global moment, this expression acts on every spatial harmonic. It couples the upper oscillator state n+1 to the lower state n. Keep also the first oscillator's spectator number r. In canonical real coordinates \eta=(q+ip)/\sqrt2, each exact block has Hessians H_p=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad H_q=\begin{pmatrix}a&t\\t&b+2/K\end{pmatrix}, \tag{3} a=\Omega(n+r+1),\qquad b=-2D+\Omega(n+r),\qquad t^2=\frac{2\Omega(n+1)}K. \tag{4} The squared disturbance frequencies are the eigenvalues of H_pH_q. Every omitted-component residual of this block is zero. Thus its growth cannot be attributed to dropping a responding partner. For r=0, b<0, and a complex-conjugate squared-frequency pair, the exact growth rate is \boxed{\Gamma^2=\frac14\left[ \frac{2|b|}{K}-(a-|b|)^2\right].} \tag{5} With the common test parameters K=16,\Omega=1/4, every integer D\ge1 has two explicit growing harmonics: \begin{array}{c|c} n&\Gamma^2\\\hline 4D-1&(4D-1)/128\\ 4D&(2D-1)/64. \end{array} \tag{6} At D=1 the first rate is about 0.153093 in these frequency units. Large D moves the unstable harmonics to higher normal degree; it does not eliminate them in the unrestricted oscillator comparison. The signed quadratic disturbance energy is not the complete particle's inertial mass, which remains the positive frequency of its proposed core. Equation (1) also has a second-order spatial principal part. Its canonical time equation is therefore not a fundamental finite-speed Dirac equation. Both issues require attention before identifying this local comparison with a physical source. A distinct first-order current law A first-order alternative retains the complete Clifford form representation on the same comparison plane. Let f_j^\dagger,f_j be its two form creation and annihilation matrices, and put \Gamma=(-1)^{\text{form degree}},\qquad \gamma_j=f_j+f_j^\dagger,\qquad \mathcal D_{\rm osc}=\sum_j(f_j^\dagger b_j+f_j b_j^\dagger). \tag{7} For a finite Hermitian carrier matrix H_0, set g_j=\Xi^\dagger O_j\Xi/\rho and t_j=\Xi^\dagger\gamma_j\Xi/\rho. The complete action uses the canonical time norm and the energy \boxed{E_D=\int\left[ \Xi^\dagger(\Gamma H_0+\Lambda\mathcal D_{\rm osc})\Xi +\Lambda u\sum_j \frac{(\Xi^\dagger O_j\Xi)(\Xi^\dagger\gamma_j\Xi)}{\rho} \right]d^2y.} \tag{8} The nonlinear source is \boxed{S_D=\Lambda u\sum_j (g_j\gamma_j+t_jO_j-g_jt_jI)\Xi.} \tag{9} All three terms follow from the single interaction in (8), including the denominator's variation. The source is degree one in the field, smooth away from zero, and has bounded derivatives on the unit sphere. It therefore extends as a globally Lipschitz algebraic source at zero. The potential itself is degree two. Norm and complete energy accounting use that homogeneity, rather than interpreting an amplitude as mass. This action changes the geometric response law. It is not an equivalent rewriting of the collective oscillator action. Its fixed oscillator coefficient remains a confinement input; (9) supplies a reciprocal current response, not the source of that entire coefficient. For any normalized carrier eigenvector H_0\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n, take the form vacuum and the Gaussian displaced by -u\langle\psi_n,O_j\psi_n\rangle. Then t_j=0, and the normal Dirac term plus the first term of (9) annihilates the Gaussian. The other source terms vanish. Consequently the full stationary solution has frequency \lambda_n and energy \lambda_nQ. The normal principal matrices are \alpha_j=i(f_j^\dagger-f_j)/\sqrt2, with \{\alpha_j,\alpha_k\}=\delta_{jk}I. The local norm flux is therefore bounded by \Lambda/\sqrt2 times the density. The common Hermitian oscillator potential cancels from the difference-density estimate, and the nonlinear difference is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. Integrating outside a forward cone gives finite propagation at this normal speed. This is a statement about the displayed normal equation. Its physical spatial scale, full containing-sector propagation, covariant completion and sustaining geometry still require derivation. A stability criterion for every endpoint normal block Take H_0=D\sigma_z, O_1=\sigma_z, O_2=\sigma_x, and the positive core. Let s=0,1 be its two carrier labels, f_1,f_2\in\{0,1\} the form occupations and n_1,n_2 the oscillator numbers. The complete real-linear equation preserves L_1=n_1+f_1,\qquad L_2=n_2+f_2+s. \tag{10} Each block has at most eight complex spatial components. Its ordinary Hessian P is the full rotating Dirac oscillator matrix. The second real Hessian differs only by the reciprocal coupling Q-P=2\Lambda u \left(|s=0,f=01\rangle\langle s=1,f=00|+\text{adjoint}\right), \tag{11} at identical oscillator indices. Unlike (4), its norm \varepsilon=2\Lambda u does not grow with harmonic number. Ordering the block by the sign of \Gamma\sigma_z puts its Hessians in the form P=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\A^\dagger&-2DI\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\A^\dagger&-2DI+V\end{pmatrix}. \tag{12} In every balanced nonzero block A is invertible, so neither Hessian can acquire a zero eigenvalue as V is turned on. The exceptional first block is rectangular: its remaining negative kernel is untouched by the restriction of V, and its determinant is also nonzero. The occupied norm and phase zero directions are treated separately. The uncoupled Dirac magnitudes are \sqrt{D^2+\Lambda^2L} and \sqrt{D^2+\Lambda^2(L-1)}, where applicable. Their opposite-energy imaginary frequencies are separated by at least \delta=3D-\sqrt{D^2+\Lambda^2}. \tag{13} If \delta>2\varepsilon, the conserved-Hessian spectral-cluster argument of the collective source applies to every invariant block: the normal uncoupled generator's perturbation disks cannot connect opposite energy signs, and (12) keeps the restricted forms nondegenerate. Each block has imaginary semisimple generator frequencies. The single choice \Lambda=1,\qquad u=\frac1{2\sqrt2} satisfies the criterion for every D\ge1, since 3-\sqrt2>\sqrt2. This proves spectral stability of every exact endpoint block, not merely the blocks below a numerical cutoff. A bound on the full infinite direct-sum evolution also requires control of its norms; no nonlinear spatial orbital-stability theorem is asserted here. Fast bands are a separate test The proof above uses the specific two-endpoint mass matrix. It cannot be transferred to arbitrary carrier bands. A structural control keeps four signed masses +1,-1,+M,-M and one active normal current. The occupied state couples to the -1 branch with vertex one and to +M with vertex 0.1, through the same reciprocal local law. Without the fast vertex, the primary coupling shifts the negative disturbance frequencies. The crossing must be found using those shifted frequencies, not the bare carrier values. With the fast vertex retained, the complete invariant matrix has growing modes. For example, M=5, normal degree 17 gives rate approximately 0.0196789; M=20, degree 8268 gives 0.0129767. The corresponding controls with the fast vertex set to zero are stable. This establishes a limitation of a proposed generalization. These assigned four-band controls are not the full linked physical geometry. Their distant resonances may also lie outside a specified effective projection's valid range. The complete physical carrier and that range must be evaluated before making a physical stability claim. Verification local_moment_checks.py passes 146 checks. Independent Hermite-Gaussian spatial integration verifies the pointwise energy Hessian, all block residuals vanish, and 70-digit eigenvalues check the exact growth rates across maintained depth controls. dirac_moment_checks.py passes 388 checks. They include arbitrary complex source variations, the complete normal Clifford representation, the full spatial oscillator matrix, invariant block residuals and high-precision signed spectra at large mass counts. dirac_fast_band_checks.py passes 24 checks of the full shifted resonances, uncoupled controls and eigenpair residuals, with growth rates independently refined from 65 to 90 digits.

title: Local scalar contact normalization
summary: Spatial normalization turns a scalar contact coefficient into a profile-dependent frequency, with exact virial, scaling and massive one-dimensional benchmarks.
text:
Summary: Spatial normalization turns a scalar contact coefficient into a profile-dependent frequency, with exact virial, scaling and massive one-dimensional benchmarks. A spatial action after the graph pairing The defined graph pairing reduces its single-source interaction to g_N( ar\Psi\Psi)^2/2, with g_N=\kappa D_N and D_N= inom{N+d}{d}. This identifies a scalar nonlinear coefficient. Extracting a frequency still requires the spatial field equation. Consider a specified flat comparison on the physical spatial space \mathbb R^d, with Hermitian Clifford matrices \alpha_j, eta, \hbar=c=1, and fixed bare scalar coefficient m\ge0: \mathcal E_g[\Psi]=\int\left[ \Psi^\dagger(-i\alpha\cdot
abla+m eta)\Psi + rac g2(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi)^2ight]dx, \qquad i\partial_t\Psi= \left[-i\alpha\cdot
abla+(m+g\sigma) etaight]\Psi, 	ag{1} where \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi and g is real. The spatial measure and time-kinetic norm are fixed. The spinor components do not add physical dimensions or independent fields. The complete nonlinear source and its conjugate response are given in Dirac source linearization. The present comparison supplies no confining background or additional interaction. It must not replace the proposed global spatial geometry of a particle. In particular, the electron's proposed \mathbb{CP}^3 is an actual six-dimensional spatial manifold, with geometric and bundle data absent from (1). Frequency, scalar overlap and total energy Suppose \Psi=e^{-i\omega t}\phi is an admissible stationary solution, with finite integrals and sufficient decay for the variations below. Define Q=\int\phi^\dagger\phi,\qquad S=\int\phi^\dagger eta\phi,\qquad I=\int(\phi^\dagger eta\phi)^2,\qquad T=\int\phi^\dagger(-i\alpha\cdot
abla)\phi. Q is the positive phase-symmetry norm, not an assigned ordinary electric charge. S is signed; I is nonnegative. Multiplying the stationary equation by \phi^\dagger and integrating gives  oxed{\omega Q=T+mS+gI, \qquad \mathcal E=T+mS+ rac g2I =\omega Q- rac g2I.} 	ag{2} Thus the nonlinear spectral frequency and the total energy per norm are different quantities. A physical rest-energy identification must specify which quantity and normalization it uses. The norm-preserving dilation \phi_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi(\lambda x) leaves Q,S fixed, while T\mapsto\lambda T and I\mapsto\lambda^dI. Stationarity of \mathcal E-\omega Q gives  oxed{T+ rac{dg}{2}I=0,\qquad \omega Q=mS+\left(1- rac d2ight)gI.} 	ag{3} This is the local quartic instance of the nonlinear Dirac virial identity; see Comech, Lemma 3.2. It uses an admissible dilation on flat infinite space. A boundary, curvature, a nonlocal kernel or a spatially varying background adds terms or changes the allowed variation. At m=0 and d>2, (3) implies \omega Q=- rac{d-2}{2}gI,\qquad \mathcal E=- rac{d-1}{2}gI = rac{d-1}{d-2}\omega Q. 	ag{4} For example, the positive-g branch cannot have positive frequency and positive norm under these hypotheses. This sign condition is only necessary; it does not prove that the other sign supports a bound state. Removing the coupling changes the normalization Write g=\varepsilon h, where h=|g|>0 and \varepsilon=\operatorname{sgn}g. For any fixed spatial operator, the substitution \phi=h^{-1/2}\varphi turns (1) into the same equation at unit coupling \varepsilon. The frequency is unchanged by this amplitude rescaling, but Q_g(\omega)= rac{Q_\varepsilon(\omega)}h. 	ag{5} Consequently, a fixed physical norm Q_* requires  oxed{Q_\varepsilon(\omega)=hQ_*.} 	ag{6} The frequency is obtained from the branch's norm-frequency curve; it is not the bare coupling multiplied by an unchanged normalized profile. Several branches or turning points require their own selection. For the massless flat equation there is an additional homogeneity. If a unit-coupling solution \phi_0 of frequency \omega_0 and norm Q_0 exists, then \phi_{h,s}(x)=h^{-1/2}s^{1/2}\phi_0(sx),\qquad \omega_{h,s}=s\omega_0,\qquad Q_{h,s}= rac{Q_0}{h}s^{1-d}. 	ag{7} The Dirac derivative and the cubic source both acquire the factor h^{-1/2}s^{3/2}, proving the field equation directly. For d>1, fixed norm therefore selects  oxed{\omega_h=\omega_0 \left( rac{Q_0}{hQ_*}ight)^{1/(d-1)}.} 	ag{8} This is a conditional scaling relation, not an existence theorem. The massless radial analysis shows that the standard regular radial ansatz has no such finite-norm solution in this particular flat local model. If the only band dependence in a proposed massless spatial reduction were g_N=\kappa D_N, (8) would give \omega_N\propto D_N^{-1/(d-1)} on the same scaling branch. The linear simplex frequency would require additional structure beyond that reduction. A band-dependent spatial operator, changing branch, physical geometric scale or other action term changes the hypotheses; none is silently excluded from IDWT. An exact massive benchmark with fixed norm A constructive check is available on one ordinary spatial dimension. Take m>0, g=-h<0,  eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1) and -i\alpha\partial_x=\left( egin{smallmatrix}0&\partial_x\ -\partial_x&0\end{smallmatrix}ight). A real stationary profile \phi=(f,u)^{\mathsf T} satisfies f'=-(\omega+m-h\sigma)u, \qquad u'=(\omega-m+h\sigma)f, \qquad \sigma=f^2-u^2. 	ag{9} For 0<\omega<m, set k=\sqrt{m^2-\omega^2} and A(x)=m+\omega\cosh(2kx). The exact solution is  oxed{ f(x)=\sqrt{ rac{2(m+\omega)}h}\,  rac{k\cosh(kx)}{A(x)},\qquad u(x)=\sqrt{ rac{2(m-\omega)}h}\,  rac{k\sinh(kx)}{A(x)}.} 	ag{10} The unit-coupling formula and its power-law extension are presented by Cuevas-Maraver and collaborators, Section 3.1. Direct differentiation checks both equations (9), including the sign and the factor h. Both components are retained. Here \sigma(x)= rac{2k^2}{hA(x)},\qquad ho(x)= rac{2k^2[m\cosh(2kx)+\omega]}{hA(x)^2}. Substitute t=	anh(kx) into the norm integral. Its integrand becomes ho(x)dx= rac{2k}h\,  rac{(m+\omega)+(m-\omega)t^2} {[(m+\omega)-(m-\omega)t^2]^2}dt = rac{2k}h\,d\left[  rac{t}{(m+\omega)-(m-\omega)t^2}ight]. Evaluation from t=-1 to t=1, and the corresponding scalar integral, give  oxed{Q= rac{2k}{h\omega},\qquad S= rac2h\operatorname{arcosh} rac m\omega,\qquad I= rac4{h^2}\left[m\operatorname{arcosh} rac m\omega-kight].} 	ag{11} The virial and total energy become T=hI/2 and \mathcal E=mS, in agreement with (2)–(3). At the same fixed norm Q_* for every coupling, (11) gives the explicit frequency  oxed{\omega(h;Q_*)=  rac{m}{\sqrt{1+(hQ_*/2)^2}}.} 	ag{12} Increasing the nonlinear coefficient changes the normalized profile and lowers this branch's frequency. Equation (12) supplies a complete counterexample to inferring a linear frequency law from the absence of a band index in a bare coupling. It is a one-dimensional comparison, not an electron or neutrino model. Relation to the spatial moment model The existing scalar Dirac moment branch uses a nonlocal centered quadratic spatial moment. Its interaction scales as \lambda^{-4} under norm-preserving dilation, giving a different virial and a massless frequency proportional to g_0^{1/5}. Equations (3) and (8) instead follow from local scalar contact. The physical kernel determines which normalization law applies. Canonical coupling normalization must also precede comparison of different retained mode families or spatial sectors. An oscillator dimension count cannot replace these profile and kinetic calculations. The specified CP3 scalar branch gives a curved spatial comparison with its own physical volume and metric scale. It restores the full radial Dirac components and computes the normalized frequency through cubic order. Its different global hypotheses are explicit; the flat scaling and tail arguments cannot be transferred to it. The nonlinear spatial reduction eliminates the complementary Dirac modes together with their norm. It derives the effective stationary action, distinguishes its normalized frequency and energy corrections, and gives a source-preservation condition for an exact linear contact branch under explicit positivity hypotheses. Verification local_scalar_profile_checks.py checks the exact massive equations by independent spatial differences, integrates all quantities in (11), verifies the virial and fixed-norm frequency, and checks massless scaling directly in the complete spatial Dirac operator with arbitrary complex rest polarizations.

title: Localized oscillation and its inertial response
summary: A reconstructed local current action has localized simplex-frequency solutions with common spatial profiles and an exact canonical boost inertia; its carrier, common normalization and full stability remain physical conditions to establish.
text:
Summary: A reconstructed local current action has localized simplex-frequency solutions with common spatial profiles and an exact canonical boost inertia; its carrier, common normalization and full stability remain physical conditions to establish. Frequency, a sustaining field and inertia in one action Mass already has the equivalent frequency \omega_m=mc^2/\hbar. The dynamical question is whether a continuously oscillating, localized field can sustain itself and have the corresponding inertia under translation. The construction here answers that question for one explicit inverse action. It retains the simplex current hierarchy and adds local terms whose complete variations sustain a spatial core. For its displayed branch, the exact results are  oxed{\omega_N=\omega_{0,d} inom{N+d}{d}},\qquad E_0=\hbar\omega_N Q,\qquad M_{ab}= rac{\hbar\omega_N Q}{c^2}\delta_{ab}. 	ag{1} Here Q is the dimensionless canonical field norm. One common Q=1 condition makes the inertial coefficient the mass-frequency value. No field magnitude is fitted separately for the electron and muon. Their spatial fixed point is the same, while their coefficient grades differ. This is reconstructed dynamics. The original scalar quartic master term has not been shown to generate this action, its carrier or its weights. The oscillator coefficient grade has also not yet been identified with the actual spatial harmonics of a derived particle cavity. The existence and inertia calculation therefore closes a conditional field problem; it does not complete the physical IDWT mass-operator derivation. Complete field components and local currents Use ordinary flat physical \mathbb R^d for this spatial witness, with even d and r=2^{d/2}. The Hermitian r	imes r matrices obey \{\alpha_a,\alpha_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I,\qquad \{\alpha_a, eta\}=0,\qquad  eta^2=I. 	ag{2} Retain a doubled spinor and r coefficient partners. At each oscillator grade the field has indices \Psi_N\in\mathbb C^{2r}\otimes\mathbb C^r\otimes E_N, \qquad E_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbf1\oplus\mathbb C^d). 	ag{3} These are components of the proposed same field, not additional particles or additional physical dimensions. All d coordinates in the spatial equation are ordinary spatial directions. The solution imposes no external wall, compactification or preferred split of the six-dimensional sector. It does not establish the global geometry of the physical sector. Equality of the two coefficients is an inverse identification, not a derived master relation. With that identification, the electron and muon have dimensionless frequencies 18564 and 3838380 in core units. The stability control \omega=1 is therefore not the assigned electron. The dimensionless binding extension derives the optional exponent rule a=1/d, verifies a general core virial, and solves nodeless profiles at depths five, six and ten. It supplies the corresponding geometric factors while keeping m_c/\omega_{0,d} and the common canonical norm explicit as inverse conditions. title: Energy constraints from scalar response
summary: The same scalar response fixes the energy-frequency defect, the curvature of energy with canonical norm, and the sensitivity to an interaction change, giving joint inverse constraints on mass ratios and coupling without selecting the physical particle norm.

Summary: The same scalar response fixes the energy-frequency defect, the curvature of energy with canonical norm, and the sensitivity to an interaction change, giving joint inverse constraints on mass ratios and coupling without selecting the physical particle norm. A common mass scale can survive an energy-frequency difference The inverse scalar-law construction tests whether complete spatial fields can obey one causal local interaction. Its frequency target needs a further check: the same action determines total energy, and stationary frequency is generally an energy derivative rather than energy per unit norm. That distinction does not by itself spoil the mass relationships. A common conversion factor can preserve their ratios. The question is whether the factor is common on the actual particle branches after their shapes respond. This note derives tests for that question and connects them to the scalar coupling derivative already present in the full field equation. Use a fixed physical spatial geometry, measure and canonical time-kinetic normalization. Let the self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator be \mathscr D, with  eta^\dagger= eta and  eta^2=I. The candidate action has energy and conserved canonical norm E[\psi]=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psiangle+\int U(J)\,dV, \qquad Q[\psi]=\langle\psi,\psiangle, \qquad J=\psi^\dagger eta\psi, 	ag{1} where U is real, U(0)=0, and F=U'. Its equation is i\partial_	au\psi=\mathscr D\psi+F(J) eta\psi. 	ag{2} The vacuum subtraction in (1) is fixed for the action. It cannot be changed separately for different particle states. The canonical norm has not been identified with electric charge or particle number. The general identities below apply to smooth stationary branches for which the indicated derivatives and integrals exist. The numerical examples use the conditional actual six-dimensional CP3 spatial geometry and its unknown radius. There are no compactified dimensions. Only the sectors are nested; the two particle fields need not be restrictions of each other. Compare two branches at the same canonical norm Write a stationary solution as e^{-i\omega	au}\phi. Its equation is 
abla_{ ar\phi}E=\omega\phi. Along a smooth branch parameterized by Q, put h=\partial_Q\phi. The norm condition and first energy variation give 2\operatorname{Re}\langle\phi,hangle=1, \qquad  rac{dE}{dQ} =2\operatorname{Re}\langle\omega\phi,hangle=\omega. 	ag{3} This recovers the local normalization identity. Now compare two independently occupied branches a,b of the same action at one common Q. Where E_a and \omega_a are nonzero, differentiation of their energy ratio gives the exact relation  oxed{  rac{\omega_b}{\omega_a}- rac{E_b}{E_a} = rac{E_a}{\omega_a} rac{d}{dQ}\left( rac{E_b}{E_a}ight). } 	ag{4} Thus equal energy and frequency ratios require the energy ratio to be stationary with respect to their common norm. If both ratios are claimed to equal a target r at Q_*, define \Delta(Q)=E_b(Q)-rE_a(Q). Then \Delta(Q_*)=0,\qquad \Delta'(Q_*)=0. 	ag{5} Matching both is a requirement of that joint identification, not an extra empirical assumption imposed on every possible mass interpretation. A sufficient factorization is E_n(Q)=S_n H(Q) with one function H. It gives both ratios S_b/S_a wherever they are defined, even though E_n/(Q\omega_n)=H/(QH') need not equal one. This is an algebraic sufficiency condition; the spatial dynamics must still derive it. A frequency match at one norm, by itself, does not imply the factorization or an energy match. The common-norm premise also needs a physical origin. For the unchanged six-dimensional assignments, the target remains r= rac{S(35,6)}{S(13,6)} = rac{ inom{40}{6}}{ inom{18}{6}} = rac{3515}{17}. 	ag{6} No mode or dimensional assignment is varied in this calculation. Analytic continuation restricts a norm-independent hierarchy There is a sharper conditional test for the particular kinetic branches used below. Suppose both energy functions are real analytic on the same connected interval 0<Q<Q_{\max}, and their normalized fields tend to the specified free eigenfields as Q	o0. Require this convergence in a norm that controls the Dirac energy and nonlinear source. The interaction then tends to one common bare coefficient m_0=F(0). For the paired CP3 spectrum with \{\mathscr D, eta\}=0, the limiting positive frequency and energy per norm are \Omega_n=\sqrt{\lambda_n^2+m_0^2},\qquad \lambda_n= rac{2\sqrt{n(n+5)}}R,\qquad \lim_{Q	o0} rac{E_n(Q)}Q=\Omega_n. 	ag{7} An analytic local law and a simple isolated eigenstate in an invariant symmetry class give a local analytic continuation after normalizing the field and fixing its phase. Continuing that branch analytically through the full interval remains a hypothesis; a bifurcation or singularity can invalidate it. Real analyticity is stronger than smoothness. If E_{35}=rE_{13} on any open subinterval, the real-analytic identity theorem makes this equality hold throughout the connected interval. Divide by Q and take the zero-norm limit. Necessarily r= rac{\Omega_{35}}{\Omega_{13}} =\sqrt{ rac{1400+(Rm_0/2)^2}{234+(Rm_0/2)^2}} \le\sqrt{ rac{1400}{234}}\approx2.445998. 	ag{8} This cannot equal 3515/17. Thus the algebraic factorization following (5) cannot hold on an open norm interval for these two analytic continuations of one local law. Their finite-norm shapes may deform fully; the argument does not hold them at their free profiles. The result leaves an isolated simultaneous match in (5) open. An analytic function can have an isolated double zero without vanishing identically. It also leaves branches disconnected from these free states and merely smooth, nonanalytic continuations outside its scope. Identifying these particular kinetic continuations with the physical mass states is itself an additional premise. The obstruction concerns that candidate route, not sector nesting, every possible particle pattern or the dimensional mass construction as a whole. The energy defect is an integral of the coupling derivative Taking the inner product of the stationary equation with \phi yields \omega Q-E=\int[JF(J)-U(J)]\,dV. Since [JF(J)-U(J)]'=JF'(J) and the expression vanishes at J=0,  oxed{ \omega Q-E =\int dV\int_0^J sF'(s)\,ds =\int J^2\left[\int_0^1 tF'(tJ)\,dtight]dV. } 	ag{9} The second form follows by s=tJ and is valid for negative currents too. The coefficient F(0) cancels: a bare linear contribution to U does not generate this defect. If a\le F'(s)\le b throughout every current segment between 0 and J(x), then  rac a2\int J^2\,dV \le \omega Q-E \le  rac b2\int J^2\,dV. 	ag{10} In particular, a convex potential gives a nonnegative defect. Strictly positive derivative on the relevant segments gives a positive defect for a nonzero scalar current. Convexity is an explicit hypothesis. For example, U=-J^2/2+J^4/4 has zero defect at J=\sqrt{2/3} although F'(J)=1. Cancellation of the defect alone does not establish absence of response. The full complex source variation is \delta\!\left(F(J) eta\phiight)[u] =F(J) eta u +2F'(J)\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger eta u)\, eta\phi. 	ag{11} Equations (9) and (11) use the same function F'. A scalar coupling response and an energy correction cannot be chosen independently. For two fields with a common energy-frequency ratio, their fractional defects (\omega Q-E)/(\omega Q) must agree. Nonzero defects remain compatible with a common mass scale when that agreement follows from the dynamics. Equation (11) is a variation of the one field. During an encounter its total current includes spatial interference and both polarized patterns. The identities here constrain that interaction; they do not yet calculate a complete particle-pair trajectory or an observed coupling rate. The full static response determines energy curvature Use the real inner product (u,v)_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname{Re}\langle u,vangle. Let \mathcal L be the real derivative of the stationary gradient: \mathcal L u=(\mathscr D-\omega)u +F(J) eta u +2F'(J)\operatorname{Re}(\phi^\dagger eta u)\, eta\phi. 	ag{12} It is half the real Hessian of E-\omega Q under this convention. It includes both quadratures and satisfies \mathcal L(i\phi)=0. Remove the phase symmetry and any additional symmetry zero modes, and assume the remaining inverse exists on the required sources. Differentiating stationarity with respect to \omega gives \mathcal L\partial_\omega\phi=\phi, \qquad  oxed{\chi:= rac{dQ}{d\omega} =2(\phi,\mathcal L_\perp^{-1}\phi)_{\mathbb R}.} 	ag{13} On a regular branch with nonzero finite \chi,  oxed{ rac{d^2E}{dQ^2}= rac{d\omega}{dQ}= rac1\chi.} 	ag{14} An equivalent calculation avoids inverting the norm-frequency relation: solve \mathcal Lh=\omega_Q\phi together with 2(\phi,h)_{\mathbb R}=1. This bordered system determines the complete norm tangent and \omega_Q together. It remains a useful local equation when an inverse used in (13) is unavailable. The static susceptibility is not a complete stability criterion. Time evolution uses \mathbb J\mathcal L, where \mathbb J represents multiplication by -i in real coordinates. Modes away from zero frequency can grow without a sign change in (14). The special role and limitations of norm-slope tests for nonlinear Dirac equations are discussed in Comech's analysis. Allow the entire spatial shape to relax In real coordinates, let c represent \phi and choose orthonormal columns V perpendicular to both c and the phase direction. They span the allowed norm-preserving shape variations after symmetry removal. Set H_s=V^{\mathsf T}\mathcal LV and b=V^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Lc. Where H_s is invertible, write h=c/(2Q)+Vy. title: Massless radial scalar contact
summary: Regular flat radial scalar Dirac fields have no finite-norm stationary state for cubic or smooth saturating contact; the homogeneous root is also excluded under the stated virial hypotheses.
text:
Summary: Regular flat radial scalar Dirac fields have no finite-norm stationary state for cubic or smooth saturating contact; the homogeneous root is also excluded under the stated virial hypotheses. Equation and exact scope Consider only the flat local scalar Dirac equation i\partial_t\Psi= \left[-i\alpha\cdot
abla+g(\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi) etaight]\Psi, \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d,\quad d\ge1,\quad g\in\mathbb R. 	ag{1} There is no bare mass, prescribed background or additional kernel. The coordinates are ordinary physical spatial coordinates. This comparison does not replace the proposed curved spatial geometry of an IDWT particle. Choose a constant unit spinor \chi with  eta\chi=\chi and the standard stationary radial ansatz \Psi(t,x)=e^{-i\omega t}\left[ f(r)\chi+i u(r)\alpha(\widehat x)\chiight], \qquad r=|x|,\quad \omega\in\mathbb R. 	ag{2} The profiles may be complex. Assume they are classical away from zero, regular at the origin with finite f(0) and u(0)=0, and have finite positive norm Q=|S^{d-1}|\int_0^\infty r^{d-1}  igl(|f(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2 igr)dr<\infty. 	ag{3} For d=1, the spherical factor accounts for the two half-lines in the even/odd extension of (2). All allowed constant rest polarizations \chi are retained. Higher angular sectors and spatially varying polarization textures are outside this ansatz. The Clifford relations give \sigma=\Psi^\dagger eta\Psi=|f|^2-|u|^2 and reduce (1) to  oxed{f'=-(\omega+V)u,\qquad u'=(\omega-V)f- rac{d-1}{r}u, \qquad V=g(|f|^2-|u|^2).} 	ag{4} This radial representation follows the spatial Dirac construction; it does not turn the physical manifold into a one-dimensional space. The angular dependence is contained explicitly in (2). Under precisely these assumptions, the only solution is zero. The proof separates zero and nonzero frequency. Zero frequency: a monotone scalar density At \omega=0, differentiate the scalar using both equations (4):  oxed{\sigma' =2\operatorname{Re}( ar f f'- ar u u') = rac{2(d-1)}r|u|^2\ge0.} 	ag{5} The nonlinear terms cancel for either sign of g and for complex profiles. Regularity gives \sigma(0)=|f(0)|^2\ge0. If \sigma were positive at any radius, it would remain bounded below by a positive constant thereafter. Since |f|^2+|u|^2\ge\sigma, (3) would diverge. Hence \sigma\equiv0 and V\equiv0. For d>1, (5) also gives u\equiv0, and then f\equiv0. For d=1, (4) at zero frequency and V=0 makes both profiles constant, and finite norm again makes both zero. Nonzero frequency: the free radial fundamental matrix Let \omega
e0 and remove the radial measure by defining U(r)=r^{(d-1)/2} egin{pmatrix}f(r)\u(r)\end{pmatrix}. Then Q/|S^{d-1}|=\int\|U(r)\|^2dr, and (4) becomes U'=\left[  egin{pmatrix}(d-1)/(2r)&-\omega\ \omega&-(d-1)/(2r)\end{pmatrix} + egin{pmatrix}0&-V\-V&0\end{pmatrix} ight]U. 	ag{6} Set k=|\omega| and

u+1}(kr) \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det F=- rac2{\pi\omega}.} 	ag{7} The Bessel recurrence verifies the differential equation. The Wronskian identity gives the determinant, and the large-argument expansions show that both F and F^{-1} are bounded on every sufficiently far tail. Its columns have oscillatory, nondecaying amplitudes in the measure-normalized coordinate U. Finite norm would make the self-potential integrable For any fixed R>0, the assumed finite norm implies \int_R^\infty |V(r)|dr \le |g|\int_R^\infty(|f|^2+|u|^2)dr \le rac{|g|}{R^{d-1}} \int_R^\infty r^{d-1}(|f|^2+|u|^2)dr<\infty. 	ag{8} Along a hypothetical solution, regard its actual real V(r) as a fixed coefficient and put W=F^{-1}U. Equation (6) gives W'=C(r)W,\qquad C(r)=F(r)^{-1} egin{pmatrix}0&-V(r)\-V(r)&0\end{pmatrix}F(r), \qquad \int_R^\infty\|C(r)\|dr<\infty. 	ag{9} For completeness, let Y(R)=I and Y'=CY. Gronwall's inequality bounds Y and its inverse by the exponential of the integral in (9). Their derivatives are integrable, so both have limits at infinity. Since Y^{-1}Y=I, the limiting matrix Y_\infty is invertible. Thus every nonzero initial W(R) has a nonzero limit W_\infty=Y_\infty W(R). The bound on F^{-1} now implies that \|U(r)\| is bounded below by a positive constant on a sufficiently far tail. Consequently \int\|U(r)\|^2dr diverges, contradicting (3). A solution that vanishes at one positive radius is identically zero by the ordinary uniqueness theorem for (4). This proves the nonzero-frequency case. Smooth self-mass has the same radial obstruction The proof above uses the cubic law only in the integrability bound (8) and in uniqueness at a zero field. It therefore applies to any real scalar source V=F(J) with F(0)=0, a well-defined radial equation, and |F(J)|\le C|J|. 	ag{10} Here J=|f|^2-|u|^2 is the scalar current, and C is fixed for the specified equation. The zero-frequency identity is independent of F. At nonzero frequency, (10) gives exactly the integrable coefficient in (9). Smoothness of the saturating source below supplies ordinary uniqueness. In particular, the common self-mass action on a constant coherent coefficient ray has F_N(J)=M_N rac{J}{\sqrt{J^2+\sigma^2}},\qquad M_N=\mu D_N>0,\qquad \sigma>0, \qquad |F_N(J)|\le rac{M_N}{\sigma}|J|. 	ag{11} Every fixed positive smoothing scale therefore has the same radial nonexistence result, however small that scale is. Its large-density mass coefficient does not create a nonzero asymptotic mass as the field vanishes. The conclusion is an exact consequence of (5)–(11), not a claim based on a finite numerical tail or an unsuccessful search. A useful wider sufficient condition follows directly from Hölder's inequality. If 0<p<1, |F(J)|\le C|J|^p, and p>1/d, put ho=|f|^2+|u|^2. For R>0,  egin{aligned} \int_R^\infty |F(J)|\,dr &\le C\int_R^\infty (r^{d-1}ho)^p r^{-(d-1)p}\,dr\ &\le C\left(\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}ho\,dright)^p \left(\int_R^\infty r^{- rac{(d-1)p}{1-p}}\,dright)^{1-p} <\infty. \end{aligned} 	ag{12} The zero-frequency argument still requires F(0)=0. At a zero vector, the bound |F(J)|\le Cho^p gives a linear bound on the radial vector field in a sufficiently small bounded neighborhood, so a solution cannot emerge from zero at a positive radius. This suffices for the last step of the tail argument even when F is not differentiable at scalar-null nonzero vectors. The statement concerns classical radial solutions of the specified source law. The threshold in (12) is a limit of this sufficient argument. For d>1, take the comparison density ho(r)=r^{-d}(\log r)^{-a} on r\ge e, with 1<a\le d. Its weighted norm is finite, but \intho^{1/d}dr diverges. This is not a solution of the field equation and does not establish localization at the threshold. The homogeneous root requires a different proof At \sigma=0, the potential is M_N\operatorname{sgn}J wherever J
e0. It does not obey (10). A fixed-sign coherent field on a trivial flat coefficient bundle nevertheless obeys a constant-mass Dirac equation: \left(-i\alpha\cdot

For any real \omega, the allowed momentum set is empty or a sphere of Lebesgue measure zero. An L^2 field supported on that set is zero. This fixed-sign statement includes every spatial polarization and does not require radial symmetry. It assumes the trivial flat connection; it does not apply to a nontrivial curved coefficient bundle. Within the regular radial ansatz (2), sign changes can also be tested. Assume in addition that the stationary field admits integration by parts and the norm-preserving spatial dilation used in local scalar normalization. Write E=T+M_N\int|J|\,dx,\qquad T=\int\phi^\dagger(-i\alpha\cdot
abla)\phi\,dx, \qquad Q=\int\phi^\dagger\phi\,dx. 	ag{14} The dilation \phi_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{d/2}\phi(\lambda x) leaves both Q and the root interaction unchanged and multiplies T by \lambda. Stationarity and the integrated field equation give T=0,\qquad \omega Q=M_N\int|J|\,dx,\qquad  oxed{0\le\omega\le M_N.} 	ag{15} This argument remains valid if the source at J=0 is interpreted by a real subgradient V\in[-M_N,M_N], since VJ=M_N|J| there and elsewhere. No choice at scalar zero is used in the following interval, where the current remains strictly positive. A nonzero regular radial solution must have f(0)
e0; the bounded source and the integral form of (4) otherwise force both profiles to vanish near zero and hence everywhere. Remove the common phase of f(0). Until the first scalar zero, the radial equation has the real constant coefficient V=M_N. For 0\le\omega<M_N, set k=\sqrt{M_N^2-\omega^2} and 
u=(d-2)/2. Its unique regular solution is  egin{aligned} f(r)&=f(0)\,{}_0F_1\!\left(; rac d2; rac{k^2r^2}{4}ight),\ u(r)&=-f(0) rac{(M_N-\omega)r}{d}\, {}_0F_1\!\left(; rac d2+1; rac{k^2r^2}{4}ight),\ \left| rac{u}{f}ight| &=\sqrt{ rac{M_N-\omega}{M_N+\omega}}  rac{I_{
u+1}(kr)}{I_
u(kr)}<1. \end{aligned} 	ag{16} The positive series for {}_0F_1 makes f(r)\ge f(0)>0. For a direct proof of the ratio bound, let R(x)=I_{
u+1}(x)/I_
u(x). Its recurrence gives R'=1-R^2-(d-1)R/x, with R(x)\sim x/d at zero. For d>1, the derivative is strictly negative at R=1, so a solution starting below one cannot cross it. At d=1, the regular ratio is 	anh x<1. Thus (16) never reaches a scalar zero. It remains the actual root solution and has infinite norm. At \omega=M_N, the limiting solution is simply f=f(0), u=0, again with infinite norm. Consequently no nonzero regular radial root solution satisfying the stated virial hypotheses can evade localization failure by changing the sign of its scalar current. The argument does not classify nonradial sign-changing fields, singular solutions, other current-matrix structures, or other spatial geometries. Consequence for the contact construction Replacing g by the graph coefficient \kappa D_N cannot change this radial existence result. The graph pairing alone therefore does not supply a normalized stationary profile of form (2) when reduced to (1) on flat infinite space. This conclusion identifies the limits of a specific spatial reduction. The cubic and smooth proofs use the flat infinite tail, zero bare mass, an integrable scalar self-potential and the stated radial form. The root case uses the additional virial hypotheses just stated. These radial arguments do not apply to the proposed global \mathbb{CP}^3 electron geometry, nonradial polarization patterns, additional same-field interactions or different asymptotic backgrounds. The fixed-sign Fourier argument (13) has its separate nonradial scope. The radial tail proof also does not apply to the nonlocal scalar moment model, whose self-generated quadratic mass profile grows at infinity. The exact massive one-dimensional solution in local scalar normalization provides a positive control: adding m>0 creates a frequency gap and admits decaying profiles. Its fixed-norm frequency is nevertheless a nonlinear function of the contact coefficient. The smooth spatial controls use their specified curved geometry and connections, so their existence is consistent with this flat-space boundary. Generating a self-mass coefficient and finding a viable localized spatial field remain separate requirements of the same proposed dynamics. The positive-current localization theorem gives a separate full-field restriction for the convex matrix-current hierarchy. Its virial and scalar identity retain every coefficient and spinor component, and identify a spatially changing mass-sign projector as a possible contribution outside a fixed positive-current decomposition. Verification local_scalar_profile_checks.py checks (4) against independent Cartesian differentiation with full Clifford matrices and complex rest polarizations, (5) for complex profiles, and (7) by independent Bessel differentiation and determinants. Representative massless radial initial-value solutions have nonzero tail norm density in the U variable. Those finite integrations illustrate the mechanism; the nonexistence result is the argument (5)–(9), not a conclusion drawn from unsuccessful numerical shooting. local_self_mass_localization_checks.py extends the verification to the smooth source bound, complex zero-frequency identity, independent Hölder integrals and illustrative smooth tails. It checks the root profiles by both spatial differences and integration of the actual sign-dependent equation in dimensions 1,2,3,5,6,10. Independent full-profile dilations include scalar sign changes and verify the norm, root energy and general smooth virial. These checks support the displayed analytic proofs with their stated scope.

title: A reciprocal matrix-current source with real uniform frequencies
summary: A reciprocal quartic matrix action has a cumulative-frequency uniform branch and real complete Fourier frequencies, while localization and the physical mode carrier remain open.
text: One conditional quartic action produces the cumulative frequency on a coherent uniform branch and admits a complete analytic test of its spatial linearization. A separate localized calculation is required before that branch can represent a particle. The retained matrix fields in this note are proposed modes of the one field, not additional particles. Their physical spatial origin, occupation and canonical normalization remain inputs to this inverse construction. All spatial derivatives act on ordinary flat R^d, with even d. The coefficient spaces below do not replace these spatial dimensions. Set hbar = c = 1. The full local Dirac principal matrices are Hermitian, and beta anticommutes with every spatial principal matrix. One action and its canonical weights Let the partner rank be r = 2^(d/2), and define F_q(C)^2=qr\operatorname{Tr}(C^2) +(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2, \qquad \mathcal L_q(C)=qrC+(1-q)\operatorname{Tr}(C)I, \quad 0<q\leq1. The identity has the full retained matrix size. The default comparison q = 1/(r+1) gives equal exchange and trace contractions, but invariance alone does not select it. Let R_k be the retained scalar current formed by the existing oscillator splitting isometries, summing target grades N >= k and tracing their discarded spectators. Choose one fixed finite ceiling K. For each k <= K retain a canonical matrix field B_k carrying the same coefficient representation as R_k. Write h_k=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1},\qquad C_k=R_k+\frac{B_k^\dagger\beta B_k}{h_k}, \boxed{U=\sum_{k=0}^{K} \left[\frac{g h_k}{2}F_q(C_k)^2 +m_B\operatorname{Tr}(B_k^\dagger\beta B_k)\right]}, \qquad g>0,\quad m_B>0. \tag{1} Every target and B_k has a unit canonical kinetic coefficient. Equivalently, b_k = B_k/sqrt(h_k) has kinetic weight h_k; that weight must be retained in both its norm and field equation. The m_B term is a common proposed source gap, not a separately chosen particle mass. All interactions in (1) are local matrix-current terms. No independent scalar exchange field or Yukawa coupling has been supplied. Variation of (1) gives the target source by lifting g h_k beta Psi L_q(C_k) through its original splitting map. The normal source is \mathcal N_{B_k}=g\beta B_k\mathcal L_q(C_k)+m_B\beta B_k. \tag{2} The same action therefore determines both responses, including the target self term. Its field source is polynomial and smooth at zero current. This does not prove global regularity of its spatial solutions. The uniform coherent branch Let z be a unit coefficient ray, and let P_z,k project onto z^k. Prepare an upper target at one grade N with scalar density a > 0, and each per-copy normal mode with density b > 0. Then R_k=\frac a r I_r\otimes P_{z,k},\qquad \frac{B_k^\dagger\beta B_k}{h_k} =\frac b r I_r\otimes P_{z,k} \quad (k\leq N). On the occupied ray L_q(C_k) acts as a+b, independently of q. The full phase equations give \boxed{\omega_N=g(a+b)D_N},\qquad D_N=\sum_{k=0}^Nh_k=\binom{N+d}{d}, \qquad \omega_{B_k}=m_B+g(a+b). \tag{3} For k > N, the normal phase is m_B+gb. The unoccupied target equations vanish. Thus the different occupied grades belong to one finite action and the same initial normal preparation. The weighted normal density is b sum_{k=0}^K h_k for all the compared grades. These a and b are uniform local densities, not finite global particle norms. On infinite spatial volume this background has infinite norm. Taking equal positive occupation to infinite coefficient order also has infinite norm independently of spatial volume. Equation (3) does not select the background, its physical carrier, its ceiling or its weights. It proves the Hockey-Stick frequency conditional on them. Complete oscillator sectors outside the occupied ray Choose a coefficient basis with z = e_0. This is a change of mathematical components, not a choice of compact spatial geometry. Give an oscillator monomial of degree n the nonnegative charge j = n - occupation(e_0). Simultaneous phase rotation of every coefficient direction orthogonal to e_0 leaves the action and the prepared state invariant. For the ordinary Hessian A and the conjugate Hessian C, invariance gives [J,A]=0,\qquad JC+CJ=0. \tag{4} All charges are nonnegative, so C has support only at j = 0. The spatial Dirac operator acts on the spinor index and preserves j. Every positive-charge block is consequently an ordinary Hermitian evolution operator, with real Fourier frequencies. This retains the oscillator components outside the coherent ray; it does not discard them. The full partner block has a positive squared-frequency form At j = 0 retain all partner matrices, upper and lower spinors, and both ordinary and conjugate variations. There is one trace block and r^2-1 traceless blocks. Label the canonical species A,B_0,...,B_N, with Q=(a,h_0b,\ldots,h_Nb),\qquad G_{AA}=gD_N,\quad G_{Ak}=G_{kA}=g,\quad G_{kk}=g/h_k, \tag{5} and all other normal cross entries zero. This symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite because x^\dagger Gx=g\sum_k h_k|x_A+x_k/h_k|^2. Define W = diag(m_i + sum_j G_ij Q_j), with m_A = 0 and m_k = m_B, and K = sqrt(Q) G sqrt(Q). In a traceless block replace K by qK. For the trace block the exact identity x^\dagger(W-K)x =\sum_i m_i|x_i|^2 +\frac12\sum_{ij}G_{ij} |\sqrt{Q_j}x_i-\sqrt{Q_i}x_j|^2 \tag{6} shows that V = W-K is strictly positive: every normal gap is positive and every normal species connects to the target. The same conclusion holds for qK with 0 < q <= 1. After a unitary lower-spinor transformation, the squared Fourier frequencies are the eigenvalues of M(p)=\begin{pmatrix} p^2I&-2pW\\ -2pV&p^2I+4W^2 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{7} H = diag(V,W) is positive and HM is Hermitian. More precisely, \begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}^{\!\dagger} HM\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix} =(px-2Wy)^\dagger V(px-2Wy) +y^\dagger(p^2W+4WKW)y. \tag{8} For p != 0 this is strictly positive. All squared frequencies are therefore positive and all Fourier frequencies are real. At p = 0, the phase and density block can have secular phase drift; no exponentially growing mode appears. Equation (8) is not a proof of nonlinear stability, uniform-in-time perturbation bounds, or stability of a nonconstant core. It also works for arbitrary positive h_k, so stability does not derive their binomial values. The complete spatial density response Consider the normal background by itself, driven by a small target scalar density delta sigma_A. Put \omega_0=gb,\qquad \mu=m_B+\omega_0,\qquad \kappa^2=4\mu\omega_0. Eliminating both lower Dirac partners and both conjugate frequency components gives \Delta(\Omega,p)=(\Omega^2-p^2)^2-4\mu^2\Omega^2+\kappa^2p^2, \frac{\delta\sigma_B}{\delta\sigma_A} =-\frac{\kappa^2p^2}{\Delta(\Omega,p)},\qquad \boxed{\frac{\delta(\sigma_A+\sigma_B)}{\delta\sigma_A} =\frac{(\Omega^2-p^2)^2-4\mu^2\Omega^2}{\Delta(\Omega,p)}}. \tag{9} The actual normal poles are real: \Omega_\pm^2=p^2+2\mu^2 \pm2\mu\sqrt{\mu^2+(1-\omega_0/\mu)p^2}. \tag{10} At zero drive frequency and nonzero momentum, (9) reduces to \delta(\sigma_A+\sigma_B) =\frac{p^2}{p^2+\kappa^2}\delta\sigma_A. \tag{11} In position space this is the screened spatial response (-Laplacian)(-Laplacian+kappa^2)^(-1). This operator was derived from the declared Dirac equations. Its static use does not replace the causal time-dependent response (9), introduce particle exchange, or establish a physical IDWT coupling. A local Dirac equation with these smooth sources has finite propagation during smooth existence. At nonzero p the complete source in (9) has zeros at Omega = sqrt(p^2+mu^2) +/- mu. They are cancellations in this specified density channel, not electric neutrality or a neutrino prediction. At p = 0, a conserved uniform normal norm cannot acquire the static density change obtained by first taking Omega = 0 and then p -> 0. These limits do not commute. The unforced lower-state singularity at Omega = 2mu must also be handled using the full equations. The small-momentum response speed is sqrt(omega_0/mu), while the static inverse length is kappa. At fixed omega_0 and m_B, increasing b and decreasing g leaves both unchanged. It reduces the local target correction relative to the background, but does not derive the background or prove that finite-particle coupling survives that limit. Verification and remaining spatial work matrix_hierarchy_checks.py verifies every finite oscillator component, both Hessians, their charge identities, the complete partner decomposition, the positive form, and independent energy and source variations. Its 20260913T204251Z report passes 168 checks through depth-two degree three. matrix_higher_depth_checks.py retains all 8192 complex components at depth six, degree two, without a dense Hessian. All 1041 checks pass in its 20260913T210031Z report, including every zero-charge column. matrix_screening_checks.py verifies the full driven spinor equations and complex susceptibility at depths two and four. Its final 20260913T204516Z report passes 208 checks. These numerical controls support the stated analytic identities; they do not supply the missing physical premises. A nonconstant target makes the local total current vary. Its background must solve its own spatial equation, and its complete energy, canonical norm and inertial response must be retained. The current localized calculation uses the same smooth binding law as the earlier root action and solves for the responding background. That is a separate conditional construction, still requiring independent matrix checks and full stability. Related research Spatial mass operator: results and remaining dynamics — connects this calculation to its premises, later corrections and the complete source question.

title: The linked shape response after geometric normalization
summary: One positive Green-function contraction gives the full endpoint coefficient, whose geometric normalization removes most of its apparent cross-depth suppression and has an explicit Gaussian limit.
text: The linked mass carrier gives different frequencies with nearly equal absolute shape responses within a depth. The coefficient written in its polynomial coordinate also becomes much smaller with increasing depth. Normalizing that coordinate by its actual geometric metric changes the second observation substantially: the normalized coefficient is already within a few percent of one common value across depths 3 through 10. This comparison retains the entire finite wave branch and its spatial normal modes. It uses the stated positive geometric metric, whose physical coefficient remains to be derived from the one field. It does not establish measured interaction strengths or neutrino suppression. One spatial integral replaces the longer source variation Let (p_d,q_d) be the positive radial components of the normalized endpoint normal mode \Phi_0: p_d'=-\frac{a}{2r}p_d-wq_d,\qquad q_d'=\frac{d-1-a/2}{r}q_d-wp_d,\qquad 2\pi\int r(p_d^2+q_d^2)dr=1. \tag{1} Use (U_d,V_d) for the distinct, horizontal geometric zero mode of P=z^d+\alpha, with M_d=2\pi\int r(U_d^2+V_d^2)dr. The metric calculation gives \delta W_h=U_d,\qquad \delta A_h=2V_d\bigl(\sin((d-1)\theta),\cos((d-1)\theta)\bigr). \tag{2} Define h_z(r)=\frac{1+r^2/2}{(1+r^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \left[-\partial_r^2-r^{-1}\partial_r+\frac{a^2}{4r^2}+1\right]Y_d =2h_zp_d. \tag{3} This is the positive-chiral Green inverse associated with the actual bounded multiplier h=z/\sqrt{1+r^2}. It retains both linked coefficients through a,w,p_d,q_d. The operator is at least one; its regular, decaying inverse is positive on this positive source. The constant-polynomial variation of the projected multiplier has one entry, \delta T=\gamma\kappa_d\alpha|0\rangle\langle d-1|. Its coefficient simplifies to \boxed{\kappa_d=-4\pi\int_0^\infty r\,(U_dp_d+V_dq_d)Y_d\,dr.} \tag{4} To obtain (4), use (2) in the complete normal Dirac variation. The positive-chiral component that can contract with D^{-1}h\Phi_{d-1} has radial coefficient U_dp_d+V_dq_d. Every other angular component is orthogonal. Reflection between the two endpoint modes makes the two wave-variation terms equal. The geometric basis phase used in (2) has angular order d, exceeding every difference of retained labels; it has no within-kernel matrix element. Thus the change of basis does not alter the endpoint entry. This also explains its sign in the stated coordinate convention: U_d,V_d,p_d,q_d,Y_d are positive, so \kappa_d<0. Changing the deformation phase changes the corresponding real source; the sign is not an assignment of negative inertia. The metric removes a coordinate dependence If the physical geometric kinetic term were \mathcal T_d M_d|\dot\alpha|^2, with a positive coefficient \mathcal T_d, the canonical real coordinate would be x=\sqrt{2\mathcal T_dM_d}\operatorname{Re}\alpha. The geometric part of its normalized vertex is therefore \boxed{\widehat\kappa_d=\frac{\kappa_d}{\sqrt{M_d}},\qquad g_{N,d}=\frac{\gamma\widehat\kappa_d}{\sqrt{2\mathcal T_d}} \,2\operatorname{Re}(v_0^*u_{d-1}).} \tag{5} Here (u,v) is the complete jointly normalized finite wave branch. The factor \mathcal T_d, spatial units and the surface normalization must be supplied before treating g_{N,d} as a physical vertex. Equation (5) displays those missing units rather than setting them to one without notice. Near the origin, write w=c_0r^d+\cdots. Switching to \tau=c_0\alpha changes \kappa_d to \kappa_d/c_0 and M_d to M_d/c_0^2, leaving \widehat\kappa_d unchanged. An independent adaptive Green solve gives: Depth \kappa_d M_d \widehat\kappa_d 3 -0.3294230571 1.0393860018 -0.3231212806 4 -0.1727356088 0.2956714215 -0.3176707294 5 -0.0802980418 0.06499949738 -0.3149560501 6 -0.03390629545 0.01168935078 -0.3136065656 10 -0.0005298856110 0.000002878106 -0.3123408322 The raw depth-three to depth-ten coefficient ratio is about 622. The metric-normalized ratio is about 1.035. Thus a small raw polynomial coefficient does not establish a weak physical coupling. In this comparison the depth-five entry is also close to the others. The mass-branch grouping within one depth remains: the exact source is \gamma\widehat\kappa_d\,2\operatorname{Re}(v_0^*u_{d-1}), and the last factor approaches a common sign at large hopping. Its finite correction is retained. No division by the particle's mass is used. The Gaussian limit follows from the linked equations The near-constant values have a mathematical explanation. In the following limit, d is the winding of the stated coefficient rule; this is not a proposal for alternative particle assignments. First, 0\le a(r)\le r^2. Integrating the first equation of the linked profile from r to \sqrt d, using w\le1, gives w_d(r)\le\left(\frac{r}{\sqrt d}\right)^d e^{(d-r^2)/2},\qquad r\le\sqrt d, \qquad c_0\le(e/d)^{d/2}. \tag{6} Hence w_d\to0 on every fixed bounded interval and a_d(r)\to r^2. With b_d(r)=w_d/(c_0r^d), integration of b_d'/b_d=-a_d/r gives b_d(r)\longrightarrow e^{-r^2/2}. \tag{7} The stable zero-mode variable Q_d=1-r^df_d is positive, decreases from one to zero, and satisfies -Q_d'(r)=4r^{2d-1}\int_r^\infty s^{1-2d}w_d(s)^2Q_d(s)ds. Bounding w_d^2 by \min(c_0^2s^{2d},1) and splitting the integral at \sqrt d gives, for fixed R<\sqrt d, 0\le1-Q_d(R)\le R^{2d}\left[c_0^2+\frac{d^{-d}}{d-1}\right]\longrightarrow0. \tag{8} The geometric mode in the \tau coordinate therefore has U_d/c_0\to e^{-r^2/2}. Its exact metric identity gives \int(V_d/c_0)^2d^2y \le\frac1d\int(U_d/c_0)^2d^2y. For control of the unbounded domain, monotonicity of a gives b_d(r)\le b_d(R)(R/r)^{a_d(R)} for r\ge R. Taking a fixed sufficiently large R supplies an integrable uniform tail bound. Thus \boxed{M_d/c_0^2\longrightarrow\pi.} \tag{9} For the normal mode, its weighted polarization identity implies \int a_dp_d^2\,d^2y+(d+2)\int q_d^2\,d^2y\le2. \tag{10} The lower component tends to zero in norm. The first term bounds the upper-component tail outside any fixed R by 2/a_d(R). Combining that bound, (1), and unit normalization gives p_d\longrightarrow p_\infty= \frac{e^{-r^2/4}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad q_d\longrightarrow0. \tag{11} The positive Green operators in (3) have lower bound one and converge locally to -\Delta_r+r^2/4+1. Their quadratic forms and the convergent sources select its regular decaying inverse. The preceding tail bounds control the source integral. Equivalently, the limiting Green function solves \left(-\Delta_r+\frac{r^2}{4}+1\right)Y_\infty =2h_zp_\infty. \tag{12} Evaluation of the limiting response Put t=r^2/2. The normalized radial functions p_j=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t/2}L_j(t) diagonalize the operator in (12) with eigenvalues 2(j+1). The Laguerre generating identity is \sum_{j=0}^\infty L_j(t)z^j =\frac1{1-z}\exp\left(-\frac{tz}{1-z}\right),\qquad |z|<1. See NIST DLMF, equation 18.12.13 for this mathematical identity. Expanding (12), using \int_0^\infty e^{-2t}L_j(t)dt=2^{-j-1}, reduces (4) to \lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{\kappa_d}{c_0} =-2\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-t}-e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{1+2t}}dt. \tag{13} One way to perform the sum is to use (j+1)^{-1}=\int_0^1s^jds in the generating function and then note h_z=(1+t)/(1+2t)^{3/2}=\partial_t[t/\sqrt{1+2t}]. All sums occur inside their radius of convergence. Finally, \int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-ut}}{\sqrt{1+2t}}dt =\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2u}}e^{u/2}\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt{u/2}), so (9) and (13) give the closed result \boxed{\lim_{d\to\infty}\widehat\kappa_d =e\operatorname{erfc}(1)-\sqrt{2e}\operatorname{erfc}(1/\sqrt2) =-0.312271559800\ldots.} \tag{14} The limit belongs to this particular bounded multiplier and linked profile. It is not a universal measured coupling constant. Changing the spatial interaction rule would require a new calculation. Verification linked_endpoint_response.py solves the normal mode and positive Green boundary problem independently of the earlier finite-difference source implementation. endpoint_metric_checks.py compares them with the complete linked variation, verifies coordinate invariance, and retains all maintained controls at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 on both surface signs. The bottom entries remain the two component controls of the maintained geometric-mean assignment. The 97-check report also compares the integral and closed form in (14) with an independent spatial solution of (12). Additional winding controls 12, 16, 20 and 24 approach that limit. Outer-domain and profile-tolerance refinements check the largest maintained depth and winding 24 separately. These are mathematical controls, not alternative particle assignments. The source reports and raw radial arrays preserve the executed equations. Neither the metric comparison nor its Gaussian limit supplies the missing same-field physical kinetic coefficient \mathcal T_d, the occupied curved equilibrium, or a complete particle-pair interaction.

title: A scale-response obstruction for the inverse current mass branch
summary: An exact bound excludes a common monotone-elasticity gap law from supplying the shared six-to-ten mass unit on the occupied inverse-current branches, and quantifies the scale-response change that an alternative would require.
text: The finite-chain inverse construction can make the occupied frequency proportional to the simplex product P_d(n)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j)=d!S(n,d) at each spatial depth. Its zero-current reference coefficient is fixed by the finite component chain, rather than by a separately fitted mass for each particle: \mu_d(h)=\frac{1}{(d-1)!\sqrt{Z_d(h)}},\qquad Z_d(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{h^{2j}}{(j!)^2}. \tag{1} Here h=g(R)R/c is the dimensionless reference edge at physical radius R. The proposed frequency unit on an occupied branch is u_d(R)=\frac{c}{R}d!\mu_d(h(R)),\qquad \omega_{n,d}=u_d(R)S(n,d). \tag{2} The inverse current function remains a conditional local design. Its master-field origin, spatial supporting energy and complete stability have not been derived. This note asks which one common positive function g(R) could at least make the reference units stationary and agree between the six-dimensional electron–muon sector and ten-dimensional tau sector. The same function is also tested at the maintained depth-two boson indices. Equal physical gap coefficients across depths are an additional hypothesis of this test; the sector-nesting premise alone does not impose it. Stationary radii and occupied-branch bounds Define the logarithmic falloff of the common edge and the elasticity of the inverse reference unit by \eta(R)=-\frac{d\log g}{d\log R},\qquad q_d(h)=-\frac{d\log\mu_d}{d\log h} =\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}j w_j, \quad w_j=\frac{h^{2j}/(j!)^2}{Z_d(h)}. \tag{3} The weights are positive and sum to one. Consequently 0<q_d(h)<d-1, and dq_d/d\log h=2\operatorname{Var}_w(j)>0. Direct differentiation of (2) gives the exact stationary-radius condition \frac{d\log u_d}{d\log R} =-1+q_d(h)(\eta-1)=0, \qquad \boxed{\eta(R_d)=1+\frac{1}{q_d(h_d)}}. \tag{4} The next derivative, evaluated at a stationary radius, is \frac{d^2\log u_d}{d(\log R)^2} =q_d(h_d)\frac{d\eta}{d\log R} -2\operatorname{Var}_w(j)(\eta-1)^2. \tag{5} A strict local minimum therefore requires positive d\eta/d\log R at that radius. This is a necessary radial condition; it says nothing about angular stress or the complete field–metric Hessian. The causal finite component chain has |\partial_n\epsilon_n|\le1. The inverse branch must therefore obey \mu_d(h)P_d'(n)<1 at every assigned index. The strongest assigned bounds in the relevant sectors are h_2>\sqrt{191^2-1}=190.99738218\quad(n=95),\qquad h_6>53.57003192\quad(n=35),\qquad h_{10}>35.21386344\quad(n=23). \tag{6} These are necessary slope bounds, not existence or stability proofs for the inverse branches. At the ten-dimensional threshold, q_{10}=8.93218749>5, and q_{10} increases with h. Equation (4) thus gives \eta(R_{10})<1.2, whereas \eta(R_6)>1.2 because q_6<5. Similarly \eta(R_2)>2 and \eta(R_6)<2 on its occupied branch. An exact bound for monotone falloff Suppose \eta(R) is nondecreasing with R across the stationary radii. The endpoint inequalities just established force the ordering R_{10}<R_6<R_2. \tag{7} Since \eta(R_{10})=1+1/q_{10}(h_{10})>10/9, integration of d\log h/d\log R=1-\eta between the first two radii gives, with r=R_{10}/R_6<1, \frac{h_{10}}{h_6}\ge r^{-1/9}. \tag{8} The same monotonicity gives \eta>1 between R_6 and R_2, so h_6>h_2>190.99738218. To turn (8) into a frequency bound, factor the highest power from (1): \mu_d(h)=\frac{h^{-(d-1)}}{\sqrt{T_d(h)}},\qquad T_d(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \left[\frac{(d-1)!}{j!}\right]^2h^{-2(d-1-j)}\ge1. \tag{9} Equations (2), (8) and (9) then imply \begin{aligned} \frac{u_{10}}{u_6} &=\frac{5040}{r}\frac{h_6^5}{h_{10}^9} \sqrt{\frac{T_6(h_6)}{T_{10}(h_{10})}}\\ &\le\frac{5040\sqrt{T_6(h_6)}}{h_6^4} <\boxed{3.788522\times10^{-6}}. \end{aligned} \tag{10} The final function decreases with h_6, so the last inequality uses only the depth-two bound (6). Even without depth two, the depth-six bound alone gives u_{10}/u_6<6.146628\times10^{-4}. The benchmark electron and tau masses and maintained counts give (m_\tau/S(23,10))/(m_e/S(13,6))\simeq1.000644. Thus a common gap law with nondecreasing logarithmic falloff cannot supply this cross-depth scale relation within the exact inverse-current reference normalization. The result covers more than one chosen power-law response, but it does not exclude a different common operator, a depth-dependent geometric conversion, or a nonmonotone supporting law. What a different common scale response would require For any common law with R_{10}<R_6, define its mean falloff on that interval by \bar\eta=\frac{1}{\log(R_6/R_{10})} \int_{R_{10}}^{R_6}\eta(R)\,d\log R. \tag{11} The exact ratio in (10), with T_{10}\ge1, shows that matching a target ratio U=u_{10}/u_6 requires \boxed{\bar\eta\le\frac{10}{9} +\frac{\log\!\left[ 5040\sqrt{T_6(h_6)}/(U h_6^4)\right]} {9\log(R_6/R_{10})}.} \tag{12} At the illustrative radius ratio R_{10}/R_6=0.2, the occupied depth-six bound limits \bar\eta to about 0.6006, and including depth two limits it to about 0.2492, for the stated benchmark U. These are necessary conditions, not a constructed supporting law. If instead \eta\ge1 throughout the interval, matching that benchmark requires R_{10}/R_6<3.7861\times10^{-6} when depth two is included. The stationary endpoints have \eta(R_{10})>10/9 and \eta(R_6)>1.2, while (12) demands a mean below 10/9 at every finite radius ratio. A smooth successful common law with these ordered radii must dip below 10/9 between them. If both stationary radii are strict local minima, (5) makes \eta rise locally at both endpoints. The intervening dip then requires at least one local maximum and one local minimum of \eta. Deriving such scale dependence from one stable same-field action is a specific remaining task. Positive power sums as candidate scale laws Two common ways to build a positive reference edge from scale-homogeneous terms have opposite, exact effects on the radial curvature. First take a direct positive sum, g(R)=g_0\sum_i a_i(R/R_0)^{-p_i},\qquad a_i>0. The weights of its terms are positive and normalized. Differentiating their weighted mean gives \eta=\sum_iw_ip_i and d\eta/d\log R=-\operatorname{Var}_w(p_i)\le0. Equation (5) is then strictly negative at every finite-gap stationary unit, because \operatorname{Var}_w(j)>0 and \eta-1>0 there. This entire additive positive-power class has only radial maxima, regardless of how many positive terms are added. Now take the reciprocal of a positive stiffness sum, g(R)=\frac{g_0}{\sum_i a_i(R/R_0)^{p_i}},\qquad a_i>0. Its weighted mean has d\eta/d\log R=+\operatorname{Var}_w(p_i)\ge0. It can create a radial local minimum if the positive first term in (5) exceeds the spectral variance term. It then falls under the cross-depth bound (10), independently of how many positive powers are included. A single stable response with a positive power-sum stiffness and a radius-independent linear source would have this reciprocal scale form after elimination, but that reduction is only a conditional model: the same-field origin and current dependence must still be derived. If its coupling to the current is affine, the eliminated response additionally has nonpositive current curvature, the opposite sign from the required convex inverse-current correction. The positive-sum batch checks three representative shared laws at two strengths across all six maintained depths. Its selected report contains 60 stationary points: 12 additive-gap maxima and 24 local minima plus 24 outer maxima for two reciprocal-stiffness examples. At the occupied-branch strength \gamma=5000, the reciprocal examples give ten-to-six unit ratios about 3.03\times10^{-10} and 1.01\times10^{-10}. The analytic variance identities, rather than this finite scan, establish the class restrictions. More generally, suppose a retained source and a stable stiffness give g(R)=J(R)/D(R), where both J and D are positive sums of radius powers. Their exponent distributions obey \eta=\langle p\rangle_D-\langle s\rangle_J, \qquad \frac{d\eta}{d\log R} =\operatorname{Var}_D(p)-\operatorname{Var}_J(s), where p and s are the denominator and numerator exponents. To produce the required dip, the numerator variance must exceed the denominator variance somewhere; at each selected strict radial minimum, equation (5) requires the denominator variance to dominate by the positive spectral threshold. This specifies a multi-scale source structure, but does not provide its field origin. With only affine current coupling to a stable eliminated amplitude, its Schur contribution remains concave in the current, so a separate direct convex current invariant is still required. A nonmonotone control and its competing branch The obstruction depends on monotonicity. To test its scope with one common law across all six maintained depths, consider the positive but nonmonotone reference edge g(R)=g_0\frac{[1+(R/10R_0)^4]^{B/4}} {[1+(R/R_0)^4]^{1.15/4} [1+(R/CR_0)^4]^{(B+1.2)/4}}. The three transitions, at R_0, 10R_0 and CR_0, make \eta(R) rise, dip and rise again. This is an inverse diagnostic, not a field-derived supporting law. For each stated trial choice of C and depth-two reference gap, the common amplitude \gamma=g_0R_0/c is set by that gap at its radial minimum, then one common shape parameter B is fitted to the benchmark u_{10}/u_6\simeq1.000644. No parameter is assigned to an individual mode. The six-depth fit finds: h_2 C B \gamma R_{10}/R_6 h_{10} Minimum \eta between radii Outer depth-ten unit / depth-six unit 220 30 1.987234 91.5040 0.070617 79.571 −0.3357 7.80\times10^{-7} 500 30 2.355061 144.560 0.068637 125.563 −0.6279 3.00\times10^{-8} 500 100 1.072244 165.062 0.023820 143.867 0.1086 2.62\times10^{-8} The selected report records the stationary radius and gap at every depth. All selected radii are strict local minima of the reference frequency unit, and every assigned mode passes the necessary singular-slope bound. Direct high-precision singular-matrix roots exist at all 16 assigned modes; sampled intermediate points retain decreasing edge and current, as required for a convex inverse density on those samples. This verifies discrete inverse-branch feasibility more strongly than the slope bound, but it does not prove regularity or stability on the whole interval. The first two trial shapes make g rise with radius across part of the interval. The third keeps g strictly decreasing everywhere: for B<1.15 and C>10, its first positive sigmoid in \eta is at least the middle sigmoid, so 1.15\sigma(R/R_0)-B\sigma(R/10R_0)>0, where \sigma(y)=y^4/(1+y^4); the final term is also positive. Thus a negative \eta is a feature of the first two fits, not a general requirement of the cross-depth unit match. The third uses a wider separation between its positive scale transitions.
