Its \eta has a local maximum at 3.191R_0 and a local minimum at 28.733R_0, satisfying the two-turning-point requirement from the stationary-frequency calculation. The fit also produces two local depth-ten minima. The small-radius minimum carries the fitted frequency unit, while the outer minimum has the far smaller unit shown in the table. The frequency curve alone has no rule selecting the inner branch. Its outer barrier is also not a complete particle energy barrier: the supporting field's energy and metric stress remain absent. The fitted equality is therefore an existence control within the inverse reference equations, not a prediction of the observed tau mass. The first fit exposes a further spatial constraint. At h_2=220, the 36-case depth-two form scan finds no resolved growth for n=76,81, but all 12 finite electric and quadrature controls at n=95 have growth around 0.862 times the particle frequency. The value is stable across angular cutoffs two, four and six and two azimuth shifts. Positive projected Hessian eigenvalues in those cases do not remove the gyroscopic growth. A one-channel gap scan places its disappearance between h_2=220 and 240 for the electric, shift-one, cutoff-six control. That scan does not establish the exact boundary for all spatial perturbations. For both fits at h_2=500, the existing 36-case exact depth-two scan already tests the same inverse-current field state at that gap and passes its finite form controls. The new radius law does not alter that fixed-metric matrix, but its own field–metric variations have not been included. The nonmonotone fit still needs a master-field source, a selection rule among its radii, compatible nested spatial states, positive complete joint stability and physical inertial normalization. A positive rational scale control The logarithmic falloff can have the required two turning points with ordinary positive power sums, without the fractional exponents in the preceding example. Take one shared reference law \boxed{\frac{g(R)}{g_0} =\frac{1+(R/bR_0)^4} {[1+(R/R_0)^4][1+(R/CR_0)^4]}.} Its logarithmic falloff is \eta=4[\sigma(R/R_0)-\sigma(R/bR_0)+\sigma(R/CR_0)], where \sigma(y)=y^4/(1+y^4). Since 1<b<C, the first difference and final term are strictly positive: g(R) decreases at every positive radius. The first bump can place the depth-ten stationary minimum before the middle dip, while depths two through six use the later rise. This is one function across all depths. When the outer transition is well separated, that first bump peaks at 4\tanh(\log b). Choosing b=1.34 puts its peak near 1.138, between the occupied depth-ten stationary falloff near 1.111 and the depth-six value above 1.2. This explains the separate radius branches but is still an inverse choice. In the rational-law batch, set b=1.34, fix the depth-two gap at h_2=500, and fit the common outer scale C to the benchmark six-to-ten unit ratio. The resulting C=18.00753138 and \gamma=179.0387654 give R_{10}/R_6=0.07325, h_{10}=116.6397, and u_{10}/u_6=1.00064435538. All six selected radii are local minima; the exact inverse singular-matrix roots exist at every assigned mode and sampled intermediate points. The two falloff turning points occur at 1.1576R_0 and 4.6846R_0, with the latter at \eta=0.03655>0. The full values and source hashes are in the selected report. The four-point robustness batch varies b from 1.332 to 1.36, refitting only C each time. All four retain the local six-depth reference checks and two depth-ten minima; C ranges from 17.740 to 18.734. This algebraic law is simpler than the previous fractional-power trial and identifies a concrete source-to-stiffness shape: J=1+(R/bR_0)^4 and D=[1+(R/R_0)^4][1+(R/CR_0)^4]. No master-field reduction has produced these functions or the required direct convex current interaction. The inner depth-ten unit still competes with an outer local minimum whose unit relative to depth six is 4.84\times10^{-8}; its selection and supporting energy remain unresolved. Matching the benchmark by fitting C is a conditional existence test, not a mass prediction. For this rational law g(R)\sim R^{-4} at large radius, so h(R)\to0 and u_d(R)\sim cd/R\to0. Its local minima are not global radial binding states without the complete supporting energy. Constraint from projecting a scalar master contact The proposed scalar master contact offers a direct action-level test. Suppose a fixed linear, canonically normalized map P_{\rm sec} embeds a sector field \psi into one master field, with no nonzero background and no eliminated dynamical modes. A pure scalar contact U_4[\Psi]\propto\int(\bar\Psi\Psi)^2 remains fourth-order after that projection: U_4[P_{\rm sec}(t\psi)]=t^4U_4[P_{\rm sec}\psi]. The inverse-current generating density used here instead obeys U_2[\psi]=\int\rho f(j/\rho),\quad \rho=\psi^\dagger\psi,\quad j=\psi^\dagger K\psi, \qquad U_2[t\psi]=t^2U_2[\psi]. These nonzero functionals cannot agree on an open amplitude cone. Linear projection of that pure quartic contact therefore does not produce this quadratic-homogeneous inverse mass current by itself. A fixed norm, a nonzero same-field background, a nonlinear reduction, or another master invariant can change the effective degree; each must enter the actual action and kinetic normalization rather than being identified with the required interaction after the fact. For example, writing \Psi=\Psi_0+P_{\rm sec}\psi inside the quartic contact produces a quadratic term proportional to J_0J_\psi+2[\operatorname{Re}(\bar\Psi_0P_{\rm sec}\psi)]^2, where J_0=\bar\Psi_0\Psi_0 and J_\psi=\overline{P_{\rm sec}\psi}P_{\rm sec}\psi. The background can supply a linearized operator, but its fixed quadratic term cannot by itself reproduce the nonlinear function f(j/\rho) across an occupied band. A same-field reduction that does produce it must also account for the background phase response, the omitted higher terms and the positive current curvature. This is a restriction on the stated pure-contact linear-projection route, not on every possible master interaction. A minimal retained-amplitude calculation makes the needed direct term explicit. At fixed positive local field density \rho, let \rho U(x,k;R) be a candidate generating energy density, where x is a dimensionless real ratio of retained components of that same field. This homogeneous form is an additional premise. With D(R)>0, write the energy per unit density near the reference as U(x,k;R)=\tfrac12D(R)x^2-J(R)x+b xk+F(k;R). Eliminating only this amplitude gives x_*(k,R)=\frac{J(R)-bk}{D(R)},\qquad U_{\rm eff}(k;R)=F(k;R)-\frac{[J(R)-bk]^2}{2D(R)}, \qquad \boxed{\partial_k^2U_{\rm eff}=F_{kk}-\frac{b^2}{D}.} At zero current the background supplies a reference edge F_k(0;R)+bJ(R)/D(R). Choosing a multi-scale source-to-stiffness ratio can make that edge's logarithmic falloff nonmonotone, but stability of the eliminated amplitude subtracts b^2/D from the needed positive inverse-current curvature at fixed \rho. The master action must therefore supply a direct F_{kk}>b^2/D on the occupied branch, as well as a geometric source and kinetic normalization for x. The exact inverse normalization also has f(0;R)=0. This reduction would require the separate value condition F(0;R)=J(R)^2/[2D(R)], in addition to its slope and curvature conditions. Otherwise the retained background adds a scalar frequency offset and spoils the fixed simplex unit. That counterterm and the background's radial energy cannot be inferred from the fitted gap coefficient alone. This calculation does not identify an available x,J,D,F in \Psi_\infty; it is an exact requirement on such a proposed reduction. A separate lead for the nonlinear current power The earlier approximate current correction has power p_d=1+2/d. A simple phase-space minimization reproduces that exponent without reproducing its normalization. For occupation 0\le v(p)\le1 of momentum states in d ordinary spatial directions, minimize the kinetic moment at fixed number density: Q=(2\pi)^{-d}\int v(p)\,d^dp, \qquad T=(2\pi)^{-d}\int |p|^2v(p)\,d^dp. \tag{13} Exchanging an occupied larger momentum with an empty smaller momentum lowers T, so the minimizer fills a ball |p|\le p_F. With V_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2+1), direct integration gives Q=\frac{V_dp_F^d}{(2\pi)^d},\qquad \boxed{T=A_d Q^{1+2/d}},\qquad A_d=\frac{d}{d+2}(2\pi)^2V_d^{-2/d}. \tag{14} For depths 2,3,4,5,6,10, the coefficient A_d in these canonical momentum units is respectively about 6.283,9.116,11.848,14.512,17.126,27.281. The inverse-current leading coefficients (d-1)^{-(1+2/d)} are respectively 1,0.31498,0.19245,0.14359,0.11696,0.07160. This shows that the power alone is not a normalization derivation. The IDWT component current k has not been identified with the occupation density Q, and a filled many-state momentum ball is an added physical premise. A field projection and kinetic normalization would have to supply that identification and its coefficient before this lead could be used as a mass interaction. Reproducible comparison The radius-law batch evaluates local stationary radii for one bounded g(R) at every maintained depth. Its selected report contains 120 depth cases and 20 complete six-depth comparisons. The scale-bound and kinetic batch computes the exact thresholds and bound above, scans 14 additional shared powers at the depth-two necessary boundary, and compares all six kinetic coefficients. Its selected report records the inputs, checks and source hash. For bounded laws g(R)=g_0/[1+(R/R_0)^q], the boundary scan runs from q=2.0001 to 1000; its largest sampled ten-to-six unit ratio is 3.77982\times10^{-6}. The formal step-response limit is (10/6)\sqrt{Z_6(h_2)/Z_{10}(h_2)} =3.78431\times10^{-6} at the necessary depth-two gap boundary. The finite scan illustrates (10); the proof does not depend on its resolution. Neither calculation derives the scale law or proves a complete supported particle state.

title: Moving support, nearby frequency zeros and the simplex branch
summary: A complex shape direction produces a nearby zero of the complete separated carrier; a positive local dynamical completion has stable periodic motion but loses the simplex index unless an additional selection law is supplied.
text: A continuously moving supporting pattern is a legitimate alternative to a frozen spatial profile. The question is whether its equations preserve the selected mass-frequency. The completed radial operator gives enough information to make a precise local test. Two results follow. First, the small wave frequency can be taken to zero by an exceptionally small allowed complex shape deformation. Second, a positive dynamical model of that deformation admits bounded periodic motion, but its frequency is determined by an additional conserved orbit action. The original simplex coefficient becomes a displacement of the orbit center. This model therefore does not select the particle masses. The first result concerns the complete infinite normal plane at one fixed surface eigenvalue. The second is an explicitly specified local effective action. Neither is a solution of the full curved particle, a prediction of zero particle inertia, or a derivation of an additional interaction field. All mode coordinates describe patterns of the same proposed field. Mass continues to mean the selected particle frequency in equivalent units. A complex deformation can close the full normal frequency gap Use the bounded completed carrier, scaled by its normal frequency unit: \mathcal H(\epsilon,\alpha) =A_g(\alpha)+\epsilon B(\alpha)+\epsilon^2 C_2(\alpha), \qquad \epsilon=\Lambda^{-1}. \tag{1} Here \alpha=\alpha_d is the actual complex centered polynomial deformation. Its two real components include the orientation of the spatial pattern. The scalar, connection and curvature coefficients vary together. A smooth local choice of their component frame is required; the frame audit specifies that requirement. At (\epsilon,\alpha)=(0,0), let P project onto the two normalized endpoint zero modes, and let Q=I-P. The complementary operator is invertible under the already verified gap conditions. Define the exact zero-energy Schur operator using the fixed reference projection: F(\epsilon,\alpha)=P\mathcal HP -P\mathcal HQ(Q\mathcal HQ)^{-1}Q\mathcal HP. \tag{2} Self-adjointness and chiral symmetry give F=\begin{pmatrix}0&\overline{f}\\ f&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} At the radial shape, angular selection and the completed radial chain give f(\epsilon,0)=a_{n,d}\epsilon^d+O(\epsilon^{d+2}), \qquad a_{n,d}=\frac{F_d(g)}{g^{d-1}} \prod_{l=0}^{d-1}(n+l). \tag{4} At the origin of this expansion, \mathcal HP=0, so the first shape derivative of the Schur correction vanishes. The complete radial endpoint calculation therefore gives \partial_{\operatorname{Re}\alpha}f(0,0)=g\kappa_d(g), \qquad \partial_{\operatorname{Im}\alpha}f(0,0)=ig\kappa_d(g). \tag{5} The coefficient \kappa_d(g) includes the texture and connection derivatives as well as the curvature derivative. It is nonzero at every maintained depth for the verified g=0.02,0.05. Consequently the real Jacobian of (\operatorname{Re}f,\operatorname{Im}f) with respect to the two shape coordinates is invertible. Assume the regular linked profiles define a smooth bounded-coefficient family in this local chart, with the complementary gap retained. The real implicit-function theorem gives a unique nearby shape \alpha_*(\epsilon) satisfying f(\epsilon,\alpha_*)=0. Its leading displacement is \boxed{ \alpha_*=-\frac{F_d(g)}{g^d\kappa_d(g)} \prod_{l=0}^{d-1}(n+l)\,\epsilon^d +O(\epsilon^{d+1}) =-\frac{F_d(g)}{\kappa_d(g)\gamma^d} \prod_{l=0}^{d-1}(n+l)+O(\epsilon^{d+1}), } \tag{6} where \gamma=g\Lambda. The expansion fixes d,g,n while \Lambda grows. It is not a uniform statement for arbitrarily large particle index. At this shape the exact Schur matrix is zero. The two corresponding full normal eigenfields are recovered with their complementary components: \psi=p-(Q\mathcal HQ)^{-1}Q\mathcal HPp, \qquad p\in\operatorname{ran}P. \tag{7} Thus this is a nearby zero of the complete separated spatial operator, rather than only a cancellation in its finite kernel compression. The theorem is local and asymptotic; the numerical coefficients used below are refined approximations, not interval-certified existence radii. Additional frame-transport terms that vanish at the radial reference and enter at order \epsilon leave (5) and the leading displacement (6) unchanged. This zero is a zero of the candidate wave frequency. The geometric support still has its own energy and stress. It is not a massless particle solution and does not identify a photon. How small is the required change of shape? In units where time is measured in R/c, write the leading endpoint coupling as t_{n,d}+s_d\alpha,\qquad t_{n,d}=\frac{F_d(g)}{\gamma^{d-1}}\prod_{l=0}^{d-1}(n+l), \qquad s_d=\gamma\kappa_d(g). \tag{8} The local frequency is its magnitude. The norm of a small geometric deformation is \sqrt{M_d}|\alpha|, with the actual horizontal metric M_d already computed from the spatial fields. At the same illustrative g=0.02,\gamma=10^7 used for the spectral bound, the leading norm of (6) is: Depth and reference mode \sqrt{M_d}|\alpha_*| 2, W 2.22\times10^{-10} 3, down 1.87\times10^{-20} 4, up 7.06\times10^{-26} 5, first neutrino 2.50\times10^{-30} 6, electron 6.48\times10^{-36} 10, tau 2.36\times10^{-58} These are dimensionless distances in the specified shape coordinate, not particle radii. The values illustrate sensitivity of a very small frequency produced by the angular chain. Improving the large-separation spectral approximation also increases this sensitivity. The same cavity radius can be retained during these deformations. Consequently common size alone does not protect the internal frequency pattern. A common displacement at one depth changes the leading complex couplings additively by s_d\alpha; it does not merely rescale their shared frequency unit. A phase perpendicular to the original coupling removes the first real frequency derivative, but both real deformation directions remain available in (5). An independent finite-carrier check makes the mechanism transparent. For diagonal entries n+l, adjacent entries \gamma h_l, and the projected endpoint derivative \gamma\kappa_{\rm proj}\alpha, T(\alpha)=T(0)+\gamma\kappa_{\rm proj}\alpha|0\rangle\langle d-1|, \qquad \det T(\alpha)=\prod_l(n+l) +(-1)^{d-1}\gamma^d\kappa_{\rm proj}\alpha\prod_lh_l. \tag{9} Here \kappa_{\rm proj} belongs to the finite normal-kernel compression; it is distinct from the fully dressed \kappa_d(g) in (5). The exact zero and its complete null vector are verified with 110-digit arithmetic for every maintained index and both surface signs. Equation (9) checks a finite operator; the infinite-radial statement follows from (2)-(7), not from a finite numerical cutoff. A positive moving-support action Rephase the endpoint and shape coordinates once at a depth so the reference frequency is t>0 and the source coefficient is s>0. Let \mathcal M>0 be a constant local geometric kinetic coefficient, and retain both complex wave polarizations c\in\mathbb C^2. An explicit local inverse action is \boxed{ L=\mathcal M|\dot\alpha|^2+\|\dot c\|^2 -|t+s\alpha|^2\|c\|^2-E_0. } \tag{10} The constant E_0 denotes the supporting energy in this flat-modulus comparison. Equation (10) retains a positive kinetic term, positive wave energy and arbitrary complex polarization. It assumes constant local metrics and the leading endpoint potential. It is not yet a controlled reduction of the entire moving spatial action. Moving-basis terms, nonlinear metric changes and the complementary field must be included before making that stronger claim. Set u=\alpha+t/s. The complete Euler equations of (10) are \mathcal M\ddot u=-s^2\|c\|^2u, \qquad \ddot c=-s^2|u|^2c. \tag{11} They possess exact solutions u=b e^{i\Omega t_{\rm time}},\qquad c=A\zeta e^{-i\omega t_{\rm time}},\qquad \|\zeta\|=1, \qquad \boxed{\omega=sb,\quad \Omega^2=s^2A^2/\mathcal M.} \tag{12} The symbol t_{\rm time} in (12) is time; t elsewhere in this section is the reference coupling in (10). The wave oscillation and the shape motion are both retained. The arbitrary constant complex vector \zeta includes the full wave polarization, not just a real ray. The positive wave phase charge and the orbit action are \mathcal Q=2\omega A^2, \qquad \mathcal J=2\mathcal M b^2\Omega. \tag{13} The latter is the conserved phase action for rotation of u in this local model. It has not been identified with the physical angular momentum of the full particle. That identification needs the actual spatial rotation law and its complete supporting field. Eliminating A,b,\Omega gives \boxed{\omega^3=\frac{s^2\mathcal J^2}{2\mathcal M\mathcal Q}, \qquad E-E_0=\frac32\mathcal Q\omega.} \tag{14} The supporting kinetic energy is \mathcal Q\omega/2, in addition to the wave's \mathcal Q\omega. No negative inertia was introduced to obtain this motion. A universal numerical factor in energy might be addressed by a derived common normalization; it must not be silently discarded. The constant supporting energy also remains part of the full particle calculation. The periodic motion has a positive stability bound Use dimensionless time \tau=t\,t_{\rm time}, displacement u=(t/s)z, and c=\sqrt{\mathcal Q/(2t)}v. Dividing the nonconstant Lagrangian by \mathcal Q t/2 gives \widehat L=\mu|z'|^2+\|v'\|^2-|z|^2\|v\|^2, \qquad \mu=\frac{2\mathcal M t^3}{\mathcal Qs^2}. \tag{15} The corresponding action is (\mathcal Q/2)\int\widehat L\,d\tau. The conserved dimensionless charges are q=-\operatorname{Im}(v^\dagger v') and j=\mu\operatorname{Im}(\bar z z'). The chosen positive-frequency wave normalization gives q=1. For arbitrary complex polarization, Cauchy's inequality and the two conserved charges give, with a=\|v\|, b=|z|, \widehat E\ge\frac{q^2}{a^2}+\frac{j^2}{\mu b^2}+a^2b^2 \ge\boxed{3(q^2j^2/\mu)^{1/3}}. \tag{16} The second inequality is the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Equality occurs at the circular solutions. For nonzero q,j, this effective potential also bounds both amplitudes away from zero and infinity at finite energy. At q=1, equilibrium has b=(j^2/\mu)^{1/3} and a=b^{-1/2}. The radial Hessian is \begin{pmatrix}8b^2&4\sqrt b\\4\sqrt b&8/b\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det=48b>0. \tag{17} Thus the orbit minimizes energy at its fixed charges, modulo its phase and polarization symmetries. Independent time integrations retain both polarizations, recover the exact solutions and conserve their charges. Nearby amplitude perturbations stay near the orbit in the tested local system. This is a stability result for (10), not for unspecified spatial or complementary modes. The bare moving model loses the particle index The translation u=\alpha+t/s removes t from (11) exactly. At one common s,\mathcal M,\mathcal Q,\mathcal J, every particle index therefore has the same frequency (14). To reproduce the prescribed simplex frequency by these orbits, their actions would have to obey \boxed{\frac{\mathcal J_n}{\mathcal J_{n_0}} =\left[\frac{S(n,d)}{S(n_0,d)}\right]^{3/2}.} \tag{18} No equation in (10) selects (18). For example, the required muon/electron orbit-action ratio is about 2.97\times10^3; the top/up ratio is about 2.31\times10^7. These are required inputs to match the frequencies, not derived predictions. The wave amplitudes in (12) merely implement the declared common phase normalization. On the full coordinate plane of this local model, the corresponding Hamiltonians at different t are related by a unitary translation of \alpha. Their quantum spectra would therefore also be identical under translated domains. Quantizing the same flat local action does not recover the missing index. Physical restrictions on the shape domain or additional metric and energy terms can break that equivalence, but must be derived rather than inserted as a separate frequency fit. Starting at the radial reference with the geometry momentarily still also fails to produce the circular solution automatically. The direct integrations retain the wave's initial oscillation and show substantial subsequent changes of the instantaneous endpoint gap. An instantaneous gap during that motion is not automatically the frequency of a persistent particle state. The available curvature stiffness is insufficient in its tested regime The ordinary tube calculation supplies an optimistic harmonic pinning term for this centered deformation. In the same R/c time units, let x=\sqrt{M_d}\alpha and E_0 be the bare geometric energy. Its leading coefficient is E_{\rm pin}=K_x|x|^2, \qquad \frac{K_x}{E_0}=\frac{A_d}{2\pi d\Lambda^2}, \qquad A_d=\frac{d(d-2)(d-3)}2. \tag{19} This follows by integrating the same geometric density and kinetic metric over the round feature. It is not an independently chosen spring. At depths two and three this leading coefficient vanishes. At higher depths the other curved shape forces remain; ignoring them here makes the single-direction test favorable to this pinning mechanism. Write s_x=\gamma|\kappa_d|/\sqrt{M_d}. In the positive branch, minimizing K_x|x|^2+\mathcal Q|t+s_xx| gives x_*=-\frac{\mathcal Qs_x}{2K_x},\qquad \omega=t-\frac{\mathcal Qs_x^2}{2K_x}, \tag{20} provided this frequency stays positive. The shift is additive and common at a depth, rather than proportional to the simplex count. Requiring a fractional shift no larger than \delta yields the necessary bound \boxed{ \frac{E_0}{\mathcal Q t}\ge \frac{\pi d\Lambda^2\gamma^2|\kappa_d|^2} {M_d A_d\delta t^2}.} \tag{21} For g=0.02,\gamma=10^7,\delta=10^{-3}, the leading bound is approximately 1.57\times10^{71} for the up reference, 4.21\times10^{79} for the first neutrino, 3.12\times10^{90} for the electron and 5.03\times10^{134} for the tau. These are conditional ratios in this particular large-separation pinning model, not physical energies. The calculation also checks a smaller separation. It does not establish that every possible same-field support has this cost. Increasing the coefficient of this bare positive geometric action can hold the shape more tightly, but its energy must then be counted. It cannot be used as cost-free rigidity while mass is read from the small wave frequency. The complete common-radius pressure test remains an additional condition. The same positive action also constrains the motion's time scale The geometric kinetic coefficient in (10) is not independent of its background energy if both come from the declared positive geometric action. Restore normal length L, feature radius R, and \Lambda=R/L. Static normal gradients scale as L^{-1}, while derivatives with respect to the chosen time coordinate scale as R^{-1}. The same horizontal metric therefore gives, to leading order in the tube expansion, \boxed{\mathcal M= \frac{E_0M_d}{2\pi d\Lambda^2}.} \tag{22} The common geometric coefficient and feature volume cancel in this ratio. The temporal connection constraint is already included in M_d. Equation (22) applies to this specified geometric action and reference profile, not to an arbitrary unknown master-field reduction. Consider the circular orbit that would retain \omega=t, and set e_0=E_0/(\mathcal Q t). Equations (12), (13) and (22) give \Omega=\frac{\gamma|\kappa_d|\Lambda}{t} \sqrt{\frac{\pi d}{e_0M_d}}. \tag{23} The leading normal operator has interior modes with frequency at most \Lambda g\sqrt d: they descend from the original normal kernel, and the perturbation has norm at most g\sqrt d. The gap conditions ensure that these modes remain in the isolated cluster. Thus a local moving-profile approximation cannot obtain separation from every retained normal frequency unless, at minimum, \frac{\Omega}{\Lambda g\sqrt d}\le\eta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\frac{E_0}{\mathcal Q t}\ge \frac{\pi\Lambda^2|\kappa_d|^2} {M_d\eta^2t^2}.} \tag{24} Here \eta<1 is the chosen separation tolerance. This is a necessary condition relative to the leading normal carrier, not a sufficient adiabatic estimate or a full finite-scale evolution theorem. With g=0.02,\gamma=10^7,\eta=0.1, the required ratio already exceeds 10^{25} for the depth-two reference and grows much larger at higher depth. Both couplings and both separations used above are checked. Consequently the stable local orbits cannot currently be promoted to controlled moving spatial solutions at a supporting energy comparable to the selected wave frequency. Making the geometric inertia sufficiently large also increases its positive energy. An exact rapid solution could evade the need for an adiabatic approximation, as the separately derived null pulses illustrate, but that would require solving its complementary spatial fields. Equation (24) does not exclude such solutions. What the calculation establishes The later periodic endpoint and temporal-frame calculation identifies a different moving possibility. A perpendicular periodic deformation preserves the leading simplex ratios through one common multiplier, with a uniform analytic error bound. Its reciprocal force still has a nonzero static component and higher temporal harmonics. Exact temporal transport can preserve all frequencies in a stated positive inverse action, but its physical connection and supporting energy remain to be derived. These results extend the moving test without turning the flat local action above into a frequency-selecting particle solution. The completed radial mass polynomial remains a valid conditional spectral result. Its nearby allowed shape zero is now explicit. Positive periodic support is possible in a stated local action, but does not by itself retain that polynomial as a selected spectrum. Ordinary curvature pinning has a quantified energy limitation in the same regime. The next supporting law must therefore preserve the relevant spatial spectrum under its own motion, with the actual component frame, complete energy and common normalization retained. This is a requirement on the joint same-field action, beyond merely choosing a cavity radius. Verification moving_endpoint_support_checks.py passes 222 checks: symbolic Euler equations, arbitrary complex-polarization energy bounds, exact and perturbed time integrations, conserved charges, and the maintained cross-depth coefficients. Its moving-support report retains the trajectories and their exact source references. endpoint_gap_closure_checks.py passes 484 checks of the exact finite determinant, complete null vectors, the complex Jacobian and the curvature-pinning estimate. Its gap-closure report identifies the complete radial input report and raw spatial coefficients. support_time_scale_checks.py passes 129 independent symbolic and numerical checks of (22)-(24), including all maintained particle indices. Its time-scale report preserves the positive-energy normalization and the restricted scope of the frequency-separation condition.

title: Canonical response of the actual moving normal modes
summary: Positive spatial Green contractions give the moving normal basis contribution to the canonical curvature, including all centered deformations and exact translation and phase controls.
text: A spatial eigenbasis changes when its supporting geometry changes. The canonical response therefore contains more than the change of the finite carrier's eigenvectors. The missing contribution can be computed from the actual normal modes and their complementary spatial inverses, without introducing a fitted kinetic coefficient. This calculation uses the ordinary unbounded normal plane, the linked geometry and both the original and geometric carriers at depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. It supplies a wave-induced geometric curvature. Its sign is not a sign of particle inertia. The orthogonal spatial derivative Let D\Phi_l=0, with an isolated chiral kernel and orthonormal modes \Phi_l. Transport them locally with \langle\Phi_i,\partial_a\Phi_j\rangle=0 at the reference point. Differentiating the kernel equation gives \boxed{\partial_a\Phi_l=-D^{-1}(I-P)(\partial_aD)\Phi_l.} \tag{1} The inverse acts only off the kernel. Since \partial_aD changes chirality, its source lies in the positive channel. The diagonal positive square L_+ in the common carrier gives \langle\partial_a\Phi_l,\partial_b\Phi_m\rangle =\langle(\partial_aD)\Phi_l,L_+^{-1}(\partial_bD)\Phi_m\rangle. \tag{2} This avoids differentiating a numerical eigenbasis. It retains the full spatial complement through its regular, decaying Green solutions. Use P(z)=z^d+\alpha_kz^{d-k}, \alpha_k=x_k+i y_k, and the polynomial gauge of the linked deformation. Write \partial_{x_k}u=f_k(r)\cos k\theta, and let U_l,V_l be the carrier's real normalized radial modes. For D=D_{t,e}, its real derivative has two positive-chiral sources, with angular labels j=l+k and j=l-k: \begin{aligned} b^+_0&=tw(r^{-k}-f_k/2)U_l +(e+1/2)(f_k'+kf_k/r)V_l/2,\\ b^+_1&=twf_kV_l/2+(e-1/2)(f_k'-kf_k/r)U_l/2,\\ b^-_0&=-twf_kU_l/2+(e+1/2)(f_k'-kf_k/r)V_l/2,\\ b^-_1&=-tw(r^{-k}-f_k/2)V_l +(e-1/2)(f_k'+kf_k/r)U_l/2. \end{aligned} \tag{3} Their spinor components are (b_0e^{i(j-d)\theta},0,0,i b_1e^{i(j+1)\theta})^T. The imaginary derivative multiplies the plus source by -i and the minus source by +i. The same relation holds after applying (1). Curvature and positive metric are different contractions Take the canonical convention A_a=i\langle\Psi,\partial_a\Psi\rangle,\qquad F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a =-2\operatorname{Im}\langle\partial_a\Psi,\partial_b\Psi\rangle. \tag{4} For a single order, angular orthogonality makes the normal curvature diagonal in l. Define the nonnegative quantities N_l^\pm=\langle b_l^\pm,L_+^{-1}b_l^\pm\rangle. Then \boxed{(F^{\rm normal}_{x_k y_k})_{ll}=2(N_l^+-N_l^-), \qquad (g^{\rm normal}_{x_k x_k})_{ll}=N_l^++N_l^-.} \tag{5} The curvature is a difference; the positive metric is a sum. Replacing one with the other would change the dynamics. Cross-order entries follow from (2), retaining every pair of matching angular labels. The numerical calculation keeps all centered orders k=2,\ldots,d, rather than freezing the other shapes while testing one endpoint. For the original carrier, the antiunitary map \Theta=\sigma_y\tau_y K sends \Phi_l to -i\Phi_{d-1-l}. It implies the exact reflection identity R F^{\rm normal}_{x_k y_h}R=-F^{\rm normal}_{x_k y_h}. This identity is checked before it is used to evaluate small differences. The geometric carrier's shifted connection does not have that symmetry. Add the retained coefficient response Let c_{\chi l} be the normalized occupied eigenvector of the full finite carrier H_P, with eigenvalue \lambda_n. Its complete wave curvature at the reference point is \boxed{ F^{\rm wave}_{ab}= \sum_{\chi,l,m}c_{\chi l}^*(F^{\rm normal}_{ab})_{lm}c_{\chi m} -2\operatorname{Im}\sum_{r\ne n} \frac{\langle n,H_a r\rangle\langle r,H_b n\rangle} {(\lambda_r-\lambda_n)^2}.} \tag{6} Here H_a=\partial_aH_P includes the complete spatial derivative. The second term is the retained-mode contribution already studied in induced geometric response. The first term is the actual moving spatial basis addition. Orthogonal transport makes their separation unambiguous at this point. All signed retained modes are included in the spectral expression. The convention (4) and the differentiated eigenvector formula underlying (6) agree with the original mathematical treatment of adiabatic phase. See M. V. Berry, Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 392 (1984), equations 6–10. The specific spatial contractions here are calculations for the stated IDWT candidate. Translation, phase and temporal connection A common translation has a useful independent check. The coefficient \alpha_1 translates the profile center by -\alpha_1/d. The normal contribution is exactly F^{\rm normal}_{x_1y_1} =-\frac{i}{d^2}[Pp_1P,Pp_2P]. \tag{7} For a complete translated wave, the retained basis contribution cancels (7). The full canonical translation curvature is zero, as also follows from commuting full spatial translation generators. Complex polarized rays test this cancellation beyond a single real eigenvector. A separate phase–scale test agrees with the derivative of the connection-charge expectation under independently recomputed scaled radial profiles. The time convention matters. Equations (1)–(6) use the polynomial spatial gauge with A_0=0. Under W\mapsto e^{i\zeta}W,\quad A_i\mapsto A_i+\partial_i\zeta, \quad\Psi\mapsto e^{-iQ_A\zeta}\Psi, one must also take A_0\mapsto A_0+\dot\zeta. The canonical term i\Psi^\dagger\dot\Psi-\Psi^\dagger Q_AA_0\Psi is then invariant. Changing the spatial representative and setting its temporal connection to zero again describes a different connection history. The physical master action has not yet selected that history or supplied the sustaining geometry's complete kinetic law. Verification normal_basis_response.py implements (1)–(6). Independent Cartesian derivatives, direct norms of D L_+^{-1}b, phase–scale profiles and the complete translation check are in normal_basis_checks.py. The 475-check report passes at all five maintained depths for both carriers. Raw spatial sources and inverses are preserved separately with their exact source hashes. The resulting curvature is tested as a proposed slow law in the complete motion calculation.

title: Nonlinear mass reduction with spatial response
summary: Eliminating complementary spatial Dirac modes gives a nonlinear effective action, its exact induced norm, and a positive source-leakage criterion for departures from a common linear contact scale.
text: Summary: Eliminating complementary spatial Dirac modes gives a nonlinear effective action, its exact induced norm, and a positive source-leakage criterion for departures from a common linear contact scale. The interaction coefficient and the occupied field The occupied-graph action retains the simplex count as a nonlinear coefficient. Determining its physical consequence requires solving the spatial field and its normalization. The calculation below eliminates complementary modes of that same field while retaining their contribution to both quantities. It does not derive the graph action from the master interaction. Let the spatial Hilbert space have a fixed physical measure and canonical time-kinetic norm. Its self-adjoint spatial Dirac operator and chirality obey \mathscr D^\dagger=\mathscr D,\qquad \beta^\dagger=\beta,\qquad \beta^2=I,\qquad \{\mathscr D,\beta\}=0. \tag{1} These are operators on actual spatial fields, not a replacement of spatial coordinates by coefficient rays. The calculation applies at any spatial depth for which the following spectral and regularity hypotheses hold; six dimensions alone do not establish them. Let P project onto the entire zero space in the problem being reduced, assume \beta P=P, and write Q=I-P. Require an invertible complementary operator \mathscr D_Q=Q\mathscr DQ. If a restricted spatial symmetry class is used, it must be invariant under the full equation, and every zero mode in that class must be retained. A negative-chirality zero mode cannot silently be inverted or omitted. For finite Galerkin systems these are finite matrix assumptions. On a smooth closed spatial manifold, an elliptic Dirac operator with a spectral gap on Q supplies the complementary inverse between the appropriate Sobolev spaces. One sufficient framework uses H^s, s>d/2, so products are controlled, and a scalar kernel bounded on that space. The local kernel is the identity. The resulting real-analytic implicit-function argument is local near zero coupling and zero frequency. It is not a claim about arbitrary coupling or continuous spectra without a gap. Use a fixed real reciprocal scalar kernel K, with \begin{aligned} \sigma_\psi&=\psi^\dagger\beta\psi,& V_\psi&=K\sigma_\psi,\\ U(\psi)&=\langle\sigma_\psi,K\sigma_\psi\rangle,& E_g(\psi)&=\langle\psi,\mathscr D\psi\rangle+\frac g2U(\psi). \end{aligned} \tag{2} The scalar potential acts by multiplication and commutes with \beta. Its complete gradient is \nabla_{\bar\psi}E_g=\mathscr D\psi+g\beta V_\psi\psi. \tag{3} Both ordinary and conjugate variations of the scalar source are part of (3). A fixed potential evaluated on an unchanging target would give a different reduction. Exact stationary elimination and the norm At a real trial frequency \omega, form \mathcal R(\psi;g,\omega)=E_g(\psi)-\omega\|\psi\|^2, \qquad \psi=u+y,\quad u=Pu,\quad y=Qy. \tag{4} Solve the full complementary equation Q[\mathscr D(u+y)+g\beta V_{u+y}(u+y)-\omega(u+y)]=0. \tag{5} The invertibility in (1) gives a unique small local solution y=y(u,g,\omega). Substitute this solution into (4), defining \mathcal R_{\rm eff}. Stationarity in y removes its implicit derivatives from every first variation. In particular, \boxed{-\partial_\omega\mathcal R_{\rm eff} =\|u+y(u,g,\omega)\|^2.} \tag{6} The reduced field's norm is therefore not generally \|u\|^2. Equation (6) is exact on the local complementary branch. This norm is the phase-symmetry norm of the written action; no ordinary electric charge or particle-number interpretation has been assigned to it. The stationary second variation has an equally exact expression. In real coordinates retaining both quadratures, let H be the full Hessian of (4). Where H_{QQ} is invertible, \boxed{H_{\rm eff}=H_{PP}-H_{PQ}H_{QQ}^{-1}H_{QP}.} \tag{7} This nonlinear stationary reduction uses the same elimination principle as the linear Feshbach--Schur method. The band-consistency calculation explains why eliminating modes and bare compression obey different consistency rules. Neither (7) nor a positive curvature in a restricted subspace establishes dynamical stability of the full Dirac field. The energy-response calculation applies this Schur reduction to the canonical norm direction. It gives the exact shape correction to the branch's energy curvature and verifies opposite correction signs on the two assigned excited radial controls. Leading effective action, including complementary normalization For u in the positive-chirality zero space define \rho_u=u^\dagger u,\qquad V_u=K\rho_u,\qquad t_u=\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q(V_uu). \tag{8} The vector t_u has opposite chirality. With \epsilon=|g|+|\omega|, expansion of (5) gives y=-g t_u -g\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q[(\omega+gV_u)t_u] +O(\epsilon^3). \tag{9} The first displayed term is negative-chirality and the second is positive-chirality. Their pointwise scalar cross term and their norm cross term vanish. Substitution into the complete functional yields \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;g,\omega) ={}&\frac g2U(u)-\omega\|u\|^2\\ &-g^2\omega\|t_u\|^2-g^3\langle t_u,V_ut_u\rangle +O(\epsilon^5). \end{aligned}} \tag{10} One can check the cubic terms directly. Write the first two terms of y as y_1,y_2. The kinetic cross term is 2\operatorname{Re}\langle y_1,\mathscr Dy_2\rangle. The scalar energy contributes 2g\operatorname{Re}\langle V_uu,y_2\rangle -g\langle y_1,V_uy_1\rangle. Because \mathscr Dy_1=-gQ(V_uu), the two terms containing y_2 cancel. The norm term contributes -\omega\|y_1\|^2. These are exactly the two cubic contributions in (10). There is no term of total degree four: the symmetry y(u,-g,-\omega)=\beta y(u,g,\omega),\qquad \mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;-g,-\omega) =-\mathcal R_{\rm eff}(u;g,\omega) \tag{11} follows from uniqueness of the local complementary solution and (1). The analytic remainder in (10) can also be differentiated. Equation (6) therefore gives \boxed{Q_{\rm eff}=\|u\|^2+g^2\|t_u\|^2+O(\epsilon^4).} \tag{12} The reduced equation must be varied together with this norm. Keeping only the last scalar-potential term of (10) would miss a contribution of the same order to the normalized frequency. A normalized branch and a criterion for an exact linear scale Let \chi be a unit vector in the retained zero space satisfying P(V_\chi\chi)=A\chi,\qquad A=U(\chi). \tag{13} This is stationarity of the restricted scalar quartic on its unit sphere. Assume a smooth parity-compatible normalized branch through \chi. For a one-dimensional complex zero space its local existence follows after fixing the phase; in a larger space the retained stationary problem must also be solved, with its symmetries and degeneracies accounted for. Define \eta=-\mathscr D_Q^{-1}Q(V_\chi\chi),\quad a=\|\eta\|^2,\quad b=\langle\eta,V_\chi\eta\rangle, \quad C=Aa+b. \tag{14} The full field is \phi_g=\chi+g\eta+g^2\zeta+O(g^3), where \operatorname{Re}\langle\chi,\zeta\rangle=-a/2 fixes the total norm. Its complementary equation at second order gives \mathscr D\zeta=(A+V_\chi)\eta. Reciprocity of K then gives \boxed{\omega(g)=gA-4g^3C+O(g^5),\qquad E_g(\phi_g)=\frac{gA}{2}-g^3C+O(g^5).} \tag{15} For example, \operatorname{Re}\langle V_\chi\chi,\zeta\rangle =-Aa/2-Aa-b. The scalar expansion is consequently U(\phi_g)=A-6g^2C+O(g^4). Together with the exact identity E_g=\omega-gU(\phi_g)/2, this proves both expressions in (15). The local scalar normalization explains why nonlinear frequency and total energy must be distinguished before a physical rest mass is identified. If A>0 and the multiplication operator V_\chi\ge0, then \boxed{C\ge A\|\eta\|^2,\qquad C=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Q(V_\chi\chi)=0.} \tag{16} Here positivity of the potential is an explicit hypothesis; a positive quadratic kernel form alone need not imply a pointwise positive potential. Under (13), vanishing source in the complement means V_\chi\chi=A\chi. Thus the unchanged field \phi_g=\chi is an exact branch with \omega=gA for every g for which the stated equation is defined. Its total energy is gA/2. Equation (16) gives a concrete route to exact linearity: the selected spatial field must make its scalar source preserve its zero-mode line. It also gives a necessary condition for exact linearity of the analytic branch under these positivity hypotheses. Existence of such a line does not establish its stability, occupied mode index or observed mass. What a common simplex coefficient would have to preserve Suppose, conditionally, that an independently derived graph interaction has supplied g_N=\kappa D_N, D_N=\binom{N+d}{d}. Applying (15) to its normalized spatial branches gives \begin{aligned} \omega_N&=\kappa D_NA_N-4\kappa^3D_N^3C_N+O(\kappa^5),\\ E_N&=\frac{\kappa D_NA_N}{2}-\kappa^3D_N^3C_N+O(\kappa^5). \end{aligned} \tag{17} The remainder here is at each fixed band; uniform control across growing bands needs its own estimates. Even if A_N is common, the next term requires control of D_N^2C_N. A common bare \kappa is insufficient to establish a common physical mass coefficient after spatial response. As a strictly specified control, take the same spatial branch family at two coefficients g_i=\kappa D_i, so A,C are identical. Then \begin{aligned} \frac{\omega_2/\omega_1}{D_2/D_1} &=1-4\frac CA\kappa^2(D_2^2-D_1^2)+O(\kappa^4),\\ \frac{E_2/E_1}{D_2/D_1} &=1-2\frac CA\kappa^2(D_2^2-D_1^2)+O(\kappa^4). \end{aligned} \tag{18} For the committed six-dimensional counts D_1=S(13,6)=18564 and D_2=S(35,6)=3838380, the coefficient ratio is 3515/17. The diagnostic holds the control action fixed and verifies both corrections in (18) without adjusting either coefficient separately. This control does not identify its fields with the physical electron and muon. Their actual band-dependent profiles, normalization and master interaction remain to be obtained. It neither changes the committed mode selections nor tests alternative particle dimensionalities. An independent six-dimensional spatial comparison The specified spatial CP3 branch provides an independent differential-equation test of the reduction. CP3 here is the candidate actual six-dimensional spatial topology with an undetermined metric radius, not compactified auxiliary dimensions. Its section degree L is not the cumulative mass-band label N. For local contact at L=1, the exact spatial coefficients are A=\frac85,\qquad a=\frac4{125},\qquad b=\frac{48}{875}, \qquad C=\frac{464}{4375}. \tag{19} Equation (15) recovers the existing cubic frequency -1856g^3/4375. The new calculation also reproduces the reduced action, the induced norm and the normalized energy. Direct complex complementary solves agree with the independent real spatial continuation, and increased Jacobi cutoffs preserve the coefficients. At L=0 the constant source has \eta=0 and gives the exact linear branch, as (16) predicts. The known local-contact instability at positive L remains present. Correctly deriving its effective frequency does not turn that branch into a viable electron. The spatial source-preservation theorem classifies the vanishing condition (16) for the specified holomorphic CP3 zero modes. It requires a constant scalar potential; a covariant kernel satisfying it also loses shape selection within that band. The theorem includes a full nonlinear stability result for the mean kernel and bounds on a finite screened-response correction. The scalar gap comparison examines a different mechanism: generating a scalar coefficient by summing occupied kinetic modes of the same field. It derives the complete collective response and tests whether the cumulative count survives at a fixed canonical norm. Its global kernel is specified independently of the occupied-graph prescription used in (17). Verification nonlinear_mass_reduction_checks.py independently solves the nonlinear complementary and normalized equations. It checks complex source derivatives, the complete real Schur Hessian, retained spaces with one to three complex modes, common-frame covariance, the exact frequency derivative (6), fourth- and fifth-order remainders, the independent norm identity dE/dQ=\omega, and the common-coefficient comparison (18). Physical six-dimensional checks use both chiral radial components at section degrees 0,1,3,6, three specified scalar kernels, and two spatial cutoffs. These finite checks support the displayed conditional derivation; they do not supply the missing master kernel.

title: A nonzero same-field background and the joint support bound
summary: A stable retained amplitude with a nonzero background can supply the missing angular force without shifting the reference spectrum, while its exact Schur complement gives a necessary joint-stability bound.
text: The spectrally transparent angular construction requires a nonzero supporting background. This note gives the minimal realization of that requirement and computes its complete quadratic consequence. A retained amplitude can supply the missing metric force while leaving the reference field equation unchanged. Eliminating the amplitude always subtracts a positive Schur term from the geometric stiffness, so force cancellation alone is not stability. This is an inverse construction. It identifies an admissible local quadratic structure and an exact test for any proposed realization in the one field. It does not derive the background, its potential, or the projected inverse angular operator from \Psi_\infty. A background coupling that is spectrally transparent Let x be a real retained amplitude of the same field and let its reference value be v\ne0. Near one of its stable minima, write U_x=\frac12\langle \xi,A\xi\rangle +\langle v+\xi,B(\Psi,g)\rangle, \qquad \xi=x-v, \qquad A>0. \tag{1} The brackets allow an angularly varying amplitude; the one-component case is obtained by replacing A by a positive number. Suppose B(\Psi,g_*)=0 \quad\hbox{as an operator on the retained field space}. \tag{2} Then the coupling energy and its field derivative vanish at the reference: U_x\big|_*=0, \qquad D_\Psi U_x\big|_*=0. \tag{3} The reference field, its frequency, and indeed the whole fixed-geometry linear field operator are unchanged. Nevertheless, D_gU_x\big|_*=\langle v,D_gB\rangle \tag{4} need not vanish. This is the nonzero-background alternative left open by the zero-background obstruction. The distinction is structural: equation (2) kills the field operator at the reference, while the background v multiplies its nonzero metric derivative. For the inverse angular channel, let the bracket in (1) be the angular L^2 pairing and take the angular source field schematically as B(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{v}\, \chi(\theta)\,\Psi^\dagger\mathcal T_0\Psi, \qquad \chi=\mathcal L_d^{-1}\left(\frac{\kappa}{\kappa_*}-1\right). \tag{5} At the round reference \chi=0 as an operator coefficient and \delta\chi=\sigma. If \langle\mathcal T_0\rangle=\beta b, equation (4) contributes \delta_gU_x=\kappa\int\rho\,\beta b\,\sigma\,dV, \tag{6} which cancels the carrier's missing -\kappa\int\rho\,\beta b\sigma\,dV channel. The ordinary local term -\kappa\int y\,\Psi^\dagger\mathcal T_1\Psi\,dV cancels the separate \mathcal L_d\sigma channel. Both coefficients are common operators; they are not fitted independently for each particle. Equation (5) does not solve the origin of \mathcal L_d^{-1}. It shows that a nonzero retained background removes the earlier first-derivative obstruction without introducing a frequency shift. Eliminating the background fixes the sign of its Hessian term The stationary amplitude is \xi_*=-A^{-1}B, \tag{7} and completing the square gives \boxed{U_{x,\mathrm{eff}} =\langle v,B\rangle-\frac12\langle B,A^{-1}B\rangle.} \tag{8} Let h be an angular metric perturbation and put F=D_gB[h]|_*. The second term in (8) contributes \boxed{\delta_g^2U_{x,\mathrm{eff}}[h,h] \supset-\langle F,A^{-1}F\rangle.} \tag{9} This sign is unavoidable for a stable amplitude that relaxes. Increasing the background stiffness suppresses the loss, but does not reverse it. For one harmonic, with background curvature a>0, background value v, cancelled carrier force F_{\rm car}, and bare geometric stiffness G, a linear coupling requires f=-\frac{F_{\rm car}}v, \qquad \boxed{G>\frac{f^2}{a} =\frac{F_{\rm car}^2}{a v^2}.} \tag{10} Thus an arbitrarily soft background destabilizes the geometry even though it cancels the first force exactly. The complete joint Hessian Field and metric perturbations can mix. Let p denote a physical field perturbation after phase and other collective zero modes have been removed. Write the uncoupled field Hessian as P, its field--metric block as M, the geometric block including vD_g^2B as G, and the mixed second derivative of B as N. The full quadratic operator on (p,h,\xi) is \mathbb H= \begin{pmatrix} P&M+vN&0\\ (M+vN)^*&G&F^*\\ 0&F&A \end{pmatrix}. \tag{11} Assuming P>0 and A>0 on the projected physical subspaces, two successive Schur complements give the necessary and sufficient quadratic condition \boxed{ G-F^*A^{-1}F -(M+vN)^*P^{-1}(M+vN)>0.} \tag{12} Equation (12) is the complete local test. Checking only (10) can miss an instability caused by field relaxation. Conversely, the negative term in (9) is not by itself a no-go theorem: sufficiently positive retained geometry and field blocks can satisfy (12). Collective position, orientation, phase, and radius directions must be projected or constrained according to their actual symmetries before using an inverse in (12). A zero eigenvalue associated with a true symmetry is not a negative mode, but it cannot be treated as a positive denominator. Angular scaling and the lowest-harmonic bottleneck For the inverse channel in (5), the force per normalized density harmonic is independent of the Jacobi eigenvalue: |F_\ell|\propto|\beta b|, \qquad \ell\ge2. \tag{13} If the retained geometric stiffness is proportional to \mathcal L_d(\ell) =-1+\frac{\ell(\ell+d-1)}d, \tag{14} then the normalized requirement |F_\ell|^2/[a\mathcal L_d(\ell)] is largest at \ell=2 and decreases strictly thereafter. The inverse channel therefore has no high-angular-degree instability forced by its Schur term. Its most demanding positive harmonic is the quadrupolar one. This conclusion depends on separating the two force channels. If a single relaxing background is made to carry the local-curvature term as well, then |F_\ell|\sim\mathcal L_d(\ell), and a background with constant A produces a penalty growing as \ell^4, faster than a second-order geometric stiffness. Such a combined realization needs angular stiffness in A or a different nonrelaxing structure. Keeping the inverse and local channels distinct is therefore dynamically meaningful. A causal background can satisfy the static bound Give the background fluctuation the quadratic action S_\xi=\frac12\int dt\left[ Z\|\dot\xi\|^2-\frac1{R^2} \langle\xi,(a_0+a_1\mathcal L_d)\xi\rangle\right], \qquad Z,a_0,a_1>0. \tag{15} On the positive angular subspace, \Omega_\ell^2=\frac{a_0+a_1\mathcal L_d(\ell)}{ZR^2}. \tag{16} Its high-degree propagation speed is c_\xi=\sqrt{a_1/(Zd)} in units where the containing-field limiting speed is one. The common sufficient choice a_1/Z\le1 is subluminal at every maintained depth. If the bare geometry has G_\ell=g\mathcal L_d(\ell), the background part of the static Schur condition becomes \boxed{ g>\frac{|F_\ell|^2} {\mathcal L_d(\ell)[a_0+a_1\mathcal L_d(\ell)]}.} \tag{17} For the inverse channel's harmonic-independent force, the right side is strictly largest at \ell=2. Hence causal propagation and positive static stiffness are algebraically compatible under one common kinetic normalization. The required coefficient must still be obtained from the physical action. Choosing it after inspecting each particle would be a fit, and equation (17) does not include the field-relaxation term in (12). A conventional local way to obtain a nonzero real background is a double-well potential V(x)=\lambda(x^2-v^2)^2/4, for which the radial curvature at either minimum is 2\lambda v^2>0. Its minimum energy can be normalized to zero, so a constant background need not carry an infinite vacuum offset. This example proves local realizability of the assumed quadratic neighborhood; it does not establish that this potential belongs to the IDWT master action. A particle-sourced positive multiplet fails transparency The previous construction leaves \mathcal L_d^{-1} explicit. It is natural to ask whether local positive modes can generate that inverse. Let their static energy instead contain U_z=\frac12\langle z,\mathcal L_dz\rangle -\langle z,S(\Psi)\rangle, \tag{18} on the projected \ell\ge2 space. Here z may be a multiplet and \mathcal L_d may include any positive component matrix. Elimination gives z_*=\mathcal L_d^{-1}S, \qquad U_{z,\mathrm{eff}}=-\frac12 \langle S,\mathcal L_d^{-1}S\rangle. \tag{19} For the required quadratic particle source, S(a\Psi)=|a|^2S(\Psi). The field-amplitude direction therefore obeys D_\Psi U_{z,\mathrm{eff}}[\Psi] =-2\langle S,\mathcal L_d^{-1}S\rangle<0 \quad\hbox{when }S\ne0. \tag{20} The positivity is strict because \mathcal L_d>0 on the projected space. At fixed canonical norm, the same nonzero component appears as a shift of the Lagrange multiplier, hence of the standing frequency. Thus every unbiased stable quadratic construction in which the particle density is the sole source of the inverse background fails spectral transparency; adding more positive response components does not cancel the sign. This narrows the viable interpretation of (1). Its nonzero background must be present independently of the occupied particle source, or a constraint, indefinite pairing, an independently derived bias satisfying the full orthogonality condition, or nonlinear structure must remove the positive amplitude overlap. An independently present background can multiply the vanishing operator in (5), but then the origin of the inverse coefficient still needs a local derivation. A particle-sourced positive quadratic multiplet does not provide both ingredients. The radius and the conformal kernel The inverse construction in (2) is used on the centered even harmonics of degree at least two, where \mathcal L_d is positive. Two scalar sectors lie outside it and require separate treatment. On the radius, \mathcal L_d(0)=-1. The inverse exists there, but with the opposite sign: \chi=-y. A uniform conformal variation \sigma_0 rescales the radius and every standing frequency as \omega\propto1/R, so \delta y=-\sigma_0 and the radius frequency shifts at first order. The \ell=0 channel is therefore not spectrally transparent, unlike the \ell\ge2 inverse. The causal background curvature on the radius is A(0)=a_0-a_1, so positive radius dynamics requires the additional condition a_0>a_1. This is strictly stronger than the positivity used on \ell\ge2 and is not implied by it: the two-parameter family a_0,a_1>0 that softens the angular Schur penalty can still give non-positive radius curvature when a_0\le a_1, and the radius Schur penalty F_0^2/(a_0-a_1) diverges as a_0\to a_1^+. On degree one, \mathcal L_d(1)=0 exactly. The operator is singular, its kernel is the degree-one scalar harmonics with multiplicity d+1, and no inverse exists. These are the conformal collective directions; they must be projected out or carried as collective coordinates rather than absorbed by an inverse. The three scalar sectors are therefore disjoint: the one-dimensional radius, the d+1-dimensional kernel, and the positive inverse on \ell\ge2. Scope across the maintained depths The identities use only positivity of \mathcal L_d(\ell) for \ell\ge2 and apply at depths 2,3,4,5,6,10. The separate depth-two form coefficients change \mathcal T_0 and \mathcal T_1, but not the background or Schur argument. This includes the maintained massive depth-two indices; it does not construct a photon state or derive physical transverse polarization. The result also does not repair the finite-chain mass-unit drift or the failed shared electron--tau unit. It preserves the existing reference frequencies deliberately. A complete candidate still needs a common background potential, the projected inverse as an actual response of \Psi_\infty, a physical origin for the radius curvature a_0-a_1, and verification of (12) using the physical field and geometry Hessians rather than symbolic positive blocks. Verification nonzero_support_background_checks.py verifies the exact force cancellation, eliminated energy, Schur determinant, stable and unstable sides of the joint bound, the causal dispersion bound, the positive particle-sourced overlap, and the lowest-harmonic monotonicity for every maintained index at depths 2,3,4,5,6,10. It also verifies the two scalar sectors outside the inverse: the opposite-sign radius response, the a_0>a_1 positivity condition with its degenerate and wrong-sign controls, the diverging radius Schur penalty, and the d+1-dimensional degree-one kernel. The rational component values are algebraic controls rather than measured physical coefficients. The selected 4,218-check report records the normal Python run; an optimized run passes the same conditions.

title: The spatial complement and positive kinetic normalization
summary: Eliminating the actual complementary spatial modes produces a positive kinetic correction and a controlled leading frequency change; projecting the full square directly gives a different spectrum.
text: The small mass-frequency branch survives the leading response of the omitted normal modes. Their contribution includes a positive correction to kinetic normalization. It must be retained together with their change to the frequency operator. This calculation uses the maintained full spatial parent. It supplies a specific improvement over a finite-band assumption, while leaving the infinite-complement remainder and the occupied supporting geometry open. The bounded angular completion then uses the same spatial structure to remove the leading mode-dependent departure from the simplex factors. Eliminate the spatial modes before squaring Let P be the kernel of the linked geometric operator D, including its two canonical blocks, and Q=I-P. At a fixed surface parameter \beta, write the maintained first-order parent as H=\Lambda D+M,\qquad M=-C\chi_1\beta-\frac12K\chi_1 -C\gamma(\chi_-h+\chi_+\bar h), \quad h=zB/2. \tag{1} Here \Lambda=R/L, \gamma=g\Lambda, K=(d+1-a)S-aI, and D is the geometric Jacobi operator. All its radial coefficients are shared by the particle indices at one depth. The normal plane remains an ordinary unbounded spatial plane. Define H_P=PMP,\qquad F=QMP,\qquad Y=D_Q^{-1}F. \tag{2} The inverse exists because |D_Q|\ge 2/\sqrt{d+1}. Splitting an eigenfunction into \psi=p+q, the exact elimination is \left[H_P-F^\dagger(\Lambda D_Q+QMQ-\omega)^{-1}F\right]p =\omega p. \tag{3} The source F has negative normal chirality, whereas Y has positive chirality. This removes the term proportional to \Lambda^{-1}. Expansion through the first nonzero order gives \boxed{ \left(H_P+\frac A{\Lambda^2}\right)p =\omega\left(I+\frac N{\Lambda^2}\right)p+\cdots, \qquad N=Y^\dagger Y\ge0,\quad A=Y^\dagger M_+Y.} \tag{4} The same coefficient follows by normalizing the complete spatial wave: q=-Yp/\Lambda+\cdots, so \|\psi\|^2=p^\dagger(I+N/\Lambda^2)p+\cdots. The omitted field adds positive norm. It does not supply negative inertia. Canonical normalization of (4) gives the Hermitian operator \boxed{H_{\rm low}=H_P+\frac1{\Lambda^2} \left(A-\frac12\{N,H_P\}\right)+\cdots.} \tag{5} The frequency shift computed from (4) agrees with (5), including both canonical blocks. The amplitude normalization fixes how this frequency enters the action; it is not a mass-fitting variable. In contrast, direct compression of the full square gives PH^2P=H_P^2+F^\dagger F. \tag{6} The additional term is positive but does not describe the low spectral subspace after its normal dressing. Numerically, it overwhelms the tiny mass branch. Equation (6) therefore cannot replace (3). The spatial inverse is explicit The polarization part uses the exact identity D(\mathcal R\Phi_l)=(K-k_l)\Phi_l, \qquad \mathcal R=-iS\alpha\cdot x,\quad k_l=d-1-2l. \tag{7} The hopping part is obtained from the positive-chiral radial Green equations of D^2, retaining both radial components, their connection terms and the subtraction of the retained projection. This is an actual spatial inverse, rather than a scalar denominator assigned to an omitted mode. The radial fields determine every entry of N and A. Angular selection then restricts the off-diagonal block of (5): its row-minus-column shift lies between -1 and 2. If an entry contains \gamma^p and has shift s, it obeys p-s\le2. Combining this rule with the small-branch endpoint vectors gives \frac{\delta\omega_{n,d}}{\omega_{n,d}} =g^2\kappa_{n,d}(\gamma)+\text{higher orders}, \qquad g=\gamma/\Lambda, \tag{8} where \kappa_{n,d} has a finite large-\gamma limit for each maintained index. The leading correction is not amplified by an inverse power of the tiny mass-frequency itself. A bound on the full operator norm would miss this angular information. For example, at \gamma=10000, the positive surface branch gives: Depth and control Coefficient \kappa_{n,d} of g^2 2, W -0.0966583 3, down -0.1550261 3, strange -0.2188834 4, up -0.3775428 4, top -0.4328352 5, first neutrino -0.6593903 6, electron -0.9628474 6, muon -0.9869815 10, tau -2.7745591 The coefficients are not exactly common within a depth. The maintained parent therefore does not preserve the simplex law exactly after this correction. Its formal zero locations shift as well. This is a limitation of that full extension, not a change to the assigned particle indices. What the larger spatial comparison establishes A finite spatial Galerkin space containing P, the range of F, and the range of Y reproduces the leading coefficient independently. It retains 6d complex basis vectors. The normal part has a positive gap, the complete matrix has the required chiral symmetry, and halving g gives the expected fourth-order frequency remainder after (8). The basis is deliberately sufficient to test this order. It is not an exhaustive discretization of the infinite normal plane. Independent radial refinement checks the spatial integrals used in the small eigenvalue; high-precision diagonalization alone would not establish that accuracy. The result supports a positive, properly normalized reduced wave action under the stated parent. It does not supply the overall physical phase normalization, the same-field source balance, or the total inertia of a localized occupied particle. Those require the supporting action as well. Verification normal_complement_expansion.py constructs the spatial inverse matrices and the larger Galerkin comparison. normal_complement_expansion_checks.py passes 384 checks across all six depths, every maintained particle control and both surface signs. The report retains the formal-root shifts, independent radial refinements, exact executed source hashes and separate raw spatial arrays. The 384-check complementary-mode report contains the complete frequency, normalization and spatial refinement results.

title: Normal Dirac extension and the canonical mass coefficient
summary: A full Dirac field on a conditional spatial half-cylinder induces the absolute tangential Dirac operator, while its kinetic norm cancels a constant bulk mass factor and local scalar contact excites complementary normal profiles.
text: Summary: A full Dirac field on a conditional spatial half-cylinder induces the absolute tangential Dirac operator, while its kinetic norm cancels a constant bulk mass factor and local scalar contact excites complementary normal profiles. Obtain a nonlocal operator from ordinary spatial continuation The Killing-spinor transfer gives a Hermitian scalar-mass candidate when its polynomial is evaluated on the absolute spatial Dirac operator: \widehat M_d=\frac{Q_d(R|\mathscr D|)}{d!},\qquad Q_d(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{d/2}(x-j)(x+j-1). \tag{1} It has the desired simplex eigenvalues on both Dirac signs, under the specified round geometry. The absolute value makes it spatially nonlocal. A natural question is whether ordinary spatial continuation of the same field can supply that absolute value. An exact product-space calculation does supply it as a map from a field's value to its perpendicular derivative. However, that same continuation induces a nontrivial time-kinetic norm. A constant bulk scalar coefficient remains constant after canonical normalization. A local nonlinear scalar source also drives normal profiles outside the initially selected decaying profile. These statements concern a conditional geometry and boundary problem. Take a six-dimensional spatial manifold Q_6 and one ordinary perpendicular coordinate y\ge0, with metric dy^2+g_{Q_6}. The six tangential directions remain equivalent in kind. No dimension is compactified and no small geometric radius is assumed. This is a local normal-direction benchmark, not an assignment of a seven-dimensional particle or a derivation of the full six-to-ten nesting. Multiple normal directions require their complete Clifford structure and cannot be supplied by independent scalar copies. A nested spatial submanifold does not itself impose a hard boundary, a one-sided domain or a decaying boundary condition. Those are explicit extra assumptions here. All retained and complementary profiles below are modes of the same Dirac field. Keep the full parent spinor Let the tangential operators satisfy \mathscr D^\dagger=\mathscr D,\qquad \beta^\dagger=\beta,\qquad \beta^2=I,\qquad \{\mathscr D,\beta\}=0,\qquad A=|\mathscr D|>0. \tag{2} Assume a positive spectral gap, as on the conditional round sphere, where A has values (k+3)/R. Initially work on smooth finite spectral sums; the integrated formulas then extend on their indicated quadratic-form domains. The parent scalar matrix must be distinct from the new spatial Clifford matrix. On the full doubled spinor bundle set \mathbb D= \begin{pmatrix}\mathscr D&0\\0&\mathscr D\end{pmatrix},\quad \alpha_y= \begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\\beta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \beta_p= \begin{pmatrix}\beta&0\\0&-\beta\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3} The two last matrices are Hermitian involutions. They anticommute with each other and with \mathbb D. For an ordinary rank-eight six-dimensional spinor, (3) retains all sixteen components of this parent Hamiltonian. These are field components, not additional spatial coordinates or particles. The massless parent spatial operator is H_0=\mathbb D-i\alpha_y\partial_y. \tag{4} This product form belongs to the standard theory of Dirac Cauchy data and their spectral projectors; see Sharma, Introduction, pages 2–3. The particular lift, norm and scalar-action calculations needed here follow directly below. Construct the complete decaying lift Define the tangential involution and the parent isometry T=i\beta\mathscr D A^{-1},\qquad T^\dagger=T,\qquad T^2=I,\qquad V=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}I\\T\end{pmatrix}. \tag{5} Write A_p=\operatorname{diag}(A,A) and K=i\alpha_y\mathbb D. Direct multiplication gives \begin{gathered} K^\dagger=K,\qquad K^2=A_p^2,\qquad KV=VA,\\ V^\dagger V=I,\qquad VV^\dagger=\Pi_+=\frac12(I+KA_p^{-1}),\\ \beta_pV=V\beta,\qquad V^\dagger\alpha_yV=0. \end{gathered} \tag{6} Thus V spans the entire decaying half of the parent data and retains every tangential polarization. The scalar matrix preserves this subspace. The last identity makes its normal flux vanish for arbitrary complex data. For a tangential trace variable f, set F(y)=V e^{-yA}f. \tag{7} Since H_0=-i\alpha_y(\partial_y+K), equations (6)–(7) give \boxed{ H_0F=0,\qquad -\partial_yF(0)=VAf. } \tag{8} The positive operator A=|\mathscr D| is therefore the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator: it maps the boundary field value to its outward derivative. A mode with A=\lambda decays over length 1/\lambda, or R/(k+3) on the round six-space. This is a field profile length under the assumed geometry, not compactification. The tangential and normal kinetic terms cancel in (8). Retaining only one of them would give a different reduced equation. Normalize the entire action The trace f does not have the canonical norm of the parent field. Integration over the normal coordinate gives \|F\|^2=\langle f,Zf\rangle,\qquad Z=\int_0^\infty e^{-2yA}dy=\frac1{2A}. \tag{9} Consequently the time-kinetic term is i\langle f,Z\partial_t f\rangle. The canonically normalized tangential variable is \chi=Z^{1/2}f,\qquad f=(2A)^{1/2}\chi. \tag{10} As a linear control, add a constant real scalar coefficient M to the parent equation, giving H_M=H_0+M\beta_p. Here M is prescribed; the local self-interaction will be tested separately. Its bulk energy is \begin{aligned} E_M(F) &=M\int_0^\infty\langle F(y),\beta_pF(y)\rangle\,dy\\ &=M\langle f,\beta Zf\rangle =M\langle\chi,\beta\chi\rangle. \end{aligned} \tag{11} The last equality uses [A,\beta]=0. The resulting canonical equation and exact lifted solution are i\partial_t\chi=M\beta\chi,\qquad F(t,y)=Ve^{-yA}(2A)^{1/2}e^{-itM\beta}\chi_0. \tag{12} Substitution verifies (12) in every component of the full parent equation, with the specified decaying boundary data. The coefficient is M, independent of tangential level. The nonlocal operator in (8) has not become a mass enhancement. Its inverse also enters the kinetic norm and cancels from (11). For comparison, a separately specified boundary quadratic form b\langle f,\beta f\rangle compresses in the same canonical variables to E_{\partial}=2b\langle\chi,A\beta\chi\rangle. \tag{13} This gives a first-degree inverse-width factor, with a new boundary coefficient. It is the compression of an additional form onto (7). Its complete boundary condition and changed normal profile must still be solved before (13) is treated as an exact physical spectrum. The full polynomial and normalization in (1) have not been derived. Specified contribution Form in the trace variable Canonical compressed form Time-kinetic norm \langle f,\frac1{2A}f\rangle \langle\chi,\chi\rangle Constant bulk scalar term M\langle f,\frac{\beta}{2A}f\rangle M\langle\chi,\beta\chi\rangle Additional boundary scalar term b\langle f,\beta f\rangle 2b\langle\chi,A\beta\chi\rangle Why a free normal extension does not select a bound particle On a complete normal line y\in\mathbb R, decay toward positive y requires data in \operatorname{Ran}\Pi_+; decay toward negative y requires data in \operatorname{Ran}\Pi_-, where \Pi_-=I-\Pi_+. Their intersection is zero. Hence a smooth zero-frequency solution of H_0F=0 cannot use both free decays across y=0 with nonzero continuous data. The same obstruction applies to the lifted scalar eigensolutions of (12) at frequencies \pm M: after selecting their scalar eigenvalue, the remaining spatial equation is again H_0F=0. An interface, a boundary law or a nonlinear binding mechanism would have to supply different matching dynamics. This concerns this product-space construction. It does not exclude different normal geometries or a fully solved nonlinear profile. It also does not replace IDWT's cylindrical free continuation by an already established localized normal profile. Vary the actual local scalar contact The round local-gap construction provides the exact spatial pair \varepsilon,\xi=\beta\varepsilon. Its Dirac eigenvalues are +\lambda and -\lambda, respectively, with \lambda=3/R. The pair is pointwise orthonormal. Its scalar-current matrix is the ordinary Pauli X, and arbitrary complex coefficients give a spatially constant scalar current. On this pair, V in (5) is represented pointwise by the same isometry as in the operator calculation. Choose a tangential field \chi=a\varepsilon+b\xi and define w_\lambda(y)=\sqrt{2\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda y},\qquad F(y,q)=w_\lambda(y)V\chi(q),\qquad j=\chi^\dagger\beta\chi,\quad \rho=\chi^\dagger\chi. \tag{14} Both j and \rho are constant on the spatial sphere. Tangential spatial measure is held fixed throughout; unit spatial measure may be used to isolate the normal normalization. The elementary normal integrals are \int_0^\infty w_\lambda^2dy=1,\qquad \int_0^\infty w_\lambda^4dy=\lambda,\qquad \int_0^\infty w_\lambda^6dy=\frac43\lambda^2. \tag{15} Consider the written local parent scalar energy \kappa\int(F^\dagger\beta_pF)^2/2. Its compression onto (14) gives E_{\rm int}^{\rm comp} =\frac{\kappa\lambda}{2}\int_{Q_6}j^2\,d\mu,\qquad N_{\rm comp}(\chi)=\kappa\lambda j\beta\chi. \tag{16} This inverse-width coefficient is obtained from the actual local quartic interaction with its canonical normal norm. But compression alone is not the complete nonlinear equation. The full local source is N(F)=\kappa w_\lambda^3 j\,\beta_pV\chi. \tag{17} Its normal profile is w_\lambda^3, not w_\lambda. Let W\chi=w_\lambda V\chi be the canonical lift on the pair. Then its projection is W^\dagger N=\kappa\lambda j\beta\chi, and the complementary normal source obeys \boxed{ \|(I-WW^\dagger)N\|_y^2 =\frac{\kappa^2\lambda^2j^2\rho}{3}. } \tag{18} Here the norm integrates the normal coordinate at a spatial point; integrating over Q_6 gives the full spatial statement. Indeed, (15) gives \|N\|_y^2=4\kappa^2\lambda^2j^2\rho/3, whereas \|W^\dagger N\|^2=\kappa^2\lambda^2j^2\rho. Their difference proves (18). For nonzero current the omitted force is one half of the full force norm, or 1/\sqrt3 times its retained part. The source stays within the spatial Killing pair, so this residual already lies in genuine complementary normal profiles; it is not an artifact of omitting angular spinor modes. The fixed decaying lift is therefore not an exact nonlinear invariant family for nonzero local scalar current. Solving those profiles can change both the effective interaction and its normalization, as the nonlinear mass reduction explains. Solve the full-line binding question within the spatial Killing channel For this spatial pair, the complete nonlinear normal problem admits a stronger conclusion than the residual (18). Retain four arbitrary complex functions of y: the two spatial Killing coefficients in each parent block. Write their vector as z(y)\in\mathbb C^4. This includes growing, decaying and oscillatory normal profiles; the lift (14) is no longer imposed. The spatial pair has constant Gram and scalar matrices, so its complete local source is still independent of the tangential point. On a full normal line the stationary equation is \begin{gathered} (D_\lambda+K_m)z=\omega z,\qquad K_m=-i\alpha_y\partial_y+m(y)\beta_p,\\ D_\lambda=I_2\otimes \begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0\\0&-\lambda\end{pmatrix}, \qquad m(y)=\kappa z^\dagger\beta_p z. \end{gathered} \tag{19} In this equation \alpha_y and \beta_p are the four-component restrictions of (3). The normal direction is free at both infinities; there is no boundary or external normal potential. Assume a bounded smooth field of finite canonical normal norm. Then m is bounded and integrable because |m(y)|\le|\kappa|\,|z(y)|^2. The stationary equation puts z in H^1. Since m depends only on y, the exact identities are \{D_\lambda,K_m\}=0,\qquad D_\lambda^2=\lambda^2I. \tag{20} Integration by parts on H^1 gives the norm identity \boxed{ (\omega^2-\lambda^2)\|z\|^2=\|K_mz\|^2\ge0. } \tag{21} Thus no nonzero bound state can have |\omega|<\lambda, even with a completely relaxed nonlinear normal profile. At |\omega|=\lambda, equation (21) requires K_mz=0. Its exact first-order solution has the form z(y)=\exp\!\left[-i\alpha_y\beta_p \int_{y_0}^{y}m(s)\,ds\right]z(y_0). \tag{22} The integral stays finite at infinity. This matrix and its inverse therefore stay bounded, so nonzero initial data cannot approach zero in norm and cannot be square integrable. Finally suppose |\omega|>\lambda. The stationary equation is z'=B_0z+m(y)Cz,\qquad B_0=i\alpha_y(\omega-D_\lambda),\qquad C=-i\alpha_y\beta_p. \tag{23} Here B_0^2=-(\omega^2-\lambda^2)I, so both e^{yB_0} and e^{-yB_0} are uniformly bounded. In the interaction variable a(y)=e^{-yB_0}z(y), a'=m(y)e^{-yB_0}Ce^{yB_0}a. \tag{24} Its coefficient has integrable operator norm. Gronwall's inequality applied in both directions gives a strictly positive lower bound on |a(y)| for every nonzero initial value. The bounded inverse free evolution gives the same lower bound on |z(y)|. Square integrability is again impossible. Equations (21)–(24) exhaust real stationary frequencies.
