title: Angular shape, finite width and responsive support of the simplex carrier
summary: Exact angular witnesses qualify restricted standing-wave stability; a zonal alternative, finite-width correction and collective support tests identify what a complete spatial carrier must supply.
text: The prescribed-surface operator supplies a useful frequency mechanism, but its supporting field and complete spatial stability must be solved. Three different tests are relevant: changing the angular shape, giving the surface finite normal thickness, and allowing the supporting scales to respond. They cannot be replaced by a test of one restricted coefficient family. The exterior-form construction uses a physical spherical feature S_R^m, m=d-2, within an ordinary spatial sector of depth d. Its angular degree is l=n+1. The separate spin construction uses S_R^{d-1}, with spin level n. Both have the same finite link matrices where applicable, but different fields and interaction actions. Neither sphere represents compactified spatial directions. 1. What the standing angular test establishes At fixed radius and gap, the weak-charge standing branch of the stipulated nonlinear Hodge action has E(Q)=Q\Omega-\frac{gQ^2}{2\kappa^2\mathcal A}\overline W+O(Q^3), \qquad \mathcal A=\operatorname{Area}(S_R^m),\quad g>0. For a real degree-l harmonic with sphere-average norm \langle f^2\rangle=1, and the stationary mixture of the two signed Hodge branches held fixed, \overline W=C_0\langle f^4\rangle,\qquad C_0=s^4+\frac{l(l+m-1)}3s^3t>0. Here s and t are the scalar endpoint and first-row response of that normalized signed mixture. The factor 1/3 follows from \int f^2|\nabla f|^2=l(l+m-1)\int f^4/3. For the real highest-weight harmonic Y\propto\operatorname{Re}(X_1+iX_2)^l, let Z be a normalized orthogonal degree-l harmonic and write A=\langle Y^2Z^2\rangle, I_4=\langle Y^4\rangle. The normalized path (Y+\epsilon Z)/\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2} has leading energy curvature proportional to 1-3A/I_4. For the azimuthal weight l-2, transverse scalar, first-Jacobi sector, beta moments give 1-\frac{3A}{I_4} =-\frac{l[(b-1)l+1]}{(2l-1)(b+l-1)},\qquad b=\frac{d-3}{2}. Depth Degrees Exact curvature factors 4 4, 21, 73 8/49,399/1681,5183/21025 5 11, 16, 23 -1/21,-1/31,-1/45 6 14, 36 -224/783,-1368/5183 10 24 -2928/2491 This direction is outside the earlier four-complex-mode family and outside rigid rotations. Thus the positive restricted Hessian remains correct, while it does not extend to an unrestricted minimum. The negative leading coefficient excludes a strict fixed-charge minimum near zero charge at depths five, six and ten, conditional on a smooth continuing branch. It does not prove exponentially growing modes or particle breakup. The full same-degree scalar/exact block scan includes both signed components and their complex phases. Other form grades, other degrees, normal fields and finite-amplitude corrections require separate tests. Depth three has only the cosine/sine pair at a given degree; depth two's old S^0 feature has no angular tower. 2. A different standing shape removes this particular obstruction The zonal harmonic, concentrated about a pole, is Y_l(x)\propto C_l^{(m-1)/2}(x). It has the same linear frequency but different contact integrals. At depth five, m=3, the normalized zonal field is the Chebyshev polynomial U_l(x), with average norm one. The product identity U_l^2=\sum_{k=0}^l U_{2k},\qquad I_4=l+1 counts the orthogonal even channels in its square. For every transverse sector j=1,\ldots,l, \frac{A_j}{I_4}=\frac1{2j+1}. One derivation uses h_j(\theta)=\sin^{j+1}\theta C_{l-j}^{j+1}(\cos\theta). It solves the Dirichlet problem with potential j(j+1)\csc^2\theta and eigenvalue (l+1)^2. Differentiating the eigenvalue in j, with l-j held fixed, gives \langle\csc^2\theta\rangle_{h_j}=2(l+1)/(2j+1). The oscillatory part of \sin^2((l+1)\theta) is orthogonal to the remaining polynomial, yielding the overlap formula. The j=1 sector is a rotation; all j\ge2 have positive energy curvature, at least 2/5 in this normalized same-ray measure. The completed signed and complex same-degree calculations also have positive nonsymmetry energy curvature for the maintained depth-five, six and ten zonal cases. Depth-four zonal controls have negative directions, so changing the shape is not a universal stability repair. Zonal symmetry and exactness of f^2df=d(f^3)/3 also pass the first cubic resonance projection; this is not a finite-amplitude existence theorem. Allowing a lower angular degree remains a separate obstruction. At frozen support, the fixed-charge quadratic energy gives \Delta E_Q=\frac{Q}{2\Omega_l} (\Omega_{l-1}^2-\Omega_l^2)\epsilon^2 +O(\epsilon^4,Q^2\epsilon^2). In the high-gap limit, \Omega_{l-1}/\Omega_l\to(l-2)/(l+d-2)<1. The negative term is order Q; the quartic is order Q^2. A regular positive-gapped support background changes this conclusion only at order Q^2, if it leaves the leading spectral ordering unchanged. A singular zero-charge limit, a derived constraint or a genuinely changed leading operator lies outside that statement. Energetic saddles need not be dynamically unstable in a conservative theory. 3. Finite radial width changes the spin carrier For the distinct spin surface define T_\pm(r)=GU+\frac c r B_\pm,\quad U_{j,j+1}=1, \quad B_+=\operatorname{diag}(n,\ldots,n+d-1), \quad B_-=-\operatorname{diag}(n+d-1,\ldots,n). A minimal radial continuation has positive action S_2=\kappa\int dt\,dr\,d\Omega\, \bigl(|\dot y|^2-c^2|(\partial_r+W)y|^2-|T_\pm(r)y|^2\bigr), \quad y=r^{(d-1)/2}x. The real scalar W is shared by every chain component. Its same-field origin is unspecified. For a common normalized radial profile, let \mu=\langle1/r\rangle and \sigma^2=\langle1/r^2\rangle-\mu^2. Exactly, \langle T_\pm^\dagger T_\pm\rangle =T_\pm(\mu)^\dagger T_\pm(\mu)+c^2\sigma^2B_\pm^2. The normal derivative adds c^2\|(\partial_r+W)f\|^2I. Replacing inverse radius by its mean misses the positive matrix correction. For n>0, no exact solution f(r)v with a fixed nonzero chain vector exists on a radial interval: the coefficient B^2 has distinct diagonal entries, forcing a coordinate vector, while BU+U^\dagger B couples every such vector to a neighbor. This excludes that separable ansatz, not a coupled vector profile v(r). At depth two the projected traces agree, while \det H_- -\det H_+=(2n+1)c^2G^2\sigma^2. For equal weights at radii 1 and 2, c=G=1, the exact splits for n=0,76,81,95 are 1/16,153/16,163/16,191/16. These are projection controls, not predicted particle masses. The positive zero-link null vector is fixed; the negative one changes direction with radius. A shared scalar normal derivative, or a shared unitary chain connection preserving their overlap, cannot transport both null lines. Sign-mixing ambient radial operators remain outside the test. Without W, trials escaping to large radius have energy tending to zero; the construction supplies no isolated positive frequency below the continuum. On the bounding circle the spin modes have half-integer rotation weights on the spin cover, whereas vector photon amplitudes have integer weights. A quadratic map can match weights but changes the kinetic metric and is singular as a vector coordinate at a vanishing helicity. Thus depth-two algebra and a two-state degeneracy do not derive photon polarization or propagation. 4. Responsive support can compress the frequency hierarchy A conditional thin-tube reduction has E=Q\Omega+R^{d-2}T(G),\qquad \Omega=\frac cR\sigma_l(GR/c),\qquad T=T_0+aG^2+bG^{-2}>0. The tension follows from a finite-energy normal texture trial if the unproved projection G\propto1/\text{width} holds. It is not a full coupled field solution. Write m=d-2 and s=d\log\sigma_l/d\log(GR/c). Joint scale balance requires mU=Q\Omega(1-s),\qquad \frac{d\log T}{d\log G}=\frac{m(-s)}{1-s}. At high gap the required slopes are 2/3,3/2,12/5,10/3,36/5 at depths 3,4,5,6,10. The three-term tension has slope strictly between -2 and 2, excluding the high-gap balances at 5,6,10 in this class. Finite-gap equilibria can exist, and must not be excluded by that asymptotic argument. With one common coefficient choice c=T_0=a=b=1, charges 100 and 300 give 26 verified collective equilibria with positive radius–gap Hessians. Their frequencies strongly compress the count ratios. At depth six the muon/electron assigned count ratio is 3515/17, but the two calculated frequency ratios are about 2.35549 and 2.45191. At depth five the extreme count ratio is 230/7, versus about 2.02328 and 2.25650. These are failures of these particular collective models, not an exhaustive result for all coefficient choices or responsive field laws. There is a general local diagnostic. For a mode-independent support E(P,y)=QP h(y)+U(y), h=h_0e^{-b\cdot y}, positive total scale Hessian H, and fixed charge, \frac{d\log\omega}{d\log P}=1-E_w b^TH^{-1}b<1. If U_{yy}>0, this equals [1+E_w b^TU_{yy}^{-1}b]^{-1}. It is a continuous-branch response identity; finite discrete ratios and changes between branches need their own calculation. Mode-dependent profiles derived from one law are not excluded. The frozen normal energy also contributes to complete inertia, as treated in the current-support ledger. Evidence and remaining task Independent verification recomputes nine exact angular signs, the three depth-five zonal overlap sequences with different quadrature, 34 signed radial projections, and all 26 collective Hessians using direct chain singular values and finite differences of the complete reduced energy. Maximum Hessian discrepancy is below 1.9\times10^{-6} in the reported normalized units. A viable spatial candidate still needs the coupled normal profile, selected frequency, finite-amplitude shape response and complete energy–momentum inertia. The useful constructive alternatives are the zonal surface family and a genuinely vector-valued radial continuation; neither is yet a physical mass operator.

title: Projecting the field kinetic term onto a surface
summary: The canonical field kinetic term gives a boundary expression for the two-normal surface coefficient; common background circulation can make it profile-independent, while a fully localized normal field has a cancelling outer contribution.
text: Summary: The canonical field kinetic term gives a boundary expression for the two-normal surface coefficient; common background circulation can make it profile-independent, while a fully localized normal field has a cancelling outer contribution. A kinetic coefficient with a stated field origin The surface-bending frequency calculation uses a geometric kinetic coefficient \Gamma. It is possible to test its origin directly from the canonical field action, independently of the curvature energy. This addresses a normalization coefficient, not a new way of solving for mass. The selected frequency already specifies mass in equivalent units. A field's fixed-point equation may determine the common background and the profile used in the kinetic projection. Their existence as solutions of the same spatial action remains necessary. Take the canonical time term L_{\mathrm{time}}=\frac{i\hbar}{2}\int \left(\Psi^\dagger\dot\Psi-\dot\Psi^\dagger\Psi\right)d^dx. \tag{1} All complex spinor components are retained. Their number does not add physical dimensions. The following comparison singles out two ordinary coordinates normal to a proposed field feature; it does not distinguish two fundamental directions in the containing sector. Let y=(y_1,y_2) denote those normal coordinates. Locally approximate a translated core by \Psi(y-X), with slow dependence along the surface. The two displacement variations are \delta_a\Psi=-\partial_a\Psi. The exterior derivative of the kinetic one-form in (1) gives the oriented coefficient per tangential area \boxed{ \Gamma_{12}=-2\hbar\operatorname{Im}\int_{\mathbb R^2} (\partial_1\Psi)^\dagger\partial_2\Psi\,d^2y. } \tag{2} The sign follows the order of the normal coordinates and the convention that the symplectic form is the exterior derivative of the kinetic one-form. Reversing their orientation reverses the sign. The positive \Gamma in the bending calculation is its magnitude after that orientation choice. Neither sign supplies an antiparticle interpretation. Equation (2) is a pullback of the existing kinetic term, rather than an independently chosen field or pair coupling. The approximation that a curved feature is represented by these translated normal profiles, and the contributions of its other field variations, still require checking. The coefficient is a boundary circulation Define the normal current one-form j_a=\operatorname{Im}(\Psi^\dagger\partial_a\Psi). \tag{3} This is a canonical phase-current expression, not an assigned ordinary electric charge. Commuting the two spatial derivatives gives \partial_1j_2-\partial_2j_1 =2\operatorname{Im}\big[(\partial_1\Psi)^\dagger\partial_2\Psi\big]. \tag{4} For a smooth core and a normal disk B_L, Stokes' theorem therefore yields \boxed{ \Gamma_{12}(L)=-\hbar\oint_{\partial B_L}j_a\,dy_a. } \tag{5} The outer field matters even when the core is narrow. Restricting the integral to a convenient inner region can change the kinetic coefficient. This is an instance of the need to retain the complete canonical normalization. A common background makes the result independent of core shape As a declared spatial control, take \Psi(r,\theta)=f(r)e^{ik\theta}\chi,\qquad \chi^\dagger\chi=1, \qquad f(0)=0, \tag{6} where k is a nonzero integer and \chi is a full complex spinor. This is a common-core ansatz for its components, not a generic zero set of an arbitrary spinor and not a solved Dirac field. Equation (5) becomes \Gamma_{12}(L)=-2\pi\hbar k f(L)^2. \tag{7} Equivalently, the bulk integrand in (2) is -2\hbar k f f'/r. Its radial integral gives the same boundary value. If f(r)^2\to\rho_\infty>0, then \boxed{|\Gamma_{12}|=2\pi\hbar|k|\rho_\infty.} \tag{8} The detailed core width and radial shape have disappeared. A common winding and background density therefore supply a coefficient independent of the occupied surface harmonic, under these assumptions. The background density could be set by one common fixed-point equation; it is not a separate value to retune for each mass. The transverse core width in this calculation is different from the round surface radius or a particle's proposed common cavity scale. Equation (8) establishes no equality between those spatial lengths. For a general multicomponent boundary pattern, the correct expression remains -\hbar\oint\operatorname{Im}(\Psi^\dagger d\Psi). Different component windings or spatial polarization textures cannot silently be replaced by (8). A localized outer field cancels the coefficient If the complete normal field decays so that its outer current circulation vanishes, (5) gives \Gamma_{12}=0. For example, a smooth localized profile f(r)=r^{|k|}\exp[-r^2/(2a^2)] has positive and negative radial contributions that cancel. Keeping only the rising core would miss the returning outer contribution. Thus a nonzero coefficient of the form (8) needs the stated nonvanishing surrounding field or a different complete kinetic reduction. A nonzero background also requires its own finite relative energy, spatial stress and global consistency analysis; (5) by itself does not provide them. What this supplies for the frequency operator With the stated positive coefficient, the bending frequency would read \omega_{n,d}= \frac{\kappa d!}{mR^d\,2\pi\hbar|k|\rho_\infty}S(n,d), \qquad m=d-2. \tag{9} This conditionally supplies the origin of one common normalization factor. It does not derive the bending energy coefficient \kappa, the particle indices, the common radius or the full inertial response. In particular, \Gamma is a first-order geometric kinetic coefficient with different units from mass; it must not be relabelled as inertia. The next dynamical requirement is a same-field fixed point and reduction that produce the needed curvature energy and its supporting terms together with (2). The unrestricted bending evolution's propagation limitation also remains. A boundary identity cannot resolve that limitation. Verification The localized oscillation calculation now supplies a different complete kinetic reduction. It pairs a spatial translation with an actual boost of a solved field, including the boost's frequency-dependent spatial phase, and obtains inertia \hbar\omega Q/c^2 in every ordinary spatial direction. This leaves the two-translation boundary cancellation in (5) intact. The new result belongs to an explicitly reconstructed local matrix-current action; it does not derive the bending energy or its surface coefficient from the original scalar quartic term. surface_kinetic_projection_checks.py verifies (5) with independent Cartesian differences of the actual complex fields and Fourier differentiation of their boundary currents. It retains all eight or thirty-two spinor components in the six- and ten-dimensional controls, and checks covariance under a complete unitary basis change. Different core widths with the same surrounding field give the same coefficient. Localized controls retain the outer contribution and give zero. Spatial-step and quadrature refinements check these conclusions. The preserved radial densities display where the contributions enter; the prescribed profiles do not establish a spatial master-field solution.

title: Separating the transverse modes of a mass core
summary: Exact contraction identities reduce every transverse coefficient mode and initially empty lower grade to a self-adjoint spatial wave equation in a fixed frame, leaving the occupied coefficient block as the nontrivial partner-response problem.
text: The complete finite current hierarchy has a useful decomposition around one coherent particle core. Its many coefficient components do not each require a separate stability calculation. Every component transverse to the occupied coefficient ray has a complex-linear, self-adjoint spatial equation. The same is true of every initially empty lower grade. Only the occupied coefficient block retains the real/conjugate partner response studied in the spatial shape calculation. This result assumes a fixed component frame and a spatially constant coherent coefficient ray. It concerns the formal linearized equation on the complete ordinary spatial domain. It does not prove nonlinear stability, settle the responding frame, or derive a physical spatial carrier for the prescribed simplex weights. Mass is the particle's selected oscillation frequency in equivalent units throughout. Complete coefficient components Use the density-normalized current action, with partner rank s, physical depth d, and q=1/(s+1)>0. At occupied grade N, write \Psi_N(x,t)=e^{-i\omega_N t}\Phi(x)\otimes z^{\otimes N}, \qquad \Phi=(\phi,0)^T,\quad \phi=fI_s+i h\alpha_{\hat x},\quad \omega_N=\omega_0 D_{N,d},\quad D_{N,d}=\binom{N+d}{d}. \tag{1} The core has \phi\phi^\dagger=\phi^\dagger\phi=cI_s, where c=f^2+h^2>0. All coefficient indices refer to the retained tensor description; they are not additional physical dimensions. Choose a constant orthonormal coefficient basis with z=e_0. A normalized occupation vector contains j indices outside that ray, with multiplicity h_{j,d}=\binom{j+d-1}{d-1},\qquad 1+\sum_{j=1}^N h_{j,d}=D_{N,d}. \tag{2} Each such coefficient retains an arbitrary complex 2s-by-s spinor/partner matrix disturbance. There is no restriction to the core's scalar/vector matrix form. A constant coefficient basis change preserves the fixed-frame spatial Dirac operator and all traced binding currents. Two exact sums determine the whole transverse mass response The normalized symmetric splitting of the graded current construction gives \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d} \frac{\binom{N-j}{k}}{\binom Nk} &=\frac{D_{N,d}}{D_{j,d}},\\ \sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d} \frac{\binom kj}{\binom Nj} &=D_{N,d}\frac d{d+j}. \end{aligned} \tag{3} Unavailable binomials are zero. For the first identity, replace the binomial ratio by \binom{N-k}{j}/\binom Nj. The convolution of \binom{k+d-1}{d-1} and \binom{N-k}{j} is \binom{N+d}{d+j}. Dividing by \binom Nj gives the stated answer. For the second, use \binom{k+d-1}{d-1}\binom kj =\binom{d+j-1}{j}\binom{k+d-1}{d+j-1} and apply the Hockey-Stick sum. For j\ge1, varying the complete mass source now gives \boxed{D S_{{\rm mass},j}[\eta] =\omega_N(a_j B_0\eta+b_jP_+\eta),\qquad a_j=1-q+\frac q{D_{j,d}},\quad b_j=\frac{qd}{d+j}.} \tag{4} Here B_0=\operatorname{diag}(I_s,-I_s) and P_+=\operatorname{diag}(I_s,0). The term with a_j comes from lifting the unvaried current gradient to the changed field. Its projector contraction is the first sum in (3). The varied current gradient supplies the second sum. The conformal-unitary relation in (1) reduces its full spinor/partner factor to P_+. Both contributions are necessary. There is no conjugate-field contribution to (4): for a transverse coefficient the first current variation joins the occupied retained ray to an orthogonal retained component. Its return to the perturbation coefficient is complex-linear. Different occupations do not mix. The equality of complete core Hessians proved in the density note also transfers (4) to the previous regular root-current action. At j=1, a_1+b_1=1. The upper rotating-frame mass shift therefore vanishes, as required for an infinitesimal change of the coherent ray. For j\ge2, 1-a_j-b_j=q\left(1-\frac1{D_{j,d}}-\frac d{d+j}\right)>0. \tag{5} This is a signed disturbance-frequency shift. It is not a negative inertia of the complete particle. Binding and spatial derivatives preserve this reduction The binding currents trace the coefficient indices. Orthogonality to z^{\otimes N} consequently gives \delta J=\delta K=\delta\rho=0 for every transverse disturbance. The complete binding derivative is simply D S_{{\rm bind},j}[\eta] =m_cB_1\eta\beta-\kappa B_1\eta F(x),\qquad F(x)=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\beta K_0)K_0} {\operatorname{Tr}K_0^2},\quad K_0=\phi^\dagger\beta\phi. \tag{6} This includes the density-denominator derivatives: their first variations vanish in precisely these directions. It is not a rule to omit them in other variations. Since K_0^2=c^2I_s, F=tK_0/c, with t=(f^2-h^2)/c. Thus F is Hermitian and \|F\|\le1 everywhere, including the decaying spatial tail. The shape source adds the complex-linear Hermitian projector \mu P_{\perp,+}\eta=(\mu P_\perp\eta_+,0)^T. The coefficient basis is spatially constant, so the actual Dirac derivative also preserves each block. In the rotating frame the whole operator is \boxed{ H_j\eta=-iA_a\partial_a\eta +\omega_N(a_jB_0+b_jP_+-I)\eta +m_cB_1\eta\beta-\kappa B_1\eta F(x) +\mu P_{\perp,+}\eta.} \tag{7} Left and right Hermitian matrix multiplication commute as operators on the matrix field. All nondifferential terms in (7) are therefore bounded and Hermitian on the canonical matrix L^2 space. The free spatial Dirac operator is self-adjoint on H^1(\mathbb R^d), and adding this bounded Hermitian multiplication preserves self-adjointness on the same domain. The evolution i\partial_t\eta=H_j\eta is unitary: \|\eta(t)\|_{L^2}=\|\eta(0)\|_{L^2}. \tag{8} This covers all ordinary spatial angles and wavelengths for these coefficient blocks. It is stronger than a finite angular or frozen-point scan. It does not apply to the remaining occupied coefficient block. Initially empty lower grades Suppose M<N is initially empty. Its first current variation is zero because the current is quadratic in that grade's field. Its complete mass Hessian is consequently D S_{{\rm mass},M,j}[\eta] =\omega_0D_{M,d}\left(1-q+\frac q{D_{j,d}}\right)B_0\eta, \qquad 0\le j\le M. \tag{9} There is no b_j term. Equations (6) and the shape projector still apply. These blocks are also complex-linear and self-adjoint, and they do not linearly force the occupied grade. In particular their coefficients are independent of the larger target grade. This is a spatial response version of the common-target identity. The formal finite-tower linearization through the highest occupied grade therefore consists of the one occupied coefficient block, the transverse blocks (7), and the lower-grade blocks (9). Empty channels above the highest occupied grade can have a Lipschitz source without a derivative at zero; this decomposition does not assert otherwise. A spatially varying coefficient ray or a responding frame requires its connection terms to be examined separately. Verification transverse_core_checks.py checks (3) with exact rational arithmetic at every maintained particle grade. It independently evaluates the complete current and binding Hessians on all coefficient, spinor and partner components at small grades in depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10. It retains arbitrary complex matrix variations, different physical radial directions and all initially empty lower grades. The 657-check report records its complete scope and source hashes. The spatial self-adjointness argument is analytic; the executable report is not a nonlinear evolution or a test of a derived physical carrier.

title: One quartic current law for conditional self frequency and pair response
summary: A same-field quartic in two scalar currents yields both a conditional simplex self frequency and a reciprocal polarized pair energy, with explicit spatial and frozen-field checks; physical support, inertia normalization and master selection remain open.
text: The rank-independent one-current excess preserves isolated occupied sources but begins at eighth order in the field. The localized action already contains several Lorentz-scalar currents of the same field. Comparing two of them gives a quartic field law with a direct spatial-pattern response. This is an inverse candidate. Its spatial carrier, mode weights and physical normalization have not been derived from the master interaction. One same-field quartic and its complete source Retain the doubled field and partner indices of the localized action. At each retained oscillator order k, let C_k be the current with B_0=\sigma_z\otimes I and let K_k use B_2=I\otimes\beta, including the same spectator trace in both. Both are Hermitian Lorentz-scalar matrices in the stated Dirac representation. Put h_{k,d}=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}. A single quartic comparison is \boxed{U_q=g_d\sum_{k\ge0}h_{k,d} \left[\operatorname{Tr}(C_k^2) -q\operatorname{Tr}(K_k^2)\right].} \tag{1} The retained-current maps and their adjoints are part of this equation. If one suppresses those maps to display the local matrix variation, the source is \frac{\partial U_q}{\partial\Psi^\dagger} =2g_d\sum_k h_{k,d} \left[B_0\Psi C_k-qB_2\Psi K_k\right], \tag{2} with each matrix lifted back into its original oscillator grade. This formula includes both complex partner and conjugate variations. At q=-1, the two current squares have equal positive coefficients: U_{-1}=g_d\sum h_{k,d} [\operatorname{Tr}C_k^2+\operatorname{Tr}K_k^2]\ge0. It is smooth even when a current vanishes. Equal coefficients are a specified symmetry choice, not yet a consequence of the master field. Conditional self frequency and its norm At a spatial point, take an upper-only coherent field \phi=\sqrt{\rho}\,U, where U is unitary in the complete partner frame, and put B=U^\dagger\beta U. Then B^2=I and at every occupied order C_k=\rho I_r\otimes P_{z,k},\qquad K_k=\rho B\otimes P_{z,k}. \tag{3} Both current squares act on the occupied field as \rho^2. The exact occupied source from (2) is 2g_d(1-q)\rho\,D_N\phi, where D_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}h_{k,d}=\binom{N+d}{d} and the maintained particle index is n=N+1. Thus a spatial zero-mode field with constant \rho has the conditional frequency \boxed{\omega_N=2g_d(1-q)\rho D_N,\qquad q=-1:\ \omega_N=4g_d\rho D_N.} \tag{4} This is mass from a self-coupling term in the standing equation, and the same term supplies the pair response below. No frequency coefficient is fitted separately for two grades at one depth. At common canonical norm Q and physical spatial volume \mathcal V_d, this square-unitary ansatz has \rho=Q/(r_d\mathcal V_d). The frequency unit is therefore 4g_d Q/(r_d\mathcal V_d) for the equal-coefficient law. The volume, common norm, cross-depth relation and suitable spatial zero modes remain physical inputs. A nonconstant upper-only density makes the right-hand side of (4) position dependent, so the earlier localized core is not a solution of (1). The existing constant-density CP3 construction shows that some noncoherent full-bundle spatial zero modes can have constant total density. It does not supply the square-unitary current pattern or the simplex enhancement required here. There is an exact energy normalization issue. Let T_{\rm sp} be the quadratic spatial kinetic energy and U the quartic (1). For a stationary field, homogeneity gives \omega Q=T_{\rm sp}+2U, while its canonical Hamiltonian is E=T_{\rm sp}+U=\omega Q-U. On a spatial zero mode, \boxed{E=\frac{\omega Q}{2}.} \tag{5} At the working one-particle norm Q=1, this energy is half the frequency-equivalent rest energy. Setting Q=2 would remove the factor algebraically on that branch, but no norm quantization or full boost stress has selected it. The finite frozen controls below do not resolve this inertial-mass identification. Reciprocal prepared-pair law For two same-depth upper fields, let their local densities be \rho,\sigma, their spatial partner involutions B_A=U_A^\dagger\beta U_A and B_B=U_B^\dagger\beta U_B, and their coherent oscillator-ray overlap be s=|z^\dagger w|^2. For a shared order k, direct substitution into (1) and subtraction of both isolated energies gives \boxed{V_{AB,k} =2g_d\rho\sigma\left[r_d-q\operatorname{Tr}(B_A B_B)\right]s^k.} \tag{6} The expression is symmetric in A,B and varies both fields. For q=-1 it becomes V_{AB,k} =g_d\rho\sigma\|B_A+B_B\|_{\rm HS}^2s^k\ge0. \tag{7} Compatible B_A=B_B patterns have the largest prepared cross energy; opposite B_A=-B_B patterns have zero. This is a shape-sensitive energy, not an observed interaction rate. The six-depth quartic calculation checks (2), isolated sources and (6) with complete complex field variations. The actual retained grade-zero tower gives the same pair formula and reciprocal derivatives at all six maintained depths, with pair formula errors below 7.2\times10^{-15}. For a larger grade N and smaller grade M, the full shared-order pair factor is F_{M,d}(s)=\sum_{k=0}^{M}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}s^k,\qquad F_{M,d}(1)=D_M,\qquad \lim_{M\to\infty}F_{M,d}(s)=(1-s)^{-d}\quad(0\le s<1). \tag{8} Thus imperfect overlap can make pair strength much less sensitive to the occupied mass grade than the self frequency. In the exact maintained depth-six comparison at s=0.5, the n=13 factor is about 0.95187 of the n=35 factor. At s=1 their ratio is 0.0048364. The law does not select s or ensure it stays away from one. Keeping only order zero would make the pair factor exactly grade independent, but that would be a different contraction rule from (1) and needs its own derivation. Transverse depth-two control and spatial separation For normalized transverse Jones vectors e,f\in\mathbb C^2, let B_e=2ee^\dagger-I_2. These are Hermitian involutions, and the rank-two factor in (7) is exactly 2+\operatorname{Tr}(B_eB_f)=4|e^\dagger f|^2. \tag{9} The depth-two control checks linear, right- and left-circular, and elliptical patterns, including their relative phases. Orthogonal linear and opposite circular states give zero, while matched states give the maximum. A common physical rotation of the transverse plane preserves (9); rotating only one linear pattern changes it as 4\cos^2\theta, while a circular pattern keeps its overlap under such a rotation. This checks the required polarization geometry if those Jones states are occupied photon patterns in the IDWT field. That identification, photon propagation and the n=0 massless boundary remain unproved. The different sign q=1 has a useful prepared spatial identity even though it gives zero coherent self frequency. On an upper field \phi, decompose its spatial spinor with P_\pm=(I\pm\beta)/2 and set A=\phi^\dagger P_+\phi, B=\phi^\dagger P_-\phi. Then \operatorname{Tr}(C^2)-\operatorname{Tr}(K^2) =4\operatorname{Tr}(AB)\ge0. \tag{10} It vanishes, with zero complete source, on a single square-unitary coherent core. For two such prepared cores, its cross energy is \rho\sigma s^k\|B_A-B_B\|_{\rm HS}^2. This provides a local quartic correction to the previous trace mass action but does not itself produce self mass. For the analytic stereographic upper-core profile of the localized action, the spatial calculation derives the exact displaced-core potential for (10). Write h=|\delta|/R, \rho(x)=A_R^2(1+|x|^2/R^2)^{1-d}, and J_d=\pi^{d/2}\Gamma(3d/2)/\Gamma(2d). One shared shell gives V_{-,k}(\delta) =4r_d A_R^4R^d\,s^k h^2J_d \,{}_2F_1\!\left(\frac{3d}{2},d;d+\frac12;-\frac{h^2}{4}\right). \tag{11} The pair energy is zero at coincidence, rises to a finite barrier, and decays at large separation. Independent shifted-profile quadrature and Feynman-parameter integration verify (11) at the tested depths and separations. The gapless analytic depth-two profile has divergent canonical norm, so its value here is only a local preparation. Odd-depth entries use the integral formula without a constructed matching Clifford spatial core. For the q=-1 positive sum, the same preparation instead has its largest cross energy at coincidence in the sampled separations; that action changes the isolated analytic core, so this is a prepared-pair comparison rather than a force between its solutions. Frozen control and remaining derivation The unified batch and report retain all real and conjugate spinor and partner directions in finite uniform-core tests at depths 2, 4 and 6, one or two oscillator columns, and momenta 0.1,1,10. For the constant-density self-mass action (1), the equal-positive choice q=-1 has no resolved imaginary frequency above 3\times10^{-14}; q=-0.5 and q=0 also pass these finite samples. The tested q=0.25,0.5,0.75 have growth approximately 0.630,1.295,2.608 respectively at momentum ten. These are frozen controls, not stability of a spatially varying core or every momentum and mode. The equal-positive quartic is the first simple trial here in which one smooth local expression supplies both a conditional simplex self frequency and a polarization-sensitive pair response. The theorem is conditional: its full spatial state, common finite-volume normalization, physical depth-two photon map, cross-depth sector embedding, particle mode selection and complete response have not been obtained. Equation (5) is a specific unresolved inertial-energy defect at the working Q=1. The retained weights and the relation of this quartic to the master field remain assumptions. It is therefore a useful one-law candidate, not yet the physical mass operator or coupling law.

title: A spatial instability of the uniform polarization source
summary: A complete uniform scalar-current polarization source has a provably growing momentum interval even after adding nonnegative constant Dirac gaps.
text: The positive scalar-current square has a growing channel even when its normal field occupies a complete isotropic spinor multiplet. The result holds for every positive current coefficient and both positive occupations. Adding nonnegative constant Dirac gaps moves the unstable momentum interval without removing it. This is a statement about a uniform source on ordinary noncompact flat space. It does not classify localized sources or a derived discrete spatial spectrum. Action and occupied background The target is a doubled spinor matrix \Psi. Each normal polarization B_A now has a complete partner multiplet of the same rank r. The scalar current is C=\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi, with F_q(C)^2=qr\operatorname{Tr}(C^2)+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2. Choose a Hilbert-Schmidt orthonormal Hermitian basis with E_1=I/\sqrt r and traceless E_A for A>1. For q>0, the real current coordinates c_1=\operatorname{Tr}C,\qquad c_A=\sqrt{qr}\,\operatorname{Tr}(E_A C)\quad(A>1) satisfy |c|^2=F_q(C)^2. The associated arrow matrix is \begin{pmatrix}0&c^T\\c&0\end{pmatrix}; its positive eigenvector defines the stated occupied normal polarization. Label its distinguished component by 0 and its remaining components by A=1,\ldots,r^2. Now put t_A=2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(B_0^\dagger\beta B_A). The interaction and optional constant gap terms are U=\frac g2|c+t|^2 +m_a\operatorname{Tr}(\Psi^\dagger\beta\Psi) +m_b\sum_{A=0}^{r^2}\operatorname{Tr}(B_A^\dagger\beta B_A), \qquad g>0,\quad m_a,m_b\geq0. \tag{1} All fields retain their canonical Dirac kinetic terms on the same ordinary spatial coordinates. The gaps in (1) are comparison parameters, not derived particle masses. Polarization labels remain hypothetical same-field modes. Write a>0,b>0 for the uniform target and normal canonical densities. The occupied upper target matrix is \sqrt{a/r}I_r. The upper normal multiplet is I_r/\sqrt r times the positive arrow eigenvector of norm b. All lower components vanish in this background. Define s=g(a+b),\qquad L_a=2(m_a+s),\qquad L_b=2m_b+s. \tag{2} The background phase frequencies are m_a+s and m_b+s. An invariant channel with every omitted component checked Choose a unit Hermitian traceless partner matrix. Its target upper variation, its lower Clifford partner along the momentum, and the corresponding normal dark upper and lower variations span four complex components. Retain their conjugate components as well. After a sign change on the conjugate lower components, the complete channel generator is \mathcal B=\begin{pmatrix}A&C_1\\-C_1&-A\end{pmatrix}, \qquad H_-=A-C_1,\quad H_+=A+C_1, \tag{3} where H_-= \begin{pmatrix} 0&p&0&0\\p&-L_a&0&0\\ 0&0&-s&p\\0&0&p&-L_b \end{pmatrix}, \tag{4} H_+= \begin{pmatrix} 2gqa&p&g\sqrt{2qab}&0\\ p&-L_a&0&0\\ g\sqrt{2qab}&0&-ga&p\\ 0&0&p&-L_b \end{pmatrix}. \tag{5} The squared frequencies are eigenvalues of H_-H_+, equivalently H_+H_-. This reduction follows by adding and subtracting the ordinary and conjugate equations in (3). The channel embedding is orthonormal in the actual canonical norm. Its invariance is checked by applying the full source derivative to every column, rather than by discarding matrix entries outside the proposed channel. A nonempty interval necessarily contains growth Set y=p^2. Direct determinants and elimination of the lower rows give \det H_-=-p^2(sL_b-p^2),\qquad \det H_+=L_aL_b\,P(y), \tag{6} P(y)=\left(2gqa+\frac y{L_a}\right) \left(-ga+\frac y{L_b}\right)-2g^2qab. \tag{7} Its constant coefficient is -2g^2qa(a+b)<0, while its quadratic coefficient is positive. It therefore has exactly one positive root y_*. At the zero of the other determinant, P(sL_b)=\frac{sL_b}{L_a}\,gb>0. \tag{8} Consequently 0<y_*<sL_b. Throughout the nonempty interval \boxed{\sqrt{y_*}<|p|<\sqrt{sL_b},} \tag{9} the product \det(H_-H_+) is negative. Its real characteristic polynomial has positive leading coefficient and even degree four. At zero it is negative, while it is positive at sufficiently negative real argument. It has a negative real eigenvalue \Omega^2, which gives an exponentially growing solution. This is sufficient to establish instability; additional growing momenta can occur outside (9). For zero added gaps, put \alpha=a/(a+b), u_*=y_*/s^2. Then u_*^2+\alpha(4q-1)u_*-4q\alpha=0, \quad u_*=\frac{\alpha(1-4q)+ \sqrt{\alpha^2(4q-1)^2+16q\alpha}}2, \quad 0<u_*<1. \tag{10} Increasing a constant gap changes the endpoints in (9); it cannot make them coincide under the stated positive-density assumptions. A spatial confinement law or a different interaction requires a separate analysis. Verification isotropic_channel_checks.py passes 314 conditions in isotropic-channel-20260913T200207Z.json. It verifies all stationary components, independent energy and source variations, the full ordinary and conjugate channel embedding at depths two, four and six, and the growing eigenmode. The depth-six test applies the exact full derivative without allocating its large dense Hessian. One hundred additional positive-parameter controls check the interval and determinant sign. These tests verify the specified field calculation. They neither identify the homogeneous source as a physical particle nor establish instability of the earlier localized inverse-action solutions. Related research Spatial mass operator: results and remaining dynamics — connects this calculation to its premises, later corrections and the complete source question.

title: A whole-depth spatial carrier and physical depth-two polarization
summary: A local shifted-Dirac polynomial on an actual d-dimensional sphere gives the simplex magnitude at every maintained depth; its inverse first-order chain is causal, while tangent-vector fields provide a separate depth-two polarization control without a photon zero.

title: Angular kernel parity
summary: The dot-square angular integral has an exact finite spectrum, while its density-sourced Hartree potential acts by multiplication and preserves parity.
text: The valid integral-operator statement On the ordinary spatial unit sphere S^{d-1}, d\geq2, use probability-normalized measure d\sigma and define (Tf)(x)=\int_{S^{d-1}}(x\cdot y)^2 f(y)\,d\sigma(y). If f(-y)=-f(y), changing y to -y proves Tf=0. In fact the complete nonzero spectrum consists of T1=\frac1d,\qquad T(y^TAy)(x)=\frac{2}{d(d+2)}x^TAx \quad(A=A^T,\ \operatorname{tr}A=0). This follows from rotational invariance and \int y_iy_jy_ky_l\,d\sigma =\frac{\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} +\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}}{d(d+2)}. Rotational invariance and index symmetry force the numerator's three delta pairings to have one common coefficient. Contracting i=j and k=l gives \int|y|^4d\sigma=1, fixing that coefficient to 1/[d(d+2)]. Contracting with the traceless matrix A gives the quadratic eigenvalue. The range contains only constants and traceless quadratics. The corresponding eigenvalues have multiplicities 1 and (d-1)(d+2)/2; all other spherical harmonics, including even degrees four and higher, lie in the kernel. The trace is 1/d+[(d-1)(d+2)/2],2/[d(d+2)]=1. Why a density interaction is different In a quartic density interaction, the mean-field operation is U_\rho(x)=g(T\rho)(x),\qquad \psi(x)\longmapsto U_\rho(x)\psi(x), rather than \psi\mapsto gT\psi. Squaring an odd wave function produces an even density, which can source U_\rho. For an exact example take \psi(x)=\sqrt d\,x_1, so \int|\psi|^2d\sigma=1. Then \rho=d x_1^2,\qquad U_\rho(x)=\frac{g}{d+2}(1+2x_1^2),\qquad \langle\psi|U_\rho|\psi\rangle =\frac{g(d+8)}{(d+2)^2}>0 \quad(g>0). Thus an even kernel gives a nonzero mean-field shift to an odd state in this explicit scalar model. An even multiplication operator preserves parity; it need not annihilate the odd subspace. Application to projected fields Using this angular nullspace for a projected field requires an explicit identification of that field with the scalar angular functions. Physical spin-one polarization has its own representation. A mass-protection argument using the nullspace must establish that the full projected action and its corrections preserve the same structure. The photon module instead keeps P_\gamma\mathcal M P_\gamma=0 as the condition on the full mass operator. The n=0 counting label alone does not prove it. Gauge invariance supplies a different constraint. For a consistently gauged, anomaly-free quantum theory with a symmetry-preserving prescription, q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}=0 permits nonzero transverse vacuum polarization. It does not require \Pi^{\mu\nu}=0 or a constant measured coupling. A regular transverse coefficient leaves the usual massless pole; singular terms or symmetry-breaking backgrounds require additional analysis. See Wingate's QED lectures, §6.2 for an explicit nonzero vacuum-polarization calculation. In a simultaneous matter-and-connection gauge transformation the covariant kinetic term is invariant: the matter phase variation and connection variation cancel. On-shell current conservation and the quantum Ward identities require their respective field and measure assumptions. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py checks the sphere spectrum and the odd-state mean-field example by independent circle and sphere quadratures, plus the nonzero transverse tensor. Interaction operator tools — summarizes the angular result and its application. Projected bilocal variation — derives the actual mean-field operation from a density action.

title: Anomaly-free charge family
summary: The one-family anomaly equations admit a hypercharge and B-minus-L family when a right-handed neutrino is included; selecting observed charges needs additional conditions.
text:
What is being checked This note gives a conditional consistency test for a complete specified charge table. It concerns representations of observed four-dimensional chiral fields, not additional physical spatial dimensions, and does not derive those fields from the nested spatial sectors. Use only left-handed Weyl fields, conjugating right-handed fields: Field SU(3)	imes SU(2) Abelian charge Q (\mathbf3,\mathbf2) q u^c (\overline{\mathbf3},\mathbf1) u d^c (\overline{\mathbf3},\mathbf1) d L (\mathbf1,\mathbf2) l e^c (\mathbf1,\mathbf1) e 
u^c (\mathbf1,\mathbf1) n The mixed non-Abelian, mixed gravitational, and cubic Abelian conditions are 2q+u+d=0,\qquad 3q+l=0, 6q+3u+3d+2l+e+n=0, \qquad 6q^3+3u^3+3d^3+2l^3+e^3+n^3=0. The cubic SU(3) anomaly cancels between two fundamentals and two antifundamentals. There are four weak doublets counting colours, satisfying the usual even-doublet condition. These checks assume precisely this field content and chirality assignment. A family of exact solutions For one scalar doublet H of charge h, invariance of the ordinary Yukawa terms QHu^c, QH^\dagger d^c, LH^\dagger e^c, and LH
u^c requires, respectively, q+h+u=0,\quad q-h+d=0,\quad l-h+e=0,\quad l+h+n=0. The weak-index contractions use the invariant alternating tensor where needed; these equations display the Abelian charge sums. Combining them with l=-3q gives the family (q,u,d,l,e,n)=(q,-q-h,-q+h,-3q,3q+h,3q-h). Every displayed anomaly vanishes for arbitrary q,h. In particular, the cubic sum reduces to 6q^3+3(-q-h)^3+3(-q+h)^3+2(-3q)^3 +(3q+h)^3+(3q-h)^3=0. In the field order (Q,u^c,d^c,L,e^c,
u^c), define the conventional vectors Y=\left( rac16,- rac23, rac13,- rac12,1,0ight), \qquad B-L=\left( rac13,- rac13,- rac13,-1,1,1ight). Then the general displayed family is X=aY+b(B-L), with a=2h, b=3q-h, by direct substitution in each entry. The two-parameter freedom and its relation to the neutrino charge are also described in Allanach, Davighi and Melville, §3.1. The calculation here is an explicit sufficient family, not a classification of every spectrum or of every solution without the Yukawa assumptions. For a compact global U(1), compatible charge lattices impose further integrality conditions; rational examples already demonstrate nonuniqueness. Imposing n=0 removes b in this family. Choosing h=1/2 then yields (q,u,d,l,e,n)=\left( rac16,- rac23, rac13,- rac12,1,0ight). Conjugation restores the usual right-handed charges. Neutrino neutrality and the normalization are extra conditions, or must follow from an independently derived geometric charge map. They do not follow solely from having three colours. Conversely, dropping 
u^c while calling the neutrino Dirac would omit a field from this anomaly calculation. V2's existing determinant-trivial gauge carrier gives a particular charge assignment by a separate construction. The freedom here neither changes that assignment nor inserts a new gauge field into V2. It specifies what anomaly cancellation alone can establish, leaving the physical carrier, chirality, and occupied-mode bridge to be derived. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py checks the polynomial identities symbolically, mixed Y/B-L sums, the neutral-neutrino specialization, and nonstandard rational solutions. Interaction operator tools — summarizes this charge-consistency tool. Auxiliary gauge carrier — the existing global charge construction and its separate mode-spectrum obligations.

title: The simplex spectrum from surface bending
summary: A conformal bending energy gives the exact simplex frequency sequence under a declared geometric time law, while ordinary tension changes its ratios and the round-surface translation response requires a different physical completion.
text:
Summary: A conformal bending energy gives the exact simplex frequency sequence under a declared geometric time law, while ordinary tension changes its ratios and the round-surface translation response requires a different physical completion. The frequency target and the spatial assumption Mass is already expressible as frequency: m_{n,d}= rac{\hbar\omega_{n,d}}{c^2},\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\omega_{0,d}S(n,d),\qquad S(n,d)= inom{n+d-1}{d}. 	ag{1} The problem is to obtain that frequency from the spatial dynamics and its corresponding inertial response. An arbitrary normalization of an eigenfunction is not a variable to fit in (1). A nonlinear fixed-point equation may additionally determine a field's physical magnitude and shape. Consider an explicit geometric comparison: a round surface \Sigma=S_R^m\subset\mathbb R^d, with m=d-2 even. The containing space has d ordinary spatial dimensions. The surface has two normal directions, represented by radial displacement u and axial displacement v. It would have to arise as a feature of the same physical field; the surface is not the whole sector, an extra particle, or a prescribed hard wall. No compactification is used. This differs from the scalar conformal operator on S^d. Here the bending energy of an embedded surface supplies the operator. Neither comparison determines the physical geometry of an IDWT particle. An explicit curvature energy Write A for the second fundamental form, H=\operatorname{tr}A for the trace mean-curvature vector, and A_H for the tensor obtained by contracting the normal index of A with H. In six containing dimensions, the four-dimensional surface has the local energy \mathcal E_4= rac18\int_\Sigma \left[|
abla^\perp H|^2-|A_H|^2+ rac7{16}|H|^4ight]dA. 	ag{2} This is the conformal bending energy in Takeuchi's normalization. Graham and Reichert, equation (1.1) give one sixteenth of (2); their H is also the trace. For a round four-sphere, |H|=4/R, |A_H|^2=64/R^4 and |
abla^\perp H|=0. Thus \mathcal E_4=16\pi^2 for every R>0. The general even-surface energy has a geometric definition and a known second variation, even when writing its full curvature integrand is impractical. The formal extension used to define this invariant is a mathematical construction; it is not an additional physical dimension. Derive the product from the surface Hessian Let m=2k, and use the nonnegative Laplacian \Delta on the unit m-sphere. Takeuchi, Theorem 1.1 and equation (6.6) give, in each normal direction,  egin{aligned} \delta^2\mathcal E(V,V)&= rac1m\int_\Sigma \langle \mathcal J V,Vangle dA,\ \mathcal J&=\prod_{j=1}^{k+1} \left[\Delta+(k+j-1)(k-j)ight]. \end{aligned} 	ag{3} The theorem first applies to a totally geodesic S^m inside the unit S^{m+2}. Stereographic projection from a pole normal to that equator maps it to the round S^m\subset\mathbb R^{m+2}. Its differential on the equator maps the two unit normals to the radial and axial unit normals, with conformal factor one. Conformal invariance of the energy, and vanishing first variation, therefore transfer the complete Hessian in (3) to this Euclidean surface. For a degree-\ell harmonic, \Delta Y=\ell(\ell+m-1)Y. Each factor in (3) becomes \ell(\ell+m-1)+(k+j-1)(k-j) =(\ell+k-j)(\ell+k+j-1). 	ag{4} The factors cover every integer from \ell-1 through \ell+m once. At physical radius R, it follows that  oxed{ \mathcal J_RY_{\ell,a} = rac{(\ell-1)\ell\cdots(\ell+m)}{R^d}Y_{\ell,a}. } 	ag{5} The degrees \ell=0,1 are zero modes of the round conformal family. The first positive degree is \ell=2. Enumerate the positive degrees by n=\ell-1. Then  oxed{ \mathcal J_RY_{n+1,a} = rac{d!}{R^d}S(n,d)Y_{n+1,a}. } 	ag{6} This is an exact eigenvalue identity from a curvature variation. It does not change any particle's assigned n or d. Identifying that positive surface-mode index with the particle index remains an additional physical identification. In particular, the surface harmonic degree is n+1, whereas the oscillator cutoff in the IDOS construction is n-1. The two charged-lepton operators are  egin{aligned} \mathcal J_{6,R} &=\Delta\left(\Delta- rac4{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac2{R^2}ight),\ \mathcal J_{10,R} &=\Delta\left(\Delta- rac8{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac6{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac{10}{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac{12}{R^2}ight). \end{aligned} 	ag{7} Containing depth Particle index n Surface degree \ell R^d\mathcal J_R/d! 6 13 14 18,564 6 35 36 3,838,380 10 23 24 64,512,240 The harmonic multiplicity is instead  inom{\ell+m}{m}- inom{\ell+m-2}{m}. Its cumulative growth is \ell^m, not \ell^d. Thus (6) reproduces the polynomial used for the proposed IDOS; it does not identify that IDOS with the count of surface harmonics themselves. Which time law makes this a frequency? An oriented surface with two normal directions admits a geometric symplectic form. Declare its physical coefficient to be \Gamma>0: \Omega_\Sigma(U,V)=\Gamma\int_\Sigma (U_uV_v-U_vV_u)dA. 	ag{8} This is the codimension-two Marsden–Weinstein form; see Song and Sun, Section 2.1. It pairs two actual normal displacements. Its occurrence in the master field is an additional dynamical hypothesis. The canonical field projection gives a conditional origin for its coefficient as a normal boundary-current integral. A common surrounding field can make it independent of core shape; a fully localized normal field has an outer contribution that cancels it. For Hamiltonian \kappa\mathcal E, the quadratic action can be written L^{(2)}= rac\Gamma2\int(u\dot v-v\dot u)dA - rac\kappa{2m}\int(u\mathcal J_Ru+v\mathcal J_Rv)dA. 	ag{9} With w=u-iv, both real equations are equivalent to i\partial_tw= rac\kappa{m\Gamma}\mathcal J_Rw. 	ag{10} Consequently this declared action gives  oxed{ \omega_{n,d}= rac{\kappa d!}{m\Gamma R^d}S(n,d). } 	ag{11} The eigenfunction normalization cancels from its frequency. Both normal coordinates and the two signed eigenvalues of the real evolution matrix are retained. The signs do not provide an antiparticle interpretation. By contrast, a quadratic time kinetic term would give \omega^2\propto\mathcal J_R, hence a square root of this sequence. The spatial product alone therefore does not choose the time law. Nor does (11) derive \kappa, \Gamma, a common radius, or their relation across depths. The common-cavity scale analysis still applies: converting the shared frequency unit into a physical length requires these coefficients. Here the displayed dependence is R^{-d}; a relation proportional to c/R would require the corresponding relation between \kappa/\Gamma, c and R. Ordinary tension changes the frequency ratios Add 	au\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma) to the same Hamiltonian. Let A_m be the area of the unit m-sphere. A round surface translates along its axis with speed v_0= rac{	au m}{\Gamma R}. 	ag{12} Linearization must use its moving frame. In radial graph coordinates, the area and axial translation momentum expand as  egin{aligned} dA={}&R^m\left[1+ rac{mu}{R} + rac{m(m-1)u^2+|
abla u|^2+|
abla v|^2}{2R^2} ight]d\Omega+O((u,v)^3),\ P_z={}& rac\Gamma{m+1}\int(R+u)^{m+1}d\Omega. \end{aligned} 	ag{13} The gradient in this expansion is on the unit sphere. Subtracting v_0P_z cancels the first variation. On degree \ell, define \lambda_\ell=\ell(\ell+m-1)/R^2 and B_\ell=\kappa p_\ell/(mR^d), where p_\ell is the product in (5). The two restoring coefficients are a_\ell=B_\ell+	au(\lambda_\ell-m/R^2),\qquad b_\ell=B_\ell+	au\lambda_\ell. 	ag{14} The complete normal pair has \omega_\ell^2= rac{a_\ell b_\ell}{\Gamma^2}. 	ag{15} Thus a common tension cannot generally be absorbed into the shared frequency unit. At depth six, in units R=\kappa=\Gamma=1, the unchanged electron and muon degrees have \lambda_e=238 and \lambda_\mu=1404. A positive tension decreases their frequency ratio. An illustrative relative ratio budget of 2	imes10^{-5} allows 	au R^4/\kappa\le0.29156255 in this particular model. This is a declared accuracy budget, not an experimental bound on a physical tension. For an ordinary hypersurface bubble the curvature factor in Young–Laplace is d-1. The factor m=d-2 here belongs to the explicitly different codimension-two surface. The soap-bubble analogy does not itself prescribe this geometry. Translation exposes a missing part of the dynamics The geometric symplectic form supplies a useful independent check. Let X\in\mathbb R^d be the center and N the unit axis of a round surface. Its translation momentum is P=p(R)N,\qquad p(R)= rac{\Gamma A_m}{m+1}R^{m+1}. 	ag{16} To derive this, at a point with radial unit vector 	heta\perp N, a change (\delta X,\delta R,\delta N) has normal components u=\delta R+	heta\cdot\delta X,\qquad v=N\cdot\delta X-R	heta\cdot\delta N. 	ag{17} Insert (17) into (8), and use \langle	hetaangle=0 and \langle	heta_i	heta_jangle=(\delta_{ij}-N_iN_j)/(m+1). The result is the canonical form \sum_i dP_i\wedge dX_i. All translation directions and surface orientations have been included. The pure conformal bending energy is constant on this round family. It has no translation velocity or restoring coefficient there. Adding area gives H(P)=\mathrm{constant} +	au A_m\left( rac{(m+1)|P|}{\Gamma A_m}ight)^{m/(m+1)}. 	ag{18} Differentiating \dot X=\partial H/\partial P gives (12). Its full inverse velocity derivative is  oxed{  rac{\partial P}{\partial\dot X} = rac{p}{v_0}\left[I-(m+2)NN^{\mathsf T}ight]. } 	ag{19} There are d-1 positive transverse eigenvalues p/v_0 and one negative longitudinal eigenvalue -(m+1)p/v_0. This is not the positive, isotropic particle inertia sought in (1). The result concerns the round translating background of this action; it is not a calculation of a fully dressed oscillating particle or a rejection of the proposed origin of mass. The nonlinear mode response shows why an oscillating field needs a further fixed-point calculation: its curvature interactions drive other modes and the round scale mode. Physical scope and verification This construction supplies a natural curvature origin for the complete simplex polynomial and a concrete frequency equation. It does not supply a derived master-field surface, a spinor realization, mode selection, a selected radius or the required complete inertia. The unrestricted first-order evolution in (10) also has a spatial operator of order d. Its commutator with a smooth nonconstant coordinate has order d-1 and is unbounded. The finite-propagation criterion therefore excludes using it unchanged as a fundamental causal equation for every spatial disturbance. A controlled effective bending response would need its same-field causal parent and frequency dependence. bending_surface_checks.py checks the exact product by independently applying the differential operator to Gegenbauer polynomials, including the assigned degrees. It also differentiates the full six-dimensional curvature integral (2) numerically, in both normal directions and their mixed spatial variations. The largest relative error in the reported curvature Hessians is below 2	imes10^{-7}; radius and quadrature refinement are retained. Independent variations of the actual area and momentum verify (14). The full two-coordinate trajectories check (15), while spatial spherical quadrature and velocity differentiation verify the complete tensor (19). These are tests of the stated geometric action, not experimental evidence that particles have the assumed surface structure.

title: Radial freedom in the gapped simplex carrier
summary: The exact polarization and translation identities hold for general radial winding profiles, including a bounded example with a proven full normal gap.
text: The equally spaced polarization values of the normal Dirac carrier do not require the unbounded coefficient W=z^n. They follow from a radial boundary identity that remains valid for a much larger profile family. This permits a bounded spatial coefficient while preserving the simplex numerator. The profile is a coefficient of the inverse spatial operator; its physical source and total supporting inertia remain open. Use the four-component ordinary planar Dirac operator defined in the holomorphic carrier, now with W=w(r) exp(i n theta), where w is real, positive away from zero, regular as r^n at zero, and supports decaying zero modes. Write q=n-1. The negative-chiral zero equations are U_l'=lU_l/r-wV_l,\qquad V_l'=(q-l)V_l/r-wU_l. \tag{1} Normalize each four-component mode by 2 pi integral r(U_l^2+V_l^2)dr=1. Direct differentiation gives \frac{d}{dr}[r^2(U_l^2-V_l^2)] =2r[(l+1)U_l^2-(n-l)V_l^2]. \tag{2} When the boundary term vanishes, this proves \|U_l\|_2^2=\frac{n-l}{n+1},\qquad \|V_l\|_2^2=\frac{l+1}{n+1},\qquad P(\sigma_3\otimes I)P=-\frac{2J_z}{n+1}. \tag{3} Here (J_z)_ll=l-q/2. Equation (2) also excludes every integer label outside l=0,...,q for a nonzero square-integrable mode. The n regular labels each have one decaying radial solution under the stated profile conditions. Their count refers to available modes, not their occupation. Two other exact identities survive the radial change. Ordinary momentum has zero within-kernel projection, P p_x P=P p_y P=0, because its adjacent-label radial integral is the boundary derivative rw(U_{l+1}V_l+V_{l+1}U_l)-2(q-l)V_{l+1}V_l =-\frac{d}{dr}(rV_{l+1}V_l). \tag{4} The complementary inverse of the polarization source is still the positive-chiral vector r(V_l,U_l)/(n+1), with the angular phases of the original carrier. These identities concern this unconnected radial operator. The connected extension has different weighted polarization and momentum formulas. A smooth bounded profile and a full gap One explicit choice is w(r)=\frac{r^n}{\sqrt{1+(r/R)^{2n}}},\qquad R=2. \tag{5} It approaches the finite positive value R^n at infinity. The positive-chiral square has diagonal -Delta+w^2 and off-diagonal magnitude |w'-nw/r|. Its full quadratic form therefore obeys Q^\dagger Q\ge-\Delta+(1-\epsilon_n)w^2, \qquad \epsilon_n=\frac{\sqrt n\,(n-1)^{(n-1)/(2n)}}{R^{n+1}}. \tag{6} To obtain (6), maximize |w'-nw/r|/w^2. Its maximum occurs at (r/R)^(2n)=n-1. Put a=(1-epsilon_n)/2. Then the scalar potential in (6) is at least a r^(2n) inside r=R and a R^(2n) outside. Use a positive test function equal to exp(-eta r^2/2) inside R and exp(-eta R r+eta R^2/2) outside. Its value and first derivative agree at R. The ground-state transform gives the full-space lower bound g_n^2\ge\min\left\{ 2\eta-(n-1)n^{-n/(n-1)}a^{-1/(n-1)}\eta^{2n/(n-1)},\; aR^{2n}-\eta^2R^2\right\},\qquad n\ge2. \tag{7} For eta=1 and R=2, the lower bounds on the nonzero Dirac frequencies are approximately 1.16350 at n=5, 1.15149 at n=6 and 1.11670 at n=10. Thus the entire complementary spectrum has a positive gap. This is an analytic operator inequality, not a finite-box eigenvalue estimate. The bounded multiplier h=z/sqrt(1+r^2) still has fixed positive adjacent integrals h_l. Their relative changes from the monomial profile are about 0.00059 at n=5, 0.00018 at n=6 and 0.0000013 at n=10. They change the shared frequency unit, while the diagonal product is unchanged: \omega_n(\beta)= \frac{\prod_{l=0}^{n-1}(\beta+l-(n-1)/2)} {\gamma^{n-1}\prod_l h_l}[1+O(\gamma^{-2})]. \tag{8} The existing assignments n=d and beta=L+(d-3)/2 give the numerator d! binomial(L+d-2,d). No particle indices or field magnitudes were adjusted. The full normal correction remains bounded by the earlier chirality-based resolvent argument with the new gap (7). The complementary response must also change For (5), the positive-chiral Green inverse is a coupled radial two-component inverse. The monomial carrier's separate scalar Green functions are no longer valid. The complete coupled calculation retains every forced angular sector and both spinor components. At n=6 and gamma=10000, the refined partial wave momentum response divided by frequency is approximately (265079.42,-265077.76) for the electron branch and (44061.20,-44059.54) for the muon branch. These signed responses belong to a wave in prescribed coefficients. They do not describe negative physical particle inertia. The phase of a partial response and the momentum of the complete sustaining field are separate calculations. The report bounded-normal-20260914T130117_970869Z.json passes 37 checks of the kernel identities, analytic bounds, coupled field residuals and second-order radial refinement. The finest-grid complete first-equation residual is about 1.26e-6 relative to its source. Source hashes and raw profiles accompany the report. Bounded coefficients improve the inverse operator, but their boundedness alone does not establish finite physical supporting energy. The next linked construction supplies a finite geometric functional as well; its reciprocal wave source must still be included in a complete model.

title: Bounded spectral perturbations
summary: A bounded self-adjoint perturbation preserves compact resolvent, bounds every ordered eigenvalue shift, and preserves isolated spectral-cluster rank under an explicit gap condition.
text: Hypotheses Let H be self-adjoint, bounded below, with compact resolvent. Let V be bounded and self-adjoint, with v=\|V\|. Then H+V is self-adjoint on the same operator domain D(H) and is bounded below by \inf\sigma(H)-v. For a nonreal z with |\operatorname{Im}z|>v, (H+V-z)^{-1}=(H-z)^{-1} \left[I+V(H-z)^{-1}\right]^{-1}. The bracket is invertible by its Neumann series. The first factor is compact, so the perturbed resolvent is compact. The resolvent identity extends compactness to every point of the perturbed resolvent set. Eigenvalue displacement Order eigenvalues increasingly, counting multiplicity, as E_j(H). For every unit u in the common domain, \langle u,Hu\rangle-v \leq\langle u,(H+V)u\rangle \leq\langle u,Hu\rangle+v. Taking the maximum over a j-dimensional trial space and then the infimum over such spaces gives \boxed{|E_j(H+V)-E_j(H)|\leq v.} The variational characterization used here is stated in Nam, Functional Analysis II, §2.3. It includes repeated eigenvalues. A perturbation may split a degeneracy while respecting every bound. An isolated cluster Suppose a finite group of eigenvalues is separated from the rest by a positive minimum gap g. If 2v<g, the perturbed cluster and the perturbed neighboring eigenvalues remain separated by at least g-2v. It has the same number of eigenvalues counting multiplicity. The associated subspace can rotate. To express its continuity, take a closed counterclockwise contour \mathcal C enclosing only the cluster and satisfying \operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma(H))\geq\delta>v along the contour. For H_t=H+tV, 0\leq t\leq1, define P_t=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\mathcal C}(z-H_t)^{-1}\,dz. Neumann inversion holds on the whole contour, so these orthogonal spectral projectors vary continuously in norm. Their finite integer rank is constant. The resolvent identity also gives the explicit estimate \|P_t-P_0\| \leq\frac{\operatorname{length}(\mathcal C)}{2\pi} \frac{tv}{\delta(\delta-tv)}. The contour condition supplies this bound directly; it is separate from the eigenvalue-count statement. Oscillator example For the confining oscillator, write w=\sqrt\lambda. Its distinct levels are E_N=(2N+d)w, separated by 2w. Every level defines a cluster of \binom{N+d-1}{d-1} eigenvalues. Any bounded self-adjoint V with \|V\|<w preserves these separated cluster counts along H+tV. Their eigenvalues need not remain equal or equally spaced. For example, a twofold level E with perturbation \begin{pmatrix}0&\epsilon\\\epsilon&0\end{pmatrix} splits into E\pm\epsilon. The level count survives and the two frequencies change. A physical interaction must supply its actual operator norm and domain before this bound can establish robustness of a sector calculation. Unbounded interactions require an appropriate relative-bound argument. Verification and related spectral_analysis_checks.py tests ordered shifts, cluster counts, subspace rotations, the contour bound, and explicit degeneracy splitting on independently constructed Hermitian matrices. The infinite-dimensional domain and compactness statements are proved above. Spectral analysis tools — navigation and scope.

title: A first-order parent for the curvature frequency operator
summary: A first-order spatial chain approaches the curvature simplex frequency with its complete canonical norm and finite-gap correction retained.
text:
The conformal surface Hessian already gives the simplex polynomial as a spatial eigenvalue. Its unrestricted higher-order evolution cannot be used as a fundamental finite-speed equation. A local tensor chain supplies an explicit first-order parent whose low-frequency branch approaches that polynomial, with its frequency dependence and canonical norm retained. This is an inverse linear construction on a specified round field feature. It does not derive that feature, its common radius, the common gap, or its support from the master field. The tensor components must still be realized as modes of that same field. They are not additional interaction particles or additional spatial dimensions. No compactification or Yukawa coupling is used. Factor the actual surface operator into first-order links Let m = d-2 be even, with d at least four. Consider a round S_R^m embedded in ordinary R^d. This is a proposed codimension-two spatial feature, rather than the entire d-dimensional sector. Write Delta for the nonnegative scalar Laplacian. The known conformal bending Hessian is \mathcal J_d=\Delta(\Delta-m/R^2) \prod_{j=1}^{m/2-1}\left[\Delta+ rac{j(m-1-j)}{R^2}ight]. 	ag{1} On a degree-ell scalar harmonic its eigenvalue is \mathcal J_dY_\ell =R^{-d}(\ell-1)\ell\cdots(\ell+d-2)Y_\ell = rac{d!}{R^d}D_{\ell-2,d}Y_\ell. 	ag{2} Takeuchi's second-variation theorem and the preceding V2 bending note give this geometric operator.[1] The construction below supplies a different issue: a full first-order evolution that approximates it over a controlled range. It does not claim that the nonlinear bending energy or its physical geometric time coefficient has now been derived. Use the following natural tensor bundles on the surface: scalars E_0, covectors E_1, and traceless symmetric two-tensors E_2. Define G_0f=
abla f,\qquad G_1v=\sqrt{ rac m{m-1}} \left[
abla_{(a}v_{b)}- rac{g_{ab}}m
abla\cdot vight]. 	ag{3} For each positive constant b in the product (1), also define A_bT=\left(
abla T, rac{\sqrt{2m+b}}R Tight), \qquad A_b^\dagger A_b=
abla^*
abla+ rac{2m+b}{R^2}. 	ag{4} The range in (4) is the direct sum of covector-valued traceless symmetric two-tensors and another traceless symmetric two-tensor. All components are retained. The second entry is an algebraic curvature coefficient; the first contains only one spatial derivative. Put lambda_ell = ell(ell+m-1). For a unit scalar harmonic, the normalized gradient and traceless Hessian generate an exactly closed chain. The needed identities are  egin{aligned} \|
abla Y_\ell\|^2&= rac{\lambda_\ell}{R^2},\ \|\operatorname{Hess}_0Y_\ell\|^2 &= rac{m-1}{mR^4}\lambda_\ell(\lambda_\ell-m),\ 
abla^*
abla(\operatorname{Hess}_0Y_\ell) &= rac{\lambda_\ell-2m}{R^2}\operatorname{Hess}_0Y_\ell. \end{aligned} 	ag{5} The first two follow by integration by parts and the Ricci curvature (m-1)g/R^2. The third follows by commuting two covariant derivatives of the Hessian and removing its trace. An independent Cartesian calculation below verifies the complete tensor equation, including its complex spatial polarization. The first-order link list is G_0,\ G_1,\ A_{b_1},\ A_{b_1}^\dagger,\ldots, A_{b_{m/2-1}},\ A_{b_{m/2-1}}^\dagger, \ G_1^\dagger,\ G_0^\dagger, \qquad b_j=j(m-1-j). 	ag{6} There are exactly d links. On the scalar-derived harmonic subspace, their positive matrix coefficients are  rac1R\left( \sqrt\lambda,\sqrt{\lambda-m}, \sqrt{\lambda+b_1},\sqrt{\lambda+b_1},\ldots, \sqrt{\lambda-m},\sqrt\lambdaight). 	ag{7} Their product is precisely (2). The intermediate tensor fields are actual sections over the same spatial surface; they are not copies introduced in numbers h_(k,d) to insert the simplex weights. The complete first-order evolution Multiply each link in (6) by one speed c, and call the resulting operator L_j, mapping E_(j-1) to E_j. The notation reuses E_j for the successive bundles in the list; E_d is again the scalar bundle. Introduce canonical fields x_j in E_j for j=0,...,d-1, and y_j in E_j for j=1,...,d. Each field has the usual positive time norm. The intermediate bundles have both an x and a y copy, coupled by one common positive frequency gap G. Define (Tx)_j=L_jx_{j-1}+Gx_j\quad(1\le j<d), \qquad (Tx)_d=L_dx_{d-1}, 	ag{8} i\partial_t egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix} =\underbrace{ egin{pmatrix}0&T^\dagger\T&0\end{pmatrix}}_{H}  egin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix}, \qquad Q=\int\left(\sum|x_j|^2+\sum|y_j|^2ight)dA. 	ag{9} This is one local first-order equation. Every intermediate equation, both spectral signs and the entire complex tensor field are present. The signs do not supply an antiparticle interpretation. Since H is self-adjoint on its natural closed-surface domain, the full linear evolution conserves Q. This linear fact does not establish nonlinear particle stability or a positive lower bound for the signed Hamiltonian. Its propagation speed is controlled directly. The principal symbols of G_0 and A_b have norm |p|. For G_1, on a unit tangent covector p, \|\sigma(G_1)(p)v\|^2 = rac{m}{2(m-1)}|v|^2 + rac{m-2}{2(m-1)}|p\cdot v|^2\le |v|^2. 	ag{10} After grouping variables, the principal matrix of (9) is a direct sum of the Hermitian pairs of these link symbols. The G couplings have no spatial derivatives. Thus its complete symbol norm is c|p|. The usual local norm-flux estimate gives propagation within the surface distance c|t| while retaining all field components.[2] The large gap does not alter that principal speed. This supplies a causal linear parent on the assumed surface. It does not identify these independent tensor components with the particular spinor and derivative carrier of the master action. Nor does it supply propagation or confinement in the two ordinary normal directions. The exact branch and its finite-gap correction On a degree-ell scalar harmonic, (8) is a d-by-d bidiagonal matrix with diagonal t_j equal to c times (7), and superdiagonal G. The positive low frequency is its smallest singular value. Put a_\ell= rac{\prod_{j=1}^dt_j}{G^{d-1}},\qquad C_\ell=a_\ell T_\ell^{-1}. 	ag{11} The matrix C has the explicit bounded entries (C_\ell)_{ij}= (-1)^{j-i} \prod_{a<i} rac{t_a}{G} \prod_{a>j} rac{t_a}{G}\quad(i\le j), 	ag{12} and zero otherwise. Its upper-right entry has magnitude one. Hence  oxed{\omega_\ell= rac{a_\ell}{\|C_\ell\|},\qquad a_\ell= rac{d!c^d}{R^dG^{d-1}}D_{\ell-2,d}.} 	ag{13} This is an exact finite-dimensional reduction of the stated spatial chain. title: Centroid-relative self-binding
summary: Centering the auxiliary scalar moment functional yields an explicit translation-covariant self-binding model with zero net self-force.
text:
Scope and reason for this addition Binding a particle's structure about its own centre differs from trapping its centre at an external origin. This distinction fits the V2 spatial premise: an electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions, treated alike by its self-binding. Its shared directions with a lower-depth observer acquire no preferred status. The existing self-consistent functional explicitly leaves a correctly varied centroid prescription open. Here is that prescription for its flat scalar model. The calculation below is a checked completion of this auxiliary model; it is not a recovered derivation of the master Dirac dynamics, a global construction on physical CP3, or the actual Coulomb-plus-precession orbit. Define the centre inside the functional Let x\in\mathbb R^d be ordinary spatial coordinates and assume a decaying field with finite kinetic energy and second moment. Write ho=|\psi|^2,\qquad Q=\intho\,dx>0,\qquad R= rac{1}{Q}\int xho(x)\,dx,\qquad z=x-R, M=\int zz^{\mathsf T}ho(x)\,dx. M is the unnormalized central second moment. For g>0, define E[\psi]= rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int|
abla\psi|^2\,dx+U[ho], \qquad U= rac g2\operatorname{tr}(M^2). Equivalently, U= rac g2\iint  ig[(x-R)\cdot(y-R) ig]^2ho(x)ho(y)\,dx\,dy. The same density-dependent R is used throughout. Translation of the whole field translates R and leaves M and E unchanged. Under a spatial rotation O, M becomes OMO^{\mathsf T} and \operatorname{tr}(M^2) is unchanged. No subset of the d directions is selected. Variation and self-force One must vary R as well as the explicit density factors. Its variation cancels because \int zho\,dx=0: \delta M =\int zz^{\mathsf T}\deltaho\,dx -\delta R\left(\int zho\,dxight)^{\mathsf T} -\left(\int zho\,dxight)\delta R^{\mathsf T} =\int zz^{\mathsf T}\deltaho\,dx. This holds even for variations that change Q, since R is defined using the current Q. Therefore  rac{\delta U}{\deltaho(x)}=g z^{\mathsf T}Mz, \qquad i\hbar\partial_t\psi =\left[- rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta+g z^{\mathsf T}Mzight]\psi for the usual scalar Schrödinger variational dynamics. At each fixed time, R and M are spatially constant coefficients in this potential. Its total self-force is -\intho\,
abla_x\!\left(g z^{\mathsf T}Mzight)\,dx =-2gM\int zho\,dx=0. With the stated decay and regularity assumptions, the continuity equation and momentum balance give P=\int\psi^*(-i\hbar
abla)\psi\,dx,\qquad \dot P=0,\qquad \dot R= rac{P}{mQ}. Thus the centre moves freely while the self-potential acts on the shape. In the rest frame R=0, choosing \hbar^2/(2m)=1 recovers the existing isotropic stationary calculation. Translating that solution gives a family of equally energetic resting centres. The time-dependent equation also admits the usual Galilean boost \psi_v(x,t)= \exp\!\left[ rac{im}{\hbar} \left(v\cdot x- rac{|v|^2t}{2}ight)ight]\psi(x-vt,t). This establishes the moving-centre claim for this specified nonrelativistic model. It does not derive relativistic dispersion, stability of every excited profile, particle mass counts, or cross-sector forces. Separately centering each species in a coupled model would require a fresh variation of the complete interaction.
