title: Chiral pseudoscalar mass term
summary: A specified leading chiral action makes pseudoscalar mass squared proportional to light-quark masses, with the response scale left as matched input.
text: Conditional symmetry protection The V2 hadronic problem needs a mechanism for light pseudoscalar masses. A useful adjacent benchmark is a leading chiral effective action. Assume spontaneous SU(3)_L\times SU(3)_R\to SU(3)_V breaking, positive light quark masses, and momenta and masses within its low-energy expansion. In natural units define \mathcal L_2=\frac{F^2}{4}\operatorname{Tr}(\partial_\mu U\partial^\mu U^\dagger) +\frac{F^2}{4}\operatorname{Tr}(\chi U^\dagger+U\chi^\dagger), \qquad \chi=2B_0 M, where M=\operatorname{diag}(m_u,m_d,m_s), U=\exp(i\Phi/F), \Phi=\sum_{a=1}^8\lambda_a\pi_a, and \operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_a\lambda_b)=2\delta_{ab}. Here F>0 has mass units and B_0>0 also has mass units. The flavour components are fields on physical space, not extra spatial dimensions. Both constants require matching to the underlying dynamics. Expansion with normalization explicit Expanding U to quadratic order gives \mathcal L_2=\frac12\sum_a\partial_\mu\pi_a\partial^\mu\pi_a +F^2B_0\operatorname{Tr}M -\frac{B_0}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(M\Phi^2)+O(\pi^4). The real-field mass matrix is therefore (\mathsf M^2)_{ab}=\frac{B_0}{2} \operatorname{Tr}\left(M\{\lambda_a,\lambda_b\}\right). For example \lambda_1 has unit entries at (1,2),(2,1), so \operatorname{Tr}M\lambda_1^2=m_u+m_d. The charged fields \pi^\pm=(\pi_1\mp i\pi_2)/\sqrt2 have m_{\pi^\pm}^2=B_0(m_u+m_d). The same calculation for the other flavour pairs gives Field Leading squared mass \pi^\pm B_0(m_u+m_d) K^\pm B_0(m_u+m_s) K^0,\bar K^0 B_0(m_d+m_s) \eta_8, with m_u=m_d \frac{B_0}{3}(m_u+m_d+4m_s) For unequal m_u,m_d, the neutral (\pi_3,\pi_8) block additionally has off-diagonal entry B_0(m_u-m_d)/\sqrt3 and must be diagonalized. In the isospin limit, 4m_K^2-m_\pi^2=3m_{\eta_8}^2 at this order. The quadratic mass vanishes with M. This is the explicit cancellation pattern supplied by chiral symmetry in this action. In the two-flavour restriction it gives F^2m_\pi^2=-(m_u+m_d)\langle\bar q q\rangle_0 with the per-flavour convention \langle\bar q q\rangle_0=-F^2B_0. This condensate relation uses chiral-limit parameters and holds to leading order in the light masses. The leading mass relations and their scale limitation are reviewed in PDG, Quark Masses, §60.5.2. The scheme dependence of B_0 compensates that of the quark masses. Electromagnetic effects and higher orders require additional terms. This benchmark identifies what a V2 pseudoscalar mechanism must reproduce if it realizes these chiral premises; it does not determine F or B_0. title: Colour singlet criterion
summary: Vanishing mean colour charge is weaker than the singlet condition; the positive total quadratic Casimir distinguishes them exactly.
text: Convention This singlet diagnostic supports V2's hadronic contact calculations by distinguishing mean charge, charge variance, and invariant states. The matrices below represent field amplitudes on the physical manifold; their sizes introduce no physical spatial dimensions. Use Hermitian fundamental generators of SU(N) with \operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b)=\delta_{ab}/2. Their completeness relation is \sum_a(T_a)_{ij}(T_a)_{kl} =\frac12\left(\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}-\frac1N\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\right). It is the orthogonal projector onto traceless matrices in this normalization. Contracting with two density matrices gives the purity relation below; contracting the middle indices gives the fundamental Casimir. For a density matrix \rho of trace one, write n_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho T_a). Completeness gives \rho=\frac{I}{N}+2\sum_a n_aT_a, \qquad \sum_a n_a^2=\frac12\left(\operatorname{tr}\rho^2-\frac1N\right). For a pure fundamental state this norm is (N-1)/(2N). In contrast, \sum_a T_a^2=C_FI,\qquad C_F=\frac{N^2-1}{2N}. For SU(3) with T_a=\lambda_a/2, the pure mean-charge norm squared is 1/3, while the quadratic Casimir is 4/3. Changing generator normalization changes both consistently; it does not equate these two quantities. Exact singlet test On a specified tensor product of particle representations, let Q_a=\sum_iT_a^{(i)}, using -T_a^* for an antifundamental factor. Then C_{\rm tot}=\sum_aQ_a^2\geq0, \qquad \langle\psi|C_{\rm tot}|\psi\rangle =\sum_a\|Q_a\psi\|^2. Consequently \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle=0 exactly when every generator annihilates \psi, equivalently when \psi is an SU(N) singlet. For a positive density matrix, zero expectation means that its support lies wholly in the singlet subspace. Merely having \langle Q_a\rangle=0 leaves the sum of variances uncontrolled: \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle =\sum_a\langle Q_a\rangle^2+\sum_a\operatorname{Var}(Q_a). Explicit SU(3) witnesses are: State Mean total charge \langle C_{\rm tot}\rangle Single fundamental \rho=I/3 Zero 4/3 Product |r\bar r\rangle Zero 2 Meson singlet (|r\bar r\rangle+|g\bar g\rangle+|b\bar b\rangle)/\sqrt3 Zero 0 Ordered product |rgb\rangle Zero 3 Normalized antisymmetric three-quark determinant Zero 0 Here r,g,b form an orthonormal basis labelled 1,2,3. The last state is |\epsilon\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt6} \sum_{i,j,k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}|ijk\rangle. For the meson, the generator action is proportional to the vectorized matrix T_a-T_a=0. For the determinant, a simultaneous basis change multiplies the state by \det U=1. Both states are therefore singlets. The ordered product states instead retain nonzero total charge variance. The distinction agrees with the determinant projection and pair-generator calculation in the hadronic ledger, §§74–76. Limits of a Casimir penalty An assumed term \kappa C_{\rm tot} with \kappa>0 has zero energy exactly on available singlets. This is a useful conditional selection operator. It does not derive that term from the master kernel, set \kappa, or prove spatial confinement, a growing separation energy, or nuclear depth three. If other coloured fields participate, the constraint concerns their total charge too; a valence-only projection requires justification. Verification and related interaction_operator_checks.py constructs all eight generators, the two- and three-particle charge operators, and the states in the table. It checks both mean charges and charge variances. Interaction operator tools — summarizes the singlet diagnostic and its verification.

title: Confining oscillator domain
summary: The harmonic spatial operator has a closed energy form, compact resolvent, and an explicit eigenbasis whose Gaussian tails justify specified boundary limits.
text: Operator and energy domain On a flat model of d ordinary spatial directions within the one nested physical manifold, consider H=-\Delta+\lambda|x|^2,\qquad \lambda>0,\qquad \mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,d^dx). This is a specified scalar confinement operator. Its use for a particular sector requires the corresponding kinetic and binding dynamics. Define its energy through the positive quadratic form q[u]=\int\left(|\nabla u|^2+\lambda|x|^2|u|^2\right)d^dx, \qquad \mathcal Q=H^1(\mathbb R^d)\cap\{u:|x|u\in L^2\}. Here H^1 requires square-integrable weak first derivatives. The form norm is (\|u\|_2^2+q[u])^{1/2}. It is complete: a Cauchy sequence converges in H^1 and its products |x|u converge in L^2; local convergence identifies the latter limit with |x| times the former. The densely defined closed form therefore defines the positive self-adjoint Friedrichs operator H. Compact resolvent Suppose a sequence is bounded in this form norm by a common constant. For every R>0, \int_{|x|>R}|u(x)|^2\,d^dx \leq \frac{q[u]}{\lambda R^2}. On each finite ball, the Rellich compactness theorem supplies an L^2-convergent subsequence of the H^1-bounded restrictions. Choose a diagonal subsequence over increasing balls. The uniform tail estimate makes this subsequence Cauchy on all of \mathbb R^d: first make both tails small, then use convergence on the chosen ball. Thus \mathcal Q\hookrightarrow L^2 is compact. The resolvent (H+1)^{-1} maps bounded L^2 sets to bounded form-norm sets. Composing with that compact inclusion proves compactness of the resolvent. The spectrum consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity tending to infinity, with a complete orthonormal eigenbasis. This is the confining-potential case of the spectral theorem discussed in Phan Thành Nam, Functional Analysis II, §2.5. Explicit basis and general states Set w=\sqrt{\lambda}. For a multi-index \alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d) of nonnegative integers, write |\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j=N and \alpha!=\prod_j\alpha_j!. The physicists' Hermite polynomials give \phi_\alpha(x)= \frac{(w/\pi)^{d/4}}{\sqrt{2^N\alpha!}} \prod_{j=1}^d H_{\alpha_j}(\sqrt w\,x_j) e^{-w|x|^2/2}, \qquad H\phi_\alpha=(2N+d)w\,\phi_\alpha. The one-dimensional Hermite differential equation proves the eigenvalue, and Hermite orthogonality proves normalization. Counting multi-indices with sum N gives \binom{N+d-1}{d-1} states at that energy. The spherical basis and radial overlaps are given in Normalized oscillator modes. Every normalizable state has an L^2-convergent expansion u=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\phi_\alpha with \sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2<\infty. Writing E_\alpha=(2|\alpha|+d)w, \begin{aligned} u\in\mathcal Q&\iff\sum_\alpha E_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2<\infty,\\ u\in D(H)&\iff\sum_\alpha E_\alpha^2|c_\alpha|^2<\infty. \end{aligned} In the corresponding scaled time, unitary evolution is u(t)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha e^{-iE_\alpha t}\phi_\alpha. It preserves the norm for every L^2 state, including superpositions. For example (\phi_0+\phi_{(1,0,\ldots,0)})/\sqrt2 has two energy components with relative phase e^{-2iwt}. Gaussian tails and boundary terms A fixed eigenfunction is a polynomial of degree at most N times e^{-w|x|^2/2}. For r\geq1 its polynomial obeys a bound Cr^N. Using \Omega_{d-1}=2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2) gives, for R\geq1, \begin{aligned} \int_{|x|>R}|\phi_\alpha|^2\,d^dx &\leq C^2\Omega_{d-1}\int_R^\infty r^{2N+d-1}e^{-wr^2}\,dr\\ &=\frac{C^2\Omega_{d-1}}{2w^{N+d/2}} \Gamma(N+d/2,wR^2). \end{aligned} Here \Gamma(s,z)=\int_z^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt is the upper incomplete gamma function. Polynomial derivatives have the same Gaussian envelope. Surface integrals of finite products of these eigenfunctions and their derivatives, with polynomially bounded coefficients, therefore tend to zero at infinity. This supplies explicit boundary control for finite oscillator-mode calculations. For general energy-domain states, the form tail bound above still applies. Pointwise Gaussian decay or a particular boundary flux requires additional regularity and decay assumptions. The fibre-integrated stress calculation states the flux condition for a conserved source. At level N, every normalized eigenstate has \langle |x|^2\rangle=\frac{N+d/2}{w}, \qquad L=w^{-1/2}=\lambda^{-1/4}. The diagonal one-coordinate identity \langle x_j^2\rangle=(\alpha_j+1/2)/w proves this for the Cartesian basis; the terms in |x|^2 that change total level have zero matrix elements within a fixed eigenspace, proving the general case. The coefficient \lambda has units of inverse length to the fourth in this scaled operator. Matching L to a physical length requires the physical coefficients of the action. Verification and related spatial_profile_checks.py checks normalized Hermite modes, differential residuals, moments, superposition evolution, and independent tail quadratures. The compactness argument is analytic; finite numerical checks test its explicit examples. Gaussian contact profiles — uses the ground-state covariance in an overlap calculation. title: A conformal spatial operator with the simplex spectrum
summary: The critical conformal scalar operator on a round even-dimensional sphere has exactly the normalized simplex spectrum, while its spinor realization, spatial geometry and master interaction remain additional requirements.
text:
Summary: The critical conformal scalar operator on a round even-dimensional sphere has exactly the normalized simplex spectrum, while its spinor realization, spatial geometry and master interaction remain additional requirements. An exact geometric occurrence of the mass-count polynomial There is a known natural differential operator whose normalized eigenvalues are exactly S(n,d)= inom{n+d-1}{d}. 	ag{1} For even d, it is the critical conformal scalar operator on a round d-sphere. The result follows from spatial conformal covariance and can also be verified by direct differentiation. It gives a distinct mathematical origin for the same sequence used in the mass-spectrum construction. This calculation specifies a round physical spatial geometry S_R^d, with undetermined radius R. It is a conditional comparison, not a replacement of the CP3 candidate or a determination of physical topology. Its directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions; there is no compactification or hidden small radius. Spherical harmonic coefficients do not add dimensions. The operator acts on scalar spatial functions. Its appearance in the master spinor interaction, and the identification of its harmonic degree with an occupied particle mode, must be derived separately. Conformal covariance fixes the recurrence Work first at unit radius. Let P commute with round-sphere rotations, and let its scalar eigenvalue on the complete degree-\ell harmonic space be p_\ell. Rotation covariance alone leaves those eigenvalues free. Impose the stronger critical conformal law P(C^*f)=\Omega^d C^*(Pf),\qquad C^*g=\Omega^2g. 	ag{2} This is the scalar law with input conformal weight zero and output weight -d. Its infinitesimal form, for \mathcal L_Vg=2\omega g, is [P,V]f=d\omega Pf. 	ag{3} Choose the height coordinate t=X_{d+1} on the unit sphere and V=
abla t. Since 
abla^2t=-tg, its conformal factor is \omega=-t. For \ell\ge1, the complex harmonic H_\ell=(X_1+iX_2)^\ell satisfies VH_\ell=-\ell\,tH_\ell. 	ag{4} The ambient polynomial tH_\ell is itself harmonic and homogeneous of degree \ell+1, because H_\ell is independent of t. Applying (3) to (4) gives -\ell(p_{\ell+1}-p_\ell)tH_\ell =-d\,p_\ell tH_\ell. Thus  oxed{ rac{p_{\ell+1}}{p_\ell}= rac{\ell+d}{\ell}} \qquad(\ell\ge1,\ p_1
e0). 	ag{5} Applying (3) to the constant function also gives p_0=0. Iteration yields  oxed{  rac{p_\ell}{p_1} =\prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1} rac{j+d}{j} = inom{\ell+d-1}{d}. } 	ag{6} The last expression is exactly the cumulative Hockey-Stick count in (1). Here it is an eigenvalue ratio forced by the specified conformal law, rather than a count being substituted for an eigenvalue. The chosen complex harmonic is a convenient way to derive the recurrence; rotation covariance gives the same value on every polarization of its harmonic space. A local differential operator realizes that law Let \Delta=-
abla^a
abla_a be the nonnegative scalar Laplacian, and write d=2h. The critical GJMS operator has order d; critical means that its differential order equals the spatial dimension. On the round sphere it is  oxed{ P_{d,R}= \prod_{j=1}^{h} \left[\Delta+ rac{(h-j)(h+j-1)}{R^2}ight]. } 	ag{7} The factors and the conformal transformation law are the standard Branson factorization, derived explicitly through stereographic projection in Graham, Proposition 1. The leading term in (7) is \Delta^{d/2}. On a degree-\ell scalar harmonic, R^2\Delta=\ell(\ell+d-1). Each factor becomes \ell(\ell+d-1)+(h-j)(h+j-1) =(\ell+h-j)(\ell+h+j-1). 	ag{8} The first factors cover \ell,\ldots,\ell+h-1 and the second cover \ell+h,\ldots,\ell+d-1. Therefore  oxed{ P_{d,R}Y_{\ell,a} = rac{\ell(\ell+1)\cdots(\ell+d-1)}{R^d}Y_{\ell,a} = rac{d!}{R^d}S(\ell,d)Y_{\ell,a}. } 	ag{9} The label a runs over the complete scalar harmonic multiplet. Its multiplicity is  inom{\ell+d}{d}- inom{\ell+d-2}{d}, with the second term zero when \ell<2. That multiplicity is separate from the eigenvalue (9). The constant harmonic has eigenvalue zero. For the two charged-lepton depths, the operators are particularly explicit:  egin{aligned} P_{6,R} &=\Delta\left(\Delta+ rac4{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac6{R^2}ight),\ P_{10,R} &=\Delta\left(\Delta+ rac8{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac{14}{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac{18}{R^2}ight) \left(\Delta+ rac{20}{R^2}ight). \end{aligned} 	ag{10} Define the dimensionless operator \widehat P_d=R^dP_{d,R}/d!, which normalizes the first positive harmonic eigenvalue to one. At the stated integer indices: Spatial dimension d Scalar harmonic degree \ell Eigenvalue of \widehat P_d 6 13 18\,564 6 35 3\,838\,380 10 23 64\,512\,240 The degrees in the table have not been selected by (2) or (7). Identifying \ell=n with a particle's occupied mode is an additional physical step. The harmonic degree \ell is also different from the oscillator cutoff N=n-1. No change of particle dimensionalities or unrestricted mode search is being used. At the level of scalar spatial operators, a trial family M_d=\mu_d\widehat P_d has precisely the proposed eigenvalue sequence. It is one differential operator for all harmonic degrees, with a common scale in each dimension. Its cumulative harmonic compressions obey the ordinary consistency law. This is not the auxiliary rank-one contact family. Normalizing by d! is an explicit spectral convention. It does not derive the dimensional coefficient \mu_d, nor the charged-lepton relation \mu_{10}=\mu_6. A master reduction must fix those physical normalizations across sectors. Verify it by differentiating spatial functions In stereographic coordinates, put s=|x|^2 and \Omega=2/(1+s). At unit radius, the critical conformal law gives P_d f=\Omega^{-d}(-\Delta_{\mathbb R^d})^{d/2}f. 	ag{11} For a zonal harmonic, f(s)=C_\ell^{(d-1)/2}\left( rac{1-s}{1+s}ight),\qquad \Delta_{\mathbb R^d}f=4s f''+2d f', 	ag{12} where C_\ell^\alpha is a Gegenbauer polynomial. Exact rational differentiation of (11)–(12) gives (9), including the assigned degrees. A second family retains a complex angular phase. title: Coulomb exponential profiles
summary: Normalized exponential profiles give exact Coulomb integrals, a two-particle variational bound, and finite-range contact estimates.
text: A specified spatial benchmark Use atomic units, \hbar=m_e=e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0)=1, and ordinary three-dimensional coordinates. The auxiliary Coulomb Hamiltonian is H_Z=\sum_{i=1}^2\left(-\frac12\Delta_i-\frac Z{r_i}\right) +\frac1{|x_1-x_2|}. The two position labels describe two particles in the same spatial region. This benchmark supplies integration and variational tools. Applying it to V2's six-dimensional electron and actual Coulomb-plus-precession orbit requires a separately justified reduction and interaction law. For \zeta>0, choose \chi_\zeta(x)=\left(\frac{\zeta^3}{\pi}\right)^{1/2}e^{-\zeta r}, \qquad p_\zeta(r)=4\zeta^3r^2e^{-2\zeta r}. The identity \int_0^\infty r^ke^{-ar}\,dr=k!/a^{k+1} gives \int p_\zeta=1, \langle r^{-1}\rangle=\zeta, and, from |\nabla\chi_\zeta|^2=\zeta^2|\chi_\zeta|^2, kinetic energy \zeta^2/2 per particle. Pair repulsion and optimized scale The angular average of 1/|x-y| for radii r,s is 1/\max(r,s): integrating (r^2+s^2-2rsu)^{-1/2}/2 over u\in[-1,1] proves the assertion. Hence \begin{aligned} J_\zeta &=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty \frac{p_\zeta(r)p_\zeta(s)}{\max(r,s)}\,dr\,ds\\ &=32\zeta^6\int_0^\infty r e^{-2\zeta r} \left(\int_0^r s^2e^{-2\zeta s}\,ds\right)dr =\frac{5\zeta}{8}. \end{aligned} For example, substituting \int_0^r s^2e^{-as}ds=[2-e^{-ar}(a^2r^2+2ar+2)]/a^3 reduces the last integral to elementary factorial integrals. The spatial product \chi_\zeta(x_1)\chi_\zeta(x_2), multiplied by a normalized antisymmetric spin singlet, is an admissible fermion trial state for this Hamiltonian. Its energy is E_Z(\zeta)=\zeta^2-2Z\zeta+\frac{5\zeta}{8} =\left(\zeta-Z+\frac5{16}\right)^2 -\left(Z-\frac5{16}\right)^2. For Z>5/16, its minimum occurs at \zeta=Z-5/16. The variational principle gives \inf\sigma(H_Z)\le -(Z-5/16)^2 Hartree. For Z=2 the trial value is -729/256. This is an upper bound on the ground energy, with both the Hamiltonian and trial family specified. A finite-range interaction bound If a multiplication potential vanishes for r>L and satisfies |V(x)|\le V_0, then |\langle V\rangle|\le V_0\,\Pr(r\le L),\qquad \Pr(r\le L)=1-e^{-2\zeta L} [1+2\zeta L+2(\zeta L)^2] =\frac43(\zeta L)^3+O((\zeta L)^4). This bounds a contact effect once its strength and range are supplied. More generally, a regular partial wave behaving as r^\ell near zero has radial weight O(r^{2\ell+2}), so its probability within L is O(L^{2\ell+3}). The exponent follows from the spatial measure; its coefficient depends on the normalized state. Gaussian contact profiles — complementary exact profile integrals. title: A spatial spinor parent for the curvature frequency
summary: The Killing-spinor transfer gives an actual surface spinor parent with both Dirac branches, the simplex product and the correct spatial polarization.
text: The curvature chain can be placed on the actual spinor bundle of its proposed surface. This uses the existing Killing-spinor transfer and retains both Dirac branches with their correct multiplicities. The scalar-derived frequency polynomial is unchanged, while the spatial currents differ from the earlier exterior-form comparison. The result is an inverse linear parent on a specified round field feature. It does not yet derive that feature, its normal extent, radius, gap or nonlinear support from the master field. Mass remains the selected particle frequency in equivalent units. This construction is not an insertion of a non-Hermitian operator into a scalar mass term. The actual spin connection Let the surface be S_R^m in ordinary R^(m+2), where m=2h is even. Its full complex spinor rank is r=2^h. A complete orthonormal family of positive Killing spinors gives a pointwise unitary frame U. With the actual spatial Dirac operator D, the previously established identity is \left(D^2-\frac D R-\frac{h(h-1)}{R^2}\right)UF =U\Delta F, \tag{1} where Delta acts componentwise on the scalar coefficient vector F. The corresponding Killing connection is flat but is not the ordinary Clifford-compatible spin connection. Equation (1) is a unitary transfer, not an identification of the two connections. The maintained Transfer of the simplex operator to spatial spinors derives (1) using the actual spin connection. The scalar/Killing construction is also described by Herzog and Shamir, Section 6.2. The present extension applies that identity to the codimension-two surface curvature operator and its causal parent. Define \boxed{B_K=D-\frac1{2R},\qquad B_K^2=U\Delta U^\dagger+\frac{k^2}{R^2},\quad k=\frac{m-1}{2}.} \tag{2} This is a local self-adjoint first-order spinor operator. The shift is essential. It makes the polynomial symmetric around the correct center of the two adjacent Dirac levels. There is a useful complete coordinate realization. At unit radius, let x belong to S^m in R^(m+1), and let Gamma_a be Hermitian ambient Clifford matrices on C^r. In the Killing frame, \boxed{B_KF=kF-\Gamma_x\Gamma_{\nabla_S}F.} \tag{3} The tangent principal symbol is -i Gamma_x Gamma_p for p perpendicular to x. It is Hermitian and squares to |p|^2 I. Direct differentiation of (3) on arbitrary complex spinor values, gradients and Hessians gives B_K^2 F=Delta F+k^2F. A separate stereographic calculation with the full spin connection agrees with (3). Thus this is a spatial spinor equation, not a replacement of spatial coordinates by form indices. The same curvature product with the full spinor multiplicity On scalar coefficient harmonics of degree L, set beta=L+k. The two orthogonal spectral projections are \Pi_\pm=\frac12\left(I\pm\frac{R B_K}{\beta}\right), \qquad R B_K\Pi_\pm=\pm\beta\Pi_\pm. \tag{4} For L=0 only the positive projection is nonzero. At higher degrees, the positive projection is ordinary Dirac level L, while the negative projection is negative Dirac level L-1. Their full dimensions are \begin{aligned} \dim\Pi_+&=r\binom{L+m-1}{m-1},\\ \dim\Pi_-&=r\binom{L+m-2}{m-1},\\ \dim\Pi_++\dim\Pi_-&= r\left[\binom{L+m}{m}-\binom{L+m-2}{m}\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{5} These unequal multiplicities must be retained. Treating a scalar and its spinor derivative as two independent copies would overcount. For the depth-six degree-14 feature, for example, the positive and negative B spaces have dimensions 2,720 and 2,240. For containing depth d=m+2, use the d first-order links L_j=c\left(B_K+\frac{j-(d+1)/2}{R}\right),\quad j=1,...,d. \tag{6} At even d their product is an even polynomial in B_K. title: Cyclic resonance spectrum
summary: A nearest-neighbour amplitude ring has exact Fourier resonances, paired levels, and a calculable response to alternating couplings.
text: Several resonances from a finite coupling operator For N\ge3 field amplitudes a_j with j taken modulo N, specify i\dot a_j=\alpha a_j-\beta(a_{j-1}+a_{j+1}),\qquad \beta>0. Here \alpha,\beta have frequency units. A common sufficiently large \alpha makes all frequencies positive if required by the application. The Fourier vectors u_k(j)=e^{2\pi ikj/N}/\sqrt N diagonalize the operator, since each shifted component multiplies by e^{\pm2\pi ik/N}: \omega_k=\alpha-2\beta\cos\frac{2\pi k}{N},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1. Norm and the Hermitian quadratic energy are conserved. These resonances arise from the couplings themselves. They need not be direct harmonics of a common frequency. The amplitudes describe field components on the one physical manifold. Degeneracy and a conditional filling rule The modes k and N-k have equal frequency. The bottom mode k=0 is a singleton; for even N, the top mode k=N/2 is another singleton. With an independently specified twofold spin multiplicity and fermion occupation, filling the bottom singleton and q complete pairs uses 2+4q particles. The rule applies before the top singleton is reached; filling that last singleton changes the count by two. Cyclic symmetry is C_N; the pair labels are not three-dimensional SO(3) shells. These energies concern the specified model; chemical stability also depends on geometry, interactions, and occupation. Alternating coupling in the four-ring Set alternating edges to t_1=\beta+\delta, t_2=\beta-\delta, |\delta|<\beta. Separating the two sublattices gives off-diagonal block -\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t_1&t_2\\t_2&t_1\end{smallmatrix}\right). Its singular values are 2\beta,2|\delta|, hence the full relative spectrum is \{-2\beta,-2|\delta|,2|\delta|,2\beta\}. The four-particle relative energy is E_{\rm fill}(\delta)=-4\beta-4|\delta|. A distortion therefore lowers this electronic contribution. If the specified structural cost is C\delta^2/2, C>0, the total has minima at |\delta|=4/C when this lies within |\delta|<\beta. title: Cylindrical barrier separation
summary: A barrier continued cylindrically has no route around it through the added coordinates; a separated Hamiltonian reduces each transverse mode to a longitudinal crossing problem.
text: Why the barrier argument belongs in V2 A barrier independent of the additional spatial coordinates cannot be evaded merely by moving through those coordinates. This is a useful consequence of the bound-within/free-without premise. The result concerns cylindrical continuation of the interaction potential. It does not require a uniform, normalizable particle wavefunction. Use a product region with coordinates (x,y), where x is the supported crossing coordinate and y denotes the additional ordinary macroscopic spatial directions within the containing sector. These are coordinates of one physical space. Their grouping is relative to the barrier, not an inherent division of the electron's six dimensions. Suppose V(x,y)=V_0(x). If the barrier occupies the interval I in x, its support in this region is I\times F, where F is the full available space of y. A continuous path from one side of I to the other must pass through I in its x coordinate, whatever its y coordinate does. There is no geometric detour in F. This does not prohibit quantum transmission through the barrier, or a path around an actual edge in the supported coordinates of a finite physical barrier. Exact separation under a specified Hamiltonian For a flat scalar diagnostic with no mixed kinetic or interaction terms, take H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(\partial_x^2+\Delta_y)+V_0(x) =H_x+H_y. Fourier transformation in y gives, for each transverse momentum k, \Psi(x,y)=\phi_k(x)e^{ik\cdot y},\qquad H_x\phi_k= \left(E-\frac{\hbar^2|k|^2}{2m}\right)\phi_k. The transmission problem is therefore the ordinary longitudinal one at energy E_x=E-\hbar^2|k|^2/(2m). At fixed E_x, adding the separated coordinates does not change its transmission coefficient. At fixed total E, changing the transverse momentum changes E_x, so transmission need not stay the same. For a wave packet, apply the mode decomposition and combine the outgoing fluxes for the prepared incident state. This is an exact statement for the specified separated operator, not a derivation of the full electron–barrier Hamiltonian. Curvature, mixed kinetic terms, additional coordinate-dependent interactions, or a moving barrier can invalidate this reduction. Any claim about a measured tunnelling time also requires a defined time observable and preparation. Verification The spatial structure checks verify the separated differential-operator identity and show explicitly that a mixed potential destroys it. title: Dipole dispersion response
summary: Second-order dipole coupling yields an attractive inverse-sixth-power energy with a coefficient fixed by the specified excitation response.
text: Model and range Use atomic units and two separated systems A,B in an ordinary spatial three-plane, with nondegenerate ground states, positive excitation gaps \Delta_a,\Delta_b, and zero permanent dipoles. Assume separation R large compared with their sizes, negligible exchange, and propagation delay short compared with the relevant response times. The leading instantaneous interaction is V=R^{-3}d_A^i T_{ij}d_B^j,\qquad T_{ij}=\delta_{ij}-3\hat R_i\hat R_j. This is a conditional ground-state response calculation. A classical field application must supply its fluctuation state and normalization; zero-point excitation weight is not implicit in the geometry. Spectral sum First order vanishes. The second-order ground energy is \Delta E^{(2)}=-\frac{C_6}{R^6},\qquad C_6=\sum_{a,b}\frac{ |\langle0_A|d_A^i|a\rangle T_{ij} \langle0_B|d_B^j|b\rangle|^2}{\Delta_a+\Delta_b}\ge0. All denominators are positive, fixing the attractive sign. Sums include complete excited multiplets and, where necessary, continuum integrals; convergence is an assumption on the response. For isotropic systems each spectral tensor is proportional to \delta_{ij} and \operatorname{Tr}T^2=6. Writing D_a=\sum_i|\langle0|d^i|a\rangle|^2 with degenerate states grouped gives C_6=\frac23\sum_{a,b}\frac{D_aD_b}{\Delta_a+\Delta_b}. Substitution into the spectral sum therefore proves \boxed{C_6=\frac3\pi\int_0^\infty\alpha_A(iu)\alpha_B(iu)\,du.} For a single-resonance response \alpha_X(iu)=\alpha_X(0)\Omega_X^2/(\Omega_X^2+u^2), C_6=\frac32\alpha_A(0)\alpha_B(0) \frac{\Omega_A\Omega_B}{\Omega_A+\Omega_B}. title: Finite-flux normal kernels and their spatial projections
summary: A finite-flux planar Dirac kernel has explicit localized modes and angular projections, but no complementary spectral gap and a logarithmically divergent second moment.
text: A finite connection flux can select a complete finite set of normalizable Dirac modes on an ordinary Euclidean plane. This gives an explicit spatial realization of a finite polynomial family. The kernel is not separated from the continuum, however, and bounded local multiplication generally forces its complement. These facts matter when using such a family in a mass-frequency operator. The connection below is a prescribed coefficient of the same-field spatial calculation. Its physical source in IDWT is not derived. No exchanged particle or Yukawa interaction is part of this test. The plane is unbounded ordinary space, without compactification. An explicit full-plane kernel Use z=x+iy, r=|z| and phi=(q+2) log(1+r^2)/2, with q a nonnegative integer. Set A=(-partial_y phi,partial_x phi). The normal Dirac operator and its chiral derivative are D_A=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q^\dagger\\Q&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q=-2i(\partial_{\bar z}+\partial_{\bar z}\phi). \tag{1} Its curvature and total flux are B=\Delta\phi=\frac{2(q+2)}{(1+r^2)^2},\qquad \int B\,dx\,dy=2\pi(q+2). \tag{2} The general regular upper-chirality zero mode is e^(-phi) f(z), with f entire. The lower chirality would contain e^(+phi) times an anti-holomorphic entire function and has no nonzero L2 mode. Angular orthogonality in the power series of f shows that its nonzero powers must have degree k<q+1. Thus the complete kernel has dimension q+1, with canonical basis \varphi_k(z)=\sqrt{\frac{q+1}{\pi}\binom qk} \frac{z^k}{(1+|z|^2)^{(q+2)/2}},\qquad k=0,\ldots,q. \tag{3} The count follows from the full spatial integrability condition; it is not a truncation of otherwise normalizable zero modes. This is an explicit case of the Aharonov–Casher zero-mode calculation. The distinction between integer flux and a marginal, non-normalizable next mode on the plane is also explained in the direct infinite-plane treatment. The complete projection kernel has diagonal \sum_{k=0}^q|\varphi_k(z)|^2 =\frac{q+1}{\pi(1+r^2)^2}. \tag{4} This is a count of available modes. It does not specify that one particle occupies all of them, or turn their count into a frequency. Bounded spatial coordinates give the angular matrices Define the three bounded real functions (n_x,n_y,n_z)= \frac{(2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,r^2-1)}{1+r^2}. \tag{5} Their unit-vector parameterization describes functions of the two ordinary coordinates. It introduces neither another physical space nor compactification of the plane. Let P project onto (3). In the basis k=0,...,q, define J_z=k-q/2 and J_+ with entries sqrt((k+1)(q-k)) from k to k+1. Direct beta integrals on the plane give Pn_iP=\frac{2J_i}{q+2},\qquad Pn_in_jP=\frac{\delta_{ij}}{q+3}I +\frac{2\{J_i,J_j\}}{(q+2)(q+3)}. \tag{6} Consequently the bounded local multiplier T(z)=beta+(q+2)[n_z+gamma(n_x+i n_y)]/2 projects to beta+J_z+gamma J_+. Its complete Hermitian pair therefore has the same projected rising-product frequency as the finite Schwinger normal band. All factors in (6) come from canonical plane integrals, not separately adjusted mode amplitudes. The same multiplication forces other normal modes Projection does not make the bounded coordinate functions preserve ker D_A. Their complete leakage is fixed by (6): \sum_i Pn_i(I-P)n_iP=\frac{2}{q+2}I. \tag{7} More generally, subtracting (Pn_iP)(Pn_jP) from the second identity in (6) gives every cross term of the omitted source. Both components of the Hermitian pair must be included. For its small positive branch at large gamma, the complete source outside P obeys \|(I-P)V\Psi\| \sim\gamma\sqrt{\frac{(q+1)(q+2)}{q+3}}. \tag{8} For q=5, beta=15.5 and gamma=10000, the projected frequency is 1.11383945e-15, while the actual complementary multiplier source has norm about 22912.877. A finite projected frequency is therefore not by itself a solution of the full spatial equation. There is no complementary normal gap The connection decays as 1/r. A normalized smooth spinor supported in a disk centered at distance R, with disk width sqrt(R), has Dirac residual bounded by O(R^(-1/2))+O(R^(-1)). Its support escapes to infinity. Removing its projection on the finite kernel changes its norm by a quantity tending to zero, and does not change its Dirac residual. This is a Weyl sequence in the complete complement. Thus zero lies in the essential spectrum, and no positive bound of the form ||D_A Q psi|| >= gap ||Q psi|| holds there. A finite numerical box can manufacture a gap that the actual plane does not possess. Controlling a perturbed finite-flux kernel instead requires an appropriate full weighted resolvent argument or additional derived supporting dynamics. The finite count alone is insufficient. Spatial width also distinguishes this band from an oscillator The highest mode has density proportional to r^(-4) at large radius. It is square integrable, but its second position moment diverges logarithmically. More explicitly, with t=R^2/(1+R^2), \int_{r<R}r^2|\varphi_q|^2\,d^2x =(q+1)\left[\log(1+R^2)- \sum_{j=1}^{q+1}\frac{t^j}{j}\right] \sim 2(q+1)\log R. \tag{9} This has a simple general explanation. If the highest polynomial zero mode had finite second moment, multiplying it by z would give an additional square-integrable holomorphic zero mode. A nonzero finite-dimensional kernel of this form cannot have finite second moment for every vector. A finite characteristic core size or a radius containing a fixed fraction of the norm still exists. Equation (9) concerns the second moment specifically; it does not by itself refute every possible notion of a particle's cavity size. finite-flux-normal-20260914T050943_681569Z.json passes 328 checks. It verifies actual Cartesian zero-mode equations, canonical plane norms, every first and second coordinate projection, the full local multiplier source, projected frequencies and the complete highest-mode tail. The separate gapped construction in A gapped finite normal kernel for the simplex parent addresses the complementary-gap requirement using a different prescribed spatial operator. title: Five-dimensional spinor bilinears
summary: Explicit five-dimensional Clifford matrices have an invariant antisymmetric bilinear and a quaternionic reality map; allowed interaction terms additionally depend on field statistics and the full symmetry representation.
text: Explicit spatial Clifford algebra Use the Hermitian Pauli matrices X,Y,Z and define \gamma_1=X\otimes I_2,\quad \gamma_2=Y\otimes I_2,\quad \gamma_3=Z\otimes X,\quad \gamma_4=Z\otimes Y,\quad \gamma_5=Z\otimes Z. \tag{1} They obey \{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I_4. These matrices describe spinor components in five ordinary spatial tangent directions. Matrix rank is not spatial dimension. Set C=\gamma_2\gamma_4. Direct multiplication gives C^T=-C,\qquad C^*=C,\qquad C^2=-I_4,\qquad C^\dagger C=I_4, \qquad C\gamma_aC^{-1}=\gamma_a^T. \tag{2} The transpose-intertwining sign in (2) is positive. In odd dimensions the admissible sign matters. The convention is the d\bmod8=5 case of Van Proeyen, Tools for supersymmetry, §3.1, equation (3.11) and Table 1. The equations here provide an explicit verification independently of the classification table. Rotation invariance of the bilinear The infinitesimal spatial spin generators are \Sigma_{ab}=\frac14[\gamma_a,\gamma_b]. Taking the transpose reverses the commutator, so (2) gives \Sigma_{ab}^T C+C\Sigma_{ab}=0. \tag{3} Exponentiating any real combination of these generators yields S^TCS=C. Therefore B(\psi,\chi)=\psi^T C\chi \tag{4} is a nondegenerate complex bilinear invariant under \operatorname{Spin}(5). On a Riemannian five-dimensional spin manifold it patches consistently under the spin-frame transition maps and is preserved by the spin connection. Additional twisting bundles or sector representations must supply their own invariant contractions. Quaternionic reality and field statistics Let \mathcal K denote componentwise complex conjugation. The antilinear map J=C\mathcal K satisfies J\gamma_a=\gamma_aJ,\qquad J^2=-I_4. \tag{5} It supplies a quaternionic structure. In particular, J\psi=\psi has only the zero solution, because applying J again gives -\psi=\psi. This is a different statement from the existence of the invariant bilinear (4). Statistics and the other field indices now matter. For commuting components, antisymmetry gives \psi^T C\psi=0, while \psi^T C\chi can be nonzero for independent component vectors. For Grassmann-odd components, \psi^T C\psi=2\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}\psi_i\psi_j \tag{6} need not vanish. A multiplet also carries whatever symmetry conditions apply to its additional labels; those conditions cannot be read from the spatial Clifford matrices alone. Under a common phase \psi\mapsto e^{i\alpha}\psi, a bilinear with two such factors has weight two. An action required to conserve that phase charge cannot contain this term with a neutral fixed coefficient. Establishing the relevant conserved charge and its full interaction content is an action-level calculation. Use in the coupling investigation Equations (2)–(6) supply concrete algebra for a five-dimensional sector calculation. They do not identify the physical neutrino field, impose its statistics, fix its mass, or settle lepton-number conservation. A physical Majorana or Dirac conclusion additionally requires the spacetime spinor structure, the occupied bundle, the complete allowed interactions, and the associated symmetries. The neutrino channel control states the separate neutral and nonzero-response conditions to test. Verification geometric_channel_checks.py checks all Clifford anticommutators, the transpose and reality relations, all infinitesimal bilinear identities, finite spin rotations, and explicit commuting and Grassmann coefficient controls. A passing matrix calculation does not establish an all-orders physical selection rule.

title: Fixed-null calibration
summary: A specified null model permits exact combination of independent match probabilities, explicit treatment of probability floors, and honest finite-simulation uncertainty.
text: Define what is random before scoring a match A numerical coincidence acquires a tail probability only after specifying a null distribution and a complete scoring procedure. For a statistic T whose larger values mean a closer match, the null tail is p(t)=\Pr_{H_0}(T\geq t). Under a continuous null distribution, the probability integral transform makes p(T) uniform on [0,1]. Discrete tails defined with inclusive ties are conservative: \Pr(p(T)\leq\alpha)\leq\alpha. As a simple conditional example, suppose the offset R from a fixed lattice target is uniform on [-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]. A match at least as close as the observed offset has p=\frac{2|R|}{\Delta}. For a multiplicative ladder with ratio r>1, a corresponding log-uniform cell has R=\log(x/x_*) and \Delta=\log r. This is an exact statement about that chosen cell distribution. A nonuniform ladder, measurement-error distribution, fitted anchor, or search across several targets must be included in its actual null model. Combining independent continuous tails Let U_1,\ldots,U_k be independent uniform null probabilities. Then Y_i=-\log U_i obeys \Pr(Y_i>y)=e^{-y} for y\geq0. Convolution, or multiplication of the Laplace transforms \mathbb E[e^{-sY_i}]=(1+s)^{-1}, gives X=\sum_iY_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(k,1),\qquad f_X(x)=\frac{x^{k-1}e^{-x}}{(k-1)!}. For observed x=-\sum_i\log p_i, repeated integration by parts yields \boxed{p_{\rm combined}=\Pr(X\geq x) =e^{-x}\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{x^j}{j!}.} Equivalently 2X has a chi-square distribution with 2k degrees of freedom. Independence is essential. Several ratios using one measured anchor, or several quantities derived from one fit, generally have a joint null that must be retained. Probability floors have atoms Suppose a scoring rule caps the evidential contribution of each match by using \widehat U_i=\max(U_i,f_i) with a fixed 0<f_i<1. Write a_i=-\log f_i. Then \widehat Y_i=-\log\widehat U_i=\min(Y_i,a_i). Its probability measure consists of density e^{-y} on 0\leq y<a_i and an atom of mass f_i=e^{-a_i} at a_i. Its Laplace transform is \mathbb E[e^{-s\widehat Y_i}] =\frac{1+s e^{-(1+s)a_i}}{1+s}, with a removable value at s=-1. In particular \mathbb E[\widehat Y_i]=1-f_i. The exact distribution of the sum is the convolution of these mixed measures; retaining the atoms matters at an inclusive tail threshold. For two contributions, let Q_a(t)=\Pr(\min(Y,a)\geq t)= \begin{cases} 1&t\leq0,\\e^{-t}&0<t\leq a,\\0&t>a. \end{cases} Then the exact inclusive tail is \Pr(\widehat Y_1+\widehat Y_2\geq x) =\int_0^{a_1}e^{-y}Q_{a_2}(x-y)\,dy +e^{-a_1}Q_{a_2}(x-a_1). At x=a_1+a_2 this equals f_1f_2, the mass of the joint atom. For any number of terms, \widehat X\leq X for the same underlying uniform variables, so the ordinary gamma tail evaluated at an observed \widehat x is a conservative upper bound on its capped null tail. A floor chosen after inspecting the result must itself be part of the selection procedure to retain such calibration. Repeat the whole procedure in simulation If a numerical analysis searches over depths, index assignments, formulas, anchors, tolerances, or subsets, apply that same search to each simulated null dataset. For example, if the reported statistic is the best score T=\max_{m\in\mathcal M}T_m, the null simulation must recompute that maximum. The null model should reproduce shared errors and fitted parameters with the same fitting procedure. This defines the object being calibrated. A selected formula cannot be treated as independently fixed merely because it can later be written without adjustable parameters. A fresh independent dataset can instead test a formula fixed before those data are examined. Two finite-simulation quantities For a fixed observed threshold, let K of N independent null simulations meet or exceed it. Conditional on that threshold, K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,p). If K=0, solving \Pr_p(K=0)=(1-p)^N=\alpha gives the one-sided confidence upper limit \boxed{p_{\rm upper}=1-\alpha^{1/N} \simeq\frac{-\log\alpha}{N}.} At 95% confidence the leading numerator is about 2.996. Zero observed exceedances therefore provide a resolution bound, not a zero tail probability. For numerical stability evaluate the exact expression as -\operatorname{expm1}(\log\alpha/N). A different question is a valid Monte Carlo hypothesis test. If the observed dataset and N null datasets produce exchangeable statistics, the rank of the observed one is uniform among N+1 distinct ranks. Its valid inclusive upper-tail Monte Carlo p-value is p_{\rm MC}=\frac{K+1}{N+1}. Inclusive ties make it conservative. The rank argument and distinction from estimating a fixed tail are discussed by Phipson and Smyth, §§2 and 4. This p-value is not the confidence upper bound above. Exchangeability must be justified; simulating from a fitted model without reproducing the fitting process does not automatically supply it. Verification and related spectral_analysis_checks.py checks gamma tails, exact capped convolutions and atoms, finite-rank calibration, and zero-exceedance binomial coverage. These are mathematical calibration examples, with no empirical significance assigned to V2 data. Spectral analysis tools — navigation and scope.

title: Spectral counts in a responsive cavity
summary: A gapped spatial band retains its cumulative count while its projector and coupling change; a reciprocal quasiperiodic phase gives a complete spatial response and nonlinear field evolution that test a low-frequency inertia reduction.
text: Summary: A gapped spatial band retains its cumulative count while its projector and coupling change; a reciprocal quasiperiodic phase gives a complete spatial response and nonlinear field evolution that test a low-frequency inertia reduction. What the integrated count protects For a discrete spatial operator H, define the cumulative count \mathcal N(E)=\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf1_{(-\infty,E)}(H). In a finite cavity this is a count of modes. An infinite-volume integrated density of states instead takes an appropriate volume-normalized limit. The two normalizations must be stated before using an IDOS as a physical factor. For d independent oscillator directions, subtract the common zero-point energy and measure frequency in oscillator units. The cumulative band through degree N has \begin{aligned} D_N&=\sum_{k=0}^N\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}\\ &=\binom{N+d}{d}. \end{aligned} \tag{1} Now add a bounded Hermitian spatial potential V. The variational eigenvalue bounds give |\epsilon_j(H_0+V)-\epsilon_j(H_0)|\le\|V\|. If \|V\|<1/2, the cutoff N+1/2 still encloses exactly D_N states. Individual frequencies and spatial shapes may change inside that band. For a smooth family with the cutoff in a gap, its spectral projector is P=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint (z-H)^{-1}dz. \tag{2} Differentiation, with R(z)=(z-H)^{-1}, gives \dot P=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint R(z)\dot H R(z)dz. \tag{3} In an eigenbasis, let p_a be one inside the band and zero outside. Only the mixed blocks contribute: (\dot P)_{ab} =\frac{p_a-p_b}{\epsilon_a-\epsilon_b}(\dot H)_{ab}. \tag{4} Thus \operatorname{Tr}\dot P=0 and P\dot P P=0, while a physical probe A may have \operatorname{Tr}(A\dot P)\ne0. A fixed count does not imply a fixed local contact or coupling. The moving-cavity sum rule provides a particular kinetic law whose occupied translation inertia is proportional to that count. Under its stated assumptions, gap protection then protects that coefficient. Counting alone does not establish the mass functional needed to make the same inference for IDWT. An actual quasiperiodically perturbed spatial band Use a two-dimensional harmonic oscillator and a potential bounded by \|V\|\le0.3: V(x)=0.1\sum_{j=1}^3\cos(k_j\cdot x+\phi_j), \tag{5} with wavevectors \begin{aligned} k_1&=(1,\sqrt2)/2,\\ k_2&=(\sqrt3,1)/2,\\ k_3&=(\sqrt5,\sqrt7)/2. \end{aligned} \tag{6} The comparison has fifteen states through degree four for every choice of the three phases. The two phase choices (0,0.7,1.3) and (0.4,1.1,-0.2) illustrate the remaining freedom: Quantity First preparation Second preparation State count 15 15 Local projector at (0.8,-0.4) 0.80485767 0.79192960 Specified normalized complex probe weight 0.68807241 0.70429964 Occupied energy sum, zero-point subtracted 41.04197026 40.77372675 The same full projector derivative has norm 0.17415824 and zero trace to numerical precision. An independent centered difference agrees with (4) to 4.61\times10^{-10} in matrix norm. The spatial cutoffs 24 and 32 agree in the reported energies and probe values to below 2\times10^{-7}. These coordinates and wavevectors describe ordinary spatial waves, rather than auxiliary physical dimensions. A lattice quasicrystal comparison For a separate one-dimensional control, take an 89-site periodic rational approximant to the quasiperiodic operator \begin{aligned} (H\psi)_j&=\psi_{j-1}+\psi_{j+1}+v_j\psi_j,\\ v_j&=1.4\cos(2\pi\alpha j+\phi). \end{aligned} \tag{7} with \alpha=55/89. A fixed cutoff in the selected gap encloses 34 states, giving per-site IDOS 34/89. Moving \phi changes the local projector. The exact phase shift \phi\mapsto\phi+2\pi\alpha translates the matrix by one site and leaves its spectrum unchanged, while the weight at a fixed site changes from 0.11477179 to 0.68962240. The integers 89, 55 and 34 specify this numerical comparison; they are not particle mode assignments. It is a finite approximant, rather than a proof about every infinite quasicrystal. The relation between Harper and Fibonacci quasiperiodic models has a useful mathematical treatment in Kraus and Zilberberg. The phase labels a spatial potential; it is not an extra spatial coordinate. Let one spatial phase respond to the wave A further inverse control makes the first phase in (5) reciprocal. Restore the oscillator zero-point energy and use \hbar=1 and unit oscillator frequency in this control. Write \begin{aligned} H(\theta)={}&H_{\rm rest}\\ &+\kappa(C\cos\theta-S\sin\theta). \end{aligned} \tag{8} where C=\cos(k_1\cdot x), S=\sin(k_1\cdot x), \kappa=0.1, and H_{\rm rest} contains the harmonic confinement and the two remaining fixed phase terms. Here \theta is a parameter of an actual spatial profile. It has no independent particle interpretation. Let \Phi be a frame of fifteen orthogonal complex occupied modes, with \Phi^\dagger\Phi=I, and put \rho=\Phi\Phi^\dagger. This occupation is a stated preparation. For the first-order canonical action i\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi^\dagger\dot\Phi)-E, take \begin{aligned} E(\rho,\theta)&=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H_{\rm rest})\\ &\quad+\kappa(c\cos\theta-s\sin\theta),\\ c&=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho C),\\ s&=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho S). \end{aligned} \tag{9} Both the field and phase vary in this one energy. With no bare phase kinetic term, the phase equation is algebraic. Its minimizing branch, for r=\sqrt{c^2+s^2}>0, has \cos\theta=-\frac c r,\qquad \sin\theta=\frac s r. \tag{10} Eliminating it gives the exact energy and field derivative \begin{aligned} E_{\rm red}(\rho)&=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H_{\rm rest})-\kappa r,\\ H_{\rm red}(\rho)&=H_{\rm rest}-\kappa\frac{cC+sS}{r},\\ i\dot\Phi&=H_{\rm red}(\rho)\Phi. \end{aligned} \tag{11} This derives the phase adjustment from the declared action. No rule steers the phase toward compatibility independently of the field variation. The resulting global moment dependence is instantaneous. A causal reduction from local master dynamics has not been supplied, and the harmonic confinement remains prescribed. Thus (11) is an inverse comparison, not a completed same-field particle model. The complete response and its low-frequency limit At a stationary lowest-band projector P, define V=\partial_\theta H, W=\partial_\theta^2H and \Delta_{ba}=\epsilon_b-\epsilon_a>0, for a occupied and b complementary. The direct curvature and relaxed curvature are \begin{aligned} K_{\rm dir}&=\operatorname{Tr}(PW),\\ K_0&=K_{\rm dir} -2\sum_{a,b}\frac{|V_{ba}|^2}{\Delta_{ba}}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} The second expression follows either by differentiating the occupied energy or by varying the complete field and phase together. Since all complementary gaps are positive, K_0>0 makes the quadratic energy positive on this occupied-subspace orbit, after its irrelevant frame rotations are removed. This establishes linear stability of this specified stationary preparation. Retaining both conjugate frequency branches gives the complete scalar phase-response kernel K(\Omega)=K_{\rm dir} -2\sum_{a,b}\frac{\Delta_{ba}|V_{ba}|^2} {\Delta_{ba}^2-\Omega^2}. \tag{13} The coupled frequencies are its zeros, together with any modes that decouple from the phase. At low frequency, \begin{aligned} K(\Omega)&=K_0-\mathcal I_\theta\Omega^2+O(\Omega^4),\\ \mathcal I_\theta&=2\sum_{a,b}\frac{|V_{ba}|^2}{\Delta_{ba}^3}. \end{aligned} \tag{14} This is a derived phase-inertia coefficient in the comparison. The expansion is controlled below the first coupled transition gap. It cannot be used to predict a frequency beyond that range merely by setting \Omega^2=K_0/\mathcal I_\theta. The spatially refined stationary phase is 3.1109292764, with K_0=0.6768828640 and \mathcal I_\theta=0.02718833687. The low-frequency estimate is 4.98959664, but the first transition gap is only 0.92383914. The full kernel has a first coupled frequency 0.92383905. Among the numerically resolved modes below 2.5, the mode with the largest phase amplitude has frequency 0.9878377084. That explicitly stated excitation is used for the time-domain control; it is not a proposed particle selection rule. Complete nonlinear spatial evolution For a coupled frequency \Omega, set the positive-frequency phase amplitude initially to one. The corresponding complete density variation has mixed eigenbasis entries \begin{aligned} (\delta\rho_+)_{ba}&=\frac{V_{ba}}{\Omega-\Delta_{ba}},\\ (\delta\rho_+)_{ab}&=-\frac{V_{ab}}{\Omega+\Delta_{ba}}. \end{aligned} \tag{15} It satisfies both the complete linearized field equation and the phase constraint. The program normalizes this whole variation and constructs the initial occupied frame by a unitary exponential, rather than dropping components or fitting a field amplitude to an eigenvalue. Direct integration of (11) retains all complex spatial coefficients. For perturbation sizes 0.002 and 0.001, the errors in the linear phase prediction are 8.29\times10^{-9} and 2.02\times10^{-9}. Their approximately fourfold decrease resolves the first nonlinear correction. The full energies are conserved to about 10^{-13} and the canonical Gram matrices to about 10^{-15} over two periods. Time refinement changes the complete fields by 5.40\times10^{-12}. Increasing the spatial cutoff from 32 to 40 changes the full trajectories by 2.32\times10^{-8}, after one fixed initial unitary alignment of the occupied spectator frame. The response equation evaluated in a larger spatial complement has residual 2.53\times10^{-8} at cutoff 40. These checks retain the changing phase and the complete spatial fields. The bounded potential keeps the instantaneous spectral count at fifteen. Unitarity separately preserves the rank of the occupied density matrix. During motion that density need not equal the instantaneous spectral projector. Equating them would discard the response being calculated. Connection to cavity mode selection Laser mathematics supplies examples of nonlinear, self-consistent mode selection in spatial cavities. Ge, Chong and Stone develop such equations, including gain saturation and changes in which modes lase. Their gain and threshold conditions are part of the stated laser system. Using that mathematics for IDWT would require the relevant energy transport and confinement to arise from its same field; laser mode selection does not itself give the particle mass law. The useful connection here is precise. The cumulative count can survive spatial changes, while the actual projector, local compatibility and reciprocal dynamics change. The frequency-resolved cavity response calculates the corresponding spatial and transition weights. The common-size balance states what additional energy and kinetic scaling is needed before this count becomes the proposed mass spectrum. spectral_count_checks.py verifies the projector, bounded perturbation and lattice controls, and records the fixed benchmark frequency units. quasiperiodic_phase_checks.py verifies the reciprocal phase action, complete spectral response and refined nonlinear complex spatial trajectories.

title: Gaussian contact profiles
summary: Normalized Gaussian spatial densities give an exact contact overlap, force, and covariance rule under marginalization onto shared coordinates.
text:

title: Gaussian mode geometry
summary: Normalized positive Gaussian profiles have an exact parameter-space metric determined by their mean and covariance, with zero Berry curvature for this real family.
text: Profiles on ordinary spatial coordinates On \mathbb R^d let a normalized density have mean X and positive definite covariance \Sigma: \rho(x)=\frac{\exp[-(x-X)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-X)/2]} {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma}}, \qquad \psi(x)=\sqrt{\rho(x)}. The coordinates x describe ordinary spatial directions of a sector in the nested physical manifold. X and \Sigma label field profiles on that space. Geometry on these parameters measures changes of profiles; it does not supply additional physical spatial dimensions or identify their parameter space with the electron's physical \mathbb{CP}^3. For parameters \theta^i, define the projected derivative tensor Q_{ij}=\langle\partial_i\psi, (I-|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\partial_j\psi\rangle, \qquad g_{ij}=\operatorname{Re}Q_{ij}. This convention measures the leading loss of squared overlap: 1-|\langle\psi(\theta),\psi(\theta+d\theta)\rangle|^2 =g_{ij}d\theta^i d\theta^j+o(|d\theta|^2). Derivation from Gaussian moments Put y=x-X and A=\Sigma^{-1}. Logarithmic differentiation gives d\log\psi= \frac12 dX^TAy +\frac14\left[y^TA(d\Sigma)Ay-\operatorname{tr}(A\,d\Sigma)\right]. Its expectation against \rho is zero. Normalization and reality also give \langle\psi,d\psi\rangle=0, so the projector subtraction vanishes. The linear and centered quadratic terms have zero cross moment by odd Gaussian parity. For symmetric B,C, Gaussian fourth moments imply \mathbb E[(y^TBy-\operatorname{tr}(B\Sigma)) (y^TCy-\operatorname{tr}(C\Sigma))] =2\operatorname{tr}(B\Sigma C\Sigma). One proof writes y=\Sigma^{1/2}z and uses independent standard normal coordinates, whose fourth moment is \mathbb E[z_i z_j z_k z_l]= \delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}+\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}. The resulting line element is \boxed{ds^2=\frac14dX^T\Sigma^{-1}dX +\frac18\operatorname{tr} (\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma).} Because d\log\psi=\tfrac12d\log\rho, this is one quarter of the classical Fisher information metric of the Gaussian density family. The mean/covariance form of that statistical metric is also given in Lawson et al., §2. Berry connection and oscillator width With convention \mathcal A=-i\langle\psi,d\psi\rangle, the connection vanishes throughout this globally positive real family. Consequently its Berry curvature d\mathcal A is zero. The metric is nonzero because neighboring normalized profiles differ even when their relative phase is fixed. Multiplying every profile by a smooth parameter-dependent common phase changes the connection by an exact differential and leaves both metric and curvature unchanged. For the ground state of H=-\Delta+\lambda|x|^2, \Sigma=I/(2\sqrt\lambda). At fixed center, \Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma=-\frac{d\lambda}{2\lambda}I, \qquad g_{\lambda\lambda}=\frac{d}{32\lambda^2}. If a specified self-consistency model imposes \lambda=(g/2)^{2/3} with g>0, the chain rule gives g_{gg}=\frac{d}{72g^2}=\frac{d}{288\lambda^3}. This is a metric on the chosen family of normalized profiles. A kinetic term for time-dependent width or a physical response coefficient must be derived from the action and its other modes. title: Green function marginal
summary: Full flat-fibre integration of a normalized Laplace Green function gives the lower-dimensional Green function, while restriction to a slice does not.
text: Physical scope This static operator benchmark specifies the source normalization and distinguishes integration from restriction. Its physical use requires a specified electromagnetic action and observer response. All coordinates here are ordinary macroscopic spatial coordinates in a flat model at finite depth within the one nested physical manifold. Writing \mathbb R^d=\mathbb R^m\oplus\mathbb R^{d-m} chooses coordinates relative to the smaller submanifold; it gives the containing particle no inherent division into different kinds of dimensions. Normalized identity For integers d>m>2, set p=d-m, r=|x|>0, and G_d(z)=\frac{\Gamma(d/2-1)}{4\pi^{d/2}}|z|^{2-d}, \qquad -\Delta_dG_d=\delta_d. The coefficient follows from unit source flux. For G_d(r)=c_dr^{2-d}, integrating -\Delta_dG_d over a ball gives -\Omega_{d-1}r^{d-1}G_d'(r)=c_d(d-2)\Omega_{d-1}=1. Using the unit-sphere area below and \Gamma(d/2)=(d/2-1)\Gamma(d/2-1) gives the displayed c_d. Then, with the full Euclidean fibre measure, \boxed{\int_{\mathbb R^p}G_d(x,y)\,d^py=G_m(x).} Indeed, polar coordinates and u=s^2/r^2 give \begin{aligned} I_{d,m}(r) &=\Omega_{p-1}\int_0^\infty s^{p-1}(r^2+s^2)^{-(d-2)/2}\,ds\\ &=\pi^{p/2}\frac{\Gamma((m-2)/2)}{\Gamma((d-2)/2)}r^{2-m}, \qquad \Omega_{p-1}=\frac{2\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2)}. \end{aligned} The integral uses Euler's beta integral, DLMF §5.12. Multiplying by the coefficient in G_d proves the boxed identity. For d=m there is no fibre integration and the assertion is immediate. The equality also holds as locally integrable distributions in x; it does not assign a finite value to the point-source singularity at x=0. At m=3, the unnormalized integral is C_d/r, with C_d=\frac{\pi^{(d-2)/2}}{\Gamma((d-2)/2)}, \qquad (C_3,C_4,C_5,C_6,C_{10}) =\left(1,\pi,2\pi,\pi^2,\frac{\pi^4}{6}\right). The normalized marginal is always 1/(4\pi r). Physical charges additionally depend on source couplings and kinetic normalization. The 1/r quantity is a potential; its radial derivative gives a 1/r^2 force. What changes the conclusion Operation Result for the stated flat kernel Full unweighted integration over \mathbb R^{d-3} 1/(4\pi r) Restriction to y=0 \Gamma(d/2-1)r^{2-d}/(4\pi^{d/2}) Integration with an integrable finite-aperture weight Generally depends on the weight; at distances large relative to its support it retains the r^{2-d} leading power For a normalized finite box weight, the weighted integral tends to zero as the box grows at fixed r; it is not the unweighted marginal. No probability normalization factor may be silently cancelled. The radial integrand at large s scales as s^{1-m}. For m=2 the potential integral diverges logarithmically, and for m<2 it diverges more strongly. A two-dimensional Green function requires its own additive-constant or reference prescription. The photon's bound depth two is not automatically the dimension of its static propagator. Curved metrics, finite boundaries, fibre weights, and dynamical currents require a new calculation. In particular, observer inaccessibility alone does not specify which operation in the table is physically realized. The theorem permits the full marginal of the ordinary flat kernel to pass the static Coulomb test; it neither selects that kernel nor proves the complete field theory. title: Spatial derivative compatibility and the current hierarchy
summary: Actual derivative compatibility restricts coherent spatial rays; complete Gaussian derivative currents distinguish available coefficient counts from a physical mode carrier.
text:
The cumulative derivative count has the desired rank, D_{N,d}=\sum_{k=0}^N inom{k+d-1}{d-1}= inom{N+d}{d}. 	ag{1} This note tests whether actual derivatives of a localized field have the coherent structure used in the reconstructed current action. The answer depends on their compatibility across physical space. It is not determined by counting coefficient slots at one point. All coordinates below are ordinary spatial coordinates of one sector. Derivative coefficients and the harmonic representations used to compute their contractions add no spatial dimensions. The flat and Gaussian calculations are conditional spatial controls, not an identified particle geometry or a replacement for the assigned particle indices. A coherent derivative ray is strongly constrained Let psi be a smooth vector or matrix field on a connected region of R^d. It may include every complex spinor component and partner column. Choose one constant derivative length L_j and define the homogeneous normalization of its ordinary derivatives through order N by (J_N\psi)_\alpha= \sqrt{ rac{N!}{(N-|\alpha|)!\,\alpha!}} L_j^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\psi, \qquad |\alpha|\le N. 	ag{2} The omitted homogeneous occupation is alpha_0 = N-|alpha|. These coefficients are a field of jets only when they obey the derivative compatibility equations. The standard jet definition is reviewed in Kolár, Michor and Slovák, Natural Operations in Differential Geometry, Sections 12.1–12.5.[1] The following conclusions follow directly from the product rule and do not require an assumed interaction. Suppose N is at least two and J_N psi is an exact coherent tensor Phi(x) tensor z(x)^N at every point of an open set where psi is nonzero. The zeroth coefficient implies z_0 is nonzero. Put xi_a = z_a/(L_j z_0). Comparing the first and second coefficients gives \partial_a\psi=\xi_a\psi,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\psi=\xi_a\xi_b\psi. 	ag{3} Differentiating the first equation and using the second yields (partial_a xi_b) psi = 0. Hence every xi_a is constant and  oxed{\psi(x)=e^{\xi\cdot x}\psi_*} 	ag{4} on each connected nonzero region. This includes complex phase gradients and every spinor component. A smooth nonzero solution cannot end on a finite boundary of that region, since (4) has a nonzero finite limit there. On all of R^d it is therefore a single exponential. No nonzero such field has finite ordinary L2 norm. This result concerns an exact coherent ray at every spatial point. An arbitrary finite jet at one point remains possible. Approximate coherence, independent mode-bundle fields, and other physical carriers are different possibilities and are not excluded by (4). A Hermitian connection does not remove the norm condition On a Riemannian spatial manifold, use symmetrized covariant derivatives of a Hermitian vector bundle. The corresponding coherent conditions are

Its confining field origin must still be derived from the same action. The Hermite differentiation and recurrence identities provide independent checks of this elementary construction.[2] Its canonical norm also needs to be retained. If an independent canonical term is assigned to every lifted coefficient and then pulled back to psi, the induced positive kinetic operator is Z_N=J_N^\dagger J_N =\sum_{k=0}^N inom Nk\widehat n^{\underline k}, \qquad \widehat n=\sum_j a_j^\dagger a_j, 	ag{10} where n-underlined-k is the falling factorial. To prove (10), expand the normal-ordered k-fold power of the total number operator: the coefficient of (a^dagger)^alpha a^alpha is k!/alpha!. Combining it with binomial(N,k) gives exactly (2)'s squared coefficient. On (9), the integrated lifted norm is (1+|zeta|^2)^N times the original field norm. In particular, \operatorname{Tr}ho_k=\sum_\ell g_{\ell,d}\|M_\ell\|_F^2=1, \qquad P_k:=\operatorname{Tr}ho_k^2 =\sum_\ell g_{\ell,d}\operatorname{Tr}[(M_\ell M_\ell^\dagger)^2]. 	ag{17} P_k equals P_(N-k), as required for a pure full coefficient state. For example, at N=2 and k=1 the Schmidt spectrum consists of 1/(1+d lambda^2) once and lambda^2/(1+d lambda^2) repeated d times. At positive lambda it is not a pure ray. What the current-root action actually sees For an isotropic partner field times this scalar coefficient state, the normalized current metric of the reconstructed action gives  rac{F_q(R_k)}{Q}=\sqrt{1-q+qP_k},\qquad  rac{U_{m root}}{\omega_0 Q} =A_{N,d}:=\sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d}\sqrt{1-q+qP_k}. 	ag{18} Here Q is the local coefficient norm for this comparison. At q>0, an entangled partial current lowers its factor from one. The endpoint currents k=0,N still have P_k=1. The following central-profile values use the previously examined q=1/(2^(d/2)+1), one common lambda=1, and the fixed derivative cutoffs from the assigned mass counts: Depth d Cutoff N Count D_(N,d) A_(N,d)/D_(N,d) 6 12 18,564 0.9653011231 6 34 3,838,380 0.9535345855 10 22 64,512,240 0.9899395562 These are current-energy coefficients at a specified spatial point. They are not particle frequencies: the full current source need not be parallel to the jet, the field has not solved a stationary equation, and the holonomic kinetic constraint has not been projected into that action. Independent complete small-cutoff calculations explicitly find a nonzero source component orthogonal to generic Gaussian jets. There is a useful exception: at N=2 and lambda=1, rho_1=I/(d+1), and the central source is parallel to the isotropic paired tensor. This is a local symmetry property, not a full spatial stationary solution. Treating (18) generally as an eigenfrequency would repeat the trace-versus-frequency error. There is also a useful analytic small-length expansion. At fixed N,d, P_k=1-2d\,k(N-k)\lambda^2+O(\lambda^4). 	ag{19} The leading entangled Schmidt block has ell=1, with singular value -lambda sqrt(k(N-k)) in each of d directions. The other first-order deformations are local to one side of the split. They do not change its purity at this order. Using the exact Hockey-Stick moment  rac1{D_{N,d}}\sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d}k(N-k) = rac{dN(N-1)}{(d+1)(d+2)} 	ag{20} in (18) yields  oxed{ rac{A_{N,d}}{D_{N,d}} =1- rac{q d^2N(N-1)}{(d+1)(d+2)}\lambda^2 +O(\lambda^4).} 	ag{21} At depth six and q=1/9 the coefficient is N(N-1)/14. The two assigned cutoffs therefore have different corrections under the same derivative metric. Letting lambda approach zero restores coherence by concentrating the actual coefficient norm into its zeroth derivative; it does not explain occupation of the counted derivative slots. The constructive outcome is a complete, efficiently computable test of a physical derivative carrier, including all its reduced currents and its induced kinetic norm. A successful mass derivation must supply a carrier and projected action that meet these conditions together. title: Hopf fibre and invariant channel projectors
summary: Circle averaging selects a definite fibre weight, while a colour singlet requires invariance under the full colour action; explicit projectors separate these conditions.
text: The geometric model and its averaging operator For the conditional Hopf model, write a point of the unit sphere as z\in\mathbb C^3, z^\dagger z=1. Its common phase defines the map S^1\longrightarrow S^5\longrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^2, \qquad z\longmapsto[z]. Complex notation packages six real embedding coordinates; the sphere has five tangent spatial dimensions. The unit radius fixes a mathematical normalization, not a physical length. Applying this model to a particle requires its actual spatial geometry and field bundle. A quotient map also does not by itself identify the quotient with a specified nested spatial submanifold. For an integer q, the fibre-weight projector on scalar functions is (P_qf)(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-iq\theta}f(e^{i\theta}z)\,d\theta. \tag{1} With the invariant sphere measure, these are orthogonal projections: P_q^\dagger=P_q,\qquad P_qP_p=\delta_{qp}P_q. \tag{2} Indeed a function with fibre weight p obeys f(e^{i\theta}z)=e^{ip\theta}f(z), so the integral in (1) is the Fourier orthogonality integral. Functions in \operatorname{Ran}P_0 descend to ordinary functions on \mathbb{CP}^2. They need not be constant there. A complete quadratic example For any complex 3\times3 matrix A, define f_A(z)=z^\dagger A z. Every such function has zero fibre weight. Its constant part is \operatorname{tr}A/3. Its remaining traceless part is an eight-dimensional complex space of functions transforming under the adjoint action: f_A(Uz)=f_{U^\dagger A U}(z),\qquad U\in SU(3). \tag{3} For example A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0) gives f_A=|z_1|^2-|z_2|^2. It survives P_0 exactly, yet an SU(3) rotation interchanging the first two axes changes its sign. Thus the quadratic zero-fibre-weight space contains both a constant singlet and a nontrivial eight-dimensional representation. Full group averaging is a different operator. With normalized Haar measure, \int_{SU(3)}U^\dagger A U\,dU =\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}I, \qquad \int_{SU(3)}f_A(Uz)\,dU=\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}. \tag{4} The first integral commutes with every fundamental group matrix, so it is scalar; its trace fixes the scalar. Equations (1) and (4) therefore remove different field components. An invariant channel is an operator condition On a specified finite-dimensional unitary representation R of a compact group G, the operator \Pi_G=\int_G R(g)\,dg \tag{5} is the orthogonal projector onto the invariant vectors. Haar invariance gives R(h)\Pi_G=\Pi_G, idempotence and self-adjointness. For Hermitian generators T_a of connected G, the equivalent test is \ker\left(\sum_aT_a^2\right)=\bigcap_a\ker T_a. \tag{6} The colour singlet criterion derives (6) and distinguishes it from merely vanishing mean colour. Fibre neutrality and the full invariant condition can both be required, but one does not replace the other. For a physical coupling calculation the action must determine the retained projector and the interaction operator. One then evaluates its action on the retained fields, including any complementary modes required by the dynamics. Declaring an average is not yet a mechanism that performs that average during an encounter. The neutrino channel control specifies the simultaneous electric, colour and surviving weak-response targets. Verification geometric_channel_checks.py checks (1) on explicit positive, negative and zero fibre weights, constructs the quadratic functions, and verifies (4) independently with a finite unitary averaging set exact on matrices. It retains a nonzero traceless function after fibre averaging and removes it under full matrix averaging. These are projector identities, not a neutrino interaction-rate calculation.

title: Interaction operator tools
summary: Self-contained tools for spatial projection, localized profiles, interaction operators, and conservation laws.
text: Scope These notes supply explicit mathematical tools for V2's interaction and field calculations. Each includes the definitions, derivation, examples, and assumptions required to apply its result. Coordinate groupings are relative to the chosen submanifold; every dimension retains the same physical character. Angular kernel parity The dot-square integral operator has a computable angular spectrum; a separate calculation gives its Hartree action on an odd state. Dirac heat curvature The local untwisted Dirac coefficient is -R/12, verified against the round-sphere spectrum with metric scale specified. Anomaly-free charge family Exact charge equations and a neutrino-inclusive solution family provide consistency checks for a specified chiral field content. Gaussian contact profiles Normalized Gaussian spatial densities give an exact contact overlap, force, and covariance rule under marginalization onto shared coordinates. Confining oscillator domain The harmonic spatial operator has a closed energy form, compact resolvent, and an explicit eigenbasis whose Gaussian tails justify specified boundary limits. Fibre-integrated stress Integrating a conserved stress tensor over ordinary spatial fibres yields a lower-depth balance law with explicit metric, boundary-flux, and sampling terms. Verification interaction_operator_checks.py checks these results using independent quadrature, symbolic algebra, finite differences, and explicit matrix states. Each note explains which operator, measure, and normalization its calculation uses. spatial_profile_checks.py checks Gaussian contact, oscillator domains and tails, and integrated stress using quadrature, differential identities, and conservation benchmarks.
