title: Causal constraint on reconstructed simplex dynamics
summary: An exact commutator on the actual curved spatial geometry proves that the reconstructed all-band polynomial dynamics have no finite propagation speed, while leaving open causal nonlinear dynamics with selected simplex particle frequencies.
text: Summary: An exact commutator on the actual curved spatial geometry proves that the reconstructed all-band polynomial dynamics have no finite propagation speed, while leaving open causal nonlinear dynamics with selected simplex particle frequencies. What the inverse frequency match does not settle The inverse construction gives local Hermitian equations with exact frequencies \pm\mu S(n,2m) on their complete first Dirac pair. Their full canonical norm is conserved. However, every member of that polynomial class fails a finite-propagation test when used as a fixed equation for all spatial modes. This conclusion follows directly on the specified physical \mathbb{CP}^m geometry with line connection \mathcal O(m-1). It does not require a flat approximation, a positive-frequency projection or a group-velocity interpretation. The physical radius R is arbitrary and finite. These remain ordinary macroscopic spatial directions; no direction is compactified. The result constrains an inverse dynamical ansatz. A nonlinear particle mass is not required to equal the frequency of every small disturbance of one fixed quadratic background. Causal dynamics that select several nonlinear particle states remain a different problem. No particle depth or assigned mass index is changed by this test. Finite propagation requires a bounded local commutator Let H be self-adjoint on the complete spatial field and U(\tau)=e^{-i\tau H} its unitary evolution. A finite propagation speed c means that every initial field supported in K satisfies \operatorname{supp}U(\tau)\psi \subseteq\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le c|\tau|\}. \tag{1} For an ordinary first-order Dirac operator, its bounded commutator with a Lipschitz scalar function expresses its local spatial speed. See McIntosh and Morris, Section 1 for the first-order propagation theorem. The necessary estimate used here can be proved without assuming that H is first order. Let f be a bounded real function with Lipschitz constant L_f. For \tau\ne0, put r=c|\tau| and \delta=L_fr, and partition the field space using the multiplication projections E_j=\mathbf1_{\{j\delta\le f<(j+1)\delta\}},\qquad f_\delta=\sum_j j\delta E_j. \tag{2} Zero values of c or L_f follow by using an arbitrarily larger positive bound or by observing that a constant function commutes. Two bins whose indices differ by at least three are separated by more than r. Equation (1) therefore gives E_jU(\tau)E_k=0 when |j-k|\ge3. For each remaining index difference \ell, the operator \sum_jE_{j+\ell}U(\tau)E_j has norm at most one: its domain blocks are orthogonal, its range blocks are orthogonal and \|U(\tau)\|=1. It follows that \begin{aligned} \|[f_\delta,U(\tau)]\| &\le\delta\sum_{\ell=-2}^{2}|\ell|=6\delta,\\ \|[f-f_\delta,U(\tau)]\|&\le2\delta. \end{aligned} \tag{3} The deliberately nonoptimal constant is sufficient: \boxed{\|[f,U(\tau)]\|\le8c|\tau|L_f.} \tag{4} For a smooth field \psi such that \psi and f\psi lie in the domain of H, differentiate at \tau=0. Equation (4) implies \boxed{\|[H,f]\psi\|\le8cL_f\|\psi\|.} \tag{5} Thus an unbounded commutator with one bounded smooth spatial function excludes a finite propagation speed for the full unitary equation. The argument applies on a compact spatial manifold as well: a finite diameter does not remove the small-time requirement. Evaluate that commutator on the actual spatial field Retain the complete inverse operator H_{a,b}=\mathscr D_c+ \mu\left[a(X_0)T_0+\beta b(X_0)\right],\qquad X_0=T_0^2,\quad T_0=\frac R2\mathscr D_0. \tag{6} The other spinor families still have their operator \mathscr D_c. All inverse candidates have Xa(X)^2+b(X)^2=P_m(X)^2,\qquad b(X)=\frac{X^m}{(2m)!}+O(X^{m-1}). \tag{7} The overall negative sign allowed in the classification changes the sign of the following commutator but not its norm. Use the global spatial function t=|Z_0|^2/|Z|^2. For the specified physical FS metric, |\nabla t|^2=\frac{4t(1-t)}{R^2},\qquad L_t=\frac1R. \tag{8} Let \phi_n be the normalized zero-form Jacobi field from the curved Dirac construction, at L=m-1. It is a legitimate smooth state of the complete field. It need not be a positive-frequency eigenstate of (6). Multiplication by t has the exact recurrence \begin{aligned} t\phi_n&=\gamma_n\phi_{n+1}+\frac12\phi_n+ \gamma_{n-1}\phi_{n-1},\\ \gamma_n&=\frac12 \sqrt{\frac{(n+1)(n+2m-1)} {(2n+2m-1)(2n+2m+1)}}. \end{aligned} \tag{9} The last term is absent at n=0. The coordinate is an actual function on physical space; the index n is a mathematical spatial mode label. On zero forms, \beta=1 and X_0\phi_n=x_n\phi_n, with x_n=n(n+2m-1). The term a(X_0)T_0 changes form degree and \mathscr D_c annihilates both \phi_n and t\phi_n. Consequently the zero-form component of the full commutator is \begin{aligned} \Pi_0[H_{a,b},t]\phi_n =\mu\bigl\{& \gamma_n[b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)]\phi_{n+1}\\ &+\gamma_{n-1}[b(x_{n-1})-b(x_n)]\phi_{n-1}\bigr\}. \end{aligned} \tag{10} This projection only supplies a lower bound on the complete response. It is the local form-degree projection, not a projection onto one frequency sign. The odd component and all complementary equations remain present and cannot cancel an orthogonal zero-form component. Define \begin{aligned} C_n^2={}&\gamma_n^2[b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)]^2\\ &+\gamma_{n-1}^2[b(x_{n-1})-b(x_n)]^2. \end{aligned} \tag{11} Equations (9)–(10) imply \|[H_{a,b},t]\phi_n\|\ge\mu C_n. \tag{12} For every root allocation in the inverse class, \gamma_n\longrightarrow\frac14,\qquad b(x_{n+1})-b(x_n)= \frac{n^{2m-1}}{(2m-1)!}+O(n^{2m-2}). \tag{13} The other difference has the opposite leading sign. Hence \boxed{C_n\sim \frac{n^{2m-1}}{\sqrt8\,(2m-1)!}\longrightarrow\infty.} \tag{14} But a finite propagation speed would require, by (5) and (8), \mu C_n\le\frac{8c}{R} \quad\text{for every }n. \tag{15} This is impossible for any fixed nonzero \mu and finite positive R,c. It proves the failure of finite propagation on the full curved equation, including all nine coefficient pairs at depth six and all eighty-one at depth ten. Real spatial depth Common growth of the lower bound C_n Six \frac{n^5}{120\sqrt8} Ten \frac{n^9}{362\,880\sqrt8} The asymptotic indices in this proof are test fields allowed by the proposed equation. They are not alternative particle assignments. What can and cannot change this conclusion The original first-order operator has [\mathscr D,t] equal to local Clifford multiplication by dt, up to the convention for i. Its norm is bounded by 1/R. This provides a direct curved-space control for the test above. The same obstruction also applies to the direct insertion H=\mathscr D+\mu\beta P_m(X_0), even though that insertion keeps the original first-order kinetic term. On the test field \phi_n, its zero-form commutator is still (10) with b=P_m; the ordinary Dirac commutator contributes only to the odd form. Thus promoting the polynomial mass coefficient to an operator on every spatial disturbance needs a causal completion as well. A coefficient obtained only on selected nonlinear stationary particle states is not covered by that promotion. A fixed smooth multiplication potential cannot cancel (10); it commutes with t. In particular, adding the specified local scalar term g(\psi^\dagger\beta\psi)\beta\psi has vanishing linearization at the zero field. Its small-amplitude equation still has the same obstruction. For a smooth local nonlinearity F(\psi^\dagger\beta\psi)\beta\psi, a nonzero F(0) adds only a multiplication term to that linearization. Likewise, a fixed positive commuting kinetic metric in the inverse action gives iZ\dot f=ZH_{a,b}f and the same evolution i\dot f=H_{a,b}f. That normalization does not repair (15). A different same-field dynamical completion would need to change the propagation equation itself. The scalar response calculation remains valid mathematics for its specified action. Its reciprocal coefficients and spatial residuals are useful inverse constraints, but this action cannot yet represent a fundamental causal particle interaction at unrestricted spatial frequencies. A controlled effective reduction may retain the polynomial over a limited regime, provided its causal parent, retained modes, frequency range and approximation error are derived. A cutoff alone is not a proof of causal support. The local Dirac retarded response already illustrates how causal propagation can survive a same-field reduction when its full frequency dependence is kept. The instantaneous interaction test addresses a different source of acausality: an explicitly nonlocal instantaneous spatial potential. Most importantly, (14) does not exclude a universal causal nonlinear equation whose distinct self-consistent particle solutions have selected simplex masses. That equation would have to generate the particle spectrum through its nonlinear spatial states and normalization, without imposing this unrestricted high-order dispersion on every disturbance. The inverse scalar-law construction develops that alternative with the original Dirac kinetics. It tests the full spatial residual and the requirement that all particle candidates obey one function of the scalar current. The original Dirac operator supplies the bounded local commutator control. title: Reconstructing dynamics with exact simplex frequencies
summary: An inverse polynomial classification gives nine local Hermitian dynamics with exact simplex frequencies on the specified six-dimensional Dirac pair, while canonical normalization fixes their action and the original unchanged kinetic term cannot realize that spectrum through a scalar polynomial alone.
text: Summary: An inverse polynomial classification gives nine local Hermitian dynamics with exact simplex frequencies on the specified six-dimensional Dirac pair, while canonical normalization fixes their action and the original unchanged kinetic term cannot realize that spectrum through a scalar polynomial alone. Reconstruct the full frequency rather than only its coefficient The geometric derivative construction supplies the dimensionless operator P(X)=\frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720},\qquad P\bigl(n(n+5)\bigr)=S(n,6). \tag{1} It acts on a specified family of spatial spinors on physical CP3 with line connection \mathcal O(2). The inverse problem here is stronger than asking for this scalar coefficient: require the complete positive frequency on that family to be \mu S(n,6), with one fixed \mu>0. There are explicit local Hermitian dynamics that satisfy that target. Within the two-polynomial class defined below, there are nine solutions at depth six up to a simultaneous sign of the two polynomials. The corresponding number at depth ten is eighty-one. They give the same frequencies while acting differently on the paired form components. These are reconstructed quadratic actions. The calculation does not derive them from the algebraic master scalar current, select occupied particle modes or prove causal propagation. The positive field norm and the full complementary spinor kinetics are retained explicitly. CP3 and CP5 remain conditional actual macroscopic spatial geometries with unknown physical radii and no compactification. The constructions at the two depths are independent sector calculations. They do not require an electron state to be a restriction of a tau state; only the sectors belong to the nested spatial chain. Preserve every form component of the spatial field On physical \mathbb{CP}^m, use the specified bundle \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(m-1) and the spatial Dirac operator \mathscr D=\sqrt2(\bar\partial+\bar\partial^\dagger). The dagger includes the physical FS metric and measure. Let \Pi_q project onto exterior degree q, and let \beta be exterior parity. Define \begin{aligned} \mathscr D_0&=\sqrt2\left(\bar\partial^\dagger\Pi_1+ \bar\partial\Pi_0\right),\\ \mathscr D_c&=\mathscr D-\mathscr D_0,\qquad T_0=\frac R2\mathscr D_0,\qquad X_0=T_0^2. \end{aligned} \tag{2} The local Hodge decomposition and \bar\partial^2=0 give \mathscr D_0\mathscr D_c=\mathscr D_c\mathscr D_0=0, \qquad \{\beta,\mathscr D_0\}=\{\beta,\mathscr D_c\}=0. \tag{3} On the complete zero/exact-one-form family, X_0 has values x_n=n(n+2m-1). On the other form families it vanishes, while \mathscr D_c retains their original kinetic equation. Harmonic components remain in the full field space. The dimensionless target polynomial at real depth 2m is P_m(X)=\frac{1}{(2m)!} \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\left[X+j(2m-1-j)\right],\qquad P_m(x_n)=S(n,2m). \tag{4} It has one zero at X=0 and distinct negative zeros at -c_j, where c_j=j(2m-1-j)>0 for 1\le j\le m-1. No particle mode or dimensionality is reassigned. What keeping the original kinetic term would require First retain \mathscr D_0 and change only a real scalar polynomial B(X_0). On its paired family, H=\mathscr D_0+\beta B(X_0) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega^2=\frac{4X}{R^2}+B(X)^2. \tag{5} Exact target frequencies at every x_n would require the polynomial identity \boxed{B(X)^2=\mu^2P_m(X)^2-\frac{4X}{R^2}.} \tag{6} Equality on infinitely many distinct x_n forces equality as polynomials. At X=0, (6) gives B(0)=0. Its left side therefore has no linear term, while the right side has coefficient -4/R^2. No polynomial B satisfies (6) at a finite physical radius. A specified spectral square root can instead be defined on the positive paired spectrum: B(x_n)=\sqrt{\mu^2P_m(x_n)^2-\frac{4x_n}{R^2}},\qquad B(0)=0. \tag{7} For (7) to be real on every positive level, its first level imposes \mu R\ge2\sqrt{2m}. This condition is sufficient because P_m(X)/\sqrt X increases for X>0. The resulting spectral operator is not a finite differential polynomial. Defining it supplies neither a local master interaction nor a causal reduction. Equation (6) identifies the constraint that a scalar-only inverse construction has to address. A local polynomial class that meets the target exactly Allow both coefficients on the paired family to change: \boxed{ H_{a,b}=\mathscr D_c+ \mu\left[a(X_0)T_0+\beta b(X_0)\right], } \tag{8} where a,b are real dimensionless polynomials with b(0)=0. The identity b(0)=0 prevents an extra scalar term on the complementary form families. Using (3) gives H_{a,b}^2=\mathscr D_c^2+ \mu^2\left[X_0a(X_0)^2+b(X_0)^2\right]. \tag{9} Thus the exact inverse condition is \boxed{Xa(X)^2+b(X)^2=P_m(X)^2.} \tag{10} Every solution gives both frequencies \pm\mu P_m(x_n) on the complete paired family. The other spinor families retain their original kinetic spectrum. Neither frequency sign is identified with an antiparticle or electric charge. Both terms in (10) are nonnegative for X\ge0. Their leading coefficients cannot cancel. Consequently \deg b=m and \deg a\le m-1. The constant and linear coefficients of (10) give, respectively, b(0)=0,\qquad a(0)=0. \tag{11} In particular none of these solutions retains the original constant coefficient a=2/(\mu R) of \mathscr D_0 while changing only the scalar polynomial. The change to the kinetic operator is part of the reconstructed dynamics, rather than a normalization convention. Classify all real polynomial solutions in this class Introduce a mathematical polynomial variable y and write C(y)=b(y^2)+iy\,a(y^2). \tag{12} For real coefficients, C(-y) is the coefficient conjugate of C(y). Equation (10) becomes C(y)C(-y) =\frac{y^4}{[(2m)!]^2} \prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(y^2+c_j)^2. \tag{13} The root at zero has multiplicity two in C. For each distinct pair \pm i\sqrt{c_j}, its two copies can be allocated in three ways: one to each root, or both to either root. Fixing the positive leading coefficient of b, all solutions are therefore \boxed{ C(y)=\frac{y^2}{(2m)!}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}F_{j,\epsilon_j}(y), \qquad \epsilon_j\in\{-1,0,1\}, } \tag{14} with F_{j,0}=y^2+c_j,\qquad F_{j,\pm1}=(y\pm i\sqrt{c_j})^2. \tag{15} Every choice has the conjugation property in (12), so its even part is a real b(y^2) and its odd part is iy times a real a(y^2). Conversely, the roots and leading coefficient in (13) leave no additional polynomial choices. A simultaneous sign change of a,b gives the remaining solutions. The count up to that sign is \boxed{3^{m-1}:\qquad 9\text{ at depth six},\quad 81\text{ at depth ten}.} \tag{16} This classification is restricted to the class (8). It does not classify all matrix-valued, nonpolynomial or nonlinear dynamics. At depth six, three illustrative members are: Choice a(X) b(X) Both factors balanced 0 \frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720} Rotate the factor X+4 \frac{4X(X+6)}{720} \frac{X(X-4)(X+6)}{720} Rotate the factor X+6 \frac{2\sqrt6X(X+4)}{720} \frac{X(X+4)(X-6)}{720} For the second row, for example, (10) follows from 16X+(X-4)^2=(X+4)^2. The two mixed examples have a nonzero odd-component coupling and an exact simplex frequency. The remaining members follow directly from (14), including opposite signs for each rotation. Reconstruct the action with the correct field norm Let f be the full field coordinates in a fixed Hilbert space, and let Z>0 be a specified, time-independent kinetic metric. For a target self-adjoint Hamiltonian H, the real quadratic action \mathcal S[f]=\int dt\left\{ \frac i2\left(\langle f,Z\dot f\rangle- \langle\dot f,Zf\rangle\right) -\langle f,Kf\rangle\right\}, \qquad K=Z^{1/2}HZ^{1/2}, \tag{17} gives iZ\dot f=Kf,\qquad u=Z^{1/2}f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad i\dot u=Hu. \tag{18} All spatial adjoints and every complex variation are included. The conserved norm is \langle f,Zf\rangle=\|u\|^2. This construction works also for noncommuting Z,H; that general formula alone does not guarantee spatial locality of K. If Z and H commute, K=ZH. Polynomial commuting data in the present construction then give a local quadratic action. The natural zero-form jet metric at depth six is Z(X)=(X^2+12X+40)/40. To obtain P(X) after canonical normalization, its energy numerator must therefore be \boxed{ Z(X)P(X)= \frac{X^5+22X^4+184X^3+688X^2+960X}{28\,800}. } \tag{19} Using Z(X_0) on the complete paired field, with value one on the complement, is a specified extension of that metric. Multiplying the complete target (8) by this Z gives the corresponding local inverse action. Its scalar energy term has spatial order ten. The earlier P/Z result used energy numerator P; (19) deliberately changes that energy to meet the inverse target. The algebraic master current has not thereby been shown to contain the additional derivatives. A field-dependent or time-dependent Z needs its complete variation and kinetic connection. Equations (17)–(18) assume fixed data; they cannot be used to omit the response of a moving geometric background. The canonical coupling calculation likewise normalizes each interaction leg using the same field metric. Physical scope of the reconstruction Each operator (8) is Hermitian on smooth spatial fields and has a self-adjoint realization defined by the complete harmonic decomposition. Its unitary linear evolution preserves the full canonical norm. Finite linear superpositions do not develop exponentially growing amplitudes under this fixed quadratic action. The complete scalar-response comparison adds the same local interaction to each reconstructed action. Equal frequencies allow different spatial responses; both frequency branches retain a fixed inclusive scalar strength. The complete nonlinear source also drives spatial components beyond a chosen pure occupied mode. That statement is not nonlinear particle stability. These equations permit every spectral level and do not select the assigned occupied states. They do not by themselves specify a nonlinear interaction between two particle structures. Locality as a differential expression also does not establish a finite propagation cone for a higher-order spatial equation. The complete curved causality test now proves that every member of (8), used on all spatial modes, lacks a finite propagation speed. The test uses a local spatial commutator and retains both frequency branches. These actions therefore need a controlled effective interpretation or a different causal completion. The inverse calculation supplies explicit actions that meet the target frequency identity and a complete classification within (8). Their physical coupling and state selection remain additional constraints. This approach is consistent with the distinction between an effective action and its deeper origin in Burgess, Section 3.3. No scale hierarchy or effective cutoff has been derived here. title: Isotropic projection fractions
summary: An isotropically prepared spatial direction has a beta-distributed squared projection onto a fixed subspace, with explicit moments and observer-relative momentum bookkeeping.
text: Geometric preparation Let v be a uniformly distributed unit vector in a D-dimensional Euclidean spatial space, and P the orthogonal projector onto a fixed q-dimensional subspace, 0<q<D. The squared projected fraction is F=\|Pv\|^2\in[0,1]. Uniformity is a preparation assumption. In a scattering application the interaction, incoming state, and detector acceptance determine whether that assumption is justified. The subspaces here are ordinary spatial directions within the single nested physical manifold. Distribution and moments Take independent standard real Gaussian coordinates z_1,\ldots,z_D. Their joint density is rotation invariant, so v=z/\|z\| is uniform on the unit sphere. In a basis adapted to P, put X=\sum_{j=1}^q z_j^2,\qquad Y=\sum_{j=q+1}^D z_j^2,\qquad F=\frac{X}{X+Y}. X and Y are independent gamma variables of common scale 2 and shapes a=q/2, b=(D-q)/2. Change variables to F and S=X+Y, whose Jacobian is S. Their density factors into a gamma density for S and \boxed{f_F(t)=\frac{t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}, \quad 0<t<1,\quad B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.} Integration gives \mathbb E[F^k]=\frac{(q/2)_k}{(D/2)_k},\qquad \mathbb E[F]=\frac qD,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(F)=\frac{2q(D-q)}{D^2(D+2)}. Here (a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1). The beta-integral formula also holds for real k>-q/2. Thus a magnitude fraction has \mathbb E[\sqrt F]=B(a+1/2,b)/B(a,b), which generally differs from \sqrt{q/D}. The endpoint cases q=0,D are deterministic. Beam-relative example in six ordinary spatial dimensions Suppose a beam direction lies within the observer's three-dimensional spatial subspace of an electron's six dimensions. Its orthogonal spatial complement has D=5 dimensions. Two of them lie in the observer's transverse plane and three are perpendicular to the observer's subspace. If the transverse direction is isotropic in that five-dimensional space, the fraction perpendicular to the observer's subspace has F\sim\operatorname{Beta}(3/2,1),\qquad \mathbb E[F]=\frac35,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(F)=\frac{12}{175},\qquad \Pr(F\leq t)=t^{3/2}. The electron has six equivalent ordinary spatial dimensions. The grouping above is relative to the beam and observer, with no inherent electron split. The 3/5 result concerns squared transverse momentum under the specified preparation. It supplies neither a scattering rate nor an energy threshold. Opposing momentum components can balance within a multi-particle event even when each has a nonzero perpendicular component. Projected mass shell If a particle satisfies the relativistic mass shell in the containing spatial sector, decompose its momentum relative to the observer as p=p_{\parallel}+p_{\perp}. Orthogonality gives E^2=c^2(|p_{\parallel}|^2+|p_{\perp}|^2)+m^2c^4. An observer reconstruction using the full particle energy E and only p_{\parallel} would therefore assign M_{\rm app}^2=\frac{E^2}{c^4}-\frac{|p_{\parallel}|^2}{c^2} =m^2+\frac{|p_{\perp}|^2}{c^2}. The qualification that E is the full particle energy matters: a partial energy deposit has its own detector model. This equation is kinematic; whether a process populates p_{\perp} requires its interaction. Verification and related spectral_analysis_checks.py checks beta moments by quadrature, the isotropic Gaussian construction, the special cumulative distribution, and the projected mass shell under rotations and changes of observer frame. title: Nested sector dynamics
summary: Cylindrical function lifts require a projection, and exact inheritance of dynamics additionally requires an invariant domain and an intertwining operator relation.
text: What nesting supplies All spatial sectors in V2 belong to one nested chain in the same infinite physical manifold. Their dimensions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions. Describing their relationship through functions needs two steps: defining the lift of a function and checking the lift of its dynamics. For an inclusion i:Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b, the canonical function map is restriction, in the opposite direction: i^*:C^\infty(Q_b)\longrightarrow C^\infty(Q_a),\qquad i^*F=F\circ i. To lift functions from Q_a to Q_b cylindrically, specify a smooth projection \pi:Q_b\to Q_a with \pi\circ i=\mathrm{id}. Then J=\pi^*,\qquad Jf=f\circ\pi,\qquad i^*Jf=f is an injective algebra map. In a product chart (x,y), this is simply Jf(x,y)=f(x). Nested inclusions alone do not supply a global \pi. The sector geometry audit already identifies this geometric limitation. When a lower-sector equation is preserved For a time-independent lift J, an exact evolution lift requires H_bJf=JH_af on a domain preserved by the relevant evolutions. For unbounded operators, domain compatibility is part of the assertion; a symbolic differential identity alone is not a complete operator theorem. A direct differential example is H_a=-\Delta_x+V_a(x),\qquad H_b=-\Delta_x-\Delta_y+V_a(x). Since \Delta_yJf=0, the displayed intertwining identity holds on smooth cylindrical fields. If instead H_b contains \kappa xy in a two-coordinate example, then H_bJf-JH_af=\kappa xyf(x), which depends on y and leaves the cylindrical class. Coordinate nesting survives, but this exact autonomous lower-sector evolution does not. A constant extension is not square-integrable over a noncompact fibre of infinite volume. In that case the preceding calculation is a statement about fields or generalized modes, not a normalized Hilbert-space embedding. For a Hilbert-space version one can instead specify a normalized transverse eigenfunction \chi and use J_\chi f=f\chi; a separated Hamiltonian then gives H_bJ_\chi f=J_\chi(H_a+\epsilon)f,\qquad H_y\chi=\epsilon\chi. Such an eigenfunction and its boundary conditions must actually exist. They are extra model data, not a derivation of cylindrical continuation. Consequence for interactions Nesting allows a shared-coordinate description; it does not guarantee that every interacting sector retains its isolated spectrum. A nonzero coupling can introduce backreaction, mix states, or shift energies. Use the explicit intertwining condition when exact inheritance is needed, and an effective reduction when it fails. The spatial structure checks verify the separated and mixed differential examples. Related Compression versus effective dynamics — explains why eliminating coupled variables differs from simply restricting an operator. Cylindrical barrier separation — applies the separated case to a concrete interaction question. Nested spatial tools — companion tools for spatial evolution and normalization.

title: Nested spatial tools
summary: Tools for common time, centred self-binding, cylindrical barriers, and inherited evolution on nested spatial sectors.

title: Restoring the normal oscillator tower
summary: Restoring the complete normal oscillator changes the finite-chain frequency and identifies the need for a controlled isolated spatial band.
text: A finite normal oscillator projection can imitate the curvature chain's simplex product. Restoring the complete ordinary spatial oscillator changes that frequency. This identifies a concrete requirement for a physical carrier: the finite chain must arise as a controlled isolated band, rather than from an imposed cutoff. The test does not change the exact surface curvature identity. It tests one possible realization of the chain components as normal modes of the same field. That realization is not derived or adopted here. Their coefficient labels count spatial modes, not physical dimensions. The second ordinary normal direction and the origin of this oscillator profile are not supplied by this test. Consider the complete normal operator and its Hermitian pair T_b=b+N+Ga,\qquad b>0,\ G>0,\qquad H_b=\begin{pmatrix}0&T_b^\dagger\\T_b&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2} All coefficients in (2) are in a common normal oscillator unit. G is the coefficient of a in this carrier test. Its identification with the earlier chain gap would require this proposed projection to hold. The number operator is second order in the actual coordinate x. Consequently (2) is a spectral carrier test, not an established fundamental first-order causal equation in all spatial directions. At cutoff q, its upper triangular matrix is (T_b^{(q)})_{nn}=b+n,\qquad (T_b^{(q)})_{n,n+1}=G\sqrt{n+1},\qquad 0\le n<q. \tag{3} Canonical normalization fixes the square roots in (3). At fixed q and large G its smallest singular frequency is \omega_q\sim \frac{(b)_q}{G^{q-1}\sqrt{(q-1)!}}. \tag{4} For q=d and b=L-1, the numerator is exactly (L-1)L...(L+d-2)=d!D_(L-2,d). Although T maps the finite polynomial subspace into itself, T^dagger does not. The complete upper equation contains the additional component \boxed{(H_b\Psi)_{{\rm upper},q} =\frac{G\sqrt q}{\sqrt2}\,y_{q-1}.} \tag{5} In the large-G finite chain, y is concentrated at its last component. The residual (5) is then large while (4) is very small. The finite subspace is not a reducing subspace of the Hermitian spatial operator. Checking the small finite-matrix residual does not check its complete normal field equation. The simpler displaced annihilator T=b+Ga gives another exact control. In the full space it annihilates the normalized coherent state with coefficients proportional to (-b/G)^n/sqrt(n!). A finite square truncation has a nonzero smallest singular value. That value must converge to zero as the full coherent field is restored. Solve the complete operator The Bargmann representation is a unitary mathematical representation of the same one-coordinate oscillator. In this representation, T_b f=(z+G)f'(z)+bf(z). \tag{6} A zero solution would be proportional to (z+G)^(-b), which is not entire for b>0. Composition by tz-G(1-t) has operator norm \|C_t\|=\exp\left[\frac{G^2(1-t)}{2(1+t)}\right]. \tag{8} One can verify (8) by unitary displacement of the contraction f(z) to f(tz); a normalized coherent state attains the norm. For t<1 the contraction is compact. The integral near t=1 tends to zero in operator norm as its interval shrinks, so (7) is compact as well. It is bounded, with norm at most exp(G^2/2)/b. Thus the complete Hermitian pair has a positive smallest singular frequency for b>0, even though it can be extremely small. For fixed b and G tending to infinity, substitution s=G^2 t shows that both bounds have the same leading value. Consequently \boxed{\omega_{\rm full}\sim \frac{G^{2b}}{\Gamma(b)}\exp(-G^2/2).} \tag{10} The degree dependence in (10) differs from (4). Holding a finite cutoff while increasing G is not a uniform approximation to the complete normal tower. The scalar oscillator comparison therefore does not realize the required common simplex frequency family. title: Oscillator rotation branching
summary: Harmonic-polynomial decomposition gives exact angular multiplicities for a flat oscillator shell and its restriction to an observer-selected spatial three-plane.
text: Shells under ordinary spatial rotations For an isotropic scalar oscillator on \mathbb R^d, d\ge3, the creation operators transform as a spatial vector. Shell N therefore has the representation \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^d). Its polynomial representation decomposes as \operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^d) =\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}r^{2k}\mathcal H_{N-2k}^{(d)}, \qquad h_d(\ell)=\dim\mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} =\binom{\ell+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{\ell+d-3}{d-1}. Here \mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} denotes homogeneous harmonic polynomials; binomial coefficients with top smaller than bottom are zero. To see the decomposition, subtract successive traces (Laplacians) of a homogeneous polynomial. The identity \Delta(r^{2k}h_\ell)=2k(2\ell+2k+d-2)r^{2k-2}h_\ell has a nonzero coefficient for k>0, permitting recursive removal of each trace. Dimensions then telescope to \binom{N+d-1}{d-1}. For the cumulative band 0\le N<n, the multiplicity of \mathcal H_\ell^{(d)} is \left\lfloor\frac{n-1-\ell}{2}\right\rfloor+1 \quad(0\le\ell<n). In particular the rotational scalar occurs once in each even shell, and \lceil n/2\rceil times in the cumulative band. A shell's parity condition and a cumulative band's scalar content are different counts. Restriction to a selected three-plane For d>3 choose a spatial three-plane O and perpendicular complement O^\perp within the same d directions. Under rotations of O that fix O^\perp, the shell representation decomposes into a sum over N_O+N_\perp=N. A three-dimensional oscillator shell N_O contains angular momenta \ell=N_O,N_O-2,\ldots, each once. The complementary shell contributes scalar multiplicity g_{d-3}(N_\perp)=\binom{N_\perp+d-4}{d-4}. Thus m_d(\ell,N)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor(N-\ell)/2\rfloor} \binom{N-\ell-2j+d-4}{d-4}, \qquad \sum_{\ell=0}^N(2\ell+1)m_d(\ell,N)=\binom{N+d-1}{d-1}. Summing m_d over N<n gives the cumulative multiplicity. At d=6,n=13, its values for \ell=0,\ldots,12 are (1036,784,581,420,295,200,130,80,46,24,11,4,1), and their (2\ell+1)-weighted sum is 18564=S(13,6). This is an exact restriction of the flat oscillator representation to a specified subgroup. Matching a dimension does not identify a unique group embedding. An observer's three-plane supplies relational data; it gives the electron no inherent split and does not replace its proposed actual CP3 spatial geometry by a flat oscillator model. Normalized oscillator modes — gives shell counts and the separated scalar functions. Zonal hybrid geometry — uses the resulting three-dimensional angular functions for directed overlaps. title: Projected bilocal variation
summary: Varying an exchange-symmetric interaction between projected densities retains the channel projector and one kernel convolution in each mean-field term.
text: Scope Work in a specified finite containing spatial region Q, with one field \Psi(t,x), fixed measure, and fixed channel projectors P_a(x). The labels x,y are two positions in the same physical space, not additional physical dimensions. Channel indices do not replace the required nested spatial embeddings; those maps must be supplied when applying this local model. Let \rho_a=\bar\Psi P_a\Psi be real, Grassmann-even scalar bilinears. Use projectors compatible with the chosen adjoint; in a Lorentzian Dirac convention this means P_a^\dagger\gamma^0=\gamma^0P_a. No positivity of \bar\Psi P_a\Psi is assumed. Vary \Psi and \bar\Psi independently. Variation Absorb coupling coefficients and coordinate identifications into a real kernel with exchange symmetry K_{ab}(x,y)=K_{ba}(y,x). Write \mathcal D=i\Gamma^A\nabla_A for the kinetic Dirac operator, where A ranges over the one time coordinate and the spatial directions in Q, and \nabla_A includes the chosen spin connection. Choose the interaction sign explicitly: S=\int dt\int_Q\bar\Psi\,\mathcal D\Psi\,d\mu -\frac12\int dt\sum_{a,b}\iint_{Q\times Q} \rho_a(x)K_{ab}(x,y)\rho_b(y)\,d\mu_xd\mu_y. At fixed projectors, kernel, and metric, U_a(x)=\sum_b\int_Q K_{ab}(x,y)\rho_b(y)\,d\mu_y, \qquad \frac{\delta S_{\rm int}}{\delta\bar\Psi(x)} =-\sum_a U_a(x)P_a(x)\Psi(x). To see the cancellation of the half, vary each density in the double integral and exchange (a,x) with (b,y) in the second contribution. The two contributions are identical. Thus the field equation is \boxed{\left(\mathcal D-\sum_a U_aP_a\right)\Psi=0.} With a plus interaction in the action the corresponding sign is plus. The projector remains attached to the varied field. The kernel occurs once inside U_a. If the kernel is not exchange-symmetric, only its symmetrized part contributes to the scalar-density functional. At density level, \frac{\delta U_a(x)}{\delta\rho_b(y)}=K_{ab}(x,y). This is the reciprocal response. It does not require equal response coefficients after changing field normalizations or identifying different coordinate spaces. Remaining physical requirements The kinetic symbol includes the appropriate geometric connection; replacing covariant derivatives by partial derivatives on a curved sector needs a justified local approximation. Dynamical projectors, metric-dependent measures, and kernels produce additional variations, including contributions to stress-energy. They are held fixed only for the variation above. For a local phase with generator \hat Q, the displayed scalar densities are invariant if [P_a,\hat Q]=0 and the adjoint transforms compatibly. More general charged bilocal factors need appropriate transport or invariant contractions. Gauge covariance is not implied by the double-integral notation. The equation is a Dirac mean-field equation. Its reduction to a positive scalar Schrödinger density, the sign of self-binding, a causal completion of the instantaneous spatial kernel, and the physical mass operator remain separate obligations. In particular, the flat scalar oscillator closure cannot be obtained merely by relabelling \bar\Psi\Psi as |\Psi|^2. Derive the inherited line connection Write a for the lower complex dimension, b=a+q for the higher one and W=\mathbb C^q. The normal-bundle calculation gives N=\mathcal O(1)\otimes W,\qquad 
abla^N=d+\alpha I_q,\qquad \alpha=\partial\log(1+|z|^2)^{-1}. 	ag{2} The Kähler metric identifies \overline N^{\,*} with N as Hermitian bundles with connection. Taking its exterior powers therefore gives \Lambda^s\overline N^{\,*} \simeq\mathcal O(s)\otimes\Lambda^sW. 	ag{3} Let \mathcal S_m(L)=\Lambda^{0,*}T^*\mathbb{CP}^m\otimes\mathcal O(L). Decomposing the ambient antiholomorphic forms along the lower submanifold now yields  oxed{ \left.\mathcal S_b(L_b)ight|_{\mathbb{CP}^a} = igoplus_{s=0}^{q} \mathcal S_a(L_b+s)\,\widehat\otimes\,\Lambda^sW. } 	ag{4} The hat records that total form degree is lower form degree plus s. This is also the induced Spin^c decomposition in Habib and Nakad, Section 3; their tautological exponent has the opposite sign from the present \mathcal O(L) convention. For a=3,q=2, all four normal components remain: Ambient line degree L_b Lower line degrees L_a Multiplicities -3, ordinary spin on CP5 -3,\,-2,\,-1 1,\,2,\,1 0, canonical Spin^c on CP5 0,\,1,\,2 1,\,2,\,1 4, first unshifted CP5 simplex family 4,\,5,\,6 1,\,2,\,1 Thus the canonical ambient choice contains the desired L_a=2 at s=2. Ordinary untwisted spin does not supply it. The full ambient spinor has rank 32=8(1+2+1). The line degree, normal degree and Dirac sign have no charge or antiparticle interpretation in this calculation. The connection in (2) has nonzero curvature. Calling the normal factor a collection of constant spinor entries would lose precisely the line shift in (4). A relative parallel factor after the twist has been absorbed into the lower bundle is a different statement. A simultaneous unshifted spectrum is not inherited directly The polynomial classification in the simplex note gives a necessary and sufficient condition on the r,r+1 paired form family: L=m-1+r 	ag{5} for a polynomial in R^2\mathscr D_L^2/4 to have exactly S(n,2m) with the same unshifted spectral integer n. All form families, rather than just the first, are included in (5). Suppose a full lower paired family comes from a fixed normal degree s of a higher paired family by the direct restriction (4). The line connections and the two form degrees must then satisfy L_a=L_b+s,\qquad r_a+s=r_b. 	ag{6} Demanding (5) at both depths gives a-1+r_a=b-1+r_b+s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad  oxed{2s=-(b-a)=-q.} 	ag{7} Since q>0 and s\ge0, this is impossible. The result is algebraic for all depths under the stated direct connection and full-pair inheritance, not a finite scan of mode labels. At depths six and ten the degree check is even more explicit. The lower allowed line degrees are 2+r_a, with r_a=0,1,2; the higher ones are 4+r_b, with r_b=0,\ldots,4. Equation L_a=L_b+s has only one permitted match: (r_a,r_b,s)=(2,0,0). 	ag{8} Its lower form degrees are 2,3, whereas the higher family has degrees 0,1. The direct component map is zero even before imposing the coexact and exact spatial conditions. A scalar identity restriction cannot bridge this mismatch. This result tests one proposed geometric origin for the new polynomial. It does not rule out a common master field with different spatial responses, a derived interaction changing form channels, or different geometric data. It also does not identify the global ambient Dirac operator with its tangential part: ambient eigenfields still have normal derivatives. Allowing mathematical index offsets changes (5), but supplies an additional mode identification. For complete pairs satisfying (6), the offsets obey s_{m index,a}-s_{m index,b}= rac q2+s. 	ag{9} This records what a changed identification would have to accomplish. No assigned particle modes or dimensionalities are changed here. Normal derivatives do not preserve one normal degree The standard inclusion is totally geodesic, so its tangential Dirac operator has precisely the connection decomposition (4). The full ambient operator additionally differentiates in all 2q ordinary normal spatial directions. Use Hermitian spatial Clifford matrices \alpha with \{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I. In a local adapted frame the complete graded tensor product is \alpha_{10,i}=\alpha_{6,i}\otimes I_4,\qquad \alpha_{10,6+
u}= eta_6\otimes\alpha_{4,
u}, \qquad  eta_{10}= eta_6\otimes eta_4. 	ag{10} Let \Pi_s project onto normal exterior degree s. Normal Clifford multiplication creates or removes one exterior factor. For a real normal covector p, it follows that \Pi_s\alpha_4(p)\Pi_s=0,\qquad  oxed{ \Pi_s\alpha_4(p)(I-\Pi_s)\alpha_4(p)\Pi_s =|p|^2\Pi_s. } 	ag{11} Thus a nonzero normal plane-wave derivative of a field in the selected grade drives complementary components with the full derivative norm. This holds for every complex spinor polarization and every normal orientation. The projectors are covariant under common unitary normal frame rotations; changing that frame does not remove (11). In particular, the s=2 summand that supplies L_a=2 is preserved by the tangential connection but is not an invariant sector of the unrestricted ambient Dirac equation. The nonzero commutator with normal Clifford matrices occurs in its principal derivative part. Connection terms cannot cancel it for arbitrary normal derivatives. Special differential constraints can make several normal derivatives cancel. In the full rank-eight top component at one point, the four independent complex normal first derivatives have 32 complex entries; their Dirac source map has rank 16 and a 16-dimensional kernel. Equation (11) is therefore not a theorem excluding every ambient extension. Such a constrained extension still needs its equation, norm and physical selection. Eliminate the complete local normal coupling A local calculation makes the missing normal dynamics concrete. Freeze the coefficients at one physical point and retain the full scalar Dirac symbol H=\alpha_{10}(p_t,p_n)+M eta_{10}. 	ag{12} Here M is a fixed real scalar coefficient. Freezing it tests the local linear operator; it does not solve a nonlinear scalar-current background or the global projective field. Retain the eight top-normal-degree components and eliminate all other 24 components at a frequency \omega away from their poles. The retained diagonal block is A=\alpha_6(p_t)+M eta_6,\qquad A^2=(|p_t|^2+M^2)I_8. 	ag{13} Normal Clifford multiplication maps the retained component isometrically into a middle-degree subspace. After conjugation by that map, the complementary diagonal action is -A. The exact Schur contribution is therefore  oxed{ \Sigma(\omega)=|p_n|^2(\omega+A)^{-1},\qquad K(\omega)=\omega-A-\Sigma(\omega). } 	ag{14} This comes from varying the full real quadratic action with respect to every complex complementary amplitude. The eliminated amplitudes are components of the same spinor field, with no new mediator field. The same reduction determines the norm. For a normalized retained eigenvector of A with eigenvalue a, the full field has squared norm  oxed{ Z_a=1+ rac{|p_n|^2}{(\omega+a)^2}, \qquad \partial_\omega K=I_8+|p_n|^2(\omega+A)^{-2}. } 	ag{15} The positive additional term is the norm in the eliminated components. It cannot be omitted when interpreting the reduced action. The complete dispersion relation is  oxed{\omega^2=|p_t|^2+|p_n|^2+M^2.} 	ag{16} Both signs have multiplicity sixteen in the original rank-thirty-two symbol. At these frequencies the discarded block itself has a decoupled eigenspace, so its unrestricted inverse is singular. The contraction in (14) has a removable pole there: the retained source is orthogonal to that eigenspace. Solving in the sourced subspace, or using the minimum-norm complementary solution, gives (15) and reconstructs full eigenvectors. The independent decoupled eigenvectors remain in the full spectrum. Normal motion contributes to the frequency and the reduced norm; this local elimination does not produce the polynomial (1). Curvature, spatial variation and a normal binding law would require a further global calculation. The normal extension analysis demonstrates the same need to derive the kinetic norm in an actual spatial profile problem. The nonlinear reduction also retains the complementary scalar response when the background depends on the field itself. Verification projective_mass_inheritance_checks.py checks all connection and form-degree matches, with finite dimensional controls accompanying the all-degree proof (7). An independently constructed five-mode exterior algebra verifies the full ten-dimensional Clifford action. Normal rotations, arbitrary complex polarizations and complete normal jets verify (10)–(11). Exact block elimination of all 24 complementary components checks (14). Independent frequency differentiation, full complex action variations, reconstructed eigenvectors and their norms check (15)–(16) on both frequency signs.

title: A local simplex operator on projective spatial spinors
summary: A local polynomial in the squared Dirac operator gives exact simplex values and a Hermitian scalar insertion on a specified CP3 spinor family, with its full additional spectrum, bundle assumptions and kinetic contribution retained.
text: Summary: A local polynomial in the squared Dirac operator gives exact simplex values and a Hermitian scalar insertion on a specified CP3 spinor family, with its full additional spectrum, bundle assumptions and kinetic contribution retained. An admissible spinor operator on the proposed physical geometry On a specified spinor bundle over physical \mathbb{CP}^3, define X=\frac{R^2\mathscr D_2^2}{4},\qquad \boxed{\mathcal M_6=\frac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720}.} \tag{1} Here \mathscr D_2 is the spatial Dirac operator on \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(2), with the Chern connection specified below. On its paired zero-form and exact one-form spectral family, \boxed{\mathcal M_6=S(n,6)=\binom{n+5}{6}.} \tag{2} Both Dirac signs have this same value. The operator is local, self-adjoint and commutes with the scalar matrix \beta. Consequently \mu\beta\mathcal M_6 is a Hermitian Hamiltonian contribution for real \mu. This resolves an operator-construction question on the specified projective geometry. The round-sphere Killing transfer has a different spectral structure and a direct scalar insertion that fails Hermiticity. That failure is not a universal obstruction to a local spinor polynomial. Equation (1), as introduced here, is a spectral candidate whose coefficients are fixed by requiring (2) on the stated family. A geometric derivative construction now obtains the zero-form polynomial from the symmetric third holomorphic covariant derivative and its physical adjoint. It also gives a local extension to the Dirac pair. The master interaction has not yet supplied that derivative energy. The connection, occupied family, physical mode identification and coefficient \mu remain to be derived. This is not a derivation of the occupied coherent-ray contact operator. Throughout, CP3 describes the candidate actual six-dimensional spatial manifold. Its directions are ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, with no compactification. The FS geometry and its undetermined radius R are assumptions. A line-bundle degree labels the field's connection, not additional physical dimensions. Specify the entire spinor bundle For mathematical complex dimension m, take the metric on \mathbb{CP}^m to have holomorphic sectional curvature 4/R^2. Let \Sigma_L=\Lambda^{0,*}T^*\mathbb{CP}^m\otimes\mathcal O(L),\qquad \mathscr D_L=\sqrt2(\bar\partial_L+\bar\partial_L^\dagger), \qquad \beta=(-1)^{\text{form degree}}. \tag{3} The line connection is the standard invariant Chern connection. Then \mathscr D_L^\dagger=\mathscr D_L,\qquad \{\mathscr D_L,\beta\}=0,\qquad [\mathscr D_L^2,\beta]=0. \tag{4} The spinor rank is 2^m; all exterior degrees are retained. On CP3 the ordinary spin bundle is \Lambda^{0,*}\otimes\mathcal O(-2). Thus the L=2 bundle in (1) is ordinary spin twisted by \mathcal O(4). Its Spin^c determinant line is \mathcal O(8). It is a specific connection choice, not the ordinary untwisted spin operator or an already selected physical magnetic flux. No chirality, form degree or Dirac sign is identified with charge or with an antiparticle. The existing spatial Dirac construction uses exactly the conventions (3), retaining its line degree as an input. Retain all projective Dirac families Put X_L=R^2\mathscr D_L^2/4. The complete positive squared spectrum is \boxed{ x_{r,k}=k(k+L+m-r),\qquad r=0,\ldots,m-1,\qquad k\ge\max(r+1,-L). } \tag{5} The label r specifies a coexact degree-r form and its degree-(r+1) Dirac partner. Each family has both opposite Dirac signs. Coincident values from different families have their multiplicities added. In the present \mathcal O(L) convention, (5) follows from Habib and Nakad, Proposition 3.2 by setting their tautological exponent v=-L and their spectral integer l=k+L. The multiplicity of x_{r,k}, including both signs, is \frac{ 2(k+L+m)!(k-r-1+m)!(2k+L-r+m) }{ (k+L)!\,r!\,m!\,(k-r-1)!\,(m-r-1)!\, k(k+L+m-r) }. \tag{6} There are also \binom{L+m}{m} zero modes for L\ge0 and \binom{-L-1}{m} zero modes for L\le-m-1. They occur in exterior degrees zero and m, respectively. There are no zero modes in the intervening line degrees. An independent check uses the ordinary-spin twist spectrum of Ginoux and Habib, Theorem 4.5 and Lemma 4.6. Their tautological spin twist is -L-2 on CP3. Combining their families recovers (5)–(6), including the zero modes. More concretely, the CP3 representations in (5) have SU(4) Dynkin labels \begin{array}{c|c} r&\text{representation for each Dirac sign}\\ \hline 0&(k,0,k+L)\\ 1&(k-2,1,k+L)\\ 2&(k-3,0,k+L+1). \end{array} \tag{7} The Weyl dimension formula \dim(a,b,c)= \frac{(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)(a+b+2)(b+c+2)(a+b+c+3)}{12} \tag{8} gives exactly one half of (6) in each row. This checks the complete polarization multiplicities independently of the spectral formula. For L=2, the three values of X are x_{0,k}=k(k+5),\qquad x_{1,k}=k(k+4),\qquad x_{2,k}=k(k+3). \tag{9} There are ten additional holomorphic zero modes. In the first family k=n gives (2), since \begin{aligned} X&=n(n+5),\\ X+4&=(n+1)(n+4),\\ X+6&=(n+2)(n+3). \end{aligned} \tag{10} The remaining families are present in the same operator: Family r Spectral label k Value of \mathcal M_6 Multiplicity per Dirac sign 0 1 1 70 1 2 \frac{24}{5} 140 2 3 \frac{66}{5} 84 0 13 18\,564 147\,560 1 13 \frac{250\,835}{16} 241\,920 2 13 \frac{589\,784}{45} 97\,614 0 35 3\,838\,380 12\,337\,650 These multiplicities are spatial degeneracies, not extra particles or the rank-one coherent-ray multiplicity. Assigning an observed particle to one field in a family remains a separate problem. No family in (9) has been discarded to obtain (2). Derive the first family by actual spatial differentiation For L\ge0, choose a coherent holomorphic section \chi=\sqrt{\binom{L+m}{m}}\,Z_0^L and let t=|Z_0|^2/|Z|^2. The exact spatial class \chi[F(t)+G(t)\bar\partial t] has arbitrary complex F,G, with both exterior degrees retained. Its physical norm uses w(t)dt=\frac{t^L(1-t)^{m-1}}{\mathrm B(L+1,m)}\,dt,\qquad \|\varphi\|^2=\int_0^1w\bigl(|F|^2+2t(1-t)|G|^2\bigr)dt. \tag{11} At unit radius the two differential squares are \begin{aligned} \mathscr D_L^2(F\chi) ={}&-4\left[t(1-t)F'' +(L+1-(L+m+1)t)F'\right]\chi,\\ \mathscr D_L^2(G\chi\bar\partial t) ={}&-4\left[t(1-t)G'' +(L+2-(L+m+3)t)G' -(L+m+1)G\right]\chi\bar\partial t. \end{aligned} \tag{12} These follow by composing the complete Dirac operator and its physical adjoint, as derived in the spatial note linked above. For p_k(t)=P_k^{(m-1,L)}(2t-1), Jacobi's equation gives \mathscr D_L^2(\chi p_k)=4k(k+L+m)\chi p_k. \tag{13} The derivative field \chi p_k'\bar\partial t has the same squared eigenvalue and vanishes for k=0. Applying all three factors in (1) to these differential expressions at m=3,L=2 gives (2) directly. The invariant operator and connection commute with physical SU(4) isometries. The orbit of a nonzero representative spans its irreducible family in (7); linear combinations therefore retain all its complex spatial polarizations. This extends the first-family identity beyond one radial profile. The other two families are independently accounted for by the complete spectrum above. At L=m-1, the weight in (11) is proportional to t^{m-1}(1-t)^{m-1}. After u=2t-1, its Jacobi equation is the zonal scalar equation on a round 2m-sphere. This explains the shared spectral factorization with the conformal scalar construction. It is an identity of these weighted differential equations, not an identification of CP3 with a round spatial sphere. Classify the polynomial condition without fitting individual modes Let c=L+m-r and suppose a polynomial p satisfies p(k(k+c))=S(k+s,2m) \tag{14} for every sufficiently large integer k, with an integer index offset s. Both sides must then agree as polynomials in k. The left side is invariant under k\mapsto-c-k. The right side has consecutive roots -s,-s-1,\ldots,-s-2m+1, whose reflection center is fixed. Therefore \boxed{c=2s+2m-1.} \tag{15} Conversely, when (15) holds, pairing the consecutive factors gives the unique polynomial \boxed{ p(X)=\frac1{(2m)!} \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \left[X+(s+j)(s+2m-1-j)\right]. } \tag{16} If c is even, no integer offset satisfies (15). This excludes every finite polynomial of X with that integer simplex sequence, not merely a trial cubic. It does not classify all non-polynomial or more general geometric operators. With no offset, s=0, the necessary and sufficient line degree is \boxed{L=m-1+r.} \tag{17} For the first family at the assigned real depths six and ten, the corresponding mathematical constructions are \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{real depth}&L& (2m)!\,\mathcal M_{2m}\\ \hline 6&2&X(X+4)(X+6)\\ 10&4&X(X+8)(X+14)(X+18)(X+20). \end{array} \tag{18} The ten-dimensional row uses a separately specified physical CP5 bundle. Neither its connection nor compatibility with the six-space connection is automatic. At its first-family degree n=23, (18) gives S(23,10)=64\,512\,240. The normal inheritance calculation obtains the required CP3 line degree from a canonical CP5 spinor. It also shows why simultaneous unshifted families at both depths do not follow by direct restriction, and retains the normal derivatives that mix the supplied components. For comparison, canonical CP3 with L=0 has a first-family polynomial X(X-4)(X+2)/720=S(k-1,6). Ordinary spin CP3 with L=-2 has the first-family polynomial X(X-2)(X-6)/720=S(k-2,6). These are different spectral-index maps and actions, not changes to the assigned particle modes. The classification concerns operator identities; it is not a scan showing that alternative particle dimensionalities fit the mass relationships. Put the operator in a real action and retain the kinetic term For the full L=2 bundle, specify the additional quadratic energy E_\mu(\psi)= \langle\psi,\mathscr D_2\psi\rangle +\mu\langle\psi,\beta\mathcal M_6\psi\rangle. \tag{19} Since (1) is a real polynomial of \mathscr D_2^2, every complex variation gives the Hermitian canonical Hamiltonian i\partial_t\psi= (\mathscr D_2+\mu\beta\mathcal M_6)\psi. \tag{20} On each paired spatial eigenspace, ordering the basis by positive then negative \beta, this is the complete matrix H_{r,k}= \begin{pmatrix} \mu p(x_{r,k})&2\sqrt{x_{r,k}}/R\\ 2\sqrt{x_{r,k}}/R&-\mu p(x_{r,k}) \end{pmatrix}. \tag{21} It is tensored with the identity on the multiplicity (8). Thus the physical frequencies are \boxed{ \omega_{r,k,\pm} =\pm\sqrt{\frac{4x_{r,k}}{R^2}+\mu^2p(x_{r,k})^2}. } \tag{22} The direct sum of these Hermitian matrices gives unitary linear evolution on its self-adjoint domain. This is a statement about the specified quadratic action, not nonlinear stability of an unconstructed master-field state. Even in the first family, \mu S(n,6) is a scalar operator coefficient; it is not the entire frequency in (22). At a common \mu,R, the positive frequency ratio for n=35 and n=13 is \frac{\omega_{35}}{\omega_{13}} = \sqrt{ \frac{4(35)(40)+(\mu R)^2S(35,6)^2} {4(13)(18)+(\mu R)^2S(13,6)^2} }. \tag{23} It lies below the simplex-coefficient ratio at finite nonzero \mu R and approaches it as |\mu R| increases. No kinetic contribution has been subtracted by convention. The nonlinear normalization analysis explains why deriving the actual interaction and occupied field can further change the relation between coefficient, frequency and energy. The added term in (19) has spatial differential order six. It is not a rewriting of the existing algebraic local scalar current. A derivation as an effective master interaction must supply its normalization, domain and relevant frequency dependence. A local way to distinguish the paired form channels A polynomial of the full X cannot vanish on both additional infinite families while remaining nonzero on the first: it would have infinitely many distinct roots. There is, however, a more specific local operator using the existing Kähler form-degree projectors \Pi_q: X_r=\frac{R^2}{2} \left(\bar\partial_L^\dagger\Pi_{r+1}\bar\partial_L +\bar\partial_L\Pi_r\bar\partial_L^\dagger\right). \tag{24} It equals X_L on the r,r+1 paired Hodge family and vanishes on the other families and on harmonic forms. The Dolbeault identity \bar\partial_L^2=0 gives X_rX_s=0\ (r\ne s),\qquad \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}X_r=X_L,\qquad [X_r,\mathscr D_L]=[X_r,\beta]=0. \tag{25} Therefore X_0(X_0+4)(X_0+6)/720 is a local Hermitian scalar candidate supported on the first family. The other polarizations remain in the full field equation and retain their kinetic action. Using (24) would specify a different interaction that distinguishes form channels. It supplies a concrete covariant possibility, but does not establish that the master action selects it. The unselected families cannot be treated as absent observed particles merely because their scalar coefficient is set to zero. Verification projective_spinor_simplex_checks.py compares two complete projective Dirac spectral descriptions, including zero modes, and checks all CP3 multiplicities against independent SU(4) Weyl dimensions. Exact polynomial identities verify (15)–(18). Repeated spatial differentiation of both Jacobi form components checks the sixth- and tenth-order operators through the assigned degrees. Independent physical quadrature retains their full canonical Gram matrices. Complex action variations, both Dirac signs and the kinetic square verify (19)–(23). Complete finite Dolbeault complexes check the local channel identities (24)–(25) under unitary changes within every form degree.

title: Radial confinement bounds
summary: The radial spatial measure fixes the centrifugal term, while a Hardy bound gives an explicit sufficient condition excluding levels below a saturating threshold.
text:
Correct radial operator Consider the scalar operator H=-\Delta+V(r) on ordinary \mathbb R^d, d\ge2, in units \hbar^2/(2m)=1. For a normalized spherical harmonic with angular eigenvalue \ell(\ell+d-2), write \psi(x)=R(r)Y_\ell(\hat x) and u(r)=r^{(d-1)/2}R(r). This transformation sends the radial norm to \int_0^\infty|u|^2dr. Differentiating R=r^{-(d-1)/2}u yields H_\ell u=-u''+ \left[V(r)+ rac{(\ell+(d-2)/2)^2-1/4}{r^2}ight]u. The term (d-1)(d-3)/(4r^2) is contributed by the radial measure. Use the Friedrichs realization inherited from the full spatial quadratic form. In particular the regular branch has u\sim r^{\ell+(d-1)/2}; the critical d=2,\ell=0 endpoint selects the regular, nonlogarithmic branch. An arbitrary half-line boundary condition describes a different operator. A form bound on attraction For d\ge3, integration by parts for smooth compactly supported \psi gives 0\le\int\left|
abla\psi+a rac{x}{r^2}\psiight|^2dx =\int|
abla\psi|^2dx+ [a^2-a(d-2)]\int rac{|\psi|^2}{r^2}dx. Choose a=(d-2)/2 and extend by form closure:  oxed{\int|
abla\psi|^2dx\ge  rac{(d-2)^2}{4}\int rac{|\psi|^2}{r^2}dx.} This is Hardy's inequality; see Nonnenmacher, Proposition 3.2.7. As an application, measure lengths in a stated range L and energies in \hbar^2/(2mL^2). For the dimensionless operator H_{m sat}=-\Delta+\lambda rac{r^2}{1+r^2},\qquad \lambda>0, subtract its limiting potential \lambda. Since (1+r^2)^{-1}\le r^{-2}, \langle H_{m sat}-\lambdaangle \ge\left[ rac{(d-2)^2}{4}-\lambdaight] \int rac{|\psi|^2}{r^2}dx. Thus \lambda\le(d-2)^2/4 excludes every spectral value below \lambda. The bound is sufficient; exceeding it alone does not establish a bound state. A first-order Dirac operator needs its own analysis. Confining oscillator domain — treats an unbounded harmonic potential with compact resolvent. Coulomb exponential profiles — illustrates how normalized spatial profiles enter energy bounds. Resonance and profile tools — overview and verification. resonance_profile_checks.py checks finite examples by quadrature, matrix evolution, and independent algebra.

title: Resonance and profile tools
summary: Tools for Coulomb profiles, angular functions, cyclic and quartic resonance, dispersion response, radial bounds, and pseudoscalar symmetry protection.
text: These conditional mathematical models support V2 calculations. Their operators, state preparation, and physical matching assumptions are stated in each note. All physical coordinates remain in one nested manifold of ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. Coulomb exponential profiles — Normalized exponential profiles give exact Coulomb integrals, a two-particle variational bound, and finite-range contact estimates. Zonal hybrid geometry — Spherical-harmonic addition gives exact directed-state overlaps and conditional trigonal, tetrahedral, and octahedral orthogonality. Cyclic resonance spectrum — A nearest-neighbour amplitude ring has exact Fourier resonances, paired levels, and a calculable response to alternating couplings. Dipole dispersion response — Second-order dipole coupling yields an attractive inverse-sixth-power energy with a coefficient fixed by the specified excitation response. Radial confinement bounds — The radial spatial measure fixes the centrifugal term, while a Hardy bound gives an explicit sufficient condition excluding levels below a saturating threshold. Chiral pseudoscalar mass term — A specified leading chiral action makes pseudoscalar mass squared proportional to light-quark masses, with the response scale left as matched input. Resonant quartet dynamics — A conservative quartic amplitude interaction has exact action invariants and a detuning-controlled exchange law under specified pump preparation. Oscillator rotation branching — Harmonic-polynomial decomposition gives exact angular multiplicities for a flat oscillator shell and its restriction to an observer-selected spatial three-plane. Spectral analysis tools — companion analytic and statistical results. resonance_profile_checks.py checks finite examples by quadrature, matrix evolution, and independent algebra.

title: Resonant quartet dynamics
summary: A conservative quartic amplitude interaction has exact action invariants and a detuning-controlled exchange law under specified pump preparation.
text: Four distinct field modes In frequency units with canonical equation i\dot a_j=\partial H/\partial a_j^*, choose H=\sum_{j=1}^4\omega_j|a_j|^2+ \kappa a_1^*a_2^*a_3a_4+kappa^*a_1a_2a_3^*a_4^*. For example i\dot a_1=\omega_1a_1+\kappa a_2^*a_3a_4 and i\dot a_3=\omega_3a_3+\kappa^*a_1a_2a_4^*; exchange 1\leftrightarrow2 and 3\leftrightarrow4 for the other two equations. The positions of the complex conjugates are essential to reciprocity. Let I_j=|a_j|^2 and Z=\kappa a_1^*a_2^*a_3a_4. Direct differentiation gives \dot I_1=\dot I_2=2\operatorname{Im}Z, \qquad \dot I_3=\dot I_4=-2\operatorname{Im}Z. Every charge Q_c=\sum c_jI_j with c_1+c_2=c_3+c_4 is conserved. These include total norm, I_1-I_2, and I_3-I_4. The Hamiltonian itself is conserved and total norm bounds every amplitude, giving global solutions for finite initial data. Mode amplitudes add no physical spatial dimensions. Frequency matching Writing a_j=b_je^{-i\omega_jt} makes the first interaction proportional to e^{i\Delta t} with \Delta=\omega_1+\omega_2-\omega_3-\omega_4. A label equality n_1+n_2=n_3+n_4 implies \Delta=0 when all four frequencies follow the same affine law \omega_j=An_j+B. It need not do so under a nonlinear count law or unequal sector scales. For example 1+4=2+3, while S(1,2)+S(4,2)=11 and S(2,2)+S(3,2)=9. In a first-order calculation that freezes the other three rotating amplitudes, the forced change is proportional to \int_0^t e^{i\Delta s}ds and is bounded by 2/|\Delta| times that fixed forcing strength. This bound belongs to that approximation. Exact exchange with undepleted pumps For independently maintained pumps b_2,b_4, the 1,3 subsystem obeys i\dot b_1=g e^{i\Delta t}b_3,\qquad i\dot b_3=g^*e^{-i\Delta t}b_1,\qquad g=\kappa b_2^*b_4. Set b_1=c_1e^{i\Delta t/2} and b_3=c_3e^{-i\Delta t/2}. Then i\frac d{dt}\begin{pmatrix}c_1\\c_3\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\Delta/2&g\\g^*&-\Delta/2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}c_1\\c_3\end{pmatrix}. The matrix square is (|g|^2+\Delta^2/4)I.
