title: Spatial mode tensors carried by the field's rest frame
summary: A same-current rest-frame connection gives a covariant spatial tensor action and preserves zero-rotation-moment branches, while polarized principal modes expose a high-wave-number limitation of this completion.
text:
Summary: A same-current rest-frame connection gives a covariant spatial tensor action and preserves zero-rotation-moment branches, while polarized principal modes expose a high-wave-number limitation of this completion. A precise transformation law for spatial coefficients The localized frequency and inertia action has an explicit spatial solution. Its initial boost calculation treats coefficient labels as spectators. If the oscillator coefficients instead represent ordinary spatial tensors, their transformations must compose consistently with the spinor boosts. One local inverse completion uses the field's own current to define its rest frame. It introduces no independent frame field, additional particle or additional spatial dimension. It gives an exactly covariant action on a stated domain. It also produces a new kinetic response for complex polarized mode rays. That response has a high-wave-number limitation, derived below, so covariance alone does not complete the physical carrier. Use natural units and the full spinor matrices A_a and canonical grade fields of the localized action. Define  egin{aligned} I_N^\mu&=\Psi_N^\dagger A^\mu\Psi_N, \qquad A^0=I,\quad A^a=A_a,\ j^\mu&=\sum_N\operatorname{Tr}I_N^\mu,\qquad s=\sqrt{j^\mu j_\mu},\qquad u^\mu=j^\mu/s. \end{aligned} 	ag{1} The metric is \eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,\ldots,-1). This construction requires j^0>0 and j^\mu j_\mu>0. At a displayed localized core, j=(ho_{\mathrm{tot}},0) at every finite point, so the condition holds. Its zero-current and null-current boundaries remain outside this definition. All spatial frames here concern the d ordinary spatial directions of one sector. A particle's local zero-momentum frame does not stop its oscillation or split its physical dimensions into different kinds. The subsequent retained-frame completion replaces the instantaneous frame response and repairs the stated principal defect. Its spatial source and mode-weight selection remain unresolved; this extension is distinct from the normal-carrier construction. The induced spatial rotation and connection For u=(u^0,\mathbf u), the canonical boost sending e_0 to u is B(u)= egin{pmatrix} u^0&\mathbf u^T\ \mathbf u&I+\dfrac{\mathbf u\mathbf u^T}{1+u^0} \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{2} It satisfies B^T\eta B=\eta. Under a proper time-preserving Lorentz transformation \Lambda, put u'=\Lambda u. The matrix B(u')^{-1}\Lambda B(u) = egin{pmatrix}1&0\0&R(\Lambda,u)\end{pmatrix} 	ag{3} defines an ordinary orthogonal spatial rotation. Matrix multiplication immediately proves the composition law R(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1,u) =R(\Lambda_2,\Lambda_1u)R(\Lambda_1,u). 	ag{4} Thus spatial tensor rotations and boosts are parts of one transformation rule. A tensor is referred to its own current's spatial rest frame; it is not assigned an unrelated spectator boost. Project the matrix one-form B^{-1}dB onto its spatial block. Direct differentiation gives the real antisymmetric connection  oxed{\mathfrak a_\mu=  rac{(\partial_\mu\mathbf u)\mathbf u^T -\mathbf u(\partial_\mu\mathbf u)^T}{1+u^0}.} 	ag{5} With the spacetime one-form transformation understood, it obeys \mathfrak a'=R\mathfrak aR^{-1}-(dR)R^{-1}. It is not generally flat. At rest its curvature evaluated on two velocity variations v,w is w v^T-v w^T. A sequence of changes of velocity can therefore rotate the spatial coefficient frame. Let D_N(R) be the normalized symmetric-tensor representation on E_N=\operatorname{Sym}^N(\mathbf1\oplus\mathbb C^d). The scalar summand is invariant and the spatial vector summand transforms by R. Its connection is \Gamma_{N,\mu}=dD_N(0\oplus\mathfrak a_\mu). 	ag{6} The partner column labels of the localized matrix core remain spectators under both rotations and boosts. Only the oscillator spatial tensors use (6). This leaves the original spinor transformation on the field's row index intact. A transformation of the independent partner labels is not needed to prove (4). In normalized occupation bases, a one-slot generator G acts through \sqrt{n_b(n_a+1)}G_{ab} between occupations differing by transfer of one index from b to a, and through \sum_an_aG_{aa} on the diagonal. This specifies (6) on every coefficient, not just a selected coherent ray. Vary the resulting action, including its frame With matrix columns carrying the tensor representation, define \Psi'_N(x')=S(\Lambda)\Psi_N(x)D_N(R)^{-1},\qquad 
abla_\mu\Psi_N=\partial_\mu\Psi_N-\Psi_N\Gamma_{N,\mu}. 	ag{7} Identity matrices on partner indices are implicit. The induced rotations are unitary, so tracing the column indices still gives j'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_{
u}j^
u. Definition (1) is therefore consistent with its own nonlinear field transformation. Replace the ordinary derivative in the canonical spinor action by (7), retaining the same current potential U. The complete extra term is  oxed{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{frame}} =-i\sum_{N,\mu}\operatorname{Tr}(I_N^\mu\Gamma_{N,\mu}).} 	ag{8} The current hierarchy's partial traces commute with the tensor rotations, so the same root-current potential and binding potential remain invariant. The kinetic term is invariant only when the derivative of the field-dependent rotation in (7) is retained as well. Independent full first-derivative data in six and ten dimensions verify this equality for the complete action. The connection is a local function of the fields and their first derivatives. It is linear in those derivatives, so this is a local first-order quasilinear action on its stated domain. Its coefficients must be varied with the fields. Holding u fixed while varying \Psi gives a different equation and would miss the effect below. Each grade's local phase leaves j, u, I_N and (8) unchanged. Only the original time and spatial terms contribute the phase-gradient change -j_N^\mu\partial_\mu	heta_N. The Noether current and conserved norm therefore remain the canonical j_N and Q_N. The general field-space kinetic two-form nevertheless changes; a conserved norm is not the entire kinetic structure. Which localized results survive exactly At a static core, u=e_0 and \partial u=0. Around it, \mathfrak a starts quadratically in variations of the spatial current velocity. Hence (8) and its first variation vanish at that field. The displayed localized solutions and their simplex frequencies remain exact stationary solutions of this completed action. The added kinetic term does not turn their amplitudes into masses. For a coherent ray write z=(z_0,z_1,\ldots,z_d), \|z\|=1, and define its spatial rotation moment M_{ab}=2\operatorname{Im}(\overline z_a z_b),\qquad 1\le a,b\le d. 	ag{9} At the core, I_N^0=ho I_r\otimes P_{z,N} and I_N^a=0. The symmetric-tensor expectation is \langle z^N,dD_N(G)z^Nangle=N z^\dagger Gz. Writing v for the first variation of \mathbf u, the entire quadratic addition is consequently  oxed{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{frame}}^{(2)} =- rac{iho_{\mathrm{tot}}N}{2} z^\dagger igl(0\oplus[\dot v v^T-v\dot v^T] igr)z =- rac{ho_{\mathrm{tot}}N}{2}v^TM\dot v.} 	ag{10} A real coherent ray has M=0. More generally, zero spatial rotation moment is the precise condition; the scalar slack component can have a separate phase without producing M. Under this condition the new action starts at cubic order in arbitrary full field perturbations, including all spinor, partner, mode and derivative directions. Its complete linear response is therefore the one already tested in the localized response calculation. For M
e0, (10) must be retained. Independent variations of the actual action verify both the vanishing quadratic coefficient at a real ray and the nonzero coefficient at a complex polarized ray. An agreement of the stationary frequencies would not reveal this difference. The exact translation/boost inertia is retained. At rest a translation changes the profile but not u=e_0, so (10) contributes zero to its pairing with a boost. The earlier coefficient \hbar\omega_NQ/c^2 is unchanged. Uniformly boosted stationary solutions also have constant u, making (8) zero on the solution. These statements do not establish the stability of the completed action. A finite probe identity with the new kinetic term For a target whose spatial rotation moment is zero, its contribution to (8) vanishes for every connection: the trace of each tensor rotation generator is zero on that ray. A fixed finite probe can change the common current u and its derivatives, but their values remain the same for different larger target grades at the same target profile. Thus the cross contribution of (8), its full probe variation and its target translation variation remain independent of target grade under the same distinct-grade conditions as the earlier coupling identity. The result uses the complete new action, rather than keeping its frame fixed during the probe variation. The diagnostic uses a unit-norm Gaussian probe with a spatially varying matrix polarization, retaining constant and linear spatial coefficient terms, their phases and a moving center. The added cross term is nonzero. Targets of grades two and three give equal values and equal arbitrary first-derivative probe variations at three points. This is a conditional functional comparison, not a solved encounter or an observed vertex. The polarized principal symbol has a defective part The nonzero coefficient in (10) permits an exact high-wave-number test. At one isotropic core point normalize ho_{\mathrm{tot}}=1 and \phi=I_r/\sqrt r. Use real canonical coordinates y=(\sqrt2\operatorname{Re}\eta,\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\eta) for all spinor and partner components of the occupied oscillator ray. The velocity variation is v=Cy, with C_a=\sqrt2 igl(\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{vec}t_a, \operatorname{Im}\operatorname{vec}t_a igr),\qquad t_a= egin{pmatrix}0\\alpha_a\phi\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{11} The canonical and additional kinetic matrices are \Omega_0= egin{pmatrix}0&-I\I&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Omega_1=-NC^TMC. 	ag{12} Actual first derivatives of (8) in two independent lower-spinor directions verify this added two-form. It is not inferred just from the frequency spectrum. Since C\Omega_0^{-1}C^T=0, the matrix Z=\Omega_0\Omega_1 satisfies Z^2=0. The kinetic form remains invertible: \Omega^{-1}\Omega_0=I+Z. Let A be the real form of the original Clifford principal matrix in one ordinary spatial direction. It obeys A^2=I and exchanges upper and lower spinor blocks. The new principal evolution matrix is  oxed{P=(I+Z)A.} 	ag{13} The correction Z acts only in the lower block, giving ZAZ=0. Consequently K=P^2-I=Z+AZA,\qquad K^2=0. 	ag{14} All characteristic roots remain +1 or -1, but for a nonzero rotation moment the matrix need not be diagonalizable. Decompose it exactly as P=P_s+P_n,\qquad P_s=P(I-K/2),\qquad P_n=PK/2, \quad P_s^2=I,\quad P_n^2=0,\quad [P_s,P_n]=0. 	ag{15} The Fourier propagator of this frozen principal equation is e^{-iktP} =(\cos kt\,I-i\sin kt\,P_s)(I-iktP_n). 	ag{16} The last factor grows with wave number when P_n
e0. For the explicit ray z_1=1/\sqrt2, z_2=i/\sqrt2, degree N=2 and d=6, the largest amplification at time 2\pi is approximately 12.645, 125.672 and 1256.638 at integer wave numbers 1, 10 and 100. Every complete spinor and partner component is included; the orthogonal oscillator directions have the original principal symbol. This proves failure of a wave-number-independent canonical norm estimate for that principal equation. It does not demonstrate superluminal characteristic speeds, and it is not a numerical claim of a particle lifetime. A lower-order mass term does not repair diagonalizability of the principal matrix. The simple induced connection therefore does not supply the general strong-hyperbolicity control required for the physical carrier. At M=0, Z=0 and the complete original Clifford symbol is recovered, but that special branch is not a proof of nonlinear regularity in a neighborhood containing polarized fields. The remaining carrier requirement This construction supplies an actual transformation law, its local action, its reciprocal kinetic response and a precise propagation restriction. A more complete kinetic reduction must address the polarized defect while retaining the mass-frequency branch and its normalization. Additional terms or constraints would need their own same-field origin and variations. It also remains necessary to identify the coefficient grades with physical spatial modes and explain their selection. Rest-frame covariance is not that identification. The derivative-carrier calculation already shows why simply declaring the coefficients to be normalized derivatives can introduce a nonlocal response. Neither a representation dimension nor a boost composition law bypasses that dynamical test. Verification rest_current_carrier_checks.py checks 60 conditions: boost-frame composition and curvature, complete tensor generators, the full field-dependent action in six and ten dimensions, phase current, full first-derivative variations, a finite textured probe, the actual kinetic two-form and the exact polarized principal propagator. The growing principal control is an expected mathematical result, not a test silently adjusted to pass stability. The action and representation calculations are in rest_current_carrier.py.

title: Round-sphere Dirac counts
summary: The round-sphere Dirac spectrum has a dimension-dependent spinor multiplicity, giving two times the simplex count on S3 and four times it on S5.
text: The operator and its multiplicity For the untwisted complex spinor Dirac operator on a round sphere S^d of radius R, d\ge2, the eigenvalues and multiplicities for each sign are \lambda_k^\pm=\pm\frac{k+d/2}{R},\qquad m_d(k)=2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots. The unit-radius result is Bär, The Dirac operator on space forms of positive curvature, Theorem 1; rescaling the metric supplies the displayed factor 1/R. Summing the positive branch through level k=n-1 gives N_+(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}m_d(k) =2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}S(n,d). This is a cumulative eigenstate count with multiplicity, not an individual Dirac eigenvalue. Including both signs doubles this count. Low-dimensional examples Sphere Spinor factor Positive cumulative count S^3 2 2S(n,3) S^5 4 4S(n,5) At the V2 neutrino indices 10,15,22, the round S^5 operator gives 8008,46512,263120 positive-branch states. Restricting to fewer components would need a specified invariant projection and its own spectrum. At radius one on S^3, the eigenvalue 7/2 belongs to k=2 and has multiplicity 12. Multiplicity 20 belongs to k=3, whose eigenvalue is 9/2. The coincidence m_3(3)=S(4,3)=20 does not equate a shell count with a cumulative count. Use in V2 These formulas provide a checked benchmark for the candidate sphere operators. The spinor factor counts field components; it introduces no additional physical spatial directions. They do not select a sphere as the actual sector geometry, construct its nesting, or derive the law m=\mu S(n,d). The mass law and the individual sphere Dirac eigenvalues remain different quantities. Existing particle depths and the neutrino mass ratios use a separately specified contact mass operator. The mode counting checks verify the cumulative sums and the explicit S^3 and S^5 examples. They check applications of the cited spectrum, not a numerical construction of the sphere Dirac operator. title: A complete finite normal band
summary: Two ordinary normal coordinates realize a complete invariant oscillator band and a local first-order parent for the rising frequency product.
text:
A finite sequence of normal modes can be a complete invariant band of an ordinary spatial operator. It need not be obtained by throwing away the end of an oscillator tower. The construction below produces the curvature simplex product in such a band and gives it a local, first-order, canonically normalized completion. This is an inverse construction. Its oscillator background, component couplings and selected normal degree are inputs. The calculation does not derive the supporting field, choose the particle bands, or establish their complete inertia. Mass remains the selected frequency. Use both ordinary normal coordinates Let a proposed surface feature have two ordinary normal coordinates y_1 and y_2, with one common profile width a. These coordinates are part of the containing physical space, not compactified directions. Set x_i=y_i/a and define a_i= rac{\partial_{x_i}+x_i}{\sqrt2},\qquad N_i=a_i^\dagger a_i,\qquad N=N_1+N_2. 	ag{1} Here the symbol a_i denotes an operator; the unindexed a denotes a length. The normal fields are the complete normalized Hermite functions in both coordinates. The eigenspace N=q is \mathcal K_q=\operatorname{span} \{\phi_n(x_1)\phi_{q-n}(x_2):0\le n\le q\}. 	ag{2} It has dimension q+1. Both J_z=(N_1-N_2)/2 and J_+=a_1^\dagger a_2 preserve it, as do their adjoints. These are operators on spatial oscillator functions. The representation dimension is not a number of additional physical dimensions. For the surface spinor operator B_K already derived in A spatial spinor parent for the curvature frequency, use a common frequency unit nu=c_t/R. Its dimensionless positive eigenvalue is beta=L+(d-3)/2. On the selected normal band consider T_q= eta+J_z+\gamma J_+, \qquad H_q= egin{pmatrix}0&T_q\T_q^\dagger&0\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{3} All components have the same canonical time coefficient. In the basis (2), T_q has diagonal beta+n-q/2 and lower diagonal gamma sqrt(n(q-n+1)). The whole Hermitian operator preserves (2). This supplies the adjoint closure missing in the single-oscillator cutoff test in Restoring the normal oscillator tower. The frequency product and its normalization The smallest positive frequency is the smallest singular value of T_q. At fixed q and beta, its exact triangular inverse gives \omega_q= rac{
u}{\gamma^q q!} \prod_{n=0}^{q}\left( eta+n- rac q2ight) \left[1- rac{( eta-q/2)^2+( eta+q/2)^2} {2q\gamma^2}+O(\gamma^{-4})ight]. 	ag{4} This formula assumes positive diagonal entries, as in the assigned controls. It follows by scaling the inverse by its largest corner entry; the two adjacent entries supply the first correction to its norm. The full singular vector, rather than only an end component, supplies the kinetic normalization. Choose q=d-1. Then beta+n-q/2=L-1+n, and  oxed{\omega_L\sim rac{d
u}{\gamma^{d-1}}  inom{L+d-2}{d}.} 	ag{5} The factorial q! in (4) is fixed by ordinary Hermite normalization. It changes the frequency unit from that of an equal-link chain. It does not change the simplex polynomial. The choice q=d-1 is still a physical selection requirement, rather than a consequence of (1). Every vector in K_q has integral (x_1^2+x_2^2)|psi|^2=q+1 at unit norm. Thus its root-mean-square normal extent is a sqrt(q+1), independent of its surface harmonic. The finite completion below has a small additional occupation in K_(q-1); that correction is retained. Complete the second-order normal operator Equation (3) contains second normal derivatives. To test a local first-order completion, retain a target two-component field psi and two additional two-component mode fields eta_1, eta_2. Each component also carries the complete surface spinor. They are proposed components of the same field, not exchanged particles. Write A psi=(a_1 psi,a_2 psi), and order the four additional components as (1x,1y,2x,2y). Define the Hermitian matrix C= egin{pmatrix} 0&1/2&0&\gamma\ 1/2&0&0&0\ 0&0&0&-1/2\ \gamma&0&-1/2&0 \end{pmatrix}. 	ag{6} In dimensionless frequency units, the complete linear equation is i\partial_t egin{pmatrix}\psi\\eta\end{pmatrix} =
u egin{pmatrix} 	au_x RB_K&\sqrt M A^\dagger\ \sqrt M A&-M C^{-1} \end{pmatrix}  egin{pmatrix}\psi\\eta\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{7} The dimensionless M is one common additional-component frequency scale divided by nu. The canonical norm includes both psi and eta. Eliminating eta at dimensionless frequency w gives the exact target operator and its kinetic metric  egin{aligned} H_{m red}(w)&=	au_x RB_K+ A^\dagger C(I+wC/M)^{-1}A,\ Z(w)&=I+ rac1M A^\dagger C^2(I+wC/M)^{-2}A. \end{aligned} 	ag{8} The second expression is positive and equals the full eliminated field norm. Its correction must not be discarded when comparing frequencies or interaction coefficients. At large M, the first expression reduces to (3). The conserved graded normal number is N on psi and N+1 on eta. Consequently the complete band is psi in K_q and eta_i in K_(q-1). Its dimension is 2(q+1)+4q=6q+2, multiplied by the actual surface spinor rank. A and A^dagger map these entire spaces into each other. No unretained normal component is generated by either equation. Check all spatial propagation directions The normal derivatives in (7) are first order. Their symbol has norm at most nu a sqrt(M/2)|p_normal|. The tangential symbol has norm c_t|p_tangent|. With epsilon=a/R, a sufficient total speed bound is v_{\max}\le c_t\sqrt{1+M\epsilon^2/2}. 	ag{9} Choosing c_t no larger than c divided by the square root in (9) therefore bounds every spatial direction by c. All spatial components, including the additional ones, enter this estimate. This is a Hermitian first-order parent with a finite propagation bound. Its principal matrices are not a full irreducible ambient Dirac Clifford representation. Equation (7) is therefore not yet a derivation from the master Dirac equation, nor a proof of Lorentz covariance. The oscillator coordinate terms are a specified background profile requiring its own same-field origin and stress calculation. Numerical controls and the remaining selection schwinger-normal-parent-20260914T033434_202537Z.json passes 128 checks. Direct Hermite derivatives verify both normal equations and both adjoints. Thus conservation of a selected q is not a derivation of its occupation or isolation under arbitrary perturbations. The ordinary Euclidean tube also changes B_K with the radial coordinate. The origin of the normal background, selection q=d-1, relation of frequency units across depths and complete particle inertia remain open. title: Curvature of the complete normal band
summary: The actual Euclidean tubular metric mixes neighboring normal bands but admits controlled spatial residuals for the specified narrow-profile trial.
text: The finite normal band in A complete finite normal band is exact on a product of its surface and normal coordinates. An ordinary Euclidean tube is different: its tangential radius varies across the normal profile. Retaining that variation mixes normal bands but gives a small, explicit correction in the tested narrow-profile regime. The calculations below concern the declared linear parent and background. They do not derive the background from the master field. A small residual in this equation is not yet a particle fixed point or an inertia proof. Keep the actual radial metric For a round S_R^m feature in ordinary R^(m+2), write r=R+y_1 and z=y_2. The containing metric is ds^2=dr^2+dz^2+r^2d\Omega_m^2,\qquad r>0. \tag{1} The unitary factor r^(-m/2) converts its radial measure to dr dz. The corresponding first radial derivative includes m/(2r) before that unitary conversion. The following normal fields and their norms use the converted representation. This keeps the physical volume factor rather than assuming an exact product metric. Set x=y_1/a and epsilon=a/R. At a fixed angular spinor eigenvalue beta, the target frequency term in the parent becomes \tau_x\frac{\beta}{1+\epsilon x}. \tag{2} The normal coefficients, R, a, gamma and M are held common between the assigned modes. This is a specific extension of the declared parent into the tube, not a derivation of its normal potentials. It uses no compactification or additional physical dimensions. Retain every forced normal band In the fixed-number basis, multiplication by x changes the target normal degree by one. It retains both chirality components. With w_0 the complete parent frequency and psi_0 its full normalized field, expand \begin{aligned} H(\epsilon)&=H_0+\sum_{j\ge1}\epsilon^jV_j, &V_j&=(-1)^j\beta\tau_x x^j,\\ w(\epsilon)&=w_0+\sum_{j\ge1}\epsilon^j w_j, &\psi(\epsilon)&=\psi_0+\sum_{j\ge1}\epsilon^j\psi_j. \end{aligned} \tag{3} V_j acts on the target components; the additional components still enter the complete resolvent and canonical norm. Use intermediate normalization <psi_0,psi_j>=0 for j>0. The coefficient equations are \begin{aligned} w_k&=\left\langle\psi_0, \sum_{j=1}^{k}V_j\psi_{k-j}\right\rangle,\\ (w_0-H_0)\psi_k &=\sum_{j=1}^{k}(V_j-w_j)\psi_{k-j}. \end{aligned} \tag{4} The inverse in the base band is restricted to the phase-orthogonal complement. In every other forced band it includes all parent branches and both signs. At order k, every possible normal degree lies between q-k and q+k. Thus a coefficient calculation has a finite complete set of paths, without dropping an infinite tail at that order. The second coefficient provides a separate useful check: w_2=\langle\psi_0,V_2\psi_0\rangle \,+\sum_{s=\pm1} \left\langle V_1\psi_0, (w_0-H_{q+s})^{-1}V_1\psi_0\right\rangle. \tag{5} Normal parity makes every odd frequency coefficient vanish. It does not make the first field correction vanish: that correction occupies both adjacent bands. The assigned modes have small relative corrections At gamma=10000 and M=10^18, write w/w_0=1+c_2 epsilon^2+c_4 epsilon^4+c_6 epsilon^6+... . The complete coefficient calculation gives Normal band and surface mode c_2 c_4 c_6 q=5, L=14 25.00584528 521.3159973 10754.83815 q=5, L=36 24.96639964 521.0972186 10761.82410 q=9, L=24 68.97118383 3328.911022 142158.6838 The first field-correction norms are 5.49399714, 5.45149742 and 11.57966292, respectively. These multiply epsilon. Their values come from the complete spatial response, not from dividing a large source by a guessed single gap. The near equality of the first two c_2 values makes their leading ratio correction only about -0.03944564 epsilon^2. This is a conditional geometric comparison at fixed coefficients. It does not select epsilon, explain why a physical particle chooses the band, or make the finite-gamma frequency law exact. schwinger-tube-20260914T034426_921830Z.json passes 54 checks. Independent 100- and 120-digit calculations agree, the full second-order resolvent agrees with the recurrence, and every generated component satisfies its coefficient equation. A separate finite-curvature control diagonalizes the complete canonical parent through different normal cutoffs. Its error relative to the sixth-order series falls from about 1.32e-15 at epsilon=.004 to 5.16e-18 at epsilon=.002. This is the expected eighth-order scaling. Normal cutoff refinement and reversal of epsilon agree independently. Bound the full spatial residual A Taylor series by itself does not prove convergence of the complete curved problem. Instead, take its explicit field through order K=6, psi_app, and its frequency w_app, and bound their residual directly. The field is a finite sum of actual Hermite functions, including every generated normal component. Keep a smooth radial cutoff chi equal to one for x>=-1/(4 epsilon) and zero for x<=-1/(2 epsilon). Its transition can be chosen with |chi'|<=2 pi epsilon. The resulting spatial field vanishes before the radial origin and has r>=R/2 wherever it is nonzero. No Gaussian is silently extended through r=0. On this retained region, the exact rational remainder obeys \left|\frac1{1+\epsilon x} -\sum_{j=0}^{K}(-\epsilon x)^j\right| \le2\epsilon^{K+1}|x|^{K+1}. \tag{6} Let r_poly be the complete residual after replacing (2) by the polynomial through degree K, with all higher powers generated by psi_app and w_app still retained. Let P_t denote the target components. The normal derivative commutator with chi then gives \begin{aligned} \|(H-w_{\rm app})\chi\psi_{\rm app}\| \le{}&\|r_{\rm poly}\| +2|\beta|\epsilon^{K+1}\|x^{K+1}P_t\psi_{\rm app}\|\\ &+2\pi\epsilon\sqrt{M/2}\, \|\psi_{\rm app}\|_{x<-1/(4\epsilon)}. \end{aligned} \tag{7} All norms are complete spatial norms. Hermite polynomial coefficient bounds and an upper incomplete-gamma bound control the final tail. The same estimate bounds the small norm removed by chi. Thus (7) can be divided by the retained full norm without losing normalization. Under the illustrative hierarchy epsilon=10^(-9), gamma=10000 and M=10^18, the computed right sides of (7), divided by the frequency and full norm, are approximately 9.39e-43, 1.09e-44 and 5.04e-29 for the three assigned controls. title: Shared time coordinate
summary: All nested spatial sectors use one time coordinate; this premise neither equates proper times nor supplies a metric or causal theorem.
text: The premise already used by V2 The time variable in the V2 evolution equations is shared across sectors. The photon module already uses shared time. There is one infinite physical manifold, with one temporal direction and one nested chain of spatial submanifolds. A sector's depth counts only its spatial dimensions. Thus a six-dimensional electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial directions and uses the same time coordinate as three-dimensional matter and a ten-dimensional tau. Its six spatial directions are six of the tau's ten. Sharing three with an observer does not make those three different in kind, and no sector acquires a separate time dimension. At a finite depth, a local evolution chart can be written (t,q_d),\qquad q_d\in Q_d,\qquad Q_a\subset Q_b\quad(a<b). The same t appears in both charts. This notation records the framework's temporal premise; it does not construct an infinite-dimensional metric or Dirac operator. A global product with a time axis is a stronger geometric choice than merely using such local charts. Shared coordinate time and elapsed time One coordinate t does not imply that every physical clock accumulates the same proper time. For example, in the finite-dimensional flat Lorentzian metric ds^2=-c^2dt^2+\sum_{j=1}^{d}(dq^j)^2, \qquad d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-\frac{\lVert\dot q\rVert^2}{c^2}}, timelike paths with different speeds have different elapsed proper times. This is a compatibility example using the usual metric definition of proper time, not a derivation of the V2 metric. See Carroll, General Relativity notes, §1, equation 1.97. Likewise, one timelike direction alone does not forbid boosts along any particular spatial direction or prove the absence of closed timelike curves. Those questions need the actual metric, global causal assumptions, and a specification of physically accessible operations. Finally, a block-diagonal metric need not be an exact product metric: ds^2=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\sum_j(dq^j)^2 has no time–space cross terms, yet its spatial block depends on time. Consequently, neither exact operator separation nor ordinary observer Lorentz dynamics follows just from the common time coordinate. title: Simplex band level moments
summary: Uniform counting over a cumulative oscillator band gives exact mean and variance of the excitation level, without selecting a physical occupation or mass correction.
text: Uniform cumulative-band counting The mean excitation level d(n-1)/(d+1) is an exact identity for uniform counting across a cumulative oscillator band. Set N=n-1 and give equal weight to each Cartesian oscillator state (a_1,\ldots,a_d) with nonnegative integer entries and K=\sum_i a_i\le N. The shell degeneracy and band size are g_d(k)=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1},\qquad B=\sum_{k=0}^{N}g_d(k)=S(n,d). Thus the probability of a shell under this specified counting measure is g_d(k)/B, not 1/(N+1). Exact first and second moments The factorial-moment identities k g_d(k)=d\binom{k+d-1}{d},\qquad k(k-1)g_d(k)=d(d+1)\binom{k+d-1}{d+1} and the hockey-stick sum give \mathbb E[K]=\frac{dN}{d+1},\qquad \mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\frac{dN(N-1)}{d+2}, \operatorname{Var}(K)= \frac{dN(N+d+1)}{(d+1)^2(d+2)}. Equivalently, append a slack coordinate a_0=N-K. The uniform set of weak compositions \sum_{i=0}^{d}a_i=N is symmetric in all d+1 entries, so each has mean N/(d+1). The slack is counting notation, not an additional physical spatial direction. For an affine diagnostic f(K)=A+BK, its counting average is therefore A+BdN/(d+1). A quadratic diagnostic additionally uses the second moment. This gives exact finite-band benchmarks before any physical occupation weights are introduced. Physical scope The coordinates being counted describe d equivalent ordinary spatial oscillator directions in an auxiliary flat model. Equal weighting of all states in the cumulative band is explicit model data. A single occupied shell, a coherent state, and a nonuniform mixture generally have different moments. Applying these moments to a physical energy correction requires the perturbing operator and the relevant physical state. The counting mixture is a mathematical benchmark for those calculations. The mode counting checks compare these expressions with direct rational shell sums and explicit weak-composition enumeration. title: Simplex heat trace
summary: The tower with one eigenvalue per simplex index has an explicit heat-trace bound and convergence domain, distinct from the spatial dimension of a sector operator.
text: Specify the tower being summed Let a positive diagonal operator A_d have one eigenvalue \lambda_n=\mu S(n,d),\qquad n\ge1,\qquad \mu>0, for each index, with no extra degeneracy. Define K_d(t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-t\mu S(n,d)},\qquad t>0. Here t is a heat parameter in inverse-eigenvalue units, not the shared physical time coordinate. This is an analytic diagnostic for the proposed count sequence; it does not identify A_d with the spatial Dirac operator. A bound that proves the asymptotic For integer d\ge1, \frac{n^d}{d!}\le S(n,d)\le\frac{(n+d-1)^d}{d!}. Put a=\mu t/d! and f(x)=e^{-ax^d}. Its integral is I_d(t)=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx =\Gamma\!\left(1+\frac1d\right) \left(\frac{d!}{\mu t}\right)^{1/d}. Since f decreases, its positive-integer sum lies between I_d-1 and I_d. The shifted sum beginning at integer d differs by at most d-1. Sandwiching K_d between these two sums gives \max(0,I_d(t)-d)\le K_d(t)\le I_d(t). In particular, K_d(t)= \Gamma\!\left(1+\frac1d\right) \left(\frac{d!}{\mu t}\right)^{1/d}+O(1) \quad(t\downarrow0). For a numerical cutoff L, the omitted positive tail obeys 0\le K_d(t)-\sum_{n=1}^{L}e^{-t\mu S(n,d)} \le\int_L^\infty e^{-ax^d}\,dx =\frac{\Gamma(1/d,aL^d)}{d\,a^{1/d}}, where the final expression uses the upper incomplete gamma function. Thus both the leading approximation and finite numerical sum have explicit error bounds. Different generating functions count different things The ordinary index generating function is also exact: \sum_{n\ge1}S(n,d)z^n=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{d+1}}, \qquad |z|<1. It weights the index by the count; the heat trace instead places the count in an exponential. Their singular exponents need not agree. Likewise, comparison with n^{-ds} shows that \sum_n S(n,d)^{-s} converges absolutely exactly when \operatorname{Re}s>1/d. The heat exponent 1/d is therefore a property of this one-eigenvalue-per-index tower. It is not evidence that the corresponding spatial dimension equals d. For example, the actual round-sphere Dirac spectrum has eigenvalues linear in its level and nontrivial multiplicities, as detailed in round-sphere Dirac counts. V2's physical depth is the number of ordinary macroscopic spatial directions in its principal-symbol construction. This diagnostic does not replace that construction or change any depth. What this does not regularize The bounds establish the displayed trace and convergence region. They do not establish analytic continuation at s=0 or finiteness of all interaction sums. Even if an operator zeta function is regular there, its regularized determinant changes under rescaling: \log\det\nolimits_\zeta(\alpha A) =\log\det\nolimits_\zeta A+\zeta_A(0)\log\alpha. This follows by differentiating \zeta_{\alpha A}(s)=\alpha^{-s}\zeta_A(s). A finite value at zero alone neither determines its derivative nor removes normalization-scale dependence. The mode counting checks check direct heat sums against both bounds and verify the index generating-function coefficients. Related Simplex reciprocal sum — gives the exact s=1 value for d>1. title: Simplex reciprocal sum
summary: Reciprocal simplex counts have an exact telescoping sum and truncation remainder, providing a conditional trace check for the V2 count spectrum.
text: A useful identity adjacent to the mass spectrum The identity below concerns the count S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d} used by the V2 mass module. It supplies a closed-form check and an exact truncation error for sums of inverse counts. No new geometry or particle assignment is needed. For positive integer n and integer d>1, \frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{d-1} \left[\frac{1}{S(n,d-1)}-\frac{1}{S(n+1,d-1)}\right]. To verify this, factor (d-1)!/[n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-2)] from the difference in brackets. The remaining factor is (d-1)/(n+d-1), giving d!/[n(n+1)\cdots(n+d-1)] after multiplication by d/(d-1). Summing the difference gives \sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{d-1} \left[1-\frac{1}{S(N+1,d-1)}\right], and hence \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{S(n,d)}=\frac{d}{d-1}, \qquad \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{S(n,d)} =\frac{d}{(d-1)S(N+1,d-1)}. The remainder tends to zero for every d>1. For d=1, S(n,1)=n, so the corresponding harmonic series diverges. Adjacent-depth recursion The factorial definition also gives the multiplicative recursion \frac{S(n,d)}{S(n,d+1)}=\frac{d+1}{n+d},\qquad S(n,d+1)=\frac{n+d}{d+1}S(n,d). At fixed n>1, S(n,d) strictly increases with d; for n=1 all counts equal one. At fixed d, the ratio decreases with n. These are count identities for any positive indices, usable alongside the additive Pascal recursion without assigning physical occupation weights. What the trace interpretation requires If a specified positive operator has exactly one eigenvalue \mu_d S(n,d) per positive integer n, with no additional degeneracy, then its inverse trace is \operatorname{Tr}(A_d^{-1})=\frac{d}{(d-1)\mu_d}. This is conditional on that operator and counting measure. The formula does not establish that the master Dirac operator has this spectrum or that all these bands are occupied particles. Restricting to the occupied particle indices gives a different finite sum; including a massless zero mode makes an ordinary inverse undefined. If each band is instead assigned multiplicity S(n,d), each band's contribution to the inverse trace is 1/\mu_d, and the infinite trace diverges. This simple example is why multiplicities must be stated. Oscillator excitation energies and cumulative counts also remain distinct, as in the existing mass analysis. Verification and related work The spatial structure checks compare direct rational finite sums with the telescoping expression across several depths and truncations. The all-N proof is the algebra above, rather than numerical extrapolation. Nested spatial tools — companion tools for spatial evolution and normalization.

text:

To obtain the last equality, take the logarithm of the gamma-function product: \log\Gamma(1+j)=-\gamma j+ \sum_{n\geq1}\left[ rac jn-\log\left(1+ rac jnight)ight]. Only finitely many j are summed. title: Spectral survival recurrence
summary: Pure-point spectral evolution has a positive mean return weight and arbitrarily accurate recurrences, while an integrable continuous spectral density permits decay of the return amplitude.
text: A specified evolution and preparation Let H be a self-adjoint frequency operator and u a normalized field profile. Time evolution is u(t)=e^{-itH}u; for an energy operator replace H by H/\hbar. The return amplitude and weight are a(t)=\langle u,e^{-itH}u\rangle, \qquad P(t)=|a(t)|^2. These are Hilbert-space diagnostics of the selected linear evolution. They apply to classical complex mode amplitudes as well as quantum states. Their interpretation as an observed survival probability requires a measurement prescription. Mode amplitudes describe fields on the one physical manifold and introduce no further spatial dimensions. For a preparation supported on the pure-point spectrum, combine each degenerate eigenspace into one orthogonal projector P_j, with distinct frequencies \omega_j. Put p_j=\|P_ju\|^2. Then p_j\geq0,\quad \sum_jp_j=1, \qquad a(t)=\sum_j p_j e^{-i\omega_jt}. The series converges absolutely and uniformly in time, because its omitted tail is bounded by the omitted sum of p_j. Time average For a finite spectral sum, integrate each pair of phases: \frac1T\int_0^T e^{-i(\omega_j-\omega_k)t}\,dt \longrightarrow \begin{cases}1&j=k,\\0&j\ne k.\end{cases} Uniform tail control extends this calculation to a countable sum. Hence \boxed{\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T P(t)\,dt =\sum_jp_j^2>0.} Degeneracies must be grouped before squaring their weights. The average of a(t) itself retains only a zero-frequency component, so it is a different quantity. A small mean return weight can coexist with eventual recurrence. For two equally weighted frequencies, a(t)=e^{-i(\omega_1+\omega_2)t/2} \cos\!\left(\frac{\omega_2-\omega_1}{2}t\right), \qquad P(t)=\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\omega_2-\omega_1}{2}t\right). The recurrence of the ray occurs every 2\pi/|\omega_2-\omega_1|. The difference of frequencies controls the beating. Approximate recurrence without commensurability Choose a finite set of occupied frequencies and a reference \omega_1. For any time unit \tau>0, consider the phase vectors k\tau(\omega_j-\omega_1)/(2\pi) modulo one, for integers k. Partition this finite-dimensional unit cube into boxes of side 1/Q. Among one more points than boxes, two share a box. Subtracting their integer times gives a positive t at which every selected relative phase is within 2\pi/Q of an integer multiple of 2\pi. For a countable spectrum choose the finite set with omitted weight \eta. If the selected phase errors have absolute value at most \epsilon, \|e^{-itH}u-e^{-i\omega_1t}u\|^2 =\sum_jp_j|e^{-i(\omega_j-\omega_1)t}-1|^2 \leq\epsilon^2+4\eta. Both terms can be made arbitrarily small. Such times are unbounded: if the approximating integer times remained bounded as the tolerance shrank, one of them would be an exact common period, whose multiples are unbounded. For any fixed tail cutoff the same argument supplies arbitrarily late returns. Exact ray recurrence requires all occupied frequency differences times t to lie in 2\pi\mathbb Z; approximate recurrence needs no such commensurability. This is the spectral recurrence setting discussed by Campos Venuti, §I. An absolutely continuous preparation The spectral theorem more generally gives a probability measure \mu_u: a(t)=\int e^{-i\omega t}\,d\mu_u(\omega). If d\mu_u=f(\omega)d\omega with f\in L^1, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma gives a(t)\to0. For a uniform density on [\omega_0-B,\omega_0+B], B>0, a(t)=e^{-i\omega_0t}\frac{\sin Bt}{Bt}. This decay describes dephasing of the return amplitude while the full evolution remains unitary. Singular continuous spectral measures require their own analysis; absolute continuity is the sufficient hypothesis used here. Selecting a physical persistent mode additionally requires its coupling and dynamics, beyond a recurrence identity. title: A complete rotation family for the depth-six fixed point
summary: A complete fixed-rotation spinor family retains all compatible harmonics and spinor components for the conditional depth-six stationary equation.
text: The actual spinor parent admits a manageable spatial symmetry class for testing a circulating nonlinear branch. Fix the two rotation quantum numbers of a highest-weight spinor pattern, then retain every spinor component and every compatible scalar harmonic. This supplies a basis for a fixed-point calculation; it does not establish the fixed point or stability against perturbations in other rotation classes. Use the unit four-sphere feature in ordinary six-dimensional space, with the spinor operator B_K in A spatial spinor parent for the curvature frequency. The underlying four-sphere sits in five ambient directions. Its second ordinary normal direction and its physical sustaining field are still outside this surface calculation. Actual coordinates and canonical measure At zero azimuths a representative point is x=(\sqrt t,0,\sqrt{1-t}\sqrt{1-u^2},0,\sqrt{1-t}\,u), \quad 0<t<1,\quad -1<u<1. \tag{1} The first and second planes also have azimuths phi_1 and phi_2. Their integration gives the measure dA_{\rm reduced}=2\pi^2(1-t)^{1/2}\,dt\,du, \qquad \int dA=\frac{8\pi^2}{3}. \tag{2} There is no replacement of physical coordinates by oscillator labels. The azimuth dependence is known exactly from the declared rotation quantum numbers and is retained in every derivative. Every compatible spinor component Choose the standard ambient Clifford frame with i Gamma_1 Gamma_2=-Z tensor I and i Gamma_3 Gamma_4=-I tensor Z. Let L_0 be the circulating base degree. For spinor components 0,1,2,3 the scalar azimuthal charges are (q_1,q_2)=(L_0,0),\ (L_0,1),\ (L_0+1,0),\ (L_0+1,1). \tag{3} Together with the spin rotation, all four have the same total rotation labels. The component-zero polynomial (x_1+i x_2)^(L_0) is a monogenic positive B_K mode. In the parity class of this initial field, all compatible scalar degrees are K=L_0+2s, s nonnegative. For one component and fixed K, choose a rest-sphere degree l satisfying K=q_1+l+2j, j nonnegative, l at least q_2. The complete scalar basis is F_{K,l}(t,u,\phi_1,\phi_2) =C\,t^{q_1/2}(1-t)^{l/2} P_j^{(l+1/2,q_1)}(2t-1)P_l^{q_2}(u) e^{i(q_1\phi_1+q_2\phi_2)}. \tag{4} Here the second P is an associated Legendre polynomial, and C normalizes (4) using (2). Jacobi and associated-Legendre orthogonality give the full canonical norm; different spinor components are also orthogonal. Up to s=J the basis has (J+1)(2J+1) scalar-spinor modes. Each coefficient may be complex. All four physical tangent derivatives are used. In particular the azimuthal gradients are i q_1/sqrt(t) and i q_2/sqrt((1-t)(1-u^2)); omitting them would remove the circulating motion and change the spinor operator. Complete first-order closure Apply the actual ambient formula B_K=3/2-Gamma_x Gamma_grad to (4) and integrate its full spinor matrix elements. Each K block closes exactly and satisfies B_K^\dagger=B_K,\qquad B_K^2=(K+3/2)^2I. \tag{5} At order s its dimension is 4s+1. Its positive and negative B_K multiplicities are respectively 2s+1 and 2s. The first block therefore contains the single monogenic positive mode; the other spinor branches enter at higher compatible spatial degree. This is a consequence of the rotation labels, not an imposed removal of their components. The same low-frequency chain supplies both positive and negative parent frequencies on each block. Both must be retained in a nonlinear fixed-point and response calculation. An efficient canonical embedding can use the two exact B projections in each block, avoiding a discretionary choice of basis inside degenerate eigenspaces. It includes complete canonical Gram matrices, direct full spatial Dirac closure, both branch multiplicities, arbitrary complex field projection and the current in every tangent direction. title: Weighted mode evaluation
summary: A weighted coefficient norm bounds point evaluation exactly when the corresponding inverse-weighted evaluation sum is finite; counts alone do not establish that condition.
text: Why the basis values matter Inverse simplex counts can control mode expansions when the basis values satisfy the evaluation criterion below. The reciprocal-sum identity supplies a useful bound. For a specified scalar readout of the mode functions, write initially for finitely supported coefficients f_c(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\phi_n(x),\qquad \|c\|_w^2=\sum_{n\ge1}w_n|c_n|^2,\qquad w_n>0. This is a norm on coefficient sequences. Calling it a spatial L^2 norm would require an additional basis and measure identification. Its use for classical fields does not introduce any extra physical spatial dimensions. Necessary and sufficient condition At a fixed evaluation point, define B(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{|\phi_n(x)|^2}{w_n}. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |f_c(x)|\le \|c\|_w\sqrt{B(x)}. Conversely, for a finite cutoff L with B_L(x)>0, choose c_n=\frac{\overline{\phi_n(x)}}{w_n\sqrt{B_L(x)}} \quad(1\le n\le L). These coefficients have norm one and evaluation \sqrt{B_L(x)}. Thus evaluation extends boundedly to the completed coefficient space if and only if B(x)<\infty, and its norm is exactly \sqrt{B(x)}. This proof also identifies the missing assumption in an argument based only on \sum_n1/w_n. Applying the simplex weights For one scalar mode per n, take w_n=S(n,d) with d>1. If |\phi_n(x)|\le C uniformly in both n and x on the region of interest, then B(x)\le C^2\frac{d}{d-1}. The exact reciprocal-count remainder gives a uniform tail bound: \left|\sum_{n>L}c_n\phi_n(x)\right| \le C\left(\sum_{n>L}S(n,d)|c_n|^2\right)^{1/2} \left[\frac{d}{(d-1)S(L+1,d-1)}\right]^{1/2}. This establishes uniform convergence for finite weighted norm under the stated uniform mode bound. It is a usable truncation estimate, not a general claim about every sector basis. If band n has several components, the actual criterion becomes B(x)=\sum_{n,\alpha}\frac{|\phi_{n,\alpha}(x)|^2}{w_n}. For example, give band n multiplicity g_d(n-1)=\binom{n+d-2}{d-1}. There exist orthonormal families with all components having unit magnitude at a point: distinct Fourier modes on a circle with normalized measure provide a mathematical example. Then B(0)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{g_d(n-1)}{S(n,d)} =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{d}{n+d-1}=\infty. The one-mode reciprocal sum converges while this evaluation is unbounded. This counterexample tests the inference from weights alone; the circle is not a replacement geometry for an IDWT particle. Limits for contact calculations V2's finite-band contact theorem uses a specified finite reproducing kernel. Passing to an infinite field requires controlling the corresponding evaluation sum and occupation weights. Derivative readouts need the sums of squared derivative values; interaction energies and determinants need their own estimates. Finite inverse-count weight alone is not a proof of universal ultraviolet control. Evaluation on a homogeneous spatial space Let a compact homogeneous space X have invariant volume \operatorname{Vol}X. Take a rank-N orthogonal projector onto smooth scalar functions or bundle sections, invariant under a transitive unitary symmetry action. For an orthonormal basis \phi_j of its range the evaluation kernel is K(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^N\phi_j(x)\phi_j(y)^\dagger. Equivariance conjugates K(x,x) by the fibre symmetry. Its trace is therefore constant on the transitive orbit. Integrating that trace gives N, so \operatorname{tr}K(x,x)=\frac{N}{\operatorname{Vol}X}. For scalar functions this is the squared norm of point evaluation, and |f(x)|^2\le N\|f\|^2/\operatorname{Vol}X in the projected space. For a spherical-harmonic shell on the unit S^2, it gives K_\ell(x,x)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi); summing shells 0\le\ell<n gives n^2/(4\pi). The identity fixes the summed evaluation weight. Individual basis values can vanish at a point. For bundle sections, a chosen source direction v probes v^\dagger K(x,x)v, while summing an orthonormal set of fibre polarizations gives the trace. Scalar proportionality on the fibre requires an additional isotropy representation condition. The compact homogeneous hypotheses must hold for this bound to replace a direct evaluation sum. The mode counting checks test saturation of the finite bound, generic complex coefficients, and the multiplicity counterexample. Related Simplex reciprocal sum — supplies the exact tail used above. title: Zonal hybrid geometry
summary: Spherical-harmonic addition gives exact directed-state overlaps and conditional trigonal, tetrahedral, and octahedral orthogonality.
text: Directed angular functions On the unit sphere of a chosen ordinary spatial three-plane, let Y_{\ell m} be orthonormal with area measure. Define a normalized angular coefficient vector for unit direction v by |\ell,v\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}} \sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\overline{Y_{\ell m}(v)}|\ell,m\rangle. The spherical-harmonic addition theorem gives \langle\ell,v|\ell,w\rangle=P_\ell(v\cdot w), \qquad \|\,|\ell,v\rangle\|=1. The normalization and addition formula are specified in DLMF 14.30.8–9. Different \ell blocks are orthogonal. Thus a directed function |h_v\rangle=\sum_\ell c_\ell|\ell,v\rangle, with the same coefficients for each direction and \sum|c_\ell|^2=1, has overlap \boxed{\langle h_v|h_w\rangle=\sum_\ell|c_\ell|^2P_\ell(v\cdot w).} These are angular functions, not trajectories or additional physical spatial dimensions. The three-plane is selected relative to the system being described; the electron's six spatial directions remain equivalent. The scalar-plus-vector case Let |h_i\rangle=a|s\rangle+b|p_{v_i}\rangle, with a,b>0, a^2+b^2=1. Suppose the n functions are orthonormal and their span contains |s\rangle. Completeness within that span implies 1=\sum_{i=1}^n|\langle h_i|s\rangle|^2=na^2. Consequently a^2=1/n, b^2=(n-1)/n, and off-diagonal orthogonality requires v_i\cdot v_j=-\frac1{n-1}\quad(i\ne j). Their direction Gram matrix has one zero eigenvalue and n-1 eigenvalues n/(n-1), so it can be realized in a three-plane only if n\le4. The sum of the directions is zero. This gives the regular simplex cases: n Scalar share a^2 Pair cosine Geometry 2 \frac12 -1 Opposite directions 3 \frac13 -\frac12 Trigonal directions 4 \frac14 -\frac13 Tetrahedral directions The simultaneous directed form, equal coefficients, orthonormality, and span condition are assumptions. Orthogonalizing arbitrary directed functions generally changes their form; it does not establish these assumptions or select nuclear equilibrium angles. A six-direction construction With squared shares (|c_0|^2,|c_1|^2,|c_2|^2)=(1/6,1/2,1/3), \frac16+\frac12x+\frac13P_2(x)=\frac{x(x+1)}2. The six directions \{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\} have distinct pair cosines 0 or -1, so their six directed functions are orthonormal. This proves an octahedral construction for the displayed shares. Selecting those shares or an actual molecular geometry requires dynamics. Multicentre orbit axes — obtains related direction geometry from an actual prescribed route. title: Chiral CP3 selection
summary: A normalized six-dimensional chiral spinor coupled to an unconstrained bivector selects a CP3 minimum family with a Berry term and nonlinear energy confinement, conditional on its master-field derivation and identification with physical spatial coordinates.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Summary: A normalized six-dimensional chiral spinor coupled to an unconstrained bivector selects a CP3 minimum family with a Berry term and nonlinear energy confinement, conditional on its master-field derivation and identification with physical spatial coordinates. Fixed-depth route using chiral polarization Electron depth six is fixed by the mass-formula assignment in this model. Instead of requiring the filled twelve-state response band of the preceding candidate model, consider one normalized chiral Spin(6) polarization z in C4 and an unconstrained real skew 6x6 bivector B. A six-dimensional Dirac spinor has chiral halves of this size; selecting one half and representing the relevant polarization by a pure normalized vector are additional premises, not consequences of dimension alone. The Pauli bilinear map already checked in the geometric-response note gives J(z)=J(zz dagger), with J squared=−I and <J,J>=3. It is linear in the density matrix. We do not impose B squared=−rho² I. The purpose of the coupling is to determine whether that condition follows for B. The chiral spinor here is a polarization variable. It must not silently be identified with a global spatial Dirac field on an already assumed CP3 base. The earlier spinor-bundle obstruction remains in force. Linear bivector coupling and exact energy minimum Let mu>0, g>0, and <A,B>=−tr(AB)/2. Define the Hermitian chiral operator h(B) by the expectation identity z^\dagger h(B)z=-g\langle B,J(z)\rangle. It is the bivector representation on the chosen chiral spinor. In the explicit traceless two-Pauli basis P_A, its checked matrix is h(B)=−(g/4) sum_A <B,J(P_A)> P_A. The total joint energy is E(B,z)=\mu\langle B,B\rangle-g\langle B,J(z)\rangle =\mu\|B-\rho J(z)\|^2-\frac{3g^2}{4\mu},\qquad \rho=\frac{g}{2\mu}. This is an exact completed square for every B and normalized z. Therefore the global minima have B=rho J(z), and B squared=−rho² I follows. The family of minima modulo the common spinor phase is CP3. The positive quadratic cost and the bilinear chiral coupling are the effective interaction assumptions; their presence and normalization remain to be derived from the master theory. For a chosen chirality and the stated signs, the map selects one component of the orthogonal-complex structures. If both chiralities are admitted symmetrically, the opposite component returns with the same energy. Thus the construction does not derive a physical chirality selection. At a minimum the source operator has the especially simple form h(\rho J(z))=-g\rho(4zz^\dagger-I_4). Its occupied ray has eigenvalue −3g rho and the other three eigenvalues are +g rho. The gap is 4g rho=2g²/mu. Unlike the preceding real-band model, there is no separately assumed twelve-state filling or externally supplied gap Delta; the gap follows from the self-consistent bivector amplitude. Normal variations in matrix space and conservative confinement The auxiliary skew 6x6 matrix B has 15 independent rotation-plane components. Six parameter variations stay tangent to the CP3 minimum family; the other nine are "normal variations in matrix space," meaning deviations away from that family. These are not nine additional spatial directions. The electron's assigned spatial depth remains six. Eliminating the spinor into the lowest eigenstate of h(B) gives E_eff(B)=mu||B||²+lambda_min(h(B)). Near a selected minimum the source ground ray is nondegenerate. The full fifteen-parameter matrix-space Hessian has six zero tangent eigenvalues and nine positive eigenvalues 2mu. These are checked through finite differences of the Hellmann–Feynman gradient 2mu B−gJ(z_ground(B)). An explicit joint action is L=i\hbar z^\dagger\dot z+\frac{M}{2}\langle\dot B,\dot B\rangle-E(B,z), \qquad z^\dagger z=1, with the phase multiplier understood. It gives the reciprocal equations M\ddot B=-2\mu B+gJ(z),\qquad i\hbar\dot z=h(B)z. Both spinor norm and the total energy are conserved. The exact square gives \mu\|B-\rho J(z)\|^2+\frac{\|\Pi\|^2}{2M} =E_{\rm total}-E_{\min}. This controls distance to the entire minimum family and the momentum for small excess energy, not merely an eigenvalue test at one point. Direct coupled evolution verifies conservation and the bound. It is conservative stability of the family, not attraction to one orientation, and not a proof of stability for an electron orbit after adding the nuclear interaction. Phase dynamics now survive For the rank-one projector P=zz dagger and horizontal variations u,v, i\operatorname{tr}\bigl(P[\delta_uP,\delta_vP]\bigr) =-2\operatorname{Im}(u^\dagger v). This is nonzero in general and is checked against an explicit canonical pair. It supplies the projective Berry/symplectic term missing from the filled real-band candidate. Direct differentiation of J under the spinor equation gives \dot J=-\frac{2g}{\hbar}[B,J], matching the existing geometric commutator convention with I_e=hbar/2. At an isolated minimum B=rho J this commutator vanishes, as it should: the self-coupling creates the geometry and gap, not a preferred moving orientation. The self-energy becomes a constant, leaving the Berry term and any added nuclear energy V_N(J). The latter then produces the previously checked first-order CP3 precession. Thus a consistent effective route to the earlier action exists within this model; a real-band source with zero Berry curvature could not do this. For small nonzero M, substituting the leading B=rho J into the kinetic term gives 4M rho² ds_FS²/dt², using <dJ,dJ>=8 ds_FS². This is the leading derivative expansion, not an exact constraint at finite frequency. Frequency scales must be small relative to the eliminated amplitude dynamics before discarding its corrections. Source and kinetic parameters are not fitted to an observed electron frequency here. What has and has not been selected The construction supplies a CP3 collective minimum family, positive stiffness for normal variations in matrix space, a self-generated polarization gap, and the projective phase term, without assuming the defining constraint on B or a filled real source band. It does assume a pure chiral polarization, a quadratic bivector cost, and their coupling. The pure chiral ray already carries CP3 polarization geometry; the nontrivial selection result is that an initially unrestricted B locks to it and acquires controlled normal variations in matrix space. This is not a derivation of CP3 without any spinorial premises. Most importantly, a CP3 polarization/collective space is not automatically the electron's spatial base. The finite normalized calculation is not a proof of spatial localization or absence of field collapse. The remaining physical identification concerns z and B, the chiral sector and its coupling, and the configuration reduction—not another particle-depth comparison. No geometry is ruled out merely because it differs from the V1 assignments. There is a useful algebraic route to examine at that next step. For an unnormalized pure chiral amplitude w, let n=w dagger w. The bilinear identity becomes ||J(ww dagger)||²=3n². Algebraically eliminating B therefore gives the local term −3g² n²/(4mu). An attractive density quartic can thus admit this auxiliary-bivector representation at the classical commuting-amplitude level. This observation does not supply an independent B kinetic term or establish an operator identity for anticommuting quantum fields. The written master-current construction uses bar(Psi)Psi, not automatically w dagger w for a single chiral amplitude. Their projection and normalization must be evaluated before claiming this auxiliary channel is already derived from the master scalar interaction. title: Collective precession branches
summary: The reciprocal tensor-response model admits uniformly precessing electron–response solutions whose rate obeys a cubic, with distinct branches and stability that must be checked rather than assumed.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Summary: The reciprocal tensor-response model admits uniformly precessing electron–response solutions whose rate obeys a cubic, with distinct branches and stability that must be checked rather than assumed. Exact collective solution This result uses the effective response channel in the linked note; it is not a derived microscopic nuclear current or a replacement for the actual-orbit target. Let K generate a planar rotation in O, put a in (0,1), q=sqrt(1−a²), and use the following time-dependent mixed blocks: A=aK,\quad C=-aK,\quad Q(t)=\operatorname{diag}\big(qR(\omega t),1\big), \qquad R(\theta)=e^{\theta K_2}. Take a response rotating at the same rate, X(t)=\operatorname{diag}\big(xR(\omega t),z\big),\qquad Y=M_X\dot X. The oscillator equation and electron equation independently require z=\chi g,\qquad x=\frac{\chi gq}{1-\omega^2/\Omega_X^2},\qquad \omega q=\frac{2ga}{\mathcal I_e}x. With kappa=chi g², the common rate must therefore obey \boxed{ \omega\left(1-\frac{\omega^2}{\Omega_X^2}\right) =\frac{2\kappa a}{\mathcal I_e}. } Unlike assigning X(t) as an external drive, this ansatz solves both reciprocal equations if the cubic holds. It constructs a family of self-consistent motions, not attraction from arbitrary initial conditions. The response has its own stored energy and momentum. The endpoint cases, zero coupling, and the response pole omega=plus/minus Omega_X are excluded from this nonzero-q derivation and require separate treatment. Branch structure Define omega_ad=2 kappa a/I_e > 0. For \omega_{\rm ad}<\frac{2\Omega_X}{3\sqrt3} there are two positive sub-resonant roots and one negative root below −Omega_X. The two positive branches merge at Omega_X/sqrt(3). Beyond that threshold only the negative real branch remains. The negative branch has an out-of-phase planar response, not a negative susceptibility parameter. This root count follows from the extrema of the cubic. For a fixed positive a and increasingly fast response, the low positive branch approaches omega_ad. This is the finite-response continuation of the static precession result. The relation determines the rate given (kappa,I_e,Omega_X,a); it does not determine those physical inputs or select an integer petal count. Full tangent stability The rotating-frame linearization includes all six CP3 tangent directions plus nine X and nine Y variables, not only the planar ansatz. Choose the dimensionless example chi=I_e=1, Omega_X=2, a=3/5, kappa=25/64. Its three self-consistent roots are \omega_- =\frac{-1-\sqrt{61}}4,\qquad \omega_{\rm low}=\frac12,\qquad \omega_{\rm high}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{61}}4. For reproducible rational algebra use U=gX and Z=gY. In the frame rotating only the O plane at rate omega, the equations are \dot J=-[B_U,J]-[\operatorname{diag}(\omega K,0),J],\qquad \dot U=Z/M_X-\omega KU,\qquad \dot Z=-U+\kappa Q-\omega KZ. At the low root, Q=diag(4/5,4/5,1), U=diag(1/3,1/3,25/64), and Z=K/24. The exact 24-dimensional characteristic polynomial, up to its positive leading normalization, factors as \lambda^4(\lambda^2+4)(4\lambda^2+1)(4\lambda^2+9) (4\lambda^2+25)(144\lambda^4+1324\lambda^2+1825)\,p_8(\lambda), where p_8(\lambda)=5435817984\lambda^8+96096780288\lambda^6 +601412116420\lambda^4+1573811889137\lambda^2+1436009168896. Exact real-root counting after setting t=lambda² shows that every nonzero factor has strictly negative real t roots. Thus the nonzero linear eigenvalues are imaginary for this example, without a numerical tolerance being used as the proof. Zero has algebraic multiplicity four, nullity three, and squared-matrix nullity four: one size-two Jordan block remains. The result is absence of exponential linear growth, not bounded linear evolution or nonlinear orbital stability. The high positive branch has no numerically resolved exponential mode in the same full tangent test. This is a numerical result only; it is not covered by the exact low-branch polynomial proof. The negative branch has a positive growth rate approximately .665240. A small constraint-preserving perturbation grows in an independent nonlinear rotating-frame integration. At amplitudes 1e-5 and 5e-6, the differences from linear evolution at time 3 are approximately 1.31e-10 and 3.56e-11. Completed Hamiltonian and target rotation Use the same six-coordinate classical Hamiltonian as the previous note, including the quadratic term: H=\sum_i\frac{|p_i-m\lambda Cq_i|^2}{2m} -\sum_i\frac{k}{|q_i|}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{\gamma}{|q_i-q_j|} +\frac{\langle C,C\rangle}{2I}.
