It therefore spans every direction with zero phase motion. Nonzero phase motion preserves the same uniform plane-wave magnitude. 3. The cross-depth contact theorem Let ho_a(x) be a density or current carried by the depth-a mode, and let ho_b(x,y) be one carried by the depth-b mode. From the higher-depth side, the lower-depth quantity is cylindrical: ho_a^{\uparrow b}(x,y)=ho_a(x). For an allowed interaction local on \Xi_b, the overlap is I_{ab} = \int_{\Xi_a}d\mu_a(x) \int_{F_{b/a}}d\mu_F(y)\, ho_a(x)ho_b(x,y). Define the pushforward, or marginal, of the higher-depth density:  arho_{b	o a}(x) = (\pi_{ba})_*ho_b(x) = \int_{F_{b/a}}ho_b(x,y)\,d\mu_F(y). Fubini's theorem then gives  oxed{ I_{ab} = \int_{\Xi_a} ho_a(x) arho_{b	o a}(x)\,d\mu_a(x) }. This is the cross-depth contact theorem. The higher-depth particle contributes through its complete marginal over the extra coordinates, and the cylindrical lower-depth extension covers the entire fibre. The overlap therefore carries the full marginal weight. If ho_b is a normalized nonnegative density, its whole weight survives the pushforward: \int_{\Xi_a} arho_{b	o a}\,d\mu_a = \int_{\Xi_b}ho_b\,d\mu_b =1. This is the precise sense in which contact is full: the interaction integrates the extra coordinates over the complete fibre. For a nonlocal or filtered interaction, replace the pointwise product by a kernel on the shared coordinates: I_{ab}[K] = \int_{\Xi_a	imes\Xi_a} ho_a(x)K_{ab}(x,x') arho_{b	o a}(x') \,d\mu_a(x)d\mu_a(x'). Unequal depth determines how the modes meet. The kernel, coupling constant, and representation content determine what they do when they meet. 4. Noncompact normalization On an infinite fibre, the cylindrical pullback \pi_{ba}^{*}\chi_a can be used as a translation-invariant generalized state or as a field/observable. These uses need distinct normalizations: a cylindrical field or observable pulled back from \Xi_a; a generalized momentum eigenstate with delta normalization; or a box-normalized approximation, whose density contains an explicit inverse fibre-volume factor. The particle's normalization over its spatial support remains \int_{\Xi_a}|\chi_a(x)|^2d\mu_a(x)=1. The cross-depth interaction of a cylindrical field is finite when the higher-depth density supplies an integrable fibre factor. This does not make it equal to the overlap of two probability-normalized states. In a box of fibre volume V_F, a normalized uniform extension has density ho_a(x)/V_F; its overlap with a fixed normalized ho_b is I_{ab}/V_F, tending to zero as the box grows. Cancelling that factor requires a specified flux, source-density, or coupling normalization in the action. It does not follow from Fubini's theorem. The contact formula above uses the cylindrical-field convention, normalized on the physical spatial sector. 5. Reciprocity Let the interaction part of the action be S_{ab}=g_{ab}\int dt\,I_{ab}. For the local form, functional differentiation gives  rac{\delta S_{ab}}{\deltaho_a(x)} =g_{ab} arho_{b	o a}(x), and  rac{\delta S_{ab}}{\deltaho_b(x,y)} =g_{ab}ho_a(x). The lower-depth mode feels the higher-depth mode through the latter's complete marginal. The higher-depth mode feels the lower-depth mode uniformly across the additional fibre. These are two variations of the same interaction term, so reciprocity follows when the action and kernel have the corresponding exchange symmetry. Both objects remain in their respective sectors. In IDWT's one-field language, ho_a and ho_b are sector components of one field \Psi_\infty. A cross-sector term is that field coupling two of its own depth-resolved structures on their shared coordinates. Particle depth as spatial geometry Read the complete source. Literal macroscopic spatial dimensions IDWT has one infinite-dimensional physical manifold, M_\infty. Every particle sector is a nested spatial submanifold of that same manifold: Q_a\hookrightarrow Q_b\hookrightarrow M_\infty,\qquad a<b. This inclusion relates spatial sectors. Individual particles are field structures associated with the sectors; it does not place one particle inside another or make it a constituent of another. In particular, an electron state need not be the restriction of a tau state. A restriction of bundles compares the available field components across sectors; identifying particular particle solutions through that restriction is an additional dynamical assumption. Depth d counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions of Q_d. They are all the same kind of physical dimension. Their coordinates specify position, separation, and motion. A sector is not an internal state space, a compactified auxiliary space, or a configuration-space substitute for physical space. There are no additional physical dimensions outside M_\infty. For the electron and tau, this means Q_6\hookrightarrow Q_{10}: the electron's six spatial dimensions are six of the tau's ten. All ten are the same kind of dimension for the tau. The electron is “flat” relative to it, meaning lower-dimensional, not that the tau has an inherent six-plus-four division. The same relationship holds between three-dimensional nuclei and six-dimensional electrons. “Flat” here describes relative dimensionality, not a claim of zero metric curvature. The photon-transversality construction illustrates this at every containing depth. The photon retains two directions of bound oscillation. There is one perpendicular direction within a three-dimensional sector, four within a six-dimensional sector, and eight within a ten-dimensional sector. These are descriptions relative to the photon; they do not create different kinds of dimensions in the containing sector. IDWT attributes the three-dimensional experience of ordinary matter and observers to the three-dimensional nuclear sector. This general premise does not require a physical division of any higher-depth particle into different kinds of dimensions. The observer map must describe what the observer's interactions register; its dynamics remains to be derived. For example, the electron has six ordinary macroscopic spatial dimensions. In the proposed geometry, Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3 is its actual spatial submanifold. Three of those dimensions are shared with us. That fact makes none of the six physically different in kind, and does not give the electron an inherent 3+3 split. Grouping coordinates by an observer's access is a choice of description, not a division in the electron. Frame-lock models that use such a grouping have additional assumptions; they do not establish the general origin of three-dimensional experience. This states the physical premise; it does not declare the proposed metric, embedding, lock, or observer response mathematically derived or experimentally established. The following vocabulary applies throughout the research record: Term Physical or mathematical meaning Sector, depth, base Q_d A nested spatial submanifold of M_\infty, with d macroscopic spatial directions. Observed and unobserved directions; formerly “visible” and “hidden” Names relative to an observer or interaction. Directions shared with us are no different in physical kind from any others. These names do not divide the electron into two physical parts. Normal or projection fibre When used for spatial nesting, directions or points of the same physical manifold omitted by a particular restriction or marginal. Spinor, vector-bundle, or mode-space dimension The number of components used to represent fields and modes on that manifold. It introduces no additional physical dimensions or independently postulated internal world. Homogeneous coordinates and coefficient rays Mathematical representations whose meaning must be specified. A homogeneous coordinate for a point of Q_6 represents spatial position; an arbitrary ray of field coefficients does not automatically do so. Multiparticle configuration space A mathematical record of several positions in the same physical manifold, not extra dimensions of physical space. “Intrinsic” in older mathematical passages Defined from a manifold's own metric or tangent bundle. It must never mean that the particle sector is internal or nonspatial. Compact projective geometry A proposed global topology of a spatial submanifold. IDWT has no compactified dimensions. Mathematical compactness sets no physical length scale; conclusions using this topology remain conditional on it and the physical metric scale remains to be derived. Inclusions of nested submanifolds, maps that marginalize spatial coordinates, and projectors acting on field components are different mathematical objects. One cannot establish the first merely by constructing either of the others. See the geometry and nesting audit for the resulting restrictions on existing calculations. The intermediate-depth obstruction sharpens that requirement: the standard \mathrm{CP}^2\subset\mathrm{CP}^3 inclusion cannot factor through a smooth five-dimensional spatial submanifold. A pointwise normal direction exists, but the nonzero normal Euler class prevents the required global line subbundle. Thus assigning candidate topologies at separate depths must be followed by a compatible global embedding construction; local spinor branchings do not supply it. 1. Geometric claim Status: spatial depth and a named geometry are separate hypotheses. The candidate sphere/projective assignments elsewhere in V2 are not proved by the dimension and principal-symbol arguments below. Those arguments also assume the sector embedding and projection stated in their hypotheses; they do not independently select a physical depth. See the geometry premise audit. A particle of depth d lives on a spatial submanifold Q_d of M_\infty with real dimension d. Each spatial coordinate supplies a derivative direction and a conjugate covector component in the principal symbol of the kinetic operator. In IDWT the depth d appears simultaneously in TQ_d, \qquad T^*Q_d, \qquad \gamma^ap_a, \qquad S(n,d), \qquad \pi_{ba}:Q_b	o Q_a, and in the integration measure used for cross-depth contact. These are linked uses of one physical spatial depth. The particle's physical spatial submanifold is Q_d. Its spinor bundle carries the spatial Dirac field. The auxiliary coherent-ray fibre \mathbb{CP}^{d} organizes the phase modes constructed from the d spatial oscillator directions, and embeds by the degree-N Veronese map into the full projective mode space \mathbb P(\mathcal E_{N,d})\cong\mathbb{CP}^{S(N+1,d)-1} at a point (for N>0). These three geometric layers are Q_d, \qquad \Sigma Q_d, \qquad \mathbb P(\mathcal E_{N,d}). Only Q_d names physical spatial dimensions. The other two objects describe the field and its modes on Q_d; their component counts add no dimensions to M_\infty. In particular the auxiliary \mathbb{CP}^{d} here is a space of mode coefficients, distinct from the physical electron submanifold Q_6=\mathbb{CP}^3. 2. Principal symbol on a base manifold Let X be a spatial manifold and F	o X a vector bundle carrying polarization or charge data. A Dirac-type field has kinetic operator \mathcal D_{m int} =i\gamma^\mu
abla_\mu\otimes I_F+A(x), where A(x) acts algebraically on F. Its principal symbol is \sigma_1(\mathcal D_{m int})(x,k) =\gamma^\mu k_\mu\otimes I_F. Additional physical spatial coordinates y^a extend the kinetic operator to \mathcal D_{m spatial} =i\gamma^\mu
abla_\mu+i\Gamma^a
abla_a+A(x,y), and its principal symbol becomes \sigma_1(\mathcal D_{m spatial})(x,y;k,p) =\gamma^\mu k_\mu+\Gamma^ap_a. The covector components p_a are their conjugate momenta. They determine the characteristic set and propagation directions; the short-time heat kernel and spectral dimension; localization and uncertainty relations; the measure over which contact and overlap are calculated; the kinetic response to gradients in those directions. Thus base dimension is read invariantly from the number of independent covector components in the principal symbol. Fibre matrices enter the lower-order algebraic structure and representation content. 8. Projected-principal-symbol theorem The decisive calculation can be made exactly once the meaning of sector projection is stated. Let i_d:Q_d\hookrightarrow M_\infty be a sector embedding with an orthogonal tangent--normal splitting along Q_d. Let P_d be a smooth zeroth-order orthogonal projector from the restricted master spinor bundle onto a sector bundle \Sigma_d. For a covector p\in T_q^*Q_d, let \iota_dp denote its tangential extension that annihilates the normal bundle. Assume the master operator is Dirac type, so \sigma_1(\mathcal D_\infty)(q,\Xi) =i\,c_\infty(\Xi), and define the sector operator by tangential compression, \mathcal D_d =P_d\mathcal D_\infty^{\parallel}P_d. Because P_d is order zero, symbol composition gives \sigma_1(\mathcal D_d)(q,p) =iP_d c_\infty(\iota_dp)P_d. Derivatives of P_d contribute to the order-zero connection and algebraic mixing terms. The principal momenta remain those in the compressed Clifford symbol. Now impose the essential compatibility condition: \Sigma_d is invariant under tangential Clifford multiplication and its identification with the spin or Spin^c bundle of Q_d obeys P_dc_\infty(\iota_dp)P_d=c_d(p). Choose a local coframe e^1,\ldots,e^d on Q_d and write p=p_ae^a. Then  oxed{ \sigma_1(P_d\mathcal D_\infty^{\parallel}P_d)(q,p) =i\gamma_d^ap_a } with exactly d independent momentum components. The inherited Clifford relation is c_d(p)c_d(r)+c_d(r)c_d(p) =2g_d^{-1}(p,r)I, and hence \sigma_1(\mathcal D_d)(q,p)^2 =-g_d^{-1}(p,p)I for the displayed i\mathcal D convention. Thus the same d-dimensional cotangent metric controls the characteristic kinetic response. For time-dependent dynamics, the same evolution parameter t is used for every sector. The count d here concerns spatial momenta on the nested submanifold; introducing a time parameter does not postulate another spatial manifold or another particle depth. 8.1 Lower-order normal geometry Tangential compression sets normal covectors to zero. The normal connection and normal Clifford products survive in the lower-order part: \mathcal D_d =i\gamma_d^a(\partial_a+\omega_a+A_a^{\perp})+\Phi_d. Here A_a^{\perp} and \Phi_d act algebraically on the lower-depth fibre as the projected gauge polarization, while the principal symbol contains the momenta tangent to Q_d. 8.2 The theorem's hypotheses The result is conditional on three geometric facts: P_d is a smooth zeroth-order bundle projector; sector restriction means tangential compression with normal covectors set to zero; the projected spinor subbundle is invariant under tangential Clifford multiplication. Tangential Clifford invariance gives a full-rank elliptic symbol. Its direct verification for every sector is the diagnostic that the projected geometry retains all d spatial directions. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Spatial operator and contact toolkit
summary: The simplex factor must arise from an actual physical spatial operator or a justified effective reduction. Mode counting, one eigenfrequency, a contact trace, and a pair vertex are different objects.
text:
The simplex factor must arise from an actual physical spatial operator or a justified effective reduction. Mode counting, one eigenfrequency, a contact trace, and a pair vertex are different objects. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Projective derivative simplex Read the complete source. Define the complete derivative and its tensor norm For a nonnegative line degree L, let \mathcal B_k: \Gamma(\mathcal O(L)) \longrightarrow \Gamma igl(\operatorname{Sym}^k T^{*1,0}\otimes\mathcal O(L) igr) 	ag{4} be the symmetric k-fold covariant derivative. The tensor norm in (4) is inherited from the full tensor product. In particular, all ordered index contractions are retained, with no extra factor of 1/k! in the norm. On the affine chart [1,z_1,\ldots,z_m], put t=(1+|z|^2)^{-1},\qquad h_L=t^L,\qquad \Gamma^k_{ij}=-t(\delta_i^k ar z_j+\delta_j^k ar z_i). 	ag{5} The line connection has holomorphic coefficient -Lt ar z_i. For any constant complex direction v, define u=t\sum_i ar z_iv_i. Then \partial_vu=-u^2. Contracting every tensor index with v gives the exact recurrence \mathcal B_{k+1}s(v^{k+1}) = igl(\partial_v+(2k-L)u igr)\mathcal B_ks(v^k). 	ag{6} The coefficient 2k includes the connection on all k tensor indices; omitting it would give a different operator. Induction in (6) gives \mathcal B_ks(v^k)= \sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^{k-j} inom kj (L-j)_{\underline{k-j}}\, u^{k-j}\partial_v^js, 	ag{7} where a_{\underline r}=a(a-1)\cdots(a-r+1), with a_{\underline0}=1. At k=L+1, every coefficient with j<k vanishes. Therefore  oxed{\mathcal B_{L+1}s=\partial^{L+1}s} 	ag{8} in this affine holomorphic line frame. Polarization of (6)–(7) recovers the complete mixed tensor, not merely its value in one chosen direction. Derive its spectrum using physical spatial fields Use the spatial Jacobi construction on \mathbb{CP}^m with line degree L. In the coherent chart frame, a representative of its zero-form spectral family is s_n=\chi p_n(t),\qquad p_n(t)=P_n^{(m-1,L)}(2t-1),\qquad X s_n=n(n+L+m)s_n. 	ag{11} The normalization of the coherent holomorphic section \chi cancels from the following norm ratio. The original radial weight is t^L(1-t)^{m-1}dt. Direct use of (5) on all tensor indices gives \mathcal B_ks_n =\chi\,t^kQ_k(t)\, ar z^{\otimes k},\qquad Q_{k+1}=(k-L)Q_k-tQ_k',\qquad Q_0=p_n. 	ag{12} The physical inverse metric contracts each copy of  ar z with squared norm 2|z|^2/(R^2t^2). Hence  rac{\|\mathcal B_ks_n\|^2}{\|s_n\|^2} = \left( rac2{R^2}ight)^k  rac{\displaystyle\int_0^1 t^{L-k}(1-t)^{m-1+k}|Q_k(t)|^2dt} {\displaystyle\int_0^1 t^L(1-t)^{m-1}|p_n(t)|^2dt}. 	ag{13} The recurrence also has the exact Jacobi form Q_k=(-1)^kt^{k-L} rac{d^k}{dt^k}(t^Lp_n) =(-1)^k(n+L)_{\underline k} P_n^{(m-1+k,L-k)}(2t-1). 	ag{14} It follows by differentiating the finite Jacobi polynomial, or its hypergeometric expression. With \alpha, eta>-1, the shifted Jacobi norm is I_n(\alpha, eta)=  rac{\Gamma(n+\alpha+1)\Gamma(n+ eta+1)} {(2n+\alpha+ eta+1)n!\,\Gamma(n+\alpha+ eta+1)}. 	ag{15} This is DLMF Table 18.3.1 after changing variables from [-1,1] to [0,1]. For 0\le k\le L, substitution in (13) immediately gives  oxed{  rac{\|\mathcal B_ks_n\|^2}{\|s_n\|^2} =\left( rac2{R^2}ight)^k (n+L)_{\underline k}(n+m)_k. } 	ag{16} Here (a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1) is the rising factorial. At the required final step k=L+1, the second Jacobi parameter in (14) is -1. This endpoint must be handled explicitly. For n\ge1, P_n^{(\alpha,-1)}(2t-1) = rac{n+\alpha}{n}\, tP_{n-1}^{(\alpha,1)}(2t-1). 	ag{17} Its factor t makes (13) finite and reduces it to the ordinary positive weight t(1-t)^\alpha. Using (15) on that polynomial proves (16) also for k=L+1. The n=0 field is annihilated separately, as required by (8). The operator and metric commute with physical SU(m+1) isometries. The zero-form section spectrum is a multiplicity-free sum of irreducible families, and an isometry orbit of the representative (11) spans its family. The adjoint square acts as a scalar on each one. Thus (16) determines its eigenvalue on every complex spatial polarization in that family, beyond the radial representative. The balanced degree gives the consecutive simplex factors Set L=m-1 and take its first annihilator, of order k=m. Equation (16) becomes  oxed{ \mathcal B_m^\dagger\mathcal B_m ig|_n = rac{2^m}{R^{2m}}\, (n)_m(n+m)_m = rac{2^m}{R^{2m}}\,(n)_{2m}. } 	ag{18} The two rising products are adjacent. Normalizing at n=1 therefore gives exactly S(n,2m) for every n\ge1. For a general L, the first annihilator instead gives (n)_{L+1}(n+m)_{L+1}. The consecutive product in (18) is a specific consequence of the relation L=m-1, which remains a physical connection requirement. The geometric operator identities at the assigned real depths are Spatial depth Line degree Derivative order Normalized adjoint square 6 2 3  rac{X(X+4)(X+6)}{720} 10 4 5  rac{X(X+8)(X+14)(X+18)(X+20)}{10!} Here X=R^2\mathscr D_L^2/4 on the zero-form channel of the corresponding physical projective geometry. In particular, \mathcal M_6(13)=18\,564,\qquad \mathcal M_6(35)=3\,838\,380,\qquad \mathcal M_{10}(23)=64\,512\,240. 	ag{19} The ten-dimensional construction has its own specified line connection. The inheritance analysis explains why simultaneous first-family connections do not follow merely by directly restricting one CP5 spinor to CP3. No particle mode or dimensionality is reassigned in (19). Projective spectral contact Read the complete source. An actual spatial band has the simplex count On physical \mathbb{CP}^3 with the specified line connection \mathcal O(3), retain every zero-form spatial spectral shell from 0 through N=n-1. The complete band has dimension  oxed{ \mathscr D_N= inom{N+3}{3} inom{N+6}{3} =20 inom{n+5}{6}=20S(n,6). } 	ag{1} Its physical point evaluation in the zero-form polarization is rank one and has nonzero eigenvalue \mathscr D_N/\mathcal V, where \mathcal V is the physical volume. Thus a specified point contact has an exact simplex coefficient with a single factor of twenty independent of the band. This is a different space of spatial fields from the holomorphic tangent-mode band: the line degree here stays fixed while nonholomorphic spatial harmonics are added. It also uses a different connection from the \mathcal O(2) derivative polynomial. The two calculations should not be combined without a map between their bundles and actions. The count and evaluation operator can be derived. A smooth local scalar current has not thereby become a point insertion. The explicit reproducing state below has a different self-contact expectation and drives complementary components. The geometry is conditional actual CP3 with ordinary macroscopic spatial directions, no compactification and unknown FS scale R. The calculations at CP5 below use a separately specified actual ten-dimensional geometry. Line and spectral labels are field data, not additional physical dimensions or charge assignments. Derive the polarized point operator Use the unit-volume spatial measure d
u first. At a physical point x, evaluation maps \mathcal K_N	o\mathcal O(L)_x, a one-dimensional fibre. Its point form is T_{N,x}=\operatorname{ev}_x^\dagger\operatorname{ev}_x. 	ag{6} Spatial homogeneity makes the diagonal reproducing kernel constant. Its trace integral is \mathscr D_N, so  oxed{ T_{N,x}	ext{ has rank one},\qquad T_{N,x}^2=\mathscr D_NT_{N,x}. } 	ag{7} With the physical measure d\mathrm{vol}=\mathcal Vd
u, the nonzero eigenvalue is instead \mathscr D_N/\mathcal V, where \mathcal V=\pi^mR^{2m}/m!. Equation (5) therefore fixes the band dependence of a specified polarized point form. The point x is a position in the actual spatial manifold. It is not the auxiliary occupied tangent-mode ray in the mass-contact construction. Matching their ranks up to a constant does not identify their representations, evaluation maps or physical sources. Evaluate the actual local scalar self-source For this unit-norm zero-form state, the local scalar interaction has occupied expectation  oxed{ \mathcal A_N=\intho_N^2d
u =m\left( rac{A_N}{B_N}ight)^2 \int_0^1t^{2L}(1-t)^{m-1}  igl[P_N^{(m,L)}(2t-1) igr]^4dt. } 	ag{14} This integral follows from the same physical norm used for (7). It can be evaluated exactly by finite beta integrals. At m=L=3: Cumulative cutoff N Point eigenvalue \mathscr D_N Local quartic \mathcal A_N \mathcal A_N/\mathscr D_N 0 20  rac{100}{21}  rac5{21} 1 140 23.170163 0.165501 12 371\,280 46\,113.932673 0.124203 34 76\,767\,600 9\,372\,719.126622 0.122092 The ratios at the unchanged electron and muon cutoffs differ. The smooth self-current of these reproducing states therefore does not reproduce the point coefficient with one exact common factor. There is also a field-equation residual. Let \mathsf P_N be the zero-form band projector and define r_N=\mathsf P_N(ho_N\psi_{N,x})-\mathcal A_N\psi_{N,x}. 	ag{15} Exact projection onto every retained Jacobi shell gives r_N
e0 at N=1,2,12,34. The scalar source also has a nonzero component outside the band at every tested cutoff, including N=0. Its full norm and both residual norms are calculated from the same polynomial source; the test does not stop at its occupied expectation. Independently, the free Dirac term satisfies  oxed{ \|\mathscr D_L\psi_{N,x}\|^2 = rac4{R^2\mathscr D_N} \sum_{k=1}^{N}X_kd_k>0 \qquad(N\ge1). } 	ag{16} A purely zero-form reproducing state consequently requires its odd Dirac component to solve a stationary scalar equation. The point-form eigenvector alone is not a complete stationary particle field. For physical norm Q, the profile is scaled by \sqrt{Q/\mathcal V}. Its occupied scalar coefficient acquires gQ/\mathcal V times \mathcal A_N. This is still an expectation of the source, rather than an exact stationary frequency in the presence of (15)–(16). Finite chain current mass Read the complete source. A strict finite-chain ratio theorem For spatial depth d\ge2, let B_n be the real lower bidiagonal component matrix (B_n)_{jj}=n+j\quad(0\le j<d),\qquad (B_n)_{j,j-1}=b_j>0\quad(1\le j<d), 	ag{1} where the b_j are independent of the harmonic label n. The current carrier has b_j=g for all j, while the linked carrier has b_j=g h_j, with one positive geometric hopping list per depth. At a fixed physical radius, the smallest singular value \epsilon_n is the positive oscillation frequency of this component carrier. Write P_{n,d}=\det B_n=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j)=d!S(n,d). 	ag{2} The adjugate identity gives an exact normalization formula:  oxed{ rac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} = rac1{\|\operatorname{adj}B_n\|_2}.} 	ag{3} Conjugating the adjugate by alternating diagonal signs makes it a nonnegative lower triangular matrix A_n. Its entries are (A_n)_{ij}= \left(\prod_{a=j+1}^{i}b_aight) \left(\prod_{a<j\,	ext{or}\,a>i}(n+a)ight), \qquad i\ge j, 	ag{4} with zero entries above the diagonal. Every entry is nondecreasing in n>0, and some entries increase strictly. The bottom row is positive, so the leading left and right singular vectors can be chosen strictly positive. Their bilinear characterization then makes \|A_n\|_2 strictly increasing. Equation (3) proves  oxed{ rac{\epsilon_{n_2}}{S(n_2,d)} < rac{\epsilon_{n_1}}{S(n_1,d)} \quad	ext{whenever }n_2>n_1>0.} 	ag{5} This holds at every finite positive hopping strength, including different positive h_j that are common to all modes at one depth. It covers the maintained depths two, three, four, five, six and ten. Depth ten has only one maintained mode, so it has no within-depth ratio test. The theorem does not cover nonlinear self-consistent hopping that changes with n, different physical radii for particles in one sector, or an added direct mass interaction. When all b_j grow at fixed positive ratios, expanding the largest singular value of the adjugate gives  rac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} = rac1{\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}b_j} \left[1-  rac12\left( rac{n^2}{b_1^2} + rac{(n+d-1)^2}{b_{d-1}^2}ight) +O(g^{-4})ight]. 	ag{6} Here the remainder is at fixed n,d as the common edge scale g increases. This correction is the positive norm of internal component content in the causal parent, rather than an error from computing a tiny singular value. The unified calculation verifies (3) independently of direct singular-value decomposition on every maintained mode. For the benchmark masses already used in the mass-spectrum comparison, the observed electron-to-muon ratio is 206.76828299, while the bare simplex ratio at depth six is 3515/17=206.76470588. The latter is low by about 0.00173\%. Equation (5) means an uncorrected finite chain at one common radius and hopping strength lowers its prediction further. At dimensionless current edge g=5000, the whole-depth current ratio is 206.75506228; the linked carrier at its specified strength 10000 gives 206.76242640. These are conditional model predictions against the stated benchmark, not uncertainty-weighted experimental exclusions. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. title: Same-field actions and canonical normalization
summary: A candidate mass and coupling mechanism must follow from one varied action with its canonical norm, retained modes and complete energy. The calculations here are conditional action constructions; they do not establish a unique master-field reduction.
text:
A candidate mass and coupling mechanism must follow from one varied action with its canonical norm, retained modes and complete energy. The calculations here are conditional action constructions; they do not establish a unique master-field reduction. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Homogeneous current mass Read the complete source. One local current and one generating functional On the stated spatial geometry, let H_0 be the first-order carrier with its adjacent component coupling removed. If J is the matrix with ones immediately below its diagonal, define the Hermitian channel K= egin{pmatrix}0&J^\dagger\J&0\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{1} It acts on the retained components of the same field and is the identity on the spatial spinor or form indices. Those components do not add physical spatial dimensions or describe additional particles. For the local density and real current, write ho=\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\qquad j=\Psi^\dagger K\Psi,\qquad k=j/ho. 	ag{2} The quotient is used where ho>0. Choose one positive strength g, with frequency units, and a dimensionless \eta>0, common to the modes being compared. The proposed photon assignment has n=0. Extending the count by S(0,2)=0 records a vanishing contribution from this mode family. The formal empty bundle \mathcal E_{-1,d}=0 has no nonzero state and therefore supplies neither a zero eigenvalue nor a propagating photon. e0. Its kinetic propagation, complete energy–momentum response and stability must follow from the same field action. The zero-count boundary alone does not prove these conditions or the protection of a massless branch. 8.2 The bottom beat The ordinary theorem gives the single-band masses m(n,3)=\mu_3S(n,3). The bottom formula m_b=\mu_3\sqrt{S(16,3)S(17,3)} requires a two-band coupling. Its closure condition is that the off-diagonal contact operator between \mathcal E_{15,3} and \mathcal E_{16,3} have a singular value equal to the geometric mean of their diagonal contact eigenvalues. 8.3 Sector scales For a band-blind master contact coefficient, one \mu_d multiplies every ordinary occupied band in a sector. Numerical projection must determine \mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_4,\mu_5,\mu_6,\mu_{10} and their cross-sector relations from the normalized master kernel and its overlap between the corresponding Q_d sectors. Observed masses provide the empirical test of those projected values. 8.4 Mode selection The operator supplies a collective mass eigenbranch for every positive integer n. A separate stability or resonance condition must select which branches occur as particles. The accuracy of the mass-depth scan is conditional on those occupied indices. 8.5 Occupied-ray and ray-averaged quartic densities The distinction between contact at the occupied ray and averaging over all rays is mathematically observable. For a normalized coherent state |w;Nangle, define its normalized phase-ray density ho_w([z]) =D_N|\langle z;N|w;Nangle|^2. It obeys \intho_w\,d
u_{m FS}=1. Because |\langle z;N|w;Nangle|^2 =|\langle z|wangle|^{2N}, the invariant moment formula gives \int_{\mathbb{CP}^{d}} |\langle z|wangle|^{4N}\,d
u_{m FS} = rac{1}{D_{2N}}, \qquad D_{2N}= inom{2N+d}{d}. A quartic energy averaged over the whole ray space is \intho_w([z])^2\,d
u_{m FS} = rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}, while occupied-ray self-contact has eigenvalue D_N. The two interactions are 	ext{occupied-ray self-contact} \quad\longrightarrow\quad D_N, 	ext{ray-averaged quartic density} \quad\longrightarrow\quad rac{D_N^2}{D_{2N}}. Of these two specified prescriptions, only the point contact has the simplex multiplier with a band-independent coefficient. This comparison does not establish uniqueness among nonlinear actions. The full smooth quartic variation establishes coherent stationary solutions, a complete mode Hessian and finite-mode orbital stability for the second action. Its nonlinear frequency retains D_N^2/D_{2N}. Deriving a coherent branch and deriving the point-contact multiplier are therefore separate requirements. The specified spatial CP3 scalar branch tests another necessary step: restoring the physical spatial Dirac complement. On that proposed geometry, the normalized local-contact branch has a nonzero cubic frequency correction and an oscillatory radial instability at every positive section degree for sufficiently small coupling. A smooth spatial moment kernel changes that response and avoids the radial instability in the same regime. The physical CP3 section count uses  inom{L+3}{3}; it must not be identified with the auxiliary cumulative count D_N= inom{N+6}{6}. That is enough to derive the rank D_N of the cumulative band. The corresponding band projection is P_{N,d}|q|^2P_{N,d} and the phase-ray contact density is D_N|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Their relation requires either a master interaction written locally on the homogenized phase-ray bundle; or a derivation showing that the coordinate-space nonlinear kernel transforms into the occupied-ray contact density after the oscillator and sector projections. This step completes the map from coordinate confinement to phase-ray self-contact. The actual spatial oscillator point form provides a separate explicit comparison: its eigenvalue is the spatial reproducing kernel on the diagonal, with a weighted Hockey-Stick central value and fixed-width growth of degree d/2. The simplex dimension is its integrated trace, so spatial point evaluation alone does not supply the projective coefficient at every point. Consistency across cumulative bands adds a test for one underlying kernel, distinguishing fixed bare compression from a dynamical Schur reduction. The specified band embeddings and any eliminated modes are part of that bridge. 9. Sector normalization The universal combinatorial part of the scalar contact projection is now fixed: P_N\delta_{[z]}P_N =S(N+1,d)|z;Nangle\langle z;N|. Write the scalar coefficient left after sector projection as \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d. Here \kappa_d is the projected master-contact coefficient, R_d is the normalized spatial-profile overlap on Q_d, and B_d is the scalar spinor contraction. Suppose the order-zero vertex is a scalar identity on the normalized non-mode factors, its coefficient is constant on the occupied contact graph, and its coefficient is independent of the band projector. Under these band-blind hypotheses, all three factors are independent of N. The contact theorem then gives m(n,d)=\kappa_dR_dB_d\,S(n,d). For the stated band-blind scalar vertex, \mu_d=\kappa_dR_dB_d is independent of N. Derivative vertices, nonconstant order-zero coefficients, finite contact width, spectral functions, mode-dependent spinor polarization, and band-dependent state normalization generate testable modifications of the mass sequence. For two sectors with equal self-couplings, the ratio of mass units is  rac{\mu_a}{\mu_b}= rac{R_aB_a}{R_bB_b}. Thus the proposed \mu_6=\mu_{10} symmetry requires both g_{66}=g_{10,10} and equality of the normalized projected overlaps. The local scalar profile calculation shows explicitly how normalization can change the frequency produced by a contact coefficient. Its virial and exact massive benchmark concern a flat local comparison; they do not replace the physical geometry and bundle terms needed for the occupied particle solutions. The nonlinear spatial reduction now derives the effective stationary action and induced norm after complementary Dirac modes respond. For a normalized chiral zero-mode branch, the frequency is gA-4g^3C+O(g^5) while the total energy is gA/2-g^3C+O(g^5). Under the stated positive-potential hypotheses, C vanishes exactly when the scalar source preserves the selected zero-mode line. A common graph coefficient g_N=\kappa D_N must therefore also control these spatial corrections before it supplies a common physical mass scale. The graph coefficient itself remains to be derived from the master action. The physical tangent-band point projection computes the complete holomorphic zero-form contact spectrum with the natural curved connection. Its eigenvalues depend on fibre polarization. At fixed line twist their maximum grows cubically with the cumulative degree on CP3, while the auxiliary simplex rank grows as its sixth power. This is a derived distinction between specified operators; it does not change the particle assignments or identify a physical rest mass. The constant-density local branch solves the written local scalar equation on that specified curved kinetic bundle. Five holomorphic polarization fields occupy five orthogonal tangent copies already in the carrier. Their total density is constant, so the scalar coefficient is exact; at common norm and volume it is independent of the carrier rank. The action also retains copy symmetries that leave the occupied pattern unselected. The coherent curved mode-bundle construction retains the natural tangent-mode connection and gives pointwise coherent spatial fields with balanced first moments. The specified scalar moment action has exact linear branches on these fields, but local scalar contact and a spatially transported graph pairing retain different normalization factors. Their master origin and full stability remain open. The balanced spatial branch supplies an exact unit-norm field with frequency g and energy g/2 for the specified smooth moment kernel. Its noncoherent holomorphic shape has an isotropic first spatial moment, and its complete spatial linearization has no exponential modes. This is a constructive solution of a conditional spatial normalization problem; the master origin of the kernel and coherent-ray coefficient, nonlinear stability and physical rest-mass identification remain to be established. On the specified physical CP3 geometry, exact source preservation forces a smooth real scalar potential on a holomorphic section to be constant. A covariant kernel preserving the coherent branch then makes every holomorphic shape in that degree degenerate. The genuine mean kernel gives an exact, nonlinearly stable phase orbit, while a finite same-field static response retains a bounded nonzero spatial correction. Exact linearity therefore does not by itself select the occupied shape. The scalar self-consistency comparison constructs a nonzero scalar coefficient and an exact collective response frequency from one specified global kernel. Its leading coefficient is M\simeq\kappa Q, where Q is the full canonical norm. A cumulative count enhances it only when that norm grows with the number of modes; at unit total norm, |M|\le\kappa for every band. This locates a normalization requirement that a physical mass derivation must supply. 9.1 The conditional common-anchor relation There is a compact way to state the scale relations that have direct mass tests. Let n_d^\star be a specified reference band in sector d and define its contact mass M_d^\star=\mu_dS(n_d^\star,d). Under the projected fixed-point condition  rac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}} =  rac{m_e^2}{g_{66}}. the sector scale is  oxed{ \mu_d =  rac{m_e}{S(n_d^\star,d)} \sqrt{ rac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}} }. The square root is the direct algebraic consequence of this quadratic fixed-point equation. The master equation of motion must supply that equation. For the proposed reference choices, the formula reads  egin{aligned} \mu_6&= rac{m_e}{S(13,6)},\ \mu_3&=m_e\sqrt{ rac{g_{33}}{g_{66}}},\ \mu_4&= rac{m_e}{S(3,4)} \sqrt{ rac{g_{44}}{g_{66}}}. \end{aligned} The electron fixes the unit. The d=3 and d=4 expressions then make conditional predictions to compare with inferred quark-mass parameters. A quantitative comparison must specify the mass definition, renormalization scheme, scale and matching to measured hadronic or scattering observables. These parameters are not directly measured free-particle masses; see the PDG quark-mass review. No common-scheme refit is performed here. The proposed d=2 formula \mu_2=m_e\sqrt{ rac{g_{22}}{g_{66}}} uses a unit-count back-reaction reference. It is testable because it predicts the absolute W, Z, and Higgs masses after their mode indices are specified. Likewise, \mu_{10}=\mu_6 is testable against the tau mass, but still requires the normalized 6\leftrightarrow10 overlap equality just identified. These are the direct empirical checks of the conditional fixed-point equation and coupling counts. 9.2 The neutrino scale is unresolved The proposed relation \mu_5 =  rac34 rac{\mu_6^3}{\mu_4^2} is a phenomenological normalization calibrated to the observed neutrino order of magnitude. V2 treats \mu_5 as an undetermined projected normalization. An operator equation must select the factor 3/4 and powers (3,-2) before this expression becomes a derived scale law. Neutrino oscillations measure mass-squared differences. Given the proposed mode indices, they constrain a common \mu_5. An absolute neutrino-mass measurement will provide the direct scale test. The current status is  oxed{\mu_5	ext{ remains an undetermined projected normalization.}} A derivation requires evaluating \kappa_5R_5B_5 from the master action. 9.3 Remaining numerical calculation The outstanding work is to evaluate (\kappa_d,R_d,B_d), \qquad d\in\{2,3,4,5,6,10\}, from one normalized projected action and recover the cross-sector relations. The simplex multiplier is derived, the non-neutrino scale relations are conditional and empirically testable, and the neutrino expression is a phenomenological ansatz. The construction also makes sharp deformation predictions: a finite ray-contact width replaces the constant diagonal evaluation with a convolution of the Bergman kernel and changes the mass sequence; derivatives of the contact delta insert powers of the representation generators and generate additional N-dependence; a band-dependent scalar coefficient spoils the scale-free family ratios; a mixed state on several projective rays splits or averages the rank-one mass eigenvalue. Order-zero self-contact at a definite projective mode ray is one operator realization of the simplex spectrum. The homogeneous coherent actions provide other exact occupied eigenvalues with different complete mode responses. Their nonconstant spatial solutions have canonical energy and full linear stability for the specified independent kinetic bundle. The functional normalization and master-field carrier remain assumptions; the direct derivative identification fails finite propagation in its stated flat control. The spectrum therefore constrains a master interaction without determining it uniquely. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Localization and same-field support
summary: The same-field interaction may sustain a finite spatial pattern and set its oscillation frequency. A radial minimum is only one necessary part of a stationary spatial field; angular stress and the response of the sustaining structure matter.
text:
The same-field interaction may sustain a finite spatial pattern and set its oscillation frequency. A radial minimum is only one necessary part of a stationary spatial field; angular stress and the response of the sustaining structure matter. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Coupling localization mass Read the complete source. A scale test of localization For a fixed normalized spatial profile in d ordinary directions, let \psi_R(x)=Q^{1/2}R^{-d/2}\phi(x/R). A first-order positive gradient estimate scales as A Q/R. A local density-square contact scales as B Q^2/R^d, where A,B>0 are profile integrals. If the contact is repulsive, both positive terms decrease as the pattern spreads. If it is attractive, the fixed-profile energy is E_2(R)= rac{A Q}{R}- rac{g B Q^2}{R^d},\qquad g>0. 	ag{1} For every d>1, its only finite stationary radius satisfies R^{d-1}=d gBQ/A, and direct differentiation gives E_2''(R_*)= rac{(1-d)AQ}{R_*^3}<0. 	ag{2} It is a maximum, with collapse as R	o0 in this ansatz. The result applies to these two scale terms and fixed profiles; it does not rule out other gradients, nonlocal response, curved geometry, or complete same-field support. A higher positive local density term offers a concrete conditional alternative in the same field. Absorb fixed positive profile and norm factors into a,B,C>0, put y=1/R, and consider E_3(y)=a y-B y^d+C y^{2d}. 	ag{3} The attractive and repulsive terms can arise from one nonlinear energy density, for example -gho^2/2+hho^3/3, with ho=\psi^\dagger\psi; they need not be separate fields. The first finite stationary pair appears when E_3'=E_3''=0. Solving those equations gives y_{m fold} =\left[ rac{a(d-1)}{2d^2C}ight]^{1/(2d-1)}, \qquad B_{m fold} = rac{2(2d-1)}{d-1}C y_{m fold}^{d}. 	ag{4} For B>B_{m fold}, a broad-radius maximum and a smaller-radius minimum occur in this scale function. The minimum first crosses the dispersed reference energy zero at y_{m bind} =\left[ rac{a(d-1)}{dC}ight]^{1/(2d-1)}, \qquad B_{m bind} = rac{2d-1}{d-1}C y_{m bind}^{d}. 	ag{5} The six-depth scale batch checks depths 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 at a=C=Q=1 and B=1.2B_{m bind}. Its selected report finds one finite scale minimum below the dispersed reference at every depth. The values of the illustrative inverse radius run from 0.930 to 1.019 in the chosen units. This is an existence result only for the scale ansatz; it has not solved a complete spatial field equation or established dynamic stability. Restoring the norm dependence makes the missing mass step explicit: E_3(Q,R)= rac{aQ}{R}- rac{g BQ^2}{R^d} + rac{hCQ^3}{R^{2d}}, \qquad \omega_{m branch}=\left. rac{\partial E_3}{\partial Q} ight|_{R=R_*(Q)} = rac a{R_*}- rac{2gBQ}{R_*^d} + rac{3hCQ^2}{R_*^{2d}}. 	ag{6} The radius derivative drops out by stationarity. In the bound examples of the batch, this first-order frequency shift relative to the chosen dispersed reference is negative. An absolute positive particle frequency, correct inertial response and complete energy require the remaining field and supporting terms. Stable radius selection alone does not prove mass generation. One interaction can also control a pair encounter For two pointwise orthogonal field components with densities ho_i,ho_j, the same nonlinear contact that supplied (3) has the mixed density \Delta U_{ij} =-gho_iho_j +hho_iho_j(ho_i+ho_j). 	ag{7} This follows by subtracting the two isolated densities from U(ho_i+ho_j). The coefficients are exactly the same ones that enter each self-energy and its localization equation. Yet the integrated pair response also depends on spatial overlap, polarization, relative phase when the components are not orthogonal, and reciprocal deformation. In particular, little overlap with ordinary matter can give rare encounters even if a pattern's own sustaining coupling is not small. This is a possible route for a neutrino-like weak encounter rate; it has not been calculated for an IDWT neutrino state. The more specific neutrino hypothesis is that its effective self-coupling itself is small, making its localized oscillation frequency small. That can be tested, but low coupling cannot simply be taken to zero in (3): below the finite threshold (4), this particular scale model has no localized stationary radius. At depth five with a=C=Q=1, the threshold is B_{m fold}=1.10616. A weakly coupled but localized neutrino would therefore need either an effective coefficient still above its profile-dependent localization threshold or a different same-field support mechanism. The toy coefficient is not a physical neutrino coupling, and the observed small neutrino mass is constrained by upper bounds and oscillation differences, not a measured positive absolute value for every state. An extended neutrino pattern is another distinct possibility. If one spatial carrier obeys \omega_d=\alpha_d c/R_d, where \alpha_d is its derived dimensionless eigenvalue, then  rac{R_
u}{R_e} = rac{\alpha_
u}{\alpha_e}  rac{\omega_e}{\omega_
u}. 	ag{8} The large observed electron-to-neutrino frequency contrast could then reflect a large support ratio, a small spectral factor, or both. This relation is conditional on each state having a meaningful characteristic radius and a common propagation speed; a diffuse or differently localized neutrino need not obey that simple carrier law. An extended physical support is also distinct from the width of a neutrino wave packet during propagation. Equation (1) gives a useful limit on one simple explanation of such extension. At depth five, the magnitude of a local density-square self-contact relative to the gradient estimate is gBQ/(A R^4). Making g weaker and R larger suppresses that ratio in both ways. Thus this particular local contact cannot by itself hold a very broad, weakly coupled state. A supporting interaction with a different scale law, a suppressed gradient term, or a different spatial solution would have to be derived from the same field. This is a restriction on the fixed-profile contact model, not on the proposal that neutrinos may be much larger. An isolated composite can likewise have rest energy that differs from the sum of its components' bare rest energies because its complete interacting field contains kinetic, stress and interaction energy. This is consistent with the measured proton-mass problem and its lattice QCD decomposition, but no IDWT proton or neutron structure has been solved here. A positive interaction term alone does not determine whether binding raises or lowers the composite's total energy relative to physically isolated constituents. The proposed strong inter-quark coupling has a clear conditional test in (7). Where the two densities satisfy h(ho_i+ho_j)>g, that local mixed term is positive: the interaction contribution to a composite can exceed the sum of the isolated self terms. Where the inequality reverses it is negative. Thus the same nonlinear interaction can be attractive in one density range, helping localization, and add positive cross energy at another. The total proton or neutron mass would still require its complete spatial kinetic energy, supporting stress and field solution. The couplings and density ranges for actual quark patterns have not been derived in IDWT. The direct test of the proposal is therefore one canonically normalized same-field action with a finite, stable particle profile; the action must give its selected frequency, full positive inertial response, and reciprocal pair response without an independently fitted interaction rule. The two-term scale obstruction and three-term example identify what such a derivation must address, rather than providing the mass operator themselves. Current supported geometry Read the complete source. Exact pressure of the finite carrier Let \epsilon_n(R,G) be the smallest positive frequency of the complete component chain with diagonal entries c(n+j)/R and common adjacent coupling G. Put \gamma=GR/c. Its homogeneity gives the exact identity  oxed{-R\epsilon_R+G\epsilon_G=\epsilon.} 	ag{1} Define the radius exponent and its logarithmic gap derivative by p=- rac{R\epsilon_R}{\epsilon},\qquad p'= rac{dp}{d\log\gamma}. 	ag{2} The complete inverse of the triangular chain has positive magnitudes proportional to \gamma^{j-i}. Let its normalized left and right Perron singular vectors assign weights w_{ji}>0 to these entries, with \sum w_{ji}=1. Differentiation of its largest singular value gives p=1+\sum_{j\ge i}(j-i)w_{ji},\qquad  oxed{1<p<d,\quad p'\ge\operatorname{Var}_w(j-i)>0.} 	ag{3} The curvature bound follows by holding the maximizing singular vectors fixed while differentiating the logarithm of their positive bilinear sum. That fixed-vector expression is a log-sum-exp function, with second derivative equal to the stated variance. Allowing the maximizing vectors to move can only increase the curvature at their smooth maximum. Thus the finite carrier interpolates from a radius exponent near one to the leading simplex exponent d. This is an exact statement about the whole finite matrix, not an assumption that its leading determinant term is already accurate. The current fixed point retains a nonzero radius force For the homogeneous current, let k=\epsilon_G, s=\sqrt{k^2+\eta^2}, G=f'(k), and C=f(k)-kf'(k), with f(k)=-g\sqrt{k^2+\eta^2}. In particular,  rac{dG}{d\log R} = rac{f''G\epsilon_{GG}}{1-f''\epsilon_{GG}},\qquad  rac{\partial\lambda}{\partial g}=-s. 	ag{9} These relations agree with independent finite differences of the full fixed point at every maintained index. Differentiating only \epsilon(R,G(R)) would omit the cancellation from C. For the positive action at fixed phase charge, its standing-wave energy is \mathcal Q\lambda. Equation (8) is therefore a real remaining radius force. The current law has closed the spatial field equation on the given geometry, while leaving the size as an input. As an explicit inverse trial, choose g(R)= rac{g_0}{1+(R/R_0)^4}. 	ag{10} Equivalently, with curvature scale \kappa=1/R, this is g(\kappa)=g_0\kappa^4/(\kappa^4+\kappa_0^4), \kappa_0=1/R_0. This function and its scales are inputs; they are not derived by writing them in curvature notation. The radius equation becomes  rac{d\log\epsilon}{d\log R}=-p+q_g(p-1)=0. 	ag{11} At a stationary point its logarithmic second derivative is  rac{d^2\log\epsilon}{d(\log R)^2} =q_g'(p-1)-(q_g-1)^2p'. 	ag{12} For (10), the tested roots are radial minima. In the leading large-gap limit their common radius within a depth is  oxed{ rac{R_*}{R_0} =\left( rac{d}{3d-4}ight)^{1/4}.} 	ag{13} The exact finite-chain radii retain mode dependence. At the illustrative g_0R_0/c=1000, the depth-two controls give radii from about 1.0118R_0 to 1.0185R_0; the depth-three controls range from 0.880114R_0 to 0.880238R_0. Independent angular stresses constrain local curvature support The nonuniform force is not specific to the bounded example (10). Allow an additional rotationally invariant functional of the geometry. At a round reference metric its first variation is isotropic, so it contributes only to the constant angular channel. The spinor n=1 control has no degree-four density component and is outside this two-harmonic obstruction; the earlier explicit radial test still applies to it under its narrower assumptions. This identifies the missing kind of supporting response for the stated states: it must carry the independent angular stresses, or the spatial state and geometry must change. title: Current mass-operator candidates
summary: The finite component carrier, inverse current law and density-current simplification are candidate routes to the assigned frequencies. Their exact finite-chain and current calculations should be read with their stated geometric and normalization assumptions.
text: The finite component carrier, inverse current law and density-current simplification are candidate routes to the assigned frequencies. Their exact finite-chain and current calculations should be read with their stated geometric and normalization assumptions. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Finite chain current mass Read the complete source. A strict finite-chain ratio theorem For spatial depth d\ge2, let B_n be the real lower bidiagonal component matrix (B_n)_{jj}=n+j\quad(0\le j<d),\qquad (B_n)_{j,j-1}=b_j>0\quad(1\le j<d), \tag{1} where the b_j are independent of the harmonic label n. The current carrier has b_j=g for all j, while the linked carrier has b_j=g h_j, with one positive geometric hopping list per depth. At a fixed physical radius, the smallest singular value \epsilon_n is the positive oscillation frequency of this component carrier. Write P_{n,d}=\det B_n=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j)=d!S(n,d). \tag{2} The adjugate identity gives an exact normalization formula: \boxed{\frac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} =\frac1{\|\operatorname{adj}B_n\|_2}.} \tag{3} Conjugating the adjugate by alternating diagonal signs makes it a nonnegative lower triangular matrix A_n. Its entries are (A_n)_{ij}= \left(\prod_{a=j+1}^{i}b_a\right) \left(\prod_{a<j\,\text{or}\,a>i}(n+a)\right), \qquad i\ge j, \tag{4} with zero entries above the diagonal. Every entry is nondecreasing in n>0, and some entries increase strictly. The bottom row is positive, so the leading left and right singular vectors can be chosen strictly positive. Their bilinear characterization then makes \|A_n\|_2 strictly increasing. Equation (3) proves \boxed{\frac{\epsilon_{n_2}}{S(n_2,d)} <\frac{\epsilon_{n_1}}{S(n_1,d)} \quad\text{whenever }n_2>n_1>0.} \tag{5} This holds at every finite positive hopping strength, including different positive h_j that are common to all modes at one depth. It covers the maintained depths two, three, four, five, six and ten. Depth ten has only one maintained mode, so it has no within-depth ratio test. The theorem does not cover nonlinear self-consistent hopping that changes with n, different physical radii for particles in one sector, or an added direct mass interaction. When all b_j grow at fixed positive ratios, expanding the largest singular value of the adjugate gives \frac{\epsilon_n}{P_{n,d}} =\frac1{\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}b_j} \left[1- \frac12\left(\frac{n^2}{b_1^2} +\frac{(n+d-1)^2}{b_{d-1}^2}\right) +O(g^{-4})\right]. \tag{6} Here the remainder is at fixed n,d as the common edge scale g increases. This correction is the positive norm of internal component content in the causal parent, rather than an error from computing a tiny singular value. The unified calculation verifies (3) independently of direct singular-value decomposition on every maintained mode. For the benchmark masses already used in the mass-spectrum comparison, the observed electron-to-muon ratio is 206.76828299, while the bare simplex ratio at depth six is 3515/17=206.76470588. The latter is low by about 0.00173\%. Equation (5) means an uncorrected finite chain at one common radius and hopping strength lowers its prediction further. At dimensionless current edge g=5000, the whole-depth current ratio is 206.75506228; the linked carrier at its specified strength 10000 gives 206.76242640. These are conditional model predictions against the stated benchmark, not uncertainty-weighted experimental exclusions. An exact depth-two inverse current law on a finite branch For d=2, put P=n(n+1) and use a common positive edge G. The two singular values \epsilon<\Omega satisfy \epsilon(P,G)=\frac12 \left[\sqrt{G^2+4P+1}-\sqrt{G^2+1}\right], \qquad \partial_P\epsilon=\frac1{\sqrt{G^2+4P+1}}. \tag{7} Consider the local homogeneous generating density \rho f(k), where \rho=\Psi^\dagger\Psi, k=\Psi^\dagger K\Psi/\rho, and the same component current matrix K acts on the full form carrier. Complete variation gives the edge G=f'(k), scalar offset C=f(k)-Gk, and standing frequency \lambda=\epsilon(P,G)+C. The envelope identity is d\lambda/dP=\partial_P\epsilon along a self-consistent branch. Choose a reference edge g>0 and set \mu=(1+g^2)^{-1/2}. Requiring \lambda(P)=\mu P through a continuous finite band makes (7) imply G(P)^2=g^2-4P, \qquad k(G)=\frac G2\left(\mu-\frac1{\sqrt{1+G^2}}\right)<0. \tag{8} The following one function of the local current supplies exactly that edge and scalar offset: \boxed{ f(k(G))= \frac{\mu(g^2+G^2)}4- \frac1{2\mu}+ \frac1{2\sqrt{1+G^2}}. } \tag{9} It has f(0)=0 at G=g and direct differentiation gives f'(k)=G. Substitution into the full frequency, including C, then gives the exact identity \boxed{\lambda_n=\mu n(n+1)=2\mu S(n,2).} \tag{10} There is no particle-index coefficient in (9). At the two tested reference strengths g=500 and g=5000, all three maintained depth-two indices 76,81,95 lie in its regular branch. In that branch, G>\sqrt{(1+g^2)^{1/3}-1}, the map G\mapsto k is one-to-one and f''(k)=\frac{2}{\mu-(1+G^2)^{-3/2}}>0. \tag{11} The branch has a finite upper mode bound because G^2=g^2-4P>0, and its one-to-one condition is slightly stronger. An extension of f outside this current interval has not been specified. The exact law therefore applies to the stated finite band, not to every harmonic and not to a derived photon zero mode. Since the interaction is local and algebraic in the normalized current, it preserves the spatial eigenspace and does not change the Dirac or form principal symbol on this branch at fixed geometry. With the already specified positive squared-wave action, its homogeneous gradient supplies exact oscillating solutions at (10) and canonical phase charge \mathcal Q=2\lambda\|\Psi\|^2. Its geometric force, full field Hessian, nonlinear continuation and origin in the master action remain to be established. On the fixed round depth-two form geometry, the complete component derivative has an additional finite control. Its real and imaginary blocks are L_x=A+2f''vv^T and L_y=A, with v=(K-kI)\phi, A=H_0+GK+C, and the entire signed component space retained. At both reference strengths and all three maintained indices, every eigenvalue outside the occupied \lambda ray has absolute value greater than \lambda. Hence the rotating component quadratic stiffness is nonnegative. The separate form spatial scan retains all four form types, electric and quadrature polarizations, azimuth shifts one and three, and angular cutoffs two, four and six. Its 72-case report has positive complete projected Hessians and no resolved growing frequency; the largest growth-to-particle-frequency value is 4.40\times10^{-11}, at numerical resolution. Doubling the quadrature order changes the complete matrix by at most 3.08\times10^{-15} after scaling by the squared strength. This is finite spatial evidence, not a theorem of full field stability. The exact proportionality also makes an on-branch radial comparison possible without moving each mode to a different size. Restore the physical radius and speed through h(R)=g(R)R/c. If the same inverse current function is scaled consistently at each radius, (10) gives \lambda_n(R)=\frac{cP_{n,2}}{R\sqrt{1+h(R)^2}}. \tag{12} As one explicit curvature trial, take the previously tested bounded law g(R)=g_0/[1+(R/R_0)^4], set x=R/R_0 and \gamma=g_0R_0/c. Every n then has the same stationary radius equation 2\gamma^2x^2(x^4-1)=(1+x^4)^3. \tag{13} At \gamma=1000 and 10000, its inner roots are respectively 1.0000010000025R_0 and 1.00000001000000025R_0. The logarithmic on-branch frequency curvatures there are approximately 3.999976 and 3.99999976, both positive. A second, outer stationary root is a maximum, and the frequency tends to zero as R\to\infty. Thus the inner branch has a common local minimum, not global binding. The curvature law and its radius scale are inputs; the full field-radius mixed Hessian and supporting energy remain open. The earlier depth-two angular-stress calculation still constrains this route. If its geometry dependence enters only through a scalar curvature function and any additional first metric variation is isotropic, the electric form's degree-two, degree-four and degree-six density components cannot all be stationary. Changing the current function changes one curvature-response coefficient but does not remove that three-component incompatibility. A patterned same-field supporting response or a different spatial state is still required. The sign in (11) matters. Eliminating a linearly coupled stable same-field response coordinate from a positive quadratic potential V(x)+xk gives f_{\mathrm{eff}}''=-1/V''<0. That elementary Schur result cannot produce the positive curvature required by (9). A direct positive current contribution or a more involved retained dynamics would be needed; the exact inverse function alone does not supply it. The sign obstruction extends to any stable set of response coordinates that enters affinely in the current: the minimized energy \inf_x[V(x)+kB(x)] is an infimum of affine functions of k, so it is concave wherever finite. At a smooth positive Hessian its curvature is -B_x^T(V_{xx}+kB_{xx})^{-1}B_x\le0. This does not exclude the direct convex current term used below, a response that remains dynamical, or nonlinear coupling to k. One dimension-aware correction across all tested depths The strong-gap calculation also suggests a simpler common formula for a candidate current source. On the negative-current branch, let p_d=1+\frac2d,\qquad a_d=(d-1)^{-p_d}, \qquad f_d(k)=gk+a_dg|k|^{p_d}. \tag{14} These are functions of the spatial depth, not fitted mode coefficients. Because k\simeq-(d-1)P_{n,d}/g^d, the second term adds P_{n,d}n^2/g^{d+1} at large n, canceling the leading -P_{n,d}n^2/g^{d+1} part of (6). The finite-index terms and the next powers of 1/g remain. Full variation gives G=g\big[1-a_dp_d|k|^{p_d-1}\big],\qquad C=-a_dg(p_d-1)|k|^{p_d},\qquad \lambda_n=\epsilon_n(G)+C. \tag{15} The unified script solves (15) rather than substituting a prescribed G. The table gives largest-to-smallest spreads of \lambda_n/S(n,d) within each maintained depth. Here the reference edge is g=\text{strength}/2; both strengths are diagnostics, not measured coupling values. Depth Fixed current, strength 1000 Corrected current, 1000 Fixed current, 10000 Corrected current, 10000 2 1.012077525 1.000000097 1.000130611 1.000000000008 3 1.001281644 1.000002078 1.000012800 1.000000001074 4 1.022002484 1.000492062 1.000215327 1.000000046360 5 1.001731997 1.000004387 1.000017280 1.000000000253 6 1.004690472 1.000024970 1.000046643 1.000000002041 Depth ten has one assigned mode, so neither formula has a within-depth spread there. All 32 tested corrected fixed points have positive frequency and positive derivative of their scalar fixed-point equation. The correction improves agreement with the bare simplex rule, not with the electron-to-muon benchmark: at strength 10000 its ratio is 206.76470546, still below the benchmark 206.76828299 and slightly below the bare simplex value 206.76470588. The complete finite-component derivative has real and imaginary blocks L_x=A+2f_d''(k)vv^T,\qquad L_y=A, \quad A=H_0+GK+C,\quad v=(K-kI)\phi. \tag{16} The component-Hessian batch uses the prior report's branch locations but recomputes the fixed points at high precision before diagonalizing all signed components. In all 32 cases every eigenvalue outside the occupied ray has absolute value greater than \lambda. The smallest ratio is 1.0000001761, at depth three and strength 10000. This supplies nonnegative rotating component quadratic stiffness at fixed geometry. The separate fractional depth-two spatial scan then evaluates 72 finite form channels with the same modes, strengths, polarizations, shifts and cutoffs as the exact-law scan. Every complete projected Hessian is positive and the largest growth-to-particle-frequency value is 5.65\times10^{-11}, at numerical resolution. Neither scan establishes stability of the full spatial field or its geometry. For d>2, the fractional term is only C^1 at k=0; the second variation there needs a smooth completion. Its dimension-dependent exponent and coefficient were chosen to cancel the known finite-gap correction. Neither their master-field origin nor the required common six/ten physical frequency unit follows from this calculation. The exponent is forced within this restricted single-current correction class. At a fixed index and large reference gap, the current scales as |k|\sim(d-1)P_{n,d}g^{-d}, while the unwanted leading frequency correction scales as g^{-(d+1)}. A first nonlinear term ag|k|^p scales as g^{1-dp}; matching these powers requires p=1+2/d. Its dependence on the harmonic index also matches the leading n^{d+2} drift. Thus one universal nonzero leading power of this scalar current cannot cancel the leading drift at two different depths. In particular, an analytic current function with a quadratic first correction can do so at depth two, but its correction decays too quickly with the gap at every higher depth. This is a restriction on a current-only cancellation mechanism, not on a master action containing other field or geometric invariants. Continuous inverse branches and the six-to-ten scale The exact depth-two function suggests a general inverse problem. For a reference dimensionless edge g, set \mu_d(g)=\|\operatorname{adj}B_0(g)\|_2^{-1},\qquad P_d(n)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+j). \tag{17} The value of \mu_d is the exact zero-mode slope of the smallest singular value divided by P_d'(0). At n=0 the adjugate has only its first column nonzero, with row-i entry (d-1)!g^i/i!. Consequently the reference unit is available without a matrix decomposition: \boxed{\mu_d(g)=\frac1{(d-1)!} \left[\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\frac{g^{2i}}{(i!)^2}\right]^{-1/2}.} \tag{17a} If a differentiable branch is to have \lambda_n=\mu_d(g)P_d(n) continuously, the envelope theorem requires \partial_n\epsilon_n(G_d(n))=\mu_d(g)P_d'(n). \tag{18} Let k_d(n)=\partial_G\epsilon_n(G_d(n)). On any interval where this current is one-to-one, the one local inverse density specified by f_d(k_d(n))=\mu_d(g)P_d(n)-\epsilon_n(G_d(n))+G_d(n)k_d(n) \tag{19} obeys f_d'(k_d(n))=G_d(n). Indeed, differentiating (19) and using (18) cancels the explicit n-derivatives, leaving df_d/dn=G_d\,dk_d/dn. Its full varied standing frequency is therefore the target \mu_dP_d. This is a constructive identity conditional on an invertible branch, not a physical origin for f_d. The exact inverse function is locally smoother at zero current than the fractional approximation in (14). Let Z_d(g)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}g^{2i}/(i!)^2, w_i=g^{2i}/[(i!)^2Z_d(g)], and a_d(g)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}w_i \sum_{j=i+1}^{d-1}\frac1j>0. \tag{19a} This is the derivative of \log\|\operatorname{adj}B_n\|_2 at n=0: only the first adjugate column contributes at first order. Writing P_d'(0)=(d-1)!, implicit differentiation of (18) at (n,G)=(0,g) gives G_d'(0)=\frac{2\mu_d(g)a_d(g)P_d'(0)} {\mu_d'(g)P_d'(0)},\qquad k_d'(0)=\mu_d'(g)P_d'(0), \quad \boxed{f_d''(0^-)= \frac{2\mu_d(g)a_d(g)} {[\mu_d'(g)]^2P_d'(0)}>0.} \tag{19b} Thus each finite-gap inverse branch has a one-sided finite positive second derivative at k=0, and the implicit-function theorem gives a smooth local continuation there. This does not supply one universal function across different depths or settle regularity at zero field density, where k=j/\rho is a separate issue. The inverse-depth batch and its selected report samples each maintained depth at both reference gaps, including points between the maintained indices. All 12 sampled depth-gap branches have decreasing positive G_d(n), decreasing negative k_d(n), and positive secant estimates of f_d''. The calculation does not prove these properties between all sampled points or beyond the assigned band. For example, at g=5000, the effective edge falls from 0.9999974952g at electron index 13 to 0.9999850569g at muon index 35. The required finite-band correction divided by g|k|^{1+2/d} approaches the dimension-aware leading coefficient in (14), while retaining finite-index variation. The exact inverse function remains depth dependent. Restoring a physical radius gives the simplex frequency unit \omega_{0,d}=\frac c{R_d}\,d!\mu_d(h_d),\qquad h_d=\frac{G_dR_d}{c}, \tag{20} where G_d here denotes the reference physical edge, rather than the self-consistent edge on a particular mode. With equal dimensionless reference gaps h_6=h_{10}=500, an equal six-to-ten frequency unit requires R_{10}/R_6=8.06309677\times10^{-8}; at h=5000, it requires 8.06399097\times10^{-12}. These are exact finite-chain reference-unit ratios, close to the leading 5040/h^4. If instead the physical reference gap is shared, so h_{10}=h_6R_{10}/R_6, solving (20) gives R_{10}/R_6=0.19519654 at h_6=500 and 0.07773980 at h_6=5000. The resulting depth-ten gaps are about 97.60 and 388.70; the index-23 inverse branch exists at both sampled values. These radius ratios are conditional requirements, not predictions of a supporting geometry. The inverse-depth batch also varies the same bounded curvature trial of (13) at every maintained depth, using one g_0 and one R_0. From (17a), define the exact dimensionless elasticity q_d(h)=-\frac{d\log\mu_d}{d\log h} =\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} i h^{2i}/(i!)^2} {\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} h^{2i}/(i!)^2}. \tag{21} With x=R/R_0, h=\gamma x/(1+x^4), and q_g=4x^4/(1+x^4), the shared radial unit in (20) is stationary precisely when (q_g-1)q_d(h)=1. The inner local minima have R_{10}/R_6=0.97330930 at \gamma=1000 and 0.97330927 at \gamma=10000. Yet their ten-to-six frequency-unit ratios are only 4.84522\times10^{-8} and 4.84564\times10^{-12}. Thus this one specified common curvature trial does not supply the charged-lepton scale relation, even after the inverse current law makes the within-depth ratios exact. These are necessary local radial minima; no full field or metric stationarity has been shown. The same-field metric stress and a compatible nested geometry still have to determine the cross-depth scales. There is also an exact boundary on the tempting equal-radius, equal-dimensionless-gap option. At one radius the reference-unit ratio is (10/6)\sqrt{Z_6(h)/Z_{10}(h)}, where Z_d(h)=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}h^{2i}/(i!)^2. It decreases from 10/6 to zero as h grows: the extra terms in Z_{10}/Z_6 have powers higher than every term of Z_6, so their ratio to Z_6 increases strictly. The unit ratio equals one only at h=6.5440289929. But B_n'(n)=I, so the smallest singular value is 1-Lipschitz in n and |\partial_n\epsilon_n|\le1. Equation (18) would require slopes 320.71 for the electron index, 27129.62 for the muon index, and 1.04565\times10^6 for the tau index at that gap. Hence the exact inverse current law with its zero-mode normalization has no occupied branch at the unique equal-radius shared-gap crossing. This excludes that restricted normalization choice, not distinct sector radii or a different same-field operator. More generally, the same slope bound imposes a minimum reference gap for every occupied inverse branch. The largest necessary bound within each maintained depth is: Depth Controlling index Necessary h above 2 95 190.9974 3 17 31.1288 4 72 116.6521 5 22 35.7856 6 35 53.5700 10 23 35.2139 Each bound solves \mu_d(h)P_d'(n)=1 using (17a). It is necessary, not sufficient for existence, invertibility or stability of the branch. The exact depth-two law (9) and the approximate common rule (14) are separate inverse actions. They must not borrow the conformal Hessian or background threshold computed for the saturated current law. The joint candidate calculation keeps all of them on the same modes and records its source fingerprints and fixed-point outputs in its report. The next physical test is to derive a current term of the required sign and depth dependence from the master field, then vary the complete metric, field and supporting background together. The common-scale response bound shows that no positive common gap law with nondecreasing logarithmic falloff can make the occupied inverse-current depth-six and depth-ten frequency units agree. It states the separate depth-two condition and the nonmonotone response required to evade that bound. Density current simplification Read the complete source. The single-grade formula Use the complete 2s-by-s matrix field \Psi=(\phi,\chi)^T, where s is the partner representation rank. The matrices and currents are those of the localized polarization core: A_a=\sigma_x\otimes\alpha_a,\quad B_0=\sigma_z\otimes I_s,\quad B_1=\sigma_x\otimes\beta,\quad B_2=I_2\otimes\beta, \qquad C=\Psi^\dagger B_0\Psi,\quad J=\Psi^\dagger B_1\Psi,\quad K=\Psi^\dagger B_2\Psi. Here the Hermitian \alpha_a,\beta anticommute and square to one. Let \rho=\operatorname{Tr}\Psi^\dagger\Psi,\qquad \Delta_C=s\operatorname{Tr}C^2-(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2. For \rho>0, the simplified potential is \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \widetilde U={}&\frac{\omega}{2\rho}\left[\rho^2+ qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2\right] +m_c\operatorname{Tr}(J\beta)\\ &-\frac{s\kappa}{\rho^2} \operatorname{Tr}(\beta K)\operatorname{Tr}(JK) +\mu\|P_\perp\phi\|_F^2. \end{aligned}} \tag{1} The physical spatial principal operator remains -iA_a\partial_a. The projector P_\perp removes the scalar and physical-vector matrix components, as defined in the shape-response calculation. The common contraction choice remains q=1/(s+1). No parameter is adjusted for an individual particle. At \Psi=0, set both the potential and its source to zero. A zero scalar or polarization current in a nonzero field no longer causes any division by zero. The density denominators do not introduce a new field, a density scale, or a mass obtained by fitting the field magnitude. Compared with the cutoff construction, (1) removes the cutoff function, both uses of it, its two threshold constants, and all derivatives of the cutoff. It also removes the square root from the occupied-grade mass potential. The binding, shape and responding-frame structures still have distinct mathematical roles. Equality of the complete core derivatives At every point of the radial core, \phi_0=fI_s+i h\alpha_{\hat x},\quad \chi_0=0,\qquad c=f^2+h^2,\quad C_0=cI_s,\quad K_0^2=c^2I_s, \quad J_0=0,\quad\rho_0=sc. \tag{2} The original mass expression was F_q(C)=\sqrt{qs\operatorname{Tr}C^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}C)^2} =\sqrt{t^2+q\Delta_C},\qquad t=\operatorname{Tr}C. The normalized mass expression satisfies the exact identity \boxed{\widetilde F=\frac{\rho^2+F_q^2}{2\rho},\qquad \widetilde F-F_q=\frac{(\rho-F_q)^2}{2\rho}\ge0.} \tag{3} It is positive at every nonzero field and even under reversal of the scalar current. There is no square root in its implemented formula. On the core, F_q=\rho and \delta F_q=\delta\rho for every complete field variation. Consequently \rho-F_q=O(\epsilon^2), so the potential difference starts at fourth order. The complete Hessian and third potential variation agree. The same argument applies to a conformal-unitary lower-only core, where C=-cI_s. Equivalently, the upper-core expansion is \widetilde F=t+q\Delta_C/(2\rho)+(\rho-t)^2/(2\rho). The last term preserves the reversed-current symmetry while having zero variation through third order at the upper core. No new coefficient is introduced. For the binding term, put D=\operatorname{Tr}K^2. At the core, D=\frac{\rho^2}{s},\qquad \delta D=2c\,\delta\rho =\delta\left(\frac{\rho^2}{s}\right). \tag{4} The numerator \operatorname{Tr}(\beta K)\operatorname{Tr}(JK) vanishes there because J_0=0, and starts at first order. Replacing D by \rho^2/s changes the potential only at third order. The binding potential, full source and complete Hessian therefore agree. These are identities for arbitrary complex spinor and partner variations, including variations outside the scalar/vector shape of the core.
