The transverse-mode reduction further separates the complete finite hierarchy into one occupied coefficient block and complex-linear spatial blocks. The complete spatial linearized differential operator is consequently the same as before, with the same canonical kinetic term. Its existing local Clifford decomposition, spatial angular equations and outgoing matching controls transfer directly. This does not turn those limited stability results into a complete stability theorem. Retaining the whole finite current hierarchy The simplification is not confined to an occupied coefficient ray. For a finite set of grades, retain the canonical fields and exact symmetric-tensor splitting maps of the graded current construction. At retained order k, let R_k be the sum of the scalar-insertion currents from grades N\ge k, and define \rho_k=\sum_{N\ge k}\|\Psi_N\|_F^2,\qquad h_{k,d}=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}. The mass action becomes \boxed{ \widetilde U_{\rm mass} =\frac{\omega_{0,d}}2\sum_k h_{k,d} \left[\rho_k+ \frac{qs\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2+(1-q)(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2} {\rho_k}\right].} \tag{6} An empty active channel contributes zero. The numerator uses the partner rank s, not the generally larger size of the retained current matrix. The binding currents instead trace the oscillator indices and sum all grades; their denominator uses the total canonical density. At an isolated coherent upper core, R_k=cI_s\otimes P_{z,k} and \rho_k=sc. The auxiliary defect s\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2-(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2 and its first field variation vanish. To see the latter, write \Pi=I_s\otimes P_{z,k}. The first current variation has no (I-\Pi)-to-(I-\Pi) block: one of its two field factors is still the occupied coherent field. Hence \delta\{s\operatorname{Tr}R_k^2-(\operatorname{Tr}R_k)^2\} =2sc\operatorname{Tr}[(\Pi-I)\delta R_k]=0. Therefore \delta F_q=\delta\operatorname{Tr}R_k=\delta\rho_k, and the exact remainder (3) includes every retained oscillator component, not just partner variations inside the occupied ray. It also includes an initially empty lower grade used as a weak probe. The same Hockey-Stick sum gives \omega_{N,d}=\omega_{0,d}\sum_{k=0}^N h_{k,d} =\omega_{0,d}\binom{N+d}{d}. \tag{7} The weights in (6) remain an inverse prescription. Rewriting the action does not derive their physical carrier. An initially empty channel above the highest occupied grade has a Lipschitz source but need not have a linear derivative at its zero field. No infinite-grade differentiability or uniform infinite-grade evolution estimate is asserted here. The polarization-sensitive interaction survives For two coherent upper cores of grades N\ge M, let \rho,\sigma be their total local canonical densities and let \tau=|z^\dagger w|^2 be the overlap of their coefficient rays. Subtracting the isolated mass energies in (6) gives exactly \boxed{ V_{\rm mass} =-\omega_{0,d}q\frac{\rho\sigma}{\rho+\sigma} \sum_{k=1}^M h_{k,d}(1-\tau^k).} \tag{8} This is a nonzero polarization-sensitive interaction under the same stated conditions as the earlier current comparison. It remains independent of the larger grade. The complete initial source seen by the lower-grade probe has the same common-target identity, because every channel accessible to that probe contains the same target current and density. Its finite-overlap numerical value differs from the original square-root interaction. In the weak-probe limit the original and new laws agree at leading order, as also follows from the complete Hessian equality. Neither expression is an observed gauge vertex or an encounter rate, and subsequent particle deformations need not be identical. Setting q=0 would remove (8) entirely. On upper-only fields, (6) would then collapse to a sum of prescribed quadratic grade masses. A mass-only comparison would miss this loss of the polarization-sensitive self-interaction. Retaining the positive contraction term is therefore part of preserving the joint mass-and-coupling construction. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Common scales across particle sectors
summary: One operator must account for frequencies at all maintained depths without fitting each particle independently. Radius, gap, spatial conversion and canonical norm must be compared under the same assumptions.
text: One operator must account for frequencies at all maintained depths without fitting each particle independently. Radius, gap, spatial conversion and canonical norm must be compared under the same assumptions. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Monotone scale obstruction Read the complete source. Stationary radii and occupied-branch bounds Define the logarithmic falloff of the common edge and the elasticity of the inverse reference unit by \eta(R)=-\frac{d\log g}{d\log R},\qquad q_d(h)=-\frac{d\log\mu_d}{d\log h} =\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}j w_j, \quad w_j=\frac{h^{2j}/(j!)^2}{Z_d(h)}. \tag{3} The weights are positive and sum to one. Consequently 0<q_d(h)<d-1, and dq_d/d\log h=2\operatorname{Var}_w(j)>0. Direct differentiation of (2) gives the exact stationary-radius condition \frac{d\log u_d}{d\log R} =-1+q_d(h)(\eta-1)=0, \qquad \boxed{\eta(R_d)=1+\frac{1}{q_d(h_d)}}. \tag{4} The next derivative, evaluated at a stationary radius, is \frac{d^2\log u_d}{d(\log R)^2} =q_d(h_d)\frac{d\eta}{d\log R} -2\operatorname{Var}_w(j)(\eta-1)^2. \tag{5} A strict local minimum therefore requires positive d\eta/d\log R at that radius. This is a necessary radial condition; it says nothing about angular stress or the complete field–metric Hessian. The causal finite component chain has |\partial_n\epsilon_n|\le1. The inverse branch must therefore obey \mu_d(h)P_d'(n)<1 at every assigned index. The strongest assigned bounds in the relevant sectors are h_2>\sqrt{191^2-1}=190.99738218\quad(n=95),\qquad h_6>53.57003192\quad(n=35),\qquad h_{10}>35.21386344\quad(n=23). \tag{6} These are necessary slope bounds, not existence or stability proofs for the inverse branches. At the ten-dimensional threshold, q_{10}=8.93218749>5, and q_{10} increases with h. Equation (4) thus gives \eta(R_{10})<1.2, whereas \eta(R_6)>1.2 because q_6<5. Similarly \eta(R_2)>2 and \eta(R_6)<2 on its occupied branch. An exact bound for monotone falloff Suppose \eta(R) is nondecreasing with R across the stationary radii. The endpoint inequalities just established force the ordering R_{10}<R_6<R_2. \tag{7} Since \eta(R_{10})=1+1/q_{10}(h_{10})>10/9, integration of d\log h/d\log R=1-\eta between the first two radii gives, with r=R_{10}/R_6<1, \frac{h_{10}}{h_6}\ge r^{-1/9}. \tag{8} The same monotonicity gives \eta>1 between R_6 and R_2, so h_6>h_2>190.99738218. To turn (8) into a frequency bound, factor the highest power from (1): \mu_d(h)=\frac{h^{-(d-1)}}{\sqrt{T_d(h)}},\qquad T_d(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \left[\frac{(d-1)!}{j!}\right]^2h^{-2(d-1-j)}\ge1. \tag{9} Equations (2), (8) and (9) then imply \begin{aligned} \frac{u_{10}}{u_6} &=\frac{5040}{r}\frac{h_6^5}{h_{10}^9} \sqrt{\frac{T_6(h_6)}{T_{10}(h_{10})}}\\ &\le\frac{5040\sqrt{T_6(h_6)}}{h_6^4} <\boxed{3.788522\times10^{-6}}. \end{aligned} \tag{10} The final function decreases with h_6, so the last inequality uses only the depth-two bound (6). Even without depth two, the depth-six bound alone gives u_{10}/u_6<6.146628\times10^{-4}. The benchmark electron and tau masses and maintained counts give (m_\tau/S(23,10))/(m_e/S(13,6))\simeq1.000644. Thus a common gap law with nondecreasing logarithmic falloff cannot supply this cross-depth scale relation within the exact inverse-current reference normalization. The result covers more than one chosen power-law response, but it does not exclude a different common operator, a depth-dependent geometric conversion, or a nonmonotone supporting law. What a different common scale response would require For any common law with R_{10}<R_6, define its mean falloff on that interval by \bar\eta=\frac{1}{\log(R_6/R_{10})} \int_{R_{10}}^{R_6}\eta(R)\,d\log R. \tag{11} The exact ratio in (10), with T_{10}\ge1, shows that matching a target ratio U=u_{10}/u_6 requires \boxed{\bar\eta\le\frac{10}{9} +\frac{\log\!\left[ 5040\sqrt{T_6(h_6)}/(U h_6^4)\right]} {9\log(R_6/R_{10})}.} \tag{12} At the illustrative radius ratio R_{10}/R_6=0.2, the occupied depth-six bound limits \bar\eta to about 0.6006, and including depth two limits it to about 0.2492, for the stated benchmark U. These are necessary conditions, not a constructed supporting law. If instead \eta\ge1 throughout the interval, matching that benchmark requires R_{10}/R_6<3.7861\times10^{-6} when depth two is included. The stationary endpoints have \eta(R_{10})>10/9 and \eta(R_6)>1.2, while (12) demands a mean below 10/9 at every finite radius ratio. A smooth successful common law with these ordered radii must dip below 10/9 between them. If both stationary radii are strict local minima, (5) makes \eta rise locally at both endpoints. The intervening dip then requires at least one local maximum and one local minimum of \eta. Deriving such scale dependence from one stable same-field action is a specific remaining task. A nonmonotone control and its competing branch The obstruction depends on monotonicity. To test its scope with one common law across all six maintained depths, consider the positive but nonmonotone reference edge g(R)=g_0\frac{[1+(R/10R_0)^4]^{B/4}} {[1+(R/R_0)^4]^{1.15/4} [1+(R/CR_0)^4]^{(B+1.2)/4}}. The three transitions, at R_0, 10R_0 and CR_0, make \eta(R) rise, dip and rise again. This is an inverse diagnostic, not a field-derived supporting law. For each stated trial choice of C and depth-two reference gap, the common amplitude \gamma=g_0R_0/c is set by that gap at its radial minimum, then one common shape parameter B is fitted to the benchmark u_{10}/u_6\simeq1.000644. No parameter is assigned to an individual mode. The six-depth fit finds: h_2 C B \gamma R_{10}/R_6 h_{10} Minimum \eta between radii Outer depth-ten unit / depth-six unit 220 30 1.987234 91.5040 0.070617 79.571 −0.3357 7.80\times10^{-7} 500 30 2.355061 144.560 0.068637 125.563 −0.6279 3.00\times10^{-8} 500 100 1.072244 165.062 0.023820 143.867 0.1086 2.62\times10^{-8} The selected report records the stationary radius and gap at every depth. All selected radii are strict local minima of the reference frequency unit, and every assigned mode passes the necessary singular-slope bound. Direct high-precision singular-matrix roots exist at all 16 assigned modes; sampled intermediate points retain decreasing edge and current, as required for a convex inverse density on those samples. This verifies discrete inverse-branch feasibility more strongly than the slope bound, but it does not prove regularity or stability on the whole interval. The first two trial shapes make g rise with radius across part of the interval. The third keeps g strictly decreasing everywhere: for B<1.15 and C>10, its first positive sigmoid in \eta is at least the middle sigmoid, so 1.15\sigma(R/R_0)-B\sigma(R/10R_0)>0, where \sigma(y)=y^4/(1+y^4); the final term is also positive. Thus a negative \eta is a feature of the first two fits, not a general requirement of the cross-depth unit match. The third uses a wider separation between its positive scale transitions. Its \eta has a local maximum at 3.191R_0 and a local minimum at 28.733R_0, satisfying the two-turning-point requirement from the stationary-frequency calculation. The fit also produces two local depth-ten minima. The small-radius minimum carries the fitted frequency unit, while the outer minimum has the far smaller unit shown in the table. The frequency curve alone has no rule selecting the inner branch. Its outer barrier is also not a complete particle energy barrier: the supporting field's energy and metric stress remain absent. The fitted equality is therefore an existence control within the inverse reference equations, not a prediction of the observed tau mass. The first fit exposes a further spatial constraint. At h_2=220, the 36-case depth-two form scan finds no resolved growth for n=76,81, but all 12 finite electric and quadrature controls at n=95 have growth around 0.862 times the particle frequency. The value is stable across angular cutoffs two, four and six and two azimuth shifts. Positive projected Hessian eigenvalues in those cases do not remove the gyroscopic growth. A one-channel gap scan places its disappearance between h_2=220 and 240 for the electric, shift-one, cutoff-six control. That scan does not establish the exact boundary for all spatial perturbations. For both fits at h_2=500, the existing 36-case exact depth-two scan already tests the same inverse-current field state at that gap and passes its finite form controls. The new radius law does not alter that fixed-metric matrix, but its own field–metric variations have not been included. The nonmonotone fit still needs a master-field source, a selection rule among its radii, compatible nested spatial states, positive complete joint stability and physical inertial normalization. A positive rational scale control The logarithmic falloff can have the required two turning points with ordinary positive power sums, without the fractional exponents in the preceding example. Take one shared reference law \boxed{\frac{g(R)}{g_0} =\frac{1+(R/bR_0)^4} {[1+(R/R_0)^4][1+(R/CR_0)^4]}.} Its logarithmic falloff is \eta=4[\sigma(R/R_0)-\sigma(R/bR_0)+\sigma(R/CR_0)], where \sigma(y)=y^4/(1+y^4). Since 1<b<C, the first difference and final term are strictly positive: g(R) decreases at every positive radius. The first bump can place the depth-ten stationary minimum before the middle dip, while depths two through six use the later rise. This is one function across all depths. When the outer transition is well separated, that first bump peaks at 4\tanh(\log b). Choosing b=1.34 puts its peak near 1.138, between the occupied depth-ten stationary falloff near 1.111 and the depth-six value above 1.2. This explains the separate radius branches but is still an inverse choice. In the rational-law batch, set b=1.34, fix the depth-two gap at h_2=500, and fit the common outer scale C to the benchmark six-to-ten unit ratio. The resulting C=18.00753138 and \gamma=179.0387654 give R_{10}/R_6=0.07325, h_{10}=116.6397, and u_{10}/u_6=1.00064435538. All six selected radii are local minima; the exact inverse singular-matrix roots exist at every assigned mode and sampled intermediate points. The two falloff turning points occur at 1.1576R_0 and 4.6846R_0, with the latter at \eta=0.03655>0. The full values and source hashes are in the selected report. The four-point robustness batch varies b from 1.332 to 1.36, refitting only C each time. All four retain the local six-depth reference checks and two depth-ten minima; C ranges from 17.740 to 18.734. This algebraic law is simpler than the previous fractional-power trial and identifies a concrete source-to-stiffness shape: J=1+(R/bR_0)^4 and D=[1+(R/R_0)^4][1+(R/CR_0)^4]. No master-field reduction has produced these functions or the required direct convex current interaction. The inner depth-ten unit still competes with an outer local minimum whose unit relative to depth six is 4.84\times10^{-8}; its selection and supporting energy remain unresolved. Matching the benchmark by fitting C is a conditional existence test, not a mass prediction. For this rational law g(R)\sim R^{-4} at large radius, so h(R)\to0 and u_d(R)\sim cd/R\to0. Its local minima are not global radial binding states without the complete supporting energy. Curvature frequency scale Read the complete source. Restore the lengths already present in the carrier Let R_d be the tangential length parameter and L_d the normal profile's length unit. These are ordinary spatial lengths, common to the particle modes at one depth. Write the dimensionless normal coordinate as y=x/L_d. The physical coefficient in the curvature-moment rule has inverse-length units: h_{\rm phys}=\frac{z_{\rm phys}B_{\rm phys}}2 =\frac1{L_d}h(y). \tag{1} With a common wave speed c and a dimensionless physical coefficient g_d, the frequency matrix therefore has diagonal entries c(\beta+j_z)/R_d and adjacent entries cg_dh_l/L_d. Equivalently, \boxed{\gamma_d=g_dR_d/L_d,\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\frac c{R_d}\lambda_{n,d}(\gamma_d).} \tag{2} The normal separation parameter is R_d/L_d. This is a restoration of the existing parameters, not an additional adjustable length for each particle. In the large-hopping limit the common unit is \boxed{\omega_{0,d}= \frac{c\,d!}{g_d^{d-1}\prod_lh_l} \frac{L_d^{d-1}}{R_d^d},\qquad \omega_{n,d}=\omega_{0,d}\binom{n+d-1}{d} [1+O(\gamma_d^{-2})].} \tag{3} Thus a measured common frequency unit constrains a combination of the lengths, coupling and computed spatial integrals. It does not determine all of them separately. The geometric factor is fixed by the operator, and cannot be dropped when comparing inferred sizes across depths. Conditional radius requirements are computable For illustration, retain a common L and g across the two depths but allow their radii to differ. Put r=R_{10}/R_6. Then \gamma_{10}=r\gamma_6, and the positive-sign anchor equation is \boxed{ \frac{\lambda_{23,10}(r\gamma_6)} {r\lambda_{13,6}(\gamma_6)} =\frac{S(23,10)}{S(13,6)}.} \tag{7} The small singular value strictly decreases as positive hopping grows: the nonnegative absolute triangular inverse increases entrywise. Thus the left side of (7) decreases from infinity to zero with r, giving a unique conditional radius ratio at each stated \gamma_6. The leading expression is r_{\rm lead}= \left[\frac{10!}{6!} \frac{\prod_lh_l^{(6)}}{\prod_lh_l^{(10)}} \frac1{\gamma_6^4}\right]^{1/10}. \tag{8} Full finite-matrix solutions give: \gamma_6 Required R_{10}/R_6 Resulting \gamma_{10} 100 0.23713045 23.7130 1000 0.10320217 103.2022 10000 0.04125312 412.5312 100000 0.01642733 1642.7334 These values impose the assigned anchor ratio under the extra common L,g assumption. They are not a forward derivation of actual particle sizes. They also do not remove the finite within-depth correction: at \gamma_6=10000, the computed muon/electron ratio is about 1.10\times10^{-5} below its ideal simplex ratio. Matching one cross-depth anchor cannot silently eliminate that remaining correction. The physical kernel must still determine the shared lengths and coupling and satisfy the normal-complement control needed for the projected spectrum. This dimensional accounting also leaves the supporting state's energy and coherent motion unresolved. Neither issue is a mass–frequency separation. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: The competing outer depth-ten branch
summary: The extra depth-ten branch is a candidate state of the same harmonic, not an established particle identification. Its local frequency, retained same-field response and shifted-radius checks are useful even though one fitted law does not reproduce every known sector.
text: The extra depth-ten branch is a candidate state of the same harmonic, not an established particle identification. Its local frequency, retained same-field response and shifted-radius checks are useful even though one fitted law does not reproduce every known sector. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Light tau branch and coupling Read the complete source. The frequency and its origin At fixed depth ten, the common simplex factor cancels between the two radii. With h=g(R)R/c, the exact ratio is \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{out}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{in}}} =\frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R_{\mathrm{out}}} \sqrt{\frac{Z_{10}(h_{\mathrm{in}})}{Z_{10}(h_{\mathrm{out}})}}, \qquad Z_{10}(h)=\sum_{j=0}^{9}\frac{h^{2j}}{(j!)^2}. \tag{1} For the fitted positive rational law with b=1.34, C=18.00753138, and h_2=500, the inner branch is at R_{\mathrm{in}}/R_0=1.06721483, h_{\mathrm{in}}=116.63970; the outer branch is at R_{\mathrm{out}}/R_0=14.18017176, h_{\mathrm{out}}=568.77005. Equation (1) gives \omega_{\mathrm{out}}/\omega_{\mathrm{in}} =4.84170206\times10^{-8}. Calibrating the fitted inner branch to the 1776.93 MeV tau benchmark gives an outer equivalent mass-energy of 86.03366 eV and a cyclic frequency of 2.08028\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{Hz}. These are conditional values inherited from the fit, not an independent experimental mass measurement. The large suppression has an exact spectral origin. Writing Z_{10}(h)=h^{18}T_{10}(h)/(9!)^2, where T_{10}(h)\to1 at large h, equation (1) becomes \frac{\omega_{\mathrm{out}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{in}}} =\frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R_{\mathrm{out}}} \left(\frac{h_{\mathrm{in}}}{h_{\mathrm{out}}}\right)^9 \sqrt{\frac{T_{10}(h_{\mathrm{in}})} {T_{10}(h_{\mathrm{out}})}}. \tag{2} Thus a reference-gap increase of a factor about 4.88 is amplified by the ninth power. The outer radius is about 13.29 times the inner radius. The calculation does not establish that either radius is realized by a physical tau structure. An independent shape grid also varies b and C separately by \pm0.5\% around the reference values, retaining only the depth-two gap anchor and not refitting C to the inner tau/electron unit. All nine trials retain two depth-ten reference-frequency minima; the outer one has positive radial frequency curvature and passes the necessary occupied-slope condition. Its energy after calibrating each inner branch to the tau benchmark spans 72.16–103.00 eV. The inner tau/electron unit ratio simultaneously ranges from 0.8353 to 1.1922 times its benchmark. The grid report therefore supports local branch existence, while the narrow 86.03348–86.03414 eV range under correlated refits is not an unfitted mass prediction. This finite grid does not establish full spatial stability or the physical probability of the state. A two-channel route to the radius law The fitted rational shape is exactly a sum of two positive response terms. Put x=(R/R_0)^4, a=b^{-4}, and c=C^{-4}. Then \frac{1+ax}{(1+x)(1+cx)} =\frac{w_s}{1+x}+\frac{w_l}{1+cx}, \qquad w_s=\frac{1-a}{1-c},\quad w_l=\frac{a-c}{1-c}. \tag{2a} Both weights are positive for the fitted 1<b<C. At b=1.34, w_s=0.68985012 and w_l=0.31014988. The two terms contribute almost equally to the gap at the inner radius, whereas the long-scale term supplies 99.99238% at the outer radius. The two-channel audit checks the identity and the branch fractions for all four fitted shapes in its selected report. This makes a long-scale same-field response a concrete candidate source of the extra branch; it does not derive that response. For example, let two retained same-field amplitudes q_i have positive stiffnesses D_s=1+x, D_l=1+cx, and local energy D_iq_i^2/2-J_iq_i+\beta_iq_i k, where k is the normalized current. Choosing J_i=\beta_i=\sqrt{\gamma w_i} and eliminating these amplitudes gives F_{\rm eff}(k,R)=F_0(k) -\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)} +\gamma\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}k -\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}k^2. \tag{2b} The coefficient of the linear current is exactly the fitted gap g(R)=\gamma[w_s/D_s+w_l/D_l], with \gamma=179.0387654 for the reference fit. However, the eliminated response subtracts g(R) from current curvature, so the direct same-field contribution must satisfy F_0''>g(R) on a convex occupied branch. The conditional lower bounds are 109.294 and 40.110 in the source units at the inner and outer radii. This is a necessary sign test, not a derivation of F_0. The eliminated response also contributes to the radial energy. At a fixed current k, its derivative is \left.\partial_R E_{\rm response}\right|_k =2\gamma(1-k)^2R^3\left[ \frac{w_s}{(1+R^4)^2} +\frac{cw_l}{(1+cR^4)^2}\right]>0, \tag{2c} in units where R_0=1. At k=0, the audit obtains 56.898 at the inner and 1.571 at the outer radius; the occupied currents change these values only slightly. The frequency minima therefore do not establish stationarity of the complete energy. Other same-field terms and shape response must balance this radial stress while preserving the occupied spectrum. The fourth power, channel scales, source amplitudes, canonical kinetic term and such a balancing term still require derivation from the master field. The preceding expression is an uncompleted response per canonical norm. Its zero-current offset would shift the particle frequency by -54.647 at the inner radius and -20.055 at the outer radius in c/R_0 units for the equal-source choice. The corresponding occupied frequencies are only 5.4732\times10^{-5} and 2.6500\times10^{-12}. This offset cannot be left out of the mass-operator calculation. A completed-square same-field action One homogeneous retained-mode alternative includes the zero-current normalization in a positive square. Per canonical norm, consider \mathcal E=\langle H_0(R)\rangle+F_0(k) +\sum_{i=s,l}\left[ \frac{D_i(R)}2\left(q_i-\frac{J_i}{D_i(R)}\right)^2 +\beta_iq_i k\right], \quad J_i=\sqrt{r\gamma w_i},\quad \beta_i=\sqrt{\gamma w_i/r},\quad r>0. \tag{2d} Here q_i are retained modes of the same field, rather than independent particles. Their kinetic terms and actual spatial profiles have not been specified. Eliminating their static values q_i=(J_i-\beta_i k)/D_i gives F_{\rm eff}(k,R)=F_0(k)+g(R)k -\frac{g(R)}{2r}k^2, \qquad g(R)=\gamma\sum_i\frac{w_i}{D_i(R)}. \tag{2e} The square cancels the uncompleted response's zero-current frequency offset and its associated zero-current radial stress. Its Schur contribution to current curvature is -g/r, so the direct term must supply F_0''=f_{\rm target}''+g/r on an occupied inverse branch. Without square completion, reducing r lowers the offset but increases the negative curvature: channel by channel, 2|E_{0,i}||F_{i,kk}|=g_i^2. For general two-channel coefficients, Cauchy's inequality gives 2|E_0||F_{kk}|\ge g^2. The same-action batch tests whether one radius-independent F_0(k) could at least match both sampled inverse-current bands. It maps target values and derivatives to F_0 at harmonics 5, 20, 22.5, 23, 23.5, 26 and 30 on each radius, plus F_0(0)=F_0'(0)=0. All adjacent secant slopes lie between their endpoint derivatives for tested r=0.001,0.01,1,100 and the zero-current matching ratio below. The selected report records the samples. These are necessary convex-interpolation checks, not a constructed smooth F_0, a full spatial state, or a test at the other depths. The same proposed action has a radial force test. At fixed canonical norm and on the stationary component field, its derivative is \partial_R\mathcal E =-\frac{\epsilon/R-Gk}{R} +g'(R)k-\frac{g'(R)}{2r}k^2, \qquad G=g(R)-\frac{g(R)}r k+F_0'(k), \tag{2f} where \epsilon is the dimensionless finite-chain singular frequency and G is the physical current edge. At the inherited inner and outer radii, this derivative is positive for all five tested positive r. At r=1 it is 3.248\times10^{-6} and 4.749\times10^{-16} in the corresponding c/R_0 energy-per-norm units. This completed-square action therefore does not make either inherited radius an exact stationary state. At r=1 the outer residual is small relative to its frequency, leaving a nearby shifted equilibrium possible; the complete field, radius and metric Hessian has not been solved. There is a sharper condition if the exact inverse current law must continue smoothly from each branch to k=0. One radius-independent direct term must then have the same F_0''(0) at both radii: f_{{\rm inv},\mathrm{in}}''(0)+\frac{g_{\rm in}}r =f_{{\rm inv},\mathrm{out}}''(0)+\frac{g_{\rm out}}r. \tag{2g} The exact zero-current inverse formula gives physical curvatures 2.31215\times10^{12} and 2.69108\times10^{17} in c/R_0 units. Equation (2g) fixes r=2.570865\times10^{-16}, rather than leaving the source/current amplitude ratio free. Its sampled convexity inequalities still pass. But its fixed-norm radial forces at the inherited radii become 4.548\times10^6 and 2.162\times10^{-9}, respectively. Thus the simple completed-square action cannot simultaneously keep the inherited radii stationary and realize one smooth zero-current direct law under that full inverse continuation. A shifted solution, additional same-field stress, or a law that applies only on occupied finite bands remains possible. The magnitude is a diagnostic in this action's chosen normalization, not a measured force. The action is a candidate construction with specific force and spatial tests remaining, not a derived physical mass operator. A local continuation of this action finds nearby stationary radii with positive restricted radial curvature on both depth-ten branches. Its scalar-current angular controls pass under an assumed nonnegative retained-mode gradient stiffness; the complete polarized field and geometric spatial variations remain open. Absolute spectrum across the maintained sectors The rational law was fitted to the depth-six electron and inner depth-ten tau frequency units; the other depths were only checked for local roots and necessary inverse slopes. To test the candidate as one common mass operator, fix the remaining physical scale c/R_0 with the observed electron mass-energy. With no further depth-dependent conversion, every assigned mode then has the definite prediction m_{n,d}^{\rm trial}c^2 =m_ec^2\frac{u_d}{u_6} \frac{S(n,d)}{S(13,6)},\qquad S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d}. \tag{3} The selected whole-spectrum calculation records all 16 maintained mode values under this one calibration. Representative results are: Assigned mode Trial mass-energy Observed comparison Depth two, W index 76 21.10 TeV 80.369 GeV PDG Depth five, neutrino index 10 5.194 MeV Sub-eV laboratory scale; effective electron-neutrino mass <0.45 eV at 90% confidence KATRIN Depth six, muon index 35 105.65655 MeV About 105.658 MeV Depth ten, tau index 23, inner radius 1776.93 MeV Fitted input Depth ten, tau index 23, outer radius 86.03366 eV Competing conditional branch The W discrepancy is over two orders of magnitude at the selected h_2=500 fit, and the neutrino discrepancy is much larger, so the common rational law with this reference normalization fails the full assigned mass spectrum. The neutrino bound cited is a measurement of an effective electron-neutrino mass, whereas the maintained depth-five assignments are model labels. The KATRIN result is an upper bound on an effective electron-neutrino mass, not a measured nonzero value or a lower bound on any neutrino mass. The MeV trial values are incompatible with treating these assigned modes as the observed light neutrinos without an additional, derived mixing or suppression mechanism. A dimension-dependent spatial conversion could change (3), but it would need to follow from the common field and geometric operator. Assigning a new fitted conversion to each depth would not repair this candidate as a predictive law for all known assignments. These comparisons do not exclude a separate, possibly unseen exotic state. They only limit the claim that this one fitted law also explains the named W and neutrino states. The outer depth-ten branch remains a mathematical solution with no derived selection or detection channel. The same script refits C at depth-two reference gaps 220, 300, 500, and 1000 with b=1.34. Across those four trials, the lightest assigned depth-five neutrino ranges from 2.286 to 10.389 MeV, and the assigned W from 0.791 to 337.6 TeV. This finite scan shows the failure is not confined to h_2=500. It is not a proof that no other common spatial law or normalization can work. The h_2=220 trial also has the independently observed depth-two n=95 finite spatial growth, so lowering that gap is not a verified stability remedy. Occupied branch and local controls The reproducible batch checks four neighboring shared-law shapes b=1.332,1.34,1.35,1.36. For each shape the one outer scale C is refitted to the same inner tau/electron unit ratio, so this variation is a local fit sensitivity test, not an independent prediction. In the selected report, the conditional outer mass-energy ranges from 86.03348 to 86.03414 eV. All four outer points are strict local minima of the reference frequency curve and pass the assigned necessary occupied-slope inequality. At b=1.34, exact finite-chain inverse roots exist at sampled harmonics 1, 5, 20, 23, 26, and 30 on the outer branch. Their edge and negative normalized current decrease in order, as required by the sampled convex inverse-current construction. At the assigned index 23, the outer normalized current is -5.9474\times10^{-13}. The inner branch current is -4.5331\times10^{-6}. The sampled controls do not prove invertibility across every intermediate point. The inner depth-ten frequency minimum and its following maximum occur at 1.0672R_0 and 1.2557R_0. That maximum is only 1.02684 times the inner minimum. The second minimum is at 14.1802R_0, with a much lower frequency. This maximum is not a calculated particle decay barrier. The complete radius energy, supporting field and collective radius inertia have not been supplied. Changing b over the four cases changes the frequency maximum over the inner minimum from 1.00222 to 1.14515, even though the outer frequency remains close under refitting. The necessary occupied-slope limit for the assigned depth-ten index is h>35.21386344. Along the outward side of the b=1.34 outer branch, the shared law reaches this limit at R/R_0=54.72550. Thus the inverse occupied branch is not established out to arbitrarily large radius. The reference-frequency curve beyond this limit cannot be interpreted as the same physical particle branch without a different current continuation. Neither the local outer minimum nor this finite domain proves global binding. The complete signed finite-component matrix at fixed geometry gives the nearest other component magnitude divided by the occupied frequency as 1.02401 for the inner branch and 1.000928 for the outer branch. Both exceed one. The local inverse-current curvature is positive on the sampled branch, so its rank-one real-component correction also has the favorable sign. This is a finite component control only: the outer branch has not passed a depth-ten spatial or full field–metric stability calculation. Shifted tau action stability Read the complete source. Action and local continuation In units R_0=c=1, write D_s=1+R^4, D_l=1+C^{-4}R^4, and g(R)=\gamma\sum_{i=s,l}w_i/D_i. The candidate energy per canonical norm is \mathcal E=\langle H_0(R)\rangle+F_0(k) +\sum_i\left[\frac{D_i(R)}2\left(q_i-\frac{J_i}{D_i(R)}\right)^2+\beta_iq_i k\right], \quad J_i=\sqrt{r\gamma w_i},\quad \beta_i=\sqrt{\gamma w_i/r}. The q_i are retained modes of the same field in this candidate, and r>0 is their source-to-current amplitude ratio. Static elimination gives q_i=(J_i-\beta_i k)/D_i and F_{\rm eff}(k,R)=F_0(k)+g(R)k-\frac{g(R)}{2r}k^2, \qquad G=\partial_k F_{\rm eff}=F_0'(k)+g(R)-\frac{g(R)}r k. At each inherited branch current k_0, the calculation supplies a local quadratic Taylor germ of F_0. Its value and slope reproduce the prior inverse branch. Its curvature is the finite secant estimate from harmonics 22.5 and 23.5, plus g(R_0)/r; this is an input, not an independently derived current law. At each trial radius the ten-component singular vector supplies k self-consistently with G. The frequency includes the complete eliminated-mode scalar offset, rather than only the lowest singular value divided by radius. The fixed-norm force after this component and retained-mode response is \partial_R\mathcal E=-\frac{\epsilon/R-Gk}{R} +g'(R)k-\frac{g'(R)}{2r}k^2. Solving this equation near each inherited radius gives the following local results. Frequencies and curvatures use the common c/R_0 units and the stated canonical norm. r Branch Shifted R/R_0 Change from inherited radius Particle frequency Radial curvature 0.01 Inner 1.05638450945 −1.01482% 5.47132994\times10^{-5} 3.32019460\times10^{-4} 0.01 Outer 14.17892438901 −0.00879661% 2.64995665\times10^{-12} 3.80719019\times10^{-13} 1 Inner 1.05672321555 −0.983084% 5.47145140\times10^{-5} 3.30340813\times10^{-4} 1 Outer 14.17892438915 −0.00879661% 2.64995665\times10^{-12} 3.80719019\times10^{-13} The force residuals are below 10^{-55} in the high-precision solve. Centered force derivatives at relative radius steps 10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6} agree within about 1.4\times10^{-7} relative. Positive curvature establishes a local minimum only along this self-consistent radius and finite-component path. Component and spatial controls At the shifted radii, F_0''-g/r remains positive: approximately 3.86\times10^4 and 4.16\times10^9 for inner and outer branches at r=0.01, with similarly positive values at r=1. The nearest other signed finite-component frequency magnitude, divided by the occupied frequency magnitude, exceeds one: about 1.0236 inner and 1.000928 outer. This is a fixed-geometry component-separation diagnostic, not a dynamical spatial-stability theorem. For a restricted spatial test, suppose the retained same-field amplitudes have a nonnegative gradient stiffness \kappa. On a round radius-R nine-sphere of angular directions in ten ordinary spatial dimensions, a scalar harmonic of degree \ell has \lambda_\ell=\ell(\ell+8)/R^2. The scalar-current Schur curvature in this stipulated extension is \mathcal C_\ell=F_0''-\frac{\gamma}{r} \sum_{i=s,l}\frac{w_i}{D_i+\kappa\lambda_\ell}. For \kappa\ge0, \mathcal C_\ell\ge\mathcal C_0=F_0''-g/r>0, so this particular scalar-current direction passes for every angular degree under the assumed positive gradient law. Direct evaluations at \ell=0,1,2,4,8 and \kappa=0,1 confirm the formula at both shifted radii and both tested r. The gradient law and round angular metric are model inputs; no ten-dimensional physical spinor or polarization carrier has been supplied for this completed-square action. Its full field, angular, metric, and nonlinear stability therefore remain unknown. Adding the two shifted current points to the earlier 15 sampled knots preserves the necessary convex Hermite secant inequalities for a radius-independent F_0 at each tested r. The smallest numerical margin is about 1.21\times10^{-7}. These are finite necessary compatibility checks. The inner and outer Taylor germs were specified separately, and no single smooth global F_0 has been constructed or shown to produce both states. In particular, the stronger requirement of a shared smooth exact inverse law down to zero current has a different, highly constrained r, which this continuation did not solve. The executed script and selected report give the self-consistent roots, force residuals, curvature step checks, finite-component separations, convexity controls, and spatial scalar-current values. A complete test needs one global direct current law and a spatial carrier for this same action, including polarized field and geometry variations. Until then, the outer branch is a supported local possibility in a restricted action, not an established particle or derived physical mass operator. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Spatial and dynamical stability
summary: Stability claims depend on which field, polarization and geometric perturbations were varied. The current-action component and angular results and the conformal background calculation belong to specified, distinct actions.
text:
Stability claims depend on which field, polarization and geometric perturbations were varied. The current-action component and angular results and the conformal background calculation belong to specified, distinct actions. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Spatial current stability Read the complete source. The positive Hessian retains the full derivative At a stationary field F[\phi]=\lambda\phi, let L=DF[\phi] be the real self-adjoint derivative. Homogeneity gives D^2F_\phi(h,\phi)=0. Symmetry of the third variation of the generating functional then removes the extra term from the second variation of the positive potential:  oxed{  rac12\delta^2\|F\|^2[h,h]=\|Lh\|^2. } 	ag{5} The identity also has a directional proof that covers the nodal fields used here. The local nonlinear map N_0=F-H_0 is globally Lipschitz for each fixed \eta>0. Indeed, \|K\|=1, and its normalized current direction obeys \|(K-kI)\Psi\|^2/ho\le1. Equation (12) of the current construction gives the uniform local bound \|DN_0\|\le g(1+\eta+2/\eta). 	ag{5a} Continuity at zero extends the Lipschitz estimate along any straight field segment, including one that crosses the origin. If the background field is nonzero almost everywhere and h lies in the domain of H_0, dominated convergence then gives F(\phi+th)=F(\phi)+tLh+o_{L^2}(t). The highest-weight zero sets have zero volume, so they satisfy this hypothesis. The generating functional has the directional expansion E_1(\phi+th)=E_1(\phi) +2t\operatorname{Re}\langle F(\phi),hangle +t^2\operatorname{Re}\langle Lh,hangle+o(t^2). 	ag{5b} Homogeneity gives E_1(\phi+th)=\operatorname{Re}\langle\phi+th,F(\phi+th)angle. Subtracting t\operatorname{Re}\langle h,F(\phi+th)angle from (5b) cancels its quadratic term. Consequently the remainder in F, paired with \phi, is o(t^2). At F(\phi)=\lambda\phi, expanding \|F(\phi+th)\|^2 now proves (5) directly. This establishes the required directional quadratic form for the stated nodal backgrounds. It does not make the local map differentiable at the origin, prove a uniform Frechet Hessian on the full field space, or establish global nonlinear well-posedness. For a normalized component ray, write v=(K-kI)\phi. The local real current part is Nh=2f''v\operatorname{Re}(v^\dagger h),\qquad  oxed{N^2=2f''\|v\|^2N.} 	ag{6} The spatial normalized eigensection is included in the local direction in (6). Its pointwise norm has been divided out, so the component \|v\| is constant on the background. Let P be an orthogonal angular projection invariant under the base spatial operator A=H_0+GK+C, and set N_P=PNP. Projecting the square of the full derivative gives the exact identity  oxed{ PL^2P=(A_P+N_P)^2+ \underbrace{2f''\|v\|^2N_P-N_P^2}_{\displaystyle (QNP)^*(QNP)\ \ge0}, \qquad Q=I-P. } 	ag{7} Thus the omitted angular square is available without truncating the nonlinear source first. Its positivity does not mean it is negligible. Squaring A_P+N_P alone would be a different calculation. For a rotating positive-frequency background, the normal and conjugate perturbations combine into \eta. Let \Sigma be plus the identity on the normal part and minus the identity on its conjugate. The complete projected squared operator \mathcal K=PL^2P gives \ddot\eta-2i\omega\Sigma\dot\eta+ (\mathcal K-\omega^2I)\eta=0. 	ag{8} For \eta\propto e^{-i\Omega t}, the actual frequency pencil is \mathcal K-(\Omega I+\omega\Sigma)^2. Positivity of \mathcal K alone is insufficient to infer stability of (8). The numerical test retains the gyroscopic term and solves this pencil. Actual spinor angular channels at every depth For b=(d-1)/2, choose z=x_1+ix_2, q=|z|^2, and a constant spinor with \Gamma_u\zeta=0, u=e_1+ie_2. Convenient raw fields are F_l=z^m q^l\zeta,\qquad G_l=z^{m+1}q^l\Gamma_x\Gamma_{ ar u}\zeta. 	ag{9} The actual shifted spatial Dirac operator acts as  egin{aligned} BF_l&=(m+b+2l)F_l-lG_{l-1},\ BG_l&=4(m+1+l)F_l-(m+b+2+2l)G_l. \end{aligned} 	ag{10} For m\ge0, the finite invariant span contains F_0,\ldots,F_L and G_0,\ldots,G_{L-1}. For m=-M<0, use F_M,\ldots,F_{M+L} and G_{M-1},\ldots,G_{M+L-1}. The latter expressions are regular fields: for example, z^{-M}q^M= ar z^M. The coefficient that would leave the span at its lower end is zero in (10). The probability-volume Gram entries are  egin{aligned} \langle F_i,F_jangle&=b\,\mathrm B(m+i+j+1,b),\ \langle F_i,G_jangle&=2b\,\mathrm B(m+i+j+2,b),\ \langle G_i,G_jangle&=4b\,\mathrm B(m+i+j+2,b). \end{aligned} 	ag{11} The normal current projector sends F_l to itself and G_l to 2F_{l+1}. The anomalous part pairs an azimuth m with m'=2n-m for a background z^n\zeta. The three corresponding cross entries are b\,\mathrm B(n+i+j+1,b),\qquad 2b\,\mathrm B(n+i+j+2,b),\qquad 4b\,\mathrm B(n+i+j+3,b). 	ag{12} These are actual spatial inner products, not independent copies of a scalar mode. Orthogonalization uses exact high-precision Gram matrices. Stable evaluation uses Jacobi polynomials in a moving two-component frame inside the physical spinor bundle. It does not reduce the sphere's dimension or assert that the complete spinor rank is two. A linear fast gap for the entire angular spectrum The linear parent admits a bound independent of angular degree. First remove the bounded diagonal geometric shifts and write T_0=xI+GJ, for any real spatial eigenvalue x. With e_d the last coordinate vector, T_0^\dagger T_0=A_0-G^2e_de_d^\dagger,\qquad A_0=(x^2+G^2)I+xG(J+J^\dagger). 	ag{13} The eigenvalues of the tridiagonal matrix A_0 are x^2+G^2+2xG\cos[r\pi/(d+1)], for 1\le r\le d. Their smallest value is at least G^2\sin^2[\pi/(d+1)]: complete the square in |x|-G\cos[\pi/(d+1)]. Rank-one interlacing in (13) then bounds the second-smallest singular value of T_0. The actual diagonal geometric shift has norm c(d-1)/(2R). Restoring it, and then the scalar current offset C, gives  oxed{\operatorname{gap}_{m linear,fast}\ge G\sin\! rac{\pi}{d+1}- rac{c(d-1)}{2R}-|C|.} 	ag{14} When positive, (14) controls all component branches except the lowest signed pair at each angular eigenvalue. It covers the complete infinite angular spectrum of this linear parent, not just the numerical cutoff. The real current derivative N still has to be included. Subtracting its norm 2|f''|\|v\|^2 gives a crude further bound, which fails to prove a gap in some of the reviewed cases. Such a failed bound is not evidence that the physical spectrum has become unstable. The current fixed point also gives a component stability criterion At one fixed spatial eigenvalue, take the normalized real component eigenvector \phi, the bare positive frequency \epsilon, and A=H(G)+C. Let \lambda=\epsilon+C>0. The current vector v=(K-kI)\phi is orthogonal both to \phi and to its chiral partner. The current derivative therefore leaves both low component rays unchanged. Its real and imaginary blocks are L_x=A+2f''vv^T,\qquad L_y=A. 	ag{15} Assume the remaining bare component eigenvalues lie outside [-\lambda,\lambda]. On that fast subspace the rank-one secular function is D(z)=1+2f''\langle v,(A_f-z)^{-1}vangle,\qquad D'(z)=2f''\|(A_f-z)^{-1}v\|^2\le0. 	ag{16} There are no poles in the specified interval. The exact second Hellmann--Feynman derivative gives \epsilon_{GG}=-2\langle v,(H_f-\epsilon)^{-1}vangle, \qquad  oxed{D(\lambda)=1-f''\epsilon_{GG}.} 	ag{17} The right-hand side is precisely the derivative of the scalar fixed-point equation G-f'(\epsilon_G)=0. If it is positive, monotonicity in (16) prevents a secular zero anywhere in the particle gap. No shifted fast component eigenvalue enters that interval. The unchanged opposite partner has magnitude \epsilon-C\ge\lambda, because this current has C\le0. Thus the complete component rotating quadratic stiffness L^2-\lambda^2 is nonnegative under these conditions. Its positive kinetic term and skew gyroscopic term exclude an exponentially growing finite-component mode. A zero stiffness can still permit a neutral or secular perturbation; this is not a claim of strict asymptotic stability. Every maintained index passes these conditions at the illustrative strengths gR/c=100 and 1000, with an independent direct component eigensystem calculation. The result explains that part of the numerical stability without an additional fitted coefficient. It does not replace the spatial test: angularly varying perturbations can mix spatial eigenspaces through the local current direction. What the numerical stability tests establish The depth-two form calculation tests the maintained indices 76, 81 and 95, two complex polarization choices, azimuth shifts one and three, and three angular cutoffs. At gR/c=1000, all 36 cases have growth rates indistinguishable from numerical zero in the tested frequency pencil. Independent finer quadrature agrees with the complete squared operator. All four form types are retained. The spinor calculation uses the same current law at depths two, three, four, five, six and ten, with the maintained indices and three axial cutoffs. Its illustration uses gR/c=100 to resolve the small frequencies more reliably. No resolved growing mode appears in those channels. A conservative squared-matrix resolution estimate reaches roughly one percent of the selected frequency for the depth-ten control; that numerical limitation is reported separately. These are finite spatial perturbation tests, including their exact positive angular-square contribution. They do not prove stability in all azimuthal channels, nonlinear stability, supporting geometry, or complete particle inertia. Increasing the spatial basis is also required when a two-mode encounter drives new angular components. Conformal background hessian Read the complete source. Exact two-direction derivatives Put \sigma=t_0+t_1q and write f_0=1, f_1=q. On the unit sphere, \widehat\Delta q=2(d+1)q-4,\qquad |\widehat
abla q|^2=4q(1-q),\qquad \kappa_\sigma=e^{-\sigma} \sqrt{1+ rac2d\widehat\Delta\sigma - rac{d-2}{d}|\widehat
abla\sigma|^2}. 	ag{5} For either basis function let k_i=-f_i+\widehat\Delta f_i/d. The second derivative of the curvature scale at the reference is k_{ij}=f_if_j-  rac{f_i\widehat\Delta f_j+f_j\widehat\Delta f_i}{d} - rac{(\widehat\Delta f_i)(\widehat\Delta f_j)}{d^2} - rac{d-2}{d}\widehat
abla f_i\cdot\widehat
abla f_j. 	ag{6} For spinors, the force vector and bare geometric Hessian per unit N follow directly from (1), (3), (5) and (6): F_i=- eta B\langle f_iangle_ho +(A-sg_0)\langle k_iangle_ho, 	ag{7} G_{ij}= eta B\langle f_if_jangle_ho +(A-sg_0)\langle k_{ij}angle_ho +s g_0\langle k_ik_jangle_ho. 	ag{8} The script evaluates the depth-two derivatives from (4), using its actual even and odd weights. All angular averages reduce to moments of q\sim\operatorname{Beta}(n+1,(d-1)/2), so the entries are exact finite-moment evaluations after the numerical singular vectors are fixed. The same script also differentiates the unexpanded energy by independent spatial quadrature for one maintained depth-two form and one depth-six spinor. This tests the curvature expansion and the distinct form transport. The same derivatives apply to an arbitrary smooth real conformal function f. Write T= eta B, and \Delta f=\widehat\Delta f. Equation (8) has the pointwise form  egin{aligned} G[f,f]=\intho\Big[& (T+A)f^2- rac{2A}{d}f\Delta f + rac{2sg_0-A}{d^2}(\Delta f)^2\ &+ rac{(sg_0-A)(d-2)}d|\widehat
abla f|^2 \Big]dV. \end{aligned} 	ag{8a} The (f,\Delta f/d) quadratic matrix is positive when T+A>0,\quad 2sg_0-A>0,\quad (T+A)(2sg_0-A)-A^2>0. 	ag{8b} All three inequalities, and the positive gradient coefficient, hold at every maintained spinor mode and both common strengths. Since ho>0 almost everywhere, (8a) proves positive bare fixed-profile conformal curvature for every nonzero smooth f, including non-zonal directions. It does not cover traceless metric changes or the depth-two form carrier. One inverse background and its common threshold A retained same-field background coordinate x=v+\xi can be coupled to the complete reference metric derivative of this same conformal current action. Distinguish the generating functional W from the complete positive wave action. For a nearby metric g, define W[\Psi,g,\xi] =E_1[\Psi,g]- rac{v+\xi}{v} D_gE_1\Psi,g_*. 	ag{9} Here the last term is the linear functional of the metric displacement at the round reference g_*; its reference operator is common to every harmonic. At g=g_*, \xi=0, it vanishes along with its field variation. Its metric force cancels D_gE_1, and the field–metric mixed block cancels as an operator identity wherever the current branch is differentiable. The reference frequencies remain \omega_{n,d}. Take F_W=\delta W/\delta\Psi^* and the candidate complete action L_+=\|\dot\Psi\|^2-\|F_W\|^2+L_{g,\xi}^{m kinetic}-a\xi^2/2, with positive geometric and background kinetic terms left as inputs. On a positive standing branch, the phase charge is \mathcal Q=2\omega N, and its wave energy at the reference is \mathcal Q\omega. Because D_gF_W=0 at the reference for every field, the fixed-profile geometric second derivative of the squared wave potential is \mathcal Q G, while its geometry–background derivative is -\mathcal Q F/v. The quadratic field–geometry block also vanishes. This uses the degree-two homogeneity of W on the specified current branch; it does not assume that the generating energy itself is the physical positive-wave potential. At unit phase charge \mathcal Q=1, the geometric and background potential block is  egin{pmatrix}G&-F/v\-F^T/v&a\end{pmatrix}. 	ag{10} When G is positive, this retained block is positive exactly when  oxed{a v^2>F^TG^{-1}F.} 	ag{11} At general phase charge the threshold is a v^2>\mathcal Q F^TG^{-1}F. At unit wave norm N=1 instead, it is 2\omega F^TG^{-1}F. One common a,v within a depth must exceed the largest threshold among its occupied modes. The background coordinate is a retained amplitude of the same field, not an additional particle. Equation (9) is an inverse action: it does not derive the background potential, its kinetic coefficient, the reference geometry, or this derivative coupling from the original master field. Maintained-mode calculation Both eigenvalues of the original two-direction G are positive for every maintained mode at all six depths and both common strengths. The table lists the largest unit-phase-charge threshold in (11) within each depth, and the largest-to-smallest spread of \omega_{n,d}/\mathcal S(n,d). Depth ten has only one maintained mode, so its within-depth spread is undefined. These are normalized candidate values, not stiffnesses or masses inferred from experiment. Depth g_0=1000: av^2> Frequency-unit spread g_0=10000: av^2> Frequency-unit spread 2 16.49 1.01208 1.821 1.000131 3 0.05471 1.001282 0.0005487 1.0000128 4 0.8968 1.02200 0.0009342 1.0002153 5 0.0007249 1.001732 7.276	imes10^{-8} 1.0000173 6 0.0006673 1.004690 6.729	imes10^{-9} 1.0000466 10 1.783	imes10^{-9} — 1.790	imes10^{-18} — The finite-strength current carrier approaches the simplex ratios as the strength increases but does not give exact count proportionality in these controls. The absolute frequency unit and common physical radius remain undetermined. The extended calculation tests the joint bare Hessian on the nine unit-sphere-normalized zonal functions of degrees 0, 2, ..., 16. Every maintained mode remains positive. The common unit-phase-charge thresholds change only modestly: Depth g_0=1000: av^2> g_0=10000: av^2> 2 16.500 1.8222 3 0.05530 0.0005546 4 0.8973 0.0009348 5 0.0007289 7.317	imes10^{-8} 6 0.0006689 6.745	imes10^{-9} 10 1.794	imes10^{-9} 1.801	imes10^{-18} The spinor pointwise result is stronger than this finite scan for the bare conformal block. title: Complete energy, inertia and causal motion
summary: Mass is the selected oscillation frequency in equivalent units, while positive inertia requires the momentum response of the complete particle and its sustaining field. Partial wave momentum and an assigned frequency do not settle that response.
text:
Mass is the selected oscillation frequency in equivalent units, while positive inertia requires the momentum response of the complete particle and its sustaining field. Partial wave momentum and an assigned frequency do not settle that response. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Localized current inertia Read the complete source. Frequency, a sustaining field and inertia in one action Mass already has the equivalent frequency \omega_m=mc^2/\hbar. The dynamical question is whether a continuously oscillating, localized field can sustain itself and have the corresponding inertia under translation. The construction here answers that question for one explicit inverse action. It retains the simplex current hierarchy and adds local terms whose complete variations sustain a spatial core. Their spatial fixed point is the same, while their coefficient grades differ. This is reconstructed dynamics. The original scalar quartic master term has not been shown to generate this action, its carrier or its weights. The oscillator coefficient grade has also not yet been identified with the actual spatial harmonics of a derived particle cavity. Set U_{\mathrm{mass}}=\omega_{0,d}\sqrt r \sum_{k\ge0} inom{k+d-1}{d-1}\|R_k\|_{\mathrm{HS}}. 	ag{12} The binding currents J,K instead trace all oscillator coefficients and sum all grades before (7) is varied. Hockey-Stick gives \sum_{k=0}^N inom{k+d-1}{d-1}= inom{N+d}{d}, \qquad \omega_N=\omega_{0,d}D_N. 	ag{13} The factor \sqrt r in (12) is one stated normalization rule across depths: \sqrt r\|ho I_r\|_{\mathrm{HS}}=rho equals the canonical density. Without it, a common unnormalized coefficient would introduce an artificial rank factor between r_6=8 and r_{10}=32. The rule preserves the proposed shared charged-lepton frequency unit if \omega_{0,6}=\omega_{0,10} is imposed. It does not derive that equality or remove the documented tau mass residual in the frequency-unit comparison. Full stress and a direct kinetic derivation of inertia For the displayed radial cores in (11), both the spatial kinetic expectation and the binding energy vanish pointwise, because they connect the upper and lower blocks. Hence  oxed{\Omega(-\partial_a\Phi,b_b)=-\omega_NQ\delta_{ab}.} 	ag{23} Restoring the time-term coefficient \hbar and the velocity factor c^{-2} gives (1). This derives the center's inertia from the actual oscillating field's canonical kinetic term. It is not a redefinition of an amplitude as mass. It also differs from the two-translation surface pairing: the second variation here is a boost, including its frequency-dependent spatial phase. What remains physical input The frequency and inertia identities do not select the shell weights. Replace the binomial weights in (12) by any positive sequence w_k, keeping one common action and the same sustaining core. The same contraction and canonical calculation give \omega_N=\omega_{0,d}\sum_{k=0}^Nw_k,\qquad E_0=\hbar\omega_NQ,\qquad M_{ab}= rac{\hbar\omega_NQ}{c^2}\delta_{ab}. 	ag{28} The spatial equation (10) does not contain these weights. This freedom tests what the inverse construction establishes; it does not propose different particle indices or a competing dimensional assignment. The Hockey-Stick identity is exact once its weights are supplied, but neither spatial existence nor the boost calculation derives them. Likewise, Q=1 is a common physical normalization condition, not an arbitrary rescaling at fixed nonlinear coefficients. The coefficient g in the unit-norm core was chosen once per depth to implement it. No quantization of Q follows. The relation m_c=\omega_{0,d} is a separate inverse identification. The relativistic kinetic structure in (6) is also supplied: the inertia calculation verifies its localized solution's response rather than deriving that kinetic structure. The displayed boosts treat the oscillator and partner column labels as spectators. This makes the written local spinor action and its boosted solutions consistent. The later same-current rest-frame completion supplies an explicit Lorentz transformation law for the spatial tensors and varies its additional kinetic connection. The stationary frequencies and inertia survive, and zero-rotation-moment rays retain the complete linear response. Complex polarized rays expose a defective principal propagation matrix, however, so this completion does not yet settle a general physical carrier. Likewise, a list of coefficient grades is not a derivation of their underlying spatial harmonics, occupations or selection. Those are distinct carrier problems. The master origin of the reconstructed terms, the common canonical norm, the relation of the core scale to \omega_{0,d}, and full spatial stability remain necessary for a physical particle interpretation. The complete response calculation gives finite normalized common-probe identities and bounded radial and angular tests. It does not yet identify observed electromagnetic or weak vertices, derive cross-depth coupling, or settle the neutrino control. The solved-core pair calculation exhibits a specific fractional-current cancellation during an allowed pair preparation. Its smooth binding comparisons remove that particular variation singularity and still have localized depth-six solutions with the exact frequencies and full boosted stress. The smoothing scale is an additional common inverse coefficient; its spatial profiles and stability tests must be kept distinct from the original fractional model. The trace-current comparison changes the current norm away from the occupied ray while preserving its complete isolated mass source, energy and spatial core. It removes a specific secular high-momentum response of the original norm and gives a positive conserved norm for the constant far-field linearization. This is a further inverse action choice. It does not select the shell weights, provide a physical energy floor, or resolve the polarized carrier's kinetic defect. Retained source energy Read the complete source. Stationary identity for a quartic action Consider canonical Dirac fields \Phi_j=e^{-i\omega_jt}\phi_j(x) with finite integrals and vanishing boundary terms. Write their complete energy as E=T+U_2+U_4, where T is the spatial Dirac kinetic energy, U_2 is quadratic in the fields, and U_4 is quartic. Here the symbols denote integrated quantities. Let Q_j=\int\phi_j^\dagger\phi_j. Multiplying each stationary field equation by its conjugate and summing gives Euler's homogeneous-function identity, \sum_j\omega_jQ_j=T+U_2+2U_4, \qquad  oxed{E=\sum_j\omega_jQ_j-U_4.} 	ag{1} Additional binding terms must contribute their actual homogeneous variations; a smoothed or fractional binding term cannot silently be counted as quartic. Equation (1) is not a formula for particle mass from amplitudes. It is a consistency test on the energy of the specified stationary solution and its canonical normalization. For a pure cross interaction between target A and retained source B, let the target's other energy terms vanish on its solved branch. Then \omega_aQ_a=U_	imes, while the normal equation gives \omega_bQ_b=T_b+U_	imes if it has no other terms. The complete energy is therefore E=\omega_aQ_a+T_b. 	ag{2} The algebraic homogeneous comparison has T_b=0. A spatial source does not acquire this identity merely by reproducing the same target source matrix. Its kinetic expectation must be evaluated, along with any binding contributions omitted from the hypotheses of (2). Spatial scaling supplies another necessary condition Suppose the geometry is ordinary flat \mathbb R^d, the coefficients are spatially constant, and all currents and boundary terms allow the norm-preserving variation \phi_j(x)\mapsto\lambda^{d/2}\phi_j(\lambda x). Then T\mapsto\lambda T, U_2\mapsto U_2, and U_4\mapsto\lambda^dU_4. Stationarity at fixed Q_j implies T+dU_4=0,\qquad E=U_2-(d-1)U_4, \quad \sum_j\omega_jQ_j=U_2-(d-2)U_4. 	ag{3} In particular, a massless canonical Dirac action with a nonnegative local quartic potential cannot have a nontrivial finite stationary solution of positive energy under these scaling hypotheses when d>1. This does not apply to the earlier inverse binding action, to a nonzero background without a justified subtraction, or to a different spatial geometry. It identifies which extra physical structure a proposed localized positive-frequency realization must account for. Equations (1)–(3) follow directly from the stated action and admissible variations.
