title: Photon geometry and physical polarization
summary: Depth-two light supplies the explicit transverse polarization control. A massive higher-depth sector may have a different polarization rule; the proposed photon zero and its radiative protection remain separate questions.
text: Depth-two light supplies the explicit transverse polarization control. A massive higher-depth sector may have a different polarization rule; the proposed photon zero and its radiative protection remain separate questions. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Photon transversality Read the complete source. 2. The physical spatial plane and its normal bundle Let x be the photon's centre and let E_{\gamma,x}\subset T_x\Xi_\infty be its oriented physical spatial two-plane. This is the local physical content of the d=2 assignment: \dim E_{\gamma,x}=2. Its orientation is a dynamical variable. At a containing depth r\geq3, write its image as E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\subset T_x\Xi_r. With the spatial metric restricted to that depth, there is an orthogonal decomposition T_x\Xi_r = E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)} \oplus N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}, where N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)} = \left(E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\right)^\perp, \qquad \dim N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}=r-2. The second summand is the normal space available for propagation relative to the photon plane. At observer depth its dimension is \dim N_{\gamma}^{(3)}=1. At deeper levels the photon plane is still two-dimensional while its normal space has more possible directions. Here “normal” is the geometric word for perpendicular to the chosen photon plane. It is a relationship to that plane, not a different kind of spatial dimension. There are four such directions within the electron's six and eight within the tau's ten. Neither containing sector acquires an inherent physical split from this description of the photon. 3. The depth-independent transversality theorem This is a conditional geometric theorem: assigning polarization to the physical spatial plane and propagation momentum to its normal space already enforces their orthogonality. The depth-two assignment alone does not derive those assignments, select the separated mode below, or establish the electromagnetic constraint equations. Free outer dynamics also allow wavepackets; constant outer intensity describes the chosen momentum eigenmode, not every photon. Choose coordinates u on the physical spatial plane and y on its normal space: u\in E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}, \qquad y\in N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}. Bound within, free without gives the two coordinate sets different jobs. The photon's physical oscillation is the spatially bound mode \chi_0(u) in its two bound spatial directions. Those same directions belong to the containing sectors. In the outer directions it has no localized envelope: a free momentum eigenmode has constant magnitude and a changing phase. The separated photon mode is \Psi_\gamma(u,y,t) = \chi_0(u)\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\, e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}, where \boldsymbol\varepsilon \in E_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}\otimes\mathbb C, \qquad \mathbf K\in N_{\gamma,x}^{(r)}. If this vector ansatz is identified directly with a source-free electric field, the full divergence constraint additionally requires \boldsymbol\varepsilon\cdot\nabla_u\chi_0=0. A real scalar envelope with constant circular polarization spanning the two bound directions must then have both transverse derivatives zero, so that particular factorization cannot provide transverse localization. Spatially varying polarization, additional components or a different reconstruction of the electric field can change the conclusion. Orthogonality alone does not solve these spatial constraints, and the Maxwell constraint must not be imposed on an unidentified master-field component without the stated field identification. Its intensity is independent of the free coordinate: |\Psi_\gamma(u,y,t)|^2 = |\chi_0(u)|^2|\boldsymbol\varepsilon|^2. This is the precise meaning of “the photon is already there.” Its support is uniform in the free direction, while its phase gradient carries energy, momentum, and the sequence of possible interactions. The polarization belongs to the physical spatial plane, \boldsymbol\varepsilon\in E_\gamma, while the phase gradient belongs to the outer free coordinates, \mathbf K\in N_\gamma. By orthogonality, \boxed{\mathbf K\cdot\boldsymbol\varepsilon=0.} This conclusion holds for every r containing the photon plane. At depth r=3, the normal space is one-dimensional, producing the familiar picture of one propagation axis and a two-dimensional transverse plane. At depth r>3, the photon may propagate along any direction in an (r-2)-dimensional normal space, but every such direction remains perpendicular to both spatial photon directions. Including the shared time coordinate, define K^A=(\omega,\mathbf K), \qquad \varepsilon^A=(0,\boldsymbol\varepsilon). Then K_A\varepsilon^A=0. If the photon is massless, its dispersion relation additionally gives K_AK^A=0, \qquad \omega^2=\|\mathbf K\|^2. Masslessness makes K null. Transversality follows from the allocation of phase propagation and physical oscillation to orthogonal parts of the nested manifold. 4. Momentum without rest mass Energy, momentum, and invariant rest mass obey E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4. For m=0 and E>0, \boxed{p=\frac{E}{c}>0.} The same result follows directly from the field stress tensor. Let u be the wave's energy density and \mathbf S its energy-flux vector. The field momentum density is \mathbf g=\frac{\mathbf S}{c^2}. For the source-free Maxwell control in three observed spatial dimensions, the general pointwise bound is |\mathbf S|\le cu. With real electric and magnetic fields \mathbf E and \mathbf B, u^2-\frac{|\mathbf S|^2}{c^2} =\frac{\epsilon_0^2}{4} \left[(|\mathbf E|^2-c^2|\mathbf B|^2)^2 +4c^2(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B)^2\right]\ge0. Equality requires a null field. For a finite pulse of total energy U, \mathbf P=\frac{1}{c^2}\int\mathbf S\,d^3x, \qquad |\mathbf P|\le\frac{U}{c}. Integrated equality additionally requires aligned energy flux wherever the energy is nonzero. Two equal-energy, disjoint packets at angles \pm\alpha to an axis have |\mathbf P|=(U/c)\cos\alpha. An individual massless excitation obeys p=E/c; a multidirectional classical pulse or an expectation four-vector need not saturate that relation. The exact plane-mode result does not establish equality for every free finite pulse. Uniform support and nonzero Noether momentum coexist because the plane-wave factor has unit magnitude and a nonzero phase gradient: \left|e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}\right|=1, \qquad -i\nabla_y e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)} = \mathbf K e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot y-\omega t)}. If the one-quantum normalization is used, the same statement is E=\hbar\omega, \qquad \mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf K, \qquad \omega=c|\mathbf K|. The ratio p/E=1/c is classical wave kinematics and is independent of the absolute value of \hbar. It is the wave's Noether momentum and energy flux. Finally, n=0 labels the unexcited spatial mass mode. External frequency \omega, wave vector \mathbf K, energy E, and momentum \mathbf p remain the freely specifiable wave data, allowing a zero-rest-mass sector mode to carry arbitrary photon energy. 5. Why there are two polarization modes Choose an oriented orthonormal basis \{\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\} of the physical spatial plane. Any photon oscillation is \boldsymbol\varepsilon = a_1\mathbf e_1+a_2\mathbf e_2. The polarization vector has component count \dim_{\mathbb C}\left(E_\gamma\otimes\mathbb C\right)=2, at every containing depth. Increasing r enlarges the possible normal propagation directions while preserving these two polarization modes. The circular basis is \mathbf e_\pm = \frac{\mathbf e_1\pm i\mathbf e_2}{\sqrt2}. Under a rotation of the photon plane through angle \alpha, \mathbf e_\pm \longmapsto e^{\mp i\alpha}\mathbf e_\pm. These are the two orientation weights \pm1 of the physical spatial SO(2)\simeq U(1) geometry. At depth r=3, where the plane is the complete spatial complement of the propagation direction, these weights are precisely the usual photon helicities \pm1. At higher depths the full massless little group is larger, and the same two circular polarization modes form the d=2 sector representation. A parity-complete solution space permits both circular modes. A particular state can occupy one or both. Reality relates positive-frequency components to their negative-frequency conjugates; it does not require both independent positive-frequency helicities to be occupied. For example, \operatorname{Re}[(\mathbf e_1+i\mathbf e_2)e^{i(kz-\omega t)}] is real and has one positive-frequency circular polarization. 6. Orientation at an arbitrary depth The space of possible orientations of the photon plane at depth r is the oriented Grassmannian \operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(T_x\Xi_r). A photon configuration at that depth consists geometrically of a pair (E_\gamma,\mathbf K), \qquad E_\gamma\in\operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(T_x\Xi_r), \qquad \mathbf K\in E_\gamma^\perp. This is the depth-independent state geometry. It reduces at r=3 to the familiar coincidence \operatorname{Gr}^{+}_2(\mathbb R^3) \simeq S^2 \simeq \mathbb{CP}^1, because an oriented plane in three dimensions is determined by its oriented unit normal. This realizes the physical photon plane in observer geometry. For the r=3 realization, the right- and left-circular polarization line bundles over the direction sphere have c_1(\mathcal L_\pm)=\pm2, and can be written, up to orientation convention, as \mathcal L_\pm\simeq\mathcal O(\pm2). This is the spin-one topology visible at that depth. The helicity bundles are \mathcal O(\pm2), while the basic amplitude Hopf line is \mathcal O(1). Thus the physical spatial plane has the required observer-level realization. 9. The dynamical masslessness condition The convention S(0,2)=0 labels the photon zero mode. Exact masslessness requires the projected action to possess a gauge symmetry or dynamical identity forbidding a scalar mass endomorphism on this mode: \boxed{P_{\gamma}\mathcal M P_{\gamma}=0}, where \mathcal M is the full radiatively corrected mass operator. Depth two boson control Read the complete source. The exact two-mode spectrum The positive surface-sign matrix reduces to T_n=\begin{pmatrix}n&0\\g&n+1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad g=\gamma h_0, \qquad h_0=0.4773956986626318. \tag{1} Both surface signs have the same singular values in this two-mode case. Put A=g^2+n^2+(n+1)^2. Then s_+^2=\frac{A+\sqrt{A^2-4n^2(n+1)^2}}2, \qquad \boxed{s_- =\frac{n(n+1)}{s_+}.} \tag{2} The numerator is 2S(n,2). Thus the common leading frequency is 2S(n,2)/g, with its finite correction retained explicitly. For n>0, \frac1{\sqrt{1+[n^2+(n+1)^2]/g^2}} \le\frac{s_-}{n(n+1)/g}\le1. \tag{3} This follows from g\le s_+\le\sqrt A. It does not treat the leading simplex expression as an exact finite-hopping law. For the endpoint deformation T_{01}'=\gamma\kappa_2, the normalized frequency-response magnitude is exactly \boxed{\frac{|s_-'|}{|\gamma\kappa_2|} =\frac{g s_+}{s_+^2-s_-^2}.} \tag{4} It lies between g/s_+ and one. To obtain (4), differentiate s_+s_-=\det T and s_+^2+s_-^2=\operatorname{Tr}T^\dagger T. The first derivative of the trace is zero in this direction. Assignment Frequency correction relative to the leading simplex law Endpoint response correction W -0.025666% -0.025660% Z -0.029129% -0.029120% Higgs -0.039987% -0.039971% The shared normalized endpoint coefficient is \kappa_2/\sqrt{M_2}=-0.55216758. The modest index dependence in the table is calculated, not removed by dividing each response by its particle frequency. These percentages are corrections to this candidate's leading law, not errors relative to measured boson masses. Physical polarization is a further spatial test For a complex spatial vector \varepsilon=a+ib, the real harmonic motion is \operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon e^{-i\omega t}) =a\cos\omega t+b\sin\omega t. \tag{6} Its trajectory lies in the real plane spanned by a,b. Collinear vectors give linear motion; orthogonal equal lengths give circular motion; the general case is elliptical. This trajectory can have a component along the propagation direction unless transversality is imposed or derived. The ellipse's rank does not determine the spatial support dimension of the complete particle field. The physical photon plane in photon transversality is perpendicular to propagation. Its two circular components have spatial rotation weights \pm1. The existing two-form coupling gives the analyzer overlap |e^\dagger\varepsilon|^2: a cosine-squared law for linear preparations and one half for a circular preparation with a linear analyzer. Direct real-space contractions verify these comparisons. Massive bosons need not inherit that transverse-plane restriction. Longitudinal W/Z polarization is part of the measured comparison, including joint longitudinal states in the ATLAS WZ measurement. The Higgs mass assignment also does not prescribe a vector polarization: the ATLAS spin study found evidence for spin zero against its tested alternatives. The depth assignment is an IDWT premise, while these measurements constrain the required mode content. Within each nonzero singular-frequency doublet, the current retained shape-source matrix is proportional to the identity. Its self-shape response therefore does not itself supply a polarization analyzer. The spatial plane identification, vector versus scalar state content and the massive longitudinal channel remain to be obtained from the full field. Higher-depth patterns can be compared with massive-boson polarization without assuming that the photon is either universal or exceptional. The formal photon zero exists, but is not protected yet Extending (1) formally to n=0 gives T_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\g&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad u_0=\frac{(1,-g)^T}{\sqrt{1+g^2}},\qquad v_0=(1,0)^T. \tag{7} The full chiral mass matrix has the two zero vectors (u_0,0) and (0,v_0). A separately specified free propagation term leaves both mass eigenvalues zero and allows nonzero wave frequency. The normal mass matrix alone does not derive that propagation law or establish the availability of the required physical surface mode. For the allowed centered deformation T_{01}=\gamma\kappa_2\alpha_2, the leading small mass-frequency becomes \boxed{s_-(\alpha_2)= \frac{|g\gamma\kappa_2|}{\sqrt{1+g^2}} |\alpha_2|+O(|\alpha_2|^2).} \tag{8} Consequently the reference zero alone is insufficient. The physical action still needs a constraint or identity that protects the photon zero under the permitted dynamics. The common kernel may eventually provide it; the current calculation has not done so. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Same-field coupling across sectors
summary: Coupling is compatibility and reciprocal response of actual spatial patterns in the one field. A response coefficient, pair vertex, encounter probability and rest frequency require separate normalizations before they can be related.
text: Coupling is compatibility and reciprocal response of actual spatial patterns in the one field. A response coefficient, pair vertex, encounter probability and rest frequency require separate normalizations before they can be related. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Generalized sector coupling Read the complete source. Physical scope There is one infinite physical manifold with one nested chain of ordinary macroscopic spatial submanifolds. Particles at different depths are structures of \Psi_\infty on that chain. All directions belonging to a given particle are of the same spatial kind. A decomposition relative to another particle's submanifold describes their relation; it does not give either particle an inherent division into different kinds of space. The following construction applies to arbitrary finite collections of sectors, including the working depths 2,3,4,5,6,10. It assumes specified spatial maps, measures, mode subspaces, and an interaction channel. It does not require accepting a particular list of global sphere or projective topologies. Actual embeddings and their domain conditions must be supplied wherever a proposed topology is used. IDWT has no mediator particles. The source profiles, response modes, and representation indices below describe the one field on this physical space. Coupling starts with its direct interaction terms. Eliminating some of its modes is a conditional reduction of those equations, not a particle-exchange mechanism. The working coupling hypothesis includes a changing geometric match: each particle can drive the other's spatial pattern toward greater compatibility or toward incompatibility during an encounter. Bilateral polarization coupling separates that physical target from a restricted orientation benchmark whose relative overlap remains constant. Both the change in compatibility and its effect on subsequent interaction must follow from the same dynamics. The concrete shape calculation is developed in Transition-density coupling, followed by Reciprocal scattering of spatial modes. For any operator O on the multiplet, \langle O\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho O). \tag{5} A common phase relative to another coherent field must still be retained in the combined field and its transition terms. To express (4) as spatial tensors, choose Hermitian Euclidean Clifford matrices \gamma_i, satisfying \{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I. They describe how the field transforms under rotations of its actual spatial coordinates. For even depth use one specified chiral representation; for odd depth use the stated irreducible spin representation. Define the Hermitian spatial operators B_{ij}=-i\gamma_i\gamma_j,\qquad C_{ijkl}=\gamma_i\gamma_j\gamma_k\gamma_l, \qquad i<j<k<l. \tag{6} Restriction to the selected chiral space is understood. Their expectation values are the two-form J_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho B_{ij}) and four-form K_{ijkl}=\operatorname{tr}(\varrho C_{ijkl}). Count and verify a complete operator basis At the depths below, the listed operators \Gamma_A form a complete Hermitian basis on the indicated polarization multiplet: physical spatial depth complex components N complete operator grades number of operators 3 2 scalar and two-form 1+3=4 5 4 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+10+5=16 6, one chirality 4 scalar and two-form 1+15=16 10, one chirality 16 scalar, two-form and four-form 1+45+210=256 In five dimensions a four-form is dual to a vector in those same five spatial directions. The table counts descriptions of fields, not additional spatial coordinates or independent particles. The Clifford trace identities give \operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_A\Gamma_B)=N\delta_{AB}. \tag{7} To see why the stated grades suffice, products of distinct Clifford generators are trace-orthogonal unless their index sets agree or are related by the top-dimensional duality. In an irreducible odd-dimensional module, the top product is scalar; on an even-dimensional chiral module it is fixed by chirality. The table selects one representative of each dual pair. Its N^2 orthogonal operators span the entire N\times N matrix algebra. Consequently \boxed{\varrho=\frac1N\sum_A \operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)\Gamma_A.} \tag{8} The scalar coefficient is one. For a single normalized coherent polarization, purity also gives \sum_{A\ne0}\operatorname{tr}(\varrho\Gamma_A)^2=N-1. \tag{9} The coefficients are constrained by the full equation \varrho^2=\varrho; (9) alone is insufficient. At six dimensions, J therefore determines the entire polarization matrix within the selected four-component multiplet: \boxed{\varrho_6=\frac14\left(I+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}B_{ij}\right).} \tag{10} For a pure ray, its J satisfies J^2=-I_6. One way to establish this for every ray is to note that the fifteen traceless B_{ij} span the Hermitian generators of SU(4). Their spin representation acts transitively on the rays, and rotates J as a physical two-form. A reference ray has three unit orthogonal planes; rotating it preserves J^2=-I_6. The normalized same-chirality family \boxed{z_{\eta,\theta} =\cos\eta\,|0\rangle+e^{i\theta}\sin\eta\,|1234\rangle} \tag{12} has \boxed{J=\operatorname{diag} (\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,\lambda J_2,J_2), \quad \lambda=\cos2\eta,\quad J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.} \tag{13} Every off-diagonal occupation transition in a two-form changes at most two matrix occupations, so it cannot connect the two components in (12). The four-form does connect them: \boxed{K_{1357}=\sin2\eta\cos\theta.} \tag{14} Thus \theta can change the field polarization without changing any component of J. At \eta=\pi/4, the fields with \theta=0,\pi are orthogonal, yet have exactly the same J. Every vector in (12) is a pure coherent state in the sense of (4). The term Cartan-pure spinor imposes a separate algebraic condition: the complex spatial vectors v satisfying \gamma(v)z=0 span a maximal five-dimensional complex annihilator. Both coefficients in (12) are nonzero in this range, and the distinct occupation grades cannot cancel each other. Only a_5 remains. On the vacuum, all five a_j annihilate the field coefficient. title: Composite and hadronic mass
summary: A composite frequency and complete energy can contain a substantial interaction contribution. The normal response, quark-pattern coupling and canonical normalization must be calculated from one action before identifying a nucleon mass mechanism.
text:
A composite frequency and complete energy can contain a substantial interaction contribution. The normal response, quark-pattern coupling and canonical normalization must be calculated from one action before identifying a nucleon mass mechanism. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Dimensional constriction and hadronic mass Read the complete source. 67. Frequency-domain correction: the hadronic problem must be stated spectrally Re-audit convention: in Sections 67--76, \varpi_d denotes the spatial sector frequency unit \mu_d/\hbar. It must not be identified with the constricted oscillator frequencies also called \omega_3,\omega_4 earlier in this exploratory ledger. The electron reference is \omega_e=m_ec^2/\hbar; natural units set c=1. Sections 73--76 correct the later Schur and color-projection exclusions. Frequency ratios are the targets; no independently fitted field amplitude is introduced. The preceding normalization discussion drifted into amplitude-domain quantities. That is not the correct observable language for the present V2 investigation. The measurable content of the theory is spectral: frequencies, masses interpreted as frequencies in natural units, and dimensionless ratios of those frequencies. Field amplitudes, profile normalizations, and current magnitudes may appear in an intermediate representation of an operator, but they are not the quantities the hadronic calculation is trying to predict. Accordingly, the cross-depth problem should be written directly in terms of spectral eigenvalues. Let \omega_e denote the measured electron frequency and let \varpi_3 denote the depth-three fundamental spectral unit. The hadronic constriction calculation seeks a frequency \omega_{34}^{m con} associated with the physical 4	o3 projected operator. The relevant unknown is therefore the dimensionless spectral ratio  oxed{ r_{34} :=  rac{\omega_{34}^{m con}}{\varpi_3}. } Equivalently, relative to the sole dimensional anchor,  oxed{  rac{\omega_{34}^{m con}}{\omega_e} =  rac{\varpi_3}{\omega_e}\,r_{34}. } No independent MeV scale has to be generated. Once the dimensionless ratio to \omega_e is known, expressing the result in MeV is merely a human unit conversion. 67.1 Static relaxation contribution versus spectral frequency The rank-one coupling matrix obeys g_{34}^2=g_{33}g_{44}. In the static quadratic comparison of Section 32, the removed relaxation contribution is  oxed{ g_{m con} =  rac{g_{34}^2}{g_{44}} = g_{33}. } The actual static Schur complement is g_{33}-g_{34}^2/g_{44}=0, whereas the clamped principal block is g_{33}. These are distinct algebraic quantities, not automatically observable frequencies. It does not by itself say that the observable frequency is \omega_{34}^{m con}=g_{33}\varpi_3. That further statement requires a spectral theorem identifying how the dimensionless coupling eigenvalue enters the physical projected frequency operator. Thus the clean frequency-domain question is  oxed{ r_{34}\stackrel{?}{=}g_{33}} or, if additional projection factors occur,  oxed{ r_{34}=F_{34}(g_{33},g_{34},g_{44},	ext{projection data}).} The task is to derive the dimensionless function F_{34} from the projected operator spectrum. 67.2 Frequency targets do not require an amplitude fit The earlier quantities introduced in this investigation such as cross-profile overlaps, current amplitudes, and an effective coefficient \mu_{34}^{m eff} are not required to state the observable problem. Their use as independently fitted amplitude inputs is abandoned. Genuine operator dependence must still be derived or shown to cancel; changing notation alone does not remove it. The physical target is the eigenfrequency ratio  rac{\omega_{34}^{m con}}{\omega_e}, not a field amplitude and not a separately postulated dimensionful coefficient. 68. Source-level spectral audit: allowed channels and a well-defined frequency operator The V2 coupling module describes the normal-polarization singlet selection rule. This identifies allowed tensor structures; allowance alone does not force every corresponding matrix element to be nonzero. Separately, under its stated locality, finite-band, coherent-ray and normalization hypotheses, the self-contact construction gives \Lambda_{N,d}=S(N+1,d)P_{[z]}, \qquad \omega_{n,d}=\varpi_d S(n,d). Its contact multiplier is exact within those hypotheses. The sector-relative and composite dynamics remain separate questions. 68.1 An off-diagonal block does not have a standalone frequency spectrum The expression P_3D_\infty P_4 generally maps one channel space into another. It must not be assigned an ordinary standalone eigenfrequency spectrum without specifying its domain, codomain and physical generator. After defining an orthogonal channel decomposition and the stationary time generator, the coupled problem has a form such as \mathsf H= egin{pmatrix}\mathsf H_3&V_{34}\ V_{34}^\dagger&\mathsf H_4\end{pmatrix}. Its full spectrum, an exact frequency-dependent reduction, or a separately justified singular-value construction can be investigated. These are not interchangeable prescriptions. If the original sector maps are not orthogonal Hilbert-space projectors, their metric and adjoint structure must be established first. Section 76 supplies the exact block-reduction identity for a specified generator. It does not assert that the V2 master blocks have already been evaluated. 69. Frequency targets without an amplitude fit The target observables are frequencies and their electron-relative ratios. No independent field-amplitude measurement is introduced. An eigenvector's arbitrary overall normalization does not affect the eigenvalues of a fixed linear operator. This allows a frequency calculation without solving for an experimentally calibrated amplitude. It does not make geometric matrix elements, operator coefficients, boundary conditions or induced interactions disappear. The earlier factorized-current example remains only a diagnostic of a particular operator representation. Couplings and spatial-profile overlaps are not all field amplitudes. Any dependence they create in a proposed generator must be derived, eliminated exactly, or proved to cancel before making a frequency prediction. 69.1 What changing units and projecting a state do not prove Writing an unknown coefficient as the electron reference times an unknown dimensionless ratio changes its units, not whether that ratio has been determined. Likewise, projecting a state and then renormalizing it does not automatically justify replacing its generator by a compressed matrix. Section 74 gives an exact example in which a projection factor changes spectral weight but not the surviving frequency. The normalized-marginal example showed no universal 7/6 multiplier for that example. Its failure is neither erased merely by using frequency notation nor promoted into a universal theorem about a different operator. The required endpoint is a derived frequency ratio, with no fitted amplitude. In a nonlinear theory, any background dependence of the linearized frequency operator also has to be specified or eliminated; eigenvalue notation alone does not establish independence from it. 74. Color projection: spectral weights, compressed generators, and observed frequencies The earlier 64/6 computation was algebraically correct for one compressed rank-one operator. Its interpretation as a universal color-induced reduction of frequency was not correct. 74.1 Carrier content does not determine the generator The proposed carrier W=\mathbb C\Omega\oplus U, with U\cong\mathbf3, has \dim W^{\otimes3}=64. Its two SU(3) singlets are the vacuum-like line \Omega^{\otimes3} and the determinant line \Lambda^3U. This is a representation statement. It does not establish that W^{\otimes3} is the baryon carrier or that its dimension is a baryon frequency multiplier. 74.2 What the identical-vector zero actually excludes The determinant projection obeys P_{\Lambda^3U}(z\otimes z\otimes z)=0. This excludes the identical-vector product as a determinant-color state. It does not exclude three particles in the same orbital mode with a separate antisymmetric color factor. Color and orbital tensor factors must not be conflated. 74.3 Compression changes the operator unless the subspace reduces it Let v=|123angle be an ordered orthonormal color tensor and let P_\epsilon project onto the normalized determinant singlet. For A=64|vangle\langle v| one obtains P_\epsilon A P_\epsilon= rac{32}{3}P_\epsilon. However, [A,P_\epsilon]
e0. This is not restriction to a reducing subspace: using the compressed operator as a closed generator discards the coupling to its complement. No master-action argument previously justified that discard. 74.4 Exact observation preserves a surviving frequency, not necessarily its weight For a time-independent linear projection P, a stationary mode satisfies P\!\left(u\,e^{-i\omega t}ight)=(Pu)e^{-i\omega t}. If Pu
e0 and the same clock is used, its frequency is unchanged. A vanishing projection removes the line; it does not divide its frequency. The distinction is explicit in the rank-one test above. In dimensionless spectral units, the exact projected resolvent is P_\epsilon(z-A)^{-1}P_\epsilon =\left[ rac{1}{6(z-64)}+ rac{5}{6z}ight]P_\epsilon. It has poles at 64 and 0, not at 32/3. The factor 1/6 is the residue of the frequency-64 pole. It is fixed geometrically in this diagnostic, not fitted from an amplitude measurement. The exact reduced generator on this line is A_{m eff}(z)= rac{32z}{3z-160}, \qquad z-A_{m eff}(z)= rac{3z(z-64)}{3z-160}. Retaining the eliminated-channel term recovers the original poles. The apparent singularity at z=160/3 is not an eigenvalue of the original matrix. This example distinguishes observation and exact elimination from physically imposing a new clamped generator. It does not claim that a non-invariant ordered-color contact is the physical baryon Hamiltonian. 74.5 A singlet constraint need not attenuate orbital eigenfrequencies If the generator factorizes as \mathsf H=I_{m color}\otimes A_{m mode}, then color-singlet restriction gives (P_\epsilon\otimes I)\mathsf H(P_\epsilon\otimes I) =P_\epsilon\otimes A_{m mode}. Every allowed mode eigenfrequency of A_{m mode} survives unchanged. More generally, in a closed three-quark model with color-neutral remaining factors, an SU(3)-invariant generator preserves its color-singlet subspace. Additional colored dynamical fields require a total-color constraint, not an unjustified valence-only truncation. Corrected result: color projection neither derives the candidate 64 nor universally suppresses it by 1/6. The claimed suppression-based exclusion is withdrawn. Whether 64 occurs must be decided from the actual invariant interacting generator, without treating proximity to a previously selected numerical target as a derivation. 75. Three-body relative coordinates: an effective domain, not a new particle depth 75.1 The observed-coordinate kinematics For three positions in a common observed \mathbb R^3, an orthogonal Jacobi transformation separates the center coordinate and two vectors ho,\lambda\in\mathbb R^3. Their relative configuration space is \mathbb R^6. With the Euclidean metric and R^2=|ho|^2+|\lambda|^2, a fixed-R surface is S^5. Mass-weighted Jacobi coordinates can be used when the kinetic metric requires them. These statements concern three-body configuration coordinates, not six spatial directions available to a single particle. 75.2 Native depth is not configuration-space dimension V2 assigns the constituent fields to their native manifolds Q_d. Observing three positions in a common three-space does not prove that the native higher-depth coordinates disappear from the dynamics. Consequently neither the six Jacobi coordinates nor their S^5 angular surface can be identified with the electron's depth-six manifold or the neutrino's depth-five sector merely by matching dimensions or manifold names. Such an identification needs an explicit map of operators, metrics, bundles, measures, and constraints. 75.3 Degeneracy is not automatically a frequency For scalar harmonics on the unit round S^5, -\Delta_{S^5}Y_{\ell}=\ell(\ell+4)Y_{\ell}, \qquad h_\ell= inom{\ell+5}{5}- inom{\ell+3}{5}. The Laplacian eigenvalue and its degeneracy are different quantities. Neither is automatically the spectrum of the composite Dirac/contact frequency generator. The previous degeneracy scan therefore did not test a specified V2 baryon operator. 75.4 A conditional valence-space representation After deriving an appropriate observed-coordinate reduction, a three-quark valence model could use a physical subspace of L^2(\mathbb R^6_{ho,\lambda}) \otimes\Lambda^3U_{m color} \otimes\mathcal H_{m spin/flavor}, with the total fermionic permutation constraint enforced. This is a possible effective representation, not a derivation of the complete baryon Hilbert space. Native coordinates and other dynamical channels must either be retained or eliminated with their induced spectral terms. 75.5 Predict the whole baryon pole The primary target is the complete rest-frequency ratio  oxed{z_B=\omega_B/\omega_e.} The earlier approximately 309--310 MeV quantity was a per-constituent allocation of a residual after subtracting chosen quark contributions. It is not, without an additional decomposition theorem, a separate measured eigenfrequency that the operator must contain. 75.6 Corrected status The Jacobi construction provides useful observed three-body kinematics. It does not establish a new particle sector, a baryon-to-neutrino identification, or the elimination of native coordinates. Passive projection alone does not generate a larger frequency. A physical frequency shift requires the interacting generator or a specified change of dynamics; exact elimination represents that interaction rather than replacing it with dimension counting. 76. Exact frequency-domain reduction and the color-singlet pair coefficient This section records the constructive result of the revised audit. The block identities are exact for the finite matrices checked here. Applying them to the full master operator additionally requires specified domains, a stationary background where needed, and a controlled treatment of its infinite-dimensional channels. 76.1 A frequency equation with no fitted field amplitude Let \mathsf H be a dimensionless stationary time-evolution generator, defined using the electron reference and the common phase variable 	au=\omega_e t: i\partial_	au\Psi=\mathsf H\Psi. An eigenvalue z is then a frequency ratio \omega/\omega_e. A covariant spacetime Dirac operator is not automatically this generator; its time direction and stationary reduction must first be specified. For an orthogonal model-space projector P_B and Q_B=I-P_B, define \mathsf H_{m eff}(z) =P_B\mathsf H P_B +P_B\mathsf H Q_B (z-Q_B\mathsf H Q_B)^{-1} Q_B\mathsf H P_B. The inverse acts on \operatorname{Ran}Q_B. Where it exists, the projected resolvent is P_B(z-\mathsf H)^{-1}P_B =\left[zI_{P_B}-\mathsf H_{m eff}(z)ight]^{-1}. Thus the bound-state calculation seeks  oxed{\ker\!\left[z_BI_{P_B}-\mathsf H_{m eff}(z_B)ight]
e\{0\}.} A determinant equation is available in a finite representation. At excluded complementary eigenvalues, the original system must be checked or the model space enlarged; denominator clearing alone is insufficient. This is standard Feshbach-Schur reduction, not a newly derived V2 interaction. See Dusson, Sigal, and Stamm, The Feshbach-Schur map and perturbation theory, Theorem 1.2 and equations (1.15)--(1.16). The independently checked two-channel example in Section 74 fixes the sign convention used here. 76.2 Derive the color factor from the specified generators The V2 gauge-block proposal uses fundamental generators T^a=\lambda^a/2. With \operatorname{tr}(T^aT^b)=\delta^{ab}/2, define C_{ij}=\sum_{a=1}^8T_i^aT_j^a = rac12\left(\mathsf X_{ij}- rac13Iight), where \mathsf X_{ij} exchanges the two color slots. The generator normalization and completeness identity are standard; see Haber, Useful relations among the generators in the defining and adjoint representations of SU(N). On the determinant singlet, \mathsf X_{ij}=-I. Therefore  oxed{P_\epsilon C_{ij}P_\epsilon=- rac23P_\epsilon,} \qquad  oxed{P_\epsilon\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}P_\epsilon=-2P_\epsilon.} The sum contains three unordered pairs. These are operator eigenvalues from representation theory, not field amplitudes and not an inserted hadron-mass fit. 76.3 What this fixes in an actual pair interaction If the derived dimensionless interaction has the form \mathsf V_{m pair}(z)=\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}\otimes K_{ij}(z), with K_{ij}(z) acting on the remaining factors, its singlet restriction is  oxed{\mathsf V_{{m pair},B}(z)=- rac23\sum_{i<j}K_{ij}(z).} It reduces to -2K(z) only when the three remaining pair operators actually coincide. It does not supply a universal frequency ratio of two or 2/3. The sign is retained; whether this is an attractive contribution depends on the remaining operator convention. This form is a conditional template for matching to the V2 master interaction. The audit has derived its color coefficient, not the existence, radial dependence, spin dependence, or normalization of K_{ij}. 76.4 What has and has not been solved The static/spectral Schur distinction, the projection-versus-frequency error, and the singlet pair coefficient have been resolved exactly. A normalized eigenvector may be used to represent a mode, but no measured field amplitude is used as an input. Electron anchoring fixes the unit. It does not, by itself, determine every dimensionless interaction coefficient. The next calculation must derive the remaining blocks and their spectral dependence from the V2 dynamics, retaining induced terms rather than guessing an integer near the desired mass. No numerical baryon-frequency prediction is claimed by this revision. Coupling localization mass Read the complete source. One interaction can also control a pair encounter For two pointwise orthogonal field components with densities ho_i,ho_j, the same nonlinear contact that supplied (3) has the mixed density \Delta U_{ij} =-gho_iho_j +hho_iho_j(ho_i+ho_j). 	ag{7} This follows by subtracting the two isolated densities from U(ho_i+ho_j). The coefficients are exactly the same ones that enter each self-energy and its localization equation. Yet the integrated pair response also depends on spatial overlap, polarization, relative phase when the components are not orthogonal, and reciprocal deformation. In particular, little overlap with ordinary matter can give rare encounters even if a pattern's own sustaining coupling is not small. This is a possible route for a neutrino-like weak encounter rate; it has not been calculated for an IDWT neutrino state. The more specific neutrino hypothesis is that its effective self-coupling itself is small, making its localized oscillation frequency small. That can be tested, but low coupling cannot simply be taken to zero in (3): below the finite threshold (4), this particular scale model has no localized stationary radius. At depth five with a=C=Q=1, the threshold is B_{m fold}=1.10616. A weakly coupled but localized neutrino would therefore need either an effective coefficient still above its profile-dependent localization threshold or a different same-field support mechanism. The toy coefficient is not a physical neutrino coupling, and the observed small neutrino mass is constrained by upper bounds and oscillation differences, not a measured positive absolute value for every state. An extended neutrino pattern is another distinct possibility. If one spatial carrier obeys \omega_d=\alpha_d c/R_d, where \alpha_d is its derived dimensionless eigenvalue, then  rac{R_
u}{R_e} = rac{\alpha_
u}{\alpha_e}  rac{\omega_e}{\omega_
u}. 	ag{8} The large observed electron-to-neutrino frequency contrast could then reflect a large support ratio, a small spectral factor, or both. This relation is conditional on each state having a meaningful characteristic radius and a common propagation speed; a diffuse or differently localized neutrino need not obey that simple carrier law. An extended physical support is also distinct from the width of a neutrino wave packet during propagation. Equation (1) gives a useful limit on one simple explanation of such extension. At depth five, the magnitude of a local density-square self-contact relative to the gradient estimate is gBQ/(A R^4). Making g weaker and R larger suppresses that ratio in both ways. Thus this particular local contact cannot by itself hold a very broad, weakly coupled state. A supporting interaction with a different scale law, a suppressed gradient term, or a different spatial solution would have to be derived from the same field. This is a restriction on the fixed-profile contact model, not on the proposal that neutrinos may be much larger. An isolated composite can likewise have rest energy that differs from the sum of its components' bare rest energies because its complete interacting field contains kinetic, stress and interaction energy. This is consistent with the measured proton-mass problem and its lattice QCD decomposition, but no IDWT proton or neutron structure has been solved here. A positive interaction term alone does not determine whether binding raises or lowers the composite's total energy relative to physically isolated constituents. The proposed strong inter-quark coupling has a clear conditional test in (7). Where the two densities satisfy h(ho_i+ho_j)>g, that local mixed term is positive: the interaction contribution to a composite can exceed the sum of the isolated self terms. Where the inequality reverses it is negative. Thus the same nonlinear interaction can be attractive in one density range, helping localization, and add positive cross energy at another. The total proton or neutron mass would still require its complete spatial kinetic energy, supporting stress and field solution. The couplings and density ranges for actual quark patterns have not been derived in IDWT. The direct test of the proposal is therefore one canonically normalized same-field action with a finite, stable particle profile; the action must give its selected frequency, full positive inertial response, and reciprocal pair response without an independently fitted interaction rule. The two-term scale obstruction and three-term example identify what such a derivation must address, rather than providing the mass operator themselves. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Orbits, binding and observed spatial patterns
summary: A projected picture, a circulating coefficient ray and an actual spatial orbit are distinct. The available orbit calculations make the observer map explicit and test a conditional Coulomb-driven spatial pattern.
text:
A projected picture, a circulating coefficient ray and an actual spatial orbit are distinct. The available orbit calculations make the observer map explicit and test a conditional Coulomb-driven spatial pattern. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Projective orbit observer map Read the complete source. 2. Projective data available to an observer Let z=(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)\in\mathbb C^4\setminus\{0\}, \qquad [z]=[cz],\quad c\in\mathbb C^*. Every physical readout must be unchanged by this common complex rescaling. The normalized coordinate occupations are p_j([z]) = rac{|z_j|^2}{z^\dagger z}, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^4p_j=1. Whenever z_i and z_j are nonzero, their relative phase is represented by \chi_{ij}([z]) = rac{z_i ar z_j}{|z_iz_j|} =e^{i(\arg z_i-\arg z_j)}. Both objects are projectively invariant. They are the occupation and relative-angle data available after the common scale and phase have been removed. Split the chosen four-state orbit into amplitude and clock planes, \mathcal V=\mathcal V_A\oplus\mathcal V_C, \qquad \mathcal V_A=\operatorname{span}(z_1,z_2), \qquad \mathcal V_C=\operatorname{span}(z_3,z_4). Conditioning on the amplitude plane gives q([z]) = rac{p_1}{p_1+p_2} = rac{|z_1|^2}{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2}. The primitive clock phase is e^{i\phi([z])} =\chi_{34}([z]) = rac{z_3 ar z_4}{|z_3z_4|}. Along the magnetic orbit, q(	heta)=\cos^2(L	heta), \qquad e^{i\phi(	heta)}=e^{i	heta}. 4. Classification of covariant plane maps Restrict the readout to the two arguments q and \phi. This is an additional measurement ansatz: projective invariance alone permits other occupations and relative phases. The classification below is complete only within this restricted class. Let W=X+iY be a complex coordinate in an observer-aligned plane. Rotating the clock by \alpha must rotate the apparatus coordinate by the same angle: W(q,\phi+\alpha)=e^{i\alpha}W(q,\phi). Set \alpha=-\phi. The covariance equation immediately gives W(q,\phi)=e^{i\phi}W(q,0). Therefore every orientation-preserving covariant plane map is  oxed{ W=R h(q)e^{i\phi} }, where R>0 is the spatial scale and h may be complex. An occupation-dependent argument of h(q) is an angular shear: points at different radii are rotated by different extra angles. If the aligned apparatus also respects reflection across its chosen axis, W(q,-\phi)=\overline{W(q,\phi)}, then h(q) is real. Write this real response as f(q). Nonnegativity is an additional radial-response condition, used below with monotonicity, rather than a consequence of reflection alone. The reflection-aligned maps are  oxed{ W=Rf(q)e^{i\phi}. } Orientation reversal replaces e^{i\phi} by e^{-i\phi}. The readout ansatz selects the arguments q and \phi; rotation covariance fixes the equivariant form. Reflection alignment removes the possible angular shear. The detector response supplies the radial function f. 5. Radial-response invariance of the lobe count Suppose the detector response satisfies f(0)=0 and is strictly increasing on [0,1]. Along the orbit, |W(	heta)| =R f\!\left(\cos^2(L	heta)ight). The occupation q(	heta) has maxima at 	heta= rac{k\pi}{L} and zeros at 	heta= rac{(k+	frac12)\pi}{L}. A strictly increasing f preserves those extrema. Hence every map in this class has exactly  oxed{2L	ext{ separated radial lobes per primitive clock turn}.} The lobe count is therefore a topological/order property of the locked amplitude and clock, invariant across the stated class of f. The theorem's response class is continuous, strictly increasing, and satisfies f(0)=0. Those conditions preserve the extrema and separate adjacent lobes at the origin. 7. Canonical occupation measure on the orbit The Hamiltonian flow uses the compact group parameter 	heta\in[0,2\pi). Its invariant probability measure is normalized Haar measure d
u(	heta)= rac{d	heta}{2\pi}. The plane curve W_L therefore carries the pushforward measure  oxed{ \mu_L(B) = rac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \mathbf1_B\!\left(W_L(	heta)ight)d	heta } for every measurable detector region B. Identifying the group parameter with uniform physical time selects this measure directly. The amplitude occupation Q=\cos^2(L\Theta), \qquad \Theta\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,2\pi), has the arcsine density  oxed{ f_Q(q)= rac{1}{\pi\sqrt{q(1-q)}} }, \qquad 0<q<1, independently of nonzero integer L. For the Born radius ho=R\sqrt Q, the radial density is  oxed{ f_ho(ho) = rac{2}{\pi\sqrt{R^2-ho^2}} }, \qquad 0<ho<R. The distribution is singular near the turning radius because the radial velocity vanishes there. Different L values share the same one-dimensional radial marginal; their distinction is the angular arrangement of the lobes. 8. From a curve measure to detector intensity The exact pushforward \mu_L is supported on a one-dimensional curve. A finite detector profile requires a normalized response kernel K_\sigma(x): K_\sigma(x)\geq0, \qquad \int K_\sigma(x)d^3x=1. If detections sample the trajectory uniformly in physical time and the apparatus response is spatially translation invariant, the registered density for a three-dimensional trajectory \Gamma_L(	heta) is  oxed{ ho_{m obs}(x) = rac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} K_\sigma\!\left(x-\Gamma_L(	heta)ight)d	heta }. It is automatically normalized. The Hamiltonian gives the time-occupation measure; identifying that with detection probability is an additional interaction assumption. The apparatus model must justify the sampling law, kernel shape, and width \sigma. Neither this convolution nor a spread in detection positions is a direct observation of the electron's physical shape. Completed coulomb petals Read the complete source. Completed Hamiltonian and target rotation Use the same six-coordinate classical Hamiltonian as the previous note, including the quadratic term: H=\sum_i rac{|p_i-m\lambda Cq_i|^2}{2m} -\sum_i rac{k}{|q_i|}+\sum_{i<j} rac{\gamma}{|q_i-q_j|} + rac{\langle C,Cangle}{2I}. The source remains a skew 6 by 6 coadjoint variable. Its magnitude and spectrum are conserved; this is not yet a mechanism that induces source angular momentum from zero. The test uses m=k=I=1, lambda=0.2 and, for two electrons, gamma=0.4. These are dimensionless model parameters rather than fitted atomic constants. Let Eab denote the unit skew generator and define A_L=- eta\{E_{12}+E_{45}+L(E_{14}+E_{25})\}. A relative equilibrium satisfies \dot q_i=A_Lq_i,\qquad \dot p_i=A_Lp_i, \qquad\dot C=[A_L,C], together with the autonomous Hamilton equations. At q1=e1, canonical momentum is fixed by p1=m(A_L+lambda C)q1. For the antipodal pair, q2=-q1 and p2=-p1. The remaining vector and commutator equations determine C and beta numerically. No target trajectory occurs in the RHS; it occurs only as the relative-equilibrium ansatz whose residual must vanish. The computed residual is at most 1.52e-13. Independent integrations over a full clock turn agree with the exact group orbit to 8.62e-9, conserve energy to 4.52e-9, and return the full state to 8.62e-9. Actual projected trajectories The first electron's first two Cartesian coordinates are exactly (x,y)=\cos(L	heta)(\cos	heta,\sin	heta), \qquad	heta= eta t, while its full six-dimensional radius is one. This is an actual smooth six-coordinate orbit with a signed linear projection, not a stationary orbital and not a curve assigned after integration. Even L gives the same planar image as the visualization's modulus-folded construction: L=2 has four petals and L=4 has eight. Odd L remains a different image: L=1 is an offset circle and L=3 is a three-petal rose rather than the displayed two and six petals. The visualization's height readout is not derived here. The corrected solved branches are: Electrons L Clock beta Source squared norm 1 1 2.12132034356 126.114105614 1 2 0.453730466088 15.0400869518 1 3 0.299230566607 5.82394386616 1 4 0.223579960826 3.33468292914 2 1 1.34164078650 47.8125019186 2 2 0.402749351016 11.8511029453 2 3 0.255225288434 5.90890775165 2 4 0.190501248180 4.05290086226 Source norm here is <C,C> in model units. These particular unconstrained solutions differ in magnitude, but that is not necessary. Constraining <C,C>=15 and resolving produces spectrally stable one-electron branches: L Clock beta at common source norm Positive eigenvalues of iC 2 0.454619168037 0.07408293, 2.01168471, 3.30872125 3 0.318698166754 1.62354101, 1.70665083, 3.07432229 4 0.162808843130 0.47026621, 2.01069745, 3.27657526 Their equilibrium residuals are below 3e-13 and apparent maximum real linear parts below 8e-7. Therefore different total source strength is not required for L=2,3,4. Their full conserved spectra still differ, so integer L remains encoded in prepared source data rather than quantized dynamically by this model. What is finished and what is not The existence question for a consistent one-electron completion now has a positive answer: the quadratically completed autonomous Hamiltonian supports actual four- and eight-petal projected orbits, and those two tested branches have no resolved exponential linear instability. The earlier claim that quadratic completion simply destroys the petals was too broad; it destroys the old preparation but admits new relative equilibria. The physical theory is not finished in three respects. First, C=0 remains C=0, so the model does not induce the required source magnitude. Second, the integer frequency ratio is encoded in conserved initial source data. Third, the tested two-electron pair is unstable. A source with canonical amplitude and momentum can in principle be driven from zero, but its action, spectrum, and stable relative equilibria must be derived and tested rather than appended to force the desired answer. Interaction 099 correction to the rank three requirement a Read the complete source. 99. Correction to the rank-three requirement: a generic rank-two orbital bivector uniquely selects an SO(3) frame by orientation-preserving Procrustes completion Section 55 correctly proved that the mixed block of one simple orbital bivector has rank at most two, E_L=x_Op_H^T-p_Ox_H^T, \qquad \operatorname{rank}E_L\le2. It then drew the stronger conclusion that rank two is insufficient to determine a complete three-frame relation. That conclusion is false once the desired frame map is restricted to Q\in SO(3). Two independent oriented vector correspondences determine the third axis by orientation. Equivalently, a generic rank-two 3	imes3 tensor has a unique orientation-preserving orthogonal Procrustes factor. This materially strengthens the scattering route. 99.1 Exact factorization of the orbital mixed block Write A_O=[x_O\;p_O], \qquad A_H=[x_H\;p_H], and J_2=  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\ -1&0 \end{pmatrix}. Then  oxed{ E_L=A_OJ_2A_H^T. } If x_O
ot\parallel p_O and x_H
ot\parallel p_H, both A_O and A_H have column rank two and J_2 is invertible. Therefore  oxed{ \operatorname{rank}E_L=2. } Its left and right null directions are exactly the two orbital-plane normals:  oxed{ E_L^T(x_O	imes p_O)=0, }  oxed{ E_L(x_H	imes p_H)=0. } Thus the missing third axis is not absent geometrically. It is already fixed, up to sign, by the oriented normals of the two rank-two planes. 99.2 Rank-two 3	imes3 tensors have a unique SO(3) Procrustes maximizer Let a real rank-two tensor have singular-value decomposition E=U  egin{pmatrix} \sigma_1&0&0\ 0&\sigma_2&0\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix} V^T, \qquad \sigma_1,\sigma_2>0. Because the third singular vectors correspond to zero singular value, their signs may be chosen so that U,V\in SO(3). Consider the orientation-preserving Procrustes problem \max_{Q\in SO(3)}\operatorname{tr}(Q^TE). Write Q=URV^T, \qquad R\in SO(3). Then \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) = \sigma_1R_{11}+\sigma_2R_{22}. Since every diagonal entry of an orthogonal matrix is at most one, \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) \le \sigma_1+\sigma_2. Equality requires R_{11}=R_{22}=1. Orthogonality then forces the first two rows and columns to be the first two coordinate basis vectors, and the condition \det R=1 forces R_{33}=1. Hence R=I_3 is the unique maximizer. Therefore  oxed{ Q_E=UV^T } is a uniquely selected element of SO(3) even though \det E=0. So full matrix rank is not required for full orientation selection in three dimensions. 99.3 Canonical exact example For E=  egin{pmatrix} 0&a&0\ -b&0&0\ 0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a,b>0, one has E=Q_0 \operatorname{diag}(b,a,0), with  oxed{ Q_0=  egin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\ -1&0&0\ 0&0&1 \end{pmatrix} \in SO(3). } For any Q=Q_0R, \qquad R\in SO(3), the trace objective is \operatorname{tr}(Q^TE) =bR_{11}+aR_{22} \le a+b, with equality only for R=I. This provides a completely elementary exact verification of the rank-two theorem. 99.4 Consequence for the scattering hierarchy The ranking in Section 55 must therefore be revised. A rank-one mixed source leaves a continuous axial ambiguity and is insufficient. But a generic rank-two source already fixes two independent directions, and the orientation condition fixes the third. Thus  oxed{ \operatorname{rank}E=2 \quad	ext{is generically sufficient to select a unique }Q\in SO(3). } The scattering-triad tensor E_{m tri} remains a valid full-rank construction, but it is no longer the minimal one. The simpler orbital bivector  oxed{ L=x\wedge p } already supplies, through its mixed block,  oxed{ E_L=x_Op_H^T-p_Ox_H^T, } a generically rank-two bifundamental tensor whose unique SO(3) Procrustes completion defines  oxed{Q_L.} This is substantially more economical because x and p are the ordinary phase-space data of one relative orbit; no independently postulated third dyadic term is needed. 99.5 Relation to the second-order lock theorem Section 95 showed that the first-order cross-depth transition itself need not contain a full (\mathbf3,\mathbf3) correlation tensor. A much smaller transition can produce P_Q and hence T_Q at second order. Section 99 now removes an analogous unnecessary requirement on the classical orientation source. The source tensor need not be full rank either. It only has to determine a unique orientation-preserving frame map. Therefore the required chain can be weakened from 	ext{full-rank }E_{m tri} \longrightarrow Q_{m scat} to  oxed{ 	ext{generic rank-two }E_L \longrightarrow Q_L \longrightarrow P_{Q_L} \longrightarrow T_{Q_L}. } This is a genuine reduction in the amount of dynamical structure V2 must derive. 99.6 Degenerate cases are now sharply classified For the orbital tensor E_L=A_OJ_2A_H^T, rank falls below two exactly when at least one orbital plane degenerates: x_O\parallel p_O or x_H\parallel p_H. Then only one or zero independent directions are correlated and a continuous frame ambiguity returns. Thus the physical distinction is not 	ext{rank three versus rank two}, but  oxed{ 	ext{two independent oriented directions versus fewer than two}. } This matches ordinary three-dimensional frame geometry: two noncollinear axes determine the third by the right-hand rule. 99.7 Revised bottleneck The source audit of Section 98 remains valid: the current non-note V2 corpus does not yet insert an orbital/scattering bifundamental into the electron--nucleus kernel. But the missing source is now simpler than Section 98 assumed. One no longer needs to derive a full-rank tensor such as E_{m tri}. It is enough to derive a nondegenerate mixed orbital block  oxed{ E_L=P_O(x\wedge p)P_H } or any equivalent rank-two bifundamental whose SO(3) Procrustes completion is unique. The next source-level test is therefore:  oxed{ 	ext{does the actual }3\leftrightarrow6	ext{ projected interaction retain the mixed orbital bivector }P_O(x\wedge p)P_H	ext{ or an equivalent two-direction correlation?} } If yes, the orientation problem is much closer to closure than the earlier full-rank criterion suggested. If every source-level cross-depth term removes or averages away this rank-two orbital information, the orientation route still fails. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. The source notes supply the full derivations, corrections and reproduction references. A physical mass operator still requires one canonically normalized same-field action, supported spatial states, positive complete inertia and agreement across the maintained particle sectors.

title: Flavor, charge and gauge geometry
summary: Mass assignments alone do not produce a mixing matrix or a physical gauge field. Candidate projected operators and bundle data give finite tests whose physical source and normalization remain to be derived.
text: Mass assignments alone do not produce a mixing matrix or a physical gauge field. Candidate projected operators and bundle data give finite tests whose physical source and normalization remain to be derived. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Ckm mixing from cross sector contact Read the complete source. 2. The occupied quark bases The committed up-type occupied modes are (n_u,n_c,n_t)=(3,20,72), at depth d_u=4, while the down-type sector contains n_d=1, \qquad n_s=4, and the bottom state is the critical adjacent-band pair (n_{b,-},n_{b,+})=(16,17). Its mass is m_b =\mu_3\sqrt{S(16,3)S(17,3)}. Thus the physical three-generation spaces may be written schematically as \mathcal F_u =\operatorname{span}\{|u\rangle,|c\rangle,|t\rangle\}, \mathcal F_d =\operatorname{span}\{|d\rangle,|s\rangle,|b\rangle\}. The first two down states are ordinary occupied coherent bands. The bottom state is already exceptional because it is represented by a two-band singular-value construction. Any CKM derivation must respect that distinction rather than replacing the bottom state by an arbitrary ordinary mode. 3. Where CKM lives in the projected operator Restrict the cross-sector weak block to the physical generation spaces: C_{34} = P_{\mathcal F_d}\mathcal C_{34}P_{\mathcal F_u}. In chosen orthonormal mass bases, (C_{34})_{ij} = \langle d_i|\mathcal C_{34}|u_j\rangle, where (d_1,d_2,d_3)=(d,s,b), (u_1,u_2,u_3)=(u,c,t). The charged-current interaction then has the form \mathcal L_W \supset \frac{g_2}{\sqrt2} \overline{d_{Li}}\gamma^\mu (C_{34})_{ij}u_{Lj}W^-_\mu +\text{h.c.} Canonical normalization is determined by the kinetic metrics, not by an arbitrary polar or singular-value decomposition of the vertex. For a transition matrix K before canonical normalization and positive kinetic metrics Z_u,Z_d, define K_c=Z_d^{-1/2}KZ_u^{-1/2},\qquad V_-=L_d^\dagger K_cL_u, where L_u,L_d diagonalize the canonically normalized left-handed mass operators. For already orthonormal mass bases, these transformations are identities. The three-generation charged current is unitary only if K_c^\dagger K_c=I \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^\dagger Z_d^{-1}K=Z_u. This is an additional property to derive, not a permission to discard the singular values of K. A deficient-rank kernel cannot be repaired by invertible kinetic normalization; its polar unitary completion is nonunique. The rows here are (d,s,b) and columns (u,c,t), so V_- is the adjoint of the usual up-row/down-column CKM matrix: V_{\rm CKM}=V_-^\dagger. Below, identity and zero-mixing conclusions are independent of this convention. See the normalization audit. 5. Why the mass hierarchy does not determine CKM The simplex mass laws determine diagonal mass eigenvalues: M_u =\mu_4\operatorname{diag} \left( S(3,4), S(20,4), S(72,4) \right), while the down sector has the schematic form M_d =\mu_3\operatorname{diag} \left( S(1,3), S(4,3), \sqrt{S(16,3)S(17,3)} \right). These spectra fix eigenvalues but not the relative orientation of the up and down eigenbases. For any unitary matrices U_u and U_d, M_u \mapsto U_uM_uU_u^\dagger, M_d \mapsto U_dM_dU_d^\dagger preserves the eigenvalue spectra. The charged-current mixing matrix is V_{\rm CKM}=U_u^\dagger U_d. This is the usual up-row/down-column W^+ convention. The down-row/up-column matrix V_- used for the preceding cross-sector kernel is its adjoint, V_-=U_d^\dagger U_u; the two must not be given the same matrix label. Therefore the successful simplex mass hierarchy alone cannot determine CKM. A separate geometric object fixing the relative orientation of the two three-dimensional flavor frames is mathematically necessary. Any proposal that constructs CKM solely from the six quark masses, with no independently derived cross-sector operator, adds an extra ansatz rather than following from the present V2 mass theorem. 6. The minimal V2 completion The minimal completion is a generation-space operator G_{34}:\mathcal F_u\to\mathcal F_d appearing in P_3D_\infty P_4 \supset g_2\gamma^\mu W_\mu^-T^-P_{(1,1)} \otimes G_{34}. Its matrix elements must be obtained from the same projected master geometry: (G_{34})_{ij} = \langle d_i| P_3D_\infty P_4 |u_j\rangle_{\rm normalized}. A successful derivation must produce all of the following without fitting CKM data: a dominant 1\leftrightarrow1, 2\leftrightarrow2, 3\leftrightarrow3 structure; a much larger 1\leftrightarrow2 transition than 2\leftrightarrow3; a strongly suppressed 1\leftrightarrow3 transition; one irreducible complex phase; unitarity after canonical normalization; the same universal weak coupling g_2 for all generations. In schematic magnitude form the target hierarchy is |V_{us}|\sim2\times10^{-1}, \qquad |V_{cb}|\sim4\times10^{-2}, \qquad |V_{ub}|\sim4\times10^{-3}. The hierarchy between these three off-diagonal amplitudes is itself a stringent geometric test. 8. A finite matrix problem The CKM calculation can be reduced to a finite operator computation. Let the up-sector normalized occupied states be |U\rangle = \left( |3,4\rangle, |20,4\rangle, |72,4\rangle \right), and let the down-sector states be |D\rangle = \left( |1,3\rangle, |4,3\rangle, |b,3\rangle \right), where |b,3\rangle is the normalized singular vector of the 16--17 bottom block. Define K_{ij} = \langle D_i| P_3D_\infty P_4 |U_j\rangle. Remove the derived universal polarization and weak-coupling factors and use the independently derived kinetic metrics and mass-basis rotations: \boxed{ V_{\rm CKM}^{\rm V2} =\left(L_d^\dagger Z_d^{-1/2}KZ_u^{-1/2}L_u\right)^\dagger. } This is a standard unitary CKM candidate only after the isometry test in Section 3 passes. Taking an arbitrary polar factor is not this calculation. No quark mass values are required to choose its mixing angles once the occupied mode projectors and master kernel are fixed. This 3\times3 calculation is the decisive CKM test. Auxiliary gauge carrier Read the complete source. 1. An explicit globally admissible bundle Let L=O(1) on CP5 and choose E_g=(L^{-2}\otimes\mathbb C^3)\oplus(L^3\otimes\mathbb C^2). The determinant is L^(-6+6)=the trivial line. Hermitian metrics and a chosen parallel determinant trivialization reduce its frame bundle to S(U(3) times U(2)). This is a real global construction, not local trace subtraction on the tangent bundle. The group is the usual (SU(3) times SU(2) times U(1))/Z6 subgroup of SU(5). The integer block charges (-2,3) are the primitive solution of 3a+2b=0, up to simultaneous sign reversal. Dividing by six gives the existing hypercharge generator Y=diag(-1/3,-1/3,-1/3,1/2,1/2). The choice of degree-one L and of this auxiliary carrier is an additional construction, not a background selection derived from the master action. For a unitary connection a on L and traceless unitary connections A_c,A_w on the displayed trivial multiplicity bundles, a compatible connection is \nabla^g=\operatorname{diag}(d-2aI_3+A_c,\ d+3aI_2+A_w). The expression is interpreted in local line frames with their transition functions; the global tensor-product connection is what is defined. Its trace is zero and its mixed blocks vanish. With A_c=A_w=0, its actual holonomy is only a U(1) subgroup; the allowed structure group is not a proof that every non-Abelian gauge interaction is dynamically generated. 2. The entire charge table is a global exterior bundle Use F_g=Lambda^even E_g, of rank 16. Its decomposition is Exterior component SU(3) x SU(2) Line factor Y Conventional field label Lambda^0 (1,1) L^0 0 nu^c Lambda^2 colour (bar3,1) L^-4 -2/3 u^c colour tensor weak (3,2) L^1 1/6 Q Lambda^2 weak (1,1) L^6 1 e^c Lambda^3 colour tensor weak (1,2) L^-3 -1/2 leptons Lambda^2 colour tensor Lambda^2 weak (bar3,1) L^2 1/3 d^c The line exponents are just sums of the five primitive weights. Their multiplicities are 1,3,6,1,2,3. This is the same fibre branching as the existing gauge module, now on a specified global bundle. If read as one family of left-handed 4D fields, the usual hypercharge, mixed, and weak-doublet anomaly checks pass; that is a representation check, not a derivation of 4D field content. 4. Fibre multiplicities are not zero-mode multiplicities If one were additionally to use the ordinary spin Dirac operator on CP5 twisted by a line L^q, its index would be \operatorname{ind}(D\otimes L^q)=\chi(\mathcal O(q-3)) =\binom{q+2}{5}, where the binomial is the polynomial extension for negative arguments and K^(1/2)=O(-3). For the charges q=(-4,-3,0,1,2,6) this gives (-6,-1,0,0,0,56), not one mode per representation. This is a conditional diagnostic of a particular twisted-Dirac interpretation, not a compactification premise imposed on V2. It prevents declaring a complete particle spectrum merely from the 16-dimensional exterior fibre. Scope These are selected calculations, not an exhaustive archive. title: Observational comparisons and remaining proofs
summary: A candidate law must pass simultaneous frequency, normalization, spatial-state, stability and response tests. This document keeps the maintained depth controls and explicit proof obligations together without promoting an inverse fit into a physical derivation.
text: A candidate law must pass simultaneous frequency, normalization, spatial-state, stability and response tests. This document keeps the maintained depth controls and explicit proof obligations together without promoting an inverse fit into a physical derivation. The equations and numerical values below retain the assumptions of their linked source notes. Results from different actions are not combined into one physical mechanism. Mass operator sector controls Read the complete source. Fixed assignments and a common calculation Use the maintained mass-spectrum assignments, with particle index n_p, cumulative degree N=n_p-1, surface degree L=N+2, and normal winding n=d. The last equality remains an inverse model premise. Distinguishing winding from particle index is essential.
