They are not two new particle assignments, nor a calculated bottom particle. Its maintained count is \sqrt{816\cdot969}=889.21538448\ldots. The connected normal operator uses the unchanged radial equations w'=\frac{d-a}{r}w,\qquad a'=2r(1-w^2), the same multiplier h=z/\sqrt{1+r^2}, canonical unit norms, and the same illustrative hopping \gamma=10^4. No coefficient is retuned for an individual mode. Its complete complementary gap remains at least one; the actual d kernel modes satisfy P[(d+1-a)S]P=-2J_z. Direct Cartesian derivatives of every normal spinor, a second application of the full Dirac operator, and radial and outer-domain refinements verify these statements at both new depths. The separate bounded unconnected profile also retains positive analytic gap bounds, approximately 1.18923 at depth three and 1.17675 at depth four. The projected diagonal factors give \prod_{l=0}^{d-1}\left(\beta+l-\frac{d-1}{2}\right) =\prod_{l=0}^{d-1}(L-1+l) =d!\binom{N+d}{d}. This includes the down assignment N=0; no large-degree approximation is used in this numerator. The full small frequency still has the previous finite-hopping correction: \omega_{N,d}= \frac{d!\binom{N+d}{d}}{\gamma^{d-1}\prod_l h_l} \left[1-\frac{(L-1)^2/h_0^2+(L+d-2)^2/h_{d-2}^2} {2\gamma^2}+O(\gamma^{-4})\right]. The correction is a property of the complete finite matrix. At the illustrative hopping, it ranges from about -1.06\times10^{-7} for down to -6.90\times10^{-6} for the upper bottom component, and from -4.56\times10^{-7} for up to -1.09\times10^{-4} for top. These numbers are mathematical departures from the simplex product, not comparisons with new mass measurements. The actual lower-dimensional surface The normal calculation uses one ordinary plane at every winding. By itself, changing that winding would not test the full physical dimension. The surface calculation must also use m=d-2 directions and the appropriate intrinsic spinor rank 2^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}. For odd m, construct the ambient Clifford matrices in m+1 directions and restrict their even products to one ambient chirality. The surface operator contains only such even products: B_K=k-\Gamma_x\Gamma_{\nabla_S},\qquad k=\frac{m-1}{2}. They preserve that chirality exactly. The resulting intrinsic rank is one on the depth-three circle, two on the depth-four sphere, and two on the depth-five three-sphere. Both choices of ambient chirality are checked; neither is assigned a particle charge or antiparticle meaning. Arbitrary complete spatial spinor jets verify B_K^2=\Delta_S+k^2, and a separate stereographic calculation with the actual spin connection agrees. The full principal symbol is Hermitian and squares to the spatial momentum norm. These controls cover depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 without interpreting matrix rank as additional physical coordinates. On the unit circle, in one of the two equivalent ambient realizations, B_K=-i\partial_\theta,\qquad \mathscr D=B_K+\frac12. Here the specified bounding spin structure has antiperiodic spinors \psi=e^{i\theta/2}F, with periodic coefficient F. The modes F=e^{\pm iL\theta} have B_K eigenvalues \pm L. Both are retained for L\ge1. At L=0, B_K=0; a formula dividing by \beta must not be used there. All assigned depth-three controls have L\ge2. The depth-three link product is B_K(B_K^2-1). It is odd in B_K, so its two surface signs give opposite signed products. The complete canonical Hamiltonian H_P=\begin{pmatrix}0&T^\dagger\\T&0\end{pmatrix} reads positive frequency from a singular value and gives the same positive frequency on both branches. More generally, if R reverses the chain and J=\operatorname{diag}((-1)^l), reflection symmetry of the actual hoppings gives T(-\beta)=-JRT(\beta)^TRJ. Thus both signs have the same complete singular spectrum at finite hopping, including at odd depth. The signed product alone is not the physical frequency or an inertia sign. The earlier positive scalar bending-Hessian interpretation requires a separate extension at odd depth. On the circle its desired positive spectrum would be that of \sqrt{\Delta_S}(\Delta_S-1), which is not a finite polynomial in the scalar Laplacian. The local first-order parent survives this parity test; the even-dimensional scalar interpretation does not transfer unchanged. The codimension-two surface construction at depth two has m=0 and is outside the differential-surface controls established here. Complete partner phases and geometric response For diagonal links D_l=\beta+l-(d-1)/2, let u_l,v_l be the positive singular vectors obtained from the absolute scaled inverse. Their canonical phases must obey s_0=1,\qquad s_l=-\operatorname{sgn}(D_l)s_{l-1},\qquad t_l=\operatorname{sgn}(D_l)s_l. The positive-frequency state is (s_lu_l,t_lv_l)/\sqrt2. An alternating-sign formula is sufficient only when all D_l>0. The implementation now retains the correct partner phases on negative and mixed-sign controls. This correction leaves the previously tested positive-branch frequencies unchanged. The complete geometric source gives the constant-polynomial deformation response F_{N,d}=2\gamma\kappa_d \operatorname{Re}(v_0^*u_{d-1}), where \kappa_d is one spatial integral shared by all grades. Here \kappa_d denotes the endpoint integral, not the core binding coefficient. At fixed positive surface branch and the common illustrative hopping: Depth Mode Geometric response F_{N,d} 3 Down -3294.23064 3 Strange -3294.22917 3 Bottom lower component -3294.21072 3 Bottom upper component -3294.20827 4 Up 1727.35553 4 Charm 1727.34007 4 Top 1727.16733 These are derivatives with respect to the stated geometric coefficient. Their units and physical canonical conversion are not yet fixed between sectors. Within each depth, they show response grouping without dividing by mass or changing the coefficients for each particle. Both surface signs and both real and imaginary shape perturbations must be retained. At fixed mode and orientation, the complete source gives F_{N,d}(-\beta)=(-1)^dF_{N,d}(+\beta). Thus the depth-three surface partners have opposite signed response, whereas the depth-four partners have the same signed response. Their positive mass-frequencies agree exactly. At normal orientation angle \vartheta, the derivatives with respect to the real and imaginary geometric coefficients are (F_{\mathrm{Re}},F_{\mathrm{Im}}) =F_{N,d}(0)(\cos(d\vartheta),\sin(d\vartheta)). The full reciprocal source verifies both components independently. For the circle's two degenerate surface modes, a normalized superposition with weights |a|^2+|b|^2=1 has response F_{\mathrm{superposition}}=(|a|^2-|b|^2)F_{N,3}(+\beta) to a surface-independent normal deformation. Cross terms vanish by the actual circle integral. Equal weights cancel this particular response for every relative phase, while other spatial deformation channels remain. Such balance is a state choice here, not a derived occupation rule or a general absence of interactions. The same parity rule applies to other odd depths and cannot by itself single out neutrinos. The sign of a geometric force depends on orientation and polarization; it is not a sign of particle inertia. The full occupied support still has to respond to the complete spatial source. The bottom assignment adds a dynamical constraint A normal deformation constant over the circle commutes with the surface operator. It cannot mix the bottom components L=17 and L=18: \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-17i\theta}e^{18i\theta}\,d\theta=0. A first surface harmonic can access that channel, since the same integral with \cos\theta inserted is 1/2. Using the previously derived normal endpoint deformation and the actual two canonical states gives a nonzero first-harmonic matrix element, approximately -1647.10475 at \gamma=10^4. This identifies a spatially allowed channel, not a stationary occupied shape or a derived bottom mass. Ordinary mixing of the two positive branches is insufficient. For 0<a<b, retain their frequencies on the diagonal and add any Hermitian off-diagonal coupling: M=\begin{pmatrix}a&g\\\bar g&b\end{pmatrix}. At \lambda=\sqrt{ab}, \det(M-\lambda I) =-\sqrt{ab}(\sqrt b-\sqrt a)^2-|g|^2<0. Consequently \sqrt{ab} is never an eigenfrequency of this matrix. In fact no eigenvalue lies strictly between a and b. The two uncoupled frequencies also give an ordinary difference frequency, not their geometric mean. The maintained bottom count therefore requires a different coupled block, changed diagonal dynamics, or an explicitly derived relation between the two canonical quadratures. Merely inserting the target off-diagonal singular value would assume the missing result. The full signed parent and its same-field nonlinear response remain available to test; this exclusion concerns the stated two-positive-branch reduction. The full core limitation persists at the new depths The separate polarization core has the same radial rule at each physical depth: \frac{h(r)}{f(r)} =\frac{I_{d/2}((\kappa-m_c)r)} {I_{d/2-1}((\kappa-m_c)r)},\qquad \kappa>m_c>0. With m_c=1,\kappa=2, its dimensionless root mean squared radii are 1.73035154 at depth three and 2.22415436 at depth four. Within each depth, all listed single-grade controls have the same profile. Full spatial variation, the canonical norm, and the complete boosted field equation and stress pass the new checks. Thus positive total inertia on that conditional branch does not depend on specializing to depth six. The full linear-response problem persists as well. At both depths the retained core representation has rank four, so the common rule q=1/(r+1) gives q=1/5. It would be inconsistent to reuse the depth-six value 1/9 without changing that rule. The full real multiplet has 64 components. Constructing its exact invariant tail block gives the same finite-wave-number Jordan chain at p_\perp=\sqrt3, with \|e^{tA}u\|/\|u\|=\sqrt{1+c_J^2t^2},\qquad c_J=\frac{2(q\omega^2+1)}{\sqrt{\omega^2+1}}. The existing translated-packet argument therefore applies at depths three and four too. This is an unbounded formal linear response, not a negative physical inertia and not a nonlinear instability theorem. The bottom component frequencies are only spectral controls of this core, as above. The cross-sector comparison supports the dimensional consistency of the specified constructions while narrowing their physical completion. The joint occupied geometry, the bottom two-grade dynamics, stability, and physical normalization across sectors remain necessary tests of a candidate mass operator. What survives and what comes next The exact representation algebra, specified analytic orbit constructions, fixed-source chart, and checked conservative equations remain useful. They are positive mathematical results for defined models. They are not a completed derivation of the physical electron, chemistry, or a unique CP3 geometry. Known unstable and rejected branches must remain in the record. title: Cross-sector moment kernel
summary: The unaveraged quadratic kernel retains the tensor data needed to investigate orientation dependence.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Source and scope Starting point: Gravity §3.10.1–2 and Appendix B §20a. The explicit rectangular identification and tensor generalization below are an adaptation derived during the import review, not a theorem quoted from V1. Retain the second moments Let x in R^d, y in R^e, and let B:R^e -> R^d be a specified identification. For unit-normalized densities define K_B(x,y)=g(x^{\mathsf T}By)^2,\qquad M_x=\int xx^{\mathsf T}\rho_x(x)\,dx,\quad M_y=\int yy^{\mathsf T}\rho_y(y)\,dy. Then, exactly, V_x(x)=g x^{\mathsf T}B M_y B^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad U_{xy}=g\operatorname{tr}(M_x B M_y B^{\mathsf T}). For fixed M_y and B, the coordinate Hessian of V_x is 2g B M_y B^T. This is not automatically the full coupled-field Hessian: the background moments can fluctuate too. For equal dimensions and B=I, write M_x=aI+Q_x and M_y=bI+Q_y, with traceless Q_x,Q_y. Then U_{xy}=g\left[dab+\operatorname{tr}(Q_xQ_y)\right]. The historical isotropic reduction sets both Q tensors to zero. Retaining them gives an explicit orientation-sensitive term. Its sign and eigenvalue structure must determine the preferred orientation; alignment is not automatic. Even a preferred quadrupole-axis alignment need not determine a unique signed frame or the electron's complex-structure polarization. Symmetry and missing inputs Under independent orthogonal frame changes x->R x and y->S y, covariance requires B->R B S^T. Holding B fixed preserves only compatible transformations. An unspecified cross-sector dot product is therefore not invariant under arbitrary independent rotations. For complex coordinates, specify a Hermitian kernel such as |x-dagger B y|^2 and its representation separately. Rank-one sector coefficients g_de=v_d v_e do not force the coordinate kernel or its projected matrix elements to be rank one. Promising next calculation: derive B and background moments from the V2 field, retain their fluctuations, and project onto the actual polarization states. Do not identify this scalar coordinate Hessian with a spin-dependent lock operator without that projection and the corresponding kinetic form. Related Self-consistent moment lock test — follow-up: the positive scalar ground-state model does not generate a mixed covariance spontaneously, but its response to a supplied source is calculable. Self-consistent functional — the isotropic background to generalize. Import boundaries — explains why older uniqueness and closure claims are not imported.

title: Import boundaries
summary: Negative results and faulty closure claims constrain what may safely be transferred from V1.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Preserve these useful restrictions Chemistry §6.1–6.4 contains a useful conditional factorization result. If H=H_obs tensor I + I tensor H_hidden, the unobserved states are orthonormal, and O=O_obs tensor I, then \langle\psi\otimes\chi_a|O|\psi'\otimes\chi_b\rangle =\langle\psi|O_{\rm obs}|\psi'\rangle\delta_{ab}. A purely unobserved contribution gives a common shift when all compared states share the same unobserved state and particle content. Under these assumptions it cannot generate orbital-dependent splittings. A mixed interaction is the place to investigate deviations. Do not import the universal chemistry claim or numerical contact bound without separately establishing their premises, range, units, amplitude, and relevant observables. Appendix B §20a and §50 record that isotropic density overlaps retain the monopole, with the mean traceless quadrupole vanishing. This is a restriction on that reduction, not on all anisotropic states, virtual transitions, or spinor operators. The imported notes do not rely on §50's separate fourth-moment formulas. Appendix D §49b records the rejection of an old rho-meson comb-root claim: a target-bracketed root among many roots does not select a physical resonance. Preserve this warning rather than the contradictory positive claim still present in Mass §10. title: Normalized oscillator modes
summary: Explicit normalized modes and density overlaps supply calculational inputs without identifying them with mixing amplitudes.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Source and scope Transcribed from Appendix B §20–20a, with representation-theory overclaims omitted. The associated historical code includes overlap_J near line 2282. These are scalar flat-space oscillator modes, not automatically V2 spinor, polarization, or orbital-section states. Explicit normalized basis For H=-Delta+lambda r^2, w=sqrt(lambda)>0, and angular harmonics normalized to unit integral on S^(d-1), \chi_{n_r\ell m}(r,\Omega)= N_{n_r\ell}r^\ell L_{n_r}^{(\ell+d/2-1)}(wr^2) e^{-wr^2/2}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega), \qquad N_{n_r\ell}^2=\frac{2w^{\ell+d/2}n_r!}{\Gamma(n_r+\ell+d/2)}. N=2n_r+\ell,\qquad E_N=w(2N+d),\qquad \langle r^2\rangle_N=\frac{2N+d}{2w}. The level degeneracy is binomial(N+d-1,d-1); the cumulative count through N=n-1 is S(n,d)=binomial(n+d-1,d). This count is not E_N. Equality of dimensions with another representation does not establish an operator intertwiner or an equivalence of physical state spaces. Density overlap versus transition matrix element For isotropic normalized densities in the same R^d, O_{ij}=\iint(x\cdot y)^2|\chi_i(x)|^2|\chi_j(y)|^2\,dx\,dy =\frac{\langle r^2\rangle_i\langle r^2\rangle_j}{d}. Isotropy must hold for the actual density, for example an s-wave or a uniform shell mixture; an arbitrary individual oscillator eigenstate need not have it. With one mode fixed, this overlap grows linearly with the other shell index, unlike the degree-d cumulative count. It is a density-density expectation, not a normalized charged-current amplitude. For actual coherent transitions use off-diagonal moments such as integral chi_i^*(x) x_a x_b chi_j(x) dx, retaining phases, angular indices, selection rules, and any spinor vertex. A reusable radial integral For s>0 and integer n_r>=0, \int_0^\infty u^{1/2}e^{-su}L_{n_r}^{(1/2)}(u)\,du =\frac{\Gamma(n_r+3/2)}{n_r!} \frac{(s-1)^{n_r}}{s^{n_r+3/2}}. At s=1 it vanishes for n_r>=1; at s=3/2 no finite radial level is eliminated. The weight must be obtained from the actual vertex before using this as a selection rule. It does not select a particle tower by itself. Product shell counts Shell degeneracies obey a useful convolution. For g_d(N)=\binom{N+d-1}{d-1}, \sum_{k=0}^{N}g_a(k)g_b(N-k)=g_{a+b}(N). The generating functions multiply as (1-z)^{-a}(1-z)^{-b}=(1-z)^{-(a+b)}. This counts product states of the specified separated oscillators with fixed total excitation. Using cumulative counts as though they were shell degeneracies would give a different convolution. The partition into a and b directions is a calculation choice among equivalent ordinary spatial directions. The a=b=3 example does not give the electron an inherent 3+3 split or prove colour neutrality. The simplex band moments instead average shell observables across a whole cumulative band. Constant-background overlaps A uniform continuation and an oscillator ground state have different overlap weights. For the physicists' Hermite polynomials in a dimensionless coordinate, \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}H_{2m}(y)e^{-y^2/2}\,dy =\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{(2m)!}{m!},\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}H_{2m+1}(y)e^{-y^2/2}\,dy=0. To derive this, integrate the generating function e^{2ty-t^2}=\sum_jH_j(y)t^j/j! against e^{-y^2/2}. The result is \sqrt{2\pi}e^{t^2}. Thus overlap against a constant background removes odd modes by parity, but every even mode has a nonzero overlap. Normalized oscillator modes add nonzero prefactors and do not change these zeros. The constant is a generalized background on the line, not a normalizable oscillator state. A ground-state bra would supply another Gaussian and a different orthogonality relation. This distinction matters for the cylindrical continuation premise: a low-degree insertion and parity alone do not exclude excitation in several added coordinates when the relevant modes are even. The actual vertex and integration weight must be supplied. Finite spatial operators The complete source marginal uses these normalized constant-background integrals in a finite matrix; its singular strengths follow a weighted Hockey-Stick identity. Physical bilinear currents must be formed before that linear map is applied. The spatial evaluation kernel uses the same paired-occupation weights at the oscillator center and fixes the distinction between spatial point contact and projective ray contact. Review checks Independent quadrature in the preceding review checked unit normalization and the radial second moment for (d,n_r,ell,w)=(3,2,0,2.195), (4,1,2,1.314), and (6,6,0,0.5), with errors below 1e-13. This was a representative check, not a rerun of the entire historical script or validation of its conclusions. The mode counting checks verify shell convolutions and independently integrate the Hermite overlaps by Gaussian quadrature. Related Self-consistent functional — supplies the harmonic background under stated assumptions. Import boundaries — prevents reinterpreting density overlaps as CKM probabilities. Counting mode tools — collects the counting and spectral identities.

title: Reference-band normalization
summary: The historical mass-scale prescription uses a fixed occupied reference count whose dynamical origin remains open.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Source Mass §10, beginning near line 633, states that the squared lightest occupied mass scales as g_dd/g_66 relative to the electron. Preserve this as a historical prescription, not an established consequence of varying the displayed action. The useful distinction Write D_d*=S(n_min(d),d) for a fixed occupied reference count and m(n,d)=mu_d S(n,d). The historical reference condition is (\mu_d D_d^*)^2=\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}m_e^2, \qquad \mu_d=\frac{m_e}{D_d^*}\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. For the d=3,4,6 comparison the reference counts are 1,15,18564. Once fixed, D_d* is a sector constant, not the variable S(n,d) of whichever excited mode is being evaluated. Consequently mu_d=C v_d/D_d*, with v_d=sqrt(g_dd) and C=m_e/sqrt(g_66), is compatible with band blindness. This supports the corrected common-anchor interpretation in the existing V2 notes: a fixed-reference relation is not ruled out merely because it contains a count. It does not prove the relation or select its reference bands. Remaining derivation Derive the stationary cross-sector equations and kinetic normalization that select the occupied-reference masses rather than the pre-count coefficients. Explain why these particular occupied modes define the reference. Do not extend this prescription indiscriminately: V1 also uses different neutrino, boson, and tau scale constructions despite some universal wording. The scalar oscillator closure lambda proportional to (gQ)^(2/3) is a different equation. Converting it into this mass-reference condition requires an explicit operator and units dictionary, not a relabeling of lambda. title: Self-consistent functional
summary: A reusable harmonic mean-field closure with explicit norm and variation assumptions.
text: Physical premise (IDWT): There is one infinite-dimensional physical manifold. All sectors form one nested chain of submanifolds within it. Particle depth counts ordinary, literal macroscopic spatial dimensions. “Observed” and “unobserved” describe an observer's access to those dimensions, not different kinds of physical dimension. See spatial meaning and mathematical scope. Source and scope Adapted from IDWT_04_Gravity.md, §3.10.2–3.10.5c, especially the explicit functional, near line 315. Status: checked algebra within a flat, scalar, fixed-norm mean-field model; not a derivation of the V2 master dynamics. Functional and stationary equation For real coordinates x,y in R^d, coupling g>0, kinetic coefficient set to one, and Q = integral |Psi|^2 fixed, retain the source functional E[\Psi]=\int |\nabla\Psi(x)|^2\,dx +\frac g2\iint(x\cdot y)^2|\Psi(x)|^2|\Psi(y)|^2\,dx\,dy. Variation of E-mu Q gives \left[-\Delta+g\int(x\cdot y)^2|\Psi(y)|^2\,dy\right]\Psi(x)=\mu\Psi(x). For an isotropic density, its second moment is integral y_i y_j |Psi(y)|^2 dy = Q delta_ij <r^2>/d. Thus V(x)=lambda |x|^2, with lambda=g Q <r^2>/d. The normalized oscillator ground state has <r^2>=d/(2 sqrt(lambda)), so \lambda=(gQ/2)^{2/3},\qquad \Psi(x)=\sqrt Q\,\lambda^{d/8}\pi^{-d/4} \exp(-\sqrt\lambda\,|x|^2/2). The historical formula lambda=(g/2)^(2/3) is the Q=1 specialization. Choosing Q=1 is not a derivation of quantum charge discreteness. Excited-shell self-consistency The same closure can be evaluated on an excited oscillator shell. Let N\geq0 be its total excitation degree, keep the conserved norm Q fixed, and require the second moment to be isotropic. A single-shell oscillator state satisfies \mu_N=(2N+d)\sqrt\lambda,\qquad \langle r^2\rangle_N=\frac{2N+d}{2\sqrt\lambda}. The second identity follows from the oscillator virial identity, or by integrating the normalized Laguerre modes. Isotropy of the second moment is the extra condition that makes the self-sourced potential scalar. It is satisfied, for example, by the radial states with even N. Self-consistency therefore gives \boxed{\lambda_N^{3/2}=\frac{gQ(2N+d)}{2d},\qquad \lambda_N=\left[\frac{gQ(2N+d)}{2d}\right]^{2/3}.} This includes the ground-state equation at N=0 and has a positive solution for every positive gQ and every positive spatial dimension. It is a property of the specified flat scalar functional; a topological Euler characteristic does not enter this calculation. At fixed g,Q, different occupied shells source different well widths. A common well for all particles at a depth consequently needs a sustaining field whose relevant moment remains common, or another derived feedback law. The single-mode closure alone does not implement that premise. For comparison, hold one well fixed and use two isotropic unit-normalized shell profiles. The dot-square pair integral is \iint(x\cdot y)^2\rho_N(x)\rho_M(y)\,dx\,dy =\frac{(2N+d)(2M+d)}{4d\lambda}. With a fixed probe M, the depth-six shell ratio for the assigned N=34 and N=12 is 74/30=37/15. Their cumulative state-count ratio is instead \binom{40}{6}/\binom{18}{6}=206+13/17. These describe different operators. A common bare coefficient does not by itself remove the spatial matrix elements from a physical coupling calculation. geometric_channel_checks.py verifies the shell moments by independent radial Laguerre quadrature and substitutes them into the full mean-field coefficient at fixed norm. Neither the norm nor the field amplitude is identified with particle mass. Transfer conditions This produces an isotropic stationary solution, not a proof that it is the unique physical background or that its full fluctuation spectrum is stable. The eigenvalue mu includes the full mean-field potential; the interaction appears with one-half its double integral in E. Do not equate mu Q with E. When expanding this functional in oscillator modes, retain the kinetic matrix and quartic term, or explicitly subtract the background potential already included in oscillator eigenvalues. Otherwise it is double-counted. A resonant-only quartic mode sum requires a justified rotating-wave or time-averaging reduction; index-resonance restrictions do not follow merely from expanding the static functional in a basis. The formula as written uses a fixed origin. The centroid-relative completion defines and varies a centred version with translation covariance and zero net self-force. That completion remains a flat scalar auxiliary model. This closure does not identify oscillator eigenvalues with cumulative state counts, select occupied particle indices, or supply a physical lock frequency. Related Cross-sector moment kernel — generalizes the isotropic moment retained here. Normalized oscillator modes — supplies the normalized stationary basis. Centroid-relative self-binding — makes the centre dynamical rather than tying the self-potential to an external origin.

title: Spatial Depth and the Three Spin Classes
summary: An exact nonlinear Dirac profile has spin-half covariance and finite bound-sector norm at depths three and above, while quadratic patterns supply scalar and vector rotation channels; a common dynamical particle spectrum remains to be derived.
text: An explicit nonlinear spinor profile provides a possible connection between spatial depth and the spin classes in IDWT. Its complete spatial pattern transforms with spin one-half, and its integrated squared amplitude is finite at every maintained matter depth: three, four, five, six and ten. The same profile has a logarithmically divergent norm at depth two. This is a concrete branch-specific correlation. It suggests that depth could affect which kinds of localized excitation are admissible. It does not yet explain why nature selects those excitations, or produce the spin-zero and spin-one particles assigned to depth two. How This Relates to the Other Correlations This is a third connection to investigate alongside the mass relationships and the electron orbit and observer map. Together they ask whether the same spatial framework can account for mass, orbital geometry and spin. Their evidential strength depends on which inputs they share and which outcomes follow independently. Here the spinor premise already supplies half-angle rotation behavior. The additional result is the finite-norm threshold of a complete nonlinear spatial profile, which aligns with the assigned matter/boson depth division. That is a concrete consistency test, rather than three independently established experimental confirmations of IDWT. In particular, this flat \mathbb R^d calculation is not yet a global solution on the proposed \mathbb{CP}^3 electron geometry; joining those constructions needs a compatible metric, profile and field equation. 1. The Physical Target Depth means ordinary physical spatial dimension in the nested sector geometry. The depth assignments below belong to IDWT; the spin values are the observed particle classifications. They must not be confused with measured evidence for those depth assignments. IDWT depth Assigned particles Required spin 2 Photon, W and Z 1 2 Higgs 0 3, 4 Quark families 1/2 5 Neutrinos 1/2 6 Electron and muon 1/2 10 Tau 1/2 The assignments are described in mass-spectrum depth selection. Experimental particle properties are compiled by the Particle Data Group. Depth two already requires two different spin values. A successful law therefore needs to determine allowed kinds of excitation at each depth, with a further distinction between scalar and vector modes. Spin describes transformation under spatial rotations. In units where Planck's reduced constant is one, its diagnostic is J^2=j(j+1),\qquad j=0,\frac12,1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J^2=0,\frac34,2. A massive spin-one particle can have zero spin projection along one chosen axis. That longitudinal state still has total spin one; it is not the spin-zero Higgs state. 2. An Exact Nonlinear Dirac Profile Let x\in\mathbb R^d describe the bound spatial directions and r=|x|. Choose Hermitian Clifford matrices \Gamma_i satisfying \Gamma_i\Gamma_j+\Gamma_j\Gamma_i=2\delta_{ij}I, \qquad D=-i\Gamma\cdot\nabla. Here D is the spatial Dirac operator. Let a>0 be a length scale, A>0 an amplitude, and \chi a constant unit spinor. Define \boxed{ \psi_\chi(x)=A\left(1+\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)^{-d/2} \left(I+i\frac{\Gamma\cdot x}{a}\right)\chi. } This is the known critical Dirac bubble, equivalent up to conventions to the profiles studied by Borrelli, Malchiodi and Wu in Ground state Dirac bubbles and Killing spinors. The construction is external mathematics. Its application to the IDWT spin–depth comparison is the conditional investigation here. Since (\Gamma\cdot x)^2=r^2I, its squared amplitude is \rho=\psi^\dagger\psi =A^2\left(1+\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)^{1-d}. Differentiating both the radial envelope and the angular matrix gives D\psi=\frac{d}{a}\left(1+\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)^{-1}\psi. Consequently it solves \boxed{D\psi=g\rho^{1/(d-1)}\psi}, \qquad gA^{2/(d-1)}=\frac{d}{a}. The exponent follows the conformal scaling rule for a first-order Dirac operator in dimension d. This gives a dimension-dependent family of comparison equations. Deriving that family from restrictions of one infinite-dimensional field action remains a separate step. A real spatial variational functional producing this equation is \mathcal F=\int_{\mathbb R^d} \left[ \operatorname{Re}(\psi^\dagger D\psi) -g\frac{d-1}{d}\rho^{d/(d-1)} \right]d^dx. This is a spatial equation and functional. A time-dependent action, nonzero rest-frequency, complete energy and stability have not been established by writing it down. 3. Where Depth Two Separates From the Matter Depths The positive norm over the bound directions is Q=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho\,d^dx. At large radius the amplitude falls as r^{1-d}. Including the volume measure, the tail contribution to Q is proportional to \int r^{1-d}\,dr. It converges precisely when d>2. For these dimensions the exact integral is \boxed{ Q=A^2a^d\pi^{d/2} \frac{\Gamma(d/2-1)}{\Gamma(d-1)}. } The \Gamma with a scalar argument denotes the gamma function, distinct from the indexed Clifford matrices. Direct integration at depth two gives \boxed{ Q(R)=\pi A^2a^2\log\left(1+\frac{R^2}{a^2}\right) \longrightarrow\infty. } Depth Exact Q/(A^2a^d) Finite bound-sector norm? 2 Logarithmically divergent No 3 \pi^2 Yes 4 \pi^2/2 Yes 5 \pi^3/12 Yes 6 \pi^3/24 Yes 10 \pi^5/6720 Yes Thus one scaling rule gives the desired separation between depth two and all the assigned matter depths, if finite Q is a physical admissibility condition. The profile remains a valid critical-equation solution at depth two in the function space used in the cited research; its critical spatial functional is finite there. Divergent Q alone is not a universal finite-energy exclusion. Other spinorial branches can have different tails. This result excludes only this profile from the finite-Q class at depth two. Also, cylindrical extension along unbounded free directions needs its own complete normalization calculation: the integral above covers the bound directions. 4. The Entire Pattern Transforms With Spin One-Half For d\geq3, take rotations in the three ordinary spatial directions shared with an observer. Their spinor generators can be written J_1=-\frac{i}{2}\Gamma_2\Gamma_3,\qquad J_2=-\frac{i}{2}\Gamma_3\Gamma_1,\qquad J_3=-\frac{i}{2}\Gamma_1\Gamma_2. Clifford algebra gives [J_i,J_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}J_k, \qquad \sum_iJ_i^2=\frac34I, \qquad e^{-2\pi iJ_3}=-I. These identities concern the spinor components. For the complete spatial solution, let R be a spatial rotation and S(R) its spinor lift. Clifford covariance additionally gives \boxed{ S(R)\psi_\chi(R^{-1}x)=\psi_{S(R)\chi}(x). } The coordinate rotation and the angular matrix transform together. The whole solution family therefore carries exactly the spinor-label rotation law, rather than acquiring an extra orbital multiplet from its angular factor. At depths three, four, five, six and ten, its restriction to those observer rotations consists of spin-one-half copies. This is a classical rotation property. It does not by itself establish fermionic quantum statistics or identify an observed particle. A full turn reverses the field amplitude; bilinear observables are unchanged. Increasing depth alone does not change a direct spinor into an integer-spin field. A depth-two spinor also has half-angle behavior under rotations in its own plane. The useful new distinction comes from this profile's norm, not from a disappearance of spinor algebra in two dimensions. 5. Why Neutrinos Fit This Part of the Calculation At depth five the explicit expressions are \rho_5=A^2\left(1+\frac{r^2}{a^2}\right)^{-4}, \qquad Q_5=\frac{\pi^3}{12}A^2a^5, \qquad gA^{1/2}=\frac5a. The profile has finite norm and spin-one-half covariance, matching the spin requirement for the depth-five neutrino assignment. The same rule also works at neighboring depths three, four and six. Nothing in this calculation makes depth five uniquely weakly interacting, neutral, unusually light or restricted to a fixed axis. Those properties need a coupling and frequency calculation. Using Dirac spinors here also does not settle whether physical neutrinos are Dirac or Majorana particles. 6. Scalar and Vector Channels of the Same Field A spinor can also produce integer-spin patterns through quadratic combinations. For an observer spinor doublet \xi, form B=\xi\xi^\dagger =\frac12\left(sI+\mathbf v\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right), \qquad s=\operatorname{Tr}B, \qquad v_i=\operatorname{Tr}(B\sigma_i), where \sigma_i are the Pauli matrices. Under a spin rotation U, \xi\mapsto U\xi,\qquad B\mapsto UBU^\dagger. The trace s is a scalar and \mathbf v is a spatial vector. The rotation Casimir on the basis I,\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3 is \mathcal J^2=\operatorname{diag}(0,2,2,2). The field algebra consequently contains all three required transformation classes: Pattern Rotation class Direct spinor amplitude Spin 1/2 Scalar quadratic component Spin 0 Vector quadratic components Spin 1 These are available mathematical channels. Establishing particles requires their actual dynamics. For a single doublet the matrix B has rank one, so s^2=|\mathbf v|^2: its scalar and vector components cannot be treated as four independent modes. A current or density is not automatically a separate propagating excitation. There is a further depth-two lead. For the bubble there, \int_{\mathbb R^2}\operatorname{Tr}(B^2)\,d^2x =\int_{\mathbb R^2}\rho^2\,d^2x =\pi A^4a^2<\infty. A quadratic pattern can therefore have finite squared norm while the parent spinor has divergent Q. This is not a license to replace the physical energy by a more convenient norm. A collective action and its complete energy must justify that change of description. The photon-plane geometry already supplies circular vector weights +1 and -1. Connecting those patterns to the collective dynamics remains open. A massive vector also needs its longitudinal polarization, whereas a scalar is a different total spin class. A common completion must account for both distinctions. 7. Relation to the Mass Operator At fixed g, the profile condition gives A=\left(\frac{d}{ga}\right)^{(d-1)/2}, \qquad Q\propto a. The family retains a continuous length scale. It does not select a discrete mass-frequency, the electron–muon harmonic relation, or the simplex spectrum. Its rotation result also needs rechecking when additional transforming mode coefficients are attached to the spatial profile. The mathematical opportunity is specific: use a common field action to support this localized spinor family and determine whether scalar and vector collective modes are physically admissible at depth two. Such an action would need finite complete energy, stable evolution, selected frequencies, and the appropriate polarization constraints. The present calculation establishes the profile and rotation identities that this proposal can use. 8. Verification and Scope The reproducible calculation and recorded results contain 69 successful checks: Clifford relations, full-profile derivatives and rotations at all six depths, radial integrals against their exact values, scalar/vector rotation algebra, orientation phases, vector polarization counts and simplex representation controls. The analytic derivations above supply the scope of the identities; sampled matrix checks support their implementation. No time-evolution or stability test is included. The conclusion is an exact mathematical correlation for one nonlinear profile, together with candidate scalar and vector channels, rather than a completed depth-to-particle-spin law.

title: The Case for Investigating IDWT's Sector Structure
summary: A case for independent investigation of IDWT's sector assignments, built from rigid combinatorial mass relationships and the reuse of spatial geometry across orbit, spin, helicity and charge constructions, with explicit tests for completing or challenging the proposal.
text: Abstract Can the dimensionality of a particle's spatial wave structure organize both its mass and its other properties? Infinite Dimensional Wave Theory (IDWT) proposes a nested sector structure and a mass-frequency law proportional to a simplex count. This paper makes the case for investigating that structure through the constraints it already satisfies. With the maintained assignments, a common sector scale gives an electron–muon mass ratio about 17.3 parts per million below the benchmark, while neighboring muon indices change the ratio by 15–17%. Fixed-index family comparisons favor the assigned depths over the tested alternatives. At those same depths, explicit geometric constructions address orbital patterns, spinorial motion, handedness and neutral channels. A recent common-connection construction realizes the target six- and ten-dimensional lepton counts as polynomials in spatial Dirac eigenvalues, on families that also contain observer half-spin states. This is an inverse construction with explicit geometric constraints. The explanatory opportunity lies in reusing structure across these questions. The paper displays what is fixed, what follows and what is additionally chosen, and proposes concrete tests of state selection, complete mass-frequency dynamics and reciprocal coupling. The results constitute a reproducible case for investigation; the occupied particle states and a common physical interaction law remain to be derived. 1. The Scientific Question A useful organizing principle earns attention when it continues to constrain new questions. If a proposed spatial structure helps organize masses, the next test is whether the same structure can also accommodate the particles' rotational and interaction properties without acquiring a separate adjustable rule for every observation. That is the question pursued here. IDWT associates particle families with depths in one nested spatial manifold. The empirical starting point is a combinatorial mass pattern. The further motivation is that the same candidate depths support explicit mathematics relevant to other properties. The research opportunity is to determine whether these pieces follow from one physical law. The case for investigation is the combination of numerical restriction and reusable geometry. Neither requires claiming that the full theory is complete. Both can be examined now, with explicit equations and reproducible comparisons. Three results give a short route into the argument: A rigid mass relationship: one exact count ratio approximates the electron–muon ratio closely, with no remaining sector-scale adjustment in that ratio and large jumps to neighboring counts. A concrete six-dimensional orbit construction: one geometric generator produces a sequence of two-, four- and six-lobed projections under a stated preparation and observer map. A common six-/ten-dimensional construction: the two target counts can be reconstructed as polynomials on actual spatial spectral families under one specified connection, and those families contain half-spin representations under the same type of observer action. The distinction between these results matters. The first compares with measurements. The second establishes a geometric mechanism for a visual pattern. The third establishes simultaneous spectral and representation compatibility. Their value together is the possibility of a common explanation, which the remaining calculations must test. What a Sector Means The depth d counts ordinary spatial dimensions of the same kind as the familiar three. Sectors form one nested chain in an infinite-dimensional physical manifold. The proposed electron sector has six such dimensions; the tau sector has ten. Sector inclusion does not make an electron a constituent of a tau. Particle patterns remain distinct, and their orientations need not define a universal fixed grid. Mass is expressed in equivalent frequency units, \omega_m=\frac{mc^2}{\hbar}. The model seeks the dynamics selecting that frequency. Physical field amplitude is not identified with mass; it remains unspecified where it cancels and must be retained where nonlinear dynamics makes it relevant. 2. Why the Combinatorial Mass Pattern Deserves a Close Look The proposed law is S(n,d)=\binom{n+d-1}{d},\qquad m_{n,d}=\mu_d S(n,d), with one scale \mu_d shared by all members of a sector. The index n selects a rung of an integer sequence. Changing \mu_d stretches the entire sequence together; it cannot adjust one family member while holding another fixed. A Worked Example: Electron and Muon The maintained depth-six assignments give S(13,6)=18564,\qquad S(35,6)=3838380, and therefore \frac{m_\mu}{m_e}=\frac{3838380}{18564} =\frac{3515}{17}\approx206.7647059. The scale has disappeared. Using the archived electron mass to evaluate the shared scale gives a muon mass of 105.656547603 MeV/c^2, against the archived benchmark 105.6583755 MeV/c^2: a signed residual of approximately -0.00173001\%, or -17.3 parts per million. Both particles are higher harmonics of the same sector fundamental; the electron is the calibration reference, not that fundamental. The exact adjacent-rung identities explain how restrictive the comparison is: \frac{S(n+1,d)-S(n,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac dn, \qquad \frac{S(n,d)-S(n-1,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac d{n+d-1}. At the muon assignment, stepping down changes the count by 15%; stepping up changes it by approximately 17.1429%. The observed residual is about 8,700 times smaller than the smaller of those steps. Moving the muon index by one cannot supply a small repair. Adjusting the sector scale also moves the electron. This is the sense in which the formula is rigid. The 8,700 comparison is a measure of local rung spacing relative to error, not a chance probability or a measure of experimental significance. The 17.3-parts-per-million discrepancy is much larger than the measurement uncertainty, so the uncorrected count ratio is not an exact mass law. It is a precise target for a dynamical explanation or a principled correction. What Is Being Counted? The count has a standard, explicit meaning: S(n,d)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1} =\#\left\{(a_0,\ldots,a_d)\in\mathbb N^{d+1}: \sum_{j=0}^{d}a_j=n-1\right\}. It counts oscillator configurations through total excitation n-1, equivalently monomials of degree at most n-1 in d variables. The extra coordinate is a slack variable, not an additional physical dimension. The sum is the Hockey-Stick Identity, and adjacent counts obey Pascal recursion: S(n,d)=S(n,d-1)+S(n-1,d). Thus the mass proposal uses an established count of available configurations. The physical questions are why the count multiplies a frequency and why particular rungs are occupied. An explanation of those two steps would connect the empirical pattern to dynamics. The Full Assignment Set Spatial depth Particle comparison Index n Count S(n,d) 2 Photon 0 0, separate massless convention 2 W 76 2,926 2 Z 81 3,321 2 Higgs 95 4,560 3 Down 1 1 3 Strange 4 20 4 Up 3 15 4 Charm 20 8,855 4 Top 72 1,215,450 5 Neutrino mass state 1 10 2,002 5 Neutrino mass state 2 15 11,628 5 Neutrino mass state 3 22 65,780 6 Electron 13 18,564 6 Muon 35 3,838,380 10 Tau 23 64,512,240 Photon n=0 denotes zero rest mass, not zero traveling-wave frequency. Bottom is an unresolved exception to the ordinary integer sequence. A nearby geometric mean of counts is not an established bottom-particle mechanism and is excluded from the family tests below. The indices and grouping are maintained hypotheses developed using known particle data. They have not been selected by a derived field equation. Once specified, however, they impose the simultaneous numerical constraints shown here. A fair evaluation should retain both facts: the construction has a selection history, and its shared scales leave genuine restrictions to explain. 3. Do the Mass Comparisons Point Toward the Proposed Depths? The first comparison holds the indices fixed and allows every trial depth from 1 to 15 its own best common scale. For benchmark masses M_i, \log\widehat\mu_d=\frac1N\sum_i\log\frac{M_i}{S(n_i,d)}, \qquad \epsilon_d=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_i \left[\log\frac{\widehat\mu_d S(n_i,d)}{M_i}\right]^2}. The proposed depths give much closer simultaneous family ratios. This makes dimensionality a meaningful part of the numerical hypothesis. The table tests the specified family groupings and indices. It does not discover either grouping or exhaust simultaneous changes of indices and depths. A stronger comparison should document the admissible index ranges, shared-scale rules and selection procedure before searching alternatives. A competing assignment must satisfy the same simultaneous constraints; matching one isolated ratio with arbitrary integers is a different test. Depth Five: A Ratio Without an Absolute Neutrino Mass Scale For the maintained neutrino indices, the scale cancels from R_\nu(d)=\frac{S(15,d)^2-S(10,d)^2} {S(22,d)^2-S(10,d)^2}. The values at depths four, five and six are approximately 0.05550, 0.0303498422349 and 0.01686. The archived splitting set \Delta m^2_{21}=7.53\times10^{-5} and \Delta m^2_{32}=2.455\times10^{-3} eV^2 gives \Delta m^2_{21}/\Delta m^2_{31}=0.0297593170770 after converting \Delta m^2_{31}=\Delta m^2_{32}+\Delta m^2_{21}. Depth five is about 1.98% high under that comparison. The neutrino module separately uses 7.49\times10^{-5} and 2.534\times10^{-3} eV^2 for the 21 and 31 splittings, giving a 2.6789% residual. These dated input sets must not be mixed. The evidence is one scale-free splitting ratio; it is not three measured absolute neutrino masses. Depth Ten: A Demanding Charged-Lepton Comparison The additional proposal \mu_{10}=\mu_6 gives \frac{m_\tau}{m_e}=\frac{S(23,10)}{S(13,6)}. It yields 1775.78576288 MeV/c^2, approximately 0.0643940% below the archived tau benchmark. Keeping the same index and scale at depths nine and eleven gives about 554.93 and 5327.36 MeV/c^2. The shared-scale assumption is doing real work: a freely adjustable scale could fit a single tau mass at any depth. This raises a further physical test. A ten-dimensional tau construction must retain the charge and spin shared by charged leptons despite the change of depth. Sections 5 and 7 develop concrete parts of that question. 4. From a Mass Assignment to Six-Dimensional Orbit Geometry The mass comparison motivates examining six dimensions for the electron and muon. Six also has a specific spin-geometric property: \operatorname{Spin}(6)\simeq SU(4),\qquad SO(6)/U(3)\simeq\mathbb{CP}^3. A projective ray with four complex homogeneous coordinates has six real dimensions. More generally, at d=2m, a chiral spinor has 2^{m-1} complex components. Its full ray space has real dimension 2^m-2; its pure-spinor orbit has dimension m(m-1). Equating either with the spatial dimension 2m selects m=3. At depths 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, the respective sequences are (0,2,6,14,30) and (0,2,6,12,20). This is a precise reason to examine the proposed six-dimensional geometry. The two equalities reflect the same representation structure and reinforce its coherence; they are not two independent experimental observations. One Generator, a Sequence of Petals The orbit construction uses degree-L sections on \mathbb{CP}^3. Their full number is \dim H^0(\mathbb{CP}^3,\mathcal O(L))=\binom{L+3}{3}. Under the same generator at every L>0, G=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,0), the four sections z_1^L,z_2^L,z_3z_4^{L-1},z_4^L have relative weights (L,-L,-1,0). Change the extremal pair to the symmetric and antisymmetric basis, u=(z_1^L+z_2^L)/\sqrt2,\qquad v=(z_1^L-z_2^L)/\sqrt2. Its diagonal weights become the generator L\sigma_x. An initially symmetric state evolves with coefficients \cos(L\theta) and -i\sin(L\theta) in this basis. The conditional u occupation supplies the changing amplitude; the last two sections supply a unit relative-phase clock. With that preparation and a nonzero clock doublet, q=\cos^2(L\theta),\qquad \phi=\theta. The radial observer readout W=R\sqrt q\,e^{i\phi} =R|\cos(L\theta)|e^{i\theta} has exactly 2L radial maxima: two, four and six petals for L=1,2,3. A strictly increasing radial response that vanishes at zero preserves that count. The generator is not changed for each pattern; the degree-L representation supplies the change. The interactive orbit visualization makes the construction inspectable. The physical value of this result is its explicit mechanism: a sequence of projected patterns follows from one flow and one stated readout. Its scope is geometric morphology. The preparation, amplitude-to-clock relation and detector interpretation still require dynamics; a primitive clock alone does not fix the amplitude-to-clock ratio. These lobes are not a calculation of measured atomic probability densities or an atomic energy spectrum. The angular label L is not the mass index n, and \binom{L+3}{3} is not S(n,6). The L=0 constant section has no relative-phase clock and needs a separate construction. A second six-dimensional control uses the observer-equivariant monogenic numerator q_\perp X-3Y, with q_\perp=d-3>0 and X,Y Clifford contractions in the observer and normal coordinates. Its norm is proportional to q_\perp^2|x|^2+9|y|^2, isotropic in the full space precisely when q_\perp=3. This is another dimension-sensitive consequence of a specified ansatz, on flat space. Identifying it with a field on physical CP3 requires further construction. The pure-spinor bridge and observer-map analysis keep the spatial point, coefficient ray and field value distinct. There is no global constant rank-four identification of the physical spatial half-spin bundle. 5. A Stronger Reuse of Structure: Counts and Spin in One Lepton Construction The next step puts count and spin into the same declared spectral setting. Propose physical \mathbb{CP}^3\subset\mathbb{CP}^5 as six- and ten-dimensional spatial submanifolds with compatible Fubini–Study metrics and undetermined scale R. This is a proposed global topology; no small curled-up extra dimensions are introduced. On \mathbb{CP}^m, use the canonical Spin-c bundle and its spatial Dirac operator, \Sigma_m(L)=\Lambda^{0,*}T^*\mathbb{CP}^m\otimes\mathcal O(L), \qquad D_L=\sqrt2(\bar\partial_L+\bar\partial_L^\dagger). Here \mathcal O(L) specifies the line connection. The integer L denotes its degree; the present spectral construction fixes L=3, independently of the varying orbital degree in section 4. For that shared connection and paired form channel r=1, x=\frac{R^2D_3^2}{4}=k(k+m+2),\qquad k\ge2. The spatial eigenvalue family follows from Habib and Nakad, Proposition 3.2, after converting their line convention to \mathcal O(3). Pairing the factors in the simplex products gives P_6(x)=\frac{x(x+4)(x+6)}{6!},\qquad P_6(k(k+5))=S(k,6), P_{10}(x)=\frac{(x-8)x(x+6)(x+10)(x+12)}{10!}, \qquad P_{10}(k(k+7))=S(k-1,10). The elementary pairing identity is (k+i)(k+m+2-i)=x+i(m+2-i). Electron and muon use k=13,35; tau's n=23 uses k=24. This shift is a spectral-label conversion from the factorization, not a rule for generating particle indices. The polynomials are reconstructed from the target count law on these actual eigenfamilies: the bare Dirac spectrum has not independently predicted the count law. The gain is a definite spatial operator problem whose count, rotation and nesting requirements can now be tested together. The Same Families Contain Actual Observer Half-Spin States Choose the global observer SU(2) action as two doublets on homogeneous \mathbb C^4 and three doublets on \mathbb C^6. It rotates spatial points and bundle fibres, so the orbital part of rotation is included. The paired modules are (k-2,1,k+3)_{SU(4)},\qquad (k-2,1,0,0,k+3)_{SU(6)}. Their full restriction contains the following numbers of observer doublets per Dirac sign: M_6(k)=2(k^2-1),\qquad M_{10}(k)=\frac{(k^2-1)(k+2)(k+3)(k^2+16k+40)}{30}. Comparison Spatial label k Target count Available half-spin doublets Electron, depth six 13 18,564 336 Muon, depth six 35 3,838,380 2,448 Tau, depth ten 24 64,512,240 13,455,000 The tensor representations use the ordinary geometric descriptions in Dolan and collaborators, Appendix A; this calculation does not adopt a fuzzy physical space. The doublet multiplicities are neither occupation probabilities nor coupling strengths. This is the paper's clearest example of constructive convergence. One connection and a consistent observer action support both count identities and half-spin availability in the same families. The spin calculation does not require a new particle-specific mass parameter. Its contribution is stronger than placing unrelated favorable formulas next to one another. The construction is still conditional on the projective topology, metric, connection, channel and observer lift. Other spectral channels, including zero modes, remain. Higher half-integer spins occur alongside half-spin. A quadratic operator H_d=D_3+a_d\beta P_d(x),\qquad \{D_3,\beta\}=0, uses form parity \beta and a real coefficient a_d, whose relation to the phenomenological sector frequency unit remains open. Its full eigenfrequencies are \omega_\pm=\pm\sqrt{4x/R^2+a_d^2P_d(x)^2}. All observer-spin components in a fixed spatial family have the same two-by-two block. This law therefore supplies neither spin-one-half selection nor the exact phenomenological mass-frequency \omega_{0,d}S(n,d). The count polynomial has been constructed on the spectrum; the kinetic completion, physical coefficient and occupation mechanism must still be derived. Those are specific mathematical targets, including the causal completion needed by the high spatial order. Six Within Ten Preserves Half-Integer Parity For the standard inclusion, the normal bundle is \mathcal O(1)\otimes W, and \Sigma_b(L)|_{\mathbb{CP}^a} =\bigoplus_{j=0}^{b-a} \Sigma_a(L+j)\otimes\Lambda^j\overline W^*. At CP3 within CP5 and L=3, the normal factors have ranks 1, 2 and 1. The complementary W=\mathbb C^2 is an observer doublet. A full central rotation acts on every block with sign (-1)^{3+j}(-1)^j=-1. Retaining the normal doublet in the middle block preserves half-integer parity throughout the restriction. This makes the proposed nesting compatible with shared lepton rotation behavior. It does not equate the full representations, select half-spin alone, or make an electron solution the restriction of a tau solution. 6. What the Other Depths Contribute The proposed organization also has to accommodate the other maintained sectors. The following constructions expose useful depth-dependent distinctions under explicit rules. A Finite-Norm Spinor Branch Has a Threshold Above Two The flat-space critical Dirac profile \psi_\chi=A(1+r^2/a^2)^{-d/2}(I+i\alpha\cdot x/a)\chi, \qquad \|\chi\|=1, obeys \rho=A^2(1+r^2/a^2)^{1-d},\qquad D\psi=g\rho^{1/(d-1)}\psi,\qquad gA^{2/(d-1)}=d/a, where D=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla and the Hermitian matrices obey the spatial Clifford algebra. Its squared norm in the bound directions is \mathcal N=A^2a^d\pi^{d/2} \frac{\Gamma(d/2-1)}{\Gamma(d-1)},\qquad d>2. The tail integral behaves as \int r^{1-d}dr. It converges above two and diverges logarithmically at two. Every maintained matter depth meets this condition, while the assigned bosonic depth lies at the threshold. Joint rotation of coordinates and components gives S(R)\psi_\chi(R^{-1}x)=\psi_{S(R)\chi}(x). The critical Dirac-bubble analysis of Borrelli, Malchiodi and Wu supplies the mathematical setting. The useful distinction is conditional on this profile, its exponent and its squared-norm criterion. It does not individually select depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10, exclude every depth-two fermion, or establish a persistent particle. The spin-depth calculation gives the full context. Depth Five Provides One Complete Normal Rotation Plane Relative to a three-dimensional observer, depth five leaves exactly two normal spatial directions. At maintained matter depths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10, the normal rotation algebras have \binom{d-3}{2}=0,0,1,3,21 generators. Only five has a nontrivial abelian normal rotation algebra \mathfrak{so}(2) with exactly one complete plane. This makes a handed normal-mode construction particularly economical there. For normal coordinates u,v and texture \zeta=\frac{(1,w)}{\sqrt{1+|w|^2}},\qquad w=((u+iv)/a)^k,\qquad A=-i\zeta^\dagger d\zeta, the curvature flux is 2\pi k. At unit coupling magnitude, normal Dirac modes take the form f_m\propto\frac{(u+iv)^m}{\sqrt{1+(r/a)^{2k}}}, \qquad 0\le m<k-1. The strict endpoint gives one mode, m=0, at the minimum allowed integer winding k=2. With general coupling magnitude |\lambda|, the condition is m<|\lambda|k-1 and the number of modes is \max(0,\lceil|\lambda|k\rceil-1). The minimum winding therefore depends on the coupling assumption. Both odd-Clifford orientation blocks \eta=\pm1 must be retained. Their handedness relation is h_\eta=\frac{\eta}{2}\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_\eta\Phi). Opposite-sign couplings can give the same handedness in both blocks; for \lambda_\pm=\lambda_0\pm\lambda_5, this requires |\lambda_5|>|\lambda_0| and normalizability. A massive neutrino permits both helicities. The relativistic unfavorable spinor weight under a left-chiral response is suppressed by m^2/(E+|p|)^2; a full interaction rate needs its vertex and kinematics. The Same Plane Admits a Conserved Neutral Channel Define K=-i\alpha_4\alpha_5 for normal spin and C=-i\alpha_1\alpha_2\alpha_3 for tangent handedness. The odd-dimensional orientation gives C=\eta K. The candidate generator Q_0=\frac{\eta+K}{3},\qquad Q_0^2=\frac49P_R,\qquad Q_0P_L=0, \qquad P_{L,R}=\frac{I\mp C}{2} has an exact neutral subspace. Including spatial motion replaces the component sign by the full normal angular momentum: J_{45}=L_{45}+K/2,\qquad Q=\frac{\eta+2J_{45}}3,\qquad [Q,D_5]=0. For the critical profile, Q\psi_\chi=\psi_{Q_0\chi}; a left-handed seed is neutral under this generator. The texture with \lambda_\eta=-\eta has the same neutral m=0 channel, the sole normalizable orbital mode when 1<|\lambda_\eta|k\le2. Here handedness and neutrality reuse the same normal plane and orientation algebra. The additional choice is important and explicit: the electric interpretation, equal coefficients in \eta+2J_{45} and normalization 1/3 are not forced by geometry alone. With a\eta+2bJ_{45} the corresponding value is (a-b)\eta. Deriving the equal weighting is the open charge problem. Five is distinguished within this construction by the one-dimensional continuous center of \mathfrak{so}(d-3), together with odd-dimensional Clifford orientation. At monogenic angular degree \ell there are 2(\ell+1) observer doublets, and selecting 2J_{45}=-\eta leaves one neutral doublet at every degree. This angular degree is distinct from the texture winding k. Neutrality can coexist with excitation without changing a degree-only eigenvalue; counting only neutral states would change the count sequence. The radial bubble and textured normal channel share this symmetry but are not yet one exact localized solution. See the charge–helicity–spin bridge. The Photon Plane Carries the Expected Rotation Weights For a rank-two bound plane E, place polarization \epsilon in E and the free phase gradient K in its orthogonal normal space. Then K\cdot\epsilon=0. The circular basis \epsilon_\pm=(e_1\pm i e_2)/\sqrt2 has rotation phases e^{\mp i\alpha}, giving helicities \pm1 in a three-dimensional containing sector. Linear and elliptical polarizations are combinations; the corresponding direction-space line bundles have Chern numbers \pm2, up to orientation convention. This is an economical match between a two-plane and transverse polarization. The assignment of the phase gradient and polarization is a premise. The photon module identifies the remaining dynamical work: a source-free field, protected zero rest mass and observed timing. A fixed circular polarization times a real localized scalar envelope does not satisfy electric divergence unless the transverse envelope is constant; full components or varying polarization must be included. 7. Shared Structure Is the Opportunity The explanatory aim is to obtain more consequences while making fewer additional choices. Shared assumptions can be a strength: once the same geometry is used for several properties, a change intended to repair one result must remain consistent with the others. This is distinct from statistical independence. Several consequences of one representation can make that representation more useful without being several independent measurements. No product of coincidence probabilities is assigned here. The relevant accounting is visible in the following table. Structure retained across questions Consequences obtained Additional physical step One simplex law and one scale per sector Family mass ratios, exact rung gaps, tested depth preferences Derive occupied indices, scales and residual corrections Six-dimensional spin geometry, fixed orbit generator and stated preparation/readout CP3 correspondence and an entire petal sequence Derive that preparation, detector response and atomic observables One O(3) connection, specified six-/ten-dimensional channels and observer lift Spectral-polynomial representations of both count laws and available global half-spin states Select the channel and occupied spin, and derive the full frequency law The same projective nesting with all normal factors Half-integer parity in every restricted block Derive compatible supported particle fields and their interaction One depth-five normal plane and orientation algebra Handed modes and a compatible conserved neutral channel Derive the charge weighting, texture and complete localized state One critical spatial spinor family Spinorial rotation and the norm threshold above depth two Supply a common origin for the exponent and persistent dynamics One photon plane with orthogonal phase gradient Transverse polarization and helicity weights Derive the full electromagnetic response and timing The present record contains several such packages. It does not yet have one action producing all of them. This is where a unification claim can be tested sharply: specify the proposed common action, retain its full kinetic and support terms, and determine which results survive together. Equal charged-lepton response gives a concrete example. For a physical mode map S, the Gram metric is G=S^\dagger S. Canonical amplitudes b=\sqrt\kappa G^{1/2}c give the scalar-phase charge Q=gq\,b^\dagger b. Equal charge per canonical action therefore need not require equal sector stiffness. Equal integrated particle charges still require a physical occupation rule. This same nonzero scalar phase cannot make a nonzero finite-norm neutrino neutral; the depth-five generator above is a different candidate. Bringing those responses into one law is an explicit coupling target, not an assumed result. 8. The Research Problems That Could Change the Assessment The useful next contributions have definite inputs and outcomes. They need not solve the whole theory at once. A. Test the Numerical Organizing Principle More Severely Reproduce the published ratios, then compare alternative depths and indices under a declared common search procedure, mass conventions and uncertainty treatment. Record every adjustable scale and the cost of selecting integers. Test whether the reported preferences survive simultaneous family constraints. A controlled alternative with comparable simplicity and accuracy would weaken the case; robust discrimination would strengthen it. B. Derive a Count-to-Frequency Mechanism Start from the explicit spatial spectral families in section 5, or a justified alternative. Derive a common kinetic and self-interaction law whose complete particle clock has the required count dependence. Account for the spatial Dirac contribution, support energy and sector scale. The observed electron–muon residual fixes the direction and size of a correction to test; an arbitrary independent correction per particle would give up the formula's central restriction. C. Select the Occupied States Determine whether one nonlinear or geometric mechanism selects the maintained indices and spin-one-half branches while treating the additional states consistently. The existing quadratic projective law leaves observer-spin components degenerate, providing a concrete starting obstruction. A successful extension must show how the degeneracy changes and why the relevant states persist. Count availability alone does not answer occupation. D. Complete the Orbit and Observer Construction Derive the preparation and observer response of section 4 from a supported electron–nucleus configuration. Compare actual spatial densities, angular observables and spectra, including the L=0 case. The present generator and robust petal count give a reproducible starting calculation; matching their silhouette alone would leave the physical identification unresolved. E. Derive Reciprocal Coupling from the Same Field Calculate interactions with each particle retaining its own isolated frequency and an evolving relative phase. Include the polarization of both participants, their responding spatial shapes, supporting stress and conserved energy–momentum. Recover the common charged-lepton response while testing the proposed neutral handed channel. Use depths two, three and four alongside five, six and ten as controls under the same law; a depth-five effect must be distinguished from a generic odd-dimensional effect. This would connect the sector geometry to a measurable interaction law. These questions call on spectral geometry, nonlinear Dirac equations, representation theory, constrained stability and particle phenomenology. Each offers a way to improve or reject a specific part of the proposal. The linked derivations and executable comparisons make it possible to contribute without accepting every IDWT premise. 9. Conclusion The mass relationships supply a restrictive numerical motivation for the sector assignments. The geometric constructions supply explicit ways in which those same depths can organize further properties. The strongest recent advance expresses both target lepton counts as spectral polynomials on families that also contain half-spin states, under one declared connection and observer action. This inverse construction links previously separate requirements in a concrete spatial setting. Shared mathematical structure is central to this case. Its scientific value grows when additional physical constraints follow without separately adjusted rules. The next test is to turn the surviving constructions into one action with selected states, complete frequency dynamics and reciprocal interactions. The sector structure merits independent investigation because it presents both a concrete pattern to explain and a growing set of mathematical constraints that a common explanation must satisfy. This paper invites that investigation through explicit calculations, visible assumptions and results that can be checked, extended or overturned. Appendix A. Absolute Masses, Scale Assumptions and Reproduction The ratio tests in the main text do not require the proposed non-neutrino scale prescription. For completeness, that prescription is g_{22}=\frac{1445}{2},\qquad g_{33}=8\sqrt7,\qquad g_{44}=\frac{12}{\sqrt7},\qquad g_{66}=g_{10,10}=\frac14. These are sector coefficients; their identification with physical coupling strengths is open. With specified reference counts C_d^\star, M_d^\star=\mu_d C_d^\star,\qquad \frac{(M_d^\star)^2}{g_{dd}}=\frac{m_e^2}{g_{66}},\qquad \mu_d=\frac{m_e}{C_d^\star}\sqrt{\frac{g_{dd}}{g_{66}}}. Depth Reference count C_d^\star \mu_d in MeV/c^2 2 1, unit-count reference 27.47064959 3 S(1,3)=1 4.701857978 4 S(3,4)=15 0.1451024874 6 S(13,6)=18564 0.00002752633861 Only the archived m_e=0.51099895000 MeV/c^2 is a measured dimensional input to this evaluation; W, down and up are outputs. The expressions were developed to explain previously fitted scales. Their one-input evaluation is therefore distinct from an independently derived scale law. The self-contact mass-operator module gives the conditional construction. The tau relation \mu_{10}=\mu_6 additionally requires equal normalized overlaps; equality of the listed sector coefficients alone is insufficient. The absolute neutrino scale remains separate. The chosen coefficients imply g_{33}g_{44}=96, g_{44}/g_{33}=3/14 and the reference up/down ratio \sqrt{3/14}. Those are consequences of this prescription, not additional empirical confirmations. No arithmetic on particle indices is used to derive them here.
